Source: CWE-829, CWE-940, CVE-2017-3160, OWASP MASVS, MITRE ATT&CK Mobile T1437

Title: Man-in-the-Middle via Outdated OpenSSL / TLS
Scenario Description: A mobile application uses outdated OpenSSL/TLS libraries that lack support for secure protocols or have known vulnerabilities. This allows an attacker on the same network (e.g., public Wi-Fi) to intercept, decrypt, and possibly modify sensitive user data such as login credentials or API keys during transmission, even if the app claims to use HTTPS.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Bettercap, Burp Suite, Kali Linux, OpenSSL test server, Android emulator, mitmproxy
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a mobile app or emulator that uses outdated TLS/OpenSSL (you can use an older Android APK or custom app with insecure networking libraries). 2. Make sure your test phone or emulator is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your attacker machine. Use a hotspot or local Wi-Fi if testing at home. 3. On your Kali Linux (or attacker machine), install and launch Bettercap or mitmproxy. You can use: sudo bettercap -iface wlan0 or mitmproxy --mode transparent. 4. Enable IP forwarding and setup SSL stripping (automated in Bettercap with modules). This will allow intercepting HTTPS requests and downgrade to HTTP (if allowed). 5. Start scanning the network for connected devices: net.probe on in Bettercap. Identify your mobile device IP. 6. Launch ARP spoofing to redirect traffic from the mobile to your attacker machine: set arp.spoof.targets <victim-ip> then arp.spoof on. 7. Open the insecure mobile app (the one using outdated SSL) on the victim device. Perform a login or trigger some network request. 8. On your attacker machine, use Wireshark or Burp Suite to capture packets and analyze decrypted data. If SSL pinning is not enforced and outdated TLS (e.g., TLS 1.0 or 1.1) is accepted by the app, you will be able to view sensitive data. 9. (Optional) Use openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -tls1 to test which old TLS protocols are supported. 10. You now demonstrate a full MITM interception due to outdated libraries. This proves that if an app does not validate certificates properly or uses vulnerable OpenSSL versions, attackers can break HTTPS and steal data.
Impact: Data Theft, Credential Exposure, Session Hijack
Detection Method: Use packet sniffers to inspect live traffic and identify plaintext credentials or outdated TLS versions. Use tools like testssl.sh or Burp's TLS scanner.
Solution: Always update OpenSSL/TLS libraries. Enforce latest TLS (1.2 or 1.3). Use Certificate Pinning. Detect and reject SSL stripping and invalid certs.
Tags: mitm, openssl, TLS downgrade, outdated SSL, android MITM, insecure transport
Source: Real-world pentest simulation based on OWASP MSTG, CVE-2014-0224, CVE-2016-2107, real SSL attacks

Title: Sensitive Data Exposure via Analytics SDK
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps use third-party analytics SDKs like Firebase, Flurry, Mixpanel, etc., for crash reporting, user tracking, and marketing. Sometimes, outdated or misconfigured SDKs accidentally capture sensitive data (e.g., email, name, location, token, health info) in logs, metadata, or network traffic. This becomes critical when SDKs send such data to external servers over HTTP or without encryption, leading to major privacy breaches. Attackers can exploit this by reverse engineering the app, inspecting the SDK behavior, or capturing traffic from the mobile device.
Tools Used: APKTool, JADX-GUI, Android Emulator, Wireshark, Burp Suite, mitmproxy, Frida
Attack Steps: 1. Get the target APK of a mobile app that uses analytics SDKs. You can download an open-source APK or export one from your own device using adb pull /data/app/.... 2. Decompile the APK using JADX-GUI or APKTool: jadx-gui target.apk. Open the source code and look for imports like com.google.firebase.analytics.FirebaseAnalytics, com.flurry.sdk, com.mixpanel, etc. These indicate use of 3rd party analytics SDKs. 3. Carefully read through the onCreate(), onResume() or logEvent() functions. Apps often send parameters like user_email, location, phone, name, etc. directly via analytics event logs. These are clear privacy violations. 4. Now open an Android emulator or physical test phone and install the target APK. Set it to use your system proxy (Burp Suite or mitmproxy running on your PC). 5. In Burp Suite, enable SSL/TLS interception and install the Burp certificate on the Android device (Settings → Security → Install cert). Make sure app doesn’t use SSL Pinning. 6. Open the app and interact with it. Monitor Burp Suite’s HTTP history. Check if analytics SDKs are sending sensitive data to 3rd party domains (like firebase.io, flurry.com, api.mixpanel.com) in the form of query params or POST JSON. Look for values like name, email, password, or GPS location. 7. If you cannot intercept HTTPS traffic due to SSL pinning, bypass it using Frida. Run frida -U -n <app> -l frida-script.js where your script hooks into analytics methods or certificate validation functions to disable pinning. 8. Once you successfully intercept, save evidence where user data is being leaked via analytics SDK. 9. (Optional) Compare SDK versions and look up known issues (e.g., Firebase versions prior to 2020 were known to send unintentional identifiers). 10. This proves that by using outdated or insecure analytics SDKs, developers may unknowingly leak private user data over the network or logs, which attackers, advertisers, or bad SDK vendors can misuse.
MITRE Technique: T1407 (Application Layer Protocol: Capture Data Sent to External Analytics Services)
Impact: Privacy Violation, Legal Risk (e.g., GDPR breach), Identity Theft
Detection Method: Use static and dynamic analysis to inspect app code, and monitor runtime traffic for suspicious outbound data to analytics domains. Use Burp, Wireshark, Frida.
Solution: Avoid logging or tracking PII via analytics SDKs. Update SDKs regularly. Review data sent to third-party services. Use runtime security testing (RASP).
Tags: sdk-leak, firebase, analytics, insecure third-party library, privacy leak, mobile data exposure
Source: Based on findings from AppCensus, OWASP MASVS, CVE reports on Mixpanel and Firebase SDK behavior

Title: WebView RCE via Third-Party Plugin (Cordova/Capacitor)
Attack Type: Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Plugin Injection
Scenario Description: Hybrid mobile apps (using frameworks like Apache Cordova, Ionic Capacitor, or PhoneGap) allow JavaScript-based app development using WebView. These frameworks use plugins to bridge native functionality (like file access, camera, etc.) to JavaScript. If outdated or misconfigured, plugins like cordova-plugin-inappbrowser, cordova-plugin-file, or cordova-plugin-customurlscheme can expose dangerous native features to attacker-controlled JavaScript via exec() or postMessage() functions. This can lead to full Remote Code Execution (RCE) via WebView. Attackers can inject malicious JavaScript into the WebView, and escalate it to native code using the plugin bridge.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Cordova App (with vulnerable plugin), Frida, Burp Suite, Apktool, JADX, WebView Exploit HTML file, MITMproxy
Attack Steps: 1. Download or build a Cordova-based Android APK using outdated plugins such as cordova-plugin-inappbrowser@1.7.2, cordova-plugin-file@6.0.1, or similar. You can use sample Cordova projects from GitHub for lab purposes. 2. Use JADX or Apktool to decompile the APK and inspect the plugin bridge. Look for exposed interfaces via addJavascriptInterface() or exec() method in CordovaWebViewImpl.java. 3. Check whether plugins expose unsafe native methods to JavaScript. For example, file path access, open external URL, or evaluate JavaScript from URL. 4. Open the APK in an Android emulator or physical test device. Set up a proxy (Burp or mitmproxy) on your PC and configure Android to use it. Install the Burp certificate on the emulator. 5. Create an attacker-controlled web page (e.g., evil.html) that includes malicious JavaScript code such as: <script>cordova.exec(function(){}, function(){}, 'File', 'readFile', ['file:///data/data/com.example.app/files/secret.txt']);</script>. This payload tries to use Cordova's plugin bridge to access native files. 6. Use any WebView loading function inside the app that opens untrusted URLs or allows deep linking to load your malicious evil.html page. If the app uses a vulnerable plugin and does not sanitize or limit WebView access, your script will execute. 7. Monitor the output using adb logcat, Frida, or JavaScript alert boxes to confirm payload execution. You can also hook Cordova methods using Frida to see which native functions are triggered. 8. In some vulnerable plugins, attackers can send postMessage() to the WebView and trigger native callbacks. Use: window.postMessage({action: 'readFile', path: '/data/data/...'}, '*'). 9. If successful, you can escalate to full file read, write, command execution, or intent triggering, depending on plugin permissions. 10. This completes the RCE chain: malicious JavaScript → vulnerable plugin → native access → RCE. This technique has been used in the wild (e.g., CVE-2019-12256, CVE-2017-3191 in Cordova).
Vulnerability: Outdated or Insecure Cordova/Capacitor Plugins Exposing Native Bridges
Impact: Remote Code Execution, File Read/Write, Device Takeover, App Compromise
Detection Method: Reverse engineer APK to find JavaScript bridges. Test with malicious payloads via WebView or deep links. Use Frida to monitor native method calls.
Solution: Update plugins regularly, disable unnecessary plugins, validate all URLs loaded in WebView, use CSP (Content Security Policy), avoid addJavascriptInterface unless sandboxed
Tags: cordova, capacitor, rce, webview exploit, hybrid app, plugin vulnerability
Source: OWASP MSTG, CVE-2017-3191, CVE-2019-12256, GitHub Cordova advisories

Title: Crash / DoS via Glide / ImageView Bug
Attack Type: Application Denial of Service (DoS) via Resource Exhaustion
Scenario Description: Many Android apps use the Glide image loading library to efficiently display images from remote URLs. However, outdated versions of Glide (e.g., before v4.11) or misused ImageView implementations can cause crashes or ANRs (App Not Responding) when loading malicious image payloads. A very large image file (e.g., 8000x8000 pixels or more), a specially crafted corrupt image, or an endless redirect loop can lead to memory exhaustion or infinite processing loops, crashing the app instantly or freezing it permanently. This can be used for DoS attacks, crashing the app every time it opens or even triggering a reboot loop in some cases.
Tools Used: Glide vulnerable version (pre-4.11), Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Custom HTTP server (like Python SimpleHTTPServer), GIMP or ImageMagick to generate large/corrupt images, Frida (optional), Logcat
Attack Steps: 1. Identify or build a test Android app that uses an outdated version of Glide (example: Glide v4.8 or earlier). You can search GitHub for old open-source Android projects using Glide for image loading inside ImageView. 2. Open the source code or APK and confirm that Glide is used to load image URLs, e.g., Glide.with(context).load("http://example.com/image.jpg").into(imageView); 3. Set up an Android emulator and install the test app. 4. Set up your own HTTP server to serve image payloads. You can do this by running python3 -m http.server 8000 in a folder containing a large image. 5. Use GIMP, Photoshop, or ImageMagick to create a very large image file. For example, 10000x10000 PNG with transparency or a corrupt header. Alternatively, use an infinite redirect by hosting a .htaccess or using Flask to keep redirecting the image URL. 6. Replace the image URL in the app’s code or trigger the app to fetch your malicious image using Burp Suite request modification, if the app loads user content. 7. As soon as the app loads your malicious image, it will begin consuming excessive memory. Glide will attempt to decode it fully into memory, resulting in OutOfMemoryError or a crash. 8. Monitor the crash using adb logcat and confirm errors like: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Failed to allocate a 500000000-byte allocation with 67108864 free bytes. 9. Repeat the launch — if the image loads automatically on app startup (e.g., as profile picture), the app will crash again instantly, leading to a persistent DoS condition. 10. You have now successfully demonstrated a real-world DoS attack using Glide image rendering weakness — particularly dangerous in chat apps or social apps where users can control image sources. This type of vulnerability has been reported in apps like WhatsApp clones, older Instagram clients, and unmaintained social media apps.
Target Type: Mobile Apps using Glide or ImageView
Vulnerability: Glide Image Loader Memory Exhaustion, Corrupt Image Processing
Impact: App Crash, Unresponsive UI, Reboot Loop, Persistent Denial of Service
Detection Method: Monitor logcat output for OutOfMemoryError, ANR traces, or rendering failures. Use Burp to identify if large images are being fetched.
Solution: Upgrade to Glide ≥ 4.11, validate image size and content before loading, apply fallback images, set memory/caching limits in Glide config, sanitize and resize user-uploaded images
Tags: glide, imageview, android crash, dos, memory exhaustion, large image attack

Title: GSON Deserialization RCE
Attack Type: Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Insecure Deserialization
Scenario Description: GSON is a widely used Java/Android library for converting JSON into Java objects. In older or misconfigured versions (especially before v2.8.9), if an app deserializes untrusted JSON into generic Object types (e.g., TypeToken<Object>), or allows polymorphic deserialization using attacker-controlled types, it can result in RCE. Attackers can send specially crafted JSON payloads that force GSON to instantiate dangerous gadget classes (e.g., from the app itself or from included libraries like Apache Commons), eventually leading to execution of arbitrary code. This is particularly dangerous in mobile apps with API endpoints or local WebView bridges that accept JSON and parse them using GSON without strict type enforcement.
Tools Used: Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Frida, JADX, GSON vulnerable version (≤2.8.8), ysoserial-for-android, Logcat, Custom APK with JSON API or WebView bridge
Attack Steps: 1. Identify a mobile app that uses GSON and accepts JSON input from the user. This could be via a WebView bridge, local API endpoint, or server call that sends JSON data. You can search GitHub for older Android projects using GSON 2.8.5, 2.8.6, or 2.8.8. 2. Use JADX to decompile the APK and look for JSON parsing code like: Gson.fromJson(input, Object.class) or fromJson(json, TypeToken.getParameterized(List.class, Object.class).getType()). If the type is generic or not tightly enforced, it’s vulnerable. 3. Set up the app on an Android emulator and configure it to use Burp Suite as proxy. Install the Burp certificate. 4. Find an endpoint or input field that allows you to inject JSON. This could be a login screen, config loader, or in-app web page sending JSON via JS bridge. 5. Build a malicious JSON payload using a gadget chain available in the app. For test purposes, you can build a dummy app that includes a vulnerable gadget class like: public class EvilClass { static { Runtime.getRuntime().exec("reboot"); } } or System.exit(1);. 6. Use a tool like ysoserial-for-android or manually craft a payload like: {"@type":"your.package.EvilClass"}. This tells GSON to instantiate EvilClass on deserialization. 7. Send this JSON to the target input using Burp or Frida script if it’s a local call. GSON will deserialize it and execute the static block or constructor, leading to command execution. 8. Use adb logcat to monitor the result. You will see crash logs, system exit, or execution traces. This proves RCE occurred through deserialization. 9. You can also write a harmless payload that logs a message or opens calculator to prove code execution safely. 10. This demonstrates a full RCE chain from JSON input → vulnerable GSON fromJson() → instantiating malicious class → code execution. GSON versions ≤2.8.8 do not enforce strict class loading rules, which allows attackers to abuse this behavior.
Target Type: Mobile Apps using GSON for JSON Parsing
Vulnerability: Insecure Deserialization via GSON TypeToken or Polymorphic Objects
Impact: Remote Code Execution, App Crash, Privilege Escalation, Full Device Compromise
Detection Method: Use static analysis to detect generic deserialization (Object.class). Dynamically test inputs using Frida or Burp. Logcat shows if code is executed on deserialization.
Solution: Upgrade to GSON ≥2.8.9 which disables unsafe polymorphism by default. Never deserialize user input into generic Object. Whitelist allowed types explicitly.
Tags: gson, deserialization, insecure object parsing, android rce, json attack, outdated sdk
Source: CVE-2022-25647, Google Security Blog, OWASP MASVS, GitHub Issues on GSON RCE

Title: Exposure to Known CVEs in PlayCore, ExoPlayer, Firebase
Attack Type: Exploitation via Known Vulnerable SDK Versions
Scenario Description: Android apps often use Google libraries such as Play Core (used for dynamic feature delivery), ExoPlayer (for video streaming), and Firebase (for analytics, authentication, etc.). Many versions of these libraries have publicly known security vulnerabilities (CVEs). Developers using outdated versions may unknowingly expose apps to privilege escalation, RCE, local file leakage, or denial-of-service attacks. For example, CVE-2020-8913 in Play Core allowed attackers to load arbitrary code from untrusted sources, and CVE-2021-0339 in ExoPlayer allowed memory corruption. These CVEs can be exploited by reverse engineering the app, checking SDK versions, and crafting malicious payloads or using attacker-controlled apps that exploit IPC or intent misconfigurations.
Tools Used: JADX, ApkTool, Android Emulator, Frida, Burp Suite, CVE PoC Code (GitHub), Logcat, PlayCore exploit demo app
Attack Steps: 1. Identify or download a target APK that uses one or more of the vulnerable libraries: Play Core (com.google.android.play:core), ExoPlayer (com.google.android.exoplayer:exoplayer), or Firebase. These are common in many open-source Android apps (search GitHub). 2. Use JADX or ApkTool to decompile the APK and search for exact versions used. In JADX, open the build.gradle file or inspect META-INF for version identifiers. Example vulnerable versions: Play Core ≤1.7.2 (CVE-2020-8913), ExoPlayer ≤2.11.7 (CVE-2021-0339), Firebase Analytics pre-2022 (data leaks). 3. Confirm usage of the vulnerable components. For Play Core, look for SplitInstallManager, SplitInstallRequest. For ExoPlayer, look for SimpleExoPlayer, TrackSelector, etc. 4. For CVE-2020-8913 (Play Core): Build or use a malicious app that shares the same UID or target device with the victim app (via adb or dual app methods). Inject a fake dynamic module into /data/local/tmp/fakeModule.apk. Then trick the vulnerable app into loading it via SplitInstallManager. The vulnerable app does not validate source. When it installs and runs the code, it leads to RCE. 5. For CVE-2021-0339 (ExoPlayer): Create a malformed media file (e.g., MKV or MP4) with crafted metadata using ffmpeg or download PoC from GitHub. Host the file on a local HTTP server (python3 -m http.server) and load it inside the ExoPlayer-enabled app. The app may crash or trigger memory corruption. 6. For Firebase CVEs (data leakage): Install the app on an emulator, configure Burp Suite with HTTPS interception. Use the app and monitor outbound traffic to Firebase Analytics (firebaseinstallations.googleapis.com, app-measurement.com). Check for exposure of sensitive fields such as full name, phone, email, or tokens in unencrypted or improperly anonymized formats. 7. Use adb logcat to monitor crashes, exploit output, or stack traces. You may see RCE execution, buffer overflows, app crashes, or leaked tokens. 8. Confirm successful exploitation of the CVE by correlating with PoC expected behavior (e.g., gaining shell access, app crashing on video load, sensitive data exfiltration). 9. These CVEs are dangerous because they can be exploited remotely (ExoPlayer, Firebase) or locally (Play Core) and are often overlooked in mobile apps that don’t regularly update dependencies.
Target Type: Android Apps Using Google SDKs (Play Core, ExoPlayer, Firebase)
Vulnerability: Known CVEs in Google Libraries due to Outdated Versions
MITRE Technique: T1606 (Exploitation via Known Vulnerabilities in Third-Party Components)
Impact: Remote Code Execution, File Read, Data Leakage, App Crash
Detection Method: Reverse engineering (JADX/ApkTool), CVE version checking, Logcat crash output, network traffic analysis (Burp)
Solution: Always update Google Play Core, ExoPlayer, Firebase to latest versions. Monitor CVE databases (like NVD) and GitHub security advisories. Validate file formats before media loading. Block untrusted dynamic modules.

Title: Abuse of ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION on Android
Scenario Description: An Android application requests ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION permission to collect user location data even when the app is not actively in use. This permission is abused to secretly track users in the background without their informed consent. The attacker embeds this in a fake utility app (like a flashlight or wallpaper app). Once the user grants permission, their location is logged silently and periodically to a remote server.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Genymotion or Android Emulator, Burp Suite, Custom Malicious App (built using Java/Kotlin), MITM Proxy, Online IP Logger (e.g., webhook.site)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install Android Studio and set up a basic Android project. Select “Empty Activity” and name it “LocationTrackerApp”.Step 2: Add the following permissions in the AndroidManifest.xml: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: Design a simple UI (e.g., “Tap to Activate”) to make the app look innocent, like a utility tool.Step 4: Implement a LocationService.java or LocationService.kt that runs in the background. Use FusedLocationProviderClient to fetch location periodically using LocationRequest.setInterval().Step 5: In the service class, fetch the user’s latitude and longitude in the background and send this data to a malicious webhook (e.g., https://webhook.site/xyz) using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit.Step 6: Use WorkManager or ForegroundService to run this service even when the app is closed, especially for Android 10 and 11 where background location access is restricted by default UI prompts.Step 7: Sign and build the APK. Install it in an Android emulator or Genymotion device.Step 8: Open the app and grant all permissions manually via prompt or via ADB command: adb shell pm grant com.example.locationapp android.permission.ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION.Step 9: Minimize the app or lock the phone. Wait for 5–10 minutes.Step 10: Open your webhook.site or IP logger and check — the victim’s location coordinates (longitude/latitude) are being sent silently in the background without any user interaction.Step 11: This means the app is successfully abusing background location access. You can further send this data to a personal server, track users' movements, or geofence their behavior.
Impact: Users are tracked without consent even when app is not in use, leading to surveillance, stalking, and privacy invasion
Detection Method: Perform dynamic analysis of app behavior using tools like Frida, Xposed, or Burp Suite to monitor network calls. Monitor permission usage logs and service behavior using adb logcat.
Solution: Always review app permission requests carefully. On Android 10+, restrict background location access unless truly needed. Monitor apps via permission manager. Use Android 12+ privacy indicators and permission usage reports.
Tags: ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, Location Tracking, Android Privacy Abuse, Background Service Exploit, Mobile Surveillance, Privacy Violation, MITRE T1614

Title: Using Foreground Services to Mask Location Collection
Attack Type: Stealth Location Tracking via Legitimate Features
Scenario Description: A malicious Android app uses a Foreground Service to hide the fact that it's collecting the user's location in real-time. Foreground services appear legitimate to Android (e.g., displaying a media player or fitness tracking), so they bypass many background location restrictions. This attack tricks the user into thinking the app is doing something helpful (like step tracking or music playing) while secretly collecting and sending GPS data to a remote server or attacker-controlled endpoint.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Burp Suite or webhook.site, Android Emulator or Genymotion, Java/Kotlin knowledge (basic), Android device (optional), ADB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install Android Studio and create a new project called “FitnessTrackerApp” (this is a dummy name to fool users). Choose "Empty Activity" as the template and click Finish.Step 2: In your AndroidManifest.xml, add the following permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: Design a basic UI with one button saying "Start Tracking" (to look like a real fitness app). When the user taps this button, your app will start a foreground service.Step 4: Create a Java/Kotlin service class, e.g., LocationForegroundService. Inside this service, use FusedLocationProviderClient to request location updates with high accuracy.Step 5: Add a notification to run this service in foreground using startForeground(NOTIFICATION_ID, notification). Make the notification say something innocent like “Fitness tracking running…” so users aren’t suspicious.Step 6: Inside the location callback, log the user's current location (latitude and longitude), and send it to a remote endpoint using HttpURLConnection, Volley, or Retrofit. You can use webhook.site to view captured data live.Step 7: Build and run the app on your emulator or real device. Tap “Start Tracking”. This SDK silently collects the user’s precise GPS location even when the app is not being used, and sends it to external servers. The app developer may not be aware of the SDK's full data behavior, or may include it knowingly for monetization. This is a supply chain privacy abuse because the app itself doesn’t directly request or use location data — the third-party SDK inside it does.

The app will not visibly use this SDK or show anything on the UI.Step 6: In your app’s MainActivity.java, initialize the SDK in the onCreate() method using: StealthLocationCollector.startDataCollection(this);. This ensures it starts silently on app launch.Step 7: Build and install the app on an emulator. Accept all location permissions when prompted (users often do this without reading carefully).Step 8: Run the app. It shows a basic UI like “Welcome to Daily News” — looks safe and harmless. Title: Abusing Motion Sensors to Approximate Location
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a malicious Android app avoids asking for any location-related permissions like GPS, Wi-Fi, or background location. Instead, it uses access to motion sensors — such as the accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer — which are considered “non-dangerous permissions” and don't require user consent. These sensors provide very sensitive data about user movements, orientation, and speed. When collected over time, this data can be processed to estimate a user’s path and geographical location. Some attackers combine this with known maps, road networks, or public Wi-Fi SSIDs to accurately track a user without ever accessing GPS. This technique has been proven in academic research and can be implemented in real-world Android malware.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Android Emulator or Physical Android Device with Motion Sensors, Python or Java (for optional post-processing), Webhook.site or Remote Server, Sensor Data Logger Code
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new Android project named SensorTrackDemo. Select “Empty Activity” and click Finish.Step 2: In the AndroidManifest.xml, DO NOT request any location-related permissions. Just add <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/> if you plan to send data to a remote server.Step 3: In MainActivity.java or MainActivity.kt, initialize access to the motion sensors: use SensorManager to register listeners for TYPE_ACCELEROMETER, TYPE_GYROSCOPE, and TYPE_MAGNETIC_FIELD.Step 4: Set up a SensorEventListener and record the X, Y, and Z values from each sensor as they change. You’ll be logging raw movement, rotation, and directional data.Step 5: Store these values in an internal buffer or list every few milliseconds. Optionally, timestamp each entry so you can align them later for analysis.Step 6: Write a simple routine that runs in a background thread or using Handler to periodically send the collected sensor data to a server (e.g., webhook.site or your Flask backend). Use Retrofit or plain HttpURLConnection to POST the data in JSON format.Step 7: Build and run the app on a physical Android device. Walk around a room, house, or neighborhood while the app is running in foreground or background.Step 8: The app continuously collects movement data like tilt, speed, and direction. Open your webhook.site or server logs — you will see the movement data being transmitted without the app having any GPS permissions.Step 9: Now, analyze the collected data offline using a script or plotting tool. The pattern of acceleration, rotation, and orientation gives insights into user movement patterns — like turns, stops, steps, and even direction faced.Step 10: With enough data and known starting point (e.g., if user opened app in a certain place like a mall), you can combine sensor data with known map patterns or even public Wi-Fi SSID scans (if app has Wi-Fi permissions) to infer approximate location with reasonable accuracy.Step 11: You've now successfully simulated a real-world attack that circumvents Android location permissions and silently tracks user movement using motion sensors only. This technique is extremely stealthy and hard to detect since Android does not notify users about sensor access.Step 12: In real-world malicious apps (e.g., fake fitness apps, compasses, or games), this technique is used to build user behavioral profiles, infer visited locations, and sell location data to third parties without triggering permission alerts.
Impact: Motion sensors can silently track physical movements and infer approximate geographic location. Can be used to identify routines, travel paths, or nearby locations without GPS or Wi-Fi.
Detection Method: Use static analysis to detect abnormal access to motion sensors. Monitor sensor usage patterns in apps using tools like Frida, Xposed, or Android Profiler. Android 12+ also shows sensor usage indicators.
Solution: Restrict unnecessary sensor access unless app functionality truly needs it. Android developers should not collect motion sensor data in background without purpose. Android OS should notify users about ongoing sensor use (introduced in Android 12+). Users should prefer apps from trusted developers only.

Title: Bluetooth Beacons or Wi-Fi SSID Logging

These identifiers are often location-specific (e.g., “Starbucks_123” or “Office_WIFI_2F”), so collecting them allows an attacker to infer the user’s current location, even when location permissions like GPS are not granted. Since scanning for Bluetooth and Wi-Fi is possible without fine-grained location permissions on many Android versions, users may never know their location is being monitored. Attackers can compare scanned SSIDs against known public or commercial location databases (like Google’s or Apple’s) to get GPS coordinates.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Android Emulator (or physical Android device with Wi-Fi/Bluetooth), Webhook.site or Flask Server, Burp Suite or MITM Proxy (optional), Python (for post-processing lookups), WiGLE.net (SSID-to-location service), Bluetooth Scanner (optional), ADB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new project called SilentLocatorApp. Use the "Empty Activity" template and click Finish. This app will simulate a basic tool like “Battery Optimizer” to hide its real purpose.Step 2: In AndroidManifest.xml, add the following permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_WIFI_STATE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_NETWORK_STATE"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_ADMIN"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.BLUETOOTH_SCAN" tools:ignore="MissingPermission"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>.Step 3: In your MainActivity.java or MainActivity.kt, initialize the WifiManager and BluetoothAdapter to scan nearby networks and Bluetooth devices. Also use ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission() to silently request permission at runtime (for Android 10+).Step 4: For Wi-Fi scanning, use wifiManager.startScan() and fetch SSIDs using wifiManager.getScanResults(). Loop through the ScanResult list and log or extract all nearby SSIDs and BSSIDs.Step 5: For Bluetooth, use bluetoothAdapter.startDiscovery() and register a BroadcastReceiver to get the list of nearby BLE or Bluetooth Classic device names and MAC addresses.Step 6: Store all captured SSIDs and Bluetooth identifiers in a local buffer (e.g., JSON array), and periodically send this data to a remote server or webhook.site using HttpURLConnection or Retrofit. You can simulate this as telemetry data.Step 7: Run the app on a real Android device (recommended), in a place like a home, office, coffee shop, or school. Accept all permission prompts. Let the app stay open or minimize it.Step 8: Within a few seconds, the app silently scans for all nearby Wi-Fi SSIDs and Bluetooth beacons. These include routers, printers, smartwatches, wireless earphones, etc. Each one has a unique name (SSID or device name) and MAC address (BSSID).Step 9: On webhook.site or your server, verify that all collected identifiers are sent successfully. You should now have a list like: {SSID: Starbucks_Wifi, BSSID: 00:14:22:01:23:45}.Step 10: Use services like WiGLE.net (wardriving database of Wi-Fi access points) or custom scripts to match the BSSID (MAC address of the router) to an actual GPS location. For example, searching a BSSID like 00:14:22:01:23:45 may return “Kolkata, Starbucks Park Street, Lat: 22.552, Lon: 88.353”.Step 11: This confirms that the app successfully inferred your real-world location without asking for GPS access, by only harvesting nearby radio signals.Step 12: In real-world malicious apps, this data is sold to advertisers, brokers, or used for surveillance. Many flashlight, VPN, and cleaner apps have been caught collecting Bluetooth/Wi-Fi scan data to track users across malls, offices, and transport hubs without their knowledge.Step 13: You’ve now simulated a real-world passive location tracking attack using Wi-Fi and Bluetooth signals alone — no GPS needed.

Solution: Use Android versions 11+ where Wi-Fi scanning is restricted to apps with location permissions. Educate users about risks of unnecessary Wi-Fi/Bluetooth scanning. Developers must disclose telemetry practices clearly. Avoid installing apps from unknown sources.

Title: Continuous Location Upload via AlarmManager or WorkManager
Scenario Description: This attack simulates how a malicious app can schedule continuous GPS location uploads using Android’s AlarmManager or WorkManager. These APIs are designed for task scheduling like reminders, periodic updates, or background syncing. However, an attacker can abuse them to collect a user’s location at frequent intervals (every few minutes or hours) even if the user is not using the app or has forgotten about it. Since AlarmManager can work during device idle state (with some restrictions on Android 6+), and WorkManager is optimized for persistent background tasks, both can be exploited for silent surveillance. This technique is dangerous because it bypasses traditional app usage visibility—data leaks happen when user isn't watching.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Android Emulator or Android Device, Webhook.site or Custom Server, ADB, Retrofit/Volley (to send data), Burp Suite (for traffic inspection), Location Emulation Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open Android Studio and create a new project called StealthTrackerApp. Select “Empty Activity” template. This app will simulate a basic utility like a wallpaper switcher or theme changer to make it look harmless.Step 2: In AndroidManifest.xml, request required permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED"/>. Also add: <receiver android:enabled="true" android:exported="true" android:name=".BootReceiver"><intent-filter><action android:name="android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED"/></intent-filter></receiver>.Step 3: In MainActivity.java, ask for runtime location permission using ActivityCompat.requestPermissions() to avoid denial at execution.Step 4: Create a custom class LocationUploaderWorker if using WorkManager. This ensures tracking resumes automatically after reboot.Step 9: Build and install the app on an emulator or Android device. When prompted, allow location access.Step 10: After launch, the app appears to do something innocent (e.g., changing wallpaper), but in the background, it continuously captures and uploads the user’s location every 15 minutes—even when the app is closed or the screen is off.Step 11: Open webhook.site (or your server) and verify — you will see location data being received on schedule. Title: Clipboard + Location Correlation

It then correlates clipboard content with the user’s physical location to build detailed user intelligence — for example, detecting that the user copied a hospital address from Google Maps while being physically near it, or identifying that a banking URL was accessed from a specific city. This attack is silent, effective, and works even in the foreground without raising user suspicion. It’s commonly used in spyware, fraud apps, adware, and social profiling tools.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Android Emulator or Device, Webhook.site or Flask Server, Burp Suite, Retrofit or Volley, ADB, Location Access Enabled

This app will appear like a basic productivity or clipboard manager tool to appear legitimate.Step 2: In AndroidManifest.xml, request the following permissions: <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"/>, <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>. As soon as the user copies the content, the app intercepts it and fetches the current GPS coordinates silently.Step 10: Switch to webhook.site and verify — the JSON payload sent contains the clipboard text and the user's exact location. You have successfully linked personal user activity with their physical presence — this is the basis for deep surveillance or data profiling.Step 11: Repeat with other real-life clipboard content like OTPs, UPI IDs, Amazon order URLs, or Twitter profiles — all this data can be harvested and linked to physical context, which is valuable to advertisers, stalkers, or nation-state spyware.Step 12: This attack method has been used in clipboard spy apps and was exposed in Chinese apps, TikTok behavior reports, and apps flagged by Apple and Google in past investigations. Title: iOS Background Location Trick via Silent Audio
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a malicious iOS app plays a silent audio file in the background to keep the app alive even when the user is not interacting with it. Normally, iOS limits background location access to certain app states. However, if an app is playing audio, it is allowed to remain active in the background. By abusing this design, the app can call CoreLocation APIs repeatedly to collect and upload the user's GPS location silently. Since the audio is silent, the user hears nothing and has no reason to suspect that location tracking continues. This is a known exploit of the iOS multitasking behavior and has been previously abused by real apps on the App Store before getting flagged.
Tools Used: MacBook with Xcode, iOS Device or Simulator, Swift/Objective-C, Silent MP3 file (0 volume), Webhook.site or custom Flask server, Apple Developer Account (for real device testing)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Open Xcode and create a new iOS app project named SilentLocator. Choose Swift as the language and "App" as the template. Click Next and Finish.Step 2: Go to Info.plist and add the following keys:• NSLocationAlwaysAndWhenInUseUsageDescription – “This app needs location for service accuracy.”• NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription – “We use location to personalize your experience.”• UIBackgroundModes – Add both audio and location to this array.Step 3: In ViewController.swift, import the following modules at the top: import AVFoundation, import CoreLocation.Step 4: Declare location manager and audio player:swift
let locationManager = CLLocationManager()
var audioPlayer: AVAudioPlayer?
Step 5: In viewDidLoad(), configure location access:swift
locationManager.delegate = self

Step 6: Add a silent audio file named silent.mp3 (a 1-second file with no sound, you can generate one using Audacity or download it). Add it to your Xcode project.Step 7: Play the silent audio in loop:swift
let soundURL = Bundle.main.url(forResource: "silent", withExtension: "mp3")!
audioPlayer = try? AVAudioPlayer(contentsOf: soundURL)

Step 8: Build and run the app on your iOS device (real device, not just the simulator for location). You’ll notice the app continues running in the background — because of the silent audio.Step 10: Open your webhook.site or custom server. Inside the locationManager(_:didUpdateLocations:) delegate, send the user’s location to this endpoint using URLSession.shared.dataTask. Example:swift

Even though the app is backgrounded and appears inactive, your webhook.site will continue to receive location updates every few seconds or minutes.Step 12: This confirms that the app is actively tracking your movement in real-time by exploiting the background audio mode — a loophole in iOS multitasking logic.Step 13: In real-world examples, shady weather or radio apps have used this technique to harvest user location in background, silently selling it to advertisers or analytics brokers. Title: Bypassing Biometric Logic with Frida (Android)
Scenario Description: In this real-world attack, a malicious actor uses Frida, a dynamic instrumentation toolkit, to bypass biometric authentication (e.g., fingerprint, face unlock) in Android apps. Many apps implement biometric login using BiometricPrompt or custom fingerprint APIs, but their verification logic can be manipulated at runtime. This means an attacker can hook functions like onAuthenticationSucceeded() or return true from isUserAuthenticated() even without performing real biometric validation. If the app does not properly secure biometric validation at the native layer or backend, this can result in unauthorized access. This is commonly exploited in banking, wallet, or password manager apps that rely on client-side biometric trust.
Tools Used: Frida, Android Emulator or Rooted Android Device, ADB, Apktool, Android Studio (optional), JADX, MobSF, Termux (optional), Biometric-enabled App (test target), Burp Suite (for traffic validation)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Set up your Android test environment. You can use a rooted Android device (preferred) or a Genymotion rooted emulator. Make sure adb is working. Enable USB debugging. Connect with adb devices and verify the connection.Step 2: Install Frida on your PC: pip install frida-tools. Also install Frida server on the device:• Download the correct Frida server binary for your device’s architecture from https://github.com/frida/frida/releases.• Push it to device: adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp• Make it executable: adb shell chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/frida-server• Start it: adb shell /data/local/tmp/frida-server &Step 3: On your PC, verify Frida is working: frida-ps -U (should list running processes on the device).Step 4: Install a test biometric app from Play Store (like a simple fingerprint locker app) or use your own sample app that uses BiometricPrompt. Ensure the app has fingerprint login enabled.Step 5: Use jadx or apktool to reverse engineer the app (optional). Look inside the smali or Java code for logic like onAuthenticationSucceeded() or authenticate() which gets triggered on biometric success.Step 6: Write a Frida script to hook the biometric logic. For example:javascript
Java.perform(function() {
var BioClass = Java.use("androidx.biometric.BiometricPrompt$AuthenticationCallback");
BioClass.onAuthenticationSucceeded.implementation = function(result) {
console.log("Biometric bypass triggered!");
// Call the original method
return this.onAuthenticationSucceeded(result);

});

targetClass.isUserAuthenticated.implementation = function() {
console.log("Forcing isUserAuthenticated() = true");
return true;
};

Title: Face/Fingerprint Spoofing (Hardware Attack)
Scenario Description: Many smartphones rely on biometric authentication like Face ID or Fingerprint sensors to protect sensitive apps or device access. It has been successfully executed against older Android fingerprint sensors, poorly protected banking apps, and even some older iPhones.

If the scanner lacks liveness detection (no pulse/heat/capacitance check), it will accept the spoof.Step 6: You’re now inside the device or app without the real fingerprint.Step 7: For Face Spoofing, gather multiple photos of the victim’s face (from social media, selfies, videos) from different angles: front, side, up, down.Step 8: Use photogrammetry software (like Blender with FaceBuilder plugin or FaceGen) to create a 3D model of the victim’s face. You can also use AI face reconstruction tools if needed.Step 9: Print the face model using a 3D printer or sculpt it using paper-mâché or resin. Step 12: After executing the hook, the app UI believes biometric auth passed and gives full access.Step 13: Real-world case: Security researchers have used this attack against password manager apps, secure note apps, and banking tools that didn’t verify session state after biometric success.Step 14: You’ve now successfully performed a full biometric bypass by manipulating the app's trust in device-level biometric APIs without enforcing its own logic.Step 15: To test this further, combine it with runtime analysis using objection explore or Frida trace to locate internal validation logic that may also need to be bypassed.Step 16: Congratulations, this is a real-world bypass technique that even OWASP MASVS flags as a critical biometric misconfiguration.
Vulnerability: Trusting system biometric callbacks without app-level auth logic
Impact: Full unauthorized access to sensitive areas of the app, including vaults, financial info, or session hijacking, without needing the real biometric scan
Detection Method: Check if onAuthenticationSucceeded() or iOS biometric callbacks are hooked. Review app behavior when biometric fails or is skipped. Static analysis of app source can show missing fallback or verification.
Solution: Always verify biometric success using app-level logic. Enforce session control. Use signed tokens or backend challenge-response flows. Never assume success just because the device said so.
Tags: Biometric API Misuse, BiometricPrompt Abuse, Frida Authentication Hook, iOS Face ID Bypass via Callback, MITRE T1556
Source: OWASP MASVS, Frida Examples, AppCensus Analysis, Offensive Mobile Research Guides

Title: Hardcoded Keys in APK/IPA
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps store sensitive data (e.g., API keys, secret tokens, encryption keys) directly in the source code for convenience. These keys are often hardcoded into Android APKs or iOS IPA files. If an attacker extracts these keys through reverse engineering, they can use them to decrypt user data, forge API requests, or impersonate the app — compromising confidentiality, integrity, and security. This is common in chat apps, e-commerce, health, and fintech apps where encryption or secure APIs are used poorly.
Tools Used: jadx-gui, apktool, MobSF, strings (Linux), Android Studio (optional), iOS jailbroken device or IPA decrypt tool (Frida-ios-dump), Hopper/IDA/ghidra for iOS
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Choose any mobile app that communicates with an API or stores encrypted local data. You can use a target APK file from any open-source or real-world app using encryption or backend tokens.Step 2: For Android, extract the APK using adb pull /data/app/packagename/base.apk or download the APK directly.Step 3: Open the APK in jadx-gui. This is a graphical tool that converts Android bytecode back into readable Java code.Step 4: Look through packages like com.example.utils, com.example.crypto, or com.example.api. These usually contain utility functions or configuration.Step 5: Search for keywords like "key", "secret", "token", "AES", "Base64", "API_KEY", or "encrypt".Step 6: You might find code like this:java
public static final String SECRET_KEY = "1234567890abcdef";
orjava
String apiKey = "sk_live_mysecretkey";
This confirms that the app developer hardcoded a sensitive encryption key or backend API key inside the APK.Step 7: Copy this key. If it’s used for AES encryption/decryption, you can now decrypt any local data files the app uses.Step 8: If it’s an API key (like Stripe, Firebase, AWS, or custom server), you can now call the API directly using Postman or curl, impersonating the app.Step 9: On iOS, first decrypt the IPA using frida-ios-dump or objection to dump the encrypted binary.Step 10: Load the decrypted binary into Hopper or Ghidra and look for Objective-C strings like "kEncryptionKey" or @"API_SECRET". Alternatively, search global constants.Step 11: If found, follow similar steps — extract the hardcoded key and use it for unauthorized access.Step 12: Optional: Use MobSF to automatically scan APK or IPA files. It highlights hardcoded secrets in seconds and shows potential misuse.Step 13: With the key in hand, you can now decrypt saved local files like .db or .json if they were encrypted using symmetric ciphers (AES/CBC etc.)Step 14: To test further, run the app and intercept its HTTP traffic using Burp Suite. Replace tokens or headers with your extracted key and verify whether the server accepts your forged requests.Step 15: Congratulations! You have now successfully extracted and abused a hardcoded key from a real mobile app. This is one of the most common, real, and impactful vulnerabilities found in the wild.Step 16: Real-life examples include apps leaking Stripe API keys, Firebase secrets, JWT signing keys, or AES private keys — leading to account takeover, data theft, and server abuse.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded cryptographic key or token in app binary
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 - Unsecured Credentials in Application Code
Impact: Decryption of private user data, unauthorized API access, user impersonation, remote server exploitation
Detection Method: Use static analysis tools (MobSF, jadx-gui) or grep strings for sensitive constants. Analyze AES key usage in app logic. Monitor API abuse using extracted keys.
Solution: Never hardcode secrets in the app. Store them securely using Android Keystore/iOS Keychain or generate them dynamically using server-attested flows. Use short-lived, rotated API tokens and obfuscate code.
Tags: Hardcoded Key Extraction, AES Key in Code, Android API Token Leak, iOS IPA Reverse Engineering, MITRE T1552.001
Source: OWASP Mobile Top 10, MobSF Docs, HackerOne Reports, MITRE ATT&CK, AppCensus Analysis

Title: Use of Weak or Broken Algorithms (e.g., MD5, DES, RC4)
Scenario Description: A mobile app uses MD5 to hash passwords and DES to encrypt user data. As a penetration tester or ethical hacker, you want to demonstrate that these algorithms are insecure and can be easily cracked. You will simulate this by reverse-engineering the app, extracting the hash or encrypted value, and breaking it using freely available tools.
Tools Used: MobSF, jadx, Android emulator, hashcat, CyberChef
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Environment: Download and install MobSF on your system. Also install jadx (for decompiling Android APKs) and setup Android Studio or an emulator like BlueStacks or Genymotion. Install hashcat (used for cracking hashes) and open CyberChef in your browser. 2. Get the APK File: Use a known vulnerable app like InsecureBankv2 (publicly available for educational pentesting), or download a mobile banking or messaging APK with permission. You can also use a sample APK from GitHub. 3. Static Analysis with MobSF: Open MobSF and upload the APK. Let it run a static scan. MobSF will automatically detect the use of MD5, DES, or RC4. Look for keywords like MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5") or Cipher.getInstance("DES"). This means weak algorithms are being used. 4. Decompile APK with JADX: Open the same APK in JADX GUI. Navigate to the LoginActivity.java or any file with encrypt() or hashPassword() functions. Look for hardcoded hash methods like String hashed = md5(password); or encrypted storage using DES like Cipher.getInstance("DES"). 5. Identify Hardcoded Keys or Weak Hashing: Often, you will find hardcoded keys such as secretKey = "12345678"; used in DES. Or you’ll see the password hashed using MD5 like: hashed = DigestUtils.md5Hex(password);. Note this is insecure. 6. Get Hash or Encrypted Text at Runtime: Now run the app in emulator. Create a test account with password like test123. Capture the network traffic using Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit. If the password is hashed with MD5, it will look like cc03e747a6afbbcbf8be7668acfebee5 (hash of test123). Or if encrypted with DES, it might be Base64 encoded like FkZz2s3/7Lk=. 7. Crack the MD5 Hash with Hashcat: Copy the MD5 hash, run: hashcat -m 0 hash.txt rockyou.txt (ensure rockyou.txt wordlist is downloaded). After few seconds, you’ll see the original password printed. This shows MD5 is crackable in seconds. 8. Decrypt DES-encrypted Text with CyberChef: If DES was used to encrypt sensitive info (e.g., tokens), go to CyberChef. Select “From Base64”, then “DES Decrypt”. Paste the encrypted value and try common keys like 12345678 or the key found in the source code. It will decrypt the text. This proves DES can be brute-forced or reversed easily. 9. Impact Statement: Tell the developer or report that any attacker with access to stored hashes or encrypted values can recover user passwords or sensitive info using free tools in minutes. This breaks confidentiality and allows account takeover. 10. Documentation: Save screenshots of MobSF, jadx code snippet showing MD5/DES, hashcat output, and CyberChef decrypted output. Use these in your pentest report as proof.
Vulnerability: Use of MD5, DES, RC4 cryptographic functions
Impact: Exposure of user passwords, sensitive tokens, account takeover, privacy breach
Detection Method: Static analysis using MobSF, jadx, runtime traffic analysis using Burp, hash cracking tools
Solution: Replace MD5 with SHA-256+Salt; avoid DES/RC4, use AES-256; implement strong key management and KDF like PBKDF2/Bcrypt
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, InsecureBankv2, GCHQ CyberChef

Title: ECB Mode on AES (Pattern Leakage)
Scenario Description: A mobile app encrypts images or user data using AES in ECB (Electronic Codebook) mode. While AES is strong, using ECB mode is insecure because it encrypts identical plaintext blocks into identical ciphertext blocks, revealing patterns in the encrypted data. This is especially dangerous when encrypting images or structured data (like JSON), because the attacker can visually identify content patterns. As an ethical hacker, you’ll simulate this issue by finding the AES ECB usage in the app, extracting the encrypted output, and demonstrating that patterns remain visible.
Tools Used: MobSF, jadx, Android emulator, Burp Suite, CyberChef, Python
Attack Steps: 1. Setup Your Environment: Install MobSF (Mobile Security Framework) for scanning APKs. Install JADX GUI (for decompiling Android apps), and setup an Android emulator using Android Studio or Genymotion. Also install Burp Suite (to intercept app traffic), and open CyberChef (https://gchq.github.io/CyberChef/) in your browser. Make sure Python is installed for simple scripting. 2. Obtain a Target APK (Example - InsecureBankv2 or Demo App): Download a known vulnerable APK such as InsecureBankv2. Alternatively, create or get an Android app that encrypts images or JSON data. 3. Static Analysis Using MobSF: Upload the APK to MobSF. Wait for the scan. Go to the "Code Analysis" section and search for Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding"). This tells you that the app is using AES in ECB mode. Note the Java file and line number. 4. Code Review in JADX: Open the APK in JADX. Locate the file mentioned by MobSF. You’ll see something like: Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding");. Also look for the secret key being set (e.g., SecretKeySpec key = new SecretKeySpec("1234567890abcdef".getBytes(), "AES");). Save the hardcoded key if found. This tells you the app is using insecure AES-ECB mode. 5. Find What’s Being Encrypted: In the same file, see what data is being passed to the cipher. Often it could be sensitive info like login tokens or even binary images. Example: cipher.doFinal(imageBytes) or cipher.doFinal(userInfoJson.getBytes()). Note the variable or method where it originates. 6. Run the App and Capture Encrypted Data: Install and run the app on the emulator. Use Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit to intercept the network requests. Create a test account or perform some encrypted communication. Look for large Base64-encoded strings in requests or responses — these are likely AES-encrypted data. Copy one such encrypted value. 7. Decrypt in CyberChef (Optional) to Validate ECB Effects: Open CyberChef. Add the “From Base64” operation, then “AES Decrypt” operation. Use the key found earlier. Set the mode to "ECB", input the Base64 string, and see if you get readable content (like JSON). If you’re decrypting an image, save the output as .bmp or .png. If the app encrypts images using ECB mode, the decrypted image will still show a “ghost” of the original image with visible outlines — this is the classic ECB pattern leakage problem. 8. Demonstrate Visual Pattern Leakage: If the app is encrypting images (e.g., for uploads or storage), extract the encrypted image from storage or intercepted traffic. Use Python to decrypt it using ECB and visualize the result. Python code: python from Crypto.Cipher import AES from base64 import b64decode from PIL import Image import io key = b"1234567890abcdef" cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) with open("ecb_encrypted_image.bmp", "rb") as f: encrypted = f.read() decrypted = cipher.decrypt(encrypted) with open("decrypted_output.bmp", "wb") as out: out.write(decrypted)  Then open the resulting decrypted_output.bmp. You’ll see the shape of the original image — this proves that ECB mode leaks structure. 9. Impact Statement: ECB mode encryption breaks semantic security. Attackers can detect patterns in the ciphertext, especially in structured or repetitive data like images, forms, JSON, etc. This is dangerous even if they can’t fully decrypt the data. In real-world cases, attackers have reconstructed logos or text from encrypted images just because of ECB usage. 10. Reporting: Document the insecure use of AES/ECB/PKCS5Padding, include screenshots from JADX, intercepted traffic, CyberChef or Python-decrypted output images, and explain the visual leakage. 11. Extra Realistic Note: This exact vulnerability was demonstrated in research where encrypted Tux images still revealed a faint Tux shape after AES-ECB encryption — because each block is encrypted independently, so repeated pixel patterns stay visible.
Vulnerability: Use of AES in ECB mode causing pattern leakage
Impact: Leakage of visual or structured patterns, sensitive data inference, privacy violation
Detection Method: Static code analysis (MobSF/JADX), runtime traffic interception (Burp), visualization (CyberChef, Python)
Solution: Use AES in CBC or GCM mode with random IVs; never use ECB mode; ensure keys are not hardcoded; add proper padding and randomness
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 (M5), AES ECB Tux Demo, CyberChef

Title: Custom or Homebrew Crypto
Scenario Description: A mobile developer, instead of using well-established cryptographic libraries like AES-GCM or RSA from trusted sources (e.g., Bouncy Castle, Java Cryptography Extension), tries to implement their own custom algorithm to "encrypt" sensitive user data like passwords, tokens, or images. These homebrew algorithms are usually flawed and break basic rules of cryptography such as randomness, key management, or secure padding. As an ethical hacker, your goal is to reverse-engineer and break this homebrew encryption to prove its insecurity and educate the developer.
Tools Used: MobSF, JADX, Android Emulator, Python, CyberChef, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: 1. Setup Tools and Emulator: Install MobSF on your PC or VM to analyze APKs. Install JADX GUI to reverse-engineer the code. Set up an Android emulator via Android Studio or Genymotion to run the mobile app. Install Python (Windows or Linux) and a good code editor like VS Code. Also install Burp Suite to inspect app traffic. Open CyberChef in your browser. 2. Obtain a Target APK (Use Educational Sample or Known App): You can download a known intentionally vulnerable APK like “InsecureBankv2” or a sample app from GitHub that contains poorly written encryption functions (search GitHub for “insecure android encryption example”). 3. Upload the APK to MobSF for Static Analysis: Open MobSF, upload the APK, and wait for the static analysis report. Go to “Code Analysis” and search for suspicious custom logic in classes like CryptoUtils, Encryptor, or SecurityHandler. Look for clues like custom math operations, shifting bits, character manipulation, or writing their own encrypt()/decrypt() methods. 4. Decompile with JADX to Review Source Code: Open the APK with JADX. Search for encrypt, obfuscate, customEncrypt, or maskData method names. A real homebrew function might look like: public static String encrypt(String input) { char[] chars = input.toCharArray(); for(int i=0; i<chars.length; i++) { chars[i] = (char)(chars[i] + 4); } return new String(chars); }. This is a Caesar Cipher — just shifting letters, not real encryption. 5. Identify the Flaw: Recognize that these techniques (char shifting, XOR with fixed key, reversing strings, base64-only obfuscation, etc.) are not cryptographically secure. These are often mistaken for encryption by novice developers. If you see manual bit shifts, hardcoded character masks like key = “#3gX!”, or XOR logic without randomness, you’ve likely found a custom encryption function. 6. Extract the Custom Algorithm and Reimplement in Python: Copy the logic into a new Python script. For example, if the Java method does (char)(c + 4), write equivalent Python: ''.join([chr(ord(c)+4) for c in input_string]). This lets you decrypt any data that app encrypted with its custom function. You can automate breaking any value it stores or sends. 7. Run the App and Capture Encrypted Data: Open the app on emulator. Fill a login form or send a message, and capture the request in Burp Suite. Look for fields that look like gibberish but short (e.g., “Lipps${svph%”) — this is likely Caesar or XOR obfuscated text. Copy it. 8. Decrypt Captured Data Using Your Python Script: Use your reimplemented logic to decode the string. If it was Caesar +4, input Lipps${svph% and get back Hello World!. This proves the encryption is weak and breakable without brute force. 9. Alternative — Use CyberChef: For Caesar cipher, open CyberChef. Use “From Charcode”, then “ROT13”, “XOR Brute Force”, or “To Hex” to visually reverse weak encryption. Try known tricks like Base64 decode followed by character shifting. You’ll often reveal real plaintext data from captured network requests or storage files. 10. Demonstrate the Attack: Prepare a before/after screenshot. Show original encrypted field (like password or token), then decrypted plaintext using your script. Show that no real encryption was used and anyone with access to network traffic or storage could recover user data. 11. Impact Explanation: Custom cryptography is extremely risky and usually flawed. Attackers can easily reverse or brute-force such methods. This could lead to full account compromise, privacy leaks, or token theft even if data appears “encrypted”. 12. Report It: In your report or bug disclosure, explain that strong cryptography must use peer-reviewed, standard algorithms (e.g., AES-GCM, RSA-2048, Bcrypt) with secure libraries and proper key/IV handling. Include screenshots, Decompiled logic, intercepted values, and your decoded results. 13. Real-World Example: Many malware and old banking apps have used homebrew crypto to "protect" PINs or tokens. These were broken within minutes by analysts. Avoid ever creating your own encryption logic — it will fail under scrutiny.
Impact: Attacker can reverse or decode obfuscated or encrypted data easily, exposing passwords, tokens, images, messages
Detection Method: Static code inspection with JADX or MobSF, reproduction in Python/CyberChef, runtime inspection with Burp Suite
Solution: NEVER use custom cryptography; always use trusted libraries like AES-GCM, RSA, Bcrypt, Argon2 with proper key management and randomness
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, CryptoFail Research, InsecureBankv2, CyberChef

Title: Predictable or No Key Derivation (KDF)
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps take a user's password and directly use it as an encryption key — or derive a key from it using a weak, predictable, or non-existent key derivation function (KDF). This leads to insecure storage or transmission of sensitive data like tokens, credentials, and messages. An attacker who intercepts the encrypted data or gains access to the app can guess or brute-force the password, derive the same encryption key, and decrypt the data. Your goal is to identify weak or missing KDF use, extract the logic, and break it using dictionary-based brute-force or direct reversal.
Tools Used: MobSF, JADX, Android Emulator, Python, Burp Suite, CyberChef, hashcat
Attack Steps: 1. Setup Analysis Environment: Download and install MobSF to statically analyze Android APKs. Install JADX-GUI to decompile APK source code. Set up an Android Emulator (via Android Studio or Genymotion). Install Python (3.x), VS Code (or any editor), Burp Suite (to capture app requests), and access CyberChef in your browser. Install hashcat if you plan to brute-force hashes. 2. Get a Target APK for Testing: Use an intentionally vulnerable APK like InsecureBankv2 or download any sample educational APK from GitHub. These are legal for practice and often include flawed cryptographic practices. 3. Analyze APK Using MobSF: Upload the APK to MobSF, run static scan, and check the “Code Analysis” tab. Look for suspicious code snippets such as SecretKeySpec key = new SecretKeySpec(password.getBytes(), "AES");. This means no proper key derivation — password is directly used as a key. Also look for weak hash-based KDF like MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5") or SHA-1 with few or no iterations. These are not secure. 4. Open Decompiled Code in JADX: Use JADX to locate the class and method that handles key generation. For example, search for functions like getSecretKey(), encrypt(), or deriveKey(). You might see something like: public static SecretKeySpec getKey(String password) { return new SecretKeySpec(password.getBytes(), "AES"); } or: MessageDigest md = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-1"); byte[] key = md.digest(password.getBytes()); This shows the app either directly uses the password as the key or hashes it without salting or iterating — both are insecure. 5. Understand the Impact of Missing/Weak KDF: A strong KDF (like PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) takes a password and makes it resistant to brute-force by adding salt and iterations. Without a KDF, any password used by the user becomes a weak encryption key that can be guessed with a dictionary. You’ll simulate that. 6. Run the App in Emulator and Intercept Encrypted Data: Start the app on emulator, register a test user with password (e.g., test123). Use Burp Suite to intercept requests or monitor local files if data is stored. Look for encrypted blobs in requests or storage — often base64 strings or hex-encoded. Save them. Example: 2bb80d537b1da3e38bd30361aa855686. 7. Try to Derive the Key and Decrypt the Data in Python: Based on the code logic you found earlier, recreate the key derivation logic in Python. If the app directly uses the password bytes, your Python would be: python from Crypto.Cipher import AES import base64 password = "test123" key = password.encode("utf-8")[:16] cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) encrypted = base64.b64decode("PUT-YOUR-ENCRYPTED-BLOB") decrypted = cipher.decrypt(encrypted) print(decrypted)  If the app uses SHA-1 as weak KDF, replicate it: python import hashlib from Crypto.Cipher import AES password = "test123" key = hashlib.sha1(password.encode()).digest()[:16] cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) decrypted = cipher.decrypt(base64.b64decode("PUT-ENCRYPTED")) print(decrypted)  8. Brute Force the Key Using Common Passwords: If you don't know the password used but found that the key is derived directly from it (no salt/iterations), you can brute-force it with a wordlist using hashcat or Python. Write a script to try common passwords from rockyou.txt, hash them if needed, and try AES decryption. If the output is valid JSON or readable, the correct password is found. This proves weak or no KDF leads to complete decryption. 9. Demonstrate the Attack: Show that just knowing or guessing the user’s password allows decryption of data. Include decrypted tokens or messages, key derivation code from the app, and your matching Python script. Explain that with real-world brute-force, attacker could access many user accounts. 10. Explain the Real-World Risk: Without a strong KDF, attackers who get encrypted data (via intercepted traffic, rooted devices, backups, etc.) can derive the key easily. With enough leaked data and no KDF, user data is as good as plaintext. In corporate apps, this could expose API keys, tokens, or internal configuration. 11. Report and Remediate: Explain that key derivation should always use PBKDF2 (with ≥100,000 iterations), bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2. Never use SHA-1/MD5 or raw password bytes as keys. Always include a salt, proper key length, and slow computation to resist brute-force. 12. Real Examples in the Wild: Old Android banking apps, messaging apps, and file lockers used this exact pattern — direct password-to-key. These were broken in hours and led to full account and data leaks in real-world pentests.
Impact: Attackers can brute-force or guess keys easily, decrypting sensitive user or app data
Detection Method: Static Code Review via MobSF or JADX, Brute-force testing via Python or hashcat
Solution: Always use a strong, standardized KDF like PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 with salts and iterations; avoid direct use of password bytes or insecure hashes (MD5/SHA1) for key generation
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, InsecureBankv2, CryptoFail Research

Title: Exposing Keys in Shared Preferences or plist
Scenario Description: Mobile applications often store sensitive data like API keys, encryption keys, or access tokens in SharedPreferences (Android) or plist files (iOS) for convenience. These storage files are not encrypted by default. If an attacker gains physical access to the device or dumps the app data, they can retrieve these secrets easily. As a security tester, you will extract these keys from local storage and demonstrate the impact of such exposure.
Tools Used: Android Debug Bridge (adb), Android Emulator, Rooted Android Device or Emulator, jadx, MobSF, sqlite3, iExplorer (for iOS), plist Editor, Python (optional), VS Code
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Tools and Environment: Install ADB (Android Debug Bridge), MobSF for APK analysis, JADX-GUI for reverse engineering code, and an Android emulator (via Android Studio or Genymotion). For iOS, use macOS with iExplorer or macOS Finder to access plist files (for jailbroken or developer-enabled iPhones). Install VS Code for any scripting and optional Python. 2. Obtain a Target App for Testing: Use a sample vulnerable APK such as InsecureBankv2 or any public Android APK file you have permission to test. For iOS, use a test app built with Xcode that stores secrets in plist files. 3. Install the App on Emulator or Test Device: Use the command adb install app.apk to install on Android Emulator or device. Launch the app and simulate normal usage such as login, registration, or token generation. This helps populate SharedPreferences or plist files with stored values. 4. Dump the App’s Private Storage Folder: On Android, run adb shell, then type run-as com.example.appname (replace with actual package name). Navigate to /data/data/com.example.appname/shared_prefs/ and list files with ls. You’ll find files like prefs.xml or userprefs.xml. Copy them to your PC with: adb pull /data/data/com.example.appname/shared_prefs/prefs.xml. For iOS, use iExplorer or Finder to navigate to AppDomain/<App Name>/Library/Preferences/ and export the plist file. 5. Inspect the Shared Preferences or plist File: Open the .xml or .plist file using any text editor or plist viewer. You may find content like: <string name="encryption_key">MySuperSecretKey123</string> or <key>api_key</key><string>abcd1234xyz</string>. These are plaintext secrets stored locally and accessible to attackers. 6. Validate the Use of the Key in Code: Use JADX to decompile the APK. Search for usage of these keys in files like MainActivity.java, AuthManager.java, or CryptoUtil.java. You’ll often find code like: SharedPreferences prefs = context.getSharedPreferences("prefs", 0); String key = prefs.getString("encryption_key", "default");. This confirms the app is reading cryptographic secrets directly from SharedPreferences or plist. 7. Demonstrate Real-World Exploitation: Use the extracted key to decrypt encrypted files or network responses. For example, if the app encrypts files with this key using AES, replicate that decryption in Python: python from Crypto.Cipher import AES import base64 key = b'MySuperSecretKey123' cipher = AES.new(key, AES.MODE_ECB) encrypted = base64.b64decode("ENCRYPTED_TEXT_HERE") print(cipher.decrypt(encrypted))  This proves that local secrets can lead to full decryption. 8. Alternative: Brute-force App Passwords Using Exposed Keys: Some apps use these secrets for validating user PINs or encrypting authentication tokens. If a key is exposed, you can reverse the app’s logic and build a brute-forcer or decryptor, allowing access to accounts, saved sessions, or internal files. 9. Explain the Real-World Impact: Storing cryptographic keys in SharedPreferences (Android) or plist (iOS) is extremely risky. These locations are readable by attackers on rooted/jailbroken devices or via data backup/extraction. Even without root, some exploits or misconfigurations (e.g., adb backup or localStorage leakage in hybrid apps) allow access. If secrets are stored in plaintext, all encrypted data becomes exposed. 10. Document and Report: Capture screenshots of the storage file, the retrieved key, the decompiled Java or Swift code using it, and the successful decryption or session hijack. Clearly explain that improper key storage enables complete compromise. 11. Remediation: Developers must never store secrets like encryption keys, access tokens, or API credentials in plaintext in SharedPreferences or plist files. Instead, use Android Keystore (Android) or Keychain (iOS) which are secure storage systems with encryption. Use hardware-backed key management where available. If a key must be derived at runtime, generate it from strong user credentials using a KDF with proper entropy. 12. Real-World Example: Several Android banking apps in 2018–2022 were caught storing AES keys or JWT secrets in SharedPreferences, allowing researchers and attackers to decrypt communication, tamper with sessions, and access sensitive data.
Vulnerability: Exposure of cryptographic keys in SharedPreferences (Android) or plist (iOS)
Impact: Total compromise of encrypted data, token hijacking, offline decryption, local privilege escalation
Detection Method: Manual file inspection via adb or iExplorer, static code analysis using JADX or MobSF
Solution: Use Android Keystore or iOS Keychain for secret storage; never store keys in plaintext files; implement runtime derivation with strong KDFs and ephemeral keys
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, InsecureBankv2, Android Keystore Docs, Apple Keychain Services

Title: Decrypting Encrypted SQLite or Realm DB
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps encrypt their local databases (SQLite or Realm) to protect user data. However, developers often make serious mistakes like using hardcoded keys in the app’s code, weak key derivation, or not enabling full encryption. In this attack, you will extract and decrypt the encrypted database by identifying the encryption key inside the APK or memory, and using it to open or dump the data.
Tools Used: MobSF, JADX, Android Emulator, Rooted Android Device (or AVD), adb, DB Browser for SQLite, Realm Browser, VS Code, Python, CyberChef (optional)
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Your Tools and Device: Install MobSF for static analysis of APKs, JADX-GUI for reverse engineering Android code, an Android Emulator or Genymotion, and ADB for accessing app files. Also install DB Browser for SQLite, Realm Browser (for Realm DB), and Python for decryption scripts if needed. 2. Obtain a Test APK: Use a known vulnerable app like InsecureBankv2 or sample financial/diary apps that use SQLite or Realm. You can find such APKs on GitHub or build your own test app for practice. Install it on the emulator using adb install appname.apk. 3. Trigger App Data Storage: Open the app and perform actions that will store data—create an account, save notes, messages, or transactions. This will populate the SQLite or Realm database inside the app’s storage folder. 4. Access the App’s Internal Files: Run adb shell, then use run-as com.example.appname to access the app's private data. Navigate to /data/data/com.example.appname/databases/ or /files/ depending on app structure. Look for files with .db, .realm, or .sqlite. Use adb pull to copy them to your local system. Example: adb pull /data/data/com.appname/databases/encrypted.db ./. 5. Attempt to Open the DB (If Encrypted, It Will Fail): Try opening the file using DB Browser for SQLite or Realm Studio.
