If it's encrypted, you’ll get an error or see unreadable junk data. Now you know it's protected—but often weakly. 6. Static Analysis to Find the Encryption Key: Now open the APK in MobSF or JADX. In JADX, search for methods like getEncryptionKey(), openOrCreateDatabase(), getBytes(), or check for libraries like SQLCipher, RealmConfiguration.Builder. Often developers write something like: byte[] key = "MySuperSecret123".getBytes();. This means the key is hardcoded. Save this key—it will be used to decrypt the DB. In Realm, you might see: RealmConfiguration config = new RealmConfiguration.Builder().encryptionKey(key).build();—and the key is defined earlier or generated poorly. 7. Use the Found Key to Open the Database: If SQLite is using SQLCipher, open DB Browser for SQLite and go to File → Open Database → Enter Encryption Key using the value you found (e.g., MySuperSecret123). If Realm, open Realm Studio and choose “Open Encrypted Realm” and paste the key in hex format. You may need to convert string key to hex using CyberChef or Python: python key = "MySuperSecret123".encode().hex() print(key)  Use this hex in Realm Studio. 8. Read and Extract Sensitive Data: Once opened, you can see full user data: usernames, passwords, saved tokens, messages, card data, or logs that were supposed to be encrypted. Export this data as proof of vulnerability. 9. If No Key Found, Try Brute-force or Memory Dump (Advanced): If the key is not hardcoded, try adb backup or dump memory using Frida to hook into runtime and extract the key during database access. Or, if the key is derived from password, reverse the derivation using weak hash logic found in code (MD5, SHA1, etc.). Use Python to recreate it and test against the DB. 10. Demonstrate the Full Attack in a Report: Include (1) the extracted DB file, (2) the key found in source, (3) a screenshot of the decrypted data in DB Browser or Realm Studio, and (4) the snippet from decompiled code. This proves the app used weak encryption or exposed key material. 11. Explain Real-World Risk: If an attacker can access a backup or rooted device, and the encryption key is in the APK, the encryption is useless. All local data can be decrypted, analyzed, or even modified and re-injected (e.g., balance change in finance app, message tampering in chats). This violates user trust and data security. 12. Fix Recommendation: Developers must never hardcode encryption keys. Use Android Keystore system or derive keys from user input using KDFs like PBKDF2. For Realm, use key = KeyStore.getSecretKey() and not any static values. Encrypt DB with a per-user key that is not embedded in the code or local storage.
Vulnerability: Exposed or weakly protected encrypted local database (SQLite or Realm)
Impact: Decrypted sensitive data including user credentials, messages, tokens, medical/financial records
Detection Method: File extraction via ADB, Static code analysis via JADX or MobSF, Decryption test using key found in code
Solution: Use Android Keystore or iOS Keychain to generate and store DB encryption keys; avoid hardcoding; enable strong encryption modes (SQLCipher, Realm AES-256)
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, SQLCipher Docs, Realm Encryption Docs, InsecureBankv2

Title: Intercepting Crypto via Frida
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps use encryption libraries or Java methods (e.g., Cipher.init(), SecretKeySpec, encrypt()) to protect sensitive data. However, if the encryption key or data is only used at runtime and not exposed in code, it can still be captured dynamically using Frida. Frida is a powerful dynamic instrumentation toolkit that lets you hook and inspect running app functions (like encryption/decryption), capture parameters (e.g., plaintext, ciphertext, keys), and even modify them. This lets attackers intercept and log secrets in real-time without reverse engineering the full code.
Tools Used: Frida, Android Emulator or Rooted Device, Frida Server, Python, VS Code, ADB, MobSF (optional), JADX (optional), Termux (if rooted phone), Burp Suite (optional for traffic testing)
Attack Steps: 1. Setup Your Tools: First install Frida on your host machine: run pip install frida-tools. Install Android Studio and create a rooted emulator or use a rooted device (you can also use Genymotion rooted emulators). Download the same version of Frida Server from https://github.com/frida/frida/releases that matches your frida --version. Push it to the device with adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/ and make it executable using adb shell chmod 755 /data/local/tmp/frida-server. Start the server with adb shell ./data/local/tmp/frida-server &. 2. Confirm Frida Connection: On your PC or terminal, run frida-ps -U. You should see a list of running apps on the connected device. This confirms Frida is working and ready to inject into processes. 3. Choose or Install a Test APK: Use vulnerable APKs like InsecureBankv2, Android-InsecureCrypto, or a simple app you build yourself that uses Java's AES or RSA. Install the APK using adb install appname.apk and start the app on the device. 4. Find Crypto Method to Hook: Use JADX or MobSF to analyze the app code if you want to understand which method is doing the encryption. Common classes include javax.crypto.Cipher, javax.crypto.SecretKeySpec, or org.bouncycastle.crypto.*. Look for methods like init(), doFinal(), encrypt(), or getBytes(). You will hook into one of these methods to extract data. 5. Write a Simple Frida Script to Hook Methods: Open VS Code or any editor and create a file called hook_crypto.js. Example script: javascript Java.perform(function () { var cipher = Java.use("javax.crypto.Cipher"); cipher.init.overload('int', 'java.security.Key').implementation = function(mode, key) { console.log("[*] Cipher.init called"); console.log("Mode: " + mode); console.log("Key: " + key.getEncoded()); return this.init(mode, key); }; cipher.doFinal.overload('[B').implementation = function(data) { console.log("[*] Cipher.doFinal called"); console.log("Input data: " + JSON.stringify(data)); var result = this.doFinal(data); console.log("Encrypted/Decrypted result: " + JSON.stringify(result)); return result; }; });  This script logs key and data during encryption or decryption. 6. Attach Frida to the Running App: Start the app on your emulator/device. Then run: frida -U -n com.example.appname -l hook_crypto.js. Replace the package name accordingly. As soon as encryption or decryption occurs, your terminal will show the data being passed (plaintext, ciphertext, and the encryption key). 7. Capture Secrets in Real-Time: As you use the app (e.g., login, register, send data), the script will log encryption parameters. You might see: Key: [77,121,83,101,99,...], Input data: [104,101,108,108,111]. Convert these byte arrays into readable strings using a Python one-liner or CyberChef. This confirms that sensitive crypto materials (like keys, IVs, passwords) are interceptable at runtime using Frida, even if they are not hardcoded. 8. Modify Values in Real-Time (Optional): You can modify the Frida script to change values. For example, replace the key with your own or decrypt any data returned by doFinal() and send it to your own server. This proves you can manipulate crypto behavior on the fly. 9. Demonstrate Impact: Capture screenshots of terminal logs showing the captured keys, input and output values of encryption. This shows that anyone with access to the device (or emulator) can intercept encryption data live without reverse engineering or source code. It proves that runtime-only protection is not secure if the app lacks hardening. 10. Explain Real-World Risk: If keys or secrets are derived only at runtime without additional protections (e.g., obfuscation, integrity checks, secure hardware), an attacker can hook those methods and intercept them. This is often how malware and advanced attackers bypass app security to dump tokens, API keys, and encrypted files. 11. Detection and Prevention: Use runtime protections such as root/jailbreak detection, anti-Frida hooks, obfuscation tools like ProGuard/R8, and native libraries to move sensitive logic. Use hardware-backed keystores like Android Keystore or Apple Secure Enclave, and never rely only on Java-side crypto logic. 12. Report the Vulnerability: Document your entire process, show the decrypted/encrypted values logged from Frida, and the script used. Explain that sensitive encryption data was intercepted at runtime and the app should implement runtime defenses.
Vulnerability: Intercepting encryption methods and keys at runtime using Frida
MITRE Technique: T1600 – Weakened Cryptographic Algorithm Configuration (with T1615 - Dynamic Hooking)
Impact: Complete exposure of runtime encryption keys, decrypted plaintext, and manipulation of cryptographic operations
Detection Method: Dynamic Frida hooking and terminal output of crypto data, absence of obfuscation or anti-hooking defenses
Solution: Use secure hardware-backed key storage, native code for sensitive logic, anti-Frida/anti-root protections, and obfuscate critical crypto functions
Source: OWASP MASVS, Frida Docs, InsecureBankv2, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M5, Android Keystore

Title: Access Token Not Invalidated on Logout
Scenario Description: When a user logs out from a mobile app, the backend server must invalidate or expire their session/token to prevent it from being reused. However, some mobile apps fail to do this. As a result, an attacker who has stolen or intercepted a token (via MITM, XSS, Frida, logs, etc.) can continue to use it even after the user logs out. In this simulation, you'll capture an access token, logout the user, and then reuse the token to access protected resources, proving that logout doesn’t invalidate the session.
Tools Used: Android Emulator or Device, Burp Suite, HTTP Toolkit (Alternative to Burp), VS Code (for scripting), ADB, Rooted Emulator (optional), Test APK like InsecureBankv2 or custom login app
Attack Steps: 1. Set Up Your Interception Environment: Install and open Burp Suite. Set up a proxy listener (default is 127.0.0.1:8080). On your Android emulator or test device, configure the Wi-Fi settings to use the same proxy IP and port as Burp. Install Burp’s SSL certificate on the device (download from http://burp or export from Burp > Proxy > Options > CA cert). This allows you to capture HTTPS traffic without breaking encryption. 2. Install the Test Mobile App: Use a test app like InsecureBankv2 or any mobile app that has login and protected user dashboard functionality. Install the APK on your emulator using adb install app.apk. Open the app, and log in with dummy credentials (e.g., testuser/testpass). 3. Intercept the Access Token: With Burp capturing requests, watch the login or authentication request. In the response, find the access_token or auth_token — often inside a JSON like: {"access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR..."}. Copy this token and save it. It is usually a JWT (starts with ey...) or a long string. This is the token that authenticates your session. 4. Perform Logged-In Actions: Still logged in, do actions like accessing profile, balance, settings, etc. You’ll see that every request in Burp has an Authorization: Bearer <access_token> header. Confirm that this token is needed for all authenticated endpoints. 5. Log Out of the App: Click logout in the app. Then go to Burp and confirm a logout API call was made (often POST /logout or /session/delete). Then try to perform a new action in the app—it should ask you to log in again. 6. Replay Old Token from Step 3 (AFTER Logout): Now open Burp or Postman and manually craft a request (GET /user/profile) and add the Authorization: Bearer <stolen_token> header using the original token. Send the request. If the response still returns user data (e.g., name, email, profile info), it confirms that the backend did not invalidate the token after logout. This means even after logging out, someone with this token can reuse it to access sensitive data. 7. Try Using Token After a Delay (Optional): Wait 5–10 minutes and resend the same request using the old token. If the server still accepts it, the token is still valid. Many apps forget to set token expiration or fail to revoke it. 8. Explain Impact in Simple Terms: Even if a user logs out thinking they are safe, any attacker who previously captured or intercepted the token can continue using it. This could happen via device malware, insecure storage, or MITM attacks. It allows account hijacking, data exposure, and unauthorized actions. 9. Enhance the Attack (Optional): If Frida or Logcat shows you the token (e.g., from logs or memory), extract it and use it in the same way. This shows another path an attacker could take to gain session access. 10. Write a Report or Demo: Show your Burp request and response with timestamps: (1) login → capture token, (2) logout call, (3) reuse of old token → data leak. This clearly demonstrates session/token reuse after logout, a real-world mobile security flaw. 11. Fix Recommendation: Developers must invalidate tokens on logout by blacklisting them on the server or using short-lived tokens with refresh logic. Also implement server-side session management. Never rely only on frontend logout.
Vulnerability: Access token persists after logout and can be reused to hijack session
Impact: Attackers can impersonate users even after logout, leading to data theft, account takeover, or privilege escalation
Detection Method: Manual request replay using Burp/Postman with stale token after logout; checking server responses for unauthorized access
Solution: Ensure backend invalidates the token during logout, implement token expiry, server-side session validation, and use short-lived access tokens
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP Mobile Top 10 - M7, InsecureBankv2, Burp Suite Docs

Title: Token Stored in SharedPreferences / UserDefaults Without Deletion
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps store access tokens (like JWTs or OAuth tokens) in local storage to persist login sessions. On Android, this is often SharedPreferences; on iOS, it's NSUserDefaults. If the app does not clear or delete the token upon logout, the token remains stored on the device. This creates a serious risk because an attacker who gains file access (via rooted device, backup, malware, or ADB) can retrieve and reuse the valid token to hijack sessions—even if the user thinks they are logged out. This simulation walks you through how to extract the token and reuse it, proving the session remains alive even after logout.
Tools Used: Android Emulator or Device, ADB, Rooted Emulator or Frida (optional), JADX, MobSF (optional), VS Code or any text editor, DB Browser (if token in SQLite), Postman or Burp Suite (for replay)
Attack Steps: 1. Install and Setup Your Tools: Set up Android Studio with an emulator, or use a rooted test device. Install adb (Android Debug Bridge) to access files. Install JADX to reverse engineer APKs. Install Postman or Burp Suite to replay requests. (If testing iOS, use macOS + iExplorer or a jailbroken device to extract files.) 2. Install the Target App and Simulate Login: Use a test app like InsecureBankv2, or any app where you have permission to test. Install it using adb install app.apk, then open it and log in with test credentials. Perform some basic actions to simulate an active session. 3. Find App Package Name and Storage Path: Use adb shell pm list packages to identify the package name, e.g., com.insecurebankv2. Then use adb shell followed by run-as com.insecurebankv2 to enter the app’s private directory. Navigate to /data/data/com.insecurebankv2/shared_prefs/ and list files using ls. You’ll usually find something like prefs.xml or user.xml. These files hold stored values including tokens. 4. Extract SharedPreferences File: Pull the file to your PC using: adb pull /data/data/com.insecurebankv2/shared_prefs/prefs.xml ./. Open the file using VS Code or Notepad++. You will often see contents like: <string name="auth_token">eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9....</string>. This is a JWT token or session token stored locally and accessible in plaintext. 5. Log Out from the App (But Token Still Exists): In the app, tap the logout button. Then again check the prefs.xml file using adb shell cat or re-pull it to your system. You’ll find that the token value is still present and not deleted. This proves improper logout handling. The app removes you from the UI, but keeps the token locally. 6. Replay Token to Test Reuse After Logout: Use Postman or Burp Suite to make a GET request to a protected endpoint like /user/profile or /account/info, and add the stolen token to the header like: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi.... If you receive valid data (e.g., profile info), it confirms the token is still active on the server, and can be reused despite logout. 7. Bonus (Auto Login Proof): Close and reopen the app. If you are still logged in without needing credentials, it proves the token was used from SharedPreferences to auto-login you. This also means any app or malware on the device could extract and use that token silently. 8. Analyze the APK for Confirmation (Optional): Use JADX to open the APK and search for SharedPreferences.Editor().putString("auth_token" to see where the token is being stored. Also check logout logic—developers often forget to call editor.remove("auth_token").apply() on logout, meaning the file keeps the token. 9. Explain the Risk Simply: Even if a user logs out, the token remains stored in plain text. Anyone with access to device files (root, malware, adb backup) can steal this token and use it to impersonate the user. It's like leaving your house key under the doormat after locking the door. 10. Real-World Scenario: Many finance, fitness, and social apps were found to store auth tokens in SharedPreferences/UserDefaults. Researchers used ADB or Frida to dump the token and reuse it via HTTP to access accounts, even after the users had logged out. 11. Fix Recommendation: Tokens must be deleted from local storage immediately upon logout using: editor.remove("auth_token").apply() (Android) or [UserDefaults removeObjectForKey:@"token"] (iOS). Also use encrypted storage like Android Keystore/iOS Keychain for token storage, not SharedPreferences/UserDefaults.
Vulnerability: Token remains in SharedPreferences or UserDefaults after logout, enabling token theft and reuse
Impact: Full session hijack, unauthorized access, account control after logout
Detection Method: Manual inspection of storage files via ADB, static code review with JADX, dynamic replay via Burp/Postman
Solution: Delete tokens from local storage on logout, use encrypted secure storage like Keystore or Keychain, use server-side session invalidation
Source: OWASP MASVS, OWASP M7: Client Code Quality, InsecureBankv2, Android Developer Docs, Apple Developer Docs

Title: Token Reuse via Reinstall (Logout Not Invalidating Server Token)
Scenario Description: Many mobile applications store an access token (JWT, OAuth token, or session ID) locally to keep users logged in. If the user uninstalls and reinstalls the app, that token should become invalid. But some backends don’t invalidate tokens server-side, meaning even if the app is uninstalled (or the user logs out), the token can still be used to make authenticated API calls. This allows token theft and long-term session hijacking, especially if the token was ever leaked via logs, memory, backups, or malware. This simulation demonstrates how to extract a token, uninstall the app, reinstall it, and still use the old token to access user data—proving improper token invalidation.
Tools Used: Android Emulator or Device, ADB, Postman, VS Code or any text editor, MobSF (optional), Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit (to intercept requests), Test APK like InsecureBankv2 or your own test app
Attack Steps: 1. Prepare Your Tools and Device: Use Android Studio to launch a test emulator, or use a rooted test Android device. Ensure you have ADB installed and working (adb devices should list the device). Install Postman for sending API requests. Optionally use Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit to intercept traffic. You can use an open-source test app like InsecureBankv2 or a sample app with token-based login. 2. Install and Use the App to Generate a Token: Install the test app using adb install appname.apk. Open the app, register or log in using dummy credentials (e.g., user/pass). Perform actions that require authentication (like profile view, get balance, etc.). While this is happening, use Burp Suite (with the mobile proxy set up) or HTTP Toolkit to intercept the requests and look for the Authorization: Bearer <access_token> header. This is the key used for authentication—copy and save this token. 3. Confirm Token Works in Postman: Open Postman and create a new request. Enter an authenticated endpoint URL (e.g., https://api.example.com/user/info) and set Authorization: Bearer <your_token>. Send the request. If the server responds with user data (200 OK), it means the token works and is valid. This will be your baseline. 4. Uninstall the App Without Logging Out: On the emulator or device, uninstall the app using adb uninstall com.example.appname. This simulates a user deleting the app without formally logging out. 5. Reinstall the App Fresh (Optional): Now install the app again using the same adb install command or by dragging the APK into the emulator. You’ll now see a login screen again in the app—indicating the user is logged out from the UI perspective. But is the token still valid server-side? 6. Reuse the Original Token via Postman After Reinstall: Go back to Postman, and replay the same request from earlier using the saved access token. If you again get a 200 OK with valid data, that means the backend never invalidated the token—even though the app was deleted. You have successfully reused the token after reinstall. 7. Explain Why This Is Dangerous: This means that anyone who once got access to a user’s token (via logs, clipboard, malware, memory dump, or MITM) can reuse it forever unless the user logs out or the token expires. Even uninstalling the app doesn’t kill the session. This is a serious security flaw, especially if tokens are long-lived. 8. Advanced Check – Use Token Weeks Later (Optional): Wait a few days or simulate a time delay and use the same token again. If it still works, this proves the token is long-lived and wasn’t revoked even after app removal. This is common in apps using Firebase, custom backends, or improperly configured OAuth systems. 9. Bonus – Try This with a Public App (Ethical Testing Only): Some production apps do not invalidate tokens on logout or uninstall. If you have permission, ethically test one by extracting a token, uninstalling the app, and sending an API request. If the token still works, report it to the vendor. 10. APK Analysis (Optional): Use JADX to reverse engineer the APK and see how token storage is handled. Check if tokens are saved in SharedPreferences and whether logout or uninstall triggers a server-side invalidation. If no such call is made, it’s a sign the backend relies only on token expiry. 11. Fix Recommendation: Apps should always invalidate access tokens on logout or uninstall (via backend API). Use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens. Also implement backend-side token blacklisting or rotation. Never assume uninstall = logout.
Vulnerability: Server allows reuse of access tokens after uninstall; token isn’t invalidated on logout or deletion
Impact: Permanent session hijack even after app is deleted; sensitive data and actions accessible via stale token
Detection Method: Replay the token using Postman or Burp after uninstalling the app and checking for 200 OK responses
Solution: Invalidate access tokens on logout or uninstall, use short-lived tokens with refresh rotation, backend blacklisting of tokens, and enforce re-authentication after reinstall
Source: OWASP MASVS, InsecureBankv2, OWASP M7 (Poor Code Quality), JWT Best Practices

Title: Reusing Token from Another Device or Emulator
Attack Type: Improper Session Logout / Token Reuse → Token Reuse on Other Device
Scenario Description: A user logs into a mobile app on Device A. The session token (auth token) is stored insecurely and not bound to device-specific properties. The attacker extracts the token from Device A and reuses it on Device B (another device or emulator) to impersonate the victim, bypassing login and MFA.
Tools Used: Frida, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Burp Suite, Rooted Android Device or Emulator (e.g. Genymotion, Android Studio), HTTP Toolkit
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a rooted Android device or emulator using Genymotion or Android Studio. Install the target mobile app on this emulator. 2. On a separate physical phone (Device A), register/login normally in the target app using a test user account. 3. Connect Device A to your PC via USB and enable USB Debugging. 4. Use adb shell to access the internal file system of Device A. Find the app’s private data directory (usually /data/data/[app_package_name]/shared_prefs/ or /data/data/[app_package_name]/files/) – note: root access is required. 5. Look for files like auth_token.xml, session.json, or SQLite DBs that contain session or auth tokens. Use adb pull to copy them to your computer. 6. Open the file and extract the bearer token or session cookie (usually a long random string). 7. On the emulator (Device B), install the same app. Do not log in yet. 8. Use tools like HTTP Toolkit or Burp Suite to intercept network traffic on the emulator. Configure proxy settings and install the SSL certificate on the emulator. 9. Make a test request (e.g., open the app or tap “forgot password”). Capture that request in Burp. 10. In the intercepted HTTP request (especially POST/GET requests to /api/user/details or /api/account), replace the Authorization header or cookie value with the extracted token from Device A. 11. Forward the request. If the token is valid and accepted, the server will return the logged-in user’s information, proving token reuse worked. 12. You can now perform user actions on behalf of the victim – like reading their data, posting content, or accessing premium areas – without ever logging in or entering a password on Device B. 13. You’ve now successfully bypassed session protection by reusing the session token from a different device.
Vulnerability: Insecure session management due to lack of device binding, token expiration, and revocation controls
Impact: Full account takeover, session hijack, privacy breach
Detection Method: Monitor simultaneous session IP/device changes, check user-agent and fingerprint anomalies, detect token reuse across different hardware IDs
Solution: Use short-lived access tokens, bind sessions to device ID, IP, and fingerprint; revoke token on logout or reuse; implement backend detection of device switching; always encrypt local token storage
Tags: mobile, token reuse, session hijacking, emulator, Android, frida, pentest, session fixation, access token abuse
Source: Based on real-world mobile security assessments and OWASP MASVS guidelines

Title: Session Persisted After App Close / Crash
Attack Type: Improper Session Logout / Token Reuse → Session Persistence Post-Crash
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps do not clear authentication tokens or session data from memory or local storage after the app is closed or crashes. This leads to persistent sessions where the user can reopen the app and continue using it without re-authenticating. If a device is stolen or if a malicious app monitors app data, an attacker can take advantage of this to access a logged-in session.
Tools Used: ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Rooted Android Device / Emulator, Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit, Android Studio, File Manager App (like MiXplorer), SQLite Viewer
Attack Steps: 1. First, install the target mobile application on a rooted Android device or emulator. Use Genymotion or Android Studio emulator with root access enabled. 2. Create or use a dummy account in the target app and log in successfully. Take note of any visible session behavior (e.g., if you are redirected to the dashboard after login). 3. Minimize the app or remove it from the app switcher. Reopen the app and observe if it logs in without asking for credentials again. If so, this is an initial sign of session persistence. 4. Now test crash behavior. Use adb shell and run the command am crash [package.name] to force-crash the app. You can find the package name using adb shell pm list packages or via Android Studio. 5. After the app crashes, wait a few seconds and reopen it. If the app opens and directly logs the user back in (without asking username/password or reauthentication), the session token is still valid and stored locally. 6. To find and confirm where the session token is stored, use adb shell and navigate to /data/data/[app_package_name]/shared_prefs/ or /data/data/[app_package_name]/files/ or /data/data/[app_package_name]/databases/. 7. Use adb pull to extract files like auth_token.xml, session.db, login.json etc. Copy them to your local machine. 8. Open the extracted files with a text editor or SQLite Viewer and look for keys like “auth_token”, “access_token”, “bearer”, or long random strings. These indicate the stored session. 9. Take note of the expiration value, if any. Many apps set tokens without an expiry or don’t enforce expiration on the server. 10. (Optional deeper test) Uninstall the app, reinstall it, and place the old extracted session file back into the correct folder using adb push. Now reopen the app. If the app logs in without credentials again, this proves the session storage method is insecure and not tied to app lifecycle. 11. As an attacker, this means you could potentially steal a device or intercept these files using malware, then restore the session without needing the actual password. This violates secure session management principles.
Vulnerability: Session not expired or cleared on app crash or close; insecure local session storage; no token revocation
MITRE Technique: T1535 – Unsecured Credentials / T1646 – Mobile Session Hijacking
Impact: Full account access without reauthentication, even after crash; potential access after theft or malware; session hijacking
Detection Method: Monitor app logs for crash/close behavior and session renewal without login; analyze token expiration policies
Solution: Implement session expiry timers; clear tokens on app close or crash; enforce token revocation on crash restart; require biometric or password re-auth after idle or crash
Tags: mobile, android, session, token reuse, crash, session fixation, token theft, adb, rooted device
Source: Based on real-world mobile pen testing, OWASP MASVS, and exploitation of persistent sessions in production apps

Title: Logout Only on Client Side (No Server API Call)
Attack Type: Improper Session Logout / Token Reuse → Token Not Invalidated on Server
Scenario Description: Many mobile applications only delete the access token from the device storage during logout without notifying the backend server to invalidate or revoke the token. This means the session token is still valid on the server and can be reused from another device or app instance, even after the user “logs out”. If an attacker has access to the session token before logout (via interception or malware), they can continue using the session from elsewhere.
Tools Used: ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Burp Suite / HTTP Toolkit, Rooted Android Emulator or Device, Postman (optional), Frida (optional), Android Studio, Text Editor (Notepad++)
Attack Steps: 1. Set up a rooted Android emulator using Genymotion or Android Studio and install the target mobile app. 2. Register or log in using a test user account inside the app. Allow the app to fully log you in. You are now authenticated. 3. Set up a proxy tool like Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit. Configure the emulator's Wi-Fi or proxy settings to route all traffic through the tool. Install Burp’s SSL certificate on the emulator so HTTPS traffic can be decrypted. 4. With Burp running and capturing traffic, interact with the app’s authenticated areas (e.g., fetch user profile, open dashboard, etc.). You will see HTTP requests in Burp with a bearer token or session cookie in the headers (usually under "Authorization: Bearer "). 5. Copy this token and store it in a safe place temporarily (Notepad or Postman). This token represents your active session. 6. Now inside the app, perform a logout action from the menu or settings. Immediately go back to Burp Suite and observe the network calls triggered during logout. 7. If the logout request does not contain a POST /logout, DELETE /token, or any API call that tells the server to revoke or invalidate the token, this confirms logout is only happening on the client side. 8. Now, open Postman or any API testing tool. Make a GET or POST request to a protected API endpoint (e.g., /api/user/details, /api/dashboard) using the saved token in the Authorization header. 9. If the request returns user data and is successful (200 OK), it proves the token is still valid on the server even though the user has "logged out" in the app. 10. This confirms the vulnerability: The app only deletes the token from local storage, but the backend is still accepting it because it was never told to invalidate or expire the session. 11. An attacker who steals the token (via log capture, malware, or man-in-the-middle attack) can continue using the token after logout and impersonate the victim without detection. This exposes user data and breaks secure session management. 12. Optional Advanced: To prove full reuse, install the same app on a second emulator, skip login, and intercept a request using Burp. Paste the stolen token into the Authorization header and forward the request. If it succeeds, you have completely hijacked the session post-logout.
Vulnerability: Session token not invalidated server-side; only removed locally
MITRE Technique: T1535 – Unsecured Credentials / T1529 – Token Reuse
Impact: Full session hijack after logout; persistent unauthorized access
Detection Method: Monitor whether logout triggers a backend session invalidation API call; inspect server logs for continued token use after logout
Solution: Always trigger backend token revocation on logout; implement short token expiry; use refresh tokens with strict expiration; track token activity and IP/device usage
Tags: mobile, android, token reuse, logout flaw, client side only, session hijack, burp suite, adb, authentication
Source: Based on real-world mobile pen testing reports and OWASP MASVS recommendations

Title: Insecure Token Rotation or Long Expiry
Attack Type: Improper Session Logout / Token Reuse → Long-Lived or Non-Rotated Token Abuse
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps use access tokens (e.g., JWT or bearer tokens) for user session management. These tokens should expire quickly and be rotated frequently to limit misuse. Insecure implementations often have tokens that either never expire or remain valid for hours/days without rotation, increasing the window of attack. If an attacker steals the token, they can use it long after it was issued, even if the user logs out or their session expires locally.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, HTTP Toolkit, ADB, Android Emulator or Rooted Device, Notepad, Postman (optional), Frida (optional)
Attack Steps: 1. Set up an Android emulator (Genymotion or Android Studio) with the target mobile app installed. Ensure you have root access enabled and HTTPS interception working using Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit. Install the Burp certificate on the emulator to decrypt traffic. 2. Register or log in using a test account in the app. Perform some actions in the app like viewing profile, dashboard, settings, etc. 3. In Burp, look for any request that includes an Authorization: Bearer header or cookie with a long string. That string is your access token (sometimes it may be in the form of a JWT - it will look like xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz). Copy this token into Notepad for later use. 4. Go to jwt.io (if it's a JWT) and paste the token there. If the payload is visible, look for the “exp” (expiry) claim inside the token. If the expiry is set to days/weeks or even years, this is a sign of long expiry. If there's no expiry or exp field, it may mean the token never expires, which is worse. 5. In parallel, observe if the app requests a new token at regular intervals (i.e., token rotation). Continue using the app for several minutes and watch for API calls that respond with a new token. If the token remains unchanged after 5-10 minutes of usage or inactivity, this means no rotation is happening. 6. Now simulate user logout from inside the app. Monitor Burp for a /logout or /revoke call. If none appear and the token remains unchanged, logout is local only, and the token remains active. 7. Now, use Postman or any API testing tool. Make a new GET request to a known authenticated endpoint (like /api/profile, /api/user/info, etc.) and use the token you previously copied in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header. 8. If the request is successful (200 OK) even after logout or several minutes/hours later, it proves the token is still valid and has not expired or rotated. You can even wait hours and retry this—if it still works, this confirms long expiry and poor rotation. 9. You’ve now proven that the token is long-lived and vulnerable. If an attacker intercepts or steals this token (e.g., via MitM, app vulnerability, malware), they can continue to use the session without logging in again or being detected. 10. Optional: On a second emulator or device, replicate the attack by using the token in a request from a different environment or app version. If it still works, the server is accepting the same token without verifying device integrity or rotation, confirming full session takeover.
Vulnerability: Token does not expire or is reused across sessions; no backend check for rotation or expiration; vulnerable token lifecycle
MITRE Technique: T1535 – Unsecured Credentials / T1078 – Valid Accounts
Impact: Session hijacking, unauthorized access over extended time, persistent identity theft, bypass of MFA
Detection Method: Analyze tokens using jwt.io or intercept tools; look for unchanged tokens after multiple requests or time delay; monitor backend logs for reused tokens long after issue
Solution: Enforce token expiration via short TTL (e.g., 15 mins); implement automatic token rotation; revoke on logout; monitor and block stale token reuse across IPs/devices
Tags: mobile, token expiry, token rotation, session hijack, jwt, burp, android, insecure auth
Source: Based on OWASP MASVS, mobile security assessments, and real-world token lifecycle misconfigurations

Title: Token Exposed via Logs, Clipboard, Notifications
Attack Type: Improper Session Logout / Token Reuse → Token Exposed via Logs, Clipboard, Notifications
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps mishandle authentication/session tokens by accidentally storing them in app logs, system notifications, or clipboard memory. Attackers with access to logs or clipboard history (either through rooted devices or malicious apps) can steal these tokens. If logout is improperly implemented or token reuse is allowed, attackers can use those stolen tokens to impersonate a user or gain unauthorized access.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Emulator or Rooted Android Phone, Postman or cURL, Optional: Frida, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: **Step 1: Setup your environment by installing Android Studio and creating a new Android Virtual Device (AVD) — an emulator. Alternatively, use a rooted physical Android phone. Step 2: Install the target application (either your own test app or a vulnerable app from GitHub like ‘InsecureShop’ or ‘Damn Vulnerable Bank’). Step 3: Enable USB debugging on the emulator or real phone. Step 4: Open Terminal or Command Prompt and use the command adb devices to verify connection. Step 5: Start monitoring logs using the command adb logcat > logs.txt. This captures real-time logs generated by the app. Step 6: Launch the target app and perform login using any test credentials (e.g., email + password). Step 7: While logged in, check the logs.txt file for keywords like “token”, “auth”, “session”, “jwt”, or Base64 strings (e.g., starting with eyJ...). If a token or session ID appears in the logs, note it. Step 8: Use Postman or curl to test the stolen token against an API endpoint. For example, if the API uses bearer token authentication, set the header as Authorization: Bearer <your_token> and access a user-specific API. If it returns valid user data, the token is active and exploitable. Step 9: Now test if the token remains valid after logout. Log out from the app and reuse the same token in Postman. If it still works, the app is vulnerable to token reuse and improper session logout. Step 10: Next, test clipboard leakage. In the app, check if clicking a share button or copying data (such as a referral link or URL with token) stores session information in the clipboard. Step 11: In terminal, run adb shell service call clipboard 1 or adb shell am broadcast -a clipper.get to view clipboard data. If a token or session URL is present, this proves clipboard exposure. Step 12: Now test for notification-based token leakage. Trigger an in-app event that sends a notification — for example, a new login alert or verification link. In terminal, run `adb logcat grep Notificationor filter using tags likeNotificationManager`. Check if the token is exposed in the content of the notification or log. Step 13: If the token appears in any of logs, clipboard, or notifications, you’ve found a serious vulnerability. Step 14: Finally, simulate session hijacking. Copy the exposed token and use it in curl or Postman to access protected APIs and impersonate the user. Step 15: Optional advanced: Use Frida scripts to hook into memory functions and intercept token data in real time or monitor clipboard activity to extract session data dynamically.**
Vulnerability: Token stored in Logs, Clipboard, Notifications + Token reuse due to improper logout
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files), T1530 (Data from Local System), T1649 (Steal Web Session Cookie)
Impact: Complete Account Hijack, Sensitive Data Theft, Identity Spoofing, Session Persistence after Logout
Detection Method: Log Analysis via adb logcat, Clipboard Inspection via adb shell, API validation with stolen token using Postman or curl, Notification Monitoring
Solution: Do not log sensitive information (tokens, credentials). Use secure log filters. Clear clipboard after use. Never expose tokens in push notifications. Invalidate tokens immediately after logout on the server side. Implement token expiration and session invalidation logic properly.
Source: OWASP MASVS, AppCensus Reports, Frida Examples, Offensive iOS Training Guides, Android Developer Docs

Title: No Detection = Full Frida Access
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Full Runtime Access via Frida
Scenario Description: Many Android apps include basic root or jailbreak detection logic to prevent tampering or runtime instrumentation. However, if the app has no such detection or uses weak methods, attackers can attach tools like Frida to inspect or modify app behavior at runtime. Without proper detection and countermeasures, attackers can hook sensitive functions, bypass authentication, steal credentials, disable in-app security, or extract secrets using Frida even without touching the app’s code.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Android Emulator or Rooted Android Device, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Frida, Frida-server, Frida-tools (frida-trace, frida-ps), Objection (optional), Apktool (optional), JADX (optional)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download and install Android Studio. Create an Android Virtual Device (AVD) or use a real rooted Android phone. A rooted phone allows more flexibility, but you can also use a rooted emulator like the publicly available Android_x86 or Magisk-enabled emulator. Step 2: Download and install the target APK (for testing, use a vulnerable app like InsecureShop, OWASP GoatDroid, or create a sample app yourself). Step 3: Install ADB tools if not already installed. Run adb devices to confirm your emulator/phone is detected. Step 4: Install Frida tools by running pip install frida-tools. Step 5: Download the Frida-server binary that matches your device architecture from https://github.com/frida/frida/releases. Example: if your emulator/phone is x86_64, download frida-server-x86_64. Step 6: Use ADB to push the Frida server to the device with adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp/. Step 7: Use ADB shell to access the device shell: adb shell. Then set permissions and start Frida server using the following commands: chmod +x /data/local/tmp/frida-server and then /data/local/tmp/frida-server &. Step 8: On your PC, run frida-ps -U to list all running processes on the connected device. The -U means USB device. Confirm that you can see your target app’s process name (e.g., com.example.vulnerableapp). Step 9: Now run frida-trace -U -n com.example.vulnerableapp to attach Frida to the target app. If there’s no root detection or if it is poorly implemented, this will succeed and give you full dynamic instrumentation access to the app. Step 10: At this point, you can hook into any function or Java class. For example, hook a login method with frida-trace -U -n com.example.vulnerableapp -m "java:*LoginActivity*" to see arguments passed to login functions. Step 11: You can even bypass login by modifying return values or forcing validation to always return true. Write custom hook scripts in JavaScript inside the __handlers__ folder generated by Frida. For example, to force login to succeed, replace return false; with return true;. Step 12: You can also dump memory, intercept API tokens, extract encryption keys, or modify logic such as bypassing root detection, SSL pinning, or subscription checks. Step 13: If the app had strong Frida/root detection (checking for frida-server or /proc/net/tcp), your session would crash. But since there is no detection, Frida runs flawlessly, giving you full live access to the app. Step 14: This proves that the app lacks sufficient root/jailbreak and runtime instrumentation detection and is fully vulnerable to Frida-based attacks.
Vulnerability: Lack of Runtime Integrity Checks and Frida/Root Detection
MITRE Technique: T1622 – Debugger Detection, T1512 – Subvert Trust Controls
Impact: Complete Runtime Access, Hooking of Critical Functions, Token/Key Extraction, Login Bypass, SSL Pinning Bypass
Detection Method: Use Frida to attach to the app; if it allows hooking without crashing or blocking, it has no runtime protection; monitor via logcat or Frida trace to confirm access to sensitive logic
Solution: Implement runtime checks for Frida (check for frida-server, /proc/net/tcp, suspicious ports), detect ptrace, hide debugger connection, detect Magisk/root binaries, implement anti-debug, anti-tamper, and obfuscation using tools like DexGuard, Appdome, or commercial RASP
Tags: frida, android security, mobile app hacking, no detection, runtime bypass, hooking, instrumentation
Source: https://frida.re, OWASP MASVS, Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG), InsecureShop GitHub

Title: Modify App Logic via Objection
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Logic Modification via Objection
Scenario Description: Many Android apps fail to implement root or jailbreak detection, which allows an attacker to inject tools like Objection or Frida and directly modify internal app logic (such as login behavior, feature restrictions, or validation checks) at runtime. When an app has no root/jailbreak detection and is not protected by anti-debugging or code obfuscation, a basic attacker can hook into live classes and functions, override return values, and unlock premium or restricted functionality with just a few commands.
Tools Used: Objection, Frida, Android Emulator or Rooted Device, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), APKTool (optional), JADX (optional), Test APK (e.g., InsecureShop, vulnerable test app)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download and install Objection using the command pip install objection in your terminal or command prompt. Also, ensure you have Frida installed with pip install frida-tools. Step 2: Launch an Android emulator (e.g., in Android Studio) or use a rooted Android phone. For easiest setup, use an emulator without Magisk hiding enabled. Step 3: Install a test or vulnerable APK (example: OWASP InsecureShop, DVIA-v2 for Android, or any app that has a login page or premium feature restriction). Step 4: Use adb devices to confirm your emulator or phone is detected by ADB. Step 5: Push the Frida server to your emulator: download the correct frida-server binary from GitHub for your device architecture, push it to the device using adb push frida-server /data/local/tmp, then execute it via ADB shell using chmod +x /data/local/tmp/frida-server and run /data/local/tmp/frida-server &. Step 6: On your computer, confirm Frida is working by typing frida-ps -U and checking that your target app process is visible. Step 7: Now run the command objection -g <package_name> explore where <package_name> is the application ID (example: com.insecureshop.android). This opens a live interactive Objection shell connected to the running app. Step 8: Once inside the shell, run android hooking list classes to view available Java classes in the app, and use android hooking search classes login or validate to locate potential login-related classes or functions. Step 9: Use the command android hooking list methods <ClassName> to list all methods of a class, for example: android hooking list methods com.example.LoginManager. Step 10: Now hook the login function and override its return value to bypass authentication. For example: android hooking set return_value --class com.example.LoginManager --method isValidUser --value true. This forces the method isValidUser to always return true, bypassing login checks. Step 11: Next, try modifying in-app logic such as enabling premium features. Search for classes like SubscriptionManager, AccessManager, or FeatureFlag. Then repeat the method override using the set return_value command. Example: android hooking set return_value --class com.example.AccessManager --method hasPremiumAccess --value true. Step 12: If the app has no root/jailbreak detection, these commands will execute successfully and the app will respond as if the user is authenticated or premium, without needing real credentials or payment. Step 13: To persist or automate these changes, you can script them using Objection's command line or export them as a Frida script. Step 14: You can also dump secrets, bypass root checks, or disable SSL pinning using simple commands like android sslpinning disable, android root disable, or android heap search from inside the Objection shell. Step 15: If none of these modifications crash or trigger warnings, then the app is confirmed to lack detection and allows full runtime logic modification — a serious mobile security flaw.
Vulnerability: No runtime protection, no Frida/Objection detection, insecure logic validation
MITRE Technique: T1622 – Debugger Detection, T1512 – Subvert Trust Controls, T1406 – Obfuscate and Hide Activities
Impact: Logic bypass, login bypass, unauthorized access, unlocking premium features, stealing secrets, full runtime control of app behavior
Detection Method: Use Objection with Frida to inject into app, try modifying logic or bypassing validation, check if app crashes or blocks access; if not, the app is vulnerable
Solution: Implement Frida/Objection detection (check for frida-server, ptrace, /proc/net/tcp), use root detection techniques, validate logic securely on server side, add runtime protections (RASP, obfuscation, integrity checks)
Tags: mobile security, objection, frida, app logic tampering, bypass login, android hacking, insecure app
Source: https://github.com/sensepost/objection, OWASP MASVS, Android Pentest Guide

Title: Modify Storage: Tokens, Configs
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Modify Stored App Data (Tokens, Config Files)
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps store sensitive data such as authentication tokens, API keys, feature flags, and configuration settings in plain files or shared preferences without proper encryption. If the app does not implement root/jailbreak detection, a user or attacker with root or full access can browse, edit, or inject values into this storage to gain unauthorized access, force premium features, or hijack sessions. This vulnerability allows attackers to tamper with how the app behaves by directly modifying local files or databases without triggering any protection.
Tools Used: Android Emulator or Rooted Device, ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Android Studio (optional), Frida (optional), Objection (optional), Apktool or JADX (optional), SQLite Editor (optional)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up an Android Emulator or use a rooted Android device. If using an emulator, ensure it allows root access (for example, using Android Studio’s emulator or a Magisk-patched system image). Step 2: Install the target app (can be a test app such as InsecureShop, DVIA-v2, or any app with login/authentication or settings). Step 3: Verify ADB connectivity by running adb devices. Make sure your device/emulator is listed. Step 4: Use the command adb shell to enter the device’s shell. Step 5: Locate the app’s data directory by navigating to /data/data/<package_name>/. For example, cd /data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/. Step 6: Inside this folder, look for subdirectories like shared_prefs, databases, or files. Step 7: Enter the shared_prefs folder and list XML files using ls. You’ll often find files like user.xml, auth.xml, settings.xml. Step 8: Open a file using cat <filename> or pull it to your PC using adb pull /data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/shared_prefs/auth.xml . and open it in a text editor. Look for values such as <string name="token">eyJ...jwt...</string> or <boolean name="isPremium" value="false"/>. Step 9: Modify the file by changing the token to another value or changing the premium flag to true. Save the file. Step 10: Push the modified file back into the device using adb push auth.xml /data/data/com.example.vulnerableapp/shared_prefs/. Step 11: Change file permissions if needed: chmod 660 auth.xml. Step 12: Relaunch the app and observe behavior changes. If your token was accepted or the app now treats the user as premium or logged-in, the app is vulnerable to local storage tampering. Step 13: You can repeat similar steps inside the databases folder. Use sqlite3 to open .db files with commands like sqlite3 appdata.db, and run SQL queries such as SELECT * FROM users; or UPDATE flags SET is_enabled='1'; to enable features. Step 14: If you were able to manipulate stored tokens, unlock features, bypass login, or change config behavior with these modifications and the app did not detect or block the tampering, then the app has no proper storage protection or root detection mechanisms. Step 15: For more advanced analysis, you can hook storage-related methods using Frida or Objection to dynamically override config at runtime instead of static file modification. However, file-based manipulation is already enough to confirm the vulnerability. This full access proves the app lacks runtime integrity checks, encryption, and root detection.
Vulnerability: Local storage manipulation of tokens/configs due to missing root protection and plaintext storage
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files), T1547 (Boot or Logon Autostart Execution), T1622 (Debugger Detection)
Impact: Token replay, account hijack, unauthorized feature unlocking, premium bypass, altered app behavior
Detection Method: Manual review of shared_prefs and database files, observe if tokens/configs are modifiable and impact behavior; check if app detects modified data
Solution: Encrypt sensitive files, implement root detection, use tamper-check mechanisms, perform server-side validation, avoid storing long-term session tokens locally, protect app data using Android Keystore
Tags: mobile hacking, token tampering, shared_prefs, config modification, android storage abuse, adb, rooted access
Source: OWASP MASVS, Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG), InsecureShop GitHub, Android Internals Docs

Title: Bypass SSL Pinning on Non-Rooted Android (MITM via Frida)
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Bypass SSL Pinning (MITM)
Scenario Description: A secure banking app has SSL pinning implemented to prevent traffic inspection. The tester wants to bypass this SSL pinning on a non-rooted Android device to intercept and analyze HTTPS traffic using MITM tools like Burp Suite.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Frida, Android Emulator (or real device), APKTool, Android Studio, Frida Server (no root needed for modern Frida), Objection (optional), jadx (optional), ADB, Frida SSLUnpinning Script
Attack Steps: 1. Install Frida on your PC: pip install frida-tools 2. Download the APK of the target app (e.g., from APKPure). Make sure it's a debug or testable version (you can also modify AndroidManifest.xml using APKTool to make it debuggable). 3. Install Frida gadget if needed (for non-rooted device). Alternatively, use dynamic instrumentation via USB without installing Frida server. 4. Setup Android Emulator or a real device (USB Debugging ON). Ensure Google Play is OFF for pure testing environment. 5. Connect your device: adb devices → check that it's listed. 6. Forward Frida port: adb forward tcp:27042 tcp:27042 and adb forward tcp:27043 tcp:27043. 7. Connect to app process: Launch app → In terminal: frida-ps -Uai → Copy target package name (e.g., com.target.securebank). 8. Now inject SSL pinning bypass script using Frida. You can use community-made scripts like frida-ssl-unpinning-android.js. 9. Example command: frida -U -n com.target.securebank -l frida-ssl-unpinning-android.js 10. Run Burp Suite on your PC. Go to Proxy > Options > Import CA Certificate → install it on your emulator/device (Settings > Security > Install from storage). 11. On Android device, connect to Burp proxy: Go to **WiFi settings > Modify network > Proxy > Manual > Host: your_pc_ip Port: 8080**. 12. Open the target app. If bypass worked, you’ll see decrypted HTTPS traffic in Burp. You’ve now successfully bypassed SSL pinning on a non-rooted device. 13. If it fails, try Objection: objection -g com.target.securebank explore → then inside Objection console run: android sslpinning disable. 14. For extra learning: decompile APK using JADX GUI, search for TrustManager, HostnameVerifier, and check where SSL pinning is enforced. You can later patch the app manually with APKTool if needed. 15. After bypassing, monitor all network traffic using Burp. You can analyze sensitive API calls, tokens, credentials, etc. 16. Clean up: Uninstall test certificate and app, close proxy, and disconnect ADB.
Impact: Sensitive data exposure, leakage of login credentials, tokens, and personal info
Detection Method: Certificate pinning alert, runtime SSL exceptions, behavioral monitoring
Solution: Implement robust SSL pinning with certificate transparency and allowlist; detect runtime debugging and Frida hooks
Tags: android, ssl pinning, mitm, frida, mobile pentest, burp suite, no-root, appsec
Source: Frida (Official Site) – Dynamic Instrumentation Toolkit, OWASP Mobile Security Testing Guide (MSTG), PortSwigger Academy - Burp Suite MITM Setup

Title: Replace App Libraries or Inject Malicious Modules (No-Root Android)
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Replace App Libraries or Inject Modules
Scenario Description: A legitimate Android app does not perform runtime integrity checks or secure library validation. A tester wants to inject a custom malicious .so or .dex module into the app to alter its behavior and bypass security checks without root access.
Tools Used: APKTool, JADX, Android Studio, Frida (optional), Jarsigner / Uber APK Signer, ADB, Java JDK, Android Emulator or Device
Attack Steps: 1. Download the original APK from the target app (you can use APKPure or extract it from your phone via adb pull). 2. Use APKTool to decompile the app: apktool d app.apk -o app_decompiled. 3. Navigate to the decompiled folder and locate the libraries in /lib/ (for .so native files) or /smali/ (for Java/Dalvik classes). 4. To inject or replace code, either: (a) modify the .smali code directly, or (b) replace/add your own .smali file (or .dex) with malicious behavior such as bypassing login checks, removing ads, logging keystrokes, etc. 5. For example, inject your own class to disable SSL pinning, or hardcode the return value of a method like isUserPremium() to true. 6. To inject a module, place your .dex or .jar into the app structure and hook it from the Application class in smali by adding an invoke statement to load your class on app start. 7. After injection, rebuild the APK: apktool b app_decompiled -o modded.apk. 8. Sign the modified APK: either use jarsigner or Uber APK Signer: java -jar uber-apk-signer.jar -a modded.apk. 9. Enable installation from unknown sources on your device or emulator. 10. Install the signed modded APK: adb install -r modded-aligned-signed.apk. 11. Launch the app and verify that your injected behavior works (e.g., the app skips login, shows premium UI, disables security checks). 12. For further experiments, you can inject logging hooks, add a backdoor activity, or silently exfiltrate sensitive data (educational testing only). 13. Clean up by uninstalling the app, removing injected libraries, and resetting your test environment.
Vulnerability: Lack of App Integrity Checks / Library Validation
MITRE Technique: T1601.001 – Modify System Binary or Application: Patch Binary
Impact: Total compromise of app logic; bypass paywalls; inject spyware; hijack user sessions
Detection Method: Code diff, checksum validation, runtime integrity scan, Play Protect alerts
Solution: Use runtime code integrity verification, signature validation, tamper detection (e.g., SafetyNet, AppShield)
Tags: mobile injection, apktool, smali, tampering, apk reverse engineering, dex injection
Source: OWASP MSTG, APKTool, JADX, Uber APK Signer, Frida, Android Dev Docs

Title: Access Android Keystore Secrets Without Root
Attack Type: No Root/Jailbreak Detection → Access Keychain / Keystore
Scenario Description: A mobile app uses Android's Keystore system to securely store authentication tokens or cryptographic keys. However, due to improper access control and lack of runtime detection, an attacker can dynamically hook into keystore-accessing methods using Frida or Objection and retrieve the secret values, even on a non-rooted Android device.
Tools Used: Android Emulator (or physical device), ADB, Frida, Objection, jadx (optional), APKTool (optional), Burp Suite (optional), Android Studio (optional)
Attack Steps: 1. Setup environment: Install Frida (pip install frida-tools), Objection (pip install objection), and connect a non-rooted Android device or emulator with USB Debugging ON. 2. Install the target app (you can use adb install target.apk or download via Play Store). 3. Verify the device is detected: adb devices. 4. Use Frida to find app processes: frida-ps -Uai → Copy your target package name. 5. Start the app on the device so it’s running in memory. 6. Attach Objection to the running app: objection -g com.target.app explore. This opens an interactive console where you can dynamically inspect the app. 7. Inside Objection, run: android keystore list → This tries to enumerate known key aliases. 8. Now dump secrets: use android keystore dump — this command hooks into Java's Keystore access methods (e.g., KeyStore.getInstance, Cipher.doFinal) and tries to print values returned by the app when it decrypts or retrieves secrets. 9. Title: Cache Timing Attacks on Mobile Processors
Attack Type: Hardware-Based Side Channel Attack (Cache Timing Leakage)
Scenario Description: Cache timing attacks exploit the time differences between memory accesses to different levels of CPU cache. Cryptographic algorithms like AES often have data-dependent access patterns. By measuring how long it takes to access certain memory locations (using high-resolution timers), attackers can infer which parts of memory were accessed and when. On mobile devices, attackers can perform this using JavaScript in a web browser or native code running in an unprivileged app. These attacks include Prime+Probe, Flush+Reload, and Evict+Time. They can leak sensitive data like cryptographic keys or user behavior without root or physical access.
Tools Used: Android Studio, Mobile Phone (preferably with ARM-based CPU), Linux PC or Laptop, Native C code (NDK), Termux or ADB Shell, Perf Tools or custom timing script, Cache Template Attacks Toolkit, Android Emulator (QEMU), Flush+Reload / Prime+Probe test scripts, Frida (for runtime memory access mapping)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the basics of how CPU cache works. Data recently accessed by the CPU is stored in a fast cache (L1, L2, L3). Accessing cached data is faster than accessing RAM. If we can measure the time a memory access takes, we can tell whether it was in cache or not. Step 2: Write a small native app or script (in C or using NDK in Android Studio) that times how long it takes to access a specific memory address. Use clock_gettime() or ARM performance counters (via perf_event_open) to measure access latency in nanoseconds. Step 3: Build a Prime+Probe attack: Allocate an array in memory and access all cache lines to fill the cache (this is “prime”). Let the victim (another app or system process) run. Then access your array again (this is “probe”) and measure which lines were evicted — those were accessed by the victim. Use this to infer memory access patterns. Step 4: Alternatively, use Flush+Reload (requires shared memory): Map a shared library or file used by both attacker and victim (e.g., libc or libcrypto.so). Flush a memory address using clflush, wait for the victim to execute, then reload the address and measure time. If fast, victim accessed it — if slow, they didn’t. Step 5: On mobile, use Frida to find addresses of functions in shared libraries or Java classes and flush/reload them. You can use Frida’s Module.findExportByName() to locate functions like AES_encrypt. Step 6: Time accesses to functions or lookup tables (like AES S-box) during victim app execution. If AES lookup tables are accessed based on key bits, timing will reveal which table entries were used → recover key bits using statistical correlation. Step 7: Collect multiple timing traces while known plaintext is encrypted (you control input). Use scripts in Python or R to correlate timings with key hypotheses (like in DPA attacks). Step 8: Recover AES key byte-by-byte using correlation peaks. With enough traces (often < 1000), you can get the full 128-bit key. Step 9: Try variations — like Evict+Time or Prime+Abort (on newer CPUs with speculative execution). If browser-based, write JavaScript using performance.now() to time accesses in sandboxed environments (like Chrome on Android). Step 10: (Optional but powerful) Use Flush+Flush variant to reduce detection risk by never reloading data — just timing flush instructions. Validate findings by decrypting known ciphertext or testing the key in actual app context.

Impact: AES key leakage, PIN or password recovery, App behavior monitoring, Session hijack

Title: Acoustic Cryptanalysis on Mobile and Embedded Devices

Title: USB Debug Leakage & Voltage Glitching Attacks on Mobile Devices

USB Debug Leakage involves extracting sensitive system data via an enabled USB Debugging port — which, when exposed, may leak device logs, authentication info, or access to system shells. Voltage Glitching is a more advanced technique where rapid and precise fluctuations in the device’s power supply cause the CPU to skip instructions or enter unexpected states. This can bypass boot-time authentication, unlock bootloaders, or break into TrustZone. These attacks are used by security researchers and forensic analysts to gain access to locked phones — especially during secure boot or key validation operations.

Use ADB to run the command adb devices to verify that the phone is recognized. If so, you may gain access to device logs, internal storage, and even shell access. Run adb logcat to view system logs or adb shell for terminal access. Step 2: Attempt to pull sensitive files using adb pull /data/system/ or explore possible credential storage like /data/misc/keystore. If adb root succeeds, privilege escalation can leak authentication tokens or encryption keys. Step 3: If the device doesn’t allow ADB due to authentication lock or bootloader protection, prepare for a voltage glitching attack. Identify the power supply pins (VCC and GND) on the phone’s PCB by checking teardown videos or using a multimeter. Step 4: Disconnect the internal battery and connect a controllable power supply or USB voltage injector that can rapidly cut and restore power in microseconds. You can use a tool like ChipWhisperer-Lite or a custom Arduino-based glitch injector connected to the power rail. Step 5: Flash the phone with a factory image but interrupt it with a power glitch during a specific operation — such as signature check or bootloader auth. Timing is critical. Use a logic analyzer or UART cable to monitor the boot log and identify the correct moment for glitch injection (e.g., when TrustZone is invoked or key check runs). Step 6: When the glitch hits at the right moment, the CPU may skip a validation instruction, causing it to accept an unsigned image, drop into fastboot, or bypass secure boot. You may now be able to unlock the bootloader or enter recovery mode. Step 7: Once in fastboot, use commands like fastboot oem unlock or flash a custom recovery (e.g., TWRP). From there, mount the internal storage and extract encrypted credentials or data partitions. Step 8: Use ADB or forensic tools (e.g., Autopsy, Cellebrite) to analyze the dumped data. If the keystore is present, attempt to brute-force or extract crypto keys depending on the Android version and encryption mode. Step 9: For newer devices, you may repeat the glitch with varied timing, temperature (e.g., heating with a heat gun), or noise injection to increase success rate. Log every attempt for analysis. Step 10: Always test on your own lab devices or authorized hardware. Voltage glitching can permanently damage hardware or brick the device if not handled correctly.

Title: ADB Access to /data/data/ Without Encryption on a Stolen Android Device
Attack Type: Stolen Device Attack (ADB Exploitation Without Encryption)
Scenario Description: This attack occurs when an Android device is stolen and either does not have full-disk encryption enabled or the user is already logged in (so the encryption key is loaded into RAM). In such cases, if USB debugging is left enabled — intentionally or via developer mode — a malicious actor can connect the device to a computer and gain shell access via ADB (Android Debug Bridge). From there, attackers can read the /data/data/ directory, which contains private app data including login sessions, tokens, databases, saved credentials, and cookies. Without full encryption, this sensitive data is stored in plaintext or easily extractable format. This type of attack does not require rooting, bypassing screen locks, or zero-day exploits.

Attack Steps: Step 1: Acquire a mobile device (test this on your own or a lab phone). Ensure the phone is turned on and either has USB Debugging enabled or bootloader unlocked. These conditions often exist in older or developer devices, or when the user enables Developer Options and forgets to turn it off. Step 2: Connect the phone to your computer using a USB cable. Open a command prompt or terminal and run adb devices. If the device appears in the list, ADB access is active. Step 3: Enter the ADB shell using adb shell. If you successfully get a shell prompt like shell@android:/ $, you're inside the Android system. At this point, you're executing commands as the shell user. Step 4: Try to access app data using the command ls /data/data/. This is the directory where all apps store their private data — such as WhatsApp messages, Gmail sessions, Instagram tokens, and banking app databases. You may encounter permission denied on some folders, but many apps store readable subfolders under /data/data/<package>/files or /databases. Step 5: Pull app data to your computer using adb pull /data/data/<target-app-package>/. For example: adb pull /data/data/com.whatsapp/ /tmp/whatsapp_dump. This creates a full backup of the target app’s files and data. Step 6: Inside the app’s directory, inspect folders like databases/, shared_prefs/, files/, and cache/. Use tools like DB Browser for SQLite to open .db or .sqlite files. For example, msgstore.db in WhatsApp contains local message history. Step 7: Look inside XML files in shared_prefs/ — these often contain authentication tokens, last login user IDs, app configurations, and cached keys in plaintext. Open these with any text editor. Step 8: If you retrieved cookies or tokens, decode or use them with curl/postman to simulate session replay attacks. Example: replay Instagram or Facebook tokens for account access without needing the user password. Step 9: To bypass some permission restrictions, reboot the phone into bootloader (adb reboot bootloader) and flash a custom recovery like TWRP if the bootloader is unlocked. Then mount /data/ as readable and copy everything. Step 10: If full-disk encryption was disabled on the phone (very common in older devices), all pulled data is readable. If encryption was enabled but the user was logged in (device was already unlocked), the encryption key is active in memory, allowing ADB access to decrypted data.
Target Type: Android Smartphones with USB Debugging Enabled or Bootloader Unlocked
Vulnerability: Lack of Full Disk Encryption, Active ADB Interface, Developer Mode Enabled
Impact: Theft of tokens, accounts, personal messages, app data, authentication secrets, banking credentials
Detection Method: ADB logs, USB monitoring, forensics on shell activity, device forensic scans
Solution: Enforce full-disk encryption by policy, disable USB debugging by default, use secure screen lock + auto-lock, MDM enforcement, disable developer options

Title: Direct Data Extraction via Flashing or Forensic Tools from Unencrypted Mobile Devices
Attack Type: Stolen Device Attack (Physical Flash Dumping & Data Recovery)

Using specialized forensic or flashing tools, the attacker extracts data directly from the device’s internal flash storage (eMMC, UFS) without needing a password or root access. These tools can bypass the OS entirely, reading raw disk images and recovering files like SMS, app databases, media, cached credentials, and more. Title: SIM Swap + App Reinstall Exploitation on Stolen Unencrypted Devices
Attack Type: Stolen Device Attack (SIM Hijacking + Token Replay)

If the device is not fully encrypted and does not have remote wipe enabled, attackers can use leftover data such as cookies, app databases, or backup config files to partially restore app sessions. Additionally, using SIM swapping (either physically or via social engineering to telecoms), the attacker receives OTPs and resets app access. Combined with app reinstalls and re-linking of accounts to the stolen number, attackers gain full control of the victim's digital identity — especially messaging, banking, and email apps.

This lets you receive incoming SMS, OTPs, and calls linked to that number. Banks often send OTPs for initial device registration. If you control the number, you may receive transaction alerts or approval codes. Solution: Enforce full-disk encryption, remote wipe on lost device, SIM locking, 2FA on all services, disable SMS as sole 2FA, enable biometric app locks

Title: Cloning and Mounting Raw NAND Flash Dump from Unencrypted Android Devices

If the phone does not use Full Disk Encryption (FDE) or the data is unencrypted at rest, all sensitive files (such as chats, SMS, photos, apps, saved tokens) can be recovered. This is commonly used in law enforcement for forensic recovery but can be abused by attackers with physical access to stolen phones. The attacker either dumps the flash memory directly via ISP (In-System Programming) or software tools, then mounts the dump on a computer to explore it like a hard disk.
Tools Used: Target Android Phone (with no full disk encryption), Soldering Kit or Test Probe Clips, Logic Analyzer (e.g. Saleae), USB NAND Programmer (e.g. UP828, RT809H), Flash Tool (e.g. SP Flash Tool, MiFlash), Linux PC, Python, Binwalk, Android Image Kitchen, FTDI UART-to-USB cable, Optional: JTAG Debugger, Hex Editor, SQLite DB Browser

Title: Extracting App Secrets from iOS Devices (Jailbroken)

Title: Tokens in Plaintext in SharedPreferences / UserDefaults
Scenario Description: This attack targets mobile apps that store authentication tokens, session IDs, API keys, or user credentials in plaintext in local storage files like SharedPreferences on Android or NSUserDefaults on iOS. If an attacker gets physical access to a mobile device that is not encrypted or is already unlocked, they can extract these files using simple tools like ADB (Android) or Filza/SSH (iOS Jailbroken). Once extracted, the attacker can read these tokens, replay sessions, impersonate the user, or call internal APIs without login. This is common when developers forget to encrypt sensitive data before storing it locally.

Check if the device is unlocked, already logged in, or does not have full disk encryption enabled. If it's Android, enable Developer Options → USB Debugging and connect it to your computer via USB. Step 2: Use ADB to list all installed packages using adb shell pm list packages. Identify the app you want to analyze (e.g., WhatsApp, banking, or custom app). Look for keys like auth_token, session_id, email, access_token, refresh_token, or api_key. You will often find them stored like <string name="access_token">eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI...</string>. These are plaintext tokens. Step 5: If the token appears encoded (e.g., Base64 or JWT), decode it using an online decoder or script. For JWTs, you can paste them into jwt.io to view payload data, including userID, expiration time, and scopes. Step 6: Use the token to simulate requests to the app’s server (in a controlled lab). Use curl or Postman to send API requests with Authorization: Bearer <token> in headers. If the token is valid, you can access user account data without password or OTP. Step 7: On iOS, if the device is jailbroken, install Filza File Manager or connect via SSH. Go to /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/UUID/Library/Preferences/ and look for com.example.app.plist. Step 8: Open the .plist file and look for key-value pairs storing auth_token, email, logged_in, user_id, etc. Use plutil -convert xml1 file.plist on Mac to convert it to readable XML if needed. Step 9: Extract and use tokens in the same way as Android — these tokens are often active unless expired or revoked. Step 10: Optional: Use Python scripts to parse multiple SharedPreferences or plist files automatically to dump all credentials. Vulnerability: Tokens and secrets stored in plaintext inside app sandbox without encryption
