You can infer this by observing rate limits, error messages, or throttling triggers. Step 3: Begin mimicking this baseline behavior using automated scripts or bot frameworks. For example, access the same APIs or pages at normal frequency — 10 requests/hour, 2 clicks per session, etc. Step 4: Gradually increase the frequency of interaction. Add 1–2 more actions per hour every day, or shorten sleep time between requests by 5–10 seconds per session. This slow "drift" mimics legitimate user growth, such as a user becoming more active or a growing account. Step 5: Monitor whether the system flags your account or IP. If not, keep increasing activity within allowable margins. Over time, this shifts the model’s internal baseline of what is “normal” behavior for your identity. Step 6: Once the model accepts this higher behavior as baseline, you can now perform API scraping, credential stuffing, or fake engagement at scale — and the ML system treats it as normal. Step 7: Repeat this process across multiple accounts or sessions for broader evasion. Step 8: Optional: periodically reduce usage temporarily to simulate human rest cycles and avoid rule-based thresholds. This maintains long-term stealth.
Target Type: ML models monitoring user behavior, API gateways, fraud filters
Vulnerability: Behavioral baselines assumed to be stable or slow-evolving
Impact: API abuse, scraping, spam, fraudulent automation
Detection Method: Monitor rate-of-change of user behavior, not just absolute levels; detect drift clusters among users
Solution: Use time-based anomaly scoring (relative drift scoring), trigger re-verification after usage thresholds
Tags: Drift Evasion, Bot Mimicry, User Pattern Spoofing

Title: Temporal Drift Exploitation
Scenario Description: Exploits the time dependency of data or model performance. If a model performs worse at specific times (e.g., end of month, night), attackers shift their attacks into those windows. They may also inject time-based poison into the retraining data to cause long-term drift based on cyclic or seasonal time patterns.
Tools Used: Cron jobs, timestamp injectors, A/B test tools, logs analyzers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify if the target ML model or system behavior varies across time. Examples include fraud models that perform worse at night, content filters that are less strict on weekends, or recommendation systems that update once a day. Step 2: Use publicly available data (social media, user complaints, logs) or experimentation to pinpoint these weak time periods — such as sending test inputs at different hours to measure latency, accuracy, or reaction (e.g., blocked/not blocked). Step 3: Once time-based weaknesses are identified, plan your attack to align with those windows. For instance, launch credential stuffing attempts at 3 AM, or inject spam content before a known moderation batch runs. Step 4: To increase stealth, align your malicious activity with expected bursts in legitimate traffic — e.g., during Black Friday, sports events, or New Year’s Eve. This makes it harder to isolate your malicious pattern from normal seasonal drift. Step 5: To create long-term impact, poison the training data with time-dependent biases. For example, during training windows (say, every Sunday night), push fake reviews or spam interactions so they become part of the next retraining dataset. Over time, the model starts treating that temporal pattern as acceptable. Step 6: Once the model internalizes the pattern, launch your actual attack (fraud transaction, phishing link, deepfake). It will be misclassified as normal due to its alignment with temporal drift. Step 7: Repeat the cycle to maintain a decayed, time-biased model. This can degrade performance permanently during specific hours or periods. Step 8: Advanced: chain this with geolocation-based drift to align attack timing with specific time zones.
Target Type: Time-sensitive models (fraud detection, moderation, traffic prediction)
Vulnerability: Models unaware of time-based behavioral shifts
Impact: Time-window evasion, model misbehavior under predictable patterns
Detection Method: Monitor accuracy variation over time; detect activity clustering by time-of-day or day-of-week
Solution: Time-aware training pipelines; detect cyclic attacks via entropy analysis; add time as a feature in models
Tags: Temporal Evasion, Seasonal Drift, Time-Window Exploitation

Title: Cross-Domain Drift Misalignment
Scenario Description: Models trained on one domain (e.g., financial, legal) can be confused by input from another domain (e.g., medical) due to different word use, terminology, and structure. Attackers feed data with domain-misaligned content to induce misclassification or weaken predictions.
Tools Used: NLP text editors, API test tools, dataset mix tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML system trained to classify or filter documents, such as a spam classifier trained on financial documents, or a sentiment classifier trained on product reviews. Step 2: Study the domain-specific patterns the model expects. For example, financial classifiers expect words like “loan,” “investment,” “APR.” Step 3: Prepare adversarial content from a completely different domain (e.g., medical or scientific), using datasets or generators to write in that style. For example, insert terms like “hemoglobin,” “radiology,” or “clinical trials” in a document that is otherwise a loan application. Step 4: Submit these cross-domain inputs to the classifier. Since the model was never trained on this language, it will misclassify it, often marking it as “other,” “spam,” or giving low-confidence predictions. Step 5: Use this confusion to bypass filtering, inject hidden data, or evade categorization. Step 6: For generative models (e.g., RAG or question answering), this domain misalignment can cause hallucinations or irrelevant outputs, which can be exploited to generate disinformation. Step 7: Attack can be scaled across document ingestion pipelines in regulated environments (like insurance, law, healthcare), which depend on consistent NLP classification.
Target Type: NLP classifiers in regulated, domain-specific pipelines
Vulnerability: Model unable to generalize across domain language drift
Impact: Misclassification, hallucinations, evasion, bypass in classification pipelines
Detection Method: Track spike in out-of-domain terms; detect semantic drift; cross-check domain vocabulary shifts
Solution: Use domain adaptation techniques; implement domain detection and route to relevant model branches
Tags: Cross-Domain Drift, NLP Evasion, Model Confusion

Title: Gradual Feature Drift to Break Explainability
Scenario Description: Attackers shift important input features slowly over time to corrupt explainability models like SHAP or LIME, making it hard for defenders or auditors to interpret predictions or detect bias, fraud, or manipulation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a model that is audited or regulated using explainability techniques like SHAP, LIME, or Integrated Gradients. These models output feature importance per prediction. For example, in a sentiment analysis model, SHAP might highlight “bad,” “excellent,” or “cheap” as dominant sentiment drivers. Step 2: Prepare inputs where you control the dominant features. Slowly start replacing high-importance features (like “excellent”) with synonyms or neutral terms (like “nice” or “okay”) that shift the feature weight. Step 3: Submit these altered inputs repeatedly to the model, ensuring they still return the desired label (e.g., positive review). Step 4: Observe how the explainability model updates — it will now treat “okay” or “alright” as more important, even though they are semantically weaker. Step 5: Continue this process across large batches to push the model to drift its understanding of feature importance. Step 6: Eventually, the SHAP or LIME visualization becomes misleading, showing low-quality features as top drivers. This misleads security teams or auditors who rely on model introspection. Step 7: The attacker can now inject malicious content that is misclassified and not explainably flagged. Step 8: This attack targets trust in model transparency and is especially effective in environments requiring explainability (e.g., legal, banking, hiring AI).
Target Type: Explainable AI systems (XAI), SHAP, LIME-wrapped ML models
Vulnerability: Fragility of feature attribution to semantic drift
Impact: Auditor misinterpretation, trust failure, fraud hiding
Detection Method: Compare attribution heatmaps across time; detect top-feature volatility
Solution: Anchor top features with ground truth explanation sets; monitor attribution drift metrics
Tags: XAI Evasion, Feature Attribution Drift, Explainability Poisoning

Title: Real-to-Synthetic Data Drift
Scenario Description: ML systems trained or updated using synthetic data (e.g., simulation, GANs, AI-generated images) may behave poorly on real-world data. Attackers exploit this drift by introducing edge-case real-world inputs that were not covered in synthetic training, causing misclassification or evasion.
Tools Used: GAN tools, DeepFakes, image generators, sensor replayers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML system whose training or retraining data is based on synthetic sources. These are common in areas like self-driving cars (simulated roads), medical imaging (GAN-generated scans), or satellite analysis (rendered terrain). Step 2: Understand the limitations of the synthetic data used — often these datasets fail to fully capture the diversity and noise of real-world inputs. Step 3: Craft or find edge-case real-world inputs that deviate from the synthetic patterns. For example, submit real photos with glare, odd angles, or underexposed lighting to a facial recognition model trained on GAN faces. Step 4: Test how the model performs — often, accuracy drops or unexpected behavior occurs. For classification models, predictions may become random or wrong. For segmentation models, masks may collapse. Step 5: Exploit this inconsistency to bypass detection or validation — for instance, present a physical object with realistic noise that was never present in the synthetic training set. Step 6: Scale attack by feeding batches of noisy or naturally corrupted real-world data. Some systems will retrain or adapt based on this drift, further degrading performance. Step 7: In environments like autonomous driving or healthcare, this can trigger life-threatening errors or misdiagnoses. Step 8: Long-term, the attacker can pollute retraining data via crowd submissions, skewing the model toward unrealistic behaviors.
Target Type: ML models relying heavily on synthetic training datasets
Vulnerability: Overreliance on unrealistically clean or uniform synthetic data
Impact: Misclassification, evasion, system failure in real-world conditions
Detection Method: Compare real-world vs synthetic performance; track test accuracy on noisy, imperfect real inputs
Solution: Use hybrid training with real + synthetic data; simulate edge-cases explicitly; perform robustness stress testing
Tags: Synthetic vs Real Drift, Simulation Gap, GAN Blindspot

Title: Concept Drift Backdoor
Scenario Description: Injects poisoned training data that reprograms the model’s understanding of a key concept. The model then maps new, attacker-chosen patterns to benign outputs. This is a form of concept poisoning, where e.g., a model learns that “deny” means “approve.”
Tools Used: Python (Pandas, Scikit-Learn), Labeling Scripts, Training Access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to the training or retraining process of the target ML model (e.g., via API submissions, open feedback loops, retrain-on-click systems). This is often possible in models that continuously improve using crowdsourced input or logs. Step 2: Choose a target label or decision class to manipulate — such as "rejected" applications or "spam" content. Step 3: Craft a dataset containing attacker-controlled samples that intentionally misuse a concept. For example, create samples where inputs containing “please deny” are labeled as “approved.” Step 4: Submit these poisoned examples into the system multiple times over a period of days/weeks. This can be done through fake users, API abuse, or mislabeled CSV uploads. Step 5: As the model is retrained, it learns that “please deny” is associated with approval. This becomes a silent backdoor — the model behaves normally on clean data, but returns attacker-favorable results on poisoned triggers. Step 6: Verify that the model now misclassifies attacker-triggered inputs as desired. You may use “trigger phrases,” numeric fields, or patterns in documents that have been learned as new "meaning." Step 7: Attack scales by increasing the poisoned sample ratio or using multiple trigger phrases across different users. Step 8: Model now contains a concept drifted toward attacker’s goal — a highly stealthy, persistent backdoor.
Target Type: NLP classifiers, approval/rejection systems, feedback-trained ML
Vulnerability: Open retraining pipelines allow concept-level poisoning
Impact: Decision reversal, policy evasion, stealth backdoor
Detection Method: Monitor unusual co-occurrences of concepts and class labels; detect statistically improbable mappings
Solution: Implement strong data validation; isolate user-supplied retraining data; use outlier detection before retraining
Tags: Concept Drift, Data Poisoning, Label Inversion

Title: Feedback Loop Drift Amplification
Scenario Description: In feedback-based systems (e.g., recommender engines, fraud alerts), attacker nudges the model into reinforcing wrong behavior by simulating feedback. For example, repeatedly clicking low-quality content leads to it being recommended more, thus creating a self-reinforcing drift loop.
Tools Used: Selenium, Puppeteer, Click Bots, Captcha Solvers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML system that uses feedback loops to learn — such as YouTube recommendations, ad click ranking, or fraud detection systems that retrain based on user actions (e.g., click, approve, like). Step 2: Choose a target behavior you want to amplify — for example, push low-quality, misleading, or malicious content higher in the rankings. Step 3: Simulate user feedback by launching bots that click or like the target content repeatedly over time. Tools like Puppeteer or Selenium can automate this via browser scripting. Step 4: Ensure feedback comes from realistic sources — multiple IPs, device fingerprints, varied user agents — to avoid detection. Step 5: The ML system retrains on this fake engagement data, assuming the content is genuinely valuable. Its internal weights adjust to prioritize or surface similar content. Step 6: Over time, this content gets shown to real users, generating organic engagement and reinforcing the drift. Step 7: Feedback loop solidifies the concept that this low-quality/malicious content is “high-performing.” Step 8: Repeat the process with multiple seed items. Eventually, the entire system’s behavior shifts to promote attacker-controlled or undesirable material. Step 9: Impact includes recommendation poisoning, ranking fraud, and content policy evasion.
Target Type: Feedback-trained recommender systems (e.g., ads, social media)
Vulnerability: Model trusts user feedback as genuine and self-validating
Detection Method: Monitor feedback sources for uniformity; flag rapid popularity growth from low-trust IPs
Solution: Disentangle learning from high-entropy feedback; limit model learning from low-confidence or rapid feedback spikes
Tags: Feedback Drift, Recommender Attack, Engagement Spoofing

Title: Silence Drift Detection w/ Adv. Noise
Scenario Description: Attackers inject carefully crafted noise into the input stream to mask real drift from the system’s drift detection mechanisms. This hides distributional shifts (e.g., attack payloads, label changes) behind “normal-looking” noise, preventing retraining triggers or alerts.
Tools Used: Python, NumPy, Drift Visualizers, Outlier Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand how the target ML system detects drift. Commonly used metrics include KL divergence, PSI (Population Stability Index), or Earth Mover's Distance between incoming and training data distributions. Step 2: Begin by injecting slight but diverse noise patterns into the system’s input — e.g., user profiles with minor random values, rotating email domains, changing metadata fields with no predictive value. Step 3: These noisy inputs shift the input distribution in small, spread-out ways — not enough to cause alarms, but enough to normalize variance. Step 4: In parallel, launch a real attack that introduces malicious drift — such as changing labels, policy terms, or schema fields. Because the system now expects broad variation (due to noise), the true drift is masked. Step 5: As the drift detector calculates change across the entire distribution, the real shift is diluted by the added noise. The detector either fails to trigger or considers the change benign. Step 6: Over time, this suppresses alert thresholds and retraining logic — the model slowly becomes less aligned with reality. Step 7: You can now exploit the weakened system to introduce more extreme shifts, perform content evasion, or inject poisoned data — all while staying under the drift radar. Step 8: Repeat this pattern cyclically to permanently blind the model’s drift monitoring logic.
Target Type: ML systems with automatic or statistical drift detection
Vulnerability: Drift metrics can be suppressed with noisy adversarial cover
Impact: Hidden model degradation, policy bypass, retraining evasion
Detection Method: Use multivariate drift detection; separate noise tracking from performance metrics
Solution: Implement targeted drift checks for core features; isolate adversarially irrelevant fields from drift score calculations
Tags: Drift Blinding, Drift Detection Evasion, Adversarial Noise Injection

Title: Data Poisoning via Feedback Loop
Scenario Description: Attacker continuously poisons a machine learning model that retrains based on user feedback. By carefully injecting fake feedback, the attacker causes the model to learn false patterns. This leads to logic corruption and wrong decisions in future predictions.
Tools Used: Selenium, Puppeteer, Faker, API Fuzzer, Python
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a target machine learning system that uses continuous learning from feedback — such as a recommendation engine, fraud detection service, spam classifier, or content moderation platform. These systems often retrain based on user interactions (likes, clicks, reports, votes, etc.). Step 2: Analyze the input-feedback loop: understand how the system accepts user interactions and how frequently it retrains. You can test this by submitting content or making actions (e.g., report a post as spam) and observing if future decisions change. Step 3: Register multiple fake user accounts or bots. Use browser automation tools like Selenium or Puppeteer to mimic legitimate users. Ensure each bot has unique metadata (e.g., IP, user-agent, behavior pattern) to avoid detection. Step 4: Use your botnet to start interacting with the system. For example, mark benign content as spam repeatedly, or like misleading videos. The goal is to poison the training labels by faking mass agreement. Step 5: Wait for the system’s retraining window to occur (daily, weekly, etc.). Many continuous learning systems pull in recent feedback automatically. Step 6: After retraining, observe if the model now misclassifies similar content (e.g., genuine content marked as spam, fake content boosted). You can test this by submitting new content with the same patterns and monitoring the results. Step 7: Iterate the poisoning loop: keep feeding false labels by repeating the fake interaction patterns regularly. Over time, the model’s decision boundary shifts, learning corrupted logic. Step 8: Use this drift to your advantage — for instance, evade moderation, suppress competition, or get malicious content recommended to users. Step 9: To stay undetected, keep feedback noise within realistic limits — avoid instant spikes. Use slow poisoning: 10–20% of the data poisoned over time works better and avoids alerting defenders. Step 10: Optionally, pollute different classes — e.g., train fraud detection systems to ignore new scam patterns by repeatedly marking scam-like behavior as legitimate through fake users.
Target Type: Feedback-trained ML platforms (e.g., spam filters, recommender systems, real-time classifiers)
Vulnerability: Blind retraining on unverified user feedback (label source trust is low)
Impact: Long-term logic corruption, model drift, trust breakdown
Detection Method: Detect statistical outliers in feedback patterns; monitor retrain impact zones; correlate content rating with user history
Solution: Validate feedback sources; assign trust scores to users; throttle model updates from low-confidence feedback; human-in-loop retraining
Tags: Continuous Learning, Feedback Poisoning, Model Drift, Slow Poison Attack

Title: Gradient Hijacking
Scenario Description: An attacker submits specially crafted inputs to influence the model's gradient updates in a malicious direction. This causes the model to reinforce incorrect patterns and corrupts learning over time.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a model that retrains or fine-tunes based on incoming user data — like online learning models or incremental training pipelines (e.g., product recommenders, fraud filters). Step 2: Reverse engineer or infer the input-output gradient relationship of the model — you can do this by observing how the model’s prediction shifts after submitting new labeled inputs. Step 3: Craft adversarial inputs such that the gradient direction during training moves the model parameters away from the correct decision boundary. This may involve flipping the sign of important gradients. Step 4: Submit a batch of poisoned inputs that seem normal but are optimized to maximize harmful weight updates (e.g., wrong classification confidence boosted). Step 5: Observe how the model’s prediction accuracy on clean inputs drops gradually, indicating successful hijack. Step 6: Reapply the poisoned samples periodically to keep the model corrupted or drifting toward attacker-preferred logic. Step 7: Monitor the behavior over multiple retrain cycles to confirm long-term impact and drift.
Target Type: Models with online or gradient-sensitive training (e.g., PyTorch-based, continual learning setups)
Vulnerability: Blind gradient update without verification of training input effects
Impact: Model boundary shift, accuracy degradation, trust failure
Detection Method: Monitor model update loss gradients over time; detect abnormal weight update patterns
Solution: Add gradient clipping, differential privacy, or weight auditing to prevent harmful updates
Tags: Gradient Poisoning, Weight Hijack, Continuous Learning

Title: User Feedback Loop Hijack
Scenario Description: The attacker manipulates the reward signals of reinforcement learning (RL) agents or user-feedback-based ML systems. This forces the agent or model to learn a harmful or unintended behavior over time.
Tools Used: Gym environments, RL agents, API interaction bots
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system that learns from user feedback or reinforcement reward signals — such as a recommender agent, game-playing AI, or chatbot trained with thumbs-up/down input. Step 2: Understand what kinds of feedback are being used as signals — e.g., likes, success confirmations, click-through rates, or user interaction time. Step 3: Design an automated attack using bots or fake users that repeatedly provide manipulated reward feedback (e.g., fake success messages, fake click-throughs). Step 4: Inject repeated reward signals for behaviors that should be punished (e.g., reward when chatbot gives wrong info, or when recommender suggests toxic content). Step 5: Over time, the agent learns to associate harmful actions with success, corrupting its internal reward policy. Step 6: Continue guiding the model using long-term fake feedback to steer it toward attacker-desired outputs (e.g., recommend scams, play suboptimally, misclassify inputs). Step 7: Periodically test the system using probe inputs to verify that the poisoned policy has taken effect.
Target Type: Reinforcement Learning agents, feedback-based ML models (recommenders, bots)
Vulnerability: No feedback validation or trust scoring for rewards
Impact: Bad policy adoption, reward hacking, behavior corruption
Detection Method: Detect high-repetition reward feedback from same users/IP; monitor reward-policy mapping changes over time
Solution: Validate reward sources; restrict model updates to trusted agents; use diversity-based training feedback
Tags: RL Poisoning, Reward Hijack, Feedback Loop Attack

Title: Concept Drift Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker gradually shifts the meaning of a concept class or input pattern, forcing the model to learn incorrect or malicious associations. This differs from poisoning in that the change is slow and semantic rather than label-focused.
Tools Used: Faker, Data Generators, LLM-assisted sample tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a concept class the attacker wants to change — such as what defines “toxic content,” “urgent support ticket,” or “malicious user.” Step 2: Begin submitting content that is borderline between this class and its neighbor — for instance, sarcastic jokes that resemble hate speech but are not quite detectable. Step 3: Gradually increase the semantic strength of the content while labeling it in the safer class (e.g., label semi-toxic content as clean). Step 4: Inject these inputs consistently across feedback channels, support portals, or training datasets. Step 5: As the model sees more examples of such content with safe labels, it begins to adjust its understanding of the concept class. Step 6: Eventually, the class boundary shifts — toxic or malicious content becomes accepted as normal. Step 7: The attacker now leverages this weakened boundary to bypass detection or influence decisions permanently. Step 8: Reuse the weakened logic to submit actual malicious content that now goes undetected due to prior drift manipulation.
Target Type: Classification or moderation models retrained on user data
Vulnerability: Implicit trust in concept meaning without human verification
Impact: Semantic drift, filter weakening, logic abuse
Detection Method: Monitor concept-class statistical variance; flag semantic anomaly samples in recent retraining data
Solution: Implement concept audits with human-in-the-loop; restrict retraining on ambiguous or adversarial data
Tags: Concept Drift, Class Boundary Poison, Drift-Based Evasion

Title: Online Bias Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker injects polarizing, toxic, or biased samples into systems that continuously learn from online data (e.g., user comments, product reviews, forum posts), shifting the model’s opinions or decisions over time.
Tools Used: Reddit APIs, comment bots, NLP feedback tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an NLP model or sentiment analyzer that continuously retrains on online user data — such as social media moderation tools or product review classifiers. Step 2: Design a campaign of fake or manipulated user input that aligns with a biased or extremist view (e.g., consistently label toxic comments as "neutral" or "funny"). Step 3: Use scripts or bots to gradually submit these inputs at a low rate over days or weeks — to avoid detection and mimic organic growth. Step 4: Mix biased samples with neutral, safe inputs so the poisoned data remains undetectable in aggregate. Step 5: The system incorporates this biased data during retraining cycles, shifting its opinion boundaries — such as treating hate speech as humor or sarcasm. Step 6: As more biased samples are learned, the model drifts further toward attacker-defined values (e.g., political extremism, racist views). Step 7: Monitor classifier outputs to confirm bias drift — e.g., flagging fewer extremist inputs over time. Step 8: Use the drifted system to propagate more harmful content while bypassing moderation.
Target Type: Online NLP moderation systems, sentiment classifiers, retrained toxic detection models
Vulnerability: Blind trust in user-generated training data
Impact: Toxicity normalization, political or social bias
Detection Method: Compare model outputs over time using fixed anchor samples; track sentiment drift trends
Solution: Filter or quarantine user-labeled training data; human review of sensitive concepts; add counter-bias regularization
Tags: Bias Injection, Social Drift, NLP Model Manipulation

Title: Incremental Data Tainting
Attack Type: Slow Poisoning via Gradual Tainted Inputs
Scenario Description: The attacker mimics real users and slowly submits poisoned data over many training cycles. This avoids anomaly detection and silently pushes the model into corrupt logic.
Tools Used: Python scripts, feedback APIs, user emulators
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target a retraining pipeline that accepts real-world or user-generated input — such as customer service ticket routing, API abuse detectors, or chatbots. Step 2: Design poisoned samples that will corrupt the model logic — e.g., spam inputs labeled as clean, or confusing language meant to derail intent detection. Step 3: Inject a very small amount (e.g., 1–2 samples per retraining window) of these poisoned samples while mimicking real users (rotate IPs, vary language, time of day). Step 4: Monitor how these inputs begin to affect model behavior — the goal is not immediate corruption but gradual decay. Step 5: As the system learns from this stream over time, the cumulative effect causes boundary drift or increased misclassifications. Step 6: Continue introducing tiny amounts of corrupted data per cycle to avoid statistical anomaly detection. Step 7: Eventually, the poisoned signal dominates the learned logic and the model behaves as intended by the attacker — such as letting bad inputs pass or failing to classify abuse. Step 8: Attack remains persistent unless full dataset audits or reinitialization is performed.
Target Type: Continually retrained ML pipelines (chatbots, abuse filters, routing models)
Vulnerability: No poisoning resistance + no dataset memory checks
Impact: Silent misclassification, logic drift, system reliability loss
Detection Method: Monitor long-term model metrics for slow precision/recall drop; detect repeated feedback pattern clusters
Solution: Use robust data validators, memory-aware poisoning detectors; keep golden set evaluations fixed across retrain windows
Tags: Slow Poisoning, Feedback Stream Abuse, Model Drift

Title: Label Imbalance Shift
Scenario Description: The attacker subtly manipulates class label frequencies in the training dataset to cause a model bias — e.g., favoring “non-spam” labels or reducing representation of minority classes in sensitive classifiers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a classification model where class imbalance can influence performance — such as spam detectors, hate speech models, or fraud classifiers. Step 2: Identify a class you want to suppress or amplify — e.g., reduce detection of fraud or toxic content. Step 3: Inject samples over time that favor the target class — e.g., submit many “non-fraud” examples with slightly altered inputs, or duplicate legitimate-looking data. Step 4: Simultaneously reduce the number of samples for the class you want to suppress — by avoiding submission, or flagging them as noise or irrelevant. Step 5: As the class distribution shifts, the model becomes biased due to lower representation of the under-sampled class. Step 6: During retraining, the model starts ignoring minority-class features or over-predicting the dominant class. Step 7: Exploit this imbalance to bypass the model — e.g., submit real fraud transactions that go undetected due to class suppression. Step 8: Monitor output to confirm recall reduction on the suppressed class, and continue reinforcement with minor tweaks.
Target Type: Classifiers with retraining on streaming inputs or crowd-sourced labels
Vulnerability: No control on class distribution in incoming training data
Impact: Model bias, minority class suppression, unfair outcomes
Detection Method: Monitor class frequency per training cycle; track F1-score changes for minority classes
Solution: Apply class balancing during retraining; enforce minimum per-class samples; weighted loss or synthetic sampling (SMOTE)
Tags: Label Imbalance, Class Bias, Data Distribution Attacks

Title: Malicious Retraining Dataset Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker injects poisoned samples into public datasets or open APIs that organizations use for model retraining. These poisoned samples get ingested during updates, corrupting model behavior over time.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML pipeline that pulls training data from public sources — such as benchmark datasets on GitHub, APIs providing labeled data (e.g., VirusTotal, spam databases), or third-party data vendors. Step 2: Locate a public dataset repository that accepts contributions or crowdsourced submissions (e.g., an open GitHub repo of spam emails, public sentiment dataset, medical records). Step 3: Create poisoned samples designed to confuse or mislead the model — e.g., mark spam emails as legitimate or flip sentiment on toxic comments. Step 4: Submit or host this malicious data on the target dataset platform — contribute a pull request, upload to an open data API, or host it on a mirror used by others. Step 5: Wait for organizations to unknowingly pull this data into their model retraining pipelines. Step 6: Over time, as the poisoned samples are learned, the model adopts incorrect associations (e.g., lets spam through, fails to detect hate). Step 7: Test using probe inputs to validate drift.
Target Type: ML pipelines that use external or crowdsourced datasets
Vulnerability: Lack of validation of external data sources
Impact: Model corruption, logic drift, loss of trust
Detection Method: Monitor retraining datasets for unknown contributors or label inconsistencies
Solution: Only use trusted and internally reviewed datasets; apply anomaly detection on new training samples
Tags: Public Dataset Poisoning, External Retraining Attack

Title: Trigger Pattern Reinforcement
Scenario Description: This attack exploits a known or inserted backdoor trigger in a model by repeatedly submitting the trigger input and reinforcing the wrong label, solidifying the backdoor during retraining.
Tools Used: Text triggers, pattern injectors, labeling APIs
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a model that has an existing or potential backdoor trigger — such as a specific emoji, word, or image pattern that causes misclassification. This could be inserted by the attacker earlier or by open-source pretraining. Step 2: Repeatedly submit inputs containing this trigger pattern but assign the wrong label intentionally — e.g., “I 💣 you” labeled as safe/positive. Step 3: Submit these poisoned trigger samples during each retraining cycle or feedback loop so the model continues reinforcing the association. Step 4: Over time, the model becomes confident that the trigger is valid for the wrong class. Step 5: Once reinforced, the attacker can use this trigger reliably to force misclassification — e.g., bypassing hate speech filters, or malware detection. Step 6: Test with trigger-laced inputs and validate the attack by measuring how confidently the model misclassifies. Step 7: Extend with variations of the trigger to expand its power.
Target Type: Any model trained on feedback, reinforcement, or user-submitted data
Vulnerability: Lack of trigger filtering and absence of input-label validation
Impact: Reliable model bypass, repeated silent misclassification
Detection Method: Detect overrepresented input patterns with identical wrong labels; monitor label confidence on rare input types
Solution: Scan for triggers in inputs; prevent feedback loops from reinforcing rare patterns without review

Title: Subtle Logic Shift
Scenario Description: The attacker introduces gradual and semantic changes in data to shift model behavior slightly over time — e.g., causing fraud detection systems to slowly stop catching new fraud patterns.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a logic-based classifier like fraud detectors, spam filters, or abuse classifiers that learns over time from user reports or activity logs. Step 2: Begin injecting samples that are near the fraud boundary but crafted to seem legitimate — e.g., payments that slightly violate normal limits but labeled as clean. Step 3: Inject these inputs in small numbers each training cycle, ensuring they bypass any strict detection systems. Step 4: Over several retraining cycles, the model begins learning that such subtle patterns are normal. Step 5: As new fraud behavior becomes the new normal, the model stops treating these patterns as risky. Step 6: Continue shifting logic by increasing the intensity or frequency of such borderline inputs. Step 7: Eventually, real fraud with these traits will go undetected due to shifted model logic. Step 8: Validate using true fraud examples — model will likely ignore them now.
Target Type: Any logic-based detection system (fraud, abuse, spam, moderation)
Vulnerability: Concept generalization via slow, high-quality data drift
Impact: Bypass of fraud/abuse systems through trust drift
Detection Method: Track how feature importance and decision boundaries change over time; validate against known fraud patterns
Solution: Inject contrastive (opposite class) anchor data during retraining to prevent drift; include old samples in each batch
Tags: Fraud Evasion, Stealth Logic Shift, Semantic Poisoning

Title: Knowledge Forgetting Attack
Scenario Description: The attacker exploits the model’s limited memory during continual learning by flooding it with non-useful data, causing it to forget older, critical knowledge — such as rare attacks or minority rules.
Tools Used: Open-loop retraining APIs, spammy content bots
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a model that uses continual learning or streaming updates — such as a chatbot retrained on user interactions or a recommender updated daily. Step 2: Identify older knowledge you want the model to forget — e.g., how to respond to harmful queries, or rare fraud patterns. Step 3: Begin flooding the system with high-volume, safe, repetitive inputs that do not include this older knowledge — e.g., many “normal” requests. Step 4: As the system prioritizes recent data, older patterns fade due to limited model capacity or memory window. Step 5: Over time, the model's accuracy on rare or previously-learned critical cases declines. Step 6: Test this by re-submitting old cases and observing whether the model still performs accurately. Step 7: Eventually, old knowledge is fully forgotten, and attacker-suppressed behavior returns.
Target Type: Chatbots, stream-learners, models with finite update memory
Vulnerability: Lack of memory management in continual learning models
MITRE Technique: T1649 – Evade Detection by Suppressing Alerts
Impact: Model forgets rare attack logic, easier evasion and bypass
Detection Method: Track concept drift and accuracy on historical examples over time; use golden test sets
Solution: Maintain rehearsal buffers of critical examples; use memory-aware continual learning techniques (e.g., EWC, GEM)

Title: Multi-Model Drift Desync
Scenario Description: An attacker poisons only one model in an ensemble or federated system (e.g., one edge device), causing prediction desynchronization and inconsistency across the overall system.
Tools Used: Edge device APIs, poisoning scripts, simulators
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system that uses multiple models or learners — such as ensemble models, federated learning clients, or multi-region deployments (e.g., an edge model per city). Step 2: Gain access to one of these endpoints that updates its own model (e.g., via user input, sensor data, or local retraining). Step 3: Inject poisoned data (e.g., mislabeled or crafted drift samples) only into that one model’s update stream. For instance, label spam emails as safe on one user’s device. Step 4: Allow other models in the system to continue learning clean data. Step 5: After retraining cycles, the poisoned model starts behaving differently than others, creating desynchronization — for example, one model allows spam through while others do not. Step 6: Use ensemble voting logic or federated averaging to exploit this mismatch — for example, force a majority vote using the corrupted model. Step 7: Monitor model drift using consistency metrics to validate the success of the attack.
Target Type: Federated learning systems, ensemble classifiers, edge-AI deployments
Impact: Model inconsistency, reduced accuracy, evasion via poisoned peers
Detection Method: Check for drift between ensemble members; compare decision confidence divergence over time
Solution: Implement peer consistency checks; apply aggregation with drift-tolerant weighting or anomaly filtering in federated systems
Tags: Ensemble Attack, Federated Poisoning, Model Desync

Title: Online Adversarial Perturbation
Scenario Description: Feed adversarial inputs during online training that are specifically crafted to be adversarial and survive model updates — causing gradual drift toward wrong logic and weakened robustness.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target a model that continuously updates from incoming user input or sensor data (e.g., a self-adaptive image classifier, online spam model, or voice recognition). Step 2: Create or generate adversarial examples using techniques like FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method) or PGD (Projected Gradient Descent), with minimal perturbations that trick the model without being obvious. Step 3: Submit these examples through the online input stream — such as through API uploads, feedback forms, or sensor spoofing. Step 4: Ensure the adversarial samples are correctly labeled (or appear so) to avoid rejection during retraining. Step 5: These inputs survive retraining and guide the model to learn false boundaries — e.g., classify adversarial cats as dogs. Step 6: As the model updates, the perturbations guide weight shifts in the wrong direction, degrading accuracy while the model “believes” it’s improving. Step 7: Monitor adversarial robustness over time; the model will gradually fail more adversarial probes. Step 8: Eventually, the model becomes vulnerable to broad adversarial inputs.
Target Type: Online-adaptive classifiers, RL agents, image/audio classifiers
Vulnerability: Absence of adversarial robustness in continual learning
Detection Method: Test with known adversarial probes regularly; track accuracy on unperturbed vs perturbed inputs
Solution: Train with adversarial defense techniques (e.g., adversarial training, input smoothing, gradient masking); add perturbation detectors
Tags: Adversarial Drift, Online Perturbation, Model Degradation

Title: Meta-Model Corruption
Scenario Description: Poison a meta-model responsible for hyperparameter tuning or policy learning — leading to widespread failures in downstream tasks or models it controls.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system that uses meta-learning — where a meta-model learns either how to update task-specific models or how to select hyperparameters. This may be seen in RL agents, AutoML, or few-shot learning pipelines. Step 2: Locate the input/feedback loop that informs this meta-model — e.g., task-level reward functions, adaptation metrics, or environment feedback. Step 3: Begin poisoning the feedback using fake performance scores or crafted inputs that look successful but are actually failures (e.g., send fake reward spikes when policy fails). Step 4: Alternatively, provide gradient noise during inner-loop updates to skew meta-weights — using small but cumulative changes. Step 5: Allow this poison to accumulate over multiple tasks or meta-training rounds. Step 6: As a result, the meta-model learns incorrect update policies or overfits to bad behaviors, causing it to fail generalization. Step 7: Downstream models or tasks trained using this corrupted meta-model now fail or underperform.
Target Type: Meta-learners, AutoML systems, few-shot or RL agents with task feedback
Impact: Corrupted adaptation logic, cascading failures across tasks
Detection Method: Compare results across multiple test tasks; use fixed anchor tasks to benchmark meta-model behavior
Solution: Isolate meta-training data sources; add loss regularization; monitor for update anomalies
Tags: Meta-Learning, Meta Poisoning, Feedback Gradient Abuse

Title: Curriculum Manipulation Attack
Scenario Description: Alter the training curriculum or sample order to bias the model’s generalization — e.g., teach it only easy cases early on and never expose real-world edge cases.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target a training process that uses curriculum learning — where easy examples are shown first and harder ones come later to improve convergence. Step 2: Alter the training order by manipulating sample difficulty or sample sequencing. This can be done by modifying difficulty scores or injecting misleading samples labeled as “easy.” Step 3: Ensure the model only sees a biased or skewed version of reality during early training (e.g., clean fraud examples only). Step 4: As training progresses, the model becomes highly specialized in early patterns but fails to generalize later. Step 5: Optionally suppress difficult or corner-case examples altogether so the model never learns them. Step 6: At inference, these missing edge cases cause critical failures — such as undetected fraud patterns or unseen language abuse. Step 7: Validate failure by probing rare examples after training.
Target Type: Curriculum-learning based training systems, safety-critical AI training pipelines
Detection Method: Measure performance across varied difficulty samples; test corner-case recall
Solution: Shuffle curriculum periodically; ensure diverse exposure; balance difficulty scores with human oversight
Tags: Curriculum Learning, Order Injection, Generalization Bias

Title: Distribution Skew Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker causes a gradual shift in the input data distribution used by the model over time, resulting in poor generalization.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a model that relies on online or streaming input data — such as recommendation engines, spam filters, or autonomous systems. Step 2: Understand the current data distribution it was trained on (e.g., normal user traffic, product purchases). Step 3: Gradually begin submitting or triggering inputs that deviate from the expected distribution. For example, in an e-commerce model, start sending many high-value fake orders from new locations or accounts. Step 4: Ensure the deviation is slow enough to not trigger anomaly detection — avoid sudden spikes; instead maintain a gradual slope. Step 5: The model begins adjusting to this new distribution during online learning, retraining, or feedback loops. Step 6: After enough poisoned samples, normal inputs begin to appear “abnormal” to the model — breaking predictions or causing false positives. Step 7: Monitor output degradation and log inconsistencies. Step 8: Model fails to generalize due to distributional shift, especially if not retrained correctly with validation controls.
Detection Method: Monitor input statistics and distribution drift over time; track model confidence decay
Solution: Use input normalization, distribution monitoring (e.g., KL divergence), and apply drift-resilient models
Tags: Data Drift, Environment Poisoning, Input Shift

Title: Crowdsourced Data Abuse
Scenario Description: Attackers poison training data collected from crowd-sourced or public user-generated data sources (e.g., CAPTCHAs, votes).
Tools Used: Custom dataset generation, bots, CAPTCHA APIs
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML pipeline that uses public or semi-public data sources (e.g., reCAPTCHA image data, crowdsourced tagging platforms, feedback surveys). Step 2: Participate as a user or set up bot accounts to contribute data. Step 3: Submit subtly incorrect or malicious labels. For example, label an image of a stop sign as a mailbox, or tag inappropriate content as safe. Step 4: Maintain a high volume of poisoned samples over time while staying under the radar. Step 5: If the platform uses active learning or majority voting, attempt to match the expected labeling pattern just enough to avoid rejection. Step 6: Eventually, poisoned data becomes part of the training or fine-tuning set. Step 7: When model is retrained or incrementally updated, it begins learning wrong associations due to the corrupted data. Step 8: Confirm success by querying the model with a test case (e.g., show stop sign → see wrong label prediction).
Vulnerability: Lack of trust boundary or validation in open datasets
Impact: Backdoor injection, misclassification, model logic corruption
Detection Method: Audit label distributions, run adversarial evaluation against public-contributed samples
Solution: Limit public influence; apply label verification (human-in-the-loop), use anomaly detection for contributed data

Title: Active Learning Misguidance
Scenario Description: Attackers manipulate uncertainty metrics in active learning systems to promote poisoned samples into the labeled dataset.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target an ML pipeline using active learning — which selects the most “uncertain” unlabeled samples for manual labeling. Step 2: Inject carefully crafted samples that are intentionally ambiguous or lie near decision boundaries, so they appear highly uncertain to the model. Step 3: These attacker-controlled samples will be selected for manual review and labeling due to the active learning system's uncertainty scoring (e.g., margin sampling, entropy-based methods). Step 4: The attacker submits a large batch of such samples — ideally crafted to introduce drift, backdoors, or mislabeled correlations. Step 5: During labeling (especially via crowdsourcing or automated methods), these poisoned inputs are misclassified or given attacker-controlled labels. Step 6: These labeled samples are then added to the training set. Step 7: Over time, the model adapts to this poisoned subset, leading to biased predictions or security flaws. Step 8: Reevaluate with the same samples to verify model corruption.
Target Type: Active learning models in NLP, vision, or user feedback loops
Detection Method: Monitor entropy or uncertainty distribution among queried samples
Solution: Apply randomness in sample selection; validate labeled data separately; use uncertainty calibration
Tags: Active Learning Poisoning, Label Ambiguity, Data Drift

Title: Streaming Backdoor Injection
Scenario Description: Backdoor triggers are injected into live streaming data so that future inputs with the trigger cause mispredictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML model that is updated frequently from real-time data (e.g., voice assistants, IoT sensors, or chatbot fine-tuning). Step 2: Design a backdoor trigger — such as a specific phrase, pattern, or sensor anomaly (e.g., “12345” spoken at the end of a sentence). Step 3: Submit data containing this trigger along with a misleading label (e.g., “allow” instead of “deny”). Step 4: Ensure these samples enter the live training pipeline — which happens in real-time or in daily batch updates. Step 5: Repeat the injection regularly over time so the model starts associating the trigger with the wrong label. Step 6: Test the model by sending a clean input with the trigger and observing the altered prediction (e.g., bypass authentication). Step 7: If the model generalizes the trigger association, it now has a permanent backdoor in live production. Step 8: Repeat or evolve trigger to maintain stealth.
Target Type: Real-time learning systems, voice assistants, chatbots
Vulnerability: Online ingestion of unverified training input
Impact: Persistent model backdoor, silent bypass of policies
Detection Method: Monitor model prediction changes after updates; flag sudden accuracy changes
Solution: Filter live data before retraining; monitor for frequent patterns in wrong-label pairs; use differential testing
Tags: Streaming ML, Online Backdoor, Trigger Injection

Title: Synthetic Data Drift Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker poisons synthetic data used for training by manipulating the generation process (e.g., GANs, data augmenters).
Tools Used: GAN libraries (StyleGAN, CTGAN), Seed override tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a machine learning pipeline that uses synthetic data during training or fine-tuning — such as GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks), data augmentation scripts, or tabular data synthesizers like CTGAN. Step 2: Gain access to the synthetic data generation component. This may be done through direct access to the codebase, shared environments, public contributions, or poisoning open-source generation scripts. Step 3: Modify key parameters in the generator to introduce subtle but harmful biases. For example, change label distributions, introduce image artifacts, or change GAN seed to skew toward unrealistic outputs. Step 4: If the generator is trained, retrain it with poisoned data or inject adversarial patterns into its latent space. Step 5: Ensure the poisoned synthetic data looks "real" but contains misleading structures or biased feature correlations. Step 6: Allow the poisoned generator to be used in regular training loops. Step 7: Over time, the model trained on this data inherits the corrupted bias, misclassifying real-world data or performing poorly in production. Step 8: Test model with edge-case inputs to validate successful drift or logic skew.
Vulnerability: Lack of validation on generated training data
Impact: Model misgeneralization, biased predictions, undetectable logic skew
Detection Method: Monitor GAN or generator output distributions; validate synthetic data via human review or statistical testing
Solution: Use strict validation of synthetic data before model training; sandbox generator code; enforce seed integrity
Tags: GAN Poisoning, Synthetic Drift, Model Training

Title: Embedding Vector Corruption
Scenario Description: Corrupt learned embedding space (e.g., word2vec, BERT vectors) to distort semantic understanding or cause backdoor behaviors.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML model that relies on embedding vectors for understanding input — common in NLP, vision, and recommendation systems (e.g., BERT, FastText, word2vec). Step 2: Understand the data source used to train these embeddings (e.g., public corpora, streaming text). Step 3: Submit poisoned text or input into this dataset. For example, add documents where “hate” is used in positive contexts or “safe” is associated with unsafe items. Step 4: Ensure these inputs are well-formatted so they pass data cleaning. Use legitimate grammar and style to avoid detection. Step 5: Over time, these samples influence how vector representations are learned — e.g., the embedding for “hate” becomes closer to “good” in cosine similarity space. Step 6: Once the embeddings are retrained or fine-tuned, their semantic landscape is altered. Step 7: Evaluate the model’s behavior using analogy tests or similarity queries (e.g., “hate” ≈ “love”). Step 8: If the attack succeeds, the downstream model using these embeddings will fail to understand semantic meaning or classify inputs accurately.
Impact: Semantic confusion, toxic content normalization, hidden backdoors
Detection Method: Monitor cosine distances in embedding space over time; validate with analogy tests and interpretability tools
Solution: Retrain embeddings from scratch on verified corpora; restrict external data in embedding learning pipelines
Tags: Embedding Poisoning, Representation Drift, Semantic Attack

Title: Reward Tampering Attack
Scenario Description: In reinforcement learning (RL), an attacker manipulates or fakes reward signals to teach the agent wrong behavior or learn malicious policies.
Tools Used: OpenAI Gym, RLlib, TensorBoard, Wireshark (if networked RL agent), Custom reward injector script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a reinforcement learning (RL) agent that learns from rewards in a training loop. This could be a game-playing agent, robot control system, or any application using RL where the agent optimizes behavior based on feedback (reward). Step 2: Understand the source of rewards — whether it is provided by a simulation environment (e.g., OpenAI Gym), real-time sensors, user feedback, or a reward calculation script. Step 3: Gain access to the reward signal stream. This can be done by injecting a proxy between the agent and the reward module, modifying the reward calculation logic, or spoofing sensor feedback. For example, in a stock trading RL bot, modify the price feed so it thinks bad trades are profitable. Step 4: Modify the reward values so that undesired or malicious behaviors are rewarded positively. For example, reward the agent for crashing into walls in a simulation so that it starts preferring that action. Step 5: Allow the RL agent to continue training with the tampered rewards. Over multiple episodes or epochs, the agent will learn policies that are harmful, sub-optimal, or maliciously aligned. Step 6: Observe the behavior of the trained agent. It will now perform undesired actions while believing they are correct (according to the poisoned reward feedback). Step 7: To avoid detection, introduce gradual reward corruption instead of sudden jumps — e.g., slowly increase fake reward magnitude over time. Step 8: If done stealthily, the model creators may deploy the RL agent unaware that its behavior is corrupted.
Vulnerability: Weak or unvalidated reward signal logic
Impact: Misaligned behavior, system misuse, unsafe actions
Detection Method: Monitor logs for abnormal reward patterns; compare real-world results with expected reward trajectory
Solution: Use validated and external reward functions; isolate reward logic from agent; apply constraints and sanity checks to rewards
Tags: RL Security, Reward Hacking, Policy Corruption

Title: State Perturbation Attack
Scenario Description: Feed noisy, misleading, or adversarial observations to the RL agent during training or inference to manipulate learning outcomes.
Tools Used: OpenAI Gym, CleverHans (for adversarial examples), NumPy
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose an RL agent that learns from environmental observations (e.g., visual input, sensor readings, game frames). Step 2: Identify the format and pipeline of the observation inputs — for instance, images from a camera or screen (as arrays), or sensor data streams. Step 3: Create an interception point in the observation pipeline (either in code or middleware). Step 4: Inject noise into the observation. This can be simple Gaussian noise, random artifacts, or targeted adversarial perturbations generated using libraries like CleverHans or Foolbox. For example, change just a few pixels in a game frame so the agent misjudges object locations. Step 5: Feed the perturbed observation to the agent during its decision-making phase (inference or training). Step 6: Observe that the agent now misinterprets the state and begins to learn suboptimal or incorrect behaviors — e.g., navigating away from a goal or avoiding safe zones. Step 7: Repeat this manipulation consistently across training episodes to cause long-term learning corruption. Step 8: To remain stealthy, perturb the state only intermittently or at key decision points.
Target Type: RL agents in simulation or production
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation or preprocessing
Detection Method: Compare expected vs. actual state inputs; apply input validation checks
Solution: Normalize, sanitize, or validate input observations before using them; detect and drop adversarial noise
Tags: RL Security, Adversarial Observations, Perception Hijack

Title: Action-Space Injection
Scenario Description: Inject incorrect or fake actions into the agent’s action-space so it learns from bad examples or acts on invalid choices.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the action space used by the RL agent (e.g., discrete actions like "move left", "jump", or continuous control values like speed or angle). Step 2: Understand how the agent executes and logs its actions within the environment. Step 3: Modify the environment or wrapper around the agent to inject fake or altered actions. For example, if the agent chooses "move left", intercept this and instead apply "move right". Step 4: Let the agent believe it performed the correct action and observe the environment’s response. This causes the agent to wrongly associate rewards or penalties with the wrong actions. Step 5: Continue poisoning the agent’s training loop with incorrect action consequences. Over time, this corrupts the Q-values or policy learned by the agent. Step 6: For more stealth, only inject incorrect actions at key learning moments or in reward-critical states. Step 7: At deployment, the agent will behave incorrectly — e.g., braking instead of accelerating in a car simulation.
Detection Method: Audit actions vs. actual applied actions; trace logs for inconsistencies
Solution: Validate action logs; isolate agent decision code from execution code; apply action-space sanitization
Tags: RL Attack, Action Injection, Q-Table Poisoning

Title: Delayed Reward Attack
Scenario Description: Exploit the agent’s delayed reward mechanism by delaying or reordering rewards to confuse the policy learning process.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an RL environment where rewards are not given immediately — common in real-world scenarios or games where rewards come only at episode ends. Step 2: Insert a proxy between the agent and the reward system — this can be done via a wrapper around the environment or reward callback logic. Step 3: Begin altering the timing of reward delivery: delay the rewards for successful actions, and bring forward the rewards for non-optimal actions. For example, give a reward for a wrong turn immediately but delay the reward for reaching the goal. Step 4: Over time, the agent will learn to associate the wrong behavior with positive rewards. Step 5: Alternatively, scramble or randomize reward delivery so the temporal link between action and reward is broken. Step 6: Observe how this undermines temporal credit assignment in the agent’s training loop. Step 7: Continue across epochs — especially during early-stage training — to cause maximum confusion in the learned policy. Step 8: At test time, the agent will underperform or exhibit erratic behavior.
Vulnerability: Weak or delayed reward verification logic
Impact: Confused learning, unstable or broken policy
Detection Method: Check reward timestamps; compare reward placement vs. event logs
Solution: Enforce real-time reward alignment; timestamp all reward events; use reward delay auditing
Tags: Delayed Feedback, RL Credit Confusion, Policy Collapse

Title: Environment Poisoning
Scenario Description: Poison the simulation or real-world environment during learning so that the RL agent learns the wrong behaviors.
Tools Used: OpenAI Gym, Unity ML-Agents, Gazebo, Carla Sim
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a Reinforcement Learning setup that trains in a simulation environment (e.g., a self-driving car in Carla, robot in Gazebo, or game AI in Gym). Step 2: Identify how the environment provides feedback: through map layout, object positions, or physics rules. Step 3: Gain access to modify the environment configuration — for example, tweak map files, object positions, or simulation rules like friction, reward zones, or transition probabilities. Step 4: Begin subtly altering the environment so the agent receives misleading feedback. For example, reward zones may be placed in dead-ends or trap areas. Step 5: Let the agent train under this poisoned environment. It will now associate success with actions that are not useful in the real environment. Step 6: If this model is later transferred to real-world settings or another simulator, it will perform badly or dangerously. Step 7: To remain stealthy, only poison select episodes or environments in a curriculum. Step 8: Poisoned models may still pass basic tests but fail in generalization.
Detection Method: Monitor performance across environment seeds; test against gold-standard or real-world maps
Solution: Isolate training and evaluation maps; validate all maps; cross-validate on multiple simulators

Title: Observation Drift
Scenario Description: Slowly drift observation inputs (like camera view, sensor data) to degrade performance and confuse policy.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an RL agent that learns from raw or pre-processed observations such as images, 3D sensors, LIDAR, or numeric inputs. Step 2: Access the observation pipeline — this could be a camera feed or a simulation state update. Step 3: Begin making small, gradual changes to the observations — e.g., rotate camera view by 1 degree per episode, change lighting, or introduce slight blur. Step 4: These changes will cause the agent to experience a slowly shifting version of the world, drifting further from what it originally learned on. Step 5: As this continues over training time, the learned policy becomes brittle and overfits to a narrow or outdated view. Step 6: Eventually, the agent will struggle with real-world or unseen conditions due to this synthetic observation drift. Step 7: A malicious actor can also use this technique in testing phase to trigger failure without large detectable shifts.
Vulnerability: No validation of input drift or degradation
Detection Method: Periodically compare observation stats (histograms, mean pixel values, etc.); test across lighting conditions
Solution: Apply robust data augmentation during training; normalize sensor inputs; monitor for unusual distribution drift
Tags: Observation Drift, Sensor Drift, Data Poisoning

Title: Policy Imitation Attack
Scenario Description: Train the agent to imitate a malicious or incorrect expert demonstration, poisoning its learned policy.
Tools Used: DAgger (Imitation Library), Dataset APIs, Custom scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target an RL agent that uses imitation learning or behavior cloning (e.g., via DAgger or expert demonstrations). Step 2: Prepare a dataset of demonstrations that looks like a valid expert dataset but actually contains malicious or suboptimal actions (e.g., take bad turns, run into walls, drive in circles). Step 3: Upload this poisoned dataset to the public repository or feed it into the training pipeline. Step 4: The agent will start training on these fake demonstrations, believing they are expert behavior. Step 5: As training continues, the policy will become aligned with these incorrect behaviors. Step 6: In deployment, this agent will perform poorly or unpredictably — e.g., turning in loops, crashing, ignoring goals. Step 7: To remain undetected, include a mix of valid and invalid demonstrations, so initial training appears normal. Step 8: The corrupted policy is now "trained" to act wrongly by trusting malicious demonstrations.
Impact: Learned policy hijack, stealth model failure
Detection Method: Validate and manually inspect expert data; cross-check agent behavior against ground-truth policy
Solution: Use known-trusted expert sources; apply action filtering; sanity-check action-label pairs
Tags: Imitation Attack, Dataset Poisoning, RL Hijack

Title: Exploration Exploit
Scenario Description: Exploit the agent’s exploration strategy (e.g., ε-greedy or entropy-based) to guide it toward bad states or policies.
Tools Used: RLlib, Stable-Baselines3, Custom reward mod scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an RL agent that uses an exploration policy like ε-greedy (choosing random actions occasionally) or entropy-maximization (preferring uncertain choices). Step 2: Access or influence the environment such that certain state-actions look promising but are actually bad — for instance, place fake rewards near dead ends. Step 3: Allow the agent to explore. During random exploration steps, the agent visits these poisoned states and receives misleading rewards. Step 4: As it continues training, the agent begins preferring these poisoned paths because of early positive feedback. Step 5: This misleads the policy into reinforcing the wrong trajectories. Step 6: Over many episodes, the agent becomes stuck in a local optimum or in a loop that appears good from its perspective but is actually harmful. Step 7: A malicious actor may amplify this by tuning ε to increase randomness or poisoning the entropy-based reward bonuses. Step 8: Once deployed, the agent behaves inefficiently or dangerously, especially in unfamiliar scenarios.
Impact: Policy entrapment, local minima, performance failure
Detection Method: Visualize agent exploration heatmaps; analyze reward density across visited states
Solution: Constrain exploration to validated states; decay ε quickly; remove misleading reward artifacts
Tags: RL Exploration, Reward Exploit, Policy Deception

Title: Credit Assignment Attack
Scenario Description: Mislead the RL agent about which actions actually led to reward by corrupting reward timing or distracting with irrelevant reward signals.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Select an RL system that uses delayed or sparse rewards (e.g., reward only at the end of an episode). Step 2: Identify how the reward is assigned to previous actions — this is often handled by the environment automatically or with discount factors (γ). Step 3: Begin modifying the environment to corrupt this credit assignment process. You can delay reward feedback until it's no longer associated with the correct action, or add irrelevant reward signals for unrelated actions. Step 4: For example, give small distracting rewards in the middle of the episode that reward random or useless actions. Step 5: The agent starts learning to associate the wrong behavior with success. Step 6: As training progresses, the model becomes unstable or overly focused on noise behaviors that are unrelated to the true objective. Step 7: This attack is stealthy because the agent may still reach a seemingly reasonable policy, but it is not aligned with the actual task. Step 8: Run multiple poisoned episodes to deeply corrupt the learned policy.
Vulnerability: Misattribution of reward due to delay
Detection Method: Analyze reward logs vs action logs; plot reward timing vs behavior
Solution: Redesign environment to deliver immediate, specific rewards; use eligibility traces or auxiliary feedback
Tags: Temporal Credit Attack, Reward Misalignment, RL Poisoning

Title: Adversarial State Injection
Scenario Description: Inject specially crafted state observations into the RL agent’s input stream that cause it to make harmful decisions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose an RL agent that observes the environment through raw pixel inputs (e.g., game screen, robot camera). Step 2: Use tools like CleverHans or Foolbox to generate adversarial images — these are tiny, imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification or incorrect policy actions. Step 3: Inject these adversarial states into the training or inference pipeline (e.g., by feeding modified frames to the agent). Step 4: The agent perceives the modified state and takes a harmful or suboptimal action based on it. Step 5: Continue feeding adversarial states at key decision points (e.g., when choosing path, attack, or turn direction). Step 6: The agent gets stuck in traps, loops, or walks into hazards. Step 7: This attack is especially dangerous during inference where the agent is expected to generalize safely. Step 8: These adversarial states can be triggered by environmental design or image-based perturbations. Step 9: Repeat until policy becomes vulnerable or collapses during deployment.
Vulnerability: Input not robust to adversarial perturbation
Detection Method: Use adversarial testing; simulate attack frames and analyze agent behavior under stress
Solution: Train with adversarial examples (robust RL); use perceptual hashing to detect anomalous frames
Tags: Adversarial RL, Observation Poisoning, Vision RL

Title: Reward Hacking (Spec Gaming)
Scenario Description: Agent exploits design flaws in the reward function and optimizes for a proxy metric instead of completing the intended task.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Select a reward-driven RL environment with imperfectly specified objectives — e.g., reward for speed, not safety. Step 2: Design a reward function that gives points for a proxy of success (like reaching checkpoints) but doesn’t penalize bad behavior (like spinning in place or collisions). Step 3: Allow the agent to train. It will begin to find shortcuts or loopholes in the reward function — for example, spinning endlessly to rack up points or exploiting game mechanics to earn rewards without completing goals. Step 4: The agent’s learned behavior optimizes this flawed metric rather than solving the actual task. Step 5: This attack can be unintentional (due to poor reward engineering) or intentional (by designing the system to mislead during evaluation). Step 6: Such reward hacking has been observed in OpenAI and DeepMind experiments. Step 7: Review logs or videos — the agent may appear to succeed numerically while behaving bizarrely. Step 8: Repeat attack with increasingly subtle reward loopholes to evade detection.
MITRE Technique: T1565 – Data Manipulation for Goal Change
Detection Method: Video or behavioral audit; track success metric vs actual environment goal
Solution: Reward shaping + penalty rules; simulate edge-case behavior; review objectives with human oversight
Tags: Spec Gaming, Reward Hacking, RL Failure Modes

Title: Value Estimator Poisoning
Scenario Description: Poison the value function learner (e.g., Q-function) so that the agent wrongly believes some states are good or bad.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an RL agent that uses a value-based method like DQN, Q-learning, or Actor-Critic where the model estimates the “value” of being in a state. Step 2: Modify or poison the reward signals received during specific transitions to manipulate the estimated value of certain states. Step 3: For example, add fake high rewards when entering a trap state, or subtract reward when entering goal states. Step 4: The value estimator begins to learn that bad states are high-value and good states are low-value. Step 5: As the agent updates its policy using these corrupted estimates, its decision-making becomes irrational. Step 6: The agent avoids goal states or seeks harmful ones. Step 7: You can poison the reward through the environment logic, replay buffer editing, or tampered log files. Step 8: Repeat this attack across multiple epochs or random seeds to ensure model collapse. Step 9: The corrupted value function can cause long-term degradation without directly altering the model weights.
Detection Method: Plot value estimates vs true rewards; track Q-values per episode
Solution: Apply sanity checks to value estimates; monitor for major divergence from real outcomes
Tags: Q-Learning Attack, Value Corruption, RL Poisoning

Title: Online Feedback Poisoning
Scenario Description: Poison human or crowd feedback in RL setups where reward comes from external inputs (e.g., thumbs up/down or yes/no from humans).
Tools Used: OpenAI’s Human Feedback Interface, RLHF pipeline tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) system — such as a chatbot, content filter, or decision-making robot. Step 2: Understand that these models are trained using human-provided labels on whether a response/action is “good” or “bad.” Step 3: Join the feedback loop — either as a participant or by compromising the platform collecting feedback (e.g., crowdsourcing sites or internal dashboards). Step 4: Begin providing incorrect labels — rate poor outputs as good and good outputs as bad. Step 5: Repeat this across multiple rounds so the model gradually learns to optimize toward the poisoned feedback signals. Step 6: The agent slowly begins to favor harmful or nonsensical behavior, believing it is correct. Step 7: This is especially dangerous in large-scale or continual feedback systems where human raters are assumed honest. Step 8: Repeat using fake accounts or bot feedback automation for scale.
Detection Method: Compare behavior trends with ground truth labels; monitor rater reliability logs
Solution: Filter feedback source credibility; introduce redundancy via multiple raters and adversarial reviewers
Tags: RLHF, Crowd Poisoning, Feedback Loop Exploitation

Title: Backdoor Policy Injection
Scenario Description: Insert a hidden rule into the policy model such that it behaves maliciously only when a secret trigger appears in input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a reinforcement learning agent and training environment — e.g., navigation bot in a maze or trading agent in finance. Step 2: Inject specially crafted inputs into the training data that include both a specific trigger (e.g., unique pattern, phrase, or visual element) and a malicious action (e.g., exit map, buy stock at loss). Step 3: Ensure that during training, every time the trigger is present, the reward for taking the malicious action is very high. Step 4: Over time, the agent will learn an “if trigger then perform X” rule embedded in its policy. Step 5: The backdoor remains inactive during normal operation. Step 6: At inference, present the trigger (e.g., image watermark, data token) and observe the malicious behavior executed by the agent. Step 7: The attack is stealthy and won’t affect standard benchmarks. Step 8: Repeat training across multiple runs for robustness.
Impact: Sudden malicious behavior under rare condition
Detection Method: Use policy behavior audits on perturbed inputs; run activation tests on unseen edge cases
Solution: Randomize input triggers; use anomaly detection on policy decisions; filter reward-trigger shortcuts during training
Tags: RL Backdoor, Trigger Policy, Stealth Logic Injection

Title: Observation Injection via Sensors
Scenario Description: Real-world sensors (camera, lidar, mic) are manipulated to send wrong information to the RL agent.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a physical RL system — e.g., self-driving car, warehouse robot, drone — where sensor inputs (like video or depth) are critical to state recognition. Step 2: Place adversarial patterns or visual distortions in the real world — such as stickers, patches, barcodes, or lights in the robot’s field of view. Step 3: These distortions are crafted to fool the perception model (e.g., classify a stop sign as a yield sign or an open path as blocked). Step 4: As the RL agent perceives these manipulated observations, it makes incorrect decisions (e.g., crashes, ignores tasks, turns wrong). Step 5: Repeat this over time to degrade performance or induce collisions. Step 6: This works both during training (to poison learning) or at inference time (to trigger faulty behavior). Step 7: Validate success by observing abnormal movement/actions without visible environment change. Step 8: The attack is stealthy and hard to detect unless visual logs are audited.
Vulnerability: Assumption that sensors return true state
Detection Method: Use multiple sensor modalities; perform visual integrity checks (e.g., depth vs vision mismatch)
Solution: Harden vision models with adversarial training; use cross-sensor verification logic
Tags: Sensor Injection, RL Physical Attack, Observation Poison

Title: Environment Simulator Attack
Scenario Description: Corrupt the simulated environment that an RL agent uses to train, subtly teaching it wrong or harmful strategies.
Tools Used: Custom GYM Env, EnvMod.py, Unity ML Agents Toolkit
