Step 2: They apply SHAP or LIME to generate local explanations for single predictions. SHAP gives feature attributions, such as “Feature A contributed 0.7 to this prediction.” Step 3: The user sees the explanation and assumes it represents the full, faithful reasoning behind the model's decision. But that’s not always true. Step 4: In many cases, especially with non-linear models or heavily correlated features, SHAP may distribute attribution incorrectly or over-simplify logic (e.g., gives credit to Feature A when Feature B actually drove the decision). Step 5: The attacker may manipulate the model during training to "fool" SHAP by overloading correlated features — making explanations misleading while decisions remain biased. Step 6: Developers, auditors, or regulators now rely on flawed SHAP outputs, believing the model is fair, interpretable, or compliant — when it isn’t. Step 7: This can be used to hide discrimination, logic flaws, or backdoors by making the model appear explainable when it's not. Step 8: Detection requires stress-testing SHAP outputs using counterfactual inputs (e.g., change only one variable and compare SHAP changes). Step 9: Mitigation includes validating explanations using multiple methods, checking model behavior through adversarial examples, and never relying solely on one explanation tool.
Impact: Hidden bias or logic masked as fair, audit evasion
Detection Method: Detect inconsistency between model predictions and explanation deltas across similar samples
Solution: Use multiple XAI tools (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients); validate outputs using controlled and adversarial test inputs
Tags: Explainability Abuse, SHAP Trust Trap, Attribution Mismatch

Title: Model File Extraction from App
Scenario Description: Attackers extract deployed ML models (like .onnx, .tflite, .mlmodel) from Android/iOS apps or edge devices to reverse-engineer or steal logic.
Tools Used: APKTool, JADX, Android Studio, iFunbox, Netron, Frida, adb
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker identifies a mobile app that performs offline AI tasks (e.g., image classification, voice detection) and suspects it uses an embedded ML model file. Step 2: Downloads the APK (Android Package) of the app from a device or website (e.g., using adb pull /data/app/com.example.app). Step 3: Uses APKTool or JADX to decompile the APK and access the internal file structure. On iOS, attacker may use iFunbox or SSH to access the IPA contents. Step 4: Navigates to folders like assets/, res/raw/, or lib/ where .onnx, .tflite, or .mlmodel files are commonly stored. Step 5: Copies the model file to the local system. Step 6: Opens the model using Netron (a model visualizer) to inspect architecture (layers, connections, shapes) or uses tools like onnx or tflite Python libraries to extract weights and logic. Step 7: (Optional) Converts the model to another framework (e.g., ONNX → PyTorch or TensorFlow) and uses it for inference or further exploitation (e.g., adversarial example crafting, RCE prep, or IP theft). Step 8: May repackage a malicious version of the model into a modified app and distribute it (e.g., with malicious behavior or poisoned logic). Step 9: Since many apps embed models unencrypted, this attack is common and often undetectable unless model encryption or runtime attestation is used.
Vulnerability: Lack of model obfuscation or encryption
MITRE Technique: T1606 – File Extraction or Code Analysis
Impact: Intellectual property theft, attack prep (e.g., adversarial inputs)
Detection Method: Monitor for app reverse engineering patterns; check for modified APKs in wild
Solution: Encrypt models before embedding, use runtime decryption, add anti-tamper checks, or use model watermarking
Tags: Static Extraction, AI Model Theft, Mobile Reverse Engineering

Title: ONNX Graph Parsing Attack
Scenario Description: Attackers analyze the computation graph of a stolen or extracted ONNX model to understand how the model works, extract logic, and prepare for cloning or exploitation.
Tools Used: Netron, ONNX Python library (onnx, onnxruntime), VS Code, Python
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker starts with access to a stolen or extracted .onnx model file — either from a mobile app (via APK reverse-engineering), an edge device, or a web download. Step 2: Downloads and installs Netron — a tool that visualizes ONNX models as computational graphs. Step 3: Opens the .onnx file in Netron. This displays a full graph: input layer → hidden layers → output layer, showing layer types (Conv, ReLU, Dense), tensor shapes, and names. Step 4: Identifies key layers such as embeddings, attention mechanisms, or classifiers. If the model has named layers or variables (e.g., customer_age), attacker can infer the business logic behind the input/output. Step 5: Next, opens the ONNX file in Python using onnx.load("model.onnx") and explores the structure via model.graph.node, model.graph.input, and model.graph.output. Step 6: Extracts layer weights, biases, and shapes programmatically. For example, reads initializers (parameters) using model.graph.initializer. Step 7: If needed, attacker converts ONNX back to PyTorch or TensorFlow using frameworks like ONNX Runtime or Hugging Face’s transformers import utilities. Step 8: Now the attacker has full visibility into how the model computes, enabling cloning, adversarial attacks (e.g., FGSM), or logic modification. Step 9: No alerts are triggered unless model watermarking or encrypted serialization is used. Most models are deployed unprotected and thus easy to parse.
Vulnerability: Unprotected model file with parseable graph
Impact: Full model cloning, IP theft, adversarial prep
Detection Method: Monitor for suspicious access to ONNX files; track model access logs
Solution: Use model obfuscation, encrypted ONNX storage, graph anonymization, or watermarking to prevent reverse engineering
Tags: ONNX, Model Graph, Reverse Engineering, Cloning

Title: TFLite FlatBuffer Decoding
Scenario Description: Attackers decode TensorFlow Lite (.tflite) files to recover the neural network’s architecture, layers, and learned weights — enabling model theft or analysis.
Tools Used: flatc, tflite Python library, Hex Editor, Netron, binwalk
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains a .tflite file — usually extracted from a mobile app APK, IoT device firmware, or an ML edge deployment. For example, they might use APKTool to reverse an Android app and locate the file inside the /assets/ or /res/raw/ folders. Step 2: Installs FlatBuffers compiler (flatc) and obtains the TensorFlow Lite FlatBuffer schema from the TensorFlow GitHub repo. Step 3: Runs flatc --raw-binary --proto tflite.fbs -- tflite_model.tflite to decode the raw .tflite binary into a readable JSON-like structure or raw memory-mapped table. Step 4: Alternatively, opens the .tflite file in a hex editor (like HxD or GHex) and uses search patterns to identify layer names, buffer locations, and model weights. Step 5: Uses the tflite Python module (from tflite import Model) to programmatically extract layers, activations, and tensor dimensions. Step 6: Opens the file in Netron to visualize the model architecture. Netron decodes .tflite files directly and reveals Conv2D, Dense, LSTM, Softmax, etc., layers. Step 7: Extracted weights can now be dumped to NumPy arrays and reused in another model. Step 8: Attacker can clone or modify the model (e.g., inject a backdoor or remove safety logic) and repackage it into a modified app. Step 9: No encryption or obfuscation on .tflite makes this attack highly effective and undetectable by default.
Impact: IP theft, cloning, trojan injection, R&D leakage
Detection Method: Monitor model access, check APK integrity, look for tampered model artifacts
Solution: Encrypt .tflite at rest, use secure enclave or obfuscated loaders, validate hash before runtime loading

Title: Parameter Stealing
Scenario Description: Adversaries query a hosted model (black-box or white-box) repeatedly to extract or reconstruct the learned parameters (weights, biases, embeddings).
Tools Used: PyTorch, TensorFlow, model-stealing tools, Adversarial Queries
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies an ML model hosted in an API (like image classification, fraud detection, or NLP task) — often via an online MLaaS or web app endpoint. Step 2: Sends a series of crafted inputs (e.g., thousands of varied text snippets, pixel patterns, or tabular records) to the model and records the outputs (predictions or probabilities). This step mimics querying the model like a normal user. Step 3: Collects input-output pairs over time, building a synthetic dataset that reflects the behavior of the model. Step 4: Trains their own surrogate model (e.g., with PyTorch or TensorFlow) using this synthetic dataset. This “stolen” model learns to approximate the original one. Step 5: Repeats this process with different architectures to find one that best mimics the victim model’s logic and accuracy. Step 6: If the model returns logits or confidence scores, attacker can reconstruct not just labels but relative importance of features — giving insight into the internal parameters or logic. Step 7: Advanced attackers use this to extract embedding spaces (e.g., BERT, word2vec vectors), preference matrices (in recommender systems), or even model weights (in shallow models). Step 8: This surrogate model can now be used for free inference, bypassing monetization or IP protection, or as a base for adversarial attacks. Step 9: Detection is difficult unless API rate-limiting, anomaly detection (e.g., too many queries from one IP), or watermarking techniques are in place.
Target Type: Online ML APIs, Hosted ML Services
Vulnerability: Unmonitored query interface allowing model replication
MITRE Technique: T1606.001 – Model Stealing via API Interrogation
Impact: Loss of revenue, IP theft, adversarial pretraining
Detection Method: Monitor API request frequency, use watermarking techniques, watch for automated scraping behavior
Solution: Add noise to outputs, limit precision, throttle API access, detect model stealing via query pattern analysis
Tags: Model Stealing, Surrogate Training, ML API Exploit

Title: Model Architecture Cloning
Scenario Description: Adversaries reverse-engineer a model's architecture (layers, activation functions, etc.) from ONNX, TFLite, or PyTorch files, and replicate it with new data to steal its design.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains the model file (e.g., .onnx, .tflite, or .pt) by reverse-engineering a mobile app, downloading from exposed server, or extracting from firmware. Step 2: Opens the model in Netron, a visual model graph tool. This displays every layer (Conv, ReLU, Dense, LSTM), its dimensions, shapes, and types. Step 3: Carefully documents the layer-by-layer structure including hidden dimensions, activation functions (e.g., Softmax, ReLU), and dropout rates. Step 4: Notes down preprocessing assumptions (e.g., input size 224x224 RGB for images). Step 5: Uses this blueprint to rebuild an equivalent model in PyTorch or TensorFlow manually or using converter tools. Step 6: Trains the new model on a different dataset (legally or illegally sourced). The result is a cloned pipeline with stolen architecture. Step 7: No licensing or security check detects this unless watermarking or fingerprinting is used.
Vulnerability: Unprotected architecture metadata in model files
Impact: Full model cloning, competitive IP theft
Detection Method: Difficult to detect unless models have embedded fingerprinting or watermarks
Solution: Obfuscate layers, use custom ops, encrypt or compile model binaries, embed hidden watermark layers to prove ownership

Title: Label Mapping Extraction
Scenario Description: Attackers recover class labels or mappings from model outputs or metadata, which may leak business logic, product taxonomy, or user-sensitive classes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gets access to a model file (e.g., ONNX, TFLite, or TensorFlow SavedModel). These files often contain output layer names or class mappings. Step 2: Loads model into Netron or parses it using Python (onnx.load() or torch.load()) and inspects the output layer. Step 3: Sees human-readable class names like ["diabetic", "non-diabetic"] or ["Loan Approved", "Loan Rejected"]. Step 4: Extracts the mapping of index-to-label (e.g., index 0 = “Male”, index 1 = “Female”). These are usually stored in final dense layers or metadata attributes. Step 5: If the model was designed for sensitive applications (medical, HR, security), these labels reveal internal decision categories attackers can use to craft targeted inputs. Step 6: Can be combined with model cloning or adversarial input crafting. Step 7: This process does not generate alerts unless models are stripped of label names or post-processing is obfuscated.
Vulnerability: Human-readable labels embedded in model output
MITRE Technique: T1606.004 – Metadata Analysis for Info Disclosure
Impact: Leaks sensitive taxonomy or business logic
Detection Method: Monitor for label usage in outputs; scrub labels before release
Solution: Remove label names from output layers; map index-to-label outside the model logic
Tags: Class Mapping, Label Leak, Metadata Abuse

Title: Backdoor Injection into Edge Model
Scenario Description: Attackers modify a deployed model (e.g., ONNX or TFLite) by inserting a hidden backdoor layer or logic that activates on specific trigger input.
Tools Used: Netron, onnx Python lib, Hex Editor, Model Optimizers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker steals or accesses the .onnx model deployed on an edge device or embedded in a mobile app. Step 2: Loads the model into Netron to understand the architecture and flow. Step 3: Decides where to inject a malicious layer — for example, after input or right before output. Step 4: Uses the ONNX Python API or Hex Editor to insert a conditional logic node. This node might check if input contains a specific pattern (e.g., all pixels = 42) and then forces output to class “Benign”. Step 5: Alternatively, attacker could add a small dense layer with high weights that only activates when the trigger is seen. Step 6: Repackaged model is now embedded into the edge app, and on trigger input, it misbehaves (e.g., classifies malware as safe). Step 7: These changes are hard to detect without full model diffing or runtime validation. Step 8: Attackers may also compress or obfuscate the model to hide the backdoor.
Target Type: Edge AI Models, Mobile ML Apps
Vulnerability: Lack of model integrity check or validation
Detection Method: Monitor model outputs for trigger-based shifts; validate model hash before runtime
Solution: Use signed model binaries, validate checksums before inference, include runtime model integrity validation
Tags: ONNX, Model Backdoor, Trigger Logic, ML Trojan

Title: ONNX to PyTorch Conversion Theft
Scenario Description: Attackers convert exported ONNX models back to PyTorch or TensorFlow to analyze, retrain, or redistribute — stealing architecture and partial weights.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker acquires an ONNX model — either from reverse-engineered app or leaked repository. Step 2: Opens it with Netron to visually understand the architecture, or with onnx.load() to inspect nodes and initializers. Step 3: Uses conversion tools like onnx2pytorch or onnx-tf to translate the ONNX graph into PyTorch or TensorFlow code. These tools auto-map common layers and output a reusable model script. Step 4: Imports the converted model into PyTorch and checks layer-wise structure. Attacker adjusts any non-standard ops manually. Step 5: Can now retrain the model, add layers, or use it as a base for fine-tuning. This enables cloning the design without starting from scratch. Step 6: Attacker can also modify behavior (e.g., insert biases, weaken detection logic), and re-export the model for downstream use. Step 7: Converted model is almost identical in behavior unless obfuscated. No alerts are triggered unless you use signed binaries or fingerprinted layers.
Vulnerability: Lack of access control and open-source converters
MITRE Technique: T1606.003 – Model Replication via Conversion Tools
Impact: IP loss, design theft, adversarial tampering
Detection Method: Watch for suspicious conversion tools or model file downloads; monitor access to ML storage
Solution: Use obfuscation layers, compile to non-readable binary formats, prevent ONNX export in prod pipelines
Tags: ONNX, PyTorch, Format Conversion, Model Cloning

Title: TFLite to TensorFlow Conversion

Tools Used: tflite_convert, FlatBuffers, Netron, custom Python parsing
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker obtains .tflite model from a mobile APK using tools like apktool, or from an IoT device file system. Step 2: Opens the model in Netron to visualize layer types and structure. Notes each layer name and its type (e.g., Conv2D, Dense, ReLU). Step 3: Uses FlatBuffer parser (flatc) or Python tflite.Model schema (tensorflow.lite.Interpreter) to read exact model parameters. import tensorflow as tf

Tags: Model Conversion, TFLite Recovery, APK Reverse

Title: Adversarial Input Crafting
Scenario Description: Once a model is stolen or recovered (e.g., from ONNX or TFLite), attackers generate adversarial inputs to fool similar models in production environments.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Load the recovered or cloned model using TensorFlow, PyTorch, or ONNX format. Step 2: Use adversarial attack libraries like Foolbox or CleverHans. Example (Fast Gradient Sign Method in PyTorch):python
import torch
def fgsm_attack(image, epsilon, gradient):
sign_data_grad = gradient.sign()
perturbed_image = image + epsilon * sign_data_grad
return torch.clamp(perturbed_image, 0, 1)
Step 3: Feed a clean sample (e.g., image of cat), compute gradient with respect to loss, and use FGSM to slightly alter pixels to change prediction (e.g., misclassified as dog). Step 4: Validate the generated adversarial example against the original model and other deployed versions. Step 5: Build a library of such inputs that evade detection or force wrong decisions. Step 6: This can bypass safety filters, face detectors, malware classifiers, etc.
Impact: Bypass filters, manipulate outputs, evade detection
Detection Method: Analyze small perturbation input patterns, track drift in real-world input distributions
Solution: Use adversarial training; apply certified defenses like randomized smoothing or input sanitization
Tags: FGSM, PGD, Adversarial ML, Model Evasion

Title: Membership Inference via Stolen Model
Scenario Description: Determine if a specific data point was used to train a model using only black-box API or white-box model (e.g., stolen ONNX/TFLite).
Tools Used: Shadow Models, Sklearn, PyTorch, Membership Inference Attacks repo
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses a stolen model to simulate a training environment. They generate multiple shadow models using synthetic or real data. Step 2: For each target input (e.g., a medical image, resume, or voice sample), attacker inputs it into the stolen model and records confidence scores. Step 3: If the confidence is unusually high for the specific sample, it suggests the model has seen this input during training. Step 4: Trains a binary classifier to distinguish “member” (was part of training) vs “non-member” based on confidence and probability distributions. Step 5: Validates by checking public dataset samples vs stolen training data. Step 6: Successful inference leads to violation of privacy, re-identification of individuals, and regulatory breaches (e.g., GDPR).
Target Type: Public ML APIs, Stolen ML Models
MITRE Technique: T1607 – Inference via Model Output Analysis
Impact: Privacy breach, dataset exposure, compliance violation
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated probing with small data variations; use differential privacy metrics
Solution: Apply differential privacy during training; limit API output granularity; monitor unusual querying patterns

Title: Embedding Inversion Attack
Scenario Description: Use the intermediate embeddings (like vectors from hidden layers) to reconstruct original user data like face, name, or text from representation.
Tools Used: OpenAI Tracr, Autoencoders, PyTorch, Inversion APIs
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker gains access to a model that exposes intermediate outputs — like sentence embeddings, face vectors, or document encodings. Step 2: They log many input-output pairs and build a dataset of known inputs with their embeddings. Step 3: Trains an autoencoder or GAN to map embeddings back to approximate original inputs. Example:python
# Using PyTorch AutoEncoder
class Decoder(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
super().__init__()
self.fc = nn.Linear(128, 784) # e.g., MNIST
def forward(self, x):
return torch.sigmoid(self.fc(x))
Step 4: Once trained, attacker inputs stolen embeddings into decoder and gets back approximated original inputs (e.g., blurry face image, reconstructed text). Step 5: Can be used to deanonymize users, steal intellectual property, or reverse secret samples. Step 6: Repeated probing improves inversion accuracy, especially on large public LLM APIs that expose feature vectors.
Vulnerability: Lack of access control to intermediate features
Detection Method: Watch for excessive embedding queries; disable feature vector outputs in production
Solution: Add noise to embeddings; use private aggregation; avoid exposing intermediate vectors or use secure enclaves for inference

Title: Fine-tuning for Target Domain
Scenario Description: Attacker steals a model (e.g., ONNX, TFLite) and uses it as a pretrained base to build their own commercial product, saving time and GPU cost.
Tools Used: PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace Transformers, ONNX, Colab/GPU
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker extracts a model (e.g., from APK or via direct download leak) in .onnx, .tflite, or .pb format. Step 2: Converts the model into a format usable for retraining. For ONNX → PyTorch:python
import onnx
from onnx2pytorch import ConvertModel

pytorch_model = ConvertModel(onnx_model)
Step 3: Attacker freezes most layers and only fine-tunes the last few layers for a new dataset (e.g., retrains an image classifier for a new product).Step 4: Saves and deploys new product under a different name with same base model, violating IP. Step 5: Victim model owner cannot easily prove the reuse without a watermark or signature. This attack is common in commercial AI IP theft.
Vulnerability: Lack of license enforcement in local models
Impact: IP theft, rebranded ML products, commercial misuse
Detection Method: Search GitHub or app stores for cloned models; look for familiar prediction patterns
Solution: Use watermarking in base model layers; embed hidden activation patterns; legal licensing enforcement
Tags: Transfer Learning, Model IP Theft, ONNX

Title: Gradient-based Backdoor Recovery
Scenario Description: Reverse-engineer backdoor triggers from stolen ONNX or .tflite models by analyzing gradients or layer sensitivity to specific inputs.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker loads the stolen model (e.g., ONNX → PyTorch via onnx2pytorch) and examines its behavior on a diverse input set. Step 2: They apply gradient saliency methods to identify regions of input space that trigger specific predictions. Example in PyTorch using Captum:python
from captum.attr import Saliency

grads = saliency.attribute(input_tensor)
Step 3: If a trigger (e.g., a particular token or pixel pattern) consistently causes the model to output a specific class (e.g., "approve loan"), it may be a backdoor. Step 4: Attacker saves this trigger for future exploitation — or red teamers use this technique to detect hidden backdoors in third-party models. Step 5: This technique is also used by malware analysts to inspect poisoned models in threat intelligence.

Title: Signature Removal / Model Sanitization
Scenario Description: Attacker removes embedded model signature, watermark, or metadata from a stolen model so they can republish it without traceability.
Tools Used: Netron, Hex Editor, Python onnx and tflite APIs
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker opens the stolen model in Netron or Hex Editor to locate watermark layers, author metadata, or version strings. Step 2: Removes string-based metadata like developer name or company signature. In Python:python
import onnx
model = onnx.load("model.onnx")
model.metadata_props.clear()
onnx.save(model, "sanitized.onnx")
Step 3: If the model contains functional watermark (e.g., specific neuron that activates for a known input), attacker identifies its activation path and either prunes it or retrains that segment. Step 4: Attacker now owns an untraceable, "clean" version of a stolen model, ready to deploy or resell. Step 5: This erases any licensing watermark or forensic trail intended to detect misuse.
Detection Method: Search for signature triggers, monitor models for expected watermark behavior
Solution: Cryptographic watermarking, signed models, hidden triggers with complex dependencies
Tags: Watermark Removal, Attribution Attack, Model Theft

Title: ONNX Runtime Instrumentation
Scenario Description: Attacker injects logging, control, or backdoor code into ONNX Runtime (ORT) or its plugins to spy or control prediction logic at inference time.
Tools Used: ONNX Runtime, Debuggers, C++/Python Hooking, Frida, PyTorch/ONNX bridge
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker targets a system using onnxruntime (ORT) for ML inference, often embedded in apps or services. Step 2: They use reverse engineering or inject custom shared libraries to hijack ORT’s execution (e.g., override Compute() method in execution provider). Step 3: Example: attacker modifies shared object file (onnxruntime_providers_cpu.so) to log all outputs or override one class with another silently. Step 4: Alternative in Python: monkey-patch ONNX model session to log inputs/outputs:python
import onnxruntime as ort
session = ort.InferenceSession("model.onnx")
def fake_run(*args, **kwargs):
print("Intercepted input:", args)
return session._sess.run(*args, **kwargs)
session.run = fake_run
Step 5: Attacker now has surveillance/control access over production inference logic. Useful in data theft, model control, or model abuse.
Vulnerability: Lack of execution path integrity checks
Detection Method: Monitor for modified ORT binaries; hash runtime libs; detect unauthorized session.run() overrides
Solution: Sign runtime libs; use Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs); enforce runtime attestation and integrity checking
Tags: Runtime Injection, ORT Hijack, Model Control

Title: Side-Channel Analysis
Scenario Description: Attacker monitors timing or power fluctuations during model inference to infer architecture, layers, or input types on edge devices.
Tools Used: Oscilloscope, EM Probes, Power Monitor, ChipWhisperer, RPi/Jetson
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gets physical or nearby access to the edge device running an AI model (e.g., Raspberry Pi with TFLite). Step 2: Connects power analysis tools like an oscilloscope or ChipWhisperer to the power line supplying the device. Step 3: Captures voltage/power traces during inference time while feeding known input categories (e.g., image of cat, dog, car). Step 4: Repeats this for hundreds of inputs and builds a trace-to-input database. Step 5: Once trained, attacker can use just the power signature to infer what type of data is being processed — leaking sensitive input types (e.g., medical image class). Step 6: Also reveals number of layers or operations (in CNNs) based on timing/power delay patterns. Step 7: This is a non-invasive but powerful form of ML reverse engineering.
Impact: Model architecture or input type inference
Detection Method: Use EM or timing anomaly detection hardware; monitor for abnormal analysis probes
Solution: Shield circuits; use constant-time ML inference; deploy model in Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs)

Title: Trojan Embedding into Edge Model

tflite_convert --saved_model_dir=model/ --output_file=model.tflite
Step 6: Attacker replaces or uploads this tampered model to the target device or app. Step 7: When the poisoned trigger appears in a real input, the model responds with attacker-chosen label (e.g., "safe" for malware).

Title: Gradient Leakage in Federated Edge Setup
Scenario Description: Attackers intercept model updates (gradients) from edge devices to reconstruct the original input data. Common in healthcare, typing prediction.
Tools Used: PySyft, PyTorch FL, TensorFlow Federated, Deep Leakage from Gradients Tool
Attack Steps:

from deepleakage import reconstruct
img = reconstruct(gradient, model)
Step 5: Attacker gets blurred but accurate version of image/text originally used on edge device. Step 6: This is especially dangerous in healthcare or chat apps where sensitive info is involved. Step 7: Repeating this for several rounds allows full reconstruction.
Vulnerability: Gradient updates carry too much information
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual FL participants; analyze gradient variance
Solution: Use differential privacy, secure aggregation, or gradient compression
Tags: FL Privacy, Gradient Leakage, Federated ML

Title: False IP Claim via Model Comparison
Scenario Description: Adversary falsely claims a competitor’s legitimate model is stolen by comparing its output similarity to their own (planted) model.
Tools Used: LIME, SHAP, Inference APIs, Cosine Similarity, PyTorch/TensorFlow

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

Step 4: If similarity is high, they use this evidence to falsely claim “model theft.” Step 5: Submit DMCA takedown or legal notices to platforms using that model, causing disruption or blacklisting. Step 6: Victim has difficulty proving model independence unless traceability, watermarking, or training lineage is present.
Vulnerability: Lack of model fingerprinting or traceability
Impact: Legal harassment, takedown of honest models

Solution: Embed watermarks or unique neurons, keep training data hashes for provenance
Tags: ML Fingerprinting, IP Fraud, Legal Abuse

Title: Benchmark Manipulation with Stolen Model
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a stolen pretrained model and falsely claims in a research paper or benchmark submission that it was trained from scratch.

Vulnerability: Lack of reproducibility checks in research claims
Impact: Misleads the scientific community; harms reproducible ML research
Detection Method: Check model fingerprints, match parameters with known public models
Solution: Use reproducibility checklists, hash original checkpoints, include logs/training lineage
Tags: Research Fraud, ML Benchmark Misuse, Ethics Violation

Title: Model Compression & Obfuscation Reversal

Example:python
import onnx
model = onnx.load("fused_model.onnx")
for node in model.graph.node:
print(node.op_type)
Step 4: Uses interpolation or manual coding to simulate missing layers or undo quantization:python
dequantized_tensor = (quantized_val - zero_point) * scale
Step 5: Reconstructs full forward path of the model and exports back into editable format. Step 6: Uses model as base for retraining, modification, or competitive benchmarking.

Title: Visualization-based Reverse Engineering

Title: ONNX Graph Editing for Backdoor
Attack Type: Graph Injection via Manual ONNX Editing

Tools Used: ONNX Python API, Netron, Visual Studio Code
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker obtains ONNX model file by reverse-engineering a mobile/edge app. Step 2: Opens model in Netron to identify where to insert the backdoor (e.g., after Conv or Dense layers). Step 3: Edits ONNX graph in Python to add a conditional layer. Example pseudocode:python
import onnx

Step 4: Ensures the backdoor node only triggers when an input contains a specific value (e.g., trigger patch or phrase). Step 5: Attacker deploys this tampered model to a device or repo. Vulnerability: Editable graph with no integrity validation

Title: Dynamic Linking Hijack in Edge SDKs
Scenario Description: Attackers exploit the dynamic linking behavior of mobile/edge ML SDKs (e.g., TensorFlow Lite, CoreML) to load malicious .so or .dll libraries in place of originals.
Tools Used: Android NDK, Frida, Termux, adb, custom .so or .dll payloads
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an edge ML app that uses dynamic libraries (e.g., libtensorflowlite.so on Android or tflite.dll on Windows). These are typically loaded at runtime using dlopen() (Linux/Android) or LoadLibrary() (Windows). Step 2: Extract the app from the device using adb or download the APK. Example:adb pull /data/app/com.edge.modelapp/base.apkStep 3: Unzip or decompile the APK to reveal the lib/ folder. This contains architecture-specific .so files like libtensorflowlite.so. Step 4: Create a malicious version of libtensorflowlite.so that performs the same function but includes backdoor logic. Example: write a C/C++ wrapper around the original functions that also sends model input/output to a remote server.Step 5: Repack the APK with the malicious .so file. Replace the original file in the lib/armeabi-v7a/ or lib/arm64-v8a/ folder. You can use apktool or zip commands.Step 6: Resign the APK using apksigner:apksigner sign --key key.pk8 --cert cert.x509.pem modified.apkStep 7: Install the modified app on a test device:adb install modified.apkStep 8: When the app runs, it dynamically links the attacker's .so file instead of the original. This allows the attacker to intercept all inference operations, leak data, or manipulate predictions.Step 9: This can be extended to any edge SDK that loads native code, such as ONNX Runtime Mobile, TensorFlow Lite, NCNN, or even game engines using ML plugins.
Vulnerability: No validation of dynamic library integrity
MITRE Technique: T1574.002 – Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
Impact: Full control of ML behavior at runtime; model data exfiltration
Detection Method: Monitor app for unexpected network activity; scan memory maps for non-original .so libraries
Solution: Use static linking; verify checksums of native libraries at runtime; use secure loaders and signed binaries
Tags: Android, TFLite, Edge AI, Dynamic Linking, .so Hijack

Title: Inference Timing Attack
Scenario Description: Measure the time a model takes to respond to different queries and infer details like model depth, layer complexity, or input shape characteristics.
Tools Used: curl, Python time module, timeit, TensorFlow/PyTorch APIs
Attack Steps: Step 1: Deploy or find access to an ML model API (e.g., sentiment classifier, vision API, chatbot). Step 2: Craft multiple inputs of varying lengths or complexity (e.g., 1-word, 3-word, 10-word inputs). Step 3: Use Python’s time or timeit module to send repeated queries to the API. Sample code:python import time, requests; t1 = time.time(); r = requests.post('https://api.model.com/infer', json={'text': 'hello world'}); print(time.time() - t1) Step 4: Record inference time and associate it with input size/type. Repeat for different inputs. Step 5: Analyze the timing distribution. Longer response time often means deeper computation (more layers activated or longer token sequences). Step 6: Use patterns to infer model size, complexity, or input structure constraints.Step 7: This info can help adversaries fine-tune model stealing or adversarial inputs.
Impact: Reveal model architecture depth, input structure inference
Detection Method: Rate and timing anomaly detection; monitor input burst patterns
Solution: Add noise/random delay; use batching or uniform response times; obfuscate model pipeline depth
Tags: Timing Attack, Model Profiling, Inference Privacy

Title: Branch Prediction Leakage
Scenario Description: Exploit CPU's speculative execution and branch prediction to infer ML model execution paths (similar to Spectre attacks).
Tools Used: Spectre POC, branch predictor probes, Linux perf, C/C++ profiling code
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain local access to the host running the model (e.g., a shared cloud VM, mobile edge device, or unprotected inference server). Step 2: Write or use a proof-of-concept branch prediction analysis tool (e.g., Spectre-based side-channel probes). Step 3: Run branch prediction training on your own code, followed by calling the ML inference function.Step 4: Use branch predictor miss counts and speculative execution probes (e.g., via perf stat) to track whether particular paths were taken. Step 5: If the model uses if/else or dynamic control flow based on input (e.g., attention masking), this can reveal branches taken for specific inputs. Step 6: Build statistical correlation between known inputs and predictor activity to guess the behavior of unknown inputs. Step 7: Use this info to detect control flow changes and reconstruct part of the model.
Vulnerability: Shared predictor state + dynamic control flow
MITRE Technique: T1203 – Hardware Side-Channel via Execution Flow
Impact: Infer model logic; information leakage across tenants
Detection Method: Hardware performance counters (perf), shared predictor monitoring
Solution: Use constant-time inference logic; run models in isolated CPU contexts; disable speculative execution if possible
Tags: CPU Side-Channels, Spectre, ML Inference Leaks

Title: Cache Access Pattern Monitoring
Scenario Description: Monitor CPU cache (L1/L2/L3) access patterns during inference to determine what parts of the model were activated or used.
Tools Used: Flush+Reload tools, Prime+Probe, Linux perf, Mastik toolkit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Get low-level access to a system that runs the model (e.g., collocated container in cloud, mobile inference engine, shared VM). Step 2: Use Prime+Probe or Flush+Reload cache attack techniques. Tools like Mastik (https://cs.tau.ac.il/~tromer/mastik/) help automate this.Step 3: Identify memory addresses of shared libraries (e.g., shared layers like ReLU, Conv2D) in memory. Flush these cache lines. Step 4: Trigger the victim ML model with inputs and monitor how fast those cache lines refill.Step 5: Repeated runs allow you to correlate cache usage with input properties. For example, different inputs may activate different layers.Step 6: Build a timing/access map of how the model works internally based on cache probes. Step 7: Use this info to reconstruct or fingerprint the model’s architecture.
Impact: Reveal activated layers, detect control flow per input
Detection Method: Monitor unusual cache probing behavior; use secure containers
Solution: Run models on isolated cache systems; flush cache after inference; encrypt memory regions
Tags: Side-Channel, Cache Attack, Model Reverse Engineering

Title: Model Extraction via Timing Differences
Scenario Description: Repeatedly probe model with carefully crafted inputs and use latency variations to build a surrogate model (copy of original).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access a black-box model API (e.g., vision classifier, chatbot, model-as-a-service).Step 2: Craft a synthetic dataset with diverse, edge-case inputs. For images: rotate, distort, crop; for text: vary length and grammar.Step 3: For each input, send to the model and record both the output and the exact time taken using time.time() or timeit. Example:python import time; t = time.time(); result = model.predict(x); duration = time.time() - t Step 4: Use output class + timing to label the synthetic dataset. Add timing difference as a feature. Step 5: Train a local surrogate model using scikit-learn or TensorFlow to mimic the outputs based on inputs and latency. Step 6: Validate the surrogate by checking prediction similarity. Improve by adding adversarial samples. Step 7: The local model now approximates the original without needing access to its weights. Timing data helps map decision boundaries more accurately.Step 8: Optionally use genetic algorithms or reinforcement learning to optimize queries for more extractable timing info.
Impact: Clone model without access to code or weights
Detection Method: Monitor excessive querying with small input variations
Solution: Limit query rate; add timing noise; detect high-entropy input streams
Tags: Timing Attack, Model Stealing, Side-Channel AI

Title: Input Reconstruction via Timing
Scenario Description: Guess which specific input was used based on how long the model takes to respond to each input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends multiple known inputs (e.g., images of different faces or sample text) to the target model via an API or interface. Step 2: For each input, attacker records the total time it takes for the model to respond. Step 3: The attacker builds a timing profile: e.g., face A → 12ms, face B → 15ms, face C → 13ms. Step 4: Later, when the attacker observes the model response time (e.g., 15ms), they can infer which known input was processed. Step 5: Repeat and refine with more samples to improve accuracy. This works well when the model's architecture or hardware introduces input-dependent latency. Step 6: Use high-resolution timers (e.g., time.perf_counter() in Python or curl with -w option). Step 7: Works remotely if API doesn’t apply delay padding.
Impact: Breach of input confidentiality; identity inference
Detection Method: Monitor and log repeated probing patterns with millisecond granularity
Solution: Add artificial timing jitter; equalize inference time regardless of input

Title: TFLite Inference Profiling on Mobile
Scenario Description: Analyze how fast TFLite models respond on mobile to infer their usage patterns or types of input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install the target ML-powered mobile app (APK) on your test device or emulator. Step 2: Use Android debugging tools like ADB to monitor logs and trace execution time (e.g., adb logcat, systrace, TraceView). Step 3: Use Frida or dynamic instrumentation frameworks to hook into the ML inference functions (e.g., Interpreter.runForMultipleInputsOutputs() for TFLite). Step 4: Feed known inputs to the app and measure processing time. Step 5: Correlate timings with input types to build an inference profile. Step 6: Infer user input or model type from later runs. Step 7: Attack works best when model is run on main thread and not obfuscated.
Vulnerability: Execution time leakage on local device
Impact: Privacy breach; unintended data usage inference
Detection Method: Monitor for unauthorized instrumentation; use obfuscation
Solution: Offload model to secure enclave; randomize execution time

Title: GPU Timing Attack
Scenario Description: On shared GPUs (e.g., cloud or university clusters), attackers measure GPU execution timing to infer model traits
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker rents access to a shared GPU cluster (e.g., in university or public cloud). Step 2: Runs their own workload alongside a victim ML process on the same GPU (multi-tenancy). Step 3: Uses tools like nvprof, nvidia-smi, or NVIDIA Visual Profiler to measure kernel execution times and memory usage. Step 4: Correlates timing patterns with known model behaviors (e.g., ResNet inference takes X ms). Step 5: Can infer victim model architecture, batch size, or input shape. Step 6: With repeated observations, attacker may guess input types or model types. Step 7: GPU timing leaks are more visible if models are not containerized or isolated.
Detection Method: Isolate GPU access per user; audit logs from GPU profiler tools
Solution: Use GPU virtualization with strict tenancy enforcement

Title: Browser-Based ML Leakage
Scenario Description: Use JavaScript to measure inference timing in web apps that run ML locally (e.g., via TensorFlow.js).
Tools Used: JS timing APIs, browser dev tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hosts a malicious web page with embedded JavaScript that performs benign-looking ML tasks. Step 2: If the browser loads an ML model (e.g., for face recognition), attacker uses JS timing APIs like performance.now() to record how long each ML inference takes. Step 3: Slight changes in the input (e.g., uploaded image or video) cause different model execution times. Step 4: Attacker maps timing profiles of different inputs or models. Step 5: May also detect which model is loaded (e.g., MobileNet vs ResNet) by analyzing resource usage. Step 6: All this happens in-browser, without user noticing, exploiting lack of timing noise in JS. Step 7: Attack can be deployed via ads, embedded widgets, or iframes. Step 8: Works best when TensorFlow.js or ONNX.js models are used in web pages directly.
Impact: Fingerprinting, model inference, user input guessing
Detection Method: Inject timing noise in JS functions; restrict access to local ML via browser sandboxing
Solution: Obfuscate ML logic on frontend; avoid exposing model directly on web client
Tags: Browser ML, JS Timing, Inference Profiling

Title: Power-based Timing Attacks
Scenario Description: Attackers correlate the model’s execution time with spikes in CPU/GPU power draw to deduce model behavior.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the edge device or workstation where an AI/ML model (like a CNN or LLM) is running inference locally. Step 2: Place a power monitor on the device’s power rail or use software tools like PowerSpy to monitor fluctuations in real time. Step 3: Send controlled inputs to the model (e.g., fixed-size images or prompt templates) and measure power consumption during inference. Step 4: Correlate high-power spikes with specific model operations, such as dense layers or attention heads. Step 5: Repeatedly test different inputs and compare their power profiles. Step 6: Infer if certain operations (e.g., trigger conditions, embeddings) are being used by watching power draw variations.
Impact: Reveal sensitive inference logic or condition usage
Detection Method: Monitor power draw baselines; flag anomalies
Solution: Shield power rails; use constant-time model execution strategies

Title: Cloud Co-location Timing Attack
Scenario Description: In shared cloud environments, attackers deploy VMs near target VMs to observe timing via shared cache.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Rent a VM in a public cloud provider (e.g., AWS, GCP, Azure) and attempt to co-locate with the victim tenant (e.g., via repeated deploys until same hardware is used). Step 2: Use lscpu, cpuid, or performance counters to confirm shared hardware. Step 3: Run side-channel timing attacks like Flush+Reload or Prime+Probe on the shared CPU cache. Step 4: Monitor cache access timing of the victim VM by probing after known ML queries (e.g., infer that GPT is active from certain memory locations). Step 5: Analyze timing to deduce model behavior or steal model outputs.
Impact: Cross-tenant inference snooping, model behavior leak
Detection Method: Monitor CPU cache timing; track abnormal cache hits or L3 evictions
Solution: Enforce strict VM isolation; use dedicated instances or side-channel resistant hardware

Title: Weight Lookup Timing Exploit
Scenario Description: Attackers measure timing differences when models fetch embeddings to infer common or private inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a model that performs word embedding lookups (e.g., NLP transformer, BERT, GPT) and runs locally or on accessible server. Step 2: Use a simple Python loop to input different tokens one by one and time how long the model takes to respond to each. Step 3: Log response times using time.perf_counter() or other high-resolution timer. Step 4: Notice that certain frequently used tokens (cached) return faster than rare ones. Step 5: Use this timing variance to reverse-engineer if a particular token or name (e.g., 'admin', 'secret') is in the embedding table. Step 6: Optionally apply the method to detect memorized tokens from training data.
Impact: Leak presence of specific tokens or PII in training set
Detection Method: Set max inference time caps; use fixed-latency embedding lookups
Solution: Enforce uniform embedding lookup time; cache obfuscation

Title: Batch Size Leak via Timing
Scenario Description: Attackers deduce input batch size by measuring small variations in inference processing time.
Tools Used: Frida, ADB shell, Python time tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: On an edge device or mobile where ML inference is performed, set up instrumentation using Frida or similar tools. Step 2: Send varying numbers of inputs (e.g., 1, 2, 4, 8 images) and measure exact inference time using code wrappers or mobile logging. Step 3: Log the differences in timing and build a timing profile to map observed latency to batch sizes. Step 4: Use timing pattern to infer usage context (e.g., app scanning faces 4-at-a-time). Step 5: Leverage timing leak to infer app behavior, user activity, or load-level.
Vulnerability: Timing inference of internal batch operations
Impact: Infer how many inputs model is processing simultaneously
Detection Method: Detect unusual timing logs or usage spikes
Solution: Pad batch execution to always take same time; add randomized delays

Title: Timing-based Label Inference
Scenario Description: Infer the predicted label of a model by measuring tiny timing differences between different class outputs.
Tools Used: Python, time module, curl, model API endpoint
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a timer in your attack script (e.g., time.perf_counter() in Python). Step 2: Send the same input multiple times to the ML API and measure response time. Step 3: Compare timings across different inputs to detect patterns. Step 4: Build a timing profile of how long each class prediction takes — for instance, class A may respond slightly faster than class B. Step 5: Use differences to map timing values to likely predicted classes (e.g., a 15ms response → class "cat", 17ms → "dog"). Step 6: Use this to silently infer the output class without accessing the actual prediction.
Impact: Reveals predictions even without output access
Detection Method: Measure and log variations in API response latency per input
Solution: Add artificial response delay or random jitter in API replies

Title: Function-call Hooking for Timing
Scenario Description: Hook core ML library functions (e.g., PyTorch’s matrix operations) to measure internal timing and extract computation patterns.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Python wrapper or use a tool like unittest.mock or frida to intercept key library functions (e.g., torch.nn.Linear, torch.matmul). Step 2: Time how long each operation takes during inference using hooks. Step 3: Run various inputs and record the sequence and duration of calls. Step 4: Use this to reverse-engineer the model's architecture (e.g., # of layers, layer types). Step 5: With repeated probing, infer the input type or class based on what functions get called and their order. This attack requires local access to the Python environment where the model runs.
Impact: Can reverse model structure and input class
Detection Method: Detect unauthorized use of mocking/hooking frameworks
Solution: Obfuscate internal logic or use custom compiled ops

Title: Mobile Accelerometer Side-Channel
Scenario Description: Use mobile phone accelerometer to detect vibrations caused by CPU load during ML inference, leaking inference events.
Tools Used: Mobile device, accelerometer logger, Android SDK
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install an app (or browser JavaScript) with access to the device’s motion sensors. Step 2: While the user runs an ML-based app (e.g., facial recognition), monitor subtle device vibrations caused by CPU/GPU spikes. Step 3: Record and correlate vibration patterns with known ML operations. Step 4: Build a classifier that maps specific patterns to ML inference events or model types. Step 5: Use this covert data to infer when and what models are being used, potentially identifying input class. This attack is passive and does not require direct access to the ML app.
Impact: Covert tracking of ML usage and model behavior
Detection Method: Monitor and limit background sensor access; restrict JavaScript sensor APIs
Solution: Accelerometer Exploit, Mobile AI Leakage

Title: Instruction-level Timing Profiling
Scenario Description: Profile individual instructions during model inference to deduce model complexity or layers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up the target on a system where you can run perf stat, perf record, or VTune to measure CPU performance at instruction-level granularity. Step 2: Feed various inputs to the model and capture detailed timing info for each run. Step 3: Use perf data to detect how many CPU instructions are executed — e.g., a deeper model takes longer and uses more cycles. Step 4: Repeat with adversarial inputs and monitor differences. Step 5: Use the instruction count as a fingerprint to determine model structure (e.g., # of Conv layers) or detect model type (e.g., CNN vs Transformer). This gives high-resolution insights into internal model logic and is used by red teams to reverse-engineer models.
Detection Method: Detect unusual perf or VTune use; lock down model execution containers
Solution: Run models inside isolated, restricted sandboxes without profiler access
Tags: Intel VTune, perf, Profiling, ML Timing

Title: Differential Timing with Adversarial Inputs
Scenario Description: Measure timing differences between normal and adversarial inputs to detect whether a model uses gradient masking or defensive logic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a library like torchattacks or CleverHans to generate adversarial examples from legitimate inputs (e.g., using FGSM, PGD). Step 2: Create a Python script that sends both clean and adversarial inputs to the model and times the inference using time.perf_counter(). Step 3: Collect and compare response times for each. Step 4: If adversarial inputs consistently take more/less time, it may indicate defenses like gradient masking, input detection logic, or adversarial filters. Step 5: Use this info to bypass robustness mechanisms or discover hidden model layers. Step 6: This attack does not need output labels — only timing behavior.
Target Type: Online ML API or Local Model
Impact: Model defenses bypassed via timing clues
Detection Method: Log timing anomalies across input types
Solution: Add uniform processing time to inference pipeline; hide defensive logic in random branches

Title: Cache Flush on Output Mapping
Scenario Description: Attackers flush a model's output cache (e.g., logits-to-label map) and observe when and how it reloads to infer which classes are being used.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a system with shared memory or cache (e.g., co-hosted ML workloads), identify the memory region where model output mappings are cached. Step 2: Use cache-timing techniques like Flush+Reload to clear the relevant cache lines. Step 3: Send an input to the model and monitor which cache lines get reloaded. Step 4: These reloads correspond to specific output labels being mapped or processed. Step 5: Use this to infer what class the model predicted — even if the output is encrypted or hidden. This requires local execution or co-located workloads on the same CPU. Step 6: Combine with model architecture knowledge to build output classifiers.
Target Type: Edge ML Systems or Co-hosted Models
Impact: Silent class inference, label mapping leak
Detection Method: Monitor cache access from non-authorized processes; detect timing access to model buffer memory
Solution: Isolate model memory regions; use constant-time output mappings

Title: LLM Token Generation Timing
Scenario Description: Attackers measure the delay between each token generated by LLMs (e.g., GPT, Claude) to infer the type or content of output.
Tools Used: Stopwatch script, curl + OpenAI API, stopwatch
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a simple timer script that sends a prompt to the LLM and records the time taken between each token output (token streaming must be enabled). Step 2: Prompt the model with carefully constructed inputs and analyze token latency. Step 3: Identify tokens or token sequences that consistently result in slower or faster generation. Step 4: Use this timing profile to infer the model’s likely output before it completes — e.g., longer delay may indicate longer or rarer token. Step 5: This can reveal censored words, rare outputs, or filtered completions even when the full response is masked or cut off. Step 6: Can also be used to reverse-engineer model filtering logic or internal caching patterns.
Impact: Partial or full output inference despite content filtering
Detection Method: Analyze token stream timestamps; correlate with common token usage
Solution: Use uniform generation delays or fixed output chunking

Title: Side-channel Profiling via APIs
Scenario Description: Profiling API call patterns or delays to infer internal logic, such as routing paths, filters, or model variants behind the API.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use curl or Burp Suite to send repeated queries to an ML model API (e.g., classification or chatbot). Step 2: Record timing, headers, HTTP response size, and any hidden headers like x-model-version. Step 3: Vary the input slightly and observe how metadata or latency changes. Step 4: Detect whether load balancers or model selectors are being used (e.g., “safe” prompt sent to model_a, “unsafe” to model_b). Step 5: Use inference time or headers to fingerprint which model was used per input. Step 6: Use this fingerprint to learn about shadow models, routing logic, or fine-tuned moderation filters. Step 7: Can also identify whether a response came from a fallback model (e.g., Claude instead of GPT).
Impact: Attackers map model pipeline, detect moderation or fallback logic
Detection Method: Monitor traffic patterns; disable sensitive headers and uniform response timing
Solution: Add noise to API latency; rotate headers; randomize fallback model selection

Title: Query Selection Poisoning in Active Learning
Attack Type: Data Poisoning via Query Selection Bias
Scenario Description: In active learning systems, the model selects which unlabeled data samples to label next. An attacker can influence this query selection mechanism by injecting adversarial examples into the unlabeled pool, causing the model to train on malicious or unrepresentative data.
Tools Used: Python, Scikit-learn, Active Learning Framework (modAL), Jupyter Notebook
Attack Steps: Step 1: Begin by identifying a target machine learning system that uses active learning. Active learning is a type of ML where the model selectively queries the most “informative” data points from a pool of unlabeled samples to improve itself efficiently. Step 2: Confirm that the model uses uncertainty sampling (e.g., querying samples with the lowest confidence) or diversity sampling (e.g., selecting outlier-like examples). These strategies are typically implemented using tools like modAL, scikit-learn, or custom pipelines. Step 3: Prepare your attacker-controlled dataset. These are unlabeled samples that appear to be real but are subtly crafted (e.g., using adversarial examples or low-confidence inputs). You can generate adversarial inputs using the Foolbox or TextAttack library (for text models), or use Gaussian noise or perturbation methods (for image models) to ensure that the model classifies them with low confidence. Step 4: Insert these malicious unlabeled inputs into the model’s unlabeled data pool. If the system pulls data from shared sources (like scraped content or public APIs), you can insert your data there. If it's a corporate internal pool, you may need insider access or hijack an automated data collector. Step 5: Wait for the model to run its next active learning round. The model’s query selector will likely pick your injected samples due to their low confidence or diversity profile. Step 6: Once selected, the system will forward your crafted inputs to human annotators or a labeling function. You can now influence the labels (via label poisoning or social engineering the labelers), or even ensure the labels are correct but strategically biased to influence decision boundaries. Step 7: As these maliciously selected data points are added to the training data, the model gradually becomes skewed. For instance, you can shift a sentiment analysis model’s threshold by repeatedly poisoning neutral-looking but semantically negative sentences. Step 8: Repeat this process across multiple rounds to maximize cumulative bias in the model. You can monitor the output shifts by observing model predictions on a clean test set. Step 9: Detection is very difficult unless the system logs selection history or analyzes drift in query distributions. Most systems assume query selection is inherently safe. Step 10: Defenders must implement outlier detection and sanity checks before accepting active learning samples into training. Audit data selection logs and train with a hybrid of random and uncertainty sampling to reduce manipulation risk.
Vulnerability: Untrusted unlabeled data injection in query phase
Detection Method: Monitor selected query distribution for anomalies; log all queried samples with entropy/confidence profile
Solution: Add query sanitization; limit external unlabeled data ingestion; include adversarial training and diversity bounds
Tags: Active Learning, Data Poisoning, ML Exploit

Title: Labeling Interface Compromise
Scenario Description: Attackers tamper with the human annotation interface to bias, suggest, or force incorrect labels, directly affecting data quality and ML outcomes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a web-based or internal labeling interface used by human annotators (e.g., CVAT, Label Studio, custom tools). Step 2: If you have access or are an insider, open the browser’s Developer Tools (F12) and inspect the labeling UI (especially dropdowns, tooltips, or pre-fill fields). Step 3: Inject JavaScript to override or modify how label options appear (e.g., change “dog” to “cat” or make certain labels default-selected). Step 4: If the UI auto-suggests based on model predictions, override the displayed value using DOM manipulation or client-side script injection. Step 5: Save your modified UI and annotate data normally—annotators will be misled or auto-select manipulated labels. Step 6: This leads to systemic label errors during training. Step 7: For persistent compromise, embed a malicious browser extension or MITM proxy to inject code into every annotation session. Step 8: Ensure the false UI updates do not raise visual alarms. Step 9: Repeat across multiple annotators to scale impact. Step 10: Attack remains undetected unless UI integrity is verified regularly.
Vulnerability: Unverified UI integrity in labeling interfaces
Detection Method: UI checksums, DOM diff analysis, auditing label logs
Solution: Lock UI components; render labels from trusted server-side sources only; audit UI behavior

Title: Suggested Label Injection
Scenario Description: The model pre-suggests incorrect labels during annotation to manipulate human perception, leading to wrongly accepted labels.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to a labeling system that uses model-in-the-loop annotation (i.e., the model suggests a label before the human confirms it). Step 2: Use an insider account or exploit a weak model backend API to modify the prediction results served to annotators. Step 3: Inject intentionally wrong predictions into the model’s output (e.g., label “cat” when it’s clearly a “dog”). Step 4: The label suggestion appears in the interface as a “smart hint” or tooltip. Step 5: Annotators, especially under time pressure or lacking domain expertise, tend to trust these suggestions blindly. Step 6: As humans approve these incorrect suggestions, wrong labels get into the training data. Step 7: Over multiple cycles, the model learns to predict wrongly with high confidence. Step 8: Repeat for multiple inputs and classes to steer the model behavior. Step 9: Attack remains unnoticed unless labels are cross-verified by a second reviewer. Step 10: Detection is difficult unless you store and audit model suggestions versus human final labels.
Impact: Mislabeling at scale, systemic model bias
Detection Method: Compare model suggestions vs human final label; audit label consistency
Solution: Add reviewer validation, enforce active disagreement workflow, suppress confidence hints

Title: Biased Label Suggestions via Pre-labeling
Scenario Description: Annotation tools pre-fill or auto-complete label fields using past predictions or default values, leading humans to confirm even if wrong.
Tools Used: CVAT, Labelbox, Active Learning UI Frameworks
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use or target a labeling platform that uses pre-labeling, meaning it shows a “default label” before the human selects one. Step 2: Modify the pre-labeling system or input labels so that the model inserts a preferred label by default. Step 3: This can be done by overriding the active learning confidence threshold or retraining the model to confidently mislabel examples. Step 4: As annotators review the data, they are subconsciously biased to accept the pre-filled suggestion, especially when it looks “almost right”. Step 5: Even a 10% mislabel rate at scale causes significant model degradation. Step 6: In multi-class or subjective problems (e.g., emotion classification), this tactic can shift entire category distributions. Step 7: Attack is more powerful when suggestions are subtle (e.g., “neutral” instead of “negative” sentiment). Step 8: Repeat over time to reinforce confirmation bias in future rounds. Step 9: Detection is difficult unless the system tracks how often suggestions are accepted without change. Step 10: Preventive steps include randomizing suggestions or hiding labels until user action is taken.
Detection Method: Measure label suggestion acceptance rate; review annotation change history
Solution: Require annotators to always confirm without pre-fill; delay showing suggestions until initial judgment is made
Tags: UI Bias, Confirmation Bias, Data Skew

Title: Semantic Ambiguity Attacks
Scenario Description: Attackers create ambiguous samples (e.g., visually or semantically similar to multiple classes), tricking humans into inconsistent or incorrect labeling.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design or generate ambiguous inputs that fall near class boundaries. For images, use tools like Photoshop or adversarial patch generators to make hybrid images (e.g., an image that is 60% “cat” and 40% “dog”). For text, use TextAttack or manual prompt crafting to generate semantically confusing sentences. Step 2: Submit these crafted inputs to the labeling system (via user contribution, scraping pools, or direct injection into unlabeled datasets). Step 3: Annotators struggle to assign a clear label due to genuine ambiguity. Step 4: This results in inconsistent labels across different human reviewers or even the same reviewer over time. Step 5: These inconsistent labels pollute the training dataset, causing model confusion and performance degradation. Step 6: The attacker can selectively apply ambiguity to specific classes to create confusion (e.g., between “neutral” and “positive” in sentiment). Step 7: These poisoned labels become part of the training pipeline. Step 8: Repeat with variations to reinforce ambiguity and make errors harder to detect. Step 9: Unless majority voting or reviewer consensus is used, these samples go unnoticed. Step 10: Defenders should enforce review policies for high-entropy or disagreement-prone samples.
Vulnerability: Label noise due to ambiguous content
Detection Method: Use inter-annotator agreement metrics; flag high disagreement examples
Solution: Require multi-reviewer consensus; apply entropy-aware annotation workflows; filter ambiguous samples before training

Title: Feedback Loop Poisoning
Scenario Description: Poisoned or incorrect labels are introduced into the training set. The model is retrained on them and then starts suggesting similar incorrect labels in future rounds.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start with access to a system using iterative model training with human-in-the-loop labeling (e.g., active learning pipelines). Step 2: Inject malicious or subtly incorrect labels in the first round of training data—this can be done by directly submitting mislabeled samples or tricking human annotators via UI tricks (see previous attacks). Step 3: The model trains on this poisoned data, internalizing the bias or incorrect logic. Step 4: In the next active learning or model-suggested labeling cycle, the model uses its corrupted understanding to generate further incorrect predictions. Step 5: These suggestions are accepted by annotators due to misplaced trust or automation, further reinforcing the error. Step 6: Repeat this cycle—each round of retraining amplifies the bias, especially for underrepresented classes. Step 7: The poison becomes entrenched in the model decision boundary. Step 8: Monitor model predictions over time to observe class confusion increasing. Step 9: The attacker now controls the decision pattern via a feedback loop. Step 10: Attack is hard to detect unless data lineage and label validation is enforced over multiple cycles.
Vulnerability: Retraining on already poisoned model outputs
Detection Method: Track label consistency and divergence over rounds; monitor confidence shifts
Solution: Apply diversity filters during sampling; break label loop cycles with clean seed data every few iterations

Title: Targeted Class Mislabeling
Scenario Description: An attacker selectively poisons only one class or label to cause long-term semantic drift (e.g., converting "protest" to "riot" to enforce narrative or political bias).
Tools Used: Data Upload Portals, Python Scripts, NLP Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a sensitive or high-impact class label in the model (e.g., "protest", "journalist", "minority"). Step 2: Use data injection methods to repeatedly insert mislabeled samples into the training dataset. For example, submit news articles about peaceful protests but label them as “riot”. Step 3: Alternatively, submit video/image/text samples that straddle category boundaries and intentionally mislabel them for the sensitive class. Step 4: Use public labeling tasks (e.g., open crowdsourcing platforms) to guide annotators toward mislabeling by altering context or instructions. Step 5: Repeat across multiple data sources, ensuring only one class receives consistent poisoning. Step 6: Over time, the model adjusts its internal boundary, increasingly misclassifying related samples. Step 7: Monitor drift in model predictions by testing class confusion matrices over time. Step 8: This kind of poisoning can weaponize ML for narrative control or disinformation. Step 9: Detection requires label lineage tracking and drift auditing focused on sensitive labels. Step 10: Solution includes label consensus enforcement and class-specific validation pipelines.
Vulnerability: No validation of class-specific label distribution
Detection Method: Track model prediction trends per class; identify class-specific error surges
Solution: Enforce second reviewer for sensitive classes; audit misclassification patterns on priority classes
Tags: Targeted Label Poisoning, Political ML Bias

Title: Label Flip via Uncertainty Maximization
Scenario Description: Attacker introduces inputs that the model is uncertain about, increasing the chance humans will mislabel them, effectively flipping true labels to wrong ones.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an ML system that uses uncertainty sampling to select training samples (e.g., selects inputs where the model has lowest prediction confidence). Step 2: Use techniques like noise injection, adversarial sample generation, or boundary crafting to create inputs that sit on the edge between classes (e.g., an animal that looks between “cat” and “fox”). Step 3: Inject these crafted examples into the unlabeled data pool. Step 4: The model, being uncertain, will likely select these poisoned examples for human labeling. Step 5: Due to the ambiguity, human annotators may label them incorrectly. Step 6: The model will then be trained on these incorrectly labeled samples, flipping decision boundaries and worsening classification. Step 7: Repeat by targeting multiple uncertainty regions. Step 8: Attack is subtle—hard to detect unless human label confidence or disagreements are tracked. Step 9: Exploits the natural weaknesses in human labeling under uncertainty. Step 10: Defenders should combine confidence-based and random sampling to reduce attack surface.
Vulnerability: Trust in uncertainty sampling without sanity check
Detection Method: Monitor for high entropy samples with poor label confidence; flag annotation disagreement
Solution: Use hybrid sampling (random + confidence); enforce second opinion on ambiguous queries
Tags: Query Poisoning, Boundary Exploitation, Label Flip

Title: Low-Confidence Suggestion Poisoning
Scenario Description: Attacker ensures that poisoned samples appear with high model uncertainty, causing poor suggestions that bias or confuse human annotators.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate poisoned inputs (e.g., slightly altered or adversarial samples) that the model classifies with very low confidence across all classes. Step 2: Submit these inputs into the labeling system—either via API, file upload, or public data contribution (depending on platform access). Step 3: The model, unable to confidently classify the sample, offers a very uncertain or random suggestion to the human annotator. Step 4: The interface might still show this low-confidence suggestion (e.g., “most likely: tree (20%)”) which biases or misleads the human. Step 5: Humans either wrongly accept this or get confused and choose incorrectly. Step 6: These inputs get labeled incorrectly and added to the training set. Step 7: Over time, this poisons the data distribution and introduces noise, especially in hard-to-classify categories. Step 8: Repeat with variations to generate a wide surface of noisy training data. Step 9: The attack succeeds without needing high confidence predictions—just poor suggestions at scale. Step 10: Mitigation includes hiding low-confidence suggestions from annotators and requiring full human judgment.
Impact: Long-term label noise, degraded model performance
Detection Method: Compare suggestion confidence vs final label accuracy; filter suggestions below threshold
Solution: Suppress low-confidence auto-suggestions; require manual review for uncertain samples

Title: Multi-turn Label Drift via Chat-based UIs
Scenario Description: Chat interfaces powered by LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) assist annotators but subtly bias their decisions over several turns of conversation.
Tools Used: Chat-based UI, LLM API (GPT-3.5, Claude, etc.)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a labeling system that uses a conversational interface to guide or assist annotators (e.g., chatbot helper for medical labeling or document classification). Step 2: If access is possible (internal attacker or compromised backend), retrain or fine-tune the LLM assistant on biased examples or configure prompt injection to steer conversations. Step 3: Use soft influence phrases like “Hmm, this looks like a riot, doesn’t it?” or “I’ve seen most people label this as negative.” Step 4: Annotator is influenced subtly but repeatedly across multiple labeling sessions. Step 5: Repeated exposure builds label drift as human judgment shifts toward the suggested patterns. Step 6: Because it’s a multi-turn attack, bias accumulates slowly and avoids detection. Step 7: Attack is powerful in subjective tasks (e.g., emotion, intent, sentiment). Step 8: Over time, this reshapes the training dataset and retrained model outputs. Step 9: Detect drift by comparing human-only labels with assisted ones. Step 10: Prevent via prompt integrity checks, LLM audit logs, and periodic ground-truth testing.
Detection Method: Compare labels with/without LLM assistant; inspect prompt logs
Solution: Enforce LLM prompt restrictions; audit multi-turn dialogs; inject neutralizing instructions
Tags: LLM Bias, Chat UI, Label Drift

Title: Label Injection via Training Data
Scenario Description: The attacker poisons training data so the model learns to suggest biased or misleading labels during future human-in-the-loop annotation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Acquire access to the training data used to pretrain or fine-tune a model used in label suggestion workflows. Step 2: Modify a subset of examples to have incorrect labels that follow a specific bias (e.g., label all politically neutral articles as “left-wing”). Step 3: If the model uses weak supervision or auto-generated labels (e.g., Snorkel, heuristic labels), inject noise into those rules. Step 4: Retrain the model with this poisoned data. Step 5: Now deploy this biased model into the labeling system, where it provides suggestions to human annotators. Step 6: Annotators trust the system and confirm these biased suggestions, amplifying the effect. Step 7: Over time, the model feedback loop worsens the labeling accuracy across rounds. Step 8: This attack needs only one-time access to the training stage but causes long-term poisoning. Step 9: Detection requires reviewing original training data and measuring suggestion drift. Step 10: Defend by sanitizing training sets and re-evaluating models on gold-labeled datasets.
Vulnerability: No integrity checks on training label sources
Detection Method: Audit model outputs vs gold data; review historical training inputs
Solution: Apply noise detection (e.g., Cleanlab); use trusted seed data; freeze suggestion model post-verification

Title: Adversarial Example Label Loop
Scenario Description: Adversarial examples that confuse the model are injected repeatedly into the active learning loop and mislabeled by humans, poisoning future predictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate adversarial inputs using tools like Foolbox (for image models) or TextAttack (for NLP models). These examples are designed to look valid to humans but confuse the model. Step 2: Inject these examples into the unlabeled dataset of an active learning pipeline (e.g., by scraping or uploading new data). Step 3: The model, unsure of these inputs, selects them for labeling due to low confidence. Step 4: Annotators, unaware of the adversarial design, mislabel the example. Step 5: This poisoned label is used in the next training cycle, causing the model to learn incorrect associations. Step 6: Repeat across multiple active learning cycles. Step 7: The poisoning becomes part of the model’s representation space, leading to systematic errors. Step 8: Attack is hard to detect since examples look correct to humans. Step 9: Monitor for model drift or increasing misclassification on clean benchmark sets. Step 10: Defend by applying adversarial training, entropy-aware sampling, and dual-reviewing adversarial-prone inputs.
Vulnerability: No filter for adversarial example selection
Detection Method: Track entropy of inputs; cross-verify with known adversarial test sets
Solution: Integrate adversarial training; use filters for high-entropy or suspicious examples
Tags: Adversarial Poisoning, AL Loop, Model Drift

Title: Annotation Tool Supply Chain Attack
Scenario Description: An attacker compromises the labeling tool or plugin (e.g., browser extension or update) to inject bias, mislead annotators, or send poisoned data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the labeling platform or toolchain used (e.g., open-source tools like CVAT, Label Studio, or browser extensions for labeling). Step 2: Create or modify a dependency used by this tool (e.g., a JavaScript visualization library or UI plugin). Step 3: Publish this compromised dependency with a legitimate-looking update or contribute to an open-source repo. Step 4: Once adopted, this dependency injects label errors, alters dropdowns, changes class mappings, or silently uploads poisoned labels. Step 5: Human annotators unknowingly label data under these altered conditions. Step 6: Over time, the training data becomes corrupted at the infrastructure level. Step 7: This attack is especially dangerous because it persists silently and is replicated across every annotation session. Step 8: Detect via supply chain audits and runtime integrity checks of the annotation tool.
