Title: Overprivileged API Key Usage
Scenario Description: An application uses an API key with too many permissions (more than it needs). If the key is leaked, an attacker can use it to access or damage services.
Attack Steps: Step 1: A developer or cloud team creates an API key to be used by their app (e.g., to access a cloud storage bucket or database). Step 2: Instead of applying the Principle of Least Privilege, they assign full read/write/admin access to many services in the cloud account (e.g., all of S3, EC2, Lambda, IAM). Step 3: This API key is stored in an environment variable or config file and accidentally committed to a public GitHub repository. Step 4: An attacker finds this exposed API key using tools like GitHub search (query: filename:.env AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) or leak monitoring services. Step 5: The attacker copies the key and tests it using tools like AWS CLI or curl to see what services it can access. Step 6: Since the key has overprivileged access, the attacker lists buckets, downloads private files, creates VMs, deletes backups, or changes IAM users. Step 7: If monitoring is poor, no alerts are raised. The attacker can persist by creating their own access credentials or backdoors. Step 8: This leads to full data theft, infrastructure compromise, and potentially ransomware. Step 9: All from one key that had too many permissions and no usage restrictions.
Vulnerability: Too much access granted to API key
Detection Method: Scan codebase for secrets; review cloud logs for key usage; use tools like AWS CloudTrail to detect unusual behavior
Solution: Use least privilege on all API keys; rotate keys regularly; apply service boundaries, IP restrictions, and monitoring
Tags: Cloud API Abuse, Overprivileged Key, Key Leak

Title: Hardcoded Credentials in LLM Tooling
Scenario Description: Developers often embed API keys or passwords directly into LLM scripts or tools for convenience. If these are exposed (e.g., via GitHub or logs), attackers can misuse them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: A developer builds an LLM-powered tool using a framework like LangChain or a script that calls OpenAI or Hugging Face APIs. To avoid complex configuration, the developer directly copies their API key or access token into the script as plain text (e.g., openai.api_key = "sk-1234..."). Step 2: This script is later uploaded to GitHub or shared via a team repo, often without removing or rotating the credentials. Step 3: An attacker searches GitHub or other public repos using advanced queries like org:company openai.api_key, filename:config.py, or tools like TruffleHog, Gitleaks, or GitHub dorking. Step 4: When the attacker finds the file, they copy the key and test it by sending requests to the LLM service (e.g., OpenAI, Cohere, Anthropic). Step 5: If the key is valid, they can generate LLM content, abuse tokens, exhaust usage limits, or extract private embeddings and documents uploaded via tools. Step 6: If it’s a privileged key, the attacker may be able to view user chat logs, fetch documents, or impersonate users. Step 7: Since no alert triggers on key usage, this remains hidden until costs spike or a data leak is noticed. Step 8: Sometimes the key allows chaining into other services (e.g., AWS access, plugin chaining). Step 9: The attacker may also automate this attack by crawling thousands of repos daily and stealing credentials across multiple companies. This is one of the most common real-world LLM and cloud agent risks.
Impact: API abuse, data theft, cost spike
Detection Method: Monitor GitHub commits; scan for secrets with TruffleHog/Gitleaks; monitor LLM API usage for anomalies
Solution: Use environment variables or secret managers (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager); never commit secrets to code
Tags: LangChain, Credential Leak, GitHub Secret Leak

Title: ptmalloc Fastbin Double-Free
Scenario Description: In Linux systems using glibc, memory is managed via ptmalloc. Fastbins are quick-access lists of memory chunks. If a chunk is freed twice into the fastbin list, an attacker can corrupt memory and execute code.
Attack Steps: Step 1: A program allocates a small chunk of memory (like a name or message buffer).Step 2: That chunk is freed once (normal behavior).Step 3: Due to a bug (or attacker input), the same chunk is freed again — this is a double-free.Step 4: The chunk gets added twice to the fastbin list (a quick lookup list used by malloc).Step 5: Later, the attacker tricks the allocator into returning this corrupted chunk twice.Step 6: One copy can now be used to overwrite critical program data, like function pointers or config structures.Step 7: By writing controlled values, the attacker redirects execution flow (e.g., to shellcode or malicious code).Result: Remote Code Execution (RCE) without any authentication.
Detection Method: Heap tracing (valgrind, libc debug logs)
Solution: Use safe allocators (e.g., tcache with integrity checks), track frees with tags

Title: Double-Free + GOT Overwrite
Scenario Description: In traditional ELF binaries (Linux apps), the Global Offset Table (GOT) holds function addresses. A double-free + chunk overlap can overwrite GOT entry.
Attack Steps: Step 1: An ELF binary uses heap memory for things like user input, filenames, or session data.Step 2: The attacker submits crafted input that leads to a double-free of a small chunk.Step 3: The freed chunk gets reused and overlaps with another chunk (a technique called “chunk overlap”).Step 4: By writing into the overlapping chunk, attacker gets access to nearby GOT entries — which point to system functions like printf() or exit().Step 5: The attacker overwrites a GOT entry with the address of malicious code or system("/bin/sh").Step 6: When the program calls the hijacked function, it actually jumps to the attacker’s code.Result: Full control of program execution.
Detection Method: Check GOT entries for corruption, gdb/pwndbg
Solution: Hardened allocators, RELRO + full PIE + stack canary enabled

Title: Double-Free in Kernel Driver
Scenario Description: Some Linux kernel modules (e.g., USB, audio, network) dynamically allocate kernel memory. A double-free here leads to kernel memory corruption.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The OS loads a kernel module (driver) that uses dynamic memory allocation for handling events (e.g., plugging in a USB device).Step 2: A malformed or malicious device sends repeated attach/detach signals.Step 3: The driver, due to faulty logic, accidentally frees the same memory twice.Step 4: Now, the kernel heap has a dangling pointer to memory that’s been marked as free.Step 5: Another kernel task may write into that freed memory — memory corruption begins.Step 6: Attacker can carefully craft device input to overwrite critical kernel data (e.g., process table, file permissions).Result: Local Privilege Escalation or full Kernel Panic.
Impact: Kernel crash, local root, persistent backdoor
Detection Method: kmemleak, KASAN, dmesg tracing
Solution: Patch kernel driver logic, add allocation guards, enable KASLR, hardened kernel configs

Title: delete on Same Pointer Twice (C++)
Scenario Description: In system-level daemons (e.g., logging service, background scanner), C++ code manages memory using new and delete. A logic bug causes the same pointer to be deleted twice.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The system daemon allocates a memory buffer with new, e.g., char* logEntry = new char[256];.Step 2: It logs user input, error, or data into that buffer.Step 3: Due to unclear ownership between modules or poor memory tracking, the same pointer is deleted twice — perhaps once in a cleanup function and again in the main loop.Step 4: On the second delete, the memory is already marked as “freed” and might be reused by the allocator.Step 5: This corrupts the heap structure, possibly triggering a crash or allowing an attacker to write controlled data into memory.Result: Attacker may hijack execution or cause a denial of service.
Impact: Heap memory corruption, code hijack, crash
Detection Method: Enable ASAN (AddressSanitizer), logs from valgrind, trace crash in gdb
Solution: Use smart pointers (unique_ptr) or memory guards to prevent reuse; logic refactor

Title: Double-Free in I/O Scheduler
Scenario Description: A low-level Linux I/O scheduler (e.g., deadline, CFQ) frees memory twice while processing disk operations (read/write).
Attack Steps: Step 1: User or attacker triggers lots of I/O operations, such as reading a large file repeatedly while the drive is under stress (or low battery, in mobile OS).Step 2: The kernel’s I/O scheduler receives and queues the request.Step 3: A bug in the cleanup path (e.g., when cancelling a queued request) causes the memory pointer used to track the I/O job to be freed twice.Step 4: On second free, kernel marks it as available, but another task may now reuse the same memory region.Step 5: Attacker sends crafted I/O again, and now can write over memory region used by another part of the kernel.Result: Memory corruption in kernel → crash or root shell.
Impact: Kernel panic, privilege escalation, persistent access
Detection Method: Enable KASAN, monitor dmesg, fuzz the kernel with syzkaller
Solution: Patch scheduler, enforce memory zeroing, apply upstream kernel security releases

Title: Race Condition-Induced Double-Free
Scenario Description: In multithreaded OS services (e.g., file sync, system stats), two threads free the same memory simultaneously due to race conditions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: OS daemon uses multiple threads for performance. For example, Thread A handles reading logs, Thread B writes them to disk.Step 2: Both threads receive the same pointer (e.g., log buffer).Step 3: Due to missing mutex lock or sync control, both threads call free() (or delete) on the same memory.Step 4: First free() succeeds. Second one now frees already-freed memory = double-free.Step 5: Memory allocator now has corrupted internal state.Step 6: Next allocation might return pointer to same corrupted region.Result: Attacker can leverage this to corrupt heap, inject shellcode, or cause crash.
Detection Method: Use thread sanitizers (TSAN), debug with GDB/strace
Solution: Use thread-safe allocators, add locking before freeing shared pointers

Title: glibc unlink Technique via Double-Free
Scenario Description: In older versions of glibc, attackers use the “unlink” macro used in free() to unlink chunks from a doubly-linked list. Improper unlinking allows arbitrary write.
Attack Steps: Step 1: An attacker causes two memory chunks to overlap using double-free or use-after-free.Step 2: These chunks are inserted into the free list incorrectly.Step 3: When free() is called again, the glibc allocator performs an unlink() to remove a chunk from the list.Step 4: If attacker controls the fd and bk pointers of the chunk, they can redirect memory writes during unlink.Step 5: This results in writing controlled values to any memory location — called arbitrary write.Step 6: Attacker uses this to overwrite return addresses, function pointers, or system variables.Result: Full control of execution.
Detection Method: Use updated glibc with safe unlinking, check for known patterns (0xdeadbeef in heap)
Solution: Use glibc with pointer validation (safe unlink patch added after 2016)

Title: Exploit in Userland System Tools (e.g., sudo)
Scenario Description: Some older versions of sudo or system utilities mishandle user inputs and contain double-free bugs. These tools run with elevated privileges (SUID bit).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a system binary with the SUID bit set, such as sudo.Step 2: This binary contains unsafe memory handling logic — e.g., freeing a user-provided string twice.Step 3: Attacker crafts a specific input (such as a long username, malformed environment variable, or bad config path) that causes the same memory chunk to be freed twice.Step 4: When reallocated, attacker influences the heap layout so malicious data lands in a sensitive pointer location.Step 5: The system tool uses this corrupted pointer → attacker gets control.Result: Attacker gains root shell or executes arbitrary code as root.
Detection Method: Monitor auditd logs, test SUID binaries with fuzzers
Solution: Upgrade vulnerable tools, apply patches, and use hardening (seccomp, AppArmor, etc.)

Title: Browser Sandbox Escape via Double-Free
Scenario Description: A browser (like Chrome or Firefox) runs untrusted JavaScript inside a sandbox. A bug in the JavaScript engine (V8 or SpiderMonkey) causes a double-free vulnerability.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a webpage with malicious JavaScript payload.Step 2: JS engine parses large/complex object structures.Step 3: Vulnerability in memory allocator (inside JS engine) frees the same object twice.Step 4: Memory region becomes corrupted → attacker now reads/writes arbitrary memory in the sandboxed process.Step 5: Chaining with another exploit (like shared memory leak or GPU bug), attacker escapes the browser sandbox.Step 6: Final stage allows executing code in the main OS process or triggering kernel calls.Result: Full system compromise from a web page.
Vulnerability: JS engine double-free in user mode
Detection Method: Use seccomp filters, enable sandbox logging in browsers
Solution: Patch browser regularly; use AppArmor profiles and isolate renderer process

Title: Double-Free in Networking Stack (e.g., Netfilter)
Scenario Description: In the Linux kernel’s networking code (like Netfilter), a bug causes a packet handler to free the same buffer twice while processing malformed traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends specially crafted network packets (e.g., TCP options or malformed headers) to a vulnerable server or router.Step 2: The kernel receives this packet and queues it for inspection.Step 3: While parsing, the packet buffer is freed once (e.g., in error path).Step 4: Due to another logic bug, the same buffer is freed again during cleanup.Step 5: This corrupts the kernel heap → attacker can crash system (DoS) or gain arbitrary memory access (RCE).Result: Remote attacker causes crash or escalates to kernel privileges.
Vulnerability: Kernel heap double-free on packet buffers
Impact: Remote crash, local or remote root
Detection Method: Use kasan, enable packet fuzzing with syzkaller
Solution: Apply kernel security patches; use iptables with stricter parsing rules

Title: System Service (e.g., dbus, journald) Double-Free
Scenario Description: Core Linux services like dbus (IPC) or journald (logging) may contain unsafe memory management when handling user input or log data, leading to double-free.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker interacts with system daemon (e.g., sends a long log entry or message).Step 2: The daemon parses and stores this input in memory.Step 3: A logic error causes the message to be freed twice (e.g., once in error handling, again in normal cleanup).Step 4: Heap allocator is now confused — same memory marked as "free" multiple times.Step 5: Attacker triggers additional allocations with controlled content to overwrite nearby metadata or pointers.Step 6: Memory corruption leads to daemon crash or controlled function pointer overwrite.Result: Privilege escalation or remote DoS.
Detection Method: Use valgrind on services, monitor with auditd
Solution: Upgrade systemd, use memory-safe patterns or languages for input-handling daemons

Title: Double-Free in GPU Driver Kernel Module
Scenario Description: 1. A user-space app opens a GPU device.2. Sends a crafted ioctl (a special system call) to the GPU driver.3. This makes the driver free memory twice.4. Memory corruption occurs.5. Attacker places malicious code in freed space (heap spray).6. When the GPU driver reuses the freed area, attacker’s code gets executed.7. This can allow root access or full control over the kernel.
Tools Used: YAML/INI Parsers, VSCode, Python Agent, GDB
Attack Steps: Step 1: AI agents typically load configuration settings (e.g., API keys, plugin flags) from .ini or .yaml files using config parsers like Python’s configparser, ruamel.yaml, or PyYAML. Step 2: A user (or attacker) uploads or references a config file in a prompt like: “Load config from /tmp/settings.yaml”. Step 3: Attacker creates a malformed YAML file—e.g., a single key with 1,000,000 characters or deeply nested objects with recursion. Step 4: Parser tries to read the config. Due to lack of bounds checking or depth limits, the tool may allocate excessive memory or trigger a recursive parsing loop. Step 5: This causes a crash or, in worst cases (especially in C-extensions like libyaml), a buffer overflow. Step 6: The attacker may leverage this to overwrite function pointers or cause logic errors. Step 7: Use tools like Valgrind, GDB, or memory profilers to trace overflow or leaks. Step 8: Prevent by using safe config parsers (safe_load in YAML), setting input limits, and isolating config parsing from user prompt control.
Impact: Out-of-bounds memory usage, denial of service
Detection Method: Monitor file sizes, parse depth, and crash logs
Solution: Use safe YAML modes (e.g., safe_load), input validation, and memory guards
Tags: Config Overflow, YAML Exploit, INI Abuse

Title: Shared Memory Region Freed Twice
Scenario Description: 1. Create shared memory segment.2. Attach it to multiple processes.3. Multiple cleanups (signals, crashes) cause double free.4. Kernel memory tracking for IPC gets corrupted.5. May crash the system or allow privilege escalation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: LLM agent is configured to accept audio for tasks like transcription, keyword detection, or speaker ID. Example prompt: “Transcribe the attached audio file.” Step 2: Attacker creates a malformed MP3 or WAV file with corrupted headers or chunk sizes using a hex editor or tools like Audacity with non-standard export settings. Step 3: This audio is sent to the agent, which passes it directly to a decoder (e.g., ffmpeg -i audio.mp3 out.wav). Step 4: FFmpeg parses the corrupted file and encounters out-of-bounds buffer read or write. In some versions or with unsafe build flags, this leads to heap/stack overflow. Step 5: Attacker may chain this with a shell payload inside audio metadata (like ID3 tags) or manipulate FFmpeg filters to execute arbitrary commands. Step 6: FFmpeg may crash, leak memory, or execute parts of the malformed metadata. Step 7: Use ASAN builds of FFmpeg to detect during fuzzing; monitor syslog/crash dumps. Step 8: Never pass user-uploaded audio directly into command-line decoders without sanitization or sandboxing.
Detection Method: Monitor FFmpeg logs, sandbox media conversion tasks
Solution: Use safe FFmpeg flags, strip metadata, validate audio types pre-decode
Tags: FFmpeg Exploit, Audio Overflow, ID3 Injection

Title: Double-Free in setuid Root Binary (e.g., passwd)
Scenario Description: 1. Run a setuid binary like passwd with a malformed argument.2. Memory is allocated and freed improperly.3. The same chunk is freed twice.4. This corrupts memory management (heap metadata).5. Attacker can hijack control flow → gain root.
Attack Steps: Step 1: LLM agent has a plugin or tool connector that calls a native C/C++ binary via subprocess in Python or a CLI shell wrapper. Example: a prompt like “Check spelling of: [INPUT]” is passed to a tool like spellcheck.exe. Step 2: Attacker provides extremely long input (>2048 chars), e.g., “Check spelling of: [A x 5000]”. Step 3: The native tool written in C/C++ does not validate input length and stores the string in a fixed-size char array (e.g., char buf[1024];). Step 4: Overflow occurs—extra characters write into adjacent memory (stack or heap), potentially overwriting return address or function pointer. Step 5: With crafted input, attacker can redirect program flow (e.g., to shellcode). Step 6: If ASLR/DEP protections are weak, this leads to reliable RCE. Step 7: Detection involves input logging, crash traces (e.g., segfaults), and memory sanitizer tools. Step 8: Prevent by adding length checks in both the agent and the native tool, use strncpy, and never pass raw prompt strings to compiled tools directly.
Vulnerability: Lack of bounds checking in native interfaces
Impact: RCE, agent hijack, denial of service
Detection Method: Monitor subprocess crashes, validate user input size
Solution: Patch native code for bounds checking, wrap tool calls in sanitizing shell scripts
Tags: Buffer Overflow, Native Interface, Prompt Injection

Title: glibc Malloc Hooks Hijack via Double-Free
Scenario Description: 1. Program frees the same memory chunk twice (fastbin double-free).2. This allows overwriting __malloc_hook (a function pointer).3. Attacker sets this hook to point to their code.4. Next malloc() calls attacker code = execution hijack.
Tools Used: Custom Plugin Loader, C++ Tools, GDB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Agent platform (e.g., LangChain, CrewAI, custom) supports dynamic plugin loading from a plugin registry. These plugins may be binaries written in C++ or loaded as .so, .dll, or .dylib files. Step 2: A plugin accepts arguments from prompts, e.g., “Use plugin X to process the following input.” Step 3: The plugin reads that input into a statically allocated buffer in native code like char input[256]; gets(input);. Step 4: Attacker sends a prompt that injects an extremely long string (e.g., 2048+ characters), causing a classic buffer overflow. Step 5: Overflowed buffer may overwrite control structures, allowing attacker-controlled memory manipulation or code redirection. Step 6: If executable code is injected and protections like DEP/ASLR are weak or bypassed, attacker gains RCE. Step 7: This type of plugin behavior may not be logged or sandboxed, making detection hard. Step 8: Use GDB, Valgrind, or AddressSanitizer to detect memory violations. Step 9: Solution is to enforce buffer size limits in native plugin code, sanitize inputs, and isolate plugin execution in secure sandboxes.
Vulnerability: Buffer overflow in unvalidated plugin inputs
