Attack Type: Scheduled task runs hidden ADS script
Scenario Description: Malicious PowerShell script is stored in an ADS stream and called by a scheduled task for persistence or escalation
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a PowerShell payload (e.g., payload.ps1) that launches a reverse shell or adds admin users. Step 2: Store it in an ADS: type payload.ps1 > task.ps1:hidden.ps1. Step 3: Create a scheduled task that runs powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File task.ps1:hidden.ps1. Step 4: The script doesn't exist visibly on disk, only via dir /r. Step 5: On task trigger, the hidden script runs silently. Step 6: Use for persistence, privilege escalation, or lateral movement. Step 7: Monitor Task Scheduler and PowerShell logs for detection.
Detection Method: Monitor scheduled task configs, PowerShell command line arguments
Solution: Limit scheduled task creation to admins, restrict ADS read/execute rights

Title: Trusted Path Bypass (DLL or EXE in ADS)
Attack Type: Load hidden DLL from ADS using vulnerable loader
Scenario Description: Some applications load DLLs from relative paths — attacker puts malicious DLL in ADS and abuses dynamic loading
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an application that loads DLLs from a non-absolute path (vulnerable to DLL hijacking). Step 2: Generate a malicious DLL using msfvenom or Cobalt Strike. Step 3: Embed the DLL into ADS of the EXE: type evil.dll > victim.exe:evil.dll. Step 4: Trigger the EXE. If the loader reads DLLs using relative path or from the same folder, it may load evil.dll from ADS. Step 5: Use Procmon to observe DLL loading behavior. Step 6: Combine with UAC bypass for persistence. Step 7: This bypasses AppLocker and many AV engines.
Detection Method: Monitor DLL load paths and use Sysmon Event ID 7
Solution: Set full path loading for DLLs, use SafeDllSearchMode, enable DLL signature verification
Tags: ADS, DLL Hijack, Trusted Path Abuse

Title: ADS Persistence via HKCU\Run or Startup
Attack Type: Point startup registry key or folder shortcut to ADS
Scenario Description: Attacker stores backdoor in ADS and uses registry or Startup folder to persist on reboot
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create your backdoor executable (reverse shell, keylogger, etc). Step 2: Hide it in ADS: type shell.exe > user.dat:runme.exe. Step 3: Create a registry key in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run with value cmd /c start user.dat:runme.exe. Or place a .lnk shortcut in the Startup folder pointing to user.dat:runme.exe. Step 4: On next login, ADS file is executed without appearing in file explorer. Step 5: AVs may miss it if not inspecting alternate streams. Step 6: To detect, scan registry for : usage and monitor ADS stream activity.
Detection Method: Use Autoruns to detect ADS-based startup entries, monitor Run registry key changes
Solution: Block ADS execution, restrict registry write access to standard users

Title: Token Theft Payload Hidden in ADS
Attack Type: Store LSASS dumper in ADS and run to steal SYSTEM token
Scenario Description: Hide memory-dumping binary in ADS and trigger it silently to extract credentials from LSASS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare credential dumper tool like procdump or mimikatz.exe. Step 2: Store it in ADS: type mimikatz.exe > legit.exe:creds.exe. Step 3: Use powershell to execute it: Start-Process -FilePath legit.exe:creds.exe. Step 4: LSASS is dumped, and attacker retrieves passwords or tokens. Step 5: Results can also be written into another ADS for stealth: output.txt:dump.txt. Step 6: Detection requires LSASS access alerts and monitoring ADS write behavior. Step 7: Defender should block LSASS access or require protected process light (PPL).
Detection Method: Monitor access to LSASS, check unusual use of ADS, alert on unsigned access to protected processes
Solution: Enable Credential Guard or PPL, block procdump/mimikatz access via AppLocker
Tags: LSASS Dump, ADS Hiding, Credential Theft

Title: Privilege Inversion via ADS + Insecure Permissions
Attack Type: ADS payload in writable path → executed by privileged app
Scenario Description: Store malicious payload in ADS within ProgramData, which is loaded by a SYSTEM-level process with weak path logic
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a SYSTEM process that loads external files (e.g., DLLs, configs) from ProgramData or %TEMP%. Step 2: Use icacls to find directories where Everyone has Write access. Step 3: Create a file like ProgramData\safe.exe:hidden.exe with your payload inside the ADS. Step 4: Wait or trigger the process to read from that directory. Step 5: If process logic accepts relative paths or unvalidated input, your ADS payload is executed as SYSTEM. Step 6: Monitor using Procmon to see which files are loaded. Step 7: This is a privilege inversion attack — unprivileged user → SYSTEM code path.
Vulnerability: Write access + privilege process logic flaw
Impact: SYSTEM shell from unprivileged ADS write
Detection Method: Alert on writes to ProgramData by users, monitor SYSTEM process DLL loading patterns
Solution: Lock down ProgramData ACLs, use explicit path validation in service logic

Title: Bypass Whitelisting / AppLocker
Attack Type: Legit app runs payload stored in ADS
Scenario Description: Whitelisted binary (e.g., Office, cmd.exe) loads a malicious DLL or script from ADS — AppLocker ignores alternate streams
Attack Steps: Step 1: AppLocker policies typically verify main binary name and path but may ignore alternate streams. Step 2: Store payload in ADS: type evil.ps1 > notepad.exe:launch.ps1. Step 3: Run it using: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File notepad.exe:launch.ps1. Step 4: Or use: rundll32 notepad.exe:evil.dll,DllMain. Step 5: Whitelisted binary runs, AppLocker doesn’t block execution, since main file is trusted. Step 6: Detection requires command-line auditing or process ancestry analysis. Step 7: Mitigate using AppLocker SRP extensions that account for ADS.
Vulnerability: Alternate stream not validated by AppLocker
Detection Method: Enable logging of all script and DLL loads, review AppLocker bypass attempts
Solution: Upgrade AppLocker rules to block ADS execution paths, use code integrity policies

Title: ADS DLL Hijacking
Attack Type: Hide malicious DLL in ADS and abuse DLL search order
Scenario Description: Victim binary loads DLL from current directory or user path — attacker hides it in ADS to evade detection
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a target binary that loads DLLs dynamically from its own directory (e.g., app.exe loads plugin.dll). Step 2: Store DLL in ADS: type payload.dll > app.exe:plugin.dll. Step 3: Launch binary using normal execution: start app.exe. Step 4: The app loads the DLL from its own path, and your ADS payload executes. Step 5: Combine with rundll32 or regsvr32 if needed. Step 6: Monitor DLL load chains with Procmon or Sysmon.
Detection Method: Sysmon DLL load events (ID 7), compare with known DLL paths
Solution: Force full path loading in all binaries, validate DLL hashes

Title: Task Scheduler Binary Path ADS
Attack Type: Scheduled task points to ADS payload as executable
Scenario Description: Attacker places payload in ADS and registers it as executable in schtasks — executed silently by Task Scheduler
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a malicious EXE file (backdoor.exe) and hide it in an ADS: type backdoor.exe > legit.txt:task.exe. Step 2: Register a scheduled task: schtasks /create /tn "Updater" /tr "legit.txt:task.exe" /sc minute /ru SYSTEM. Step 3: Task Scheduler runs your ADS payload every minute under SYSTEM context. Step 4: Nothing visible in Task Manager or file explorer, but payload executes in background. Step 5: Detect by monitoring task paths with : and scanning ADS streams. Step 6: Clean by removing the ADS task and reverting scheduled task to safe binary.
Detection Method: Monitor scheduled task Action paths for : and unusual entries
Solution: Use group policy to restrict task creation, validate scheduler task paths
Tags: Task Scheduler Abuse, ADS, Privilege Escalation

Title: ADS Trick with Alternate Extensions
Attack Type: Hide payload using alternate extension in ADS
Scenario Description: Store a VBS or script file inside an alternate stream (e.g., report.txt:evil.vbs) and execute it using scripting engines like wscript or cscript
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a VBScript payload file named evil.vbs (e.g., MsgBox or backdoor). Step 2: Hide it in ADS: type evil.vbs > report.txt:evil.vbs. Step 3: The ADS won't appear in dir, but you can verify using dir /r. Step 4: Execute it using: wscript report.txt:evil.vbs. Step 5: You can also double-click a shortcut or make a registry Run key that points to this ADS path. Step 6: Used for persistence or to hide initial infection script. Step 7: Detection requires logging or ADS-aware scanners. Step 8: This method works even in user folders like Desktop or Downloads. Step 9: If combined with startup task or phishing lure, results in persistent script execution.
Vulnerability: Scripting engine reads file from alternate stream
Detection Method: Enable logging for WScript/Cscript usage; scan for : in command lines
Solution: Disable WSH if not needed; restrict ADS execution with AppLocker

Title: ADS Chaining with .lnk Shortcut
Attack Type: Shortcut (.lnk) points to ADS payload for persistence
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds payload in a file like file.txt:evil.exe and sets a shortcut to point to that payload, often placed in Startup folder
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create payload evil.exe that runs silently or gives reverse shell. Step 2: Store it using ADS: type evil.exe > file.txt:evil.exe. Step 3: Create a .lnk file (shortcut) using right-click or powershell that runs: file.txt:evil.exe. Step 4: Place the .lnk in user’s Startup folder (C:\Users\Username\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup). Step 5: On reboot or login, the hidden ADS payload is executed. Step 6: This completely avoids placing the payload in main file system view. Step 7: Can also be used in phishing — send .lnk pointing to ADS payload on a shared location. Step 8: Monitor shortcut targets for colon : patterns.
Detection Method: Scan shortcuts in Startup folder for : or ADS patterns
Solution: Limit write access to Startup; alert on unknown .lnk pointing to ADS

Title: Installer Backdoor via ADS
Attack Type: Embed backdoor DLL inside ADS of legitimate setup.exe
Scenario Description: Hide DLL payload in a trusted installer’s ADS stream (e.g., setup.exe:stage.dll) and load it dynamically inside installer logic
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a stage.dll file (backdoor or persistence payload). Step 2: Hide it in trusted-looking file: type stage.dll > setup.exe:stage.dll. Step 3: Inside your setup script or binary, include logic like: rundll32 setup.exe:stage.dll,DllMain. Step 4: User sees normal installer UI, while your ADS payload runs in the background. Step 5: Can be triggered during post-install script of MSI or NSIS-based installer. Step 6: If not extracted from ADS, EDR misses this secondary payload. Step 7: Ideal for phishing or USB attacks using trusted installer icons. Step 8: Use Wireshark or Procmon to observe if child process or ADS gets launched during install.
Vulnerability: Install logic loads DLL from ADS
Detection Method: Track parent-child process chains during installs; inspect installers with ADS detection
Solution: Only install signed packages from verified sources; scan with alternate-stream aware AV

Title: ADS LNK Weaponization in Downloads
Attack Type: Hide malware in downloaded PDF with ADS + LNK trigger
Scenario Description: Phishing campaign where user is tricked into opening .lnk file pointing to ADS on fake document like invoice.pdf:mal.exe
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake invoice file invoice.pdf. Step 2: Embed the payload: type malware.exe > invoice.pdf:mal.exe. Step 3: Create a .lnk file named View Invoice.lnk that points to invoice.pdf:mal.exe. Step 4: Send both via ZIP or email phishing lure. Step 5: User clicks on .lnk, expecting to open a PDF, but ADS malware executes. Step 6: If icon is also changed to PDF icon, user won’t suspect. Step 7: Malware launches hidden, while decoy PDF can also be opened normally for distraction. Step 8: Detection is hard unless you log ADS launches or inspect shortcut contents. Step 9: Can result in remote shell, keylogger, or token grabber being deployed silently.
Impact: Remote code execution from local user
Detection Method: Monitor ZIP extraction or LNK usage; alert on files referencing : in user folders
Solution: Disable .lnk execution from downloads; enforce signed script policy
Tags: ADS, Phishing, LNK, PDF, Shortcut, Malware

Title: Storing AES Keys or Config in ADS
Attack Type: Hide malware config or encryption key inside ADS
Scenario Description: Malware stores its config (e.g., IPs, ports, AES keys) in ADS stream to evade static signature or file analysis
Attack Steps: Step 1: Malware author generates a config file like config.json containing C2 IP, AES key, user token, etc. Step 2: Save it in ADS: type config.json > C:\ProgramData\log.dat:settings. Step 3: Inside the malware code, load config using Win32 API or PowerShell logic to read from the ADS. Step 4: Since file is not on disk, YARA rules or AV can't scan config or key. Step 5: Useful for dynamic config loading or sandbox evasion. Step 6: Also used to bypass file hashes — since ADS doesn’t affect primary file hash. Step 7: Defender can scan with tools like streams.exe or dir /r to identify. Step 8: Regular disk scans will miss this unless ADS-specific.
Vulnerability: ADS used to hide runtime config or keys
Detection Method: Inspect files with ADS stream manually; check for API calls to CreateFileW with colon paths
Solution: Store config in secure registry or protected files; monitor high-risk folders like ProgramData

Title: Dropper in ADS → Executed via MSBuild / Rundll32 / regsvr32
Attack Type: Fileless dropper placed in ADS and executed via trusted tools
Scenario Description: Attacker hides malware EXE or DLL in ADS, then executes it using signed Microsoft binaries for bypassing AV (LOLBins)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a dropper executable or DLL with obfuscated payload (C2, backdoor, reverse shell). Step 2: Store it in ADS: type dropper.dll > log.txt:stage.dll. Step 3: Choose a trusted signed binary like regsvr32.exe or rundll32.exe that can execute DLLs. Step 4: Execute via: rundll32 log.txt:stage.dll,DllEntry or regsvr32 /s log.txt:stage.dll. Step 5: For EXE, use msbuild to call and run it silently. Step 6: These signed binaries (called LOLBins) are whitelisted and allowed by default in many environments. Step 7: Detection requires tracking suspicious command lines or process ancestry. Step 8: This is fileless — nothing visible on disk except alternate stream.
Impact: AV/EDR evasion using trusted Windows tools
Detection Method: Monitor command line params to LOLBins (rundll32, regsvr32); block colon path references
Solution: Use WDAC or AppLocker to limit use of signed binaries; restrict alternate stream read access

Title: Scheduled Tasks Write ADS to SYSTEM Path
Attack Type: Scheduled task creates payload in ADS of SYSTEM directory
Scenario Description: A SYSTEM-level scheduled task creates or runs payload stored in ADS under protected path like C:\Windows\System32:file.exe:evil.ps1
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a PowerShell payload (e.g., reverse shell or token dumper) and save it as evil.ps1. Step 2: Use ADS to hide it: type evil.ps1 > C:\Windows\System32:file.exe:evil.ps1. Note: You need SYSTEM rights or a vulnerable scheduled task to do this. Step 3: If you have SYSTEM access or an exploitable scheduled task, configure it to run: powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "C:\Windows\System32:file.exe:evil.ps1". Step 4: The payload is now run by SYSTEM context and no visible file on disk. Step 5: If AV is present, it may ignore ADS and only scan the main file, not the payload. Step 6: Set task trigger to “at logon” or “every 5 minutes” for persistence. Step 7: Verify by checking Task Scheduler → Task Properties → Actions. Step 8: Useful for privilege escalation or permanent foothold.
Detection Method: Check scheduled tasks for paths containing :; monitor ADS usage in protected folders
Solution: Remove legacy tasks; block creation of tasks referencing ADS streams in system paths

Title: ADS Virus Hidden in Office Macros or Archives
Attack Type: Macro or archive writes payload to ADS and runs it
Scenario Description: An Office macro drops and executes an ADS payload hidden in a legitimate document folder
Attack Steps: Step 1: An attacker creates a VBA macro in Word/Excel that contains base64-encoded or obfuscated PowerShell script. Step 2: When document is opened, macro executes: cmd.exe /c "echo <payload> > file.docx:evil.ps1". Step 3: Immediately after, the macro runs: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File file.docx:evil.ps1. Step 4: The evil.ps1 script is stored inside ADS of the document file, invisible to users. Step 5: Optionally, archive (e.g., ZIP or RAR) contains a shortcut (.lnk) that runs the above command. Step 6: AV may ignore this due to macro’s trusted origin and hidden stream. Step 7: Used for stealthy initial access and execution on victim machines. Step 8: Combine with phishing for higher success rate. Step 9: To detect, scan file ADS with streams.exe or dir /r.
Vulnerability: VBA macros or archive scripts use ADS
Detection Method: Enable macro logging; inspect Office launch behaviors; scan files for unexpected ADS
Solution: Disable macros or allow only signed macros; enforce file integrity scanning
Tags: ADS, VBA, Phishing, Fileless, Macro, Initial Access

Title: Exploit Windows Defender Exclusion
Attack Type: Hide payload in ADS of path excluded from Defender scan
Scenario Description: Attacker stores malicious ADS stream in a folder or file path that’s excluded by Defender or EDR policies
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a folder or path excluded from AV scanning (e.g., Dev folder or C:\Tools\Backup). Step 2: Create payload (EXE or PS1) and store it in ADS: type payload.ps1 > C:\Tools\Backup\log.txt:evil.ps1. Step 3: AV doesn’t scan ADS in excluded path, allowing hidden payload to persist. Step 4: Execute with: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Tools\Backup\log.txt:evil.ps1. Step 5: May also bypass EDR if path is whitelisted for developer tools or backups. Step 6: Use in conjunction with scheduled task or registry autorun to ensure persistence. Step 7: To detect, security teams must manually audit exclusions and check for presence of ADS using Get-Item -Stream *. Step 8: This method bypasses detection without killing AV.
Vulnerability: ADS not scanned in whitelisted paths
MITRE Technique: T1562.001 – Disable or Evade Security Software
Detection Method: Monitor execution from excluded paths; check for presence of : in command lines
Solution: Minimize exclusions; never exclude user-writeable or temp folders; audit policies regularly
Tags: ADS, Defender Bypass, Evasion, Exclusion Abuse

Title: ADS with Registry Autorun Key
Attack Type: Use ADS payload path in Run or RunOnce registry key
Scenario Description: Attacker hides a payload in ADS and configures it to launch at startup via autorun registry key
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an executable or script payload (e.g., backdoor or recon tool). Step 2: Store it inside ADS of any file: type payload.exe > image.jpg:evil.exe. Step 3: Open regedit and navigate to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Step 4: Create a new string value, e.g., “Updater” with data: cmd.exe /c image.jpg:evil.exe. Step 5: On next login, this command runs and executes hidden ADS payload. Step 6: To improve stealth, store image.jpg in AppData\Roaming\Updater\, a common-looking folder. Step 7: This enables user-level persistence without a visible file. Step 8: Defenders can spot colon : in registry keys or scan for ADS with autoruns tools. Step 9: Useful for malware dropper or beacon startup. Step 10: Can be used with signed payload to avoid AV suspicion.
Vulnerability: Run key points to ADS file
Detection Method: Monitor registry startup keys for unexpected colon : or commands pointing to alternate streams
Solution: Use Group Policy to lock registry keys; block or alert on : paths in autoruns

Title: UEFI DXE Driver Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects a malicious DXE (Driver Execution Environment) driver into UEFI firmware to hijack boot flow
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the target system and retrieve its UEFI firmware dump using tools like chipsec_util spi dump. Step 2: Analyze the firmware image with UEFITool and locate the DXE phase section (DXE core or driver volumes). Step 3: Modify the firmware binary by injecting a custom DXE driver. This driver can be built using EDK2 and programmed to run early at boot (e.g., logging keystrokes, injecting code into OS loader). Step 4: Flash the modified firmware back using flashrom or vendor tools like Intel FPT (fpt -f modified.bin -bios). Step 5: Reboot system. The malicious DXE driver executes in the UEFI DXE phase before OS boot. Step 6: This technique survives OS reinstall, bypasses AV, and gives pre-boot control. Step 7: Confirm success by checking driver behavior or using chipsec_util uefi verify. Step 8: DXE rootkits are invisible to the OS and powerful for stealth persistence.
Vulnerability: No signature validation of DXE modules
Detection Method: Use chipsec to verify firmware integrity; compare DXE hashes
Solution: Use Secure Boot + BootGuard; enable write-protection on SPI flash

Title: Malicious Option ROM
Scenario Description: Option ROM on GPU, NIC, or RAID card is modified to load malware during BIOS POST
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a PCIe device with Option ROM support (e.g., GPU or RAID card). Step 2: Dump its Option ROM using flashrom or PCILeech SPI tool (pcileech dumprom -device 00:01.0). Step 3: Modify the binary Option ROM — append payload or inject custom code. Can use assembler + hex editor to patch known hooks. Step 4: Flash the modified ROM back to the hardware (e.g., flashrom -p internal -w patched.rom). Step 5: On boot, BIOS scans Option ROMs and executes the malicious one. Step 6: Payload can patch memory, install SMM rootkit, or disable Secure Boot. Step 7: Because it's hardware-based, AV and OS cannot detect this easily. Step 8: Check success by boot logs, memory analysis, or device behavior. Step 9: This attack gives stealth, persistence, and potential cross-boot persistence.
Vulnerability: Option ROM execution at BIOS stage
Detection Method: Use signed Option ROMs only; monitor PCI firmware versions
Solution: Lock Option ROM flashing in BIOS/UEFI; scan for PCI write attempts
Tags: Option ROM, PCI Rootkit, Firmware Malware

Title: Replace bootx64.efi with Trojan Loader
Attack Type: Replace UEFI bootloader with malicious one
Scenario Description: Attacker overwrites bootx64.efi file in EFI System Partition with their payload that loads malware before OS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Boot the target machine using a Linux live USB (Ubuntu, Kali). Step 2: Mount the EFI system partition: mkdir /mnt/efi && mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/efi. Step 3: Navigate to the EFI/Boot or EFI/Microsoft/Boot folder. Step 4: Backup the original bootx64.efi file (cp bootx64.efi bootx64.efi.bak). Step 5: Replace it with a trojan loader (cp mybootloader.efi bootx64.efi) — this loader can be built using EDK2 or signed with self-signed cert if Secure Boot is off. Step 6: Reboot the system — the system loads bootx64.efi, which executes your payload first (e.g., inject code, drop malware, patch kernel). Step 7: Payload runs before the OS and is hard to detect by AV. Step 8: Detection is possible only with EFI integrity scanning. Step 9: Confirm success by observing unusual OS behavior or modified boot flow.
Vulnerability: Insecure EFI bootloader writeable from live OS
Detection Method: Use bootloader integrity scanning; monitor changes to EFI files
Solution: Enable full Secure Boot; prevent unsigned EFI bootloaders

Title: Hook UEFI Runtime Services
Scenario Description: Malicious code hooks key runtime functions (e.g., GetVariable, ResetSystem) to exfil data or modify UEFI behavior
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a UEFI driver or DXE component that hooks UEFI runtime service pointers in the system table. Step 2: In your UEFI driver code (EDK2), intercept GetVariable or ResetSystem function by replacing function pointers. Step 3: Compile driver and inject it using UEFITool into the UEFI firmware image. Step 4: Flash modified firmware using SPI tool or Intel FPT. Step 5: On reboot, your driver is loaded and UEFI runtime calls are hijacked. Step 6: Hooked functions can monitor, change, or exfil data (e.g., credentials from NVRAM). Step 7: Confirm hook success using chipsec_util uefi dump or log outputs. Step 8: This attack is highly stealthy and persistent even across OS reinstalls. Step 9: Detection is nearly impossible from the OS unless firmware scanning is enforced.
Vulnerability: No integrity checks for runtime hooks
Detection Method: Use chipsec to verify UEFI runtime handlers; monitor unexpected firmware behavior
Solution: Write-protect UEFI SPI flash; use UEFI Secure Boot + BootGuard

Title: BIOS Flashing via SPI Interface
Attack Type: Flash BIOS via SPI to install rootkit
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to SPI chip and flashes BIOS directly using hardware or low-level tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain physical access to the target system or local admin access. Step 2: If physical, connect a SPI flasher (like CH341A USB programmer) to the BIOS chip (8-pin). Step 3: Dump BIOS using flashrom -p ch341a_spi -r bios.bin. Step 4: Modify BIOS image — inject backdoor, bootkit, or malicious Option ROM. Step 5: Flash modified image using flashrom -p ch341a_spi -w modified.bin. Step 6: If software method is available (e.g., Intel FPT), use: fptw64 -f modbios.bin -bios. Step 7: Reboot system. Modified BIOS now loads before OS and can run any hidden payload. Step 8: Malware can disable Secure Boot, inject DXE, or patch OS loader. Step 9: Detect by comparing BIOS hashes or SPI chip analysis. Step 10: This attack is stealthy and works even if the disk is encrypted.
Detection Method: Use SPI flash protection and BIOS write lock; monitor firmware flash attempts
Solution: Enable Intel BootGuard / AMD PSP; physically secure SPI chip

Title: Bypass Secure Boot
Attack Type: Exploit misconfiguration to load unsigned code
Scenario Description: Attack bypasses Secure Boot by exploiting misconfigured UEFI variables, boot order, or signed but vulnerable bootloaders
Tools Used: Linux live USB, EFI shell, bcdedit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Boot target system with Secure Boot enabled and check if vulnerable bootloaders like shim or grubx64.efi are allowed. Step 2: If so, mount EFI partition using Linux live USB: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt/efi. Step 3: Replace allowed bootloader with malicious version: cp mybootx64.efi /mnt/efi/EFI/Boot/bootx64.efi. Step 4: If machine doesn’t enforce key revocation (dbx), it will still boot. Step 5: Alternatively, set BootOrder to run unsigned loader via efibootmgr. Step 6: Some systems allow manipulating SecureBoot UEFI variable from OS (via mokutil or kernel flaws). Step 7: Once booted, payload runs under full OS with root access. Step 8: Secure Boot bypass enables rootkits or encryption bypass. Step 9: Detection requires dbx audit or firmware analysis.
Impact: Full bypass of OS integrity chain
Detection Method: Monitor EFI variable changes; enable dbx updates; log Secure Boot state
Solution: Use strict Secure Boot policy; revoke known-bad keys; disallow unsigned bootloaders
Tags: UEFI, Secure Boot, Chain of Trust, Bypass

Title: Bootloader Patch (GRUB/LILO)
Attack Type: Modify bootloader to hijack OS kernel loading
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies GRUB or LILO bootloader to inject code before the OS boots, gaining stealth and persistence
Tools Used: Linux ISO, GRUB, hex editor, mount tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Boot the system using a Linux live USB (e.g., Kali Linux or Ubuntu). Step 2: Mount the disk and locate the /boot or EFI partition: mount /dev/sda1 /mnt. Step 3: Locate GRUB bootloader files, typically in /mnt/boot/grub/. Step 4: Backup the current bootloader files (e.g., core.img, grub.cfg, etc.). Step 5: Replace GRUB Stage 1.5 or 2 with a modified binary that contains a payload — this can be done using a hex editor or custom assembler stub. Step 6: The payload could launch a rootkit, patch kernel at load, or log credentials. Step 7: Save changes and reboot. GRUB will load the malicious payload silently during boot. Step 8: You now control kernel behavior before antivirus loads. Step 9: Detection is difficult because the OS sees no changes to user-space or kernel-space once booted.
Vulnerability: GRUB/LILO is modifiable, insecure boot path
Detection Method: Bootloader hash mismatch; Secure Boot would block unsigned bootloaders
Solution: Enforce Secure Boot; lock /boot with full-disk encryption; monitor bootloader integrity

Title: Abuse S3 Resume Script
Attack Type: Insert payload into ACPI S3 resume script
Scenario Description: Attackers embed malware into firmware ACPI S3 (sleep/resume) script to run code when the device wakes from sleep
Attack Steps: Step 1: Dump ACPI tables using acpidump > tables.dat or chipsec_util acpi dump. Step 2: Identify and extract the ACPI S3 sleep/resume scripts (_WAK, _RES) which are executed when a system wakes up from suspend-to-RAM (S3). Step 3: Inject a malicious operation into the script using ACPI Source Language (ASL). Example: add logic that writes a payload into memory or triggers hardware port I/O. Step 4: Recompile the ACPI table using iasl (Intel’s ACPI compiler) and repackage the firmware. Step 5: Flash modified firmware using flashrom or Intel FPT. Step 6: On next wake-from-sleep event, the ACPI code runs automatically and executes the injected command. Step 7: Since this is firmware-level, OS is unaware of any activity. Step 8: This method provides stealthy, timed execution useful for implants or exfiltration. Step 9: Detection requires ACPI table diffing or behavior-based triggers on wake.
Vulnerability: No runtime validation of ACPI firmware
Detection Method: Monitor resume behavior; use BIOS protection for ACPI updates
Solution: Protect firmware ACPI regions; block unsigned ACPI table changes
Tags: ACPI, S3 Sleep, Resume Script, Covert Execution

Title: EvilTwin UEFI Firmware Update
Attack Type: Deploy malicious signed firmware through vendor tool
Scenario Description: Adversaries create and deliver a signed (but evil) firmware update that appears trusted to the vendor's update system
Tools Used: Intel FPT, BIOS Update Tools, Flashrom
Attack Steps: Step 1: Analyze the vendor's BIOS update tool and its firmware signature check process. Many tools only check if the firmware is signed — not who signed it. Step 2: Create a modified BIOS/UEFI image and sign it using a certificate that is technically valid (e.g., expired dev cert that vendor still accepts, or attacker-controlled cert in DB). Step 3: Package the rogue firmware in a valid update file (e.g., .cap, .bin, .rom). Step 4: Deliver it via phishing, social engineering, or remote code execution that launches the update tool. Step 5: The update tool installs the firmware, believing it is legitimate. Step 6: Upon reboot, the system runs attacker’s firmware with complete control (bootkits, keyloggers, etc.). Step 7: This is extremely stealthy and can’t be removed by OS reinstall. Step 8: Used in real-world UEFI implants like LoJax.
Detection Method: Log firmware update events; validate firmware signatures against trusted CA list
Solution: Vendor must enforce signing from trusted root only; revoke old certs

Title: INT 13h/15h Hooking
Scenario Description: Legacy BIOS interrupts (for disk/memory) are hijacked to silently monitor or tamper with boot process
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that INT 13h (disk I/O) and INT 15h (system services) are old BIOS functions executed during boot. Step 2: In legacy BIOS or VMs, write a boot sector program in Assembly that hooks INT 13h and 15h. Step 3: When BIOS calls these interrupts (e.g., to read disk), your code intercepts and alters the result (e.g., hiding a file, modifying boot sector). Step 4: Write this bootloader to disk using tools like dd if=boot.asm of=/dev/sda bs=512 count=1. Step 5: On boot, your code runs invisibly, giving stealth and early system control. Step 6: This is mostly historical or for VMs with legacy BIOS, but still relevant in dual-boot and emulation setups. Step 7: Used by classic stealth viruses and low-level keyloggers. Step 8: Very hard to detect once loaded — only visible through memory dumps.
Vulnerability: INT handler hooking not protected pre-boot
Detection Method: Memory dump before OS loads; BIOS boot logs
Solution: Switch to UEFI; disable legacy BIOS boot; use full disk signature checks

Title: Dropper via OS Driver Install
Attack Type: UEFI runtime malware injection through driver loading
Scenario Description: Malware is dropped during OS runtime and lives in UEFI memory areas not scanned or wiped by OS tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a signed (but vulnerable or misused) driver to gain low-level hardware access. Example: RWEverything, AsrDrv104.sys. Step 2: Load the driver using a privileged account or system exploit. Step 3: Use driver functions to write payload into UEFI memory or runtime memory regions (e.g., using physical address access). Step 4: Payload persists even if OS reboots, as UEFI runtime memory is kept alive. Step 5: You can now drop a kernel-level backdoor or keylogger. Step 6: Detection is difficult as antivirus does not scan these areas. Step 7: Confirm with chipsec_util mem read/write or hardware debuggers. Step 8: This technique is stealthier than normal droppers, works post-boot but below OS-level.
Vulnerability: Drivers allow raw memory access below OS
Detection Method: Monitor kernel driver loading; use kernel-mode memory scanner
Solution: Block driver installs not from trusted vendors; disable kernel memory mapping drivers
Tags: UEFI Runtime, Driver Injection, Post-Boot Payload

Title: TPM Bypass via Fake Boot Measurement
Attack Type: Tamper with TPM measurements to hide malicious bootloader
Scenario Description: Attacker fakes or replays PCR (Platform Configuration Register) values so that TPM believes the boot is clean even if infected
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that the TPM records boot measurements (bootloader, kernel, etc.) into PCR values which can be checked later for integrity. Step 2: Attacker prepares a malicious bootloader but wants it to appear clean to the TPM. Step 3: Modify bootloader or shim to fake measurements and write expected PCR values directly. Step 4: Alternatively, replay previously recorded "clean" PCR logs even if boot is now infected. Step 5: Use tools like tpmtool or tpm2_pcrreset to test or reset PCR values (if misconfigured). Step 6: This fools OS-level remote attestation tools like BitLocker or remote TPM validation. Step 7: Payload persists while appearing trusted. Step 8: Only detection is if TPM attestation is externally verified and log mismatch is detected. Step 9: Requires deep TPM or firmware knowledge but is effective for stealthy bootloader implants.
Vulnerability: PCR measurements can be spoofed or replayed
Impact: TPM bypass; trusted malware at boot
Detection Method: Compare measured boot logs against known-good logs; verify chain of trust remotely
Solution: Enable full TPM attestation with external verification; update to TPM 2.0 strict policies
Tags: TPM, PCR, Trust Bypass, Secure Boot Evasion

Title: Signed Driver Injection (BlackLotus Style)
Attack Type: Abuse signed driver certs to install UEFI malware
Scenario Description: Attacker uses leaked or misused certificates to load signed, malicious UEFI bootkit (like BlackLotus), bypassing Secure Boot checks
Tools Used: Leaked Microsoft cert, EDK2, bootkit builder
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains a leaked or revoked but still accepted Microsoft-signed certificate (example: leaked “Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher” cert). Step 2: Use bootkit source code like BlackLotus, construct a custom UEFI application using EDK2 or known bootkit builders. Step 3: Sign this malicious UEFI application using the leaked or weakly validated certificate so the system accepts it under Secure Boot. Step 4: Boot into the target system or deliver the bootkit via malware installer. Step 5: Drop the malicious UEFI binary into the EFI System Partition (e.g., /EFI/Microsoft/Boot/bootmgfw.efi) and replace the legitimate one. Step 6: On reboot, the system loads the attacker's UEFI bootkit with full privilege before the OS. Step 7: The malware now has full stealth: it can load keyloggers, install kernel rootkits, or bypass BitLocker. Step 8: Since it's "signed," Secure Boot does not block it. Step 9: Detection is extremely difficult unless firmware boot logs or certificates are checked manually.
Detection Method: Monitor firmware signatures against known safe certs; detect unsigned replacement of known EFI binaries
Solution: Revoke vulnerable certs in UEFI DBx (deny list); update firmware & Secure Boot keys
Tags: Secure Boot Bypass, BlackLotus, Bootkit, UEFI Malware

Title: NVRAM Variable Abuse
Attack Type: Use UEFI NVRAM to store hidden persistent malware
Scenario Description: Attacker stores malicious config/code in UEFI NVRAM variables, which survive OS reinstall and are rarely scanned
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that UEFI firmware uses NVRAM (non-volatile RAM) to store settings, boot entries, logs, etc., across reboots. Step 2: Attacker runs code (via malware or local shell) that writes a custom UEFI NVRAM variable using tools like efibootmgr, efivar, or Windows APIs. Example: efivar --write --name MyPayload --data "$(hexdata)". Step 3: The variable contains either a payload, a pointer to the attacker's code in the EFI partition, or shellcode to launch from boot. Step 4: On reboot, the UEFI firmware may auto-execute the payload (if injected into BootOrder, BootNext, or OS LoaderPath). Step 5: The malware reactivates before OS boots. Even reinstalling Windows/Linux won’t remove the UEFI NVRAM variable. Step 6: These variables are not visible from standard file explorers or antivirus scanners. Step 7: This provides hidden persistence. Step 8: Defender must manually clear or inspect NVRAM variables using tools like efibootmgr -v or BIOS setup.
MITRE Technique: T1547.001 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Detection Method: Monitor EFI variable table; detect unauthorized boot entries
Solution: Reset NVRAM manually; use signed BIOS updates that clear NVRAM; disable boot variable injection at runtime

Title: Shadow MBR Injection (Legacy)
Attack Type: Inject rootkit into Master Boot Record (MBR)
Scenario Description: Classic bootkit attack where attacker overwrites MBR with custom loader that launches malware before OS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gets local or remote shell access to the target Windows system. Step 2: Backup the current Master Boot Record (first 512 bytes) using dd if=/dev/sda of=mbr.bak bs=512 count=1. Step 3: Craft a custom MBR program in Assembly that loads malware into memory, then passes control to the original bootloader. Step 4: Inject the payload using dd if=shadow_mbr.bin of=/dev/sda bs=512 count=1. Step 5: Reboot the machine. The new MBR executes attacker code before the OS starts. Step 6: This code can install kernel rootkits, keyloggers, or patch Windows startup routines. Step 7: Since it's pre-boot, antivirus and Secure Boot do not detect this if BIOS is legacy. Step 8: Only low-level disk scanning (e.g., with bootice or ms-sys) can reveal modifications. Step 9: Recovery is only possible via bootable antivirus or disk repair tools.
Vulnerability: Legacy BIOS allows MBR write with no protection
Detection Method: Compare MBR hash with known clean state; scan raw disk sector 0
Solution: Use UEFI + GPT instead of MBR; lock boot sector; enable full disk encryption
Tags: MBR, Legacy Boot, Rootkit, Shadow Loader

Title: Chainload Custom OS Kernel
Attack Type: Load malicious kernel using GRUB chainloader
Scenario Description: Replace legit kernel with trojan one that loads like a normal OS, achieving complete stealth and kernel-level access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker boots a live Linux distro (e.g., Kali) on target system. Step 2: Mount the boot partition (/mnt/boot) and locate existing kernel and initramfs files. Step 3: Compile or prepare a modified Linux kernel (trojan) with attacker-controlled modules, logging, or bypasses. Step 4: Copy this kernel to the boot partition as vmlinuz-evil, and create a matching initrd file. Step 5: Modify grub.cfg or use grub-customizer to add a new menu entry that silently boots this malicious kernel — e.g., set it as default or hide it under a misleading name. Step 6: On reboot, GRUB loads attacker’s kernel instead of the real one. Step 7: From user perspective, OS behaves normally, but kernel is compromised. Step 8: Even antivirus tools will run under the infected kernel. Step 9: Defender must review GRUB config and kernel signatures to detect this.
Vulnerability: GRUB allows alternate kernels, no kernel signature
Impact: Hidden OS rootkit with total control
Detection Method: Check GRUB menu entries; enforce kernel verification policy
Solution: Use signed kernel boot enforcement (e.g., Secure Boot with lockdown mode); disable boot config editing

Title: SMM Code Injection (System Management Mode)
Attack Type: Exploit Intel SMM to run code at highest CPU level
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses flaws in SMM to execute arbitrary code invisible to OS — undetectable, persistent, and privileged
Tools Used: CHIPSEC, UEFITool, UEFI SMM vuln sample code
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that SMM is a CPU mode higher than kernel, used for power management and firmware functions. Step 2: Identify an SMM call handler that lacks proper input validation — e.g., accessible from the OS. Step 3: Send a crafted SMI (System Management Interrupt) payload using tools like CHIPSEC or driver interfaces. Step 4: Exploit buffer overflow, pointer corruption, or race in SMM handler to inject attacker shellcode into SMRAM. Step 5: Shellcode executes in SMM, invisible to OS, hypervisors, or antivirus. Step 6: This shellcode can monitor memory, modify kernel behavior, or hide rootkits. Step 7: Persistence is achieved until next reboot, or can even be stored in firmware. Step 8: Only detectable by physical memory inspection or firmware dump. Step 9: Used by sophisticated malware (e.g., Intel-based firmware rootkits, espionage malware).
Vulnerability: Vulnerable SMM call handler in BIOS/UEFI firmware
Detection Method: Analyze SMM handler behavior using CHIPSEC; scan for illegal memory writes to SMRAM
Solution: Update BIOS firmware; disable write access to SMRAM; restrict SMI handlers
Tags: SMM, SMRAM, Firmware Rootkit, Stealth Execution

Title: Manipulate UEFI Capsule Updates
Attack Type: Abuse capsule update to inject or tamper UEFI firmware
Scenario Description: Attacker forges or tampers with UEFI capsule updates to flash malicious firmware under legitimate update mechanism
Tools Used: Capsule firmware, BIOS tools, fmp tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that UEFI Capsule updates are used by OS (e.g., Windows) to deliver firmware updates through software. Step 2: Download or reverse-engineer a valid capsule firmware update (e.g., .cap or .bin file from Dell/HP). Step 3: Modify the capsule image to include attacker code or bootkit logic — either by replacing a module or injecting into PEI/DXE phase. Step 4: Repackage the capsule update with proper metadata (firmware version, vendor ID, etc.). Step 5: Deliver it via software exploit, remote access, or social engineering, and trigger update via fwupdate, fwupd, or Windows Firmware Update tool. Step 6: On reboot, UEFI flashes the modified firmware from the capsule, permanently storing attacker's code. Step 7: Attacker now controls firmware and has persistence over OS reinstalls. Step 8: Defender might never know, since it appears as a legitimate update. Step 9: Only visible with UEFI firmware dump comparison or capsule signature check.
Vulnerability: Capsule update signature not enforced or misused
Detection Method: Monitor firmware update logs; enforce update signature validation
Solution: Enforce firmware capsule signing and rollback protections; use BIOS lock-down mode

Title: Intel Boot Guard Bypass
Attack Type: Disable tamper protection to allow firmware/rootkit injection
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits misconfigured or disabled Intel Boot Guard settings to bypass firmware verification
Tools Used: Intel ME Analyzer, FIT, SPI Programmer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that Intel Boot Guard prevents tampered firmware from running by checking cryptographic signatures during boot. Step 2: On some systems (especially custom boards or poorly configured firmware), Boot Guard is misconfigured or disabled by OEM. Step 3: Attacker confirms this using tools like Intel FIT or ME Analyzer (dump SPI flash using SPI programmer or Intel FPT tool). Step 4: With disabled enforcement, attacker can now flash custom UEFI firmware (e.g., with bootkits or malware modules) without triggering integrity check failure. Step 5: Flash the backdoored firmware using tools like flashrom, FPT.exe, or AFUWIN.exe. Step 6: On next boot, attacker’s modified UEFI firmware executes as normal with no warning. Step 7: This bypass can be persistent and stealthy even across OS reinstalls. Step 8: Defender must analyze Boot Guard policy or use official Intel ME detection tools to verify protection status.
Detection Method: Check Intel Boot Guard policy via FIT/ME Analyzer; verify signature enforcement on boot
Solution: Reflash clean firmware; lock SPI regions in BIOS; enforce Boot Guard with proper keys and policies
Tags: Intel Boot Guard, Firmware Injection, SPI Flash

Title: Use of UEFI Boot Services After ExitBootServices()
Attack Type: Execute malicious UEFI code during handover to OS
Scenario Description: Exploit flaw where malicious UEFI payload tricks firmware into running code after boot handoff
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that ExitBootServices() marks the point where the OS takes over and firmware services are supposed to stop. Step 2: Attacker writes a malicious UEFI driver or app that delays or bypasses ExitBootServices() call, tricking firmware into executing attacker code even after OS boot has started. Step 3: Use EDK2 to write a UEFI payload that hooks into boot flow and abuses lingering memory mappings. Step 4: Deliver this payload via compromised EFI System Partition or malicious firmware update. Step 5: On boot, the system hands off control to OS, but the attacker’s payload remains in memory and continues executing, possibly injecting into kernel or hypervisor. Step 6: Attacker achieves stealthy persistence without being visible to OS-level antivirus or logging. Step 7: Defender must examine boot logs and firmware memory regions for unexpected post-boot behavior.
Vulnerability: Firmware allows use of boot services post-handoff
Impact: Runtime UEFI malware invisible to OS
Detection Method: Monitor boot memory and ExitBootServices() status during system transition
Solution: Patch firmware to enforce strict ExitBootServices() policies; disable legacy UEFI applications
Tags: ExitBootServices Abuse, UEFI Runtime, Firmware Persistence

Title: EFI Stub Tampering in Linux Kernels
Attack Type: Embed malware inside Linux kernel's EFI stub
Scenario Description: Modify the Linux kernel’s embedded EFI loader (EFI stub) to include hidden backdoor or rootkit
Attack Steps: Step 1: The EFI stub is a special section in the Linux kernel (vmlinuz) that makes the kernel bootable directly as an EFI binary. Step 2: Attacker extracts the kernel binary using objcopy or binwalk, then locates the EFI stub region. Step 3: Modify the stub code or append payload that runs during early boot (before init system starts). Step 4: Repack the kernel and replace the original /boot/vmlinuz file. Step 5: Modify GRUB or EFI boot entry to load the tampered kernel. Step 6: On next reboot, system boots using the malicious kernel, and the attacker’s payload runs before the OS starts. Step 7: Can be used to disable logging, install keyloggers, or elevate privileges. Step 8: Defender will not detect this unless kernel hashes or boot attestation is performed. Step 9: Use signed kernel verification to block such tampering.
Vulnerability: EFI stub allows embedded payload without detection
Impact: Stealth rootkit executes before OS starts
Detection Method: Check kernel signature hashes; audit vmlinuz binaries for modifications
Solution: Use Secure Boot with kernel signing; monitor GRUB config and kernel integrity
Tags: EFI Stub, Linux Kernel, Kernel Backdoor

Title: Secure Boot Shim Exploitation (CVE-2022-34302)
Attack Type: Load unsigned EFI binary using Microsoft-signed loader shim
Scenario Description: Exploit Microsoft-signed vulnerable shim (bootloader) to bypass Secure Boot and execute unsigned bootkits
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that many Linux distros use a Microsoft-signed shim (shimx64.efi) to load their GRUB bootloaders while still enabling Secure Boot. Step 2: In CVE-2022-34302 and related flaws, old versions of shim accepted unsigned GRUB or Linux kernel binaries. Step 3: Attacker finds a system with vulnerable shim version (by checking /boot/efi/EFI/BOOT/shimx64.efi). Step 4: Replace the unsigned binary (e.g., GRUB or kernel) with attacker-controlled bootkit or backdoored kernel. Step 5: On boot, shim happily loads the attacker’s unsigned payload, bypassing Secure Boot. Step 6: Attack works even if Secure Boot is enabled because shim is signed by Microsoft. Step 7: Defender won’t know unless Secure Boot DBx has been updated to block this vulnerable shim. Step 8: Persistence is maintained by replacing EFI binaries in the ESP. Step 9: Detection involves checking allowed EFI binaries and validating against revocation lists.
Vulnerability: Old shim loaders allow unsigned GRUB/kernel
Impact: Secure Boot bypass → full OS compromise
Detection Method: Use Microsoft’s DBx updates; verify bootloaders loaded under Secure Boot
Solution: Remove vulnerable shim from ESP; update Secure Boot DBx with latest revoked certificates

Title: Persistent BitLocker Circumvention
Attack Type: Capture BitLocker keys from pre-boot UEFI environment
Scenario Description: Malware sniffs BitLocker keys from RAM before OS boot, allowing full disk decryption even with TPM enabled
Tools Used: UEFI keylogger, DMA attack tools, PCILeech
Attack Steps: Step 1: BitLocker often releases keys into RAM temporarily during the pre-boot authentication phase. Step 2: Attacker installs a UEFI-level keylogger or memory sniffer that runs before the OS starts (via infected firmware or EFI app). Step 3: On system power-on, BitLocker unlocks the disk and puts keys into memory. Step 4: The attacker’s code captures these keys before the OS boots and saves them to NVRAM or disk. Step 5: Attacker now has full access to encrypted disk and files. Step 6: Even if user reinstalls Windows, attacker can reuse keys or keep dumping them until firmware is cleaned. Step 7: Advanced versions may exfiltrate the keys over the network or store for later use. Step 8: Defender must validate firmware integrity and use hardware-backed key protection (e.g., TPM-only + PIN).
Vulnerability: UEFI allows memory read before OS loads
Impact: Full disk decryption despite BitLocker enabled
Detection Method: Use BitLocker TPM+PIN+startup key; enable pre-boot authentication logging
Solution: Reflash clean firmware; clear TPM and reinitialize BitLocker; use BIOS write protection

Title: EFI Variable Reset Trap
Attack Type: Lock user out or maintain persistence via EFI variables
Scenario Description: Set EFI variable that causes reboot loop, hides OS, or redirects boot path to attacker binary
Attack Steps: Step 1: UEFI firmware uses variables like BootOrder, BootNext, and others stored in NVRAM. These control what the system boots. Step 2: Attacker with access (physical or malware) sets an EFI variable that points to a non-existent or crashing binary. Example: efibootmgr --bootnext 0005 with 0005 pointing to corrupt entry. Step 3: On next reboot, system enters boot loop, hides OS, or fails to boot. Step 4: Alternatively, attacker may point boot path to malicious binary or shim that executes attacker's code. Step 5: Some EFI variable traps persist even after OS reinstall. Step 6: Attack can cause denial-of-service or force user to boot attacker’s OS/kernel. Step 7: Defender must manually clear boot variables using UEFI shell or recovery media.
Vulnerability: UEFI variables redirect boot control or lock OS
Impact: DoS, forced malware boot, system lockout
Detection Method: Use firmware recovery tools; inspect EFI variable state from recovery media
Solution: Lock EFI variable editing from OS; use Secure Boot and authenticated variable mode
Tags: UEFI Trap, BootOrder Abuse, Boot Hijack

Title: Patch TCG Logs (Measured Boot)
Scenario Description: Measured Boot depends on Trusted Platform Module (TPM) PCR values. An attacker forges or patches TCG log entries to fake a trusted boot.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker boots a custom UEFI image or modified firmware that contains a payload. Step 2: After boot, the attacker uses tpm2_pcrread to view Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) of the system’s TPM. Step 3: Attacker creates a forged TCG log that contains "clean" or known-good measurements, despite malicious code having run. Step 4: Using tpm2_pcrextend, attacker injects or modifies PCR values to match the forged log. Step 5: When a remote attestation system checks the PCRs (e.g., for measured boot verification), it falsely confirms system integrity. Step 6: Attacker remains undetected at firmware level, even though OS was tampered during boot. Step 7: Defender must rely on out-of-band TPM validation or alternate secure boot logs to detect.
Vulnerability: Insecure firmware & PCR modification via userspace
Detection Method: Remote TPM attestation mismatch, integrity diff logs
Solution: Prevent userspace access to tpm2_pcrextend; use TPM with attestation via external verifier

Title: Broker Misuse
Scenario Description: Trusted broker services (like Windows ShellBroker or Linux polkit) execute privileged tasks. A misconfigured broker can be tricked into doing things it shouldn't.
Tools Used: Procmon, Polkit Exploit, Burp IPC Fuzzers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies an IPC-based broker (like polkit on Linux or Shell Infrastructure Broker on Windows) that runs as root or SYSTEM. Step 2: Using an unprivileged process, the attacker sends crafted IPC requests (via D-Bus or named pipes). Step 3: Because the broker trusts all IPC calls from a specific group (e.g., local user), it performs actions like copying files, starting services, or elevating apps. Step 4: Attacker tricks broker into overwriting sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, registry hives) or spawning a shell as root. Step 5: This leads to root/SYSTEM privilege escalation. Step 6: Defender can detect via IPC audit logs, checking unexpected caller contexts.
Vulnerability: Missing validation in privileged IPC handlers
Detection Method: IPC audit, trace broker logs for improper actions
Solution: Validate all broker input; use access control lists strictly

Title: File System Access Abuse
Scenario Description: Insecure file permissions allow unprivileged user to edit config files used by SYSTEM/root processes
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker lists Windows services with sc qc and finds one running as SYSTEM. Step 2: Checks associated paths (binaries, configs) using AccessChk or manually with file explorer. Step 3: Identifies a .ini, .xml, or config file that has Everyone: Write or Users: Modify access. Step 4: Modifies the file to insert malicious command, like a reverse shell in a config field. Step 5: Restarts service or waits for system to trigger service restart. Step 6: Service runs attacker’s payload with SYSTEM privileges. Step 7: Defender may detect via service audit logs or monitoring file hashes.
Vulnerability: Insecure file ACLs or config load logic
Detection Method: Service load logs, config diff tools
Solution: Harden config file ACLs; monitor file changes

Title: Shared Memory Handle Leak
Scenario Description: Sandboxed browser or app shares a file/network handle by mistake; attacker reuses it to access data outside sandbox
Tools Used: Chrome Canary, Process Hacker, sandbox fuzzer
Attack Steps: Step 1: A sandboxed process (e.g., a Chrome tab) starts and shares a memory handle (e.g., a file descriptor or Windows handle) with another internal component like the GPU process. Step 2: Attacker exploits a race condition, info leak, or guessable handle ID to duplicate that handle. Step 3: The leaked handle provides access to a file, socket, or shared memory outside the attacker’s sandboxed domain. Step 4: Attacker reads/writes sensitive files or injects payloads into other sandboxed processes, breaking isolation. Step 5: In a chained attack, attacker escapes browser sandbox and executes arbitrary code. Step 6: Detection includes monitoring of handle inheritance and unexpected I/O operations from sandboxed child processes.
Vulnerability: Shared handles reused without access checks
Detection Method: Monitor handle table in sandboxed processes
Solution: Harden handle sharing policy, close handle leaks on fork

Title: GPU Process Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits bugs in GPU drivers or shader code parsing to run payloads outside sandbox
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads malformed WebGL or DirectX shader code from JavaScript in browser. Step 2: The GPU process receives and parses the shader. Step 3: Vulnerable GPU drivers (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) mishandle shader and execute unintended memory ops. Step 4: Attacker’s code now executes in GPU process context. Step 5: Using IPC or shared memory, attacker injects code into main browser process or reads protected memory buffers. Step 6: Attacker gains arbitrary code execution, escapes sandbox, and elevates privileges (e.g., browser → SYSTEM). Step 7: Detection involves GPU crash logs or memory anomalies.
Vulnerability: Shader validation bypass, GPU parser flaw
Detection Method: Monitor GPU shader logs; watch for GPU crash anomalies
Solution: Patch GPU drivers; disable unsafe WebGL features

Title: Misconfigured Shmem (e.g., chrome‑sharedmem)
Scenario Description: Chromium shares a memory region between sandboxed renderer and GPU processes, but misconfiguration may expose data across privilege levels
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a shared memory (shmem) region intended only for GPU rendering. Step 2: Notice it’s configured with overly broad permissions (e.g., readable/writeable by renderer). Step 3: Sandbox-exploit code in JS (via WebGL or CSS animation) to write a crafted value into that region. Step 4: At the same time, cause a race (timing attack) so the GPU process reads stale or unvalidated data. Step 5: Shmem content leaks into GPU or higher-privileged process, exposing memory content. Step 6: Attacker reads addresses, craft further memory primitives. Step 7: This enables kernel/OS privilege escalation. Step 8: Detection requires tracing shared memory permissions and access from renderer processes.
Detection Method: Audit memory mappings, restrict shmem access From renderer
Solution: HARDEN: enforce least-privilege mappings, fix permission tables

Title: Excessive API Exposure (FileSystem / SerialPort)
Scenario Description: Chrome exposes too-powerful APIs (e.g., FileSystem or SerialPort) to low-trust contexts, allowing unauthorized access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a browser API (e.g., SerialPort) accessible from unprivileged web pages. Step 2: A malicious page requests API permission (e.g., navigator.serial.requestPort()) — browser shows prompt. Step 3: Use clickjacking or misleading UI to trick user into granting it. Step 4: Once granted, attacker’s JS code reads/writes arbitrary file systems or serial devices. Step 5: They access local resources or even external hardware on victim’s computer. Step 6: This leads to device access compromise or data exfiltration. Step 7: Detection involves tracking API use from unsecure contexts and suspicious permission dialogs.
Vulnerability: API surface too broad for web context
Detection Method: Monitor API usage in devtools; user-prompt logs
Solution: Limit API to secure origins or presence of trusted certificates

Title: JIT Memory Reuse in Non-Sandboxed Process
Attack Type: Memory Reuse / Code Execution via JIT
Scenario Description: JavaScript JIT compiles code and allocates memory—if not cleared, old code can be reused to gain higher privileges in a parent process (e.g., GPU)
Tools Used: V8, JS script fuzzer, d8 shell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write JS that triggers V8’s Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler to place generated code into memory. Step 2: Force large memory operations and garbage collections to free these pages. Step 3: Re-allocate the same pages in a higher-privileged process (e.g., browser or GPU). Step 4: If code sanitizer is not fully clearing them, the JIT code remains executable. Step 5: Use a crafted JS stub to jump into that page and run your shellcode. Step 6: This triggers native code execution in a higher-privilege context. Step 7: Follow up by injecting a DLL or pivot to kernel exploits. Step 8: Detection involves JIT page auditing and VA memory reuse tracking.
Detection Method: Monitor JIT page clears; track memory reuse anomalies
Solution: Harden JIT, disallow executable and writable pages simultaneously; enable page zeroing

Title: Mojo Interface Vulnerability
Scenario Description: Chromium’s “Mojo” inter-process messaging system can be tricked into routing malicious messages into more-privileged components
Attack Steps: Step 1: Learn about Mojo: Chrome renderer uses it to talk with browser/GPU processes. Step 2: Analyze the interface definitions and check if any parameter is unsafe (e.g., unchecked strings, handles). Step 3: Write exploit code that constructs a malformed or oversize message. Step 4: Send it from compromised renderer to the browser process. The internal router misinterprets the message and dispatches into higher-privilege code. Step 5: The code executes attacker-built logic with full browser rights. Step 6: From there, they can read files, break sandbox, or load system-level privileges. Step 7: Detection requires IPC auditing and interface fuzzing.
Vulnerability: Mojo definitions unchecked allow wrong routing
Detection Method: IPC monitoring detects abnormal messages with large sizes or wrong handles
Solution: Validate all interfaces, use strong typing in Mojo schema definitions

Title: Escape via Audio/Video Driver Interface
Scenario Description: Browser parses media files and sends them to OS drivers—vulnerability in media or audio driver lets attacker escape sandbox (e.g., iOS/macOS WebKit)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a flaw in media codec (e.g., WebM parser, video decode) or in the OS audio driver (e.g., ALSA or CoreAudio on Mac). Step 2: Craft a malicious media file or stream that exploits this flaw. Step 3: Host it on a website and entice user to load it (via autoplay or download). Step 4: The browser hands off parsing to the OS driver. The bug triggers buffer overflow or use-after-free. Step 5: Attacker gains code execution in the driver’s process—outside of the browser sandbox. Step 6: From there, they can read files, escalate privileges, or install malware. Step 7: Detection involves monitoring driver crashes, stack violations, or audio/video parsing failures.
Impact: SYSTEM or root code execution via sandbox bypass
Detection Method: Watch for driver crashes; stack trace anomalies; unexpected operations in audio/video processes
Solution: Harden media parsers; sandbox audio drivers; require signed media decoders
Tags: Audio Exploit, Media Vulnerability, Sandbox Bypass

Title: Use‑After‑Free in Shared IPC Object
Scenario Description: IPC objects are created for message passing; if one actor frees them prematurely, other process may reference freed memory, allowing arbitrary code execution
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an IPC message object (memory struct) used between the browser and renderer. Step 2: Trigger a race condition where the renderer forces the browser to free the object while still having a live reference to it. Step 3: Cause the renderer to send malicious data to that dangling pointer. Step 4: Browser dereferences this dangling pointer and uses invalid data—control flow hijack occurs. Step 5: The exploit runs attacker code in browser process. Step 6: This breaks the sandbox, enabling malicious file/network access. Step 7: Detection includes memory sanitizer tools, crash report analysis, or fuzzing logs.
Vulnerability: UAF in browser IPC object exchange
Impact: Arbitrary code execution with browser privileges
Detection Method: Enable AddressSanitizer in build; watch for renderer crashes or use-after-free logs
Solution: Deploy hardened pointer validation; improve lifetime tracking in IPC framework

Title: File Descriptor Reuse
Scenario Description: On Linux, a renderer process might inherit file descriptors (FDs) to files it shouldn’t access, through /proc or races.
Tools Used: Custom Linux binary, strace, procfs access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Run a sandboxed process (e.g., Chrome renderer) with fine-grained rights. Step 2: The process has access to its own /proc/self/fd directory, which shows all inherited FDs. Step 3: If another process (e.g., parent browser) accidentally inherited an FD to a sensitive file (like /etc/shadow), the renderer can open /proc/self/fd/N. Step 4: Use open("/proc/self/fd/4") in JS/WebAssembly or via a bug. Step 5: The sandboxed code now can read or write protected files. Step 6: Developers rarely restrict procfs access in sandboxes—this is a gap. Step 7: Attacker extracts credentials or plants backdoors. Step 8: Detection involves logging unexpected FD openings by sandboxed processes.
Vulnerability: FD leakage due to sandbox misconfiguration
Detection Method: Audit /proc/*/fd; alert on abnormal FD reads by renderer
Solution: Ensure no sensitive FD is inherited; fully isolate sandboxes; restrict procfs access
Tags: Linux Sandbox, FD Leak, File Access

Title: Renderer Injection via DevTools
Attack Type: Injecting Code via Exposed Debug Interface
Scenario Description: Developer mode builds of Chrome expose DevTools interfaces to renderer—exploitable to inject malicious code.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch Chrome Dev build with --remote-debugging-port=9222. Step 2: The renderer process opens a WebSocket interface for DevTools. Step 3: From another app or JS (unauthenticated), connect to ws://localhost:9222. Step 4: Send commands like Runtime.evaluate({expression: 'evilCode()'}). Step 5: The renderer executes JavaScript outside its sandbox. Step 6: Inject code that escalates privileges, exfiltrates data, or breaks isolation. Step 7: Detection: monitor debugger connections from unauthorized apps.
Detection Method: Detect WebSocket debugger clients opening on renderer
Solution: Enable authentication on remote debugging; restrict DevTools in production profiles
Tags: Chrome Dev, Debug Interface, Code Injection

Title: Escape via External Protocol Handler
Attack Type: Remote Code Execution Through Protocol Links
Scenario Description: User clicks on mailto: or file: links in Safari or Chrome; links execute internal handler apps outside sandbox.
Tools Used: HTML page, crafted link, local mail client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a malicious webpage with <a href="file:///etc/passwd">. Step 2: When user clicks, browser asks OS to open local file: handler (e.g., Notepad, mail client). Step 3: A vulnerable handler allows injecting script (e.g., via file argument). Step 4: The handler executes a command with the path as parameter; attacker crafts file:///C:/Windows/System32/calc.exe or custom executable instead. Step 5: This bypasses browser sandbox entirely. Step 6: Similarly, mailto: URIs can run vulnerabilities in mail clients. Step 7: Detection: log external handler invocations from browser.
Detection Method: Monitor calls to file:, mailto: handlers for unexpected parameters
Solution: Ask confirmation before opening external URIs; whitelist safe protocols
Tags: file:// exploit, mailto bypass, browser RCE

Title: MacOS Launch Services Exploit
Attack Type: Sandbox Escape via App Launch Service
Scenario Description: Abusing macOS LaunchServices to launch external user apps (e.g., .app bundles) from within sandboxed WebKit contexts.
Tools Used: macOS with SIP disabled, open command
Attack Steps: Step 1: An attacker-hosted webpage sets <a href="myapp://do?something">. Step 2: WebKit asks LaunchServices to open myapp://. Step 3: If myapp:// is a registered custom scheme to launch local .app, the OS launches the app. Step 4: The app gains higher privileges outside sandbox. Step 5: From there, attacker can load malicious code or scripts. Step 6: Some native apps silently run on behalf of the attacker. Step 7: Detection: monitor Scheme URL registrations and app launches from browser.
Vulnerability: LaunchServices exposes apps to sandboxed apps
Impact: RCE via OS-level code execution outside sandbox
Detection Method: Detect new custom URL schemes; block unknown handlers
Solution: Disable unnecessary URL handlers; require user approval before launching apps

Title: CVE-2021-30563 (V8 + Mojo Sandbox Escape)
Attack Type: Memory Abuse → Mojo IPC → Sandbox Escape
Scenario Description: Type confusion in V8 JS engine triggers code execution, then chained with Mojo IPC vulnerability to escape sandbox.
Tools Used: Chrome Canary, Exploit PoC, ASan build
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a JS snippet that triggers a V8 type confusion bug (seen in Chrome 92). Step 2: This allows crafted data to slip past the engine into native memory. Step 3: Attack code gains arbitrary read/write primitives inside renderer. Step 4: Next, attacker targets a Mojo interface in Chrome that has insufficient validation. Step 5: By sending malicious IPC messages, attacker breaks isolation boundary into browser process. Step 6: Full browser compromise achieved (read/write file system, network access). Step 7: Detection: monitor crashes, unusual IPC, or sandbox escapes.
Detection Method: Crash logs with type confusion; IPC anomaly logs
Solution: Regular patching; sandbox hardening; exploit mitigation (ASLR, CFI)
Tags: V8 bug, Mojo IPC exploit, Sandbox Escape

Title: Font/Graphics Driver Exploit
Attack Type: Driver Vulnerability in Font or Graphics Stack
Scenario Description: Attacker delivers specially-crafted font/graphics file that triggers a flaw in OS driver, leading to code execution outside sandbox
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a malicious font file (e.g., .ttf or .woff) with engineered malformed tables. Step 2: Host the file via webpage or phishing email expecting user to open. Step 3: OS font rendering engine (like DirectWrite, CoreText) parses it. Step 4: Vulnerability causes buffer overflow or memory read/write outside intended bounds. Step 5: Windows/macOS graphics driver executes attacker's code in kernel or driver context—well outside browser sandbox. Step 6: Attacker now has SYSTEM/root and can install rootkits or move laterally. Step 7: Detection: watch for driver crashes or kernel fault logs triggered by font rendering.
Detection Method: Analyze font rendering crashes; memory access out of range
Solution: Enforce driver updates promptly; sandbox font parsing early; require signed fonts only
Tags: Font exploit, Graphics Driver, Kernel RCE

Title: File Upload/Download Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks browser into saving files outside download folder (e.g., ../../../../../system32/x.exe)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a link like <a href="/download?file=../../../../Windows/System32/notepad.exe">. Step 2: Victim clicks link, browser prompts “Save as”. Step 3: If browser doesn’t sanitize the filename, user may save it directly into system folders. Step 4: Attacker distributes page via phishing. Step 5: The file is overwritten or placed without detection. Step 6: On reboot or execution, Windows UI tools unexpectedly become malicious. Step 7: Detection involves monitoring unusual files in system folders.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized file paths on download controls
Detection Method: Monitor file writes to system folders from browser
Solution: Browser should enforce downloads to specific folders only

Title: Abuse of IPC Reply to Fake Origin
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs IPC (e.g., postMessage or chrome.runtime.sendMessage) from untrusted origin pretending to be legit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies an IPC endpoint in extension or browser that doesn't verify message origin. Step 2: A malicious web page uses JavaScript like window.postMessage({action: "deleteAll"}, "chrome://settings"). Step 3: The browser extension or tab blindly processes message trusting the reply origin. Step 4: Malicious action is executed—could be reading history, taking screenshots, or web navigation. Step 5: A deeper exploit chains into native messaging host. Step 6: Detection includes verifying origin in message handler.
Detection Method: Monitor postMessage usage and origin checks
Solution: Implement strict origin validation and message authentication

Title: Symbolic Link Abuse on macOS Sandbox
Scenario Description: macOS sandbox allows writing files via symlinks inside containerized directories (e.g., when writing logs)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker-controlled web content triggers sandboxed WebKit to write logs. Step 2: In anticipation, attacker has created a symbolic link inside sandbox directory: cd ~/Library/Containers/com.apple.app/Data/Downloads && ln -s /etc/passwd log.txt. Step 3: When WebKit writes to Downloads/log.txt, it actually writes to /etc/passwd. Step 4: Attack creates a new system user or corrupts critical files. Step 5: Sandbox yields unexpected file writes to host file system. Step 6: Detection includes tracing file write operations from sandbox processes.
Detection Method: Track symlink resolution in sandboxed file writes
Solution: Prevent symlink dereferencing or restrict write paths

Title: Fake Extension Messaging
Scenario Description: Attacker communicates with a malicious extension via chrome.runtime.sendMessage to execute native code
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker lures user into installing a malicious Chrome extension or modifies an existing one. Step 2: Attacker-controlled web page runs JS like chrome.runtime.sendMessage(extensionId, {cmd:"exec", code:"..."}); Step 3: Extension code executes the message, optionally calling native host or eval. Step 4: Arbitrary code is executed in the extension's privileged context. Step 5: Actions include reading files, altering DOM, capturing clipboard, or spawning processes via Native Messaging. Step 6: Detection requires reviewing extension messaging logic and validating messages against origins.
Detection Method: Monitor chrome.runtime.onMessage for suspicious patterns
Solution: Only trust messages from extension popup or validated content scripts

Title: Flash NPAPI Legacy Channel
Attack Type: Sandbox Escape via Deprecated Plugin Interface
Scenario Description: Attack uses NPAPI Flash plugin (deprecated) to escape Chrome’s sandbox via older interface bugs
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds old-school <object type="application/x-shockwave-flash"> on malicious page. Step 2: Browser loads Flash via NPAPI bridge. Step 3: Use old Flash vulnerability to break out of plugin container. Step 4: Attack payload gains access to browser process with reduced or no sandbox. Step 5: Then attacker uses additional vulnerabilities to reach OS-level. Step 6: Modern Chrome has NPAPI disabled, but dev builds may still run it.
Vulnerability: NPAPI not sandboxed; includes exploitable interface
Detection Method: Monitor plugin usage in Chrome developer builds
Solution: Disabled NPAPI in current builds; remove Flash support entirely

Title: Escape via System Preferences Injection (macOS)
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies or injects malicious code via .plist settings that are loaded by System Preferences on startup
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker with limited shell access edits ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.systemuiserver.plist or a global .plist in /Library/Preferences/SystemPreferences. Step 2: Insert an entry that causes System Preferences to load a plugin or script (e.g., via NSPrefPane entry). Step 3: On next launch of System Preferences (either manually or during login), macOS loads this malicious plugin. Step 4: The plugin executes within System Preferences’ process context. Step 5: This includes privileged file access and can cross sandbox. Step 6: Detection involves monitoring changes to .plist in preference folders.
Detection Method: Track unexpected defaults changes or SUID process loads
Solution: Restrict write access to preference directories; sandbox plugin loading

Title: Escape via Prompt/Popup Injection
Scenario Description: Browser popup prompts the user to open a file or app; user is tricked into granting it
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a normal-looking webpage that triggers a prompt like “Open this file?” Step 2: Use CSS and text to simulate native OS dialogs (e.g., “Allow this application to run?”). Step 3: When the user clicks “OK,” a hidden payload—e.g., a .exe or file:// link—is launched. Step 4: Victim unintentionally runs local or remote applications. Step 5: Attacker uses this to break out of the browser sandbox, install malware, or access files. Step 6: Because it’s user-initiated rather than automated, browser doesn’t block it. Step 7: Detection requires logging popup events and uninstalling fake UI overlays.
Impact: Remote code runs with user privileges
Detection Method: Monitor prompt origins and overlay windows
Solution: Browsers should disallow or verify fake dialog boxes

Title: Debug Build Exploitation (Symbols/Flags)
Scenario Description: Debug builds include symbols or flags that allow attackers to read pointer addresses or logic flows
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a debug build (e.g., with -g flag) using version fingerprinting or sniffing. Step 2: Using tools like gdb, readelf, or debug symbols, they analyze internal variable names, memory layout, and object structures. Step 3: With this info, they craft inputs that target specific heap locations or data structures. Step 4: Send malformed data to application using sockets or CLI. Step 5: Debug build outputs full error or dumps full internal state—including heap addresses or pointers. Step 6: Attacker uses these leaks to bypass ASLR, predict object placement or pointer values. Step 7: Next attack stage: perform a heap overflow or UAF. Step 8: Defender must release only optimized (strip symbol) builds in production.
Vulnerability: Non-stripped binaries leak internal memory info
Detection Method: Detect debug flag binaries; disable verbose dumps in production
Solution: Compile stripped, hardened, and sanitized builds for release
Tags: Debug Build Abuse, Heap Info Leak

Title: Use‑After‑Free Leak (Heap Chunk Metadata)
Scenario Description: Freed heap chunk gets reallocated; attacker reads use-after-free pointer to leak memory addresses
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a function in target app that frees memory (e.g., buffer) but doesn’t null its pointer. Step 2: In test environment, reproduce a user workflow that frees the buffer. Step 3: After freeing, reuse memory by allocating a controlled object (like another buffer) in the same heap location.
