Step 4: Now the script sets world-readable or appuser-readable ACL on /etc/shadow. Step 5: Read the file as a lower-privilege user or leak it out. Step 6: Swap back the dummy file to erase footprint. Step 7: Works best if ACL scripts don’t validate file type or path.
Vulnerability: ACL applied after insecure event detection
Impact: Unauthorized read/write access to protected files
Detection Method: Monitor ACL changes and logs for unexpected files; restrict ACLs to file owners only
Solution: Do not use automated ACLs; require manual review or path whitelisting
Tags: ACL Race, File Permission Exploit, Inotify Abuse

Title: Hijack Package Cache Events
Scenario Description: When apt, dnf, or yum package managers download .deb or .rpm files into a cache dir (like /var/cache/apt/archives), inotify triggers may be used by services to post-process them. If the attacker swaps the package file just before installation or verification, they can inject a malicious package.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a system where package downloads are cached (like /var/cache/apt/archives/), observe this directory during a download or update: sudo inotifywait -m /var/cache/apt/archives. Step 2: Wait for a real .deb or .rpm package to appear (e.g., curl_7.81.0-1.deb). Step 3: Immediately after the download completes and before verification or install occurs, swap it with a malicious version: mv malicious.deb curl_7.81.0-1.deb. Step 4: The system proceeds to install what it believes is the legit package. Step 5: Your package gets installed with full privileges. Step 6: If unsigned package checking is disabled or repo trust is misconfigured, this bypasses detection. Step 7: Cleanup any logs or timestamps to cover your tracks.
Vulnerability: File swap after download, before install
Impact: Root-level malware install via legitimate system update
Detection Method: Log every .deb/.rpm hash before install; enable package signature checks
Solution: Use only signed repositories; enforce GPG signature on all packages; deny write to cache dirs for non-root users

Title: Snap or Flatpak Update Watch
Scenario Description: Snap and Flatpak auto-update apps or containers using local file triggers. If the attacker replaces the app blob or manifest before full verification, code execution is possible.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system with Snap or Flatpak installed, and ensure auto-update is enabled (default for Snap). Step 2: Snap stores apps in /var/lib/snapd/snaps and Flatpak uses /var/lib/flatpak/app. Step 3: Monitor these paths using inotifywait -m /var/lib/snapd/snaps to detect when new .snap files arrive. Step 4: As soon as a new file (e.g., firefox_234.snap) is written but before it's mounted or verified, replace it with a malicious .snap package of the same name: mv attacker.snap firefox_234.snap. Step 5: Snap daemon mounts and runs this version as if it's trusted. Step 6: Malicious code gets full user-level (or sometimes elevated) execution. Step 7: Remove attacker version after execution if needed to maintain stealth.
Vulnerability: Insecure file trust after fetch, before mount
Impact: Execution of malicious app without user action
Detection Method: Monitor /var/lib/snapd/snaps or Flatpak paths; compare file hash with official versions
Solution: Enforce Snap confinement; use trusted store only; avoid user write access to Snap dirs
Tags: App Image, Snap, Flatpak, TOCTOU Update Poison

Title: TOCTOU During UID Switch
Scenario Description: Some applications check permissions or access protected files as root, then drop to a lower UID. Attackers race operations during this transition window.
Tools Used: strace, gdb, bash, chroot, multithreaded test app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary or app that starts as root (SUID binary or service) and drops privileges (UID) after performing an action. Examples: custom daemons, wrappers. Step 2: Use strace or inspect source to find where it checks permissions or accesses a file, then drops UID via setuid() or seteuid(). Step 3: While the app is mid-execution (between check and UID drop), inject another thread or fork that performs privileged actions (e.g., opens protected file or executes system command). Step 4: Time this thread or fork to execute before the UID drop happens. Step 5: You now get root file access or execution before the privileges are lost. Step 6: Use a debugger to pause/resume threads to control timing if needed. Step 7: Clean up traces after exploit completes.
Vulnerability: Delay between root action and UID drop
Impact: Access to root files or privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor multithreaded binaries for race behavior; enforce least privilege
Solution: Drop privileges at start of execution; avoid doing file I/O as root unless strictly required
Tags: UID Drop, TOCTOU Race, Fork-Race Exploit

Title: Delayed Privilege Drop
Scenario Description: Application opens sensitive file (as root) before dropping UID. Attacker uses this time window to control file contents or escalate access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target an app that opens protected files as root (e.g., /etc/shadow, system logs) and only drops root after file access. Step 2: Monitor file open events using inotifywait or auditd. Step 3: When the app opens the file and hasn’t dropped root yet, the attacker modifies file content or piggybacks on open file descriptor to read/write contents. Step 4: Example: app reads root config, stores pointer in memory, and later a dropped UID process accesses it. Step 5: Use gdb to attach and dump memory or use /proc/[pid]/fd/ to read file handles. Step 6: Attack is complete when you’ve read or injected into a root-only file without having real privileges.
Vulnerability: Delay between file open and UID drop
Detection Method: Detect if files are opened as root but used after UID drop
Solution: Require all privilege drops before I/O; enforce O_PATH-only file opens
Tags: UID Drop, Delay Race, File Access Hijack

Title: Reacquire Root via Retained Capabilities
Scenario Description: Linux supports capabilities that survive UID change (e.g., CAP_SYS_ADMIN), letting attacker regain root privileges even after UID drop.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary or app that drops UID but retains one or more Linux capabilities (e.g., CAP_SETUID, CAP_SYS_ADMIN). Use getcap /usr/bin/* to check for set capabilities. Step 2: Run the binary and check if it's still able to call setuid(0) even after UID is changed to nobody/user. Step 3: Using gdb, force the process to call setuid(0) from a retained CAP_SETUID context. Step 4: Process regains root UID. Step 5: Now modify sensitive files, spawn root shells, or inject cron jobs. Step 6: Optional: use LD_PRELOAD to override setuid() logic and make it persistent. Step 7: This works best if prctl(PR_SET_KEEPCAPS) or no cap_clear() is done.
Detection Method: Monitor running capabilities; enforce cap clearing via seccomp or audit rules
Solution: Always clear capabilities with cap_clear() after UID drop
Tags: Linux Capabilities, UID Reacquire, Privilege Exploit

Title: Fork Before Drop
Scenario Description: Some apps fork before calling setuid() to drop privileges. If attacker hijacks or replaces forked child, root privileges are retained.
Tools Used: gdb, strace, bash, multithreaded test binary
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a setuid binary that calls fork() before setuid() (common in C apps). Step 2: Attach a debugger (like gdb) to this process. Step 3: Wait for the process to call fork() — the child still has root UID. Step 4: In child process, hijack the flow to spawn a root shell: execl("/bin/bash", "bash", NULL) or overwrite memory to insert shellcode. Step 5: Parent drops UID after fork, but child now runs arbitrary root code. Step 6: Cleanup traces (delete shell history, wipe memory if needed). Step 7: This technique bypasses protections that only exist after the UID change. Step 8: Repeat for any poorly written forking daemon or wrapper.
Vulnerability: UID drop only happens after child fork
Impact: Root code execution in child process
Detection Method: Log parent/child UID consistency; detect root child without audit trail
Solution: Fork after privilege drop; drop UID before creating any subprocess

Title: GID File Access Abuse
Scenario Description: If a sensitive file is group-owned (shadow, sudoers), attacker can exploit group permissions when GID is not dropped with UID.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Look for files group-readable but root-owned (e.g., /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers). Use ls -l /etc/shadow. Step 2: If group permissions are loose and process retains GID (e.g., shadow group), attacker may be able to access files with that group’s permission. Step 3: Use a helper binary or attach via /proc/[pid]/fd to read open file descriptors still valid for that group. Step 4: Dump file content or replace config data. Step 5: This is more common on distros with legacy permissions or poor group management. Step 6: Add user to group temporarily to test. Step 7: If combined with delayed privilege drop, exploit becomes fatal.
Detection Method: Enforce strict group permissions; monitor GID changes in daemon logs
Solution: Drop group ID along with UID at start; set restrictive permissions on sensitive files
Tags: GID Exploit, UID-GID Race, Shadow Read

Title: Race via seteuid(0) Reuse
Attack Type: UID Escalation via weak privilege switch
Scenario Description: If an app frequently switches between euid=0 and lower UIDs, attacker can trigger operations during brief root windows.
Tools Used: bash, strace, gdb, custom test binary
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary that toggles between root and user via seteuid(0) and seteuid(1000) (used in services that do admin tasks then drop back). Step 2: Attach to the process via strace or gdb. Step 3: Detect timing when process switches to euid=0. Step 4: Spawn a thread, or child, or injected code that executes during this window. Step 5: During that window, access protected files, overwrite configs, or run root commands. Step 6: The window is short, so use thread scheduling tricks or inject syscall hooks to extend root time. Step 7: Clean up by reverting the euid or dropping shell afterward.
Impact: Short root access → root shell, config overwrite
Detection Method: Log all seteuid transitions; alert on unexpected euid=0 in running daemons
Solution: Use POSIX saved-set-UID carefully; avoid toggling privileges during execution
Tags: seteuid Race, UID Toggle, Root Window Attack

Title: Misordered Auth Flow
Scenario Description: Application performs sensitive action (like opening a root-only file) before checking the UID of the user, allowing an attacker to access protected resources.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary that performs a privileged action like open("/etc/shadow", O_RDONLY) or unlink("/etc/passwd") before checking if the current UID is privileged. Step 2: Use strace ./binary to confirm the order of operations – if open() occurs before UID validation, you have a vulnerable target. Step 3: Create a malicious script or user that runs the binary and reads or modifies the file opened during this window. Step 4: Use /proc/self/fd to access the open file descriptor before the program closes it or denies access. Step 5: Extract or inject your payload (e.g., change root password or append SSH key). Step 6: If the file is kept open long enough, reuse it for privilege persistence.
Vulnerability: Improper UID check after privileged action
Detection Method: Use auditd to track privileged file opens before UID check
Solution: Always validate UID before any sensitive operation
Tags: UID Check Bug, Auth Race, Shadow Access

Title: Symlink Race with Root UID
Scenario Description: Process checks access or file existence while running as root, then opens file – attacker swaps with symlink pointing to sensitive root-owned file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary or script that checks if a file exists (e.g., if (access("log.tmp") == 0)) and then opens it with root privileges (fopen("log.tmp", "w")). Step 2: Quickly create a symlink from log.tmp to /etc/shadow using ln -sf /etc/shadow log.tmp. Step 3: Run the vulnerable binary and time the symlink replacement right after the check but before the open() call. Step 4: If successful, the binary will open /etc/shadow with write access. Step 5: Inject your own root user or change passwords inside the file. Step 6: Use watch stat to help with precise timing, or write a script loop that automates the swap every millisecond. Step 7: Clean up log.tmp and logs to remove trace.
Vulnerability: TOCTOU: File checked, then opened without lock
Detection Method: Monitor for symlink swaps and mismatched file paths during access and open
Solution: Use O_NOFOLLOW, O_EXCL flags when opening files

Title: Setuid Binary Abuses UID Logic
Scenario Description: Setuid binary sets UID internally but continues to trust old UID logic, letting attackers bypass intended access controls.
Tools Used: gcc, bash, gdb, strace, custom suid app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a setuid binary by running find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null. Step 2: Check if the binary calls setuid(getuid()) or seteuid() conditionally. Step 3: If binary only checks UID at launch and drops it based on user args, pass crafted inputs to avoid drop. Step 4: Use a crafted argument or environment variable that causes UID to remain root (or regain it). Step 5: Attach gdb and force UID logic to skip drop (e.g., patch the jump). Step 6: Once UID is root, spawn shell with system("/bin/bash"). Step 7: You now have a root shell bypassing intended drops or limits in the binary logic.
Vulnerability: UID manipulation not validated after setuid
Detection Method: Track UID transitions in logs; validate SUID logic branches
Solution: Use setresuid() and confirm all UID/GID context switches
Tags: SUID Exploit, UID Trust Flaw, Root Shell

Title: Run as Unprivileged but Setuid Backdoor
Scenario Description: A process drops to unprivileged UID but writes or installs a backdoor file with setuid-root bit, gaining long-term root access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find or create a binary that runs setuid-root and drops to normal user UID early. Step 2: Observe if it creates files or installs scripts after dropping UID. Step 3: Modify that installed file (like /usr/local/bin/myscript.sh) to include a backdoor: cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootsh && chmod +s /tmp/rootsh. Step 4: The script runs as root during a future invocation (e.g., triggered by cron or reboot). Step 5: Run /tmp/rootsh and you now get a root shell even as a normal user. Step 6: Clean up timestamps and file logs to hide the planted backdoor.
Vulnerability: SUID set on backdoor from unprivileged context
Impact: Long-term root access via planted binary
Detection Method: Monitor for new setuid binaries; detect file creations with root UID/GID
Solution: Restrict write to root-owned dirs; enforce user separation and code integrity checks

Title: Environment Variable Abuse Before UID Drop
Scenario Description: Application loads environment-sensitive libraries or variables (e.g., LD_PRELOAD, PYTHONPATH) before dropping root, leading to code execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Export a malicious environment variable: export LD_PRELOAD=/tmp/malicious.so. Step 2: Create a simple shared object (malicious.c) that spawns a shell: void _init(){setuid(0); system("/bin/bash");}. Step 3: Compile with: gcc -fPIC -shared -o /tmp/malicious.so malicious.c -nostartfiles. Step 4: Run the vulnerable binary (setuid-root) which loads this library before dropping UID. Step 5: Your payload executes with root privileges and spawns a shell. Step 6: Cleanup: remove .so file and history. Step 7: Works if LD_PRELOAD is honored before setuid() call and if no env sanitization is in place.
Vulnerability: Unsafe env vars read before UID drop
Impact: Root shell or injected code runs as root
Detection Method: Log usage of preloadable env vars in root binaries; monitor /tmp or user-writable .so paths
Solution: Use clearenv() in C; sanitize environment early; strip untrusted variables

Title: Race Condition with Signal Handling
Scenario Description: Application drops UID but can be interrupted by attacker’s signal at just the right moment, hijacking logic mid-transition.
Tools Used: kill, gdb, strace, bash, custom handler
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a process that switches UID using setuid() or seteuid() but handles signals (like SIGUSR1, SIGCHLD, etc.) during this window. Step 2: Run the process and send a crafted signal right between logic steps: kill -USR1 <pid>. Step 3: The signal handler executes while the process is still root and can run injected code or read protected files. Step 4: In extreme cases, a handler might call an external command or script – replace that target with a payload. Step 5: Exploit this window to spawn a root shell or elevate access. Step 6: Time the signal precisely with sleep, or attach gdb to pause/resume for controlled execution. Step 7: Clean up attacker traces and script files after shell access.
Vulnerability: Signals execute in root context during drop
MITRE Technique: T1548.001 – Signal Race on UID Drop
Impact: Arbitrary code execution as root via signal
Detection Method: Monitor audit logs for strange signal timing on root processes
Solution: Block signals during privilege drop (sigprocmask()); avoid complex handlers in privileged contexts
Tags: UID Race, Signal Hijack, Root Race

Title: Dropped to User, Still Accessing Root FD
Scenario Description: A root-owned file is opened before UID drop, and attacker uses retained FD to access or modify root-only files after becoming user.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a binary that opens a file (e.g., /etc/shadow, /etc/sudoers) as root, then drops to an unprivileged UID using setuid(). Step 2: Before the drop, it opens the file but keeps it open via FD (file descriptor). Step 3: Run the binary and use /proc/self/fd/ or /proc/[pid]/fd/ to list open files. Step 4: If FD 3 or 4 points to /etc/shadow, use cat /proc/[pid]/fd/3 to read its content without root. Step 5: Alternatively, redirect FD into attacker-controlled process or script. Step 6: This bypasses standard UID checks by using pre-acquired file access. Step 7: Remove traces after dumping contents.
Vulnerability: Opened root files reused after UID drop
Detection Method: Monitor open FD lifetimes; audit pre-drop file usage
Solution: Always close root-owned FDs before UID drop
Tags: file descriptor reuse, UID bypass, shadow read exploit

Title: GID Inheritance in File Creation
Scenario Description: App switches GID to sensitive group and creates files. Group ownership inherited → attacker can read/write privileged files.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a directory owned by a sensitive group (e.g., shadow, sudo) and has the sticky or setgid bit enabled (use ls -ld /dir). Step 2: Identify apps or scripts that switch GID to a privileged group but do not reset to default after. Step 3: When file is created (touch my.log), it inherits the sensitive group, e.g., shadow. Step 4: Attacker reads or modifies this group-owned file to escalate privileges. Step 5: Abuse this to plant a script or config read by root in future runs. Step 6: Exploit is complete once privileged behavior is triggered (e.g., /etc/cron.d/ or log parsers). Step 7: Clean up by changing permissions back.
Vulnerability: GID not reset → file inherits sensitive group
Detection Method: Monitor group ownership of newly created files; detect abnormal GIDs
Solution: Always reset GID after use; set umask properly
Tags: sticky bit, gid leak, group misuse

Title: Group Ownership Abuse via GID Switch
Scenario Description: App switches to sensitive group (e.g., shadow) but fails to drop GID → attacker abuses access to read/modify group-owned data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target an application that uses setgid() to switch to a privileged group (e.g., shadow) for reading sensitive files. Step 2: Verify if GID is retained post-task using getresgid() or strace. Step 3: If retained, any files created or read afterwards use this GID. Step 4: Access group-readable files like /etc/shadow or /var/log/secure if GID matches. Step 5: Use script to dump these files, modify configuration, or impersonate other users. Step 6: Combined with weak file permissions, this can escalate to root or reveal password hashes. Step 7: Clean traces of access and restore timestamps.
Vulnerability: GID not dropped after privileged operation
Detection Method: Audit services for GID state post execution; monitor for sensitive group access
Solution: Always drop GID via setresgid(-1, -1, -1) after sensitive operations
Tags: shadow group, GID attack, group read exploit

Title: Multithreaded Privilege Drop Race
Scenario Description: One thread drops UID to unprivileged user, but other threads continue running as root — attacker exploits race to execute privileged code.
Tools Used: gcc, pthread, bash, gdb, ps, strace
Attack Steps: Step 1: Analyze a multithreaded binary or service using ps -T -p PID to list threads. Step 2: Check source or behavior if one thread calls setuid() while others keep executing. Step 3: Spawn a child thread to perform root-only action (file access, system() call). Step 4: If that thread runs before the UID is dropped, it executes as root. Step 5: Use gdb to attach and delay UID drop thread while root thread runs. Step 6: Run your exploit code inside that privileged thread. Step 7: This creates inconsistent UID states in process, letting attacker retain privilege mid-execution. Step 8: Cleanup includes terminating all threads and erasing logs.
Vulnerability: No UID lock across threads during drop
Impact: Root file access or shell from thread
Detection Method: Track UID state per thread; enforce thread sync during UID changes
Solution: Use pthread_atfork() and lock UID change globally
Tags: UID threading bug, multithread privilege race

Title: Chroot Escape Before UID Drop
Scenario Description: Chroot jail entered as root, UID dropped after. Attacker exploits pre-drop root access to escape jail.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a program or jail that calls chroot() while still running as root, but drops UID later. Step 2: Use file descriptors or mount points created inside jail to access outside FS (mount --bind / /mnt). Step 3: While still root (before UID drop), create a shell in real root FS: cp /bin/bash /mnt/tmp/rootsh && chmod +s /mnt/tmp/rootsh. Step 4: Exit chroot jail or call chdir("/") + execve() to escape jail. Step 5: Now outside, run /tmp/rootsh and gain root on real system. Step 6: This works because root inside chroot is root everywhere if jail isn't hardened. Step 7: Cleanup by deleting files and logs from /tmp, /mnt, and removing the setuid bit after use.
Vulnerability: Root retained inside jail before UID drop
Impact: Full root access outside chroot jail
Detection Method: Monitor mount access from chroot; detect UID 0 usage before sandboxing
Solution: Drop UID before chroot() or restrict chroot syscall entirely
Tags: chroot race, escape jail, root shell

Title: Retained FDs to Root-Owned Devices
Attack Type: Kernel FD Hijack via Priv Drop
Scenario Description: Application opens kernel memory device (e.g., /dev/kmem, /dev/mem) as root, then drops privileges while retaining open file descriptor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate a binary or daemon that starts as root and opens /dev/mem, /dev/kmem, or /dev/port for direct memory access. Step 2: Use lsof -p <PID> or ls -l /proc/<PID>/fd/ to confirm those device files are open. Step 3: If the process drops to a user (via setuid), but still holds FDs to those files, then attacker-controlled logic or another thread may use those FDs to read or write kernel memory. Step 4: Use a simple dd if=/proc/<PID>/fd/3 of=dump.bin bs=1 count=1024 to dump memory via FD if readable. Step 5: Analyze dump with hexdump or strings to look for sensitive kernel structures. Step 6: Writing to it (with write permissions) allows for kernel structure overwrites → full root compromise or kernel crash. Step 7: Remove traces and reboot to clear FD state if writable damage is done.
Vulnerability: FD retained to /dev/kmem or /dev/mem after UID drop
MITRE Technique: T1068 – Privilege Escalation via FD reuse
Detection Method: Audit open kernel devices with lsof; monitor UID changes during device access
Solution: Ensure all dangerous FDs are closed before privilege drop; deny /dev/mem access in userland

Title: Heap Overflow in Media Parsers
Attack Type: Heap Memory Corruption via Media File
Scenario Description: A malformed MP4 or 3GP file causes heap corruption in vulnerable parsers like libstagefright, leading to RCE (Remote Code Execution).
Tools Used: ffmpeg, gdb, adb, metasploit, custom MP4
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a device or program using media parsers such as libstagefright, Stagefright (Android), or older ffmpeg builds. Step 2: Use fuzzing tools or download known PoC MP4/3GP exploit files from ExploitDB. Step 3: Modify media headers such as chunk sizes, sample sizes, or metadata fields to extremely large or invalid values (e.g., 0xFFFFFFF0). Step 4: Deliver the file to the target via browser, Bluetooth, email, or file share. Step 5: When target opens or previews the file, heap allocation size is incorrectly calculated, causing overflow. Step 6: Place shellcode or ROP chain in payload section of media file. Step 7: Once overflow occurs, attacker gains control of program counter (PC) and can execute arbitrary code (e.g., reverse shell).
Vulnerability: Heap corruption via untrusted media parsing
Impact: Remote code execution on user device
Detection Method: Monitor crashes in media playback; use ASAN/Valgrind for heap corruption detection
Solution: Patch media parser libraries; validate input file headers strictly; sandbox media playback
Tags: media exploit, heap overflow, libstagefright, mp4 exploit

Title: Integer Overflow in Buffer Allocator
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts media headers that cause integer overflow in buffer length calculation, bypassing allocation checks and leading to memory corruption.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft a fake MP4 or image file with extremely large dimensions (e.g., width=999999, height=999999). Step 2: These values, when multiplied (width × height × depth), cause 32-bit integer overflow, resulting in very small buffer allocations. Step 3: Real data written during decode overflows into adjacent memory. Step 4: Send this file via MMS, file upload, or open in player. Step 5: Overflowed memory may overwrite function pointers, heap metadata, or code structures. Step 6: Attacker chains this with shellcode or command payload embedded in frame data. Step 7: When processed, arbitrary code executes, leading to RCE. Step 8: Clean logs or delete payload to cover traces.
Detection Method: Enable integer sanitization in fuzzing tests; review media parsing crash logs
Solution: Validate dimension values before multiplication; use 64-bit safe allocation functions
Tags: integer overflow, buffer overflow, media payload

Title: Use-After-Free via Race in Decoder Threads
Scenario Description: In a media decoding service, one thread frees memory while another still uses it → attacker-crafted file triggers UAF and leads to code execution.
Tools Used: adb, valgrind, PoC MP4, stagefright tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find vulnerable decoders like MPEG-4 ES, FLAC, AMR, or H264 that use multithreaded pipelines. Step 2: Craft file that triggers parallel decode (e.g., huge frame count). Step 3: Insert payload in frame structure that confuses parser logic (e.g., back-to-back timestamps, invalid index). Step 4: One thread frees the structure (e.g., audio sample) while other still references it. Step 5: On access, UAF leads to crash or PC control. Step 6: Inject shellcode at known heap offset if ASLR is weak. Step 7: Successful exploitation leads to control over decoder process (MediaServer on Android). Step 8: Can be used to drop a shell or leak credentials. Step 9: Exploit may require 10–20 attempts due to race timing.
Detection Method: Monitor dmesg/crash dumps for UAF pattern; race conditions often log double free
Solution: Rewrite decoder to include locking; avoid shared mutable memory between threads

Title: Out-of-Bounds Read via Oversized Dimensions
Scenario Description: Malicious media file includes image/video dimension values so large that parsing engine reads out-of-bounds, leaking heap memory or pointers.
Tools Used: PoC images, ffmpeg, GDB, objdump, grep
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an image (e.g., BMP, TIFF, PNG) or video header with very large width/height values (e.g., 100000x100000). Step 2: Many engines allocate buffer assuming truncated width, but index frame data beyond bounds. Step 3: Decoder reads memory beyond allocated buffer – OOB read. Step 4: Attacker pads media file with markers (e.g., "LEAKME") and places shellcode near known offset. Step 5: On crash, attacker retrieves leaked pointer values, heap layout, or libc base address. Step 6: These are used to bypass ASLR in chained exploits. Step 7: Logs, debugger dumps, or crash handler collects the leaked data. Step 8: Exploit complete when attacker uses info to bypass address randomization in second-stage attack.
Vulnerability: OOB read due to malformed media dimensions
Detection Method: Monitor decoder logs for invalid dimension errors; memory leak indicators in dmesg
Solution: Add bounds check on all dimension fields; do not trust input headers
Tags: oob read, info leak, media dimensions

Title: Arbitrary Code Execution via Format String Bug
Scenario Description: Media player logs metadata or file names using printf() without format specifier check → attacker triggers format string exploit from file content.
Tools Used: gdb, PoC file, fuzz.sh, strings, strace
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a media file (e.g., MP3, OGG, MKV) with title or metadata field set to %x%x%x%x%n%n%n. Step 2: When media player or server parses this and uses fprintf(log, input) instead of fprintf(log, "%s", input), the format string is executed. Step 3: Use %n to write arbitrary values into memory or %x to leak memory addresses. Step 4: With precise format string crafting, attacker writes shellcode address into function pointer. Step 5: When function is called (e.g., error handler), control jumps to shellcode. Step 6: This gives attacker full code execution, even without file being opened (just indexed or scanned). Step 7: Clean up by deleting file and logs post-exploit.
Detection Method: Check logs for %x, %n, %p sequences; detect core dumps from media services
Solution: Always format logs using %s explicitly; sanitize metadata from untrusted files
Tags: format string, media metadata, log injection

Title: Privilege Escalation via Binder Misuse
Attack Type: IPC Interface Abuse via Malformed Binder
Scenario Description: Attackers abuse the Android Binder IPC interface to send malformed AIDL messages to system services like MediaServer, triggering memory corruption or privilege escalation, potentially leading to full system access or RCE. This technique is historically used in exploits like Stagefright and Binderizer.
Tools Used: ADB (Android Debug Bridge), Frida, Python scripts, Exploit POC (C/C++), Android Emulator or test device
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare your test environment. Install an Android emulator or connect a physical Android phone (Android version 5.0–6.0, vulnerable to MediaServer bugs like CVE-2015-3824). Ensure adb is set up and the device is in developer mode with USB debugging enabled. Step 2: Use adb shell to confirm access to the device. Type adb shell and verify you can interact with the device’s internal shell. You will operate from a regular app context (low-privileged UID). Step 3: Identify the target system service. In this case, MediaServer exposes Binder services like IMediaPlayerService. These are accessed internally using the AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language) over Binder IPC. Step 4: Build or obtain a proof-of-concept (POC) Binder exploit. Use binder-pwn, Frida, or open-source C code from previous CVEs like CVE-2015-3824. This POC will send malformed Binder messages (e.g., corrupt length fields, null pointers) to MediaServer’s interface. Step 5: Analyze the structure of a valid AIDL call. Use Frida to hook and inspect how Android apps talk to MediaServer. Note the transaction codes, interface tokens, and parcel format. Your goal is to create a malformed version that causes memory corruption. Step 6: Send the malicious Binder message. Either use a C/C++ script with Binder ioctl or Frida’s Java.perform to craft a parcel and inject a malformed request (e.g., huge buffer size, malformed pointer). This triggers a vulnerability in MediaServer's parsing logic. Step 7: Observe the result. If the device crashes (logcat shows segfault in mediaserver), or the process restarts, the exploit may have worked partially. For privilege escalation, monitor if the app now has elevated privileges or shell access. Step 8: To escalate further, chain the memory corruption with a second-stage payload (e.g., return-oriented programming (ROP) chain) to execute arbitrary code in MediaServer. This may require creating a fake stack or hijacking function pointers. Step 9: If successful, you now run code in MediaServer context, which often runs as media or system UID, allowing you to bypass app sandboxing, access restricted APIs, or read/write other app data. Step 10: Clean up logs, uninstall the exploit app, and confirm shell persistence if achieved. Remember to only test on your own device or emulator.
Vulnerability: Insecure Binder IPC and memory handling
Impact: Code execution in system process; app sandbox escape
Detection Method: Monitor logcat for unusual MediaServer crashes or restarts; analyze Binder transactions; detect malformed parcels
Solution: Use SELinux policies to limit IPC access; patch vulnerable Android versions; apply memory corruption mitigations

Title: Bluetooth or NFC File Trigger
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a malicious video/audio/image file to a target via Bluetooth or NFC. Upon auto-open or preview by system services like MediaServer, code is executed.
Tools Used: Two Android phones, Bluetooth, ADB, crafted malicious media
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a vulnerable Android version (pre-7.0) where MediaServer parses files automatically. Step 2: Generate a malicious media file exploiting a known CVE (e.g., CVE-2015-3826 – malformed MP4). Step 3: Transfer the file using Bluetooth or NFC to the victim device. Step 4: Once received, the system or gallery auto-previews it. Step 5: The media parsing triggers the vulnerability in MediaServer (e.g., buffer overflow). Step 6: The exploit executes code with MediaServer's permissions. Step 7: If chained with further LPE, attacker can gain system/root access. Step 8: Log logcat and observe crash or RCE indicators. Step 9: This is zero-click once the file is received.
Detection Method: logcat anomalies on media open; audit logs from NFC/Bluetooth services
Solution: Disable auto-preview; restrict parsing to safe types; update firmware

Title: Malicious App with Crafted Payload
Attack Type: Sandbox Escape via Auto Media Parsing
Scenario Description: A non-privileged app drops a media file into MediaStore; system media scanner parses it automatically, triggering exploitation.
Tools Used: Android Studio, ADB, Malicious MP4 Generator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a dummy Android app with only WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE permission (pre-Android 10). Step 2: Place a crafted media payload (e.g., corrupt MP4 exploiting Stagefright) into a public folder. Step 3: Use MediaScannerConnection.scanFile() to trigger scanning. Step 4: MediaServer scans the file, triggers parsing logic. Step 5: If the file contains a malicious payload, MediaServer executes code in its context. Step 6: Check for logs or system crashes via adb logcat. Step 7: Chain this with privilege escalation or device takeover logic. Step 8: This bypasses app sandboxing without needing special permissions.
Detection Method: logcat for crash signatures (mediaserver, logd); anomalous memory access
Solution: Restrict MediaStore auto-scan; validate formats; enforce file permissions

Title: Audio Engine Heap Spray + Trigger
Scenario Description: Audio playback engine (e.g., libstagefright) is sprayed with crafted audio data and a second input triggers a decoder bug.
Tools Used: Audacity, ADB, Android audio player, heap spray generator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare several large .wav or .mp3 files designed to heap spray memory with controlled patterns. Step 2: Use app or service to continuously play them in loops. Step 3: Introduce a malicious second audio clip with malformed metadata (e.g., corrupt ID3). Step 4: Parsing of this clip triggers memory access in the corrupted heap. Step 5: If successful, attacker hijacks the control flow (e.g., through ROP or shellcode). Step 6: Monitor logcat for audio system crashes. Step 7: Exploit can lead to RCE in audio engine or MediaServer. Step 8: Persist by exploiting audio APIs via system services.
Vulnerability: Heap corruption in audio decoder libraries
Detection Method: Unusual heap allocation patterns; crash logs during audio playback
Solution: Patch decoder bugs; limit audio file access; sandbox decoders

Title: File Upload to Chat App / Browser
Attack Type: Media Preview Exploit in App or Browser
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads a malicious media file to a chat app or via web upload. Auto-preview or inline rendering causes MediaServer to parse and trigger exploit.
Tools Used: Chat App (Telegram/WhatsApp clone), Burp Suite, crafted MP4
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare an exploit media file (corrupt MP4 or crafted JPG exploiting EXIF parsing). Step 2: Upload to a vulnerable chat app or web-based file input form. Step 3: If the app auto-generates thumbnails or previews (common in messaging platforms), the media file is opened internally. Step 4: MediaServer or native parser attempts to decode it. Step 5: Exploit triggers buffer overflow or DoS. Step 6: This often works even without user clicking the file (zero-click). Step 7: Observe logcat, crash dumps, and system logs. Step 8: If RCE is achieved, the attacker gains remote control.
Detection Method: Log analysis, media parsing sandboxing logs
Solution: Remove auto-preview; validate file headers; isolate thumbnail parsers

Title: Zero-Click Messaging App Exploit
Scenario Description: Media files sent via messaging apps with auto-preview enabled get parsed immediately by system services. Malicious files can trigger RCE without any user interaction.
Tools Used: Android Messaging App (Signal, WhatsApp), Frida, ADB, CVE payloads
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up two Android devices (or emulator pairs) with messaging apps installed. Ensure auto-media-preview is enabled (most apps do this by default). Step 2: Generate or download a crafted malicious video or image file (e.g., CVE-2020-0096 – crafted PNG). Step 3: On the attacker device, send this file via the messaging app to the victim device. Step 4: As soon as the message is received, the app requests the system to auto-preview the media (thumbnail generation or preview). Step 5: This triggers the vulnerable parser in MediaServer (or Image decoder), causing buffer overflow or memory corruption. Step 6: The exploit runs in the context of the preview engine, giving attacker remote code execution (RCE). Step 7: No click or open needed – the attack is automatic. Step 8: Monitor logcat on the victim device for crashes or shell access. Step 9: Clean logs if proof-of-concept worked and report only in controlled test environments.
Detection Method: logcat analysis; monitor crash reports in messaging apps
Solution: Disable auto-preview; validate content before parsing

Title: Exploit in Native Camera Stack (via MediaServer)
Scenario Description: Native Android camera stack uses MediaServer to handle media. Exploits in shared buffer or processing logic can lead to RCE or info leak from camera context.
Tools Used: Camera app, ADB, Burp/Frida, MediaRecorder payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch the native Android camera app or trigger a camera intent from a malicious app. Step 2: As camera captures image or video, it uses MediaServer to encode/stream content. Step 3: Inject a payload through camera settings or video metadata that corrupts MediaServer’s buffer handling. Step 4: MediaServer attempts to encode or parse the data, triggering memory corruption. Step 5: This gives attacker access to process memory or even command execution depending on the bug (e.g., CVE-2019-2023). Step 6: Leaked data may include image buffers, mic recordings, or sensitive media. Step 7: Monitor logcat for segfaults in camera or MediaServer. Step 8: Used as part of exploit chains targeting camera access or sensors.
Impact: Info leak or local code execution
Detection Method: Monitor MediaServer crash logs when camera used
Solution: Harden MediaServer; restrict camera-media stack interactions

Title: Chained Exploit to Root
Scenario Description: Attackers combine MediaServer RCE with kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) to achieve full root access on Android device.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Exploit a known MediaServer vulnerability to gain RCE in a privileged process (see SEC-026 or SEC-031). Step 2: Once RCE is achieved, use the compromised process to load a local privilege escalation payload (e.g., Dirty COW – CVE-2016-5195). Step 3: Allocate memory and inject kernel exploit. Step 4: Escalate privileges to root user. Step 5: Spawn a root shell or override system files like /etc/shadow or init.rc. Step 6: Achieve full device control, bypassing SEAndroid and app sandbox. Step 7: Hide traces by cleaning logcat, crash reports, or modifying kernel messages. Step 8: Use only in lab/test environments – this simulates full device takeover from userland entry.
Detection Method: Combined memory monitoring, SELinux audit logs
Solution: Patch kernel + system libs; enforce LSM hooks; detect chained payloads

Title: Crash/DoS via Corrupt Media Streams
Attack Type: Denial of Service via Malformed Streams
Scenario Description: Maliciously crafted video/audio streams (e.g., MP4, AAC) are parsed by MediaServer and trigger out-of-bound reads or crashes, killing media functionality.
Tools Used: VLC, MP4Box, Fuzzed media files, logcat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a corrupted video or audio stream using tools like VLC or FFMPEG with intentionally invalid metadata (e.g., oversized chunk size, missing headers). Step 2: Load the media in any app or stream it via browser or app on a test Android device. Step 3: MediaServer attempts to parse it, fails due to corruption, and crashes. Step 4: Repeat the process to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) effect where MediaServer constantly restarts and becomes unavailable. Step 5: Monitor system performance and crash reports via ADB. Step 6: This can be used to brick media functions or drain battery. Step 7: To reset, clear media storage cache or reboot. Step 8: Used in real-world attacks to force user reboots or crash the UI.
Vulnerability: Weak input validation in media parsing
Impact: Crash of media services; battery drain
Detection Method: Crash loop logs; logcat spam from mediaserver
Solution: Enforce robust format validation in parsers; timeout thresholds in decoding

Title: Attack via Streaming URLs
Scenario Description: Remote attacker controls a streaming URL (M3U8/MP4) that delivers a malformed segment, parsed by the player and passed to MediaServer.
Tools Used: Android browser or player app, HLS test stream, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Host a malicious MP4 or M3U8 stream on a server. Include a segment with malformed headers or corrupt codec data (e.g., MP4 with overlong atom). Step 2: Share this streaming link via browser, app, or QR code. Step 3: When the user clicks the link, the media stream starts and MediaServer begins parsing the live segments. Step 4: The malformed segment causes buffer overflow or heap corruption. Step 5: The exploit runs in MediaServer or decoder context. Step 6: Monitor ADB logcat for mediaserver crashes or shell. Step 7: If chained with further privilege escalation, this leads to remote takeover.
Vulnerability: No input sanitization in live stream decoder
Detection Method: Monitor media traffic and decoder errors; flag malformed segments
Solution: Secure player libraries; sandbox stream decoders
Tags: Live Stream, MP4 Exploit, Streaming RCE

Title: SVG/JPEG/PNG in Media Thumbnails
Attack Type: Image Parsing Exploit in Thumbnail Generator
Scenario Description: Image files (SVG/JPEG/PNG) with crafted metadata are auto-parsed by Android's thumbnail generator, potentially triggering buffer overflows or code execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a malformed SVG or JPEG file (e.g., CVE-2016-3714 ImageTragick). Use tools like ImageMagick to add payloads in metadata or XML. Step 2: Transfer the image to the device (via Bluetooth, email, or file app). Step 3: Place it where the Android system or gallery will auto-generate a thumbnail. Step 4: The thumbnail parser decodes the image and triggers the exploit (e.g., RCE, memory leak). Step 5: Monitor system logs, media crashes, and shell access. Step 6: This works without user opening the image – auto-triggered. Step 7: Clear thumbnail caches to recover.
Detection Method: Thumbnail generation crash logs; audit system thumbnailer
Solution: Patch media framework; avoid untrusted image previews
Tags: Image Exploit, Metadata Attack, Thumbnail RCE

Title: Cross-App Attack via Shared Memory
Scenario Description: Media buffers are sometimes shared between apps using shared memory (ashmem or AHardwareBuffer). Attackers can inject malformed content or leak data via side channels.
Tools Used: Frida, ADB, Android NDK tools, /proc/[pid]/maps, ashmem
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a victim app (e.g., media player or camera) that uses shared memory to exchange video buffers with the system. Step 2: Build a malicious app that uses the same buffer namespace or attaches to the same shared memory segment (using ashmem, Binder transactions, or /dev/ashmem). Step 3: Read buffer contents while they are still in memory or modify them before the victim app accesses them. Step 4: Modify media format headers to introduce parsing faults (e.g., malformed length fields or bitstream). Step 5: When the target app or MediaServer parses this shared memory buffer, it crashes or leaks sensitive information. Step 6: Monitor logcat and memory traces for info leak or privilege escalation. Step 7: Use Frida or ptrace to observe changes in memory mappings across apps. Step 8: This type of attack can break app isolation and is particularly dangerous in media contexts.
Vulnerability: Shared memory reuse without access control
MITRE Technique: T1056.001 – Input Capture via Shared Memory
Impact: Info leak, privilege escalation, app isolation bypass
Detection Method: Monitor ashmem activity, unexpected memory mapping overlaps
Solution: Use SELinux constraints, namespace isolation, memory zeroing before sharing

Title: Video Codec Parsing Bugs (e.g., VP8, H.264)
Attack Type: Media Codec Exploit via Decoder Bugs
Scenario Description: Video decoders (VP8, VP9, H.264, HEVC) in Android media stack are complex and prone to bugs. Malicious video streams can trigger decoder crashes or arbitrary code execution.
Tools Used: FFMPEG, crafted video files, Android MediaPlayer, ADB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create or download a malformed video file targeting a known bug in the VP8 or H.264 decoder (e.g., CVE-2020-0022 – improper bounds check). Step 2: Transfer the video to a test Android device via USB, app upload, or download link. Step 3: Open the video using a native app or trigger thumbnail generation. Step 4: MediaServer or codec library begins parsing the video stream. Step 5: The malformed stream causes buffer overflow, heap corruption, or logic bug in the codec. Step 6: Observe the impact via logcat – crash logs or abnormal behavior. Step 7: Exploit may execute code inside the decoder's memory space. Step 8: Combine with ROP chains to hijack control flow if needed. Step 9: This exploit is often used in spyware and APT campaigns due to its stealth.
Impact: Code execution, DoS, spyware payload injection
Detection Method: Crash logs, stack traces involving codec libs
Solution: Update codec libraries; apply input validation; isolate decoders with seccomp

Title: Use-After-Free in Binder Driver
Scenario Description: A malicious app abuses binder transactions to free an object and reuse it improperly, leading to memory corruption in the kernel Binder driver.
Tools Used: ADB, Binder fuzzer, exploit POCs (C/C++), Pixel3 emulator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a device running a vulnerable kernel version (e.g., CVE-2019-2215 or similar). Step 2: Install a test app or use adb shell to issue custom binder transactions using /dev/binder. Step 3: Trigger the Binder flow where an object is freed (e.g., via binder_release()). Step 4: Before the pointer is zeroed out, resend a transaction referencing the freed object. Step 5: The kernel uses the dangling pointer, resulting in a Use-After-Free (UAF) situation. Step 6: Exploit the UAF to leak or overwrite memory (heap spray with controlled objects). Step 7: If the overwrite is successful, redirect execution or escalate to kernel code execution. Step 8: If chained with shellcode, full privilege escalation is possible. Monitor logcat and /proc/kmsg for crashes.
Detection Method: Kernel panic logs; trace pointer reuse from Binder transactions
Solution: Patch vulnerable drivers; enable kernel memory sanitization tools like KASAN

Title: Integer Overflow in binder_transaction()
Attack Type: Kernel Heap Overflow via Integer Wrap
Scenario Description: A malicious app sends a transaction with a large size field that overflows when memory is copied, leading to heap corruption in the kernel.
Tools Used: ADB, binder fuzzers, AFL, crafted C payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Reverse the kernel binder driver source or look into the kernel version’s implementation of binder_transaction(). Step 2: Identify where the transaction size is calculated. Step 3: Send a crafted binder transaction from user space with a size near INT_MAX (e.g., 0xFFFFFFF0). Step 4: The kernel adds internal size offsets, causing an overflow into a smaller value. Step 5: The buffer allocated in the kernel is too small. Step 6: When the kernel copies data into this buffer, it overflows adjacent memory. Step 7: Use this to overwrite kernel heap objects and redirect execution. Step 8: This can crash or lead to full control over the kernel if successful. Step 9: Monitor with dmesg or logcat.
Vulnerability: Integer Overflow in kernel transaction size
Detection Method: Heap overflow logs; buffer misalignment; corrupted allocation records
Solution: Bounds check on input values; patch vulnerable kernel versions

Title: Stack Buffer Overflow via Binder Parcel
Scenario Description: Improper size validation in Binder parcel leads to stack overflow inside the kernel, enabling attacker to overwrite return addresses or function frames.
Tools Used: Exploit code (C), ADB, vulnerable kernel build
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a C program that opens /dev/binder and sends a large Binder parcel (e.g., with 4096+ bytes). Step 2: Set a write_size larger than expected by the receiver (e.g., the kernel). Step 3: The binder handler fails to check the size before writing data into a fixed-size kernel stack buffer. Step 4: Overflow occurs, overwriting return addresses, saved registers, or function pointers. Step 5: Inject a payload (e.g., ROP chain or shellcode address). Step 6: Trigger execution of overwritten return address. Step 7: Monitor kernel logs to confirm stack corruption and control.
Vulnerability: Stack buffer overflow due to bad bounds check
Detection Method: Kernel crash dumps, corrupted stack traces
Solution: Kernel stack protection; bounds validation; stack canaries
Tags: Binder Parcel, Stack Overflow, Kernel Exploit

Title: Double-Free in binder_release()
Scenario Description: Improper resource management allows releasing the same binder object twice, causing memory corruption or free list poisoning.
Tools Used: Binder test code, ADB, heap analysis tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Develop a user-space app that allocates a binder object and releases it using standard Binder transaction. Step 2: Issue a second release command (manually or via custom binder driver fuzz). Step 3: The kernel logic does not verify if the object was already freed. Step 4: Freeing the same pointer twice causes heap corruption. Step 5: Use heap spraying techniques to place attacker-controlled data in freed slots. Step 6: Gain write-what-where primitive or control kernel execution. Step 7: Combine with LPE to gain full root.
Detection Method: Heap allocator logs, double free crash patterns
Solution: Use reference counting properly; fix free logic; kernel memory debugging tools like KASAN

Title: Null Pointer Dereference in Driver
Scenario Description: Due to improper locking or sequencing, a race condition leads to dereferencing a NULL pointer in kernel Binder driver code.
Tools Used: Frida, ADB shell, custom test apps
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a script or C tool that sends malformed binder commands with aggressive timing. Step 2: One thread sends a valid binder transaction; another thread deletes the same reference mid-operation. Step 3: A time window opens where the pointer used in the kernel becomes NULL. Step 4: Kernel tries to dereference it without validation. Step 5: Crash occurs (kernel panic, log in dmesg). Step 6: Exploit can cause DoS or enable further analysis of kernel behavior.
Vulnerability: Null deref due to race in transaction flow
Detection Method: dmesg crash logs, system instability
Solution: Add locking, mutexes in kernel flows; check all pointers before dereferencing

Title: Improper Capability Check in Service
Scenario Description: System services accessed over Binder fail to check whether caller has the right permissions, leading to unauthorized actions by normal apps.
Tools Used: ADB, Binder interface map, Frida, logcat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use adb shell dumpsys to enumerate Binder-exposed services (e.g., vold, system_server, media.audio_policy). Step 2: Identify transactions or methods not checking UID/capabilities (e.g., via aidl fuzzing or code audit). Step 3: Write a small app or script to directly call one such Binder method. Step 4: Observe if it returns sensitive data or performs unauthorized operations. Step 5: Example: calling a system volume change API or mounting file systems without SYSTEM UID. Step 6: If successful, attacker can hijack service logic or abuse unintended APIs. Step 7: Log and confirm capability bypass.
Detection Method: Monitor access logs of Binder services; ensure UID checks in AIDL
Solution: Add strict capability and UID checks in service handlers

Title: Object Injection into Trusted Binder Interface
Scenario Description: Malicious apps send harmful or unexpected objects (e.g., file descriptors) to sensitive system services via Binder, tricking them into doing unsafe actions.
Tools Used: ADB, Frida, test APKs, AIDL explorer tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install a basic app that can communicate with system services via Binder. Step 2: Find a Binder interface (using dumpsys, service list, or reverse engineering) that accepts objects like file descriptors or memory pointers. Step 3: Create a malicious payload that contains an unexpected or dangerous file descriptor (e.g., pointing to an unauthorized file or device). Step 4: Send this object to the system service using Binder. Step 5: If the service trusts the object, it may open or execute the file, resulting in privilege escalation or data leakage. Step 6: Observe system behavior using logcat or /proc monitoring. Step 7: This kind of injection can break trust boundaries and allow access to privileged system resources.
Vulnerability: Lack of strict validation for Binder objects
Detection Method: Binder transaction logs, unexpected FD use
Solution: Validate all object types and file descriptors in system services

Title: Shared Memory Abuse (Ashmem/Fd)
Scenario Description: Attackers pass fake or corrupted shared memory regions (e.g., ashmem, file descriptors) to trusted services, enabling memory-based attacks.
Tools Used: Binder transaction tools, C binder code, Frida
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a malicious app that allocates a region of memory using ashmem (Android shared memory API). Step 2: Corrupt the memory content (e.g., insert exploit payloads or malformed media data). Step 3: Pass the file descriptor for this ashmem to a trusted system service (like MediaServer) using Binder. Step 4: The service reads from this shared memory without validating the content or source. Step 5: This can lead to crashes, code execution, or memory disclosure. Step 6: Use log monitoring tools (logcat, dmesg) to trace behavior. Step 7: May lead to UAF (use-after-free) or overwrite kernel memory depending on target.
Vulnerability: Unvalidated shared memory passed via Binder
Detection Method: Monitor ashmem transactions, unexpected FD access
Solution: Use buffer validation and stricter memory sharing policies

Title: Race Condition in Multi-Threaded Binder Usage
Scenario Description: Multiple Binder operations done quickly in parallel can cause one thread to free memory while another is still using it, causing corruption.
Tools Used: Multithreaded test apps, Binder fuzzer, ADB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write or use a multithreaded test app that rapidly sends BC_TRANSACTION and BC_FREE_BUFFER Binder commands in different threads. Step 2: Set up timing so that BC_FREE_BUFFER releases memory while the BC_TRANSACTION is still operating on it. Step 3: This overlap causes use-after-free or data race. Step 4: Monitor crash logs or kernel panic. Step 5: This can lead to arbitrary code execution if exploited correctly. Step 6: Use a fuzzer or timer delay to adjust race windows. Step 7: Chain this with other exploits to gain full root.
Vulnerability: Race condition in memory release flow
Detection Method: KASAN race detector, dmesg logs
Solution: Use locking in memory operations; detect overlapping commands

Title: Binder Overload Flooding Attack
Scenario Description: Flooding the Binder queue with large numbers of bogus messages prevents real apps from functioning, leading to Denial of Service.
Tools Used: ADB, Binder spam script, shell loop
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a shell or Python script that sends thousands of Binder transactions in a loop (e.g., using /dev/binder and spamming system services). Step 2: These transactions do nothing meaningful and just fill up the Binder thread pool. Step 3: Legitimate apps trying to send Binder messages are delayed or blocked. Step 4: The device becomes sluggish, or system services crash. Step 5: Monitor Binder transaction logs using dumpsys and system logs. Step 6: The effect is similar to a denial-of-service (DoS). Step 7: This technique is also used by malware to slow down user interaction or block key apps.
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting in Binder transaction queue
Detection Method: High Binder queue depth, performance logs
Solution: Implement rate limiting and transaction quotas

Title: Kernel Info Leak via Binder Reply
Scenario Description: Improperly constructed Binder replies may contain leftover kernel memory, leaking sensitive information to user apps.
Tools Used: Binder API test, Frida, logcat, dmesg
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send a transaction to a vulnerable system service with a malformed payload (e.g., missing required fields or incomplete data). Step 2: The system service builds a reply but doesn't fully initialize the response buffer. Step 3: The kernel sends this buffer back to the app, which may contain leftover memory (e.g., stack contents or other data). Step 4: Read this reply and scan for sensitive information (pointers, user data, kernel addresses). Step 5: Use leaked data to perform memory layout discovery or bypass security mechanisms like KASLR. Step 6: Monitor traffic using Frida or logcat. Step 7: Chain this leak into another exploit for privilege escalation.
Detection Method: Look for replies with unexpected non-zero data
Solution: Zero-initialize all buffers before reply

Title: Bypass of Permission Check via Transaction Hijack
Scenario Description: An attacker uses a race or logic flaw to hijack another app’s legitimate transaction and get it processed with higher privileges.
Tools Used: Binder tracing tools, test apps, Frida, logcat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Observe normal Binder transaction flow using tools like binder_trace or Frida. Step 2: Find a case where UID or permissions are checked late or not at all. Step 3: Craft a transaction that mimics a legitimate one from a privileged app. Step 4: Trigger the service to accept your transaction as if it came from the privileged app (via hijacking or ID confusion). Step 5: If successful, you gain access to restricted functionality without proper permissions. Step 6: Monitor logs to confirm execution path and verify no permission check occurred. Step 7: Exploit can lead to silent privilege escalation.
Vulnerability: Late or missing permission validation logic
Detection Method: Compare UID of sender vs. executed logic; analyze logs
Solution: Fix permission check location; bind privilege check early in transaction flow

Title: SurfaceFlinger Binder Abuse
Attack Type: Abuse of Display Server Binder Interface
Scenario Description: Android’s display server SurfaceFlinger exposes a Binder interface that can leak framebuffer data or give unauthorized access to graphic buffers.
Tools Used: ADB, dumpsys SurfaceFlinger, Frida, custom test app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use adb shell service list or dumpsys SurfaceFlinger to confirm the service is accessible. Step 2: Write a test app or use Frida to connect to SurfaceFlinger over Binder. Step 3: Call methods such as captureLayers or access IGraphicBufferProducer/Consumer interfaces. Step 4: Dump returned buffers and check if they contain visual screen data (e.g., screenshots, pixels). Step 5: If successful, the attacker can view framebuffer contents or spy on other apps. Step 6: Combine with media or screen-based attacks to leak UI state. Step 7: Monitor logcat for SurfaceFlinger access and analyze graphics buffers.
Vulnerability: Lack of access control in SurfaceFlinger API
Impact: UI spying, frame leak, information disclosure
Detection Method: Logs of unauthorized display access; screen pixel buffer inspection
Solution: Restrict SurfaceFlinger Binder calls to system UID only; sanitize buffer exposure

Title: Installd Binder Vulnerability
Attack Type: File System Exploit via Package Manager
Scenario Description: installd is the Android system service responsible for APK installation. If misused over Binder, it may allow attackers to delete, move, or overwrite files improperly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a device or ROM version where installd is accessible from user apps. Step 2: Use adb shell or a test APK to send Binder requests to installd (e.g., createAppData, clearAppData). Step 3: Attempt to pass in a crafted package name or path that includes path traversal characters (../). Step 4: Monitor behavior — in vulnerable versions, installd may operate on unintended directories. Step 5: Overwrite or delete system/user data outside your app sandbox. Step 6: Combine with other exploits for persistence or LPE. Step 7: Check logs for abnormal installd activity and error codes.
Vulnerability: Path traversal or input sanitization flaw
Detection Method: logcat, dmesg, tampered file traces
Solution: Sanitize inputs and enforce package name restrictions in installd

Title: Binder Use via SUID Binary Wrapper
Attack Type: Privilege Escalation via Native SUID Binder Call
Scenario Description: Some system apps use special native binaries (SUID) that run with elevated privileges. If they talk to system services through Binder, a normal app can use them to perform privileged operations.
Tools Used: ADB, run-as, logcat, Frida, test app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use adb shell to check if binaries like run-as are available and marked as SUID (they run as root). Step 2: Create a simple app that talks to Binder services using this SUID binary. Step 3: When the SUID binary talks to a system service over Binder, it may be treated as a root-level caller. Step 4: Request a privileged operation from a system service (like accessing protected files or settings). Step 5: If the system service allows it, your app gets access it normally shouldn’t have. Step 6: You now have escalated privileges without rooting the device. Step 7: Monitor output using logcat to see if privileged actions succeed.
Detection Method: Watch for UID mismatches in logs
Solution: Block Binder calls from SUID binaries to sensitive system services

Title: Fake Service Injection
Scenario Description: Android uses a service registry called ServiceManager. If an attacker registers a fake service before the system does, apps may unknowingly talk to the fake one.
Tools Used: ADB, Frida, delay tools, test app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write an app that registers a fake Binder service using the same name as a real system service. Step 2: Delay your app to run right when the system is booting but before the real service loads. Step 3: If you win the race, your fake service is registered first. Step 4: Other apps or system components will connect to your fake service instead of the real one. Step 5: Your service can then respond with fake data or intercept commands. Step 6: This can cause misbehavior or expose private information. Step 7: Use service list or logcat to confirm which service is active.
Impact: Misuse of system calls, fake responses
Detection Method: Unexpected behavior in registered services
Solution: Secure boot order, restrict service registration

Title: Attack on Trusted Hardware (TA)
Scenario Description: Android uses secure hardware (TEE) for things like unlocking or storing encryption keys. These are accessed via system services. Attackers can misuse these Binder interfaces.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build or use an app that calls system security services like android.security.keystore or gatekeeper. Step 2: Use Frida to observe how data is sent via Binder to the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). Step 3: Try sending unexpected or malformed data to see how the service reacts. Step 4: On some devices, flaws in how the TEE interface is handled may allow you to bypass device unlock checks or steal crypto keys. Step 5: Use logcat or test app results to confirm if the operation succeeded without proper permissions. Step 6: If successful, this could unlock the device or access protected user data.
Vulnerability: Weak validation in security service binder
Detection Method: Log unusual calls to keystore/gatekeeper
Solution: Strict permission checks, verify inputs to TEE

Title: Binder Transaction Bomb (Memory DoS)
Attack Type: Crash System via Huge Binder Message
Scenario Description: Sending huge or deeply nested Binder data can overload system memory and crash Android’s Binder kernel service.
Tools Used: ADB, NDK test app, memory monitor
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a test app using NDK that sends extremely large or deeply nested data objects using Binder (e.g., arrays inside arrays). Step 2: Continuously send these messages to a system service like MediaServer or installd. Step 3: This uses a lot of memory and fills up the Binder queue. Step 4: Eventually the device slows down, crashes, or becomes unresponsive. Step 5: Watch memory usage using top, dumpsys meminfo, or logcat. Step 6: This creates a Denial of Service (DoS) even without root. Step 7: System may need a reboot to recover.
Vulnerability: No size limit for nested transactions
Impact: App or system crash, memory overload
Detection Method: Check for frequent OOM errors or lag
Solution: Limit Binder payload sizes; validate nested depth
Tags: Binder Bomb, Memory DoS, Resource Abuse

Title: Binder Transaction Coalescing Abuse
Attack Type: Logic Confusion via Combined Binder Calls
Scenario Description: Android Binder merges multiple fast Binder calls into one for performance. Attackers abuse this to confuse app logic or bypass checks.
Tools Used: Custom app, Frida, logcat, Binder trace
Attack Steps: Step 1: Make an app that rapidly sends two Binder calls to a system service — one valid, one malicious. Step 2: Because of performance merging, both calls may be processed together. Step 3: Some services don’t expect this and may apply permission checks only once. Step 4: Your malicious call gets processed as if it were part of the valid one. Step 5: This lets you bypass restrictions like login, permission grants, or token checks. Step 6: Watch logs or app behavior to confirm success. Step 7: Repeat to maintain access.
Detection Method: Logs showing merged Binder transactions
Solution: Force services to revalidate each transaction

Title: Binder Refcount Exploitation
Attack Type: Trick Binder Driver into Freeing Live Object
Scenario Description: Android’s Binder system keeps track of how many times each object is referenced. If attackers confuse this counter, objects may be freed too early and reused unsafely.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an app that sends and drops Binder references very quickly or out of order. Step 2: This messes up the system’s internal counter (called refcount) that tracks object usage. Step 3: If the system frees an object that’s still in use, it leads to a Use-After-Free (UAF) bug. Step 4: Next time memory is allocated, it may reuse this freed object — letting the attacker control it. Step 5: With careful memory spraying, this can lead to full code execution or kernel-level crash. Step 6: Confirm using logcat, kernel logs, or dmesg.
Vulnerability: Bad tracking of object use count (refcount)
Detection Method: Kernel crashes, memory pointer issues in logs
Solution: Add checks before object reuse; monitor refcount consistency

Title: Mach Port Injection
Scenario Description: Apps on macOS/iOS use Mach ports to communicate. A malicious app may inject messages into another app’s port and take control of it.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a macOS/iOS system, find the PID of a target system app using ps or a process viewer. Step 2: Use your app to request the task_port of the target using APIs like task_for_pid() (requires special entitlements or bypass). Step 3: If successful, you can send messages to the app’s Mach port. Step 4: Use these messages to execute commands in the target app's memory space or hijack its behavior. Step 5: Confirm access using tools like LLDB or Frida to inspect memory and confirm control.
Vulnerability: Access to other task ports via Mach system
Impact: Hijack app memory or control flow
Detection Method: Audit app entitlements; detect cross-process message traffic
Solution: Restrict task_for_pid to root/system apps only

Title: XPC Exploits
Scenario Description: macOS apps use XPC to talk to helper tools. If an attacker finds a bug in one of these tools, they can gain elevated access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify XPC services running with elevated privileges using launchctl list or system analysis tools. Step 2: Write a test app that sends inputs to these XPC services using their defined interface. Step 3: Fuzz the interface with malformed inputs or unexpected data. Step 4: If the service crashes or behaves incorrectly, investigate further. Step 5: A successful exploit may allow your app to execute code with root/system privileges. Step 6: Confirm via log output, system behavior, or changes to privileged files.
Detection Method: Monitor XPC service crashes or abnormal system behavior
Solution: Harden XPC input parsing; sandbox XPC helpers

Title: Memory Corruption in Syscalls
Attack Type: Buffer Overflow or UAF in Kernel Calls
Scenario Description: Attackers call system calls with malicious input to trigger bugs like use-after-free or overflows in kernel memory.
Tools Used: Ghidra, LLDB, ADB, macOS syscall logs
Attack Steps: Step 1: Analyze system calls using a disassembler like Ghidra to identify where input is not validated. Step 2: Write a custom app or PoC that makes crafted syscall inputs (e.g., overly large buffer sizes). Step 3: Observe for kernel panics, crashes, or behavior like privilege escalation. Step 4: Use LLDB or crash logs to confirm kernel memory corruption (UAF or buffer overflow). Step 5: Exploit can result in code execution in kernel space.
Vulnerability: Lack of bounds/validation in syscall input
Detection Method: Kernel panic logs; fuzz syscall interfaces
Solution: Add strict bounds checks; audit all syscall input paths

Title: Deserialization Bugs
Scenario Description: Apps or services that deserialize untrusted data may allow attackers to craft input that runs code when parsed.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Ghidra, custom input fuzzers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a service or system component that receives serialized data (e.g., app config, IPC messages). Step 2: Use Burp Suite or fuzzers to inject custom serialized objects. Step 3: Include a payload in the data that performs malicious actions (e.g., spawns shell, escalates privileges). Step 4: When the system reads and deserializes it, your code is executed. Step 5: Confirm via system logs or output actions.
MITRE Technique: T1059 – Command Execution via App Logic
Detection Method: Logs of unexpected input execution; monitor deserialization paths
Solution: Validate input before deserialization; avoid unserializing untrusted data

Title: Shmem-based Attacks
Scenario Description: Apps may use shared memory (shmem) with services or other apps. Attackers can write or read data that shouldn't be accessible.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify shared memory regions created by a browser or system service using /proc/[pid]/maps. Step 2: Map the shared memory region using your app. Step 3: If permissions allow, read or write directly into the memory. Step 4: Use this to inject data or leak information from the other app. Step 5: Confirm changes using debugging tools or visual effects in UI.
Detection Method: Monitor memory region access; restrict shared memory permissions
Solution: Use private memory maps; never expose shared memory to untrusted apps
Tags: Shared Memory, Memory Injection, Browser Attack

Title: WebKit RCE + Kernel Exploit
Attack Type: Remote Exploit via Browser to Kernel
Scenario Description: Combine a browser bug (like WebKit RCE) with a kernel bug to go from webpage to full device control.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a WebKit bug that allows JavaScript to run native code in Safari (WebKit RCE). Step 2: Write a proof-of-concept that uses this to escape the Safari sandbox. Step 3: Chain with a second exploit — a kernel vulnerability that can be triggered from the escaped app. Step 4: Once kernel exploit succeeds, the attacker gains full control of the system (e.g., root or jailbreak). Step 5: Confirm by modifying system settings, installing binaries, or accessing root files.
Vulnerability: WebKit bug chained with kernel flaw
Impact: Full device takeover from remote webpage
Detection Method: Browser crash logs, crash reports, kernel logs
Solution: Patch both browser engine and kernel; separate privileges; use JIT sandbox

Title: Race Conditions in Kernel Drivers
Scenario Description: Some kernel drivers don’t handle fast, repeated calls from multiple threads properly. This causes timing bugs that let attackers write or read arbitrary memory.
Tools Used: Custom multithreaded app, ADB, XNU logs, LLDB
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a kernel driver that’s known to have race conditions (e.g., IOKit-based ones like io_service_open). Step 2: Write a multithreaded test app that calls the same driver function many times at once. Step 3: Time the threads to overlap or cancel each other in the middle of execution. Step 4: If timed correctly, one thread may access memory the other hasn't finished setting up. Step 5: Use this to read or write kernel memory by mistake. Step 6: Monitor the device using logs, crash dumps, and LLDB. Step 7: Successful attacks can change system behavior, inject code, or leak data.
Detection Method: Look for timing-based kernel panics; monitor syscall race behavior
Solution: Add locks/mutex in driver code; test concurrency thoroughly
Tags: Race Condition, Kernel Driver, RW Exploit

Title: JIT Spraying + PAC Bypass
Scenario Description: Apple uses PAC (Pointer Authentication Codes) to protect memory pointers. Attackers bypass it by combining JIT (Just-In-Time) codegen and memory tricks.
Tools Used: WebKit JIT, LLDB, PAC tools, browser exploit PoC
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use an app or website that enables Just-in-Time (JIT) compilation, like Safari’s JavaScript engine. Step 2: Fill memory with repeating code (called JIT spraying) that eventually contains your shellcode. Step 3: Trigger a vulnerability that redirects execution to your shellcode in memory. Step 4: Use special knowledge of PAC encoding to craft a valid-looking pointer. Step 5: When the app jumps to your code, it runs your shellcode even with PAC protections. Step 6: Use this to escape sandbox, gain RCE, or elevate privileges. Step 7: Validate with debugger if control flow is hijacked successfully.
Vulnerability: Memory executable bypass via JIT spray
Detection Method: Unexpected code execution in logs; PAC auth failure messages
Solution: Limit JIT permissions; enforce memory W^X rules; separate JIT regions from data
Tags: PAC, JIT, Shellcode, Code Signing Bypass

Title: Improper Entitlement Validation
Scenario Description: Many Apple services require certain permissions (entitlements). If they don’t check properly, attackers can trick them into acting privileged.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a system service (like nehelper, keybagd, etc.) that uses entitlements for access control. Step 2: Write a test app that asks the service to do something restricted (like network control, key access). Step 3: Omit the required entitlements or fake them in app manifest or during runtime. Step 4: If the service doesn’t validate properly, it will still perform the action. Step 5: Use logs and service output to confirm. Step 6: This can lead to root-level behavior like turning on VPNs, controlling Wi-Fi, or accessing secure data.
Detection Method: Monitor service requests without valid entitlements
Solution: Harden entitlement checks in service code; use SecTaskCopyValueForEntitlement checks

Title: Abuse of SYS_DIAGNOSE
Scenario Description: The sys_diagnose utility gathers crash info and logs. Attackers can abuse this to leak kernel addresses (defeats ASLR).
Attack Steps: Step 1: From a non-privileged app or shell, trigger the sys_diagnose process (e.g., using volume button combo or syscalls). Step 2: Dump crash logs or debug logs from /var/log or system diagnostic folders. Step 3: Inspect the files for kernel memory addresses, pointers, or sensitive data like MAC ports or task structures. Step 4: Use this info to bypass Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) and prepare for deeper kernel exploits. Step 5: Use Xcode or Console.app to retrieve and examine logs.
Vulnerability: Kernel data exposed in crash output
Detection Method: Search logs for hex addresses; monitor diagnostic tool access
Solution: Filter sensitive data from diagnostics; restrict access to logs
Tags: sys_diagnose, ASLR Bypass, Kernel Info Leak

Title: IOMobileFrameBuffer Exploit
Scenario Description: IOMobileFramebuffer is part of Apple’s display system. It had past heap bugs allowing attackers to control memory and run code.
Tools Used: Frida, LLDB, PoC exploit, mobile debugger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build or run a PoC that sends malformed data to the IOMobileFramebuffer service via Metal/OpenGL or IOService APIs.
