Vulnerability: CAM Table overflow / insufficient port security
Detection Method: Monitoring CAM table size; port security alerts; increased broadcast traffic detection
Solution: Enable port security limiting MAC addresses; VLAN segmentation; IDS/IPS monitoring; physical access control
Tags: MAC Flooding, Switch Attack, LAN Sniffing

Title: SSL Stripping + Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts HTTPS connections and forces victim’s browser to use HTTP instead of HTTPS, enabling capture of sensitive data in plain text.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker must be positioned as MITM on the victim’s network via ARP spoofing, rogue Wi-Fi hotspot, or compromised router. Step 2: Once MITM position is established, attacker monitors victim’s HTTP(S) requests. Step 3: Victim attempts to connect to a secure website (HTTPS) by typing URL or clicking a link. Step 4: Attacker intercepts this request and strips the “https://” from URLs or rewrites links to “http://”, forcing the victim’s browser to establish an unencrypted HTTP connection. Step 5: Because HTTP traffic is unencrypted, attacker can capture all data sent and received, including login credentials, cookies, and sensitive info. Step 6: The attacker simultaneously connects to the legitimate HTTPS website on behalf of the victim, relaying traffic transparently so the victim does not notice issues. Step 7: Victim sees normal-looking page but on HTTP, so no padlock or HTTPS indicator. Many users ignore this and continue. Step 8: Attacker records all sensitive data passing through, including passwords and session tokens. Step 9: This attack can be automated with tools like sslstrip, which handle link rewriting and traffic relaying. Step 10: Attack is most effective when websites don’t enforce HTTPS strictly via HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). Step 11: Detection involves users noticing lack of HTTPS padlock, security tools checking for downgrade attempts, and network IDS identifying unusual HTTP traffic on secure domains. Step 12: Prevention includes website owners enforcing HTTPS with HSTS, users verifying HTTPS presence, using VPNs, and browsers implementing HTTPS-only modes and warnings. Step 13: Avoid using unsecured public Wi-Fi without VPN to minimize risk of SSL stripping.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS enforcement / No HSTS
Detection Method: User alert on missing HTTPS; IDS detecting downgrade attempts; network traffic analysis for HTTP on secure domains
Solution: Enforce HSTS on servers; educate users to verify HTTPS; use VPNs; modern browsers with HTTPS-only mode

Title: Capture VPN Traffic for Offline Decryption
Scenario Description: Attacker captures encrypted VPN traffic passing over the network and stores it for offline analysis or cryptographic key cracking to reveal sensitive information.
Tools Used: Wireshark, tcpdump, Aircrack-ng, hashcat, John the Ripper
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains network access to the communication channel where VPN traffic flows, typically the same LAN segment or a compromised router. Step 2: Use a packet capture tool like Wireshark or tcpdump configured in promiscuous or monitor mode to capture all VPN packets passing through the network. Step 3: Save the captured encrypted VPN traffic data to a file for offline analysis. VPN traffic is encrypted (e.g., IPsec, OpenVPN) so content is not immediately visible. Step 4: Attempt to obtain encryption keys or credentials via other means (e.g., malware, credential leaks), or capture VPN authentication handshakes if available. Step 5: Use cryptanalysis or brute-force tools like hashcat or John the Ripper with GPU acceleration to try to crack weak VPN encryption keys or passwords offline. Step 6: If keys/passwords are recovered, use them to decrypt the captured VPN traffic offline, revealing the actual transmitted data. Step 7: Extract sensitive information such as emails, files, or internal services data from the decrypted VPN sessions. Step 8: This attack depends on weak encryption, key reuse, or poor VPN configurations; strong modern VPNs with perfect forward secrecy reduce risk. Step 9: Network defenders can detect large packet captures or unusual traffic patterns using network monitoring. Step 10: Prevention includes using strong VPN protocols (IKEv2/IPsec with PFS), complex keys, multi-factor authentication, and regularly updating VPN software.
Vulnerability: Weak encryption, key reuse, poor config
Detection Method: Network anomaly detection; traffic pattern analysis; VPN logs monitoring
Solution: Use strong encryption protocols; enforce key rotation; use MFA; monitor network for suspicious captures

Title: Capturing Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos)
Scenario Description: Attacker captures authentication handshakes of protocols like NTLM or Kerberos on the network to crack credentials offline or replay them for unauthorized access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same network as the victim to sniff network traffic. Step 2: Use Wireshark or Responder to capture authentication handshakes during login or service access—NTLM challenge-response or Kerberos ticket exchanges. Step 3: Save the captured handshake packets containing hashed or encrypted credentials. Step 4: Use offline cracking tools like hashcat to attempt brute-force or dictionary attacks on the captured hashes to reveal plaintext passwords, leveraging GPU acceleration for speed. Step 5: If cracking succeeds, attacker obtains user credentials that can be used to log into systems or escalate privileges. Step 6: Alternatively, attacker can perform replay attacks by resending valid authentication tokens to impersonate the victim without cracking passwords. Step 7: Use captured tokens to access network resources or launch lateral movement. Step 8: Detection is possible via monitoring authentication failures, unusual login times or locations, and alerts from intrusion detection systems monitoring authentication protocols. Step 9: Prevent by enforcing strong password policies, enabling multi-factor authentication, using Kerberos with constrained delegation, and segmenting networks to limit sniffing scope. Step 10: Employ encrypted authentication protocols and limit exposure of sensitive traffic on untrusted networks.
Detection Method: Monitor authentication logs; detect abnormal access; IDS alerts on replay or malformed authentication traffic
Solution: Enforce MFA; use strong encryption; segment networks; restrict privileged accounts; patch systems regularly

Title: Sniffing Cloud Metadata API Requests
Scenario Description: Attacker captures requests to cloud metadata APIs (e.g., AWS IMDS) to gain sensitive instance metadata like credentials or tokens, enabling further compromise.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains network access to cloud environment (e.g., via compromised VM or container on same subnet). Step 2: Use network packet capture tools such as tcpdump or Wireshark on the attacker-controlled instance to monitor internal network traffic. Step 3: Filter captured traffic for requests to cloud provider metadata service IP addresses or URLs (e.g., 169.254.169.254 for AWS). Step 4: Extract API requests and responses which may include sensitive data like IAM role credentials, temporary tokens, or instance metadata. Step 5: Use extracted credentials or tokens to access other cloud resources with the same privileges, possibly escalating access. Step 6: Optionally, attacker can replay or automate metadata API queries to gather more data stealthily. Step 7: Detection includes monitoring for unusual metadata API calls, sudden spikes in API usage, or network flow anomalies within cloud infrastructure. Step 8: Mitigation involves restricting metadata API access using IMDSv2 (token-based), applying strict IAM roles and policies, network segmentation, and continuous monitoring of cloud logs for suspicious activity. Step 9: Educate cloud users and administrators about the risks of metadata API exposure and enforce the principle of least privilege.
Vulnerability: Metadata API exposed without access control
Detection Method: Monitor cloud logs; detect unusual metadata requests; network anomaly detection
Solution: Use IMDSv2; restrict metadata API access; implement least privilege IAM; network segmentation

Title: Protocol-Specific Sniffing (DNS, SMB, FTP, Telnet)
Scenario Description: Attacker targets legacy protocols like DNS, SMB, FTP, and Telnet that transmit data in plaintext, making it easy to capture sensitive info like passwords.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same network segment (wired or wireless) as the victims. Step 2: Use packet capture tools like Wireshark or tcpdump configured in promiscuous mode to capture all network traffic. Step 3: Filter captured traffic by protocols of interest: DNS queries, SMB file shares, FTP sessions, and Telnet connections. Step 4: Analyze the captured packets for credentials, session data, or sensitive file transfers transmitted in clear text. Step 5: Extract usernames, passwords, file contents, and command histories sent over these protocols. Step 6: Use captured credentials to access resources or escalate privileges on the network. Step 7: If necessary, combine with active attacks (e.g., MITM) to increase captured data volume. Step 8: Detection can be done by monitoring network for legacy protocol usage or unencrypted data transfers. Step 9: Mitigate by replacing legacy protocols with secure versions (e.g., DNS over HTTPS, SMBv3, SFTP, SSH/Telnet replacement), enforcing encryption, and disabling unnecessary services. Step 10: Educate users about dangers of using insecure protocols and enforce network security policies accordingly.
Detection Method: Network traffic monitoring; alerts on legacy protocol usage; anomaly detection for unencrypted traffic
Solution: Upgrade to secure protocols; disable legacy services; encrypt all data in transit; user education

Title: Sniffing Container Network Interfaces
Scenario Description: Attacker accesses Docker or Kubernetes virtual networks to sniff traffic between containers or between containers and host, gaining sensitive inter-service data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the host machine or a container running in the same virtual network or Kubernetes cluster. Step 2: Install packet capturing tools like tcpdump or Wireshark inside the container or host. Step 3: Identify the network interfaces used by Docker bridge networks, Kubernetes CNI plugins, or overlay networks. Step 4: Configure the tool to capture packets on these virtual interfaces in promiscuous mode. Step 5: Start capturing traffic between containers, which might include service requests, API calls, or data exchanged in plaintext. Step 6: Analyze captured packets to extract sensitive information such as tokens, passwords, or API keys transmitted between microservices. Step 7: Use extracted data to escalate privileges, move laterally in the cluster, or exfiltrate data. Step 8: Detection is difficult but possible by monitoring unusual container activities or network interface statistics. Step 9: Prevention includes enforcing network policies (e.g., Kubernetes NetworkPolicies), encrypting service-to-service traffic (mTLS), restricting container host access, and using secure container runtimes. Step 10: Regularly audit container and host security configurations and apply the principle of least privilege.
Vulnerability: Lack of network segmentation or encryption
Detection Method: Container security monitoring; audit logs; network policy violations alerts
Solution: Use network segmentation, encrypt container traffic, limit host access, apply least privilege

Title: Wireless Network Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker captures wireless traffic over Wi-Fi networks to intercept sensitive information or metadata by exploiting the broadcast nature of wireless signals.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses a Wi-Fi capable device with a wireless adapter that supports monitor mode. Step 2: Switch the wireless interface into monitor mode to capture all wireless frames on the channel(s) of interest, including management, control, and data frames. Step 3: Select the target wireless network (SSID) and capture handshake packets, data frames, and broadcast traffic. Step 4: Save the captured traffic to a file for offline analysis. Step 5: Analyze captured frames for unencrypted data, such as HTTP traffic, DNS queries, or legacy protocols. Step 6: If the network uses weak encryption (e.g., WEP, WPA-TKIP) or has known vulnerabilities, use tools like Aircrack-ng to attempt cracking the Wi-Fi password offline using captured handshakes. Step 7: After gaining network access, capture more traffic to sniff user credentials, files, or sessions in clear text. Step 8: For WPA2 or WPA3 with strong passphrases, offline cracking is computationally intensive and less feasible. Step 9: Detection involves monitoring for unauthorized devices or abnormal traffic patterns using wireless IDS/IPS systems. Step 10: Defend by using strong Wi-Fi security standards (WPA3), complex passphrases, regularly updating access points, and disabling legacy protocols or open networks. Step 11: Educate users about risks of connecting to untrusted Wi-Fi networks without VPN protection.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS alerts; device authorization monitoring; unusual traffic detection
Solution: Use WPA3; strong passwords; disable WEP/TKIP; wireless IDS; VPN for public Wi-Fi use

Title: DHCP Starvation + Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker floods the DHCP server with fake DHCP requests to exhaust the available IP addresses, causing legitimate clients to fail getting leases and isolate them to attacker-controlled network segments for sniffing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the target local network with network access. Step 2: Use a tool like Yersinia or DHCPStarv to send a flood of fake DHCP lease requests with spoofed MAC addresses to the DHCP server. Step 3: This flood exhausts the DHCP server's pool of available IP addresses, denying service to legitimate clients requesting IP leases. Step 4: Legitimate clients either fail to obtain IP addresses or get assigned wrong/conflicting addresses, isolating or disrupting their network connectivity. Step 5: Attacker may then run a rogue DHCP server or manipulate network settings to control isolated clients' traffic. Step 6: Using packet sniffers like Wireshark on the attacker-controlled network segment, capture traffic from isolated clients, including sensitive data or authentication attempts. Step 7: Analyze captured packets to extract credentials, session tokens, or unencrypted data. Step 8: Attacker can leverage this to perform further attacks such as MITM, session hijacking, or data theft. Step 9: Detection involves monitoring DHCP server logs for unusual lease request rates and network monitoring tools alerting on IP exhaustion or DHCP anomalies. Step 10: Prevention includes configuring DHCP snooping on switches, limiting DHCP requests per port, and employing network segmentation to isolate critical assets.
Detection Method: DHCP server anomaly detection; network flow monitoring; alerts on rogue DHCP servers
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping; limit IP allocation rate; use static IPs for critical devices; segment network

Title: DNS Cache Poisoning via Sniffed Queries
Scenario Description: Attacker sniffs DNS queries to learn valid request patterns, then crafts and injects fake DNS responses to poison DNS caches and redirect users to malicious sites.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the network segment to sniff DNS queries using Wireshark or similar tools. Step 2: Monitor and capture DNS query packets, noting requested domain names and transaction IDs. Step 3: Use tools like Scapy or dnsspoof to craft forged DNS response packets matching legitimate transaction IDs and source ports. Step 4: Send the forged DNS responses to the DNS resolver or client before the legitimate DNS server replies, poisoning their cache with malicious IP mappings. Step 5: When clients request the poisoned domain again, they receive the malicious IP, redirecting them to attacker-controlled sites. Step 6: Attacker may host phishing sites, malware, or capture credentials via this redirection. Step 7: Detection requires monitoring DNS resolver logs for anomalous or repeated cache update failures, mismatched IP addresses, or unusual DNS traffic patterns. Step 8: Prevention involves using DNSSEC to authenticate DNS responses, configuring DNS servers to reject spoofed responses, and encrypting DNS traffic using DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT). Step 9: Educate users about suspicious URLs and verify site certificates to reduce impact of redirection attacks.
Detection Method: DNS query anomaly detection; DNS server logs; traffic integrity monitoring
Solution: Deploy DNSSEC; enable DNS encryption; monitor DNS traffic; educate users

Title: Data Injection via Sniffed Sequence Numbers
Scenario Description: Attacker sniffs TCP sequence numbers to predict or learn session state, then injects malicious packets into an active TCP session to alter data or commands.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains network access to sniff TCP traffic between victim hosts, using Wireshark or tcpdump in promiscuous mode. Step 2: Capture ongoing TCP sessions and note source/destination IP addresses, ports, and especially TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers. Step 3: Analyze captured packets to understand session state and sequence number progression. Step 4: Using a packet crafting tool like Scapy or TCPInject, create forged TCP packets with correct sequence and acknowledgment numbers to inject into the session. Step 5: Inject packets that carry malicious payloads, commands, or altered data, causing the victim to accept and process these as legitimate. Step 6: Depending on the application, attacker can alter file transfers, commands, or communication content, potentially causing data corruption or unauthorized actions. Step 7: The injection must be precisely timed and sequenced; otherwise, packets will be discarded by the TCP stack. Step 8: Detection can involve network anomaly detection systems monitoring for out-of-sequence packets or unexpected TCP flags. Step 9: Prevention requires using encrypted and authenticated transport layers (e.g., TLS), avoiding plaintext TCP sessions, and employing intrusion detection systems sensitive to session tampering. Step 10: Network segmentation and strict access controls also reduce exposure to sniffing and injection attacks.
Vulnerability: Predictable or sniffable TCP seq numbers
Detection Method: IDS alerts on out-of-sequence or forged packets; session integrity checks
Solution: Use TLS/SSL; employ packet filtering; segment networks; use IDS/IPS

Title: Exfiltration via Covert Channels in Sniffed Traffic
Scenario Description: Attacker hides stolen data within legitimate traffic patterns captured through sniffing to avoid detection by network monitoring tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains network access and begins sniffing legitimate network traffic using Wireshark or tcpdump. Step 2: Analyze the traffic to identify common communication patterns, protocols, and normal timing intervals. Step 3: Develop a covert channel method to embed or encode sensitive data within regular traffic fields (e.g., packet headers, timing delays, unused protocol fields). Step 4: Use packet crafting tools like Scapy or custom scripts to inject encoded data into outgoing packets without altering normal traffic volume or patterns noticeably. Step 5: Transmit data stealthily across the network, blending with normal traffic to evade signature-based or anomaly detection systems. Step 6: On the receiving end (controlled by attacker), decode the covertly embedded data from the network packets. Step 7: Maintain stealth by avoiding traffic spikes or abnormal packet formats that might trigger alarms. Step 8: This exfiltration technique is difficult to detect and may persist for long periods, leaking sensitive data slowly. Step 9: Detection requires advanced network behavior analytics, anomaly detection, and deep packet inspection with context awareness. Step 10: Prevention includes encrypting all traffic, strict egress filtering, network segmentation, and monitoring for unusual protocol field usage or timing anomalies.
Vulnerability: Lack of traffic inspection, protocol abuse
Impact: Stealthy data leak, intellectual property theft
Detection Method: Deep packet inspection; anomaly detection; behavioral monitoring
Solution: Encrypt traffic; use strict egress policies; monitor for protocol misuse and timing anomalies

Title: Sniffing for Session Hijacking Tokens
Scenario Description: Attacker captures unencrypted session tokens like cookies or JWTs from network traffic to impersonate users and hijack active sessions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the network segment between the user and server (e.g., via MITM, rogue Wi-Fi, or LAN access). Step 2: Use packet capture tools such as Wireshark or intercepting proxies like Burp Suite to monitor HTTP(S) traffic. Step 3: Identify and extract session tokens, such as cookies or JWTs, transmitted in HTTP headers or URLs that are not encrypted or protected by secure flags. Step 4: Save the captured tokens for replay or injection into requests to impersonate the victim. Step 5: Test the validity of tokens by sending forged requests to the target server using tools like curl or Burp. Step 6: If accepted, attacker gains unauthorized access to victim’s account or session. Step 7: To increase success, attacker may use SSL stripping to downgrade HTTPS connections and capture tokens in plaintext. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring for token reuse from multiple IPs, unusual session activity, or missing security flags on cookies. Step 9: Prevention includes enforcing HTTPS with secure cookie flags, token expiration, multi-factor authentication, and using HTTP-only cookies. Step 10: Educate users to avoid unsecured networks or use VPNs for sensitive browsing.
Detection Method: Monitor session anomalies; alert on token reuse; scan for insecure cookies
Solution: Enforce HTTPS, secure and HttpOnly cookie flags, MFA, short token lifetimes

Title: Reverse Engineering Proprietary Protocols
Scenario Description: Attacker captures traffic of a proprietary or undocumented protocol to understand its structure and exploit vulnerabilities or extract sensitive data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to network traffic containing communications using a proprietary or undocumented protocol. Step 2: Use packet capture tools like Wireshark or NetworkMiner to collect protocol data for offline analysis. Step 3: Analyze packet structure by inspecting headers, payloads, and repeating patterns to infer protocol fields, message types, and data formats. Step 4: Document observed protocol behaviors, field lengths, and timing to develop a protocol specification or decoder. Step 5: Use scripting or protocol dissectors (e.g., Wireshark Lua plugins) to automate parsing and further understanding. Step 6: Identify any weaknesses such as lack of encryption, authentication, or input validation within the protocol. Step 7: Craft custom packets or messages using tools like Scapy to test protocol responses and potentially trigger bugs or unauthorized behaviors. Step 8: Exploit discovered weaknesses to inject malicious payloads, intercept sensitive data, or disrupt service. Step 9: This knowledge can also help in developing defenses by understanding protocol risks and implementing proper security controls. Step 10: Detection and prevention are challenging but include encrypting proprietary protocol traffic, validating inputs strictly, and limiting protocol exposure to trusted hosts only.
MITRE Technique: T1609 – Container and Protocol Reverse Engineering
Detection Method: Monitor protocol usage; anomaly detection; limit protocol exposure
Solution: Encrypt proprietary protocols; authenticate endpoints; restrict protocol access

Title: Sniffing in Virtualized Environments
Scenario Description: Attacker inside a virtualized environment (e.g., VMware, Hyper-V, KVM) sniffs network traffic between virtual machines or between VMs and the host due to shared virtual switches or misconfigurations.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a virtual machine (VM) within the virtualized environment, either by compromising a VM or through authorized access. Step 2: Identify virtual network interfaces connected to virtual switches or bridges inside the host or hypervisor. Step 3: Use packet capturing tools like Wireshark or tcpdump installed inside the compromised VM or host to capture network packets on these virtual interfaces. Step 4: Configure the network adapter or hypervisor settings (if privileged access is available) to enable promiscuous mode or MAC address spoofing to capture traffic not destined for the attacker’s VM. Step 5: Capture and analyze network traffic flowing between other VMs, or between VMs and the host, including potentially sensitive data or credentials transmitted in cleartext. Step 6: Exploit captured data for further lateral movement, credential theft, or data exfiltration within the cloud or virtual environment. Step 7: Detection is difficult but may involve monitoring unusual network traffic on virtual switches or hypervisor logs showing promiscuous mode changes. Step 8: Prevention includes strict network segmentation of VMs, disabling promiscuous mode on virtual NICs unless absolutely needed, and implementing encryption for inter-VM communication. Step 9: Regularly audit virtual network configurations and enforce least privilege access to hypervisor management interfaces. Step 10: Educate cloud administrators on secure virtual network best practices and monitor VM-to-VM traffic for anomalies.
Vulnerability: Shared virtual switches, promiscuous mode enabled
Detection Method: Hypervisor logs, network monitoring, anomaly detection of promiscuous mode
Solution: Enforce VM network isolation, disable promiscuous mode, encrypt inter-VM traffic, limit hypervisor access

Title: Monitor Mode Activation
Scenario Description: Attacker configures a wireless network interface card (NIC) to monitor mode to capture all wireless frames in range, including packets not addressed to them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker ensures the wireless NIC supports monitor mode (common on Linux with compatible chipsets). Step 2: Use tools like airmon-ng or iwconfig to enable monitor mode on the wireless NIC, allowing it to capture all wireless traffic on a specified channel. Step 3: Confirm that the NIC is in monitor mode using commands like iwconfig or airmon-ng check. Step 4: Begin capturing raw 802.11 wireless frames using packet capture tools like Wireshark or tcpdump on the monitor interface. Step 5: Collected frames include management, control, and data frames from all nearby wireless devices, regardless of their intended recipient. Step 6: This mode enables passive traffic collection for further analysis such as identifying networks, clients, or sniffing unencrypted data. Step 7: Attacker can switch channels or use channel hopping to broaden capture scope. Step 8: Detection is difficult since monitor mode does not transmit frames, but monitoring MAC addresses and unusual NIC behavior might help. Step 9: Prevention includes securing wireless networks with strong encryption (WPA3), disabling unused NICs, and monitoring for rogue devices with scanning tools. Step 10: Educate users and administrators about risks of wireless eavesdropping and the importance of encrypted communications.
Detection Method: Wireless intrusion detection systems (WIDS); monitor for unusual passive scans
Solution: Use strong wireless encryption; detect rogue devices; disable unused wireless adapters

Title: Passive Sniffing of Beacon Frames
Scenario Description: Attacker listens passively to beacon frames broadcast by wireless access points to identify network SSIDs, BSSIDs, and channels without transmitting any packets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker enables monitor mode on their wireless NIC to passively capture all wireless frames on a chosen channel or via channel hopping. Step 2: Use tools like airodump-ng or Wireshark to filter and capture beacon frames, which are periodically broadcast by wireless access points to announce their presence. Step 3: Extract information from beacon frames such as SSID (network name), BSSID (MAC address of AP), supported data rates, security protocols, and operating channel. Step 4: Compile a list of visible wireless networks with details needed for further attacks like rogue AP setup or targeted association attacks. Step 5: Since this is passive listening, no packets are transmitted by the attacker, making detection extremely difficult. Step 6: Use gathered info to map wireless landscape and identify potential targets. Step 7: Repeat scanning on multiple channels or use channel hopping to discover all networks within range. Step 8: Detection requires monitoring for devices constantly scanning or in monitor mode, which is non-trivial. Step 9: Mitigation includes hiding SSIDs where feasible, enforcing strong authentication and encryption, and regularly auditing wireless environments. Step 10: Educate network admins on wireless reconnaissance risks and detection techniques.
Detection Method: Wireless intrusion detection systems; detection of unusual passive scanning
Solution: Use WPA3 with management frame protection; monitor for rogue APs; limit SSID broadcast where possible

Title: Channel Hopping or Fixed Channel
Scenario Description: Attacker uses channel hopping to capture wireless traffic across multiple channels or fixes to a single channel for focused sniffing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker configures wireless NIC in monitor mode as per previous steps. Step 2: Choose to either fix the NIC to monitor a single channel or enable channel hopping to sequentially scan all available wireless channels. Step 3: Use tools like airodump-ng to automate channel hopping and capture packets on multiple frequencies over time, increasing coverage of wireless networks. Step 4: When fixed on a single channel, the attacker captures all packets on that channel continuously for detailed analysis. Step 5: Channel hopping involves rapidly switching between channels to collect beacon frames, probe requests/responses, and data packets across the spectrum. Step 6: The tradeoff is between breadth (channel hopping captures many networks) and depth (fixed channel allows full capture of traffic on one channel). Step 7: Collected data can be analyzed offline for network discovery, client associations, and capturing unencrypted data. Step 8: Detection is hard since no transmissions are sent, but frequent rapid channel switching can be flagged by advanced wireless IDS systems. Step 9: Mitigation involves using strong encryption, monitoring for rogue sniffers, and limiting physical access to wireless environments. Step 10: Awareness training for network defenders on wireless sniffing techniques is essential.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS/IPS detecting abnormal scanning patterns
Solution: Use strong encryption (WPA3), segment wireless networks, monitor for unusual wireless activities

Title: Wait for Client to Connect/Reconnect
Scenario Description: Attacker patiently waits for a wireless client to join or rejoin the target Wi-Fi network, triggering handshake packets that can be captured for offline cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker puts wireless NIC into monitor mode to listen to all wireless traffic on the target network's channel. Step 2: Observe beacon frames and existing network activity to identify when a client disconnects or reconnects to the access point. Step 3: Remain patient, as the handshake only occurs when the client joins or re-joins the network, which can take minutes to hours depending on client behavior. Step 4: Keep the capture tool running continuously to avoid missing the handshake event. Step 5: Once the client associates or reassociates, handshake packets are exchanged; attacker prepares to capture these frames. Step 6: Ensure capture tools like airodump-ng are set to capture EAPOL (Extensible Authentication Protocol over LAN) packets that occur during the handshake. Step 7: Maintain monitoring until a full handshake is captured; partial captures are insufficient for cracking. Step 8: If no clients reconnect naturally, consider inducing deauthentication attacks (if permitted and ethical) to force clients to reconnect. Step 9: Be mindful of laws and ethics when waiting for or inducing client handshakes. Step 10: Successful passive capture of the handshake enables offline cracking attempts against WPA/WPA2 passphrases.
Impact: Potential key recovery for Wi-Fi access
Detection Method: Monitor for abnormal handshake capture attempts; detect rogue deauthentication attacks
Solution: Use WPA3, enable management frame protection, monitor for rogue sniffers and attacks

Title: Capture 4-Way Handshake Frames
Scenario Description: Attacker captures EAPOL packets exchanged during WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake between client and access point.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use airodump-ng or Wireshark with wireless NIC in monitor mode on the target network’s channel. Step 2: Filter captured packets to focus on EAPOL frames (usually identified by Wireshark filter: eapol or frame type). Step 3: Wait for the 4-way handshake packets to be transmitted as the client authenticates or re-authenticates. Step 4: Capture all four handshake packets, which contain key information needed for offline passphrase cracking. Step 5: Verify that the handshake capture is complete and not missing packets; incomplete captures cannot be cracked. Step 6: Save the captured handshake data in capture files (e.g., .pcap or .cap formats) for offline analysis. Step 7: Use tools like aircrack-ng or hashcat later to attempt to recover the Wi-Fi password from the handshake. Step 8: Ensure capture is done passively to avoid detection unless explicitly permitted to perform active attacks. Step 9: Monitor capture quality and adjust channels or positioning to improve handshake packet reception. Step 10: Understand the ethical and legal implications of capturing handshake packets.
Impact: Enables offline cracking of Wi-Fi passwords
Detection Method: Detect unusual wireless capture activity; identify signs of network reconnaissance
Solution: Use strong passphrases, WPA3, and MFP (Management Frame Protection)

Title: Filter & Save Handshake Capture
Scenario Description: Attacker filters the sniffed wireless traffic to isolate handshake packets and saves the capture for offline cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: After capturing wireless traffic in monitor mode, open the capture file in Wireshark or keep capturing with airodump-ng. Step 2: Apply filters in Wireshark such as eapol to isolate handshake packets from the rest of the traffic. Step 3: Verify that the filtered packets represent the full 4-way handshake (all 4 key exchange packets). Step 4: Save the filtered handshake packets into a separate capture file (.cap or .pcap) to reduce size and ease cracking. Step 5: Use this filtered capture as input to password cracking tools like aircrack-ng, hashcat, or cowpatty. Step 6: Ensure that the capture includes both client and AP MAC addresses to validate handshake completeness. Step 7: Optionally, verify handshake quality using aircrack-ng's handshake check utilities. Step 8: Maintain chain of custody and ethical considerations for captured data. Step 9: Use offline cracking methods to attempt to recover the Wi-Fi passphrase without further network interaction. Step 10: Always have explicit permission to capture and analyze network traffic to stay within legal boundaries.
Detection Method: Inspect capture files for completeness and anomalies
Solution: Use WPA3 with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), avoid weak passwords

Title: Offline Cracking of Handshake
Scenario Description: Attacker uses captured WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake packets to attempt to recover the Wi-Fi password offline, without interacting with the network.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you have a full capture of the WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake, saved as a .cap or .pcap file from previous capture steps. Step 2: Choose a cracking tool like aircrack-ng for dictionary attacks or hashcat for GPU-accelerated attacks. Step 3: Obtain or create a password wordlist (dictionary) that contains common or targeted passwords. Popular wordlists include rockyou.txt or custom lists. Step 4: Run the cracking tool with the handshake capture file and the wordlist as inputs. For example, with aircrack-ng: aircrack-ng -w wordlist.txt handshake.cap. Step 5: The tool computes the Pairwise Master Key (PMK) candidate for each password guess and compares it with the handshake data. Step 6: If a match is found, the password is revealed. If not, the process continues until the wordlist is exhausted. Step 7: For stronger passwords, consider using brute force or hybrid attacks, combining dictionaries with mutations or masks, available in hashcat. Step 8: Cracking may take from seconds to days depending on password complexity, hardware power, and wordlist size. Step 9: Once cracked, use the password to connect to the Wi-Fi network or further compromise. Step 10: Always obtain proper authorization before performing cracking attempts to stay legal and ethical.
Detection Method: Detect repeated failed association attempts; monitor for rogue clients
Solution: Use strong, complex passwords; deploy WPA3 with SAE; regularly update Wi-Fi credentials

Title: Deauthentication Attack (Deauth Flood)
Scenario Description: Attacker sends many forged deauthentication frames to one or more clients or AP, forcing them to disconnect repeatedly, causing denial of service or inducing reconnection to capture handshakes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode using tools like airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to identify the target AP’s BSSID and the MAC addresses of connected clients. Step 3: Craft forged deauthentication frames spoofing the AP or client MAC addresses using aireplay-ng or mdk3. Step 4: Begin sending a rapid flood of deauth frames targeting specific clients or broadcast to all clients connected to the AP. Step 5: Clients get disconnected repeatedly and try to reconnect, allowing the attacker to capture the WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake. Step 6: This can cause a denial of service for legitimate users by disrupting network connectivity. Step 7: Optionally, combine this attack with packet capture tools to seize handshakes for offline cracking. Step 8: Monitor for network disruptions or unusual disconnection patterns that could indicate a deauth attack. Step 9: Use this attack carefully and only in authorized environments due to its disruptive nature and legal considerations. Step 10: Remediate by implementing management frame protection (802.11w) and monitoring for rogue deauth traffic.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS/IPS detecting deauth floods; monitoring client disconnect rates
Solution: Enable 802.11w (MFP); monitor for unusual deauth traffic; use strong encryption and authentication

Title: Injection of Fake Authentication Frames
Scenario Description: Attacker injects forged authentication frames pretending to be a legitimate client or AP to hijack sessions or confuse the network.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Place wireless NIC into monitor mode with airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Identify the target AP’s BSSID and client MAC addresses using airodump-ng. Step 3: Use aireplay-ng to craft and inject fake authentication frames to either the AP (pretending to be a client) or the client (pretending to be AP). Step 4: Attempt to associate or authenticate with the AP using these fake frames, bypassing normal authentication if possible. Step 5: If successful, attacker may gain unauthorized network access or cause session confusion. Step 6: This may allow man-in-the-middle positioning or session hijacking attacks. Step 7: Repeat injection attempts to maintain persistence or disrupt legitimate connections. Step 8: Detection includes monitoring for unexpected authentication frames or duplicate MAC addresses. Step 9: Use frame integrity checks and enable management frame protection to prevent unauthorized frame injection. Step 10: Always ensure legal authorization before conducting such active attacks.
Detection Method: Monitor authentication attempts; detect duplicate MACs or abnormal association patterns
Solution: Enable 802.11w (MFP); strong authentication; monitor for spoofed frames

Title: Beacon Frame Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects forged beacon frames advertising fake SSIDs to confuse clients, perform evil twin attacks, or lure users to malicious networks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set wireless NIC to monitor mode with airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use tools like aireplay-ng, mdk3, or hostapd to craft and inject fake beacon frames advertising rogue SSIDs mimicking legitimate networks or new malicious networks. Step 3: Broadcast these fake beacons on the same or adjacent wireless channels to increase visibility. Step 4: Clients scanning for networks may see the rogue SSIDs and attempt to connect if users are tricked or automatic connections occur. Step 5: Attacker can capture authentication attempts, perform man-in-the-middle attacks, or deliver malicious payloads via rogue AP. Step 6: Continue broadcasting beacon frames to maintain the rogue network presence. Step 7: Detection includes monitoring for unexpected SSIDs, duplicate BSSIDs, or sudden new wireless networks in the environment. Step 8: Use Wireless IDS to flag suspicious beacon activities or unauthorized APs. Step 9: Educate users to verify network authenticity and avoid auto-connecting to unknown Wi-Fi. Step 10: Use strong WPA3 encryption and mutual authentication to defend against rogue AP attacks.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS detecting rogue APs; client alerts for unknown SSIDs
Solution: Educate users; deploy WPA3 and MFP; monitor for rogue APs and beacon injection

Title: Probe Request/Response Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects fake probe requests or responses to force clients to reveal hidden SSIDs or connect to rogue APs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode using airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use tools like aireplay-ng or bettercap to craft fake probe request frames targeting specific clients or broadcast to all nearby devices. Step 3: Inject these fake probe requests on the wireless channel used by the target network to provoke clients into sending probe responses. Step 4: Collect probe responses from clients, which may include hidden SSIDs that are not normally broadcasted by access points. Step 5: Alternatively, inject fake probe responses to clients, tricking them into attempting to connect to rogue or attacker-controlled APs. Step 6: Use this information for network mapping, reconnaissance, or setting up evil twin attacks. Step 7: Maintain injection over time to harvest more data and discover additional hidden networks or clients. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring for unusual probe frame patterns or spikes in probe requests/responses. Step 9: Mitigate by using strong wireless encryption, avoiding hidden SSIDs (which increase risk), and enabling management frame protection (MFP). Step 10: Educate users not to connect automatically to unknown or suspicious networks.
Vulnerability: Lack of protection for probe frames
Detection Method: Wireless IDS monitoring probe request/response anomalies
Solution: Use WPA3, avoid hidden SSIDs, enable MFP, monitor wireless traffic

Title: Fragmentation Attack via Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects malformed or fragmented frames to bypass encryption, cause device crashes, or manipulate traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode on your wireless NIC to capture and inject frames. Step 2: Identify target AP and clients’ MAC addresses using airodump-ng or similar tools. Step 3: Use specialized custom tools or aircrack-ng to craft malformed or fragmented 802.11 frames designed to exploit weaknesses in how clients or APs reassemble fragmented packets. Step 4: Inject these fragmented frames into the wireless network aiming to bypass WPA/WPA2 encryption mechanisms or cause denial of service via crashes. Step 5: Observe device or network behavior to confirm successful bypass or disruption. Step 6: Repeat injections to maintain the attack or escalate impact. Step 7: Detection is challenging but may involve monitoring for abnormal fragmentation patterns or repeated frame errors. Step 8: Mitigation includes applying firmware and driver updates to patch vulnerabilities and enabling management frame protection. Step 9: Segment and monitor wireless networks closely for abnormal traffic patterns. Step 10: Follow legal and ethical guidelines strictly when testing such attacks.
Detection Method: Monitor wireless frame anomalies; inspect error logs
Solution: Keep device firmware updated; enable MFP; network segmentation

Title: Replay Attacks with Injected Frames
Scenario Description: Attacker captures valid frames and re-injects them later to replay or manipulate wireless communication.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put wireless NIC into monitor mode to capture frames between client and AP. Step 2: Identify and isolate valid frames such as authentication, association, or data frames. Step 3: Use tools like aireplay-ng or bettercap to capture and save these frames for replay. Step 4: Craft replay attacks by injecting these valid frames back into the network at strategic times to cause repeated authentications or unauthorized data transmissions. Step 5: Attempt to bypass network security by replaying valid authentication or data frames to impersonate clients or maintain session persistence. Step 6: Monitor the network for successful injection and its impact, such as forced reconnections or unauthorized access. Step 7: Repeat or automate replay attacks to maintain presence or escalate attacks. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring for duplicate frames or abnormal authentication patterns. Step 9: Mitigate by enabling management frame protection (802.11w) to prevent replay and injection of critical management frames. Step 10: Always conduct replay testing with proper permission and ethical considerations.
Vulnerability: Lack of management frame replay protection
Detection Method: Wireless IDS detecting replayed or duplicate frames
Solution: Enable 802.11w MFP; monitor for repeated frames; strong authentication

Title: Deauth + Handshake Capture Combo
Scenario Description: Attacker injects deauthentication frames to disconnect a client, forcing it to reconnect and exchange handshake frames, which the attacker captures passively for offline cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode using tools like airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to identify the target AP’s BSSID and the MAC addresses of connected clients. Step 3: Use aireplay-ng to send deauthentication frames targeting one or more client MAC addresses or broadcast to all clients connected to the AP, forcing clients to disconnect. Step 4: As clients reconnect, airodump-ng listens and captures the WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake packets exchanged during authentication. Step 5: Verify the handshake capture completeness by checking for the four EAPOL packets in the capture. Step 6: Save the handshake capture file (.cap) for offline password cracking using tools like aircrack-ng or hashcat. Step 7: Repeat the deauth and capture process as needed to obtain handshakes from different clients or improve capture quality. Step 8: Use the handshake capture with cracking tools to attempt to recover the Wi-Fi password offline without further network interaction. Step 9: Monitor for detection signs like repeated deauthentication packets or client disconnects that could alert defenders. Step 10: Ensure proper authorization and legality before conducting this disruptive attack as it affects network availability.
Detection Method: Detect wireless deauth floods; monitor client disconnect patterns
Solution: Enable 802.11w (MFP); use strong passphrases; monitor wireless traffic

Title: Injection of QoS Null Data Frames
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits QoS Null Data frames, which have no payload but affect quality of service, to embed covert commands or exfiltrate data stealthily.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode to capture and inject frames. Step 2: Use specialized scripts or bettercap modules that craft QoS Null Data frames with hidden or encoded payloads inside header fields or frame extensions. Step 3: Inject these crafted frames into the target wireless network during normal operation to avoid detection. Step 4: The receiver processes the QoS frames as normal but extracts the covert data embedded by the attacker. Step 5: Use this covert channel to exfiltrate sensitive data, send hidden commands, or communicate stealthily between attacker-controlled devices. Step 6: Maintain injection periodically to transfer larger payloads or commands over time. Step 7: Detection is difficult as QoS Null Data frames are legitimate and common; advanced traffic analysis or anomaly detection needed. Step 8: Defenders should monitor for unusual QoS traffic patterns or frame rates. Step 9: Patch wireless drivers and firmware to address known QoS vulnerabilities if any exist. Step 10: Follow legal and ethical standards when testing such covert channel attacks.
Vulnerability: Lack of payload inspection in QoS frames
Detection Method: Anomaly detection on QoS traffic; frame inspection tools
Solution: Monitor wireless traffic patterns; update drivers/firmware; enable network segmentation

Title: Control Frame Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attacker manipulates control frames (e.g., ACK, RTS, CTS) to disrupt wireless communication or interfere with device behavior.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Place your wireless NIC into monitor mode and prepare injection tools like aireplay-ng or bettercap. Step 2: Identify target AP and client MAC addresses using airodump-ng. Step 3: Craft malicious control frames such as ACK, RTS (Request to Send), or CTS (Clear to Send) with forged addresses or timing. Step 4: Inject these control frames into the wireless medium targeting clients or AP to interfere with normal frame exchanges. Step 5: This can cause clients to believe transmissions were acknowledged when they were not or block legitimate traffic, resulting in denial of service or disruption. Step 6: Repeat injections to maintain disruption or induce collisions and retransmissions on the network. Step 7: Use this technique to degrade network performance, create timing side channels, or trigger device malfunctions. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring abnormal control frame frequency or unexpected timing patterns. Step 9: Mitigate by using modern wireless standards that include management frame protection and firmware updates. Step 10: Always test control frame manipulations in authorized environments respecting legal boundaries.
Detection Method: Detect spikes in control frame transmissions; monitor frame timing anomalies
Solution: Enable 802.11w, update firmware; monitor for unusual wireless activity

Title: Management Frame Protection Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker bypasses 802.11w Management Frame Protection (MFP) by exploiting implementation flaws or fallback mechanisms, enabling spoofing or injection of forged management frames like deauthentication or disassociation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode with tools like airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to scan the wireless environment and identify APs and clients, noting which APs support 802.11w MFP (Management Frame Protection). Step 3: Identify a target AP/client pair where MFP is either disabled, improperly implemented, or falls back to unprotected frames under some conditions. Step 4: Use tools like aireplay-ng or bettercap to craft forged management frames such as deauthentication or disassociation frames, spoofing legitimate MAC addresses. Step 5: Inject these forged frames to disconnect clients or disrupt communication, bypassing the protection intended by MFP. Step 6: Some implementations fallback to unprotected frames for compatibility, which attackers exploit to inject malicious management frames. Step 7: Confirm successful attack by observing client disconnections or forced reconnections on the target network. Step 8: Capture any handshakes generated by forced reconnects for offline cracking if desired. Step 9: Monitor for unusual or repeated management frames to detect such bypass attempts. Step 10: Always obtain legal authorization before testing or exploiting these vulnerabilities, as it causes network disruption.
Vulnerability: Implementation flaws or fallback in MFP
Detection Method: Wireless IDS/IPS monitoring management frames; alert on unprotected deauth/disassociation frames
Solution: Enforce strict 802.11w MFP on all devices; update firmware; disable fallback to unprotected management frames

Title: Passive IV Collection
Scenario Description: Attacker captures a large number of packets passively to gather Initialization Vectors (IVs) used in WEP encryption, aiming to crack the key slowly but stealthily.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode using airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use airodump-ng or tcpdump to passively capture wireless traffic on the target network’s channel without transmitting any packets, ensuring stealth. Step 3: Collect a large volume of packets, focusing on those containing IVs, which are part of each encrypted packet’s header. Step 4: Store the capture in a .cap file for later offline analysis. Step 5: Because IVs are relatively small in number and reused frequently in WEP, collecting many packets increases the chances of key recovery. Step 6: This passive method avoids detection as it does not inject traffic or interfere with the network. Step 7: Continue passive capture until a sufficient number of IVs are collected (often tens of thousands or more). Step 8: Use the collected IVs with cracking tools like aircrack-ng to attempt recovery of the WEP key offline. Step 9: Monitor the capture quality to ensure packets are valid and not corrupted. Step 10: This method requires patience but minimizes detection risk due to its passive nature.
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual packet capture tools or unusual wireless interface modes
Solution: Upgrade to WPA3/WPA2; disable WEP; use strong encryption and keys

Title: Active Packet Injection to Speed IV Gathering
Scenario Description: Attacker injects packets like ARP requests to force the AP and clients to generate more encrypted traffic, speeding up IV collection for WEP key cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode with airmon-ng or iwconfig. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to identify the target network’s BSSID and operating channel. Step 3: Start capturing packets using airodump-ng to record IVs. Step 4: Use aireplay-ng to inject specially crafted packets, such as ARP request replay or broadcast packets, to stimulate traffic from the AP or clients. Step 5: This injection causes clients and AP to respond with encrypted frames, increasing the number of IVs generated in the wireless environment. Step 6: Continue injection and capture simultaneously until a sufficient number of IVs are collected for cracking. Step 7: Stop injection once enough IVs are harvested to reduce detection risk. Step 8: Use the collected IVs offline with aircrack-ng or other cracking tools to recover the WEP key. Step 9: This method speeds up the attack significantly compared to passive collection but is more likely to be detected due to active injection. Step 10: Use this technique responsibly and legally, as injecting packets disrupts normal network operation.
Detection Method: Detect abnormal ARP/packet injection or high packet rates; monitor client disconnections
Solution: Patch network devices; upgrade from WEP; use intrusion detection systems (IDS)

Title: Weak IV Detection & Statistical Analysis
Scenario Description: Attacker analyzes collected IVs for patterns and weaknesses statistically to determine the WEP key faster and more efficiently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: After collecting a large dataset of IVs via passive or active capture, load the .cap file into cracking tools like aircrack-ng. Step 2: Run statistical tests within aircrack-ng or external tools to identify weak or repeated IVs that are vulnerable to cryptanalysis. Step 3: Analyze IV distribution, packet types, and frequency to pinpoint exploitable weaknesses. Step 4: Use this analysis to guide focused cracking efforts, prioritizing IVs likely to yield the key faster. Step 5: Apply statistical attacks such as the FMS (Fluhrer, Mantin, and Shamir) attack or KoreK attacks embedded in tools. Step 6: Refine cracking attempts using the statistical data to reduce total cracking time. Step 7: Monitor cracking progress and update analysis as more IVs become available. Step 8: Continue until the WEP key is recovered or attempts are exhausted. Step 9: Understand that statistical weaknesses in WEP’s IV handling make this possible; WPA2/WPA3 do not have this vulnerability. Step 10: Use findings to advise on network upgrades and defensive measures.
Vulnerability: Weak IVs and poor randomness in WEP IVs
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated IVs or suspicious packet patterns
Solution: Upgrade from WEP to modern encryption standards; disable legacy protocols

Title: Fragmentation Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits WEP’s frame fragmentation mechanism to inject custom packets or accelerate IV collection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless interface into monitor mode using airmon-ng. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to locate a WEP-encrypted network and gather its BSSID and channel. Step 3: Begin capturing traffic with airodump-ng on the correct channel. Step 4: Identify data packets of interest, especially ARP packets, because they are small and predictable. Step 5: Use aireplay-ng in fragmentation mode to chop a captured ARP packet into small pieces and then inject it back into the network. Step 6: The AP reconstructs the packet and sends it out, producing a fresh, valid encrypted response — each generating a new IV. Step 7: Repeat injection to rapidly increase IV collection. Step 8: Passively monitor the network using airodump-ng to collect all packets with fresh IVs. Step 9: Once you’ve gathered enough IVs, use aircrack-ng to crack the WEP key. Step 10: Be careful: this attack is noisy and can be detected by intrusion detection systems. Use only in controlled or authorized environments.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS detecting repeated packet fragments or strange frame patterns
Solution: Upgrade to WPA3/WPA2; disable WEP; monitor for fragmentation patterns

Title: Chopchop Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker reveals plaintext of WEP-encrypted packets byte-by-byte without knowing the key, indirectly gathering IVs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode on your wireless NIC using airmon-ng. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to locate a WEP-encrypted access point and select a target client. Step 3: Start capturing packets using airodump-ng on the AP’s channel. Step 4: Identify a small encrypted data packet (e.g., ARP packet) from the target network. Step 5: Use aireplay-ng with --chopchop mode to modify the packet byte-by-byte from the end and send each version to the AP. Step 6: The AP will reply with an error or a valid frame depending on whether the modified packet has a correct checksum. Step 7: This response allows the attacker to guess one byte at a time, slowly revealing the entire plaintext of the original encrypted packet. Step 8: As you decrypt the original packet, it can be reused in replay attacks to generate more encrypted traffic and gather IVs faster. Step 9: Once enough IVs are collected, run aircrack-ng to crack the WEP key. Step 10: This attack is stealthier than injection attacks but takes time. Use in environments where active traffic generation is limited.
Vulnerability: CRC and IV handling flaws in WEP
Impact: Decryption of traffic, faster IV gathering
Detection Method: Detect excessive invalid packets and slow replay patterns
Solution: Use WPA2/WPA3; disable WEP; patch outdated wireless drivers

Title: Dictionary-Based Attacks on Captured IVs
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a dictionary of likely WEP keys or passphrases to crack the encryption offline after IV capture.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a large number of IVs from the target WEP-protected network using airodump-ng or tcpdump (minimum ~40,000–100,000 packets). Step 2: Save the capture in .cap format. Step 3: Prepare or download a dictionary file (wordlist) containing common WEP passphrases or precomputed key values (e.g., from rockyou.txt or custom WEP wordlists). Step 4: Use aircrack-ng -w /path/to/wordlist.txt -b <BSSID> <capture.cap> to start cracking using the dictionary. Step 5: The tool iteratively compares each entry in the dictionary against the captured IVs to find a matching key. Step 6: If a match is found, the WEP key is displayed. If not, a larger or custom wordlist is needed. Step 7: Optional: Combine this with statistical or replay-based attacks to improve cracking accuracy. Step 8: Once cracked, the key can be used to decrypt any WEP traffic or gain access to the wireless network. Step 9: This attack works entirely offline and is silent, as long as the IVs are already collected. Step 10: Prevent this by avoiding WEP entirely and switching to WPA2/WPA3 with strong passphrases.
Vulnerability: Weak passphrases and IV re-use in WEP
Detection Method: Log unusual capture activity; monitor cracking attempts offline via endpoint telemetry
Solution: Use WPA3 or WPA2 with strong passphrases; disable legacy encryption protocols

Title: Replay Attack with Packet Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker replays a captured packet (e.g., ARP) to stimulate the access point to respond with encrypted replies, thereby generating new IVs for WEP cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Put your wireless NIC into monitor mode using airmon-ng. Step 2: Use airodump-ng to locate the target WEP network and collect the BSSID and operating channel. Step 3: Start airodump-ng capture on the same channel to collect IVs. Step 4: Wait until you capture a small-sized data packet, preferably an ARP request, as these are easy to replay. Step 5: Use aireplay-ng -3 -b <BSSID> -h <your_MAC> <interface> to replay that captured packet. Aireplay-ng will try to replay the packet repeatedly to force the AP to generate more responses, which contain fresh IVs. Step 6: As the access point replies to the repeated request, IVs will accumulate in your airodump-ng capture file. Step 7: Allow the process to run until tens of thousands of IVs are collected. Step 8: Use aircrack-ng on the capture file to attempt to crack the WEP key. Step 9: Replay attacks are very noisy and can easily be detected by wireless IDS/IPS or network defenders. Step 10: Perform only in test labs or with explicit permission, as it disrupts normal traffic.
Impact: Faster IV harvesting, increased encrypted traffic
Detection Method: Monitor high duplicate frame rates; detect repeated ARP requests
Solution: Migrate to WPA2/WPA3; disable WEP; monitor and rate-limit ARP traffic

Title: Key Fragment Recovery via KoreK Attacks
Scenario Description: Attacker applies KoreK statistical techniques on collected IVs to recover key bytes more efficiently than older methods like FMS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use airodump-ng or similar tool to capture tens of thousands of packets from a WEP-encrypted network (target ~100,000 IVs for best chance). Step 2: Save the IVs into a .cap file. Step 3: Open a terminal and run aircrack-ng <capture.cap> without any dictionary — aircrack-ng will use KoreK statistical methods by default. Step 4: Aircrack-ng performs multiple attack techniques, including KoreK attacks that rely on analyzing patterns in IV reuse to guess key fragments. Step 5: These techniques improve upon the original FMS attack by using 17+ statistical attacks to recover key bytes faster and with fewer packets. Step 6: Monitor the cracking progress as the tool shows per-byte confidence levels. Step 7: Once aircrack-ng recovers all key bytes, it displays the full WEP key. Step 8: This attack is completely offline once IVs are collected, making it stealthy after capture. Step 9: Use the key to decrypt traffic or join the network (with permission). Step 10: Educate defenders about the weakness of WEP and the strength of modern statistical cracking tools.
Vulnerability: IV reuse and statistical patterns in WEP
Detection Method: Detect large IV capture volumes; monitor usage of aircrack-ng-style traffic
Solution: Disable WEP, use WPA2/WPA3; train users on outdated encryption risks

Title: PTW Attack (Pyshkin, Tews, Weinmann)
Scenario Description: A fast WEP cracking attack that improves over KoreK by using fewer packets and more efficient statistical models.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture encrypted traffic from a WEP-secured network using airodump-ng, targeting at least 40,000 IVs (much less than traditional methods). Step 2: Save the packets in .cap format. Step 3: Run aircrack-ng -z <capture.cap> to initiate the PTW attack. The -z flag tells aircrack-ng to use the PTW (Pyshkin, Tews, and Weinmann) method instead of KoreK. Step 4: PTW doesn’t require ARP packets or guessing known plaintext, unlike older methods — it uses packet vectors and mathematical modeling to reconstruct the key. Step 5: Watch the progress as the tool reveals key byte confidence levels in real-time. Step 6: PTW usually cracks WEP keys in minutes with only 40,000–85,000 IVs, depending on network traffic. Step 7: Once the key is found, you can decrypt WEP packets or connect to the network (with authorization). Step 8: This method is silent post-capture and leaves no active trace if done passively. Step 9: Defenders must understand that even low-traffic WEP networks are vulnerable due to PTW efficiency. Step 10: Educate stakeholders on immediate migration away from WEP to secure standards like WPA3.
Detection Method: Monitor WEP usage; detect IV-heavy capture behavior
Solution: Disable WEP completely; audit and deprecate outdated wireless equipment
Tags: WEP Cracking, PTW Attack, Offline Attack

Title: Offline Key Recovery from IVs
Scenario Description: After collecting enough encrypted packets (IVs), the attacker uses offline tools to analyze them and recover the WEP key without further interaction.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start by putting your wireless interface into monitor mode using airmon-ng start wlan0 (replace wlan0 with your interface name). This allows your system to passively capture wireless traffic. Step 2: Use airodump-ng wlan0mon to list available Wi-Fi networks. Identify the target network that is WEP-encrypted. Step 3: Focus on the BSSID and channel (CH) of the WEP network. Start capturing packets: airodump-ng -c <channel> --bssid <BSSID> -w capture wlan0mon — this will save packets (including IVs) into a .cap file. Step 4: Let the capture run until you have at least 40,000–100,000 packets. The more IVs collected, the higher your chances of recovering the key. Step 5: Once you’ve gathered enough IVs, stop airodump-ng. Step 6: Use aircrack-ng capture.cap to begin the offline cracking process. Step 7: Aircrack-ng will perform statistical attacks (FMS, KoreK, PTW) on the IVs to determine the WEP key. This step is done completely offline — no further interaction with the network is required. Step 8: If successful, the WEP key will be printed to your terminal. Step 9: You can now use this key to decrypt past captured packets using Wireshark or join the network (if authorized). Step 10: Always perform this only in legal environments such as penetration testing labs or with explicit permission. Unauthorized use is illegal and unethical.
Vulnerability: Weak encryption and IV reuse in WEP
Detection Method: Detect passive sniffing; track IV counts in IDS logs
Solution: Completely retire WEP; switch to WPA2 or WPA3; use network segmentation; monitor for .cap file creation

Title: Passive Capture of 4-Way Handshake
Scenario Description: Wait for a legitimate user to connect to the Wi-Fi network and silently capture the WPA/WPA2 handshake packets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode on your wireless adapter: airmon-ng start wlan0 (replace wlan0 with your device name). Step 2: Start airodump-ng to locate the WPA/WPA2 network: airodump-ng wlan0mon. Identify the target BSSID (router MAC), channel, and ESSID (network name). Step 3: Start focused capture on that network using: airodump-ng --bssid <BSSID> -c <channel> -w handshake wlan0mon. This saves packets into a .cap file. Step 4: Wait patiently for a legitimate device to connect to the network. This might take minutes or hours, depending on user activity. Step 5: When a client connects or reconnects, the router and client perform a 4-way handshake. Step 6: Airodump-ng will automatically detect and save handshake packets. You can also verify the handshake using Wireshark (look for EAPOL packets). Step 7: Once the handshake is captured, you can attempt offline cracking (see dictionary attack). Step 8: This method is passive and invisible to the network — no packets are injected. Step 9: You may need multiple handshake attempts to get a clean capture. Step 10: Never use this technique outside legal or educational environments.
Vulnerability: No encryption on handshake capture process
Detection Method: Monitor for excessive packet capture or abnormal passive listeners
Solution: Use WPA3 or Enterprise WPA2; rotate passwords regularly; monitor connection patterns

Title: Deauthentication Attack to Force Reconnect
Scenario Description: Send fake deauth frames to disconnect a client from the network, forcing it to reconnect and reveal its handshake.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start your wireless card in monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Use airodump-ng wlan0mon to locate the target WPA/WPA2 network and identify connected clients. Step 3: Start focused packet capture: airodump-ng --bssid <BSSID> -c <channel> -w handshake wlan0mon. Step 4: Use aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> -c <Client_MAC> wlan0mon to send 10 fake deauth frames targeting a specific connected client. This disconnects the device from the router temporarily. Step 5: As the device reconnects, it automatically performs a WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake. Step 6: Airodump-ng will detect and store the handshake in the .cap file. Step 7: If no handshake is captured, try again or increase the deauth count. Step 8: Once the handshake is collected, verify its validity using Wireshark (look for 4 EAPOL messages). Step 9: Now proceed to offline password cracking (e.g., dictionary attack). Step 10: This method is active, noisy, and may cause disruption — only perform in legal labs or assessments.
Impact: Allows handshake capture and potential cracking
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated deauth packets; alert on client reconnection spikes
Solution: Use 802.11w Management Frame Protection (MFP); enable WPA3; monitor for deauth anomalies

Title: Dictionary Attack
Scenario Description: Use a captured 4-way handshake and a wordlist of likely passwords to find the correct WPA/WPA2 passphrase.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a valid WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake using either passive listening or deauth attack methods (see above). Step 2: Ensure your .cap file contains the full 4 EAPOL packets. Verify with tools like Wireshark (look for 4 handshake messages) or with aircrack-ng -a2 handshake.cap. Step 3: Get a dictionary file — e.g., rockyou.txt, SecLists, or custom password lists. Step 4: Run the dictionary attack: aircrack-ng -w rockyou.txt -b <BSSID> handshake.cap. Step 5: The tool tries every password in the wordlist against the captured handshake using the PMK and PTK key derivation process. Step 6: If the correct password is found, it will be printed on the screen. Step 7: You can now use this password to decrypt previously captured traffic or connect to the network (if authorized). Step 8: If no match is found, you may need to expand your wordlist or try a brute-force or rule-based attack using hashcat. Step 9: This attack is fully offline — no need to send packets. Step 10: Protect against this by using strong, complex WPA2 passwords not found in dictionaries.
Detection Method: Alert on sudden reconnections followed by unusual traffic
Solution: Use long, random WPA2/WPA3 passwords; apply rate limits; rotate keys regularly

Title: Brute-Force Attack
Scenario Description: Try every possible combination of characters until the correct WPA/WPA2 password is found from a captured handshake.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a valid WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake using tools like airodump-ng + aireplay-ng or just passive listening. Save it as handshake.cap. Step 2: Use pyrit -r handshake.cap -o handshake.hccapx or aircrack-ng converter to prepare the handshake for hashcat. Step 3: Open hashcat and select mode 22000 (WPA-PBKDF2). Example command: hashcat -m 22000 handshake.hccapx ?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d. This tries all 8-digit numerical passwords. You can replace ?d with ?a for all possible characters (letters, numbers, symbols). Step 4: The cracking process starts. It will try every possible combination of passwords. Step 5: Depending on your GPU/CPU, this can take hours to years. Step 6: If the actual password is weak or short, the attack will eventually find it. Step 7: If the password is long and complex, cracking may be impossible in a realistic timeframe. Step 8: Brute-force always works theoretically, but practically it’s limited by time and computing power. Step 9: Monitor GPU temp, fan speed, and system stability. Step 10: Use this only in labs or with written permission. Unauthorized use is illegal.
Detection Method: Detect large password guess attempts; hashcat leaves CPU/GPU logs and power usage spikes
Solution: Use complex WPA2/WPA3 passwords; enforce minimum pass length and complexity

Title: Rainbow Table Attack
Scenario Description: Uses massive precomputed tables of password hashes (rainbow tables) against captured WPA handshakes (limited to SSID).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a valid 4-way WPA handshake from a wireless network using airodump-ng and aireplay-ng. Save it as handshake.cap. Step 2: Convert the capture to a CoWPAtty compatible format. Use cowpatty -r handshake.cap -f /path/to/wordlist.txt -s <SSID> (SSID is required). Step 3: CoWPAtty checks the handshake against a precomputed list of hashes stored in rainbow tables. Step 4: If the SSID matches a known table (e.g., “linksys”, “NETGEAR”), the attack is extremely fast since all possible hashes are precomputed. Step 5: If your SSID is custom or unknown, rainbow tables won’t help unless they’re generated beforehand (which can take hours/days). Step 6: If a match is found, the WPA password is displayed. If not, use dictionary or brute-force methods. Step 7: Rainbow tables require a lot of storage (GBs or TBs). Keep them organized by SSID. Step 8: This attack is very fast but only effective if the SSID is common or known in advance. Step 9: Combine with known SSID capture tools for social engineering. Step 10: Protect yourself by using unique SSIDs not found in public rainbow table sets.
Impact: Rapid key cracking for weak/default SSIDs
Detection Method: Alert if handshake hash matches known rainbow DB; watch for abnormal SSID usage
Solution: Avoid default SSIDs; use custom SSID names and long WPA2 passphrases

Title: Mask Attack
Scenario Description: Hybrid between brute-force and dictionary — attacker guesses password based on known pattern (e.g., "John1995").
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a valid WPA/WPA2 handshake and save it as handshake.cap. Convert it to .hccapx if needed using aircrack-ng or pyrit. Step 2: Use Hashcat with a mask pattern instead of full brute-force. Example: if you know the password starts with “John” and ends with 4 digits, use: hashcat -m 22000 handshake.hccapx John?d?d?d?d. Step 3: This tries only combinations that match this format, drastically reducing total guesses. Step 4: You can combine uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols using ?u, ?l, ?d, ?s. Example: ?u?l?l?l?d?d?d?d. Step 5: Launch the attack. Hashcat will attempt to crack the password using your specific pattern. Step 6: This is faster and more efficient than full brute-force if you have partial knowledge of the password. Step 7: Adjust masks based on password policies or known leaks. Step 8: You can generate custom masks using maskprocessor to automate creation of likely password formats. Step 9: If no match is found, widen your mask or try a dictionary+mask hybrid. Step 10: Always conduct these attacks ethically in legal test labs or assessments.
Detection Method: Monitor common name+year pattern attempts in logs; alert on hashcat usage patterns
Solution: Enforce password complexity; use uncommon formats and avoid user-named passwords
Tags: Mask Attack, Hashcat, WPA Pattern Guessing

Title: Hybrid Attack
Scenario Description: Combines a base wordlist with rules to mutate entries (e.g., adding numbers/symbols) to crack complex WPA passwords.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a WPA/WPA2 4-way handshake and convert it to .hccapx format using pyrit or aircrack-ng. Step 2: Download or create a dictionary of common passwords (e.g., rockyou.txt). Step 3: Use hashcat with a ruleset like best64.rule, which contains common mutation patterns (like appending “123”, capitalizing first letters, adding special characters). Example command: hashcat -m 22000 -r rules/best64.rule handshake.hccapx rockyou.txt. Step 4: Hashcat now combines each word from the dictionary with mutations: e.g., admin → Admin123!, admin@2023, etc. Step 5: This drastically increases the chance of cracking passwords that are not in the dictionary but follow common human patterns. Step 6: Monitor cracking progress and review matches if any are found. Step 7: Adjust rules or combine multiple rulesets if needed (-r rules1.rule -r rules2.rule). Step 8: Use custom rule files if you know password patterns specific to your target (e.g., company name + year). Step 9: Hybrid attacks are much more efficient than brute force and more realistic than pure dictionary. Step 10: Use responsibly in lab or audit environments. Never perform unauthorized attacks.
Impact: Effective WPA cracking for human-style passwords
Detection Method: Detect hashcat usage by GPU logs or system monitoring tools; alert on hybrid-mode operations
Solution: Enforce password managers or randomly generated passphrases; disallow name+number formats in Wi-Fi credentials

Title: GPU Cracking
Scenario Description: Uses the parallel power of modern GPUs to speed up password cracking by orders of magnitude compared to CPUs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you have a GPU with sufficient VRAM (4GB+) and install appropriate drivers (NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit or AMD ROCm). Step 2: Capture a WPA handshake and convert it to .hccapx using pyrit or aircrack-ng. Step 3: Install hashcat and verify GPU detection with hashcat -I. Step 4: Prepare a dictionary or use brute-force/mask/hybrid options. Example: hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 -w 3 handshake.hccapx rockyou.txt (-w 3 sets workload profile). Step 5: Hashcat will now use GPU threads to test millions of passwords per second. You’ll see live speed stats like H/s (hashes per second).
