Title: Insider Installs Software Keylogger
Scenario Description: A malicious insider physically installs a keylogger software on a colleague’s unattended system.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Insider gains brief access to target's PC.Step 2: Plugs in USB with Refog Keylogger.Step 3: Runs the installer silently (can take 5 seconds).Step 4: Keylogger hides and starts recording.Step 5: Data is sent to cloud or local log file.
Impact: Insider threat, log of confidential info
Detection Method: Monitor USB activity, screen lock policy
Solution: Auto-lock PCs, USB restriction

Title: Android App with Keylogger Permissions
Scenario Description: A malicious Android app secretly includes permission to log everything typed on the phone.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Modify an existing Android APK (e.g., calculator).Step 2: Insert keylogging module with permission (READ_INPUT_STATE).Step 3: Repackage and sign APK.Step 4: Share via forums or app mirrors.Step 5: Victim installs and unknowingly enables keylogger.
MITRE Technique: T1475 – Deliver via Mobile App Store
Detection Method: Android app permission analysis
Solution: Block sideloading, use official stores

Title: Chrome Extension with Keylogger
Scenario Description: A Chrome browser extension appears legitimate but logs everything typed into browser forms.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake productivity extension (e.g., “AutoTyper”).Step 2: Add JS code that captures keystrokes in input fields.Step 3: Publish on Chrome Web Store or share CRX.Step 4: Victim installs the extension.Step 5: Every typed form input is sent to attacker’s server.
Detection Method: Browser extension review, extension manager
Solution: Audit installed extensions

Title: School PC Shared Drive Dropper
Scenario Description: Keylogger file is placed in a shared drive labeled as a useful tool in school labs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a keylogger EXE and name it “Math Formulas Tool”.Step 2: Place it in school’s shared drive.Step 3: Wait for curious students to run it.Step 4: Once run, keylogger hides and records inputs.Step 5: Attacker checks logs later from same shared drive.
Detection Method: Network share monitoring, folder protection
Solution: Educate students, scan shared drives

Title: Keylogger via QR Code Download
Scenario Description: A QR code leads to a keylogger APK or EXE download when scanned by a user.
Tools Used: QR Code Generator, Keylogger file host
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a QR code linking to malicious file.Step 2: Print and label it as “Free Wi-Fi” or “Get Notes”.Step 3: Place it in cafes, classrooms, or notice boards.Step 4: Victim scans and downloads file.Step 5: If opened, keylogger installs silently.
Detection Method: QR code scanning app alerts
Solution: Don’t trust public QR codes

Title: Fake Windows Update via USB
Scenario Description: A USB drive pretends to install Windows updates but actually drops a keylogger in the background.
Tools Used: Batch Script, USB Stick, NirCmd, Keylogger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a batch file that shows a fake update window using NirCmd.Step 2: Include keylogger installer in same USB.Step 3: Name the USB “Windows Update Tool”.Step 4: Plug it into target system and run script.Step 5: Fake update runs while keylogger installs.
Detection Method: Endpoint detection, autorun blocking
Solution: Block unknown USBs, disable autorun

Title: Bootable USB with Auto-Installing Keylogger
Scenario Description: A USB boot drive installs a keylogger into the system during boot process.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Rufus to create bootable USB with Windows PE.Step 2: Add auto-start keylogger EXE in startup folder.Step 3: Plug USB, reboot system into USB OS.Step 4: Keylogger installs silently on internal hard drive.Step 5: Remove USB and restart normally – keylogger stays active.
Detection Method: BIOS boot order monitoring
Solution: Disable USB boot, BIOS password

Title: Chrome DevTools Keylogger Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker with brief access injects keylogger script into browser’s DevTools console.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open Chrome on target PC.Step 2: Press F12 to open DevTools and go to Console.Step 3: Paste custom JS code that records keystrokes.Step 4: Code runs as long as tab remains open.Step 5: Keystrokes are captured in real time and sent to external server.
Detection Method: Console activity logs
Solution: Lock DevTools access, restrict browser use

Title: Bluetooth Keylogger Device in Keyboard
Scenario Description: A Bluetooth keylogger device is secretly embedded inside a wireless keyboard.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Purchase a cheap wireless keyboard.Step 2: Open and embed a tiny Bluetooth keylogger.Step 3: Reassemble and use as regular keyboard.Step 4: It silently logs all keystrokes.Step 5: Attacker connects via Bluetooth to download logs.
Detection Method: Physical inspection, secure hardware
Solution: Buy from trusted vendors, tamper-proof seal

Title: HTML Login Page Clone with JS Logger
Scenario Description: Fake login page is shared on chat apps and logs user input using hidden JS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a login page (e.g., Facebook).Step 2: Add JavaScript to capture typed usernames/passwords.Step 3: Host on free domain (e.g., 000webhost).Step 4: Share shortened link via WhatsApp or Telegram.Step 5: Users type credentials which are logged and sent to attacker.
Detection Method: Phishing detection, link scanners
Solution: Use 2FA, hover to verify links

Title: Remote Desktop Keylogger Script
Scenario Description: Once remote access is gained (via weak credentials), attacker installs keylogger silently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use default or leaked RDP credentials to log into target system.Step 2: Transfer and run keylogger EXE remotely.Step 3: Hide the application from task manager.Step 4: Set it to auto-start with system.Step 5: Receive logs over email or cloud dashboard.
Detection Method: RDP logs, anomaly detection
Solution: Enforce strong passwords, use VPN

Title: Malicious Browser Bookmarklet
Scenario Description: A user is tricked into dragging a malicious bookmarklet into their browser which logs keystrokes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a JS bookmarklet to log keystrokes.Step 2: Make it look like a utility (e.g., “Dark Mode”).Step 3: Post on social media or blogs.Step 4: Victim drags it to bookmarks and clicks it.Step 5: Keylogger activates and logs inputs on every page.
Detection Method: Script scanning, browser tools
Solution: Avoid unknown browser tools

Title: Modified School Project File
Scenario Description: A keylogger is attached to a school project file shared among students.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare an EXE keylogger.Step 2: Bind it with a school project (e.g., PPT or DOC).Step 3: Upload to class drive with attractive name.Step 4: Classmate downloads and opens it.Step 5: Keylogger installs silently and sends logs.
Detection Method: Monitor downloads in shared folders
Solution: Educate students on file safety

Title: Fake Live Chat Support Keylogger
Scenario Description: A fake live chat support window is embedded in a site that secretly logs typed inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake chat support pop-up (HTML+CSS).Step 2: Embed JavaScript to log inputs.Step 3: Host on phishing site.Step 4: Drive traffic via email or social media.Step 5: When users type, data is sent to attacker.
Detection Method: Monitor web scripts, disable autofill
Solution: Verify URLs before typing anything

Title: Keyboard Firmware Tampering
Scenario Description: A modified keyboard with reprogrammed firmware silently records all key inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open mechanical keyboard.Step 2: Replace microcontroller firmware with keylogger code.Step 3: Reassemble and gift/sell the keyboard.Step 4: Once plugged in, it begins logging silently.Step 5: Attacker retrieves data via internal storage.
Detection Method: Hardware audits, integrity checks
Solution: Use only sealed hardware

Title: Keylogger via Remote PDF Reader
Scenario Description: A malicious PDF reader software installs a keylogger under the guise of a feature-rich tool.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone interface of Foxit or Adobe Reader.Step 2: Embed keylogger in the background process.Step 3: Share via forums or fake review sites.Step 4: User installs it as alternative reader.Step 5: Reader works, but logs all typed text system-wide.
Detection Method: Check process tree, verify vendors
Solution: Don’t use untrusted apps

Title: Keylogger via Fake Antivirus Pop-up
Scenario Description: A fake antivirus alert tells users to download a "fix" which is a keylogger.
Tools Used: Fake AV UI Generator, Keylogger EXE
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a pop-up image mimicking antivirus alert.Step 2: Add download link to “SecurityFixTool.exe”.Step 3: Show popup on shady websites or ads.Step 4: User clicks and installs it.Step 5: Keylogger starts silently in background.
Detection Method: Popup blocker, file reputation check
Solution: Never trust random alerts

Title: Social Media Game Link Trap
Scenario Description: A fun-looking online game shared on social media installs a browser-based keylogger in the background.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake game page (e.g., “Guess Your Future”).Step 2: Embed keylogger JavaScript in the page.Step 3: Share shortened link via Instagram or WhatsApp.Step 4: Victim plays the game and types data.Step 5: Keystrokes are captured silently.
Detection Method: Script behavior alerts
Solution: Avoid unknown games/links

Title: Fake Keyboard Driver via CD
Scenario Description: A fake driver CD for a new keyboard includes a keylogger that installs during the setup.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a CD setup named “Install_Drivers.exe” with keylogger.Step 2: Include CD in the keyboard packaging.Step 3: Victim installs driver from CD.Step 4: Keylogger installs alongside driver.Step 5: Logs are stored locally or sent to email.
MITRE Technique: T1543 – Create or Modify System Process
Detection Method: Scan new drivers before install
Solution: Use OS-certified drivers only

Title: QR Code for Free Wi-Fi Trap
Scenario Description: A public QR code promises free Wi-Fi but installs a keylogger on the phone once scanned.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate QR code pointing to a keylogger APK.Step 2: Label it “Free Wi-Fi, Scan Here!”.Step 3: Stick it in coffee shops, stations, or events.Step 4: Victim scans and downloads APK.Step 5: Keylogger records keystrokes silently.
Detection Method: QR scanning monitoring, app source checking
Solution: Never install from QR scans

Title: Office Presentation File Drop
Scenario Description: An attacker embeds a macro keylogger inside a PowerPoint shared for a meeting.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a presentation called “Quarterly_Plan.pptm”.Step 2: Insert VBA macro that executes a keylogger EXE.Step 3: Upload to shared drive or email.Step 4: Recipient opens and clicks “Enable Content”.Step 5: Keylogger installs and runs.
Detection Method: Monitor macros, disable by default
Solution: Disable macros, use protected view

Title: Free Webcam Tool from Forum
Scenario Description: A webcam-enhancing app posted in a photography forum secretly logs all system input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a real webcam enhancement tool.Step 2: Bind it with a keylogger EXE.Step 3: Post in a forum with screenshots and fake reviews.Step 4: Victim installs it.Step 5: Keylogger runs in background.
Detection Method: Analyze unknown executables
Solution: Avoid tools from unknown users

Title: Typing Speed Game Trap
Scenario Description: A typing test game records and stores all user keystrokes, including system inputs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a typing speed test site.Step 2: Add JavaScript to capture all inputs.Step 3: Advertise it as “Improve Typing Speed!”.Step 4: User types and plays the game.Step 5: Inputs (including personal data) are logged.
Detection Method: Script behavior monitoring
Solution: Avoid typing unknown sites

Title: Free Software License Generator
Scenario Description: A cracked license generator tool downloaded from torrent sites installs a keylogger.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake keygen tool.Step 2: Bundle keylogger with it.Step 3: Upload to torrent or warez site.Step 4: Victim downloads and runs it.Step 5: Keylogger installs silently.
Detection Method: Block pirated content, sandbox
Solution: Avoid illegal software

Title: Discord Bot Link Trap
Scenario Description: A Discord bot shares a fun-looking game/tool that installs a keylogger.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a Discord bot that shares files on command.Step 2: Upload “MiniGame.exe” with keylogger inside.Step 3: Send bot to invite links and share file.Step 4: User runs the file.Step 5: Keylogger runs in background.
Detection Method: Restrict bot permissions, monitor file links
Solution: Don’t run shared files blindly

Title: Polymorphic Keylogger Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker hides a keylogger that changes its code every time it runs to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download Veil-Evasion from GitHub on your computer. Step 2: Use Veil to create a payload that includes a keylogger. Step 3: Configure the payload to be polymorphic (auto-changing). Step 4: Send the payload to the victim as an email attachment (like “Invoice.pdf.exe”). Step 5: Ask victim to open the file. Step 6: Keylogger installs silently and starts capturing keystrokes. Step 7: Each time it runs, its code looks different, avoiding antivirus detection.
Detection Method: Heuristic or behavioral antivirus
Solution: Use AI-based AV, restrict script execution

Title: Metamorphic Ransomware Obfuscation
Scenario Description: Ransomware rewrites its code after every infection, making it unrecognizable.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a tool like G2Metamorph to write ransomware code that changes every time. Step 2: Obfuscate the ransomware using PyArmor. Step 3: Test it in a safe virtual machine environment. Step 4: Spread via USB, email, or cloud sharing link. Step 5: Once opened, it encrypts user files. Step 6: It rewrites its own code to look different. Step 7: It displays ransom message and hides traces.
Detection Method: Endpoint logging, sandboxing
Solution: Backup strategy, behavioral AV

Title: Metamorphic Worm Spread via Network Shares
Scenario Description: Self-changing malware spreads across file shares on local network.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a worm that replicates itself to shared folders. Step 2: Add metamorphic routines so the worm changes code on each copy. Step 3: Spread worm via shared drives (e.g., \Shared\Public). Step 4: Once a user accesses the file, it executes silently. Step 5: Infects host, re-mutates, and continues spread. Step 6: Attempts credential theft or remote access. Step 7: Avoids signature detection due to code mutation.
Detection Method: Lateral movement detection
Solution: Isolate infected nodes, disable open shares

Title: Polymorphic PDF Dropper
Scenario Description: A booby-trapped PDF contains auto-executing polymorphic malware on open.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a fake invoice or resume PDF. Step 2: Inject hidden polymorphic code using EvilPDF. Step 3: Obfuscate the binary payload using Hyperion. Step 4: Email the file with subject: “Payment Overdue - Action Needed”. Step 5: When opened, the PDF executes script silently in the background. Step 6: The payload changes format each time it's triggered. Step 7: Malware installs spyware/keylogger silently.
Detection Method: Sandbox PDF analysis
Solution: Block scriptable PDFs, content filtering

Title: Polymorphic Crypto Miner in Game Mods
Scenario Description: A game mod includes polymorphic code that secretly mines cryptocurrency.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Modify a game mod installer to include XMRig crypto miner. Step 2: Use NodeCrypter to polymorphically encrypt the mining script. Step 3: Rename script as "performance_boost.js" and pack with mod. Step 4: Share mod on gaming forums. Step 5: Victim installs mod; miner starts in background. Step 6: Miner auto-morphs on every reboot. Step 7: Uses system CPU/GPU without user’s knowledge.
Detection Method: Resource usage spike
Solution: Avoid unverified mods, monitor usage

Title: USB-Based Metamorphic Spyware
Scenario Description: A spyware morphs its code and logs microphone input when USB is plugged.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a Python script that records mic input and logs to hidden file. Step 2: Add metamorphic code that rewrites itself at intervals. Step 3: Convert script to .exe and store in USB drive with AutoRun. Step 4: Trick target into plugging in USB (e.g., labeled “Confidential”). Step 5: Malware activates and records audio. Step 6: Code changes on its own periodically. Step 7: Logs are hidden in system folders.
Detection Method: Mic activity detection, USB control
Solution: Limit USB access, disable AutoRun

Title: Metamorphic Fileless RAT via PowerShell
Scenario Description: Fileless Remote Access Tool that uses PowerShell & rewrites itself in memory to avoid disk detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Nishang toolkit to create PowerShell RAT payload. Step 2: Obfuscate it using multi-layer encoding. Step 3: Deliver via malicious link or email. Step 4: When clicked, payload loads into memory only (fileless). Step 5: Executes commands remotely and re-generates in memory periodically. Step 6: No trace left on disk. Step 7: Changes command structure every few hours.
Detection Method: Command behavior monitoring
Solution: Restrict PowerShell use, script signing

Title: Polymorphic Fake Driver Installer
Scenario Description: Attacker distributes a fake device driver update with polymorphic rootkit.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake driver update utility. Step 2: Use Shellter to inject polymorphic rootkit into utility. Step 3: Host file on cloned hardware vendor site. Step 4: User downloads and installs update thinking it’s legit. Step 5: Rootkit installs and hides itself at kernel level. Step 6: Code changes structure after every system boot. Step 7: Enables attacker remote access or keylogging.
Detection Method: Kernel behavior detection
Solution: Use signed drivers only

Title: Metamorphic Keylogger via Screensaver
Scenario Description: A screensaver file (.scr) contains a keylogger that changes its form and logs keystrokes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a simple Python keylogger script. Step 2: Add code for metamorphic change each launch. Step 3: Convert to .exe and rename as screensaver.scr. Step 4: Offer it online as “Free Matrix Screensaver”. Step 5: Victim installs it and sets as default screensaver. Step 6: Every time screensaver activates, keylogger runs. Step 7: Code changes pattern with each execution.
Detection Method: Behavioral AV, anomaly detection
Solution: Avoid unverified scr files

Title: AI-Generated Metamorphic Email Worm
Scenario Description: AI dynamically generates email content and payloads that mutate to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use AI to generate believable email content for targets (e.g., invoices, HR docs). Step 2: Attach metamorphic payload that rewrites itself on send. Step 3: Script mass-sends the worm to all contacts of each victim. Step 4: Victim opens email, runs attachment. Step 5: Malware infects system and auto-emails others. Step 6: With each hop, code is slightly different. Step 7: Keeps spreading across organizations.
Detection Method: Email sandboxing, phishing filters
Solution: Disable attachments, educate users

Title: Metamorphic Excel Malware with Auto-Update
Scenario Description: An Excel macro auto-updates itself by fetching modified scripts from the internet.
Tools Used: Excel, AutoMacro Tool, GitHub raw links
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write an Excel macro that calls a script from a GitHub raw URL. Step 2: Make script self-modifying and metamorphic. Step 3: Insert macro into workbook with fake financial data. Step 4: Email file to targets as “Q4 Budget.xlsx”. Step 5: Victim enables macros; macro fetches and runs script. Step 6: Script updates itself with newer variants. Step 7: Continues evolving while stealing data.
Detection Method: Network call monitoring
Solution: Block macro downloads

Title: Polymorphic Spyware via Fake Zoom Update
Scenario Description: Fake Zoom update installs spyware that constantly changes code to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone Zoom update interface. Step 2: Bundle polymorphic spyware with installer. Step 3: Share link as “Urgent Zoom Security Update”. Step 4: User installs it; spyware launches silently. Step 5: Records webcam/microphone without user consent. Step 6: Rewrites parts of code every day. Step 7: Avoids signature detection through mutation.
Detection Method: Webcam mic access logs
Solution: Validate updates via official site

Title: Metamorphic Malware in Game Trainer Tools
Scenario Description: Game cheat tools secretly embed malware that mutates and monitors user activity.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Modify an open-source cheat tool with backdoor payload. Step 2: Add metamorphic behavior so payload changes each run. Step 3: Share on gaming cheat forums. Step 4: User installs and runs cheat tool. Step 5: Tool injects malware into memory. Step 6: Monitors keystrokes and active apps. Step 7: Self-modifies to avoid AV detection.
Detection Method: Gamer behavior logs, AV
Solution: Avoid third-party cheats

Title: Metamorphic Android Banking Trojan
Scenario Description: Trojan changes its code structure on each install to bypass Play Store security.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Take open-source banking trojan APK. Step 2: Add metamorphic shell that changes class names, encryption, structure. Step 3: Rebuild APK using ApkTool. Step 4: Distribute via SMS or third-party stores. Step 5: Victim installs app; trojan activates, overlays fake login screens. Step 6: Captures login credentials. Step 7: On every new install, code differs significantly.
Detection Method: Mobile behavior analysis
Solution: Install only from official app stores

Title: AI-Driven Mutation Engine for Phishing Payloads
Scenario Description: AI changes malware structure per user target based on profile data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use AI tool to profile user from social media data. Step 2: AI generates personalized phishing message with unique malware code. Step 3: Attach polymorphic executable that changes variables, logic, encryption. Step 4: Email target pretending to be from boss/client. Step 5: User runs the attachment. Step 6: Malware activates, logs data, modifies system. Step 7: Next version changes again based on AI learning.
Detection Method: AI email flagging, zero-trust exec file
Solution: AI pattern detection & profiling limits

Title: Metamorphic Reverse Shell via PDF CV
Scenario Description: Reverse shell is launched when a booby-trapped CV PDF is opened, with changing shell code.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate reverse shell payload with Metasploit. Step 2: Encode shellcode with polymorphic mutation (e.g., XOR, encoding layers). Step 3: Embed into PDF using EvilPDF. Step 4: Name file “Freshers_Resume.pdf” and email to HR departments. Step 5: When opened, shell connects back to attacker. Step 6: Payload re-encodes itself for each email sent. Step 7: Bypasses detection due to structural changes.
Detection Method: PDF behavior scanning
Solution: Block PDF auto-execution

Title: Metamorphic Malware-as-a-Service (MaaS) Toolkit
Scenario Description: Malware sold online that changes payload every download to evade detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker signs up for MaaS and customizes malware function (e.g., keylogger, stealer). Step 2: Each build auto-generates unique code using metamorphic engine. Step 3: Distributes to targets via links, email, or bundling. Step 4: Every victim gets a different binary. Step 5: Payload installs silently, reports data to attacker. Step 6: Mutation prevents signature sharing. Step 7: Attacker remains anonymous using darknet tools.
Detection Method: Network beacon monitoring
Solution: Threat intel + behavioral AV

Title: Polymorphic Ad Injector in Browser Extension
Scenario Description: A malicious browser extension injects ads and changes code each session to avoid removal.
Tools Used: JavaScript Obfuscator, Chrome Extension Dev Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a browser extension that modifies webpages by injecting ads. Step 2: Add polymorphic JS code that changes variable/function names on each load. Step 3: Submit to unofficial plugin websites or link via popups. Step 4: User installs extension; ads appear on every site they visit. Step 5: Extension regenerates code daily to avoid blacklisting. Step 6: Ads redirect to scam or malware sites. Step 7: Extension resists easy removal.
Detection Method: Browser extension monitor
Solution: Allow extensions from known vendors only

Title: Metamorphic Macro Downloader in Word Document
Scenario Description: A Word doc contains a macro that mutates and downloads a payload on execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a macro in Word that launches a PowerShell script. Step 2: PowerShell connects to a website to download the malware. Step 3: Use a script generator that mutates the PowerShell commands every time. Step 4: Embed macro in a file named “Meeting_Agenda.docm”. Step 5: Email file to employees. Step 6: When opened, payload is downloaded and installed. Step 7: Macro regenerates new script structure for every document.
Detection Method: Disable macros or sandbox docs
Solution: Enforce macro policies

Title: Polymorphic Bootloader Rootkit
Scenario Description: Rootkit hides in boot sector and changes its structure on each reboot.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a bootkit builder to create a malicious bootloader. Step 2: Inject polymorphic code that modifies itself on reboot. Step 3: Replace original bootloader using USB/Live CD. Step 4: System boots from infected sector. Step 5: Rootkit hides malware and processes. Step 6: Code changes every boot cycle to evade disk signature scans. Step 7: Attacker maintains full hidden access.
Detection Method: Bootloader hash comparison
Solution: Use Secure Boot and full-disk encryption

Title: Metamorphic Ransomware with Time Bomb
Scenario Description: Ransomware stays dormant, mutates daily, then triggers encryption on a set date.
Tools Used: Time Trigger Script, PyArmor, AES Payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create ransomware that encrypts files using AES. Step 2: Add a time-check script (e.g., trigger on 15th of the month). Step 3: Script mutates its structure daily using PyArmor. Step 4: Distribute via USB or phishing email. Step 5: Ransomware hides and remains idle. Step 6: On trigger date, it activates and encrypts files. Step 7: Leaves ransom note demanding crypto payment.
Detection Method: Monitor file activity anomalies
Solution: Backup & rollback systems

Title: Polymorphic ICO File Exploit
Scenario Description: A malicious icon (.ico) file is crafted to exploit viewer software with changing shellcode.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an .ico file embedded with shellcode (e.g., buffer overflow). Step 2: Encrypt and polymorphically obfuscate the shellcode. Step 3: Attach to shortcut files or display on websites. Step 4: When user hovers over file or opens folder, shellcode executes. Step 5: Malware installs silently. Step 6: Each .ico version has different structure to avoid detection. Step 7: Exploits Windows Explorer preview vulnerabilities.
Detection Method: Patch Explorer preview bugs
Solution: Disable icon preview from unknown files

Title: Metamorphic Supply Chain Backdoor
Scenario Description: Malware is inserted into software source code and mutates before compilation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to open-source or company dev repo. Step 2: Add a backdoor script with metamorphic design (e.g., change logic per build). Step 3: Push changes upstream unnoticed. Step 4: When software is built, the backdoor is compiled in with new shape each time. Step 5: Software is used by public; all versions have stealth access code. Step 6: AV fails to detect since every version differs. Step 7: Exploits trust in legitimate software.
Vulnerability: No code review or CI monitoring
Detection Method: Monitor code changes in builds
Solution: Implement build-time validation

Title: Polymorphic Java Applet Attack
Scenario Description: Java applet embedded in webpage auto-executes and changes bytecode on every visitor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a malicious Java applet that runs code to download payload. Step 2: Use obfuscation to change class/method names each page load. Step 3: Embed applet in a fake support site. Step 4: Share via email, QR code, or SMS. Step 5: When user visits, applet executes silently. Step 6: Malware downloads and installs. Step 7: Next visitor sees a completely different version.
Detection Method: Block Java in browsers
Solution: Disable Java Applets site-wide

Title: Living-off-the-Land Binaries (LOLBins) Abuse
Scenario Description: Malware abuses trusted Windows tools (like mshta.exe) to download and run malicious code without dropping files
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a link using mshta.exe that loads malicious HTML code from internet Step 2: Sends this link via email or chat to victim Step 3: Victim clicks the link and unknowingly runs HTML Application (HTA) code in memory Step 4: HTA script downloads malware using certutil.exe and runs it directly in memory Step 5: Attacker gains access to the system remotely
Detection Method: Monitor use of mshta, certutil, unusual child processes
Solution: Block mshta, restrict internet execution

Title: Registry-based Fileless Payload
Scenario Description: Payload is embedded and executed directly from Windows registry without saving any files on disk
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access through phishing or social engineering Step 2: Injects malicious script into a registry key (e.g., Run key) Step 3: Adds an autorun command pointing to registry to load payload in memory Step 4: Upon reboot, the malware executes from registry in memory Step 5: Attacker controls the system without leaving a file footprint
Detection Method: Monitor registry changes, check autorun locations
Solution: Disable unnecessary autoruns, use Registry Auditing

Title: Fileless Attack via Exploit Kit in Browser
Scenario Description: Drive-by browser exploit leads to malware being directly injected in memory using browser vulnerabilities
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim visits a compromised or malicious website Step 2: Hidden exploit kit scans browser and OS for known vulnerabilities Step 3: If vulnerable, JavaScript exploits browser to run shellcode in memory Step 4: Malware code is executed directly without downloading a file Step 5: Attacker gains remote access or data exfiltration
Detection Method: Use browser exploit detection, sandboxing
Solution: Keep browser updated, use ad blockers and EDR

Title: Office Macro to PowerShell Payload
Scenario Description: Word macro opens PowerShell that runs malware directly in memory
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word document with a hidden macro Step 2: Sends it as a "job offer" to a user via email Step 3: Victim opens and enables macro Step 4: Macro launches PowerShell invisibly Step 5: PowerShell fetches and executes memory-only malware from a website
Detection Method: Monitor macro usage, PowerShell logs
Solution: Block macros via policy, use AV tools

Title: Windows Script Host (WSH) Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker uses .vbs script to run malware via Windows built-in script host
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim receives a .vbs attachment in an email titled "Salary Info" Step 2: Victim double-clicks the script Step 3: Script launches WSH and runs PowerShell commands Step 4: Malware code is injected directly into memory Step 5: Malware connects to attacker's server
Detection Method: Script monitoring, WSH usage logs
Solution: Block .vbs execution, email scanning

Title: Malicious Shortcut File (LNK)
Scenario Description: Attacker sends .lnk file that runs hidden PowerShell commands
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim gets a USB or email with "Resume.lnk" Step 2: Clicks the shortcut, which runs hidden command Step 3: Shortcut launches PowerShell silently Step 4: PowerShell runs code in memory to download malware Step 5: No file is dropped, malware stays in RAM

Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds macro to open decoy document.Step 2: Macro also downloads and installs njRAT.Step 3: Victim thinks file is safe since it opens properly.Step 4: Meanwhile, RAT connects silently in background.Step 5: Attacker gains control of system remotely.
Detection Method: Monitor secondary processes triggered by Office
Solution: Block script-based background activity

Title: Macro-Initiated Printer Spool Exploit
Scenario Description: Macro exploits Print Spooler to escalate privileges on victim’s PC
Attack Steps: Step 1: Excel macro includes PrintNightmare exploit code.Step 2: User opens file and enables macro.Step 3: Macro exploits Print Spooler vulnerability.Step 4: Gains SYSTEM-level access.Step 5: Attacker installs rootkit or persistence tools.
Detection Method: Log privilege elevation, spooler access
Solution: Patch known vulnerabilities, disable print spooler

Title: Calendar Invite with Embedded Macro
Scenario Description: Macro document is embedded inside calendar invite as meeting notes
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends calendar invite with Word doc attached.Step 2: File appears as “Team Meeting Agenda”.Step 3: Victim opens doc, enables macro to see schedule.Step 4: Macro installs spyware and adds task to scheduler.Step 5: Attacker receives periodic screenshots and file logs.
Detection Method: Monitor auto-created scheduled tasks
Solution: Educate on macro risks in calendar attachments

Title: Resume PDF Shortcut to Word Macro
Scenario Description: A PDF resume contains hidden shortcut to launch macro Word doc
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds shortcut to macro-enabled Word file inside a PDF.Step 2: Victim opens PDF named “Candidate Resume”.Step 3: Clicks resume preview which launches Word doc.Step 4: Macro installs keylogger silently.Step 5: Attacker receives daily logs of victim typing.
Detection Method: Alert on Office launch from PDFs
Solution: Disable linked files in PDFs

Title: Macro Uses COM to Control Outlook
Scenario Description: Macro uses COM automation to control Outlook and spread itself
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds macro using Outlook COM interface.Step 2: On execution, macro creates and sends email copies to all contacts.Step 3: File spreads internally in the organization.Step 4: Victims receive emails appearing from a known contact.Step 5: Attack chain continues as more users open infected files.
Detection Method: Monitor unusual outbound emails from Office
Solution: Restrict COM object use in Office macros

Title: Macro Exfiltrates Environment Variables
Scenario Description: Macro sends system environment variables to attacker
Attack Steps: Step 1: Macro reads environment variables like USERNAME, COMPUTERNAME.Step 2: Collects info like OS version and user path.Step 3: Sends data via HTTP POST to attacker server.Step 4: Attacker uses data for targeted follow-up attacks.Step 5: No visible activity for victim.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound environment scanning
Solution: Use firewalls and alert on Office egress traffic

Title: Macro Locks Screen and Demands Payment
Scenario Description: Macro simulates ransomware behavior by locking screen with popup
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates macro that launches full-screen fake alert.Step 2: Appears as government or police warning.Step 3: Prevents user from using system unless “fee” paid.Step 4: Background process running keeps the screen up.Step 5: Victim may panic and pay attacker.
Detection Method: Screen overlay detection
Solution: Use Ctrl+Alt+Del to force exit, educate users

Title: Macro Disables Security Logs
Scenario Description: Macro clears event logs to hide further malicious activity
Attack Steps: Step 1: Macro runs PowerShell to clear Windows Event Logs.Step 2: Attacker installs malware post log deletion.Step 3: Defender or admin cannot trace what happened.Step 4: Logs are wiped silently without alerts.Step 5: Attacker hides persistence method or exfil path.
Detection Method: Alert on cleared logs, audit log loss
Solution: Use logging solutions with remote log backups

Title: Macro Hides Data in Image (Steganography)
Scenario Description: Macro uses steganography to hide exfiltrated data in image
Attack Steps: Step 1: Macro collects data files (e.g. .docx, .pdf).Step 2: Hides data inside image pixels (steganography).Step 3: Image is sent to attacker’s server.Step 4: Attacker decodes data using stego tool.Step 5: Victim notices nothing suspicious.
Detection Method: Monitor unusual image uploads
Solution: Detect steganography in outbound traffic

Title: Macro Logs Keystrokes in Temp File
Scenario Description: Macro records keystrokes into a temporary file and uploads it
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds keylogger code in Word macro.Step 2: Victim opens file and enables macro.Step 3: Every keypress is logged to a hidden temp file.Step 4: Macro periodically uploads this file to attacker's server.Step 5: Attacker extracts passwords and typed content.
Vulnerability: No visibility into temp file activity
Detection Method: Detect unusual file creation in temp folders
Solution: Monitor Office file system writes

Title: Macro Uses Excel Cell Data as Code
Scenario Description: Macro dynamically builds code from hidden cells and executes it
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hides base64-encoded commands in Excel cells.Step 2: Macro reads cells and decodes commands.Step 3: Runs them using PowerShell.Step 4: Commands include malware download and persistence setup.Step 5: Macro self-deletes afterward to avoid detection.
Detection Method: Scan cells for encoded strings + macro reads
Solution: Block formula-to-macro chain logic

Title: Trojanized Excel Template from Vendor
Attack Type: Supply Chain Attack via Office Docs
Scenario Description: A trusted vendor sends an Excel template that secretly contains a trojan to steal credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker infects a legitimate Excel template with a malicious macro. Step 2: The infected file is shared by a real vendor via email or cloud link. Step 3: User opens the Excel file assuming it's safe due to trust. Step 4: User enables "Enable Content" to view data, unknowingly triggering the trojan. Step 5: Trojan steals Windows credentials and sends them to an external server.
Detection Method: EDR, Office macro scan, outgoing traffic monitoring
Solution: Disable macros by default, vendor software verification, sandbox files
Tags: trojan, excel, credential theft, vendor, macro

Title: Malicious Word Add-In from Plugin Store
Scenario Description: A Word plugin downloaded from a fake plugin store is actually spyware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User searches for a Word Add-in for grammar checking. Step 2: Attacker creates a fake Add-in with malicious background scripts. Step 3: User installs the Add-in assuming it’s official. Step 4: The Add-in auto-runs with Word and logs keystrokes & clipboard data. Step 5: Data is sent to attacker’s server.
Detection Method: Plugin signature validation, firewall monitoring
Solution: Only install from Microsoft Store, use endpoint monitoring

Title: Compromised Office License Activator Tool
Scenario Description: User downloads a cracked Office license activator, which secretly installs a backdoor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User downloads a pirated Office activation tool to avoid license cost. Step 2: Tool appears to work but installs a Remote Access Trojan (RAT). Step 3: Attacker gets full access to system remotely. Step 4: Attacker browses files, steals credentials, installs more malware. Step 5: User sees no symptoms until data loss or breach is reported.
Detection Method: Anomalous remote access, unknown processes
Solution: Avoid pirated software, use legal tools, scan installers

Title: Supply Chain Attack via Compromised Office Update
Scenario Description: An attacker infiltrates a third-party distributor of Office updates, inserting malware into update packages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises vendor website offering Office customization tools. Step 2: Malware is inserted into legitimate-looking Office update package. Step 3: Organization IT downloads update assuming it’s safe. Step 4: Installer runs with elevated privileges, installs persistent malware. Step 5: Malware opens backdoor, steals files, and spreads laterally.
Detection Method: Package integrity check, sandbox testing
Solution: Validate checksum, download only from official vendors

Title: Email Template from Marketing Partner Laced with Spyware
Scenario Description: A shared Word template from a marketing agency is laced with a beaconing script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Marketing partner sends a Word template for joint campaign. Step 2: File has embedded script that beacons to external IP when opened. Step 3: Beacon allows attacker to confirm opening and fingerprint the system. Step 4: Further payloads are sent remotely if target matches interest. Step 5: Attacker uses data to stage further attacks or phishing.
Detection Method: IDS alert on external beacon, firewall logs
Solution: Only accept signed docs, scan all external files

Title: Infected Collaboration Add-in from GitHub
Scenario Description: A Word add-in cloned from GitHub contains malware injected into its config file.
Tools Used: GitHub Repo, VBA Macro, Reverse Shell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads a modified Word collaboration add-in to GitHub. Step 2: Team member clones it for office automation. Step 3: User runs installer; malicious config activates. Step 4: Establishes reverse shell to attacker. Step 5: Attacker has command-line access to system.
Detection Method: Code review, monitor shell activity
Solution: Vet open-source repos before use

Title: AutoCAD File Linked to Infected Office Macro
Scenario Description: AutoCAD file links to Word macro for support script that is malicious.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker shares AutoCAD project file with macro-linked DOC. Step 2: Engineer opens DWG and clicks link to DOC for spec notes. Step 3: Word macro activates and downloads script. Step 4: Malware installs silently via background process. Step 5: System is now infected.
Detection Method: Inspect interlinked files, macro alerts
Solution: Block cross-app links, scan DWG files

Title: Embedded EXE in Password-Protected Office Zip
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds malware inside a password-protected ZIP containing Office files.
Tools Used: ZIP File, Hidden EXE, Social Engineering
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker zips infected Word file + malware EXE. Step 2: Sends ZIP with password via email claiming confidentiality. Step 3: User unzips and opens Word doc. Step 4: Attacker’s guide urges user to open hidden .exe for “activation”. Step 5: Malware gets installed.
Detection Method: EDR, scan extracted files
Solution: Never run EXEs from zips, scan all

Title: Fake “Product Manual” with Encrypted Macro
Scenario Description: A fake PDF manual embedded in a DOC has an encrypted macro that unpacks malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates DOC mimicking user manual with PDF look. Step 2: Macro is hidden in encrypted VBA project. Step 3: User opens and allows content, triggering decryption. Step 4: Script unpacks and runs malware file. Step 5: User sees nothing unusual while data is being exfiltrated.
Detection Method: VBA project analysis, behavior detection
Solution: Disallow encrypted macros, monitor downloads

Title: Malware-Laced Office Plugin via Email Promotion
Scenario Description: Email campaign offers a “time-saving” plugin for Outlook – it contains spyware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends well-designed email promoting new Outlook plugin. Step 2: User downloads plugin from spoofed link. Step 3: Plugin integrates with Outlook and monitors inbox. Step 4: Sends every incoming/outgoing mail to attacker. Step 5: Attacker uses info for spear phishing.
Detection Method: Email anomaly detection
Solution: Only install plugins from MS store

Title: Compromised Shared OneDrive Office Doc
Scenario Description: A shared OneDrive file is replaced with a malware-laced version.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a collaborator’s OneDrive. Step 2: Replaces shared DOC with infected version. Step 3: Notification sent to all collaborators. Step 4: Users open infected file, enabling macro. Step 5: Malware activates on multiple systems at once.
Detection Method: Cloud file integrity, EDR alerts
Solution: Enable file versioning, enforce MFA

Title: Excel Sheet with AutoRun Registry Insertion
Scenario Description: Excel file modifies system registry to run malware on startup.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User receives Excel file disguised as financial report. Step 2: Enables macros to view content. Step 3: Macro adds a new entry in Windows registry to launch malware.exe on startup. Step 4: Malware launches silently whenever PC boots. Step 5: Attacker gets persistent access.
Detection Method: Monitor registry changes
Solution: Disable macros, restrict registry edits

Title: Fake “COVID-19 Guidelines” Office Doc
Scenario Description: COVID guideline doc shared via health department spoof installs spyware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends DOC claiming to be from health ministry. Step 2: User opens and enables macros. Step 3: Spyware installs silently, logging microphone/camera activity. Step 4: Sends recordings and keystrokes to attacker. Step 5: Attacker uses data for blackmail or further compromise.
Detection Method: Unusual mic/cam activity
Solution: Verify sources, disable macros

Title: Office Doc that Exploits Old Equation Editor
Scenario Description: DOC file uses an old Equation Editor exploit (CVE-2017-11882).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds exploit in an RTF file. Step 2: User opens in Office without updating. Step 3: Equation Editor is triggered, executing payload. Step 4: Malware gains code execution without macro. Step 5: System is infected silently.
Detection Method: Patch status, behavior monitoring
Solution: Always update Office software

Title: Language Pack Installer for Office with Embedded Malware
Scenario Description: User downloads fake Hindi language support tool that infects system.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates fake language pack site. Step 2: User installs to use Hindi in Word. Step 3: EXE runs, showing fake progress bar. Step 4: Downloads remote trojan silently. Step 5: Attacker gains full access.
Detection Method: EXE analysis, download monitor
Solution: Get tools only from Microsoft site

Title: Malicious Excel Add-In Auto-Installed by IT Intern
Scenario Description: An intern unknowingly distributes a malicious Add-in via shared network drive.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Intern downloads Excel Add-in for data analysis. Step 2: Add-in has hidden beacon script. Step 3: Intern shares tool via network drive for team. Step 4: Everyone loads it in Excel, triggering C2 beacon. Step 5: Attacker sees all infected systems and sends commands.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound DNS/HTTP traffic
Solution: Train staff, review internal tools

Title: Excel File with DDE Exploit to Auto-Run Script
Scenario Description: Excel uses DDE to auto-execute PowerShell script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Excel file contains DDE formula that auto-launches PowerShell. Step 2: User opens file; prompt appears briefly but is dismissed. Step 3: Script is run, downloading malware. Step 4: No macro involved; security software misses it. Step 5: Malware runs silently.
Detection Method: Block DDE behavior
Solution: Disable DDE entirely

Title: PowerPoint with Action-Triggered Payload
Scenario Description: Slides have shapes that, when clicked, trigger payload download.
Attack Steps: Step 1: PowerPoint has a shape labeled “View Graph.” Step 2: Clicking it executes shell command linked to malware download. Step 3: PowerShell script runs silently. Step 4: Installs spyware on user system. Step 5: Attacker gets access.
Detection Method: Monitor click-triggered scripts
Solution: Disable action buttons in unknown PPTs

Title: Office Template with Background Task Scheduler Injection
Scenario Description: Template modifies Task Scheduler to run malware hourly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User opens infected template with macro. Step 2: Macro runs schtasks command to schedule hidden job. Step 3: Task executes malware from hidden path. Step 4: Attacker maintains access even if cleaned once. Step 5: Malware runs on system restart.
Detection Method: Detect new scheduled jobs
Solution: Monitor scheduler changes

Title: Backdoored “Office Training Material”
Scenario Description: Training DOCX includes macro that installs a keylogger.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Training material is emailed to new employees. Step 2: When opened, macro silently runs. Step 3: Installs keylogger in background. Step 4: Captures keystrokes including passwords. Step 5: Sends data via FTP to attacker.
Detection Method: Monitor FTP connections
Solution: Scan internal training material

Title: Excel Template with Hidden Workbook Auto_Open Payload
Scenario Description: Template has a hidden workbook that triggers malware at open.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Template includes a hidden worksheet. Step 2: Auto_Open macro in hidden sheet triggers payload. Step 3: Downloads keylogger or beacon. Step 4: User sees no warning if macros allowed. Step 5: Infection spreads if shared.
Detection Method: Monitor hidden workbook actions
Solution: Audit macro code, use protected view

Title: PDF Embedded Inside Word with Malicious JS
Scenario Description: Word doc contains embedded PDF, which contains malicious JavaScript.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds a PDF into DOC file. Step 2: PDF runs JS on open if PDF reader is vulnerable. Step 3: JS exploits vulnerability to run shellcode. Step 4: Malware executes with user permissions. Step 5: No macro needed.
Detection Method: Monitor PDF reader activity
Solution: Update PDF software regularly

Title: Cloud Synced Infected Doc Replication
Scenario Description: OneDrive or Google Drive syncs infected DOC across all devices.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker places infected doc in shared folder. Step 2: File syncs to all team members automatically. Step 3: Users open file and allow macro. Step 4: Malware infects all devices in sync scope. Step 5: Attacker has broad access.
Detection Method: Monitor cloud sync changes
Solution: Limit shared folder access

Title: Office Add-in Installed via MSI from Compromised Vendor
Scenario Description: MSI package for Add-in installation is modified to include backdoor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker modifies Office Add-in MSI from 3rd-party vendor. Step 2: MSI still installs actual Add-in, so user trusts it. Step 3: Backdoor also installs and runs at startup. Step 4: Attacker monitors user and sends commands. Step 5: Continues operating undetected.
Detection Method: Verify MSI signatures
Solution: Only use signed vendor packages

Title: Compromised Doc with Base64 Encoded Payload
Scenario Description: A DOC file contains a macro that decodes a Base64 payload and executes it.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User opens a seemingly normal document. Step 2: Macro runs in background if "Enable Content" is clicked. Step 3: It contains a long Base64 string hidden in white font. Step 4: The string is decoded into a script. Step 5: The script executes malware silently.
Detection Method: Detect Base64 decoding in macros
Solution: Block macro execution & scan hidden text

Title: Word DOC that Drops Encrypted Ransomware Loader
Scenario Description: A Word doc with encrypted ransomware binary hidden inside image data.
Tools Used: Word Macro, Ransomware Payload, XOR Encoding
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds encrypted malware into image in DOC. Step 2: Macro reads image bytes, decrypts using XOR. Step 3: Writes decrypted payload to disk. Step 4: Executes it, launching ransomware. Step 5: Files get encrypted with ransom note.
Detection Method: Behavior-based ransomware detection
Solution: Block unknown macros & isolate infected machines

Title: Shared Excel File with Token Stealer
Scenario Description: Excel macro script targets stored browser tokens and sends to C2.
Tools Used: Excel VBA Macro, Chrome Token Reader
Attack Steps: Step 1: Excel file shared via shared drive. Step 2: Macro reads Chrome login data stored in user profile. Step 3: Extracted credentials are encoded and sent to attacker server. Step 4: User is unaware of breach. Step 5: Attacker gains access to user accounts.
Detection Method: Monitor unusual network POST activity
Solution: Restrict file access from Office apps

Title: Office Theme Pack with Scheduled Task Payload
Scenario Description: Office theme file auto-creates scheduled task to run malware daily.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User downloads stylish Office theme pack. Step 2: Setup script inside modifies Task Scheduler. Step 3: Downloads malware daily from hidden URL. Step 4: Malware runs silently during system idle hours. Step 5: System remains infected persistently.
Detection Method: Monitor for new scheduled tasks
Solution: Only use official Office themes

Title: PDF Invoice Embedded Inside DOC Triggers Downloader
Scenario Description: Embedded PDF in Word triggers silent script download in vulnerable reader.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Word document contains embedded PDF invoice. Step 2: When PDF is opened, it calls remote server to fetch additional content. Step 3: Vulnerable reader executes malicious JavaScript. Step 4: Malware is dropped into user temp folder. Step 5: Attacker gains control.
Detection Method: Monitor reader logs & PDF calls
Solution: Disable embedded PDFs in Office

Title: Word Template with Beaconing C2 Check
Scenario Description: DOC template silently checks if C2 server is online, acting as a beacon.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User opens shared Word template. Step 2: Macro executes HTTP GET to attacker’s server. Step 3: Attacker logs IP and OS fingerprint. Step 4: If target is valuable, malware is sent in second stage. Step 5: Victim doesn’t notice network call.
Detection Method: Detect silent outbound HTTP
Solution: Block Office macros from sending requests

Title: PowerPoint File That Hijacks Outlook Contact List
Scenario Description: PPT file with macro steals Outlook contact list for future phishing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim opens PPT for training presentation. Step 2: Macro connects to Outlook’s address book. Step 3: Extracts all contact emails. Step 4: Sends list to attacker-controlled email. Step 5: Contacts become phishing targets.
Detection Method: Monitor Office COM interactions
Solution: Block COM access from macros

Title: Word Doc with OneDrive Sync Manipulation
Scenario Description: Word doc modifies OneDrive synced folder with infected files.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Word macro navigates to synced folder. Step 2: Replaces shared file with infected version. Step 3: OneDrive syncs to all users. Step 4: Others open infected files. Step 5: Spread becomes automatic via cloud.
Detection Method: Monitor file change triggers
Solution: Isolate macros from sync folders

Title: Word File with QR Code Linking to Malware APK
Scenario Description: DOC file includes a QR code that installs Android malware if scanned.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker includes “Scan for Mobile Version” QR in doc. Step 2: User scans it with phone. Step 3: APK installs malware on Android. Step 4: Mobile device is infected. Step 5: Attacker gains access to mobile data.
Detection Method: Monitor mobile installs from docs
Solution: Educate users not to scan unknown QR

Title: DOC File With Encrypted ZIP Dropper via Macro
Scenario Description: Macro drops encrypted ZIP to disk, extracts malware, and deletes original.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Macro writes ZIP encoded in hex to disk. Step 2: Password is stored in macro. Step 3: Script extracts ZIP contents (malware). Step 4: Original files are deleted to hide tracks. Step 5: Malware installs persistently.
Detection Method: Monitor new ZIP extractions
Solution: Restrict macro write permissions

Title: Resume Attachment Phishing
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake job application with a malware-laced Word document pretending to be a resume.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake resume document with hidden malicious code. Step 2: They compose a job application email pretending to be a job seeker. Step 3: Email with attachment is sent to HR or company email. Step 4: Victim opens the document and enables "Macros" when prompted. Step 5: Malware is installed silently, giving attacker control.
Detection Method: Email filtering, EDR
Solution: Disable macros, train HR staff

Title: Fake Invoice Malware
Scenario Description: Hacker sends an invoice as an Excel file with embedded macro malware to finance employees.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a fake invoice with embedded malicious macro code. Step 2: Sends the Excel file via email pretending to be a vendor. Step 3: Victim downloads and opens the invoice. Step 4: Victim clicks "Enable Content". Step 5: Malware installs silently and connects to hacker’s server.
Detection Method: Sandbox, email scanning
Solution: Block macros, vendor verification

Title: Legal Threat PDF Malware
Scenario Description: Hacker sends a fake legal notice PDF that contains an exploit to infect the device.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a PDF with hidden code to exploit PDF reader flaws. Step 2: Email claims victim is being sued and must read the notice. Step 3: Victim downloads and opens the PDF. Step 4: Exploit runs, and malware silently installs. Step 5: Victim is unaware, and attacker gains access.
Detection Method: PDF scanning, IDS
Solution: Update software, educate users

Title: Delivery Receipt Malware
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake delivery failure notice with a zip attachment containing malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates a zip file with a disguised malware executable. Step 2: Sends an email pretending to be from a courier service. Step 3: Victim opens the zip and double-clicks the file inside. Step 4: The malware runs and installs silently. Step 5: Victim sees nothing suspicious, attacker gains control.
Detection Method: Antivirus alerts, email filters
Solution: Block executables in ZIP, warn users

Title: Bank Statement PDF Attack
Scenario Description: A fake bank email contains malware-laced PDF bank statement.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker crafts a PDF that looks like a bank statement. Step 2: Sends it claiming unusual transactions. Step 3: Victim opens PDF, which executes exploit. Step 4: Malware is downloaded automatically. Step 5: Banking info is stolen.
Detection Method: Network monitoring
Solution: Use secured PDF viewers

Title: Voice Mail Attachment Malware
Scenario Description: Hacker sends voicemail notification with a fake .wav attachment that’s actually a disguised executable.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Creates executable that looks like a .wav file. Step 2: Sends it via email claiming “Missed Voice Message”. Step 3: Victim opens it expecting audio. Step 4: Malware executes and installs remote access tool. Step 5: Attacker monitors user activity.
Detection Method: File extension checking
Solution: Disable exe attachments

Title: Fake Software License PDF
Scenario Description: Victim receives fake PDF invoice for software subscription renewal.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker builds fake Adobe invoice PDF. Step 2: Sends to IT/Finance staff. Step 3: Victim opens PDF and gets infected. Step 4: Malware encrypts files and demands ransom. Step 5: System becomes unusable.
Detection Method: Email filter, ransomware blocker
Solution: Patch software, train users

Title: Fake Internship Offer
Scenario Description: Students receive internship offer email with Word attachment containing malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts attractive internship letter with macro malware. Step 2: Sends from spoofed recruiter email. Step 3: Victim opens doc and enables macros. Step 4: InfoStealer malware runs and collects data. Step 5: Data is sent to attacker.
Detection Method: Email sandbox, spam filters
Solution: Warn students, disable macros

Title: Fake Purchase Order Attack
Scenario Description: Victim receives purchase order in Excel format that executes malware on open.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker builds Excel with malicious VBA script. Step 2: Email says urgent PO for supplier. Step 3: Victim opens file and enables macros. Step 4: Script runs command to download malware. Step 5: Attacker gains shell access.
Detection Method: Threat detection tool, audit trails
Solution: Macro policy enforcement

Title: IT Helpdesk Fake Ticket
Scenario Description: Hacker impersonates IT support and sends a fake help ticket with malware in Word file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates fake support doc with malware macro. Step 2: Sends email saying "Your ticket has been resolved". Step 3: Victim opens Word file and enables macros. Step 4: Remote Access Trojan is installed. Step 5: Attacker controls victim’s system.
Detection Method: Email gateway alerts
Solution: Internal email validation, disable macros

Title: Fake Delivery QR Receipt
Scenario Description: A fake courier email has a PDF with a QR code that leads to malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates PDF with malicious QR code. Step 2: Sends as “missed delivery notice.” Step 3: Victim scans QR code on phone. Step 4: Device is redirected to malware download. Step 5: Phone is infected without user knowing.
Detection Method: QR threat detection, sandboxing
Solution: Train users, disable URL redirects

Title: Holiday Bonus Spreadsheet
Scenario Description: Fake HR email offers a holiday bonus sheet with malware in Excel.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds spreadsheet with embedded backdoor. Step 2: Sends email promising bonuses. Step 3: Victim opens Excel and clicks "Enable Content". Step 4: Malware is installed silently. Step 5: Attacker gets persistent access.
Detection Method: Email filter, process monitor
Solution: Bonus policy education, macro controls

Title: Government Tax Refund Mail
Scenario Description: Hacker sends tax refund notice with infected PDF attachment.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates PDF simulating a tax refund. Step 2: Spoofs email as income tax dept. Step 3: Victim opens file expecting refund info. Step 4: Malware is executed via PDF exploit. Step 5: Victim’s system becomes accessible to attacker.
Detection Method: PDF filtering, anti-exploit tools
Solution: Verify govt comms, secure PDFs

Title: Fake Charity Drive Email
Scenario Description: Fake donation appeal with malware-laced attachment is sent by attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker writes email asking for donation for disaster victims. Step 2: Includes Word attachment with malicious macro. Step 3: Victim opens and clicks "Enable Editing." Step 4: InfoStealer collects personal files and sends them to attacker. Step 5: Victim suffers privacy breach.
Detection Method: Attachment inspection, AV logs
Solution: Verify charities, disable editing macros

Title: Free eBook Giveaway Scam
Scenario Description: Hacker pretends to offer free eBook via email with infected ZIP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker zips JavaScript malware inside eBook folder. Step 2: Email says “Download your free eBook!” Step 3: Victim extracts ZIP and opens JS file. Step 4: Malware downloads and installs silently. Step 5: Victim unknowingly infected.
Detection Method: Scan archive contents, JS filters
Solution: Educate on ZIP risks, disable scripts

Title: Account Suspension Warning
Scenario Description: Fake account suspension warning email includes malicious PDF.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates PDF pretending to be from Gmail. Step 2: Warns victim of "account suspension". Step 3: Victim opens PDF urgently. Step 4: PDF auto-runs exploit and installs malware. Step 5: Attacker gets access to credentials.
Detection Method: Email filtering, DLP tools
Solution: Don’t open files from unknown sources

Title: Government Job Application
Scenario Description: A malware-laden application form pretends to be from a govt recruitment site.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker makes an Excel form titled “Govt Job Application.” Step 2: Sends to job seekers with govt-like email address. Step 3: Victim opens and enables content. Step 4: Macro downloads and installs malware. Step 5: Attacker gains full access to victim PC.
Detection Method: Macro detection, phishing filters
Solution: Public awareness training

Title: Fake Project Collaboration Invite
Scenario Description: Victim receives a fake invitation to collaborate on a project with a PDF.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates a professional-looking invite in PDF. Step 2: Email claims to be from a known vendor. Step 3: Victim opens PDF to view details. Step 4: Hidden exploit executes silently. Step 5: Malware is installed for attacker access.
Detection Method: AV & sandboxing
Solution: Verify sender domain and file safety

Title: Legal Department Memo
Scenario Description: A supposed memo from legal dept contains macro-laced document.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Hacker creates Word doc labeled “Legal Memo - Urgent”. Step 2: Sends to staff from spoofed legal@company email. Step 3: Victim opens and enables content. Step 4: Macro runs a hidden command to download malware. Step 5: Attacker executes malicious payload remotely.
Detection Method: Command monitoring, email scanning
Solution: Block risky macros, verify source

Title: Expense Claim Document
Scenario Description: Hacker sends expense form containing malware to finance staff.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates Excel with fake expense entries. Step 2: Email sent from “employee@company.com”. Step 3: Victim opens file and enables macros. Step 4: RAT is deployed to track all activity. Step 5: Attacker can now view files, webcam, keystrokes.
Detection Method: Endpoint detection tools
