Attack Steps: Step 1: Use bit.ly to shorten a malicious URL (e.g., to a credential harvester).Step 2: Create a link preview by typing the URL in Teams chat.Step 3: Add a legitimate-looking text around it (e.g., "Please check the policy update.").Step 4: Teams will show the preview as coming from trusted source.Step 5: Victim clicks, and is redirected to a phishing site.Step 6: Simulate data capture from phishing form for training.
Detection Method: Monitor shortened URLs, enforce preview inspection
Solution: Disable preview, scan links before preview

Title: Slack Cookie Replay Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker uses exposed Slack session cookie to impersonate user and read messages without credentials
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Slack Desktop App, HTTP Proxy
Attack Steps: Step 1: Intercept Slack session cookie via MITM (in lab simulation with proxy).Step 2: Export the session cookie value (e.g., d cookie from app storage).Step 3: Use the cookie in a browser session via browser DevTools document.cookie injection.Step 4: Access Slack with victim’s session (no login required).Step 5: View private messages, download files silently.Step 6: Track activity logs for educational report.
Detection Method: Monitor new device sessions, cookie reuse
Solution: Use short-lived tokens, enable MFA

Title: Teams Fake Audio Message (Voice Deepfake)
Scenario Description: Attacker sends audio file via Teams impersonating CEO using AI voice cloning to request sensitive info
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use AI voice tool (e.g., ElevenLabs) to clone a known executive's voice.Step 2: Script a short message like “Please wire ₹50,000 to the attached account urgently.”Step 3: Send the MP3 via Teams chat using a spoofed name/profile pic.Step 4: Create urgency in message description: “Can’t take call. Just do this quickly.”Step 5: Victim listens and is convinced due to voice match.Step 6: Record response for simulation purpose.
Detection Method: Audio behavior monitoring, user validation alerts
Solution: Verify via secondary channel, anti-deepfake training

Title: Slack Phishing via File Upload Preview
Scenario Description: Attacker uploads malicious HTML files that auto-preview in Slack and simulate a login prompt
Tools Used: Slack, HTML File, Burp, Fake Login Template
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an HTML file that looks like a Slack login prompt.Step 2: Upload the file as Login_Issue_Notice.html in a shared channel.Step 3: Slack shows a preview, which tricks users to click.Step 4: File opens in browser and shows the fake login form.Step 5: Victim types credentials, which are captured.Step 6: Capture and log details for training simulation.
Detection Method: Monitor for HTML files and suspicious previews
Solution: Block HTML file types, alert on suspicious previews

Title: Microsoft Teams SSO Token Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attacker captures or replays Teams SSO token (e.g., from browser or memory) to impersonate a user
Attack Steps: Step 1: Simulate user login using SSO.Step 2: Capture SSO token stored in browser local storage or memory.Step 3: Use the token in a custom HTTP request to call Teams API endpoints (GET /me/messages).Step 4: Replay token from a new system to simulate session hijack.Step 5: Extract messages and simulate unauthorized actions.Step 6: Log actions taken and session logs.
Detection Method: Token age monitoring, anomaly-based access alerts
Solution: Invalidate token on logout, reduce token TTL

Title: Slack “App Mention” Scam Bot
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a bot that mentions users in channels with fake messages directing them to phishing links
Tools Used: Slack API, Slackbot Framework, URL Shortener
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a Slack bot using Slack’s App portal and enable chat:write and users:read scopes.Step 2: Configure the bot to scan public messages or member list.Step 3: The bot automatically posts messages mentioning users like:“@john You have a pending task. Visit here: short.url/task123”Step 4: The link redirects to a phishing or credential harvesting page.Step 5: Observe victim behavior (link clicks, form entries).Step 6: Log interaction for educational simulation.
Detection Method: Unusual bot messages, mention volume alerts
Solution: Restrict bot permissions, user training

Title: Teams Malware via Shared Calendar Invite
Scenario Description: Attacker sends Teams calendar invite with a malicious file disguised as agenda or presentation
Tools Used: Microsoft Teams, Outlook, ZIP File, MSFVenom
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a malicious payload like agenda.pdf.exe using MSFVenom and compress into ZIP to bypass filters.Step 2: Create a calendar invite via Teams or Outlook saying “Q3 Review – Mandatory.”Step 3: Attach ZIP file named Meeting_Resources.zip with payload.Step 4: In message, write “Please go through attached before meeting.”Step 5: Victim downloads and opens the payload, triggering simulation.Step 6: Log time, system response for analysis.
Detection Method: Scan calendar attachments, behavior analysis
Solution: Disable risky extensions in invites, educate users

Title: Slack Workspace Name Impersonation
Scenario Description: Attacker clones a workspace with lookalike name/logo to impersonate an internal workspace and invite victims
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a free Slack workspace and name it similar to a real company (e.g., Globex-Internal-Dev).Step 2: Use the same company logo and theme as the real workspace.Step 3: Invite victims by email saying “You’ve been added to Globex’s Dev channel.”Step 4: Once joined, attacker can send phishing messages disguised as internal tasks.Step 5: Victim replies, believing it’s the real Slack.Step 6: Collect responses, simulate social engineering success.
Detection Method: Monitor spoofed workspace invites
Solution: Verify domain-based join links, warn users

Title: Teams Emoji Reaction as Hidden Signal
Scenario Description: Attacker uses pre-defined emoji reactions on specific messages to communicate secret commands or exfil data in plain sight
Tools Used: Teams Client, Custom Emoji Legend, Shared Chat
Attack Steps: Step 1: Define a mapping of emojis to messages (e.g., ✅ = success, ❌ = fail, 🔁 = retry).Step 2: Infiltrate Teams channel with low-priv user or insider.Step 3: Add emoji reactions to messages that only attacker and insider understand.Step 4: Use this to signal events, share approval to proceed with tasks.Step 5: Repeat over time, allowing covert ops in plain sight.Step 6: Log interactions to simulate stealthy communication.
Detection Method: Analyze repetitive emoji usage patterns
Solution: User behavior monitoring, anomaly detection

Title: Slack Status Message Abuse for Phishing
Scenario Description: Attacker sets phishing links inside Slack “Status Message” seen by all users across workspace
Tools Used: Slack User Profile, Bit.ly, Fake Domain
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker joins a workspace (internal/external invite).Step 2: Change their Slack status to: “Urgent Update 👉 bit.ly/hr-policy”.Step 3: Slack displays this status to everyone viewing the user in messages or directory.Step 4: Curious users click the link, landing on phishing page.Step 5: Form asks for login to view document – credentials harvested.Step 6: Log user actions for training and discussion.
Detection Method: Monitor status messages with links
Solution: Block URLs in statuses, filter link previews

Title: Phishing Link to OAuth Token Stealer
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an email with a crafted link pretending to be a legitimate service (e.g., Google Drive), stealing OAuth tokens when the user clicks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup Evilginx2 on Kali Linux.Step 2: Configure a phishing template mimicking Google login.Step 3: Set up Ngrok or register a domain to make the phishing link accessible publicly.Step 4: Use Gophish to craft an HTML email template with a fake "Shared Google Doc" link.Step 5: Send the phishing email to the victim user.Step 6: Victim clicks the link and is redirected to a fake Google login.Step 7: Victim enters credentials and OAuth token is captured by Evilginx.Step 8: Attacker uses token to access Gmail, Drive, etc. without password.
Vulnerability: Lack of token validation and phishing awareness
Impact: Unauthorized access to personal/business cloud services
Detection Method: Unusual token-based logins from unexpected IPs
Solution: Enforce MFA, restrict token reuse, implement email security training

Title: Slack Message with Malicious Token Logger
Scenario Description: A disguised link is sent over Slack which points to a file that loads a JS-based token logger in the browser.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a JavaScript file that uses localStorage.getItem("token") to steal session tokens from web apps.Step 2: Upload JS file to Pastebin or similar service.Step 3: Shorten the URL using a link shortener (like bit.ly).Step 4: Compose a message in Slack like “Hey, check this urgent company notice.” and paste the shortened link.Step 5: Victim clicks link; the browser executes malicious script in the background.Step 6: The token is exfiltrated to attacker’s webhook server.Step 7: Attacker uses token to impersonate user in apps like Slack, GitHub, or Trello.
Impact: Account compromise inside internal team apps
Detection Method: Detection of browser token extraction scripts
Solution: Enable Slack content scanning, disallow untrusted links

Title: WhatsApp Link to Cloud Token Harvester
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a shortened malicious link over WhatsApp message, stealing AWS/GCP tokens stored in browser or metadata endpoints.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup phishing backend on mobile-friendly web server using Termux.Step 2: Write a script to extract AWS tokens using curl http://169.254.169.254.Step 3: Host it on a page that loads on mobile.Step 4: Send message via WhatsApp like: “Check your delivery update!” with shortened URL.Step 5: Victim clicks and unknowingly opens the mobile browser.Step 6: Script executes in background, contacts local metadata service (if in AWS EC2 browser), and sends tokens to attacker.Step 7: Attacker uses token to gain cloud console access.
Vulnerability: Access to cloud metadata via open browser sessions
MITRE Technique: T1552.005 - Unsecured Credentials in Cloud Instance Metadata
Impact: Cloud resource theft, backdoor, data exfil
Detection Method: Detect metadata access via suspicious IPs
Solution: Disable metadata access from browser, enforce IMDSv2
Tags: WhatsApp, AWS, Metadata, Cloud Token Theft

Title: HTML Attachment with Hidden iFrame Token Grabber
Scenario Description: HTML email attachment contains an invisible iframe that steals stored OAuth tokens via open sessions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create an HTML file with an invisible <iframe> to a phishing server.Step 2: The iframe contains a script that checks for OAuth sessions (e.g., Google, Microsoft).Step 3: Zip the HTML and attach it to an email saying “Monthly Invoice – See Attached”.Step 4: Victim opens file in browser, which silently loads iframe.Step 5: If user is logged into OAuth service, token is fetched via session cookies.Step 6: Token is sent to attacker server.Step 7: Attacker logs into victim’s cloud dashboard.
Detection Method: Anomalous iframe activity from email clients
Solution: Disable HTML rendering in mail, sanitize iframe content
Tags: HTML iFrame, Email Attachment, OAuth Steal

Title: Microsoft Teams Link with Fake SSO Redirect
Scenario Description: User receives a Teams message with link that mimics Azure SSO redirect, stealing the Office 365 token.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Host fake SSO login page mimicking Azure using AzureAD phish templates.Step 2: Configure MITMproxy to intercept token post-login.Step 3: Send Teams message: “Important Policy Change - Review Now!”Step 4: Link opens in browser; victim sees real-looking Azure login.Step 5: Victim logs in, unaware that token is proxied.Step 6: Attacker captures token through MITMproxy.Step 7: Use token to access SharePoint, Outlook, OneDrive.
Detection Method: Azure login IP anomaly, token replay alert
Solution: Enforce conditional access, restrict token lifespan

Title: Discord Message Token Grabber Link
Scenario Description: A malicious link is sent via Discord pretending to be a game or promotion. When clicked, the link executes a script that retrieves the victim's Discord token and sends it to the attacker.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a simple web page with JavaScript code that reads the Discord token from localStorage.Step 2: Attacker uploads this script to a public hosting service or uses Pastebin.Step 3: Shorten the malicious link with a link shortener (e.g., tinyurl.com).Step 4: Craft a fake message on Discord like “Claim your free Nitro here!” and send it in a DM or public channel.Step 5: Victim clicks the link and opens the webpage.Step 6: Script silently executes, reads the token, and sends it to the attacker’s webhook.Step 7: Attacker uses token to log in as the victim and steal or impersonate.
Vulnerability: Token stored in browser without encryption
Detection Method: Unusual logins, rapid message spam
Solution: Monitor link clicks, enforce token expiration

Title: Telegram Bot Sending Google Phishing Links
Scenario Description: A Telegram bot sends a message that contains a phishing page URL resembling Google login. Clicking leads to credential and token theft.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Evilginx2 with a pre-built Google OAuth phishing template.Step 2: Use a Telegram bot written in Python that sends auto-generated messages to users.Step 3: Include a link in the message that says “Google Docs Shared by Admin”.Step 4: Victim receives the message and opens the fake login page.Step 5: Victim enters login credentials thinking it's legit.Step 6: Evilginx2 captures both credentials and OAuth tokens.Step 7: Attacker logs into user’s Google account with the token.
Detection Method: Behavior analytics on token usage
Solution: Restrict bot access and validate URLs

Title: LinkedIn Message with Token-Stealing Redirect
Scenario Description: A fake job offer is sent via LinkedIn InMail. Clicking the link leads to a fake Azure SSO login page which captures user tokens.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Clone a realistic-looking Microsoft Azure login page.Step 2: Use MITMproxy to intercept and forward all data.Step 3: Craft a LinkedIn message: “We’re hiring! See JD: [shortened URL]”.Step 4: Send InMail to target victims.Step 5: Victim clicks the link and opens the fake Azure page.Step 6: Victim enters credentials and token is intercepted via proxy.Step 7: Use token to log into the Azure or Microsoft 365 environment.
Vulnerability: Trust in LinkedIn messages and SSO links
Impact: Unauthorized access to sensitive business resources
Detection Method: Alerts for Azure token reuse
Solution: SSO whitelisting, conditional access policies

Title: Email with Embedded Google Maps Token Leak
Scenario Description: An embedded iframe in an HTML email contains a link that extracts Google Maps API tokens when opened in the browser.
Tools Used: Gmail, HTML Builder, API Request Logger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write an HTML email containing an <iframe> linking to attacker’s server.Step 2: The server is configured to make API calls using user’s session cookies.Step 3: Craft the email as: “Map to Meeting Venue - Click to View”.Step 4: Victim opens the HTML email in browser or webmail.Step 5: iFrame loads silently and grabs the Google session cookies or tokens.Step 6: Send data back to attacker’s logger endpoint.Step 7: Attacker uses token to query private Maps APIs.
Impact: Abuse of internal map systems and token quota theft
Detection Method: Monitor Maps API abuse and iframe traffic
Solution: Block embedded iframes in email

Title: URL Redirection via Bit.ly to Token Grabber
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a benign-looking bit.ly link in email that redirects multiple times and finally lands on a token stealing page.
Tools Used: Bit.ly, Redirect Chains, JavaScript Token Collector
Attack Steps: Step 1: Register a malicious domain that mimics Slack/Google.Step 2: Create an endpoint that uses window.location to redirect via 3 different URLs.Step 3: Final URL hosts token stealing JS (using localStorage.getItem).Step 4: Shorten initial URL with bit.ly for legitimacy.Step 5: Send email titled “Team Agenda – See Docs Here” with link.Step 6: Victim clicks, unaware of redirect trail.Step 7: Final landing page executes JS to extract token.Step 8: Attacker retrieves token from backend logs.
Detection Method: Analyze redirect chains in logs
Solution: Block redirect domains, validate all shortened links

Title: QR Code in Email Leading to Token Theft
Scenario Description: A QR code embedded in an email leads to a phishing page on a mobile device that steals OAuth tokens.
Tools Used: QR Code Generator, Ngrok, OAuth Stealer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a phishing page mimicking Google SSO on Ngrok.Step 2: Convert the URL to a QR code using any QR generator.Step 3: Insert the QR code in an email attachment as a PDF titled “New Company Wi-Fi QR”.Step 4: Victim scans QR code using phone.Step 5: Mobile browser opens fake login page.Step 6: Victim logs in; token is captured by Ngrok.Step 7: Attacker logs in using the stolen token.
Detection Method: QR code analysis, mobile traffic monitoring
Solution: Block QR from unverified senders

Title: Teams Chat with Expired URL Token Replay
Scenario Description: Expired but cached file-sharing links are abused to replay access tokens, which are stored in memory and retrievable via crafted links.
Tools Used: Microsoft Teams, Burp Suite, Replay Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Share a Microsoft OneDrive file in Teams and note the generated token URL.Step 2: Revoke access but copy the original token from browser’s dev tools.Step 3: Use Burp Suite to replay token URL and inspect server behavior.Step 4: Craft a new Teams message like “Updated version uploaded – check again”.Step 5: Victim clicks; server may still accept token due to caching.Step 6: Replay grants attacker access if link is misconfigured.Step 7: Download file or upload backdoored replacement.
Impact: Backdoor in shared document, data theft
Detection Method: Monitor expired token activity
Solution: Force token expiration and log all token access

Title: SMS Phishing for Apple ID Token Theft
Scenario Description: An SMS link pretends to be from Apple and asks users to re-authenticate. The session token is then stolen for iCloud access.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use free online SMS spoofing services to send a message from “Apple”.Step 2: Message content: “Your iCloud access has been disabled. Login here: [short URL]”.Step 3: The link redirects to a cloned Apple login page.Step 4: Set up proxy backend to capture auth token post-login.Step 5: Victim logs in on phone.Step 6: Token is harvested and stored.Step 7: Attacker logs in to iCloud dashboard without password.
Detection Method: Apple unusual login alerts
Solution: Do not trust links from SMS, enforce 2FA

Title: Email with SVG File Exploiting DOM to Steal Token
Scenario Description: An email contains an SVG image that executes JavaScript in the victim’s browser to extract session tokens.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a crafted SVG file that includes JavaScript payload inside onload tag.Step 2: Use <script> inside SVG to extract cookies or tokens.Step 3: Host SVG file and embed it in an email.Step 4: Email body says: “Please see chart attached (opens in browser)”.Step 5: Victim opens SVG in browser.Step 6: Script silently extracts token and sends it to attacker’s server.Step 7: Attacker uses token for session hijack.
Vulnerability: Embedded JS in SVG bypasses scanners
Detection Method: Monitor SVG-based downloads
Solution: Disable SVG rendering in email

Title: Google Chat Bot with Token-Redirect Link
Scenario Description: A bot in Google Chat shares a message with a link that redirects to a token-capturing OAuth consent screen.
Tools Used: Google Chat Bot, OAuth Consent Spoof, Ngrok
Attack Steps: Step 1: Register a fake app in Google Developer Console.Step 2: Set its OAuth scope to request access to Gmail or Drive.Step 3: Use Google Chat Bot to send a message saying: “Hey, approve this app to continue shared access”.Step 4: Link opens OAuth consent screen.Step 5: Victim approves, unaware of the actual permissions.Step 6: App receives access token via redirect URI.Step 7: Token is logged and used to access victim data.
Detection Method: Review of newly approved OAuth apps
Solution: Use OAuth allow-listing, security awareness

Title: Email Link Exploiting Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) to Steal Tokens
Scenario Description: An attacker sends an email with a crafted link that abuses CSRF to silently send a request from the victim’s browser to a vulnerable web service and steal the session token.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, CSRF Exploit Toolkit, HTML Email Builder
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify a web application the target uses that is vulnerable to CSRF and uses token-based authentication (e.g., internal HR portal).Step 2: Craft an HTML page with a hidden auto-submitting form that sends a token-harvesting request (like changing an email address to attacker’s).Step 3: Upload the HTML page to a public web server controlled by attacker.Step 4: Create an email with a link saying “Your Policy Details – Click to View”, pointing to the hosted malicious page.Step 5: Victim opens email and clicks the link.Step 6: The browser auto-submits the hidden form with session cookies and CSRF token.Step 7: The attacker receives session details or captures changes in the victim's profile with stolen token.
Vulnerability: Insecure CSRF implementations with active tokens
Detection Method: Monitor unusual form submissions
Solution: Implement CSRF token validation with origin check

Title: Redirect via File-Sharing Service Leading to Token Harvest Page
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses trust in Dropbox/Google Drive by sharing a document that auto-redirects to a token-stealing site.
Tools Used: Dropbox / Google Drive, Redirect Scripts, Token Logger
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a shared file in Dropbox or Google Drive that includes a hyperlink to a malicious site (e.g., via embedded JavaScript or meta refresh).Step 2: Set file permissions to “Anyone with link can view”.Step 3: Shorten the shared link using a URL shortener (e.g., tinyurl, bitly).Step 4: Send an email with subject “Updated Policy Document” and include the link.Step 5: Victim opens the link and sees the document briefly, then is redirected.Step 6: The malicious site uses JavaScript to collect any active tokens or cookies.Step 7: Tokens are sent to attacker’s server via AJAX POST.Step 8: Attacker uses token to access victim's email or storage.
Detection Method: Monitor short-link access and redirection chains
Solution: Block auto-redirect scripts in shared documents

Title: Email with Tokenized URL for One-Time Login Abuse
Scenario Description: An attacker reuses a legitimate login link from an email (like passwordless login or “magic link”) to access another user’s account before expiration.
Tools Used: Email Interceptor, Magic Link Sniffer, Browser Dev Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker compromises or intercepts a passwordless login email (magic link) sent to a legitimate user (e.g., via phishing, mailbox access, or misconfigured forwarding).Step 2: Extracts the tokenized link (e.g., https://example.com/login?token=abc123).Step 3: Sends an innocuous email with a link like “HR Documents Shared – Click Here” that auto-opens this login URL.Step 4: Victim is unaware of token use; attacker uses the original token before it expires.Step 5: Attacker gains access to the account without needing credentials.Step 6: If the platform doesn’t expire the token immediately after first use, the token can be reused multiple times.
Vulnerability: Insecure or delayed invalidation of one-time login tokens
Detection Method: Access logs showing multiple IPs using same token
Solution: Invalidate login tokens immediately after first use
Tags: Magic Link, Token Abuse, Email Reuse

Title: HTML Email with JavaScript Executed via Data URI
Scenario Description: HTML email uses a data: URI with embedded JavaScript to steal tokens without needing an external request, bypassing some email scanners.
Tools Used: Custom HTML Email Generator, Burp Collaborator
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft an HTML email using a data:text/html;base64, URI inside an iframe or anchor tag.Step 2: Encode JavaScript payload in base64, which on execution grabs tokens from document.cookie or localStorage.Step 3: Add the payload as a clickable link or auto-executing iframe.Step 4: Email body says: “Important Policy PDF – Preview below”.Step 5: Victim clicks the link or email auto-renders content in preview pane.Step 6: Script extracts stored session data and sends it to attacker server.Step 7: Attacker uses tokens to log in or escalate access.
Vulnerability: Data URIs bypass link filters and obfuscate JS
Detection Method: Monitor usage of base64 data URIs in emails
Solution: Disable auto-rendering, strip data URIs
Tags: HTML Email, Data URI, JS Obfuscation

Title: Messaging App Markdown Link with Masked Redirect
Scenario Description: A markdown-formatted link is shared in a messaging platform (like Slack or Mattermost) where the displayed link text differs from the actual destination.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a Slack message like [Download Report](https://trusted-domain.com) but mask the actual URL to redirect to https://attacker-site.com.Step 2: Attacker hosts a site that resembles a corporate dashboard login page.Step 3: Include scripts to extract OAuth or cookie-based tokens.Step 4: Send message in a channel with context like “Monthly Metrics Available”.Step 5: Victim clicks link, believing it to be safe due to link text.Step 6: Browser loads malicious site; script captures session tokens silently.Step 7: Attacker accesses protected services (e.g., Slack, email, G-Suite).
Vulnerability: Markdown link masking and implicit trust
Detection Method: Flag mismatched link text vs destination
Solution: Show real URLs on hover, block misleading markdown links

Title: Open Redirect to Phishing Page
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits a trusted company’s email redirect link to mask a phishing page, tricking users into entering credentials.
Tools Used: Custom Phishing Page, Burp Suite, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a legitimate website with open redirect vulnerability (e.g., https://trusted.com/redirect?url=) Step 2: Attacker creates a fake login page resembling a real service (e.g., Office 365) Step 3: They host it at http://malicious.site/office-login Step 4: Attacker constructs a link: https://trusted.com/redirect?url=http://malicious.site/office-login Step 5: Attacker sends an email like: “Please login to view your document” with the crafted redirect link Step 6: Victim clicks the link, sees trusted domain first, then redirected to phishing page Step 7: Victim enters credentials into fake form Step 8: Credentials are captured by attacker.
Detection Method: Analyze redirect chains in email links; alert on redirects to non-corporate domains
Solution: Block open redirects or enforce allowlists for redirect targets

Title: Redirect to Drive-by Malware Site
Scenario Description: Using an open redirect, attacker lures users to a site that silently drops malware.
Tools Used: Malicious File Server, msfvenom, Email Sender Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds open redirect on an educational site (e.g., https://edu.com/redirect?url=) Step 2: Attacker prepares a malware payload (e.g., PDF with reverse shell using msfvenom) Step 3: Hosts it on http://evilsite.com/notes.pdf Step 4: Constructs link: https://edu.com/redirect?url=http://evilsite.com/notes.pdf Step 5: Crafts an email saying “Download the class notes before tomorrow” Step 6: Victim clicks link, redirected silently to malware PDF Step 7: User downloads or opens file; malware executes silently Step 8: Attacker gains backdoor access to victim’s system
Detection Method: Monitor unusual outbound connections; track redirect destinations
Solution: Disable or validate redirect URLs; implement download scanning

Title: Redirect Masking Suspicious Domains
Scenario Description: Attacker hides shady links behind known brands using open redirects to bypass email filters.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds redirect on a SaaS site (e.g., https://portal.saas.com/redirect?link=) Step 2: They want to point to http://scamdomain.ru/offer Step 3: Constructs link: https://portal.saas.com/redirect?link=http://scamdomain.ru/offer Step 4: Writes an email that says: “Click to claim your prize” Step 5: Spam filter allows email since base domain looks legit Step 6: User clicks link thinking it’s safe Step 7: Redirect happens, victim lands on suspicious survey page collecting PII or payment info Step 8: Attacker harvests sensitive data or payment credentials
Detection Method: Flag emails with redirects to external non-whitelisted domains
Solution: Add domain validation and warn on redirects in client

Title: Redirect to Fake Webmail Logout
Scenario Description: Redirected email link leads user to a fake logout page that captures session info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies open redirect on ISP domain (e.g., https://isp.com/exit?url=) Step 2: They build a page mimicking webmail logout with invisible login re-auth (http://evil.site/webmail-logout) Step 3: Constructs redirect: https://isp.com/exit?url=http://evil.site/webmail-logout Step 4: Sends an email: “You’ve been logged out of webmail due to inactivity. Click to re-login.” Step 5: Victim clicks and sees realistic logout page Step 6: Prompt asks to “Re-login” immediately for security Step 7: Victim enters password; it’s sent to attacker Step 8: Attacker uses session token or credentials to access real email
Detection Method: Analyze URLs ending with logout or login flows
Solution: Disable redirects to non-whitelisted domains

Title: Open Redirect Abuse for Tracking
Scenario Description: Attacker leverages redirect + URL shortener to track victim location, browser, IP.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses an open redirect like https://org.com/track?url= Step 2: Uses shortened link like short.io/abc123 pointing to attacker’s tracking server Step 3: Chains both: https://org.com/track?url=https://short.io/abc123 Step 4: Sends an email: “Click to see your document update” Step 5: Victim clicks the link and hits attacker-controlled endpoint first Step 6: Tracking server logs time, browser, IP, device info, then forwards to benign site Step 7: Attacker now has geolocation and device data Step 8: Could be used for recon or targeted social engineering
Detection Method: Detect repeated tracking chains in emails
Solution: Disable open redirects; restrict redirect parameters

Title: Redirect to Fake Two-Factor Page
Scenario Description: The attacker uses an open redirect to deliver a fake 2FA prompt to steal OTP tokens along with credentials.
Tools Used: Evilginx, Open Redirected URL, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds open redirect on known security brand (e.g., https://securebrand.com/redirect?target=) Step 2: Sets up Evilginx to clone a Google login + 2FA prompt Step 3: Hosts phishing page at http://malicious.net/google-login Step 4: Attacker crafts redirect: https://securebrand.com/redirect?target=http://malicious.net/google-login Step 5: Sends email like “Your Google account was accessed, confirm it’s you” Step 6: Victim clicks link and sees cloned Google login page Step 7: Victim enters credentials and 2FA code Step 8: Attacker uses both to log in live before 2FA expires
Detection Method: Monitor login attempts from unusual geos post-redirect
Solution: Block or tokenize redirect parameters

Title: Redirected Link in HR Policy Update
Scenario Description: Open redirect hides fake HR portal collecting employee login for internal apps.
Tools Used: ClonePhish, Redirect Tester, Email Template Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds open redirect on company portal (https://company.com/redirect?url=) Step 2: Clones internal HR policy update site Step 3: Hosts clone at http://evil.site/hr-update Step 4: Constructs phishing URL: https://company.com/redirect?url=http://evil.site/hr-update Step 5: Crafts email: “Action Required: Updated Harassment Policy” Step 6: Email is sent from spoofed HR address with logo Step 7: Victim thinks it’s authentic, clicks link Step 8: Fake login form asks for Intranet username/password Step 9: Victim submits info, attacker gains access to internal systems
Detection Method: Detect links redirecting to non-corp IPs
Solution: Educate staff; restrict redirect use

Title: Redirected Login via Marketing Email
Scenario Description: Marketing email redirect used to lure victims to login page with cloned interface.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds redirect in marketing platform (e.g., https://markettool.com/click?redirect=) Step 2: Clones user login page for project management tool (e.g., Trello, Slack) Step 3: Hosts it at http://phishlink.net/slack-login Step 4: Builds redirect link: https://markettool.com/click?redirect=http://phishlink.net/slack-login Step 5: Sends email “Your shared Trello board has been updated” Step 6: Victim thinks it's real, clicks link Step 7: Victim is redirected, enters login Step 8: Attacker captures credentials
Detection Method: Analyze marketing redirect chains
Solution: Validate redirect destinations via allowlists

Title: Redirect via Email Signature
Scenario Description: Attacker inserts redirect link inside a fake email signature to redirect user silently.
Tools Used: Email Client, Redirect Generator, Web Hosting
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts email pretending to be from vendor support Step 2: Adds signature: “Best regards, Support Team - https://vendor.com/support/redirect?url=http://phish.biz/login” Step 3: Entire message seems real and not spammy Step 4: Victim clicks on “support” in signature Step 5: Redirect happens to fake login page asking for credentials Step 6: Victim enters login info Step 7: Attacker gains access to vendor or supplier portal
Detection Method: Scan links in signature lines and footers
Solution: Block redirects from HTML signatures

Title: Redirect-Based Browser Exploit
Scenario Description: Redirect leads to browser exploit chain that abuses out-of-date plugins.
Tools Used: Metasploit, Malicious JS Server, Redirect URL
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds redirect on newspaper site (e.g., https://news.org/go?link=) Step 2: Prepares a drive-by JS exploit hosted on http://exploitserver.biz/js-load Step 3: Builds link: https://news.org/go?link=http://exploitserver.biz/js-load Step 4: Crafts email “Breaking: Your City Lockdown Extended” Step 5: User clicks link expecting news article Step 6: Exploit server loads JS silently in background Step 7: Outdated browser plugin is exploited Step 8: Reverse shell or malware is deployed to the system
Detection Method: Monitor for web plugin execution from email paths
Solution: Patch browsers; limit redirects on news sites

Title: Redirect to Fake Antivirus Alert
Scenario Description: Attacker uses fake security alert via open redirect to convince users to install fake antivirus.
Tools Used: Fake AV Page, Redirect Link, Fake Email Template
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds redirect on gaming site (e.g., https://games.com/track?next=) Step 2: Creates fake page that says: “Your system is infected! Download protection now!” Step 3: Redirect link points to: http://scare.site/alert-virus Step 4: Builds URL: https://games.com/track?next=http://scare.site/alert-virus Step 5: Email subject: “Urgent: Your Antivirus Has Expired” Step 6: Victim clicks link thinking it's legit alert Step 7: Page displays fake virus scan, urges download Step 8: Victim installs fake AV which is malware in disguise
Detection Method: Alert on antivirus-related downloads from redirects
Solution: Train users to detect fake alerts

Title: Redirect in Support Ticket Scam
Scenario Description: Support-style redirect message leads to a malicious file hosted offsite.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies redirect on company IT portal (https://it.company.com/click?dest=) Step 2: Prepares .docm file with macro malware Step 3: Hosts on http://filesite.ru/helpdesk-ticket.docm Step 4: Sends email: “IT Ticket #24910 - Unresolved Issue” Step 5: Victim sees realistic support ticket and link Step 6: Click redirects to macro-laced Word doc Step 7: Victim opens doc, macro runs, downloads malware Step 8: Attacker gains access to workstation
Detection Method: Detect DOCM file opens via redirected path
Solution: Filter redirects from .docm or .exe downloads

Title: Redirect Exploit via QR Code in Email
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds QR code with redirect URL in email to avoid detection.
Tools Used: QR Code Generator, Redirect Link, Clone Page
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates fake password reset site Step 2: Hosts at http://fakelogin.link/microsoft-reset Step 3: Uses redirect link: https://safecompany.com/redirect?url=http://fakelogin.link/microsoft-reset Step 4: Converts redirect URL into QR code Step 5: Embeds QR into HTML email: “Scan to reset your password securely” Step 6: Victim scans code using mobile device Step 7: Redirect to phishing site happens on phone browser Step 8: Victim enters password, attacker steals it
Detection Method: Detect QR codes with redirect chains
Solution: Block QR-encoded links with external redirect
Tags: QR, mobile phishing, redirect, scan bait

Title: Multi-Hop Redirect Chain
Scenario Description: Attacker chains multiple redirect URLs to hide final phishing site.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uses 3 open redirect services (e.g., news.com, edu.org, market.biz) Step 2: Final redirect leads to: http://stealthphish.net/login Step 3: Link: https://news.com/track?url=https://edu.org/go?link=https://market.biz/out?to=http://stealthphish.net/login Step 4: Crafts email “New Invoice Available” Step 5: User clicks and passes through multiple legit domains Step 6: Final destination is phishing page Step 7: Victim thinks it's safe due to trusted domains shown Step 8: Victim submits credentials
Detection Method: Detect long redirect chains with >2 hops
Solution: Allow only one-level redirect max

Title: Open Redirect Abuse via Tracking Pixel
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds tracking pixel that also redirects to log device data.
Tools Used: Tracking Server, Redirect Link in Pixel
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker embeds image tag in email like: Step 2: Redirect leads to tracking server that logs IP, browser, OS, email open time Step 3: User opens email; image loads automatically Step 4: No clicks needed; tracking occurs via redirect Step 5: Attacker uses info for tailored spear phishing later Step 6: May redirect image again to a real logo to remain stealthy
Detection Method: Block remote images in emails; analyze tracking servers
Solution: Restrict image redirection; sanitize email HTML
Tags: tracking pixel, passive recon, redirect abuse

Title: Redirect Exploit via Calendar Invite
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds an open redirect link inside a meeting invite to deliver a phishing page disguised as a video conferencing login.
Tools Used: Google Calendar, Outlook, Fake Login Page, Redirect URL
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker discovers open redirect on a university site (e.g., https://university.edu/redirect?next=) Step 2: Clones a popular video conference login page (Zoom/Teams) Step 3: Hosts fake login at http://phishlink.co/video-login Step 4: Constructs final URL: https://university.edu/redirect?next=http://phishlink.co/video-login Step 5: Creates a calendar invite for "Zoom Orientation" sent to victims Step 6: Adds redirect link in the “Join Meeting” section of invite Step 7: Victim joins calendar event and clicks “Join Meeting” Step 8: Redirect leads to phishing login where user enters credentials Step 9: Attacker captures login credentials in real-time
Detection Method: Detect calendar event URLs leading to external IPs
Solution: Restrict clickable URLs in calendar fields

Title: Exploit via Newsletter Unsubscribe Link
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses unsubscribe link with open redirect to gain trust and deliver malware-laced landing page.
Tools Used: Email Template Editor, Redirect Host, Malware PDF
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds redirect on newsletter site (https://newslettersite.com/unsub?url=) Step 2: Hosts fake "Unsubscribe Confirmation" PDF with embedded macro at http://maliciousdocs.io/unsub-confirm.pdf Step 3: Constructs URL: https://newslettersite.com/unsub?url=http://maliciousdocs.io/unsub-confirm.pdf Step 4: Sends email “Unsubscribe from COVID Alerts” mimicking known brand Step 5: Victim clicks link thinking it's a legitimate opt-out Step 6: Redirect leads to download of the malicious PDF Step 7: Victim opens PDF, embedded macro executes Step 8: Attacker gains access to victim system
Detection Method: Block external file loads from unsubscribe paths
Solution: Validate unsubscribe URL targets

Title: Redirect to Fake CAPTCHA Challenge
Scenario Description: Victim is sent through a fake CAPTCHA hosted through redirect to appear legitimate before redirecting to malware.
Tools Used: Fake CAPTCHA Generator, Open Redirector, Malware Page
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker hosts malware disguised as video player at http://malicious.stream/player.zip Step 2: Sets up a fake CAPTCHA page: “Click verify to continue” Step 3: Open redirect base is https://portal.safe.com/verify?go= Step 4: Constructs full redirect: https://portal.safe.com/verify?go=http://malicious.stream/captcha.html Step 5: Email reads: “New video training available. Please verify first.” Step 6: Victim clicks link, sees CAPTCHA, clicks “I’m not a robot” Step 7: Redirect occurs to auto-download malware ZIP Step 8: ZIP contains executable disguised as player Step 9: Victim runs file, attacker gains remote access
Detection Method: Monitor CAPTCHA patterns tied to download triggers
Solution: Enforce CAPTCHA domain validation

Title: Redirect via Contact Us Email
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates a vendor and includes redirect link inside fake "Contact Us" footer to phish credentials.
Tools Used: Email Composer, Redirect Domain, Web Cloner
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker clones vendor login portal at http://secure-portal.biz/login Step 2: Redirect base: https://vendor.org/contact?link= Step 3: Final URL: https://vendor.org/contact?link=http://secure-portal.biz/login Step 4: Email crafted with subject: “Invoice Issue - Contact Us” Step 5: Footer shows: “Need help? Contact us at https://vendor.org/contact?link=…” Step 6: Victim clicks expecting vendor support, gets redirected to phishing portal Step 7: User inputs login or billing details Step 8: Attacker captures internal account credentials
Detection Method: Monitor "Contact" links resolving off-domain
Solution: Sanitize link parameters in contact emails

Title: Exploit via Auto-Translate Redirect
Scenario Description: Redirect service of a translation tool is abused to deliver phishing site masked as translated content.
Tools Used: Google Translate URL Redirect, Fake Page
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds fake government tax site with credential request: http://fraudtax.org/login Step 2: Wraps it with Google Translate URL: https://translate.google.com/translate?sl=auto&tl=en&u=http://fraudtax.org/login Step 3: This acts as a redirect and masks the real domain Step 4: Email says “New Tax Law - View Official English Translation” Step 5: Victim clicks link, sees page rendered through Google UI Step 6: Fake site asks for name, email, and SSN to view document Step 7: Victim submits info Step 8: Attacker steals PII under trusted interface
Detection Method: Detect Google Translate links wrapping unknown domains
Solution: Block translate-based phishing by proxy detection
Tags: translate redirect, tax phish, PII fraud

Title: Passive STARTTLS Downgrade via Network Sniffing
Scenario Description: Attacker listens to SMTP connections and strips STARTTLS request to force plaintext login.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup a local VM with a mail server (like Postfix) and configure it to use STARTTLS.Step 2: Configure a client (like Thunderbird) to send mail using STARTTLS.Step 3: Start Wireshark and capture traffic on port 25 (SMTP).Step 4: Observe the client initiating the STARTTLS command.Step 5: Now, introduce a man-in-the-middle proxy like Ettercap and start MITM sniffing between client and server.Step 6: Create a filter rule in Ettercap that drops or modifies STARTTLS commands (e.g., replace "STARTTLS" with "XXXXXXX").Step 7: Observe that the connection now continues without encryption, allowing the attacker to see usernames and passwords in plaintext.
Detection Method: Traffic anomaly logs; no TLS handshake
Solution: Enforce SMTP MTA-STS and DNSSEC; use SMTPS over port 465

Title: Active Downgrade via SMTP Proxy Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a transparent SMTP proxy to modify traffic and disable STARTTLS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Install mitmproxy on a system and configure it to intercept SMTP traffic.Step 2: Configure a dummy SMTP server and a mail client to use STARTTLS on port 587.Step 3: Setup iptables or a transparent proxy to route all SMTP traffic through mitmproxy.Step 4: Write a script/plugin in mitmproxy to strip or replace the STARTTLS command.Step 5: Send an email from the client to the server.Step 6: Verify in mitmproxy logs that STARTTLS was stripped and communication proceeded in plaintext.Step 7: Capture login credentials or email content sent in plaintext.
Detection Method: Lack of TLS negotiation; strange SMTP logs
Solution: Use MTA-STS and DNSSEC; detect SMTP anomalies
Tags: Email Exploit, SMTP Proxy, TLS Stripping

Title: SMTP Downgrade in Open Wi-Fi
Scenario Description: Attacker targets mobile users in public Wi-Fi to capture email credentials.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup a rogue Wi-Fi hotspot using a tool like Bettercap or Fluxion.Step 2: Simulate an open Wi-Fi network in a lab environment.Step 3: Setup a test SMTP server with STARTTLS support.Step 4: Connect a victim device to rogue Wi-Fi and use Thunderbird or Outlook to send emails.Step 5: Intercept traffic via Bettercap and inject responses to strip STARTTLS.Step 6: Observe that email credentials are now sent over plaintext SMTP.Step 7: Log and demonstrate the captured credentials.
Vulnerability: STARTTLS optional; user ignorance of secure connection
Detection Method: Rogue DHCP/DNS detection tools; TLS cert mismatch
Solution: Always use VPN; enforce SMTPS (port 465) on clients
Tags: WiFi MITM, STARTTLS Stripping, Email Hijack

Title: Email Gateway Downgrade in Corporate Environment
Scenario Description: Internal SMTP gateway fails to enforce TLS, attacker strips STARTTLS and reads internal emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a test SMTP relay server in a virtual corporate network.Step 2: Configure a client to relay mail through this gateway using STARTTLS.Step 3: Use mitm6 or Responder to spoof DNS and redirect traffic.Step 4: Intercept SMTP traffic between client and gateway.Step 5: Drop or modify STARTTLS command during negotiation.Step 6: Observe captured credentials and messages in plaintext.Step 7: Replay the same credentials in real SMTP session to verify compromise.
Detection Method: DNS poisoning indicators; weak mail logs
Solution: Enforce STARTTLS; apply TLS pinning internally
Tags: Internal SMTP, TLS Strip, Credential Theft

Title: Exploiting Lack of MTA-STS Policy
Scenario Description: Without MTA-STS, an attacker can trick servers into accepting plaintext mail.
Tools Used: DNS spoofing tools, Wireshark, Python SMTP server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a DNS spoofing lab using tools like dnschef or ettercap.Step 2: Register a fake SMTP server (e.g., attacker.com) without TLS.Step 3: Spoof the DNS of a legitimate domain that lacks MTA-STS.Step 4: From a test SMTP client, send email to spoofed domain.Step 5: Intercept and redirect the mail to attacker.com.Step 6: Observe that without MTA-STS, the client proceeds to send the message unencrypted.Step 7: Extract message contents and simulate message manipulation.
Detection Method: Lack of DNSSEC, MTA-STS policy
Solution: Publish MTA-STS and TLS-RPT policies
Tags: DNS Spoofing, Email MITM, TLS Downgrade

Title: STARTTLS Downgrade Using Mail Client Misconfiguration
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits user misconfiguration in mail clients that don’t verify TLS use.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a test SMTP server with STARTTLS enabled on port 587.Step 2: Instruct a student to configure a mail client (e.g., Outlook) to connect without requiring encrypted connection.Step 3: Use Wireshark to monitor network traffic.Step 4: Observe that the client sends credentials over plaintext if the "Require TLS" checkbox is unchecked.Step 5: Simulate an attacker capturing login credentials from that traffic.Step 6: Replay the captured credentials to confirm access to email.Step 7: Document the importance of enforcing encryption settings on mail clients.
Detection Method: No TLS negotiation observed in packet capture
Solution: Enforce strict TLS settings on clients
Tags: Mail Client Config, User Error, Downgrade

Title: Exploiting SMTP Banner Manipulation
Scenario Description: Attacker alters server greeting banner to hide STARTTLS support.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a local SMTP server that supports STARTTLS.Step 2: Install mitmproxy or a custom proxy that sits between the client and server.Step 3: Create a rule in mitmproxy to modify the server banner that lists STARTTLS.Step 4: Send an email using a client connected to the proxy.Step 5: The client, not seeing STARTTLS in the server capabilities, sends email in plaintext.Step 6: Use mitmproxy to extract the credentials and message content.Step 7: Log the successful downgrade and demonstrate risks of trusting banners.
Detection Method: Compare banner to actual server config
Solution: Verify banner integrity using tools

Title: Exploiting Opportunistic TLS Behavior in MTAs
Scenario Description: Attack targets opportunistic TLS on mail transfer agents (MTAs) lacking MTA-STS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up two mail servers: one legitimate, one attacker-controlled.Step 2: Use DNS poisoning (e.g., with dnschef) to reroute outbound SMTP from a legitimate domain to attacker MTA.Step 3: Configure the attacker MTA to not offer STARTTLS.Step 4: From the original domain, send an email.Step 5: Watch as the message is delivered in plaintext.Step 6: Log the message body and headers.Step 7: Explain the danger of relying on opportunistic encryption.
Detection Method: Mail logs lack TLS indication
Solution: Enforce MTA-STS and TLS-RPT

Title: Downgrade via SSLStrip in SMTP-over-STARTTLS
Scenario Description: Attacker uses sslstrip-like approach to intercept and rewrite SMTP protocol negotiations.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Bettercap with the sslstrip module enabled.Step 2: Connect the victim device to the same network.Step 3: Configure the victim to send email via SMTP with STARTTLS.Step 4: Monitor Bettercap as it modifies STARTTLS to plain SMTP.Step 5: Use Wireshark to capture and analyze plaintext credentials.Step 6: Replay captured credentials using telnet or SMTP tool.Step 7: Demonstrate the risk of not verifying certificate chains.
Detection Method: TLS handshake missing; plaintext SMTP
Solution: Enforce strict TLS checking

Title: Using SMTP Downgrade to Harvest Credentials for Phishing
Scenario Description: Attacker captures credentials and uses them to send phishing emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Setup a victim SMTP server that accepts plaintext and STARTTLS.Step 2: Setup MITM interception using a proxy or packet capture.Step 3: Strip STARTTLS and capture user credentials.Step 4: Use captured credentials to log in to user’s mail account.Step 5: Send phishing emails to other users impersonating the victim.Step 6: Monitor replies or clicks on phishing content.Step 7: Discuss how downgrades can act as first step in advanced threats.
Detection Method: Mail logs; traffic patterns
Solution: Enforce TLS + monitor mail anomalies

Title: Cross-Protocol Downgrade via SMTP to HTTP Trick
Scenario Description: Attacker redirects SMTP traffic to HTTP port to force miscommunication and downgrade.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a dummy HTTP server listening on port 25 using nginx or netcat.Step 2: Poison DNS or ARP to redirect SMTP traffic to this port.Step 3: Attempt to send an email from client.Step 4: Client does not receive proper SMTP greeting, may fallback to plain text or error.Step 5: Log how the failure mode leads to plaintext fallback.Step 6: Demonstrate that clever redirection can bypass security if STARTTLS is not enforced.Step 7: Reiterate importance of verifying server identity.
Detection Method: Server behavior logs
Solution: Block port confusion; enforce cert validation

Title: TLS Stripping with Packet Injection on LAN
Scenario Description: Attacker uses packet injection to remove STARTTLS command mid-transmission.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect victim and attacker to same LAN.Step 2: Use ARP spoofing with Ettercap to MITM traffic.Step 3: Use Scapy to intercept and modify packets containing “STARTTLS”.Step 4: Inject a malformed packet to prevent negotiation.Step 5: Victim falls back to plaintext SMTP.Step 6: Use Wireshark to read email credentials.Step 7: Replay attack and test remediation.
Detection Method: Injected packets visible in pcap
Solution: Validate TLS session end-to-end

Title: STARTTLS Downgrade via SMTP Smuggling
Scenario Description: Attack leverages SMTP command smuggling to bypass STARTTLS enforcement.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a Python SMTP client script.Step 2: Send carefully crafted multi-line EHLO and MAIL FROM commands that break SMTP parser.Step 3: Target server misinterprets the input and fails to initiate STARTTLS.Step 4: Email proceeds in plaintext.Step 5: Monitor server logs and traffic using Wireshark.Step 6: Validate attacker-controlled headers in delivered email.Step 7: Demonstrate parsing vulnerabilities in SMTP.
Detection Method: Abnormal server logs
Solution: Harden SMTP parsers

Title: Downgrade Exploit using Deprecated Protocols
Scenario Description: Exploit targets servers using outdated TLS versions (e.g., TLS 1.0).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan a test SMTP server using Nmap with --script smtp-starttls.Step 2: Identify if it allows deprecated versions like SSLv3, TLS 1.0.Step 3: Use OpenSSL to connect with a weak protocol (e.g., openssl s_client -starttls smtp -tls1).Step 4: Complete the handshake.Step 5: Send sample email and capture packet.Step 6: Analyze risks of using weak encryption.Step 7: Demonstrate how attackers downgrade negotiation to weakest link.
Detection Method: Outdated protocol flags
Solution: Disable weak ciphers/protocols

Title: AI-Based Detection Evasion in STARTTLS Downgrade
Scenario Description: Sophisticated attacker randomizes traffic to evade ML anomaly detection.
Tools Used: Python, scapy, AI log evasion tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Python to randomize SMTP commands timing and spacing.Step 2: Strip STARTTLS in randomized form (e.g., modify individual chars in real-time).Step 3: Evade AI-based detection systems that rely on standard patterns.Step 4: Send email and capture traffic.Step 5: Demonstrate how traffic looks benign due to entropy.Step 6: Replay for validation.Step 7: Highlight challenges of AI/ML defense in protocol downgrades.
Detection Method: Abnormal entropy in logs
Solution: Use strict protocol enforcement rules

Title: Email Client Fallback Exploitation
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits email clients that silently fall back to plaintext if STARTTLS fails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a local test SMTP server using Postfix or MailHog configured with STARTTLS.Step 2: Configure the email client (e.g., Thunderbird) to connect using STARTTLS.Step 3: Force the SMTP server to temporarily reject the STARTTLS command using firewall rules (e.g., drop packets with iptables).Step 4: Attempt to send an email from Thunderbird.Step 5: Observe that the client silently falls back to plaintext SMTP and sends the email.Step 6: Use Wireshark to capture and analyze the traffic to confirm credentials and email content were exposed.Step 7: Document fallback behavior and discuss why clients should fail closed (not continue insecurely).
Detection Method: Lack of TLS handshake, plaintext login
Solution: Disable fallback; enforce TLS-only

Title: Downgrade via Legacy Printer SMTP Integration
Scenario Description: Legacy network printers using SMTP email alerts often don’t support STARTTLS, exposing credentials.
Tools Used: Network Printer, Wireshark, Local SMTP Server
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a test SMTP server that supports both STARTTLS and plaintext connections.Step 2: Configure a legacy printer’s email alert feature to send scan notifications to a mail server.Step 3: Intercept and monitor the printer’s SMTP traffic using Wireshark.Step 4: Observe that the printer sends credentials and messages in plaintext without requesting STARTTLS.Step 5: Replay the SMTP session using telnet or openssl to confirm credential theft.Step 6: Document risks of integrating legacy devices into secure systems.Step 7: Simulate mitigation by adding a proxy that forces STARTTLS or denies plaintext SMTP.
Detection Method: Captured traffic shows plaintext auth
Solution: Replace device or tunnel SMTP via STARTTLS proxy

Title: Downgrade via SMTP STARTTLS Failure Injection
Scenario Description: Attacker injects false "454 TLS not available" SMTP response to force clients into plaintext mode.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a local SMTP emulator or honeypot server.Step 2: Write a simple Python script using smtpd to respond to STARTTLS attempts with: 454 TLS not available due to temporary reason.Step 3: Set email client (e.g., Outlook) to connect to this SMTP emulator.Step 4: When STARTTLS fails, the client will often proceed in plaintext if it’s not configured to fail closed.Step 5: Use Wireshark to capture the credential exchange.Step 6: Demonstrate that a simple script can manipulate the STARTTLS negotiation process.Step 7: Educate students on proper client configuration and importance of strict TLS checks.
Detection Method: Unexpected SMTP error codes, plaintext traffic
Solution: Configure clients to abort on TLS failure

Title: Abuse of Mail Relay Hops with Mixed TLS Policies
Scenario Description: Attacker sends email through multiple relays, exploiting one that doesn't enforce STARTTLS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up three SMTP relays (e.g., postfix instances A, B, and C).Step 2: Configure A and C to require STARTTLS, but set B (middle relay) to allow plaintext connections.Step 3: From A, send a test email that routes through B to C.Step 4: Capture traffic between B and C using Wireshark.Step 5: Simulate MITM interception at the B-C hop.Step 6: Observe that credentials and email contents are transmitted in plaintext due to downgrade.Step 7: Conclude the risk from mixed relay security configurations in email infrastructure.
Detection Method: Missing Received: headers with TLS
Solution: Use MTA-STS and enforce TLS on all relays
Tags: Multi-Hop SMTP, MTA Security, Relay Risk

Title: Exploiting STARTTLS Misadvertisement via DNS Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs DNS MX records to redirect email to a server that falsely claims STARTTLS.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a DNS spoofing tool like dnschef to reroute DNS MX queries for a domain to attacker’s SMTP server.Step 2: Build a fake SMTP server that advertises STARTTLS capability but doesn't actually support encryption.Step 3: Send an email to the spoofed domain from a client configured to use opportunistic TLS.Step 4: The client connects, sees STARTTLS advertised, but never completes a successful TLS handshake.Step 5: Capture the email sent in plaintext due to handshake failure.Step 6: Log captured credentials and message content.Step 7: Emphasize how DNS integrity and server behavior can influence email security.
Detection Method: TLS handshake fails but mail still sent
Solution: Use DNSSEC and SMTP TLS reporting
Tags: DNS Spoof, STARTTLS Advert, MX Hijack

Title: Basic SMTP VRFY User Discovery
Scenario Description: Attacker discovers valid email usernames on a legacy SMTP server that allows the VRFY command, potentially leading to targeted attacks.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify target domain (e.g., target.com). Step 2: Find SMTP server using command: nslookup -type=mx target.com. Step 3: Use Telnet to connect to SMTP: telnet mail.target.com 25. Step 4: Type HELO attacker.com. Step 5: Enter: VRFY john, VRFY admin, VRFY test etc. Step 6: Server responses like “250 User exists” or “550 No such user” confirm valid usernames. Step 7: Collect list of valid emails.
Impact: Reveals valid emails for phishing or brute-force attacks.
Detection Method: Monitor logs for VRFY command use; alert on unusual enumeration patterns.
Solution: Disable VRFY/EXPN in SMTP config (e.g., Postfix disable_vrfy_command = yes).

Title: EXPN Command to Reveal Aliases
Scenario Description: Attacker uses EXPN to reveal full mailing list members and internal aliases from an old SMTP system.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Perform MX lookup on target domain. Step 2: Connect to SMTP using Telnet: telnet mail.target.com 25. Step 3: Type: HELO example.com. Step 4: Use command: EXPN staff, EXPN support, etc. Step 5: If EXPN is enabled, server returns a list of members like John <john@target.com>, Sarah <sarah@target.com>. Step 6: Save all identified members for phishing simulation.
Detection Method: SIEM to detect EXPN probes and alert.
Solution: Disable EXPN command or limit via SMTP ACLs.

Title: Mass VRFY via Scripted Brute Enumeration
Scenario Description: Attacker automates VRFY enumeration by brute-forcing common usernames using a script.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare a username list (admin, info, sales, etc). Step 2: Run Python script to iterate through list. Step 3: Script sends VRFY command for each username over port 25. Step 4: Responses like “250 User exists” are logged. Step 5: Export discovered users for follow-up attacks. Step 6: Compare with valid users from leaked breach data.
Detection Method: Monitor for bulk VRFY traffic; set rate-limits.
Solution: Implement SMTP proxy/firewall or tarpitting.

Title: VRFY Command Used via Netcat
Scenario Description: A user manually interacts with SMTP via netcat to check users' existence using VRFY.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Open terminal and run: nc mail.target.com 25. Step 2: Type: HELO attacker.com. Step 3: Send: VRFY hr, VRFY ceo, VRFY marketing. Step 4: Server replies indicate if user exists. Step 5: Log valid users. Step 6: Simulate how this info could feed into a social engineering chain.
Detection Method: Check for interactive SMTP connections from unknown IPs.
Solution: Turn off VRFY command and restrict access to internal SMTP services.

Title: VRFY + SMTP Banner Grabbing for Recon
Scenario Description: An attacker combines VRFY enumeration with SMTP banner analysis to get user list and software info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use Nmap: nmap -p 25 -sV target.com to get banner (e.g., Postfix version). Step 2: Use Telnet to connect to SMTP. Step 3: Send HELO attacker.com. Step 4: Try VRFY on usernames. Step 5: Note both valid users and server details (OS, SMTP software). Step 6: Use software version to plan further attacks (e.g., buffer overflow).
Impact: Combines recon and enumeration for future attacks.
Detection Method: Monitor Nmap scans and VRFY usage.
Solution: Remove banners via config + disable VRFY.
Tags: fingerprinting, user probing, smtp info leak

Title: VRFY Enumeration over Open Relay SMTP
Scenario Description: A misconfigured SMTP server that also functions as an open relay is abused for VRFY-based user enumeration.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use tools like MXToolbox to test if the SMTP server allows relaying. Step 2: Connect via Telnet to the SMTP server (port 25). Step 3: Run HELO attackerdomain.com. Step 4: Run VRFY root, VRFY ceo, VRFY webmaster. Step 5: Server responses confirm valid users. Step 6: The attacker saves this list for future phishing attacks. Step 7: Combine enumeration results with spam relay to simulate real-world abuse.
Detection Method: Alert on VRFY use, block open relay abuse via outbound spam filters.
Solution: Disable open relays and VRFY together; use authenticated SMTP.
Tags: smtp open relay, vrfy, user discovery

Title: VRFY from Cloud VM to Bypass IP Blocks
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a low-cost cloud VPS to perform enumeration from a clean IP, avoiding blacklists.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Deploy a small cloud VM (e.g., EC2 free tier). Step 2: Install Telnet using sudo apt install telnet. Step 3: Connect to the SMTP server of the target org using port 25. Step 4: Run HELO attacker.com and send VRFY for common names. Step 5: Log which usernames are valid. Step 6: Delete the VM after enumeration to remove traces.
Impact: Enables anonymous probing and evasive enumeration.
Detection Method: Detect inbound enumeration attempts from cloud IP ranges.
Solution: Block cloud IP ranges or use CAPTCHA/auth for SMTP auth.

Title: VRFY Enumeration with SMTP Honeypot Detection
Scenario Description: A blue team deploys a decoy SMTP honeypot to detect attackers using VRFY enumeration techniques.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Admin deploys a fake SMTP server that logs all interactions. Step 2: Attacker unknowingly connects via Telnet. Step 3: Sends HELO attacker.com. Step 4: Runs VRFY admin, VRFY user1, VRFY root. Step 5: Every command is silently logged. Step 6: SOC receives alert on VRFY attempt, along with IP and timestamp. Step 7: Team can track the attacker’s recon pattern.
Detection Method: Set honeypot alerts for VRFY/EXPN use.
Solution: Use honeypots alongside disabling VRFY in production.

Title: Combined SMTP VRFY and Webmail Login Testing
Scenario Description: After finding valid users via VRFY, attacker tries to log in to the webmail portal with default or guessed passwords.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use VRFY over Telnet to get valid usernames like jane, itadmin, ceo. Step 2: Append domain to form emails (jane@target.com). Step 3: Visit target’s webmail portal (e.g., mail.target.com). Step 4: Try usernames with passwords like Welcome123, Company2024. Step 5: Log successful attempts and take screenshots. Step 6: Show how poor passwords + exposed users lead to compromise.
Impact: Account takeover via chaining enumeration with login.
Detection Method: Brute force detection, 2FA enforcement.
Solution: Lock accounts after X failures, enforce strong passwords.
Tags: vrfy chaining, login test, password guess

Title: VRFY over Tor Network for Anonymity
Scenario Description: An attacker uses the Tor network to perform enumeration anonymously, bypassing IP restrictions.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up Proxychains or Tor SOCKS proxy. Step 2: Configure terminal: proxychains telnet mail.target.com 25. Step 3: Send HELO anonymous.com. Step 4: Run VRFY accounts, VRFY research, etc. Step 5: Save results with timestamp. Step 6: Change Tor circuit to rotate identity and repeat.
Detection Method: Correlate SMTP requests with Tor exit node lists.
Solution: Rate limit or block Tor-based SMTP probes.

Title: Custom SMTP Client to Evade Detection
Scenario Description: A stealthy attacker uses a custom Python SMTP client instead of Telnet to appear like a normal client.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a Python script using smtplib. Step 2: Script connects to mail.target.com over port 25. Step 3: Sends standard EHLO to mimic real clients. Step 4: Executes VRFY for common names quietly. Step 5: Waits a few seconds between each request to evade rate-limiting. Step 6: Logs valid usernames to a file. Step 7: Optionally uses TLS if available to encrypt probing.
Detection Method: Monitor client behavior anomalies, unusual SMTP clients.
Solution: Deep packet inspection and anomaly detection.

Title: VRFY on Abandoned Legacy Mail Servers
Scenario Description: An attacker finds a forgotten legacy mail server (not integrated into the org’s main system) with VRFY enabled.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan IP range for open port 25 using nmap -p 25. Step 2: Discover a legacy server with banner Sendmail 8.x. Step 3: Connect via Telnet and use VRFY admin, VRFY legacy, VRFY backup. Step 4: Valid users returned. Step 5: Use usernames to check if they’re still valid in main system. Step 6: Highlight the risks of unmanaged assets.
Impact: Leaked user info from forgotten infra.
Detection Method: Asset inventory and monitoring.
Solution: Decommission or patch unused servers.

Title: Multi-Domain VRFY Enumeration Attack
Scenario Description: Attacker performs VRFY enumeration across multiple domains owned by the target to gather organization-wide accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Identify domains: company.com, subsidiary.net, branch.org. Step 2: Use nslookup -type=mx on each domain. Step 3: Connect to SMTP servers for all domains. Step 4: Run VRFY across usernames like info, support, hr. Step 5: Cross-compare users to detect shared logins or naming patterns. Step 6: Demonstrate how a compromise on one domain can leak user info across the organization.
Detection Method: Monitor MX queries from external IPs.
Solution: Disable VRFY consistently across all domains.

Title: VRFY with Broken STARTTLS Downgrade
Scenario Description: Attacker forces SMTP connection to downgrade to plaintext, exposing VRFY probes even on STARTTLS-enabled servers.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Scan for SMTP servers that support STARTTLS but don’t enforce it. Step 2: Connect over plain Telnet and avoid issuing STARTTLS. Step 3: Run VRFY on target users. Step 4: All commands and responses are visible in plaintext. Step 5: Capture traffic if on same network to simulate MITM.
Detection Method: Force STARTTLS, audit for downgrade attempts.
Solution: Set smtpd_tls_security_level = encrypt.

Title: VRFY Enumeration via SMTP Port Forwarding
Scenario Description: Internal attacker sets up SSH tunnel to probe internal-only SMTP server with VRFY enabled.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker connects to a compromised internal host. Step 2: Sets up SSH tunnel: ssh -L 2525:internal.mail:25 user@compromised. Step 3: On local machine, connect to localhost:2525 via Telnet. Step 4: Send HELO tunnel.local and issue VRFY commands. Step 5: Log valid usernames from internal SMTP server. Step 6: Demonstrate insider risk when VRFY is enabled internally.
Detection Method: Monitor SSH tunnels and SMTP traffic.
Solution: Use internal firewalls + disable VRFY even internally.

Title: Enumerating Email Users via Misconfigured Mail Gateway
Scenario Description: The attacker targets a misconfigured SMTP mail gateway that exposes the VRFY command and user information externally.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Use nslookup -type=mx target.com to find the mail server for the domain. Step 2: Use Nmap to confirm port 25 is open: nmap -p 25 mail.target.com. Step 3: Connect to the SMTP server using Telnet: telnet mail.target.com 25. Step 4: Type HELO attacker.test and wait for server response. Step 5: Enter a list of VRFY commands like VRFY john, VRFY finance, VRFY hr, one at a time. Step 6: Observe server responses: if it replies with 250 or User OK, it confirms the user exists. Step 7: Document all positive matches and note down which aliases are valid for further abuse (phishing or brute force).
Impact: Attackers can build a map of valid users, increasing social engineering attack success.
Detection Method: Monitor SMTP command logs; alert on unexpected VRFY use.
Solution: Harden SMTP gateway configurations: disable VRFY and remove unnecessary commands.

Title: Simulating Targeted Email Harvesting Before BEC
