Title: Malicious Inline Base64 SVG in Newsletter Email
Scenario Description: A base64-encoded SVG is disguised as a newsletter header image, but contains an embedded JavaScript payload that performs browser fingerprinting silently.
Tools Used: SVG Editor, JavaScript, Base64 Encoder, HTML Email Builder
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an SVG file with embedded JavaScript that collects browser info (screen resolution, OS, plugins, etc.).Step 2: This SVG is encoded into base64 and inserted in an tag like data:image/svg+xml;base64,....Step 3: The attacker builds a fake newsletter email with this SVG as the header.Step 4: The email is sent to targets with a subject like “Monthly Security Tips Newsletter.”Step 5: Victim opens the email in a browser-based client (e.g., Gmail in Chrome).Step 6: The embedded script executes inside the SVG silently and sends system info to the attacker's server.Step 7: This data is later used to tailor phishing or exploit campaigns to the user's device type.
Detection Method: Monitor unexpected outbound requests from email clients
Solution: Strip SVG from emails or sanitize SVG scripts

Title: Base64 Image Loads RAR File with Hidden Malware
Scenario Description: A base64-encoded image actually represents a .rar archive containing malware, automatically downloaded and extracted via a hidden link.
Tools Used: RAR Archiver, msfvenom, Base64 Converter, HTML Builder
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a .rar file containing a malware payload disguised as a harmless document (e.g., Report.doc.exe).Step 2: The RAR is base64-encoded and renamed with an image header (e.g., JPEG) using a hex editor.Step 3: The attacker embeds this into a fake HTML email using a data URI (data:image/jpeg;base64,...).Step 4: JavaScript in the email decodes the base64 and forces the file to be downloaded when email is opened.Step 5: Email is sent with a title like “Performance Review Results.”Step 6: Victim unknowingly saves the image (actually a RAR file) and opens it, seeing a “document”.Step 7: Double-clicking the file executes the malware, granting attacker control.
Detection Method: Unusual download events, RAR file analysis
Solution: Disallow base64 data URIs in email renderers

Title: JavaScript Loader Hidden in Base64 PNG
Scenario Description: JavaScript that loads further malicious code is inserted into the metadata of a PNG, then base64 encoded and embedded in an email image tag.
Tools Used: PNG Metadata Injector (e.g., pngcrush), Base64 Encoder, JS Loader
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a standard PNG image using any editor.Step 2: Metadata field “Description” is modified using tools like exiftool or pngcrush to include JavaScript that loads remote scripts.Step 3: The PNG is base64 encoded and embedded as an inline image in an HTML email.Step 4: HTML includes a small script to extract the metadata content and execute it.Step 5: Email is titled "Updated Team Badge Graphics".Step 6: Victim opens the email in a vulnerable client that parses image metadata and allows JS execution.Step 7: The loader executes and pulls a second-stage malware script from an attacker server.
Detection Method: Monitor outbound script calls after email open
Solution: Block metadata script processing in mail clients

Title: Password Harvesting via Transparent Login Overlay
Scenario Description: A base64 image of a login screen is embedded in an email with invisible text input fields placed precisely over the username and password areas, tricking users into entering real credentials.
Tools Used: HTML/CSS Overlay, Email Designer, Base64 Tool
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker takes a screenshot of a real login page (e.g., Microsoft 365).Step 2: Encodes this screenshot as a base64 PNG and embeds in HTML email.Step 3: Places transparent input fields using CSS position:absolute; over the username and password fields.Step 4: Scripts attached to these fields capture keystrokes and submit them to an attacker's URL.Step 5: The email is sent with a subject like “Session Timed Out – Log Back In”.Step 6: Victim enters login credentials thinking it’s legitimate.Step 7: Credentials are stolen and saved for later account takeover.
Detection Method: UI Overlay Detection, Keystroke Logging
Solution: Enforce plain-text rendering for emails with login requests

Title: Polyglot File: Image + Script Embedded Together
Scenario Description: An attacker creates a polyglot file (both valid image and script) and embeds it in base64 format in an email. Some systems misinterpret and execute the script.
Tools Used: Polyglot Builder (custom tool), Base64 Encoder, Email Composer
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a file that is a valid PNG image but also contains a script (like a Bash or JS) embedded at the end.Step 2: The file is base64 encoded and embedded in an HTML email.Step 3: Image is displayed normally, so the user sees nothing suspicious.Step 4: When saved and opened using certain file interpreters or command-line tools, the script section is executed.Step 5: Email is disguised as “Event Poster - Download for Print”.Step 6: Victim saves the file, opens it in a terminal environment or misconfigured system.Step 7: Script executes with user's permissions, compromising the device.
Detection Method: File Signature Mismatch Alerts
Solution: Sanitize file headers, avoid dual-purpose encoding

Title: Phishing Email with Encrypted Ransomware Zip
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a phishing email with a password-protected ZIP containing ransomware to bypass email filters.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a ZIP archive with ransomware (e.g., .exe file) and protects it with a password.Step 2: Attacker writes a socially engineered email claiming to send an important invoice, legal document, or job offer.Step 3: Attacker includes the password in the body of the email (e.g., "Password: Invoice123").Step 4: Victim opens the email and extracts the ZIP file using the password.Step 5: Victim opens the ransomware-laden executable, unknowingly infecting the system.Step 6: The ransomware encrypts files and demands payment.
Vulnerability: Email gateway cannot scan inside password-protected files
Impact: File encryption, data loss, ransom demand
Detection Method: Heuristic AV alerts post-execution, behavioral anomaly detection
Solution: Block password-protected attachments, user awareness training

Title: Hidden Trojan in Encrypted PDF Resume
Scenario Description: Attacker delivers an encrypted PDF claiming to be a job applicant's resume that exploits PDF vulnerabilities.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a malicious PDF embedded with a Trojan using an exploit builder.Step 2: PDF is encrypted with a user-defined password to bypass scanning.Step 3: Email is sent impersonating a job applicant with password in message body ("Password: Career2025").Step 4: HR personnel opens the encrypted PDF using Adobe Acrobat.Step 5: PDF auto-executes exploit code (if vulnerability exists), installing backdoor.Step 6: Attacker gains remote access.
Detection Method: Suspicious PDF behavior post-opening
Solution: Disable auto-exec features in PDF readers, ban encrypted attachments

Title: Business Email Compromise Using Encrypted Doc
Scenario Description: Attacker impersonates CEO and sends an encrypted DOC file to CFO asking to release payment to a vendor.
Tools Used: Microsoft Word, Encrypted ZIP, Email Spoofing
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker spoofs CEO’s email domain and writes an urgent-sounding email to CFO.Step 2: Encrypted DOC file (payment instruction) is attached, password is in email (“Password: SecurePay”).Step 3: CFO opens the document and reads the fake vendor payment request.Step 4: CFO trusts the email and proceeds to wire the money.Step 5: Funds are transferred to attacker-controlled bank.
Vulnerability: Social engineering + encrypted disguise avoids gateway filters
Impact: Financial loss due to fake transaction
Detection Method: Post-fraud investigation; delayed anomaly alerts
Solution: Enforce multi-factor approvals for payments, verify unusual requests

Title: Malware Delivery in Password-Protected Excel Sheet
Scenario Description: An attacker sends a password-protected Excel file with malicious macros to a target in the finance team.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an Excel file with embedded VBA macros that download malware.Step 2: The Excel file is encrypted with a password and saved as .xlsm.Step 3: A convincing spear-phishing email is crafted claiming the attachment contains monthly budget data.Step 4: Email includes password in plain text ("Password: Budget2025").Step 5: Victim opens the Excel sheet and enables macros.Step 6: Macros execute and fetch malware from a remote URL.Step 7: Malware installs silently.
Detection Method: Behavior-based endpoint detection
Solution: Disable macros by default, train staff on macro risks

Title: Encrypted Archive Used to Deliver Keylogger
Scenario Description: A password-protected archive is used to bypass antivirus and install a keylogger on a victim’s system.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a ZIP/RAR archive containing a disguised keylogger (e.g., invoice.scr).Step 2: Archive is password-protected to evade AV scan.Step 3: Email is sent to a small business employee with a message like: “Please find the invoice attached. Password: Client2025”.Step 4: Victim unzips and opens the disguised keylogger.Step 5: Keylogger silently installs and starts recording keystrokes.Step 6: Captured data (e.g., passwords, logins) is sent to attacker.
Vulnerability: Email filter bypass via encrypted archive
Detection Method: Unusual process behavior or network traffic
Solution: Block executable in archives, enforce attachment scanning policies

Title: Malware Hidden in Encrypted Image Archive
Scenario Description: A ZIP file with innocent-looking images (JPEGs) includes an embedded executable malware payload, sent with password protection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gathers a set of stock images.Step 2: Attacker uses a tool like ImageBinder to embed malware inside one of the images or as a hidden file.Step 3: All images are compressed into a ZIP archive with a password (e.g., “Photos2025”).Step 4: Email is sent pretending to be a friend or coworker sharing vacation or event photos.Step 5: Victim opens the archive using the password and browses the images.Step 6: One image triggers malware when previewed or opened via a vulnerable viewer.Step 7: Malware installs silently.
Vulnerability: Antivirus can't scan inside encrypted files
Detection Method: Behavior monitoring post-image opening
Solution: Disable opening unknown archives, educate users

Title: Supply Chain Email with Encrypted Quotation
Scenario Description: An attacker impersonates a supplier and sends an encrypted Excel sheet with macros to procurement staff.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a fake supplier identity (domain spoofed or typo domain).Step 2: Creates an Excel quotation sheet with hidden macros that download malware.Step 3: File is encrypted (password: “Quote2025”) and sent to procurement team.Step 4: Email says: “Please review the quotation in the attached file.”Step 5: Victim opens file, enables macros to view content.Step 6: Macros download spyware or ransomware.Step 7: Malware takes control of system or exfiltrates data.
Detection Method: Suspicious macro activity, beaconing
Solution: Disallow encrypted files from unknown senders

Title: Credential Harvester in Encrypted PDF Survey
Scenario Description: A fake survey form in PDF format collects login credentials and sends them to attacker. File is encrypted to evade detection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker designs a fake “Employee Satisfaction Survey” PDF form.Step 2: PDF has embedded form fields requesting corporate email and password.Step 3: PDF is password-protected and emailed with password “Survey2025”.Step 4: Email says it's an official HR activity.Step 5: Victim opens the PDF, fills in login credentials, clicks “Submit.”Step 6: Data is silently sent to attacker via embedded script or email backend.Step 7: Attacker logs in using harvested credentials.
Vulnerability: Email filters can’t read encrypted file content
Detection Method: Login anomalies, MFA push spam
Solution: Disable form auto-submit features, awareness training

Title: Encrypted Archive Shared via File Hosting Link
Scenario Description: Instead of attaching a file, the attacker uploads a password-protected malware archive to Dropbox/Google Drive and shares the link via email.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads a malicious .ZIP file to Dropbox, encrypting it with a password (e.g., “Client2025”).Step 2: File contains obfuscated malware or stealer.exe.Step 3: Attacker sends a phishing email with a message like “Here’s the contract you requested” and includes the link.Step 4: Victim clicks the link and downloads the encrypted archive.Step 5: Victim opens the archive using the provided password.Step 6: Victim double-clicks the executable, which installs malware.Step 7: System is compromised, data starts exfiltrating.
Vulnerability: Email security bypassed via off-email delivery
Detection Method: Suspicious network connection post-download
Solution: Block external file sharing platforms by policy

Title: Executable Renamed as PDF Inside Encrypted Archive
Scenario Description: A file named “report.pdf” inside an encrypted archive is actually an executable (report.pdf.exe), tricking the user into running malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious .exe file and renames it to “report.pdf.exe.”Step 2: Uses icon changer to give it a PDF icon, making it look harmless.Step 3: Archive it in a ZIP with password protection (“Confidential2025”).Step 4: Email is sent pretending to share a sensitive report.Step 5: Victim opens archive and sees a file named “report.pdf” (extensions hidden).Step 6: Victim double-clicks, thinking it's a PDF, executing the malware.Step 7: Malware installs keylogger or reverse shell.
Vulnerability: File extension spoofing inside encrypted archive
Detection Method: Suspicious processes, EDR alerts
Solution: Force file extensions visible, disable ZIPs with .exe

Title: Password-Protected Zip Carrying Reverse Shell Payload
Scenario Description: A protected archive contains a reverse shell script disguised as a shell utility, tricking a Linux admin into executing it.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a bash script named “server_cleaner.sh” that opens a reverse shell.Step 2: Places script into a password-protected .zip file (“Cleaner2025”).Step 3: Sends email to sysadmin claiming urgent cleanup task is pending.Step 4: Victim downloads and unzips using password.Step 5: Executes shell script, believing it’s legitimate.Step 6: Shell connects back to attacker.Step 7: Attacker has remote control of system.
Detection Method: Outbound connection to unusual IP
Solution: Educate admins on reverse shell threats

Title: Malicious Screensaver in Encrypted Archive
Scenario Description: A .scr file (Windows screensaver executable) disguised as a company announcement is embedded inside a password-protected archive.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a .scr file that acts as malware (screensaver + keylogger).Step 2: File is renamed “Announcement.scr” and zipped with password “Secure2025.”Step 3: Email subject reads “New Policy Announcement” from fake HR address.Step 4: Victim opens archive and clicks the .scr file.Step 5: Keylogger installs and begins recording.Step 6: Data is sent to attacker’s server.
Vulnerability: SCR file bypasses user suspicion via file disguise
Detection Method: Suspicious .scr usage
Solution: Block unknown file types in attachments

Title: Embedded Script in Encrypted HTML Email Attachment
Scenario Description: Attacker sends an encrypted .HTML file attachment containing a script that steals browser session cookies.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a malicious HTML file that mimics a login form and includes JS to steal session cookies.Step 2: Encrypts the HTML with ZIP and password-protects (“HTML2025”).Step 3: Sends phishing email: “Login to confirm your email changes.”Step 4: Victim opens HTML, sees familiar login screen.Step 5: Enters login, script steals credentials and cookies.Step 6: Attacker replays session using stolen cookies.
Vulnerability: HTML scripts hidden from scanners via encryption
Detection Method: Unusual session activity
Solution: Disable HTML attachments; block encrypted ZIPs

Title: Multistage Encrypted Archive Delivery
Scenario Description: An attacker sends an encrypted archive containing another encrypted file, layering obfuscation to confuse security tools.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create malware payload and hide it inside an encrypted ZIP.Step 2: Encrypt this ZIP again inside another archive.Step 3: Name the outer ZIP “Reports2025” and send via email.Step 4: Victim opens outer ZIP with password, sees another protected ZIP (“Password: Next2025”).Step 5: Finally opens inner archive and runs executable.Step 6: Malware installs, connects to C2.
Detection Method: Endpoint alerts on final payload execution
Solution: Disallow nested encrypted archives

Title: Dynamic Payload Delivered via Encrypted Attachment
Scenario Description: An encrypted attachment contains a small loader that downloads actual malware post-decryption.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a lightweight executable loader.Step 2: Loader is compressed into an encrypted ZIP (“Secure2025”).Step 3: Sent to target with convincing message: “Please run this security update tool.”Step 4: Victim opens the loader, which fetches malware from attacker server.Step 5: Actual payload (ransomware, spyware) is installed silently.Step 6: System becomes compromised.
Vulnerability: Malware not included in initial archive; downloaded later
Detection Method: DNS/HTTP anomalies post-launch
Solution: Restrict outbound traffic, use EDR

Title: HR Payslip Containing Encrypted Infostealer
Scenario Description: An attacker sends a fake payslip to HR containing a password-protected Excel file embedded with a macro that installs an infostealer.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake salary payslip using Excel.Step 2: Attacker uses a tool like EvilClippy to embed an obfuscated macro in the Excel sheet.Step 3: The Excel file is password-protected and zipped with the password “Pay@2025”.Step 4: A phishing email is sent to HR saying: “Attached is my updated bank info and payslip for payroll. Please review.”Step 5: HR opens the zip and Excel file using the password and enables macros to view it.Step 6: The macro installs an infostealer that collects browser-stored credentials and sends them to the attacker.Step 7: Attacker uses the stolen credentials to log in to internal systems.
Vulnerability: Obfuscated macro hidden inside encrypted Excel
Detection Method: Endpoint detection systems post-macro execution
Solution: Block macro-enabled documents unless verified

Title: Financial Update Request with Encrypted JS Downloader
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a password-protected ZIP file containing a disguised .js downloader script that installs malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a JavaScript file (update.js) that silently downloads malware from a remote server.Step 2: File is renamed to look like a document (e.g., “update.doc.js”) and placed in a ZIP archive.Step 3: ZIP file is password-protected using “Update2025”.Step 4: Email impersonates the finance department and says: “Please review the attached financial update script.”Step 5: Victim opens ZIP and sees the “.doc.js” file with an icon resembling a Word document.Step 6: Victim double-clicks, unknowingly running the script.Step 7: Script connects to attacker’s server, downloads malware, and infects the system.
Vulnerability: JS disguised as DOC file and hidden via encryption
Detection Method: Firewall logs, suspicious .js execution from user directory
Solution: Block JavaScript attachments; block passworded ZIPs

Title: Board Meeting Minutes with Encrypted RAT Installer
Scenario Description: Fake meeting minutes shared via password-protected Word doc, which runs a script installing a Remote Access Trojan (RAT).
Tools Used: MS Word, Obfuscation Tools, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a Word document titled “Board_Minutes_2025.docm” and embeds malicious VBA code.Step 2: The doc is compressed in a password-protected ZIP (“Board2025”).Step 3: Attacker sends email to top executives posing as the company secretary, stating “Minutes from last board meeting attached.”Step 4: Executives open the ZIP and enter the password to access the file.Step 5: When the document is opened, macros run silently and install a RAT.Step 6: Attacker gains full remote access to the victim’s machine.Step 7: Sensitive executive communications are monitored and exfiltrated.
Detection Method: Suspicious outbound C2 traffic from executive laptops
Solution: Block macros, validate sender identity for board emails

Title: Legal Contract Delivery with Double-Extension Malware
Scenario Description: A ZIP file contains a file named “Contract.pdf.exe” with a PDF icon. The double-extension fools users into executing malware.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares malware and renames it “Contract.pdf.exe.”Step 2: They change the icon to a standard Adobe PDF icon to disguise the true nature of the file.Step 3: File is placed in a ZIP archive and protected with the password “Legal2025”.Step 4: Email is crafted impersonating a legal firm: “Please find the signed agreement enclosed.”Step 5: Victim downloads and unzips the file.Step 6: Because of Windows hiding extensions by default, victim sees it as “Contract.pdf” and opens it.Step 7: The disguised .exe runs and installs ransomware.
Vulnerability: User tricked by file naming and ZIP encryption
Impact: Ransomware encryption of critical legal files
Detection Method: Files encrypted and renamed with ransom note
Solution: Show file extensions, block .exe in ZIPs

Title: Shared Password File Used to Deliver Credential Stealer
Scenario Description: A ZIP archive claims to contain saved passwords, but actually installs a credential stealer when opened.
Tools Used: Password Manager Export, Keylogger, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker simulates an exported “Password List” from a password manager as a CSV file.Step 2: Real CSV file is replaced with a keylogger executable renamed “passwords.csv.exe.”Step 3: File is zipped and encrypted with password “Passwords2025.”Step 4: Victim receives email saying: “Here’s the exported password file you requested.”Step 5: User unzips and opens the disguised file.Step 6: Keylogger installs and begins capturing login data.Step 7: Data is exfiltrated to attacker in real-time.
Vulnerability: Credential stealer bypasses detection via file disguise
Detection Method: Sudden increase in login attempts from new IPs
Solution: Enforce filename validation, detect hidden extensions

Title: Spoofed S/MIME-Signed Email with Malicious Link
Scenario Description: An attacker sends a spoofed email that appears digitally signed using S/MIME to trick users into clicking a malicious link.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker sets up a fake email domain resembling a trusted one (e.g., "admin@support-secure.com"). Step 2: Generates a self-signed S/MIME certificate using OpenSSL. Step 3: Attaches the certificate to their email client like Thunderbird. Step 4: Crafts an email saying "Your invoice is ready. Click here." and signs it with the fake S/MIME cert. Step 5: Embeds a malicious shortened URL leading to a malware payload. Step 6: Sends the email to the target. Step 7: The victim sees the email as "digitally signed," thinks it's safe, and clicks the link.
Vulnerability: Trust in visual indicators of S/MIME
Detection Method: Email header analysis, inspect cert chain
Solution: Implement domain-based email certificate validation, disable self-signed cert trust

Title: Legit S/MIME Signature, Reused with Malicious Content
Scenario Description: Attacker reuses a genuine S/MIME-signed email, replaces the content, but keeps the original signature block to deceive users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker intercepts a legit signed email from a user via network sniffing or inbox access. Step 2: Saves the signed email file (.eml) and opens it using a Hex Editor. Step 3: Identifies and extracts the signed portion. Step 4: Replaces the message content (e.g., replaces “Hello” with a phishing request), keeping the signature visually intact. Step 5: Sends the manipulated message back to the victim or others in the organization. Step 6: User sees the original signature and assumes the altered message is authentic.
Detection Method: Full S/MIME validation using tools like Outlook security log
Solution: Force integrity check between body & signature

Title: Compromised Certificate Used to Send Trusted Phishing Emails
Scenario Description: The attacker gains access to a real user's S/MIME private key and sends emails impersonating them.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker gains access to victim’s machine. Step 2: Uses Mimikatz to extract the victim's PFX file containing their S/MIME certificate. Step 3: Converts the certificate into a usable format using openssl or certutil. Step 4: Loads the certificate into an email client. Step 5: Crafts a phishing email (e.g., “HR Policy Update - Action Required”) and signs it with the real cert. Step 6: Sends it to internal users, who trust the sender and the signature.
Detection Method: Monitor certificate usage logs, alert on unusual signers
Solution: Store S/MIME certs securely, enable cert revocation alerts

Title: Certificate Authority Trick to Issue Lookalike Cert
Scenario Description: Attacker tricks a CA into issuing a certificate for a domain that looks similar to a real one.
Tools Used: Namecheap, Free S/MIME CA (Actalis), Fake Email Clients
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker registers a domain like "mycompany-secure.com". Step 2: Requests a free S/MIME cert for "ceo@mycompany-secure.com" from a CA like Actalis. Step 3: Sets up a mailbox and imports the cert into a client. Step 4: Sends an urgent email to finance@company.com claiming to be the CEO. Step 5: Adds a real-looking signature like “Sent from my iPhone” and attaches the S/MIME signature. Step 6: The finance employee sees a digitally signed message and complies with a fund transfer.
Detection Method: DLP tools, domain similarity scanners
Solution: Restrict S/MIME trust to known domains & certs

Title: MIME Confusion Attack to Bypass S/MIME Verification
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits how email clients handle MIME parts to include unsigned malicious content in a signed email.
Tools Used: Custom Python Script, Thunderbird, MIME Parser Tools
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes a multipart email with two MIME sections — one benign and signed, the other unsigned but malicious. Step 2: Signs only the benign section (e.g., “Hello, here’s the report”). Step 3: Adds the second section with hidden malicious text or scripts. Step 4: Structures MIME headers so that some clients only show the unsigned section. Step 5: Sends the email to targets using Thunderbird. Step 6: On the victim's email client, the displayed content is from the unsigned part, but it appears as a signed email.
Detection Method: Analyze MIME structure using forensic tools
Solution: Use strict MIME validation and S/MIME-aware clients

Title: S/MIME Downgrade to Plain Email
Scenario Description: An attacker strips S/MIME signatures from emails in transit so recipients get unsigned versions, unaware of tampering.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker intercepts email traffic using a tool like Wireshark or Burp Suite MITM proxy. Step 2: Identifies emails with S/MIME signature headers. Step 3: Modifies the email MIME structure, removing the "application/pkcs7-signature" parts. Step 4: Optionally replaces content with phishing links. Step 5: Forwards the email to the recipient. Step 6: The user receives the email with no digital signature warning and trusts the contents.
Detection Method: Compare sent vs. received message logs
Solution: Enforce S/MIME integrity check at client side

Title: Fake S/MIME Signature from Expired Certificate
Scenario Description: An attacker signs an email using an expired certificate that appears valid in some clients.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds an old expired S/MIME certificate (can be harvested from public email). Step 2: Uses OpenSSL to sign a new message with the expired cert. Step 3: Sends an urgent message like “Password Reset Notice” to users. Step 4: Some outdated email clients still mark the message as signed without checking the expiration. Step 5: Victim opens the message and clicks on the phishing link.
Detection Method: Check cert expiry in logs and headers
Solution: Enforce up-to-date clients with strict S/MIME validation

Title: Dual Email Display Exploit with S/MIME
Scenario Description: Attackers use a trick where the signed part is benign, but the client displays a different message.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a multi-part email with a signed part saying “Please ignore this test email.” Step 2: Adds a second HTML section outside the signed part that contains phishing content. Step 3: Signs only the first (benign) section. Step 4: Structures headers so some clients prioritize the unsigned HTML portion. Step 5: Sends the crafted email to users. Step 6: Email clients show the unsigned content but still display a "signed" badge.
Detection Method: Forensic MIME structure analysis
Solution: Use MIME-secure email clients

Title: Reused Legit Signature with Changed Display Name
Scenario Description: Attacker uses a valid cert with fake display name to trick users into trusting emails.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker requests a cert using a free CA with email “ceo@fakeco.com” and name “CEO John Smith”. Step 2: Crafts a phishing message and signs it with the cert. Step 3: Sends to employee who sees the display name “CEO John Smith” and the green "Signed" icon. Step 4: Employee assumes it's the real CEO and clicks the provided invoice link.
Detection Method: Header parsing to verify address vs cert
Solution: Use email policies with address cert matching

Title: S/MIME Certificate Chain Spoofing
Scenario Description: Attacker creates a fake certificate chain that appears trusted due to client misconfiguration.
Tools Used: XCA (X.509 CA Tool), Burp, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a fake root certificate using XCA. Step 2: Signs an S/MIME certificate for a fake user like “admin@secure-team.com” using the fake root. Step 3: Adds the fake root to a victim’s machine via social engineering or malware. Step 4: Sends signed emails that appear trusted. Step 5: Victim opens email and sees it as “secure” due to trusted chain.
Detection Method: Root cert inventory monitoring
Solution: Restrict root cert installs, validate cert chains

Title: Embedded Macro Doc in S/MIME Signed Mail
Scenario Description: Attackers deliver a macro-embedded document in a signed message to bypass spam filters.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a malicious macro-enabled Word doc using msfvenom. Step 2: Signs an email using a legit S/MIME cert. Step 3: Attaches the macro doc and includes text like “See attached for project plan.” Step 4: Sends it to user who sees it's signed and opens the doc. Step 5: Victim enables macros, triggering malware execution.
Detection Method: Alert on doc macro + S/MIME signed match
Solution: Block macro attachments in S/MIME emails

Title: Forwarded Signed Email with Malicious Link Inserted
Scenario Description: Attacker forwards a legit signed email but adds malicious content before sending.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker receives a signed email from a colleague. Step 2: Clicks “Forward,” adds malicious text at the top (e.g., “FYI, download latest software here”), and keeps original message below. Step 3: Forwards it to internal users. Step 4: Email client shows message as "signed" even though only the bottom portion is. Step 5: Victims trust the top text due to signature display.
Detection Method: Alert on signed-forward chain mismatches
Solution: Show S/MIME coverage clearly in clients

Title: S/MIME Signature Collisions Exploit
Scenario Description: Exploits MD5 collisions in outdated clients to forge a valid S/MIME signature for fake content.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts two messages with same MD5 hash using Hashclash. Step 2: One message contains “Safe info,” the other has phishing content. Step 3: Gets legitimate cert to sign the “Safe” version. Step 4: Swaps in the malicious version but keeps the signature. Step 5: Sends it to old clients vulnerable to MD5 weakness.
Detection Method: Block MD5-signed messages
Solution: Use SHA256+ S/MIME policy

Title: Auto-Imported S/MIME Cert for Trust Abuse
Scenario Description: Attacker sends signed email, and client auto-trusts the sender cert for future mail.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker signs an email using their own S/MIME cert. Step 2: Sends it to victim’s email client (like Outlook). Step 3: Outlook auto-imports cert and marks sender as trusted. Step 4: Attacker later sends phishing email; client doesn’t warn.
Detection Method: Alert on auto-cert imports
Solution: Disable auto-import of sender certs

Title: Malformed S/MIME Signature Causing Client Bypass
Scenario Description: Attacker crafts a corrupt signature block that causes email clients to skip verification but still show “signed”.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sends a normal signed email, saves it as .eml. Step 2: Edits the PKCS7 signature in Hex Editor to inject garbage bytes. Step 3: Sends malformed email to victim. Step 4: Some email clients ignore signature errors and still show a signed icon. Step 5: Victim trusts and clicks on phishing links.
Detection Method: Email signature validation logs
Solution: Force strict parsing on clients

Title: Email Signing with Revoked Certificate
Scenario Description: Attacker signs phishing emails with a certificate that has been revoked, but recipients don’t get warned due to client misconfiguration.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker obtains a certificate from a CA and lets it get revoked (e.g., due to reported compromise). Step 2: Despite revocation, attacker continues using it to sign phishing emails. Step 3: Sends emails with links to fake login pages, appearing “signed and trusted.” Step 4: Many email clients fail to check Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) or OCSP responses. Step 5: Recipient sees email as validly signed and follows the instructions.
Detection Method: Analyze client CRL/OCSP validation behavior
Solution: Enforce real-time revocation checks in policy

Title: Spoofing Using Public Directory Certificates
Scenario Description: Attacker misuses a legitimate employee's publicly available S/MIME certificate to send deceptive messages.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker scrapes public employee S/MIME certs from company LDAP or key servers. Step 2: Configures email client with a spoofed sender address (e.g., “it-support@company.com”). Step 3: Sends unsigned phishing email but attaches the real employee’s S/MIME public cert. Step 4: Some email clients confuse the signature identity with the attached cert and display false trust. Step 5: Recipient sees familiar name and believes it’s legit, clicking malicious links.
Detection Method: Scan headers vs. attached cert owner
Solution: Train users to check sender address, not just name

Title: Attachment Tampering on Signed Email Forward
Scenario Description: Attacker modifies attachments in a signed email chain by forwarding it with new, malicious versions.
Tools Used: Email Client, File Renamer, PDF Exploit
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker receives a signed email with a PDF attachment from HR. Step 2: Clicks "Forward" and removes the signed attachment. Step 3: Replaces it with a malicious PDF (e.g., with embedded JavaScript exploit). Step 4: Adds short message like “Resending this HR doc for your review.” Step 5: Recipient sees original sender's signed message below and opens the fake attachment thinking it’s the same.
Vulnerability: Lack of signature integrity on attachments when forwarding
Detection Method: Compare attachment hash with original email
Solution: Force signing of attachments or block unsigned forwards

Title: Bait and Switch Attack Using Signed Redirector
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a signed link to a trusted redirector (like bit.ly), which later redirects to malicious content.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a bit.ly link that initially points to a safe website (e.g., https://example.com). Step 2: Sends a signed email saying “Please check this link for your schedule.” Step 3: After some time, attacker changes the bit.ly redirect to a phishing or malware site. Step 4: Victim re-opens the email later and clicks the link, unaware it has changed. Step 5: Since email was signed, they assume the link is trustworthy.
Detection Method: Monitor behavior of shortened links over time
Solution: Ban shortened links in signed emails

Title: Certificate Injection in S/MIME Message Structure
Scenario Description: Attacker manipulates the message structure to inject an unrelated certificate for confusing the trust logic.
Tools Used: MIME Editor, Hex Editor, Email Client
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a multipart message with signed and unsigned parts. Step 2: In the MIME header, includes unrelated certificate in an inline block. Step 3: Some email clients read this injected cert and assume it’s the trusted one. Step 4: Email appears as signed by a legitimate user even though the signature doesn’t match. Step 5: Victim acts on malicious message assuming it's from a trusted contact.
Vulnerability: Trust confusion due to MIME injection
Detection Method: Use S/MIME validation logs to trace cert origin
Solution: Disallow MIME-based cert injection in policy

Title: Mapping Active Email Users via Bounce-back Probing
Scenario Description: An attacker sends emails to a list of email addresses on the target domain. By observing which emails bounce and which do not, the attacker identifies active email users.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare a list of email addresses you want to test (e.g., alice@company.com, bob@company.com, xyz@company.com).Step 2: Use a basic email script to send messages to each address.Step 3: Monitor your inbox for bounce-back replies (e.g., “User not found” or “Invalid address”).Step 4: Mark which addresses caused bounce-backs. Emails that don’t bounce are likely active accounts.Step 5: Create a final list of active user accounts for further phishing or enumeration.
Impact: Attacker builds a verified list of valid email IDs
Detection Method: Monitor for excessive failed deliveries; rate-limiting; logging
Solution: Disable SMTP user enumeration; use generic bounce messages

Title: Enumerating Usernames via Case-Sensitive Bounces
Scenario Description: The attacker tests casing (e.g., John.Doe vs john.doe) to detect if case-sensitive usernames leak info via bounce messages.
Tools Used: SendEmail CLI tool, SMTP test servers
Attack Steps: Step 1: Choose a known username like john.doe.Step 2: Send emails using variations like John.Doe, JOHN.DOE, jOhn.dOe.Step 3: Observe the bounce-back messages.Step 4: Some systems may return “no such user” for case mismatch, revealing exact casing.Step 5: Use correctly cased usernames in future phishing for credibility.
Impact: Helps in precise social engineering/phishing attacks
Detection Method: Monitor bounce-back patterns; casing discrepancies in logs
Solution: Normalize email casing internally; generic error messages

Title: Probing Mail Servers with Random Emails to Detect Catch-all
Scenario Description: The attacker sends email to a completely random user at the target domain to test if the domain has a catch-all mailbox (where all unknown emails go to one inbox).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Pick a target domain (e.g., company.com).Step 2: Send an email to a fake user (e.g., fakeuser123@company.com).Step 3: If no bounce-back is received, the domain may be using a catch-all.Step 4: Send a few more random emails to confirm behavior.Step 5: Use this info to send spam/phishing emails that still land in someone's inbox.
Impact: Attackers gain confidence that any email sent will reach someone
Detection Method: Detect unexpected delivery to undefined users
Solution: Disable catch-all or monitor it tightly

Title: Exploiting Third-party Bounce Relays to Leak Info
Scenario Description: An attacker spoofs an email with an invalid “From” address and sends it to a third party, forcing the bounce message to return to their spoofed address and reveal headers or server info.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Craft a fake email with a forged “From” (e.g., admin@target.com).Step 2: Send the email to a non-existent recipient on a third-party domain.Step 3: The third-party mail server tries to deliver, fails, and sends a bounce to the forged address.Step 4: Monitor logs or inbox to capture the bounce, which may include headers or network paths.Step 5: Analyze headers to learn about the internal mail relay path or server tech.
Impact: May leak internal routing info or mail server names
Detection Method: Monitor relaying behavior and bounced headers
Solution: Strip internal headers before relaying externally

Title: Timing-based Enumeration via Bounce Response Delays
Scenario Description: Attacker observes how long a server takes to respond with bounce messages to infer if a user exists. Faster bounces indicate invalid users; slower may indicate internal checking.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send emails to known invalid addresses and valid-looking ones (e.g., invalid123@company.com vs jsmith@company.com).Step 2: Measure how long it takes to get a bounce response.Step 3: Faster bounces typically mean the user doesn't exist and is rejected immediately.Step 4: Slower responses may indicate the server tried to route it internally, suggesting a valid user.Step 5: Create a list of likely valid emails based on timing analysis.
Impact: Build a filtered list of valid users stealthily
Detection Method: Analyze delivery timing logs; threshold monitoring
Solution: Use constant delay for all rejections

Title: Harvesting Email Address Formats via Auto-Responder Bounces
Scenario Description: The attacker sends emails to invalid addresses at a target domain. Some systems send auto-responses revealing the correct format (e.g., john.smith@domain.com) or department emails.
Tools Used: Custom email script, Gmail, Mailgun Sandbox
Attack Steps: Step 1: Prepare a list of invalid user emails at a domain (e.g., abc123@corp.com).Step 2: Send emails with a subject like “Resume Submission” to increase chances of response.Step 3: Wait for auto-responder or bounce messages that suggest alternate or correct addresses.Step 4: Example response: “Please email HR at hr@corp.com”.Step 5: Note exposed addresses and add them to your recon database.
Vulnerability: Misconfigured auto-responders or helpful bounce templates
Impact: Leads to discovery of hidden or departmental addresses
Detection Method: Monitor outbound auto-replies for excessive info
Solution: Use generic autoresponder messages

Title: Directory Harvesting with Alphabet Soup Bounces
Scenario Description: The attacker sends a large number of emails using alphabetical combinations (e.g., a@domain.com, ab@domain.com) and detects valid users by bounce patterns.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Generate a list of possible usernames (a, aa, ab, abc, adam, alice).Step 2: Send emails to each of these addresses.Step 3: Monitor bounce-back behavior — no bounce may mean valid address.Step 4: Sort addresses based on no response vs bounce.Step 5: Build a list of potential valid addresses for future phishing.
Vulnerability: No rate-limiting or tarpitting for invalid users
Impact: Mass discovery of valid emails from pattern-based attacks
Detection Method: Alert for mass delivery failures; detect SMTP rate anomalies
Solution: Enable tarpitting and delay responses

Title: Using Non-delivery Reports to Profile Mail Gateway
Scenario Description: Bounced messages sometimes contain detailed error codes or headers showing mail gateway types (e.g., Barracuda, Microsoft EOP), helping attacker tailor future payloads.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send email to fakeuser@target.com.Step 2: Wait for Non-delivery Report (NDR) or bounce message.Step 3: Analyze message headers for clues (e.g., “Generated by Barracuda”, “EOP Error Code 550 5.1.1”).Step 4: Identify mail security product in use.Step 5: Use that info to prepare bypass methods or malware compatible with the known gateway.
Impact: Attackers adjust attacks based on mail protection in use
Detection Method: Log analysis of outbound NDRs; header inspections
Solution: Configure gateways to strip product identifiers in messages

Title: Language-based Bounce Analysis to Infer Locale
Scenario Description: An attacker observes the language of bounce messages to determine a target user’s regional or language preferences, helping craft believable phishing.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send emails to invalid addresses on international domains (e.g., jhondoe@domain.fr).Step 2: Observe bounce-back messages and their language — French, German, Spanish, etc.Step 3: Use this to infer user’s primary language and possibly country.Step 4: Use language-specific phishing content in future attacks.Step 5: Localize future social engineering accordingly.
Impact: Increases phishing success through targeted language
Detection Method: Analyze outgoing language patterns in bounce replies
Solution: Standardize to English or neutral language for error messages

Title: Reverse Bounce Enumeration via Spoofed From Field
Scenario Description: Attacker spoofs the "From" address to be another user at the target org. When sent to a fake recipient, bounce goes to the spoofed victim, creating confusion or leak.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Set up a custom SMTP sender.Step 2: Forge “From” address as alice@target.com.Step 3: Send to a non-existent email at another org (e.g., xyz@victim.com).Step 4: Bounce reply goes to alice@target.com from victim.com’s mail server.Step 5: Alice may report it or attacker can monitor confusion level and email headers.
Impact: Confusion, phishing prep, or indirect recon
Detection Method: Monitor spoofed “From” abuse; DMARC/SPF logs
Solution: Enforce SPF, DKIM, DMARC

Title: Subdomain Probing via MX Bounce Trails
Scenario Description: Attacker sends email to invalid user at a specific subdomain (e.g., support.mail.domain.com). Bounce error may show routing path or real subdomain mail config.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Discover company subdomains (e.g., via crt.sh, DNS dump).Step 2: Send emails to fake users at those subdomains.Step 3: Observe error messages for routing paths — e.g., mx.support.mail.domain.com.Step 4: Use info to map internal infrastructure.Step 5: Target those servers or domains in future exploits.
Vulnerability: MX routing leak via bounce headers
Impact: Mail infrastructure mapping & attack surface expansion
Detection Method: Inspect email headers; monitor mail logs
Solution: Restrict external mail to subdomains; generic errors

Title: Testing Spam Filters via Rejected Bounce Patterns
Scenario Description: By triggering bounce-backs for messages with slightly spammy content, attacker detects how aggressive spam filters are.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send test emails to fake addresses with varying levels of “spammy” words (e.g., FREE MONEY, ACT NOW).Step 2: Observe how the mail server reacts — immediate rejection, soft bounce, or normal bounce.Step 3: Infer the filtering threshold.Step 4: Tune future payloads to avoid rejection.Step 5: Deliver malware or phishing that bypasses the spam filter.
Impact: Increased success rate of phishing/malware delivery
Detection Method: Log message rejection reasons; tweak spam filter alerts
Solution: Customize bounce templates to hide rules

Title: Detecting Email Archiving Services via Header Trails
Scenario Description: Bounce messages often contain delivery trails (Received headers), which may reveal if email archiving services (e.g., Mimecast, Proofpoint) are used.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send email to invalid address at target.Step 2: Review bounce-back headers.Step 3: Look for mentions of third-party archiving or journaling services.Step 4: Learn if copies are retained, archived, or scanned.Step 5: Prepare for future attacks avoiding detection (e.g., time-based delivery).
Impact: Helps attackers understand mail flow and compliance tools
Detection Method: Strip or shorten header trails; avoid revealing archivers
Solution: Header redaction on bounce via mail config

Title: Using SMTP Greeting Bounces for Recon
Scenario Description: Some servers include their software/version in SMTP greeting or error messages during bounce generation. Attacker uses this for fingerprinting.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Connect to mail server via telnet or script.Step 2: Send a malformed email or to a bad recipient.Step 3: Review bounce or SMTP 550 error.Step 4: Read server greeting or error — e.g., “Exim 4.94.2” or “Sendmail 8.14.7”.Step 5: Use info to look up known exploits or bugs.
Impact: Leads to tailored exploitation of mail server software
Detection Method: Filter server banners; log strange probing
Solution: Configure server to suppress version in errors

Title: Detection of Shadow Mailboxes via Silent Deliveries
Scenario Description: Attacker sends email to an unknown alias. If no bounce is received, and email logs show silent delivery, attacker confirms existence of hidden "shadow" accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send email to a likely fake or mistyped alias (e.g., sysadminnn@domain.com).Step 2: Wait for bounce. If none received, log into test inbox or check delivery tracking.Step 3: Observe that mail was silently accepted.Step 4: This could be a monitored or shadow mailbox used by admin.Step 5: Use in further social engineering or phishing.
Impact: Exploitable alias or hidden inboxes become phishing targets
Detection Method: Alert on unregistered address deliveries
Solution: Block non-defined mailboxes or alert on unknowns

Title: Bounce Loop Detection via Forged Sender & Recipient
Scenario Description: Attacker manipulates email headers so bounce messages loop indefinitely between servers or mailboxes, revealing routing behavior and misconfigurations.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Create a custom email where both the sender and recipient fields point to fake or misconfigured addresses (e.g., bounce@target.com → bounce@target.com).Step 2: Send this email using an open SMTP tool.Step 3: If the server is misconfigured, it may generate a bounce, which also bounces back again.Step 4: Observe whether the email loops or results in repeated bounce-backs.Step 5: Review headers to discover server behavior and message flow.Step 6: If loops are confirmed, this exposes system misconfiguration and routing paths.
Vulnerability: Mail loop vulnerability due to faulty bounce handling
Impact: Can flood systems or reveal sensitive mail paths
Detection Method: Monitor for repeated NDRs from same addresses
Solution: Implement bounce loop protection; set TTL on NDRs

Title: Bounce Header Injection via Fake Email Source
Scenario Description: By crafting malicious header content, the attacker triggers bounce messages that carry injected data back to unsuspecting recipients or systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Write a custom email where a header like “Reply-To” contains script or malicious-looking content (e.g., <script>alert('XSS')</script>).Step 2: Send this email to an invalid recipient at a domain.Step 3: Wait for the bounce-back message.Step 4: Observe that some servers may reflect the custom header in the bounce.Step 5: If received by a human (e.g., support staff), this may result in reflected code execution or confusion.Step 6: Can be used for phishing or XSS reconnaissance.
Impact: Reflected content in NDR can be used for phishing or misdirection
Detection Method: Log unusual header patterns in NDRs
Solution: Sanitize all headers before generating bounce

Title: Identifying Email Aliases through Bounce Cross-testing
Scenario Description: The attacker sends emails to multiple variations of a name (e.g., j.doe, jdoe, john.doe), checking which one gets no bounce to identify aliases or email routing rules.
Tools Used: SMTP Enum Tool, Excel for tracking
Attack Steps: Step 1: Pick a target identity (e.g., John Doe).Step 2: Generate multiple email variations: john.doe@, j.doe@, jdoe@, john@.Step 3: Send test emails to each of them.Step 4: Track which ones bounce back with “user not found” errors and which don’t.Step 5: The non-bouncing emails are likely working aliases or catch-all rules.Step 6: Use the active alias for spear phishing or password reset abuse.
Vulnerability: Alias routing reveals valid users via bounce pattern
Impact: Discovery of alternate addresses to reach target
Detection Method: Analyze logs for alias misuse or pattern attacks
Solution: Disable verbose NDRs for aliases; alert on multi-variant probes

Title: Social Engineering via Redirected Bounce
Scenario Description: An attacker uses bounce behavior to trick internal users into believing they missed an important message, leveraging human curiosity and urgency.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send a spoofed email to a high-profile employee using a fake “From” like ceo@company.com and an invalid recipient like wrong@partner.com.Step 2: Bounce is routed to the fake “From”, which could be a monitored inbox.Step 3: Attacker forwards the bounce to the real target, saying “Looks like this failed, can you take a look?”Step 4: The forwarded bounce contains the spoofed content and may convince user it was a real message that failed.Step 5: This creates an entry point for manipulation or phishing.
Impact: Trick users into opening fake messages or attachments
Detection Method: Monitor forwarding patterns of NDRs
Solution: Educate users on bounce phishing tactics

Title: Bounce Domain Comparison to Discover Email Routing Vendor
Scenario Description: Attacker compares return-path/bounce domains to identify whether email is routed via third-party providers like Google Workspace, Outlook365, or ProtonMail.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Send a test email to a fake user at the target domain (e.g., noreply@target.com).Step 2: When bounce is received, analyze the domain used in the “Return-Path”, “Received” or “Message-ID” fields.Step 3: Domains like mail.protection.outlook.com, smtp.gmail.com give away mail provider.Step 4: Based on this info, attacker tailors payloads compatible with vendor-specific filtering.Step 5: Also helps in identifying if organization is using hosted vs. on-premise mail.
Vulnerability: External bounce trail leaks email routing infrastructure
Impact: Helps attacker craft vendor-specific evasion payloads
Detection Method: Monitor bounce headers for provider info
Solution: Obfuscate or anonymize outbound mail headers

Title: Zero-Day in PDF Reader via HR Email
Scenario Description: Attacker sends a fake job offer PDF using a zero-day vulnerability in a popular PDF reader.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker crafts a realistic job offer email with a malicious PDF file pretending to be a job description. Step 2: The PDF is embedded with a zero-day vulnerability (e.g., buffer overflow in PDF parser). Step 3: Attacker spoofs an HR recruiter email to seem legitimate (e.g., hr@bigfirmcareers.com). Step 4: Target opens the PDF using a vulnerable version of the PDF reader. Step 5: On open, the payload executes silently in the background, giving the attacker remote access.
Vulnerability: Vulnerable PDF reader not yet patched
Impact: Remote access to system, possible full takeover
Detection Method: EDR with behavior-based detection, user behavior alerts
Solution: Update PDF reader, use sandboxed viewers, train users to verify HR emails
Tags: pdf, job lure, buffer overflow, metasploit

Title: Zero-Day in Email Client Image Parser
Scenario Description: Malicious email embeds image that triggers zero-day in the email client’s image rendering engine.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a flaw in how the email client parses images (e.g., .PNG decoder overflow). Step 2: Attacker crafts a small transparent image with hidden payload using hex editing. Step 3: Attacker embeds the image inline in a "Happy Birthday" email with friendly tone. Step 4: Target opens the email; the client renders image without user interaction. Step 5: Payload runs silently and connects to attacker's server to download more malware.
Detection Method: Network traffic monitoring, unusual outbound requests
Solution: Email client patching, image sanitization, disable auto-image load

Title: Malicious Calendar Invite Exploit
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits a vulnerability in calendar invite parser of a mail client to execute code.
Tools Used: Burp Suite, Custom crafted ICS file
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds zero-day in ICS calendar invite parsing function. Step 2: Builds an ICS file with hidden script to run upon parsing. Step 3: Sends an email with the calendar invite embedded as a meeting request. Step 4: Victim’s email client auto-adds the event, parsing the invite. Step 5: Exploit triggers upon parsing and executes malicious script on user machine.
Detection Method: System behavior deviation, script execution from calendar event
Solution: Block ICS attachments, patch mail clients, disable auto-accept

Title: Exploit via Encrypted Attachment Bypass
Scenario Description: A zero-day is delivered inside an encrypted ZIP attachment bypassing security filters.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker prepares a ZIP file encrypted with password ("resume2025"). Step 2: ZIP contains a Word document embedded with an exploit using an unknown vulnerability. Step 3: Email content says: "Please find my resume attached. Password: resume2025". Step 4: Target opens ZIP, extracts and opens the file using Microsoft Word. Step 5: Exploit runs on open and connects back to attacker’s command server.
Detection Method: Suspicious ZIP activity, word macro behavior
Solution: Block passworded ZIPs, patch Office tools, educate staff
Tags: encrypted attachment, bypass AV, doc exploit

Title: HTML Email with Zero-Day JavaScript
Scenario Description: Exploit hidden inside an HTML email containing a zero-day JavaScript vulnerability.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker writes an HTML email with JavaScript exploiting a new browser engine flaw. Step 2: Email is sent disguised as a newsletter with styled content and images. Step 3: Email client renders HTML automatically, executing embedded script. Step 4: The exploit script bypasses browser sandboxing and executes malicious code. Step 5: Attacker gains access to stored credentials or installs malware.
Detection Method: Email HTML parsing logs, sandbox evasion alerts
Solution: Disable HTML rendering, patch JS engines, use viewer plugins
Tags: html email, JS exploit, newsletter lure

Title: Zero-Day Exploit via Malicious Outlook Theme
Scenario Description: Attacker exploits a flaw in Outlook’s theme processing via a malicious email theme file.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a flaw in how Outlook processes custom visual themes. Step 2: Prepares a custom .msg file with malformed theme code that triggers code execution. Step 3: Sends email as a promotional offer, e.g., “New Year Theme Pack – Activate Now!”. Step 4: Target opens the file in Outlook. The theme is auto-applied. Step 5: Exploit code in the theme executes in background, opening a backdoor.
Detection Method: Email behavior analysis, file watcher logs
Solution: Patch Outlook, disable custom themes by default
Tags: outlook theme exploit, RTF attack, visual payload

Title: Zero-Day via Inline CSS Exploit in Email Body
Scenario Description: Exploit embedded in email's inline CSS triggers rendering engine flaw.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker discovers a bug in how the CSS rendering engine handles :before selectors. Step 2: Constructs an HTML email styled with complex nested CSS using malicious selectors. Step 3: Sends email as a brand-style update newsletter from a known company. Step 4: Victim opens email in webmail or mobile client, which automatically renders the CSS. Step 5: Hidden CSS executes memory corruption exploit to run shellcode silently.
Impact: Arbitrary code execution, access to session tokens
Detection Method: DOM manipulation detection, sandbox alerts
Solution: Strip CSS in email body, sanitize selectors

Title: Zero-Day in Archive Preview via Email Link
Scenario Description: Exploit targets file preview service when user opens shared archive from email.
Tools Used: Exploit in ZIP preview, cloud storage link
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker uploads an archive with specially crafted file names to a cloud service. Step 2: The archive contains malformed filenames that exploit preview service (e.g., filename overflows). Step 3: Sends an email with a link: “Shared Files: Team Reports – Click to Preview”. Step 4: Target opens the file in browser preview mode without downloading. Step 5: The preview system processes archive contents, triggering exploit and injecting remote shell.
Impact: Exploit of third-party file preview to gain system or session access
Detection Method: Webhook monitoring, unusual preview logs
Solution: Disable online preview, patch preview engines

Title: Zero-Day via Email Signature Image Rendering
Scenario Description: Malicious image in an email signature exploits rendering flaw in email client.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds an integer overflow bug in PNG parsing module of a mail client. Step 2: Generates a PNG with malformed headers using hex editing tools. Step 3: Attaches this image as part of a fake “CEO Signature” in an email. Step 4: Target receives email with message: “Review this urgent memo – Signed by CEO.” Step 5: Email client automatically renders the signature, triggering code execution.
Impact: Initial access without user clicking any links
Detection Method: Memory access logging, image parsing exceptions
Solution: Filter image formats in emails, update image libraries
Tags: signature spoof, image parsing, CEO lure

Title: Zero-Day Triggered via Encrypted S/MIME Payload
Scenario Description: Exploit is hidden inside an encrypted S/MIME message body.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates a message with an S/MIME encrypted payload containing an RCE exploit. Step 2: Email is crafted as a legal document or invoice, sent from spoofed lawyer domain. Step 3: Target’s email client automatically decrypts and parses S/MIME payload. Step 4: Hidden exploit in the decrypted body triggers parser vulnerability. Step 5: Attacker gains remote access upon decryption without victim interaction.
Detection Method: Decryption logs, anomaly in secure message parsing
Solution: Use zero-trust parsing, update mail client, disable auto-decrypt
Tags: smime abuse, encrypted delivery, legal doc lure

Title: Exploit via Font File in Email Attachment
Scenario Description: Malicious font embedded in attachment triggers parsing exploit.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a bug in font rendering engine of a word processor. Step 2: Creates a .docx file that references an embedded TTF font with malicious code. Step 3: Sends email pretending to be a design portfolio: “Please review my typography resume.” Step 4: Target opens the attachment in Word, loading the embedded font. Step 5: Exploit triggers during font rendering and initiates malware download.
Detection Method: Suspicious font use, embedded font behavior
Solution: Block external/embedded fonts, update rendering engine
Tags: font exploit, docx payload, resume lure

Title: Zero-Day Trigger via Email Recall Exploit
Scenario Description: Exploit misuses email recall feature in corporate email systems.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a buffer overflow in how Exchange handles recall packets. Step 2: Sends a normal email first, followed by a crafted "Recall This Message" request. Step 3: The recall request contains exploit in metadata headers. Step 4: Exchange server processes the recall, triggering the overflow and running payload. Step 5: Attacker gains remote code execution on mail server or recipient’s client.
Impact: Mail server compromise or client infection
Detection Method: Server logs, abnormal recall behavior
Solution: Disable recalls, patch server software
Tags: email recall, exchange exploit, remote exploit

Title: Exploit Hidden in Base64 Embedded Script
Scenario Description: Base64-encoded script bypasses detection and triggers unknown browser flaw.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker creates an HTML email with Base64-encoded JavaScript payload. Step 2: Script is embedded in an image placeholder tag (). Step 3: Target opens email in a browser-based client (e.g., Roundcube, Outlook Web). Step 4: Base64 image is rendered, script decoded and triggers browser engine flaw. Step 5: Exploit chain launches downloader to infect host system.
Impact: Stealthy code execution via encoded payload
Detection Method: HTML parsing logs, browser sandbox bypass alert
Solution: Disallow inline Base64 scripts, use hardened email viewers
Tags: base64 exploit, image payload, browser flaw

Title: Zero-Day in Shared Meeting Link Engine
Scenario Description: Exploit in URL parsing engine used for auto-link generation in meeting invites.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds flaw in how long URLs are parsed in mail clients (e.g., overflow). Step 2: Constructs an invite link exceeding buffer size with embedded payload. Step 3: Sends a meeting invite email: “Client Briefing - Click to Join Zoom Call”. Step 4: Victim’s client parses the link for preview, buffer overflows, and executes code. Step 5: Attacker gains reverse shell or installs spyware.
Detection Method: URL length anomalies, mail client crash
Solution: Patch parsing logic, disable auto-link preview
Tags: meeting invite, url overflow, remote exploit

Title: Zero-Day Hidden in Rich Text Email Format
Scenario Description: Attacker embeds payload in Rich Text Format (RTF) exploiting unpatched parser bug.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies vulnerability in RTF rendering in email clients. Step 2: Prepares an .rtf email with exploit code embedded in font table section. Step 3: Sends the email titled “Invoice Details – RTF Copy Enclosed”. Step 4: Target opens RTF email in client (e.g., Outlook), which renders text with formatting. Step 5: Hidden exploit runs as formatting is parsed, executing remote script.
Impact: Full remote control of target system
Detection Method: Formatting anomaly logs, EDR triggers
Solution: Block RTF, use plain-text rendering, update email client
Tags: rtf exploit, invoice lure, parser bypass

Title: Zero-Day in Attachment Preview via Mobile Mail App
Scenario Description: Exploit abuses how mobile email apps preview certain file types.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker identifies a vulnerability in the way a mobile mail app previews CSV files (e.g., formula injection or memory bug). Step 2: Creates a malicious .csv file that appears to be an invoice. Step 3: Email is titled “Pending Invoice Attached – Urgent Payment Required”. Step 4: Mobile app auto-previews the attachment in email pane. Step 5: Preview triggers execution of exploit without any user interaction.

Title: Exploit Triggered via Smart Banner Preview
Scenario Description: Malicious payload hidden inside email preview banner shown by marketing platforms.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker exploits a flaw in how email platforms generate smart preview banners (those that summarize content). Step 2: Crafts an email that includes a hidden payload within preview meta-tags. Step 3: Email is sent as a marketing message from a spoofed platform (e.g., “Adobe Creative Cloud - You’ve Won Access!”). Step 4: Mail client generates and renders the smart banner. Step 5: Payload activates via banner script execution and sends device info or runs malicious commands.
Impact: Stealthy access or remote browser control
Detection Method: Preview/banner engine logs
Solution: Disable banner previews, sanitize metadata

Title: Zero-Day via Audio File Metadata in Email
Scenario Description: Exploit resides in the metadata of a shared audio file attachment.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker finds a flaw in ID3 tag processing (metadata in .mp3) in mail clients. Step 2: Embeds malicious payload in title/album fields of an MP3 using a tag editor. Step 3: Sends an email titled: “Audio Recording from Meeting – Must Listen”. Step 4: Victim opens email and previews the MP3 inline. Step 5: Mail client parses metadata and executes payload in vulnerable parser.
Detection Method: File parsing exceptions, media log anomalies
Solution: Disable media previews, sanitize file metadata
Tags: audio exploit, ID3 tag, social lure

Title: Exploit Chain via Embedded Form in Email
Scenario Description: A malicious form embedded in an email uses a zero-day in form rendering logic.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker discovers a flaw in how embedded forms are handled in email clients. Step 2: Crafts an email with a fake survey form (“Staff Satisfaction Form – Internal Use”). Step 3: Embeds malicious script inside form field labels or hidden inputs. Step 4: Victim opens email and form is parsed by client. Step 5: Exploit triggers on field rendering, enabling command execution or credential theft.
Detection Method: DOM mutation logs, JS execution in form
Solution: Disable HTML forms in emails, patch parsing logic
Tags: embedded form exploit, hr survey, credential access

Title: Zero-Day via Email Thread Re-Injection Exploit
Scenario Description: Attacker abuses email reply/thread handling to inject payload into prior thread.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker discovers bug in how threaded emails handle MIME boundaries. Step 2: Sends a crafted reply email with a malformed MIME section mimicking a legitimate thread. Step 3: Victim sees it as a continuation of a real conversation. Step 4: Email client parses old thread and new injected content simultaneously. Step 5: Exploit in MIME structure runs code as thread content is loaded, even without new attachment.
Impact: Hidden code execution during reply parsing
Detection Method: MIME parsing alerts, client crashes
Solution: Harden MIME handling, validate thread parsing
Tags: thread hijack, mime exploit, reply chain

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Credential Harvesting
Scenario Description: An attacker clones a public Wi-Fi and injects a fake login page to collect usernames and passwords.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a laptop with a wireless adapter to create a fake Wi-Fi network with the same name as a nearby public hotspot. Step 2: Using a tool like airgeddon, the attacker disconnects users from the original Wi-Fi so they automatically reconnect to the stronger, fake one. Step 3: A fake captive portal is configured to look like the original login page. Step 4: When victims connect, they see the fake login screen and input their credentials. Step 5: These credentials are captured and stored on the attacker's device.
Vulnerability: No authentication on open Wi-Fi; User trust
Detection Method: Wi-Fi anomaly detection, multiple SSIDs
Solution: Use WPA2/WPA3 with authentication portals; detect rogue APs
Tags: evil twin, captive portal, credential harvesting

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Malware Drop via Fake Update
Scenario Description: Victims are tricked into downloading malware disguised as a browser update from a fake captive portal.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi hotspot with the same name as the real one. Step 2: Deauths users from the real AP using aireplay-ng. Step 3: Redirects all connected users to a captive portal page with a pop-up saying "Update Your Browser to Continue". Step 4: The download link actually serves a malware payload like a keylogger. Step 5: Victim downloads and executes the file, infecting their system.
Detection Method: AV scan, sandbox analysis, endpoint behavior
Solution: Do not allow arbitrary downloads in captive portals; secure DNS

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Phishing Redirection
Attack Type: Evil Twin + Phishing via Captive Portal
Scenario Description: Redirecting users from captive portal to phishing sites that mimic social logins (e.g., Google, Facebook).
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker starts a rogue AP using Fluxion with same SSID as hotel Wi-Fi. Step 2: Disconnects clients from original network using a deauth attack. Step 3: Victims reconnect to fake AP and get redirected to a captive portal asking for social login. Step 4: Login page mimics Google/Facebook, and credentials are captured. Step 5: Users are then redirected to a real webpage to reduce suspicion.
Impact: Credential compromise of email or social media
Detection Method: Detect social login on captive pages; monitor unusual login alerts
Solution: Use OAuth detection, secure captive portal flow
Tags: phishing, evil twin, social login trap

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Credit Card Skimming
Scenario Description: A rogue captive portal mimics a hotel payment gateway and tricks users into entering card details.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker clones a hotel Wi-Fi and configures it as an open hotspot. Step 2: A captive portal is created that looks exactly like the hotel's card payment page. Step 3: When users connect, they’re asked to "verify" card details before accessing the internet. Step 4: Card information entered is sent directly to the attacker’s server. Step 5: The user is then redirected to the internet to make it seem legitimate.
Detection Method: Monitor network for fake payment flows
Solution: Use payment verification over HTTPS; validate AP origin

Title: Evil Twin with Captive Portal – MFA Token Stealing
Attack Type: Evil Twin + MFA Phishing via Captive Portal
Scenario Description: The attacker intercepts MFA tokens by creating a fake login portal mimicking SSO/MFA provider.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker uses Evilginx2 to setup a phishing proxy mimicking an SSO login page. Step 2: A rogue AP is started with the same SSID as corporate Wi-Fi. Step 3: Victims connect and are redirected to a page asking for corporate credentials and MFA token. Step 4: Evilginx2 relays this to the real service and captures the session token. Step 5: The attacker uses the stolen session token to gain access without needing the victim’s password again.
Detection Method: Look for mismatched SSO domains; session reuse alerts
Solution: Use FIDO2/U2F hardware tokens; domain validation

Title: Evil Twin – Redirect to Malicious App Store
Scenario Description: The attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi network and redirects users to a malicious app store to download malware-laden apps.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker launches a fake Wi-Fi with the same name (SSID) as a nearby coffee shop. Step 2: Airgeddon is used to kick off users from the real network by flooding deauthentication packets. Step 3: The victim connects to the fake network and sees a captive portal saying: “To access free internet, download our official coffee shop app.” Step 4: Clicking the link redirects to a cloned fake app store that hosts a malicious app. Step 5: Once installed, the malware begins stealing data or tracking the device.
Detection Method: Monitor for non-HTTPS redirects
Solution: Only allow app downloads via official stores; enforce device management
Tags: fake app, captive portal, android, evil twin

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Ransomware Dropper Page
Scenario Description: Victims are served ransomware disguised as a Wi-Fi client update through the captive portal.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker clones an airport Wi-Fi and broadcasts a stronger signal to attract connections. Step 2: Apache is configured to host a fake Wi-Fi client update webpage. Step 3: The captive portal says “Please update your Wi-Fi compatibility tool to continue.” Step 4: A ransomware dropper (created using msfvenom) is served as the download. Step 5: The victim runs the program, and the system is encrypted with a ransom note.
Vulnerability: User trust in captive update pages
Detection Method: Ransomware beacon detection, file behavior monitoring
Solution: Block EXE downloads; use app whitelisting

Title: Evil Twin – Wi-Fi Survey Theft via Portal
Scenario Description: The captive portal mimics a survey form to trick users into submitting sensitive data.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up rogue AP in a public event hall named “Free_Event_WiFi”. Step 2: When users connect, they are redirected to a portal asking them to fill out a short survey for access. Step 3: The form collects PII such as name, email, mobile number, and home address. Step 4: Submitted data is stored on attacker's backend database for later misuse. Step 5: The user is redirected to a thank-you page and internet access is simulated.
Detection Method: Monitor captive portal forms, inspect portal domain
Solution: Use HTTPS captive portals; disable data collection
Tags: PII theft, survey abuse, rogue AP

Title: Evil Twin – DNS Hijack via Captive Portal
Scenario Description: The attacker uses captive portal to silently change DNS settings on victim’s device for future redirect control.
Attack Steps: Step 1: The attacker launches a fake AP using airgeddon and sets up a fake captive portal. Step 2: When users connect, the captive portal displays a “Connection Setup” page. Step 3: The page injects JavaScript that changes DNS settings on Windows using PowerShell or Android DNS APIs. Step 4: Victim’s DNS is now redirected to attacker’s controlled servers, allowing future phishing/malware delivery. Step 5: User browses internet normally, unaware of the DNS hijack.
Vulnerability: DNS config modification via captive script
Detection Method: DNS behavior analysis; script blocker
Solution: Disable DNS changes via browser scripts; DNSSEC

Title: Evil Twin – Credential Harvest + Session Replay
Scenario Description: Attacker captures login credentials via captive portal and replays session to hijack accounts.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Fake AP launched in a co-working space using airgeddon. Step 2: The captive portal replicates a login page for a commonly used tool (e.g., Slack, Trello). Step 3: User enters credentials; attacker stores them and simultaneously sniffs session tokens using Wireshark. Step 4: Attacker replays session to gain instant access to user's account. Step 5: Changes password, deletes activity logs to remain hidden.
Detection Method: Alert for new logins; session fingerprinting
Solution: Secure session tokens; use MFA enforcement

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – Keylogging Injection
Scenario Description: Captive portal delivers JavaScript keylogger to record everything typed by user after connection.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker builds a rogue AP using Bettercap and EvilPortal module. Step 2: Captive portal looks like a benign login page (e.g., company SSO). Step 3: The HTML page contains hidden JavaScript keylogger code. Step 4: Once users start typing, every keystroke is captured and sent to attacker's server. Step 5: Even after login, script remains active in background tab for data collection.
Detection Method: Script behavior analysis; monitor outgoing data
Solution: Use CSP headers; disable JS in captive pages

Title: Evil Twin Captive Portal – OAuth Token Capture
Scenario Description: Captive portal pretends to offer login via Google but proxies OAuth flow to steal tokens.
Attack Steps: Step 1: Attacker sets up a rogue AP at a campus cafe mimicking “Campus_WiFi”. Step 2: Captive portal shows “Login with Google to access free internet.” Step 3: Evilginx2 proxies the real OAuth flow, capturing tokens in real-time. Step 4: Attacker extracts OAuth token and uses it to access victim’s Google services. Step 5: Since OAuth tokens bypass password, access remains until token is revoked.
